profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-12-05T12:36:08.584+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.
Input text:

p.seg: The Hanlín Xuéshì, Cháosàn Dàfū, Yòu Jiànyì Dàfū, Zhī Zhìgào, concurrently Shìjiǎng, concurrently Tíju Wànshòuguān Gōngshì, concurrently Pàn Jíxiányuàn, Shànghùjūn, Hénèi Jùn Kāiguó Hóu, with a fiefdom of one thousand three hundred households, bestowed with a purple-gold fish pouch, your servant
by imperial decree compiles
Hòu Xué Tiāntái
When Xiàng Yǔ divided the world
and enthroned the various generals,
he enthroned Pèi Gōng in Bā, Shǔ, and Hànzhōng,
calling him the Hàn Wáng.
The king was angry,
wishing to attack Yǔ.
Xiāo Hé remonstrated, saying:
"The saying goes, 'Tiānhàn,'
its appellation is extremely beautiful."
Thereupon, he proceeded to his domain.
When he later destroyed Xiàng Yǔ
and possessed the world,
he then used the name of his initial enfeoffed state and called himself Hàn.
【Chapter:
"Xiàng Yǔ zhì yuē Hàn"
- the Yǐ Shíyī Háng Běn lacks these fifty-nine characters.
Tàizǔ Gāohuángdì, Shàngzhīshàng,
surnamed Liú,
personal name Bāng,
courtesy name Jì;
a native of Zhōngyáng Lǐ, Fēngyì, Pèi.
Zhāng Yàn said: "There is no 'Gāo' in the methods of posthumous titles.
Because the emperor's achievements were the highest, and he was the great ancestor of the emperors,
therefore this name was specially given."
【Chapter: The Yǐ Shíyī Háng Běn,
after "rén"
has
"In the first year of Qín Èrshì,
Chén Shè rose in Qí.
The elders of Pèi established Jì as Pèi Gōng.
In the second year,
Xiàng Yǔ re-established him as Hàn Wáng.
The next year was called Hàn Yuánnián.
In the fifth year, he ascended the imperial throne."
(Thirty-seven characters.)
It lacks
"Zhāng Yàn"
to
"míng yān"
(twenty-five characters).
1. In winter,
in the tenth month,
anciently there were three starts to the year (zhèng): zǐ was the Celestial Zhèng,
which the Zhōu used,
taking the eleventh month as the start of the year;
chǒu was the Terrestrial Zhèng,
which the Yīn used,
taking the twelfth month as the start of the year;
yín was the Human Zhèng,
which the Xià used,
taking the thirteenth month as the start of the year.
Qín,
having the virtue of Water,
held that the month of jiànhài (the tenth month) was when water obtained its position,
hence they took the tenth month as the start of the year.
Gāozǔ arrived at Bāshàng in the tenth month,
and consequently did not change this.
It was not until the first year of Tàichū under Wǔdì
that the calendar was fixed,
and the Xià zhèng was adopted,
beginning to take yín as the start of the year;
this has been followed ever since.
Kǎoyì says: Shǐjì, Hànshū, and Xún Yuè’s Hàngjì
all state,
“In this month, the Five Planets gathered in Dōngjǐng.”

According to Wèi Shōu’s Hòu Wèishū, in the biography of Gāo Yǔn: Cuī Hào assembled various astrologers to examine and verify the records of solar and lunar eclipses and the movements of the Five Planets since the first year of Hàn,
and criticized the errors of previous historians,
creating a separate Wèi calendar,
which he showed to Yǔn.
Yǔn said,
“One who speaks well of the distant must first be verified by what is near.
Moreover, in the tenth month of winter in the first year of Hàn, the Five Planets gathered in Dōngjǐng—
this is a trivial matter in calendrical calculations.
Now, to criticize the Hàn histories without noticing this error
suggests that later criticisms of the present will be like present criticisms of the past.”
Hào said,
“What is the error you speak of?”
Yǔn said,
“According to astronomical treatises: the two planets Jīn (Venus) and Shuǐ (Mercury) always travel close to the sun.
In the tenth month of winter,
the sun rises in Wěi and Jī,
and sets at dusk south of Shēn,
while Dōngjǐng is just rising north of Yín.
How could these two planets travel against the sun?
This shows that the historians wanted to deify the event,
and did not deduce it based on reason.”
Hào said,
“For one who wishes to make changes,
what is impossible?
Why do you not doubt the gathering of the three planets,
but marvel at the arrival of the two?”
Yǔn said,
“This cannot be debated with empty words;
it should be re-examined carefully.”
All those present at the time were surprised.
Dōnggōng Shàofù Yóu Yǎ said,
“Master Gāo is skilled in calendrical science;
he would not speak falsely.”
More than a year later,
Hào said to Yǔn,
“What was discussed before
was not originally given much thought;
but upon further investigation,
it is indeed as you said:
they gathered in Dōngjǐng three months earlier,
not in the tenth month.”
We now follow this,
and therefore the tenth month does not mention the gathering of the Five Planets.
Zǐyīng tied a cord around his neck,
sealed the emperor’s seal, tally, and credentials,
and surrendered beside Zhǐdào.
Yīng Shào says: Zǐyīng did not dare assume the title of emperor,
but merely called himself king.
A plain carriage and white horses
are the attire of mourners.
Zǔ refers to
the emperor’s ceremonial apron.
Tying it around the neck
means he intended to commit suicide.
Shī Gǔ says: This zǔ
refers to a sash (shòu),
which is used to carry the seal.
Zǔ is
pronounced zǒng (五翻).
Today’s sashes and tassels are this.
Yīng Shào says: Xǐ (seal)
means trustworthiness;
in ancient times, it was used by both noble and common.
The Zuǒzhuàn states: When Xiānggōng was in Chǔ,
Jì Wǔzǐ sent Gōngyě to ask for a sealed letter (xǐshū),
and pursued him to give it.
Qín and Hàn designated it for the honored as a sign of trust (xìn),
and only then did the common people avoid its use.
Hànguān Yí says: Zǐyīng presented Shǐhuáng’s seal,
which was then used by the emperor;
it was passed down through generations,
and called
“Hàn Chuánguó Xǐ” (the Imperial Seal of the Han Dynasty).
Shěn Yuē says: When Gāozǔ entered the Pass,
he obtained Qín Shǐhuáng’s blue-jade seal,
with a coiled dragon and tiger knob,
inscribed with the words
“Received the mandate of Heaven,
the Emperor’s longevity and prosperity.”
Later generations called it the Chuánguó Xǐ.
Shǐjì Zhèngyì says: The Son of Heaven had six seals: Huángdì Xíngxǐ (Emperor’s Traveling Seal),
Huángdì Zhīxǐ (Emperor’s Seal),
Huángdì Xìnxǐ (Emperor’s Trust Seal),
Tiānzǐ Xíngxǐ (Son of Heaven’s Traveling Seal),
Tiānzǐ Zhīxǐ (Son of Heaven’s Seal),
Tiānzǐ Xìnxǐ (Son of Heaven’s Trust Seal).
All matters used them,
and imperial decrees (xǐlìng) were enacted.
The Tiānzǐ Xìnxǐ
was for transfers of office and enfeoffing feudal lords, and the seals
for deploying troops
were all sealed with purple mud from Wǔdū.
Yú Xǐ Zhìlín says: The Chuánguó Xǐ was outside the six seals;
the Son of Heaven had a total of seven seals.
Fú (tally),
Shuōwén says: It means trustworthiness.
Wéi Zhāo says: Fú
refers to tallies for deploying troops.
Shī Gǔ says: Fú
refers to all things used as a token of agreement.
The Zhōulǐ,
in the section on Earth Officials, has a manager of jié (credentials).
Zhèng Xuán’s commentary says: Jié
is like xìn (trust/token),
a token held by travelers.
Sānlǐ Yìzōng says: Jié was one chi two cun long;
from Qín and Hàn onwards, it was changed to the shape of a banner.
Wéi Zhāo says: Jié
is what an envoy holds.
Shìmíng says: It is a token for commands, rewards, and punishments.
Shī Gǔ says: Jié were made of feathers,
stacked one upon another,
resembling bamboo nodes.
Envoys held them as a token of trust.
Xú Guǎng says: Zhǐdào
is in Bālíng.
Sū Lín says: It is a pavilion name,
thirteen lǐ east of Cháng’ān.
Hàngōngdiàn Shū says: Zhǐdào Tíng is four lǐ east of Bāchéng Guān,
and Guān is a hundred paces east of Bāshuǐ.
Kuòdìzhì: Zhǐ,
pronounced zhǐ.
Zhǐdào is in the park sixteen lǐ northeast of Wànnián Xiàn, Yōngzhōu.
Pèigōng said,
“When King Huái sent me,
he firmly intended for me to be lenient and tolerant.
This event is found in the previous volume, second year of Qín Èrshì.
To kill him would be inauspicious.”
So he handed him over to his officials.
Shǔ means
to entrust.
Shǔlì means
to hand over to officials,
to have them guard him.
Shǔ, pronounced zhīyù fān.
Jiǎ Yì Lùn says: Qín, with its small territory, achieved the power of ten thousand chariots,
summoned the eight provinces and held court over its peers,
for over a hundred years,
and then made the Six Directions its home.
The Six Directions are
Heaven, Earth, East, West, South, North.
Yet a single man's rebellion
caused the seven ancestral temples to fall,
he died at the hands of others,
and became a laughingstock to the world.
Why?
It is because benevolence and righteousness were not extended, and the circumstances of offense and defense had changed.
2 Pèi Gōng entered Xiányáng from the west.
All the generals rushed to seize the treasuries of gold, silk, and valuables and divide them.
Xiāo Hé alone was the first to enter and collect the maps and documents from the Qin Prime Minister’s office and store them.
Through this, Pèi Gōng was able to fully understand all the strategic passes in the realm,
the population figures, and the strengths and weaknesses of different places.
Pèi Gōng saw that the Qin palaces, tapestries, dogs, horses, precious treasures, and women numbered in the thousands.
He intended to stay and reside there.
Fán Kuài remonstrated, saying:
“Does Pèi Gōng wish to possess the realm,
or merely become a wealthy elder?
All these luxurious and extravagant things
were the very reason for Qin’s downfall.
What use are they to Pèi Gōng?
I beg you to return quickly to Bàshàng,
and not remain in the palace!”
Fán Kuài rose from being a dog butcher,
yet his insight was thus.
I say that Kuài’s greatest achievement was his remonstrance to prevent Pèi Gōng from staying in the Qin palace.
His reprimand of Xiàng Yǔ at Hóngmén comes second.
Family Genealogy: King Xuān of Zhōu enfeoffed Zhòng Shānfǔ at Fán,
and his descendants later took this as their clan name.
Zhāng Liáng said:
“Qin acted without the Way,
which is why Pèi Gōng was able to reach this point.
Indeed, to eliminate evildoers and tyrants for the realm,
one should make plain white clothing one's provision.
Plain white clothing
is mourning attire;
it means to sympathize with the people.
為 [wèi]
is pronounced yú wěi.
縞 [gǎo]
is pronounced gōng lǎo.
If you immediately indulge in its pleasures,
this is what is called ‘aiding Jié in his tyranny.’
Moreover, loyal words may grate on the ear but are beneficial for action,
and bitter medicine may taste unpleasant but is beneficial for illness.
I beg Pèi Gōng to heed Fán Kuài’s words!”
Pèi Gōng then returned his army to Bàshàng.
In the eleventh month,
Pèi Gōng summoned all the elders and prominent local figures from the various counties
and said:
“The elders have long suffered from Qin’s harsh laws!
I made a pact with the feudal lords
that the first to enter the Pass would rule it;
I ought to rule Guānzhōng.
I make a pact with the elders that
there will be only three laws: one who kills shall die;
one who injures or steals shall be punished accordingly.
Fú Qián said: The law is determined according to the severity.
Lǐ Qí said: Injuries have circumstances,
and stolen goods vary in amount,
so the specific punishment cannot be predetermined;
thus, ‘punished accordingly’
does not specify what punishment it refers to.
Shī Gǔ said: 抵 [dǐ]
means to reach,
to be fitting.
Fú and Lǐ’s explanations are both correct.
抵 [dǐ]
is pronounced dīng lǐ.
All officials and common people shall settle down as before.
案 [àn]
means in order;
堵 [dǔ]
means wall: it means not to move or relocate.
去 [qù]
is pronounced qiāng lǚ.
I am eliminating harm for the elders,
not invading or oppressing you;
have no fear!
Moreover, the reason I returned the army to Bàshàng
was merely to await the arrival of the feudal lords and then establish the regulations.”
He then sent people with Qin officials to travel through the counties, townships, and villages
to announce and explain this.
Qin system: a county was generally a hundred square li,
with one ting every ten li,
and one xiāng for every ten ting.
This refers to the enfeoffed and self-sufficient areas.
為 [wèi]
is pronounced yú wěi.
行 [xíng]
is pronounced xià mèng.
People vied to bring cattle, sheep, wine, and food to offer to the soldiers.
Pèi Gōng again declined to accept them,
saying:
“The granaries have plenty;
we are not lacking,
and I do not wish to burden the people.”
The people were even more delighted,
fearing only that Pèi Gōng would not become the King of Qin.
Xiàng Yǔ, having pacified Héběi,
led the armies of the feudal lords, intending to enter the Pass from the west.
Previously,
when the officials, soldiers, conscripted laborers, and garrison troops of the feudal lords passed through Qínzhōng,
the Qin officials and soldiers often treated them improperly.
It means they did not treat them well.
先 [xiān]
is pronounced xī jiàn.
繇 [yóu]
is read as yáo.
The officials and soldiers of the feudal lords, taking advantage of their victory, often enslaved and used them,
and lightly humiliated the Qin officials and soldiers.
Many Qin officials and soldiers resented this and
secretly said:
“General Zhāng and others deceived us into surrendering to the feudal lords.
If they can now enter the Pass and defeat Qin,
that would be excellent;
but if they cannot,
and the feudal lords enslave us and go east,
and Qin also completely slaughters our parents, wives, and children,
what then?”
The generals faintly heard their plan
and reported it to Xiàng Yǔ.
Xiàng Yǔ summoned Qíng Bù and General Pú and discussed, saying:
“The Qin officials and soldiers are still numerous,
and their hearts are not submissive.
If they do not obey at the Pass,
the situation will surely be perilous.
It would be better to strike and kill them,
and I alone, with Zhāng Hán, Grand Scribe Xīn, and Commandant Yì, will enter Qin.”
Thereupon, the Chu army attacked at night and buried alive over two hundred thousand Qin soldiers south of the city of Xīn'ān.
Bān Zhì: It was subordinate to Hóngnóng Commandery.
Shī Gǔ said: It is today's Gǔzhōu County.
Kuòdì Zhì: The old city of Xīn'ān
is twelve li east of Mǐnchí County in Luòzhōu.
3 Someone advised Pèi Gōng, saying:
“Qin’s wealth is ten times that of the realm,
and its terrain is strong.
I hear Xiàng Yǔ has proclaimed Zhāng Hán as King of Yōng,
to rule Guānzhōng.
If he comes now,
Pèi Gōng may not be able to possess this territory.
You should quickly dispatch troops to guard Hángǔ Pass,
and not allow the feudal lords’ armies to enter;
gradually conscript Guānzhōng soldiers to augment your own strength
and resist him.”
Pèi Gōng agreed with this plan
and followed it.
Soon after, Xiàng Yǔ arrived at the Pass,
where the gates were closed.
Hearing that Pèi Gōng had already pacified Guānzhōng,
he was furious
and ordered Qíng Bù and others to attack and break Hángǔ Pass.
In the twelfth month,
Xiàng Yǔ advanced to Xì.
Pèi Gōng’s Left Marshal, Cáo Wúshāng, sent someone to speak to Xiàng Yǔ, saying:
“Pèi Gōng wishes to be King of Guānzhōng,
has appointed Zǐ Yīng as Chancellor,
and possesses all the treasures.”
He wished to gain enfeoffment by this.
Xiàng Yǔ was greatly angered.
He feasted his soldiers
and set a date for the next morning to attack Pèi Gōng’s army.
At this time,
Xiàng Yǔ had an army of four hundred thousand,
claiming a million,
stationed at Hóngmén in Xīnfēng.
Xīnfēng County was originally Qin’s Líyì,
only established in the seventh year of Gāozǔ,
the historian wrote it using the later county name.
Yīng Shào said: The Grand Supreme Emperor longed to return east,
so Gāozǔ rebuilt the city walls, streets, and neighborhoods to resemble Fēng,
and moved the people of Fēng to populate it,
hence it was named Xīnfēng.
Mèng Kāng said: Hóngmén is seventeen li east of Xīnfēng,
it is the name of the slope at the old main road.
Yáo Chá said: East of the old city of Xīnfēng,
before reaching the Xì River,
south of the road there is a broken plateau,
and the north-south cavernous gate is it.
Shuǐjīng Zhù: Today, east of the old city of Xīnfēng there is a slope
over two li long,
with a trench opening up a passage through the plateau,
open north-south,
with a twin gate,
called Hóngmén.
Mèng Kāng’s statement that it is seventeen li east of Xīnfēng
is incorrect;
it probably refers to the county seat
and not the city itself.
From the old city of Xīnfēng west to Bàchéng is fifty li,
ten li west of Bàchéng is the Bà River,
and twenty li further west is Cháng'ān City.
Pèi Gōng's army numbered two hundred thousand, stationed at Bàshàng.
Fàn Zēng said to Xiàng Yǔ:
"When Péigōng was in Shāndōng,
he was greedy for wealth
and fond of women.
Now that he has entered the Pass,
he has taken none of the valuables,
nor has he indulged in any women.
This indicates his ambition is not small.
I sent someone to observe his aura,
and it was like dragons and tigers,
forming five colors.
This is the aura of a Son of Heaven.
The Zhōu Lǐ states: The Shìjìnshì is in charge of the method of ten luminosities,
to observe omens and portents,
and discern good from ill fortune.
This is what later generations referred to as 'observing the aura.'
The Jìn Tiānwén Zhì states: The aura of a Son of Heaven
is red inside and yellow outside;
a king will emerge from the places where it manifests in the four directions.
If the Son of Heaven intends to travel to a place,
that place will also first emit this aura,
sometimes like a city gate dimly visible in a misty aura,
or an aura resembling a man in green robes without hands,
in the west of the sun,
or like a dragon-horse,
or mixed colors rising majestically to the sky –
all are auras of an emperor.
Xiàng Bó, the Left Yǐn of Chǔ,
(in Chǔ, officials included Left Yǐn and Right Yǐn)
had long been friendly with Zhāng Liáng.
So he rode overnight to Péigōng's army,
secretly met Zhāng Liáng,
and fully informed him of the situation,
wanting to call him to leave together,
saying:
"Lest you both die!"
Zhāng Liáng said:
"I, your servant, was sent by Hán Wáng to accompany Péigōng.
Péigōng is now in peril;
to flee
would be unrighteous,
so I cannot but tell him."
Liáng then went in
and fully informed Péigōng.
Péigōng was greatly alarmed.
Liáng said:
"Do you reckon your soldiers are sufficient to withstand Xiàng Yǔ?"
Péigōng was silent and said:
"Indeed, they are not as good.
What should we do about it?"
Zhāng Liáng said:
"Please go and tell Xiàng Bó
that Péigōng dared not rebel."
Péigōng said:
"How is it that you, sir, have an old acquaintance with Xiàng Bó?"
Zhāng Liáng said:
"During the Qín dynasty, he traveled with your servant.
He once killed someone,
and your servant saved his life.
Now that he is in urgent need,
he fortunately came to inform Liáng."
Péigōng said:
"Who is older, he or you, sir?"
Liáng said:
"He is older than your servant."
Péigōng said:
"Sir, please call him in for me;
I shall treat him as an elder brother."
Zhāng Liáng went out
and indeed invited Xiàng Bó.
Xiàng Bó immediately entered to see Péigōng.
Péigōng offered a cup of wine as a toast,
and pledged an alliance through marriage,
saying:
"When I entered the Pass,
I dared not touch even a single autumn hair.
Wén Yǐng said: 'Háo' (hair),
in autumn it grows well.
It speaks of abundance.
Shī Gǔ said: At the time when hair grows,
its tip is extremely fine,
just enough to metaphorize smallness,
not speaking of its abundance.
Jìn (to approach),
its pronunciation is 'jìn'.
I sealed the treasuries and waited for the general.
The reason I sent a commander to guard the Pass
was to prevent other bandits from entering and exiting, and to prepare for unusual circumstances.
Day and night I hoped for the general's arrival,
how could I dare to rebel!
I wish Bó would fully convey that I dare not betray virtue."
Xiàng Bó agreed,
and said to Péigōng:
"Tomorrow morning, you must not fail to come early to apologize."
Péigōng said:
"I agree."
Thereupon, Xiàng Bó left again that night,
arrived at the army,
and fully reported Péigōng's words to Xiàng Yǔ.
He then said:
"If Péigōng had not first broken through Guānzhōng,
how could you, sir, have entered!
Now to attack someone who has rendered a great service
would be unrighteous;
it is better to treat him kindly instead."
Xiàng Yǔ agreed.
The next morning, Péigōng came with over a hundred cavalrymen to see Xiàng Yǔ at Hóngmén,
and apologized, saying:
"I and the general united our strength to attack Qín.
The general fought north of the river,
and I fought south of the river.
I did not expect to be able to enter the Pass and defeat Qín first,
and be able to see the general again here.
Now there are words from a petty man
that have caused a rift between the general and your servant."
Xiàng Yǔ said:
"This was said by Péigōng's Left Sīmǎ, Cáo Wúshāng.
Otherwise,
how could Jí have come to this!"
Xiàng Yǔ then kept Péigōng and drank with him.
Fàn Zēng repeatedly signaled Xiàng Yǔ with his eyes,
and three times raised the jade 'jué' he wore to show him.
(A 'jué' is like a ring but with a gap.)
Fàn Zēng raised it to show Yǔ,
likely wishing him to decide to kill Péigōng.
Fàn Zēng stood up,
went out,
and summoned Xiàng Zhuāng,
saying:
"The king is not a man of resolution.
You, enter and offer a toast.
(Ruò means 'you.')
(Shī Gǔ said: Generally, 'offering a toast'
means presenting a cup to an honored person
and wishing boundless longevity.)
Then request to perform a sword dance,
and in doing so, strike Péigōng at his seat
and kill him.
If not,
you all will be captured by him!"
Zhuāng then entered to offer a toast.
After the toast,
he said:
"There is no entertainment in the camp,
I request to perform a sword dance."
Xiàng Yǔ said:
"Agreed."
Xiàng Zhuāng drew his sword and began to dance.
Xiàng Bó also drew his sword and began to dance,
constantly shielding Péigōng with his body,
so Zhuāng could not strike him.
Thereupon Zhāng Liáng went to the camp gate to see Fán Kuài.
Kuài said,
"What is the situation today?"
Liáng said,
"Now Xiàng Zhuāng is brandishing his sword and dancing,
his intention is always against Pèi Gōng."
Kuài said,
"This is urgent!
I request to enter
and share the same fate as him!"
Kuài immediately donned his sword and shield and entered.
A shield
is for protecting oneself.
The character 盾 is pronounced "shí yǐn fān."
Fán Kuài turned his shield sideways and rammed it,
and the guards fell to the ground.
He then entered,
pushed aside the curtain and stood.
A curtain [帷] is something on the side.
The Shìmíng says: 帷 (wéi)
means "to enclose" (wéi),
used for self-enclosure.
His hair stood on end,
and his eye corners were completely split.
Xiàng Yǔ pressed his sword and knelt, saying,
"Who is this guest?"
Zhāng Liáng said,
"He is Fán Kuài, Pèi Gōng's charioteer."
Xiàng Yǔ said,
"A brave warrior!
Grant him a goblet of wine!"
So they gave him a large goblet of wine.
Kuài bowed in thanks,

The King of Hàn selected those in the army who could serve as cavalry generals.
Everyone recommended Lǐ Bì and Luò Jiǎ, former Qín cavalrymen from Chóngquán.
Bān Zhì: "Chóngquán County belonged to Féngyì."
Kuòdì Zhì: "Chóngquán ancient city,
is forty-five Lǐ southeast of Púchéng County in Tóngzhōu."
Xìng Pǔ: "Descendants of Qí Tàigōng included Gōngzǐ Luò,
whose descendants adopted the surname."
Also, Shǐjì: "Āi Lái Gè's great-great-grandson was called Dà Luò."
Bì and Jiǎ said:
"We are former Qín commoners;
we fear the army will not trust us.
We wish to have one of the King's close attendants who is skilled in cavalry to command us."
Thereupon, Guàn Yīng was appointed Zhōng Dàfū Lìng,
and Lǐ Bì and Luò Jiǎ were appointed Zuǒ Yòu Xiàowèi,
to lead the cavalry to attack the Chǔ cavalry east of Xíngyáng.
They decisively defeated them,
and because of this, Chǔ could not pass Xíngyáng to the west.
The King of Hàn's army was at Xíngyáng,
and built a covered road extending to the Hé River,
to fetch grain from Áocāng.
Kuòdì Zhì: "Áocāng is fifteen Lǐ northwest of Xíngyáng in Zhèngzhōu."
"The county gate's northeast faces the Biàn River,
and its south borders Sānhuáng Mountain."
Shǔ (屬),
read as zhī yù fān.
18 Zhōu Bó, Guàn Yīng, and others said to the King of Hàn:
"Chén Píng, though beautiful as a jade crown,
Mèng Kāng said: "Decorating a crown with jade means its brilliance is visible externally,
but there is nothing within."
Your servants hear that Píng, when at home, committed adultery with his sister-in-law;
he served Wèi but was not tolerated,
and fled to Chǔ;
finding it unsuitable,
he again fled to Hàn.
Today, Your Majesty has given him a high official position,
making him Commander of the Guards.
Your servants hear that Píng accepts gold from generals;
those with much gold get good positions,
and those with little gold get bad positions.
Píng
is a deceitful and disruptive minister;
we ask Your Majesty to investigate him!"
The King of Hàn suspected him,
and summoned Wèi Wúzhī to reprimand him.
Wúzhī said:
"What I recommended was his ability,
what Your Majesty questions is his conduct.
If there were someone with the conduct of Wěishēng or Xiàojǐ,
Wěishēng,
an ancient man of integrity;
some say
he is Wēishēng Gāo.
Xiàojǐ,
son of Shāng Gāozōng,
known for his filial conduct.
Xíng (行),
read as xià mèng fān.
How could Your Majesty have leisure to employ them now!
Chǔ and Hàn are at odds;
I presented a man of extraordinary strategizing ability.
I only considered whether his plans were truly sufficient to benefit the state or not.
Adultery with a sister-in-law and accepting gold,
what is there to doubt about that!"
The King of Hàn summoned Píng and reprimanded him, saying:
"Sir, you served King Wèi unsuccessfully,
served Chǔ and left,
and now you follow me.
Is it true that faithful men are inherently fickle?"
Píng said:
"I served King Wèi,
but King Wèi could not use my advice,
so I left to serve Xiàng Wáng.
Xiàng Wáng cannot trust people;
those he relies on and loves
are either members of the Xiàng clan
or his wife's brothers.
Even if there were extraordinary men, he could not employ them.
I heard that the King of Hàn is able to employ people,
so I came to Your Majesty.
I came empty-handed;
if I did not accept gold, I would have no funds.
If my plans are truly worthy of adoption,
I hope Your Majesty will use them;
if they are not useful,
all the gold is here;
I ask to seal it and deliver it to the officials,
and request to retire."
The King of Hàn then apologized,
generously rewarded him,
and appointed him Hùjūn Zhōngwèi,
giving him command over all generals.
The generals then dared not speak further.
19 Wèi Wáng Bào requested leave to return and visit his sick parents;
Yuègūi (謁歸),
means to request leave and return.
He instead turned against Hàn for Chǔ.
Bào's capital was Píngyáng,
which was in Hédōng,
so he blocked the ferries and crossings to resist the Hàn army.
Wéi (為),
read as yú wèi fān.
The 20th day of the sixth month,
King of Hàn, Hàn Wáng, returned to Lìyáng.
On the 21st day, Rénwǔ,
Yíng was made crown prince;
criminals were pardoned.
The Hàn army diverted water to flood Fèiqiu;
Fèiqiu surrendered,
and Zhāng Hán committed suicide.
The entire Yōng territory was pacified,
and it was established as Zhōngdì, Běidì, and Lǒngxī Commanderies.
From the establishment of Zhōngdì Commandery,
until its abolition in the ninth year [of the reign],
it was subordinate to the Nèishǐ.
In the sixth year of Jiànyuán of Emperor Wǔ,
it was divided into Yòu Nèishǐ;
in the first year of Tàichū,
the Zhǔjué Dūwèi was renamed Yòu Fúfēng.
There was a great famine in Guānzhōng,
with a measure of rice costing ten thousand cash,
and people resorted to cannibalism.
The people were ordered to seek food in Shǔ and Hàn.
Initially,
when Qín perished,
the powerful and heroic contended for gold and jade,
but the Rèn clan of Xuānqǔ alone stored grain in cellars.
The Hàn had the Chángshuǐ Xuānqǔ cavalry,
and among Gāozǔ's meritorious officials was the Marquis of Xuānqǔ,
which was probably a place name.
Zhāng Yī said: Xuānqǔ
is the name of a palace,
west of Kūnmíng Lake.
Shīgǔ said: Xuānqǔ
is the name of a watchtower.
Suǒyǐn said: The "Shànglín Fù" states: "Riding west to Xuānqǔ."
It should be in the capital region,
but its exact location is now unknown.
Jiào (窖),
pronunciation: gōng xiào fān;
to dig a pit in the ground to store grain.
The people could not farm,
and all the gold and jade of the powerful and heroic went to the Rèn clan;
the Rèn clan rose to prominence this way,
remaining wealthy for several generations.
In autumn,
in the eighth month,
the King of Hàn went to Xíngyáng,
ordering Xiāo Hé to guard Guānzhōng and attend to the crown prince,
to establish laws and regulations,
and to erect ancestral temples, altars of soil and grain, palaces, and towns.
If matters required urgent action without time to report and decide,
he could act expediently and implement them,
reporting them to the Emperor
upon his return.
He counted the households in Guānzhōng,
transported grain, and mobilized troops to supply the army,
never once running short.
The King of Hàn sent Lì Yìjī to persuade Wèi Wáng Bào,
and also to summon him.
Bào did not listen,
saying:
"The King of Hàn is arrogant and insults people,
cursing feudal lords and ministers as if they were slaves.
I cannot bear to see him again!"
Thereupon, the King of Hàn appointed Hán Xìn as Left Chancellor,
and together with Guàn Yīng and Cáo Cān, attacked Wèi.
The King of Hàn asked Lì Yìjī:
"Who is the great general of Wèi?"
He replied:
"Bǎi Zhí."
Xìng Pǔ says: Bǎi
is a descendant of Bǎi Huáng Shì.
Zhuānxù's teacher was Bǎi Zhāo;
Dìkù's teacher was Bǎi Jǐng.
During the Spring and Autumn period, the state of Bǎi was destroyed by Chǔ.
"He still smells of mother's milk,"
meaning he is young and inexperienced,
too weak for the task,
as if he has not left his nurse's embrace.
"Who is the cavalry general?"
He said:
"Féng Jìng."
He said:
"He is the son of Qín general Féng Wúzé.
Although capable,
he is no match for Guàn Yīng."
"Who is the infantry general?"
He said:
"Xiàng Tā."
He said:
"He is no match for Cáo Cān.
I have nothing to worry about!"
Hán Xìn also asked Lì Shēng:
"Has Wèi not appointed Zhōu Shú as their great general?"
Lì Shēng said:
"It is Bǎi Zhí."
Xìn said:
"He is just a young fellow!"
And so, he advanced his troops.
The King of Wèi amassed troops at Púbǎn to block Línjìn.
Xìn then created a diversion,
arranging boats as if to cross at Línjìn,
while his hidden troops crossed the river from Xiàyáng using wooden pots,
and attacked Ānyì by surprise.
Bān Zhì says,
Xiàyáng County belonged to Féngyì,
it was Shǎoliáng of Qín,
renamed in the eleventh year of Qín Huìwén Wáng.
Shǐjì Zhèngyì says: Xiàyáng is in the Hánchéng district north of Tóngzhōu.
Wooden pots,
Fú Qián said: Bundling pots with wooden planks to cross.
Wéi Zhāo said: Using wooden vessels shaped like pots to ferry troops,
without boats,
and also keeping it secret.
Shīgǔ said: Fú's explanation is correct.
Yīngfǒu refers to large-bellied, small-mouthed jars.
Yīng (罌),
pronunciation: yī zhèng fān,
kāng yú gēng fān.
He led his troops to intercept Xìn.
In the ninth month,
Xìn attacked and captured Bào,
sending him to Xíngyáng;
he completely pacified the Wèi territory,
establishing Hédōng, Shàngdǎng, and Tàiyuán Commanderies.
When Hàn was defeated at Péngchéng and retreated west,
Chén Yú also realized that Zhāng Ěr was not dead,
and immediately rebelled against Hàn.
After Hán Xìn had pacified Wèi,
he sent someone to request thirty thousand soldiers,
wishing to move north to take Yān and Zhào,
strike Qí to the east,
and cut off Chǔ's grain supply to the south.
The King of Hàn granted his request,
and dispatched Zhāng Ěr to go with him,
leading the troops east,
and north to attack Zhào and Dài.
At that time, Zhào Wáng Xiē ruled Zhào,
and Chén Yú ruled Dài.
Xìn defeated the Dài army
and captured Xià Yuè at Èyǔ.
Whenever Xìn conquered Wèi or defeated Dài,
Hàn immediately sent people to collect their elite troops and send them to Xíngyáng to resist Chǔ.
Collated by Niè Chóngqí, reviewed by Gù Jiégāng

Hanlin Scholar, Cháosàn Dàfū, Yòu Jiànyì Dàfū, Zhī Zhìgào and concurrently Shìjiǎng, concurrently Tíju Wànshòu Guān Gōngshì, concurrently Pàn Jíxián Yuàn, Shàng Hùjūn, Marquis of Hénèi Commandery, granted a fief of 1,300 households, bestowed with a purple-gold fish-pouch, your servant
Compiled by imperial decree
Hòu Xué Tiāntái
Volume 1, Part 2 of Tàizǔ Gāohuángdì
1. In winter, the tenth month,
Hán Xìn and Zhāng Ěr, with several tens of thousands of soldiers, moved east to attack Zhào.
Zhào Wáng and Chéng'ān Jūn Chén Yú heard of this,
and gathered their troops at Jǐngxíng Pass.
Dù Yòu said: Jǐngxíng Pass is in Lùquán County, Zhènzhōu,
now called Tǔmén.
According to Sòng Bái's Xù Tōngdiǎn.
Shíyì County of Zhènzhōu has Jǐngxíng Mountain,
which is very steep and secure.
Also,
Lùquán County,
originally the land of Shíyì County of Hàn,
was established in the sixteenth year of Kāihuáng of Suí,
and renamed Huòlù in the early Zhìdé period.
Also,
Jǐngxíng County,
the Mù Tiānzǐ Zhuàn
states "The Son of Heaven hunted at Xíng Mountain,"
which is this place.
The commentary says: Yān and Zhào call a mountain ridge a xíng.
Xíng Mountain is eighteen lì southeast of the county,
high on four sides,
low in the middle,
like a well,
hence it is called Jǐngxíng.
Guǎngwǔ-jūn Lǐ Zuǒchē (李左車) persuaded Chéng'ān-jūn (成安君), saying:
“Hán Xìn (韓信) and Zhāng Ěr (張耳), taking advantage of their victory, have come far from their homeland to fight.
This means to take advantage of the prevailing victorious momentum.
說 (shuō)
is pronounced shū ruì.
I have heard that ‘when provisions are sent a thousand *lǐ*,
the soldiers show signs of hunger;
when firewood and kindling are gathered after the meal,
樵 (qiáo)
means to gather firewood;
蘇 (sū)
means to gather grass.
Now, the road through Jǐngxíng (井陘)
is too narrow for chariots to travel abreast.
方軌 (fāng guǐ)
means chariots traveling abreast.
Having traveled several hundred *lǐ*,
their provisions must be far behind.
Zhèng Kāngchéng (鄭康成) said: Food for traveling is called 糧 (liáng),
referring to dry rations;
food for staying is called 食 (shí),
referring to rice.
If we cut off their baggage train from a side path,
Shīgǔ (師古) said: 間路 (jiānlù)
means a minor path.
間 (jiān)
is pronounced gǔ xiàn.
Shīgǔ (師古) said: 輜 (zī)
refers to a clothing wagon;
重 (zhòng)
refers to a wagon carrying heavy goods;
hence, the supplies of travelers
are collectively called 輜重 (zīzhòng).
The Shìmíng (釋名) states: 輜 (zī)
means 'mixed,'
because clothes and miscellaneous items are mixed within.
重 (zhòng)
is pronounced zhí yòng.
They will be unable to fight in front,
unable to retreat,
and there will be nothing to plunder in the countryside.
Within ten days,
the heads of both generals can be delivered to your banner.
Otherwise, you will certainly be captured by these two men.”
Chéng'ān-jūn (成安君) had always called his army a righteous force,
and would not use deceptive or cunning strategies.
He said:
“Hán Xìn's (韓信) army is small and exhausted.
If we avoid striking them like this,
the various lords will consider us timid and lightly come to attack us.”
Hán Xìn (韓信) sent spies to observe,
and knowing that Chéng'ān-jūn (成安君) would not use Guǎngwǔ-jūn's (廣武君) plan,
he was greatly pleased,
and then dared to lead his troops forward.
When they were thirty *lǐ* from the Jǐngxíngkǒu (井陘口),
he stopped and encamped.
This means stopping the army and resting in camp.
舍 (shè)
is pronounced as written.
He issued orders,
selecting two thousand light cavalry.
傳發 (chuánfā)
means transmitting orders throughout the army to dispatch troops.
The Hàn (漢) banners were all red.
幟 (zhì)
is pronounced chāng zhì.
He commanded:
“When Zhào (趙) sees us flee,
they will surely empty their camp to pursue us.
If you swiftly enter the Zhào (趙) camp,
若 (ruò)
means 'you.'
疾 (jí)
means 'swiftly.'
plant the Hàn (漢) red banners.”
He ordered his deputy generals to pass around a meal,
saying:
Fú Qián (服虔) said: 立 (lì)
means to establish.
傳餐 (chuáncān)
means to eat.
Rú Chún (如淳) said: A small meal is called 餐 (cān).
It means that after defeating Zhào (趙), they would all eat their fill.
餐 (cān)
is pronounced qiān ān.
“Today, after we defeat Zhào (趙), we will feast together!”
All the generals did not believe him,
but pretended to agree, saying,
“Yes.”
Hán Xìn (韓信) said:
“Zhào (趙) has already occupied a favorable position and fortified it.
Moreover, they have not yet seen our great general's banners and drums,
so they will not readily attack our vanguard,
fearing that we might reach a dangerous terrain and then turn back.”
Hán Xìn (韓信) probably meant that Zhào (趙) had gathered troops to block the mouth of Jǐngxíng (井陘),
intending to wait for Hán Xìn (韓信) to emerge from the difficult terrain before attacking him.
If they saw the vanguard and immediately engaged in battle,
Hán Xìn (韓信) would certainly retreat from the difficult terrain.
還 (huán)
is pronounced xuán,
and also as written.
He led his troops out,
arraying them with their backs to the water.
The Shǐjì Zhèngyì (史記正義) says: The Miánmàn (綿蔓) River flows from the north of Bìngzhōu (幷州) into the Jǐngxíng (井陘) county boundary,
which is where Hán Xìn (韓信) arrayed his troops with their backs to the water.
背 (bèi)
is pronounced pú mèi.
陳 (chén)
is read as zhèn.
At dawn,
Hán Xìn (韓信) raised the great general's banners and drums,
and marched with drums beating out of the Jǐngxíngkǒu (井陘口).
Zhào (趙) opened their camp and attacked them,
fighting fiercely for a long time.
Thereupon, Hán Xìn (韓信) and Zhāng Ěr (張耳) pretended to abandon their drums and banners,
and fled towards the army stationed by the water.
The army by the water opened their ranks to let them in,
and then fought fiercely again.
Zhào (趙) indeed emptied their camp to seize the Hàn (漢) banners and drums,
pursuing Hán Xìn (韓信) and Zhāng Ěr (張耳).
Hán Xìn (韓 Xìn) and Zhāng Ěr (張耳) had already entered the army by the water,
and the entire army fought to the death.
Shīgǔ (師古) said: 殊 (shū)
means 'extreme';
it means a determined fight to the death.
The two thousand cavalry of Hán Xìn's (韓信) extraordinary force, who had been waiting for Zhào (趙) to empty their camp and pursue the advantage,
then galloped into the Zhào (趙) camp,
removed all the Zhào (趙) banners,
and planted two thousand Hàn (漢) red banners.
The Zhào (趙) army, unable to capture Hán Xìn (韓信) and his men,
wanted to return to their camp.
But seeing their camp filled with Hàn (漢) red banners,
they were greatly astonished,
thinking that the Hàn (漢) had already captured the Zhào (趙) king and generals.
Their troops fell into disarray
and fled.
Although the Zhào (趙) generals executed some of them,
they could not stop the rout.
Thereupon, the Hàn (漢) army attacked from both sides,
greatly defeating the Zhào (趙) army,
and beheading Chéng'ān-jūn (成安君) by the Zhǐ (泜) River.
The Shuǐjīngzhù (水經註) says: The Zhǐ (泜) River is the water from the Jǐngxíng (井陘) Mountain,
commonly called the Lùquán (鹿泉) River.
It flows northeast,
bends past Chén Yú's (陳餘) stronghold,
and then flows east to join the Miánmàn (綿蔓) River.
Shīgǔ (師古) said: 泜 (zhǐ)
is pronounced zhī,
also dīng jì,
and also dīng lǐ.
The generals presented the heads of the captured and the prisoners,
and then offered congratulations,
asking Hán Xìn (韓信):
“The art of war states: ‘To the right, face mountains and hills;
to the front-left, face water and marshes.’
Yet today, the general ordered us to array our troops with our backs to the water,
saying ‘After defeating Zhào (趙), we will feast.’
We were not convinced,
yet we ultimately won.
What strategy was this?”
Hán Xìn (韓信) said:
“This is in the art of war;
it is merely that you gentlemen did not observe it closely!
Does not the art of war say: ‘Plunge them into a death ground, and they will live’?
Sūnzǐ (孫子) in 'Nine Grounds': A death ground is where fighting fiercely means survival, and not fighting means death.
Cáo Cāo (曹操) noted: A situation where there are high mountains in front and large waters behind, making advance impossible and retreat obstructed.
Moreover, I have not had the opportunity to consistently nurture and train these officers and gentlemen.
This is what is meant by ‘driving market people to battle.’
Shīgǔ (師古) said: It means like suddenly entering a marketplace and driving its people to battle, not those who are accustomed to training.
It makes every person fight for themselves.
If I were to give them a life ground,
they would all flee.
How could I still make use of them then!”
予 (yǔ)
is read as yǔ;
the same below.
All the generals were convinced,
saying:
“Excellent!
This is beyond what we could have achieved.”
Xìn 韓信 offered a thousand gold pieces to whoever could enlist Kuǎngwǔ-jūn 廣武君.
When someone brought him bound to his command,
Xìn 韓信 untied him,
seated him facing east,
and treated him as his teacher.
He asked,
"I wish to campaign north against Yān 燕 and
east against Qí 齊.
What should I do to achieve success?"
Héruò 何若
is equivalent to Hé rú 何如.
replied the prisoner, "a defeated and vanished captive,
how can I weigh important matters?"
Quán 權
is used to measure things,
to see their weight.
Zuǒchē Gài 左車蓋 meant that military affairs are a great matter for the state,
and someone like himself, a survivor of defeat and destruction,
was not capable of discerning and handling their relative importance.
"I have heard that Bǎilǐ Xī 百里奚 resided in Yú 虞 and Yú 虞 perished;
he was in Qín 秦 and Qín 秦 became hegemon.
Bǎilǐ Xī 百里奚 was a grandee of Yú 虞,
but the Duke of Yú 虞 could not use him, and so perished.
Duke Mù of Qín 秦 trusted and employed him,
and consequently dominated the Xīróng 西戎.
'Used or not used'
means 'listened to or not listened to'.
If Chéng'ān-jūn 成安君 had indeed listened to your counsel,
then someone like Xìn 韓信 would already have been captured.
Because he did not use your counsel,
Xìn 韓信 was able to serve."
This means he was able to serve by his side to seek instruction.
"I beg you, please do not refuse!"
Kuǎngwǔ-jūn 廣武君 said,
"Now, General, you have crossed the Xīhé 西河,
captured King Wèi 魏王,
and seized Xià Yuè 夏說.
You marched east through Jǐngxíng 井陘,
and in less than a morning, routed Zhào's 趙 two hundred thousand troops
and executed Chéng'ān-jūn 成安君.
Your fame is heard throughout the land,
your might shakes the world.
Farmers cease their plowing and put down their hoes,
dressing in fine clothes and eating delicious food,
leaning in to await your command.
This is the General's strength.
However, your troops are weary and exhausted;
in reality, they are difficult to employ.
Now, the General wishes to take these tired and worn-out soldiers and deploy them beneath the strong walls of Yān 燕.
If you wish to fight, you cannot;
if you attack, you cannot take it.
Your intentions will be revealed and your strength exhausted."
Bīng 兵,
the way of strategy,
relies on exploiting opportune situations.
Jiàn 見
means "exposed" or "revealed."
Qū 屈
means "exhausted."
If our intentions are revealed, the enemy will know how to prepare;
if our strength is exhausted, the enemy can exploit our weakness.
Jiàn 見,
pronounced xián biàn.
Qū 屈,
pronounced qí wù.
Your provisions will be depleted and exhausted.
Dān 單
is the same as dān 殫,
meaning "exhausted."
Qí 齊 will certainly resist at its borders to strengthen itself.
If Yān 燕 and Qí 齊 stand firm and do not submit,
then the power of Liú 劉 and Xiàng 項 will not yet be divided.
This is the General's weakness.
A good strategist does not use his weakness to attack the enemy's strength, but rather uses his strength to attack the enemy's weakness."
Hán Xìn 韓信 asked,
"So, what course should I follow?"
Yóu 由
means "from,"
referring to what plan one should follow.
"For the General now,
there is nothing better than to put down your armor and rest your troops,
and to pacify the people of Zhào 趙.
Within a hundred *lǐ* 里,
cattle and wine should arrive daily
to feast the officers and gentlemen.
Face north towards the Yān 燕 road,
and then dispatch persuasive speakers bearing letters of咫尺 zhǐchǐ."
Shīgǔ 師古 says: "Eight *cùn* 寸 is called a *zhǐ* 咫."
Zhǐchǐ 咫尺
means that the bamboo slips or wooden tablets
were either a *zhǐ* 咫 long
or a *chǐ* 尺 long,
metaphorically referring to something hasty.
Bào 暴
means "to display,"
"to show,"
"to reveal."
Once Yān 燕 has submitted, then march east to approach Qí 齊.
Even if there are wise men,
they will not know how to plan for Qí 齊.
If this is done,
then all affairs under Heaven can be achieved.
It is a truism that in warfare, 'sound comes before substance';
this is what is meant here."
Hán Xìn 韓信 said,
"Excellent!"
He followed this strategy,
sending envoys to Yān 燕.
Yān 燕 submitted as if swayed by the wind,
sending envoys to report to Hàn 漢,
and also requesting that Zhāng Ēr 張耳 be made King of Zhào 趙.
The King of Hàn 漢 agreed.
Chǔ 楚 repeatedly sent surprise troops across the river to attack Zhào 趙.

'Ér' (而)
means 'you'.
'Gōng' (公)
is an honorific title.
Gāozǔ (高祖), when rudely scolding people,
often said
'ér gōng' (而公)
or
'nǎi gōng' (迺公),
which were self-aggrandizing terms.
Jī (幾) is pronounced jū yī (居依) in a reversed fanqie spelling.
Xún Yuè (荀悅) commented: The art of devising strategies and determining victory
has three essentials: first, *xíng* (形) (form);
second, *shì* (勢) (circumstance);
third, *qíng* (情) (sentiment).
*Xíng* (形)
refers to the general balance of gains and losses;
*shì* (勢)
refers to the appropriateness of the moment and the opportune timing for advance or retreat;
*qíng* (情)
refers to the true state of hearts and minds, whether they agree or disagree.
Therefore, when plans are similar and situations equal, yet achievements differ,
it is because
the three arts differ.
Initially,
Zhāng Ěr (張耳) and Chén Yú (陳餘) persuaded Chén Shè (陳涉) to restore the Six States,
in order to form their own faction;
this event is recorded in Volume 7, Qin Èr Shì (秦二世) First Year.
The reason why similar persuasions led to different outcomes
is that when Chén Shè (陳涉) rose up,
everyone in the world wished to destroy Qín (秦);
but the division between Chǔ (楚) and Hàn (漢) was not yet settled,
and the world might not necessarily wish to destroy Xiàng (項) now.
Therefore, establishing the Six States,
for Chén Shè (陳涉),
was what is called increasing his own faction and augmenting Qín's (秦) enemies;
furthermore, Chén Shè (陳涉) was not yet able to exclusively control the lands of the world,
so it was called taking what he did not possess to give to others,
performing an empty kindness to gain real fortune.
Establishing the Six States,
for the King of Hàn (漢王),
was what is called carving up what he possessed to aid the enemy,
setting up an empty name to suffer real disaster.
This is an instance of the same matter with different *xíng* (形).
As for Sòng Yì (宋義) waiting for Qín (秦) and Zhào (趙) to perish,
this event is recorded in Volume 8, Qin Èr Shì (秦二世) Third Year.
Biàn Zhuāngzǐ (卞莊子) was about to stab a tiger.
Guǎn Shùzǐ (管豎子) stopped him, saying:
"Two tigers are currently eating an ox;
the ox meat is delicious, they will surely fight,
then the larger will be wounded,
and the smaller will die;
if you stab after they are wounded,
one attempt will surely yield two catches."
Zhuāngzǐ (莊子) agreed,
and indeed caught two tigers.
Neighboring states attacking each other,
without immediate urgency,
then this is permissible.
The Warring States period
had lasted for a long time;
one battle's victory or defeat
did not necessarily determine survival or destruction;
its *shì* (勢) (circumstance) was not one of urgent need to destroy enemy states;
advancing was for profit,
retreating was for self-preservation;
therefore, accumulating strength and waiting for the opportune moment,
to take advantage
of the enemy's demise,
was its natural *shì* (勢).
Now, the uprising of Chǔ (楚) and Zhào (趙)
meant that their *shì* (勢) with Qín (秦) could not stand side-by-side;
the critical moment of safety or danger
could change in an instant;
advancing would secure success,
retreating would incur disaster.
This is an instance of the same matter with different *shì* (勢).
During the campaign against Zhào,
Hán Xìn's army was stationed on the Jīshuǐ river, and Zhào was unable to defeat them.
This event is detailed in the third year of the previous volume.
King of Hàn fought on the Suīshuǐ river,
where all his soldiers plunged into the Suīshuǐ and the Chǔ army won a great victory.
This event is detailed in the second year of the previous volume.
Nán,
pronounced dàn.
The Zhào soldiers came out of their state to engage in battle;
they advanced when they saw an opportunity,
and retreated when they knew it was difficult.
They harbored thoughts of looking back to their homeland
and had no intention of fighting to the death.
Hán Xìn's army, isolated on the river,
had no choice but to fight to the death,
with no wavering in their resolve.
This is why Hán Xìn was victorious.
The King of Hàn penetrated deep into enemy territory,
held feasts and grand assemblies;
his soldiers were at ease and complacent,
their fighting spirit not firm.
Chǔ, with its powerful might, had lost its capital,
and all its soldiers were filled with indignation
and the urgency to save themselves from defeat and ruin,
prepared to stake their lives on a single battle.
This is why Hàn was defeated.
Furthermore, Hán Xìn selected elite troops for defense,
while Zhào attacked with soldiers who were concerned about their homeland.
Xiàng Yǔ selected elite troops for offense,
while Hàn responded with complacent and lazy soldiers.
These are similar situations with different outcomes.
Therefore it is said: Strategies cannot be predetermined,
and changes cannot be planned beforehand.
To shift with the times
and adapt to changing circumstances
is the key to formulating policies.

when will it be settled?"

Jū,
pronounced zǐ yú.

The King of Hàn said:

the fourth month,

Cǎo,

Jiàn,
