and a left plume.
Lǐ Fěi says: The Son of Heaven's carriage has a canopy lined with yellow silk.
Dào,
is a feathered banner,
placed on the upright pillar to the left of the carriage yoke.
Cài Yōng says: It is made of yak tails,
as large as a dou measure,
sometimes on the outer horse's head,
sometimes on the yoke.
Yīng Shào says: It is made of pheasant tails,
on the left outer horse,
above the bit.
Shīgǔ says: Yīng's explanation is incorrect.
Ěryǎ Yì: Máo,
is a long-haired ox from the southwestern barbarians.
It resembles an ox,
with reddish hair over a foot long on all four joints, under its belly, and at its elbows,
but its tail is especially fine,
and as large as a dou.
The Son of Heaven's carriage has a left plume (dào)
made from this ox's tail,
tied to the yoke of the left outer horse.
Horses in the middle are called fú,
those on the outside are called fēi.
Fēi
is also cān.
It is placed on the outermost horse's head
to confuse the horses' vision,
preventing them from seeing each other.
Dào,
pronounced tú dǎo,
also pronounced dú.
"The food is exhausted,
the King of Hàn surrenders."
Chǔ all shouted "Long live!"
and went to the eastern observation tower of the city.
Because of this, the King of Hàn was able to escape with several tens of horsemen through the west gate.
He ordered Hán Wáng Xìn, Zhōu Kē, Wèi Bào, and Cóng Gōng to defend Xíngyáng.
Yǔ saw Jǐ Xìn
and asked:
"Where is the King of Hàn?"
He replied:
"He has already left."
Yǔ burned and killed Jǐ Xìn.
Zhōu Kē and Cóng Gōng said to each other:
"A king who has betrayed his state
is difficult to hold the city with!"
They then killed Wèi Bào.
King Hàn (Hàn Wáng) left Xíngyáng,
arrived at Chénggāo,
entered the Pass,
and gathered troops, intending to return east.
Yuán Shēng persuaded King Hàn, saying:
Yuán
is a surname.
The Book of Surnames states: a descendant of Yuán Táotú (Yuán Táotú), a grandee of Chén.
Considering its origin,
it is also related to the surnames Yuán (Yuán) and Yuán (Yuán).
“Hàn and Chǔ have been stalemated at Xíngyáng for several years,
and Hàn has often been in distress.
I wish that Your Majesty would exit through Wǔguān.
King Xiàng (Xiàng Wáng) will surely lead his troops south.
Your Majesty should build strong defenses and not engage in battle,
allowing the areas between Xíngyáng and Chénggāo to rest for a while,
and enabling Hán Xìn (Hán Xìn) and others to pacify and settle the Zhào territory north of the Yellow River,
and to ally with Yān and Qí.
Shī Gǔ (Shī Gǔ) said: Jí (輯)
is the same as Jí (集),
meaning to harmonize and unite.
The Preface to the Book of Odes says:
‘Bring comfort and restore peace and stability.’
The Zuǒ Zhuàn (Zuǒ Zhuàn) of the Spring and Autumn Annals says:
‘Ministers gather in harmony.’
Other instances are similar.
If this is done,
Chǔ will have many places to guard,
and its strength will be divided;
Hàn will gain rest.
When we engage them in battle again,
we will surely defeat them!”
King Hàn followed his plan,
and led his army between Wǎn and Yè.
The Bān Zhì (Bān Zhì) states that
these two counties belonged to Nányáng Commandery.
The Shǐ Jì Zhèng Yì (Shǐ Jì Zhèng Yì) states: Wǎn
is a county in Dèngzhōu.
Yè
is a county in Rúzhōu.
Wǎn
is pronounced 'yú yuán'.
Yè
is pronounced 'shì shè'.
Yǔ (Yǔ) heard that King Hàn was in Wǎn,
and indeed led his troops south;
King Hàn strengthened his defenses and did not engage in battle.
When King Hàn was defeated at Péngchéng,
and retreated west,
Péng Yuè (Péng Yuè) lost all the cities he had conquered.
He alone led his troops north, stationed along the Yellow River,
and constantly acted as a mobile force for Hàn, attacking Chǔ
and cutting off its rear supplies.
In this month,
Péng Yuè crossed the Suī River,
fought Xiàng Shēng (Xiàng Shēng) and Xuē Gōng (Xuē Gōng) at Xiàpī,
defeated them,
and killed Xuē Gōng.
Yǔ then sent Zhōng Gōng (Zhōng Gōng) to guard Chénggāo.
Zhōng
is a surname.
The Book of Surnames states: a descendant of Lù Zhōng (Lù Zhōng).
King Hàn led his troops north,
defeated Zhōng Gōng,
and re-garrisoned Chénggāo.
In the sixth month,
Yǔ had already defeated and routed Péng Yuè,
and upon hearing that Hàn had re-garrisoned Chénggāo,
he led his troops west and captured Xíngyáng City,
capturing Zhōu Kē (Zhōu Kē) alive.
Yǔ said to Kē:
“If you serve me,
I will appoint you as a supreme general
and grant you a fief of thirty thousand households.”
Zhōu Kē cursed, saying:
“If you don't quickly surrender to Hàn,
you will now become a captive;
you are no match for King Hàn!”
Yǔ boiled Zhōu Kē alive,
and also killed Cóng Gōng (Cóng Gōng) and captured King Hán Xìn (Hán Wáng Xìn),
then besieged Chénggāo.
King Hàn escaped,
alone with Téng Gōng (Téng Gōng), they rode out of Chénggāo through the Yùmén Gate.
Zhāng Yàn (Zhāng Yàn) said: Yùmén
is the north gate of Chénggāo.
They lodged at a post station in Xiǎoxiūwǔ.
Jìn Zhuó (Jìn Zhuó) said: It is east of Dàxiūwǔ City.
He claimed to be a Hàn envoy
and galloped into the Zhào encampment.
Zhāng Ěr (Zhāng Ěr) and Hán Xìn (Hán Xìn) had not yet risen.
He immediately entered their sleeping quarters
and seized their seals and tallies to summon the generals,
replacing them.
When Xìn (Xìn) and Ěr (Ěr) rose,
they then realized that King Hàn had come,
and were greatly astonished.
After King Hàn had seized the armies of the two men,
he immediately ordered Zhāng Ěr to patrol
and guard
the Zhào territory.
He appointed Hán Xìn (Hán Xìn) as chancellor
and gathered the Zhào soldiers who had not yet been deployed to attack Qí.
The generals gradually managed to leave Chénggāo and follow King Hàn.
Chǔ then captured Chénggāo,
and intended to move west;
Hàn sent troops to defend against them at Gǒng.
The Bān Zhì (Bān Zhì) states:
Gǒng County belonged to Hénán Commandery,
which was where the Lord of Eastern Zhōu (Dōng Zhōu Jūn) resided.
The Rǔ Luò Dì Tú (Rǔ Luò Dì Tú) says: Gǒng (鞏)
means solid.
Gǒng County is located between the Luò Rivers,
meaning it is surrounded by mountains
and can be consolidated.
6. Autumn,
seventh month.
A comet (bèi) appeared near Dàjiǎo.
The Suí Tiānwén Zhì (Suí Tiānwén Zhì) says: Bèi
is a type of huì (comet);
one that points to a specific direction is called huì,
while one with its radiance spreading in all four directions is called bèi.
Bèi,
meaning rampant,
is born from unusually malevolent qi.
If there is no great internal chaos,
there will surely be a great war.
When the world conspires together,
it becomes dark and unclear,
and harm will occur.
Yàn Zǐ (Yàn Zǐ) said:
“If the lord does not change,
a bèi star will appear,
what is there to fear about a huì!”
From this, it can be said that
this disaster is more severe than a huì.
Bèi
is pronounced 'pú nèi',
and also 'pú mò'.
The Bān Zhì (Bān Zhì) says: The numerous stars south of Fáng are called Qíguān;
the left horn governs justice,
and the right horn governs generals.
Dàjiǎo
is the court of the Heavenly King, the Imperial Seat.
7. King Língjiāng (Língjiāng Wáng) Áo (Áo) died;
his son Wèi (Wèi) succeeded him.
8. King Hàn (Hàn Wáng) obtained Hán Xìn's (Hán Xìn) army,
and his forces greatly revived.
In the eighth month,
he led his troops to the Yellow River,
facing south,
and encamped at Xiǎoxiūwǔ,
intending to fight Chǔ again.
The Lángzhōng Zhèng Zhōng (Zhèng Zhōng) advised King Hàn to stop.
The Hàn system: Yìláng and Zhōngláng,
rank equivalent to 600 dàn of grain;
Shìláng,
equivalent to 400 dàn;
Lángzhōng,
equivalent to 300 dàn;
all belonged to the Lángzhōnglìng.
Shuì (說)
is pronounced 'shì ruì'.
King Hàn heeded his plan,
and sent Generals Liú Jiǎ (Liú Jiǎ) and Lú Wǎn (Lú Wǎn) with twenty thousand infantry
and several hundred cavalry
across the Báimǎ Jīn ford,
to enter Chǔ territory,
assist Péng Yuè (Péng Yuè),
burn Chǔ's accumulated stores,
and thus destroy their livelihood.
Shī Gǔ (Shī Gǔ) said: Jījù (積聚)
refers to accumulated military provisions, fodder, and similar items.
Jī (積)
is pronounced 'zǐ cì'.
Jù (聚)
is pronounced 'cái yù'.
Chǔ troops attacked Liú Jiǎ,
but Jiǎ (Jiǎ) always maintained strong defenses and refused to fight,
instead securing his position with Péng Yuè.
9 Péng Yuè (彭越) attacked and captured the territory of Liáng (梁).
He conquered seventeen cities, including Suīyáng (睢陽) and Wàihuáng (外黃).
Suīyáng (睢陽)
was a Qín (秦) county,
belonging to Dàng (碭) Commandery.
Under the Hàn (漢), it belonged to the State of Liáng (梁國),
and was the state where Wēizǐ (微子) was originally enfeoffed.
In the Táng (唐) dynasty, it became Sòngchéng (宋城) County of Sòng (宋) Prefecture.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: The old city of Wàihuáng (外黃) of the Hàn (漢)
was east of Yōngqiū (雍丘) County in Chénliú (陳留) Commandery.
The Spring and Autumn
passage, "Duke Huán (桓) of Qí (齊) met the feudal lords at Kuíqiū (葵丘),"
refers to this place.
Xiàng Wáng (項王) said to Grand Marshal Cáo Jiù (曹咎):
"Guard Chénggāo (成皋 diligently)!
If the King of Hàn (漢王) wants to challenge you to battle,
by no means engage him,
just prevent him from advancing eastward.
I will definitely pacify the Liáng (梁) territory in fifteen days,
and then return to the general."
Yǔ (羽) led his troops eastward,
attacking Chénliú (陳留), Wàihuáng (外黃), Suīyáng (睢陽) and other cities,
and conquered them all.
The King of Hàn (漢王) wished to abandon the area east of Chénggāo (成皋),
and garrison Gǒng (鞏) and Luò (洛) to resist Chǔ (楚).
Lì Shēng (酈生) said:
"I have heard, 'He who knows the heaven of Heaven,
can accomplish the king's enterprise.'
A king takes the people as his heaven,
and the people take food as their heaven.
The Dà Dài Lǐ (大戴禮) says: Those who eat grains are wise and skillful.
The Gǔ Shǐ Kǎo (古史考) says: In ancient times, people ate raw meat and drank blood.
Suìrénshì (燧人氏) drilled for fire,
and then people began to wrap meat and roast it, calling it 'páo' (炮).
In the time of Shénnóng (神農),
people began to eat grains,
adding rice on top of hot stones and eating it.
By the time of Huángdì (黃帝),
there were finally pots and steamers,
and the way of cooking with fire was perfected.
The world has been transporting supplies for a long time,
and I hear that there are very large grain reserves below.
The Chǔ (楚) people captured Xíngyáng (滎陽),
but did not firmly hold Àocāng (敖倉),
instead withdrawing eastward,
ordering their crack troops to guard Chénggāo (成皋).
This is what Heaven provides to Hàn (漢).
At present, Chǔ (楚) is easy to defeat, yet Hàn (漢) retreats,
giving up its advantage.
I humbly think this is a mistake!
Moreover, two heroes cannot stand together.
Chǔ (楚) and Hàn (漢) have been locked in a stalemate for a long time,
the world is in turmoil,
farmers have abandoned their plows.
Lěi (耒)
refers to a curved wooden tool used for hand-plowing.
The hearts of the people under Heaven have not yet settled.
I wish Your Excellency would swiftly advance your troops again,
recapture Xíngyáng (滎陽),
seize the grain of Àocāng (敖倉),
block the strategic pass of Chénggāo (成皋),
obstruct the road through Tàiháng (太行),
and guard the mouth of Fēihú (蜚狐).
Rú Chún (如淳) said: This is Húguān (壺關) in Shàngdǎng (上黨).
Minister Zàn (瓚) said: The Fēihú (飛狐) mouth is in Dài (代) Commandery.
Shīgǔ (師古) said: Zàn's (瓚) explanation is correct;
Húguān (壺關) has no name of Fēihú (飛狐).
The Dì Dào Jì (地道記) says: Mount Héng (恒山) is one hundred and forty li northwest of Shàngqǔyáng (上曲陽) County.
Going north four hundred and fifty li,
one reaches the gully of Mount Héng (恒山),
called Fēihú Kǒu (飛狐口).
North of it is Dài (代) Commandery.
The Shuǐ Jīng Zhù (水經註) says: Forty li south of Dài (代) Commandery is Fēihú Guān (蜚狐關).
The Shǐ Jì Zhèng Yì (史記正義) says: According to Wèi (蔚) Prefecture, Fēihú (飛狐) County, one hundred and fifty li north, there is the old city of Dài (代) Commandery from Qín (秦) and Hàn (漢) times.
To the southwest there is a mountain,
commonly called Fēihú Kǒu (蜚狐口).
Sè (塞),
pronounced 'sī zé' in 'fān' (悉則翻).
Xíng (行),
pronounced 'hù gāng' in 'fān' (戶剛翻).
This will demonstrate to the feudal lords the strategic advantage of our formation,
meaning to occupy strategic terrain to control the enemy.
The King agreed,
and then reconsidered taking Àocāng (敖倉).
Shíqí (食其) further advised the King, saying:
"Currently, Yān (燕) and Zhào (趙) are settled,
only Qí (齊) has not yet submitted.
The various Tián (田) clans are strong.
They rely on the sea and Mount Dài (岱),
and are protected by the Hé (河) and Jì (濟) Rivers.
Qí (齊) territory extends eastward to the sea,
and southward to Mount Tài (太山),
hence it is said they 'rely on the sea and Mount Dài (岱)'.
To the west, they are protected by the clear Jì (濟) River,
and to the north by the muddy Hé (河) River,
hence it is said they are 'protected by the Hé (河) and Jì (濟) Rivers'.
Jì (濟),
pronounced 'zǐ lǐ' in 'fān' (子禮翻).
Their people are full of deceit;
even if Your Excellency sends tens of thousands of troops,
it cannot be conquered in a matter of months or years.
I request permission to take your clear edict to persuade the King of Qí (齊),
to make him serve Hàn (漢) and declare himself an eastern vassal."
Kǎo Yì (考異) says: The Shǐ Jì (史記) and Hàn Shū (漢書) combine Shíqí's (食其) advice to take Àocāng (敖倉) and his request to persuade Qí (齊) into one event.
Only Liú Xiàng's (劉向) Xīn Xù (新序) divides them into two.
Your servant believes that dividing them into two is correct.
"Good!"
Then Lì Shēng (酈生) was sent to persuade the King of Qí (齊), saying:
"Does Your Majesty know to whom the world belongs?"
The King said:
"I do not.
To whom does the world belong?"
Lì Shēng (酈生) said:
"To Hàn (漢)!"
He asked:
"How does Master say this?"
He replied:
"The King of Hàn (漢王) entered Xiányáng (咸陽) first;
Xiàng Wáng (項王) broke his covenant,
and made him king of Hànzhōng (漢中).
Xiàng Wáng (項王) moved and then killed Emperor Yì (義帝);
the King of Hàn (漢王), hearing of this,
raised troops from Shǔ (蜀) and Hàn (漢) to attack the Three Qín (秦),
emerged from the pass, and demanded an accounting for the Emperor Yì's (義帝) fate.
He gathered the armies of the world,
and established the descendants of the feudal lords.
When a city surrenders, he immediately enfeoffs its general;
when he obtains bribes, he immediately distributes them to his soldiers.
He shares his benefits with the world,
and all heroes and talented individuals are happy to serve him.
Xiàng Wáng (項王) has the reputation of breaking covenants,
and the guilt of killing Emperor Yì (義帝).
Máo Huàng (毛晃) said: To be ungrateful and lacking in virtue is 'fù' (負).
Bèi (倍)
is the same as bèi (背),
pronounced 'pú mèi' in 'fān' (蒲妹翻).
There is nothing forgotten of his crimes against people.
When he wins battles, his men do not get their rewards;
when he captures cities, they do not get their fiefs.
No one but a member of the Xiàng (項) clan can hold office.
The world revolts against him,
and the talented resent him,
and no one serves him.
Therefore, the affairs of the world belong to the King of Hàn (漢王);
this can be determined sitting down!
Indeed, the King of Hàn (漢王) launched from Shǔ (蜀) and Hàn (漢),
pacified the Three Qín (秦);
crossed the Xīhé (西河),
and defeated Běi Wèi (北魏).
The Hé (河) River, from Dǐzhù (砥柱) upstream to Lóngmén (龍門) downstream, is called Xīhé (西河).
Suǒ Yǐn (索隱) says: Běi Wèi (北魏)
refers to Wèi Wáng Bào (魏王豹),
because Bào's (豹) state was north of the Hé (河) River.
It was also called Xī Wèi (西魏),
because Dàliáng (大梁) was east of Ānyì (安邑).
He executed Chéng'ān Jūn (成安君).
This is not human strength;
it is a blessing from Heaven!
Now he has seized the grain of Àocāng (敖倉),
blocked the strategic pass of Chénggāo (成皋),
guarded the ford of Báimǎ (白馬),
obstructed the slopes of Tàiháng (太行),
and defended the mouth of Fēihú (蜚狐).
Those in the world who submit later will be the first to perish.
Lì Shēng's (酈生) persuasion
is a persuasion based on strategic terrain and constrained circumstances.
Indeed, by occupying Àocāng (敖倉)
and blocking Chénggāo (成皋),
Xiàng Yǔ (項羽) cannot advance westward.
By guarding Báimǎ (白馬),
obstructing Tàiháng (太行),
and defending Fēihú (蜚狐),
the territory of Yān (燕) and Zhào (趙) north of the Hé (河) will all belong to Hàn (漢).
Where will Qí (齊) and Chǔ (楚) go then!
Báimǎ Jīn (白馬津) is in Táng (唐) Huázhōu (滑州).
Tàiháng Bǎn (太行阪) is in Táng (唐) Zézhōu (澤州) territory.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: Wèi (蔚) Prefecture's Fēihú (飛狐) County
was the land of Hàn (漢) Guǎngchāng (廣昌) County.
Fēihú Kǒu (飛狐口) is north of the county,
which is the Hàn (漢) Fēihú Dào (飛狐道),
connecting to Guīchuān (媯川) Commandery's Huáiróng (懷戎) County.
The state of Qí (齊) can be preserved.
Otherwise,
peril and destruction can be awaited immediately!"
Previously,
Qí (齊), hearing that Hán Xìn (韓信) was about to march eastward,
sent Huá Wúshāng (華無傷) and Tián Jiě (田解) to lead heavy troops to garrison Lìxià (歷下),
and encamp
to resist Hàn (漢).
When they accepted Lì Shēng's (酈生) words
and sent an envoy to make peace with Hàn (漢),
they then withdrew the defensive preparations at Lìxià (歷下)
and indulged in daily feasting with Lì Shēng (酈生).
Hán Xìn 引兵東 (led his troops east),
未度平原 (before crossing Píngyuán),
聞酈食其已說下齊 (heard that Lì Yìjī had already persuaded Qí to surrender),
欲止 (and wanted to stop).
辨士蒯徹說信曰 (The debater Kuǎi Chè persuaded Xìn, saying):
「將軍受詔擊齊 (“General, you received an edict to attack Qí),
而漢獨發間使下齊 (but Hàn alone sent an envoy to persuade Qí to surrender).
寧有詔止將軍乎 (Is there an edict stopping you, General),
何以得毋行也 (why should you not proceed)?
且酈生 (Moreover, Lì Shēng),
一士 (a mere scholar),
伏軾掉三寸之舌 (leaned on his carriage rail and wagged his three-inch tongue),
軾 (Shì),
車前橫木 (the horizontal bar at the front of a carriage),
人所憑者 (what people lean on).
掉 (Diào),
徒釣翻 (tú diào fān),
搖也 (to wag or sway).
將軍以數萬衆 (You, General, with tens of thousands of troops),
歲餘乃下趙五十餘城 (took over a year to conquer more than fifty cities of Zhào).
為將數歲 (Having been a general for several years),
反不如一豎儒之功乎 (your accomplishments are instead inferior to those of a single junior scholar)!”
於是信然之 (Thereupon, Xìn believed him),
遂渡河 (and crossed the river).
1 冬 (In winter),
十月 (the tenth month),
信襲破齊歷下軍 (Xìn launched a surprise attack and defeated Qí’s forces at Lìxià),
遂至臨淄 (and then reached Línzī).
齊王以酈生為賣己 (The King of Qí, believing Lì Shēng had betrayed him),
乃烹之 (then boiled him alive);
引兵東走高密 (he led his troops east to Gāomì),
高密縣在膠西 (Gāomì County was in Jiāoxī),
宣帝本始元年為高密國 (and in the first year of Xuāndì's Běnshǐ reign, it became Gāomì Kingdom).
宋白曰 (Sòng Bái said): 高密 (Gāomì),
春秋時晏平仲所食邑 (was the fief of Yàn Píngzhòng during the Chūnqiū period).
田橫走博陽 (Tián Héng fled to Bóyáng),
此據史記也 (this is according to the Shǐjì).
班書作 (Bān Shū writes)
「橫走博」(“Héng fled to Bó”).
博陽近清河博關 (Bóyáng is near Bóguān in Qīnghé),
此正韓信自趙進兵之路 (this was precisely Hán Xìn’s route of advance from Zhào).
臨淄既破 (Once Línzī was breached),
君、相皆出走 (the king and his chancellor both fled).
其後韓信既虜田廣於濰水 (Afterwards, Hán Xìn captured Tián Guǎng at Wéishuǐ),
灌嬰又敗田橫於嬴下 (and Guàn Yīng further defeated Tián Héng at Yíngxià).
嬴縣亦屬太山郡 (Yíng County also belonged to Tàishān Commandery).
括地志：故嬴城在兗州博城縣東北百里 (Kuòdìzhì: The former Yíng city was a hundred *lǐ* northeast of Bóchéng County in Yǎnzhōu).
唐之博城 (Bóchéng in Táng times),
漢太山之博縣 (was Bó County of Tàishān in Hàn times);
此博陽 (this Bóyáng),
即博城之陽 (is the south side of Bóchéng).
將軍田既軍於膠東 (General Tián Jì was stationed in Jiāodōng).
括地志：即墨故城在萊州膠水縣南六十里 (Kuòdìzhì: The former city of Jìmò was sixty *lǐ* south of Jiāoshuǐ County in Láizhōu),
古齊地 (ancient Qí territory),
漢為膠東國 (which became Jiāodōng Kingdom in Hàn),
以其地在膠水之東也 (because its land was east of the Jiāo River).
2 楚大司馬咎守成皋 (The Grand Marshal of Chǔ, Cáo Jiù, defended Chénggāo),
漢數挑戰 (Hàn repeatedly challenged them to battle),
楚軍不出 (but the Chǔ army did not come out).
使人辱之 (Hàn sent people to insult them),
數日 (after several days),
咎怒 (Cáo Jiù became enraged),
渡兵汜水 (and crossed the Sìshuǐ River with his troops).
張晏曰 (Zhāng Yàn said): 汜水在濟陰界 (Sìshuǐ is on the border of Jìyīn).
如淳曰 (Rú Chún said): 汜 (Sì),
音祀 (pronounced Sì).
左傳曰 (Zuǒzhuàn says):
「鄙在鄭地汜 (“My humble abode is in Sì, a territory of Zhèng”).”
臣瓚曰 (Minister Zàn said): 高祖攻曹咎於成皋 (Gāozǔ attacked Cáo Jiù at Chénggāo),
咎渡汜水而戰 (Cáo Jiù crossed the Sìshuǐ River to fight),
今成皋城東汜水是也 (it is the Sìshuǐ east of Chénggāo city today).
師古曰 (Shīgǔ said): 瓚說得之 (Zàn's explanation is correct),
此水不在濟陰也 (this river is not in Jìyīn).
「鄙在鄭地汜」(“My humble abode is in Sì, a territory of Zhèng”),
釋者云在襄城 (commentators say it is in Xiāngchéng),
則亦非此汜水 (then it is also not this Sìshuǐ).
舊讀音凡 (It used to be pronounced Fán),
今彼鄉人呼之音祀 (now the local people pronounce it Sì).
索隱曰 (Suǒyǐn said): 此水今見名汜水 (This river is still called Sìshuǐ today),
音似 (pronounced Sì);
臣瓚說是 (Minister Zàn's statement is correct).
張晏曰 (Zhāng Yàn said): 在濟陰亦未全失 (Being in Jìyīn is also not entirely wrong).
按古濟水當此截河而南 (According to ancient maps, the Jǐshuǐ River at this point intersected the river and flowed south),
又東流溢為滎澤 (and then flowed east, overflowing into Xíngzé).
水南曰陰 (South of a river is called *yīn*),
此亦在濟之陰 (this is also south of the Jǐ River),
非彼濟陰郡耳 (but not that Jìyīn Commandery).
括地志：汜水源出洛州汜水縣東南三十二里方山 (Kuòdìzhì: The source of Sìshuǐ is in Fāngshān, thirty-two *lǐ* southeast of Sìshuǐ County in Luòzhōu).
山海經：浮戲之山 (Shānhǎijīng: Fúxì Mountain),
汜水出焉 (Sìshuǐ flows from it).
漢擊之 (Hàn attacked them),
大破楚軍 (and utterly defeated the Chǔ army),
盡得楚國金玉、貨賂 (capturing all of Chǔ's gold, jade, and valuables).
咎及司馬欣皆自剄汜水上 (Cáo Jiù and Sīmǎ Xīn both committed suicide by cutting their throats by the Sìshuǐ).
漢王引兵渡河 (The King of Hàn led his troops across the river),
復取成皋 (retook Chénggāo),
軍廣武 (and camped at Guǎngwǔ).
孟康曰 (Mèng Kāng said): 於滎陽築兩城相對為廣武 (Two cities built facing each other in Xíngyáng were called Guǎngwǔ),
在敖倉西三皇山上 (on Sānhuáng Mountain, west of Áocāng).
括地志：東廣武、西廣武在鄭州滎陽縣西二十里 (Kuòdìzhì: Dōng Guǎngwǔ and Xī Guǎngwǔ are twenty *lǐ* west of Xíngyáng County in Zhèngzhōu).
戴延之西征記曰 (Dài Yánzhī's Xīzhēngjì says): 三皇山上有二城 (There are two cities on Sānhuáng Mountain),
東曰東廣武 (the eastern one called Dōng Guǎngwǔ),
西曰西廣武 (the western one called Xī Guǎngwǔ),
各在一山頭 (each on a mountaintop),
相去百步 (a hundred paces apart).
汴水從廣澗中東南流 (The Biànshuǐ River flowed southeast through the broad valley),
今涸無水 (now it is dry and has no water).
城各有三面 (Each city has three sides),
在敖倉西 (west of Áocāng).
郭緣生述征記曰 (Guō Yuánshēng's Shùzhēngjì says): 一澗橫絕上過 (A ravine cut across it from above),
名曰廣武 (named Guǎngwǔ),
相對皆立城塹 (fortifications were built facing each other),
遂號東、西廣武 (thus they were called Dōng and Xī Guǎngwǔ).
項羽下梁地十餘城 (Xiàng Yǔ had conquered more than ten cities in Liáng territory),
聞成皋破 (when he heard Chénggāo had fallen),
乃引兵還 (he then led his troops back).
漢軍方圍鍾離昧於滎陽東 (The Hàn army was then besieging Zhōnglí Mèi east of Xíngyáng),
聞羽至 (when they heard Yǔ had arrived),
盡走險阻 (they all fled to strategic strongholds).
羽亦軍廣武 (Yǔ also encamped at Guǎngwǔ),
與漢相守 (and faced off against Hàn).
數月 (For several months),
楚軍食少 (the Chǔ army's food supply dwindled).
項王患之 (King Xiàng worried about this),
乃為俎 (so he set up a chopping board),
置太公其上 (placed Tàigōng upon it),
告漢王曰 (and told the King of Hàn, saying):
「今不急下 (“If you do not surrender quickly now),
吾烹太公 (I will boil Tàigōng alive)!”
漢王曰 (The King of Hàn said):
「吾與羽俱北面受命懷王 (“You and I both faced north and received orders from King Huái),
約為兄弟 (and pledged to be brothers).
吾翁即若翁 (My father is your father);
必欲烹而翁 (if you must boil your father alive),
幸分我一桮羹 (please be kind enough to share a cup of the broth with me)!”
如淳曰 (Rú Chún said): 俎 (Zǔ),
高几之上也 (is the top of a tall table).
李奇曰 (Lǐ Qí said): 軍中巢櫓謂之俎 (In the army, watchtowers are called *zǔ*).
師古曰 (Shīgǔ said): 俎者 (A *zǔ*),
所以薦肉 (is used for offering meat),
示欲烹之 (to show an intention to boil him),
故置俎上 (thus he was placed on the *zǔ*);
如說是 (Rú's explanation is correct).
俎 (Zǔ),
在呂翻 (zài lǚ fān).
方言：周、晉、秦、隴謂父為翁 (Fāngyán: In Zhōu, Jìn, Qín, and Lǒng, father is called *wēng*).
若 (Ruò),
汝也 (is you);
而 (ér),
亦汝也 (is also you).
古者以桮盛羹 (In ancient times, broth was served in a *bēi*),
今之盃側有兩耳者也 (which is like today's cup with two handles on the side).
欲殺之 (He wanted to kill him).
項伯曰 (Xiàng Bó said):
「天下事未可知 (“The affairs of the world are uncertain);
且為天下者不顧家 (and he who seeks to rule the world disregards his family).
雖殺之無益 (Even if you kill him, it will be of no benefit),
祇益禍耳 (it will only increase disaster)!”
項王從之 (King Xiàng followed his advice).
項王謂漢王曰 (King Xiàng said to the King of Hàn):
「天下匈匈數歲者 (The chaos in the world for several years),
徒以吾兩人耳 (is merely due to the two of us).
願與漢王挑戰 (I wish to challenge the King of Hàn to single combat),
決雌雄 (to decide the victor),
毋徒苦天下之民父子為也 (and not unnecessarily torment the fathers and sons of the common people under heaven)!”
漢王笑謝曰 (The King of Hàn smiled and replied with a refusal, saying):
「吾寧鬬智 (“I would rather compete in wisdom),
不能鬬力 (I cannot compete in strength).”
項王三令壯士出挑戰 (King Xiàng three times ordered strong warriors to come out and challenge),
漢有善騎射者樓煩輒射殺之 (but Hàn had Lóufán, skilled in cavalry and archery, who immediately shot and killed them).
應劭曰 (Yìng Shào said): 樓煩 (Lóufán),
胡人也 (is a Hu person).
李奇曰 (Lǐ Qí said): 後為縣 (Later it became a county),
屬鴈門 (belonging to Yànmén).
此縣人善騎射 (People from this county were skilled in cavalry and archery).
謂士為樓煩 (Calling the warrior Lóufán),
取其稱耳 (is taking his honorific title),
未必樓煩人也 (he is not necessarily a Lóufán person).
師古曰 (Shīgǔ said): 李奇說是 (Lǐ Qí’s explanation is correct).
射 (Shè),
而亦翻 (ér yì fān).
乃自被甲持戟挑戰 (Then Xiàng Yǔ himself donned armor and held a *jǐ* (halberd) to challenge).
樓煩欲射之 (Lóufán wanted to shoot him),
項王瞋目叱之 (but King Xiàng glared and shouted at him),
樓煩目不敢視 (Lóufán dared not look him in the eye),
手不敢發 (and dared not release his arrow),
遂走還入壁 (so he fled back into the rampart),
不敢復出 (and dared not come out again).
漢王使人間問之 (The King of Hàn secretly sent someone to inquire about it),
間問 (Jiànwèn),
微問也 (to inquire secretly).
間 (Jiàn),
工莧翻 (gōng xiàn fān).
漢王大驚 (The King of Hàn was greatly astonished).
Thereupon Xiàng Wáng then approached the King of Hàn.
Jí
means "to approach"
and "to follow."
Xiàng Yǔ desired to challenge the King of Hàn to a duel in person.
The King of Hàn enumerated Xiàng Yǔ's offenses, saying:
"Yǔ broke the pact,
and made me King in Shǔ and Hàn—
that is offense one;
he falsely killed Qīngzǐ Guànjūn—
that is offense two;
he rescued Zhào but did not report back,
but instead coerced the feudal lords' troops into the Pass—
that is offense three;
he burned the Qín palaces,
dug up the First Emperor's tomb,
and privately appropriated his wealth—
that is offense four;
Shōusī means
to take someone's wealth for oneself.
That is offense five;
he fraudulently buried alive 200,000 Qín youths at Xīn'ān—
that is offense six;
he enfeoffed his generals with good lands while exiling the former kings—
that is offense seven;
he drove out and exiled Emperor Yì,
made Péngchéng his own capital,
seized the King of Hán's territory,
and annexed the kingdoms of Liáng and Chǔ,
taking much for himself—
that is offense eight;
he sent men to secretly assassinate Emperor Yì south of the Jiāng—
that is offense nine;
his governance was unjust,
and he was untrustworthy in his promises—
he is not tolerated by Heaven,
a great rebel and lawless—
that is offense ten.
I, with a righteous army, am following the feudal lords to punish the cruel brigands.
Why should I trouble myself to challenge you, Duke,
by sending a mutilated criminal to fight you!"
Xiàng Yǔ was greatly enraged,
and shot the King of Hàn with a crossbow, hitting him.
The King of Hàn was wounded in the chest,
but covered his foot and said:
"The bandit hit my toe."
The King of Hàn, sick from his wound, lay down.
Zhāng Liáng strongly urged the King of Hàn to get up and tour the army
to reassure the soldiers,
lest Chǔ take advantage of their victory.
The King of Hàn went out and toured the army,
but his illness was severe.
He then galloped into Chénggāo.
3 Hán Xìn had already pacified Línzī,
and then pursued the King of Qí eastward.
Xiàng Wáng sent Lóng Jū to lead an army,
numbering 200,000,
to rescue Qí,
and he joined forces with the King of Qí at Gāomì.
A guest then advised Lóng Jū, saying:
"The Hàn army has fought a long way and is exhausted from battle;
their vanguard is irresistible.
Qí and Chǔ are on their own territory,
and their troops are easily defeated and dispersed.
Sūnzǐ's Nine Grounds states:
When feudal lords fight on their own territory, it is a 'dispersive ground.'
Cáo Cāo said: 'Soldiers are attached to their homes,
and those who are close to home are easily dispersed.'
Yì
is pronounced with the same tone as 'chǐ';
the same below.
Let the King of Qí send his trusted ministers to summon back the lost cities;
Xìnchén means
a minister in whom one has always placed close trust.
When Chǔ comes to rescue,
they will surely turn against Hàn.
The Hàn army is a guest on Qí territory, two thousand lǐ away.
If all the Qí cities turn against them,
they will have no source of food.
They can be made to surrender without a fight."
Lóng Jū said:
"I have known Hán Xìn's character my whole life;
he is easy to deal with!
He depended on a washerwoman for food,
showing no stratagem for self-reliance;
he suffered humiliation under a ruffian's crotch,
showing no courage to surpass others.
The event is found in volume one, first year.
Moreover, in rescuing Qí,
if we make them surrender without fighting,
what merit will I have?
If we fight now and win,
half of Qí can be obtained."
In the eleventh month,
Qí and Chǔ arrayed their forces against Hàn, flanking the Wéishuǐ.
Xú Guǎng said: The Wéishuǐ originates in Dōngguǎn and flows northeast,
entering the sea at Dūchāng County in Běihǎi.
Suǒyǐn says: The Wéishuǐ originates northeast of Jī County in Lángyá,
and enters the sea at Dūchāng.
Shuǐjīng Zhù: The Wéishuǐ passes west of the old city of Gāomì County;
Hán Xìn and Lóng Jū arrayed their forces flanking the river
at this very spot.
Wéi
is pronounced wéi.
Chén
is read as zhèn.
Hán Xìn filled sandbags,
blocking the upstream flow of the water;
he led his army to half-cross and attack Lóng Jū,
feigning defeat, and retreated.
Lóng Jū, as expected, rejoiced and said:
"I knew Xìn was a coward!"
Then he pursued Xìn.
Xìn sent men to breach the sandbag dam,
and the water surged down.
More than half of Lóng Jū's army could not cross.
Hán Xìn immediately attacked and killed Lóng Jū.
The army east of the water dispersed and fled.
King Guǎng of Qí fled.
Xìn then pursued the defeated army to Chéngyáng
and captured King Guǎng of Qí.
Shǐjì Zhèngyì says: Chéngyáng
is Léisé County,
91 lǐ southeast of Púzhōu.
I, the commentator, based on Bān Zhì,
note that Léisé, Chéngyáng County, Jìyīn Commandery, is to the northwest;
this is Liáng territory.
To pursue the defeated army from the Wéishuǐ to Chéngyáng
would be the territory of the Hàn state of Chéngyáng.
This note from Zhèngyì is erroneous,
similar to Tián Héng's uprising in Chéngyáng in volume one, second year.
He advanced to Bóyáng.
Tián Héng heard that the King of Qí was dead,
and established himself as King of Qí.
He then counterattacked Yīng.
Yīng defeated Tián Héng's army at Yíngxià.
Tián Héng fled to Liáng
and took refuge with Péng Yuè.
Yīng advanced and attacked the Qí general Tián Xī at Qiānchéng.
Qiānchéng County belonged to Běihǎi Commandery;
Gāozǔ later divided it to establish Qiānchéng Commandery.
Kuòdì Zhì: The old city of Qiānchéng
is 25 lǐ north of Gāoyuàn County in Zībō.
Chéng
is pronounced shéng zhèng fān.
He killed all of them
and completely pacified the Qí territory.
4 Zhāng Ěr was established as King of Zhào.
5 The King of Hàn recovered from his illness
and entered the Pass from the west.
Upon reaching Lìyáng,
he impaled the head of Xīn, the former King of Sài, in the Lìyáng marketplace.
Shīgǔ said: To impale a head on a wooden pole is called xiāo.
Suǒyǐn says: Xīn committed suicide at Fànshuǐ;
now, to impale him at Lìyáng
is because it was his former capital,
thus he was impaled there as a display.
He then returned to the army,
which was stationed at Guǎngwǔ.
6 Hán Xìn sent someone to tell the King of Hàn:
"Qí is a treacherous and constantly changing country;
it borders Chǔ to the south."
Shīgǔ said: Biān
means "near."
The King of Hàn opened the letter
and was furious,
cursing:
"I am in distress here,
expecting you day and night to come assist me;
yet you want to establish yourself as king!"
Zhāng Liáng and Chén Píng trod on the King of Hàn's foot,
and then whispered in his ear:
"Hàn is currently at a disadvantage;
how can you forbid Xìn from making himself king!
It would be better to take this opportunity to establish him,
treat him well,
and let him defend his own territory;
otherwise,
trouble will arise."
The King of Hàn also understood,
and then cursed again:
"A true man, when he pacifies the feudal lords,
becomes a genuine king,
why bother with a 'provisional' one!"
In spring,
the second month,
he dispatched Zhāng Liáng with the seal to establish Hán Xìn as King of Qí,
and summoned his troops to attack Chǔ.
7 Xiàng Wáng heard that Lóng Qíe had died,
and was greatly alarmed.
He sent Wǔ Shè, a man from Xūtái,
to go and persuade Qí Wáng Xìn, saying:
"The world has long suffered under Qín;
everyone worked together to attack Qín.
Once Qín was broken,
we calculated merits and partitioned land,
dividing territories to enfeoff kings,
so as to give the soldiers rest.
Now the King of Hàn has again raised troops and moved east,
invading others' divisions [territories],
seizing others' lands.
He has already defeated the Three Qín,
led his army out of the pass,
gathered the armies of the various lords to attack Chǔ in the east.
His intention is not to stop until he has completely swallowed the world;
his insatiable greed is indeed extreme!
Moreover, the King of Hàn cannot be trusted: he has been in Xiàng Wáng's grasp many times,
and Xiàng Wáng, out of pity, spared his life.
Yet, once he escaped,
he immediately broke his promise [pact],
and again attacked Xiàng Wáng.
He is thus untrustworthy.
Now, although Your Excellency considers yourself
to have a close friendship with the King of Hàn,
and exert your full effort in warfare for him,
you will certainly eventually be captured by him.
The reason Your Excellency has been able to remain safe until now [literally: for a moment]
is because Xiàng Wáng is still alive.
At this moment, the affair of the two kings
rests in Your Excellency's hands.
If Your Excellency throws to the right, the King of Hàn wins;
if you throw to the left, Xiàng Wáng wins.
If Xiàng Wáng perishes today,
then next it will be Your Excellency's turn.
Your Excellency has old ties with Xiàng Wáng,
why not turn against Hàn and ally with Chǔ,
to divide the world into three and reign over it?
Sānfēn [參分],
means 'to divide into three.'
And is this how a wise person ought to act? "
Hán Xìn bowed and said:
"When I served Xiàng Wáng,
my office was no more than Lángzhōng,
my rank no more than Zhí Jǐ.
Lángzhōng [郎中],
Zhí Jǐ were palace guards.
Xìn first served Chǔ as a Lángzhōng,
hence this statement.
My plans were not used,
so I turned my back on Chǔ and returned to Hàn.
The King of Hàn granted me the seal of Grand General (Shàng Jiàngjūn),
gave me tens of thousands of troops,
took off his clothes and clothed me,
pushed his food and fed me.
My words were heard, my plans were used.
Thus I was able to reach this point.
That man has deeply trusted me;
it would be inauspicious for me to betray him.
I would not change [my loyalty] even if I died!
Please be so kind as to decline for Xìn to Xiàng Wáng."
Wǔ Shè had left.
Kuǎi Chè knew that the balance of power in the world lay with Xìn,
so he used the art of physiognomy to persuade Xìn, saying:
"My reading of your face
indicates no more than being enfeoffed as a marquis,
and that precarious and insecure;
my reading of your back,
however, shows a nobility beyond words."
With these subtle words, he moved Xìn,
implying that if he turned his back on Hàn, he would achieve great nobility.
相 (xiàng),
read as "xī liàng fān".
"What do you mean?"
Kuǎi Chè said:
"When the world first erupted in chaos,
the only concern was the downfall of Qín.
Shīgǔ said: The intention was to destroy Qín,
and that was the only concern.
It caused the people of the world to shed their blood and guts on the ground,
and fathers and sons to expose their bones in the wilderness,
countless in number.
The Chǔ people rushed to
Péngchéng,
fighting and pursuing the fleeing enemies,
sweeping everything before them with their advantage,
their might shaking the world;
yet their troops are bogged down between Jīng and Suǒ,
pressed against Xīshān and unable to advance,
for three years now.
The Hàn King leads an army of ten
thousand men,
resisting at Gǒng and Luò,
relying on the natural defenses of mountains and rivers,
fighting several battles a day,
achieving not an inch of merit,
suffering repeated defeats and unable to recover.
折 (zhé),
means 'frustrated' or 'defeated'.
北 (bèi),
means 'to flee'.
不救 (bù jiù),
means 'unable to save oneself'.
折 (zhé),
read as 'ér shè fān'.
The common people are exhausted and utterly resentful,
with no one to turn to or rely on;
in my estimation,
the situation is such that if not for a sagely and virtuous person, the world's calamity cannot be quelled.
Today, the fate of the two lords
hangs upon your feet;
if you side with Hàn, Hàn will win;
if you side with Chǔ, Chǔ will win.
If you can truly listen to my plan,
there is nothing better than to benefit both and preserve both,
dividing the world into three,
standing like the legs of a tripod,
in which situation none would dare to make the first move.
With your sagely wisdom,
your numerous armed forces,
holding the strong state of Qí,
supported by Zhào and Yān,
attacking from a vulnerable flank to control their rear,
and relying on the people's desires,
heading west to plead for the lives of the common people—
Shīgǔ said: Qí is in the east,
hence "heading west".
To stop the battles of Chǔ and Hàn,
so that soldiers do not die,
hence "plead for lives".
鄉 (xiāng),
read as 'xiàng';
same below.
Who would dare not listen!
To divide the strong and weaken the powerful to establish feudal lords,
once the feudal lords are established,
the world will submit and obey,
and virtue will return to Qí.
Considering the former state of Qí,
it possessed the lands of Jiāo and Sì;
Jiāo and Sì
are two river names.
Then the kings of the world will lead each other to pay homage to Qí.
Shīgǔ said: 深拱 (shēn gǒng) is like 高拱 (gāo gǒng).
朝 (cháo),
read as 'zhí yáo fān'.
'If one fails to act when the time is ripe,
they will suffer the consequences;
if the opportunity comes and they do not seize it, they will ultimately be harmed.'
I wish you to consider this thoroughly!"
Hán Xìn said:
"The Hàn King has treated me with great kindness;
how can I pursue profit and betray righteousness!"
Kuǎi Shēng said:
"When the King of Chángshān and Lord of Chéng'ān were commoners,
they were sworn brothers, 'neck-cutting friends';
later, they quarreled over the affair of Zhāng Yǎn and Chén Zé,
and the King of Chángshān killed the Lord of Chéng'ān south of the Zhī River,
his head and feet separated.
These two were
the closest of friends in the world,
yet they ended up capturing each other—
why?
Trouble arises from excessive desires, and human hearts are difficult to fathom.
Now you wish to act with loyalty and sincerity in your relationship with the Hàn King,
but you certainly cannot maintain it more securely than those two lords did with each other;
and your affairs are far greater than those of Zhāng Yǎn and Chén Zé.
Therefore, I believe that your assumption that the Hàn King will not endanger you
is also mistaken!
Dàfū Wén saved the state of Yuè from ruin,
and helped Gōujiàn become hegemon,
establishing merit and achieving fame, yet he himself died.
'When the wild beasts are gone, the hunting dog is cooked.'
If we speak of friendship,
it is not as good as that between Zhāng Ěr and the Lord of Chéng'ān;
if we speak of loyalty and sincerity,
it does not surpass that of Dàfū Wén towards Gōujiàn.
These two examples are sufficient for observation;
I wish you to ponder this deeply!
Moreover, I have heard that 'he whose courage and strategy shake the lord endangers himself,
and he whose achievements overshadow the world goes unrewarded.'
Now you bear the power that shakes the lord,
and possess achievements beyond reward.
If you return to Chǔ,
the Chǔ people will not trust you;
if you return to Hàn,
the Hàn people will be alarmed and afraid.
Where do you intend to take this and find security?"
Hán Xìn declined, saying:
"Sir, please rest for a moment;
I shall consider it."
A few days later,
Kuǎi Chè again tried to persuade him, saying:
"Listening [to advice]
is the sign of an affair's potential;
Shīgǔ said: meaning being able to listen to good counsel.
復 (fù),
read as 'fú yòu fān'.
It is the crucial moment of an affair;
few are those who miss the counsel and err in their plans, yet can long remain safe!
鮮 (xiǎn),
read as 'xī shàn fān'.
To decide, or to cut off;
斷 (duàn),
read as 'dīng luàn fǎn'.
It is the harm of an affair.
To deliberate over a tiny detail of a plan,
豪 (háo),
is a long hair.
Ten 'hao' make one 'lí'.
Though wisdom truly understands it,
to hesitate and not dare to act
is the calamity of a hundred affairs.
Achievements
are difficult to make but easy to ruin;
opportunities
are hard to obtain but easy to lose.
Oh, opportunity,
it does not come again!"
Hán Xìn hesitated,
unable to bear betraying Hàn;
he also believed that his achievements were great,
and that Hàn would ultimately not take Qí from him.
So he dismissed Kuǎi Chè.
謝去 (xiè qù),
means to dismiss and send away.
He feigned madness and became a shaman.
8. In the autumn,
seventh month,
Qíng Bù was established as King of Huáinán.
9. In the eighth month,
the northern Mò and Yān people came and offered owl cavalry to assist Hàn.
Yīng Shào said: 北貉 (Běi Mò)
is a state.
梟 (xiāo)
means 'strong' or 'brave'.
Zhāng Yàn said: 梟 (xiāo)
means 'brave',
like the 'xiāo' in liùbó.
Shīgǔ said: The Mò were in the northeast,
belonging to the Sān Hán group,
all of whom were Mò-type people.
It means both the Mò people and Yān came to assist Hàn.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: Scriptures and commentaries often refer to 貊 as Eastern Yi,
thus the Zhí Fāng (Bureau of Regional Administration) managed the Jiǔ Yí and Jiǔ Mò.
Zhèng Zhì replied to Zhào Shāng saying: The Jiǔ Mò
are the Jiǔ Yí.
Also, the Zhōu Guān mentions 'Mò attendants',
with a note that they were captured from expeditions against the northeastern Yi.
貉 (háo),
is read the same as 貊 (mò).
10. The Hàn King issued an order: For soldiers who unfortunately died,
officials were to provide clothing, shrouds, and coffins,
and have their bodies transported back to their families.
People from all directions pledged their loyalty to him.
In that year,
Zhōu Chāng, the commandant of the capital (zhōngwèi), was made Grandee Secretary (yùshǐ dàfū).
Bān Biǎo states: The commandant of the capital,
a Qin official,
was in charge of patrolling the capital.
In the first year of Emperor Wǔ's Tàichū era, this office was renamed Executive of the Capital (zhí jīn wǔ).
He was [Xiāo] Hé's younger cousin.
Xiàng Yǔ knew he had little support;
his provisions were exhausted,
and Hán Xìn again advanced his troops to attack Chǔ.
Yǔ was troubled by this.
Hàn sent Hóu Gōng to persuade Yǔ to release Grandfather (Tàigōng).
Grandfather and Empress Lü (Lǚ Hòu) had been captured by Chǔ,
as seen in volume 1, year 3.
The world was divided in half,
with the land west of Hónggōu allocated to Hàn,
and that east of it to Chǔ.
Wén Yǐng said: The Hónggōu was drawn southeast from the Hé River near Xíngyáng,
to connect Sòng, Zhèng, Cài, Cáo, and Wèi,
and meet the Jì, Rú, Huái, and Sì rivers in Chǔ.
This is the modern Guāndù River.
Yīng Shào said: Twenty *lǐ* southeast of Xíngyáng,
it was probably drawn from the Hé River southeast into the Huái and Sì rivers.
Zhāng Huá said: The city of Dàliáng was in Jùnyí county.
Northwest of this county,
a canal ran east, passing south of this city,
then curved north,
dividing into two canals: one canal flowed southeast;
Qín Shǐhuáng dug it
to draw water from the Hé River to irrigate Dàliáng,
and it was called the Hónggōu;
the other canal ran east, passing south of Yángwǔ county, and was the Guāndù River.
Dù Yòu said: West of Xíngyáng county in Zhèngzhōu is Hónggōu,
the place where Chǔ and Hàn divided their territories.
Chǔ returned Grandfather and Empress Lü,
and withdrew its troops, returning east.
King of Hàn wanted to return west,
but Zhāng Liáng and Chén Píng persuaded him, saying:
"Hàn possesses more than half of the world.
Wéi Zhāo said: In general,
two-thirds is considered more than half,
and one-third is considered less than half.
Chǔ's army is exhausted and its provisions are depleted;
this is Heaven's time for its destruction.
If we release them now without attacking,
this is what is called 'raising a tiger to invite disaster upon oneself.'
The King of Hàn followed their advice.
Nie Chongqi punctuated, Rong Zhaozu proofread.

Academician of the Hanlin Academy (Hànlín Xuéshì), Grand Master of Court Discussion (Cháosàn Dàfū), Right Remonstrance Official (Yòu Jiànyì Dàfū), Drafter of Imperial Edicts (Zhī Zhìgào) and concurrently Lecturer (Shìjiǎng), concurrently Supervisor of Wànshòuguān Temple (Tíjǔ Wànshòuguān Gōngshì), concurrently Administrator of the Jíxián Academy (Pàn Jíxián Yuàn), Superior Pillar of State (Shàng Hùjūn), Founding Marquis of Hénèi Commandery (Hénèi Jùn Kāiguó Hóu) with a fief of 1,300 households, bestowed with a purple-gold fish-pouch, your servant
commanded to compile.
Hòu Xué Tiāntái
Tàizǔ Gāohuángdì Zhōng
1. Winter,
tenth month.
The King of Hàn pursued Xiàng Yǔ to Gùlíng.
Xú Guǎng said: Gùlíng is in Yángxià.
Jìn Zhuó said: It is Gùshǐ county.
I follow Bān Zhì: Gùshǐ and Yángxià are two counties,
both belonging to Huáiyáng Commandery.
Liú Zhāo Zhì says: There is Gùlíng Jù in Yángxià county, Chén Commandery.
Kuòdì Zhì says: Gùlíng,
a county name,
is forty-two *lǐ* northwest of Wǎnqiū county, Chénzhōu.
Hán Xìn and Péng Yuè did not arrive,
and Chǔ attacked the Hàn army,
utterly defeating them.
The King of Hàn then strengthened his defenses and held his position,
saying to Zhāng Liáng:
"The feudal lords are not following.
What should be done?"
He replied:
"The Chǔ army is about to be defeated,
but the two men (Hán Xìn and Péng Yuè) have not yet received their allocated lands.
Lǐ Qí said: This means Hán Xìn and Péng Yuè have not yet been allotted additional territory.
Wéi Zhāo said: Although Hán Xìn and others are nominally kings,
their boundaries have not yet been drawn.
Fēn
is pronounced fú wèn.
I agree with Wéi's explanation.
If Your Majesty can share the world with them,
you can achieve it immediately.
The establishment of King of Qí (Hán Xìn)
was not Your Majesty's intention.
It means Hán Xìn himself asked to be acting king,
and then he was established,
which was not Your Majesty's original intention.
Péng Yuè had originally pacified the Lìang region.
Initially,
Your Majesty appointed Yuè as chancellor because of Wèi Bào.
See volume 1, year 2.
Yuè also hoped to be king,
but Your Majesty did not settle it early.
Now, if you can take all the land from Suīyáng north to Gǔchéng and make Péng Yuè its king,
Bān Zhì says: Suīyáng county belongs to Liáng Commandery.
Liú Zhāo Zhì says: Gǔchéng county belongs to Dōng Commandery,
which was the Little Gǔ of the Spring and Autumn period.
Kuòdì Zhì says: The old city of Gǔchéng
is twenty-six *lǐ* east of Dōng'ē county, Jìzhōu.
Suīyáng is Sòngzhōu.
All the land from Sòngzhōu north to Gǔchéng in Jìzhōu, bordering the Huáng Hé,
should be enfeoffed to Péng Yuè.
Enfeoff Hán Xìn.
Chén,
the ancient Chén state,
is the Huáiyáng Commandery of Bān Zhì;
in the Táng dynasty, it was Chénzhōu.
All the land from Chén eastward to the sea, including the old territory of Qí,
should be given to King of Qí (Hán Xìn).
Their intention is to regain their former territories.
If you can make a sacrifice and give them this land,
allowing each to fight on their own,
then Chǔ will be easily defeated."
The King of Hàn followed his advice.
Thereupon, Hán Xìn and Péng Yuè both led their armies to come.
Eleventh month.
Liú Jiǎ crossed the Huái River south,
besieged Shòuchūn,
and sent someone to entice Zhōu Yīn, the Grand Marshal of Chǔ (Chǔ Dàsīmǎ).
Yīn defected from Chǔ,
slaughtered Liù in Shū.
Shū was the Shū state of the Spring and Autumn period.
Bān Zhì says: Shū county belongs to Lújiāng Commandery.
Kuòdì Zhì says: Shū is the old Shūchéng of modern Lújiāng.
Shǐjì Zhèngyì says: Jiǔjiāng Commandery is Shòuzhōu.
In the twenty-second year of King Kǎoliè of Chǔ, he moved to Shòuchūn,
calling it Yǐng;
until King Fùchú,
it was destroyed by Qin,
and Jiǔjiāng Commandery was established;
in the Táng dynasty, it became the territory of Lú, Shòu, Chú, Háo, and other *zhōu*.
All met with Liú Jiǎ.
In the twelfth month,
King Xiàng arrived at Gāixià.
Lǐ Qí said: "Pèixiáo Xiàn's settlement and town name."
Xiáo,
read xià-jiāo.
Zhāng Yī's Sāncāng commentary states: "Gāi
is the name of a dike,
in Pèi Jùn."
Shǐjì Zhèngyì states: "According to Gāixià, it is a high ridge and sheer cliff;
it is still three or four zhàng high today.
Its settlement and dike are on the side of Gāi,
hence the name was taken.
It is now ten lǐ east of Zhēnyuán Xiàn, Bó Zhōu."
Gāi,
sounds gāi.
When their provisions were exhausted,
they fought against the Hàn and were defeated,
so they entered their encampment.
The Hàn army and the armies of the various lords surrounded them several layers deep.
King Xiàng heard from all four sides of the Hàn army at night that they were singing Chǔ songs.
Yīng Shào said: "Chǔ songs
are songs sung at cock-crow."
"The Hàn has already largely acquired Chǔ territory,
so there are many Chǔ singers,
singing at cock-crow."
Shīgǔ said: "Chǔ songs
are songs of the Chǔ people,
just like Wú Yú and Yuè Yín."
"If 'cock-crow' refers to the name of a song,
that is logically plausible,
but one cannot say 'at the time of cock-crow'."
"When Gāozǔ ordered Qī Fūrén to perform the Chǔ dance,
and personally composed Chǔ songs for her,
how could there have been a 'time of cock-crow'?"
"Has the Hàn already obtained all of Chǔ?
Why are there so many Chǔ people?"
So he rose at night,
drank in his tent,
and sang mournfully and spiritedly.
Tears streamed down in several lines.
His attendants all wept,
unable to look up.
Thereupon King Xiàng mounted his swift horse named Zhuī,
with over eight hundred stalwart riders under his command following him.
In the dead of night,
they broke through the encirclement and galloped southwards.
At dawn,
the Hàn army became aware of this,
and ordered the cavalry general Guàn Yīng to pursue them with five thousand cavalrymen.
King Xiàng crossed the Huái River,
with only over a hundred riders able to keep up.
They reached Yīnlíng.
Bān Zhì states,
Yīnlíng Xiàn belonged to Jiǔjiāng Jùn.
Kuòdì Zhì: "The old city of Yīnlíng
is sixty lǐ northwest of Dìngyuǎn Xiàn, Háo Zhōu."
He asked a farmer,
and the farmer deceived him, saying
"Left."
Going left,
they became trapped in a large swamp,
which is why the Hàn caught up with them.
King Xiàng then led his troops eastward again.
They reached Dōngchéng.
Bān Zhì states,
Dōngchéng Xiàn belonged to Jiǔjiāng Jùn.
Kuòdì Zhì: "The old city of Dōngchéng
is fifty lǐ southeast of Dìngyuǎn."
Several thousand Hàn cavalrymen were in pursuit.
King Xiàng judged that he would not escape,
and said to his riders:
"I raised an army until now,
eight years have passed.
I have personally fought over seventy battles;
I have never been defeated,
and thus I dominated the world.
Yet now I am finally trapped here.
This is Heaven destroying me,
not a fault of my fighting!
Today I am determined to die,
and I wish to fight a thrilling battle for you all,
to surely break through the encirclement,
slay generals,
cut down flags,
and achieve three victories,
to let you all know that Heaven is destroying me,
not a fault of my fighting."
He then divided his cavalry into four detachments,
in four directions.
The Hàn army surrounded them several layers deep.
King Xiàng said to his riders:
"I will capture a general for you."
He ordered the cavalry on all four sides to charge down,
intending to meet at three locations east of the mountain.
Thereupon King Xiàng shouted loudly and charged down,
and the Hàn army all scattered and recoiled.
He then slew one Hàn general.
At this time,
the Lángzhōng cavalry Yáng Xǐ pursued King Xiàng.
"Lángzhōng cavalry"
refers to the Hàn official known as Qí Láng.
Xǐ and his horse were both startled,
and recoiled several lǐ.
King Xiàng and his riders reunited at three locations.
The Hàn army did not know King Xiàng's whereabouts,
so they divided their army into three,
and surrounded them again.
King Xiàng then charged,
and again slew one Hàn Dūwèi,
killing dozens or hundreds of people.
He then regrouped his riders,
having lost only two riders.
He then said to his riders:
"How was that?"
The riders all prostrated themselves and said:
"Just as Your Majesty said!"
Thereupon Xiàng Wáng wanted to cross the Wūjiāng River to the east.
Chén Zàn said: The Wūjiāng River is at Niúzhǔ.
Suǒyǐn says: According to Jìn, in the early days it belonged to Línhuái.
Kuòdì Zhì says: Wūjiāng Tíng,
is the Wūjiāng County of Hézhōu;
in early Jìn it was a county.
Shuǐ Jīng says: The Jiāng River then goes north and reaches Huánglǜ Kǒu,
which is the place where the Hán Shū says the Wūjiāng Tíng Zhǎng moored a boat waiting for Xiàng Wáng.
This is that place.
I believe Wūjiāng Pǔ is fifty lǐ east of today's Wūjiāng County in Hézhōu,
which is the place where the Tíng Zhǎng moored a boat waiting for Yǔ.
He said to Xiàng Wáng:
"Though Jiāngdōng is small,
its territory is a thousand lǐ,
and its people number several hundred thousand;
it is also sufficient for a king.
I wish Your Majesty would cross quickly!
Only your servant has a boat now;
when the Hàn army arrives,
there will be no means to cross."
Xiàng Wáng laughed and said:
"Heaven is destroying me,
why should I cross?
Moreover, Jí crossed the river to the west with eight thousand young men from Jiāngdōng,
and now not a single one has returned;
even if the elders and brothers of Jiāngdōng pity me and make me king,
what face do I have to see them?
Even if they do not speak,
would Jí alone not be ashamed in his heart?"
Thereupon, he bestowed his personal mount, the zhuī horse, upon the Tíng Zhǎng,
and ordered all his cavalry to dismount and fight on foot,
wielding short weapons.
Jí alone killed several hundred Hàn soldiers,
and his body also sustained more than ten wounds.
He looked back and saw Lǚ Mǎtóng, a cavalry Sīmǎ of Hàn,
and said:
"Are you not my old friend?"
Mǎtóng turned his face away.
Zhāng Yàn says: It was difficult to personally strike down an old friend,
so he turned his back.
Rú Chún says: Miàn [face],
means not looking directly.
Shīgǔ says: Rú's explanation is wrong.
Miàn [face],
means turning one's back,
not facing directly;
Miànfù [bound face-to-face] also means bound with their backs to each other;
Dù Yuánkǎi thought it merely meant seeing his face,
which is incorrect.
Gòngfù says: Miàn zhī,
simply means facing him.
"This is Xiàng Wáng."
Xiàng Wáng then said:
"I heard that a reward of a thousand jīn of gold for my head,
and an estate of ten thousand households;
Shǐ Jì Zhèngyì says: Hàn considered one jīn of gold to be a thousand jīn,
equal to ten thousand coins.
I believe that one jīn of gold and an estate of ten thousand households are disproportionate in value,
so the explanation of Zhèngyì [proper meaning]
cannot be taken as a basis.
In Bān Shū,
'dé' [virtue]
is written as
'dé' [obtain];
Dèng Zhǎn says: It means letting the duke obtain me for his achievement.
Shǐ Jì writes
'dé' [virtue];
Xú Guǎng says: It can also be the 'dé' of merit and virtue.
Shǐ Jì Zhèngyì says: Wèi,
is pronounced yú wěi fān.
It means Lǚ Mǎtóng and he were old friends,
and he had previously received kindness from him.
I believe Yǔ probably meant, 'I will take my own life for your benefit.'
He slit his throat and died.
Wáng Yì took his head;
the remaining cavalry trampled over each other
struggling for Xiàng Wáng,
and dozens of people killed each other;
ultimately,
Yáng Xǐ, Lǚ Mǎtóng, and Langzhōng Lǚ Shèng and Yáng Wǔ each obtained one part of his body;
the five men assembled his body,
and it was all there.
Therefore, they divided his household,
and all five were enfeoffed as Lièhóu.
Lǚ Mǎtóng was enfeoffed as Zhōngshuǐ Hóu,
Wáng Yì as Dùyǎn Hóu,
Yáng Xǐ as Chìquán Hóu,
Yáng Wǔ as Wúfáng Hóu,
and Lǚ Shèng as Nièyáng Hóu.
All the Chǔ territories were pacified,
except for Lǔ, which did not surrender.
Qín,
Lǔ County belonged to Xuē Jùn,
Xiàng Yǔ was first enfeoffed here;
Hàn made it Lǔ Guó.
When they reached its city walls,
the sound of stringed instruments and chanting could still be heard;
because it was a state that upheld rites and righteousness,
and its people died for their lord,
they brought Xiàng Wáng's head to show the elders and brothers of Lǔ,
and Lǔ then surrendered.
The Hàn Wáng buried Xiàng Wáng with the rites of Lǔ Gōng at Gǔchéng.
Sòng Bái says: Gǔshú County in Sòngzhōu,
was ancient Gǔchéng.
Hàn established Bó County here,
and later changed it to Gǔyáng County.
He wept for him and departed.
None of Xiàng's collateral relatives were executed.
Xiàng Bó and four others were all enfeoffed as Lièhóu,
and granted the surname Liú;
all the people who had been in Chǔ were returned to them.
Grand Historian says: Yǔ rose from amongst the fields,
Mǔ,
is the ancient character for Mǔ.
Then he led the five feudal lords to destroy Qín.
At this time, among the six states east of the mountains,
Qí, Zhào, Hán, Wèi, and Yān all rose,
following Yǔ to attack Qín,
hence it says 'five feudal lords'.
Government matters originated from Yǔ;
though his position did not last,
it had been unprecedented since ancient times!
But Yǔ turned his back on Guān and yearned for Chǔ.
Shīgǔ says: Bèi Guān [turning back on Guān],
means breaking the agreement not to enthrone Pèigōng in Guānzhōng;
Huái Chǔ [yearning for Chǔ],
means longing to return east to Péngchéng.
I believe Bèi Guān Huái Chǔ [turning back on Guān and yearning for Chǔ] is a consistent idea,
meaning Yǔ abandoned the strategic advantage of Guānzhōng and yearned for his homeland of Chǔ.
There is no need to divide it into two sections.
Bèi,
pronounced Pú Mèi Fān.
He resented the kings and marquises for betraying him—
how difficult!
He boasted of his achievements,
indulged his own private wisdom and did not learn from antiquity.
It refers to his ambition for a hegemonic enterprise,
desiring to rule the world by military conquest.
In five years,
he ultimately lost his state,
and died at Dōngchéng;
yet he did not awaken or blame himself,
but instead cited,
"Heaven is destroying me,
it is not the fault of my military strategy,"
how absurd!
Yángzǐ Fǎyán: Someone asked:
"When Chǔ was defeated at Gāixià,
just before dying,
he said, 'It is Heaven!'
Was it truly so?"
He replied:
"Hàn exhausted its strategies,
and its strategies exhausted its strength;
Liàng,
means truly.
Qū,
means exhaust.
Those who exhaust others overcome,
those who exhaust themselves lose;
what part did Heaven play in it?"
Wēngōng says: How is it Heaven's business?
2 The Hàn Wáng returned,
and arrived at Dìngtáo.
Bān Zhì says,
Dìngtáo County belonged to Jìyīn Jùn,
ancient Táoyì;
during the Sòng, it was the administrative seat of Guǎngjì Jūn.
He seized its army.
3 Gòng Wèi, the king of Línjiāng, did not surrender.
Gòng Áo,
was enfeoffed as King of Línjiāng by Xiàng Yǔ;
Wèi,
was his son.
4 In spring,
the first month,
Qí Wáng Xìn was re-established as King of Chǔ,
ruling Huáiběi,
with his capital at Xiàpī.
Péng Yuè, the Chancellor of Wèi and Marquis of Jiànchéng, was enfeoffed as King of Liáng,
ruling the former territory of Wèi,
with his capital at Dìngtáo.
5. An edict stated:
"Soldiers have not rested for eight years,
and the myriad people have suffered greatly.
Now that the affairs of the realm are settled,
let all in the realm below the crime of 'shūsǐ' be pardoned."
Rú Chún said: 'Shūsǐ'
is a clear death penalty.
The 'Zuǒ Zhuàn' says: "cut down its trees but do not 'shū' them."
Wéi Zhāo said: 'Shūsǐ'
is beheading.
Shī Gǔ said: 'Shū'
means to sever,
to separate;
it refers to the body and head being severed and placed in different locations.
Gòng Fù said: I consult the 'Shuō Wén': "The Hàn barbarians are 'shū'."
Therefore, 'shū' is a name for a death penalty.
6. All the feudal kings submitted memorials requesting to honor the King of Hàn as emperor.
In the second month, on the 'jiǎwǔ' day,
the King ascended the imperial throne on the sunny side of the Fànshǔi.
Cài Yōng said: In ancient times, the Son of Heaven was called 'Huáng',
next was 'Dì',
next was 'Wáng'.
Qín inherited the end of the Three Kings,
and considered its virtue to encompass the Three 'Huáng' and Five 'Dì',
so it combined them into a title.
When Hàn Gāozǔ received the mandate,
he continued this practice without change.
Zhāng Yàn said: The Fànshǔi is in the Jìyīn region,
named for its extensive and profound benevolence that nourishes from above.
Shī Gǔ said: According to the biography of Shúsūn Tōng: "was made emperor in Dìngtáo,"
then this water being in Jìyīn is correct.
The 'Kuòdì Zhì' says: The altar where Hàn Gāozǔ ascended the throne
is in the region of Jìyīn County, Cáozhōu.
Fàn,

Rú Chún said: 'Zhào'

From Qín and Hàn onwards,

The Hàn system of institutions: there were four types of imperial documents: first was 'cèshū',
second was 'zhìshū',
third was 'zhàoshū',
fourth was 'jièchì'.
A 'cèshū'
was made of bamboo slips,
its length was two 'chǐ',
a shorter one was half that;
written in seal script,
starting with the year, month, and day,
referring to the Emperor when issuing commands to feudal kings;
when the Three Dukes were dismissed due to crime,
they were also given a 'cè',
but in clerical script,
using one 'chǐ' one 'cùn' wood,
in two lines,
this was the difference.
A 'zhìshū'
was an imperial decree concerning institutions.
Its text read
"An imperial decree to the Three Dukes,"
all were sealed with the imperial seal,
the Director of the Imperial Secretariat would additionally seal them,
and they were openly proclaimed to the prefectures and commanderies.
A 'zhàoshū',
'zhào'
means to announce,
its text read
"Announce to a certain official as per custom."
A 'jièchì'
referred to an order to an Inspector or Grand Administrator,
its text read
"There is an imperial edict,
ordering a certain official."
All others followed this pattern.
"The former King of Héngshān, Wú Ruì,

Pān,

Shī Gǔ said: 'Biàn gào' means

Cài Yōng said: "Shàng" (上)
is where the honored position resides.
Just saying "shàng,"
one dares not speak of the honored title.
"Chèhóu and all generals, dare not conceal anything from朕,

Chè (徹)
means 'through' or 'penetrating.'

Gāo Qǐ and Wáng Líng replied:

As for devising strategies within a tent,

Xiàng Yǔ had one Fàn Zēng yet could not employ him.
This is why he was captured by me."
All the officials were convinced.
Hán Xìn went to Chǔ,
summoned the washerwoman (piāomǔ),
and gave her a thousand *jīn*.
He summoned the youth who had humiliated him by making him crawl between his legs

This event is found in Juan 9, Yuánnián.
Piāo (漂), pronounced pǐ miào.
"This is a brave man.

A mountain in the sea is called an island (dǎo).

eighty *lǐ* from the shore.
I (the author) note that according to the Běishǐ,

Dǎo (島), pronounced dīng lǎo.

The Zhōulǐ states: The Sījié is in charge of guarding the *bāngjié*,

The commentary states: *Jié* (節)
are held to indicate trustworthiness when traveling.
*Bāngjié* are the *Zhēnguī*, *Yázhāng*, *Gǔguī*, *Wǎnguī*, and *Yǎnguī*.
To guard *bāngguó*, jade *jié* are used,
made of jade.
To guard *dūbǐ*, horn *jié* are used,
made of horn.
Envoys of *bāngguó* use golden *jié*.
For gate passes,
*fú* (tallies) are used.
For goods and bribes,
*xǐ* (seals) are used.
For road passes,
*jīng* (banners) are used.
Examining this,
all that was held as a token of trust in antiquity
was called *jié*.
Since Qín,
there have been *xǐ*, *fú*, and *jié*,
thus *xǐ* are distinct from *xǐ*,
*fú* from *fú*,
and *jié* from *jié*;
they were divided into three.
The Hàn *jié*
is the ancient *jīngjié*.
Zhèng Shì's commentary considers *fújié* to be the edict tallies of various palaces in the Hàn court,
*xǐjié* to be the Hàn seals,
and *jīngjié* to be the *jié* carried by Hàn envoys.
From this, we know that what the Hàn called *jié*
was probably the ancient *jīngjié*.
Xián said: *Jié*
are used for trustworthiness,
made of bamboo,
with an eight-foot long handle,
made with yak tails,
with three layers of tufts.
This was the Hàn system.
"If Tián Héng comes,
