Tián Héng 乃與其客二人乘傳詣洛陽。
Rú Chún 曰：四馬，
高足為置傳，
中足為馳傳，
下足為乘傳；
一馬、二馬為軺傳。
急者乘一乘傳。
Shīgǔ 曰：蓋今之驛，
古者以車，
謂之傳車；
其後單置馬，
謂之驛騎。
漢律：諸當乘傳及發駕置傳者，
皆持尺五寸木傳信，
封以御史大夫印章；
其乘傳，
參封之，
參，
三也；
有期會，
累封兩端，
端各兩封，
凡四封；
乘置馳傳，
五封之，
兩端各二，
中央一；
軺傳，
兩馬再封之；
一馬一封，
以馬駕軺車而乘傳曰一封軺傳。
Shǐ Zhào 所謂依乘符傳而行者本此；
但擇焉而不精，
語焉而不詳耳，
終不若 Yán Shuō 簡而明。
傳，
張戀翻。
至 Shīxiāng ⿸广既置。
Yìng Shào 曰： Shīxiāng，
在 Yǎnshī 城西。
臣 Zàn 曰：按⿸广既置，
謂置馬以傳驛者。
「人臣見天子，
當洗沐。」
因止留，
謂其客曰：
「 Tián Héng 始與漢王俱南面稱孤；
Shīgǔ 曰：王者自稱曰孤，
蓋為謙也。
老子道德經曰：貴以賤為本，
高以下為基，
是以侯王自謂孤、寡、不穀。
而 Tián Héng 乃為亡虜，
北面事之，
其恥固已甚矣。
且吾烹人之兄，
與其弟併肩而事主；
縱彼畏天子之詔不敢動，
我獨不媿於心乎！
且陛下所以欲見我者，
不過欲一見吾面貌耳；
今斬吾頭，
馳三十里間，
形容尚未能敗，
猶可觀也。」
遂自剄，
令客奉其頭，
從使者馳奏之。
The Emperor 曰：
「嗟乎！
起自布衣，
兄弟三人更王，
豈不賢哉！」
為之流涕，
而拜其二客為都尉；
發卒二千人，
以王者禮葬之。
Shǐjì Zhèngyì 曰： Tián Héng 墓在 Yǎnshī 西十五里。
二客穿其冢傍孔，
皆自剄，
下從之。
The Emperor 聞之，
大驚。
以 Tián Héng 客皆賢，
餘五百人尚在海中，
使使召之；
至，
則聞 Tián Héng 死，
亦皆自殺。
12 In the beginning,
the man from Chǔ, Jì Bù, was a general for Xiàng Jí.
Jì is a surname.
Among the eight worthies of Zhōu, there were Jì Suí and Jì Guā.
In Lǔ, there was the Jì clan.
After Xiàng Jí was defeated,
the Emperor offered a reward of a thousand catties of gold for Jì Bù;
anyone who dared to shelter or hide him
would have their
three generations of relatives punished.
Shè means to stop.
Nì means to hide.
Jì Bù sold himself to Zhū Jiā of Lǔ.
Zhū Jiā knew in his heart that it was Jì Bù,
bought him, and placed him in his farmhouse.
He himself went to Luòyáng to see Téng Gōng,
and said:
"What crime has Jì Bù committed?
Each minister serves his own lord,
it is simply their duty.
Shīgǔ 曰: Zhí means normal;
it means this is the normal way.
Another explanation: Zhí means to be in charge of a matter.
Wèi, read yú wěi.
Now that the Emperor has just gained control of the empire,
to seek out one man due to a private grudge,
how does this not show a lack of magnanimity?
Moreover, with Jì Bù's talent,
and the Hàn's urgent pursuit of him,
he will either flee north to the Hú or south to the Yuè.
To shun a valiant man and thus strengthen an enemy state,
this is why Wǔ Zǐxū flogged the tomb of King Píng of Chǔ.
Wǔ Zǐxū was the son of Wǔ Shē, a grand master of Chǔ.
King Píng of Chǔ believed slanderous words and killed Wǔ Shē.
Zǐxū fled to Wú,
used the army of Wú to defeat Chǔ,
entered Yǐng,
dug up King Píng's tomb, and flogged his corpse.
Téng Gōng waited for an opportune moment
to speak to the Emperor,
following Zhū Jiā's suggestion.
The Emperor then pardoned Jì Bù,
summoned him, and appointed him as a Lángzhōng.
Zhū Jiā subsequently never met him again.
Jì Bù's maternal younger brother, Dīng Gōng,
was also a general for Xiàng Yǔ.
He pursued and cornered the Emperor west of Péngchéng.
With weapons clashing at close quarters,
the Emperor, in distress,
looked back at Dīng Gōng and said:
"Why should two worthy men impede each other?"
Mèng Kāng 曰: Dīng Gōng and Lài Yǐ from Péngchéng pursued the Emperor,
hence he said "two worthy men."
Shīgǔ 曰: Mèng's explanation is incorrect.
The "two worthy men" refers to Emperor Gāozǔ himself and Dīng Gōng,
meaning "I and Dīng Gōng are both worthy,
why should we obstruct each other?"
Therefore, Dīng Gōng was moved by these words and stopped.
Although he pursued with Lài Yǐ,
Emperor Gāozǔ spoke only to Dīng Gōng.
Xìngpǔ says: The Dīng family originally had the surname Jiāng.
Qí Tàigōng was posthumously titled Dīng Gōng,
and the family took this as their surname.
When King Xiàng was defeated,
Dīng Gōng requested an audience.
The Emperor paraded Dīng Gōng before the army,
saying:
"Dīng Gōng was disloyal as a minister to King Xiàng,
and he caused King Xiàng to lose the empire."
He then executed him,
saying:
"Let no future minister emulate Dīng Gōng!"
Minister Guāng said: Since Emperor Gāozǔ rose from Fēng and Pèi,
he had gathered many heroes,
recruited fugitives, and accepted rebels.
Yet, upon ascending the imperial throne,
Dīng Gōng alone suffered execution for disloyalty.
Why?
The situation for gaining power and for maintaining power
is different.
During a time when heroes contended
and the people had no fixed lord,
accepting those who came
was certainly appropriate.
But when he became the Son of Heaven,
within the Four Seas,
everyone was his subject.
If he did not clarify propriety and righteousness to them,
and allowed ministers
to harbor disloyal thoughts in pursuit of great personal gain,
how could the state long remain stable?
Therefore, he decisively acted according to great righteousness,
making it clear to all under heaven that disloyal ministers would find no place for themselves;
and those who harbored private feelings and formed personal ties,
even if it meant saving their own lives,
would not be tolerated on grounds of righteousness.
Executing one person to instill fear in ten thousand,
was his consideration of the matter not deep and far-reaching?
It is fitting that his descendants enjoyed the mandate of heaven for over four hundred years!
13 Lóu Jìng (婁敬) of Qí (齊) was garrisoned in Lǒngxī (隴西).
The Genealogy states: Lóu (婁)
is descended from the state of Zhūlóu (邾婁);
one account says: descended from Lí Lóu (離婁).
He slipped off his wheeled carriage,
wearing a sheepskin coat,
and through General Yú (虞), a Qí (齊) man, sought an audience with the Emperor.
General Yú (虞) wanted to give him fine clothes.
Lóu Jìng (婁敬) said:
“If I wear silk,
I will be seen wearing silk;
if I wear coarse cloth,
I will be seen wearing coarse cloth.
Yī (衣)
means to wear.
Bó (帛)
means silk.
Hè (褐)
is a garment made of woven wool.
Thereupon, General Yú (虞) entered and spoke to the Emperor;
the Emperor summoned Lóu Jìng (婁敬) for an audience
and questioned him.
Lóu Jìng (婁敬) said:
“Your Majesty has made Luòyáng (洛陽) your capital;
do you wish to rival the prosperity of the Zhōu (周) dynasty?”
The Emperor said:
“Yes.”
Lóu Jìng (婁敬) said:
“Your Majesty’s acquisition of the empire differs from that of Zhōu (周).
The ancestors of Zhōu (周),
starting from Hòu Jì (后稷) who was enfeoffed in Tái (邰),
according to Bān Zhì (班志),
Tái (邰) county belonged to Yòu Fúfēng (右扶風).
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: This is today’s Wǔgōng (武功) old city.
Shǐjì Zhèngyì (史記正義) says: Twenty-three lǐ (里) southwest of Wǔgōng (武功) county in Yōngzhōu (雍州),
is the old Chíláng (漦城) city.
Shuōwén (說文) says: Tái (邰),
the state enfeoffed to the Jiāng (姜) clan, descendants of Yán Dì (炎帝),
was the ancestral home of Qì (棄).
Máo Cháng (毛萇) says: Tái (邰)
was the state of Jiāng Yuán (姜嫄);
Yáo (堯) enfeoffed Hòu Jì (后稷) in Tái (邰) because Heaven caused Hòu Jì (后稷) to be born there;
hence he was enfeoffed in Tái (邰);
the sound is Tǔ cái fān.
Léi (絫)
is the ancient character for lěi (累).
By the time of Tàiwáng (太王), Wáng Jì (王季), Wénwáng (文王), and Wǔwáng (武王), the feudal lords spontaneously submitted to them,
and thus they overthrew Yīn (殷) and became Son of Heaven.
When Chéngwáng (成王) ascended the throne,
the Duke of Zhōu (周gōng) acted as his prime minister,
and then built Luòyì (洛邑),
believing this to be the center of the world,
where feudal lords from all four directions would bring their tribute,
and the distances would be equitable.
With virtue, it is easy to rule as king;
without virtue, it is easy to perish.
Thus, during the prosperous period of Zhōu (周),
the empire was harmonious,
and all the feudal lords and the Four Barbarians submitted,
presenting their tribute.
But when it declined,
no one in the empire came to court,
and Zhōu (周) could not control them;
this was not only because its virtue was thin,
but also because its strategic position was weak.
Now, Your Majesty rose from Fēng (豐) and Pèi (沛),
swept through Shǔ (蜀) and Hàn (漢),
pacified the Sān Qín (三秦),
and fought Xiàng Yǔ (項羽) between Xíngyáng (滎陽) and Chénggāo (成皋),
engaging in seventy major battles
and forty minor skirmishes;
causing the people of the empire
to have their livers and brains smeared on the ground,
and fathers and sons to have their bones exposed in the wilderness,
countless in number,
the sounds of weeping have not ceased,
and the wounded have not yet risen;
yet you wish to rival the prosperity of the time of Chéng (成) and Kāng (康).
Your servant secretly believes this is not comparable.
Furthermore, the land of Qín (秦) is surrounded by mountains and bordered by rivers,
secured by four natural barriers;
if an emergency suddenly arises,
a million troops can be assembled instantly.
Relying on the legacy of Qín (秦),
it is endowed with very beautiful and fertile land;
this is what is called a ‘heavenly storehouse.’
Fǔ (府)
means to gather;
a place where all things gather
is called a ‘heavenly storehouse.’
Even if east of the mountains is in chaos,
the former territory of Qín (秦) can be completely held.
When fighting a person,
if you do not grasp his throat
and pat his back,
you cannot fully secure victory.
Zhāng Yàn (張晏) says: È (搤)
is the same as è (扼),
meaning to hold tightly.
Kàng (亢),
pronounced gāng (岡),
also xià láng fān (下郎翻),
means throat.
This is also to grasp the throat of the empire and pat its back.”
The Emperor asked his ministers.
His ministers were all people from east of the mountains,
and they argued:
“The Zhōu (周) kings lasted several hundred years,
while Qín (秦) perished in its second generation.
Luòyáng (洛陽) has Chénggāo (成皋) to its east,
and Yáo (殽) and Miǎn (澠) to its west.
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: Yáo (殽)
refers to Mount Yáo (殽山),
which is the two Mount Yáo (殽山) east of today’s Shǎnzhōu (陝州).
Miǎn (澠)
is Miǎnchí (澠池).
It faces the Yī (伊) and Luò (洛) rivers.
The Hé (河) river is north of Luòyáng (洛陽) city,
hence it is said to be ‘behind’ (倍);
the Yī (伊) and Luò (洛) rivers are south of Luòyáng (洛陽) city,
hence it is said to ‘face’ (鄉).
Bèi (倍)
is Pú mèi fān (蒲妹翻).
Xiāng (鄉)
is read xiàng (嚮).
The Emperor asked Zhāng Liáng (張良).
Liáng (良) said:
“Although Luòyáng (洛陽) has these defenses,
its interior is small, no more than several hundred lǐ (里),
the land is barren,
and it is vulnerable to attack from four sides;
this is not a country for military endeavors.
Guānzhōng (關中) has Yáo (殽) and Hán (函) to its left,
and Lǒng (隴) and Shǔ (蜀) to its right,
with a thousand lǐ (里) of fertile land.
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: Wò (沃)
means irrigated;
it means its land has the benefit of irrigation,
hence it is called fertile land.
To its north are the advantages of the Hú (胡) pastures.
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: Refers to the areas of Āndìng (安定), Běidì (北地), and Shàngjùn (上郡) that border the Hú (胡),
suitable for animal husbandry.
Raising birds and beasts is called yuàn (苑),
pronounced yú ruǎn fān (於阮翻).
It can control the feudal lords to the east from just one side;
when the feudal lords are at peace,
the Hé (河) and Wèi (渭) rivers can transport goods for the entire empire,
supplying the capital in the west.
During the Hàn (漢) dynasty’s transportation from east of the pass,
it entered the Wèi (渭) from the Hé (河),
and went upstream from the Wèi (渭) to Cháng'ān (長安).
Transporting downstream,
it is sufficient to accumulate and distribute.
Kāng (康) says: Wěi (委),
yú wěi qiē (於偽切),
is the wěi (委) of wěi jī (委積).
Shū (輸),
is the shū (輸) of zhuǎn shū (轉輸).
Shū (輸),
chōng yù fān (舂遇翻).
It is a land of heavenly storehouses.
Fǔ (府)
is where things gather.
Where heavenly things gather,
without human effort,
hence it is called a ‘heavenly storehouse.’
The Emperor immediately drove west that day
and made Cháng'ān (長安) his capital.
He appointed Lóu Jìng (婁敬) as Lángzhōng (郎中),
conferred upon him the title Fèngchūn Jūn (奉春君),
and granted him the surname Liú (劉).
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: Wherever ‘chē jià’ (車駕) is mentioned,
it means the Son of Heaven traveling by carriage,
and is used as a respectful avoidance.
Cháng'ān (長安)
was originally a Qin (秦) district name;
Gāozǔ (高祖) made it the capital.
Fèngchūn Jūn (奉春君),
Zhāng Yàn (張晏) says: Chūn (春)
is the beginning of the year;
now Lóu Jìng (婁敬) initiated this matter,
hence he is called Fèngchūn Jūn (奉春君).
14 Zhāng Liáng (張良) had always been sickly.
After following the emperor into the pass,
he immediately began practicing Dàoyǐn (道引),
abstained from grains,
and kept his doors shut, not going out.
He said,
"My family served Hán (韓) for generations.
When Hán (韓) was destroyed,
I spared no expense in gold
to avenge Hán (韓) against the mighty Qín (秦),
shaking the whole world.
The matter can be found in Volume 7, Qín Shǐhuáng (秦始皇) 29th year.
Now, I have been enfeoffed as a Marquis of ten thousand households;
this is the utmost for a commoner,
and it is enough for me.
I wish to abandon worldly affairs
and roam with Chìsōngzǐ (赤松子)."
Shīgǔ (師古) said: Chìsōngzǐ (赤松子)
is the name of an immortal.
During the time of Shénnóng (神農), he served as the Master of Rain,
consumed 'water jade,'
taught Shénnóng (神農),
and could enter fire and burn himself.
He often dwelled in the stone chamber of Xīwángmǔ (西王母)
on Kūnshān (昆山),
ascending and descending with the wind and rain.
Yándì's (炎帝) young daughter pursued him
and also attained immortality, going with him.
Minister Guāng (光) said: The certainty of life having death
is like the certainty of night following day.
From ancient times until now,
there has indeed
been no one who transcended and existed alone.
With Zǐfáng's (子房) keen discernment and understanding of principles,
he was surely capable of knowing that the immortals were a false illusion.
However, his desire to roam with Chìsōngzǐ (赤松子)
shows his wisdom.
Indeed, the juncture of功名 (gōngmíng, achievement and fame)
is a difficult position for a minister to be in.
Those praised by Gāodì (高帝)
were only the Three Heroes;
Huáin (淮陰) was executed and annihilated,
Xiāo Hé (蕭何) was imprisoned –
was it not because they trod the path of excessive fullness without stopping?
Therefore, Zǐfáng (子房) sought refuge in the immortals,
abandoned human affairs,
regarded achievement and fame as external things,
and disregarded honor and profit.
This is what is called
"the wise protecting themselves."
The Classic of Poetry says: "Be both discerning and wise,
to protect your person."
15 In the sixth month,
on the day Rénchén (壬辰),
a great amnesty was granted to the world.
16 In autumn,
the seventh month,
Yān (燕) King Zāng Tú (臧荼) rebelled.
The emperor personally led a campaign against him.
17 Zhào (趙) King Jǐng (景) Ěr (耳) and Chángshā (長沙) King Wén (文) Ruì (芮) both passed away.
18 In the ninth month,
Zāng Tú (臧荼) was captured.
On the day Rénzǐ (壬子),
Grand Commandant Cháng'ān (長安) Marquis Lú Wǎn (盧綰) was enthroned as King of Yān (燕).
Bān Biǎo (班表) says: The Grand Commandant
was a Qín (秦) official
in charge of military affairs.
The Hàn (漢) system made him one of the Three Ducal Ministers, along with the Chancellor and the Grandee Secretary.
Yīng Shào (應劭) says: "Wèi" (尉) means "to stabilize from above."
According to the biography of Lú Wǎn (盧綰) in the Shǐjì (史記),
Cháng'ān (長安)
was formerly Xiányáng (咸陽).
Zhèngyì (正義) says: Qín (秦) Xiányáng (咸陽) was north of the Wèi (渭) River;
Cháng'ān (長安) was south of the Wèi (渭) River,
the place where Xiāo Hé (蕭何) built the Wèiyāng (未央) Palace.
Wǎn (綰) was born on the same day as the emperor.
The emperor favored Wǎn (綰) so much
that no other minister dared to hope for such a position,
so he was specially made a king.
Kǎoyì (考異) says: Both the Shǐjì (史記) and the Hànshū (漢書) (Gāojì (高紀))
state here:
"He sent Chancellor Kuài (噲) to lead troops to pacify the Dài (代) region."
However, according to Fán Kuài's (樊噲) biography: he was promoted to Left Chancellor after pacifying Hán (韓) King Xìn (信).
At this time, he was not yet Chancellor,
and there was no rebellion in the Dài (代) region,
nor is this matter mentioned in Kuài's (噲) biography.
It is suspected that the record is mistaken.
19 Xiàng Wáng's (項王) former general, Lì Jǐ (利幾), rebelled.
Lì Jǐ (利幾) had surrendered as the Prefect of Chén (陳)
and the emperor had enfeoffed him in Yǐngchuān (潁川).
When the emperor arrived in Luòyáng (洛陽),
he summoned him;
Lì Jǐ (利幾) became afraid and rebelled.
Fēngsú Tōng (風俗通) says: Lì (利)
is a surname.
Xìng Pǔ (姓譜) says: A son of the Chǔ (楚) royal house was granted a fief in Lì (利),
and later took it as his clan name.
20 Later in the ninth month,
the Chánglè (長樂) Palace was renovated.
Chéng Dàchāng (程大昌) in his Yōnglù (雍錄) says: Chánglè (長樂) Palace
was originally Qín's (秦) Xīnglè (興樂) Palace,
twenty *lǐ* (里) in circumference.
Gāozǔ (高祖) renovated it and resided there;
it was in the eastern corner of Cháng'ān (長安) city.
Lè (樂)
is pronounced as Luò (洛).
21 Xiàng Wáng's (項王) general Zhōnglí Mèi (鍾離昧)
had always been close to Chǔ (楚) King Xìn (信).
After Xiàng Wáng's (項王) death,
he fled to Xìn (信).
The Hàn (漢) King resented Mèi (昧) and,
hearing that he was in Chǔ (楚),
issued an edict to Chǔ (楚) to arrest Mèi (昧).
When Xìn (信) first went to his state,
he toured the counties and cities,
deploying troops upon entering and exiting.
1 In winter,
the tenth month,
someone submitted a memorial accusing Chǔ (楚) King Xìn (信) of rebellion.
The emperor questioned his generals,
and they all said,
"Quickly dispatch troops and bury that boy alive!"
The emperor remained silent.
He then asked Chén Píng (陳平).
Chén Píng (陳平) said,
"The person who submitted the memorial accusing Xìn (信) of rebellion,
does Xìn (信) know about it?"
The emperor said,
"He does not know."
Chén Píng (陳平) said,
"Between Your Majesty's elite troops and Chǔ's (楚), which are superior?"
The emperor said,
"They cannot surpass Chǔ's."
Píng (平) said,
"Among Your Majesty's generals, is there anyone skilled in warfare who can surpass Hán Xìn (韓信)?"
The emperor said,
"None can match him."
Píng (平) said,
"Now, your troops are not as elite as Chǔ's (楚) and your generals cannot match his.
If you raise an army to attack him,
it is to hasten a battle,
and I secretly fear for Your Majesty!"
The emperor said,
"What should be done about it?"
Píng (平) said,
"In ancient times, the Son of Heaven made inspection tours
and met with the feudal lords.
Báihǔ Tōng (白虎通) says: Why did the Son of Heaven make inspection tours?
'Xún' (巡) means to follow;
'shòu' (狩) means to gather.
It refers to traveling throughout the realm,
gathering the virtues and peace of the people,
fearing that distant and near places might differ,
and that governance and transformation might be hidden,
leading to some not finding their proper place.
Therefore, he must personally undertake it,
with reverence and respect for the people's intentions.
Mèngzǐ (孟子) said: The Son of Heaven going to the feudal lords is called 'xúnshǒu' (巡守);
'xúnshǒu' (巡守) means to inspect what they protect.
Pretend to tour Yúnmèng (雲夢).
'Dì' (第)
means 'just' or 'only'.
Chén (陳) is the western border of Chǔ (楚).
When Xìn (信) hears that the Son of Heaven is merely traveling for pleasure,
he will inevitably, without reason, go out to the suburbs to welcome and pay respects.
When he pays respects, Your Majesty can then capture him.
This is merely the task of one strong man."
The emperor thought this was a good idea.
So he dispatched envoys to inform the feudal lords to meet at Chén (陳),
saying, "I will travel south to Yúnmèng (雲夢)."
The emperor then proceeded with this plan.
Chǔ Wáng Xìn heard of this,
and became suspicious and fearful himself,
not knowing what to do.
Someone advised Xìn, saying:
"Behead Zhōnglí Mèi and present his head to the emperor,
the emperor will surely be pleased,
and you will have no worries."
Xìn followed this advice.
In the twelfth month,
the emperor met with the regional lords in Chén.
Xìn brought Mèi's head to present to the emperor;
the emperor ordered his warriors to bind Xìn,
and put him in the rear carriage.
Xìn said:
"It is indeed as people say: 'When the cunning hare dies,
the swift hound is cooked;
when the soaring birds are gone,
the good bow is put away;
when the enemy state is defeated,
the strategizing minister perishes.'
Shī Gǔ said: These are the words from Huáng Shí Gōng's Sān Lüè.
I am indeed due to be cooked!"
The emperor said:
"Someone accused you of rebellion."
He then shackled and bound Xìn and returned with him.
As for 'xiè' (shackles),
it refers to adding handcuffs and leg-irons;
as for 'jì' (binding),
it refers to adding ropes.
Tián Kěn congratulated the emperor, saying:
"Your Majesty has gained Hán Xìn,
and also controls Qín Zhōng.
Rú Chún said: People from Shān Dōng refer to Guān Zhōng as Qín Zhōng.
Shī Gǔ said: It refers to Guān Zhōng,
which is Qín territory.
It is a country of strategic advantage,
Zhāng Yàn said: It means gaining the advantage of geographical features.
with convenient terrain;
for it to deploy troops against the regional lords,
it is like standing on a high roof and pouring water from a 'líng' vase.
Rú Chún said: 'Líng'
is a bottle for holding water.
Standing on a high roof and overturning a 'líng' vase of water
describes the ease of its downward flow.
'Jiàn'
is read 'jū yǎn fān'.
'Líng'
is pronounced 'líng'.
To its east are the riches of Láng Yá and Jì Mò,
Shī Gǔ said: These two counties are near the sea,
a source of wealth and supplies.
Tài Shān is in the southern border of Qí,
and Qí relies on it as a stronghold.
Jìn Zhuó said: To the west of Qí is Píng Yuán.
The Hé Shuǐ (Yellow River) flows northeast past Gāo Táng;
Gāo Táng,
is Píng Yuán.
Mèng Jīn is also called Huáng Hé (Yellow River),
hence it is called the Turbid River.
I believe Mèng Jīn is in Hé Nèi,
quite far from Píng Yuán,
so Jìn's explanation is too restrictive;
probably because the river water is turbid,
it is called the Turbid River.
Suǒ Yǐn said: Cuī Hào stated: 'Bó'
means 'spreading out sideways'.
That which spreads out sideways
lies across Jì Běi,
therefore the 'Qí Dū Fù' states: "The sea that spreads out sideways is 'Bó',
named Bó Hǎi Jùn."
I refer to Bān Zhì:
Qí territory extends north to Bó Hǎi,
comprising the lands of Gāo Lè, Gāo Chéng, Yáng Xìn, and Chóng Hé.
[Qí has] a million men bearing halberds;
this is an eastern Qín,
meaning Qí's strategic geographical advantage is comparable to Qín's.
No one should be made king of Qí."
The emperor said:
"Excellent!"
and bestowed five hundred catties of gold.
The emperor returned,
arriving at Luò Yáng,
pardoned Hán Xìn,
and enfeoffed him as Huái Yīn Hóu.
Xìn knew that the Hàn Wáng feared and disliked his abilities,
so he often claimed illness,
and did not attend court or follow the emperor;
he was often resentful and dissatisfied,
ashamed to be ranked with [Marquis of] Jiàng and [Marquis of] Guàn.
Once, he visited Fán Jiāng Jūn Kuài.
Kuài knelt and bowed, welcoming and seeing him off,
addressing himself as "your servant,"
and said:
"Your Highness, you actually deign to visit your servant!"
When Xìn left the door,
he laughed and said:
"To think that I, alive, am in the company of the likes of Kuài!"
This laid the groundwork for Xìn's resentment, frustration, and eventual plotting of rebellion.
The emperor once casually discussed with Xìn the military capabilities of various generals and how many troops they could command.
The emperor asked:
"As for me, how many troops can I command?"
Xìn replied:
"Your Majesty can command no more than a hundred thousand."
The emperor said:
"What about you?"
He replied:
"As for your servant, the more the better."
The emperor laughed and said:
"If the more the better,
why then were you captured by me?"
Xìn replied:
"Your Majesty cannot command troops well, but you are good at commanding generals.
This is precisely why Xìn was captured by Your Majesty.
Moreover, Your Majesty,
is what is called 'bestowed by Heaven,
not by human effort.'
2 Jiǎshēn,
[the emperor] first carved tallies and enfeoffed various meritorious officials as chèhóu.
Shīgǔ said: pōu
means 'to break';
it means to combine tallies with them and then distribute them.
Pōu,
pronounced pǔkǒu.
According to the Bān Zhì,
Cuán county belonged to Nányáng Jùn.
Méng Kāng said: Cuán,
pronounced zàn.
According to Bān Shū's table of meritorious officials: Xiāo Hé was enfeoffed in Cuán,
with eight thousand households,
while Cáo Cān was enfeoffed in Píngyáng, and Zhāng Liáng in Liú,
both with ten thousand households.
It is inappropriate to say that Hé's enfeoffment was uniquely large.
Cān was enfeoffed on the twelfth month, Jiǎshēn.
Hé was enfeoffed on the first month, Bǐngwǔ;
the reason why the meritorious officials said Hé was superior and they were displeased
was specifically regarding Fán, Lì, Jiàng, and Guàn and others who were enfeoffed on the same day.
Zhāng Liáng was also enfeoffed on Bǐngwǔ.
The reason why these people mentioned Hé but not Liáng
is probably that Gāozǔ first allowed Liáng to choose thirty thousand households in Qí,
but Liáng only accepted ten thousand households in Liú,
so they dared not speak of him.
"We, your subjects, donned armor and held sharp weapons,
some fighting over a hundred battles,
others dozens of engagements.
Now, Xiāo Hé has never had the labor of a sweating horse,
merely holding literary documents and making arguments,
yet he is placed above us, your subjects.
Why is this?"
The Emperor said:
"Do you gentlemen understand hunting?
In hunting,
those who chase and kill beasts and rabbits
are dogs;
but those who release them and indicate the location of the beasts
are people.
Now, you gentlemen are merely capable of catching running beasts,
you are 'meritorious dogs';
as for Xiāo Hé,
he releases and indicates,
he is a 'meritorious person'."
Shīgǔ said: Fāzòng
means to untie and release them.
Zhǐshì means
to point to them with a hand.
Today, people popularly say fàng gǒu (release dogs).
Zòng,
pronounced zǐyòng;
but readers pronounce it as zōng,
which is the 'zōng' of zōngjì (tracks),
which is incorrect.
All original texts do not write
the character zōng
there are dogs that track on their own,
not requiring a person to release them.
Hóng Shì's Lì Shì says: In the Yuányòu period,
when Luòzhōu was managing river dikes,
a Han stele of Běihǎi Chúnyú Zhǎng Xià Jūn was unearthed,
its inscription stating
"following the path of previous tracks (shào zòng xiān guǐ)."
Also, the stele of Běijūn Zhōnghòu Guō Zhòngqí
states
"having the tracks of Shānfǔ (yǒu Shānfǔ zhī zòng),"
and also states
"magnificent tracks are evident (huī zòng xiǎn),"
and furthermore, the stele of Sīlì Xiàowèi Lǔ Jùn
states
"comparing tracks with Bào and Chǎn (bǐ zòng Bào, Chǎn),"
and also the stele of Yǔlì Zhào Jūn
states
"envying his tracks (xiàn qí zòng),"
and the stele of Wàihuánglì Gāo Biāo
states
"none can compare with his tracks (mò yǔ bǐ zòng)."
In all these,
zòng
is used as
zōng.
Xiāo Hé Zhuàn:
"Releasing and indicating the location of beasts,"
Yán Shīgǔ's commentary says: All original texts do not write
the character zōng
readers pronounce it as zōng,
which is the 'zōng' of zōngjì (tracks),
which is incorrect.
According to these steles,
Han people indeed frequently used it interchangeably;
Yán Shì's commentary is probably not entirely accurate.
Zhāng Liáng was a strategist,
and also had no combat achievements;
the Emperor allowed him to choose thirty thousand households in Qí.
Liáng said:
"Originally,
I rose from Xiàpī,
met with Your Majesty in Liú,
and saw the eight-volume (book) from the second year of Qín Èrshì.
Your Majesty used my plans,
and fortunately they were often successful.
I wish to be enfeoffed in Liú, that is enough,
I dare not accept thirty thousand households."
Thereupon, Zhāng Liáng was enfeoffed as Liú Hóu.
Chén Píng was enfeoffed as Hùyǒu Hóu.
Hùyǒu
was a township name,
belonging to Yángwǔ Xiàn in Chénliú Jùn.
Xú Guǎng said: Yángwǔ belonged to Wèi territory.
Hùyǒu is now Dōnghūn Xiàn,
belonging to Chénliú.
Suǒyǐn said: Xú Guǎng said: Yángwǔ belonged to Wèi,
but the Dìlǐ Zhì assigns it to Hénán Jùn.
Perhaps Yángwǔ later belonged to Liáng Guó.
Xú also said: Hùyǒu is now Dōnghūn Xiàn,
belonging to Chénliú,
which is consistent with Bān Shū's Dìlǐ Zhì.
This is correct;
in Qín times, Hùyǒu Xiāng belonged to Yángwǔ,
but in Han, Hùyǒu Xiāng became Dōnghūn Xiàn,
administered by Chénliú Jùn.
Kuò Dì Zhì: The old city of Dōnghūn
is ninety lì northeast of Chénliú Xiàn in Biànzhōu.
Chén Píng was also enfeoffed on the twelfth month, Jiǎshēn.
"This is not my achievement."
The Emperor said:
"I used your strategies,
won battles and defeated enemies;
if not an achievement, what is it?"
Píng said:
"If not for Wèi Wúzhī,
how could I have advanced?"
The Emperor said:
"You, sir,
can be said not to forget your roots!"
Thereupon, Wèi Wúzhī was again rewarded.
Píng's matter of being introduced to the Emperor by Wúzhī is found in volume nine, second year.
Bèi,
pronounced pūmèi.
Fù,
pronounced fúyòu.
3 The Emperor, seeing that the realm had just been pacified,
his sons were young,
and his brothers were few,
and having learned from Qin’s isolated downfall,
wished to greatly enfeoff his kinsmen to secure and soothe the empire.
In spring,
the first month,
on the *bǐngwǔ* day,
he divided the territory of Chǔ Wáng Xìn into two states: he established his paternal cousin, General Jiǎ, as the King of Jīng, ruling fifty-three counties east of the Huái River.
Suǒ Yǐn says: This refers to the King of Wú,
whose territory was east of the Huái River.
I follow Bān's history,
which states that at that time, Jiǎ was made king over fifty-three counties of the former Dōngyáng, Zhāng, and Wú Commanderies.
Dōngyáng
was the land of Xiàpī in Hàn;
Zhāng Commandery
was the land of Dānyáng in Hàn;
Wú Commandery
was Kuàijī territory;
presumably its land extended from east of the Huái River southward,
encompassing Dānyáng and Kuàijī.
After Jiǎ's death,
Wú Wáng Bì was made king over his territory,
which is why Suǒ Yǐn says it was Wú territory.
Rú Chún says: Jīng
is also Chǔ.
Jiǎ Kuí says: Qín Zhuāngxiāng Wáng's personal name was Chǔ,
so it was renamed Jīng,
and this became customary.
Jìn Zhuó says:
"Fènfá Jīngchǔ" (fiercely attack Jīng and Chǔ),
from Qín's ancestors, it was already called Jīng.
Suǒ Yǐn says: Yáo Chá, citing Yú Xǐ, says: The general term Jīng
is a state named after a mountain.
Today, to the southwest, there is Jīng Shān,
located in the vicinity of Yángxiàn.
Jiǎ was enfeoffed with Wú territory and titled King of Jīng,
taking this meaning.
The *Tàikāng Dìzhì* states: Yángxiàn County
was originally named Jīngxī.
The character '從' (cóng),
pronounced as 'cái yòng' (*cai yong*) in fanqie.
Xuē Commandery
was Lǔ Guó in Hàn;
Dōnghǎi
was Tán Commandery in Qín;
Péngchéng
later became Chǔ Guó: presumably, at the time of enfeoffment, they received the land of three commanderies.
After Jǐng and Wǔ,
Chǔ Guó consisted only of Péngchéng and a few counties.
On the *rénzǐ* day,
his elder brother, the Marquis of Yíxìn, Xǐ, was made King of Dài, ruling fifty-three counties of Yúnzhōng, Yànmén, and Dài Commanderies.
Féi, the son of the Emperor's concubine from his humble days, was made King of Qí, ruling seventy-three counties of Jiāodōng, Jiāoxī, Línzī, Jìběi, Bóyáng, and Chéngyáng Commanderies.
According to this,
Bóyáng must also have been a commandery at some point during the Qín, Chǔ, and Hàn wars.
From the Huái River east to here, ancient place names are used mixedly,
not purely using the commandery names established by Qín and Hàn.
Shī Gǔ says: "Wàifù"
refers to one with whom one has an illicit relationship.
Mèng Kāng says: At this time, the populace was migrating,
so those who could speak the Qí dialect were returned to Qí.
*Shǐjì Zhèngyì* says: It is said that the strategic advantage of Qí Guó was second only to Qínzhōng,
hence it was enfeoffed to his son Féi.
Over seventy cities near the Qí capital,
those who could speak the Qí dialect were all assigned to Qí.
As his own son,
he made his capital large.
Mèng's explanation is probably incorrect.
4 The Emperor considered Hán Wáng Xìn to be capable and martial.
The territory he was made king over was north, near Gǒng and Luò,
south, bordering Wǎn and Yè,
and to the east, it included Huáiyáng.
When Hán was divided from Jìn,
its territory extended south to Wǎn and Yè,
northwest encompassed Gǒng and Luò,
adjoined Xīn'ān and Yíyáng,
and to the east, it included Yǐngchuān.
However, the land of Huáiyáng then belonged to Chǔ.
When Hàn pacified the realm,
Hán Wáng Xìn was enfeoffed as king of Yǐngchuān,
and his territory eastward also included Huáiyáng.
What is called
"north near"
and
"south bordering"
means their borders were close to each other,
not that they belonged to Hán.
The character '宛' (wǎn),
pronounced as 'yú yuán' (*yu yuan*) in fanqie.
The character '葉' (yè),
pronounced as 'shì shè' (*shi she*) in fanqie.
He then made Tàiyuán Commandery, with thirty-one counties, into the State of Hán,
and moved Hán Wáng Xìn to rule north of Tàiyuán,
to defend against the Hú,
making Jìnyáng his capital.
Xìn submitted a memorial, saying:
"My state borders the frontier,
and the Xiōngnú frequently raid it.
Jìnyáng is far from the frontier passes,
I request to govern Mǎyì."
Bān's Record states that
Tàiyuán Commandery governed twenty-one counties;
now thirty-one counties are made into the State of Hán.
Presumably, Dìngxiāng Commandery had not yet been established,
so the territory of Tàiyuán
bordered the frontier to the north,
also encompassing Mǎyì of Yànmén.
*Jìn Tàikāng Dìjì* says: When this city was built in Qín times, it always collapsed
and could not be completed.
There was a horse that circled back and forth;
the elders considered this strange,
and so built the city based on its movements,
hence it was named Mǎyì.
Dù Yòu says: Qín's Mǎyì city
is within the boundaries of Shōuzhōu Shànyáng County.
Lǐ Qí says: The character '被' (pí),

Shī Gǔ says: '被' (pí)

The character '數' (shuò),
pronounced as 'suǒ jiǎo' (*suo jiao*) in fanqie.
5 The Emperor had already enfeoffed over twenty great meritorious ministers,
but the others disputed their achievements day and night without resolution,
and had not yet been enfeoffed.
The Emperor was in the Southern Palace in Luòyáng.
From the covered walkway, he looked down and saw his generals
often sitting together in the sand, talking.
The Emperor said:
"What are they talking about?"
The Marquis of Liú said:
"Does Your Majesty not know?
This is a conspiracy to rebel!"
The Emperor said:
"The realm is nearing stability."
'屬' (shǔ)
means 'near';
it means it is nearing stability.
The character '屬' (shǔ),
pronounced as 'zhī yù' (*zhi yu*) in fanqie.
The Marquis of Liú said:
"Your Majesty rose from commoner status,
and by this method, seized the realm.
Now Your Majesty is the Son of Heaven,
but those you enfeoff are all old acquaintances and those you cherish,
and those you execute are all enemies from your former life.
Now, the military officials are calculating merits,
thinking that the realm is not enough to enfeoff everyone.
These men fear that Your Majesty cannot enfeoff them all,
and are afraid of being suspected for past mistakes or being executed.
Hence, they are gathering to conspire rebellion."
The Emperor then worried and said:
"What should be done about it?"
The Marquis of Liú said:
"Among those Your Majesty has always hated,
and whom all your ministers know, who is the most extreme?"
The Emperor said:
"Yōng Chǐ and I have an old grudge;
he frequently humiliated me.
Fú Qián says: Before I rose,
he and I had an old grudge.
Shī Gǔ says: He often used his strength to humiliate Gāozǔ.
I observe that when the Emperor first rose,
he ordered Yōng Chǐ to guard Fēng;
Chǐ was inherently unwilling to submit to the Emperor,
and so surrendered Fēng to Wèi.
This shows that there was an old grudge.
The character '雍' (yōng),
pronounced as 'yú yòng' (*yu yong*) in fanqie.
The character '數' (shuò),
pronounced as 'suǒ jiǎo' (*suo jiao*) in fanqie.
Because of his many merits,
I cannot bear to execute him."
The Marquis of Liú said:
"If we urgently enfeoff Yōng Chǐ first now,
then all your ministers will be reassured."
Thereupon, the Emperor held a banquet
and enfeoffed Yōng Chǐ as the Marquis of Shífāng.
Sū Lín says: Shífāng
is a county in Hànzhōng.
Shī Gǔ says: The *Dìlǐ Zhì* states
it belonged to Guǎnghàn,
not Hànzhōng;
now it belongs to Yìzhōu.
The character '什' (shí)
is pronounced as 'shí' (ten).
I note that in the Táng Record,
Shífāng County belonged to Hànzhōu.
This was probably when Hànzhōu was again separated from Yìzhōu during the Chuígǒng era.
Sòng Bái says: Shífāng County
was formerly governed from Yōng Chǐ City;
now the county seat is established forty paces north of that city.
All the ministers concluded the banquet
and were all pleased,
saying:
"Even Yōng Chǐ is a marquis,
we have nothing to worry about!"
Chén Guāng 曰: Zhāng Liáng 為 Gāodì 謀臣，
委以心腹，
宜其知無不言；
安有聞諸將謀反，
必待 Gāodì 目見偶語，
然後乃言之邪！
蓋以 Gāodì 初得天下，
數用愛憎行誅賞，
或時害至公，
群臣往往有觖望自危之心；
故 Liáng 因事納忠以變移帝意，
使上無阿私之失，
下無猜懼之謀，
國家無虞，
利及後世。
若 Liáng 者，
可謂善諫矣。
6 列侯畢已受封，
詔定元功十八人位次。
Shīgǔ 曰: 謂 Xiāo Hé, Cáo Cān, Zhāng Áo, Zhōu Bó, Fán Kuài, Lì Shāng, Xī Juān, Xiàhóu Yīng, Guàn Yīng, Fù Kuān, Jìn Liǎn, Wáng Líng, Chén Wǔ, Wáng Xī, Xuē ōu, Zhōu Chāng,
Dīng Fù, Chóng Dá，

余謂此但定 Xiāo Hé 等元功十八人位次耳。
至 Lǚ Hòu 時，

Shīgǔ 所謂自 Xiāo Hé 至 Chóng Dá 十八人，

Zhāng Áo 於 Gāozǔ 九年始自 Zhào Wáng 廢為 Xuānpíng Hóu，
安得預元功十八人之數哉？
故 Shīgǔ 註功臣位次云：Zhāng ěr 及 Áo 並為無大功，
蓋以 Lǔ Yuán 之故，
Lǚ Hòu 曲升之耳。
此說則得之。
「 Píngyáng Hóu Cáo Cān，
身被七十創，
攻城略地，
功最多，
宜第一。」
謁者、關內侯 è Qiānqiū 進曰：
「群臣議皆誤，
è 本出 Jī 姓，
Jìn è Hóu 之後。
關內侯位次列侯，
爵第十九。
Shīgǔ 曰：言有侯號而居京畿，
無國邑。
此特一時之事耳。
上與 Chǔ 相距五歲，
失軍亡眾，
跳身遁者數矣；
Shīgǔ 曰：謂輕身走出也。
數，
所角翻；
下同。
非上所詔令召，
而數萬眾會。
上之乏絕者數矣，
又軍無見糧；
Xiāo Hé 轉漕 Guānzhōng，
給食不乏。
陛下雖數亡 Shāndōng，
Xiāo Hé 常全 Guānzhōng 以待陛下。
此萬世之功也。
今雖無 Cáo Cān 等百數，
何缺於 Hàn；
Hàn 得之，
不必待以全。
奈何欲以一旦之功而加萬世之功哉！
Xiāo Hé 第一，

上曰：
於是乃賜 Xiāo Hé 帶劍履上殿，
入朝不趨。
古者君子必帶劍，
所以衛身，
且昭武備也。
Qín 法：群臣上殿，
不得持尺寸之兵。
草曰菲，
麻曰屨，
皮曰履。
屨、履所以從軍，
軍容不入國，
故皆不許以上殿。
君前必趨，
崇敬也。
今賜何劍履上殿，
入朝不趨，
殊禮也。
「吾聞『進賢受上賞』。
Xiāo Hé 功雖高，
得 è Jūn 乃益明。」
於是因 è Qiānqiū 所
食邑，

悉封何父子兄弟十餘人，

7 上歸 Lìyáng。
五月，
丙午，
尊太公為 Tàishàng Huáng。

皇，
君也。
天子之父，

Xiōngnú 畏 Qín，

及 Qín 滅，

此北河也，
在 Shuòfāng 北。
Chányú Tóumàn 有太子曰 Mòdún。
後有所愛 Yānzhī，
Xiōngnú 之 Yānzhī，
猶中國之皇后。
閼，
於連翻。
氏，
音 zhī；
下 Yuèzhī 同。
Tóumàn 欲立之。
是時，
Dōnghú 強而 Yuèzhī 盛，
Kuòdì Zhì：Liáng, Sù, Gān, Shā, Tíngzhōu，
本 Yuèzhī 地。
既而 Tóumàn 急擊 Yuèzhī，

Mòdún 盜其善馬騎之，
亡歸；
Tóumàn 以為壯，
令將萬騎。
Mòdún 乃作鳴鏑，
Yīng Shào 曰：髐箭也。
Wéi Zhāo 曰：矢鏑飛則鳴。
余見今軍中亦有鳴鏑，
於近笴之處開小竅，
矢飛急則凌風而鳴。
鏑，
音 dí。
髐，
呼交翻。
勒其所部，
使習其令也。
「鳴鏑所射而不悉射者，
斬之！」
Mòdún 乃以鳴鏑自射其善馬，
既又射其愛妻；
左右或不敢射者，
皆斬之。
最後以鳴鏑射 Chányú 善馬，
左右皆射之。
於是 Mòdún 知其可用；
從 Tóumàn 獵，
以鳴鏑射 Tóumàn，
其左右亦皆隨鳴鏑而射。
遂殺 Tóumàn，
盡誅其後母與弟及大臣不聽從者。
Mòdún 自立為 Chányú.
When the Dōnghú heard that Mòdún had been enthroned,
they sent an envoy to Mòdún, saying:
"We wish to acquire the swift horse that belonged to Tóumàn during his time."
Mòdún consulted his ministers,
who all said:
"This is a treasured horse of the Xiōngnú;
do not give it!"
Mòdún said:
"How can we, being neighbors to another country, begrudge a single horse?"
So, he gave it to them.
After a short while,
the Dōnghú again sent an envoy to Mòdún, saying:
"We wish to acquire one of the Chányú's Yānshì."
Mòdún again asked those around him,
who were all enraged and said:
"The Dōnghú are without principle,
to demand an Yānshì!
We request to attack them!"
Mòdún said:
"How can we, being neighbors to another country, begrudge a single woman?"
So, he took his beloved Yānshì and gave her to the Dōnghú.
The King of Dōnghú became even more arrogant.
Between the Dōnghú and the Xiōngnú,
there was a deserted land, uninhabited,
over a thousand *lǐ* in extent.
Each side resided on its own border,
making *ōutuō*.
Fú Qián said: *ōutuō*
means making earthen chambers to live in together;
Shī Gǔ said: It refers to lookout posts on the border,
like today's ambush points.
*ōu*,
rhymes *yī hóu fān*.
*tuō*,
rhymes *tǔ huó fān*.
"[This deserted land,]
we wish to possess it."
Mòdún asked his ministers.
Some ministers said:
"This is deserted land;
giving it is acceptable,
and not giving it is also acceptable."
Thereupon, Mòdún was greatly enraged and said:
"Land
is the foundation of a state;
how can we give it away!"
All those who had said to give it away
were beheaded.
Mòdún mounted his horse,
and issued an order:
"Anyone in the state who falls behind shall be beheaded!"
Then, he launched a surprise attack on the Dōnghú.
The Dōnghú initially underestimated Mòdún
and were unprepared;
Mòdún consequently annihilated the Dōnghú.
After returning,
he then attacked the Yuèzhī to the west and drove them away,
and in the south, he annexed the kings of Lóufán and Báiyáng in Hénán.
Shī Gǔ said: The residences of the two kings of Lóufán and Báiyáng were in Hénán.
He completely re-occupied the former Xiōngnú lands that Méng Tián had seized.
Méng Tián's seizure of Xiōngnú land
is recorded in Volume 7, Qín Shǐhuáng's 31st year.
The Bān Zhì states that
Cháonà County belonged to Āndìng Commandery,
and Fūshī County belonged to Shàng Commandery.
The Shǐjì Zhèngyì says: The former city of Hàn Cháonà
is seventy *lǐ* west of Bǎiquán County in Yuánzhōu.
Fūshī County
was established by Zhào,
Qín retained it without change,
and now it belongs to Yánzhōu.
As the Hàn army was just then engaged in battle with Xiàng Yǔ,
and China was exhausted by warfare,
Mòdún was thus able to strengthen himself,
commanding over 300,000 archers.
*Kòngxián*
means drawing a bow.
*Kòng*,
rhymes *kǒu nòng fān*.
In autumn,
the Xiōngnú besieged Hán Wáng Xìn at Mǎyì.
Xìn repeatedly sent envoys to the Hú,
seeking a peaceful settlement.
Hàn dispatched troops to rescue him;
suspecting Xìn of frequently sending secret envoys,
having two minds,
they sent someone to reproach Xìn.
Fearing execution, Xìn,
in the ninth month,
surrendered Mǎyì to the Xiōngnú.
Mòdún of the Xiōngnú then led his troops south, crossing Jùzhù.
The Jùnguó Zhì says: Jùzhù
is a treacherous mountain pass,
located in Yànmén's Yīnguǎn County.
The Kuòdì Zhì says: Jùzhù Mountain is thirty *lǐ* northwest of Yànmén County in Dàizhōu.
Dù Yòu said: Jùzhù Mountain
is the Xīxíng Pass in Yànmén County of Dàizhōu.
*Jù*,
pronunciation *gōu*,
also as written,
and also pronunciation *jū*.
They reached Jìnyáng.
The Emperor entirely abolished the harsh Qín rituals
and made the laws simple and easy.
Ministers drank wine and vied for credit,
and when drunk,
some shouted wildly,
drew swords and struck pillars.
The Emperor became increasingly disgusted by this.
Shú Sūn Tōng advised the Emperor, saying:
Shú Sūn's ancestry was from the Jī surname,
descendants of the Shú Sūn clan of Lǔ.
"Indeed, scholars are difficult to advance with in conquering,
but they can be partnered with in maintaining what has been established.
Your servant wishes to recruit the scholars of Lǔ
to work with my disciples to establish court ceremonies."
The Emperor said:
"Won't that be difficult?"
Shú Sūn Tōng said:
"The Five Emperors had different music,
and the Three Kings had different rituals;
rituals
are regulations and refinements made according to the times, the age, and human sentiment.
Your servant wishes to somewhat adopt ancient rituals
and combine them with Qín ceremonies to complete them."
The Emperor said:
"You may try to make them,
make them easy to understand,
and adapt them to what I am capable of implementing!"
Thereupon, Shú Sūn Tōng acted as envoy
and recruited over thirty scholars from Lǔ.
Shī Gǔ said: Tōng acted as an envoy to recruit the scholars from Lǔ.
*shǐ*,
rhymes *shū lì fān*.
They said:
"The lord you have served is almost ten rulers,
all of whom you flattered to gain intimacy and honor.
Tōng served Qín Shǐhuáng, Èr Shì, Chén Shè, Xiàng Liáng, Chǔ Huái Wáng, Xiàng Yǔ, and the Emperor,
in total seven rulers.
*qiě*,
means 'nearly';
it means nearly ten rulers.
The dead are not yet buried,
the wounded are not yet recovered,
yet you wish to establish rituals and music.
The establishment of rituals and music
can only be undertaken after a hundred years of accumulated virtue.
Shī Gǔ said: It means after practicing virtuous teachings for a hundred years,
only then can rituals and music be established.
Sir, go away,
do not defile us!"
Shú Sūn Tōng laughed and said:
"You are truly a coarse scholar,
you do not understand the changes of the times!"
Shī Gǔ said: *ruò*,
means 'you'.
*bǐ*,
means 'not astute'.
Shī Gǔ said: Entered the pass to the west.
Shī Gǔ said: *zuǒyòu*,
refers to close ministers.
To study,
means to have academic knowledge.
With his more than one hundred disciples,
he made *miáncuì*,
and practiced in the wild.

is the same as *cuì*,

erecting markers to form *cuì*.
*cuì*,
rhymes *zī huì fān*.

is the modern character *zhuǎn*,

also pronounced *zhuǎn*.

he said:

was a Qín official,
in charge of ancestral temple rituals;

Originally,
when Qín possessed the empire,
it incorporated all the rituals of the six states,
selecting and retaining those that honored the ruler and suppressed officials.
When Tōng devised the rituals,
he made some additions and deletions,
but mostly followed Qín's old practices,

little was changed.
His writings
were later recorded together with the laws and ordinances,

was the Fǎguān (legal office).

Your servant Guāng says: Ritual is a great thing!
Applied to oneself,
one's actions have standards, and all conduct is perfected;
applied to the family,
there is distinction between inside and outside, and the nine kindred are harmonious;
applied to the community,
there is order between old and young, and customs become refined;
applied to the state,
there is proper order between ruler and ministers, and governance is achieved;
applied to the empire,
the feudal lords submit, and the proper order is established;
how can it be limited to merely obtaining order on the ceremonial mat or within the household without chaos!
Indeed, with Gāozǔ's clear understanding,
he praised Lù Jiǎ's words,
as seen in Volume 10, Year 11.
However, the reason he could not stand shoulder
with the kings of the Three Dynasties
was simply his lack of learning.
At that time,
if a great Ru (Confucian scholar) had assisted him,
and governed the empire with ritual,
would his achievements have stopped there!
Alas,
Master Sūnshū's
capacity was small!
He merely purloined the husks and empty grains of ritual,
to conform to the age, harmonize with customs, and gain favor, that is all.
The skin of grain is called kàng;
grain that fails to ripen is called pǐ;
pǐ
is the same as bǐ.
And to this day,
is it not deeply regrettable!
Therefore, Yáng Zǐ criticized him, saying:
"Long ago, Lǔ had a great minister,
whose name the historian lost.
He said: 'How great was he?'
He said: 'Shūsūn Tōng wanted to establish the rituals for ruler and minister,
and invited masters from Lǔ,
but there were two whom he could not induce to come.'
He said: 'If so,
then was Zhòngní's (Confucius') journeying among the feudal lords not right?'
He said: 'Zhòngní journeyed
to put his principles into practice.
Sòng Xián said: It means to spread his footsteps among the states of the feudal lords,
similar to "visiting various courts."
Although he had his compass and square,
how could he put them to use!'"
Excellent indeed are Yáng Zǐ's words!
How could a great Ru be willing to destroy his compass and square to achieve a temporary success!
2 The Emperor personally attacked Hán Wáng Xìn,
defeating his army at Tóngdī.
Bān Zhì:
Tóngdī County belonged to Shàngdǎng Commandery.
Shàngdǎng Jì: Jìn’s Tóngdī,
which Bóhuá took as his fief,
was twenty *lǐ* from the old palace of Tóngdī;
in the Táng Dynasty, it belonged to Lùzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: The county has the Tóngdī River,
hence its name.
鞮,
pronunciation *dīng xī* (Tīngxī).
Xìn fled to the Xiōngnú;
the Bátǔ natives Mànqiū Chén and Wáng Huáng and others enthroned Zhào Lì, a descendant of the Zhào royal house, as king.
Bān Zhì:
Bátǔ County belonged to Shàngjùn.
Kuòdì Zhì: The old city of Bátǔ

Shīgǔ said: Yuán
is pronounced *yín*;

It should be noted that
the character 圜
is a mistake for
圁.
Tōngdiǎn: The Yín River is northeast of Rúlín County in Yínzhōu,

Xìngpǔ: Qí had Mànqiū Bùzé.
[They] plotted with Xìn and the Xiōngnú to attack Hàn.

Bān Shǐ: The Xiōngnú appointed Left and Right Xiánwáng,

Guǎngwǔ County belonged to Tàiyuán Commandery.
Shǐjì Zhèngyì: The old city of Guǎngwǔ was south of Jùzhù Mountain on the border of Yànmén in Dàizhōu.
Dù Yòu said: Yànmén Commandery in Dàizhōu governed Yànmén County;

The Xiōngnú were repeatedly defeated and fled,

The Hàn army pursued them, taking advantage of their victory.
It happened to be extremely cold,
and it snowed.
Dà Dài Jì said: The *qì* of extreme Yin resides in rain and water,
which then condenses into snow.
雨,
pronunciation *yú jù*.
What falls from above is called *yǔ*;
later derived from its meaning.
Shīgǔ said: Two or three out of ten people suffered frostbitten fingers.
The Emperor stayed in Jìnyáng
and heard that Mòdú Chányú was in Dàigǔ.
Shǐjì Zhèngyì said: Dàigǔ
is now Guīzhōu.
I rely on the fact that Táng Dynasty’s Guīzhōu was northwest of Yōuzhōu,
and this Dàigǔ was north of Jùzhù.
The Later Wèi capital was Píngchéng,
established as the capital of Dài,
likely named after Dàigǔ;
in the Táng Dynasty, it belonged to Yúnzhōu.
He sent people to scout the Xiōngnú.
Mòdú hid his strong men and fat cattle and horses,
showing only the old and weak and emaciated animals.
Ten groups of envoys returned,
all saying the Xiōngnú could be attacked.
The Emperor again sent Liú Jìng as an envoy to the Xiōngnú.
Before he returned,
Hàn had assembled 320,000 troops to drive them north,
crossing Jùzhù.
Liú Jìng returned
and reported:
"When two countries attack each other,
they should boast and
show their strengths.
Now, when I went,
I only saw the emaciated, old, and weak.
This must be to show weakness
and conceal elite troops to gain advantage.
I foolishly believe the Xiōngnú cannot be attacked."
At this time,
the Hàn army had already set off.
Fán Shì Yǐ Wéi Ér Wèi Chéng Yuē Yè (凡事已為而未成曰業): "All matters already done but not yet completed are called *yè*."
The Emperor cursed Liú Jìng, saying:
"This Qí captive gained office by his glib tongue,
and now he makes wild statements to discourage my army!"
He had Jìng shackled in Guǎngwǔ.
The Emperor first arrived at Píngchéng,
but his troops had not all arrived.
Mòdú unleashed 400,000 elite cavalry
and surrounded the Emperor at Báidēng for seven days.
Bān Zhì: Píngchéng County belonged to Yànmén Commandery.
Fú Qián said: Báidēng
was the name of a terrace,

more than ten *lǐ* from Píngchéng.
Kuòdì Zhì: Shuòzhōu’s Dìngxiāng County
was originally Hàn Píngchéng County;
thirty *lǐ* to its northeast is Mount Báidēng,
and on the mountain is a terrace
called Báidēngtái.
The Emperor used Chén Píng’s secret strategy,
sending an envoy to heavily bribe the Chányú’s Yānzhī.
Yìng Shào said: Chén Píng had an artist draw a beautiful woman,
and secretly sent it to the Yānzhī, saying:
"Hàn has such a beautiful woman;
now the Emperor is in dire straits
and wishes to present her."
The Yānzhī feared losing her favor,
and spoke to Mòdú,
telling him to lift the siege.
I say the "secret strategy"
was because it was against the etiquette of the Central Kingdom,
so it was kept secret and not passed down.
間,
pronunciation *gǔ xiàn* (Gǔxiàn).
遺,
pronunciation *yú jì* (Yújì).
"The two rulers should not distress each other.
Even if you obtain Hàn territory,
the Chányú will ultimately not be able to inhabit it.
Moreover, the Hàn ruler also has divine power;
the Chányú should consider this!"
Mòdú had an agreed date with Wáng Huáng and Zhào Lì,
but Huáng and Lì’s troops did not arrive,
making him suspect they were conspiring with Hàn,
so he opened up one corner of the siege.
It happened to be very foggy,
and Hàn envoys went back and forth,
undetected by the Xiōngnú.
Chén Píng requested that the strong crossbows be fitted with two arrows,
facing outwards,
and directly exit from the opened corner.
The Emperor exited the siege
and wished to speed away;
the Grand Coachman Téng Gōng insisted on proceeding slowly.
Upon reaching Píngchéng,
the main Hàn army also arrived,
and the Hú cavalry then retreated.
Hàn also withdrew its troops and returned,
ordering Fán Kuài to remain and pacify Dàidì.
When the Emperor arrived at Guǎngwǔ,
he pardoned Liú Jìng,
saying:
"I did not heed your words,
and was consequently trapped at Píngchéng;

He then enfeoffed Jìng with two thousand households as a Guānnèihóu,
named Jiànxìnhóu.
The Emperor traveled south past Qūnì.
Bān Zhì:
Qūnì County belonged to Zhōngshān State.
Zhāng Yàn said: The Rú River curves north of the city and flows west,
hence the name Qūnì;
later, Hàn Emperor Zhāng disliked its name
and changed it to Púyīn.
Dù Yòu said: Běipíng County of Zhōngshān Commandery
was Qín Qūnì County,
and later Hàn Púyīn County.
Qūnì
should both be read as written.
Wénxuǎn Gāozǔ Gōngchén Zàn Zhù says: Qū
is pronounced *qū jù* (Qūjù);
Nì
is pronounced *yù*;
this is incorrect.
Yán Zhītuī said: Common scholars read Qūnì Hóu as *qù yù*;
Piàoyáo Xiàowèi as *piāo yáo*.
Piàoyáo,
scholars have two pronunciations;
the most baseless
is Qūnì as *qù yù*.
He said: "What a magnificent county!
I have traveled throughout the world,
and have seen only Luòyáng and this one."
He then re-enfeoffed Chén Píng as Qūnì Hóu,
granting him the entire revenue.
Píng accompanied the Emperor on campaigns,
and for all six of his extraordinary strategies,
his fiefdom was increased.
3 Twelfth month,
the Emperor returned,

Zhào Wáng Áo (趙王敖) treated him with extreme deference, observing the etiquette due to a son-in-law;

which is why he observed the etiquette due to a son-in-law.
Shīgǔ (師古) said: "Jījù (箕倨) refers to,
stretching out both legs,
the posture resembling a winnowing basket (jī)."
The Qūlǐ (曲禮) says: "Do not sit in a jī (箕) posture."
Kǒng Yǐngdá (孔穎達) said: "Jī (箕),
means to stretch out both feet,
its shape resembling the tongue of a winnowing basket."
Guàn (貫),
is a surname;
descended from Yuánbó Guàn (原伯貫).
"Our King,
is a weak king!"
Then he persuaded the King, saying:

and the capable ones are establishing themselves first.

Zhāng Áo (張敖) bit his finger until it bled,
saying:
Shīgǔ (師古) said: "Biting one's finger until it bleeds,
is to show utmost sincerity and make a vow,
pledging not to betray Hàn."
Wéi (為),
pronounced Yúwěi (于偽).
"How mistaken your words are!
Our ancestors lost their state,
but thanks to the Emperor, we recovered it.
The matter of Zhāng Ěr's (張耳) state being lost can be seen in Volume 9, Year 1,
and the matter of its recovery in Volume 10, Year 3.
Every tiny bit of it was due to the Emperor's power.
Há (豪) refers to hair that grows fine and sharp in autumn.
Qiūháo (秋豪),
means something extremely subtle or minute."
Guàn Gāo (貫高), Zhào Wǔ (趙午), and others all said to each other:
"It is we who are wrong.
Our King is a gentleman,
he will not betray kindness;
and moreover, we, by our principles, cannot be humiliated.
Now the Emperor insults our King,
so we wish to kill him.
Why would we defile the King?
If the deed succeeds, it will benefit the King;
if it fails, we alone will bear the consequences."
Meaning: they alone would bear the crime of assassinating the Emperor.
4 The Xiōngnú (匈奴) attacked Dài.
Dài Wáng Xǐ (代王喜) abandoned his state and returned by himself.
Xǐ (喜),

Xǐ (喜) was established as King of Dài (代) in the Dài (代) region,
the former state of Hán Wáng Xìn (韓王信).

Héyáng Xiàn (郃陽縣) belonged to Zuǒfēngyì (左馮翊),

"on the south bank of Hé"

Hé (郃),
pronounced as hé (合).

Rúyì (如意),

5 Spring,
second month,
the Emperor arrived at Cháng'ān.
Xiāo Hé (蕭何) had been building the Wèiyāng Gōng (未央宮).
Wèiyāng Gōng (未央宮) was in the southwestern corner of Cháng'ān (長安) city,
with a circumference of twenty-eight lǐ.
Yuánhé Zhì (元和志) says: "Its eastern side is one lǐ from Chánglè Gōng (長樂宮),
separated by the military arsenal."
Kuòdìzhì (括地志): Wèiyāng Gōng (未央宮),
is ten lǐ northwest of Cháng'ān Xiàn (長安縣) in Yōngzhōu (雍州), within the old city of Cháng'ān (長安).
[The Emperor] was very angry,
and said to Hé (何):
"The world is in turmoil,
having suffered hardships for several years,
and success or failure is still uncertain.
Why are you building palaces to such an excessive degree!"
Hé (何) replied:
"The world is still unsettled,
so this is an opportune time to complete the palaces.
Moreover, the Son of Heaven considers the four seas his home;
without grandeur and splendor, he cannot command grave authority,
and furthermore, this will prevent future generations from having to improve upon it."
The Emperor was pleased.
Chén Guāng (臣光) says: "A king takes benevolence and righteousness as his splendor,
and morality as his authority.
I have never heard of him subduing the world with palaces.
When the world is unsettled,
one should exercise self-restraint and economize to meet the urgent needs of the people;
yet to prioritize palaces instead,
how can this be called knowing what is important!
In the past, Yǔ (禹) had humble palaces, while Jié (桀) built extravagant ones.
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said: 'Yǔ (禹) had humble palaces but exerted all his effort on irrigation ditches.'
'Jié (桀) built magnificent palaces and jade terraces, exhausting the wealth of the common people.'
To personally practice frugality as an example to one's descendants,
even then its later consequences might still lead to extravagance and decadence,
how much more so if one sets an example of extravagance!
Yet to say,
'prevent future generations from having to improve upon it,'
is it not absurd!
As for Xiàowǔ (孝武),
he eventually exhausted the empire with palaces.
It may not be unrelated to Zuǎ Hóu (酇侯) initiating it!"
6 The Emperor moved the capital from Lìyáng (櫟陽) to Cháng'ān.
Although he had earlier decided to establish the capital in Guānzhōng (關中) to the west, based on the advice of Lóu Jìng (婁敬) and Zhāng Liáng (張良),
the capital city was not yet completed;
thus, he still resided in Lìyáng (櫟陽).
Now that Wèiyāng Gōng (未央宮) was complete,
he formally moved the capital from Lìyáng (櫟陽) to Cháng'ān.
7 For the first time, the office of Zōngzhèng (宗正) was established,
to manage the imperial clan.
Bān Biǎo (班表) says: "Zōngzhèng (宗正),
a Qín (秦) official post,
managed relatives;
in the first year of Yuánshǐ (元始) of Píng Dì (平帝),
its name was changed to Zōngbó (宗伯)."
8 Summer,
fourth month,
the Emperor traveled to Luòyáng.

The Hànlín Academician, Cháosàn Dàfū (朝散大夫), Right Grand Master Remonstrant, Compiler of Edicts, concurrently Imperial Lecturer, concurrently Supervisor of Wànshòu Guān (萬壽觀) affairs, concurrently Acting Head of the Jíxián Yuàn (集賢院), Supreme Protector of the Army, Founding Marquis of Hénèi Jùn (河內郡) with an estate of one thousand three hundred households, bestowed with a purple-gold fish bag, your servant

Hòu Xué Tiān Tái
Under Tàizǔ Gāohuángdì (太祖高皇帝).
1 Winter,
the Emperor

Zhēndìng Guó (真定國) was established.
Yuán (垣),
pronounced yuán (轅).

Bǎirén Xiàn (柏人縣) belonged to Zhào Guó (趙國).

Bǎirén (柏人) was renamed Yáoshān (堯山).
[They] wished to ambush the Emperor.

Yāo (要),

and he asked:

Twelfth month,

third month,

Qǐ

4 In autumn,
ninth month,

The King of Huáinán, the King of Liáng, the King of Zhào, and the King of Chǔ all accompanied him.
5 Mòdú Chányú of the Xiōngnú repeatedly troubled the northern frontier.
The Emperor was worried about this and
asked Liú Jìng.
Liú Jìng said:
"The empire has just been settled,
and the soldiers are exhausted from warfare;
it is not yet possible to subdue them by force.
Mòdú killed his father and usurped the throne,
and took his stepmother as his wife,
relying on strength for his authority;
it is not yet possible to persuade him with benevolence (rén) and righteousness (yì).
Only through a long-term strategy can
his descendants become our vassals;
however, I fear Your Majesty cannot implement it."
The Emperor said:
"What should be done?"
He replied:
"If Your Majesty can sincerely give your eldest princess (zhǎnggōngzhǔ) to him in marriage,
and provide lavish tributes,
he will certainly be pleased
and make her his Yānzhī.
If she bears a son,
he will certainly become the Crown Prince.
Each year, Your Majesty can send gifts of what the Hàn has in abundance and what they lack,
and
also dispatch eloquent persuaders to subtly instruct them in rites and etiquette.
Fēng is equivalent to fěng.
He will be a solid son-in-law;
when he dies,
his grandson will become the Chányú.
Has anyone ever heard of a maternal grandson daring to challenge his maternal grandfather with equal rites!
In this way, war can be avoided, and they can gradually be made vassals.
If Your Majesty cannot send the eldest princess,
but instead sends a woman from the imperial clan or the inner palace falsely claiming to be a princess,
once they discover the deception,
they will not value her or hold her in high regard,
and it will be of no benefit."
The Emperor said:
"Excellent!"
and wanted to send the eldest princess.
Empress Lǚ wept day and night, saying:
"I have only the Crown Prince and one daughter.
How can I abandon her to the Xiōngnú!"
The Emperor ultimately could not send her.
1 In winter,

and sent Liú Jìng to conclude a treaty of harmonious kinship.

How contradictory are his前后之相违 (before and after)!

Jiànxìn Hóu's strategy

Qínzhōng has recently been devastated,
