he fully explained why he had acted as he did;
King Wǎn of Yān then falsely denounced others,
released Shèng's family members,
and allowed him to act as a spy for the Xiongnú.
He secretly sent Fàn Qí to Chén Xī's location,
wanting to prolong the rebellion,
and keep the fighting unresolved.
He wanted them to engage in prolonged fighting,
with the outcome remaining undecided for a long time.
When Hàn attacked Qíng Bù,
Xī often led troops and resided in Dài.
When Hàn attacked and executed Xī,
his deputy generals surrendered,
saying that Yān Wáng Lú Wǎn had sent Fàn Qí to communicate strategy with Xī.
The Emperor sent an envoy to summon Lú Wǎn,
but Wǎn claimed illness.
He then sent Pìyáng Hóu Shěn Shíqí
and Bān Zhì.
Pìyáng Xiàn belonged to Xìndū Guó.
Pì,
also pronounced bì.
The Xìng Pǔ has the surname Shěn.
Shíqí,
pronounced yì jī.
They were to investigate and question his attendants.
Wǎn grew even more fearful,
shut himself away and hid.
This means he concealed his whereabouts
and hid himself.
He said, "Of those who are not of the Liú clan but have become kings,
there are only me and Chángshā.
Last year,
in spring,
Hàn annihilated Huái'yīn;
in summer,
Péng Yuè was executed.
These were all the schemes of the Lǚ clan.
Now the Emperor is ill,
entrusting affairs to Lǚ Hòu.
Lǚ Hòu is a woman
who is determined to use these matters to execute kings of other surnames and great meritorious officials."
So he continued to claim illness and did not go,
and all his attendants fled and hid.
The conversation was quite leaked,
and Pìyáng Hóu heard of it.
He returned
and reported it fully to the Emperor,
who became even more furious.
They also captured a Xiongnú defector
who said that Zhāng Shèng had fled to Xiongnú and was serving as Yān's envoy.
Thereupon the Emperor said,
"Lú Wǎn has indeed rebelled!"
In spring,
the second month,
Fán Kuài was sent as Xiàngguó to lead troops to attack Wǎn,
and Imperial Prince Jiàn was established as Yān Wáng.
10 An edict stated:
"Nánwǔ Hóu Zhī,
also a descendant of Yuè,
is to be established as Nánhǎi Wáng."
Wén Yǐng said: In the fifth year of Gāozǔ,
Yàngjùn, Guìlín, Nánhǎi, and Chángshā were used to establish Wú Ruì as Chángshā Wáng.
Yàngjùn, Guìlín, and Nánhǎi belonged to Wèi Tuó;
Tuó had not yet surrendered,
so they were remotely taken to enfeoff Ruì.
Later, when Tuó surrendered to Hàn,
in the eleventh year,
Tuó was re-established as Nányuè Wáng.
From then on, he ruled the three commanderies,
while Ruì only obtained Chángshā and Guìyáng.
Now to enfeoff Zhī as Nánhǎi Wáng,
one commandery is again remotely taken from Tuó,
and Zhī has not yet obtained the kingship.
11 When the Emperor attacked Bù,
he was struck by a stray arrow.
On the journey,
his illness became severe.
Lǚ Hòu sent for a good physician.
The physician entered and saw him,
saying,
"The illness can be cured."
The Emperor scoffed and cursed him, saying,
"I, a commoner, took the world with a three-foot blade.
Shīgǔ said: Three-foot refers to a sword.
Zhōng,
pronounced zhú zhòng.
Jiàn,
pronounced xián biàn.
My fate is in heaven;
even Biǎn Què, what good would he be!"
Biǎn Què was a renowned physician of antiquity.
Biǎn,
pronounced bǔ biàn.
He bestowed fifty catties of gold
and dismissed him.
Lǚ Hòu asked,
"After Your Majesty's hundred years,
and Xiāo Xiàngguó has died,
who should replace him?"
The Emperor said,
"Cáo Cān can."
She asked for the next,
he said,
"Wáng Líng can;
however, he is a bit simple-minded.
Shǎo zhě,
refers to the shǎo of duōshǎo.
Shīgǔ said: Zhuàng (戇) means foolish;
in ancient times it was pronounced xià gàn,
now it is zhú hàng.
Chén Píng has more than enough wisdom,
but he is difficult to entrust with sole responsibility.
Zhōu Bó is solid and unadorned,
yet it is certainly Bó who will secure the Liú clan;
he can be made Tàiwèi."
Lǚ Hòu asked again for the next,
the Emperor said,
"After this, it is not within your knowledge either."
Shīgǔ said: Nǎi (乃) means you (汝);
implying that after this,
you too will have reached your end,
and will no longer know.
In the fourth month,
on the jiǎchén day,
the Emperor passed away in Chánglè Gōng.
He was fifty-three years old.
Kǎoyì said: The Hànshū states:
"Lǚ Hòu and Shěn Shíqí plotted to execute all the generals.
Lí Shāng met Shěn Shíqí
and persuaded him, saying: 'If this happens,
the great ministers will rebel internally,
and the generals will revolt externally.
Ruin can be awaited with folded arms.'
Shěn Shíqí went in and reported this,
and then the mourning was announced on the dīngwèi day."
According to this, although Lǚ Hòu was cruel,
how could she dare to execute all the great ministers at once?
Moreover, at that time Chén Píng was not in Xíngyáng,
and Fán Kuài was not in Dài.
This account is likely false,
and is not accepted here.
On the dīngwèi day,
mourning was announced,
and a great amnesty was granted to the world.
12 Lú Wǎn, with several thousand people, stayed below the frontier pass, watching and waiting,
hoping the Emperor's illness would improve,
so he could enter and apologize himself.
Shīgǔ said: He hoped the Emperor's illness would improve, and he himself would enter to apologize, considering it his good fortune.
He then fled into Xiongnú territory.
13 In the fifth month,
on the bǐngyín day,
Gāo Dì was buried at Cháng Líng.
Bān Zhì: Chánglíng Xiàn was established by Gāo Dì and belonged to Zuǒ Fēngyì.
Huángfǔ Mì said: Cháng Líng is north of the Wèi Shuǐ,
thirty-five lǐ from Cháng'ān Chéng.
Chén Zàn said: It is forty lǐ north of Cháng'ān.
Kuòdì Zhì: It is thirty lǐ east of Xiányáng Xiàn in Yōngzhōu.
Hàn Guān Yí says: In ancient times, there were no tomb sacrifices;
Qín Shǐhuáng built a sleeping chamber beside his tomb,
and Hàn followed this custom without changing it.

For all imperial mausoleums and sleeping chambers, food was offered on the last day and first day of the month, during the twenty-four solar terms, the three hottest periods (Sānfú), during the Shè and Lù festivals, and in the four seasons.
The palace women near the imperial tombs would,
according to the drum and water clock, arrange quilts and pillows,
prepare washing water,
and lay out toiletries.
Towns were built next to the mausoleums,
and officials such as Lìng, Céng, and Wèi were appointed to guard them.
Initially,
Gāozǔ did not cultivate literary learning,
but his nature was clear-sighted and intelligent.
He was good at strategy
and able to listen.
From his gatekeepers to his border guards,
he treated them as old acquaintances.
At first, he complied with the people's will by establishing the three-chapter covenant.
See Volume 9, Year 1.
He ordered Xiāo Hé to organize the statutes and ordinances.
After the emperor had defeated Xiàng Yǔ,
the four barbarian tribes were not yet submissive,
and military campaigns had not yet ceased.
The three-chapter law
was insufficient to guard against treachery.
Xiāo Hé collected and selected from Qín's laws,
taking those suitable for the time,
and composed the Nine Chapters of Statutes.
The emperor ordered Zhāng Liáng and Hán Xìn to arrange military treatises,
totaling one hundred and eighty-two schools;
he then abridged and selected the essential and practical ones,
settling on thirty-five schools.
The Lǚ clan, when in power, illicitly seized these.
Rú Chún said: "Zhāng (章)
refers to the chapter-methods of reckoning numbers.
Chéng (程)
refers to the standard measures of weights, balances, rulers, dou, and hu."
Shīgǔ said: "Chéng (程)
means regulations or standards."
See Upper Volume, Year 6 and Year 7.
Red-written documents and iron tallies,
golden caskets and stone chambers,
were used to store them in the ancestral temple.
"Carving tallies and making oaths"
means carving tallies to enfeoff meritorious officials,
slaying a white horse, and making a "mountain-river, sash-girdle" alliance with them.
"Red-written documents and iron tallies"
means making tallies of iron
and writing on them in red.
Rú Chún said: "Jīnkuì (金匱)
is like jīnténg (金縢)."
Shīgǔ said: "Making caskets of gold
and chambers of stone,
sealing them heavily,
signifies extreme caution.
It probably refers to writing the words of oaths on iron tallies with red ink,
enclosing them in golden caskets and stone chambers, and storing them in the ancestral temple."
"Guīmó (規摹)" means grand and far-reaching.
Dèng Zhǎn said: "It's like an artist outlining an object."
Wéi Zhāo said: "A guī (規) is an instrument for drawing perfect circles.
Mú (摹)
is like when a painter hasn't applied the brush yet,
but has already outlined it with red clay."
Shīgǔ said: "Using guīmó (規摹) as a metaphor
refers to establishing systems and models."
"Jǐ (給)" means sufficient.
"Rì bù xiá jǐ (日不暇給)"
means that there were too many affairs,
and one was constantly busy.
I believe "rì bù xiá jǐ"
probably means that after Xiàng Yǔ had been pacified,
the feudal lords rebelled again.
14 On the day Jǐsì,
the Crown Prince ascended the imperial throne,
honoring the Empress as Empress Dowager.
15 Previously,
when Emperor Gāo was gravely ill,
someone slandered Fán Kuài, saying:
"He is allied with the Lǚ clan.
If the emperor passes away even one day from now,
he intends to use troops to execute Zhào Wáng Rúyì and his kin."
The emperor was greatly enraged.
Following Chén Píng's counsel,
he summoned Jiànghóu Zhōu Bó to receive the edict by his bedside,
saying:
"Chén Píng, quickly ride an express post-horse,
carrying Bó, to replace Kuài as commander!
When Píng arrives at the army,
immediately cut off Kuài's head!"
The two, having received the edict,
rode express post-horses.
Before they reached the army,
Rú Chún said: "Four horses
with high legs constitute a 'zhìchuán' (置傳), while those with medium legs constitute a 'chíchuán' (馳傳).
According to the law,
all those authorized to use a 'chuán' (post-horse) or dispatch a 'zhìchuán'
must carry a five-inch ruler-length wooden 'chuánxìn' (信, tally),
sealed with the imperial censor's seal.
When using a 'chuán,'
three seals are applied.
Cān (參)
means three.
If there is a scheduled meeting,
the two ends are sealed repeatedly,
each end with two seals,
for a total of four seals."
Chuán (傳)
is pronounced zhu-liàn.
"Fán Kuài
is an old acquaintance of the emperor,
and has rendered great service.
Moreover, he is the husband of Empress Lǚ's younger sister, Lǚ Xū.
Lǚ Xū
is pronounced xū.
Shīgǔ said: 'Xíngjì' (行計)
means to consider and plan while traveling on the road.
The emperor, out of anger, wanted to execute him,
but might later regret it.
It would be better to imprison him and bring him before the emperor
to be executed by the emperor himself."
Before reaching the army,
they erected an altar
and summoned Fán Kuài with a tally.
Kuài received the edict,
immediately bound his hands behind his back.
Shīgǔ said: "Binding both hands behind the back."
And ordered Jiànghóu Bó to replace him as commander,
leading the troops to pacify the rebellious county of Yān.
Chén Píng was on his way
when he heard of the emperor's demise.
Shīgǔ said: "He heard of Emperor Gāo's demise on the road,
before reaching the capital."
Thereupon, he rode an express post-horse
and rushed ahead first.
He met an envoy
who delivered an edict for Píng and Guàn Yīng to garrison Xíngyáng.
Píng received the edict,
then immediately rode back to the palace,
weeping with extraordinary sorrow.
Consequently, he firmly requested to be allowed to stay and guard the palace interior.
He requested to be allowed to stay and guard the forbidden palace.
Fù (復)
is pronounced fú-yòu;
the same applies below.
Bān Biǎo: "Lángzhōnglìng
was a Qín official,
in charge of the palace gates and side entrances.
In the first year of Emperor Wǔ's Tàichū era,
it was renamed Guānglùxūn."
Thereafter, Lǚ Xū's slander could not take effect.
When Fán Kuài arrived,
he was pardoned
and his rank and fief were restored.
16 The Empress Dowager ordered Qī Fūrén to be imprisoned in the Yǒngxiàng (Eternal Lane),
her head shaved and neck collared,
dressed in ochre clothes,
and made to pound grain.
Ochre clothes
were prison garments,
dyed with red earth.
Zhě (赭)
is pronounced zhǐ-yě.
Envoys were sent three times,
and Zhào Xiàng Zhōu Chāng told the envoy:
"Emperor Gāo entrusted Zhào Wáng to your servant.
The king is young.
I secretly hear that the Empress Dowager resents Qī Fūrén
and wishes to summon Zhào Wáng and execute them together.
Your servant dares not send the king.
The king is also ill,
and cannot comply with the edict."
The Empress Dowager was angry,
and first sent someone to summon Chāng.
When Chāng arrived in Cháng'ān,
she then sent someone to summon Zhào Wáng again.
When the king was coming,
but had not yet arrived,
the emperor, knowing the Empress Dowager's anger,
personally went to Bàshàng to meet Zhào Wáng,
and brought him into the palace,
personally keeping him by his side for daily life and meals.
The Empress Dowager wanted to kill him,
but could not find an opportunity.
Emperor Xiàohuì
Xún Yuè said: "The taboo character for 'Yíng' (盈)
is 'Mǎn' (滿)."
Shīgǔ said: "Subordinates using 'Mǎn'
to replace 'Yíng'
indicates that the emperor's taboo name was Yíng.
Other instances are similar."
He was Emperor Gāo's legitimate eldest son.
Yīng Shào said: "According to the Rites' posthumous title rules: 'Gentle in character and compassionate to the people' is called Huì (惠)."
Shīgǔ said: "A filial son is good at carrying on the will of others.
Therefore, the posthumous titles of the Hàn dynasty,
from Emperor Huì onwards, all include 'Xiào' (孝)."
1 In winter,
the twelfth month,
the Emperor rose early to hunt.
King Zhào (趙) was
young
and could not rise early.
The Grand Empress Dowager sent someone to give him poisonous wine to drink.
Guǎngzhì (廣志) says: The zhèn (鴆) bird is as large as an owl,
its feathers are purple and green,
and it is poisonous.
Its neck is seven or eight cùn (寸) long,
and it eats vipers.
The male is named Yùnrì (運日),
and the female is named Yīnxié (陰諧).
If its feathers pass through food or drink, it will kill people.
Fàn Chéngdà (范成大) said: The zhèn (鴆)
is heard to exist in Cháotiānpù (朝天鋪) in Yōngzhōu (邕州) and in the deep mountains.
Its form is like a slightly larger crow,
with a black body
and red eyes,
and its sound is like a羯鼓 (jiégǔ) drum.
It only eats venomous snakes,
and when it encounters a snake, it calls out with a "bāng bāng" sound.
If a snake enters a rock cave,
it performs ritual steps (Yǔbù, 禹步) outside the cave.
After a while,
the rock shatters,
and it pecks and swallows the snake.
Where there are zhèn (鴆) in the mountains,
grass and trees do not grow.
It sheds its feathers between autumn and winter.
In former times, people used silver claws to pick them up
and placed them in silver bottles.
Otherwise, their hands would rot and fall off.
If zhèn (鴆) droppings touched a person, they would die instantly.
If it perched on a rock,
the rock would also crack.
This bird is extremely vicious and poisonous.
What is called dàn (酖)
is zhènjiǔ (鴆酒), or zhèn (鴆) wine.
Lù Diàn (陸佃) in Píyǎ (埤雅) says: The zhèn (鴆)
resembles an eagle but is purple,
with a black beak,
seven or eight cùn (寸) long,
and appears bronze-colored.
It eats snakes; as soon as a snake enters its mouth, it rots.
Its droppings and urine, if they touch a rock,
will also cause the rock to rot.
Its feathers and quills are poisonous.
If steeped in wine,
drinking it will kill people.
Only rhinoceros horn can neutralize it,
hence wherever there is zhèn (鴆), there must be rhinoceros.
Yǐn (飲),
is pronounced "yú jìn" (於禁).
Xú Guǎng (徐廣) says: lí (犂)
is like bǐ (比);
bǐ (比) means until dawn.
All who say lí míng (犂明)
refer to the time just before dawn.
Lǚ Jìng (呂靜) says: lí (犂)
means "knot" or "tie";
it is pronounced "lì xī" (力奚).
Chéng Dàchāng (程大昌) says: Xú's (徐) explanation is incorrect.
Lí (犂) and Lí (黎)
were interchangeable ancient characters.
Lí (黎)
means black;
black and light intermingle,
it is the juncture of wanting to be dawn but not yet dawn,
which is also called mèishuǎng (昧爽).
Mèi (昧)
is dark;
shuǎng (爽)
is bright;
it also means a mix of light and dark.
Chímíng (遲明)
means not yet quite dawn.
Jué míng (厥明) and zhímíng (質明)
mean it is already dawn.
Kāng (康) says it is pronounced "lì zhuī" (力追).
It is unknown what this is based on.
King Zhào (趙) was already dead.
The Grand Empress Dowager then cut off Madame Qī's (戚夫人) hands and feet,
gouged out her eyes,
scorched her ears,
gave her a mute-inducing potion to drink,
and made her live in the latrine,
naming her
"human swine" (rénzhī, 人彘).
After several days,
she summoned the Emperor to observe the "human swine."
When the Emperor saw her
and learned she was Madame Qī (戚夫人),
he wept bitterly,
then fell ill,
and for over a year he could not recover.
He sent someone to appeal to the Grand Empress Dowager, saying:
"This is not something a human being should do.
As your son, I
cannot rule the world."
Shīgǔ (師古) says: He meant for the Grand Empress Dowager to manage affairs,
while he himself would be like a Crown Prince.
I believe Emperor Huì's (惠) intention
was to say that as the Grand Empress Dowager's son,
he could not tolerate his father's favored concubine,
and therefore could not ultimately rule the world.
Zhì (治),
is pronounced "zhí zhī" (直之).
He ceased to attend to government.
Minister Guāng (光) says: For a son,
if parents err, one should admonish them.
If they do not listen to the admonition,
one should weep aloud and follow them.
This is recorded in Qūlǐ (曲禮).
Háo (號),
is pronounced "hù gāo" (戶高).
As the ruler of All Under Heaven,
he could not bear his mother's cruelty,
and so abandoned the state without concern,
indulging in wine and women to harm his life!
Someone like Emperor Huì (惠)
may be said to be devoted to minor benevolence but ignorant of great righteousness.
2 Liú Yǒu (劉友), King of Huáiyáng (淮陽), was transferred to become King of Zhào (趙).
In the eleventh year of Gāozǔ (高祖),
Yǒu (友) was enfeoffed in Huáiyáng (淮陽).
3 In spring,
the first month,
construction began on the northwestern part of Cháng'ān (長安) city.
Although Xiāo Hé (蕭何) built palaces for the Han capital Cháng'ān (長安),
there was no time to build the city walls.
The Emperor began constructing them,
and it was completed in the fifth year,
hence the record of its beginning.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) says: The Cháng'ān (長安) city built by Emperor Huì (惠)
is now in the northwestern garden of Dàxīngchéng (大興城).
1 In winter,
the tenth month,
Qí Dàohuìwáng (齊悼惠王) came to court.
He was Féi (肥), Gāozǔ's (高祖) eldest illegitimate son.
Cháo (朝),
is pronounced "zhí yáo" (直遙).
The Emperor, considering the King of Qí (齊)
his elder brother,
seated him in the place of honor.
This was likely arranged according to brotherly seniority within the palace,
not according to the etiquette for ruler and minister at the outer court.
Zuò (坐),
is pronounced "cú wò" (徂臥).
Poisonous wine was poured and placed before him,
as a toast to the King of Qí (齊).
When the King of Qí (齊) rose,
the Emperor also rose to take his cup.
The Grand Empress Dowager, afraid,
rose herself and overturned the Emperor's cup.
The King of Qí (齊) found this strange,
and consequently dared not drink,
feigning drunkenness and leaving.
When he inquired and learned it was poisonous wine,
he was greatly frightened.
The Household Minister (Nèishǐ, 內史) of Qí (齊), Shì (士)
advised the King.
Shīgǔ (師古) says: Nèishǐ (內史)
is an official in a kingdom;
Shì (士)
is his given name.
Bān (班) states: Kingdoms have Nèishǐ (內史)
who manage the people.
The Grand Empress Dowager was pleased
and then dismissed the King of Qí (齊) to return home.
2 In spring,
the first month,
on the guǐyǒu (癸酉) day,
two dragons were seen in a commoner's well in Lánlíng (蘭陵).
Bān (班) states: Lánlíng (蘭陵) county belonged to Dōnghǎi (東海) commandery.
Shīgǔ (師古) says: Jiārén (家人)
refers to a commoner's household.
Wǔhángzhì (五行志) says: Wēnlíng (溫陵) household.
Jiàn (見),
is pronounced "xián biàn" (賢遍).
3 An earthquake occurred in Lǒngxī (隴西).
4 In summer,
there was a drought.
5 Hépánghóu Zhòng (郃陽侯仲) died.
Zhòng (仲)
was Liú Xǐ (劉喜), King of Dài (代);
his enfeoffment as Hépáng (郃陽) is mentioned in volume 7, Gāozǔ (高祖) era.
6. Xiāo Hé (蕭何), the Marquis Wénzhōng (文終) of Zàn (酇), fell ill.
According to the posthumous naming system: "One who has a beginning and an end is called zhōng (終)."
Méng (蒙) said: "One who achieves an excellent reputation is called zhōng (終)."
(Emperor Gāo Dì 漢高帝) then asked:
"If you were to pass away in a hundred years,
who could replace you?"
(Xiāo Hé) replied:
"No one understands a minister better than the ruler."
The Emperor said:
"What about Cáo Cān (曹參)?"
Xiāo Hé bowed his head (in assent) and said:
"Your Majesty has found him!
I can die without regret!"
In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the xīnwèi (辛未) day,
Xiāo Hé passed away.
Xiāo Hé, when acquiring fields and residences,
always chose poor and remote places.
For his home,
he did not build high walls.
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: "Pì (僻) means
'hidden'."
"Yuán (垣) means
'wall'."
"Zhì (治) is pronounced zhí zhī (直之) fanqie."
(Xiāo Hé said:) "If future generations are worthy,
they will emulate my frugality;
if unworthy,
they will not be plundered by powerful families."
On the guǐsì (癸巳) day,
Cáo Cān (曹參) was appointed Chancellor of State (xiàngguó 相國).
When Cān (參) heard of Xiāo Hé's (蕭何) death,
he told his attendants:
"Hurry and prepare for the journey!"
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: "Shèrén (舍人) is
like saying 'family members'."
"One interpretation is: 'private officials who manage household affairs'."
"I believe that in the Warring States period,
Sū Qín (蘇秦) had his shèrén (舍人) provide funds and escort Zhāng Yí (張儀) into Qín (秦),
and Lǐ Sī (李斯) was a shèrén (舍人) for Lǚ Bùwéi (呂不韋).
It is permissible to call them 'private officials',
but to confine it to 'managing household affairs' is too restrictive."
"Qù (趣) is
pronounced cù (促),
meaning 'swiftly'."
"Zhì xíng (治行) means
'to prepare one's travel baggage'."
"Jū wú hé (居無何),
jū wú hé (居無何),
means 'after a short while'."
"Xiāng (相) is
pronounced xī liàng (息亮) fanqie;
the same below."
Initially,
when Cān (參) was of humble status,
he was on good terms with Xiāo Hé (蕭何);
but after they became generals and chancellors,
a rift developed.
However, when Hé (何) was about to die,
the only worthy person he recommended was Cān (參).
"The words 'recommended as worthy' refer to that."
(Cáo Cān) made no changes in the administration.
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: "Jǔ (舉) means
'all';
meaning 'there were no changes in any matters'."
"Gèng (更) is
pronounced gōng héng (工衡) fanqie."
When selecting county and state officials who were slow-witted in their speech and writing,
"Mù (木) means
'simple and unadorned'."
"Nà (訥) means
'stammering in speech'."
(and) summoned and appointed them as Secretaries to the Chancellor (chéngxiàng shǐ 丞相史);
"The Hàn (漢) system stipulated: among the Chancellor's subordinates,
below the Chief Secretary (zhǎngshǐ 長史) were clerks (yuánshǐ 掾史), record keepers (lìngshǐ 令史), etc."
he would immediately dismiss them.
Day and night, he drank pure wine.
"Chì (斥) means
'to reject', 'to expel'."
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: "Chúnjiǔ (醇酒) means 'undiluted wine',
referring to strong wine."
"Qù (去) is
pronounced qiāng lǚ (羌呂) fanqie."
"Meaning he did not attend to the Chancellor's affairs."
Whenever his subordinates tried to report on official matters, Cān (參) would offer them pure wine;
if they intended to say something,
he would offer them more to drink,
and they would leave after becoming drunk,
never getting a chance to speak,
this became his routine.
"Kāi (開) means
'to initiate';
referring to initiating reports or petitions."
"Yǐwéi cháng (以為常) means
'offering them wine became his routine'."
"Yǐn (飲) is
pronounced yú jìn (於禁) fanqie."
"Fù (復) is
pronounced fú yòu (扶又) fanqie."
(Cáo Cān) would specially conceal and cover up (such reports);
so there was nothing to do in the Chancellor's office.
Cān's (參) son, Zhú (窋), was a Grandee of the Middle (zhōng dàfū 中大夫).
The Emperor was puzzled that the Chancellor of State (xiàngguó 相國) did not attend to affairs,
thinking,
"Could it be that he looks down on me for being young?"
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: "Meaning 'could it be because he takes me for being young?'"
"Zhì (治) is
pronounced zhí zhī (直之) fanqie."
"Yǔ (與) is
pronounced yú (歟)."
(The Emperor) privately asked Cān (參) through his son.
Cān (參) was enraged,
flogged Zhú (窋) two hundred times,
and said:
"Hurry up and attend to the Emperor!
Affairs of state are not for you to speak of!"
When it was time for court,
the Emperor reproached Cān (參) saying:
"Just now I sent someone to remonstrate with you."
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: "Nǎizhě (乃者) is
like saying nǎngzhě (曩者) 'formerly'."
"Cháo (朝) is
pronounced zhí yáo (直遙) fanqie."
"(Cáo Cān replied:) "Your Majesty, please consider, how does your sagely martial prowess compare to that of Emperor Gāo Dì (高帝)?"
The Emperor said:
"How dare I even hope to compare to the late Emperor!"
(Cān) then said:
"Your Majesty, how do you view my abilities? Am I more capable than Xiāo Hé (蕭何)?"
The Emperor said:
"You seem not to be as good."
Cān (參) said:
"Your Majesty speaks correctly.
Emperor Gāo Dì (高帝) and Xiāo Hé (蕭何) pacified the realm,
and the laws and decrees are already clear.
Now, Your Majesty rules by merely folding your hands,
and I, Cān (參), and others perform our duties,
adhering to them without deviation.
Is this not acceptable!"
The Emperor said:
"Excellent!"
Cān (參) served as Chancellor of State (xiàngguó 相國)
for three years, entering and leaving office.
The common people sang of him, saying:
"Xiāo Hé (蕭何) established the laws,
clear and uniform like a single stroke.
"Jiàoruò (較若) is
like saying 'jiàorán (較然)' today."
"Huàyī (畫一) means
'orderly and uniform'."
(Cáo Cān) upheld them without deviation;
(he) embodied purity and tranquility.
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: "Zài (載) is
like saying 'chéng (乘)' (to ride, to carry)."
1. In spring,
146,000 men and women from within 600 lǐ (里) of Cháng'ān (長安) were conscripted to build the city of Cháng'ān (長安).
They were dismissed after thirty days.
2 A woman from the imperial clan was made a princess
and married to Mòdú Chányú of the Xiōngnú.
At this time,
Mòdú was strong.
He wrote a letter
and sent an envoy to present it to Gāohòu,
using extremely disrespectful and crude language.
Gāohòu was furious.
She summoned her generals, chancellors, and high ministers
to discuss beheading the envoy
and dispatching troops to attack him.
Fán Kuài said:
"I wish I could have a hundred thousand men to march unimpeded through Xiōngnú territory!"
Zhōnglángjiàng Jì Bù said:
"Kuài should be executed!
The Hàn dynasty has the Wǔguān, Zuǒ, and Yòu Zhōngláng, three generals,
with a salary of two thousand *dàn* of grain,
who lead the *zhōngláng* (Palace Gentlemen),
and are subordinate to the Lángzhōnglìng (Prefect of Palace Gentlemen).
See Volume 7, Gāozǔ's reign.
*Kǎoyì* says: The biography of Jì Bù states:
'Previously, when Chén Xī rebelled in Dài,
the Xiōngnú besieged Gāodì at Píngchéng.'
However, the siege of Píngchéng
was due to the rebellion of Hán Wáng Xìn,
not Chén Xī's rebellion.
Kuài, as a supreme general,
was unable to lift the siege.
Now, the sounds of mourning have not yet ceased,
and the wounded are just beginning to recover,
yet Kuài wishes to stir up the world
and speaks wildly of marching unimpeded with a hundred thousand men.
This is a direct insult.
Moreover, barbarians are like birds and beasts;
their kind words are not worth rejoicing over,
and their foul words are not worth getting angry about."
Gāohòu said:
"Excellent!"
She ordered the Grand Yèzhě, Zhāng Shì, to reply to the letter.
Yèzhě was
a Qín official,
in charge of receiving guests, assisting in ceremonies, and handling affairs,
with seventy members.
The Grand Yèzhě
was probably their chief.
*Kǎoyì* says: *Shǐjì* (Annals of Emperor Wén), the table of marquises during the reign of Huì and Jǐng, and *Hànshū* (Biography of the Xiōngnú) all write
"Zé";
*Shǐjì* (Annals of Empress Lǚ) says:
"In the eighth year,
the Grand Yèzhě Zhāng Shì..."
*Hànshū* (Annals) writes
"Shì Qīng,"
while the Table of Marquises of Enzé and the Biography of Zhōu Bó all say
"Zhāng Shì";
Yán Shīgǔ notes: The Biographies of Jīng, Yān, and Wú say
"Zhāng Zé."
We follow *Shǐjì* (Annals of Empress Lǚ), *Hànshū* (Table of Marquises of Enzé), and the Biography of Zhōu Bó.
*Xùn*
is the same as *xùn*,
meaning "submissive."
Two teams of four horses each.
Mòdú again sent an envoy to apologize,
saying:
"I have never learned the rites and righteousness of the Central Kingdom.
May Your Majesty graciously forgive this."
Thereupon he offered horses,
and then a peace-and-kinship alliance was established.
3 Summer,
fifth month.
Yáo, the lord of Mǐnyuè, was established as the King of Dōnghǎi.
Yáo and Wúzhū
were both descendants of Yuè King Gōujiàn.
They followed the feudal lords in destroying Qín,
achieved great merit,
and their people were inclined to attach themselves to them,
hence he was established.
He made his capital at Dōngōu,
and was generationally known as the King of Dōngōu.
Wúzhū, King of Mǐnyuè,
was enfeoffed in Gāozǔ's fifth year,
with his capital at Yě,
which is present-day Fúzhōu Hóuguān.
The emperor also enfeoffed Yáo in Dōnghǎi.
Dōnghǎi is
Dōngōu,
which is present-day Wēnzhōu Yǒngjiā.
Yìng Shào says: Yáo was enfeoffed in Dōnghǎi,
on the coast southeast of Wú Jùn.
This is where Mǐnyuè and Dōngyuè were divided.
4 Sixth month.
Twenty thousand conscripts from among the feudal kings and marquises' household slaves were dispatched to build the city of Cháng'ān.
Construction of the northwest part of Cháng'ān city began in the first year;
this spring,
men and women from within six hundred *lǐ* of Cháng'ān were again conscripted for labor;
unwilling to trouble them again,
household slaves of kings and marquises were dispatched instead.
5 Autumn,
seventh month.
The Dūjiù storage facility suffered a fire.
Dūjiù
refers to the great *jiù*,
under the Taìpú.
6 This year,
the Jiān Dǐ of Shǔ rebelled.
Bān Zhì says:
The Jiān Dǐ Dao belonged to Shǔ Jùn's Mǐnshān,
outside the western frontier,
where the Jiāng River originates.
Also, the Table of Official Posts states: Barbarians are called a *dào*,
so that territory was inhabited by the Jiān Dǐ,
hence it is called a *dào*.
Jiān
is pronounced *qián*;
Péi Sōngzhī pronounces it *jiǎn*.
Dǐ
is pronounced *dī*.
1 Winter,
tenth month.
Empress Zhāng was established.
The empress was
the daughter of the emperor's elder sister, Princess Lǔyuán.
The Grand Empress Dowager wished for a strong marital alliance,
hence she was matched with the emperor.
The empress
was Zhāng Áo's daughter.
Princess Lǔyuán married Áo and gave birth to the empress.
Due to the later mention of "strong marital alliance,"
it is directly written as "daughter of the emperor's elder sister, Princess Lǔyuán";
this is to record the change in human relations
and also to show how external relatives solidified their favor.
*Zhòng*
is pronounced *chóng*.
2 Spring,
first month.
People exemplary in filial piety (*xiào*), fraternal duty (*dì*), and diligence in farming (*lìtián*) were nominated,
and their personal obligations were remitted.
Filial piety means serving one's parents well;
fraternal duty means serving one's elder brothers well;
diligence in farming means
exhausting one's efforts in agricultural work.
Filial piety and fraternal duty are the greatest of human relations;
diligence in farming is the foundation of human life;
therefore, commanderies and kingdoms were ordered to nominate such people.
Remitting their personal obligations
was to encourage and inspire the whole empire.
*Dì*
is pronounced *tì*.
*Fù*
is pronounced *fù*.
3 Third month,
*jiǎzǐ* day.
The emperor was capped,
and a general amnesty was granted to the empire.
The emperor ascended the throne at the age of seventeen,
and only now was capped for the first time.
Kǒng Yǐngdá says: According to a brief explanation: The Duke of Zhōu told King Chéng that in ancient times, people wore *mào* and *jùlǐng*.
The note says: "ancient people" refers to the time of the Three Sovereigns, when *mào* covered the head and *jùlǐng* wrapped around the neck.
By the time of the Yellow Emperor, there were *miǎn* (ceremonial caps).
The *Shìběn* says the Yellow Emperor invented cooked food and the *zhānmiǎn* (felt cap),
meaning *miǎn* originated with the Yellow Emperor.
However, before the Yellow Emperor,
crowns were made of feathers and hides;
after the Yellow Emperor,
cloth and silk were used.
As for the age for capping,
emperors and feudal lords were capped at twelve.
Therefore, *Zuǒzhuàn* (Duke Xiāng, ninth year) says: In ancient times, a ruler begot a son at fifteen;
to beget a son after capping
was according to ritual.
For scholars,
capping was at twenty.
In ancient times, the capping ceremony was held in the ancestral temple.
First, a black cloth cap was added;
next, a deerskin cap was added;
third, a sparrow-cap was added,
which is called
"three additions make it increasingly esteemed,
each addition representing an achievement."
Feudal lords had four additions, which included the dark cap;
thus *Dàdàilǐ* says
"a duke has four additions to his cap."
Since feudal lords had four additions,
the Son of Heaven would have five additions,
which included the *gǔnmiǎn* (emperor's ceremonial cap).
Zhèng Qiáo says: The Hàn dynasty changed the emperor's capping ceremony to "adding the prime attire";
first, a black cloth *jìnxián* cap was added;
next, a sparrow cap;
next, a martial cap;
next, a "reaching heaven" cap;
after capping,
all would pay respects at the ancestral temple of Gāozǔ according to ritual.
4. Abolished laws and decrees that hampered officials and common people.
The law against possessing books was abolished.
Yìng Shào said: "Jiá" (挾)
means to hide.
Zhāng Yàn said: According to Qín laws,
those who hid books were exterminated with their families.
Now it was finally abolished.
5. The Emperor went to pay respects to the Empress Dowager at Chánglè Gōng and also went there frequently in between,
and the frequent imperial clearances annoyed the people.
Shīgǔ said: "Jiān wǎng" (間往) means to visit occasionally, not for a grand audience.
When the Son of Heaven went in or out, a clearance was announced,
stopping pedestrians;
frequent clearances,
therefore, made people feel annoyed.
Zhèng Shì's commentary on the Zhōu Lǐ says: When the state had affairs,
and the King was to go out,
travel was forbidden,
just like the imperial guards filling the streets for a clearance nowadays.
Jiǎ Gōngyàn's commentary says: According to Hàn etiquette: when the imperial carriage made a procession,
guards were sent to fill and block the streets and alleys,
to guard against emergencies.
pronounced "bì jí" (壁吉).
The Military Arsenal was located between Chánglè and Wèiyāng,
so a covered walkway was built starting from the south of the Arsenal.
"This was the path where Gāodì's (高帝) ceremonial robes and crowns were taken out for monthly processions,"
Fú Qián said: The ceremonial robes and crowns from Gāo Miào (高廟) were taken
and paraded to various temples on the first day of the month,
and then returned.
Yìng Shào said: On the first day of the month,
Gāodì's ceremonial robes and crowns were taken out,
prepared with imperial equipage,
and called "parading the robes and crowns."
Rú Chún said: Gāozǔ's (高祖) robes and crowns were stored in the imperial sleeping quarters,
and taken out for a procession every three months.
The path was directly beneath the covered walkway now being built,
hence the saying
"traveling on the path of the imperial ancestral temple."
Jìn Zhuó said: According to the Huáng Tú: Gāo Miào was on the east of Cháng'ān city gate street,
and the sleeping quarters were north of Guì Gōng (桂宮);
Fú's statement that the robes and crowns were stored in the temple,
and Rú's statement that they were in the palace,
are both incorrect.
Shīgǔ said: The explanations of all these scholars are not satisfactory.
It refers to the robes and crowns being brought out from Gāodì's mausoleum and sleeping quarters,
and paraded to Gāo Miào,
once a month,
as was the Hàn system.
Later scholars did not understand its meaning,
saying that it was at the time of the moon's emergence,
a night procession of robes and crowns,
all of which is wrong.
The Emperor said in alarm:
"Quickly demolish it!"
Tōng (通) said:
"A ruler has no missteps;
now it has been built,
and the common people all know about it.
I wish Your Majesty would establish a Yuán Miào (原廟) north of the Wèi River,
Shīgǔ said: Yuán (原) means 'repetition' or 'addition';
a temple already existed,
and now another is being built,
hence it is called 'repetition.'
and parade to it.
This would expand the ancestral temples,
and is the essence of great filial piety."
Thereupon, the Emperor ordered the relevant authorities to establish a Yuán Miào.
Zhèng Shì said: The word "miào" (廟) refers to "mào" (貌, appearance);
the spirits of the deceased cannot be seen,
but based on their dwellings during life,
palaces and chambers are built to resemble them.
Commentary on the Xiàojīng: Zōng (宗) means 'honored.'
Miào (廟) means 'appearance.'
Your servant Guāng (光) says: Mistakes
are inevitable for humans;
only sages and worthies can recognize and correct them.
The sage kings of antiquity,
fearing that they would have faults and not realize them,
therefore set up the 'tree for criticism' and installed the 'drum for daring remonstrance';
The Hòu Hànshū says: Yáo (堯) set up the drum for daring remonstrance.
Jiǎ Yì said: The rulers of the Three Dynasties
had the banner for advancing goodness,
the tree for criticism,
and the drum for daring remonstrance.
This is why Zhòng Huǐ (仲虺) praised Chéng Tāng (成湯) saying:
"He does not begrudge correcting his mistakes."
Fù Yuè (傅說) admonished Gāozōng (高宗) saying:
"Do not be ashamed of your faults and commit wrongs."
From this perspective,
then, a ruler
is certainly not considered worthy for being faultless,
but rather admirable for correcting his faults.
Now, Shūsūn Tōng (叔孫通) admonished Xiàohuì (孝惠),
yet said
"a ruler has no missteps."
This is teaching a ruler to gloss over mistakes and persist in wrongs.
How absurd is that!
6. The Hóng Tái (鴻臺) in Chánglè Gōng caught fire.
The Sān Fǔ Huáng Tú says: Hóng Tái was in Chánglè Gōng.
It was built by Qín Shǐhuáng (秦始皇) in the 27th year [of his reign],
forty zhàng high,
with pavilions on top;
the Emperor once shot flying wild geese from the platform,
hence it was called Hóng Tái.
7. In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the Yǐhài day,
the Líng Shì (凌室) in Wèiyāng Gōng caught fire;
on the Bǐngzǐ day,
the Zhī Shì (織室) caught fire.
Líng Shì was the chamber for storing ice;
Zhī Shì was the place in charge of weaving silk fabrics.
Bān Biǎo (班表) says: The Shǎofǔ (少府) had the Dōng Zhī (東織) and Xī Zhī (西織) (Eastern Weaving Office and Western Weaving Office).
Líng (凌),
pronounced "lì zhèng" (力證),
also rhymes with "líng" (陵).
1. In winter,
there was thunder;
The Hóngfàn Lùn (洪範論) says: Yang operates for one hundred eighty-three days and ends,
Yin operates for one hundred eighty-three days and ends.
Thunder emerges from the ground for one hundred eighty-three days and then re-enters the ground,
and after one hundred eighty-three days in the ground, it re-emerges,
this is its normal course;
thunder in winter is a deviation from the norm.
Jujubes bore fruit.
2. In spring,
in the first month,
another 145,000 men and women from within six hundred lǐ of Cháng'ān were conscripted to build the city of Cháng'ān;
they were dismissed after thirty days.
3. In summer,
there was a great drought,
the Jiāng and Hé rivers had low water,
and the streams and valleys ran dry.
4. In autumn,
in the eighth month,
Píngyáng Yì Hóu (平陽懿侯) Cáo Cān (曹參) passed away.
The law on posthumous titles says: "Gently virtuous and kind" is called Yì (懿).
1. In winter,
in the tenth month,
Wáng Líng (王陵) was made Right Chancellor,
and Chén Píng (陳平) was made Left Chancellor.
2. Qí Dàohuì Wáng Féi (齊悼惠王肥) passed away.
3. In summer,
Liú Wénchéng Hóu (留文成侯) Zhāng Liáng (張良) passed away.
The Duke of Zhōu's (周公) law on posthumous titles: "Bringing peace to the people and establishing governance" is called Chéng (成).
Hè Chēn (賀琛) on posthumous titles for ministers: "Assisting the premier and seeing through to the end" is called Chéng (成).
4. Zhōu Bó (周勃) was made Grand Commandant.
1. In winter,
chariots and cavalry, and skilled officers were dispatched to Xíngyáng,
commanded by Grand Commandant Guàn Yīng (灌嬰).
2. In spring,
in the first month,
on Xīnchǒu (辛丑) day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
3. In summer,
in the fifth month,
on Dīngmǎo (丁卯) day,
there was a solar eclipse,
which was total.
4. In autumn,
in the eighth month,
on Wùyín (戊寅) day,
the Emperor passed away in Wèiyāng Gōng.
A general amnesty was declared throughout the empire.
In the ninth month,
on Xīnchǒu day,
he was buried at Ān Líng (安陵).
Chén Zàn (臣瓚) said: He was twenty-four years old.
Ān Líng is thirty lǐ north of Cháng'ān.
Shīgǔ said: It is ten lǐ from Cháng Líng (長陵).
Originally,
Empress Dowager Lǚ (呂) ordered Empress Zhāng (張) to adopt another person's child,
and killed its mother,
making him the Crown Prince.
After the burial,
the Crown Prince immediately ascended the imperial throne,
being young;
the Empress Dowager held court and issued decrees.
Shīgǔ said: The words of the Son of Heaven
are of two kinds: one is a "zhìshū" (制書), and the other is a "zhàoshū" (詔書).
"Zhìshū" refers to commands regarding systems and regulations,
which an Empress is not entitled to issue.
Now the Empress Dowager held court,
performing the duties of the Son of Heaven,
hence she "issued decrees."
Niè Chóngqí (聶崇岐) punctuated, Róng Zhàozǔ (容肇祖) reviewed.

Hanlin Academician, Cháosàn Dàfū, Right Jiànyì Dàfū, Zhī Zhìgào, concurrent Shìjiǎng, concurrent Tí Jǔ Wànshòu Guān Gōngshì, concurrent Pàn Jíxián Yuàn, Shànghùjūn, Hénèi Jùn Kāiguó Hóu, with an allocated fief of one thousand three hundred households, bestowed with a purple-gold fish pouch, your servant
respectfully compiled by imperial decree.
Hòu Xué Tiān Tái
Gāo Huánghòu
Xún Yuè said: The character
“zhì” (pheasant)
was tabooed by calling it
“yě jī” (wild chicken).
Suǒ Yǐn said: Her courtesy name was Éxǔ.
Yīng Shào said: According to the rites,
a woman takes her husband’s posthumous title,
hence she is called
“Gāo” (high).
Shī Gǔ said: As “zhì” was tabooed,
so her subjects avoided using “zhì”.
Xǔ,
read as Xǔ Yú fān.
1 In winter,
the Grand Empress Dowager discussed her wish to make various Lǚ clan members kings.
She asked the Right Chancellor, Líng,
who replied:
“Emperor Gāo Dì sacrificed a white horse and swore an oath, saying:
‘Gāo Zǔ sacrificed a white horse and swore an oath with his ministers, saying:
“Those who are not of the Liú clan shall not be kings;
those without merit shall not be marquises.” ’
All under heaven struck down those who violated this.
Now to make the Lǚ clan kings
is not in accordance with the oath.”
The Grand Empress Dowager was displeased.
She asked the Left Chancellor, Píng, and the Grand Commandant, Bó,
who replied:
“Emperor Gāo Dì established the empire
and made his sons and younger brothers kings.
Now the Grand Empress Dowager holds court,
and to make the Lǚ clan kings
is entirely permissible.”
The Grand Empress Dowager was pleased.
After court was dismissed,
Wáng Líng reproached Chén Píng and Jiàng Hóu, saying:
“When we swore the blood oath with Emperor Gāo Dì,
were you gentlemen not present?
Now Emperor Gāo Dì has passed away,
the Grand Empress Dowager is the female ruler,
and wishes to make the Lǚ clan kings.
You gentlemen indulge her wishes and betray the oath.
How will you face Emperor Gāo Dì in the underworld?”
Chén Píng and Jiàng Hóu replied:
“As for now,
to openly contend at court
means to remonstrate and contend in the presence of the court.
To preserve the altars of soil and grain
and secure the succession of the Liú clan,
you are also not as good as we are.”
Líng had no answer.
In the eleventh month,
on a jiǎzǐ day,
the Grand Empress Dowager appointed Wáng Líng as Grand Tutor to the Emperor,
effectively stripping him of his chancellorial power.
Líng subsequently fell ill and was dismissed to return home.
Thereupon, the Left Chancellor Píng was made Right Chancellor.
At this time, the right was esteemed,
hence Chén Píng moved from Left Chancellor to Right Chancellor.
He did not manage affairs,
but was ordered to oversee the imperial palace,
like a Lángzhōng Lìng.
It means that he did not attend to the duties of a chancellor,
but often oversaw the palace like a Lángzhōng Lìng.
Jiān,
read as gǔ xián fān.
All the dukes and ministers consequently decided matters through him.
The Grand Empress Dowager resented Zhào Yáo for plotting on behalf of Zhào Yǐnwáng,
and so condemned Yáo to death.
Yáo plotted for the King of Zhào;
the matter is seen in the previous volume, Gāo Zǔ, year 10.
Zhào Wáng Rúyì
was posthumously titled Yǐn.
The posthumous title rules: Yǐn refers to something that is not fully manifested or accomplished;
Yǐn refers to being obscure and holding a state;
Yǐn refers to being beautiful, firm, and long-lasting.
Wéi,
read as yú wěi fān.
The Administrator of Shàngdǎng, Rèn Áo, had once been a prison official in Pèi
and had shown kindness to the Grand Empress Dowager.
Thereupon, he was made Grandee Secretary.
Rèn Áo,
a man from Pèi,
was a prison official in his youth.
Gāo Zǔ often avoided officials;
an official once arrested Lǚ Hòu,
and treated her disrespectfully.
Áo struck and injured the official who was detaining Lǚ Hòu,
which is why the Empress favored him.
The Grand Empress Dowager also posthumously honored her father, the Marquis of Línsì, Lǚ Gōng, as Xuānwáng,
and her elder brother, the Marquis Wǔ of Zhōulǚ, Zé, as Dàowǔ Wáng,
wishing to make this a gradual step towards making the Lǚ clan kings.
Marquis of Línsì,
Bān Biǎo: A title bestowed on the Empress's father.
Suǒ Yǐn said: Yīng Shào said: Zhōulǚ
is a state.
According to this, Zhōu and Lǚ are both state names.
There is Lǚdū county in Jìyīn.
Jìn Zhuó said: Lǚ
is a county name,
made into a marquisate.
I rely on Bān Zhì: Lǚ county belonged to the state of Chǔ.
Lìngwǔ
is a posthumous title.
2 In spring,
the first month,
the punishments of three kindreds and 'seditious speech' were abolished.
Qín, in its tyranny and cruelty,
had among its gravest crimes the execution of three kindreds;
and erroneous words
were considered seditious speech.
Therefore, all these were abolished.
3 In summer,
the fourth month,
Princess Lǔyuán passed away.
The princess's son, Zhāng Yǎn, was enfeoffed as King of Lǔ,
and the princess was posthumously titled Grand Empress Dowager Lǔyuán.
4 On a xīnmǎo day,
Xiàohuì’s son, Shān, whom she had named, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Xiāngchéng.
Bān Zhì: Xiāngchéng county belonged to Yǐngchuān Commandery.
Zhǐ county belonged to Hénèi Commandery.
Húguān county belonged to Shàngdǎng Commandery.
The Grand Empress Dowager wished to make the Lǚ clan kings,
and so first established Xiàohuì’s son, Qiáng, whom she had named, as King of Huáiyáng,
and Bùyí as King of Héngshān.
In the first year of Huì Dì,
King Yǒu of Huáiyáng was transferred to be King of Zhào;
now Qiáng is enfeoffed with this.
Héngshān Commandery originally belonged to the state of Zhào;
now it is carved out to enfeoff Bùyí.
Héng,
read as hù dēng fān.
[Kǎo Yì says: In Shǐjì, Wén Dì Běnjì],
“Zé.”
Shǐjì, Lǚ Hòu Běnjì:
“In the eighth year,
Zhāng Shì, Zhongdà Yèzhě,”
Hànshū Jì reads
“Shì Qīng.”
Ēnzé Hóu Biǎo and Zhōu Bó Zhuàn both state
“Zhāng Shì.”
Yán Shīgǔ notes: Jīngyàn Wú Zhuàn states
“Zhāng Zé.”
Now we follow Shǐjì, Lǚ Hòu Běnjì, and Hànshū, Ēnzé Hóu
[Biǎo].
The ministers then requested to establish Dàowǔ Wáng’s eldest son, the Marquis of Lì, Tái, as King of Lǚ,
carving out Qí’s Jìnán Commandery as the state of Lǚ.
5 In the fifth month,
on a bǐngshēn day,
the Congtái terrace of the King of Zhào’s palace caught fire.
Liú Zhāo Zhì: In Hándān county of Zhào state, there is Congtái.
6 In autumn,
peaches and plums bloomed.
1 In winter,
the eleventh month,
King Sù of Lǚ, Tái, passed away.
Kǎo Yì says: Shǐjì Běnjì:
“In the first year of Gāo Hòu,
Xiàohuì’s son, Bùyí, was established as King of Héngshān,
and Lǚ Tái as King of Lǚ.”
“In the second year,
the King of Héngshān passed away.”
“In the eleventh month,
King Lǚ Tái passed away.”
The Niánbiǎo states
both passed away in the first year.
Hànshū Běnjì:
“In the first year,
Bùyí, Lǚ Tái, Chǎn, Lù Tōng were established as kings.
In the second year,
Bùyí passed away.”
The Niánbiǎo:
In the first year,
Bùyí and Lǚ Tái became kings,
and both passed away in the second year.
Perhaps in the Shǐjì Niánbiǎo,
the character “hōng” (passed away)
should have been in the second year,
but was mistakenly written in the first year.
In reality, both passed away in the second year.
The Hànshū Běnjì saying
“Chǎn, Lù Tōng were established as kings”
is also a mistake.
2. In spring,
in the first month,
on the Yǐmǎo day,
there was an earthquake;
mountains collapsed in Qiāngdào and Wǔdōudào.
Qiāngdào,
according to Bān Zhì,
was a xiàn,
belonging to Lǒngxī Jùn.
Wǔdōu
was a xiàn at that time.
Hàn Zhì states: xiàn mixed with barbarians are called dào.
Emperor Wǔ established Wǔdōu Jùn.
3. In summer,
in the fifth month,
on the Bǐngshēn day,
Yǐngkè, a son of King Chǔyuán, was enfeoffed as Shàngpī Hóu;
Zhāng, a son of King Qídàohuì, was enfeoffed as Zhūxū Hóu.
Bān Zhì states:
Xiàpī Xiàn was in Dōnghǎi.
Yìng Shào says: Pī was originally in Xuē,
its later relocation here
is why it is called Xiàpī.
Chén Zàn says: There was Shàngpī,
hence it was called Xiàpī.
Shīgǔ says: Zàn's explanation is correct.
Bān Zhì states:
Zhūxū Xiàn belonged to Lángyá Jùn.
Kuòdì Zhì states: The old city of Zhūxū
is sixty lǐ east of Línqú Xiàn in Qīngzhōu;
this is the Hàn Zhūxū.
Shísān Zhōu Zhì states: Dān Zhū roamed its old ruins (xū),
hence it is called Zhūxū.
Xū
is like qiū (mound);
zhū
is like dān (cinnabar).
Suǒyǐn: Xū
is pronounced "xū."
Kǎoyì says: The Shǐjì Gāohòu Jì places this in the first year,
but we follow the Hànshū Wángzǐ Hóu Biǎo here.
Also, Lǚ Lù's daughter was given in marriage to Zhāng.
4. In the sixth month,
on the Bǐngxū huì day,
there was a solar eclipse.
5. In autumn,
in the seventh month,
Hángshān Āiwáng Bùyí passed away.
6. Eight-zhū coins were put into circulation.
Yìng Shào says: Originally Qín coins,
their quality was like Zhōu coins,
inscribed with "bàn liǎng,"
weighing as inscribed,
which was eight zhū.
Hàn, considering them too heavy,
minted jiáqián;
what common people now call yújiáqián are these.
The people suffered from them being too light,
so by this time, eight-zhū coins were circulated again.
7. On the Guǐchǒu day,
Shān, the Marquis of Xiāngchéng, was established as King of Hángshān,
and his name was changed to Yì.
1. In summer,
the Jiāngshǔi and Hànshǔi overflowed,
flooding over four thousand households.
Bān Zhì states: The Jiāngshǔi originates from a mountain outside the jǐao (frontier pass) of Jiāndīdào in Shǔ Jùn,
flows southeast to Jiāngdū and enters the sea.
Yǔgòng states: Bōzhǒng guides the Yàng,
which flows east to become the Hàn.
Kǒng Ānguó commented: A spring initially emerging from a mountain is called Yàngshuǐ,
flowing southeast it becomes Miǎnshuǐ,
reaching Hànzhōng and flowing east it becomes Hànshuǐ.
Bān Zhì states: Dīdào Xiàn in Lǒngxī,
is where the Yàngshuǐ mentioned in Yǔgòng originates;
upon reaching Wǔdōu it becomes the Hàn.
Furthermore, under Wǔdōu it states: The eastern Hànshuǐ receives the Dīdàoshuǐ,
also named Miǎn,
passing Jiāngxià,
it is called Xiàshuǐ,
and enters the Jiāng.
Also,
Hànzhōng Jùn has Miǎnyáng Xiàn.
Rú Chún commented: The people of this region call the Hànshuǐ the Miǎnshuǐ.
Shīgǔ says: Above the Hàn is called Miǎn.
The Shuǐjīng, however, considers Miǎn and Yàng to have different sources.
The Yàng emerges from Bōzhǒng Shān in Dīdào, Lǒngxī,
flows east to Jǔ Xiàn in Wǔdōu to become the Hànshuǐ.
Its course,
southeastward passes Báishuǐ and Jiāměng,
then southeastward past Lángzhōng in Bājùn to Jiāngjīn Xiàn where it enters the Jiāng;
the Fúshuǐ flows into it;
this is what Yǔ Zhòngyōng called "inner water."
The Miǎnshuǐ emerges from Lánggǔ, east of Jǔ Xiàn in Wǔdōu,
also named Jǔshuǐ,
flows east past Miǎnyáng, Nánzhèng, Chénggù, and other xiàn in Hànzhōng Jùn,
then east past Xīchéng and Xī Xiàn,
then east past Xiāngyáng and Zhōnglú in Nánjùn,
which is Dāngyáng Xiàn in Yíchéng Jùn,
then east past Yúndù Xiàn in Jiāngxià,
then south to Shāxiàn Xiàn and enters the Jiāng.
I rely on Yǔgòng,
where it says the Yàng is guided to flow east as the Hàn,
and further east as the Cāngláng river,
passing three xiè (fords),
reaching Dàbié and entering the Jiāng from the south;
this means the Hànshuǐ originates from the Yàng.
According to Shuǐjīng,
the Yàng meets the Fú,
and the Miǎn enters the Jiāng;
they have different sources
and different mouths.
According to Bān Zhì,
the Yàng emerges from Dīdào, Lǒngxī,
and upon reaching Wǔdōu becomes the Hànshuǐ;
and the eastern Hànshuǐ receives the Dīdàoshuǐ,
generally called Miǎn,
passing Jiāngxià and entering the Jiāng.
So, Yàng and Miǎn seem to be combined as one,
yet it also states that the Jǔshuǐ emerges from Jǔ Xiàn and flows south to Shāxiàn to enter the Jiāng,
which seems inconsistent with the Shuǐjīng's statement that Miǎnshuǐ is Jǔshuǐ, but in fact it is consistent.
2. In autumn,
a star was seen during the day.
3. The Yīshuǐ and Luòshuǐ overflowed,
flooding over sixteen hundred households.
Bān Zhì states: The Yīshuǐ emerges from Xióng'ěr Shān in Hóngnóng Jùn,
flows northeast into the Luòshuǐ.
Shuǐjīng states: The Yīshuǐ emerges from Mànqú Shān in Nányáng Xiàn.
Lì Dàoyuán commented: The foothills are largely the same,
only the ridges and peaks differ.
Also, Bān Zhì states: The Luòshuǐ emerges from Shàngluò Xiàn in Hóngnóng Jùn,
flows northeast to Gǒng Xiàn in Hénán and enters the river.
It flooded over eight hundred households.
Yìng Shào says: The Rǔshuǐ emerges from Hóngnóng Xiàn,
and enters the Huái.
Shuǐjīng states: The Rǔshuǐ emerges from Dàyú Shān in Lǔyáng Xiàn, Nányáng,
flows southeast through Jiá, Dìnglíng, and Yǎn in Yǐngchuān,
then southeast past Shàngcài and Píngyú in Rǔnán,
and enters the Huái from the south.
1. In spring,
in the second month,
on the Guǐwèi day,
Tài, a son of Emperor Xiàohuì, was established as Chāngpíng Hóu.
Bān Zhì states:
Chāngpíng Xiàn belonged to Shànggǔ Jùn.
2. In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the Bǐngshēn day,
the Empress Dowager enfeoffed her younger sister Xū as Línguāng Hóu.
Xū,
is pronounced "xū."
3. The Young Emperor gradually grew up,
and knowing that he was not the Empress's son (Empress Zhāng of Emperor Huì was the daughter of Princess Lǔyuán),
(the Empress Dowager, seeing she had no son,
had her feign pregnancy,
took a son of a court lady and named him hers,
and killed the mother.
The Young Emperor, Yì, Cháo, Qiáng, and Bùyí were all like this.)
When he grew up,
he knew:
"How could the Empress have killed my mother and named me hers!
When I am grown,
I will cause trouble!"
The Empress Dowager heard of this,
confined him in the Yǒngxiàng (Side Alley),
and announced that the Emperor was ill.
None of his attendants were allowed to see him.
The Empress Dowager said to her ministers:
"The present Emperor has been ill for a long time,
demented and confused,
unable to succeed and govern the world;
he should be replaced."
All the ministers bowed their heads and said:
"Her Imperial Majesty the Empress Dowager considers the welfare of all people under heaven,
and her measures to secure the ancestral temple and altars of soil and grain are profound;
all ministers bow their heads and respectfully obey the decree."
Thereupon, the Emperor was deposed,
confined and killed.
In the fifth month,
on the Bǐngchén day,
Yì, King of Hángshān, was established as Emperor,
and his name was changed to Hóng;
the regnal year was not renamed to 'first year,'
because the Empress Dowager controlled all affairs of the world.
Cháo, the Marquis of Zhì, was made King of Hángshān.
4. In this year,
Cáo Zhú, the Marquis of Píngyáng, was made Grandee Secretary.
5. The officials requested to prohibit trade and ironware with Nányuè at the border passes.
The Hàn had trade with barbarians at the border passes,
which was called Guānshì (Pass Markets).
"Emperor Gāo established me,
and allowed envoys and goods to pass.
Now Empress Gāo listens to slanderous ministers,
treating barbarians differently,
cutting off instruments and goods;
this must be the plan of the King of Chángshā,
who wishes to rely on China to attack and destroy Nányuè and annex it,
taking the credit for himself."
1 In spring,
Zhào Tuó 自稱 Nányuè Wǔdì.
Wéi Zhāo 曰: "To claim the title of Wǔ in life [as a personal name],
is not in accordance with ancient practices."
Shī Gǔ 曰: "This statement is incorrect.
Tāng 曰:
'My martial prowess is great,
so I style myself Wǔwáng.'
That Tuó calls himself Wǔdì
is just like that.
How can it be said that he does not follow ancient practices?"
Gòng Fù 曰: "Although Yán cites the words of Chéng Tāng,
it is still unknown whether Tāng himself assumed the title of Wǔwáng.
The Sages,
it was others who gave them their names.
The Shī calls Tāng Wǔwáng,
just as the Shū calls Wénwáng Níngwáng.
The statements in the Shǐjì
are not necessarily credible."
[He] defeated several counties and departed.
2 In autumn,
eighth month,
Huáiyáng Huáiwáng Qiáng 薨;
Húguān Hóu Wǔ was made Huáiyáng Wáng.
3 In ninth month,
cavalry from Hédōng and Shàngdǎng were dispatched to garrison Běidì.
4 For the first time, garrison soldiers were rotated annually.
The Qín cruelly used their people,
garrisoning the Wǔlǐng mountains in the south,
and building the Great Wall in the north.
Many garrison soldiers died, not returning home for years.
By this time,
it was decreed for the first time that they be rotated once a year.
Gèng,
工衡 fan.
1 In winter,
tenth month,
the Empress Dowager, because Lǚwáng Jiā's living was arrogant and self-indulgent,
deposed him.
Jiā
was Tái's son.
In the second year,
Tái 薨,
and Jiā succeeded.
Chǔ,
昌呂 fan.
Sùwáng's younger brother Chǎn was made Lǚwáng.
Tái
was posthumously named Sù.
2 In spring,
a star was seen in daytime.
3 In summer,
fourth month,
on the dìngyǒu day,
a general amnesty was declared throughout the realm.
4 Zhūxū Hóu Zhāng's younger brother Xīngjū was enfeoffed as Dōngmóu Hóu.
The Bān Zhì states:
"Dōngmóu County belongs to Dōnglái Commandery."
Xián 曰: "The old city of Dōngmóu
is now in the northwest of Wéndēng County, Láizhōu."
5 The Xiōngnú raided Dí Dào
and attacked Āyáng.
The Bān Zhì states:
"Dí Dào County belongs to Lǒngxī Commandery;
Āyáng County belongs to Tiānshuǐ Commandery."
6 Five-fen coins were circulated.
Yìng Shào 曰: "These are the so-called jiáqián."
7 Xuānpíng Hóu Zhāng Áo 卒.
The Kǎoyì 曰: "The Shǐjì Lǚhòu Běnjì states that
Áo 卒 in the sixth month of the following year.
According to the Shǐjì Gōngchénbiǎo:
'In the sixth year of Gāohòu,
Áo 卒';
the Hànshū Gōngchénbiǎo states that
Áo was enfeoffed in the ninth year of Gāozǔ
and 薨 in the seventeenth year.
This is probably an error in the Běnjì.
Zhāng Áo originally succeeded his father's noble rank as Zhào Wáng.
When the plot of Guàngāo was exposed,
Áo was deposed and made Xuānpíng Hóu,
and continued to be married to Princess Lǔyuán.
During the reign of Huìdì,
Qí Dàohuì Wáng offered Chéngyáng Commandery to support Lǔyuán.
When Áo died,
he was posthumously granted the title Lǔyuán Wáng because of the princess."
1 In winter,
twelfth month,
the Xiōngnú raided Dí Dào
and plundered over two thousand people.
2 In spring,
first month,
the Empress Dowager summoned Zhào Yōuwáng Yǒu.
In the first year of Huìdì,
Yǒu was transferred from Huáiyáng to rule Zhào.
[He] did not love [the Lǚ woman],
loving other concubines.
The women of the Lǚ clan were angry,
departed,
and slandered him to the Empress Dowager, saying:
"The King said, 'How could the Lǚ clan possibly rule!
After the Empress Dowager passes away,
I will certainly attack them.'"
Because of this, the Empress Dowager summoned the King of Zhào.
When the King of Zhào arrived,
he was lodged in a residence,
and was not allowed an audience.
This means he was placed in the Zhào residence.
Shī Gǔ 曰: "Residences in the capital for lords of commanderies and states who come for court are generally called dì.
Dì
means to arrive,
referring to the place where one returns and arrives."
Dì,
丁禮 fan.
He was not given food;
if any of his trusted retainers secretly provided food,
they were immediately arrested and punished.
Those who provided him food were arrested
and judged guilty.
On the dīngchǒu day,
the King of Zhào starved to death.
He was buried with the rites of commoners in the burial ground for commoners in Cháng'ān.
3 On the jǐchǒu day,
there was a solar eclipse,
and it was dark during the day.
The Empress Dowager was displeased by it,
and said to her attendants:
"This is for me!"
4 In second month,
Liángwáng Huī was transferred to be Zhào Wáng,
and Lǚwáng Chǎn was made Liáng Wáng.
The King of Liáng did not go to his state,
but served as Grand Tutor to the Emperor.
5 In autumn,
seventh month,
on the dīngsì day,
Píngchāng Hóu Tài was made Jìchuān Wáng.
In the fourth year,
Tài was enfeoffed as Chāngpíng Hóu;
the Bān Biǎo also has
"Chāngpíng,"
this is an error with the character
"Píng"
placed above.
Jìchuān
was the territory of Jìnán and Jìběi,
presumably carved out from Qí and granted as a fief.
At that time, Tài was young
and had not yet gone to his state.
Jì,
子禮 fan.
6 A woman of the Lǚ clan was the wife of General and Yínglíng Hóu Liú Zé.
The Bān Zhì states:
"Yínglíng County belongs to Běihǎi Commandery,"
or it is called Yíngqiū.
Yìng Shào 曰: "Shī Shàngfǔ was enfeoffed at Yíngqiū."
Líng
is also a qiū.
Chén Zàn 曰: "Yíngqiū,
which is Línzī and Yínglíng,
was called Yuánlíng in the Chūnqiū."
Shī Gǔ 曰: "Línzī and Yínglíng were both former Yíngqiū territory."
The Kuòdì Zhì: "The old city of Yínglíng
is thirty lǐ south of Běihǎi County, Qīngzhōu."
[Liú Zé] was a paternal cousin of Gāozǔ.
Tián Shēng of Qí spoke to Dàyèzhě Zhāng Qīng on his behalf, saying:
Zhāng Qīng
is the former Dàyèzhě Zhāng Shì.
Shuō,
式芮 fan.
"When the Lǚ clan became kings,
the various ministers were not entirely convinced.
Now Yínglíng Hóu Zé,
is the eldest among the various Liú;
if you now tell the Empress Dowager to make him a king,
the Lǚ clan's rule will be even more secure."
Zhāng Qīng entered and spoke to the Empress Dowager,
and the Empress Dowager agreed.
So she carved out Lángyá Commandery from Qí and enfeoffed Zé as Lángyá Wáng.
When Qín destroyed Qí,
it established Lángyá Commandery with the coastal land;
Hàn continued this.
The Kǎoyì 曰: "The Shǐjì Shìjiā and Hànshū Lièzhuàn
all say that Tián Shēng first persuaded Zhāng Qīng to hint to the ministers to establish Lǚ Chǎn as Lǚ Wáng,
and then persuaded [them] to make Zé a king.
However, the Empress Dowager herself deposed Lǚ Wáng Jiā for his arrogance and indulgence,
and replaced him with Chǎn as Lǚ Wáng,
not making him a king of Lǚ for the first time;
moreover, the Lǚ clan had been kings for a long time,
so why would they need Tián Shēng's plan!
Therefore, this [account] is not adopted."
7 Zhào Wáng Huī's
heart was unhappy when he was moved to Zhào.
The Empress Dowager made Lǚ Chǎn's daughter the queen,
and all the queen's retinue were members of the Lǚ clan.
They seized power
and secretly watched the King of Zhào,
so the King of Zhào could not act as he pleased.
The King had a beloved concubine;
the queen sent someone to poison her to death.
In the sixth month,
the King, unable to bear his grief and indignation,
committed suicide.
When the Empress Dowager heard of this,
she believed the King had abandoned the rites of the ancestral temple for a woman,
and that vassal kings had their states
to serve the ancestral temple.
Now Huī, for the sake of a beloved concubine,
had gone so far as to commit suicide,
so she condemned him for abandoning the rites of the ancestral temple.
8 At this time,
the Lǚ clan seized power and managed affairs.
The Marquis of Zhūxū, Zhāng,
then twenty years old,
possessed strength and vigor,
and resented that the Liú clan could not hold office.
He once entered to attend the Empress Dowager at a banquet.
The Empress Dowager ordered Zhāng to be the wine officer.
Zhāng requested, saying:
"I am a descendant of a general;
please allow me to administer the wine according to military law."
The Empress Dowager said:
"You may."
When the drinking was well underway,
Zhāng requested to sing a song about farming;
the Empress Dowager granted it.
Zhāng sang:
"Plow deeply and sow densely,
but when the seedlings stand, they should be sparse.
Those that are not of the right species,
weed them out and remove them!"
Shī Gǔ said: Jì means
dense.
'Sow densely' means
to have many descendants.
'Stand sparsely' means
to place them scattered,
making them into a screen and support.
'Weed out and remove those not of the right species'
is to denounce the Lǚ clan.
Jì is pronounced
jì.
Qù is pronounced
qiāng lǚ fān.
A short while later,
one of the Lǚ clan, being drunk,
fled from the wine.
Zhāng pursued him,
drew his sword, cut him down, and returned,
reporting:

Third year before [the era name]
(*Jiǎzǐ*, 177 BCE)
1 In winter,
the tenth month,

on the *Dīngmǎo* (丁卯) new moon,

3 The emperor issued an edict:
"Previously, I sent the marquises to their states.
This matter can be found in the previous year of the upper volume.
The Chancellor,
whom I greatly esteem,
shall lead the marquises to their states on my behalf!"
In the twelfth month,
Chancellor Zhōu Bó was dismissed
and sent to his state.
On the *yǐhài* day,
the Grand Commandant Guàn Yīng was appointed Chancellor;
the office of Grand Commandant was abolished
and its functions were attached to the Chancellor.
The Hàn dynasty inherited the Qín system,
with the Chancellor, Grand Commandant, and Grandee Secretary as the Three Excellencies.
Now, Zhōu Bó was dismissed from the chancellorship and sent to his state,
and Guàn Yīng became Chancellor from Grand Commandant,
whereupon the office of Grand Commandant was abolished;
this suggests that it was not deemed necessary to always have all Three Excellencies,
and also that military authority should not be lightly entrusted.

the fourth month,
Jǐng Wáng Zhāng of Chéngyáng passed away.
The posthumous epithet law states: "Jǐng" means achieving through righteousness;
"Jǐng" means having profound foresight and great deliberation;
"Jǐng" means propagating righteousness and acting with firmness.

He frequently disregarded the law;

hence "deceived."
"I was not given any duties,
and was dismissed and sent away;
this person must have defamed me.
If Your Majesty summons a servant based on one person's praise,
and dismisses a servant based on one person's slander,
I fear that those with discernment under Heaven, hearing this,
will be able to gauge the depth of Your Majesty's character!"
The Emperor remained silent,
felt ashamed,
and after a long time said:
"Hédōng
is a vital commandery to me,
so I specifically summoned you, that's all."
4 The Emperor discussed appointing Jiǎ Yì to a position among the high officials.
Many high officials disparaged him, saying:
"This person from Luòyáng
is young and a novice scholar,
solely desirous of monopolizing power
and throwing everything into confusion."
Consequently, the Son of Heaven later also became distant from him,
did not adopt his proposals,
and made him Grand Tutor to the King of Chángshā.
The King of Chángshā
was Wú Chāi.
The Han system stipulated that feudal kingdoms had a Grand Tutor to assist the king.
"Shū"
is the same as "shū" (meaning 'distant').

漢承秦制，

行，

吏

提，

Jiǎ Yí (賈誼) remonstrated, saying:
"The law allows everyone in the world to publicly hire and rent to cast copper and tin into coins.
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: 'Hiring and renting'
refers to the direct cost of hiring
or renting the principal.
The crime for this is tattooing (黥).
However, the nature of coin casting is such that
without mixing and adulterating to make it skillful,
one cannot profit.
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: 'Mixing' (殽)
means to confuse and adulterate;
'cannot profit' (不得贏)
means there is no surplus profit;
it means if lead and iron are not mixed in, there is no profit.
殽
is pronounced 'yáo'.
The profit is extremely high.
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: 'Wēi' (微)
means subtle and exquisite;
it means that mixing lead and iron,
the technique is subtle and exquisite,
undetectable,
yet yields very high profits,
thus encouraging people to lightly commit fraud and making it unstoppable.
I (Yú, 余) say 'wēi' (微)
means small;
it means that when unscrupulous people mix lead and iron,
their cost is very small,
but their profit is very high.
Now, allowing common people to wield the power of currency creation,
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: 'Cāo' (操)
means to hold;
everyone can cast coins.
操
is pronounced 'qiān gāo fān'.
If one then wishes to forbid their greatly profitable subtle fraud,
even if the tattooing punishment is meted out daily, the trend will not stop.
Sū Lín (蘇林) says: 'Bào' (報)
means to judge.
I (Yú, 余) note that in the biography of Zhāng Tāng (張湯), there are 'xùn' (訊), 'jū' (鞫), 'lùn' (論), 'bào' (報);
in the biography of Yán Yánnián (嚴延年), there is 'bào qiú' (報囚);
Shī Gǔ's (師古) annotations all take them to mean 'to report and submit a judgment'.
However, Yuán Fù's (原父) annotation states that 'bào' (報) means to decide on prisoners,
just as today, officials record the crimes of prisoners,
and the chief magistrate approves and decides;
this is correct.
The number of common people who incur crimes is hundreds in a single county,
and those suspected by officials, flogged, beaten, and forced to flee are very numerous.
Indeed, what is more egregious than establishing laws to lure people
into a trap?
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: 'Jǐng' (阱)
is a pit dug to trap beasts.
Jǐng (阱)
is pronounced 'cái xìng fān'.
Counties differ: some use light coins,
adding a certain amount per hundred.
Yīng Shào (應劭) says: At that time, a coin weighed four zhū (銖);
one hundred legal coins
should weigh one jīn (斤) and sixteen zhū (銖);
if light, a certain number of coins are added
to make up the full weight.
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: 'Ruògān' (若干)
is a provisional numerical expression.
'Gān' (干)
is like 'gè' (箇),
meaning 'this many units'.
Hú Guǎng (胡廣) says: 'Ruò' (若)
means 'to comply';
'gān' (干)
means 'to seek';
meaning 'one should comply with what is sought and give it.'
If the weight is standard, they are not accepted.
Yīng Shào (應劭) says: If heavy coins are used, the standard weight will have a surplus,
making them unacceptable.
Minister Zǎn (瓚) says: Qín (秦) coins weighed half a liǎng (兩);
in the early Hàn (漢) dynasty, 'jiáqián' (莢錢) were cast;
Emperor Wén (文) later cast four-zhū (銖) coins.
Qín (秦) coins and 'jiáqián' (莢錢) were both supposed to be abolished,
but they circulated alongside the four-zhū (銖) coins.
The people, knowing they were to be abolished,
therefore added a certain number per hundred when using light coins;
if using heavy coins, even if one counted as one, they would still not be accepted;
this is why counties differed.
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: Yīng's (應) explanation is correct.
Chēng (稱)
is pronounced 'chǐ yùn fān'.
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: These are coins according to the law.
Then it becomes greatly troublesome and burdensome, and one's strength cannot endure it;
if we let it be and do not stop it?
Then markets will use different currencies,
and coin denominations will be in great disorder;
if this is not the right method,
how can it be acceptable anywhere!
Now, agricultural work is abandoned, and copper miners increase daily;
they lay aside their plows and hoes,
smelting and burning charcoal.
Counterfeit coins become more numerous daily,
but the five grains do not increase.
This means people abandon farming to smelt copper and burn charcoal,
thus the five grains do not increase.
Wéi (為)
is pronounced 'yú wěi fān'.
I fear the people will fall into penal servitude;
penal servitude will be extremely inauspicious,
how can we ignore it!
The state knows this problem,
and officials will certainly propose 'to ban it.'
If the ban is not implemented skillfully,
the harm will certainly be great.
If coin casting is banned,
then coins will certainly become heavy;
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: 'Lìng' (令)
refers to laws and decrees.
Counterfeiters will rise up like clouds,
and the punishment of public execution will again be insufficient to stop them.
The number of fraudsters constantly wins, and legal prohibitions constantly collapse;
copper causes this to happen.
Copper is distributed throughout the world,
and its harm is widespread;
therefore, it is better to collect it."
Jiǎ Shān (賈山) also submitted a memorial,
believing that:
"Coins
are useless objects.
Wáng (亡)
is interchangeable with wú (無).
Wealth and nobility
are the handles of the ruler;
allowing the people to make them
is to share the handles with the ruler,
which cannot be allowed to continue."
The Emperor did not heed them.
At this time,
Grand Master of the Palace Dèng Tōng (鄧通) was in great favor,
and the Emperor, wishing him to be wealthy,
bestowed upon him the copper mountain of Yándào (嚴道) in Shǔ (蜀).
He was allowed to cast coins.
The Bān Zhì (班志) states that
Yándào (嚴道) belonged to Shǔjùn (蜀郡).
The Kuòdì Zhì (括地志) states: Three lǐ (里) north of Róngjīng (榮經) County in Yǎzhōu (雅州) there is a copper mountain,
which is the copper mountain Dèng Tōng (鄧通) was granted to cast coins.
Táng (唐) Róngjīng (榮經) is
Hàn (漢) Yándào (嚴道).
Yùzhāng (豫章)
was the territory of Qín (秦) Zhāngjùn (鄣郡);
Emperor Gāo (高) divided it to establish Yùzhāngjùn (豫章郡).
In the east, seawater was boiled to make salt;
thus, there were no taxes, and state finances were abundant.
The historian says that Wú (吳) became strong and wealthy, leading to rebellion.

Now, Cháng (長), arrogant and overbearing,

Guānnèi Hóu (關內侯)
was the nineteenth rank of nobility.
Titles originated from the Emperor;

The Emperor severely criticized himself for this,
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: 'Zhòng' (重)

citing Guǎn (管) and Cài (蔡), as well as Qǐng Wáng (頃王) of Dài (代) and Xīngjū (興居) of Jìběi (濟北), as warnings.

Yuán Àng remonstrated:

Bān Zhì:

Yōng,

'suī.'

Xīnqī County belonged to Rǔnán Commandery.

Lǐ Xīnchuán said: Both the fourth year and the middle fourth year of Hàn Jǐng Dì had solar eclipses in the tenth month.
Now, the *Tōngjiàn* records this after summer and autumn.
Perhaps the editor extracted it from the records of signs,
without considering that in the early Hàn, the tenth month was the start of the year,
hence it was mistakenly placed at the end of the year.
I comment that Liú Gòngfù has already pointed out this error,
and the *Tōngjiàn* likely adopted it from the Basic Annals of the *Hàn Shū*.

is pronounced *yú kuàng fān*.

is pronounced *zǐ xù fān*;
the same below.
The rule of the empire ultimately does not allow private matters to disrupt public affairs.
Now, Your Majesty is ranked among the feudal lords,

violating imperial prohibitions

King Liáng was afraid,

'Your younger sister'
refers to the Empress.

Truly, a benevolent person's attitude toward his brothers

no lingering resentment,

This uses the meaning of Mèngzǐ's words.

Wáng Xìn said:
"Agreed."
He seized an opportunity to speak,
and the emperor's anger gradually subsided.
At this time,
the Empress Dowager, worried about the Liáng affair, refused to eat
and wept incessantly day and night.
The emperor was also troubled by this.
Coincidentally, Tián Shū and others, having investigated the Liáng affair, returned.
They arrived at Báchāng,
Báchāng is east of Cháng'ān.
The Kuòdì Zhì states: it is thirty-eight *lǐ* northeast of Wànnián County in Yōngzhōu.
They appeared before the emperor empty-handed.
The emperor asked:

Shū replied:
