saying:
"King Liáng was unaware;
those who engineered this
were only his favored ministers Yáng Shèng, Gōngsūn Guǐ, and their ilk.
They have already been duly executed,
and King Liáng is unharmed."
When the Empress Dowager heard this,
she immediately rose, sat down, and ate,
her spirits recovering.
Liáng Wáng (梁王) then submitted a memorial requesting an audience.
When he reached the pass,
Máo Lán (茅蘭) advised the king,
telling him to enter in a plain cloth carriage with only two attendants,
and hide in the garden of the eldest princess.
Fú Qián (服虔) said: Máo Lán (茅蘭) was
a grand master of Xiào Wáng (孝王).
Zhāng Yàn (張晏) said: A cloth carriage
indicated submission, equating oneself to a person in mourning.
The eldest princess
was Dòu Piáo (竇嫖), the Guǎntáo (館陶) eldest princess.
After the king had entered the pass,
all his chariots and cavalry remained outside,
unaware of the king's whereabouts.
The Empress Dowager wept, saying:
"The Emperor has indeed killed my son!"
The Emperor was filled with anxiety and fear.
Thereupon, Liáng Wáng (梁王) knelt before an axe and a chopping block below the palace gate to apologize.
The Empress Dowager and the Emperor were greatly pleased,
weeping together,
and relations were restored to as before.
All of the king's retinue were summoned to enter the pass.
However, the Emperor became increasingly distant from the king,
and no longer rode in the same carriage with him.
Shū (疏)
is the same as shū (疎);
the same applies below.
He was promoted to be Chancellor of Lǔ (魯).
He was the Chancellor to Lǔ Wáng Yú (魯王餘).
1 In winter,
in the eleventh month,
the offices of the Censor-in-Chief for the feudal lords were abolished.
2 In summer,
in the fourth month,
there was an earthquake.
3 There was a drought,
and the sale of alcohol was prohibited.
4 In the third month,
on the day Dīng-sì (丁巳),
Imperial Prince Chéng (乘) was enfeoffed as Qīnghé Wáng (清河王).
Gāo Dì (高帝) had established Qīnghé Jùn (清河郡) between Qí (齊) and Zhào (趙);
now it was made a kingdom.
5 In autumn,
in the ninth month,
there was a locust plague.
6 A comet appeared in the northwest.
7 On the last day of the month, Wù-xū (戊戌),
there was a solar eclipse.
8 Initially,
the Emperor had deposed Crown Prince Lì (栗),
and Zhōu Yàfū (周亞夫) had strongly argued against it,
but to no avail;
the Emperor became distant from him because of this.
And when Liáng Xiào Wáng (梁孝王) came to court,
he often spoke ill of Tiáohóu (條侯) to the Empress Dowager.
Liáng Wáng (梁王) and Tiáohóu (條侯) had a grudge,
as seen three years prior.
"The Empress's brother, Wáng Xìn (王信), can be enfeoffed as a marquis."
The Emperor declined, saying:
"Initially,
Nánpí (南皮) and Zhāngwǔ (章武),
the former Emperor did not enfeoff them.
Nánpí Hóu (南皮侯) Dòu Péngzǔ (竇彭祖) was
the son of the Empress Dowager's younger brother, Zhǎngjūn (長君);
Zhāngwǔ Hóu (章武侯) Dòu Guǎngguó (竇廣國) was
the Empress Dowager's younger brother.
The Bān Zhì (班志) records that
Nánpí (南皮) and Zhāngwǔ (章武) both belonged to Bóhǎi Jùn (勃海郡).
Xìn (信) has not yet been enfeoffed."
Empress Dowager Dòu (竇) said:
"People's lives unfold according to their time.
During the lifetime of Dòu Zhǎngjūn (竇長君),
he ultimately was not enfeoffed.
After his death,
his son Péngzǔ (彭祖) was, on the contrary, enfeoffed.
I deeply regret this!
Your Majesty should quickly enfeoff Xìn (信)."
The Emperor said:
"Please allow me to discuss this with the Chancellor."
The Emperor discussed it with the Chancellor.
Yàfū (亞夫) said:
"Gāo Huángdì (高皇帝) decreed: 'Those who are not of the Liú (劉) clan may not be kings,
and those who have not rendered meritorious service may not be marquises.'
Now, although Xìn (信) is the Empress's brother,
he has no meritorious service.
To enfeoff him as a marquis
would be contrary to the decree."
The Emperor remained silent and ceased the discussion.
Later, six Xiongnú (匈奴) kings, including Xú Lú (徐盧), surrendered.
The Emperor wished to enfeoff them to encourage others in the future.
Chancellor Yàfū (亞夫) said:
"They betrayed their lord and surrendered to Your Majesty.
If Your Majesty enfeoffs them,
then how can you admonish subjects who do not uphold their integrity?"
The Emperor said:
"The Chancellor's advice is unusable."
Thereupon, he enfeoffed Xú Lú (徐盧) and the others as marquises.
Xú Lú (徐盧) was Róngchéng Hóu (容城侯);
Cì (賜) was
Huán Hóu (桓侯);
Lù Qiáng (陸彊) was
Qiú Hóu (遒侯);
Pú Tán (僕䵣) was
Yì Hóu (易侯);
Fàn Dài (范代) was
Fànyáng Hóu (范陽侯);
Hándān (邯鄲) was
Xī Hóu (翕侯).
Tán (䵣),
Shīgǔ (師古) pronounces it Dá (怛).
In the ninth month,
on the day Wù-xū (戊戌),
Yàfū (亞夫) was dismissed;
Liú Shè (劉舍), the Táohóu (桃侯) Censor-in-Chief, was made Chancellor.
Suǒyǐn (索隱) says: Táoxiàn (桃縣) belonged to Xìndū Jùn (信都郡).
1 In summer,
there was a locust plague.
2 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the day Wù-wǔ (戊午),
there was a solar eclipse.
1 In summer,
Imperial Prince Shùn (舜) was enfeoffed as Chángshān Wáng (常山王).
Gāo Dì (高帝) had established Chángshān Jùn (常山郡),
which belonged to Zhào Guó (趙國);
Empress Lǚ (呂) divided it into a kingdom;
Emperor Wén (文) merged it into Zhào Guó (趙國);
now it was again made a kingdom for Wáng Shùn (王舜).
2 In the sixth month,
on the day Dīng-sì (丁巳),
a general amnesty was granted to the empire.
3 There was a great flood.
4 In autumn,
in the eighth month,
on the day Jǐ-yǒu (己酉),
there was a fire at the East Gate of Wèiyāng Gōng (未央宮).
5 In the ninth month,
an edict stated:
"For all doubtful cases in prisons,
even if the wording of the law leads to a conviction,
meaning that after considering the circumstances to determine guilt,
it was originally not a capital offense,
but was arbitrarily applied by legal text to achieve that result,
these cases shall be reported for review."
6 There was an earthquake.
1 In winter,
in the tenth month,
Liáng Wáng (梁王) came to court, and submitted a memorial wishing to stay;
the Emperor did not permit it.
Chǔ Shǎosūn (褚少孫) said: Feudal lords who came to court to see the Son of Heaven,
according to Hàn (漢) law, generally had four audiences: Upon arrival,
they entered
for a minor audience.
On the first day of the first month,
they presented an offering of deerskin, jade, and a jade bi to congratulate the new year,
which was a formal audience.
Three days later,
a banquet was held for the king, and he was bestowed gold, cash, and valuables.
Two days later,
he again had a minor audience
to take his leave.
The total stay in Cháng'ān (長安)
did not exceed twenty days.
A minor audience meant
a private audience within the forbidden gates,
and drinking within the palace chambers.
(The Emperor's) mood was restless and unhappy.
2 In the eleventh
month,
the titles of various officials such as Tíngwèi (廷尉) and Jiàngzuò (將作) were changed.
At this time, Tíngwèi (廷尉) was changed to Dàlǐ (大理),
Jiàngzuò Shǎofǔ (將作少府) to Dàjiàng (大匠),
Fèngcháng (奉常) to Tàicháng (太常),
Diǎnkè (典客) to Dàxíng Lìng (大行令),
Chángxìn Zhànshì (長信詹事) to Chángxìn Shǎofǔ (長信少府),
Jiāngxíng (將行) to Dàchángqiū (大長秋),
and Zhǔjué Zhōngwèi (主爵中尉) to Dūwèi (都尉).
3 In spring,
in the second month,
on the day Yǐ-mǎo (乙卯),
the Emperor journeyed to Yōng (雍)
and sacrificed at the Wǔzhì (五畤).
4 In the third month,
it snowed.
5 In summer,
in the fourth month,
Liáng Xiàowáng died.
Dòu Tàihòu heard of it,
and wept with extreme sorrow,
refusing to eat.
She said,
“The emperor has indeed killed my son!”
The emperor was saddened and fearful,
not knowing what to do.
He consulted with the Cháng Gōngzhǔ,
and then divided Liáng into five states,
appointing all five of Xiàowáng’s sons as kings: Mǎi as Liángwáng,
Míng as Jìchuānwáng,
Pénglí as Jìdōngwáng,
Dìng as Shānyángwáng,
and Bùshí as Jìyīnwáng.
Liáng continued to have Suīyáng as its capital.
The state of Jìchuān was located between Chénliú and Dōngjùn.
The state of Jìdōng later became the Hàndàhéjùn,
and later still, the Dōngpíng Guó.
Shānyáng Guó was the same as Shānyáng Jùn.
Jìyīn Guó was the same as Jìyīn Jùn.
Jì
is pronounced "zǐ lǐ fān".
When this was presented to the Tàihòu,
the Tàihòu was pleased,
and took an extra meal for the emperor.
Before Xiàowáng died,
his wealth was counted in the tens of millions.
When he died,
there were still over 400,000 catties of gold remaining in his treasury,
and other valuables in proportion.
6 The emperor had already reduced the flogging penalty,
as seen in the first year of the previous volume.
He now further reduced 300 strokes of flogging to 200,
and 200 strokes to 100.
He also standardized the regulations for the rod:
Shīgǔ said: The rod,
or cane,
is what is used for striking.
Chuí
is pronounced "zhǐ ruǐ fān".
Its base was one inch in diameter,
made of bamboo;
its tip was half an inch thick,
and all its nodes were flattened.
Those to be flogged were to be flogged on the buttocks;
Rú Chún said: This implies that before this, they were flogged on the back.
Duī
is pronounced "tú mén fān".
This was changed to spare the person.
From then on, those who were flogged survived.
However, as the death penalty was severe and the life penalties were light,
the people easily committed crimes.
7 In the sixth month,
the Xiongnú invaded Yànmén,
reached Wǔquán,
entered Shàngjùn,
and seized imperial horses.
Yànmén has the strategic passes of Gōujù.
Rú Chún said: The Hàn Yízhù states: The Tàipú managed thirty-six imperial ranches,
distributed along the northern and western borders,
with láng serving as ranch overseers,
30,000 official slaves,
and 300,000 horses.
Shīgǔ said: Wǔquán
is a county in Yúnzhōng.
Rearing birds and beasts is generally called yuàn,
hence a place for pasturing horses is called yuàn.
The Shíhuò Zhì states: Jǐngdì first created imperial ranches to expand their use.
Lǒngxī Lǐ Guǎng, as the Tàishǒu of Shàngjùn,
once went out with a hundred cavalry,
and encountered several thousand Xiongnú cavalry.
Seeing Lǐ Guǎng,
they thought he was a decoy,
a decoy being
a small force used to lure the enemy.
Yòu
is pronounced "yòu";
same below.
They ascended a hill and formed a battle array.
Shīgǔ said: They formed an array to await Lǐ Guǎng.
Chén
is read as zhèn;
same below.
Lǐ Guǎng wanted to gallop back and flee.
He said,
“I am dozens of li from the main army.
If I flee now with a hundred cavalry,
the Xiongnú will pursue and shoot us all down immediately.
If I stay now,
the Xiongnú will certainly think I am a decoy for the main army,
and will surely not dare to attack me.”
Lǐ Guǎng ordered his cavalry,
“Advance!”
Before reaching the Xiongnú array by about two li,
he stopped,
and gave the order:
“All dismount and unbridle your saddles!”
His cavalry said,
“The barbarians are many and close.
If there is an emergency,
what then?”
Lǐ Guǎng said,
“Those barbarians think we are fleeing;
having
everyone unbridle their saddles shows we are not fleeing,
which will strengthen their suspicions.”
Shīgǔ said: To show firmness, so that the enemy knows it.
A white-horse general came out
to supervise his troops.
Shīgǔ said: A general riding a white horse.
Hù
means to monitor.
Jiāng
is pronounced "jí liàng fān".
He rode with more than ten cavalry,
shot and killed the white-horse general, and returned.
Upon reaching his cavalry, he unbridled his saddle
and ordered his soldiers to release their horses and lie down.
It was then evening,
and the Hu soldiers remained suspicious,
not daring to attack.
Around midnight,
the Hu soldiers also believed that the Hàn had an ambush nearby,
intending to attack them at night,
so the Hu all withdrew their troops and left.
At dawn,
Lǐ Guǎng returned to his main army.
8 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the last day of the month, Xīnhài,
there was a solar eclipse.
9 Since the death of Zhì Dū,
many imperial relatives in and around Cháng’ān often violently violated the law.
The emperor then summoned Jìnán Dūwèi Nányáng Níng Chéng to be the Zhōngwèi.
His governance was as effective as Zhì Dū’s,
though his incorruptibility was not as great;
nevertheless, the imperial relatives and powerful figures were all terrified.
10 Chéngyáng Gòngwáng Xǐ died.
Gòngwáng Xǐ,
in the fourth year before Wéndì’s reign, succeeded his father Zhāng to the title of king,
in the eighth year, he was moved to rule Huáiyáng,
and four years later, returned to Chéngyáng.
He died at this time.
Gòng
is read as gōng.
The first year after
(Wùxū, 143 BCE)
1 In spring,
in the first month,
an edict stated:
“Prisons
are serious matters.
People vary in intelligence,
and officials in rank.
Cases with doubts should be referred to the relevant authorities for deliberation;
if the authorities cannot decide,
they are transferred to the Tíngwèi for deliberation;
and if afterward it is deemed inappropriate,
the deliberator is not considered to have erred.”
Shīgǔ said: For example, after deliberation,
if the reasoning is found to be inappropriate,
the person who deliberated is not held culpable.
Yàn
is pronounced "yú liè fān",
and also "yú jiǎn fān".
2 In the third month,
a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
3 In summer,
there was a great feast for five days,
and people were allowed to sell alcohol.
In the middle three years, the people were forbidden to sell alcohol,
now this ban is lifted.
Pú
is pronounced "pú".
4 In the fifth month,
on the day Bǐngxū,
there was an earthquake.
Shàngyōng experienced an earthquake for twenty-two days.
The Bān Zhì states that
Shàngyōng County belonged to Hànzhōng Jùn.
5 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the day Bǐngwǔ,
the Prime Minister Shě was dismissed.
6 On the last day of the month, Yǐsì,
there was a solar eclipse.
7 In the eighth month,
on the day Rénchén,
Wèi Wǎn, the Grandee Secretary, was made Chancellor,
and Zhí Bùyí of Nányáng, the Commandant of the Palace Guard, was made Grandee Secretary.
According to the Book of Surnames, he was a descendant of Zhí Gōng of Chǔ.
When Bùyí was a court gentleman,
a colleague went home on leave.
He mistakenly took the gold of another colleague.
Later, the colleague whose gold was missing became aware of its absence
and suspected Bùyí.
Shī Gǔ said: He suspected him of stealing it.
Shī Gǔ said: It means to report that he actually took it.
Afterward, the one who went home on leave arrived and returned the gold,
and the colleague whose gold was missing was greatly ashamed.
Because of this, he was praised as a magnanimous person
and gradually rose to the position of Middle Grandee.
Someone publicly slandered Bùyí.
Shī Gǔ said: Slandering him when he was present in court.
When Bùyí heard this,
he said:
“I truly have no elder brother.”
However, he never explained himself.
8 The Emperor was in the forbidden palace.
He summoned Zhōu Yàfū and offered him food,
placing only large chunks of meat (dà zì) before him,
Shī Gǔ said: Zì
means large pieces of meat.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: Cooked meat with bones cut into pieces is called yáo;
pure meat cut into pieces is called zì.
Zì,
pronounced cè lì fān.
and also did not provide chopsticks.
Yàfū felt displeased in his heart.
He looked at the supervisor of the席 (shàng xí) and asked for chopsticks.
Yīng Shào said: Shàng xí
is the one in charge of the mats.
“Is this not enough for Your Majesty?”
Mèng Kāng said: To serve chunks of meat without chopsticks, is this not insufficient for Your Majesty?
He resented him.
Rú Chún said: It was not intentionally lacking in the Emperor’s dining implements,
but accidentally overlooked.
Shī Gǔ said: Mèng’s explanation is closer.
The Emperor said, “I grant you food but do not provide chopsticks.
This is by my will.
Is there something insufficient for you?”
The Emperor said:
“Rise!”
Yàfū then hurried out.
The Emperor watched him leave and said:
“This man is discontented (yāngyāng).
He is not a minister for a young ruler.”
Not long after,
Yàfū’s son bought five hundred sets of armor and shields (jiǎ dùn) from the imperial armory (Gōngguān Shàngfāng) for his father,
which could be used for burial.
He oppressed the laborers he hired and did not pay them.
Shī Gǔ said: Yōng
refers to wages;
kǔ
means to make them suffer extremely.
I say that Yàfū’s son was ignorant.
By oppressing his workers and not paying them wages,
he caused their resentment, which brought disaster upon his father.
Although Yàfū’s death was due to Jǐngdì’s lack of kindness,
his son is also deeply blameworthy.
Resentful, the laborers reported the matter to the authorities (shàng biàn),
accusing the son,
and the affair implicated Yàfū.
When the report reached the Emperor,
Yàfū was handed over to the officials.
The officials interrogated Yàfū.
Rú Chún said: They questioned the circumstances of his statements.
Shī Gǔ said: Bó zé means
to write it down in a register and question him about each point.
Wū,
pronounced wū gù fān.
Xià,
pronounced hù jià fān.
The Emperor cursed him, saying:
“I will not use you!”
Mèng Kāng said: Meaning he would not accept his explanation, wishing to kill him.
Rú Chún said: Fearing that the prison officials might hesitate to humiliate him due to his past influence.
Shī Gǔ said: Mèng’s explanation is correct.
Another account says: The Emperor rebuked the officials,
saying they were incompetent,
“I will not use you,”
and therefore summoned Yàfū to the Grand Judge’s court.
The Grand Judge questioned him:
“Does Your Lordship intend to rebel?”
Yàfū said:
“The items your servant bought
are burial articles.
How can you call that rebellion?”
The official said:
“Even if you do not intend to rebel on the ground,
you intend to rebel underground!”
The officials’ harassment became increasingly severe.
Initially,
when the officials arrested Yàfū,
Yàfū wanted to commit suicide.
His wife stopped him,
which is why he did not die.
He was then taken to the Grand Judge’s court
and, refusing to eat for five days,
he vomited blood and died.
9 In this year,
Jìyīn Āiwáng Bùshí died.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
the earth quaked three times in one day.
2 In the third month,
the Xiongnu invaded Yànmén.
Grand Administrator Féng Jìng fought them
and died.
Chariots and elite soldiers were dispatched to garrison Yànmén.
3 In spring,
due to poor harvests,
the inner commanderies were prohibited from feeding horses with grain;
it was confiscated.
4 In summer,
in the fourth month,
an edict stated:
“Elaborate carvings and engravings
harm agricultural affairs;
brocades, embroideries, weaves, and ribbons
are detrimental to women’s work.
Yìng Shào (應劭) said: *Zuǎn* (纂),
today’s five-colored adornments,
is *cuì* (綷).
today’s sash tassels and cords, is this.
Minister Zàn (瓚) said: Xǔ Shèn (許慎) stated: *Zuǎn* (纂)
is a red ribbon.
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: Zàn (瓚)’s explanation is correct.
*Cuì* (綷)
means 'to gather';
to gather five colors
is now called 'mixed colors' (*cuò cǎi* 錯綵),
it is not *zuǎn* (纂).
*Cuì* (綷),
read *zǐ nèi* (子內) (fanqie).
*Tāo* (絛),
read *tā láo* (他牢) (fanqie).
When women’s work is harmed, it is the origin of cold.
When hunger and cold arrive together, few can avoid doing wrong.
*Wáng* (亡),
is used for the ancient character *wú* (無).
The Empress personally tends the mulberry trees
to provide grain offerings and sacrificial robes for the ancestral temple,
setting an example for the empire;
we do not accept tributes,
we reduce the provisions of the Grand Steward,
and we lighten the corvée and taxes.
We desire that the empire engage in farming and sericulture,
and maintain reserves to prepare for disasters.
The strong should not bully the weak,
the many should not oppress the few;
the aged should die of old age,
and young orphans should be able to grow to maturity.
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: *Suí* (遂)
means 'to complete'.
*Zhǎng* (長),
read *zhī liǎng* (知兩) (fanqie).
The people’s food is rather scarce,
where lies the fault?
Some, by fraud and deceit, become officials.
Zhāng Yàn (張晏) said: It means that deceitful people become officials.
Minister Zàn (瓚) said: It is what the law refers to as 'those who become officials by rectifying wrongs.'
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: Both explanations are incorrect;
it simply means falsely claiming to be an official.
They plunder the common people,
and encroach upon the myriad folk.
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: *Yú* (漁)
means acting like fishing or hunting.
Lǐ Qí (李奇) said: *Móu* (牟)
is an insect that eats the roots of sprouts.
To 'encroach and eat the people' (*qīn móu shí mín* 侵牟食民)
is likened to beetles and thieves.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: *Móu* (牟)
means 'to take'.
They are senior officials;
to violate the law in collusion with thieves,
is utterly senseless!
Lǐ Fěi (李斐) said: *Jiān fǎ* (姦法) means committing wrongdoing through the law.
Wén Yǐng (文穎) said: *Yǔ dào* (與盜) means that when thieves should be punished,
those who know the situation instead assist them,
which is no different from being a co-conspirator in theft.
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: *Yǔ dào dào zhě* (與盜盜者)
means to conspire with thieves in theft.
Those who do not attend to their official duties and cause disorder,
the Grand Chancellor shall report
and request their punishment.
Proclaim this throughout the empire,
so that all may clearly know Our intention.”
5 In the fifth month,
an edict ordered that one could obtain official positions by having four *suàn* (算) of wealth.
Fú Qián (服虔) said:
Ten thousand *qián* (錢) in wealth is one hundred and twenty *suàn* (算).
Yìng Shào (應劭) said:
In ancient times, despising the greed of officials,
one would know honor and disgrace when adequately clothed and fed.
A limit of ten *suàn* (算) of wealth was set to become an official;
ten *suàn* (算) was one hundred thousand.
Merchants with wealth could not become officials,
and upright scholars without wealth could not obtain official positions.
Therefore, the wealth requirement was reduced to four *suàn* (算) to obtain an official position.
6 In autumn,
there was a great drought.
1 In winter,
in the tenth month,
both the sun and moon were eclipsed,
and were red for five days.
2 On the last day of the twelfth month,
there was thunder;
the sun appeared purple;
the five planets retrograded and guarded the Tàiwēi (太微) enclosure;
The *Jìn Tiānwén Zhì* (晉天文志) states: Tàiwēi (太微)
is the court of the Son of Heaven,
the seats of the Five Emperors,
and the residences of the twelve feudal lords.
Its outer wall
represents the nine ministers;
the space between the two stars in the southern wall is called Duānmén (端門);
to the east is Zuǒ Zhífǎ (左執法),
symbolizing the Grand Judge;
to the west is Yòu Zhífǎ (右執法),
symbolizing the Imperial Censor-in-chief.
To the east of Zuǒ Zhífǎ (左執法)
is Zuǒ Yèmén (左掖門);
to the west of Yòu Zhífǎ (右執法)
is Yòu Yèmén (右掖門).
The four stars in the eastern wall:
the first star in the south is called Shàng Xiàng (上相),
to its north is Dōng Tàiyángmén (東太陽門);
the second star is called Cì Xiàng (次相),
to its north is Zhōnghuá Dōngmén (中華東門);
the third star is called Cì Jiàng (次將),
to its north is Dōng Tàiyīnmén (東太陰門);
the fourth star is called Shàng Jiàng (上將),
these are the so-called Four Aids.
The four stars in the western wall:
the first star is called Shàng Jiàng (上將),
to its north is Xī Tàiyángmén (西太陽門);
the second star is called Cì Jiàng (次將),
to its north is Zhōnghuá Xīmén (中華西門);
the third star is called Cì Xiàng (次相),
to its north is Xī Tàiyīnmén (西太陰門);
the fourth star is called Shàng Xiàng (上相),
these are also the Four Aids.
3 In spring,
in the first month,
an edict stated:
“Agriculture
is the foundation of the empire.
Gold, pearls, and jade
cannot be eaten when hungry,
nor worn when cold.
They are used as currency.
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: Currency
is used to facilitate trade,
and to exchange valuables.
Every few years, there may be poor harvests.
We believe that those engaged in secondary occupations are numerous,
and farmers are few.
Therefore, instruct the commanderies and states to diligently encourage agriculture and sericulture,
and to increase the planting of trees,
so that food and clothing may be obtained.
If officials deploy people or take their wages
Wéi Zhāo (韋昭) said: To deploy people means to use their labor;
to take their wages means to take their funds to hire laborers.
and are found guilty of corruption, they are treated as thieves.
If the Grand Administrator (Èrqiānshí 二千石) hears of this
and condones it, he shall share the same guilt.”
4 On the *jiǎyín* (甲寅) day,
the Crown Prince came of age.
5 On the *jiǎzǐ* (甲子) day,
the Emperor passed away in the Wèiyāng (未央) Palace.
Minister Zàn (瓚) said: He lived for forty-eight years.
He was sixteen years old.
The Empress Dowager was honored as the Grand Empress Dowager,
and the Empress as the Empress Dowager.
6 In the second month,
on the *guǐyǒu* (癸酉) day,
Emperor Xiàojǐng (孝景) was buried at Yánglíng (陽陵).
Minister Zàn (瓚) said: From his passing to his burial, it was ten days in total.
7 In the third month,
Tián Fěn (田蚡), the maternal younger brother of the Grand Empress Dowager, was enfeoffed as Wǔ’ān Hóu (武安侯).
The *Bān Zhì* (班志) states that Wǔ’ān (武安) County belonged to Wèi (魏) Commandery.
Also according to the *Gōu Xù Zhì* (溝洫志),
Fěn (蚡) was enfeoffed as Wǔ’ān (武安),
but his enfeoffed territory for sustenance was in Yú (鄃) of Qīnghé (清河).
Fěn (蚡),
read *fáng wěn* (房吻) (fanqie).
The *Shǐjì Zhèngyì* (史記正義) states: Twenty-nine *lǐ* (里) east of Wénxǐ (聞喜) County in Jiàng (絳) Prefecture, there is the old city of Zhōuyáng (周陽).

言今此時之人,
亦夏、殷、周之所馭,

傷今不然.
周、秦之敝,

掃除煩苛,

至于 Xiàowén,

Xiàojǐng 遵業.
五六十載之間,

黎民醇厚.
Shīgǔ 曰: 黎,
眾也.
醇,
不澆雜.
漢言文、景,
美矣!
2 漢興,
接秦之弊,
作業劇而財匱,
自天子不能具鈞駟,
四馬一色,
謂之鈞駟.
Shīgǔ 曰: 以牛駕車也.
余據漢時以牛車為賤,
魏、晉以後,
王公始多乘牛車.
Sū Lín 曰: 無物可蓋藏.
Gāozǔ 乃令賈人不得衣絲、乘車,
重租稅以困辱之.
Xiàohuì、Gāohòu 時,
為天下初定,
復弛商賈之律;
然市井之子孫,
亦不得仕宦為吏.
量吏祿,
度官用,
以賦於民.
Shīgǔ 曰: 纔取足.
量,
音良.
度,
徒洛翻.
自天子以至於封君湯沐邑,
皆各為私奉養焉,
不領於天子
之經費.
Shīgǔ 曰: 言各收其所賦稅以自供,
不入於國朝之倉廩府庫也.
經,
常也.
Shīgǔ 曰: 中都官,
京師諸官府也.
繼以 Xiàowén、Xiàojǐng,
清淨恭儉,
安養天下,
七十餘年之間,
國家無事,
非遇水旱之災,
民則人給家足.
都鄙廩庾皆滿,
而府庫餘貨財;
京師之錢累鉅萬,
貫朽而不可校;
Shīgǔ 曰: 累巨萬,
謂數百萬萬也.
校,
謂計數也.
Shīgǔ 曰: 陳,
謂久舊也.
至腐敗不可食.
眾庶街巷有馬,
而阡陌之間成壠,
Shīgǔ 曰: 謂田中之阡陌也.
Mèng Kāng 曰: 皆乘父馬,
有牝馬間其間則踶齧,
故斥出不得會同.
Shīgǔ 曰: 言時富饒,
恥乘字牝,
不必以其踶齧也.
為吏者長子孫,
Rú Chún 曰: 時無事,
吏不數轉,
至于生長子孫而不轉職也.
長,
知兩翻.
Rú Chún 曰: 《貨殖傳》倉氏、庫氏是也.
先行義而後詘
辱焉.
Shīgǔ 曰: 以行義為先,
以愧辱相絀也.
行,
下孟翻.
罔疏而民富,
役財驕溢,
或至兼併、豪黨之徒,
以武斷於鄉曲.
Shīgǔ 曰: 恃其豪富則擅行威罰也.
斷,
丁亂翻.
Shīgǔ 曰: 謂國之宗姓受封邑土地者也.
爭於奢侈,
室廬、輿服僭於上,
無限度.
物盛而衰,
固其變也;
自是之後,
Xiàowǔ 內窮侈靡,
外攘夷狄,
天下蕭然,
財力耗矣!

Jiànyuán 元年
(辛丑、前一四〇)自古帝王未有年號,
始起於此.
Gòngfù 曰: 《封禪書》云:
「其後三年,

所謂
「其後三年」
者,
蓋盡 Yuánshòu 六年至 Yuándǐng 三年也.
然 Yuándǐng 四年方得寶鼎,
又無緣先三年稱之.
以此而言,
自 Yuándǐng 以前之年,
皆有司所追命;
其實年號之起在 Yuándǐng,
故 Yuánfēng 改元則始有詔書也.
十月,
詔舉賢良方正直言極諫之士,
上親策問以古今治道,
對者百餘人.
Guǎngchuān Dǒng Zhòngshū 對曰:
「道者,
所繇適於治之路也,
Shīgǔ 曰: 繇,
從也.
適,
往也.
治,
直吏翻.
繇,
古由字.
皆其具也.
故聖王已沒,
而子孫長久,
安寧數百歲,
此皆禮樂教化之功也.
夫人君莫不欲安存,
而政亂國危者甚眾;
所任者非其人而所繇者非其道,
是以政日以僕滅也.
夫 Zhōu Dào 衰於 Yōu、Lì,
非道亡也,
Yōu、Lì 不繇也.
至于 Xuānwáng,
思昔先王之德,
興滯補敞,
明文、武之功業,
周道粲然復興,
此夙夜不懈行善之所致也.
Kǒngzǐ 曰: “It is man that can make the Way great;
it is not the Way that can make man great.”
Shīgǔ said: The Analects record Kǒngzǐ’s words.
It means that intelligent people can practice the Way;
if one does not possess the inner quality,
one will not be transformed by the Way.
If Heaven’s mandate is not bestowed,
it cannot be reversed;
what they hold to is perverse and mistaken,
losing its proper order.
For a ruler,
by rectifying one’s mind, one rectifies the court;
by rectifying the court, one rectifies the hundred officials;
by rectifying the hundred officials, one rectifies the myriad people;
by rectifying the myriad people, one rectifies the four directions.
When the four directions are rectified,
those near and far dare not fail to be unified in righteousness,
and there will be no evil influences or treachery among them.
Thus, yin and yang are harmonious and wind and rain are timely,
all living things flourish in harmony and the myriad people thrive,
all things that bring blessings,
and auspicious omens that can be brought about,
all arrive without fail,
and the Kingly Way is complete!
Kǒngzǐ 曰: “The phoenix does not arrive,
the Yellow River does not bring forth its chart;
it is all over for me!”
The Analects record Kǒngzǐ’s words.
And his status was humble and lowly, preventing him from bringing them about.
Shīgǔ said: The phoenix and the River Chart
are all auspicious omens for a king.
Zhòngní sighed that he possessed virtue but lacked a position,
hence they did not appear.
To possess the wealth of the four seas,
to occupy a position that can bring these about,
to wield power that can bring these about,
and also to have the ability to bring these about;
with lofty conduct and profound benevolence,
clear understanding and noble intentions,
loving the people and fond of scholars,
one can be called a righteous ruler.
Yet, if Heaven and Earth do not respond and no beautiful auspicious signs arrive,
why is this?
It is all because moral education is not established and the myriad people are not rectified.
The myriad people’s pursuit of profit
is like water flowing downwards;
if not dammed and prevented by moral education,
it cannot be stopped.
The ancient kings were clear about this,
therefore, when facing south to govern the world,
none failed to make moral education their most important task.
They established the Grand Academy to teach in the state,
and set up xiáng and xù schools to transform the districts.
The Xuéjì says: In ancient education,
a family had its shú,
a xiáng in the xiǎng,
then an xù in the suì,
and a xué in the state.
They guided the people with righteousness,
and regulated the people with propriety.
Thus, their punishments were very light, yet prohibitions were not violated,
because moral education was effective and customs were beautiful.
When a sage king succeeded a chaotic age,
he swept away its traces and completely removed them,
then revived and promoted moral education.
Once moral education was clear,
and customs were established,
descendants would follow them.
Shīgǔ said: Xún
means to follow;
to follow and practice it.
Qín abolished the Way of the former sages,
and adopted a makeshift governance.
Therefore, it lasted fourteen years and perished.
Counting from Shǐhuáng’s initial unification of the world,
until its demise, was fourteen years.
This made customs shallow and evil,
and the people stubborn and ignorant,
defiant, disrespectful, and rebellious,
rotten to such an extreme.
Wényǐng said: Gǎn
means to rush out.
Shīgǔ said: Those whose mouths do not speak loyal and trustworthy words are yín,
and those whose hearts do not conform to the principles of virtue and righteousness are wán.
Dǐ
means to collide.
Mào
means to transgress.
Shū
means to sever.
Hǎn
means to resist.
Yín,
pronounced yú jīn.
Mào,
pronounced as written,
also pronounced mò kè.
For extreme cases, they must be untied and re-strung,
then they can be played;
for governance that is ineffective,
for extreme cases, it must be changed and reformed,
then it can be put in order.
Therefore, since Hàn gained the world,
it has always wished to govern well, yet until today it cannot be governed well,
this is due to failing to reform when reform was necessary.
Your servant heard that when sage kings governed the world,
From this point downwards,
it belongs to the second strategy.
Those of greater ability were placed in positions,
meaning they were given positions to test their abilities.
Shǎo,
pronounced shī zhǎo.
Zhǎng,
pronounced zhī liǎng.
Punishments were used to deter their evil,
thus the people understood propriety and righteousness and were ashamed to offend their superiors.
Wǔwáng practiced great righteousness,
pacified the cruel and wicked,
and Zhōugōng created rites and music to civilize them.
During the flourishing era of Chéng and Kāng,
the prisons were empty for over forty years.
The Éryǎ says:
[Liú Xī]
Lǐng means to lead;
Yǔ means to restrain;
to lead and record prisoners for confinement and restraint.
The Lǐjì Zhèngyì says: Chóngjīng asked:
“A prison,
Zhōu called it yuántǔ,
Yīn called it Yǒulǐ,
Xià called it jūntái;
what era does língyǔ belong to?”
Jiāoshì answered:
“The Yuèlìng
and Qínshū
refer to prison names.
Hàn called it Ruòlú,
Wèi called it Sīkōng;
such are they.”
This too was a gradual influence of moral education and a flow of benevolence and righteousness,
not merely the effect of physical harm.
But Qín was not like this.
They followed the laws of Shēn Bùhài and Shāng Yāng,
who were Shēn Bùhài and Shāng Yāng.
They abhorred the Way of emperors and kings,
adopting greed and avarice as custom.
Shīgǔ said: Wolves are all greedy,
therefore greedy people are called "greedy wolves."
Shīgǔ said: Zhū
means to blame.
Thus, all officials adorned themselves with empty words and disregarded reality,
outwardly showing the etiquette of serving the ruler,
but inwardly harboring intentions to betray their superiors,
fabricating falsehoods and embellishing deception,
shamelessly pursuing profit.
Therefore, those punished were extremely numerous,
and those who died were seen everywhere,
yet treachery did not cease,
as custom and transformation made it so.
Now Your Majesty has unified the world,
and all submit,
yet the achievements do not benefit the common people;
perhaps the king’s heart has not yet been applied.
Zēngzǐ said: “If one honors what one has heard,
one becomes lofty and enlightened;
if one acts upon what one knows,
one becomes glorious and great.
To be lofty and enlightened, glorious and great,
does not lie in anything else,
but in the intention to apply oneself.”
Shīgǔ said: This is from Zēngzǐ’s writings.
Zēngzǐ was Zēng Shēn.
If one is truly sincere within and acts upon it,
then how would one differ from the Three Kings?
To seek out the worthy without first cultivating scholars
is like seeking beautiful patterns without first carving jade.
Therefore, the greatest means of cultivating scholars
is none other than the Tài-Xuē (太學);
the Tài-Xuē
is where worthy scholars are selected.
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: Guān (關)
means "from."
Now, with the multitude of an entire commandery or kingdom responding,
there are none who answer the call of the "shū" (書).
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: Shū (書)
refers to the imperial edicts for recommending worthy and learned individuals.
Wáng (亡)
is interchangeable with the ancient character wú (無);
the same applies below.
Your servant wishes that Your Majesty would establish the Tài-Xuē (太學),
appoint enlightened teachers,
to cultivate the scholars of the realm,
and frequently examine and question them to fully discover their talents,
then the brilliant and outstanding can surely be obtained.
The present commandery governors (Jùn-Shǒu 郡守) and county magistrates (Xiàn-Lìng 縣令)
are the teachers and leaders of the people,
tasked with upholding traditions and propagating enlightenment.
Therefore, if the teachers and leaders are not worthy,
the ruler's virtue will not be proclaimed,
and his benevolence will not flow.
Now, officials not only lack instruction for the people below,
but some also fail to implement the laws of the sovereign above.
They tyrannize the common people,
engage in illicit dealings.
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: This means that when petty officials engage in fraud,
the governors and magistrates do not expose them,
but instead trade with them to seek profit.
The wronged and suffering lose their positions,
which greatly displeases Your Majesty.
This is why the Yīn (陰) and Yáng (陽) are in disharmony,
malefic qi (qì 氣) fills the air,
all things are born but few succeed,
and the common people are not saved.
All this is due to the lack of discernment of the senior officials!
Senior officials (zhǎng-lì 長吏) mostly come from among the Lang-Zhōng (郎中), Zhōng-Láng (中郎), and the children of officials of two thousand dàndàn (dàn 石).
The selection of Lang-Lì (郎吏) is also based on wealth,
not necessarily on worthiness.
Moreover, what the ancients called "merit"
was determined by holding office and fulfilling one's duties,
not by accumulating days and duration.
Thus, a person of small talent, even if they accumulate days,
will not depart from a small office.
A worthy person, even if they have not served long,
is not hindered from becoming an assistant.
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: Hài (害)
means "hinder."
Lí (離),
read as lì zhì (力智).
They should diligently attend to their duties and strive for merit.
Today, this is not the case.
One attains nobility by accumulating days,
and obtains office by prolonged service.
This causes integrity (lián-chǐ 廉恥) to be confused and disordered,
the worthy and unworthy to be mixed and indistinct,
and the true talent not to be obtained.

Your servant humbly believes that if all the enfeoffed nobles (liè-hóu 列侯), commandery governors (jùn-shǒu 郡守), and officials of two thousand dàndàn (dàn 石) were to each select two of their worthy subordinates (lì-mín 吏民)
and offer them annually to serve in the imperial guard (sù-wèi 宿衞),
this would also be a way to observe the abilities of the high ministers.
Those who recommend worthy individuals
would be rewarded,
and those who recommend unworthy individuals
would be punished.
If this were done,
all officials of two thousand dàndàn (dàn 石) would wholeheartedly seek out the worthy,
and the talented individuals of the realm could be appointed to office and employed.
Grant them office and employ them.
Then the flourishing age of the Sān-Wáng (三王) would be easy to achieve,
and the reputation of Yáo (堯) and Shùn (舜) could be matched.
Do not take days and months as merit;
instead, truly test the worthy and able as the priority.
Assign offices according to ability,
and determine positions based on virtue.
Then integrity (lián-chǐ 廉恥) and disgrace will take separate paths,
and the worthy and unworthy will be in different places!
Your servant has heard that many small things make a multitude,
and accumulating small things leads to greatness.
From this point onwards,
it belongs to the third strategy.
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: Jù (鉅)
means "great."
Àn (晻)
is the ancient character for àn (暗).
Therefore, Yáo (堯) began among the feudal lords,
and Shùn (舜) rose from the deep mountains.
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: Yáo (堯) here
refers to his ascent from Marquis of Táng (Táng-Hóu 唐侯) to the position of Son of Heaven.
Mèng Kāng (孟康) says: Shùn (舜) tilled fields at Lì-Shān (歷山).
There was a gradual process by which this was achieved.
Words spoken from oneself
cannot be stopped.
Actions initiated by oneself
cannot be concealed.
Speech and action
are the greatest elements of governance,
by which a noble person (jūn-zǐ 君子) moves heaven and earth.
Therefore, one who perfects the small becomes great;
one who is careful in the subtle becomes manifest.
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: One who can perfect many small things
will achieve greatness;
one who can be careful in the subtle
will have their goodness clearly manifested.
It is like a person growing taller day by day without others realizing it.
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: Cháng (長)
refers to the length of a person's body,
from childhood to adulthood.
It is like a fire consuming wax without people seeing it.
This is why Táng (唐) and Yú (虞) obtained excellent reputations, while Jié (桀) and Zhòu (紂) are to be lamented and feared.
To be joyful but not chaotic,
to return but not be weary—
this is called the Dào (道).
The Dào (道)
is imperishable for ten thousand generations.
Perishability
is a deviation from the Dào (道).
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: It means that if there is perishability, it is not the Dào (道),
but rather it arises from losing the Dào (道).
Wáng (亡)
is interchangeable with the ancient character wú (無);
the same applies below.
There must be partial and inactive areas,
so government policies become unclear and ineffective.
One only needs to address these partial aspects to remedy their failings.
The Dào (道) of the Sān-Wáng (三王)
had different ancestors,
but they were not contradictory.
They intended to rectify excesses and support decline,
which was dictated by the changes they encountered.
Jiù (捄)
is the same as jiù (救).
They reformed the calendar and the beginning of the year,
and changed the color of ceremonial robes,
simply to comply with the mandate of Heaven.
As for the rest, they all followed the Dào (道) of Yáo (堯);
why make further changes?
Therefore, rulers have the name of reformulating systems,
but no reality of changing the Dào (道).
However, the Xià (夏) dynasty valued loyalty,
the Yīn (殷) dynasty valued reverence,
and the Zhōu (周) dynasty valued refinement.
This was the appropriate remedy for what they inherited.
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: Jì (繼)
refers to the succession from previous generations.
Jiù (捄)
refers to remedying its flaws.
What was added or subtracted is discernable.
The Zhōu (周) dynasty followed the rites of the Yīn (殷) dynasty;
what was added or subtracted is discernable.
And for those who succeed the Zhōu (周),
even after a hundred generations, this can be known.
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: This is recorded as the words of Kǒng-Zǐ (孔子) in the Lún-Yǔ (論語).

Nevertheless, the Xiongnú (匈奴) feared Lǐ Guǎng (李廣)'s strategy,

This means that managing a multitude without laws

Lǐ Guǎng (李廣) as a general
allowed everyone to do as they pleased.
Given Lǐ Guǎng (李廣)'s talent,
this might have been acceptable;
but it cannot be taken as a model.
Why not?
Because his successors would find it difficult;
much less those who were generals at the same time as him!
The nature of small-minded people

Since they regarded Chéng Bùshí (程不識) as bothersome and preferred to follow Lǐ Guǎng (李廣),

Thus, it is said,

As for a general,

So, if one emulates Chéng Bùshí (程不識),

if one emulates Lǐ Guǎng (李廣),

'In the second year of Jiànyuán, Máolíng yì was first established,'
and 'In the third year, money was granted to those relocated to Máolíng.'
At that time, Wèi Qīng and Gōngsūn Hóng were not yet prominent.
Moreover,
'In the second year of Yuánsò, the powerful figures from the commanderies and states were moved to Máolíng.'
This is therefore the time when Guō Jiě was moved."
Bān Gù 曰 (said): In ancient times, the Son of Heaven established states,
feudal lords established households,
from ministers and grand masters down to common people,
each had their ranks and distinctions.
Thus, the people served their superiors, and inferiors had no covetous desires.
Shī Gǔ 曰 (said):
Jì (覬),
means to hope for;
Yú (覦),
means to desire;
to hope to obtain what one desires.
Jì (覬),
pronounced as Jì.
Yú (覦),
pronounced as Yú,
also pronounced as Yù.
Rites and music, and punitive expeditions, emanated from the feudal lords.
After Huán (桓) and Wén (文),
grand masters held power for generations,
and subordinate ministers wielded authority.
Shī Gǔ 曰 (said): Péi (陪),
means secondary or subordinate.
Grand masters holding power for generations refers to
the Six Ministers of Jìn (晉), the Three Huán (桓) of Lǔ (魯), and the Tián (田) clan of Qí (齊).
Subordinate ministers wielding authority refers to
the likes of Yáng Hǔ (陽虎).
The vassals of a feudal lord
were considered subordinate ministers to the Son of Heaven;
the retainers of a grand master
were considered subordinate ministers to a feudal lord.
Forming alliances and intricate networks of influence,
this led to the princes of various states –
Wèi (魏) had Xìnlíng (信陵),
Zhào (趙) had Píngyuán (平原),
Qí (齊) had Mèngcháng (孟嘗),
Chǔ (楚) had Chūnshēn (春申) –
all leveraging the power of kings and dukes,
competing to become roving knights-errant.
The matter of "cock crows and dog thieves"
is seen in Volume 3, during the 17th year of King Nǎn (赧).
And Zhào (趙) Chancellor Yú Qīng (虞卿),
abandoned his state and deserted his lord
to assist Wèi Qí (魏齊) in his dire straits, brought on by poverty;
the matter is seen in Volume 5, during the 56th year of King Nǎn (赧) of Zhōu (周).
(There was also) the case of (Xìnlíng Jūn) secretly appropriating a tally and falsely issuing an order,
executing a general and monopolizing the army
to rescue Píngyuán (平原) from his predicament;
the matter is seen in Volume 5, during the 57th year of King Nǎn (赧).
Jiàng (將),
pronounced as Liàng (亮).
(These men) achieved widespread fame,
and those who talked with admiration, wringing their wrists,
referred to the Four Grandees as their chief representatives.
At this point, the doctrine of "betraying the public and dying for one's faction" prevailed,
while the principle of "upholding one's duty and serving one's superiors" was abandoned.
When the Hàn (漢) dynasty arose,
the prohibitions and laws were lax and broad,
and there was no effort to rectify this.
For this reason, Chén Xī (陳豨), the Chancellor of Dài (代), traveled with a thousand chariots,
and Wú Bì (吳濞) and Huáinán (淮南) both recruited thousands of retainers;
powerful maternal relatives and high ministers, such as Wèiqí (魏其) and Wǔ'ān (武安), competed fiercely in the capital,
while common roving knights-errant, like Jù Mèng (劇孟) and Guō Jiě (郭解), galloped through the villages and alleys, their power extending across regions,
able to defy dukes and marquises.
The common people glorified their names and deeds,
coveting and admiring them.
Even if they fell into criminal punishment,
they considered it achieving fame by sacrificing their lives,
like Jì Lù (季路) and Qiú Mù (仇牧),
who died without regret.
Jì Lù (季路) died in the calamity of Marquis Zhé (輒) of Wèi (衞).
Qiú Mù (仇牧) died in the calamity of Duke Mǐn (閔) of Sòng (宋).
Both matters are seen in the Zuǒ Zhuàn (左傳).
"When the superior loses the Way,
the people have been dispersed for a long time."
Seen in the Lún Yǔ (論語).
If they are shown what to like and dislike,
and regulated by rites and laws,
how can the people know what is forbidden and return to the right path!
According to the ancient correct law: The Five Hegemons
were criminals of the Three Kings;
and the Six States
were criminals of the Five Hegemons;
these Four Grandees
were moreover criminals of the Six States.
How much more so the likes of Guō Jiě (郭解),
who, as mere commoners,
usurped the power of life and death,
their crimes already intolerable of leniency.
Observing them, they were gentle and kind, widely benevolent,
aiding the poor and helping the distressed,
humble and not boastful,
indeed all possessing extraordinary qualities.
What a pity!
Not entering into the Way and virtue,
they merely indulged in deviant trends,
leading to their own deaths and the destruction of their clans—
this was no misfortune.
Xún Yuè (荀悅) discussed, saying: The world has three types of wanderers,
who are the thieves of virtue: The first is Yóuxiá (遊俠) (roving knights-errant),
the second is Yóushuì (遊說) (itinerant persuaders),
and the third is Yóuxíng (遊行) (itinerant schemers).
Those who establish their influence and power,
create awe and blessings,
and form private connections to become strong in the world
are called Yóuxiá (遊俠);
those who embellish their arguments,
devise deceptive schemes,
and rush throughout the world to seize opportunities and power
are called Yóushuì (遊說);
those who feign benevolence to conform to popular tastes,
gather factions and cliques,
and establish false reputations to gain influence
are called Yóuxíng (遊行).
These three
are the source from which disorder arises;
they harm the Way and damage virtue,
corrupt laws and delude the world,
and were matters of caution for the former kings.
The state has four classes of people,
each cultivating their own occupation;
those who do not follow the occupations of the four classes
are called traitorous people.
The four classes are
scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants.
Only then can the kingly way be achieved.
All these three types of wanderers arose
in later generations,
especially prevalent at the end of the Zhōu (周) and Qín (秦) dynasties.
When superiors are not enlightened,
inferiors are not upright,
institutions are not established,
and the governing principles are lax and abandoned;
when praise and blame determine honor and disgrace, without verifying their truth;
when love and hate determine benefit and harm, without discussing their reality;
when joy and anger determine rewards and punishments, without examining their reason.
Superiors and inferiors deceive each other,
all affairs are askew and erroneous,
thus those who speak calculate advantage and disadvantage before uttering words,
those who make selections measure closeness and distance before putting pen to paper,
good and evil are confused by popular opinion,
and merits and crimes are mixed up with the king's law.
In such circumstances, benefit cannot be sought through righteousness,
nor can harm be avoided through the Way.
For this reason, noble persons transgress rites,
and common people violate laws,
rushing and galloping about,
overstepping their duties and exceeding their stations,
adorning superficiality and abandoning substance,
competing to pursue timely gains.
They disregard the respect due to fathers and elders,
but elevate the rituals for guests;
they treat the kindness of family lightly,
but are devoted to the love of friends;
they forget the Way of self-cultivation,
but seek the praise of the multitude;
they cut back on their livelihood to provide for lavish feasts and entertainment.
Gifts and offerings fill their courtyards,
and visits and inquiries crisscross the roads.
Wrapping is called Bāo (苞),
using mats is called Jū (苴).
The commentary on the Shī Jīan (詩箋) says: Those who present fruits as gifts are called Bāojū (苞苴).
It also says: Bāojū (苞苴) means
wrapping fish and meat,
either with reeds
or with straw.
The commentary on the Zuǒ Zhuàn (左傳) says: Pìn (聘) means
holding jade and silk to make mutual inquiries.
Private affairs outweigh public duties,
thus corrupt customs are formed and the righteous Way is corrupted.
Therefore, when a sagely king is in power,
he manages the state and orders the people,
correcting its institutions;
good and evil are judged by merits and crimes, and not swayed by praise or blame.
He listens to their words and demands accountability for their actions,
he names them and points to their reality.
Therefore, when the reality does not match the reputation, it is called emptiness (xū);
when the inner feelings do not cover the outer appearance, it is called falsehood (wěi);
when praise and blame lose their truth, it is called slander (wū);
when words and deeds lose their proper category, it is called deception (wǎng).
Empty and false conduct cannot be established,
slanderous and deceptive words cannot be practiced.
Those with crimes and transgressions have no hope of escape,
and those without crimes and transgressions do not fear.
Petitions and requests have no effect,
Qǐng (請) means
to seek.
Yè (謁) means
to report.
Superficial expressions are curbed,
extravagant rhetoric is removed,
false arguments are prohibited,
excessive cleverness is abolished,
the chaos of the Hundred Schools is banished,
and the supreme Way of the sages is unified.
When people are nurtured with benevolence and kindness,
and refined with rites and music,
then customs will be settled and great transformation will be achieved.
7 Yān Wáng Dìngguó (燕王定國) committed incest with his father, Kāng Wáng (康王), and his concubine;
he seized his younger brother's wife as a concubine.
He killed the magistrate of Féirú (肥如), a man from Yǐng (郢).
Féirú (肥如)
was a dependent county of Yān (燕).
The kingdom of Yān (燕) was abolished,
absorbed into Hàn (漢),
and became part of Liáoxī (遼西) Commandery.
Yìng Shào (應劭) said: "Féizǐ (肥子) fled to Yān (燕),
and Yān (燕) was enfeoffed here."
Zhǔfù Yǎn (主父偃) was instrumental in uncovering these matters.
The high officials and ministers requested Dìngguó's (定國) execution.
The emperor granted it.
Dìngguó (定國) committed suicide,
and the kingdom was abolished.
In the early years of Wén Dì (文帝),
Wáng Zé (王澤) was first enfeoffed as King of Yān (燕).
He was succeeded by his son, Kāng Wáng Jiā (康王嘉).
In the ninth year of Wén Dì (文帝),
Jiā (嘉) died,
and Dìngguó (定國) succeeded him.
He had reigned for forty-two years.
Qí Lì Wáng Cìchāng (齊厲王次昌) also had an affair with his elder sister, the princess Jì Wēngzhǔ (紀翁主).
Qí Xiào Wáng Jiānglǘ (齊孝王將閭)
was enfeoffed in the sixteenth year of Wén Dì (文帝).
He was succeeded by his son, Yì Wáng Shòu (懿王壽),
and Shòu (壽) was succeeded by Cìchāng (次昌).
Qí Jì Tàihòu (齊紀太后) disapproved.
Yǎn (偃) then spoke to the emperor, saying:
"Qí Línzī (齊臨菑) has a hundred thousand households,
market taxes of a thousand catties of gold,
and a prosperous and numerous population,
larger than Cháng'ān (長安).
Unless one is the emperor's own brother or beloved son,
one should not rule this kingdom.
Now, the King of Qí (齊) is increasingly distant in kinship.
'Shū' (疏)
is the same as 'shū' (疎).
I request that he be investigated!"
Thereupon, the emperor appointed Yǎn (偃) as the Chancellor of Qí (齊),
and also to rectify the situation.
When Yǎn (偃) arrived in Qí (齊),
he promptly investigated the eunuchs in the king's inner palace.
Their testimony implicated the king.
The king, in fear,
drank poison and committed suicide.
In his youth, Yǎn (偃) traveled through Qí (齊), Yān (燕), and Zhào (趙).
When he became powerful,
he caused the downfall of Yān (燕) and Qí (齊) consecutively.
Zhào Wáng Péngzǔ (趙王彭祖) was afraid.
Péngzǔ (彭祖)
was Jǐng Dì's (景帝) son;
two years earlier, he was enfeoffed as Guǎngchuān (廣川),
and five years later, he was moved to Zhào (趙).
Because of this, many sons and younger brothers of the feudal lords were able to be enfeoffed.
When the King of Qí (齊) committed suicide,
the emperor heard about it
and was greatly angered.
He believed that Yǎn (偃) had coerced the king into committing suicide,
so he summoned him and handed him over to the officials.
Yǎn (偃) admitted to having accepted gold from the feudal lords,
but denied coercing the king into suicide.
The emperor wanted to spare him from execution,
but Gōngsūn Hóng (公孫弘) said:
"The King of Qí (齊) committed suicide
without an heir.
The kingdom was abolished, becoming a commandery and absorbed into Hàn (漢).
Zhǔfù Yǎn (主父偃) was fundamentally the chief culprit.
If Your Majesty does not execute Yǎn (偃),
there will be no way to appease the world."
Thus, Zhǔfù Yǎn (主父偃) was exterminated with his clan.
8 Zhāng Ōu (張歐) was dismissed.
The emperor wanted to appoint Liǎohóu Kǒng Zāng (蓼侯孔臧) as Grandee Secretary (Yùshǐ Dàfū).
Zāng (臧) declined, saying:
"My family has for generations made classical studies its profession.
I beg to be appointed Grand Master of Sacrifices (Tàicháng),
to oversee my family's profession,
along with my cousin, the Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) Ānguó (安國),
Hundred Officials' Table: Shìzhōng (侍中)
is an additional office,
allowing entry and exit from the Forbidden Palace.
Yìng Shào (應劭) said: 'They attend the Son of Heaven,
hence called Shìzhōng (侍中).'
The Xù Hànshū (續漢書) says: 'Shìzhōng (侍中) ranks equivalent to two thousand piculs,
with no fixed number.'
The Hàn Guānyí (漢官儀) says: 'Shìzhōng (侍中) wears left cicada and right sable ornaments;
originally they were Qin chancellors' clerks,
who went in and out of the palace halls,
hence called Shìzhōng (侍中).
They were in charge of the emperor's carriage and apparel,
down to intimate items like the urinal (hǔzǐ).
During Wǔ Dì's (武帝) time,
Kǒng Ānguó (孔安國) was a Shìzhōng (侍中).
As a scholar,
he was specially permitted to manage the imperial spittoon on the throne,
which the court considered an honor.'
Cóng (從),
pronounced Cái Yòng (才用) fan.
so that it may forever be passed down to our descendants."
The emperor then appointed Zāng (臧) as Grand Master of Sacrifices (Tàicháng),
bestowing upon him the same courtesies as the Three Ducal Ministers (Sān Gōng).
1 In winter,
the Xiongnú (匈奴) Chányú (單于) Jūnchén (軍臣) died.
His younger brother, the Left Gǔlí Wáng (左谷蠡王) Yīzhìxié (伊稚斜), established himself as Chányú (單于).
Among the Xiongnú (匈奴), the Left and Right Gǔlí Wáng (谷蠡王)
were below the Left and Right Xián Wáng (賢王).
Gǔlí (谷蠡)
is pronounced Lùlí (鹿黎).
Suǒyǐn (索隱) says: "Zhì (稚),
pronounced Chí Lì (持利) fan.
Xié (斜),
pronounced Shì Jiē (士嗟) fan.
Zōu Dànshēng (鄒誕生) pronounced it Zhí Yá (直牙) fan.
Probably
'Yīzhìxié' (稚斜)
is a Xiongnú (匈奴) word,
which approximates its true meaning."
Yú Dān (於單) fled and surrendered to Hàn (漢).
2 Gōngsūn Hóng (公孫弘) was appointed Grandee Secretary (Yùshǐ Dàfū).
At this time,
the southwest Yi (西南夷) were being opened up,
Cānghǎi (蒼海) Commandery was established in the east,
and Shuòfāng (朔方) Commandery was built in the north.
Gōngsūn Hóng (公孫弘) repeatedly remonstrated,
believing that exhausting the central plains to serve useless lands
was unwise, and he wished to abolish these projects.
The emperor sent Zhū Mǎchén (朱買臣) and others to argue the benefits of establishing Shuòfāng (朔方),
presenting ten arguments.
Hóng (弘) could not refute a single one.
Shīgǔ (師古) says: "He spoke of ten points of its advantages and disadvantages,
and Hóng (弘) had nothing to respond with."
Nán (難),
pronounced Nǎi Dàn (乃旦) fan.
"[As] a rustic from Shāndōng (山東),
I was unaware of such benefits.
I wish to abandon the southwest Yi (西南夷) and Cānghǎi (蒼海),
and concentrate on maintaining Shuòfāng (朔方)."
The emperor then agreed.
In spring,
Cānghǎi (蒼海) Commandery was abolished.
Hóng (弘) used quilts made of plain cloth
and did not eat meat more than once (or did not eat multiple meats at one meal).
It means not having multiple meat dishes.
Zhòng (重),
pronounced Zhí Lóng (直龍) fan.
"[They said:] Hóng (弘)'s position is among the Three Ducal Ministers (Sān Gōng),
and his salary is very generous;
yet he uses plain cloth quilts –
this is deception."
The emperor asked Hóng (弘).
Hóng (弘) apologized, saying:
"It is true.
Among the Nine Ministers (Jiǔ Qīng), no one is closer to me than Àn (黯).
Yet today, he publicly rebuked me in court,
truly hitting my weak point.
Indeed, for a Three Ducal Minister (Sān Gōng) to use plain cloth quilts
is no different from a petty official,
truly an act of feigning and deception,
intended to gain fame.
Shīgǔ (師古) says: 'Diào' (釣),
means 'to obtain';
it refers to the act of fishing.
Moreover, without Jí Àn's (汲黯) loyalty,
how could Your Majesty hear such words!"
The emperor considered him modest and humble,
and increasingly held him in high esteem.
3 In the third month,
a general amnesty was declared.
4 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the bǐngzǐ (丙子) day,
the Xiongnú (匈奴) crown prince Yú Dān (於單) was enfeoffed as Shè'ān Hóu (涉安侯).
He died a few months later.
5 Initially,
a Xīongnú defector said:
“The Yuèzhī’s former abode was between Dūnhuáng and Qílíán.
They were a powerful nation.
Mòdú Chányú of the Xīongnú attacked and defeated them.
Lǎoshàng Chányú killed the Yuèzhī king,
and used his head as a drinking vessel.
The remaining multitudes fled far away,
resenting the Xīongnú,
and having no one to jointly attack them with.”
The Emperor sought someone who could be an envoy to the Yuèzhī.
Zhāng Qiān of Hànzhōng, as a Láng, answered the call,
departing from Lǒngxī,
passing through the Xīongnú territory.
The Chányú captured him,
detaining Qiān for over ten years.
Qiān found an opportunity to escape,
heading west towards the Yuèzhī,
and after several tens of days,
he reached Dàyuān.
The *Xīyù Chuán* states: The Kingdom of Dàyuān is governed from Guìshān City,
12,570 *lǐ* from Cháng’ān;
to the southwest, it is 690 *lǐ* to where the Dà Yuèzhī reside.
Wǎn,
read as yú yuán.
Though they wished to establish communication, they could not,
but upon seeing Qiān,
they rejoiced
and provided guides and interpreters to reach Kāngjū.
A guide
is one who leads the way;
an interpreter
is one who conveys words.
The Kingdom of Kāngjū is governed from Lèyuè’nìdì,
which is also Bēitián City,
12,300 *lǐ* from Cháng’ān.
Wéi,
read as yú wěi.
The Dà Yuèzhī crown prince became king.
Having already attacked Dàxià,
they divided its territory and settled there.
The Kingdom of Dàxià was southwest of Dàyuān,
its capital south of the Guīshǔi.
The Yuèzhī resided north of the Guīshǔi.
They suffered few raids,
and had absolutely no desire to avenge themselves against the Hú.
Qiān stayed for over a year,
but ultimately could not obtain the Yuèzhī’s core intent.
Lǐ Qí said: Yàolǐng
means the essential agreement.
Shī Gǔ said: Yào
refers to the waist of a garment;
lǐng
refers to the collar of a garment.
Anyone holding a garment grasps it by the waist and collar;
it means Qiān could not grasp the Yuèzhī’s true intentions,
having nothing to bring back to Hàn,
hence the metaphor of *yàolǐng*.
Yào,
read as yī yáo.
Following the Nánshān,
the *Shǐjì* states: Nánshān is the Lián Zhōngnánshān,
extending from south of the capital eastward to Huàshān,
then northeastward to the sea,
which is the Zhōngtiáoshān.
From south of the capital westward,
it connects to Cōnglíng for over ten thousand *lǐ*,
hence it is called "following the Nánshān."
The *Xīyù Chuán* says: Its Nánshān emerges from Jīnchéng in the east,
and is connected to Hàn’s Nánshān.
Huán,
read as cóng xuān,
also as written;
same below.
Bìng,
read as bù làng.
He was again captured by the Xīongnú,
and detained for over a year.
At that time, Yīzhìxié was pursuing Yú Dān,
and there was internal strife within the Xīongnú.
Qiān then escaped with Tángyì-shì’s slave Gānfù and returned.
Fú Qián said: Tángyì
is a surname.
A Hàn person;
his slave’s name was Gānfù.
Fù,
sound is fǔ.
Gānfù was an envoy.
When Qiān first set out, there were over a hundred people.
Thirteen years later,
only two returned.
The *Kǎoyì* states: The *Shǐjì* *Xīnán Yí Chuán* says:
“In the first year of Yuánshòu (122 BCE),
Zhāng Qiān came from Dàxià,
speaking of the benefits of opening communication with Shēndú.”
According to the chronological tables,
Qiān was enfeoffed as Bówàng Hóu in the second month of the *jiǎchén* day of the sixth year of Yuánshuò (123 BCE).
Therefore, he certainly did not return in the first year of Yuánshòu.
Perhaps in the first year of Yuánshòu,
the Son of Heaven first ordered Qiān to open communication with Shēndú.
The doubt cannot be clarified,
thus the account concludes with the enthronement of Yīzhìxié in that year.
6 Tens of thousands of Xīongnú cavalry entered the pass,
killing the Grand Administrator of Dàijùn, Gōng.
Dàijùn,
is the area of Táng’s Wèizhōu and Wǔzhōu.
7 In the sixth month,
on the *gēngwǔ* day,
the Empress Dowager passed away.
She was Empress Wáng, Emperor Wǔ’s mother.
8 In autumn,
the Western Yi were disbanded,
and only two counties, Nányí and Yèláng, and one commandant were established.
Jiànwéi was gradually allowed to manage itself.
Shī Gǔ said: Bǎo
is the same as bǎo (保);
meaning to allow them to govern themselves,
and establish their own commanderies and counties.
9 The Xīongnú again entered Yànmén,
killing and abducting over a thousand people.
That year,
Zhōng Dàfū Zhāng Tāng (張湯) was appointed Tíngwèi (廷尉).
Tāng (湯) was by nature cunning,
skilled at using cleverness to control others.
At that time, the Emperor was partial to scholarship and literature,
so Tāng (湯) feigned admiration,
serving Dǒng Zhòngshū (董仲舒), Gōngsūn Hóng (公孫弘), and others.
He appointed Ér Kuān (兒寬) of Qiānchéng (千乘) as a Zuòyàn Yuán (奏讞掾).
Ér (兒)
was originally surnamed Ní (郳).
They took their state as their clan name,
later removing
the "Yì" (邑) radical.
He was made Tíngwèi Yuán (廷尉掾),
specifically in charge of judicial reviews.
Ér (兒),
pronounced wǔ-xī-fān (五奚翻).
Yàn (讞),
pronounced yú-jiǎn-fān (魚蹇翻).
Yuán (掾),
pronounced yú-juàn-fān (俞絹翻).
What he handled: cases where the Emperor intended to convict,
working with Jiān (監) and Shǐ (史) to deeply implicate people;
Bān Biǎo (班表) states: The Tíngwèi (廷尉) had a Left and Right Jiān (監),
with a salary of one thousand shí (石).
Hànbǎiguānzhì (漢百官志) says: The Tíngwèi (廷尉) had twenty-seven prison clerks (獄史).
"Deeply implicate" (深禍)
