He was to be executed,
but was redeemed as a commoner.
At this time,
the soldiers, horses, and weapons of the veteran generals were all inferior to those of the Piàojì.
The Piàojì always led picked men;
Shīgǔ said: He selected the brave and sharp.
Suǒyǐn said: "Xuǎn"
is read as "yí biàn".
He always went ahead of the main army with strong cavalry;
his army also had heavenly luck,
and was never in distress or at an impasse.
But the veteran generals often lagged behind and were unlucky,
Shīgǔ said: "Liú"
means to delay;
"luò"
means to fall;
thus they were not in harmony and had no achievements.
This was similar to the Grand General.
The Xiongnu invaded Dài and Yànmén,
killing and plundering several hundred people.
4. Jiāngdū Wáng Jiàn
Jiàn was the son of Yì Wáng Fēi and the grandson of Jǐngdì.
Jiàn was boating on Léipí.
Léipí
is Léitáng in Guǎnglíng,
located north of present-day Yángzhōu Bǎochéng,
on Pínggāng.
Jiàn ordered two officials to take a small boat into the lake.
The boat capsized,
and the two officials drowned.
They clung to the boat,
appearing and disappearing intermittently;
"jiàn"
is read as "xián biàn".
He ordered that they not be rescued,
and they both died.
In total, he killed thirty-five innocent people,
and indulged in depravity and cruelty.
Knowing his many crimes,
and fearing execution,
he and his empress Chéng Guāng together used Yuè slave women to call forth spirits
and curse the emperor.
He also heard of the conspiracies of Huáinán and Héngshān,
so Jiàn also made weapons,
carved an imperial seal,
and prepared for rebellion.
When the matter was discovered,
the authorities requested his arrest and execution;
Jiàn committed suicide,
and his empress Chéng Guāng and others were all executed in the marketplace,
and the kingdom was abolished.
5. Jiāodōng Kāng Wáng Jì passed away.
Jì was the son of Jǐngdì,
and was enfeoffed in the second year of Zhōng.
6 In the autumn,
the Xiongnú Húnyé Wáng surrendered.
At this time,
the Chányú was enraged that Húnyé Wáng and Xiūtú Wáng, who were residing in the west, had allowed tens of thousands of their people to be killed or captured by the Hàn.
He intended to summon them and put them to death.
Húnyé Wáng and Xiūtú Wáng were afraid,
and plotted to surrender to Hàn.
They first sent envoys to the border to intercept Hàn people,
ordering them to report to the Tiānzǐ.
At this time,
Dàlǐ Lǐ Xī was about to construct a city on the Hé,
when he received the envoy of Húnyé Wáng.
He rode
a post-chaise to report this.
When the Tiānzǐ heard of it,
fearing that they might be feigning surrender to attack the border,
he ordered Piàojì Jiāngjūn to lead troops to meet them.
Xiūtú Wáng later regretted his decision,
so Húnyé Wáng killed him,
and absorbed his forces.
Once Piàojì had crossed the Hé,
he faced Húnyé Wáng’s forces.
Húnyé Wáng’s deputy generals saw the Hàn army,
and many did not wish to surrender.
Shī Gǔ said: "They feared being enveloped."
Piàojì then galloped in,
managed to meet Húnyé Wáng,
and executed eight thousand of those who wished to flee.
He then sent Húnyé Wáng alone by post-chaise to
the imperial residence,
and led all his forces across the Hé.
Over forty thousand people surrendered,
though they were claimed to number one hundred thousand.
When they arrived in Cháng’ān,
the Tiānzǐ bestowed rewards amounting to several tens of millions.
Húnyé Wáng was enfeoffed with ten thousand households,
as Luòyīn Hóu.
The Bān Zhì says,
Luòyīn Xiàn was subordinate to Píngyuán Jùn.
Luò,
pronounced as tā hé fān.
Hūdúní was made Xiàmó Hóu,
Yīngpì was made Huīqú Hóu,
Qínlí was made Héquí Hóu,
Wéndānghù Diàosuī was made Chánglè Hóu.
Wén Yǐng said: Yīng,
sounded as yīng.
Pì,
sounded as pì in pìyīnzhībì.
Shī Gǔ said: Pì,
pǐ lǚ fān.
When Húnyé surrendered,
Hàn dispatched twenty thousand carts to welcome him.
Kǎoyì said: "The Hànshū: Shíhuòzhì states
'thirty thousand carts.'
We now follow the Shǐjì: Píngzhǔnshū and Jí Àn Zhuàn."
Horses were requisitioned from the populace,
but some people hid their horses,
so the full number was not met.
The Emperor was angry,
and intended to execute the Cháng’ān Lìng.
Yòu Nèishǐ Jí Àn said:
"The Cháng’ān Lìng is innocent.
If you must execute someone, execute me, Àn,
and then the people will be willing to turn out their horses.
Furthermore, the Xiongnú rebelled against their lord and surrendered to Hàn.
Hàn should gradually transfer them via counties.
Why should the whole empire be thrown into turmoil,
exhausting Zhōngguó
to deal with these foreign people?"
The Emperor remained silent.
When Húnyé arrived,
over five hundred merchants and market traders were condemned to death.
Àn requested a private audience at Gāomén.
Jìn Zhuó said: "The Sānfǔ Huángtú states that
there was a Gāoméndiàn in Wèiyānggōng."
Jiǎ,
sounded as gǔ.
Jiàn,
xián biàn fān.
"The Xiongnú attacked the vital passes,
meaning the barricades obstructing the Xiongnú's entry route.
Zhōngguó mobilized troops to punish them,
and the dead and wounded were innumerable,
with expenses running to hundreds of millions.
Shī Gǔ said: 'This means several hundreds of millions.'
All captured individuals were made into slaves
and bestowed upon the families of those who died in military service.
The spoils of war
were given to them,
lǔ is the same as lǔ.
yǔ is
read as yù.
This would satisfy the hearts of the common people.
Shī Gǔ said: 'Sè means full.'
Sè,
xī zé fān.
Húnyé led tens of thousands of his people to surrender,
emptying the imperial coffers for rewards,
and mobilizing good citizens to serve and care for them.
It's like serving a spoiled child.
How could ignorant people know that buying goods in Cháng’ān
and then, according to the strictures of scribes, taking property out through the border passes is prohibited?
Yìng Shào said: Lán means arbitrary.
The law states: for Xiongnú markets,
officials and common people are not allowed to take weapons or money out of the pass.
Even if they buy in the capital,
the law is the same.
Chén Zàn said: Entering or exiting without a seal or credential is lán.
Moreover, to use petty regulations to kill over five hundred ignorant people,
this is what is called 'protecting its leaves but harming its branches.'
I humbly submit to Your Majesty that this is not right."
The Emperor remained silent and did not agree,
saying:
"I have not heard Jí Àn’s words for a long time.
Now he is speaking nonsense again!"
A short while later,
the surrendered people were divided and settled outside the old frontier of the five border commanderies,
all of which were south of the Hé.
Their former customs were preserved, and they were established as five dependent states.
The five commanderies
were Lǒngxī, Běidì, Shàngjùn, Shuòfāng, and Yúnzhōng.
The old frontier
refers to the frontier passes that Qín first established against the Xiongnú.
From the time Qín sent Méng Tián to seize Xiongnú land and expand the border passes,
during the chaos of Qín and Xiàng,
Mòdú Nánqīn
and Zhōngguó faced each other at the old frontier.
When Wèi Qīng recovered the land south of the Hé,
the border passes reverted to Méng Tián’s old lines.
The "outside the old frontier" referred to
the area south of the Běi Hé.
Shī Gǔ said: Generally, "dependent state" means
preserving their state name but making them subordinate to the Hàn court,
hence "dependent state."
The Shǐjì: Zhèngyì said: "The surrendered people were moved to the five commanderies,
each following their original customs but subordinate to Hàn,
hence 'dependent state'."
The Hé River flows out from Jīnchéng, Hégōng Xiàn, southwest of the frontier, from Jīshí Shān,
flowing east through the border of Jīnchéng Jùn.
West of Yǔnwú,
it is generally called the Jīnchéng Hé.
Crossing the river to the west
are the lands of Wǔwēi and the other four commanderies.
However, Jīnchéng Jùn was only established by Emperor Zhāo in Yuánshǐ year six,
so the historian wrote it in retrospect.
The area was empty of Xiongnú;
Xiongnú scouts occasionally arrived, but rarely.
Xiūtú Wáng’s crown prince, Rìdī, along with his mother Yānshī and younger brother Lún, were all confiscated by the government
and sent to the Huángmén to raise horses.
After a long time,
the Emperor was enjoying a banquet
and inspected the horses.
Shī Gǔ said: "He summoned and reviewed the horses during the banquet."
Rìdī and several tens of others led horses past the front of the hall.
None failed to steal glances.
Shī Gǔ said: "Looking at the palace women."
Rìdī was eight feet two inches tall,
with a very stern appearance,
and his horses were fat and good.
The Emperor was surprised and asked about him.
He recounted his original situation truthfully.
The Emperor marveled at him,
and that very day bestowed upon him bathing supplies, clothes, and a cap,
and appointed him Mǎjiān.
The Huángmén had a Mǎjiān and a Gǒujiān.
He was made Shìzhōng,
allowed to enter and exit the forbidden palace.
He was made Fùmǎ Dūwèi.
This was established by the Emperor,
with a rank comparable to a Two-Thousand-Picul official.
Shī Gǔ said: Fù means auxiliary horse;
not driving the main carriage,
all are auxiliary horses.
Another explanation: Fù means close,
or swift.
He was made Guānglù Dàfū.
Originally Zhōng Dàfū,
the Emperor changed its name.
He never made any mistakes,
and the Emperor trusted and loved him deeply.
His rewards amounted to thousands of gold.
When the Emperor went out, Rìdī would ride in his entourage,
and when he entered, he would attend by his side.
Many imperial relatives secretly complained, saying:
"Your Majesty has inexplicably taken a Xiongnú boy
and made him so important."
When the Emperor heard this,
he treated him even more generously.
Because Xiūtú had made a golden statue to worship the god of heaven,
Rìdī was given the surname Jīn.
This laid the foundation for the Jīn clan's prominence.
In the
third
year (Xīnyǒu, 120 BCE):
1. In spring,
a comet appeared in the east.
2. In summer,
in the fifth month,
there was a general amnesty throughout the empire.
3. When the King of Huáinán, Liú Ān, conspired to rebel,
Kāng Wáng Jì of Jiāodōng, having vaguely heard of the matter,
privately prepared for battle and defense.
When officials investigated the Huáinán affair,
his deposition was revealed.
Shī Gǔ said: The depositions in the case implicated and
revealed his actions.
He was the younger brother of the Empress Dowager,
and thus extremely close to the emperor.
Distressed by this,
he fell ill and died,
not daring to appoint a successor.
The emperor heard of this and pitied him,
and so established his eldest son, Xián, as King of Jiāodōng.
Kāng Wáng Jì had died the previous year,
and a successor was only appointed this year.
The king's former territory was that of the King of Héngshān.
The Héngshān kingdom had six commanderies,
so it was renamed Liù'ān.
4. In autumn,
the Xiōngnú invaded Yòuběipíng and Dìngxiāng,
each with tens of thousands of cavalry,
killing and plundering over a thousand people.
5. There were great floods in Shāndōng,
and many people suffered from hunger and destitution.
The Son of Heaven dispatched envoys to empty the granaries of commanderies and states to relieve the poor,
but it was still insufficient.
He then recruited wealthy officials and commoners who could lend to the poor, and had their names reported.
As they still could not help each other,
the poor were moved to west of the passes and to the south of Shuòfāng, in Xīnqínzhōng.
Yì Shào said: Qín sent Méng Tián to repel the Xiōngnú,
and obtained a thousand *lǐ* of their fertile Hénán Zàoyáng land.
The land was excellent,
so cities and walls were built there,
and people were moved to settle it.
It was named Xīnqín.
People from all four directions were mixed together,
and their extravagance and frugality differed.
Today, the custom is to call newly rich people
"Xīnqín,"
and this name comes from that.
Their food and clothing were all supplied by the county officials,
and they were given property for several years.
Envoys were divided into groups to protect them,
their carriages and hats visible to each other.
The expenses were counted in *yì*,
innumerable.
6. After the Hàn obtained the territory of King Húnyé,
Lǒngxī, Běidì, and Shàngjùn had fewer incursions by the Hú.
An edict reduced the garrison troops of the three commanderies by half,
to ease the corvée labor of the empire.
7. The emperor was about to attack Kūnmíng,
because they had obstructed the Hàn envoys.
Thus, he constructed Kūnmíng Chí (Kūnmíng Lake) to practice naval warfare.
Kūnmíng Chí was southwest of Cháng'ān,
with a circumference of forty *lǐ*.
According to old records of the Sānfǔ,
Kūnmíng Chí covered three hundred and twenty *qǐng* of land.
Many officials were dismissed.
Military campaigns were frequent,
and many commoners bought exemptions.
Shī Gǔ said: They paid money to the government to obtain exemption from service.
The character *fù*,
read *fāng mù fān*.
The rank of Wǔdàfū was
the ninth level of the old twenty ranks of nobility.
According to Hàn law,
upon reaching this rank, one was exempt from corvée labor.
Therefore, those with the ranks of Qiānfū and Wǔdàfū were made officials;
those who did not wish to serve contributed horses.
Shī Gǔ said: Those of Qiānfū and Wǔdàfū who did not wish to be officials
were made to contribute horses.
Qiānfū was
the seventh rank of military merit.
All were conscripted to cut thornbushes in the Shànglín Park
and excavate Kūnmíng Chí.
8. In this year,
a divine horse was obtained from the waters of Wòwā.
Lǐ Fěi said: In Xīnyě, Nányáng, there was a *bàolìzhǎng* (overseer of profitable enterprises) named Bào Lìcháng.
During Emperor Wǔ's reign, he was punished and
stationed to farm the land in the Dūnhuáng region.
He often saw wild horses near this water,
among them a strange horse different from ordinary horses,
which came to drink from this water.
Lìcháng first made a clay figure holding a bridle by the water,
and later the horse became accustomed to it.
After a long time,
he replaced the clay figure, holding the bridle himself,
captured the horse,
and presented it.
Wishing to make this horse appear divine,
he claimed it emerged from the water.
*Wò*,
pronounced *wò*.
*Wā*,
read *yú jiā fān*.
The Yuèfǔ (Music Bureau) had seventeen chapters of the Ānshì Fángzhōng Gē and
nineteen chapters of the Jiāosì Gē,
performed by seventy boys and girls.
Shī Gǔ said: This was when it was first established.
The name Yuèfǔ probably originated here,
and it was abolished during Emperor Āi's reign.
The eunuch Lǐ Yánnián was appointed Xiélǜ Dūwèi (Prefect of Harmonizing Pitches).
Xiélǜ Dūwèi,
this official position did not exist before;
Emperor Wǔ first established it here.
He composed the initial poems with strings to harmonize the melodies of the eight tones.
Many of the poems were in the elegant style of the *Ěryǎ*.
The initial poems
were newly created poems.
The eight tones are
metal, stone, silk, bamboo, gourd, earth, leather, and wood.
*Diào*,
read *tú diào fān*.
The *Ěryǎ* in three scrolls and twenty chapters
was listed among the academic officials during Emperor Wén's reign.
Zhāng Yàn said: *Ěr* means
"near."
*Yǎ* means
"correct."
One must gather scholars of the Five Classics to jointly discuss, learn, and read it,
only then can one fully understand its meaning.
When the divine horse was obtained,
a song was composed for it.
Jí Àn said:
"Whenever a ruler composes music,
it is to honor ancestors above
and to transform the myriad people below.
Now Your Majesty has obtained a horse,
and a song is made of it,
harmonizing with the ancestral temple.
How could the former emperors and the common people understand its tune?"
The emperor remained silent and displeased.
The emperor recruited and welcomed scholars and officials,
always as if it were not enough;
however, his nature was stern and severe.
If his favored and trusted ministers
committed even a small violation of the law,
or deceived him,
he would immediately punish them by execution,
showing no leniency.
Jí Àn advised:
"Your Majesty works hard to seek out worthy people,
but before fully utilizing them,
you have already killed them.
To inflict endless punishments on a limited number of talented individuals,
I fear that all the worthy talents in the empire will be exhausted.
With whom will Your Majesty govern?"
Àn spoke with great anger.
The emperor smiled and enlightened him.
Àn spoke with great anger;
the emperor then smiled and enlightened him.
Observing the intent of the interaction between the ruler and minister in that moment of anger and smile,
it shows that the emperor, towards Àn,
not only tolerated his directness,
but also calmly and unhurriedly
enlightened him with his own views.
If another person were in this situation,
they would surely not have time to merely comply.
Yet Àn, speaking his mind, still considered it wrong.
How could this be someone who outwardly agreed but later spoke behind one's back?
Àn's service to his ruler was indeed difficult for others to match;
and the emperor's tolerance of Àn
is also beyond what later rulers could achieve.
*Zhì*,
read *zhí lì fān*.
"What era lacks talent?
The problem is people's inability to recognize it.
If one can recognize it,
why worry about a lack of people?
Those called talented
are like useful tools.
If one has talent but is unwilling to use it fully,
it is no different from having no talent.
If not killed, what use are they?"
Àn said:
"Although I cannot refute Your Majesty with words,
my heart still believes it to be wrong.
I wish Your Majesty would change from now on,
and not consider me foolish and ignorant of reason."
The emperor looked at his ministers and said:
"Àn claims to be a *biànpì*—that is not acceptable."
Zhū Xī said: *Biàn* means
to cater to what people like.
*Pì* means
to avoid what people dislike.
*Biàn*,
read *pí lián fān*.
*Pì*,
read *pì*.
"Is that not truly so?"

pronounced dài (徒計翻).

means to secretly estimate.

Zhān,
pronounced zhān (之贍翻);
the same below.

used to string coins.

I think it means that for every two thousand *mín qián*, one tax unit was levied,

Mín,
pronounced mín (眉巾翻).
All were subject to tax.

Nì,
means to hide.
Xī,
means to exhaust.

Half of it was given to the informer.
This law was largely proposed by Zhāng Tāng.
Each time Zhāng Tāng presented matters at court,
discussing state expenses,
it would be late in the day.
Shī Gǔ said: Because many matters were discussed,
it would reach late in the day.
Zhāo (朝),
pronounced zhāo (直遙翻).
The Chancellor merely filled his position,
without offering any constructive suggestions.
The common people were restless,
uneasy in their lives,
and all pointed their resentment at Zhāng Tāng.
2 Previously,
Bǔ Shì from Hénán,
repeatedly requested to donate his wealth to the government to aid the border.
The Son of Heaven sent an envoy to ask Bǔ Shì:
“Do you wish for an official position?”
Bǔ Shì replied:
“I am young and used to farming and herding,
not accustomed to officialdom,
I do not wish for it.”
The envoy asked:
“Is there some injustice in your family that you wish to speak about?”
Bǔ Shì replied:
“I have never had disputes with others in my life;
I lend to the poor in my village,
and teach those who are not virtuous.
Everyone in my locality follows my example.
How could I suffer injustice from anyone?
There is nothing I wish to speak about.”
The envoy said:
“If this is so,
what do you desire then?”
Bǔ Shì replied:
“The Son of Heaven is punishing the Xiongnú.
I foolishly believe that the virtuous should die heroically at the border,
and those with wealth should contribute it.
If this is done, the Xiongnú can be defeated.”
The emperor considered him worthy for this,
and wished to honor and promote him to inspire the populace.
So he summoned and appointed Bǔ Shì as a Court Gentleman (Zhōng Láng),
conferred upon him the rank of First Rank of Commoners (Zuǒ Shù Cháng),
bestowed ten *qǐng* of land,
and proclaimed it throughout the realm
to make it widely known.
Not long after,
Bǔ Shì was again promoted to Grand Tutor of Qí (Qí Tài Fù).
King Cìchāng of Qí,
died without heir in the third year of Yuánsāk,
and the state was abolished.
In the sixth year of Yuánshòu, Prince Hóng was first enfeoffed as King of Qí.
Bǔ Shì was probably the tutor of Hóng.
The historian recorded this because of his donation and subsequent official appointment.
Jī (幾),
pronounced jī (居豈翻).

is the desert.
Shīgǔ said: It means treating the Han army lightly,
remaining there and not leaving.
Another says: It means the Han army could not lightly enter and remain for a long time.
I think the latter explanation is correct.
Their position will surely achieve what they desire."
So, ten thousand horses were fed with grain.
Shīgǔ said: To feed horses with grain.
Privately, another forty thousand horses were carried as baggage.
Shīgǔ said: Those who privately carried their own baggage and privately brought their own horses
were all beyond the limits set by the state.
Cóng,
pronounced cái yòng fān.
Shīgǔ said: Zhuǎn refers to
transporting supplies.
Zhǒng,
connecting.
The Pjàoqí initially set out from Dìngxiāng,
to confront the Chányú;
captives reported the Chányú was to the east,
so the Pjàoqí was instead ordered to depart from Dàijùn,
and the Dàjiàngjūn was ordered to depart from Dìngxiāng.
Lángzhōnglì Lǐ Guǎng repeatedly requested to go,
but the Son of Heaven considered him old,
and did not permit it;
after a long time,
he finally permitted it,
appointing him Qiánjiàngjūn.
Tàipú Gōngsūn Hè was the Zuǒjiàngjūn,
Zhǔjuédūwèi Zhào Shíqí was the Yòujiàngjūn,
Píngyánghóu Cáo Xiāng was the Hòujiàngjūn,
all subordinate to the Dàjiàngjūn.
Zhào Xìn advised the Chányú, saying:
"Once the Han troops have crossed the Mù,
their men and horses will be exhausted,
and the Xiongnú can capture them effortlessly."
Shīgǔ said: It means capturing the Han army's men and horses would require no effort,
hence "sit" (坐) is used.
Bà,
read as pí.
Shīgǔ said: To send supplies far away,
to the north.
The Dàjiàngjūn, having exited the pass,
learned the Chányú's location from captives,
and personally led his elite troops to pursue him,
while ordering Qiánjiàngjūn Guǎng to join with the Yòujiàngjūn's army,
and proceed via the eastern route.
Shīgǔ said: Bìng
means to combine;
to combine armies and follow the same route.
Guǎng personally requested, saying:
"My division is the Qiánjiàngjūn,
but now the Dàjiàngjūn has instead transferred me to take the eastern route.
Moreover, I have fought the Xiongnú since my hair was bound,
and now I finally have a chance to confront the Chányú.
'Binding hair' means
being on the battlefield as soon as one comes of age,
and now having a chance to confront the Chányú.
I wish to die fighting the Chányú first."
Shīgǔ said: To exert oneself to the death to capture the Chányú.
He thought,
"Lǐ Guǎng is old,
and his fate is unlucky."
Mèng Kāng said: Qí means
singular and unmatched.
Rú Chún said: Being defeated by the Xiongnú multiple times is considered unlucky and mismatched.
Shīgǔ said: It means Guǎng's fate is singular and unmatched;
Mèng's explanation is correct.
Shù,
pronounced suǒ jiǎo fān.
Qí,
pronounced jū yí fān.
"I fear he may not achieve what he desires."
Shīgǔ said: It means he may not defeat the enemy.
I think it refers to wishing to capture the Chányú,
and if by chance he loses him,
that would be not achieving what he desires.
The Dàjiàngjūn also wanted to have Áo confront the Chányú with him.
Áo had lost his marquisate two years prior.
Qīng was originally friends with Áo,
and had also saved Qīng from peril,
so Qīng wanted to have him confront the Chányú and earn merit.
Guǎng knew this,
and firmly excused himself to the Dàjiàngjūn;
the Dàjiàngjūn did not listen,
and Guǎng departed without saying goodbye,
feeling very resentful and angry.
The Dàjiàngjūn departed from the pass and traveled over a thousand lǐ,
crossing the Mù,
and saw the Chányú's troops arrayed and waiting.
It means forming a battle array to await the enemy.
Chén,
same as zhèn.
Zhāng Yàn said: Wǔgāngchē are
military chariots.
Shīgǔ said: Huán
means to surround.
Xù Hàn Zhì: All armies had spears and halberds,
their decorations included pennants and banners,
with cloths and covers,
called Wǔgāngchē.
Huán,
pronounced huàn.
The Xiongnú also deployed about ten thousand cavalry.
As the day was setting,
meaning the sun was about to go down,
sand and gravel struck their faces,
and the two armies could not see each other.
The Han further deployed their left and right wings to encircle the Chányú.
Shīgǔ said: Yì
means extending their troops left and right,
like a bird spreading its wings.
Judging that he could not fight as well as the Han army,
the Chányú then rode six mules,
with several hundred strong cavalry,
directly breaking through the Han encirclement,
and fled northwest.
Shīgǔ said: Luó are
the offspring of donkeys and horses,
sturdy and enduring.
The Chányú himself rode fast-running mules,
and strong cavalry followed him.
Mào
means to assault.
Luó,
pronounced lái gē fān.
Mào,
pronounced mò kè fān.
The Han and Xiongnú engaged in a chaotic struggle,
Shīgǔ said: Fēnná
means a chaotic struggle and grappling with each other.
Ná,
pronounced nǚ jū fān.
Casualties on both sides were roughly equal.
The Chányú departed before dusk,
and the Han army dispatched light cavalry to pursue him by night,
with the Dàjiàngjūn's army following close behind.
The Xiongnú troops also scattered and fled.
At dawn,
having traveled over two hundred lǐ,
they did not find the Chányú,
but captured and beheaded nineteen thousand enemy troops,
then reached Zhènyánshān Zhào Xìn Chéng,
where they found accumulated Xiongnú grain and fed their army.
After staying for one day, they burned all the remaining grain in the city and returned.
The armies of General of the Vanguard Lǐ Guǎng and General of the Right Gōngsūn Shíqí had no guide,
got lost and confused,
and fell behind the Grand General.
Shīgǔ said: "Huò" (惑)
means confused.
To be behind is to miss the appointed time.
The Grand General led his army back,
and passing south of the encampment,
he encountered the two generals.
The Grand General ordered his Chief Clerk to question Lǐ Guǎng and Gōngsūn Shíqí about getting lost.
He urgently ordered Lǐ Guǎng to come to his headquarters to answer the charges.
Shīgǔ said: "Bó" (簿)
refers to the written charges.
"The various colonels are innocent;
it was I who got lost.
I will now personally submit to the charges at the Grand General's headquarters."
Lǐ Guǎng said to his subordinates:
"I, Lǐ Guǎng, since I came of age, have fought over seventy battles, large and small, against the Xiongnú.
Now, by good fortune, I followed the Grand General to engage the Chányú's forces,
but the Grand General moved my division,
making our route circuitous and long, and then we got lost.
Is this not fate?
Moreover, I, Lǐ Guǎng, am over sixty years old,
and I certainly cannot face the scribes and officials again!"
Thereupon, he drew his sword and slit his own throat.
Lǐ Guǎng was a man of integrity;
whenever he received rewards and gifts, he would immediately distribute them to his subordinates.
He shared food and drink with his soldiers.
Though he served as an official receiving two thousand shí of grain for over forty years,
his family had no surplus wealth.
He had long arms,
and was skilled in archery.
Rú Chún said: His arms were like an ape's, extending all the way to his shoulders.
When leading troops,
in places where there was scarcity and destitution,
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: "Fá" (乏) means temporary lack,
"jué" (絕) means not continuing.
if the soldiers had not all drunk,
Lǐ Guǎng would not approach water;
if the soldiers had not all eaten,
Lǐ Guǎng would not taste food.
Because of this, the soldiers loved and were willing to serve him.
When he died,
the entire army wept;
when the common people heard of it,
whether they knew him or not,
old and young alike, all shed tears.
Shīgǔ said: "Zhī" (知) refers to those who knew each other previously.
"Wéi" (為) pronounced yúwěi.
He deserved to die,
but was ransomed to become a commoner.
When the Chányú fled,
his soldiers scattered, often mixing with Han soldiers, and followed the Chányú.
The Chányú was separated from his main force for a long time.
His Right Gǔlí Wáng thought the Chányú was dead,
and so he proclaimed himself Chányú.
After more than ten days,
the true Chányú regained his forces,
and the Right Gǔlí Wáng then abandoned his title of Chányú.
The cavalry and heavy baggage of General of Agile Cavalry Huò Qùbìng's army were equal to those of the Grand General's army,
but he had no deputy generals.
He made Lǐ Gǎn and others chief colonels,
to serve as deputy generals.
He went out more than two thousand lǐ beyond Dài and Yòuběipíng,
crossed the Great Desert,
and directly engaged the forces of the Left Flank.
Shīgǔ said: "Zhí" (直)
means to be opposite to.
The Xiongnú divided their country into left and right: all the Left Kings and generals resided in the east,
directly opposite Shànggǔ and to its east,
bordering the Huìmò and Cháoxiǎn;
the Right Kings and generals resided in the west,
directly opposite Shàngjùn and to its west,
bordering the Dǐ and Qiāng;
therefore they were called the Left and Right Flanks,
or also the Left and Right Territories.
He captured eighty-three generals, chancellors, dānghù, and commandants,
performed the Fēng sacrifice on Wángjūxū Shān,
the Shàn sacrifice on Gūyǎn,
and ascended to Hánhǎi.
Zhāng Yàn said: Ascending a mountain by the sea to gaze upon the sea.
There was a great infant,
so the mountain was elevated and the territory expanded.
Rú Chún said: Hánhǎi
is the name of the Northern Sea.
Cuī Hào said: It is where the fēi bird sheds its feathers,
hence it is called Hánhǎi.
Guǎng Zhì says Hánhǎi is north of the desert.
Shīgǔ said: To pile earth to raise height is "fēng" (封);
to make an altar for the earth sacrifice is "shàn" (禪).
The Son of Heaven increased the General of Agile Cavalry's enfeoffment by five thousand eight hundred households;
he also enfeoffed four people from his command, including Lù Bódé, the Administrator of Yòuběipíng, as marquises.
Lù Bódé became the Marquis of Pīlí,
Wèi Shān became the Marquis of Yìyáng,
Fùlù Zhī became the Marquis of Dù,
and Yī Jíjǐn became the Marquis of Zhònglì.
Colonel Lǐ Gǎn became an Inner-Pass Marquis,
with an allotted territory.
Many military officials and soldiers received official positions and abundant rewards.
However, the Grand General was not granted an additional enfeoffment,
and none of his military officials or soldiers were enfeoffed as marquises.
When the two armies marched out of the pass,
the pass censused a total of one hundred forty thousand official and private horses,
but fewer than thirty thousand returned into the pass.
Thereupon, the position of Grand Minister of War (Dà Sīmǎ) was established.
The Grand General and the General of Agile Cavalry both became Grand Ministers of War.
A decree was established,
stipulating that the General of Agile Cavalry's rank and emolument should be equal to those of the Grand General.
Yìng Shào said: The Sīmǎ manages military affairs,
and various military officials also used this title.
Hàn Guān Yí says: At the time, it was discussed that there were Sīmǎ (marshals) among the marquises in the army,
so the character
"dà" (大)
(grand) was added to make "Dà Sīmǎ" to distinguish them.
From this point, the General of Agile Cavalry held the same rank and position as the Grand General,
his status being second only to the Chancellor.
Grand General Wèi Qīng declined day by day, while General of Agile Cavalry Huò Qùbìng grew more prominent.
Many of Grand General Wèi Qīng's old friends and retainers left to serve General of Agile Cavalry Huò Qùbìng,
and immediately received official positions and noble titles.
Only Rèn Ān refused.
The General of Agile Cavalry was a person
of few words and not given to leaking secrets.
Kǒng Wénxiáng said: This means he was steady and quiet,
with courage within.
The Son of Heaven once wanted to teach him Sūnzi's and Wú Qǐ's Art of War,
Sūn
refers to Sūn Wǔ;
Wú
refers to Wú Qǐ.
(He replied): "It is only a matter of strategy;
there is no need to study ancient military texts."
The Son of Heaven had a grand residence built for him,
and ordered the General of Agile Cavalry to inspect it.
He replied:
"As long as the Xiongnú are not exterminated,
I have no need for a home!"
Because of this, the emperor esteemed and loved him even more.
However, having become noble at a young age,
he was inconsiderate of his soldiers.
Shīgǔ said: "Shěng" (省)
means to observe;
it means he did not care for or look after his soldiers.
"Shǎo" (少) pronounced shàozhào.
The Son of Heaven sent the Grand Provisioner (Tàiguān) to bring dozens of carts.
Bān Biǎo says: The Tàiguān has a chief and a deputy,
who are in charge of meals.
Shīgǔ said: "Jī" (齎)
is the same as "zī" (資).
I think the pronunciation zéxī is also acceptable,
meaning to load.
"Wéi" (為) pronounced yúwěi.
"Chéng" (乘) pronounced shéngzhèng.
The heavy carts had leftover meat and grain,
but there were hungry soldiers.
When they were beyond the frontier,
the soldiers sometimes ran out of provisions and could not recover themselves,
while the General of Agile Cavalry was still digging fields and playing cújú.
Fú Qián said: "Chuān yù" (穿域)
means to build a cújú field.
Shīgǔ said: "Jú" (鞠)
is made of leather,
filled with wool,
and kicked as a game.
Liú Xiàng's Biélù says: Cújú
is traditionally believed to have been created by the Yellow Emperor,
or some say it originated in the Warring States period,
used to practice martial skills and identify talent.
"Tà" (蹋) pronounced túlà.
"Jú" (鞠) pronounced jūliù.
The Grand General was benevolent,
fond of scholars, humble,
and pleased the emperor with his mild and gentle nature.
Such were the characters and dispositions of the two men.
At this time,
the Hàn had killed and captured 80,000 to 90,000 Xiōngnú in total,
while the Hàn soldiers who died from natural causes also numbered several tens of thousands.
Wèi Tái discussed and consulted: Gāotáng Lóng said:
"I heard from my former teacher that,
'wù' (物)
means 'nothing,'
'gù' (故)
means 'affair,'
meaning one can no longer do anything regarding the affair."
Suǒ Yǐn said: Since the Hàn dynasty, death has been called 'wùgù' (物故),
referring to decay and becoming old.
Shī Gǔ said: 'Wùgù' (物故)
means to die;
it refers to becoming like a ghost and perishing.
It is said that the Hàn army also suffered tens of thousands of deaths.
However, there was no royal court south of the desert.
Mòdú Chányú, in his strength,
completely recovered the Xiōngnú lands taken by Méng Tián,
and established his royal court south of the desert.
Now, the Xiōngnú, attacked by the Hàn,
had fled far north of the desert,
hence there was no royal court south of the desert.
The Bān Zhì says
that Língjū county belonged to Jīnchéng Commandery.
Líng (令)
is pronounced líng.
(The Hàn) established 'tián guān' (田官, agricultural officials),
establishing officials to manage military agricultural colonies.
They gradually 'silkworm-fed' on the Xiōngnú to the north;
'Silkworm-fed' (cánsī)
means like a silkworm eating leaves,
gradually encroaching on their territory.
They no longer made large expeditions to attack the Xiōngnú.
The Xiōngnú, using Zhào Xìn's plan,
sent envoys to Hàn,
with good words requesting a 'hèqīn' (和親, peace and kinship alliance).
The Son of Heaven put it to discussion;
some spoke of a 'hèqīn,'
others spoke of making them vassals.
The Chéngxiàng Chángshǐ Rèn Chǎng said:
Bān Biǎo: The Chéngxiàng had two Chángshǐ,
with a salary of two thousand dàn.
Rèn (任)
is pronounced rén.
"The Xiōngnú have just been defeated and are in distress;
it would be appropriate to make them outer vassals,
coming to the border for audience."
The Hàn sent Rèn Chǎng to the Chányú,
who was greatly enraged
and detained him, not sending him back.
At this time,
the Bóshì Dí Shān argued that 'hèqīn' was more convenient.
Xìng Pǔ: Dí (狄)
is a descendant of the Dís state of the Chūnqiū period;
it also says: King Wén of Zhōu enfeoffed his youngest son in Díchéng.
Tāng said:
"This is an ignorant and foolish scholar."
Dí Shān said:
"I am indeed foolish,
foolishly loyal;
whereas Yùshǐ Dàfū Tāng
is deceptively loyal."
Thereupon, the Emperor became angry and said:
"I will have you govern a commandery."
Shī Gǔ said: Bóshì
was a scholarly official,
hence he was called 'shēng' (sir).
He replied:
"I cannot."
(The Emperor) said:
"Govern a county?"
He replied:
"I cannot."
Again (the Emperor) said:
"Govern a barrier post?"
Shī Gǔ said: A 'zhàng' (障)
refers to a strategic and dangerous place on the frontier,
where a separate wall was built,
and officials and soldiers were stationed,
serving as a screen to ward off invaders.
'Zhàng' (障) is pronounced zhī-shàng (平).
Also, under the Hàn system,
a separate wall was built at every crucial point on the frontier,
with people stationed to defend it,
which was called a 'hòuchéng' (候城, watchtower city);
this is what a 'zhàng' (障) is.
(Dí Shān) was cornered in the debate and about to be handed over to the authorities.
Shī Gǔ said: 'Dù' (度)
means 'to estimate';
being questioned and running out of arguments,
one should be handed over to the authorities.
'Xià' (下) is pronounced xiá-jià (去).
(Dí Shān then said) "I can."
Thereupon, the Emperor sent Shān to take charge of a barrier post.
Shī Gǔ said: 'Chéng' (乘)
means to ascend,
to ascend and guard it.
The Xiōngnú cut off Shān's head and left.
From then on,
all officials were deeply intimidated and trembled.
Shī Gǔ said: 'Zhèn' (震)
means to move.
'Shè' (慴)
means to lose spirit.
'Shè' (慴)
is pronounced zhī-shè (入).
That year,
Jí Àn was dismissed due to legal issues,
and Yì Zòng, the Tàishǒu of Dìngxiāng, was appointed Yòu Nèishǐ,
while Wáng Wēnshū, the Tàishǒu of Hénèi, was appointed Zhōngwèi.
Previously,
Níng Chéng served as the Guāndūwèi,
the Dūwèi of Hángǔguān.
'Xiān' (先)
is pronounced xī-jiàn (去).
"Better to see a lactating tiger
than to encounter Níng Chéng's wrath."
Shī Gǔ said: A fierce tiger, when nursing its young,
will attack and bite excessively in protection,
hence this metaphor.
'Rǔ' (乳)
is pronounced rén-yù (上).
Yì (義)
is the surname.
Zòng (縱)
is his given name.
Níng Chéng would walk sideways in greeting and welcoming;
(this means) he dared not walk upright,
expressing extreme deference.
(Yì Zòng) then impeached Níng Shì,
crushing his family;
the officials and common people of Nányáng were 'heavy-footed with one footprint.'
It means their feet were piled up,
extremely terrified.
'Chóng' (重)
is pronounced zhí-lóng (平).
Upon his initial arrival,
he rounded up over two hundred people in the Dìngxiāng prison,
who were either serious offenders or lightly held,
and also over two hundred guests, relatives, and brothers who had secretly come to visit.
In one sweep, he arrested them,
and interrogated them, saying:
"You were helping death row prisoners escape."
He arrested and interrogated them all.
Fú Qián said: The law states: Any prisoner who secretly frees himself from shackles, fetters, or chains,
will have his crime increased by one degree;
those who help others escape are subject to the same punishment.
Zòng interrogated two hundred people who had offered bribes,
treating their actions as helping death row prisoners escape,
and killed them all.
Shī Gǔ said: 'Jū' (鞫)
means to exhaust,
referring to thorough investigation and prosecution.
He reported and killed over four hundred people in total.
Shī Gǔ said: He submitted a request and received approval for the executions.
Yuán Fù said: Zòng rounded up the Dìngxiāng prison,
arresting and interrogating everyone,
and it says that on that day, all were executed after being reported,
so it was not a report of a request that received approval,
rather, it was the final judgment that was considered the report.
At that time,
Zhào Yǔ and Zhāng Tāng were among the Jiǔ Qīng (Nine Ministers) for their severity,
yet their governance still relied on law;
Zòng solely governed with an 'eagle strike' approach.
Shī Gǔ said: It means like the strike of a hawk or falcon.
'Zhì' (治)
is pronounced zhí-lì (去).
Wáng Wēnshū began as the Commandant of Guǎngpíng.
Guǎngpíng originally belonged to the state of Zhào.
Between the reigns of Jǐng and Wǔ,
it was divided into Guǎngpíng Commandery.
In the first year of Zhēnghé,
it was established as the state of Pínggān.
Shīgǔ said: Those who are heroes and men of resolute character, who act decisively without any hesitation,
he appointed as officials.
He held their serious secret crimes
and then allowed them to supervise bandits and thieves.
Shīgǔ said: Zòng
means to release.
Dū
means to inspect and observe.
Even if these individuals had a hundred crimes,
he did not punish them by law.
Shīgǔ said: This means that if the apprehended bandits and thieves were the right persons and it was satisfactory,
Wēnshū would then not inquire into their previous crimes.
Fú fǎ
means not to apply the law.
If they were killed in the course of their duties,
their clans were also exterminated.
Shīgǔ said: Bì
means not to fully exert oneself in apprehending and attacking.
Along the borders of Qí and Zhào, bandits dared not approach Guǎngpíng.
Guǎngpíng gained the reputation of a place where things dropped on the road were not picked up.
He was promoted to Grand Administrator of Hénèi.
He arrived in the ninth month,
and ordered the commandery to prepare
fifty horses as relays.
Shīgǔ said: This means setting up relays with private horses at various points along the road,
from Hénèi to Cháng’ān.
More than a thousand families were implicated and punished by association.
He submitted a memorial requesting
that the most serious cases lead to the extermination of the clan,
and minor cases result in death,
with all family property confiscated to compensate for ill-gotten gains.
Shīgǔ said: Those who committed crimes involving ill-gotten gains, their property was confiscated,
and they were also ordered to pay double the amount of the ill-gotten gains,
which was either taken into the official coffers
or returned to its owner.
I believe that confiscating their family property to compensate for the ill-gotten gains they received
seems to be the direct meaning.
Zāng
is read as zāng.
He presented the memorial and the Son of Heaven approved it,
which was called "obtaining approval."
Everyone in Hénèi found his memorial strange,
considering it divinely swift.
By the end of the twelfth month,
there was no sound in the commandery;
no one dared to travel at night.
Gǔ Wú and Wú are interchangeable.
If some were not caught,
they were lost,
and pursued in neighboring commanderies and states.
When spring arrived,
Wēnshū stomped his foot and sighed:
"Alas!
If only this winter month could be extended by one more month,
my task would be complete!"
Shīgǔ said: This is because executions were no longer carried out after the beginning of spring.
That is why he said so.
Zhǎn
means to extend.
The Son of Heaven heard this,
and everyone considered him capable.
Therefore, he was promoted to an official of the Middle Two Thousand Piculs rank.
A Grand Administrator was of the Two Thousand Piculs rank,
while chief ministers and high-ranking ministers were all of the Middle Two Thousand Piculs rank.
6. Shàowēng of Qí,
gained an audience with the Emperor through arts of ghosts and spirits.
The Emperor's favored Lady Wáng had died.
Lady Wáng was the mother of Wáng Hóng, King of Qí.
He made an appearance resembling Lady Wáng,
which the Son of Heaven saw from behind a curtain.
Kǎoyì said: The Hànshū places this event in the biography of Lady Lǐ.
From ancient times to the present, it has always been considered an event involving Lady Lǐ.
The "Treatise on the Feng and Shan Sacrifices" in the Shǐjì says:
"When Shàowēng met the Emperor,
the Emperor's favored Lady Wáng had died.
Shàowēng used his arts to conjure the likeness of Lady Wáng and the kitchen god at night."
However, when Lady Lǐ died,
Shàowēng had already been dead for a long time.
The Hànshū is mistaken.
We now follow the Shǐjì.
He received many rewards
and was treated with the courtesy of a guest.
Wénchéng also persuaded the Emperor to build Gānquán Palace,
with a terraced chamber inside,
where images of Heaven, Earth, Tàiyī, and various ghosts and spirits were painted,
and sacrificial implements were placed
to summon the celestial spirits.
After more than a year,
his arts increasingly failed,
and the spirits did not arrive.
He then wrote a book on silk and fed it to an ox.
Shīgǔ said: This means mixing it with grass to feed the ox.
Fàn
is pronounced fú wǎn fān.
He said:
"There is something extraordinary in this ox's belly."
When the ox was killed and examined,
the book was found.

“Yì” (瘞)
is pronounced “yù” (於計) as in 'yú jì'.
He (Tāng) made an agreement with Tāng (湯) to both apologize.
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: This agreement was made when they were about to enter court.
“Cháo” (朝)
is pronounced “zhāo” (直遙) as in 'zhí yáo'.
Upon reaching before the Emperor,
Tāng believed that as Chancellor (Chéngxiàng), he should apologize when performing the seasonal rites at the imperial mausoleums.
The Grandee Secretary (Yùshǐ Dàfū) was not involved in mausoleum affairs,
and therefore did not apologize.
Tāng wanted to add to his memorial the phrase
“the Chancellor (Chéngxiàng) was aware of it,”
intending to implicate the Chancellor (Chéngxiàng) with the crime of leniency due to prior knowledge.
The Chancellor's (Chéngxiàng) Chief Clerks (Zhǎngshǐ) Zhū Mǎichén (Zhū Mǎichén), Wáng Cháo (Wáng Cháo), and Biān Tōng (Biān Tōng),
were all former nine ministers (jiǔqīng) or officials earning two thousand bushels (èr qiān dàn).
Zhū Mǎichén (Zhū Mǎichén) had served as Chief Commander of State Revenues (Zhǔjué Dūwèi);
Wáng Cháo (Wáng Cháo) had reached the position of Right Internal Historian (Yòu Nèishǐ);
Biān Tōng (Biān Tōng) had reached Minister of Jìnán (Jìnán Xiàng).
The Chénliú Fēngsú Zhuàn (陳留風俗傳) states: Biān (邊) was descended from Prince Róng (Róng), courtesy name Zǐbiān (Zǐbiān), of Sòng (Sòng) in the Spring and Autumn period.
I note from the Zuǒ Zhuàn (左傳)
that there was a Grandee (Dàfū) Biān Bó (Biān Bó) in the Zhōu (Zhōu) dynasty.
Tāng often conducted the Chancellor's (Chéngxiàng) affairs.
Knowing that the three Chief Clerks (Zhǎngshǐ) had always been noble,
he therefore treated them disdainfully.
The Chancellor's (Chéngxiàng) staff treated him (Tāng) similarly.
All three Chief Clerks (Zhǎngshǐ) resented him
and wanted to die.
They wanted to expose Tāng's (湯) treachery through their deaths.
They sent officials to arrest and investigate the merchant Tián Xìn (Tián Xìn) and others,
saying:
“Tāng (湯) was about to submit a memorial.
Xìn (信) always knew about it beforehand,
and accumulated wealth by hoarding goods.”
Fú Qián (服虔) said: “Jū” (居)
means 'to store'.
“Jiǎ” (賈)
is pronounced “gǔ” (古);
the same below.
The details of the matter were somewhat known (to the emperor).
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: It was known to the Son of Heaven.
“What I do,
the merchants always know about it first,
and increase their hoarding of those goods.”
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: “Yì” (益)
means 'many'.
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: “Lèi” (類)
means 'similar'.
He (Tāng) again feigned surprise and said:
“It must be so.”
Jiǎn Xuān (Jiǎn Xuān) also memorialized the affair of Yè Jū (謁居) and others.
The Emperor believed Tāng (湯) was treacherous and deceitful to his face.
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: Deceiving and slandering face-to-face.
Tāng then wrote a letter of apology,
and then said:
“Those who entrapped this minister
are the three Chief Clerks (Zhǎngshǐ).”
He then committed suicide.
After Tāng (湯) died,
his family's property was worth no more than five hundred gold pieces.
His brothers and sons wished to give Tāng (湯) a lavish funeral.
Tāng's (湯) mother said:
“Tāng (湯) was a great minister of the Son of Heaven,
and died under false accusations and slander.
Why a lavish funeral?”
He was carried in an ox-cart,
with a coffin but no outer coffin.
When the Emperor heard of this,
he thoroughly investigated and executed all three Chief Clerks (Zhǎngshǐ).
In the twelfth month,
on the day Rénchén (壬辰),
Chancellor (Chéngxiàng) Qīng Dí (Qīng Dí) was imprisoned
and committed suicide.
2 In spring,
the Báiliáng Tái (柏梁臺) was built.
Fú Qián (服虔) said: A terrace built with one hundred cypress beams,
hence its name.
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: The Sānfǔ Jiùshì (三輔舊事) states that
it was made of fragrant cypress.
The current texts all write
“bǎi” (柏),
so Fú's (服) statement is incorrect.
It was twenty zhàng high and seven wéi in circumference,
made of copper;
on top was a celestial immortal's palm,
used to collect dew,
which was mixed with jade powder and drunk,
said to grant immortality.
The repair of palaces
became increasingly prevalent from this point on.
3 In the second month,
Zhào Zhōu (Zhào Zhōu), Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàifù), was appointed Chancellor (Chéngxiàng).
4 In the third month,
on the day Xīnhài (辛亥),
Shí Qìng (Shí Qìng), Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Tàifù), was appointed Grandee Secretary (Yùshǐ Dàfū).
The state of Wèi (Wèi) had a Grandee (Dàfū) named Shí (石).
5 There was a heavy snowfall.
6 In summer,
there were great floods,
and thousands of people starved to death east of the passes (Guāndōng).
7 In this year,
Kǒng Jǐn (Kǒng Jǐn) was appointed Grand Minister of Agriculture (Dà nóng Lìng),
and Sāng Hóngyáng (Sāng Hóngyáng) was appointed Middle Assistant Secretary of Agriculture (Dà nóng Zhōngchéng).
Bān Biǎo (班表) states: The Grand Minister of Agriculture (Dà nóng) had two Assistant Secretaries (chéng).
In the fourth year of Yuánshòu (Yuánshòu),
Dōngguō Xiányáng (Dōngguō Xiányáng) and Kǒng Jǐn (Kǒng Jǐn) were appointed to these positions.
Now a Middle Assistant Secretary (Zhōngchéng) is appointed,
whose position should be above the two Assistant Secretaries (chéng).
This was to circulate goods.
At that time, offices for Equalization and Transportation (Jūnshū Guān) were established in commanderies (jùn) and kingdoms (guó),
ordering distant regions to transport their local products.
A Level Standard (Píngzhǔn) office was established in the capital (Jīngshī),
to receive all goods transported from throughout the empire.
When prices were high, it would sell;
when prices were low, it would buy,
preventing wealthy merchants and great traders from profiting.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: Emperor Wǔ (Wǔdì) of Hàn (Hàn) established the Equalization and Transportation (Jūnshū) system,
meaning that whatever was due to the government,
people were to transport the produce abundant in their local areas.
The government would then price it according to the local market rate
and sell it elsewhere.
The transporters benefited,
and the government also profited.
8 The white metal was slightly devalued,
and the people did not cherish or use it.
Eventually, it was abolished.
The casting of white metal
is mentioned in the previous volume, Yuánshòu Fourth Year.
Orders were given exclusively to the three officials of the Shànglín imperial park to mint coins,
and it was decreed that no coins other than those of the three officials of the empire should circulate.
Péi Yīn said: "The 'Table of Hundred Officials' states: 'The Grand Administrator of the Waterways and Parks (Shuǐhéng Dūwèi)
is in charge of the Shànglín Park.'
Its subordinate officials include the Shànglín, Jūnshū, Zhōngguān, and Biàntóng prefects.
Therefore, the 'three officials of Shànglín' must be these three prefects!
Considering their expenses, they could not balance the accounts,
so only true artisans and great villains would illicitly counterfeit them."
9 After Húnyé Wáng surrendered to Hàn,
as mentioned in the previous volume, Yuánshòu First Year,
as mentioned in the previous volume, Yuánshòu First Year,
the Western Regions route became accessible.
Thereupon, Zhāng Qiān suggested:
"The Wūsūn King Kūnmò was originally a subject of the Xiōngnú.
Later, his army became somewhat stronger,
and he refused to again pay homage to the Xiōngnú.
The Xiōngnú attacked but failed to defeat him and so kept their distance.
Now the Chányú is newly troubled by Hàn,
and the former territory of Húnyé is empty and uninhabited.
The custom of the barbarians is to cling to their old lands,
and they are also greedy for Hàn's treasures.
If we now at this time generously bribe Wūsūn with valuable gifts,
and persuade them to move further east,
to settle in the former territory of Húnyé—
(Zhāng Qiān's Biography states: Kūnmò's father, Nàndōumí, was originally with the Dà Yuèzhī in the area between Dūnhuáng and Qílián,
a small state.
The Dà Yuèzhī attacked and killed Nàndōumí,
seizing his land.
But the Dà Yuèzhī were in turn defeated by the Xiōngnú,
who attacked the Sài kings to the west and seized their country.
Kūnmò avenged his father's death
by attacking and defeating the Dà Yuèzhī kingdom to the west,
and then remained there to establish the Wūsūn kingdom.
Qiān wished to induce them to return to their former lands.)
—their situation makes it suitable for them to agree.
If they agree, it will be severing the right arm of the Xiōngnú.
Once Wūsūn is allied with us,
all states to their west, such as Dàxià, can be invited to become our outer vassals."
The Son of Heaven considered this to be true,
and appointed Qiān as Zhōnglángjiàng.
He led three hundred men,
each with two horses,
and cattle and sheep numbering in the tens of thousands.
He carried gold, silk, and other valuables worth tens of thousands of *jùwàn*.
Many vice-envoys, bearing credentials, were dispatched.
(Shīgǔ said: "They were vice-envoys to Qiān,
and each was ordered to carry credentials.")
They were sent to other neighboring countries.
Along the way, if there was an opportune path to communicate with another country, an envoy was dispatched there.
When Qiān arrived in Wūsūn,
Kūnmò met Qiān with
very arrogant rites.
Qiān explained his purpose, saying:
(Shīgǔ said: "He explained the intentions of the Son of Heaven to him.")
"If Wūsūn can settle to the east in its old lands,
then Hàn will send a princess to be your wife,
and we will become brothers,
jointly resisting the Xiōngnú.
The Xiōngnú will not be able to withstand us."
Wūsūn, considering itself far from Hàn,
did not know its size;
it had long been subject to the Xiōngnú,
and furthermore, it was close to them.
All its chief ministers feared the Xiōngnú
and did not wish to relocate.
Qiān stayed for a long time
but could not achieve his objective.
He then dispatched his vice-envoys to Dàyuān, Kāngjū, Dà Yuèzhī, Dàxià, Ānxī, Shēndú, Yútián, and other neighboring countries.
Wūsūn sent interpreters and guides to escort Qiān back,
sending dozens of men
and dozens of horses
to follow Qiān to express their gratitude,
and also to observe the size of Hàn.
In that year,
Qiān returned.
Upon arrival,
he was appointed Dàxíng.
After more than a year,
the envoys Qiān had dispatched to Dàxià and other related countries all returned, bringing some of their people with them.
(Jìn Zhuó said: "People from their countries.")
The Western Regions generally comprised thirty-six states.
There were great mountains to the north and south,
and a river in the center.
(The Western Regions, when first connected with Hàn, comprised thirty-six states.

Later, over fifty states were established: Ruòqiāng, Shànshàn, Qiěmò, Xiǎoyuān, Jīngjué, Rónglú, Xúmí, Qúlè, Píshān, Wūchá, Xīyè, Púlí, Zǐhé, Yī'nài, Wúlèi, Nàndōu, Jìbīn, Wūyìshānlí, Líqiān, Tiáozhī, Ānxī, Dà Yuèzhī, Dàxià, Kāngjū, Yǎncài, Dàyuān, Táohuái, Xiūxún, Juǎndǔ, Shāchē, Shūlè, Wèitóu, Wūsūn, Gūmò, Wēnsù, Qiūcí, Wūlěi, Qújī, Wèilí, Wēixū, Yānqí, Wūtánzīlí, Bēilù, Bēilù Hòuguó, Yùlìshī, Dānhuán, Púlèi, Púlèi Hòuguó, Xīqiěmí, Dōngqiěmí, Jiéguó, Shānguó, Húhú, Chēshī Qián, and Hòu Wáng, are these.)
(The "great mountains to the north and south" refers to:
the Southern Mountains, which are south of Yútián, extend eastward to Jīnchéng,
and connect with the Southern Mountains of Hàn;
the Northern Mountains are north of Chēshī,
which are the same as the Liǔgǔ Jīnshālǐng and other mountains north of Jiāohé County in Xīzhōu, as mentioned in the Tang records.)
("A river in the center" refers to:
the river has two sources,
one originating from Cōnglíng,
and one from the Southern Mountains of Yútián.
Its northern branch flows and merges with the Cōnglíng River,
emptying into Púchānghǎi.
From Yútián westward,
all waters flow west,
passing through Xiūxún, Jìbīn, Dà Yuèzhī, Ānxī, and other countries before entering the Western Sea.
The waters of Púchāng flow underground
and emerge south of Jīshí,
forming the Central Plain's river.
The waters of the Western Sea merge southeastward into the Zhǎnghǎi of Jiāozhōu.)
(The Western Regions) were a thousand *lǐ* or more from north to south.
To the east, they bordered Hàn's Yùmén and Yángguān.
(Bān Zhì states: "Dūnhuáng Commandery's Lónglè County has Yùmén Guān and Yáng Guān."
Jiǔquán Commandery has Yùmén County.
Kàn Yīn said: "Hàn abolished the garrison at Yùmén Guān,
and settled its people here."
Kuòdì Zhì states: "Shāzhōu's Lónglè Mountain
is 165 *lǐ* south of the county.
Yùmén Guān
is 118 *lǐ* northwest of the county."
Xīhé Jiùshì states: "Cōnglíng
is a tall and vast mountain,
where onions (cōng) grow everywhere,

(One source originates from Cōnglíng,
one from Yútián,
and they merge to flow eastward into Yánzé.)
(Yánzé is over 300 *lǐ* from Yùmén and Yáng Guān.)

From Shànshàn, skirting the north of the Southern Mountains,
following the river westward to Shāchē,

(Shànshàn is also called the Lóulán Kingdom.
Its capital is Yúní City,
1,600 *lǐ* from Yáng Guān.)
(Shàn,
pronounced "shàn" [上扇翻].)
(Bàng,
pronounced "bàng" [步浪翻].)
(Shāchē,

9,950 *lǐ* from Cháng'ān.)
(Shā,
pronounced "shā" [素河翻].)
This route led to Dà Yuèzhī and Ānxī.
From the court of the King of Chēshī Qián, following the Northern Mountains and the river westward to Shūlè,
was the Northern Route.
(The King of Chēshī Qián,
his capital is Jiāohé City,
8,150 *lǐ* from Cháng'ān;
this is the same as the Jiāohé County of Xīzhōu in Tang.)
(Shūlè,

9,350 *lǐ* from Cháng'ān,
and it lies to the west on the route to Dà Yuèzhī, Dàyuān, and Kāngjū.)
This route led to Dàyuān, Kāngjū, and Yǎncài.

later became Sù
All these states were subject to the Xiōngnú.

who established a Commander of Servants (Tóngpú Dūwèi).
The Xiōngnú evidently regarded the various states of the Western Regions as servants,
hence the name of the official.
He usually resided between Yānqí, Wēixū, and Wèilí,
(Yānqí,

7,300 *lǐ* from Cháng'ān.)
