Since the Wūsūn king was unwilling to return east,
Hàn then established Jiǔquán Commandery in the former territory of Húnyé Wáng.
(Yìng Shào said: "Its water is like wine,
hence it is called Jiǔquán.")
(Shīgǔ said: "There is a golden spring below the city,
whose water tastes like wine;
in Tang, it was Sùzhōu.")
(Sòng Bái said: "It is 2,900 *lǐ* southeast to Cháng'ān.")
Later, Wǔwēi Commandery was also established.
(This was originally the territory where the Xiōngnú Xiūtú Wáng resided.
In the fourth year of Tàichū, Wǔwēi Commandery was established.
The Liángzhōu of Tang was this area.)
(Sòng Bái said: "It is 2,800 *lǐ* southeast to Cháng'ān.")
The Son of Heaven obtained a *Hànxuèmǎ* from *Wǎn*,
loved it,
and named it
"Heavenly Steed" (*Tiānmǎ*).
Envoys were constantly seen on the roads, seeking them.
Among those sent to foreign countries,
the large retinues numbered several hundred,
the small ones over a hundred people.
The provisions and supplies each person carried were generally similar to the time of the Marquis of *Bówàng*.
*Jī*
means "resources."
*Cāo*
means "to hold."
*Fàng*
means "to rely on."
This states that the quantities of imperial credentials and silk carried by the envoys were generally in accordance with those carried when the Marquis of *Bówàng* was dispatched.
*Fàng*
is read as *fǎng*.
*Shīgǔ* said: Because they were accustomed to this task,
not many people were sent.
*Shǎo*
is pronounced *shīzhǎo* (*shào*).
The smaller groups were five or six retinues;
those going far returned after eight or nine years,
and those going near returned after several years.
1. In winter,
the *Hángǔ Guān* was moved to *Xīn'ān*.
According to *Bān*'s history,
the old pass became *Hóngnóng* County.
*Yīng Shào* said: *Hóngnóng* is three hundred *lǐ* from *Xīn'ān*.
The *Shùzhēngjì* states: *Xīn'ān* County
is still called *Xīnguān* today.
2. In spring,
in the first month,
on the *wùzǐ* day,
the *Yánglíng Yuán* caught fire.
3. In summer,
in the fourth month,
there was a hailstorm.
4. More than ten commanderies and kingdoms east of the pass suffered famine,
and people cannibalized each other.
5. *Chángshān Xiànwáng Shùn* passed away.
*Shùn*
was a son of Emperor *Jǐng*,
and was enfeoffed in the fifth year of the middle era.
The rules for posthumous titles state: "Broadly learned and highly capable is *Xiàn*."
Those who were deposed for not attending to the sick *Xiànwáng* during his illness or for being disrespectful during mourning
were banished to *Fánglíng*.
The *Bānzhì* states that *Fánglíng* County belonged to *Hànzhōng* Commandery.
*Sòng Bái* said: *Kàn Yīn* said,
this is the land of *Fángzhǔ* from the Spring and Autumn period.
Emperor *Xiàn* of *Hàn* changed
*Fáng*
to
*Fáng*,
and also established *Fánglíng* Commandery;
it is now *Fángzhōu*.
The Son of Heaven re-enfeoffed *Xiànwáng*'s son, *Píng*, as King of *Zhēndìng*.
*Zhēndìng* County originally belonged to *Chángshān*.
Now the four counties of *Zhēndìng*, *Miánmàn*, *Gǎochéng*, and *Féilèi* were separated to form a kingdom.
Thus, all Five Sacred Mountains were within the Son of Heaven's domain.
*Huàshān* and *Sōnggāo*
were originally in the Son of Heaven's commanderies.
The Southern Marchmount, Mount *Huò*, belonged to *Lújiāng*.
*Huáinán* and *Héngshān* conspired to rebel,
their kingdoms were abolished,
and they were incorporated into *Hàn* as commanderies.
In the first year of *Yuánshòu*,
the King of *Jìběi* presented *Tàishān* and its surrounding settlements.
Now, *Chángshān* was again made a commandery,
and then all were within the Son of Heaven's domain.
6. The King of *Dài*, *Yì*, was moved to become King of *Qīnghé*.
*Yì*
was the grandson of *Wén dì*'s son, King *Cān* of *Dài*,
and the son of King *Dēng*.
King *Chéng* of *Qīnghé*,
a son of Emperor *Xiàojǐng*,
died
without issue,
his kingdom was abolished,
and the King of *Dài* was moved there.
7. In this year,
*Yīzhìxié Chányú* of the *Xiongnu* died,
and his son, *Wūwéi Chányú*, ascended.
1. In winter,
in the tenth month,
the Emperor traveled to *Yōng*
to sacrifice at the Five *Zhì* altars.
An edict stated:
"Now I personally offer sacrifice to the Supreme Deity in the southern suburb,
but the Earth Deity (*Hòutǔ*) is not sacrificed to,
then the rites are not reciprocated."
*Shīgǔ* said: *Dá*
means "to respond."
Sacrificing to Heaven without sacrificing to Earth
loses the meaning of the pair.
Another interpretation: neglecting the sacrifice to the Earth Deity
means it will not be answered by the spirits.
A shrine to the Earth Deity was established on a circular mound in a marsh.
The *Jiaosì Zhì* states: Officials deliberated that the sacrifice to the Earth Deity should be on a circular mound in a marsh,
forming five altars.
The *Bānzhì* states: *Xiàyáng* County belonged to *Zuǒfēngyì*.
*Fényīn* County belonged to *Hédōng* Commandery.
The Son of Heaven began to tour the commanderies and kingdoms;
the Administrator of *Hédōng*, not expecting the imperial visit,
failed to prepare
and committed suicide.
Not expecting the Emperor's visit to the commandery,
he could not prepare the provisions.
On the *jiǎzǐ* day,
a shrine to the Earth Deity was established on the *Fényīn Shuī*.
*Rú Chún* said: The *Shuī*
is a unique, towering mound on the eastern bank of the *Hé* (Yellow River),
about four or five *lǐ* long,
over two *lǐ* wide,
and over ten *zhàng* high.
*Fényīn* County seat was on the *Shuī*;
the Earth Deity shrine was west of the county seat.
The *Fén* River was north of the *Shuī*,
flowing west to join the *Hé*.
*Shīgǔ* said: The *Shuī*
is so named because its shape is high and raised,
like a person's buttocks (*kāoshuī*).
Another theory: this is above the *Fén* River,
the place was originally named *Huì*,
pronounced the same as *kuí*.
Locals there pronounce *kuí* like *shuí*,
so it transformed into the character *shuī*.
Hence, the *Hàn Jiùyí* calls it *Huìshàng*.
*Shuī*
is pronounced *shuí*.
The rites were performed as for the Supreme Deity.
After the rites,
he traveled to *Xíngyáng*,
and returned
to *Luòyáng*.
The *Bānzhì* states: *Xíngyáng* and *Luòyáng* both belonged to *Hénán* Commandery.
Minister *Zàn* said: The *Jízhǒng Gǔwén* calls *Wèi Jiāngjūn Wénzǐ* "Lord *Nán Mímóu*,"
and later there were *Zǐnán Gù* and *Zǐnán Jìng*.
The *Jìnián* states that *Jìng* paid court to *Wèi*.
Later, King *Huìchéng* went to *Wèi*
and appointed *Zǐnán* as a marquis.
*Qín* unified the Six States,
and *Wèi* was the last to fall.
It is suspected that *Jiā* was a descendant of *Wèi*,
hence he was surnamed *Zǐnán* and called "Lord."
*Shīgǔ* said: *Zǐnán*
was the name of his enfeoffment;
because he was a descendant of *Zhōu*,
he was generally referred to as *Zhōu Zǐnán Jūn*.
*Zàn*'s explanation is incorrect.
It is not customary to state the surname first and then call him "Lord."
Moreover, from *Jiā* downwards, all were surnamed *Jī*,
as recorded in historical accounts.
I rely on the *Ēnzé Hóubiǎo*, which states that *Zhōu Zǐnán Jūn* was enfeoffed in *Chángshè*, *Yǐngchuān*.
2. In spring,
in the second month,
*Zhōngshān Jìngwáng Shèng* passed away.
*Shèng*
was a son of Emperor *Jǐng*,
and was enfeoffed in the second year of the middle era.
3. Lèchéng Hóu Dīng Yì
Yì
was the great-grandson of Dīng Lǐ, a meritorious minister of Gāozǔ.
The Bān Zhì
states that Lèchéng
was a marquisate
belonging to Nányáng Jùn.
Kǎoyì says: The Hànshū Jiāosì Zhì records
"Lèchéng Hóu Dēng."
However, according to the Shǐjì and Hànshū Gōngchén Biǎo, it should be
"Dīng Yì."
He claimed to have studied under the same master as the Wénchéng Jiāngjūn.
The Emperor was regretting the execution of Wénchéng,
(The execution of Wénchéng is found in the previous volume, Yuánshòu Sī Nián.)
and was greatly pleased.
Dà had previously served Jiāodōng Kāng Wáng,
Kāng Wáng Jì
was the Emperor's younger brother.
Shī Gǔ says: "Shàn (善)" means sweet and pleasing words.
Yet he dared to speak grandly,
without any doubt.
Dà grandly declared:
"Your servant has often traveled to the sea,
and met those like Ānqí and Xiànmén.
They considered your servant lowly
and did not trust him;
they also thought Kāng Wáng was merely a feudal lord,
not worthy of comparison.
My master says: 'Gold can be made, and the breach of the Yellow River can be stopped;
the elixir of immortality can be obtained,
and immortals can be summoned.'
However, your servant fears meeting the same fate as Wénchéng;
if so, all the fangshì would cover their mouths,
how would they dare to speak of such methods!"
The Emperor said:
"Wénchéng died from eating horse liver, that's all.
Suǒyǐn says: The Lùnhéng states: The qi was violent and the poison potent,
so eating the liver of a galloping horse;
horse liver is fatal.
The Rúlín Chuán says: 'When eating meat, do not eat horse liver.'
This is correct.
What do I begrudge?"
Dà replied:
"My master does not seek out people;
people seek him.
If Your Majesty truly wishes to summon him,
then honor his messenger,
make him a relative,
and treat him with the courtesies due to a guest.
Only then can he be sent to communicate with the divine beings."
Thereupon, the Emperor ordered a test of a minor technique:
fighting flags,
where the flags struck each other.
Kǎoyì says: The Fēngshàn Shū and Jiāosì Zhì both write
"qí (棊)" (board game piece),
only the Shǐjì Xiàowǔ Jì writes
"qí (旗)" (flag).
According to the Hànwǔ Gùshì,
"Dà once erected several hundred flags in front of the palace.
Dà ordered the flags to strike each other,
fluttering throughout the courtyard,
more than ten zhàng above the ground.
All who watched were astonished."
Thus, the character
"qí (旗)"
is correct.
The Emperor was worried about the breach of the Yellow River and the failure to produce gold,
so he appointed Dà as Wǔlì Jiāngjūn.
He was also appointed Tiānshì Jiāngjūn,
Dìshì Jiāngjūn,
and Dàtōng Jiāngjūn.
In the summer,
fourth month,
on the day Yǐsì,
Dà was enfeoffed as Lètōng Hóu.
Ēnzé Hóu Biǎo: Lètōng Hóu's fief was in Gāopíng Xiàn, Āndìng Jùn.
He was bestowed a grand residence,
a thousand child-servants,
imperial carriages and horses, canopies, and artifacts to fill his home.
Shī Gǔ says: "Chì (斥)" means unused.
He was given a hundred thousand jīn of gold.
The Son of Heaven personally visited Wǔlì's residence;
messengers paid respects and provided supplies,
lining the road.
From the Tàizhǔ and the generals and ministers downwards,
(Tàizhǔ was the Emperor's aunt, Dòu Tàizhǔ.)
all presented gifts to him.
The Son of Heaven also carved a jade seal that read
"Tiāndào Jiāngjūn,"
and sent an envoy dressed in feathered robes
to stand on white reeds at night;
Wǔlì Jiāngjūn also dressed in feathered robes,
stood on white reeds,
and received the seal,
to demonstrate his non-subservience.
Feathered robes
are garments woven from feathers and down;
modern Daoists wear them.
Shǐyī, yìyī (使衣、亦衣),
read yú (於) and jì (既) respectively.
He wore six seals:
the five generals — Wǔlì, Tiānshì, Dìshì, Dàtōng, and Tiāndào —
together with Lètōng Hóu, made six seals.
At this, between the sea and Yān and Qí,
none failed to clasp their wrists and declare themselves possessing secret methods,
capable of achieving immortality.
4. In the sixth month,
Wū Jǐn of Fén'yīn,
Yìng Shào says: Jǐn was the name of the shamaness.
Shī Gǔ says: Fénshuí was originally the mound (墳) of the land of Wèi,
hence it was called Wèishuí.
The "camp" (營)
refers to the auspicious site (兆域) of the Hòutǔ Temple.
The Emperor sent someone to investigate and inquire;
the shamaness found the tripod to be without deception,
so sacrifices were offered with proper rites,
and the tripod was welcomed to Gānquán.
Following the Emperor's procession,
Rú Chún says: The tripod was taken to Gānquán following the procession.
It was stored in Gānquán Gōng;
all the ministers offered felicitations.
5. In autumn,
Shāng, the son of Chángshān Xiàn Wáng, was established as Sīshuǐ Wáng.
Sīshuǐ controlled Líng, Sīyáng, and Yú three counties.
It originally belonged to Dōnghǎi Jùn,
but the Emperor divided it to create a kingdom.
6. Previously,
Tiáohóu Zhōu Yàfū was Chancellor.
Zhōu Yàfū became chancellor seven years before Jǐngdì,
and was dismissed three years into his term.
Everyone in the chancellery praised his integrity and fairness.
However, Yàfū did not employ [Zhào] Yǔ,
saying:
"I know very well that Yǔ is harmless,
but his interpretation of law is too deep,
and he cannot be placed in a high office."
Yìng Shào says: Yǔ upheld legal statutes with deep scrutiny.
He was considered cruelly severe compared to the nine ministers;
meaning that when compared to the nine ministers of his time,
Yǔ was cruel and severe.
Officials strove to be stern and severe,
but Yǔ was even more renowned for his strictness and severity.
The Zhōngwèi Yǐn Qí was known for his daring executions.
The Xìng Pǔ says: The son of Shàohào was enfeoffed in Yǐnchéng,
and his descendants took this as their surname.
According to the Yǐn clan,
they were hereditary ministers of Zhōu.
Officials and common people became increasingly impoverished and exhausted.
In this year,
Qí was found incompetent and punished.
The Emperor then reinstated Wáng Wēnshū as Zhōngwèi,
and Zhào Yǔ as Tíngwèi.
Four years later,
Yǔ, due to old age,
was demoted to Yān Xiàng.
At this time, all officials prized cruelty and harshness in governance.
Only the Zuǒ Nèi Shǐ Ér Kuān
promoted agriculture,
eased punishments,
and managed lawsuits
with the aim of gaining the people's trust.
He selected benevolent and magnanimous scholars,
showed empathy to his subordinates,
and did not seek fame.
Officials and common people greatly trusted and loved him.
When collecting taxes,
he adjusted the "breadth and narrowness,"
lending to the people.
Shī Gǔ says: This means when poor or weak farmers needed it,
he did not immediately collect taxes.
I (the annotator) believe "breadth"
refers to times when collection was somewhat lenient and restrictions loose;
"narrowness"
refers to times of urgent pressure and strict enforcement.
During "broad" times, he did not urgently collect taxes,
but lent to the people,
allowing them to carry on their livelihoods.
Later, when a military expedition was launched,
the Zuǒ Nèi Shǐ's tax collection was deficient,
and he was to be dismissed.
When the people heard he was to be dismissed,
they all feared losing him.
Wealthy families with ox-carts and poorer families carrying burdens transported their taxes,
a continuous stream without interruption.
Shī Gǔ says: "Qiáng (繈)" means rope.
It means the taxpayers formed an unbroken line on the road,
like ropes connected to each other,
similar to today's "successive ropes."
Shuǐ (屬) is read zhīyù.
His tax collection was reported as excellent.
7 In the beginning,
Wénwáng of Nányuè sent his son Yīngqí to serve in the imperial guard.
King Hú of Nányuè passed away,
posthumously named Wénwáng.
Yīngqí, while serving in the imperial guard,
saw the seventeen-chapter text from the first year of Jiànyuán.
He had a son named Xīng.
After Wénwáng passed away,
Yīngqí ascended the throne.
He then hid the seal of his predecessor, Emperor Wǔ.
Zhào Tuó had styled himself Emperor Wǔ of Nányuè.
Lǐ Qí said: Remove his pretentious title.
Xīng was designated as heir.
The Hàn repeatedly sent envoys to persuade Yīngqí to come to court.
Yīngqí still enjoyed his unrestricted indulgence in killing,
and feared that if he entered the court, he would be required
to be treated like an inner vassal according to Hàn law.
So he steadfastly claimed illness
and thus did not come for an audience.
Yīngqí passed away,
posthumously named Míngwáng.
Crown Prince Xīng took his place,
and his mother became the Empress Dowager.
The Empress Dowager, even before she became Yīngqí's concubine,
had an affair with Ānguó Shǎojì from Bālíng.
Shīgǔ said: His surname was Ānguó,
and his courtesy name was Shǎojì.
Shǎo
is pronounced shīzhào.
The emperor sent Ānguó Shǎojì to persuade the King and the Empress Dowager to come to court,
and to be treated like inner vassals.
He ordered the eloquent debater and Grandee Remonstrant Zhōng Jūn and others to expound on these words.
A hundred officials submitted a memorial: In the fifth year of Yuánshòu,
Grandee Remonstrants were first established,
with a salary of eight hundred shí.
Shīgǔ said: To assist in making policy decisions.
Bān Zhì: Guìyáng County belonged to Guìyáng Commandery.
In the Táng dynasty, it was the territory of Guìyáng and Liánshān counties in Liánzhōu.
The King of Nányuè was young,
and the Empress Dowager was a Central Plains person.
When Ānguó Shǎojì went there,
he resumed his secret affair with her,
which the people of the country largely knew about,
and many did not support the Empress Dowager.
The Empress Dowager feared that unrest would arise,
and also wished to rely on Hàn power.
She repeatedly urged the King and her favored ministers to request incorporation into the empire.
She then, through an envoy, sent a letter
requesting to be treated like an inner vassal,
to come to court once every three years,
and to abolish the border passes.
Thereupon the Son of Heaven granted her request,
bestowing a silver seal upon her Chancellor Lǚ Jiā,
as well as seals for the Imperial Clerk, Commandant of the Capital, and Grand Tutor.
The remaining officials they could appoint themselves.
He abolished their former tattooing and nose-cutting punishments,
using Hàn law,
treating them like inner vassals.
The envoys all remained there
to pacify and stabilize the region.
According to Hàn regulations,
all officials of two thousand shí or above in vassal kingdoms were appointed by the Hàn court;
the rest could be appointed by the kingdom itself.
Now, the seals for Nányuè's Chancellor, Imperial Clerk, Commandant of the Capital, and Grand Tutor were bestowed,
making them comparable to inner vassals.
The Hàn, since Emperor Wén, had abolished corporal punishment,
not using the methods of tattooing or nose-cutting,
so they also ordered Nányuè to abolish them.
Qì
is pronounced yúqì,
also niúlí.
Tián
is pronounced zhèn.
This laid the groundwork for Lǚ Jiā's rebellion.
8 The emperor went to Yōng
to perform the suburban sacrifice.
Someone said:
"The Five Emperors
are assistants to Tàiyī.
Tàiyī should be established,
and the emperor should personally perform the suburban sacrifice."
The emperor was doubtful and had not yet decided.
Gōngsūn Qīng from Qí said:
"This year, a precious ding was obtained.
In the winter, on the first day of the Xīnsì month, it will be the winter solstice,
which is the same as in the time of the Yellow Emperor."
Qīng had a bamboo slip text.
Shīgǔ said: Děng means same.
Zhá are thin, small wooden slips.
"The Yellow Emperor obtained a precious ding.
In that year, on the first day of the Jǐyǒu month, it was the winter solstice.
After exactly three hundred and eighty years,
the Yellow Emperor ascended to heaven as an immortal."
He then presented it through a favored attendant.
The emperor was greatly pleased,
summoned him, and asked.
Qīng replied:
"I received this text from Shēn Gōng.
Shēn Gōng said:
'When the Hàn arose, it was destined to be like the time of the Yellow Emperor.
The sage of Hàn will be a grandson or great-grandson of Gāozǔ.
When a precious ding appears, it will communicate with the spirits.
The Yellow Emperor received all spirits at the Míngtíng,
and Míngtíng is Gānquán.
The Yellow Emperor collected copper from Shǒushān.
Bān Zhì: In Púbǎn County, Hédōng, there is Shǒushān.
Bān Zhì: In Huáidé County, Féngyì, there is Jīngshān.
There were dragons with drooping beards descending to welcome the Yellow Emperor,
Shīgǔ said: Hú refers to the fleshy dewlap under the chin;
xú refers to its hair.
Xú is pronounced rénzhān.
And he, along with seventy-odd favored ministers and imperial concubines, ascended to heaven.' "
Thereupon the Son of Heaven said:
"Ah!
If I could truly be like the Yellow Emperor,
I would regard leaving my wife and children as easily as shedding a shoe!"
Shīgǔ said: Xǐ are small shoes.
Shedding a shoe means it is convenient and easy,
and one has no concerns.
Xǐ is pronounced shān'ěr.
He sent someone eastward to seek spirits at Tàishì.
Shīgǔ said: Tàishì Mountain is in Chónggāo County, Yǐngchuān,
and is the Central Peak.
1 In winter,
in the tenth month,
the Emperor worshipped the Wǔzhì at Yōng.
Then he crossed Lǒng.
Lǒng is a mountain plateau,
located in Lǒng County, Tiānshuǐ Commandery.
The Sānqín Jì says: "Its slopes have nine bends,
and it takes seven days to cross Lǒng."
The Táng Dìlǐ Zhì states,
Kōngtóng is west of Yìlè County, Mínzhōu.
Mínzhōu
was the territory of Hàn Líntáo.
The Shǐjì writes it as
“Kōngtóng”.
Zhèngyì says: Kōngtóng Mountain
is one hundred *lǐ* west of Pínggāo County, Yuánzhōu.
The imperial entourage could not get food,
became panicked,
and committed suicide.
Thereupon, the Emperor headed north, exiting Xiāoguān,
and with tens of thousands of cavalry, hunted in Xīnqínzhōng,
then returned after reviewing the border troops.
Xīnqínzhōng was perhaps a thousand *lǐ* without a single watchtower or border marker,
so the Grand Administrator of Běidì and others below him were executed.
The seat of Táng Línzhōu was Xīnqín.
Dù Yòu: "It was the land of Hàn Xīnqínzhōng."
I say that the Táng merely adopted the name of Hàn Xīnqínzhōng for its commandery,
and Línzhōu could not fully encompass the territory of Hàn Xīnqínzhōng.
Běidì bordered Shuòfāng;
at that time, Shuòfāng had just been established as a commandery.
Presumably, Běidì was made to jointly exert effort in constructing watchtowers and border markers.
Jiǎo,
pronounced jídiào.
A sacrificial altar for Tàiyī was erected,
and the sacrificial implements used were like those for one *zhì* at Yōng, but with additions.
Yōng has Wǔzhì;
the implements used for worshipping Tàiyī now
were like the sacrificial implements for one *zhì* at Yōng.
The "additions"
refer to added sweet wine, jujubes, and dried meat.
This was for sacrificial meals for the divine attendants and the Northern Dipper.
The Shuōwén says,
zhuì,
is to offer pure wine in sacrifice.
Shīgǔ says: "It refers to a series of connected sacrifices."
Zhuì,
pronounced zhúrèi.
Shí,
read as sì.
Cóng,
pronounced cáiyòng.
On the *xīnsì* day, the first day of the month,
it was the winter solstice;
at dawn,
mèi
means dimness.
Shuǎng
means brightness.
It means when the sun is still dim but the sky is gradually brightening.
In the morning, the sun was greeted;
in the evening, the moon was greeted.
Yīng Shào says: "The Son of Heaven greets the sun in spring mornings
and the moon in autumn evenings;
the sun is greeted in the morning,
the moon in the evening."
Minister Zàn says: "According to the Hàn Yízhù: 'When sacrificing at Tàizhì,
the Emperor emerges from the bamboo palace at daybreak,
faces east and greets the sun;
that evening, he faces southwest and greets the moon.
This is done on the day of the sacrifice,
not specifically in spring or autumn.'"
Shīgǔ says: "Greeting the sun in spring mornings
and the moon in autumn evenings
was probably the usual custom;
but greeting the sun and moon during the sacrifice at Tàizhì
is another distinct ceremony."
Cháo cháo,
the second character is pronounced zhíyáo;
the same below.
Fires filled the altar,
and cooking utensils were heated by the altar.
Officials reported:
"There was a light above the altar."
They also reported:
"During the day, a yellow vapor ascended to the sky."
The Grand Astrologer Tán and the sacrificial officer Kuānshū, etc.,
presented memorials. The Grand Astrologer was subordinate to the Grand Minister of Ceremonies.
The Liú Zhāo Zhì states: "His rank was six hundred *dàn* of grain;
he was in charge of celestial phenomena and the calendar,
and all national sacrifices, funerals, and marriages."
Tán
was Sīmǎ Tán.
Cíguān was the officer in charge of sacrifices.
Kuānshū:
His surname was omitted by the historians.
An imperial edict approved this.
2 The King of Nányuè and the Queen Dowager prepared their travel arrangements,
carrying abundant tribute
to equip themselves for entering the court.
Their Chancellor, Lǚ Jiā,
was old;
he had served three kings.
More than seventy members of his clan held official positions as senior administrators.
All his sons had married royal daughters,
and all his daughters had married princes, royal kinsmen,
and also had ties with the King of Cāngwú-Qín.
Mèng Kāng says: "Cāngwú
was a king in Yuè,
who styled himself King of Qín."
Lián
means matrimonial kinship.
Jìn Zhuó says: "The King of Qín
was the later Zhào Guāng;
the Zhào originally shared the same surname as Qín,
hence he was called King of Qín."
I say, since the King of Nányuè's surname was Zhào,
why was he not called the King of Nányuè-Qín?
Jìn's explanation is not convincing.
Zhǎng,
pronounced zhīliǎng.
He commanded more popular support than the king.
Shīgǔ says: "Yù
means to surpass."
He repeatedly advised the king to stop,
but the king did not listen.
He harbored rebellious intentions,
frequently feigned illness,
and refused to see the Hàn envoys.
The envoys all paid close attention to Jiā,
but were unable to execute him.
The King and Queen Dowager also feared that Jiā and others would act first,
and wished to rely on the authority of the Hàn envoys
to conspire to execute Jiā and others.
Wéi Zhāo says: "They relied on the envoys as their armor."
Suǒyǐn says: "The Zhìlín states: 'Jiè means to rely on;
they wished to rely on the envoys' authority to execute Lǚ Jiā.'
Wéi Zhāo takes jiè to mean to rely on.
Jiè also means 'between';
it means to use the power 'between' them and the Hàn envoys—
this interpretation seems correct.
However, to say 'relying on as armor' is incorrect.
Yú Xǐ takes jiè to mean 'to rely on',
which also has a basis;
jiè is what connects guest and host."
All the high officials were seated, drinking.
Jiā's younger brother was a general,
and his troops were stationed outside the palace.
As the wine was circulating,
the Queen Dowager said to Jiā:
"Nányuè becoming an inner dependency
is beneficial to the state;
why does Your Excellency find it so inconvenient?"
This was to provoke the envoys.
The envoys hesitated and looked at each other,
and thus no one dared to act.
Jiā saw that the atmosphere was unusual,
Shīgǔ says: "It means different from the usual."
The Queen Dowager was enraged
and wanted to stab Jiā with a spear,
but the King stopped her.
Jiā then left,
armored his brother's troops and went to his residence.
Lǐ Qí says: "Jiè
means 'to wear'."
Shīgǔ says: "Jiè
means 'armor';
to wear armor to protect oneself.
Brother's troops
refers to those mentioned above, his brother's general and troops stationed outside."
He refused to see the King or the envoys,
and secretly plotted rebellion with the high officials.
The King had never intended to execute Jiā,
and Jiā knew this,
which is why he did not act for several months.
The Son of Heaven heard that Lü Jiā
would not obey the command, that the King and Grand Empress Dowager were isolated and weak, unable to control him,
and that the envoy was timid and indecisive.
He also believed that the King and Grand Empress Dowager had already sided with Han,
and that Lü Jiā alone was causing trouble,
which was not reason enough to raise an army.
He wished to send Zhuāng Cān with two thousand men as an envoy.
Cān said:
"If going in good faith,
a few people are enough;
if going by force,
two thousand men will not be sufficient."
He declined, and
the Son of Heaven dismissed Cān.
Hán Qiānqiū, a brave warrior from Jiá and former Chancellor of Jìběi,
(Bān Zhì:
Jiá county belongs to Yǐngchuān Commandery.
Shǐ Jì Zhèngyì says: Now Rǔzhōu Jiáchéng county.
Jiá,
pronounced jiá.
Qiānqiū
was probably the Chancellor of Jìběi Chéng Wáng Hú.
Hú was
Zhēn Wáng Bó's son.)
said: "With the small state of Yuè,
and with the King and Grand Empress Dowager supporting us,
only Chancellor Lü Jiā is causing harm.
I request three hundred brave warriors,
and I will surely behead Jiā to repay you."
Thereupon, the Son of Heaven dispatched Qiānqiū and Jiū Lè, the Grand Empress Dowager's younger brother, leading two thousand men.
They entered the Yuè territory.
Lü Jiā and others then rebelled,
issuing an order throughout the country:
"The King is young.
The Grand Empress Dowager
is a woman from the Central Plains,
and she is also having illicit relations with the envoy.
She is intent on annexing our state to Han,
offering all the precious treasures of the former kings to the Son of Heaven to ingratiate herself;
she takes many people with her
to Cháng'ān,
where they are enslaved and sold as servants;
she seeks temporary personal gain,
with no regard for the Zào clan's altars of soil and grain, nor any thought for the welfare of future generations."
He then, with his younger brother, led troops to attack and kill the King, the Grand Empress Dowager, and the Han envoys,
and sent people to inform Qín Wáng of Cāngwú and the various commanderies and counties under him.
He established Míng Wáng's eldest son, Yuè Zǐ Zǐ Shùyáng Hóu Jiàndé, as King.
(Jiàndé surrendered to Han and
was first enfeoffed as Shùyáng Hóu;
the historian probably added this later.
Bān Biǎo says
Shùyáng Hóu's fief was in Xiàpī, Dōnghǎi.
Zhǎng,
pronounced zhī liǎng.
They captured several small towns.
Afterwards, Yuè opened up a direct road and supplied provisions.
(Shīgǔ said: They allowed them to penetrate deep,
then attacked and annihilated them.)
Pānyú,
the capital of Nányuè.
Fān,
pronounced Pān.
They then annihilated them;
they sent someone to seal the Han envoy's credential in a box and place it on the border,
making a deceptive apology,
and dispatched troops to guard strategic locations.
In spring,
in the third month,
on the day Rénwǔ,
the Son of Heaven heard of Nányuè's rebellion,
and said:
"Although Hán Qiānqiū had no achievement,
he was still the vanguard of the army.
Enfeoff his son Yánnián as Chéng'ān Hóu."
(Bān Biǎo says:
Chéng'ān Hóu's fief was in Jiá county of Yǐngchuān Commandery.)
"As for the one who first desired to attach himself to Han,
enfeoff his son Guǎngdé as Lóngkàng Hóu."
(Bān Zhì:
Lóngkàng county belongs to Pèiguó.
Kàng,
pronounced gāng.
Kǎoyì says: In Hàn Shū Gōngchén Biǎo, it is written
"Lóng Hóu,"
and in Nányuè Zhuàn, it is written
"Lóng Hóu."
Jìn Zhuó said:
"Lóng"
is the ancient
character for
"Lóng."
Shǐ Jì Jiàn Yuán Yǐ Lái Hóu Zhě Biǎo and Nányuè Zhuàn both write
"Lóngkàng Hóu";
we now follow this.)
In summer,
in the fourth month,
a general amnesty was declared throughout the empire.
On the last day of Dīngchǒu,
there was a solar eclipse.
In autumn,
Fúbō Jiāngjūn Lù Bódé
(Huán Jì Yàolüè says: Fúbō Jiāngjūn means 'General Who Calms the Waves', wishing to make the waves subside when navigating rivers and seas with ships.)
descended the Huáng Shuǐ.
(Shuǐ Jīng: Huì Shuǐ originates from Lú Jù in Guìyáng county,
flows south out of Zhēnnǚ Xiá,
joins Quàng Shuǐ,
passes southeast through Hán Quàng county,
and flows south out of Quàngpǔ Guān as Guì Shuǐ.
Shānhǎi Jīng considers Quàng Shuǐ to be Huáng Shuǐ.
Xú Guǎng said: Huáng Shuǐ,
also known as Quàng Shuǐ,
originates from Guìyáng
and connects to Sìhuì.
Shīgǔ said: Huáng,
pronounced huáng.)
He descended the Zhēn Shuǐ.
(Yìng Shào said: Zhēn Shuǐ originates from the west of Lóngchuān in Nánhǎi
and enters Qín Shuǐ.
Shuǐ Jīng: Zhēn Shuǐ flows past the south of Zhēnyáng county in Guìyáng Commandery
and then branches right into Zhēn Shuǐ.
Zhēn,
Zhèng Shì said: Zhēn,
pronounced chēng;
Mèng Kāng said: Zhēn,
pronounced zhēn;
Shīgǔ said: Zhēn,
pronounced zhàng gēng.)
From Línglíng,
Xià Lí Shuǐ
(Zhāng Yàn said: Yán, a former Yuè person,
surrendered
and became Guīyì Hóu.
Yuè people carry people's boats in the water,
and there are also dangers from dragons.
Therefore, spears were placed under the boats,
hence the name.
Chén Zàn said: Wǔ Zǐxū Shū mentions 'spear-boats' (gēchuán),
which carried spears and halberds,
hence they were called spear-boats.
Shīgǔ said: Judging by the example of 'tower-boats' (lóuchuán),
it does not mean carrying spears and halberds.
This probably refers to placing spears under the boats to defend against the harm from crocodiles and other aquatic creatures,
and Zhāng's explanation is close.
Gòngfù said: Placing spears under a boat is difficult to arrange
and also makes it impossible to move;
many boats are built today,
but none have spears placed under them.
Yán, being a northerner,
did not understand how to operate boats,
so he believed Zhāng's explanation;
Zàn's explanation is probably correct.
I refer to the table which has no Guīyì Yuè Hóu Yán.)
Línglíng originally belonged to Guìyáng;
the emperor divided it and established a commandery;
during the Táng dynasty, it was Yǒng and Dào two prefectures.
Lí Shuǐ,
Bān Zhì: originates from the southeast of Yánghǎi mountain in Línglíng county,
and enters Yù Shuǐ at Guǎngxìn.
Xià Cāngwú
(Fú Qián said: Jiǎ was a former Yuè person who returned to Han.
Chén Zàn said: Lài means rapids;
in Wú and Yuè it is called lài,
in the Central Plains it is called qì.
Wǔ Zǐxū Shū mentions 'river-descent boats' (xiàlài chuán).
Lài,
pronounced lài.)
Cāngwú was originally Yuè territory;
the emperor first established a commandery there,
which had Lì Shuǐ Guān;
in the Táng dynasty, it was the land of Wú, Hè, Kāng, Duān, and Fēng prefectures.
He sent a hundred thousand men in tower-boats south of the Jiāng and Huái rivers.
Yuè Chíyì Hóu Yí separately led criminals from Bā and Shǔ,
and mobilized troops from Yèláng,
who descended the Zāngkē Jiāng,
all to rendezvous at Pānyú.
Qí Xiàng Bǔ Shì wrote a memorial,
requesting that he, his son, and the mariners from Qí go to their deaths in Nányuè.
The Son of Heaven issued an edict commending Bǔ Shì,
granting him the title of Guānnèi Hóu,
sixty catties of gold,
ten qǐng of land,
and publicized it throughout the empire;
yet no one responded.
At this time, the liehou numbered in the hundreds,
but none sought to join the army to attack Yuè.
It happened that in the ninth month, during the chou ritual,
when sacrifices were offered at the ancestral temple,
the liehou, as commanded, offered gold to assist in the sacrifices.
The Shaofǔ inspected the gold,
and if the gold was light or of poor color,
the Emperor ordered all involved to be impeached for disrespect,
and one hundred and six were stripped of their titles.
Rú Chún said: "According to the Hàn ceremonial regulations: 'Princes who become marquises
annually offer yellow gold for the chou ritual at the Hàn temples.
The Emperor personally receives the offered gold.
If the gold is insufficient,
not matching the required weight,
or of poor color,
a king's county is reduced,
and a marquis is stripped of his domain.' "
I infer that among those who lost their marquisates at that time, liehou and princely marquises together numbered one hundred and six,
so it was probably not only princely marquises who had to provide chou gold.
Chou,
read zhí yòu fān.
Shěng,
read xī jǐng fān.
Hái,
read hù gài fān.
Xīnsì
Chéngxiàng Zhào Zhōu was impeached for knowing that the chou gold of the liehou was light,
was imprisoned,
and committed suicide.
6 Bǐngshēn,
Shí Qìng, the Yùshǐ Dàfū, was made Chéngxiàng
and enfeoffed as Mùqiū Hóu.
According to the Ēnzé Hóu Biǎo,
Mùqiū Hóu's fief was Píngyuán.
Sāng Hóngyáng and others generated profits,
Wáng Wēnshū and his like enforced strict laws,
and Ér Kuān and others promoted literature,
all becoming Jiǔqīng,
taking turns holding power;
matters were not decided by the Chéngxiàng,
Chéngxiàng Qìng merely remained pure and circumspect.
Shī Gǔ said: "Chún means 'sincere and substantial'."
7 Wǔlì Jiāngjūn prepared to depart,
heading east into the sea to seek his master.
However, he did not dare to enter the sea,
and instead went to Tàishān to perform sacrifices.
The Emperor sent men to verify,
but in reality, nothing was seen.
Wǔlì falsely claimed to have seen his master,
but most of his methods proved ineffective,
Shī Gǔ said: "Shòu means 'effective' or 'corresponding';
bù shòu means 'no verification'."
and he was cut in two at the waist;
Lèchéng Hóu was also publicly executed.
8 The Xīqiāng, numbering one hundred thousand, rebelled,
sent envoys to the Xiōngnú,
attacked Gù'ān,
and besieged Báohǎn.
Gù'ān County belonged to Zhuójùn;
how could the Xīqiāng army reach here!
It should be
"Ān Gù".
According to the Bān Zhì,
the two counties of Ān Gù and Báohǎn
both belonged to Lǒngxī Jùn.
Báohǎn was
formerly a Qiāng settlement.
Sòng Bái said: "The old city of Ān Gù
is south of Lánzhōu.
Báohǎn is
the present seat of Hézhōu."
Bá,
pronounced fū.
Hǎn,
as written.
Wǔyuán,
was Qín's Jiǔyuán Jùn,
renamed by the Emperor;
in the Táng dynasty, it was Yánzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: "Wǔyuán Jùn had five plains,
hence the name.
These were Lóngyóu Yuán, Qǐdìyú Yuán, Qīnglǐng Yuán, Kělánzhēn Yuán, and Héngcáo Yuán."
The old city of Wǔyuán
is within the present Yúlín County boundaries.
1 In winter,
one hundred thousand troops were mobilized,
and Jiāngjūn Lǐ Xī and Lángzhōnglìng Xú Zìwéi were sent to suppress the Xīqiāng,
which they accomplished.
2 General of the Towered Warship, Yáng Pú, entered Yuè (Yue) territory.
First, he captured Xúnhá (Xunha),
and broke through Shímén (Shimen).
Shímén (Shimen) was twenty lǐ northwest of Pānyú (Panyu).
The Jùn Guó Zhì (Jun Guo Zhi) states: Lǚ Jiā resisted Hàn (Han),
piling stones in the river to form a gate,
hence it was named Shímén (Shimen).
Yáng Pú waited with several tens of thousands of men for the General Fúbō (Fubo), Lù Bódé, to arrive, then advanced together.
The Towered Warship division led the way,
reaching Pānyú (Panyu).
Nányuè (Nanyue) King Jiàndé (Jiande) and Prime Minister Lǚ Jiā defended the city.
The Towered Warship division was positioned on the southeast face,
and Fúbō (Fubo) on the northwest face.
As evening fell,
the Towered Warship division attacked and defeated the Yuè (Yue) people,
setting fire to the city.
Fúbō (Fubo) set up a camp.
Shīgǔ (Shigu) said: "He established a camp and fortifications to await those who surrendered."
He bestowed seals and ribbons,
and then released them to invite others.
Shīgǔ (Shigu) said: "Those who surrendered were immediately given marquis seals,
then released to return
and persuade others to surrender."
Fù (Fu),
pronounced fú yòu fān.
They were driven into Fúbō's (Fubo's) camp.
At dawn,
everyone in the city surrendered.
Jiàndé (Jiande) and Jiā (Jia) had fled into the sea during the night.
Fúbō (Fubo) sent men to pursue them.
Colonel Sīmǎ Sū Hóng captured Jiàndé (Jiande),
and Yuè (Yue) Lang Dū Jī captured Jiā (Jia).
Mèng Kāng said: "These were lang (court gentlemen) appointed by the Yuè (Yue) themselves."
Kǎo Yì (Kao Yi) states: "The tables in the Shǐ Jì (Shi Ji) and Hàn Shū (Han Shu) both write
'Sūn Dū,'
but the Nányuè Chuán (Nanyue Chuan) all say
'Dū Jī.'
We now follow the biography."
Nányuè (Nanyue) was thus pacified.

Its territory was then made into nine commanderies: Nánhǎi (Nanhai), Cāngwú (Cangwu), Yùlín (Yulin), Hépǔ (Hepu), Jiāozhǐ (Jiaozhi), Jiǔzhēn (Jiuzhen), Rìnán (Rinan), Zhūyá (Zhuya), and Dān'ěr (Dan'er).
Nánhǎi (Nanhai)
was the land of Guǎngzhōu (Guangzhou) and Xúnzhōu (Xunzhou) during the Táng (Tang) dynasty.
Cāngwú (Cangwu):
notes seen above.
Yùlín (Yulin)
was the land of Guìzhōu (Guizhou), Yùlín (Yulin), Dǎngzhōu (Dangzhou), and Xiùzhōu (Xiuzhou) during the Táng (Tang) dynasty.
Hépǔ (Hepu)
was the land of Liánzhōu (Lianzhou), Léizhōu (Leizhou), and Pánzhōu (Panzhou) during the Táng (Tang) dynasty.
Jiāozhǐ (Jiaozhi)
was the land of Ānnán (Annan) during the Táng (Tang) dynasty.
Dù Yòu said: "The southern barbarians
have large feet with widely splayed toes;
if they stand with their feet together,
their toes interlock,
hence the name Jiāozhǐ (Jiaozhi) ('interlocking toes')."
Liú Xīnqī's Jiāozhōu Jì (Jiaozhou Ji) states: "The people of Jiāozhǐ (Jiaozhi) from Nándìng (Nanding) county
have boneless feet,
hairy bodies,
and can only rise after being helped when lying down."
The Shān Hǎi Jīng (Shan Hai Jing) says: "The Jiāojǐng (Jiaojing) people have interlocking shins."
Guō Pú said: "Their shins are bent and crossed,
which is what is meant by
'diāotí (diaoti) and jiāozhǐ (jiaozhi).'"
Jiǔzhēn (Jiuzhen)
was the land of Àizhōu (Aizhou) during the Táng (Tang) dynasty.
Rìnán (Rinan)
was the land of Huānzhōu (Huanzhou) during the Táng (Tang) dynasty.
Shīgǔ (Shigu) said: "It means 'south of the sun,'
referring to those who 'open their northern doors towards the sun.'"
Zhūyá (Zhuya) and Dān'ěr (Dan'er)
were the lands of Qióngguǎn (Qiongguan) during the Táng (Tang) dynasty.
Yīng Shào said: "These two commanderies are on the cliffs and shores of the great sea,
and produce pearls,
hence the name Zhūyá (Zhuya) ('pearl cliff').
As for Dān'ěr (Dan'er),
the people have large ears,
and their chiefs call themselves kings;
their ears are especially drooping,
hanging three inches below their shoulders."
Zhāng Yàn said: "The Yì Wù Zhì (Yi Wu Zhi) states that
these two commanderies are in the sea,
a thousand lǐ from east to west,
and five hundred lǐ from north to south.
The people of Dān'ěr (Dan'er)
carve the skin of their cheeks,
connecting it to their earlobes,
dividing it into several branches,
shaped like sheep's intestines,
hanging down from their ears."
Xián (Xian) said: "The old city of Dān'ěr (Dan'er)
is now Yìlún (Yilun) county in Dānzhōu (Danzhou)."
Dān (Dan),
pronounced dīng gān fān.
Chén Zàn said: "The seat of Zhūyá (Zhuya) commandery was Shèndū (Shendu),
7,324 lǐ from Cháng'ān (Chang'an).
Dān'ěr (Dan'er) was 7,335 lǐ from Cháng'ān (Chang'an),
as seen in the Máo Líng Shū (Mao Ling Shu)."
The emperor increased the enfeoffment of Fúbō (Fubo);
Yáng Pú, General of the Towered Warship, was enfeoffed as Jiāngliáng Hóu (Jiangliang Hou);
Sū Hóng as Hǎicháng Hóu (Haichang Hou);
Dū Jī as Líncài Hóu (Lincai Hou).
Xú Guǎng said: "Hǎicháng (Haichang) is in Dōnglái (Donglai)."
I, the humble one, have consulted the Wángzǐ Hóu Biǎo (Wangzi Hou Biao)
and found that Hǎicháng Hóu (Haichang Hou) should have his fief in Lángxié (Langxie).
The Gōngchén Biǎo (Gongchen Biao) states that
Líncài Hóu (Lincai Hou) had his fief in Hénèi (Henei).
Zhào Guāng was enfeoffed as Suítáo Hóu (Suitao Hou);
Shǐ Dìng as Āndào Hóu (Andao Hou);
Bì Qǔ as Liáo Hóu (Liao Hou);
Jū Wēng as Xiāngchéng Hóu (Xiangcheng Hou).
Kǎo Yì (Kao Yi) states: "For all these enfeoffments as marquises,
the annual tables all have months and days.
Because their chronological order is difficult to ascertain,
they are all appended to the place where their meritorious service was performed;
the following instances will be similar."
3 Gōngsūn Qīng, awaiting the gods in Hénán (Henan),
said he saw footprints of immortals on Gōushì (Goushi) city wall.
The Bān Zhì (Ban Zhi) states that
Gōushì (Goushi) county belonged to Hénán (Henan) commandery.
Sòng Bái said: "The old city of Hàn (Han) Gōushì (Goushi) county
is twenty-five lǐ southeast of the present county."
Gōu (Gou),
pronounced gōng hóu fān.
The Son of Heaven personally visited Gōushì (Goushi) city to inspect the footprints,
and asked Qīng (Qing):
"Are you not imitating Wénchéng (Wencheng) and Wǔlì (Wuli)?"
Qīng (Qing) replied:
"Immortals do not seek human lords;
human lords seek them.
Their way is not easily accessible;
if not leniently accommodated,
the gods will not come.
If matters concerning spirits are spoken of as circuitous and fantastical,
Shīgǔ (Shigu) said: 'Yū (Yu) means distant;
dàn (dan) means grand speech.'
then they can be attracted."
The emperor believed him.
Thereupon, each commandery and kingdom cleared roads,
repaired palaces, temples, famous mountains, and spirit shrines, awaiting a visit.
4 To offer sacrifices to Nányuè (Nanyue),
and to worship Tàiyī (Taiyi) and Hòutǔ (Houtu),
music and dance were first used.
According to the Jiāosì Zhì (Jiaosi Zhi),
in the autumn of the fifth year,
a prayer was made to Tàiyī (Taiyi) for the campaign against Nányuè (Nanyue),
hence the current commemorative sacrifice.
Sài (Sai),
pronounced xiān dài fān.
5 The Marquis Chíyì (Chiyi) mobilized southern Yí (Yi) troops
intending to attack Nányuè (Nanyue).
However, the ruler of Qiělán (Qielan), fearing a long journey,
(Qiělán (Qielan) was also a southern Yí (Yi) tribe.
The emperor established it as a county,
belonging to Zāngkē (Zangke) commandery.
Qiě (Qie),
pronounced jū;
zǐ lǘ fān.)
rebelled with his followers,
killing the envoy and the Administrator of Jiànwéi (Jianwei).
The Hàn (Han) then mobilized eight colonels of criminals from Bā (Ba) and Shǔ (Shu) who were designated
to attack Nányuè (Nanyue),
and dispatched Central Palace Grandees Guō Chāng and Wèi Guǎng to lead them and attack Qiělán (Qielan), as well as the rulers of Qióng (Qiong) and Zuò (Zuo).
(The ruler of Qióng (Qiong) was the ruler of Qióngdū (Qiondu).
The Marquis of Zuò (Zuo) was the ruler of Zuòdū (Zuodu).
Zuò (Zuo),
pronounced cái gè fān;
same below.)
The ruler of Yèláng (Yelang), who had initially relied on Nányuè (Nanyue),
after Nányuè (Nanyue) was destroyed,
subsequently submitted to the court.
The emperor made him King of Yèláng (Yelang).
Rǎnmáng (Ranmang) were all terrified,
requesting to become subjects and to have officials appointed.
So Qióngdū (Qiondu) was made Yuècuì (Yuecui) commandery,
Zuòdū (Zuodu) was made Shěnlí (Shenli) commandery.
Fú Qián said: "The seat of the present Shu commandery's Northern Commander was originally Zuòdū (Zuodu)."
Chén Zàn said: "The Máo Líng Shū (Mao Ling Shu) states that Shěnlí (Shenli) was governed from Zuòdū (Zuodu),
3,335 lǐ from Cháng'ān (Chang'an)."
During the Táng (Tang) dynasty, it was the land of Lízhōu (Lizhou).
Bái Mǎ (Bai Ma) west of Guǎnghàn (Guanghan) was made Wǔdū (Wudu) commandery.
Gāozǔ (Gaozu) established Guǎnghàn (Guanghan) commandery;
during the Táng (Tang) dynasty, it was Zǐzhōu (Zizhou).
Bái Mǎ (Bai Ma) resided in Wǔdū (Wudu) Qiúchí (Qiuchi),
which the Bān Zhì (Ban Zhi) called Tiānchí Dàzé (Tianchi Daze).
The Kuò Dì Zhì (Kuo Di Zhi) states: "Chéngzhōu (Chengzhou) and Wǔzhōu (Wuzhou) in Lǒngyòu (Longyou) were all Bái Mǎ Dī (Bai Ma Di),
and their prominent family, the Yáng (Yang) clan, resided on Qiúchí (Qiuchi) mountain in Chéngzhōu (Chengzhou)."
Wǔdū (Wudu) commandery
was the land of Jiēzhōu (Jiezhou), Chéngzhōu (Chengzhou), Wǔzhōu (Wuzhou), etc., during the Táng (Tang) dynasty.
6 Initially,
Yúshàn (余善), the King of Dōngyuè, submitted a memorial
requesting to lead 8,000 troops to follow the 'Towered Warship General' to attack Lǚjiā (呂嘉).
When the troops reached Jiēyáng (揭陽),
Bān Zhì (班志) states,
Jiēyáng County belonged to Nánhǎi (南海) Commandery;
in the Táng (唐) dynasty, it was Cháozhōu (潮州).
Wéi Zhāo (韋昭) said: Jiē (揭),
pronounced as qì shì fān (其逝翻).
Sū Lín (蘇林) pronounced it jiē (揭),
Shīgǔ (師古) pronounced it jié (竭).
Yúshàn did not proceed,
but held both ends,
secretly sending envoys to Nányuè (南越).
When Hàn (漢) later broke Pānyú (番禺),
he did not arrive.
Yáng Pú (楊僕) submitted a memorial, wishing to immediately lead troops to attack Dōngyuè;
the emperor, considering the soldiers weary,
did not permit it,
ordering all commanders to garrison in Yùzhāng (豫章) and Méilǐng (梅嶺) to await orders.
Xú Guǎng (徐廣) said: Méilǐng is in Huìjī (會稽) Commandery.
Suǒyǐn (索隱) said: Xú's (徐) statement is incorrect.
According to current knowledge, thirty *lǐ* (里) from Yùzhāng there is Méilǐng,
on Hóngyá (洪崖) Mountain,
along the ancient post road.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: Méilǐng is in Qiánzhōu (虔州) Qiánhuà (虔化) County.
Kuòdìzhì (括地志) states: It is one hundred twenty-eight *lǐ* northeast of Qiánhuà County.
Jiào (校),
pronounced as hù jiāo fān (戶教翻).
When the Hàn (漢) army approached his border,
Yúshàn then rebelled,
dispatching troops to block the Hàn (漢) roads,
naming generals such as Zōu Lì (騶力) as "Swallow-Hàn Generals",
and entering Báishā (白沙), Wǔlín (武林), and Méilǐng.
Suǒyǐn (索隱) said: According to current knowledge, two hundred *lǐ* north of Yùzhāng borders Pányáng (番陽),
the place name is Báishā,
eighty *lǐ* southeast of Báishā there is Wǔyáng (武陽) Pavilion,
thirty *lǐ* southeast is a place named Wǔlín,
along the main road between Mǐn (閩) and Yuè (越).
Liú Xù (劉昫) said: Wǔlín,
is within Cāngwú (蒼梧) Ménglíng (猛陵) County;
the Suí (隋) dynasty divided Ménglíng to establish Wǔlín County,
belonging to Yǒngpíng (永平) Commandery;
the Táng (唐) dynasty established Gōngzhōu (龔州).
At this time,
Hàn (漢) envoys, Grand Minister of Agriculture Zhāng Chéng (張成) and the former Marquis Chǐ (齒) of Shānzhōu (山州), were ordered to garrison.
Chǐ (齒),
son of the King Gòng (共) of Chéngyáng (城陽),
lost his marquisate for an offense regarding "tribute gold",
hence the text refers to him as "former marquis".
Jiàng (將),
pronounced as jí liàng fān (即亮翻);
the *jiàng* (將) in *pú jiàng* (僕將) below is the same.
They retreated to a convenient location,
and all were executed for cowardice.
Yúshàn (餘善) proclaimed himself Emperor Wǔ (武帝).
The emperor wished to again appoint Yáng Pú (楊僕) as general.
For his previous efforts,
he sent him a letter of reprimand, saying:
“The only merit your generalship has is the prior capture of Shímén (石門) and Xúnxiá (尋陿);
there is no real achievement of beheading generals or capturing banners.
Shīgǔ (師古) said: Qiān (搴) means to pull out and take.
Previously, when Pānyú was captured,
you took the surrendered as captives,
and excavated the dead as trophies;
this is one fault.
You allowed Jiàndé (建德) and Lǚjiā (呂嘉) to use Dōngyuè as an ally;
Shīgǔ (師古) said: Because Pú (僕) did not pursue them relentlessly,
they were able to use Dōngyuè as an ally.
The soldiers were exposed for successive years,
but you, general, did not consider their hard work,
and instead requested to ride post carriages to cross the passes,
thus returning home,
carrying silver and gold seals,
wearing three cords,
to boast in your hometown.
These are three faults.
Shīgǔ (師古) said: Yín (銀) refers to the silver seal;
Huáng (黃) refers to the gold seal.
Pú (僕) was Chief Commandant for Ceremonials,
and also 'Towered Warship General',
and simultaneously commanded Liáng Hóu (梁侯),
hence 'three cords'.
Zǔ (組) means official ribbons.
Shīgǔ (師古) said: It means he was thinking of his wives and concubines.
This is the fourth fault.
When asked the price of a Shǔ (蜀) knife, you feigned ignorance.
Shǔ (蜀) knife refers to knives made in Shǔ.
Shīgǔ (師古) said: Shǔ (蜀) knives are those with rings.
Shīgǔ (師古) said: Gān (干) means to violate.
You received the imperial edict but did not go to Lánchí (蘭池).
Lánchí Palace is in Wèichéng (渭城).
Rú Chún (如淳) said: Originally, when the army was dispatched, he was supposed to go to Lánchí Palace,
but he stopped and did not arrive.
If your subordinates, general,
do not respond when asked,
and do not comply when ordered,
what would their crime be?
Extending this attitude to outside matters,
can you be trusted in the regions of the rivers and seas?
Now Dōngyuè has advanced deeply;
can you, general, lead the troops to cover your faults or not?”
Pú (僕) replied in trepidation:
“I wish to die to atone for my crimes!”
The emperor then dispatched General of the Transverse Seas Hán Yuè (韓說) from Gōuzhāng (句章).
Bān Zhì (班志) states: Gōuzhāng County belonged to Huìjī (會稽) Commandery.
Shǐjì Zhèngyì (史記正義) states: The ancient city of Gōuzhāng

ordering distant regions to transport their local products, similar to how merchants transferred goods in different seasons,
as a tax to mutually supply each other.
A 'balancing standard prices' office was established in the capital,
receiving all tributes from across the empire.
The various officials of the Grand Minister of Agriculture
monopolized all goods in the empire.
When prices were high, they sold;
when prices were low, they bought,
intending to prevent rich merchants and great traders from profiting excessively.
Rú Chún said: Móu
means to take.
By this time,
when the Son of Heaven toured the commanderies and counties,
the rewards and gifts he bestowed along the way
amounted to over a million rolls of silk,
and money and gold in the tens of thousands,
all drawn from the Grand Minister of Agriculture.
Hóngyáng also requested
that officials be allowed to supply grain to obtain office and criminals to redeem their crimes.
The grain transported by boat from east of the mountains increased by six million shí annually.
Within a year,
the Tàicāng and Gānquán granaries were full,
the border regions had surplus grain,
all goods were equally distributed,
and there were five million rolls of silk.
The people's taxes were not increased, yet the empire's resources were abundant.
Thereupon, Hóngyáng was granted the title of Zuǒshùzhǎng
and two hundred jīn of gold.
At this time, there was a minor drought.
The emperor ordered officials to pray for rain.
Bǔ Shì said:
"The county officials should only eat rent and wear taxes.
Now Hóng Yáng orders his subordinates to set up markets and shops,
buying and selling goods to seek profit.
If Hóng Yáng is cooked,
then Heaven will send rain."

The same below.

Zhēnxīng
is S Saturn.

"Your Majesty established the Hàn dynasty's Fēngshàn sacrifices,

1. In winter,
in the tenth month,
the emperor traveled to Yōng
and sacrificed at the Wǔzhì;
upon returning,
he offered a prayer and sacrifice to Tàiyī,
and bowed to Déxīng.
Shīgǔ said: Bowing and sacrificing to it,
with added prayers.
2. In spring,
in the first month,
Gōngsūn Qīng said:
"I saw an immortal on Mount Dōnglái,
who seemed to want to see the Son of Heaven."
The Son of Heaven then went to Guīshì Chéng,
appointed Qīng as Zhōng Dàfū,
and then proceeded to Dōnglái,
staying there for
several days,
but saw nothing,
though he saw footprints of a great man.
He again sent alchemists to seek spirits and wonders,
collecting thousands
of magic mushrooms and herbs.
At this time, the year was dry.
The Son of Heaven, having come out without success,
then prayed at Wànlǐ Shā.
Yīng Shào said: Wànlǐ Shā is a spirit shrine
in Qǔchéng, Dōnglái.
Mèng Kāng said: The sandy path is over three hundred *lǐ* long.
Dù Yòu's Tōngdiǎn: Wànlǐ Shā is in Lái Zhōu, Yè Xiàn district.
In the fourth month,
he returned,
passing by Mount Tài to offer sacrifices.
3. Originally,
the Yellow River breached at Húzi;
the initial breach of the Yellow River is mentioned in chapter 18, Yuánguāng 2nd year.
The lands of Liáng and Chǔ were particularly affected.
In this year,
the emperor sent the two ministers Jí Rén and Guō Chāng to dispatch tens of thousands of soldiers to dam the breach at Húzi.
The Son of Heaven returned from Mount Tài,
personally oversaw the breached river,
sank white horses and jade disks into the river,
and ordered all his retainers and accompanying officials, from generals downwards, to carry firewood,
and the soldiers to fill the breached river.
A palace was built above it,
named Xuānfáng Gōng.
Two canals were guided north from the Yellow River,
restoring Yǔ's old course.
Gōuxù Zhì: Yǔ guided the Yellow River from Jīshí,
passed through Lóngmén,
south to Huáyīn,
east down to Dǐzhù, and Mèngjīn, Luò, Ruì,
reaching Dàpēi.
Thereupon Yǔ thought that the source of the river was high,
and the water was turbulent and fierce,
difficult to flow on flat ground,
often causing damage.
So he dug two canals to divert the river,
carrying it north to higher ground,
past Hòngshuǐ,
to Dàlù,
dividing it into Jiǔhé,
all flowing into the Bohai Sea as Yínghé.
Mèng Kāng said: Of the two canals,
one emerges southwest of Bèiqiū,
and then turns south;
the other is the Luò Chuān.
Since the time of Wáng Mǎng, the Yellow River dried up,
only the Luò was used.
Shī
is pronounced 'shān zhī'.
Luò
is pronounced 'tǔ hé'.
There were no water disasters.
4. The emperor returned to Cháng'ān.
5. He first ordered Yuè shamans to sacrifice to the High God and the hundred spirits,
and used chicken divination.
Yuè customs use chicken divination.
Lǐ Qí said: Holding chicken bones for divination,
like rat divination.
Shǐjì Zhèngyì said: The method of chicken divination
uses one chicken and one dog.
After offering live prayers,
the chicken and dog are killed,
cooked, and then offered again.
Only the two eye-bones of the chicken are taken;
they naturally have holes.
If they split into shapes resembling human figures, it is auspicious;
if not, it is inauspicious.
This method is still practiced in Lǐngnán today.
Fàn Chéngdà's Guìhǎi Yúhéng Zhì: Chicken divination is
a method of fortune-telling used by southerners.
They take a young rooster, hold its two feet,
burn incense, and pray for the matter to be divined.
They kill the chicken by beating it,
pluck the two thigh bones,
wash them clean,
tie them with a thread,
insert a bamboo stick into the tied part,
so that the two bones are at the ends of the stick, facing away from each other.
They hold the bamboo and pray again.
The left bone represents *nóng* (I),
*nóng*
means "I".
The right bone represents *rén* (person),
*rén*
means the matter being divined.
They observe the small holes on the sides of the two bones,
and insert small bamboo splints, about an inch long, into all of them.
The angle, straightness, and alignment of these splints
naturally vary according to the holes,
determining good or ill fortune.
There are eighteen variations of this method.
Generally, if splints are mostly straight and aligned, or close to the bone,
it is auspicious;
if they are crooked and slanted, or far from the bone,
it is inauspicious.
There are also those who use chicken eggs for divination.
They hold an egg for divination,
write ink on the shell
to mark its four directions;
after boiling it, they cut it horizontally,
and observe the thickness of the white inside the shell
at the inked parts to determine the fortune of *nóng* and *rén*.

whose multitude numbered tens of thousands,

Láo Shēn and Mí Mò repeatedly encroached upon the envoys and officials.
Thereupon, the Emperor dispatched General Guō Chāng and Imperial Household Grandee Wèi Guǎng to raise troops from Bā and Shǔ to attack and destroy Láo Shēn and Mí Mò,
and then brought troops to Diān.
The Diān King surrendered with his entire kingdom,
requesting the establishment of officials and permission to attend court.
Therefore, it was established as Yìzhōu Commandery.

during Táng, it was the land of Kūnzhōu and Yáozhōu;

Jiàng,

Cháo,

And he (the Diān King) was allowed to continue to govern his people.
The Son of Heaven considered the two generals besieging the city to be at odds,

When Suí arrived,

The reason it hasn't been taken for so long

He fully explained his long-held view,

He then ordered the General of the Left's subordinates to seize the General of the Fleet,

Bān Gù says: Xuántú and Lèlàng

He taught its people civility and righteousness,
farming, sericulture, and weaving.
He established eight prohibitions for the people:
one who kills another
must repay with their own life;
one who injures another
must compensate with grain;
one who steals
becomes a male slave of the victim's family,
and a female becomes a maidservant.
Those who wish to redeem themselves must pay fifty million *qián*,
and even if they are freed to be commoners,
the custom is still to shame them,
making it impossible for them to marry.
Because of this, its people never stole from each other,
there was no need to lock doors,
and women were chaste, trustworthy, and not promiscuous.
Their rural diet was served in bamboo and wooden vessels (biān dòu).
In the cities, they somewhat imitated officials,
often eating with cups and bowls.
When the commanderies first took officials from Liáodōng,
the officials saw that the people had no locked storage,
and when merchants visited,
they committed theft at night.
The customs gradually became less virtuous,
and now the number of violations of prohibitions has steadily increased
to over sixty articles.
How commendable

Emperor Xiàowǔ first established thirteen Cìshǐ,

The *Gǔjīn Zhù* says: They typically traveled through their circuits at the spring equinox,
and each commandery and kingdom sent an official to meet them at the border.
The *Hàn Jiùyí* says: According to imperial decrees and old regulations,
the Cìshǐ, after publicly declaring their duties,
traveled through the commanderies and kingdoms,
inspecting governance,
demoting or promoting according to ability,
and resolving wrongful lawsuits,
using six articles to inquire into affairs.
Matters not covered by these articles
were not inspected.
Article one:
Powerful clans and influential magnates whose land and residences exceeded regulations,
who oppressed the weak with their strength,
and brutalized the few with their numbers.
Article two:
Officials of two thousand *shí* who did not obey imperial decrees, conform to established regulations,
betrayed public interest for private gain,
used their influence to seek profit,
extorted the common people,
and amassed wealth through illicit means.
Article three:
Officials of two thousand *shí* who did not attend to doubtful cases,
recklessly executed people,
applied punishments arbitrarily when angry,
bestowed rewards arbitrarily when pleased,
were vexatious and cruel,
and slaughtered the common people,
thus incurring the hatred of the populace;
as well as landslides and rockfalls,
ominous signs and rumors.
Article four:
Officials of two thousand *shí* who made unfair selections and appointments,
indulged their favorites,
and obscured the worthy while favoring the dull.
Article five:
Sons and younger brothers of officials of two thousand *shí* who relied on their family's glory and power,
and sought favors from those they supervised.
Article six:
Officials of two thousand *shí* who violated public interest to collude with subordinates,
flattered influential magnates,
facilitated bribery,
and curtailed government decrees.
The *Xùhàn Zhì* also says: The Cìshǐ of the various prefectures regularly toured the commanderies and kingdoms in the eighth month,
recorded prisoners,
and evaluated performance.
Initially,
