all the ranks and positions of the marquises were fully ordered,
stored in the ancestral temple,
with a duplicate held by the relevant officials.
Shī Gǔ said: Fù (副),
means duplicate.
The records of merit for the marquises were stored in the ancestral temple,
and a duplicate of the original was also with the relevant officials.
Within four or five generations,
the displaced people had returned,
and the household population also increased.
The largest marquisates reached three or four tens of thousands of households,
while smaller states doubled.
Shī Gǔ said: This refers to former five hundred households,
which now reached a thousand households.
Cáo Cān (曹參) was initially enfeoffed with ten thousand six hundred households;
when his descendant Zōng (宗) was dismissed,
he had twenty-three thousand households.
This is why the population multiplied.
Others were all similar.
Shī Gǔ said: It means their wealth also increased as much as their population.
Many violated laws and prohibitions,
lost their lives and their states.
By this time, only four active marquises remained:
Xiāo Shòuchéng (蕭壽成), Marquis of Zuǎn (酇); Lì Shìzōng (酈世宗), Marquis of Miù (繆); Jìn Shífēng (靳石封), Marquis of Fényáng (汾陽); and Zhāng Chāng (張昌), Marquis of Suīlíng (睢陵) — these were the four.
Jiàn (見),
pronounced xián biàn.
6 After the Hàn (漢) had lost the battle at Zhuóyě (浞野),
all the Gōngqīng (公卿) who deliberated wished to withdraw the army from Wǎn (宛)
and concentrate their strength on attacking the Hú (胡).
The Son of Heaven had already dispatched troops to punish Wǎn;
if Wǎn, a small state, could not be subjugated,
then the states like Dàxià (大夏) would gradually despise Hàn,
and Wǎn's excellent horses would certainly not come.
Wūsūn (烏孫) and Lúntái (輪臺) would easily treat Hàn envoys with contempt.
Jìn Zhuó (晉灼) said: Yì (易),
means light (contemptuous).
Shī Gǔ said: Lúntái (輪臺),
is also a state name.
Yu (余) notes that Lúntái (輪臺) is over a thousand lì (里) west of Chēshī (車師),
and further west of that is Dàyuān (大宛).
Yì (易),
pronounced yǐ shì.
Thus, Dèng Guāng (鄧光) and others, who argued that attacking Wǎn was particularly inconvenient, were investigated.
Shī Gǔ said: To investigate their crimes and inflict punishment.
Then, young ruffians and frontier cavalry were mobilized;
after more than a year, sixty thousand men emerged from Dūnhuáng (敦煌).
Shī Gǔ said: Deployment and mobilization took over a year to be ready for action.
Shī Gǔ said: Those carrying private provisions and followers were not included in the sixty thousand men.
Cóng (從),
pronounced cái yòng.
Yǔ (與),
read as yù.
There were thirty thousand horses,
and tens of thousands of donkeys and camels,
carrying a large supply of provisions and weapons (bows and crossbows).
Shī Gǔ said: The arrangements were very complete.
More than fifty captains were transferred to supply and attack Wǎn.
There were no wells inside Wǎn city;
water was drawn from a stream outside the city.
So, hydraulic engineers were sent to divert the water below the city,
and hollow out (attack) the city through holes.
Shī Gǔ said: Kōng (空),
is kǒng (孔, hole).
To divert the water below the city meant to make it flow through another path,
not close to the city.
To hollow out (attack) the city through holes meant to besiege and attack it,
making holes to bore through.
Later it says 'cut off and move its water source',
and also 'besieged and attacked its city';
both describe the same event twice.
One interpretation is: after diverting the water so it would not flow beneath the city,
they then used the old holes that drew water into the city,
attacked and bored through them.
I (Yu) believe this text states that hydraulic engineers were sent to divert the water and bore into the city,
and the later text about cutting off the water source and attacking the city
was merely carrying out the initial plan,
not describing the event twice.
Gūyán (居延) and Xiūtú (休屠) garrisons were established to protect Jiǔquán (酒泉).
The Bān Zhì (班志) states that
Gūyán (居延) County belonged to Zhāngyè (張掖) Commandery,
and Xiūtú (休屠) County belonged to Wǔwēi (武威) Commandery.
Tú (屠),
pronounced chú.
They were suitable for military service;
and dried rations were transported to supply the Èrshī (貳師).
The cart drivers and laborers were continuously connected.
And two experienced horsemen were appointed as Zhímǎ Xiàowèi (執馬校尉) and Qūmǎ Xiàowèi (驅馬校尉).
Shī Gǔ said: Xí (習),
is like biàn (便, skilled).
One was appointed Zhímǎ Xiàowèi (執馬校尉),
the other Qūmǎ Xiàowèi (驅馬校尉).
Thereupon, Èrshī Hóu then set out again.
With a large army,
wherever he went, no small state failed to welcome him
and provide food for the army.
When they reached Lúntái,
Lúntái did not surrender.
They attacked for several days
and massacred its inhabitants.
From here westward,
they proceeded smoothly to Yuānchéng.
Shīgǔ said: “’Píngxíng’ (proceeded smoothly)
means there were no bandits or difficulties.”
The Yuān army met and attacked the Hàn army.
The Hàn army defeated them with arrows,
and the Yuān army fled inside
to defend their city.
Èrshī wanted to attack Yùchéng city,
but feared that delaying his advance would allow Yuān to become more deceptive.
Shīgǔ said: “’Liúxíng’ (delaying his advance)
means stopping the army and neglecting its movement.”
If he cut off their water source and diverted it,
then Yuān would certainly be worried and distressed.
He besieged their city
and attacked it for more than forty days.
The Yuān nobles plotted, saying:
“King Wúguǎ
has secretly hoarded good horses and
killed the Hàn envoy.”
Shīgǔ said: “Wúguǎ
is the name of the King of Yuān.”
The Hàn army ought to withdraw.
If they do not withdraw,
then we will fight with all our might and die;
it is not too late.”
All the Yuān nobles agreed,
and together they killed their king.
Their outer wall was broken.
They captured Jiānmí, a brave general and Yuān noble.
Shīgǔ said: “The brave general among the Yuān nobles
was named Jiānmí.”
Jiān
is pronounced Zǐyán Fān.
They fled into the city,
holding the head of King Wúguǎ,
and sent an envoy to Èrshī, proposing:
“If Hàn does not attack us,
we will bring out all our good horses for you to take as you please,
and supply food to the Hàn army.
If you do not agree,
we
will kill all the good horses,
and the relief force from Kāngjū will soon arrive.
When they arrive,
we will be inside,
and Kāngjū will be outside,
to fight the Hàn army.
Consider this carefully:
which will you choose?”
Shīgǔ said: “This means letting Èrshī weigh his options carefully:
Does he want to attack and fight, or
does he want to not attack and get the horses?”
Shú,
is the same as shú;
the ancient characters were interchangeable.
Kāngjū, observing that the Hàn army was still strong,
dared not advance.
Èrshī heard that the city of Yuān had recently acquired Hàn people
who knew how to dig wells,
and that they still had plenty of food inside.
He calculated, thinking:
“I came to punish Wúguǎ, the chief culprit.
Wúguǎ’s head has already been delivered.
If I do not agree to this, they will hold out steadfastly,
and Kāngjū, observing that the Hàn army is exhausted, will come to aid Yuān.
The Hàn army will surely be defeated.”
Thereupon, he agreed to Yuān’s proposal.
Yuān then brought out their horses,
allowing Hàn to choose them,
and generously supplied food to the Hàn army.
The Hàn army took several dozen of their best horses,
and more than three thousand medium and inferior horses, both mares and stallions.
They then installed a Yuān noble named Mòcài, who had previously shown goodwill towards Hàn, as the King of Yuān,
made an alliance with him, and withdrew their troops.
Initially,
Èrshī set out westward from Dūnhuáng.
Qǐ
means “to set out.”
It means setting out from Dūnhuáng and heading west.
They took both the southern and northern routes.
Colonel Wáng Shēnshēng led over a thousand men to Yùchéng separately.
The King of Yùchéng attacked and annihilated them.
A few men escaped
and fled to Èrshī.
Èrshī ordered Sōusù Dūwèi Shàngguān Jié to go and attack
Yùchéng.
The emperor established the Sōusù Dūwèi,
subordinate to the Dàsīnóng.
The Xìngpǔ states: The youngest son of King Zhuāng of Chǔ became Shàngguān Dàfū,
and his descendants adopted this as their surname.
When Qín destroyed Chǔ,
they were moved to Shàngguī in Lǒngxī.
Jié pursued them to Kāngjū.
Kāngjū, hearing that Hàn had already defeated Yuān,
handed over the King of Yùchéng to Jié.
Jié ordered four cavalrymen to bind him and bring him before Èrshī.
Zhào Dì, a cavalryman from Shàngguī, feared losing the King of Yùchéng.
The Bānzhì states:
Shàngguī County belonged to Lǒngxī Commandery,
formerly the settlement of the Guī Róng.
Guī
is pronounced guī.
He pursued and caught up with Èrshī.
1 In spring,
General Èrshī arrived at the capital.
The small states that Èrshī had passed through, hearing that Yuān had been defeated,
all sent their sons and younger brothers to accompany him, presenting tributes.
They met the Son of Heaven
and served as hostages.
When the army returned,
they brought in over a thousand horses.
The Hànshū, Lǐ Guǎnglí Zhuàn states: "When the army returned,
over ten thousand men entered Yùmén,
and over a thousand horses."
The text is more detailed and clear.
Having returned to Dūnhuáng and then setting out again,
it is thus called "hòuxíng" (later expedition).
Not many died in battle,
but the generals and officials were greedy,
did not care for their soldiers,
and extorted them.
Shīgǔ said: "This means they preyed on them like caterpillars on crops."
The Son of Heaven, for having campaigned over ten thousand *lǐ*,
did not record their faults.
Instead, he issued an edict enfeoffing Lǐ Guǎnglí as Hǎixī Hóu.
The Bānzhì states:
Hǎixī County belonged to Dōnghǎi Commandery.
The Gōngchén Biǎo states:
The Shī Hóu of Xīnzhì held a fief in the land of Qí.
Zhì
is pronounced zhǐ.
Three military officers became Jiǔqīng,
over one hundred became lords' chancellors, commandery governors, or officials of two thousand *shí*,
and over a thousand became officials of one thousand *shí* or less.
Those who performed bravely received offices beyond their expectations.
Méng Kāng said: "Fèn means swift;
those who acted willingly and enthusiastically."
All those who had endured hardship
had their merits dismissed.
Shīgǔ said: "This refers to those who were demoted due to crimes;
they were acquitted of their offenses,
but their merits were not rewarded."
Shīgǔ said: "Or they were compensated with other valuables,
hence it is called 'zhí' (straight/fair)."
The Xiongnú, hearing that Èrshī was campaigning against Dàyuān,
wanted to intercept him.
However, Èrshī’s army was strong,
and they dared not confront him.
Instead, they sent cavalry through Lóulán to intercept subsequent Hàn envoys
and prevent them from passing.
At that time, Hàn general Rèn Wén was stationed with troops at Yùmén Pass.
He captured a prisoner,
learned of the situation, and reported it.
The Emperor ordered Rèn Wén to take his troops by a convenient route to capture the King of Lóulán
and bring him to the imperial court for questioning.
The King replied:
“Our small country is caught between great powers.
If we do not belong to both, we cannot be safe.
I wish to move my country and reside in Hàn territory.”
The Emperor found his words reasonable.
Shīgǔ said: “He considered his words to be truthful.”
He also used him to observe and spy on the Xiongnú.
From then on, the Xiongnú did not fully trust Lóulán.
After the defeat of Dàyuān,
the Western Regions were greatly shaken and fearful.
Hàn envoys entering the Western Regions increasingly gained respect.
Shīgǔ said: “They were rewarded for their diligence,
and all received official appointments.”
I believe Yán Yuè’s explanation is incorrect.
This means that when Hàn envoys entered the Western Regions,
the various states dared not slight or insult them,
because they had gained their proper standing.
“Gained respect” means they did not lose their due respect.
At Lúntái and Qúlí,
Qúlí was east of Lúntái,
its southeast bordering Qiěmò,
and its south bordering Jīngjué.
Envoys and colonels were stationed
to supervise and protect
agricultural colonies.
Shīgǔ said: “This refers to supervising and protecting affairs related to garrison farming.”
Shīgǔ said: “They collected the five grains to supply them.”
Shǐ is pronounced shūlì fān.
More than a year later,
the nobles of Yuān thought that Rìmò Cài was good at flattery,
and that he had gained his kingship because of his good relations with Hàn.
So they conspired together to kill Rìmò Cài,
and set up his younger brother Chánfēng, who was not of the same mother, as the King of Yuān,
then sent his son to serve
in Hàn.
Hàn then sent envoys with gifts and rewards,
to pacify them.
Chánfēng made a pact with Hàn,
to offer two Heavenly Horses annually.
In the autumn of the 2nd year,
the Míngguāng Palace was built.
According to the Sānfǔ Huángtú: The Míngguāng Palace was behind the Chánglè Palace,
connected to the Chánglè Palace in the south,
and extended north to the Guì Palace.
In the winter of the 3rd year,
the Emperor traveled to Huízhōng.
In the 4th year, the Xiongnu Chulihú Chányú died,
and the Xiongnu established his younger brother, the Left Grand Commandant Qiědīhóu, as Chányú.
The Son of Heaven wished to use the prestige of the campaign against Yuān to further humble the Hú,
so he issued an edict saying:
"Emperor Gāo left me with the trouble of Píngchéng,
(The affair of Píngchéng is seen in volume 11, Gāozǔ year 7.)
(Yí,
read as Jì in Yú,
also as written.)
and the Chányú's letters are completely rebellious.
(The matter is seen in volume 12, Huìdì year 3.)
(Bèi,
Pú nèi fan.)
The Spring and Autumn Annals magnify such deeds."
(Gōngyáng Zhuàn: In the spring of Zhuāng year 4,
Qí Xiānggōng destroyed Jì,
in an act of revenge.
Xiānggōng's ninth-generation ancestor was slandered by the Marquis of Jì and boiled to death in Zhōu,
therefore Xiānggōng destroyed Jì.
Can one still seek revenge after nine generations?
It is said: Even after a hundred generations, it is permissible.)
Fearing that Hàn would attack him,
he said:
"I, your son,
how dare I hope for the Son of Heaven of Hàn?
The Son of Heaven of Hàn,
is like my father-in-law."
(Shīgǔ said: Zhàngrén is
a respectful term for an elder.
Háng,
Hù làng fān.)
Chōngguó was detained (seen above in Yuánfēng year 4).
He sent an envoy to offer tribute.
In the first year of Tiānhàn
(Xīnsì, 100 BCE) (Yìng Shào said: At that time, there were successive years of severe drought,
so the era name was changed to Tiānhàn,
to pray for sweet rain.
Shīgǔ said: The Dàyǎ has a poem called Yúnhàn,
composed by Zhōu Grandee Réng Shú,
to praise King Xuān who, when faced with drought,
cultivated virtue and diligently governed, thereby bringing rain;
hence, it was used as the era name.)
In the spring,
in the first month,
the Emperor traveled to Gānquán,
and performed the suburban sacrifice to Tàizhì.
In the third month,
he traveled to Hédōng,
and sacrificed to Hòutǔ.
The Emperor commended the Xiongnu Chányú's righteousness,
and sent Lieutenant-General Sū Wǔ to escort the Xiongnu envoy who had remained in Hàn,
and generously rewarded the Chányú,
responding to his goodwill.
Wǔ went with Deputy Lieutenant-General Zhāng Shèng and acting official Cháng Huì and others.
(Shīgǔ said: Jiǎlì means
a concurrent official;
at that time, they temporarily served as officials for the mission,
like today's assigned personnel acting as envoys.)
(Xìngpǔ: The Cháng surname
is descended from Cháng Xiān, the minister of the Yellow Emperor.)
They presented gifts to the Chányú.
The Chányú became even more arrogant,
which was not what Hàn had hoped for.
(Hàn hoped he would change his heart and incline towards goodness,
but now he became even more arrogant,
hence it says not what Hàn had hoped for.)
At that time, Gōu Wáng and Chángshuǐ Yú Cháng and others
(Gōu Wáng was
the nephew of the Xiongnu Húnyé Wáng,
and descended to Hàn with Húnyé Wáng,
later following Zuóyě Hóu and being lost among the Xiongnu.
Hàn had a Chángshuǐ Commandant,
who commanded the Chángshuǐ Hu cavalry.
Shīgǔ said: Chángshuǐ
is a Hu name.
In his commentary on the Lì Tàizǐ Zhuàn, he also says: There is a Chángshuǐ east of present-day Hù County.
I, Yú, based on the Shuǐjīng Zhù,
Chángshuǐ originates from Báilùyuán in Dù County,
and flows north into Bàyáng.
The Hu cavalry were likely stationed here,
so it is not a Hu name.
The Lìzhuàn is correct.)
(Yú Cháng was probably also lost among the Xiongnu earlier.)
(Gōu,
Gōng hóu fān.)
secretly conspired to kidnap the Chányú's mother, the Yānzhī, and return her to Hàn.
Wèi Lǜ's
father was a former Chángshuǐ Hu person.
Lǜ was skilled in harmonious music and acquainted with Commandant Lǐ Yánnián.
Yánnián recommended Lǜ as an envoy to the Xiongnu.
When the envoy returned,
he heard that Yánnián's family had been arrested,
and so he fled and defected to the Xiongnu.
(Kǎoyì says: The Yánnián Zhuàn states: Yánnián's brothers and clan were executed.
However, Lǐ Guǎnglì was still a general commander after this,
so it was probably only Yánnián and his younger brother Jì's wives and children who were executed.)
He participated in national affairs,
and was established as the King of Dīnglíng.
(Wèilüè says: Dīnglíng is
north of Kāngjū,
seven thousand li from the Xiongnu court, near the Xí River.)
(The Xiongnu probably enfeoffed Wèi Lǜ as the King of Dīnglíng.)
He secretly said to Shèng:
"I hear the Son of Heaven of Hàn greatly resents Wèi Lǜ.
If I can set an ambush with crossbows for Hàn and kill him,
my mother and brother are in Hàn,
(referring to his mother and his younger brother.)
Zhāng Shèng agreed,
and gave goods to Cháng.
A month or so later,
when the Chányú went hunting,
leaving only the Yānzhī and the Chányú's sons and younger brothers,
Yú Cháng and more than seventy others wanted to act,
but one of them fled during the night and reported it.
The Chányú's sons and younger brothers dispatched troops to fight,
Gōu Wáng and the others were all killed,
and Yú Cháng was captured alive.
(Shīgǔ said: Was apprehended and seized.)
Chányú sent Wèi Lǜ to handle the matter.
Zhāng Shèng heard of this,
fearing his previous words would be revealed,
so he told Wǔ the situation.
Wǔ said:
"Things have come to this;
this will surely reach me.
To be captured and then die
would be a great disservice to the state."
He wanted to commit suicide.
Shèng and Huì together stopped him.
Yú Cháng indeed implicated Zhāng Shèng.
To be captured,
meaning to say, "I was attacked by the Xiōngnú, and only then did I die,"
would be to further betray the Hàn state.
Therefore, he wanted to commit suicide first,
but Shèng and Huì stopped him.
Yǐn (引),
means to implicate or involve in one's testimony.
Zhòng (重),
read with a straight yòng fan sound.
Chányú summoned his nobles for a discussion,
wanting to kill the Hàn envoy.
Zuǒ Yīzhìzī said:
"If we conspire against Chányú,
what could be a greater crime!"
Chén Zàn says: Zuǒ Yīzhìzī
is a title of a Hú official.
According to the Xiōngnú Biography,
when Hūhánxié was defeated,
his Yòuyīzhìzī Wáng (右伊秩訾王) sent him to surrender to Hàn.
Thus, this is a title of a Hú Wáng.
Shīgǔ says: He means that to conspire against Wèi Lǜ and kill him
would be too severe a punishment.
Fù (復),
read with a fú yòu fan sound.
Chányú sent Wèi Lǜ to summon Wǔ to receive his instructions.
Shīgǔ says: To convey Chányú's command and take his reply.
Wèi (謂),
is like yǔ (語);
Wǔ spoke to Huì and others.
"To betray one's principles and disgrace one's mission,
even if I live,
what face would I have to return to Hàn!"
He drew his scabbard knife and stabbed himself.
Wèi Lǜ was shocked;
he embraced Wǔ himself,
rushed to summon a doctor,
dug a pit in the ground,
placed warm coals in it.
Shīgǔ says: Wēn (熅)
refers to gathered fire without flames.
Wēn (熅),
read yú yún fan.
Shīgǔ says: To cover the body over the pit.
Fù (覆),
pronounced fāng mù fan.
Wǔ stopped breathing,
but after half a day, he revived.
Shīgǔ says: Xī (息)
means to exhale.
He was carried back to the camp.
Chányú admired his integrity.
Morning and evening, he sent people to inquire about Wǔ,
and arrested and imprisoned Zhāng Shèng.
Wǔ gradually recovered.
Chányú sent an envoy to enlighten Wǔ,
wanting him to surrender.
Shīgǔ says: To persuade and enlighten Wǔ to surrender.
He wanted to use this opportunity to make Wǔ surrender.
After Yú Cháng was beheaded,
Lǜ said:
"The Hàn envoy Zhāng Shèng conspired to kill Chányú's close minister.
Shīgǔ says: Jìnchén (近臣)
refers to Wèi Lǜ himself.
Chányú offers a pardon to those who surrender."
He raised his sword, intending to strike him.
Shèng requested to surrender.
Lǜ said to Wǔ:
"Your deputy has committed a crime;
you should be implicated."
Wǔ said:
"I had no part in the conspiracy,
nor am I a relative.
How can I be implicated?"
Lǜ again raised his sword and aimed at him.
Wǔ did not move.
Lǜ said:
"Sū Jūn!
I, Lǜ, formerly betrayed Hàn and submitted to the Xiōngnú.
Fortunately, I received great favor, was granted a title and called a Wáng,
commanding tens of thousands of people,
with horses and livestock filling the mountains.
Shīgǔ says: Mí (彌)
means full.
Xù (畜),
read xǔ yòu fan.
If Sū Jūn surrenders today,
tomorrow it will be the same;
you will merely leave your body to fertilize the wilderness.
Who will ever know of it again!"
Wǔ did not respond.
Lǜ said:
"If you surrender through me,
I will treat you as a brother.
If you do not listen to my plan now,
later, even if you wish to see me again,
will you be able to?"
Wǔ cursed Lǜ, saying:
"You, as a minister and son of man,
disregarded kindness and righteousness,
betrayed your lord and abandoned your kin,
becoming a surrendered slave to barbarians.
Why should I see you!
Shīgǔ says: Meaning, what good is there in seeing you?
You hold the power over people's lives and deaths,
yet you do not act with fairness and justice.
Instead, you want to incite conflict between two lords
and watch their ruin.
Nányuè killed a Hàn envoy,
and was annihilated into nine commanderies.
The Wáng of Yuān killed a Hàn envoy,
and his head was hung at the Northern Gate.
Cháoxiǎn killed a Hàn envoy,
and was immediately exterminated.
The Nányuè affair can be seen in the previous volume, Yuándǐng (元鼎) 5th and 6th years.
The Yuān affair can be seen above, Tàichū (太初) 3rd year.
The Cháoxiǎn affair can be seen above, Yuánfēng (元封) 2nd year.
Xiàn (縣),
read xuán.
If you know that I will not surrender,
Shīgǔ says: Ruò (若)
means you (汝).
He means, you know I will not surrender.
Then the disaster of the Xiōngnú will begin with me."
Lǜ knew that Wǔ could not be intimidated in the end,
so he reported to Chányú.
Chányú became even more eager to make him surrender.
Then he imprisoned Wǔ in a large cellar.
Shīgǔ says: An old cellar for rice and grain, but now empty.
Jiào (窖),
read gōng xiào fan.
It rained and snowed.
Wǔ lay down,
gnawing on snow and swallowing the felt with it.
After several days, he did not die.
The Xiōngnú considered him a god.
So they moved Wǔ to an uninhabited place on the North Sea,
made him herd rams,
and said:
"You may return when the rams lactate."
Shīgǔ says: Dī (羝)
is a male sheep.
Rams do not lactate,

in the second month,
Wáng Qīng (王卿) committed a crime and committed suicide.
Dù Zhōu (杜周), the Commandant of the Gilded Plumes (執金吾), was appointed Grandee Secretary (御史大夫).
Bān (班) states: The Commandant of the Capital (中尉) was in charge of patrolling the capital.
In the first year of Tàichū (太初), its name was changed to Zhíjīnwú (執金吾).
Yīng Shào (應劭) says: Wú (吾),
means to resist.
He was in charge of wielding metal and leather [weapons] to resist extraordinary events.
Shīgǔ (師古) says: Jīnwú (金吾),
is the name of a bird,
which wards off misfortune.
When the emperor traveled,
he was responsible for leading the procession to guard against emergencies,
hence he held the image of this bird;
and the office was named after it.
2. For the first time, a state monopoly on brewing and selling wine was established.
3. In the third month,
the emperor traveled to Tài Shān (泰山),
performed the Feng sacrifice (脩封),
worshipped in the Míngtáng (明堂),
and received reports [from local officials].
Upon his return,
he sacrificed at Cháng Shān (常山)
and buried a black jade.
Dèng Zhǎn (鄧展) says: Yì (瘞),
means to bury.
The Erya (爾雅) says: To sacrifice to the earth is called *yì mài*.
Burying the object [of sacrifice]
indicates returning it to the earth.
Yì (瘞),
pronounced *yú lì fān*.
However, Gōngsūn Qīng (公孫卿) still used the "footprints of the great man" (大人跡) as an explanation.
The "footprints of the great man" were seen in the twentieth juan, Yuánfēng (元封) first year.
Nevertheless, the connection [to the immortals] was not completely severed.
Shīgǔ (師古) says: Jīmí (羈縻),
means to be tied and connected.
A horse's halter is called *jī*,
and an ox's harness is called *mí*.
After this,
the number of fangshi (方士) who spoke of spiritual sacrifices increased greatly,
but their efficacy could be seen [to be limited].
4. In summer,
in the fourth month,
there was a great drought.
An amnesty was granted throughout the empire.
5. In autumn,
the Xiongnú (匈奴) invaded Yànmén (鴈門).
Yànmén Jùn (鴈門郡) belonged to Bǐngzhōu (幷州).
Rú Chún (如淳) says: According to military law,
those who hesitate or are cowardly in battle are to be beheaded.
Nuǎn (愞),
pronounced *rú chuán fān*;
Shīgǔ (師古) says: also pronounced *nǎi guǎn fān*.
1. In spring,
in the first month,
the kings of the feudal states paid court at Gānquán Gōng (甘泉宮).
2. The empire's seven categories of exiles (七科讁) were raised.
Zhāng Yàn (張晏) says: Officials who committed crimes,
one;
fugitives,
two;
sons-in-law who lived in their wives' homes,
three;
merchants,
four;
those who previously had commercial household registration,
five;
those whose parents had commercial household registration,
six;
those whose grandparents had commercial household registration,
seven;
these are the seven categories in total.
The General Ershī (貳師將軍) Lǐ Guǎnglì (李廣利) was sent with sixty thousand cavalry and seventy thousand infantry out of Shuòfāng (朔方).
Shuòfāng Jùn (朔方郡) belonged to Shuòfāng Zhōu (朔方州),
and was the territory of Líng (靈) and Xiàzhōu (夏州) in the Táng (唐) dynasty.

The General Yóujī (游擊將軍) Hán Shuō (韓說) was sent with thirty thousand infantry out of Wǔyuán (五原); the General Yīnyú (因杅將軍) Gōngsūn Áo (公孫敖) was sent with ten thousand cavalry and thirty thousand infantry out of Yànmén (鴈門).
When the Xiongnú (匈奴) heard of this,
they moved all their dependents and valuables north of the Yúwú Shuǐ (余吾水).
Shīgǔ (師古) says: Lěizhòng (累重),
refers to wives, children, and assets.
Lěi (累),
pronounced *lì ruì fān*.
Zhòng (重),
pronounced *zhí yòng fān*.
Yúwú Shuǐ (余吾水) is north of Shuòfāng (朔方).
The Shānhǎi Jīng (山海經) says: From the mountains of Běixiān (北鮮), the Xiānshuǐ (鮮水) flows out,
flowing north into Yúwú (余吾).
[The Xiongnú] engaged in battle with General Ershī (貳師).
General Ershī (貳師) disengaged and returned,
having fought continuously with the Chányú (單于) for over ten days.
The Kǎoyì (考異) states: The "Treatise on the Xiongnú" (匈奴傳) in the Shǐjì (史記) says that Guǎnglì (廣利) surrendered to the Xiongnú (匈奴) here,
which is incorrect.
Yīnyú (因杅) fought with the Left Worthy King (左賢王),
was at a disadvantage,
and withdrew.
At that time, the emperor sent Áo (敖) deep into Xiongnú (匈奴) territory to welcome Lǐ Líng (李陵).
Áo's (敖) army returned without achieving anything,
and then said:
"We captured a prisoner
who said that Lǐ Líng (李陵) taught the Chányú (單于) how to deploy troops to prepare for the Hàn (漢) army,
which is why your subject gained nothing."
The emperor then exterminated Líng's (陵) family.
Later, it was learned that
it was Lǐ Xù (李緒), a Hàn (漢) general who had defected to the Xiongnú (匈奴),
and not Líng (陵).
Líng (陵) sent someone to assassinate Xù (緒).
The Grand Yānzhī (大閼氏) wanted to kill Líng (陵).
Shīgǔ (師古) says: The Grand Yānzhī (大閼氏),
is the Chányú's (單于) mother.
Yānzhī (閼氏),
pronounced *yān zhī*.
When the Grand Yānzhī (大閼氏) died,
[Líng] returned.
The Chányú (單于) gave his daughter to Líng (陵) in marriage,
and established him as the Right 校 King (右校王).
Both he and Wèi Lǜ (衞律) were highly esteemed and held important positions.
Wèi Lǜ (衞律) was always by the Chányú's (單于) side;
Líng (陵) resided outside,
and only entered to discuss major affairs.
3. In summer,
in the fourth month,
the imperial prince Bó (髆) was established as King of Chāngyì (昌邑王).
In the first year of Tàishǐ
(yǐyǒu, 96 BCE), Yīng Shào said: It means to cleanse the world,
and for the people to make a fresh start,
hence it is used to crown the beginning of the era.
1. In spring,
in the first month,
Gōngsūn Áo was executed by beheading because his wife practiced wūgǔ.
Wū
refers to a zhù (prayer officiant);
gǔ
refers to yān (curse),
or huò (bewitchment);
it means to use witches to offer sacrifices, make prayers and curses, and perform enchantments to bewitch people.
Gǔ
is pronounced gǔ.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: Gǔ
is a term for damage and destruction,
thus the Zuǒzhuàn says: "Insects in a vessel constitute gǔ";
this refers to gǔ (worms) in tableware,
and witches practicing evil arts
to harm people.
Yāo
is the same as yāo (waist/to cut off the waist).
2. The local magnates and heroes from the commanderies and kingdoms were moved to Máolíng.
3. In summer,
in the sixth month,
a general amnesty was granted to the empire.
4. In this year,
the Xiongnú Chědīhóu Chányú died;
he had two sons,
the elder was the Zuǒ Xián Wáng,
and the younger was the Zuǒ Dà Jiàng.
Among the twenty-four chiefs of the Xiongnú,
the Zuǒ Xián Wáng ranked first,
and the Zuǒ Dà Jiàng ranked fifth.
Cháng is pronounced zhīliǎng fān.
The nobles thought the elder son was ill,
and instead established the Zuǒ Dà Jiàng as Chányú.
When the Zuǒ Xián Wáng heard of this,
he dared not come forward;
the Zuǒ Dà Jiàng sent someone to summon the Zuǒ Xián Wáng and offered him the position.
The Zuǒ Xián Wáng declined, citing illness,
but the Zuǒ Dà Jiàng would not listen,
saying:
"If by ill fortune I should die,
it will be passed on to you."
The Zuǒ Xián Wáng agreed,
and was consequently enthroned
as Húlùgū Chányú;
he appointed the Zuǒ Dà Jiàng as Zuǒ Xián Wáng.
Several years later,
the Húlùgū Chányú died of illness;
his son Xiānxiándǎn could not succeed him,
and was instead made Rìzhú Wáng.
The Chányú himself appointed his own son as Zuǒ Xián Wáng.
1. In spring,
in the first month,
the Emperor toured to Huízhōng.
2. Dù Zhōu died,
and Guānglù Dàfū Bào Shèngzhī became Yùshǐ Dàfū.
3. In autumn,
there was a drought.
4. Zhào Zhōng Dàfū Bái Gōng proposed digging a canal to divert the Jīng river's water,
starting from Gǔkǒu
and ending in Lìyáng.
Bān Zhì states that
Gǔkǒu and Lìyáng counties belonged to Zuǒ Féngyì.
Shīgǔ said: Gǔkǒu
is present-day Yúnyáng County.
Dù Yòu said: The present Yúnyáng County seat is Gǔ.
He also said: Lǐquán was
Han Gǔkǒu County territory,
in the Suí dynasty it became Lǐquán County,
and the old city of Gǔkǒu County is northwest of the county seat.
Lì is
pronounced yào.
The canal was two hundred lǐ long,
irrigating over four thousand five hundred qǐng of fields,
and was thus named the Bái Qú;
the people benefited greatly from it.
1. In spring,
in the first month,
the Emperor toured to Gānquán Gōng.
In the second month,
he toured to Dōnghǎi,
where a red goose was caught.
He toured to Lángyá.
The two commanderies of Dōnghǎi and Lángyá both belonged to Xúzhōu.
Lángyá was
the Táng dynasty's Yí and Mì Prefectures.
Mèng Kāng said: Lǐ Rì
means to worship the sun.
Rú Chún said: He worshipped the sun at Chéng Shān.
Shīgǔ said: Chéng Shān is in Dōnglái Bùyè County,
and juts into the sea.
Chén Zàn said: The Dìlǐ Zhì states that
Dōnglái Chuí County has Zhīfú Shān.
Shīgǔ said: Fú
is pronounced fú.
2. In this year,
Imperial Prince Fúlíng was born.
Fúlíng's mother was called Hújiān Zhào Jiéyú.
Hújiān Kingdom belonged to Jìzhōu,
which was the Táng dynasty's Yíng and Mò Prefectures.
The Emperor appointed Jiéyú,
a position equivalent to a high minister,
with a rank comparable to a marquis.
Shīgǔ said: Jié
means to receive the Emperor's favor frequently.
Yú
means beautiful appearance.
Jié
is pronounced jiē.
Yú
is pronounced yú.
Shīgǔ said: The Huángtú states that
the Gōuyì Gōng was outside the city;
the Hàn Wǔ Gùshì states
it was south of the Zhímén.
The Emperor said:
"I heard that in ancient times Yáo was born after fourteen months,
and now Gōuyì is the same,"
so he named the gate through which she gave birth the Yáomǔ Mén.
Chén Guāng said: As a ruler,
one's every action and movement must be undertaken with extreme caution,
for what emanates from within will surely manifest externally,
and there will be nothing unknown to the world.
At that time,
the Empress and the Crown Prince were both safe and sound,
yet to name Gōuyì's gate "Yáomǔ"
was improper.
Consequently, wicked individuals
probed the Emperor's intentions,
knowing his extraordinary love for his youngest son
and his desire to make him heir,
thus giving rise to the intention to endanger the Empress and the Crown Prince,
which ultimately led to the disaster of wūgǔ.
Alas!
3 A man from Zhào, Jiāng Chōng, was appointed Commandant of Waterways and Parks (Shuǐhéng Dūwèi).
The state of Zhào belonged to Jìzhōu;
in the Táng Dynasty it was Jìzhōu,
but its territory was also divided and entered the borders of Shēnzhōu and Dézhōu.
In the second year of Yuándǐng,
the office of Commandant of Waterways and Parks was first established,
in charge of the Shànglín Imperial Park.
Yīng Shào said:
"In antiquity, the official for mountains and forests was called 'Héng';
since he managed all pools and parks,
he was therefore called 'Shuǐhéng' (Water and Parks)."
Zhāng Yàn said: "He was in charge of all waterways and Shànglín,
hence called 'Shuǐhéng';
he was in charge of various officials,
hence 'Dū' (Chief);
he had soldiers and martial affairs,
hence 'Wèi' (Commandant)."
Shīgǔ said: "'Héng'
means 'balance' (píng),
he was in charge of balancing the tax revenues;
his position ranked among the Nine Ministers,
with a salary of two thousand bushels of grain."
Jiāng Chōng was a retainer of King Jìngsù of Zhào.
King Jìngsù's
personal name was Péngzǔ;
upon his death,
he was given the posthumous title Jìngsù.
He absconded;
he went to the palace gate and reported secret affairs of the Zhào Crown Prince,
and the Crown Prince was consequently deposed.
The Emperor summoned Jiāng Chōng for an audience.
Jiāng Chōng's appearance was impressive and imposing,
his clothes were light and elegant.
Shīgǔ said: "'Kuí'
means 'large.'
'Àn' refers to
having sharp edges like a cliff.
'Bèifú' means
clothing.
'Qīng'
means 'light and fine.'
'Mǐ'
means 'beautiful and luxurious.'
'Bèi'
is pronounced Pí Yì."
When the Emperor spoke with him about governmental affairs,
he was greatly pleased.
From then on, Jiāng Chōng enjoyed favor,
and was appointed Inspector-Investigator of the Embroidered Uniform (Zhízhǐ Xiùyī Shǐzhě),
to supervise and investigate powerful relatives and close ministers who were extravagant.
Jiāng Chōng impeached without avoiding anyone,
and the Emperor considered him loyal and upright,
everything he said was to the Emperor's liking.
Shīgǔ said: "'Zhòng'
means 'fitting.'
'Zhòng'
is pronounced Zhú Zhòng."
When he encountered the Crown Prince's household servant driving a carriage on the imperial thoroughfare (chídào),
Jiāng Chōng handed him over to his subordinates.
Yīng Shào said: "The chídào
is the road used by the Son of Heaven,
like the central road of today."
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: "The chídào
is the main road, the imperial carriage road.
It is the place where the Son of Heaven's carriages and horses rush,
hence it is called 'chídào'."
Rú Chún said: "Order B;
if riders or drivers travel on the chídào,
those already judged shall have their carriages, horses, and equipment confiscated."
Shīgǔ said: "The 'household servant'
was someone sent by the Crown Prince to inquire at Gānquán.
'Shǐ'
is pronounced Shū Lì.
'Zhǔ'
is pronounced Zhī Yù."
The Crown Prince sent someone to apologize to Jiāng Chōng, saying:
"It's not that I cherish the carriage and horses;
I truly do not wish for the Emperor to hear of it,
so as to instruct those who have not been taught before."
Shīgǔ said: "It means that he had not previously instructed his attendants.
In ancient script,
'wáng' (亡) and 'wú' (無) are interchangeable."
Jiāng Chōng did not listen,
and consequently reported it to the Emperor.
The Emperor said:
"A subject should be like this!"
He was greatly trusted and employed,
and his prestige shook the capital.
1 In spring,
the third month,
the Emperor made an imperial tour to Mount Tài.
On the day Rénwǔ,
he sacrificed to Gāozǔ in the Bright Hall (Míngtáng) to match him with the Supreme Deity (Shàngdì),
and consequently received the annual reports.
On the day Guǐwèi,
he sacrificed to Emperor Xiàojǐng in the Bright Hall.
On the day Jiǎshēn,
he renewed the Feng Sacrifice.
On the day Bǐngxū,
he performed the Shan Sacrifice at Shílǘ.
In summer,
the fourth month,
he visited Bùqí.
In the fifth month,
he returned,
visited Jiànzhāng Palace,
and granted a general amnesty to the empire.
2 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the last day, Jiǎyín,
there was a solar eclipse.
3 In the twelfth month,
the Emperor made an imperial tour to Yōng,
to sacrifice at the Five Zhì altars;
he went west to Āndìng and Běidì.
These two commanderies belonged to Shuòfāngzhōu.
Āndìng was
the land of Jìng and Yuán in the Táng Dynasty.
Běidì was
the land of Bīn, Níng, Huán, Qìng, Yán, and Yòuzhōu in the Táng Dynasty.
Zhēnghé first year
(Jǐchǒu, 92 BCE). Yīng Shào said: "It means that the four barbarian tribes were subjugated by military campaigns, and the world was at peace."
1 In spring,
the first month,
the Emperor returned
and visited Jiànzhāng Palace.
2 In the third month,
King Jìngsù of Zhào, Péngzǔ, died.
Péngzǔ had taken Nàojī, a favored concubine of King Yì of Jiāngdū.
Péngzǔ,
a son of Emperor Jǐng,
was enfeoffed as Guǎngchuān two years prior,
and transferred to Zhào five years later.
The story of Nàojī can be found in Volume 19, Yuánshòu second year.
'Nào'
is pronounced Nú Jiào.
She was called Nàozǐ.
At that time, Nàojī's elder brother was a Han eunuch,
and the Emperor summoned him and asked:
"What is Nàozǐ like?"
He replied:
"She is very ambitious."
The Emperor said:
"Being ambitious is not suitable for ruling a state and governing the people."
He asked about Marquis Wǔshǐ, Chāng.
Chāng was also a son of Péngzǔ.
Bān Zhì: Wǔshǐ County belonged to Wèijùn.
[He replied:] "Neither blameworthy nor praiseworthy."
The Emperor said:
"This will do."
He sent an envoy to install Chāng as King of Zhào.
3 In summer,
there was a great drought.
4 The Emperor was residing in Jiànzhāng Palace
when he saw a man with a sword enter the Zhōnglónghuá Gate.
Suspecting him to be an unusual person,
he ordered him to be arrested.
The man dropped his sword and ran,
and they pursued him but did not catch him.
The Emperor was enraged
and executed the gate guard.
The gate guard
was in charge of the palace gate's entry and exit prohibitions;
Xù Hàn Zhì states,
his rank was six hundred bushels of grain.
In the eleventh month,
knights from the Three Fǔ regions were dispatched for a large search in Shànglín,
and the city gates of Cháng'ān were closed for a search;
Minister Zàn said: "'Sōu'
refers to searching for wicked persons.
Shànglín Park had a circumference of several hundred *lǐ*,
fearing that wicked persons might hide there,
hence a large search was conducted.
'Suǒ'
is pronounced Shān Kè."
The witchcraft (wūgǔ) incident began.
5. Chancellor Gōngsūn Hè's (公孫賀) wife, Jūnrú (君孺),
was Empress Wèi's (衞皇后) elder sister.
Hè (賀) was consequently favored.
Hè's (賀) son, Jìngshēng (敬聲), succeeded his father as Grand Coachman (太僕),
and was arrogant, extravagant, and disregarded the law.
He embezzled nineteen million cash from the Northern Army (北軍).
When this was discovered,
he was imprisoned.
At this time, an imperial edict urgently sought the capture of Zhū Ānshì (朱安世), a great brigand from Yánglíng (陽陵).
Hè (賀) personally requested to pursue and capture Ānshì (安世) to atone for Jìngshēng's (敬聲) crime,
and the Emperor granted his request.
Afterwards, Ānshì (安世) was indeed captured.
Ānshì (安世) laughed and said:
"The Chancellor's (丞相) misfortune extends to his whole clan!"
Thereupon, from prison, he submitted a memorial,
accusing
"Jìngshēng (敬聲) of having an illicit affair with Princess Yángshí (陽石公主).
Princess Yángshí (陽石公主)
was the Emperor's (帝) daughter."
Bān Zhì (班志) states: Yángshí (陽石) belonged to Běihǎi (北海) Commandery.
"Shàngshū" (上書)
is pronounced shí zhǎng fān (時掌翻);
both xià (下) and shàng (上) are similar.
"He also made a sorcerer bury effigies along the imperial road,
cursing the Emperor,
uttering vile words."
Shīgǔ (師古) said: Carving wood to make a person,
in the likeness of a human form,
is called an effigy (偶人).
Ǒu (偶)
means "together" (並),
and "opposite" (對).
Zhù (祝)
is pronounced zhí jiù fān (職救翻).
Zǔ (詛)
is pronounced zhuāng zhù fān (莊助翻).
1. In spring,
the first month,
Hè (賀) was imprisoned,
and the case was investigated.
Both father and son died in prison,
and their clan was exterminated.
Their whole family was put to death.
The Chancellor (丞相)
was enfeoffed as Marquis of Péng (澎侯).
Zhuó (涿) Commandery
was established by Emperor Gāo (高帝),
and belonged to Yōuzhōu (幽州).
It is the land of Táng Yíng (唐瀛), Mò (莫), Yōu (幽), Zhuó (涿), Shēn (深), and Qí (祁) Prefectures in the Táng (唐) dynasty.
Qū (屈)
is pronounced qiū wù fān (丘勿翻).
Lí (氂)
is pronounced lì zhī fān (力之翻).
Jìn Zhuó (晉灼) said: Péng (澎)
is a county in Dōnghǎi (東海).
Upon examination, Bān Zhì (班志) does not mention this.
Fú Qián (服虔) said: Péng (澎)
is pronounced péng (彭).
He was the son of Jìng Wáng (靖王) of Zhōngshān (中山).
Jìng Wáng Shèng (靖王勝)
was Emperor Jǐng's (景帝) son.
2. In summer,
the fourth month,
there was a great wind
that unroofed houses and broke trees.
3. In the intercalary month,
Princess Zhūyì (諸邑公主), Princess Yángshí (陽石公主), and the Empress's (皇后) nephew, Marquis Chángpíng Kàng (長平侯伉), were all executed for witchcraft.
Zhū (諸)
was a county in Lángyá (琅邪),
used to enfeoff the princess,
hence called Yì (邑).
Both she and Princess Yángshí (陽石公主) were daughters of Empress Wèi (衞皇后).
Marquis Chángpíng Kàng (長平侯伉)
was Wèi Qīng's (衞青) son.
Kàng (伉)
is pronounced kàng (抗),
and also gāng (剛).
4. The Emperor traveled to Gānquán (甘泉).
5. Originally,
the Emperor was twenty-nine years old when Crown Prince Lì (戾太子) was born,
and he loved him greatly.
As he grew older, he was benevolent, forgiving, gentle, and prudent.
The Emperor, however, felt his talent and ability were somewhat lacking
and unlike his own.
Moreover, the favored Lady Wáng (王夫人) bore him a son, Hóng (閎);
Lady Lǐ (李姬) bore sons Dàn (旦) and Xū (胥);
Lady Lǐ (李夫人) bore a son, Bó (髆).
The Empress's (皇后) and Crown Prince's (太子) favor gradually declined,
and they often felt insecure.
The Emperor noticed this
and said to General-in-Chief Qīng (青):
"The Hàn (漢) dynasty's various affairs are still in their initial stages.
Zhū Xī (朱熹) said: Cǎo (草)
means "rough" (略).
Chuàng (創)
means "create" (造).
If I do not change the system and institutions,
future generations will have no laws.
If I do not dispatch armies to conquer,
the world will not be at peace.
To do these things, I cannot avoid burdening the people.
If future generations act as I have,
they will be following in the footsteps of the fallen Qín (秦).
The Crown Prince (太子) is steady and fond of tranquility,
and will surely be able to bring peace to the world
and spare me worry.
If one seeks a ruler who can preserve established order,
how can there be anyone more worthy than the Crown Prince (太子)?
I hear the Empress (皇后) and Crown Prince (太子) feel insecure.
Is this true?

Numbers being short is because

Major affairs include divining the establishment of a ruler, divining major enfeoffments, major sacrifices, dispatching military expeditions, mourning rituals,
and the eight commands of the tortoise:
First is zhēng (征) (expedition),
second is xiàng (象) (image),
third is yǔ (與) (giving),
fourth is móu (謀) (plan),
fifth is guǒ (果) (fruit/outcome),
sixth is zhì (至) (arrival),
seventh is yǔ (雨) (rain),

The Shìrén (筮人) (yarrow diviner) manages the nine sayings of yarrow divination:

xián (咸)

referring to divining about establishing regulations;

referring to having many affairs,

If Fú's advice had been followed,
the state would have been spared the expense of splitting territories and bestowing titles,
and Your subjects would have avoided the disaster of rebellion, rebellion, and extermination.
The past events are already done,
but Fú alone has not received his due merit.
May Your Majesty examine this
and value the strategy of moving firewood and bending the chimney,
placing him to the right of those with scorched hair and burned faces!"
The Emperor then bestowed upon Fú ten rolls of silk,
and later appointed him as a Láng.
When the Emperor first ascended the throne,
he paid homage at the Gāomiào.
Grand General Huò Guāng rode alongside the carriage
(According to Hàn regulations,
for the imperial carriage,
the Grand General rode alongside).
(Chéng,
pronounced shéng zhèng fān;
same below.)
The Emperor felt as if there were thorns in his back.
Later, when General of Chariots and Cavalry Zhāng Ānshì rode alongside Guāng,
the Son of Heaven relaxed his body at ease,
feeling very comfortable and close.
When Guāng himself died and his clan was ultimately exterminated,
it was popularly said that the disaster of the Huò clan originated from the side-riding.
(Shī Gǔ said: 'Méng'
means 'the beginning of life'.)
Empress Huò was later moved to the Yúnlín Guǎn,
and then committed suicide.
Bān Gù's encomium says: Huò Guāng received a trust from the cradle,
undertaking the responsibility for the Hàn dynasty.
He rectified the state,
brought peace to the altars of soil and grain,
supported Zhāo Dì,
and established Xuān Dì.
Even Zhōu Gōng and Āhéng could not have done more!
(Shī Gǔ said: 'Āhéng'
was the official title of Yī Yǐn.
means 'to lean on'.
'Héng'
means 'to balance'.
It means that upon him the world leaned,
and by him all below were made balanced.)
(Wáng,
an ancient character used interchangeably with wú.)
The wicked schemes of his hidden wife,
(Jìn Zhuó said: Not to expose their faults.)
indulging in overflowing desires,
thereby increased the disaster of overthrow.
Three years after his death,
his clan was exterminated.
Alas!
Minister Guāng says: Huò Guāng's assistance to the Hàn imperial house
can be called loyal;
yet he ultimately could not protect his own clan.
Why?
For power and authority
are the tools of the ruler;
when a minister wields them
and does not return them for long,
few avoid disaster.
With Xiào Zhāo's intelligence,
at fourteen he knew of Shàngguān Jié's deceit,
and could certainly have taken charge of government.
Moreover, Xiào Xuān ascended the throne at nineteen,
intelligent and resolute,
understanding the people's sufferings.
Yet Guāng long monopolized great power,
not knowing how to avoid or withdraw.
He appointed many private
partisans,
filling the court,
causing the ruler to harbor resentment above,
and officials and people to accumulate grievances below,
gnashing teeth and glaring sideways,
waiting for the opportune moment to act.
That he himself escaped harm was fortunate;
how much more so for his descendants who pursued pride and extravagance!
Nevertheless,
had Xiào Xuān simply enriched his descendants with official salaries and rewards,
allowing them to govern large counties
and attend court as honored guests,
that would have been sufficient to repay his great virtue.
But instead, he again entrusted them with governance
and bestowed upon them military power.
When problems accumulated and conflicts grew,
and then he further cut them back,
it led to resentment and fear, giving rise to wicked schemes.
How could it be merely the Huò clan bringing disaster upon themselves?
It was also Xiào Xuān who fostered it to completion.
Formerly, Dòu Jiāo caused rebellion in Chǔ
(The collateral branch of Ruò'áo of Chǔ became the Dòu clan.
It was thought that if Zǐwén had no descendants,
how could good deeds be encouraged.
This event is seen in Zuǒ Zhuàn, Xuān's fourth year.
Zǐwén was Dòu Gǔyútu.
Zhēn Yǐn was a Chǔ official title.
Kè Huáng was Zǐwén's grandson.
Zhēn,
pronounced zhī jīn fān).
Although they deserved extermination,
Guāng's loyal service could not go without sacrifices.
(Though Dòu Jiāo and his kin deserved extermination),
(It should read: Although Dòu Jiāo and his kin deserved extermination, but
the loyal services of Zǐwén should not be left un-sacrificed. To cause a family to have no survivors and
have no descendants)
It was also Xiào Xuān who lacked compassion!
6 In the ninth month,
an edict was issued to reduce salt prices throughout the empire.
It was also ordered that commanderies and kingdoms annually report prisoners
who died from flogging, scourging, or starvation,
specifying their county of origin, name, title, and village.
(Hàn Shū Běnjì states "name, county, title, village".)
(Shī Gǔ said: 'Name'
refers to the person's name;
'county' refers to their affiliated county;
'title' refers to their official rank;
'village' refers to their place of residence.)
(Shī Gǔ said: Whenever 'diàn zuì' is mentioned,
'diàn'
means 'last',
meaning the performance is last;
'zuì'
means 'foremost of all essentials',
meaning the performance is first.)
(Diàn,
pronounced dīng jiàn fān.)
7 In the twelfth month,
Qīnghé Wáng Nián was deposed for internal misconduct
and exiled to Fánglíng.
(In the second year of Wǔ Dì's Yuánguāng era,
Qīnghé Wáng Yì was established to succeed Xiào Wáng.
Nián
was Yì's grandson.)
8 That year,
Zhū Yì (朱邑) of Lújiāng (廬江), the Administrator of Běihǎi (北海), for being ranked first in governance, entered [the court] as Grand Minister of Agriculture (Dàsīnóng, 大司農).
Gōng Suí (龔遂), the Administrator of Bóhǎi (勃海), entered as Chief Commandant of Waterways and Parks (Shuǐhéng Dūwèi, 水衡都尉).
Prior to this,
the surrounding commanderies of Bóhǎi (勃海) suffered famine for years.
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: "Surrounding"
refers to those adjacent and contiguous.
Prior,
pronunciation is Xī Jiàn (悉薦).
The officials receiving salaries of two thousand dàn (dàn, 石) could not control [the situation].
The Emperor selected competent administrators.
The Chancellor (Chéngxiàng, 丞相) and Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ, 御史) recommended Gōng Suí (龔遂), former Prefect of the Palace Affairs (Lángzhōnglìng, 郎中令) of Chāngyì (昌邑).
The Emperor appointed him Administrator of Bóhǎi (Bóhǎi Tàishǒu, 勃海太守).
He was summoned for an audience
and asked:
"How will you govern Bóhǎi (勃海)
and pacify its bandits?"
He replied:
"The seacoast is remote
and not touched by the sagely transformations.
Its people suffer from hunger and cold, and the officials do not care,
thus Your Majesty's infants (chìzǐ, 赤子) play with Your Majesty's weapons in a stagnant pool (huángchí, 潢池).
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: Chìzǐ (赤子)
is like saying "newborn,"
meaning young and small.
Infants are red when first born,
hence called chìzǐ (赤子).
A pool of water is called huáng (潢),
pronounced huáng.
How will they be pacified?"
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: Shèng (勝)
means to overcome and kill with power and might.
Ān (安)
means to soothe and pacify with virtue and transformation.
"Selecting and employing the virtuous and good,
one certainly wishes to pacify them."
Suí (遂) said:
"I have heard that governing a chaotic populace is like untangling a tangled rope;
it cannot be rushed.
Only by slowing down
can it then be governed.
I request that the Chancellor (Chéngxiàng, 丞相) and Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ, 御史) temporarily do not restrict me with laws and regulations,
but allow me to act according to expediency in all matters."
The Emperor agreed to this,
and additionally bestowed gold upon him for his journey.
He traveled by post-chaise to the border of Bóhǎi (勃海).
The commandery, hearing of the new Administrator's arrival,
dispatched troops to welcome him.
Suí (遂) sent them all back.
He issued a letter instructing the subordinate counties:
"Dismiss all officials who pursue and arrest bandits.
Those who carry hoes, sickles, and farming implements
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: Gōu (鉤)
is a sickle.
officials are not to question them;
those who carry weapons are then bandits."
Suí (遂) arrived at the prefecture in a single carriage alone.
The bandits, hearing Suí's (遂) commands,
immediately dispersed,
abandoned their weapons and crossbows, and carried sickles and hoes.
Thereupon, everything was pacified.
The people were content in their homes and happy in their work.
Suí (遂) then opened the granaries and lent [grain] to the poor.
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: Jiǎ (假)
means to give.
Suí (遂) observed that the customs of Qí (齊) were extravagant
and fond of minor crafts,
not engaging in farming.
He therefore personally led by example in frugality,
encouraging the people to diligently pursue agriculture and sericulture,
each planting trees and raising livestock according to their household size.
Suí (遂) ordered the people to plant one elm tree per person,
one hundred scallions,
fifty onions,
and one bed of leeks;
each household was to have three sows
and five chickens.
Xù (畜),
pronunciation is Xǔ Lù (許六).
He made them sell swords to buy oxen,
and sell knives to buy calves,
saying:
"Why wear an ox or carry a calf?"
He traveled around to encourage and inspect,
and soon the entire commandery had accumulated livestock and provisions,
and litigation ceased.
The Zīzhì Tōngjiàn (資治通鑑) records Gōng Suí (龔遂) entering [the court] as a high official from Bóhǎi (勃海),
and thus describes his administrative achievements.
9 The daughter of the Wūsūn (烏孫) princess became the夫人 (fūrén) of Jiàngbīn (絳賓), the King of Qiūcí (龜茲).
Jiàngbīn (絳賓) submitted a memorial, stating:
"Having the honor of marrying a Han (漢) descendant,
I wish to enter the court together with the princess's daughter."
Yuánkāng (元康) first year
(bǐngchén, 丙辰; 65 BCE)
1 In spring,
the first month,
the King of Qiūcí (龜茲) and his夫人 (fūrén) came to court;
both were bestowed with seals and ribbons,
and the夫人 (fūrén) was titled princess.
They received very generous rewards.
2 Construction of Dùlíng (杜陵) began.
Chancellors (Chéngxiàng, 丞相), generals, marquises, officials receiving salaries of two thousand dàn (dàn, 石), and those with assets of one million (zì bǎiwàn, 訾百萬) were moved to Dùlíng (杜陵).
At that time, the eastern plateau of Dù (杜) County in Jīngzhào (京兆) was designated as the initial imperial mausoleum,
and Dù (杜) County was renamed Dùlíng (杜陵).
Zī (訾),
read as Cī (貲).
3 In the third month,
an edict was issued because phoenixes gathered at Tàishān (泰山) and Chénliú (陳留),
and sweet dew descended upon Wèiyāng (未央) Palace,
proclaiming a general amnesty.
4 Officials again proposed that the Dàoyuán (悼園) should be honored with the title Huángkǎo (皇考, Imperial Deceased Father);
in Běnshǐ (本始) first year, the deceased parent was posthumously titled Dào (悼) and a cemetery town was established.
Fù (復),
pronunciation is Fú Yòu (扶又).
In the fifth month,
the temple for the Huángkǎo (皇考) was established.
5 In winter,
the Commandant of the Guard (Wèiwèi, 衞尉) for Jiànzhāng (建章) was established.
Wèiyāng (未央), Chánglè (長樂), Jiànzhāng (建章), and Gānquán (甘泉) all had a Commandant of the Guard (Wèiwèi, 衞尉),
each responsible for guarding their palace gates and garrisoning troops.
6 Zhào Guǎnghàn (趙廣漢) liked to employ descendants of officials and young, newly advanced individuals.
Shīgǔ (師古) said: This means descendants of old official families,
who later emerged to seek advancement,
and were also young.
Hǎo (好),
read Hū Dào.
Shào (少),
read Shī Zhào.
Shīgǔ (師古) said: It is the same as fēng (鋒),
referring to a sharp and incisive spirit.
They avoided nothing,
Shīgǔ (師古) said: "Fēng shēng (風生)" means their speed was irresistible.
Huí (回),
means crooked.
No one could obstruct them,
but ultimately, he was ruined by this.
Guǎnghàn (廣漢) used a private grudge to sentence to death a man named Róng Xù (榮畜).
Originally,
Guǎnghàn’s (廣漢) guest privately sold wine in the Cháng'ān (長安) market,
and a prime minister’s (chéngxiàng 丞相) official drove him away.
The guest suspected a man named Sū Xián (蘇賢) had reported it,
told Guǎnghàn (廣漢),
who then investigated Xián (賢).
Xián’s (賢) father submitted a memorial to protest the charges,
and Guǎnghàn (廣漢) was demoted in rank for it.
He suspected his fellow townsman Róng Xù (榮畜) had instigated it,
and sentenced Xù (畜) to death under another law.
Róng (榮) is a surname;
during the Zhōu (周) dynasty, there was Róng Gōng (榮公),
whose descendants took Róng as their surname.
The matter was referred to the prime minister (chéngxiàng 丞相) and the imperial censor (yùshǐ 御史) for investigation.
Guǎnghàn (廣漢) suspected the prime minister’s (chéngxiàng 丞相) wife had killed a maid,
and wished to use this to threaten the prime minister (chéngxiàng 丞相).
The prime minister (chéngxiàng 丞相) investigated him even more urgently.
Guǎnghàn (廣漢) then led officials and soldiers into the prime minister’s (chéngxiàng 丞相) residence,
summoned his wife to kneel in the courtyard to receive questioning.
Shīgǔ (師古) said: To receive her responses.
The prime minister (chéngxiàng 丞相) submitted a memorial to explain himself.
The case was sent to the Minister of Justice (Tíngwèi 廷尉) for judgment.
In reality, the prime minister (chéngxiàng 丞相) had personally reprimanded and flogged his maid for a transgression,
and she died after being sent out to the outer residence,
not as Guǎnghàn (廣漢) had stated.
The Emperor (Dì 帝) disliked this,
and sent Guǎnghàn (廣漢) to the Minister of Justice's (Tíngwèi 廷尉) prison.
Tens of thousands of officials and common people stood before the palace gate, weeping loudly:
"We, your subjects, are of no benefit to the county (xiànguān 縣官) while alive;
we wish to die in place of Zhào Jīngzhào (趙京兆),
so that he may shepherd and nourish the common people!"
In the "Hàn Shū (漢書) Biography,"
above "chéng shēng (臣生)"
are
the two characters "huò yán (或言)."
[Zhāng (章): The Jiǎ Shíwǔ Háng Běn (甲十五行本)
has exactly
the two characters
"huò yán (或言)"
above "chéng (臣)";
the Yǐ Shíyī Háng Běn (乙十一行本) is the same;
the Kǒng Běn (孔本) is the same;
the Tuìzhāi Jiào (退齋校) is the same.
Yāo (要),
is the same as yāo (腰).
Kǎo Yì (考異) said: In the "Běnjì (本紀)":
"In the second year of Yuánkāng (元康)
winter,
Guǎnghàn (廣漢) committed a crime and was executed by severing at the waist (yāozhǎn 腰斬)."
"Bǎiguān Biǎo (百官表)":
"In the third year of Běnshǐ (本始),
Guǎnghàn (廣漢) became the Magistrate of Jīngzhào (Jīngzhào Yǐn 京兆尹);
in the sixth year,
he was executed by severing at the waist (yāozhǎn 腰斬).
In the first year of Yuánkāng (元康),
he served as Magistrate of Jīngzhào (Jīngzhào Yǐn 京兆尹) and Grand Administrator of Péngchéng (Péngchéng Tàishǒu 彭城太守), posthumously."
According to Guǎnghàn’s (廣漢) biography,
Sīzhí (司直) Xiāo Wàngzhī (蕭望之) impeached Guǎnghàn (廣漢) for humiliating high officials.
Wàngzhī (望之) moved from Sīzhí (司直) to become Grand Administrator of Píngyuán (Píngyuán Tàishǒu 平原太守).
In the first year of Yuánkāng (元康),
he moved from Grand Administrator of Píngyuán (Píngyuán Tàishǒu 平原太守) to become Minister Steward (Shǎofǔ 少府).
Therefore, Guǎnghàn’s (廣漢) death must have occurred in the first year of Yuánkāng (元康),
so the "Běnjì (本紀)" is erroneous.
Guǎnghàn’s (廣hàn) biography also states:
"In the seventh month of the third year of Dìjié (地節),
the prime minister’s (chéngxiàng 丞相) maid hanged herself."
Presumably, the maid had died several years earlier,
and Guǎnghàn (廣hàn) later brought up the matter.
He was honest and upright,
controlling the powerful and influential,
and the common people found their proper places.
Shīgǔ (師古) said: "Dé zhí (得職)" means each found their usual position.
7 In this year,
the Minister Steward (Shǎofǔ 少府) Sòng Chóu (宋疇) was demoted for discussing,
"'A phoenix (fènghuáng 鳳皇) descended at Péngchéng (彭城),
but it did not reach the capital (Jīngshī 京師),
so it is not enough to be called beautiful',"
and was reduced to Grand Tutor (Tàifù 太傅) of Sìshuǐ (泗水).
He tutored Wáng Zōng (王綜) of Sìshuǐ (泗水).

8 The Emperor (Shàng 上) selected scholars of broad learning (bóshì 博士) and Grand Masters of Remonstrance (jiàndàfū 諫大夫) who were proficient in governance to fill positions as Grand Administrators (shǒuxiàng 守相) of commanderies and states,
appointing Xiāo Wàngzhī (蕭望之) as Grand Administrator of Píngyuán (Píngyuán Tàishǒu 平原太守).
Wàngzhī (望之) submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your Majesty (Bìxià 陛下) has compassion for the common people,
fearing that virtue will not be fully realized.
Shīgǔ (師古) said: "Jiū (究)" means to complete.
Referring to its prevalence throughout the world.
If there are no contentious ministers in court,
then Your Majesty (Bìxià 陛下) will not know Your faults.
This is what is called worrying about the branches and forgetting the root."
The Emperor (Shàng 上) then summoned Wàngzhī (望之) to enter and serve as Minister Steward (Shǎofǔ 少府).
9 Yǐn Wēngguī (尹翁歸) of Hédōng (河東), Grand Administrator of Dōnghǎi (Dōnghǎi Tàishǒu 東海太守),
entered to serve as Right Fúfēng (Yòu Fúfēng 右扶風) due to his excellent administration of the commandery.
Wēngguī (翁歸) was public-spirited, honest, and keen-sighted.
He knew all the officials and common people in the commandery, the worthy and unworthy, as well as their cunning and crimes.
Each county had its own record book,
and he personally heard their cases.
Shīgǔ (師古) said: This means he personally judged the cases of cunning and wickedness in the various counties, not entrusting them to the magistrates or chiefs.
When officials and common people were slightly negligent,
he would open the register.
Fú Qián (服虔) said: To open the register of those who have committed crimes.
Shīgǔ (師古) said: "Jiě (解)" is read xiè (懈).
Shīgǔ (師古) said: During large assemblies or when inspecting counties,
he would present criminals to warn the public.
Háng (行),
read xià mèng.
The subsequent gǎi háng (改行) and yǐ háng (以行)
are the same.
What he sought to achieve was
to warn a hundred by means of one.
All officials and common people respected
and feared him,
changing their ways and reforming themselves.
When he was Fúfēng (扶風),
he selected honest, fair, and detestable officials to serve as "right-officials" (yòuzhí 右職).
A "right-official" (zhí 職) was placed above other officials
and called a yòuzhí (右職).
He treated
their likes and dislikes as his own;
if they offended Wēngguī (翁歸),
punishment would certainly be carried out.
Yet he was gentle, kind, humble, and modest,
not boasting of his conduct or abilities to others,
and therefore gained even greater renown at court.
10 Initially,
the youngest son of the Wūsūn (烏孫) Princess (Gōngzhǔ 公主), Wànnián (萬年), was favored by the King of Shāchē (Shāchē Wáng 莎車王).
Bān Shū (班書) said, the King of Shāchē (Shāchē Guó 莎車國) governed Shāchē Chéng (莎車城),
which was nine thousand nine hundred and fifty lǐ (里) from Cháng'ān (長安).
Shā (莎),
read sū hé.
At that time, Wànnián (萬年) was in Hàn (漢).
The people of Shāchē (Shāchē Guó 莎車國) considered
that they wished to rely on Hàn (漢),
and also wished to gain the favor of Wūsūn (烏孫),
so they submitted a memorial requesting Wànnián (萬年) to be their king.
Hàn (漢) agreed,
and dispatched an envoy, Xī Chōngguó (奚充國), to escort Wànnián (萬年).
The "Xìng Pǔ (姓譜)" states: The Xī (奚) surname
descends from Xī Zhòng (奚仲), the chariot master (chēzhèng 車正) of the Xià (夏) dynasty.
He was cruel and wicked,
and the people of the kingdom were displeased.
The Emperor ordered his trusted ministers to recommend someone who could be sent to the Western Regions.

The former General, Hán Zēng 韓增, recommended Féng Fèngshì 馮奉世 of Shàngdǎng 上黨 to serve as a Wèihóu 衞候 (Imperial Guard Commander) with a staff, to escort guests from Dàyuān 大宛 and other kingdoms to Yīxún Chéng 伊循城.
Wèihóu 衞候,
means "Imperial Guard Commander."
Yīxún Chéng 伊循城 was in the kingdom of Shànshàn 鄯善,
where the Hàn 漢 established agricultural garrisons with officers and soldiers.
使 (shǐ),
pronounced shū lì fān 疏吏翻.
He proclaimed himself king.
At that time, the Xiōngnú 匈奴 again dispatched troops to attack Chēshī Chéng 車師城,
but they failed to capture it and withdrew.
Shāchē 莎車 sent envoys to spread rumors,
saying, "The kingdoms of the Northern Route have already submitted to the Xiōngnú 匈奴!"
Yángyán 揚言,
means "to openly declare one's words to the outside."
They made a blood-oath alliance and rebelled against the Hàn 漢,
cutting off communication with all regions west of Shànshàn 鄯善.
The Protector-General, Zhèng Jí 鄭吉, and Colonel Sīmǎ Xǐ 司馬憙 were both among the kingdoms of the Northern Route.
Fèngshì 奉世 and his deputy, Yán Chāng 嚴昌, deliberated,
believing that if they did not attack quickly,
Shāchē 莎車 would grow stronger day by day,
its power would become difficult to control,
and it would surely endanger the Western Regions.
So, he used his staff of authority to issue a proclamation to the kings of the various kingdoms,
and then raised their troops.
The Northern and Southern Routes combined to form fifteen thousand men,
who advanced to attack Shāchē 莎車,
besieging and capturing its city.
The King of Shāchē 莎車 committed suicide,
and his head was sent to Cháng'ān 長安.
Another of his younger brothers or nephews was then installed as the King of Shāchē 莎車.
All the kingdoms were pacified,
and his prestige shook the Western Regions.
Fèngshì 奉世 then disbanded his troops and reported the matter.
The Emperor summoned Hán Zēng 韓增 and said:
"I congratulate the General; the person you recommended was indeed the right one."
Fèngshì 奉世 then traveled west to Dàyuān 大宛;
Dàyuān 大宛, hearing that he had beheaded the King of Shāchē 莎車,
respected him more than other envoys,
and he returned with their famous horse, Xiànglóng 象龍.
Shīgǔ 師古 said: It refers to a horse whose form resembles a dragon.
Zhòng Féng 仲馮 said: This horse's name was Xiànglóng 象龍.
宛 (Yuān),
pronounced yú yuán fān 於元翻.
還 (huán),
pronounced cóng xuān fān 從宣翻,
also as written.
There was a discussion about enfeoffing Fèngshì 奉世.
The Chancellor and generals all thought it permissible,
but only the Grand Steward, Xiāo Wàngzhī 蕭望之, believed
that "Fèngshì 奉世, when carrying out his mission, had specific instructions
Shīgǔ 師古 said: The original purpose was to escort guests from various kingdoms.
but [he] presumptuously
violated orders,

要 (yāo),

1 In spring,
the first month,

華 (Huá),

Qīn 欽.

邛 (Qióng),

傳 (chuán),

傳 (chuán),

過 (guò) here

4 He further said:

If the Hàn 漢 obtains it,
they will farm widely and accumulate grain,

Because of this, they repeatedly sent troops to attack the farmers of Chēshī 車師.
Zhèng Jí 鄭吉 led seven thousand soldiers from Qúlí 渠犂 to rescue them,

Jí 鄭吉 reported:
"Chēshī 車師 is more than a thousand *lǐ* from Qúlí 渠犂,

They are unable to help each other,

The Emperor discussed with the Rear General, Zhào Chōngguó 趙充國, and others,

"Your servant has heard:
to rescue the chaotic and punish the violent
is called a righteous army (yì bīng);
an army that is righteous will rule as king.
When an enemy attacks oneself,
and one is compelled to rise up,
this is called a responsive army (yìng bīng);
an army that is responsive will be victorious.
If one disputes over minor grievances
and cannot bear one's anger,
this is called an angry army (fèn bīng);
an angry army will be defeated.
Those who covet others' land, goods, and treasures
are called a greedy army (tān bīng);
a greedy army will be annihilated.
Relying on the greatness of one's state
and
the multitude of its people,
wishing to display one's might to the enemy,
this is called an arrogant army (jiāo bīng);
an arrogant army will be destroyed.
These five [categories]
are not merely human affairs,

Recently, the Xiongnú have shown goodwill,

Although there was a dispute over the garrison farms in Jūshī,

This means it is not worth worrying about.
The Chancellor did not participate in the discussions of the Central Court,

Now the border commanderies are in distress,

Shīgǔ said: One cannot move them with military affairs.
There will surely be a year of famine.
Shīgǔ said: This quotes a saying from Lǎozi's Dàodé Jīng.
Even if the troops sent out are victorious,
there will still be future worries,
and I fear that disasters and calamities may arise from this.

Shīgǔ said: It means they are not the right people.

According to this year's records,
there are a total of two hundred and twenty-two cases of sons and younger brothers killing their fathers and elder brothers, and wives killing their husbands.
Your foolish servant believes this is no small change.
Now the attendants at court do not worry about this.
Shīgǔ said: Attendants (zuǒyòu) refers to close officials around the Son of Heaven.
This is probably what Kǒngzǐ meant by, 'I fear Jì Sūn's trouble is not in Zhuānyú, but within his own palace.' "
Shīgǔ said: In the Lúnyǔ, when Jì Shūn was about to attack Zhuānyú,

Zhuānyú

Xiāoqiáng (蕭牆)

[The emperor] merely dispatched Cháng Luóhóu Cháng Huì to lead cavalry from Zhāngyè and Jiǔquán to Jūshī,

6 Wèi Xiàng enjoyed studying Hàn historical precedents and memorials of expediency.

Hào (好)

Ever since his great-grandson encountered his good fortune,

he never spoke of his past favors,

It happened that a palace maid from the Yè Tíng Palace, named Zé Lìng Mínfū, submitted a memorial,

He immediately feigned illness.

8 Initially,

the Yè Tíng Director Zhāng Hè frequently praised the talent and virtue of the imperial great-grandson to his younger brother, the General of Cavalry and Chariots, Ānshì, and also spoke of strange omens.
Shīgǔ said: Zhēng (徵) means proof.
Shù (數) is pronounced Suǒ Jiǎo.

[Ānshì] believed that with the young lord on the throne,

The emperor, recalling Hè's kindness,

Shīgǔ said: Since he died and was posthumously enfeoffed, it is called enfeoffing the tomb.
Hè had a son who died early,

Shīgǔ said: 'Son' (zǐ) means he was adopted as a son.
Wishing to enfeoff him,

The emperor said:

The emperor [Xuān] deeply resented the former King Hè of Chāngyì.

Shī Gǔ said: It was a secret order for surveillance,
not meant to be publicly announced.
Xià, pronounced xiá jià.
To make evident the consequences of his deposition and ruin.

to make clear.
"The former King Hè of Chāngyì
was dark-skinned,
with small eyes,
a sharp and low nose tip,

Your servant Chǎng once spoke with him,

The owl (xiāo) is
an unfilial bird,

Once their wings and feathers are formed,

The mother has nothing to give in response,

Hàn envoys from Dōngjùn would send owls,

Xiāo is pronounced jiān yáo,
also yú jiāo.
Nǎi fù is pronounced fú yòu.
'He is 'qīngkuáng' and not intelligent.'
Sū Lín said: Generally, for a mad person, both yin and yang pulses are completely turbid.
This person is not mad but resembles a mad person,

Some say: It means a clear and calm complexion and demeanor, but an unintelligent mind, hence 'qīngkuáng'.
Qīngkuáng
is like today's 'báichī' (idiocy).

'When he was kept to guard the garden of King Āi,
Hè's father, Bó,

Shī Gǔ said: Xǐ means
to like.

1. In spring,
the third month,
an edict ennobled the former King Hè of Chāngyì as the Marquis of Hǎihūn.

the Grandee Secretary Bǐng Jí, the Gentleman-of-the-Household-General Shǐ Zēng, Shǐ Xuán, the Chánglè Guard Commander Xǔ Shùn, and the Palace Attendant and Grandee of the Palace Xǔ Yánshòu all had old kindnesses toward Us,

Their benevolence and kindness were exceptional,
and their merits were abundant.
Does not the Shī Jīng say: 'No virtue goes unrequited'?

Therefore, Zhāng Hè is posthumously granted the title of Marquis Āi of Yángdū,

At the age of seven,
he was appointed Scattered Cavalry Gentleman-of-the-Household-General

Shī Gǔ said: Fú is
the cord for attaching a seal;
pronounced fú.
"This man is not yet dead!
Your servant has heard that those with hidden virtue will surely enjoy their happiness,

Later, he indeed recovered.
Zhāng Ānshì, considering that both he and his son had been enfeoffed as marquises,
making their position in office too prominent,

An edict ordered the treasury to separately store an unspecified number of millions of Zhāng family money.
Wén Yǐng said: Dū nèi is
the official in charge of storing.
Zhāng Yàn said: Ānshì returned it to the office,
and the office did not record it.

Whenever major policies were decided,
once settled,
he would always feign illness and withdraw.
Upon hearing an imperial edict,
he would be startled
and send an official to the Chancellor's office to inquire about it.
From among the court ministers,
no one knew he had participated in the discussions.
He once recommended someone,
and that person came to thank him.
Ānshì was greatly displeased,
thinking,
"When recommending the worthy and promoting the capable,

He completely cut off communication with him.
Shī Gǔ said: He did not allow anyone who wished to thank him to communicate.
One interpretation says: He informed this person and cut him off,
no longer meeting with him.
Fù is pronounced fú yòu;
the same below.
Wèi is pronounced yú wěi.
I believe "jué fú wèi tōng" means
Ānshì instructed his gatekeeper to refuse the person.
Someone spoke of Ānshì (to his face),
and Ānshì replied:
"Your accomplishments are great,
known to the enlightened ruler.
What is the point of a minister discussing his own merits or shortcomings?"
He absolutely refused.
Afterward, the gentleman (láng) was indeed promoted.
Shī Gǔ said: Ānshì outwardly rejected him but actually caused his promotion.
Feeling uneasy,
he sought an outside posting for his son Yánshòu as an official.
The emperor appointed him Administrator of Běidì.
After more than a year,
the emperor, pitying Ānshì's old age,

This means he was made Left Cao in addition to Grand Coachman.
3 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day of bǐngzǐ,
Imperial Prince Qīn was established as Huáiyáng Wáng.
The Crown Prince, aged twelve,
was proficient in the Lúnyǔ and Xiàojīng.
Grand Tutor Shū Guǎng said to Junior Tutor Shòu:
"I have heard, 'He who knows contentment will not be disgraced;
he who knows when to stop will not be imperiled.' "
Shīgǔ said: These are the words of Lǎozǐ, cited by Guǎng.
"With office achieved and reputation established,
if we do not withdraw now,
I fear there will be regrets later."
On that very day,
father and son both feigned illness
and submitted a memorial requesting to retire.
The Emperor granted their requests,
adding a reward of twenty jīn of gold,
and the Crown Prince presented them with fifty jīn.
The high officials, nobles, and old acquaintances set up a farewell feast and decorations outside the eastern gate of the capital,
with hundreds of carriages escorting them.
Spectators along the road all said:
"How worthy are these two grandees!"
Some sighed and shed tears for them.
Guǎng and Shòu returned to their hometown.
Guǎng and Shòu
were from Lánlíng in Dōnghǎi.
Shīgǔ said: "rì rì shè zhī yě" (They set it up daily).
"Gòng"
is read as "gōng";
the same below.
They enjoyed themselves together.
Someone advised Guǎng to use his gold to establish some properties for his descendants.
Guǎng said:
"How could I be so old and muddled as not to think of my descendants!
But we already have our old fields and dwellings,"
Shīgǔ said: Gù (顧) means to think of.
"which are sufficient for our food and clothing,
making us equal to common people.
If I were now to add to them for surplus,
it would only teach my descendants to be lazy and degenerate.
If they are worthy and have much wealth,
it will diminish their ambition;
if they are foolish and have much wealth,
it will increase their faults.
Furthermore, the wealthy are resented by the multitude.
Since I have nothing to teach and enlighten my descendants,
I do not wish to increase their faults and create resentment.
Moreover, this gold
is what the sagely ruler uses to favor and nourish old officials.
Therefore, I am happy to share its bounty with my fellow villagers and clansmen,
to live out my remaining days.
Is this not acceptable!"
Thereupon, his clansmen were pleased and convinced.
4 Yǐngchuān Grand Administrator Huáng Bà ordered all post stations and village officials to raise chickens and pigs.
Shīgǔ said: "Yóutíng" (郵亭) refers to a relay station, a place where documents are transmitted and where one stops, similar to today's postal inns.
"Xiāngguān" (鄉官) refers to the administrative center of a village.
Shěn Yuè said: Under the Hán system: five families formed a wǔ,
overseen by a wǔzhǎng;
two wǔ formed a shí,
overseen by a shízhǎng;
ten shí formed a lǐ,
overseen by a lǐkuí;
ten lǐ formed a tíng,
overseen by a tíngzhǎng;
