In autumn,
the Qiāng (羌) tribes Ruòlíng (若零), Líliú (離留), Qiězǒng (且種), and Érkù (兒庫)
collectively beheaded the great chiefs of the Xiānlíng (先零), Yóufēi (猶非) and Yáng Yù (楊玉),
and presented their heads.
Wén Yǐng (文穎) said: 'Yóufēi (猶非) is a person's name.'
Shīgǔ (師古) said: 'Yóufēi (猶非) and Yáng Yù (楊玉) are two people.'
The Hàn (漢) enfeoffed Ruòlíng (若零) and his brother Zé (澤) as Kings Who Lead the Multitude,
and all the others as marquises or lords.
Líliú (離留) and Qiězǒng (且種) were made marquises;
Érkù (兒庫) was made a lord;
Yángdiāo (陽雕) was made Marquis Who Speaks of War;
Liáng'ér (良兒) was made a lord;
Míwàng (靡忘) was made Lord Who Presents Cattle.
An imperial edict was issued to recommend candidates for the Protector of the Qiāng Commander (hùqiāng xiàowèi).
The office of Protector of the Qiāng Commander (hùqiāng xiàowèi)
first appeared here.
Fàn Yè said: During the time of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn (Hàn Wǔdì),
the various Qiāng tribes communicated with the Xiōngnú,
attacked Lìngjū and Āngù,
and besieged Bàohǎn.
Lǐ Xī and Xú Zìwéi were sent to attack and pacify them,
and the Protector of the Qiāng Commander (hùqiāng xiàowèi) was first established.
The Four Offices recommended Xīn Wǔxián's younger brother, Tāng.
The Four Offices
were those of the Chancellor (chéngxiàng), Imperial Censor (yùshǐ), General of Chariots and Cavalry (chējì jiāngjūn), and General of the Vanguard (qián jiāngjūn);
together with the Office of the General of the Rear (hòu jiāngjūn),
they constituted the Five Offices.
A memorial stated:
"Tāng is given to intoxication and
cannot govern the barbarians."
Yán Shīgǔ said: "Given to intoxication" (shǐjiǔ)
means acting impulsively due to alcohol,
like what is now called 'bad drunk'.
The character "使" (shǐ)
is pronounced as written.
At that time, Tāng had already been appointed and received the insignia of authority.
"Appointed" (bài) here means
appointed as Protector of the Qiāng Commander (hùqiāng xiàowèi),
holding the insignia to protect the various Qiāng tribes.
Later, he was dismissed due to illness while in office.
The Five Offices again recommended Tāng.
Tāng repeatedly got drunk and humiliated the Qiāng people.
The Qiāng people revolted,
exactly as Chōngguó had predicted.
The historian ultimately mentioned this matter.
The character "卒" (zú)
is pronounced zǐ-xù.
Hoping for rewards by defeating the Qiāng,
but the regulations were not followed.
Áng leaked words from within the central government offices.
When Xīn Wǔxián was in the army,
he and Áng conversed at a banquet.
Áng said
that Zhāng Ānshì initially displeased the Emperor,
and the Emperor wanted to execute him;
Áng's family general believed that Zhāng Ānshì should be completely spared,
and thus Zhāng Ānshì was pardoned.
Wǔxián resented Chōngguó
and reported Áng for this offense.
He committed suicide.
3 The Superintendent of the Capital (sīlì xiàowèi) of Wèi Commandery (Wèijùn), Gài Kuānráo.
(From "Table of Officials"): The Superintendent of the Capital (sīlì xiàowèi)
was a Zhōu dynasty official;
Emperor Wǔ (Wǔdì) first established it in the fourth year of Zhēnghé (Zhēnghé),
holding the insignia of authority,
with 1,200 inmates from the capital offices under him,
to arrest practitioners of witchcraft and sorcery,
and supervise major scoundrels;
later his troops were disbanded,
and he investigated the Three Commanderies of the Capital Region (Sānfǔ), Three Rivers Region (Sānhé), and Hóngnóng Commandery (Hóngnóng).
Yán Shīgǔ said: "Because he managed prisoners and patrolled,
he was called Sīlì."
The character "蓋" (Gài)
is pronounced gǔ-hé.
Grandee Chén Dài of Qí (Qí) held an estate in Gài,
and his descendants took this as their surname.
By the early Hàn dynasty,
Qí had Gài Gōng.
Gài Kuānráo frequently offended the Emperor's will.
At that time, the Emperor was enforcing legalism,
and appointed Central Secretaries (zhōngshū guān).
Emperor Wǔ (Wǔdì), while feasting in the rear palace,
used eunuchs as Central Secretaries (zhōngshū guān).
Emperor Xuān (Xuāndì) followed this practice,
thus laying the foundation for the calamities brought by Gōng and Xiǎn.
Xú Guǎng said: "Central Secretary (zhōngshū)
refers to documents within the inner court."
Gài Kuānráo said: "Currently, the sagely Way is gradually diminishing,
and Confucianism is not practiced.
Those who are 'remnants of punishment' are made to be like [the Dukes of] Zhōu and Shào."
Yán Shīgǔ said: "This means making eunuchs hold power."
The character "召" (Zhào)
is read Shào.
Yán Shīgǔ said: "This means using penal law to achieve moral transformation."
He also said:
"The Five Emperors (Wǔdì) held the realm as an office,
the Three Kings (Sānwáng) held the realm as a family estate.
A family estate is passed down to descendants,
an office is passed down to the worthy and sagely."
When this memorial was submitted,
the Emperor considered Kuānráo's words to be resentful slander,
and sent his memorial down to the officials receiving two thousand dàn of salary.
At that time, the Bearer of the Golden Mace (zhíjīnwú) deliberated,
according to the memorial from the high officials and ministers—
in that year,
Grand Administrator Xián of Nányáng (Nányáng tàishǒu Xián) served as Bearer of the Golden Mace (zhíjīnwú).
The verdict was: "Kuānráo's intention is to seek abdication,
which is an act of great rebellion and unrighteousness!"
Yán Shīgǔ said: "This means he wanted the Son of Heaven to cede the throne to himself."
When officials spoke of matters that were not to the Emperor's liking, they were defamed and suppressed by the scribes.
Yán Shīgǔ said: "詆" (dǐ)
means to slander.
"挫" (cuò)
means to break.
"Litigation" (sòng) refers to litigating one's injustice.
Another official said:
"I have heard that when a mountain has fierce beasts,
one does not gather the wild greens from it;
when a country has loyal ministers,
evildoers will not arise.
Superintendent of the Capital (sīlì xiàowèi) Gài Kuānráo
does not seek comfort in his dwelling,
nor satiety in his food."
Yán Shīgǔ said: The Analects quotes Kǒngzǐ as saying:
"A junzǐ does not seek satiety in food,
nor comfort in dwelling."
Therefore, this is cited.
"He has the righteousness of dying for his integrity;
above, he has no connections like the Xǔ or Shǐ families,
below, he has no patrons like the Jīn or Zhāng families."
Yīng Shào said: Xǔ Bó
was the father of Emperor Xuān's (Xuāndì) empress.
Shǐ Gāo
was from Emperor Xuān's (Xuāndì) maternal family.
"Jīn" refers to Jīn Rìdī.
"Zhāng" refers to Zhāng Ānshì.
These four families' recommendations were always followed.
Yán Shīgǔ said: "This explanation is incorrect.
The Xǔ family and Shǐ family
had the grace of being the Emperor's maternal relatives;
the Jīn family and Zhāng family
relied on their status as close attendants."
The character "屬" (shǔ)
is read as its original character.
"He follows a straight path,
has many enemies and few allies."
Yán Shīgǔ said: "仇" (chóu)
refers to resentment and animosity.
"與" (yǔ)
refers to partisans and allies.
"The authorities impeached him, recommending the death penalty.
I am fortunate to be among the Grandees,
and my office is named for its function of remonstrance,
so I dare not remain silent!"
The Emperor did not listen.
In the ninth month,
Gài Kuānráo was handed over to the officials;
Gài Kuānráo drew his belt knife and slit his own throat below the Northern Watchtower (Běiquè),
and none among the multitude did not pity him.
4 The Xiongnú Chányú, Xūlǘ Quánqú, led over 100,000 cavalry in a hunt along the frontier,
intending to invade the border as bandits.
Before they arrived,
it happened that his subject Tí chú Qú Táng defected and surrendered to Hàn, reporting the situation.
Hàn considered his words and dispatched troops to Lùxī Lùlú
Hóu.
This marqués is not seen in the tables,
likely because he had no fief.
He was similar to the previous Qiāng Yángdiāo, who was also a Marqués of Military Advice.
Wén Yǐng said: "It belongs to Wǔyuán, Shuòfāng, and the like."
Shīgǔ said: "The nine commanderies were
Wǔyuán, Shuòfāng, Yúnzhōng, Dàijùn, Yànmén, Dìngxiāng, Běipíng, Shànggǔ, and Yúyáng."
Over 40,000 cavalry were divided and stationed there,
and Chóngguó was in overall command.
According to Chóngguó's biography,
this matter was recorded before the campaign against the Qiāng;
the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, due to the Xiongnú's internal strife,
recorded it here as a preliminary event.
After more than a month,
the Chányú fell ill and vomited blood.
Consequently, he dared not enter,
returned and left,
and then withdrew his troops.
He then sent the Tí Wáng Dūlíhúcì and others to Hàn to request a heqīn alliance.
Before a response was given,
the Chányú died.
When Xūlǘ Quánqú Chányú was first enthroned,
he deposed Zhuānqú Èshì.
This event is found in volume 24, Dìjié second year.
Èshì,
pronounced yān zhī.
The Right Xiánwáng met at Lóngchéng and departed.
Zhuānqú Èshì told him that the Chányú was gravely ill,
and that he should not go far.
A few days later,
the Chányú died.
The influential noble Hǎosù Wáng Xíngwèiyāng sent men to summon the various kings,
but before they arrived,
Zhuānqú Èshì conspired with her younger brother, the Zuǒ Dàjiàng
Jùqú Dūlóngqí,
to enthrone the Right Xiánwáng as Wòyǎnqúshī Chányú.
Wòyǎnqúshī Chányú
was a great-great-grandson of Wūwéi Chányú.
Yīng Shào said: "Èrsūn (ear-grandson)
is the son of a xuánsūn (great-great-grandson);
it means that they are so far removed from their high ancestors
that they only hear of them."
Lǐ Fěi said: "Èrsūn
is a zēngsūn (great-grandson)."
Jìn Zhuó said: "Èrsūn
is the zēngsūn of a xuánsūn (great-great-grandson's great-grandson)."
The Table of Feudal Kings
indicates eight generations.
Shīgǔ said: "Regarding èrsūn,
the various explanations differ.
According to the Bình Jì and the Table of Feudal Kings,
Liáng Xiàowáng's xuánsūn's son is èrsūn,
pronounced réng;
also, the Xiongnú biography states that Wòyǎnqúshī Chányú
was Wūwéi Chányú's èrsūn;
comparing these,
Lǐ's explanation of zēngsūn is correct.
However, various places in the Hànshū also consistently use zēngsūn,
so it should not mix two terms.
According to the Ěryǎ,
'the son of a zēngsūn is a xuánsūn,
the son of a xuánsūn is a láisūn,
the son of a láisūn is a kūn sūn,
the son of a kūn sūn is a réngsūn.'
Counting from oneself,
this is eight generations,
which is consistent with Jìn's explanation.
Réng and ěr are close in pronunciation,
so they are likely the same term.
However, Bān Shì only retained the ancient name,
but his calculation of generations is incorrect."
When Wòyǎnqúshī Chányú was enthroned,
he was cruel and wicked.
He killed Xíngwèiyāng and others and appointed Dūlóngqí.
He also dismissed all the sons and close relatives of Xūlǘ Quánqú and replaced them with his own sons and relatives.
Xūlǘ Quánqú Chányú's son Jīhóu Pī
(Shīgǔ said: Pī,
pronounced xiān ān fān,
also pronounced suǒ jiān fān;
Dù Yòu pronounced shān jiàn fān)
had failed to be enthroned.
The Wūchánmù were originally a small state between Kāngjū and Wūsūn,
frequently invaded and harassed.
They led their several thousand people to surrender to the Xiongnú.
Húlùgū Chányú married his younger brother's daughter, the Rìzhúwáng's sister, to him,
making him their chief
and placing him in the western territory.
Shīgǔ said: "Zhǎng qí zhòng (to be their chief)
means to be their leader."
Qī (to marry)
pronounced qī xì fān.
Zhǎng (chief)
pronounced zhī liǎng fān.
His father, the Zuǒ Xiánwáng, was supposed to be the Chányú,
but he yielded to Húlùgū Chányú,
and Húlùgū Chányú promised to enthrone him.
This event is found in volume 22, Wǔdì Tàichū first year.
The Rìzhúwáng had long been at odds with Wòyǎnqúshī Chányú.
He immediately led his people, intending to surrender to Hàn,
and sent someone to Qúlí
to communicate with the Cavalry Commandant Zhèng Jí.
Zhèng Jí dispatched 50,000 men from Qúlí, Qiūcí, and other states to meet the Rìzhúwáng, who brought 12,000 people and 12 xiǎowángjiàng.
The xiǎowángjiàng were those who assisted the xiǎowáng in commanding troops.
One account says that among the Xiongnú, the Zuǒ/Yòu Xiánwáng, Zuǒ/Yòu Gǔlíwáng, Zuǒ/Yòu Dàjiàng, and below,
all 24 chiefs were dàwángjiàng;
the rest were xiǎowángjiàng.
Jiàng (to command)
pronounced jí liàng fān.
The Yellow River makes a thousand-li bend.
This should be within Jīnchéng Commandery.
Zhèng Jí pursued and killed him,
then brought him to the capital.
Jiàng (to bring)
pronounced as written,
meaning to lead,
or to take with.
The Table of Meritorious Officials: Guīdé Hóu's fief was in Rǔnán.
After Zhèng Jí defeated Jūshī,
(This event is found in the previous volume, Dìjié third year.)
his prestige shook the Western Regions.
He then simultaneously protected Jūshī and the Northwest Road,
hence he was called Dūhù (Protector-General).
The establishment of the Dūhù office
began with Zhèng Jí.
Shīgǔ said: "He protected both the northern and southern routes,
hence he was called Dū."
Dū
is like dà (great)
or zǒng (general).
The Table of Meritorious Marquises: Ānyuǎn Hóu's
fief was in Shèn County of Rǔnán.
Shīgǔ said: "Zhōng Xīyù (Central Western Regions)
means being most centrally located among the various states,
equidistant from far and near."
Zhōng (central)
pronounced zhú zhòng fān.
Kǎoyì says: The Table of Officials states:
"The Protector-General of the Western Regions
was an additional office,
first established in the second year of Dìjié."
This is likely a mistake, confusing Shénjué with Dìjié.
The Western Regions chapter also says
"third year of Shénjué,"
which is also a mistake.
It was over 2,700 li from Yángguān.
Wūlěi City
was near the Qúlí agricultural office.
Yángguān
was west of Dūnhuáng Lónglè County.
Sòng Bái said: Yīzhōu Yīwú Commandery
was the Hàn territory of Yīwúlú;
during Emperor Xuān's reign,
Zhèng Jí was Protector-General of the Western Regions,
governing from Wūlěi City,
which is this place.
At the end of Yǒngpíng,
this territory was taken and the Yíhé Commandant was established.
They dared not contest the Western Regions,
and the Tóngpú Dūwèi (Protector-General of Slave Servants) was consequently abolished.
The various states of the Western Regions had previously been vassals of the Xiongnú.
The Xiongnú's western border Rìzhúwáng established the Tóngpú Dūwèi
to administer the Western Regions,
who resided between Yānqí, Wēixū, and Wèilí,
taxing the various states
to provide for his wealth.
The Xiongnú regarded the Western Regions as their servants.
Now that the Rìzhúwáng had surrendered,
all the states of the Western Regions submitted to Hàn,
thus the Tóngpú Dūwèi was abolished.
If there was any change, it was reported.
If it could be pacified,
it was pacified;
if not, it was punished and attacked,
and Hàn's decrees were issued throughout the Western Regions.
Shīgǔ said: Bān
means to distribute.
Wòyǎnqúshī Chányú then appointed his paternal cousin Bóxūtáng as Rìzhúwáng.
This laid the groundwork for Bóxūtáng to be enthroned as Túqí Chányú.
Cóng
pronounced cái yòng fān.
5. The Wūsūn Kūnmí Wēngguīmí
submitted a memorial through Chángluó Hóu Cháng Huì: “I wish to establish
Yuánguìmí, the Han emperor’s external grandson, as my successor.
Yuánguìmí is the eldest son of Chǔ Zhǔ Jiěyōu.
By uniting in marriage and deepening our kinship,
we can break away from the Xiōngnú.”
The edict was sent down to the Gōngqīng for discussion.
Dàhónglú Xiāo Wàngzhī believed:
“Wūsūn is a remote region;
its volatile nature is hard to guarantee,
so this should not be permitted.”
The emperor praised Wūsūn for their recent great achievement
(referring to their defeat of the Xiōngnú in the second year of Běnshǐ).
Shīgǔ said: “重 [zhòng] (serious)
means difficult.”
“故業 [gùyè]” (former ties)
refers to their prior marital ties with the Xiōngnú.
Extravagant provisions were sent with them,
and Cháng Huì was ordered to escort them to Dūnhuáng.
Before they had left the pass,
news arrived that Wēngguīmí had died.
The Wūsūn nobles collectively followed the original agreement and enthroned Cénqǔzǐ Nímí as Kūnmí.
He was called the Mad King.
The original agreement is found in Chapter 24, Běnshǐ 2nd year.
“Cénqǔ”
is written as
“Cénzōu” in the *Hànshū*.
“[I] request that the young lord remain in Dūnhuáng.”
Huì rushed to Wūsūn,
reprimanded them for not establishing Yuánguìmí as Kūnmí,
and returned to welcome the young lord back.
The matter was sent to the Gōngqīng.
Wàngzhī again stated:
“Wūsūn
is playing both sides,
and it is difficult to form an alliance.
Now that the young lord has returned because Yuánguìmí was not enthroned,
we are certainly not indebted to the barbarians.
This is a blessing for the Central Kingdom.
If the young lord is not stopped,
corvée labor will likely arise.”
Yáo (繇)
is interchangeable with the ancient character yáo (傜).
The young lord was summoned back.
Kǎoyì states: The Wūsūn biography says
the marriage request was in the second year of Yuánkāng.
Wàngzhī’s biography says
“second year of Shénjué.”
Based on the second year of Yuánkāng,
Wàngzhī was not yet Hónglú.
This is probably a mistake, confusing Shénjué with Yuánkāng.
1. In spring,
the third month,
on the day Bǐngchén,
Gāopíng Xiànhóu Wèi Xiàng passed away.
The Énzé Hóu Biǎo states that
Gāopíng Hóu was enfeoffed in Zhè Xiàn of Huáiyáng.
According to the *Shìfǎ*: “One who is widely learned and highly capable is called Xiàn.”
In the fourth month,
on the day Wùchén,
Bǐng Jí became Chancellor.
Jí was magnanimous,
fond of propriety and yielding,
and did not involve himself in trivial matters;
people at the time considered him to understand the great principles.
2. In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the day Jiǎzǐ,
Dàhónglú Xiāo Wàngzhī became Grandee Secretary.
3. In the eighth month,
an edict stated:
“If officials are not honest and impartial,
then the path of governance declines.
Now, minor officials are all diligent in their duties, but their salaries are meager.
It is difficult
for them not to exploit the common people!”
Rú Chún said: “Yú (漁)
means to seize;
it refers to seizing their benefits.”
Jìn Zhuó said: “Xǔ Shèn said it is the character for fishing.”
Shīgǔ said: “Yú (漁)
is like saying 'fishing and hunting' (yúlìe).
Jìn’s explanation is correct.”
Rú Chún said: “The law states: for 100 *shí* [of grain],
the monthly stipend is 600 [coins].”
Wéi Zhāo said: “If one eats 1 *shí*,
then an additional 5 *dòu* [is given].”
Kǎoyì states: Xuān Jì says:
“Officials below 100 *shí* in rank had their stipend increased by 15.”
Wéi Zhāo said: “If one eats 1 *shí*,
then an additional 5 *dòu* [is given].”
Xún Jì says:
“Officials below 100 *shí* in rank had their stipend increased by 50 *hú*.”
Perhaps because 15 was difficult to understand,
it was changed.
However, the edict says “below,” so it might be difficult to refer to 50 *hú*.
4. In this year,
Hán Yánshòu, the Administrator of Dōng Jùn, became Zǔo Fēngyì.
Originally,
Yánshòu was the Administrator of Yǐngchuān.
Yǐngchuān, following Zhào Guǎnghàn’s incitement of officials and common people,
(the matter of inciting officials and common people is found in Chapter 24, Běnshǐ 3rd year)
Shīgǔ said: “Gòu (搆)
means to bind/form.”
Yánshòu made reforms,
teaching them propriety and yielding.
He summoned respected elders
to discuss and set standards for marriage, funerals, and sacrificial rites,
roughly following ancient rites,
and not exceeding the legal limits.
The common people followed his teachings.
Those who sold clay figurines of carriages and horses, or vulgar counterfeit goods,
discarded them in the market.
Zhāng Yàn said: “Xiàlǐ (下里)
refers to fake goods from the underworld, *haolǐ*.”
Shīgǔ said: “Ǒu (偶)
refers to those made of earth and wood,
shaped like real carriages and horses.”
“Ǒu (偶)”
means pair/likeness.
They discarded their goods on the market roads.
Bá (referring to Hán Yánshòu’s successor) followed his footsteps and governed excellently.
As an official, Yánshòu
highly valued propriety and righteousness,
and was fond of ancient teachings and moral transformation.
Wherever he went, he would invite worthy scholars,
treat them with respect,
use them to broaden his deliberations,
and accept their remonstrances.
He commended those filial and fraternal in conduct,
repaired and managed educational institutions,
Shīgǔ said: “Xuéguān (學官)
refers to the buildings of schools (xiángxù).”
“Zhì (治)”
is pronounced with a straight tone (zhí zhī fān).
He displayed bells, drums,
and wind and string instruments, strictly observing the rituals of ascending and descending, bowing and yielding.
The *Zhōulǐ*, Dìguān, states: “The Xiāng Dàfū, using the five elements of the village archery ritual, inquired of the common people:
first, harmony (hé); second, composure (róng); third, hitting the target (zhǔpí);
fourth, harmonious composure (héróng);
fifth, starting the dance (xìngwǔ).”
He set up axes and battle-axes, flags and banners,
and practiced archery and charioteering.
The Han commanderies all held military exercises in the eighth month,
lecturing on military affairs.
Rú Chún said: “The Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu), Commandant (Dūwèi), Magistrates (Lìng, Zhǎng), and their subordinates (Chéng, Wèi)
all attended the comprehensive drill
to assess performance.”
When collecting taxes and rent,
he first clearly announced the dates,
treating scheduled meetings as a major affair.
Officials and common people respected and feared him,
and flocked to him.
He also established Zhèng and Wǔzhǎng.
Shīgǔ said: “Zhèng (正)
is like today’s xiāngzhèng and lǐzhèng.”
“Wǔzhǎng (伍長)”
means that within a group of five, one person is appointed as leader.
“Zhǎng (長)”
is pronounced zhǐ liǎng fān.
Criminals were not allowed to stay,
Shīgǔ said: “Shè (舍)
means to stop.”
and officials immediately became aware.
Criminals dared not enter his jurisdiction.
Although it seemed troublesome at first,
later officials were spared the hardship of chasing and apprehending,
and the common people were free from the worries of flogging and beating.
Shīgǔ said: “Chuí (箠)
means staff.”
“Chǔ (楚)
means荆木 [jīngmù] (thornwood);

Shī Gǔ said: Jiǎ
means to rent or hire.
Yánshòu was ultimately executed in the marketplace
for being cunning and immoral.
Thousands of officials and common people escorted him to Wèichéng.
The old and young clung to the chariot wheels,
vying to offer wine and roasted meat.
Shī Gǔ said: Zòu
means to present.
Zhì,
pronounced 'zhī yè fān',
is roasted meat.
Everyone offered a drink,
totaling over one *shí* of wine.
He sent his clerks to thank the escorts, saying,
"You have suffered greatly, officials and common people.
Yánshòu dies with no regrets!"
None of the common people did not shed tears.
1. In spring,
the first month,
the emperor visited Gānquán
and performed the suburban sacrifice to Tàizhì.
Kǎoyì says: Xuān Jì states:
"In the third month,
he traveled to Gānquán."
Xún Jì records
"the first month."
According to Hàn regulations,
suburban sacrifices were usually held in the first month.
Presumably, when Xún Yuè wrote the chronicle,
the original text was not yet mistaken.
Also, Yáng Yùn's biography states:
"The journey will surely not reach Hédōng."
Presumably, at that time, he also visited Hédōng to sacrifice to Hòutǔ,
which the historian omitted.
2. The Chēqí Jiāngjūn, Hán Zēng, died.
In the fifth month,
Jiāngjūn Xǔ Yánshòu was made Dà Sīmǎ and Chēqí Dàjiāngjūn.
3. Chéngxiàng Bǐng Jí was old,
and the emperor respected him greatly.
Xiāo Wàngzhī often held Jí in low regard,
which displeased the emperor.
The Chéngxiàng Sīzhí impeached Wàngzhī for treating the Chéngxiàng with arrogant disrespect.
At that time, Fán Yánshòu was Chéngxiàng Sīzhí.
Shī Gǔ said: Fán
is pronounced 'pó'.
(Wàngzhī) privately added an extra 103,000 to his accounts.
Shī Gǔ said: He had his officials conduct purchases and sales for Wàngzhī's household,
and the officials augmented these with their private funds,
to enrich Wàngzhī.
In autumn,
the eighth month,
on the *rénwǔ* day,
an edict demoted Wàngzhī to Tàizǐ Tàifù;
and Tàizǐ Tàifù Huáng Bà was made Yùshǐ Dàfū.
4 The Xīongnú Chányú Hūhánxié dispatched his younger brother, the Right Gǔlí Wáng, and others to attack the Chányú Túqí in the west,
stationing troops and killing and plundering over ten thousand people.
When Chányú Túqí heard of this,
he personally led sixty thousand cavalry to attack Chányú Hūhánxié.
Chányú Túqí's army was defeated,
and he committed suicide.
Dūlóngqí then fled to Hàn with Túqí's young son, the Right Gǔlí Wáng Gūmòlóutóu.
Chányú Chēlí surrendered to Chányú Hūhánxié in the east.
In winter,
in the eleventh month,
Chányú Hūhánxié's Left Dàjiàng Wūlìqū and his father Hūsuǒlěi Wūlìwēndūn, seeing the Xīongnú in chaos,
led their tens of thousands of followers to surrender to Hàn;
Wūlìqū was enfeoffed as Xīnchéng Hóu,
and Wūlìwēndūn as Yìyáng Hóu.
Shīgǔ said: Hūsuǒlěi
was his official title.
Suǒ (遫)
is an ancient form of the character sù (速).
Lěi (累)
is pronounced lìzhuī fān.
The record of meritorious ministers states that
Xīnchéng Hóu's fiefdom was Xìyáng in Rǔnán;

Kǎoyì says: The Xuān Chronicle
states: "The Xīongnú Chányú Hūsuǒlěi led his followers to surrender."
The Meritorious Ministers' Table says:
"Xìnchéng Hóu,
Wáng Dìng, with the Xīongnú Wūhuán Túmò Chányú's son, the Left Dàjiàngjūn, led his followers to surrender,
and became a Marquis.
Yìyáng Hóu,
Lìwēndūn, with the Xīongnú Hūliánlěi Chányú, led his followers to surrender,
and became a Marquis."
These are Qū and Dūn.
They were never Chányú;
perhaps they styled themselves Chányú when they surrendered,
or both the Chronicle and the Table are incorrect.
Chányú Hūhánxié captured and executed them;
he then re-established the Chányú's court,
but his followers numbered only several tens of thousands.
Chányú Túqí's paternal cousin, the Xiūxún Wáng, established himself as Chányú Rùnzhèn,
residing in the western region;
Chányú Hūhánxié's elder brother, the Zuǒxián Wáng Hūtúwúsī, also established himself as Chányú Zhìzhīgǔdūhóu,
residing in the eastern region.
5 The Guānglùxūn Píngtōng Hóu Yáng Yùn,
according to the Meritorious Ministers' Table,
Píngtōng Hóu's fiefdom was Bóyáng in Rǔnán.
However, he boasted of his conduct and ability.
Fá (伐)
means to boast.
Xíng (行)
refers to one's actions.
Néng (能)
refers to one's talent.
Xíng (行)
is pronounced xiàmèng fān.
He liked to expose people's hidden faults,
and for this reason, he incurred much resentment at court.
He fell out with Tàipú Dài Chánglè;
someone submitted a memorial accusing Chánglè of a crime.
Chánglè suspected Yùn had instigated the accuser,
and also submitted a memorial accusing Yùn, saying:
"Yùn submitted a memorial in defense of Hán Yánshòu.
Lángzhōng Qiū Cháng asked Yùn: 'I heard you, Marquis, defended Hán Féngyì.
Will he be saved?'
Yùn said: 'How easy is this matter?
Even the 'jìngjìng' (straightforward) ones may not be safe!'
Shīgǔ said: Jìngjìng (脛脛)
describes a straightforward appearance.
Jìng (脛)
is pronounced xiàdǐng fān.
Shīgǔ said: It means, 'I cannot even protect myself, how can defending someone else save them?'
The rat cannot enter its hole,
carrying its 'jùshù' (basketware).'
Lǐ Qí said: Zhēnrén (真人)
means an upright person.
Rú Chún said: The reason it cannot enter its hole is precisely because it obstructs itself by carrying the 'jùshù',
thus it cannot enter the hole.
Shīgǔ said: Jùshù (窶數)
is a head-pad for carrying basins.
When carrying objects in a basin on one's head, one places the jùshù as a cushion.
It is like what people who sell white round cakes use today.
Jù (窶)
is pronounced qíyǔ fān.
Shù (數)
is pronounced shānyǔ fān.
'Since the first month,
the sky has been overcast without rain.
This is recorded in the Chūnqiū
and spoken of by Lord Xiàhóu.' "
Zhāng Yàn said: Xiàhóu Shèng advised King Chāngyì, saying:
"If the sky is overcast for a long time without rain,
there must be ministers plotting against the ruler."
The Chūnqiū does not record long periods of overcast weather without rain as an omen.
The Hàn Shǐjì records what Shèng said,
hence it is called "Chūnqiū suǒjì" (recorded in the Chūnqiū),
meaning it discusses the omens and calamities of the Chūnqiū period.
Shīgǔ said: There are records of lack of rain in the Chūnqiū,
and commentators then discuss prolonged overcast weather,
attaching it to these.
Zhāng Yàn calling the Hàn Shǐjì the Chūnqiū
is a mistake.
Tíngwèi Dìngguó reported Yùn for resentment and hope,
and for making ominous and evil statements.
This refers to Yú Dìngguó.
Yāo (訞)
is the same as yāo (妖).
The Emperor could not bear to execute him,
so an edict was issued to dismiss both Yùn and Chánglè as commoners.
Kǎoyì says: The Xuān Chronicle:
"In the twelfth month,
Yáng Yùn, for crimes committed as former Guānglùxūn,
was dismissed as a commoner.
He did not repent,
but held resentment and hope,
which was great treason and impiety,
and was to be executed by beheading."
The Xún Chronicle followed this.
Yùn's biography states:
"Yùn wrote to Sūn Huìzōng, saying: 'It has been three years since I incurred guilt.'"
Also, due to the anomaly of a solar eclipse,
Zhōumǎ Wěizuǒ Chéng submitted a memorial accusing Yùn of crimes.
He was imprisoned and died.
Furthermore, Yáng Tán states Dù Yánnián became Yùshǐ Dàfū.
According to the Baǐguān Table,
Yùn became Guānglùxūn in the first year of Shénjué,
and was dismissed in the fifth year.
Dài Chánglè also became Tàipú in that year,
and was dismissed in the fifth year.
Dù Yánnián became Yùshǐ Dàfū in the third year of Wǔfèng,
in the sixth month,
on the day Xīnyǒu.
Also according to Xiāo Wàngzhī's biography:
"Guānglùxūn Yùn was ordered to dismiss Wàngzhī,"
which event occurred in the eighth month of this year,
so Yùn was still Guānglùxūn.
It was not until the fourth month of the fourth year
that the solar eclipse anomaly occurred.
Presumably, Yùn was dismissed as a commoner in the twelfth month of this year,
and died in the fourth year.
The Xuān Chronicle is mistaken.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the day Guǐmǎo,
Bóyáng Dìng Hóu Bǐng Jí passed away.
Bān Gù praised, saying: The ancients' way of naming

is a constant principle throughout antiquity and modernity,
a natural order of things.
Looking at the Hàn prime ministers,
when Gāozǔ established the foundation,
Xiāo and Cáo were preeminent.

I believe this means their prime ministerial achievements were preeminent among later generations.
Guān (冠)
is pronounced gǔwán fān.
Bǐng and Wèi had renown.
At this time, promotions and demotions were orderly,
chù (黜)
means to demote.
zhì (陟)
means to promote.
High officials often lived up to their positions,
and within the seas (the empire), politeness and humility flourished.
Reviewing their conduct and deeds,
how could it be without substance!

was the reason for achieving good governance,
not merely by chance.
2 In the second month,
on the day *Rénchén*,
Huáng Bà was appointed Chancellor.
Bà's talent lay in governing the people,
but when he became Chancellor,
his reputation for achievement diminished compared to his time governing commanderies.
At that time, Zhāng Chǎng, the Metropolitan Superintendent of Jīngzhào, had a *héfēn* bird fly from his residence and perch on the Chancellor's office.

Shīgǔ said, "Sū's statement is incorrect.
This *hé*
is pronounced *fēn*,
and the character was originally written as 鳻.

The *fēnfèn* bird is large and green,
found in the Qiāng regions,
not the one worn by the Imperial Guards.
The *hé* of the Imperial Guards is black,
found in Shàngdǎng.
Because they fight to the death without stopping,
their feathers were used to adorn the helmets of military officials.
This is what is now popularly called the *hé* chicken.
It is pronounced *hé*,
not this *fēnfèn* bird."
An impeachment was intended to be reported.
Chǎng submitted a memorial to Bà, saying:

"I humbly observe that the Chancellor has invited the officials of Two Thousand *Shí* and the Erudites to jointly question the Chief Clerks and Assistant Governors from the commanderies and kingdoms about how they promote benefits and eliminate harms for the people,

Their responses were itemized.
Those who practice sharing field boundaries,
men and women walking on separate paths,
not picking up lost items on the road,

and brought to the front of the hall first.
Shīgǔ said: This refers to the house where the Chancellor sat.

not necessarily a palace.
Furthermore, according to Zhèng Xuán's commentary on the *Zhōu Lǐ*,
the Hàn Minister of Works' office had a great assembly hall for the Son of Heaven and below.
The Minister of Works' office of the Later Hàn
was the Chancellor's office of the Former Hàn.
Others followed;
those who did not make such specific proposals were at the back.
They bowed their heads in thanks to the Chancellor,
though their mouths spoke no words,
their hearts wished for him to do so.
While the Chief Clerks and Assistant Governors were giving their responses,
a *héfēn* bird from my residence flew and perched on the roof of the Chancellor's office.
Hundreds of people, including the Chancellor, saw it.
Many border officials knew what a *héfēn* bird was,
but when asked,
they all feigned ignorance.
The Chancellor discussed and deliberated reporting this
Shīgǔ said: *Tú* means 'to plan'.
Shīgǔ said: Whenever *tiáo* is mentioned,
it means to enumerate each item individually,
like branches of a tree.
Later, when it was known that the bird came from my residence,
the matter was dropped.
The officials of the commanderies and kingdoms secretly laughed at the Chancellor's benevolence, magnanimity, and insight.
*Zhī*
is synonymous with 智 (*zhì*).
I do not dare to disparage the Chancellor,
but I truly fear that his humble subordinates dare not speak out,
fearing that his humble subordinates dare not report the truth of the matter.
They return to their offices' regulations,
each creating private instructions,
striving to add more and more,
thereby watering down the pure and dispersing the simple.
Shīgǔ said: 'Pure' means unmixed;
watering it makes the flavor thin and weak.
'Simple' refers to the original, unadorned state.
'Cutting' means dispersing.
There is name without substance.
亡 (*wáng*) is anciently interchangeable with 無 (*wú*).
The most extreme cases become absurdities.
If the capital first implements sharing field boundaries, separate paths, and not picking up lost items,
but in reality, it does not benefit the conduct of the honest and greedy, or the chaste and lewd,
亡 (*wáng*) is anciently interchangeable with 無 (*wú*).
行 (*xíng*) is pronounced *xià mèng fān*.
This is certainly not acceptable.
If the feudal lords implement it first,

The Hàn dynasty, inheriting a flawed system, adapted and changed,
establishing laws and regulations,
which serve to encourage good and prohibit evil.
Their provisions are detailed and comprehensive,

to return and inform the officials of Two Thousand *Shí*
to recommend the Three Elders, Filial and Fraternal, Industrious Farmers, Filial and Incorrupt, and Incorrupt Officials,
ensuring they find the right people.
All commandery affairs should use laws and regulations as
standards and models,
and they should not be allowed to concoct private instructions.
Those who dare to engage in fraud and deceit to gain a reputation
must first be punished,

The Son of Heaven praised and accepted Chǎng's words.
He summoned the reporting officials,
and had the Grand Imperial Secretary oversee and instruct them,

Bà was deeply ashamed.
Moreover,
Shǐ Gāo, Marquis of Lèlíng, was a Grand Imperial Secretary due to his old favor as a maternal relative.
He was highly esteemed.
Lèlíng County
belonged to Píngyuán Commandery.
Shīgǔ said: Lè
is pronounced *lái gè fān*.

The Son of Heaven had the Grand Scribe summon and question Bà:
"The office of Grand Commandant has been abolished for a long time."

belonged to the Minor Treasury.

five additional members were appointed.

During Emperor Wǔ's reign,
Tián Fén was appointed Grand Commandant;

it was never re-appointed.
To reach the hidden and obscure,
to ensure no innocent people are unjustly punished in prisons,
and no thieves or robbers in towns,
is your duty.
The offices of general and chancellor
are for me to appoint.
Shīgǔ said: He means that appointing generals and chancellors
is up to him.
Intimate and close officials,
I personally attend to them.
Shīgǔ said: He means he fully knows their abilities.
The Chancellor's duty
is to oversee all officials,
to promote the worthy and dismiss the unworthy.
Bà recommended Shǐ Gāo.
To recommend the wrong person might be acceptable,
but to consider it exceeding his authority is incorrect.
Indeed, since Emperor Wǔ,
the Chancellor has long neglected his duties.
The *Hòu Hàn Zhì* says: The Chief Grand Scribe
was an office established by Qín.
Emperor Wǔ used eunuchs to change it to the Chief of the Central Scribes and Attendants.
Emperor Chéng used scholars,
restoring its former state,
and it was responsible for all selections and appointments, as well as submitting and distributing documents to the Grand Scribe bureaus.

were two different offices.

Several days later,
a decision was made.

the Emperor visited Hédōng
to sacrifice to the Empress Earth.

of twenty-three *qián* per person: twenty *qián* for feeding the Son of Heaven;

All but those condemned to capital punishment.

and sent his younger brother, the Right Gǔlí Wáng (右谷蠡王),

3. Gěng Shòuchāng (耿壽昌), the Grand Minister of Agriculture's Aide (大司農中丞), submitted a memorial stating:
"For several years, the harvests have been abundant,
grain prices are low,
and farmers have little profit.
At present, a shí (石) of grain costs five qián (錢),
which is what is meant by 'cheap grain harms farmers.'
Shù (數) is pronounced suǒ jiǎo (所角).
Shǎo (少) is pronounced shī zhǎo (詩沼).
This involves 60,000 conscripted laborers.

fourth month,

The hardship of farm life,

so gēng (庚) days must be Fú (伏) days.

Roasted lamb,
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: Páo gāo (炰羔) is roasted meat,
which is what is now called áo (爊).

one that has not yet been weaned;

Páo (炰) is pronounced bù jiāo (步交).
After drinking wine, with ears hot,
I look up at the sky, beat a fǒu (缶) and cry 'Wū wū (烏烏),'

"Beating jugs,

遭值匈奴乖亂，
推亡固存，
李奇曰：推亡者，
若紂為無道，
天下苦之，
有滅亡之形，

固存，
譬如鄰國以道蒞民，
上下一心，
勢必能存，
因就而堅固之。
今匈奴內自紛爭，
宣帝能朝呼韓邪而固存之；
走郅支使遠遁，
是謂推亡也。
師古曰：尚書仲虺之誥曰：推亡固存，
邦乃其昌。
言有亡道者則推而滅之，
有存道者則輔而固之，
王者如此，
國乃昌盛。
故此贊引之。
推，
吐雷翻。
單于慕義，
稽首稱藩。
功光祖宗，
業垂後嗣，
可謂中興，
侔德殷宗、周宣矣！
師古曰：侔等殷之高宗及周之宣王也。

to leverage the momentum of the rising fires.
The Kāngjū soldiers retreated;
the Hàn soldiers pushed their shields from all four sides,
entering the earthen city simultaneously.
Over a hundred of the Chányú's men and women fled into the Dà Nèi.
Shīgǔ said: Dà Nèi refers to
the Chányú's private chambers.
Officers and soldiers rushed in,
and the Chányú, wounded, died.
Dù Xūn, an acting aide to a Jūnhòu, beheaded the Chányú.
According to Hàn regulations,
during military campaigns, each department had a Xiàowèi;
below a department was a Qū,
and each Qū had one Jūnhòu.
Furthermore, a Dūhù had a Fù Xiàowèi,
with a salary equivalent to two thousand *dàn* of grain;
one Céng,
and two Sīmǎ, Hòu, and Qiānrén each.
Dù Xūn was originally a Jūnhòu and served as acting Céng.
All spoils of war
were distributed to those who obtained them.
In total, one thousand five hundred and eighteen heads were taken, including Yānzhī, crown princes, and Míngwáng;
one hundred and forty-five captives were taken alive,
and over a thousand surrendered captives
were distributed among the fifteen kings from the surrounding city-states who had been mobilized.
1 In spring,
the first month,
the head of Zhìzhī arrived at the capital.
Yánshòu and Tāng submitted a memorial, saying:
“We, your subjects, have heard that it is the great righteousness of All Under Heaven to be unified.
In the past, there were Táng and Yú;
now, there is the mighty Hàn.
Hūhánxié Chányú of the Xiōngnú has already declared himself a northern vassal;
only Zhìzhī Chányú rebelled
and has not paid for his crime.
West of Dàxià,
he believed that the mighty Hàn could not make him its subject.”
Dàxià
is the name of a Western Regions state,
southwest of Dàyuān.
Shīgǔ said: It means that Hàn could not make Zhìzhī submit.
“His great evil reached up to heaven.
Your subject Yánshòu
and your subject Tāng,
leading righteous troops,
executed the punishment of Heaven.
Relying on Your Majesty's divine power,
with yin and yang responding in unison,
and the weather clear and bright,
we breached their formations and defeated the enemy.
We cut off the head of Zhìzhī and those of his famous kings and below.
It is fitting to display their heads at Gǎojiē, between the barbarian residences.”
Jìn Zhuó said: Gǎojiē,
according to the Yellow Map, is inside the gates of Cháng'ān city.
Shīgǔ said: Gǎojiē
is a street name,
and the barbarian residences are on this street.
Dǐ
is like today's guesthouse.
He also said: The barbarian residences
are like today's Hónglú Guǎn.
Cuī Hào believed
that "gǎo"
should be
"tuó";
Tuójiē
is the same as Tóngtuó Jiē.
This theory is mistaken.
Tóngtuó Jiē is in Luòyáng;
there is none in the Western Capital.
Xuàn
is read as xuán;
the same applies below.
“Let it be clear that anyone who defies the mighty Hàn,
though distant, shall surely be punished!”
Chancellor Kuāng Héng and others believed:
“It is precisely spring, the time to cover exposed bones and bury rotten flesh.”
The Lǐjì Yuèlìng states: In the first month of spring,
cover exposed bones and bury rotten flesh.
The commentary says: This refers to the death qi opposing the life qi.
Yīng Shào said: The bones of birds and beasts are called gé;
gé
means large.
The bones of birds and rats are called zì;
zì
means hateful.
Your subject Zàn said: Dry bones are called gé;
bones with flesh are called zì.
Shīgǔ said: Zàn's explanation is correct.
Gé,
pronounced gōng kè fān.
Zì,
pronounced cái cì fān.
An edict ordered them displayed for ten days,
then buried.
Sacrifices were then offered at the suburban altars and ancestral temples,
and a general amnesty was declared.
All officials offered congratulations,
and a feast was held.
2 In the sixth month,
on the day jiǎshēn,
Zhōngshān Āiwáng Jìng passed away.
Āiwáng was
the emperor's younger brother,
who grew up studying and socializing with the crown prince.
Yóu
refers to banqueting.
Xué
refers to studying.
Shīgǔ said: They lived together and grew up to adulthood.
Shǎo,
pronounced shī zhào fān.
Zhǎng,
pronounced zhī liǎng fān.
The crown prince went to offer condolences.
The emperor saw the crown prince from afar,
and was moved by the memory of Āiwáng.
His grief was uncontrollable.
When the crown prince arrived before him,
he showed no sorrow.
The emperor was greatly displeased and said:
“How can someone who is not compassionate and benevolent
be able to serve the ancestral temples
and be a parent to the people?!”
At this time, Fùmǎ Dūwèi and Shìzhōng Shǐ Dān was supervising the crown prince's household.
Hù,
means supervision.
Shīgǔ said: Zhě means to speak.
“Your subject truly saw Your Majesty's sorrow and pain for Zhōngshān Wáng,
to the point of being affected and weakened.”
It means being saddened and emotionally affected, causing one's spirit to be depleted.
“Your subject secretly warned him
not to weep,
so as not to distress Your Majesty;
the fault lies with your subject,
who deserves death!”
The emperor considered this true,
and his anger subsided.
3 In Lántián, there was an earthquake,
mountains collapsed,
blocking the Bàshǔi.
The bank of Ānlíng collapsed,
blocking the Jīngshǔi,
and the Jīngshǔi flowed backward.
Lántián County belongs to Jīngzhào.
The Shuǐjīng: The Bàshǔi flows out of Lántián Valley in Lántián County,
passes through Bàlíng County,
and flows northwest into the Wèishǔi.
Mèng Kāng said: The bank of Ānlíng
is the bank of the Jīngshǔi beside Emperor Huì's mausoleum.
1 In spring,
the third month,
a general amnesty was declared.
2 In summer,
the sixth month,
on the day gēngshēn,
Lìyuán was restored.
3 On the last day of the month, rénshēn,
there was a solar eclipse.
4 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the day gēngzǐ,
the ancestral temples and gardens of Tàishàng Huáng, the Yuán Miào, Zhāolíng Hòu, Wǔ'ài Wáng, Zhāo'āi Hòu, and Wèi Sī Hòu's gardens were restored.
At this time, the emperor was ill,
and had not recovered for a long time.
He believed it was due to the reproof and anger of his ancestors,
thus he restored them all;
only the temples in the commanderies and states remained abolished.
In the fourth year of Yǒngguāng,
the Yuán Miào was abolished.
5 In this year,
Jìyáng Wáng Kāng was transferred to become Shānyáng Wáng.
6 Hūhánxié Chányú of the Xiōngnú, hearing that Zhìzhī had been executed,
was both happy and fearful.
He was happy
because with Zhìzhī executed, he had no future troubles.
He was fearful
because of Hàn's might and power,
fearing he might offend again and be destroyed like Zhìzhī.
He wished to enter the court and pay homage.
Jìngníng First Year
(wùzǐ, 33 BCE) Yīng Shào said: Hūhánxié Chányú wished to protect the frontiers,
and the border regions could thus be peaceful and tranquil,
hence it was used to name the era.
Shīgǔ said: According to Yīng's explanation,
jìng is read as jìng (border).
In ancient usage,
jìng (border) and jìng (finally) were indeed interchangeable.
However, the imperial edict stated,
“There shall be no more military affairs for a long time,”
and jìng means
finality,
meaning eternal peace and tranquility.
With no military affairs, both the interior and exterior are peaceful and tranquil;
it is not limited to just the border.
If one reads according to the original character,
the meaning is even broader.
1. In the spring,
the first month,
Hūhánxié Chányú of the Xiōngnú came to court,
stating his desire to become a son-in-law of the Hàn imperial clan to foster closer ties.
Shīgǔ said: He meant he wanted to marry a Hàn woman and himself become a son-in-law of the Hàn family.
The Chányú was delighted
and submitted a memorial,
"I wish to protect the border from Shànggǔ westward to Dūnhuáng,
Shīgǔ said: Bǎo (保),
means to guard.
He voluntarily requested to guard and protect it,
to prevent bandits and thieves.
Dūn (敦),
read as túmén.
I request to dismiss the border garrisons and officials,
to give rest to the Son of Heaven's people."
The Son of Heaven referred the matter to his officials for deliberation.
All those who deliberated thought it was advantageous.
Lángzhōng Hóu Yīng, who was familiar with border affairs,
believed it should not be permitted.
The Emperor asked for his reasoning.
Yīng replied:
"Since the Zhōu and Qín dynasties, the Xiōngnú have been arrogant and cruel,
raiding and invading the borders.
Since the rise of the Hàn,
they have suffered especially from this.
I have heard that the northern border, from the fortresses to Liáodōng,
has the Yīnshān Mountains to its north.
Spanning over a thousand *lǐ* east to west,
with lush vegetation
and abundant birds and beasts,
this was originally where Mòdún Chányú relied on and blocked himself in,
making bows and arrows.
They would sally forth to raid,
making it their hunting ground.
By the time of Emperor Wǔ,
armies were dispatched to campaign and conquer,
seizing this territory,
pushing them back to the north of the *mù* (desert).
Shīgǔ said: Chì (斥),
means to open.
Rǎng (攘),
means to repel;
pronounced rén-yáng.
Guard posts and signal towers were erected,
outer walls were built,
and garrisons were stationed to defend it.
Only then did the border regions enjoy a little peace.
The land north of the *mù* is flat,
with sparse vegetation,
and many large sands,
what is called the Great Desert.
Shǎo (少),
pronounced shī-zhǎo;
same below.
There are few places for concealment.
South of the fortresses,
one passes through deep mountains and valleys,
making travel quite difficult.
Border elders say: 'Since the Xiōngnú lost the Yīnshān Mountains,
they have never crossed it without weeping!'
If we dismiss the border garrisons and officials,
it would show great advantage to the barbarian tribes,
which is the first reason not to do so.
Now the Sagely Virtue is widely extended,
covering the Xiōngnú like heaven.
Shīgǔ said: Like heaven covering them.
Bèi (被),
pronounced pí-yì.
Fù (覆),
pronounced fū-yòu.
They bow their heads and come to submit.
The nature of barbarians is such that
when in distress, they are humble and compliant,
but when strong, they are arrogant and rebellious.
This is their inherent nature.
Previously, the outer walls were already dismantled—
this incident is mentioned in chapter 24, Dìjié 2nd year of Emperor Xuān.
They were barely sufficient for observation
and transmitting烽火 (signal fires).
The ancients, in peace, did not forget danger.
They must not be dismantled again;
this is the second reason.
The Central Plain has the teachings of rites and righteousness,
and the punishments of law.
Even ignorant people still violate prohibitions.
How much more so the Chányú?
Can he guarantee that his multitude will not violate the agreement?
This is the third reason.
Shīgǔ said: Bì (必),
means to exhaust;
to exhaustively guarantee it.
Máo Huàng said: Bì (必),
is a definitive word.
Passes and bridges
are set up at important junctions of water and land.
Barriers are set up based on narrow mountains to inspect land travelers, forming *guān* (passes).
Sometimes stones are erected,
sometimes wood is laid,
or boats are moored across water to inspect boat travelers, forming *liáng* (bridges).
Setting up fortresses and outposts,
and stationing garrisons,
is not solely for the Xiōngnú.
It is also for the various tributary states and surrendered people,
who were originally Xiōngnú.
We fear they might remember their past and flee.
This is the fourth reason.
Recently, the Western Qiāng, protecting the fortresses,
interacted with the Hàn people.
Officials and commoners, coveting profit,
encroached upon their livestock, property, wives, and children.
Due to this resentment,
they rose up and rebelled.
If we now dismiss those guarding the fortresses,
it will create a gradual trend of insolence, contempt, and disputes.
This is the fifth reason.
Shīgǔ said: Chéngsài (乘塞),
means to climb upon and guard them.
Mányì (嫚易),
is similar to bullying.
Yì (易),
pronounced yì-chǐ.
If their descendants become impoverished,
and one day flee,
they will join their relatives.
This is the sixth reason.
Moreover, many slaves and bondservants on the border, suffering hardship,
wish to flee,
saying:
'We hear that it is pleasant among the Xiōngnú,
but what can be done about the strict surveillance?'
Nevertheless, there are still occasional escapes beyond the fortresses.
This is the seventh reason.
If bandits and cunning scoundrels
gather in groups and violate the law,
and if they are in distress,
they might flee north.
Then they would be uncontrollable.
This is the eighth reason.
It has been over a hundred years since the fortresses were erected.
From the time Emperor Wǔ erected the fortresses
until now, it has been over a hundred years.
Sometimes relying on mountains, cliffs, rocks, wood, valleys, and water gates,
they were gradually leveled.
Soldiers and laborers built and repaired them.
The effort and expenditure have been long-lasting,
beyond calculation.
I fear that the deliberators have not deeply considered the ultimate consequences,
wishing to save on labor and garrisons with a single stroke.
Shīgǔ said: Yīqiè (壹切) means
a temporary measure,
not a permanent one.
Just like cutting an object with a knife,
one seeks immediate neatness,
without regard for length, shortness, vertical, or horizontal,
hence the term *yīqiè*.
Yáo (繇),
is interchangeable with the ancient character *yáo* (傜).
Within a century,
should any other change suddenly occur,
leading to the destruction of the barriers and fortresses,
and the disappearance of the guard posts and signal towers,
we would have to redeploy garrisons and carry out repairs again.
The accumulated years
of effort cannot be restored quickly.
This is the ninth reason.
If we dismiss the garrisons
and reduce surveillance,
the Chányú will consider himself solely responsible for protecting and defending the fortresses.
He will certainly deeply feel indebted to the Hàn.
Shīgǔ said: He will claim the favor and virtue from the Hàn for himself.
If he is slightly displeased,
his intentions will become unpredictable.
This would open a gap for the barbarians
and undermine the security of the Central Plain.
This is the tenth reason.
This is not the long-term strategy
for maintaining lasting peace and asserting authority over all barbarian tribes!"
After the memorial was presented,
the Son of Heaven issued an edict:
"Do not deliberate on dismissing the border garrisons."
He ordered the Chējì Jiāngjūn, Jiā, to orally instruct the Chányú,
Shīgǔ said: Jiāngjūn Xǔ Jiā.
Yù (諭),
means to inform and explain.
"The Chányú submitted a memorial wishing to dismiss the officials and soldiers guarding the northern fortresses,
with his descendants guarding the fortresses for generations.
The Chányú admires rites and righteousness,
and his plans for his people are very considerate.
This is a long-term strategy.
I greatly commend it!
The four borders of the Central Plain all have passes, bridges, barriers, and fortresses.
This is not solely to guard against those outside the fortresses.
It is also to prevent wicked and unrestrained individuals from the Central Plain
from going out and causing harm as bandits.
Therefore, clear laws and regulations are established to unify the hearts of the people.
Zhuān (專),
means to unify.
Shīgǔ said: He means he already understands his intentions.
For the Chányú to wonder why they are not dismissed,
Thus, he sent Jiā Xiǎo Chányú.”
Máo Huàng said: Xiǎo
means to clarify and explain.
“I, your foolish servant, do not understand this great plan.
The Son of Heaven has mercifully sent his high minister to inform and advise me.
This is truly generous!”
Initially,
Zuǒ Yīzhīzī had advised Hūhánxié to return to Hàn.
This event is recorded in Volume 27, Xūandì’s Gānlù first year.
Later, some slandered Yīzhīzī, saying he boasted of his own accomplishments.
Shīgǔ said: Fá
means to boast of one's achievements and efforts.
I believe this refers to his boasting about his plan that settled the Xiōngnú,
not his physical effort.
Hūhánxié became suspicious of him;
Yīzhīzī, fearing execution,
led over a thousand of his followers and surrendered to Hàn.
Hàn made him a Guānnèi Hóu,
granted him an estate of three hundred households,
and ordered him to wear his princely seal and ribbon.
Shīgǔ said: Although he was a Guānnèi Hóu in Hàn,
he still followed the Xiōngnú royal title and wore the seal and ribbon.
He met with Yīzhīzī and
apologized, saying:
“Your Majesty’s plan for me was truly profound,
allowing the Xiōngnú to live in peace to this day.
This is Your Majesty’s strength,
and your virtue can never be forgotten!
I lost Your Majesty’s favor,
causing Your Majesty to leave,
and did not try to keep you.
Shīgǔ said: He meant he did not think about keeping him in Xiōngnú.
Now I wish to report to the Son of Heaven
and request Your Majesty to return to the court.”
Meaning, return to the Chányú court.
“The Chányú, relying on Heaven’s decree,
personally surrendered to Hàn
and thereby achieved peace.
This is due to the Chányú’s divine spirit
and the Son of Heaven’s protection.
How could I claim credit for this power?
Having already surrendered to Hàn,
to return to the Xiōngnú again
would be to have a divided heart.
I wish to serve the Chányú as an envoy in Hàn,
but I dare not obey your command to return!”
Shīgǔ said: He meant to serve as the Chányú’s envoy in Hàn,
unable to return to the Xiōngnú.
使 (shǐ),
read as shū lì fān.
He could not be persuaded to return.
The Chányú named Wáng Zhāojūn Nínghú Èshì;
Shīgǔ said: This meant that because the Hú obtained her,
their nation became peaceful.
He made her the Yòurìzhú Wáng.
2. The Crown Prince came of age.
3. In the second month,
Yùshǐ Dàfū Lǐ Yánshòu passed away.

Shí Xiǎn saw that Fèng Fèngshì and his son were prominent amongst the high officials,

Féng Zhāoyí,
that is Féng Jiéyú,

He recommended, saying:

The Son of Heaven summoned him

“Among the Jiǔqīng, none surpasses Yěwáng;

and I fear that future generations will certainly regard Your Majesty as having surpassed all wise men
Shīgǔ said: Duó
means to exceed.
The Emperor said:
“Excellent,
I had not considered that!
Shīgǔ said: He meant he had not seen this principle.
“If I appoint Yěwáng as a Sāngōng,

In the third month,
on the day Bǐngyín,
an edict stated:
“Strong and firm,
resolute and without desire,
Dàhónglú Yěwáng is such a man.
Wáng
is an ancient variant of wú (無).
Fluent in distinguishing right from wrong and skilled in rhetoric,
Biàn
means to distinguish.

Honest and thrifty,

Why,

calling him

the Huìyuán was abolished.

means to allow or approve.
The captured wealth brought into the passes

They sent letters to the commanderies and counties along the route he passed,

After a triumphant return from thousands of miles,

now the Sīlì, instead, arrests and investigates us.

Chóng,

Zhāng Yàn 曰: In Hépíng second year,

Sū Lín 曰: If advice is not followed,
this is called disorder,
and then metal will not conform to transformation.
Jǐng (景)
means omen;
what omen?
It means impending danger and ruin.
Wèi (為)
is pronounced yú wěi fān.
The altars of soil and grain (state) face three perils: Lǚ,
Huò,
and Shàngguān.
All were families of empresses dowager.
The way of cherishing relatives
is to preserve them as paramount,
Shīgǔ 曰: Striving to keep them safe and secure,
this is supreme.
Teach them the way of loyalty and filial piety.
Now, instead, their positions are honored and cherished,
and they are given the "big dipper's handle" (power).
Shīgǔ 曰: Using the dipper as a metaphor.
The body of the dipper is the kuí (魁).
This leads to their annihilation.
Shīgǔ 曰: Yí (夷)
means level,
referring to their complete removal.
Even a worthy man like Huò Guāng
could not plan for his descendants,
thus powerful ministers are easily endangered from generation to generation.
The Shū says: "Do not be like fire,
which starts faintly."
Shīgǔ 曰: This is a phrase from the Zhōu Shū Luò Gào.
Yōngyōng (庸庸)
describes something tiny and insignificant.
It means that fire, when initially small,
if not extinguished early,
will become blazing.
Similarly, when high officials become powerful and arrogant,
one should plan early,
and curb their power.
If their power becomes greater than the ruler's,
then trying to prevent it
will be too late!"
Shīgǔ 曰: Yǐ (已) is a final particle.

È (戹)

Kǒng Yǐngdá (孔穎達) says: The cycle of floods and droughts

According to the Lǜlì Zhì (律曆志), nineteen years make one Zhāng (章),
four Zhāng (章) make one Bù (部),
twenty Bù (部) make one Tǒng (統),
and three Tǒng (統) make one Yuán (元).
Thus, one Yuán (元) has 4,560 years.
In the first year of a Yuán (元), there is Yángjiǔ (陽九),
meaning nine years of drought.
Next, after 374 years, comes Yīnjiǔ (陰九),
meaning nine years of floods.
Adding 106 years and 374 years makes 480 years.
The commentary says:
This is the number six multiplied by eight.
Next, after 480 years, there is Yángjiǔ (陽九),
meaning nine years of drought.
Next, after 720 years, comes Yīnqī (陰七),
meaning seven years of floods.
Next, after 720 years, comes Yángqī (陽七),

Another commentary says: 720
is the number nine multiplied by eight.
Next, after 600 years, comes YīnWǔ (陰五),

Next, after 600 years, comes YángWǔ (陽五),

The commentary says: 600 years
is obtained by multiplying eight by eight,
which is sixty-four.

which is fifty-six,
totaling 1200 years.
In the Yì (易), seven and eight do not change,

therefore, they are combined and counted,
each yielding 600 years.
Next, after 480 years, comes Yīnsān (陰三),
and next, after 480 years, comes Yángsān (陽三).
Excluding the years from the beginning of the Yuán (元) until Yángsān (陽三),

there are a total of 4,560 years.
The calamity years include
two Yángjiǔ (陽九) years,
one Yīnjiǔ (陰九) year,
one set of seven Yīn (陰) and Yáng (陽) years each,
one set of five Yīn (陰) and Yáng (陽) years each,
and one set of three Yīn (陰) and Yáng (陽) years each,
totaling 57 years.
Together with the previous 4,560 years,
this makes a total of 4,617 years.
Here, the Qì (氣) of one Yuán (元) concludes.
This is the great calculation of Yin and Yang, floods and droughts.
The reason for using seven, eight, nine, and six as multipliers
is that the number for water is six,
for fire is seven,
for wood is eight,
and for metal is nine.
These interact and multiply each other.
Because the numbers of Yīn (陰) and Yáng (陽) naturally correspond to seven, eight, nine, and six,
there are calamities of nine, seven, five, and three years.
