Collated and punctuated by Róng Zhàozǔ (容肇祖), reviewed by Gù Jiégāng (顧頡剛) and Niè Chóngqí (聶崇岐).

Hànlín Xuéshì (翰林學士), Cháosàn Dàfū (朝散大夫), Yòu Jiànyì Dàfū (右諫議大夫), Zhī Zhìgào (知制誥) concurrently Shìjiǎng (侍講), concurrently Tíjiǔ Wànshòuguān Gōngshì (提舉萬壽觀公事), concurrently Pàn Jíxián Yuàn (判集賢院), Shàng Hùjūn (上護軍), Hénèi Jùn Kāiguó Hóu (河內郡開國侯), with a fief of 1300 households, bestowed with the purple-gold fish-pouch, your servant
compiled by imperial command.
Hòu (後) Xué (學) Tiān (天) Tái (台)
Emperor Xiào’āi (孝哀) Middle
Jiànpíng (建平) Second Year
(Bǐngchén (丙辰), 5 BCE)
1 In spring,
the first month,
a comet appeared in Qiānniú (牽牛).
The Jìn Tiānwén Zhì (晉天文志) says: "The six stars of Qiānniú (牽牛) are the celestial bridge,
governing matters of sacrifice."
Bèi (孛)
is pronounced pú nèi (蒲內).
2. The clans of the Dīng and Fù were extravagant and arrogant.
They all envied Fù Xǐ’s deference and frugality.
Moreover,
Empress Dowager Fù wanted to be granted an honorable title,
equal in status to Emperor Chéng’s mother.
Xǐ, along with Kǒng Guāng and Shī Dān, together insisted that this was impermissible.
The Emperor was reluctant to go against the righteous counsel of his senior ministers.
Shī Gǔ said: “重 (zhòng),
means difficult.”
He wavered for several years.
Rú Chún said: “依違 (yī wéi),
refers to not making a decision.”
I (the compiler) believe the preceding two phrases
express the meaning of 依違 (yī wéi).
The Emperor, having no choice,
first dismissed Shī Dān to influence Xǐ.
Shī Dān’s dismissal is recorded in the previous year of the preceding volume.
Zhū Bó, allied with the Marquis of Kǒngxiāng, Fù Yàn,
conspired to secure the honorable title for the Empress Dowager.
They frequently met in private audience,
presenting secret memorials
that slandered Xǐ and Kǒng Guāng.
毀短 (huǐ duǎn) means
to slander and speak of one's shortcomings.
On the day Dīngchǒu,
the Emperor then issued an edict dismissing Xǐ,
sending him back to his marquisate.
The office of Grandee Secretary had been abolished.
In the first year of Suīhé of Emperor Chéng’s reign,
the Grandee Secretary office was abolished,
and the Grand Minister of Works (Dà Sīkōng) was established.
This event is recorded in Volume 32.
From the title of Son of Heaven down to the assistant clerks in the Hán dynasty,
all differed from antiquity.
Hán officials stopped at the rank of Dòu Shí and assistant clerk.
It means that the Hán inherited the title of Emperor from the Qín,
and down to the titles of the hundred officials,
none were the same as in antiquity.
Their duties were difficult to distinguish clearly,
providing no benefit to good governance or disorder.
Thereupon, Zhū Bó presented a memorial, stating:
“According to former practice, outstanding prefects and chancellors of commanderies and states were selected to be Middle Two-Thousand-Picul officials.
Middle Two-Thousand-Picul officials were selected to be Grandee Secretaries.
Those who performed their duties well became Chancellors.
This means that if a Grandee Secretary was capable of his duties,
he would be promoted to Chancellor.
This was to honor virtuous sagely rulers
and give weight to the Chancellor of the state.
Now, Middle Two-Thousand-Picul officials are made Chancellors without first serving as Grandee Secretaries.
Their authority is diminished,
which is not the way to give weight to state affairs.
I, your humble servant, believe that the office of Grand Minister of Works (Dà Sīkōng) can be abolished,
and the Grandee Secretary restored,
following the old system.
I am willing to exert my full effort to serve as Grandee Secretary and be a leader for all officials!”
The Emperor assented.
In the summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day Wùwǔ,
Bó was reappointed as Grandee Secretary.
Furthermore, the Empress Dowager Dīng’s elder brother, Míng, Marquis of Yáng’ān, was appointed Grand Marshal and General of the Guards (Dà Sīmǎ Wèi Jiāngjūn),
with a full staff.
The Grand Marshal’s title followed old practice.
This restored the system from before Suīhé.
冠 (guān),
read as Gǔwán.
3. Empress Dowager Fù again issued an edict to the Chancellor and Grandee Secretary, saying:
“Gāowǔ Hóu Xǐ has sided with inferiors and deceived superiors,
and, in concert with the former Grand Minister of Works Dān, has disloyally betrayed us,
abandoned orders and disgraced his clan.
Yīng Shào said: ‘It means abandoning instructions,
and disgracing one’s kin.’
背 (bèi),
read as Púmèi.
圮 (pǐ),
read as Píměi.
Send him back to his enfeoffed state!”
4. Chancellor Kǒng Guāng,
since the time of the previous emperor, had a disagreement regarding the succession,
and had further greatly offended Empress Dowager Fù’s wishes.
The matter of his disagreement is recorded in Volume 32, first year of Suīhé of Emperor Chéng.
To "greatly offend Empress Dowager Fù’s wishes" refers to his not allowing her to reside in the northern palace,
presenting a memorial to move Fù Qiān,
and opposing the proposal to grant her an honorable title.
Shī Gǔ said: “重 (zhòng),
pronounced zhíyòng.”
忤 (wǔ),
pronounced wǔgù.
They conspired to slander Guāng.
表 (biǎo),
means outer.
裏 (lǐ),
means inner.
The Fù clan slandered him internally,
and Zhū Bó slandered him externally.
On the day Yǐhài,
Guāng was dismissed by edict and became a commoner.
Shī Gǔ said: “According to the old Hán rituals, if a Chancellor committed other offenses,
an envoy would present an edict.
He would immediately walk out of the office
and return to his hometown in a simple cart.”
He was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yángxiāng.
The List of Favored Marquises states: “Marquis of Yángxiāng
was enfeoffed in Húlín, Shānyáng.”
The *Kǎo Yì* states: “The *Gōngqīng Biǎo* says:
‘On the Yǐwèi day of the fourth month,
Kǒng Guāng was dismissed,
and Zhū Bó became Chancellor.’
It also says:
‘In the fourth month,
on the Wùwǔ day,
Bó became Grandee Secretary;
on the Yǐhài day,
he was promoted.’
The *Wǔxíng Zhì* says:
‘In the fifth month,
on the first day Yǐhài,
Bó became Chancellor.’
The *Xún Jì* says:
‘On the Yǐhài day,
Kǒng Guāng was dismissed.’
According to the *Cháng Lì*,
the first day of that month was Dīngsì,
so there was no Yǐwèi.
The nineteenth day was Yǐhài,
not the first day of the month.
Both the *Biǎo* and *Zhì* have errors.”
In the first year of Suīhé of Emperor Chéng’s reign,
Zhào Xuán was demoted from Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince;
now he was again promoted,
all according to the wishes of the Dīng and Fù families.
Shī Gǔ said: “To usher in and ascend the hall.”
The *Hàn Jiù Yí* says: “When the Chancellor and Grandee Secretary are first appointed,
the Emperor ushers them in and personally issues the edict.”
“The palace attendants and guards on the steps all heard it.”
Shī Gǔ said: “陛者 (bì zhě),
refers to those holding weapons arrayed at the side of the steps.”
The Emperor consulted Huángmén Shìláng, Yáng Xióng of Shǔjùn.
The *Xù Hàn Zhì* says: “Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng,
six hundred *shí* salary,
in charge of attending the Emperor,
serving as an intermediary,
connecting internal and external affairs and all noblemen when they had audience in the palace,
and escorting princes to their seats.”
This is what Yáng Xióng referred to in his *Jiě Cháo* as
“My office does not exceed Shìláng,
my talent is merely enough for Gěishì Huángmén.”
Yáng Xióng himself said that his ancestor was a certain Zhōu Bóqiáo who lived in the early years of the Zhōu dynasty,
who was enfeoffed in Yáng in Jìn,
and thus took the surname.
I don’t know Bóqiáo;
what distinction was he from Zhōu?
He promptly replied:
“This is what the *Hóngfàn* calls ‘drum demons.’
The *Shī Fǎ* states that if a ruler is not discerning,
and is misled by the multitude,
and empty names are promoted,
then there will be sound without substance,
whose origin is unknown.
The *Hóngfàn Wǔxíng Zhuàn* says: ‘If listening is not discerning,
this is called not deliberating,
and then there will be drum demons.’
If the ruler is stern and severe and closes off his inferiors,
and ministers are fearful and block their ears,
then the qi of deluded hearing will manifest in sounds,
hence there are drum demons.
妖 (yāo),
read as Yújiāo.
Then the chief ministers receive it.
Now, the anomalies in the fourth month, on the days chén and sì,
correspond to the center.
If a year is divided into three parts,
then the fourth month is already the middle of the year.
If a day is divided into three parts,
then chén and sì are already the middle of the day.
This refers to the high-ranking ministers.
It is advisable to dismiss the Chancellor and Grandee Secretary
to respond to the celestial changes.
However, even if they are not dismissed,
within a year,
those individuals will suffer the consequences themselves.”
Shī Gǔ said: “期年 (qī nián),
means twelve months.”
蒙 (méng),
is like 被 (bèi, to suffer).”
期 (qī),
pronounced jī.
“Drum demons
are an omen of impaired hearing.
Zhū Bó is strong and resolute,
with many stratagems.
He is fit to be a general, not a chancellor.
I fear there will be fierce and swift anger.”
The Emperor did not heed him.
Once Zhū Bó
became Chancellor, the Emperor adopted his proposal.
He issued an edict saying:
"The title of Dìngtáo Gòng Huáng
should no longer be referred to as Dìngtáo;
the Gòng Huáng Tàihòu is to be honored as Dì Tàitàihòu,
and called Yǒngxìn Gōng;
the Gòng Huánghòu is to be called Dì Tàihòu,
and known as Zhōng'ān Gōng;
a memorial temple is to be established for Gòng Huáng in the capital,
following the system of Xuān Dì's father, Dào Huángkǎo."
Eight years after Xuān Dì's enthronement,
the relevant officials stated: "According to the rites,
if the father was a scholar,
and the son became the Son of Heaven,
sacrifices should be offered as to a Son of Heaven.
Dào Yuán should be called Huángkǎo,
and a temple should be erected,
using the garden as a resting place,
where offerings are made at the appropriate times."
However, Dào Yuán was in Guǎngmíng Chéngxiāng,
outside the eastern suburb of Cháng'ān.
Dìngtáo Gòng Wáng was buried in Dìngtáo, but his temple was established in the capital,
which means it was not a resting place within the garden.
All ranks were Zhōng Èrqiān Shí.
Fù Tàihòu, Dīng Tàihòu, and Zhào Tàihòu, along with the Tàihuáng Tàihòu, constituted the four Tàihòu.
They were especially arrogant,
and when speaking with the Tàihuáng Tàihòu,
they even called her an old woman.
At that time, the Dīng and Fù families had risen rapidly and become exceptionally prominent within one or two years;
there were many who became Gōng Xiāng Lièhóu;
however, the Emperor did not grant them much power,
and their influence was not comparable to that of the Wáng clan during Chéng Dì's reign.
5 Chancellor Bó and Grandee Secretary Xuán memorialized, saying:
"Previously, Gāochāng Hóu Hóng
first proposed the discussion of honoring the title,
but was impeached by Guānnéi Hóu Shī Dān,
and dismissed as a commoner.
The incident can be found in the upper卷 of Suíhé second year.
劾,
read as 'hù gài fān'.
In his grief,
he entrusted governance to Dān.
Shī Gǔ says: it means that because of the recent mourning for Chéng Dì,
wearing coarse mourning clothes,
the Son of Heaven did not personally attend to state affairs.
衰,
read as 'cāng huí fān'.
惟,
means 'to think'.
He suppressed and demoted the honored title,
thereby diminishing filial piety.
There is no greater disloyalty!
Your Majesty is benevolent and sagacious,
and has clearly established the honored title.
Hóng, for his loyalty and filial piety, has been reinstated as Gāochāng Hóu;
Dān's evil and rebellious actions are evident.
Although he received a pardon,
he should not hold a title or fiefdom.
We request that he be dismissed as a commoner."
The memorial was approved.
They also memorialized:
"Xīndū Hóu Mǎng, formerly Grand Minister of War,
did not broadly promote the principle of honoring the revered,
suppressed and demoted the honored title,
and diminished filial piety.
This incident is also found in the upper卷 of Suíhé second year.
Fortunately, he received a pardon,
but he should not hold a title or land.
We request that he be dismissed as a commoner."
The Emperor said:
"Since Mǎng is related
to the Huáng Tàihòu,
he shall not be dismissed,
but sent to his feudal state."
As for Píng'ā Hóu Rén, who harbored relatives of Zhào Zhāoyí,
they were all sent to their feudal states.
Rén was
Tán's son.
臧,
is interchangeable with the ancient character for 藏.
Many in the empire felt wronged by the Wáng clan!
This laid the groundwork for Wáng Mǎng's regaining control of the state in Yuánshòu second year.
"Emperor Xiàochéng deeply considered the importance of the ancestral temple,
and praised Your Majesty's supreme virtue in succeeding to the heavenly mandate.
Heavenly mandate
refers to the succession order of emperors and kings,
ordained by Heaven.
上,
read as 'shí zhǎng fān'.
His grace and benevolence were exceedingly profound.
Reflecting on the late emperor's intentions,
how could he not have wished to replace himself with Your Majesty
to serve and attend to the Eastern Palace?
Shī Gǔ says: it means to provide for the Tàihòu.
Having repeatedly suffered sorrow,
referring to first suffering the mourning for Yuán Dì and then weeping for Chéng Dì.
數,
read as 'suǒ jiǎo fān'.
更,
read as 'gōng héng fān'.
Shī Gǔ says: 'yǐnlǐng' means to pull one's collar and retreat.
[This sentence is missing from the original translation context, but based on the Chinese it seems to be an interjection about the Emperor's feelings]
Moreover, when Your Majesty ascends to a high place and looks far into the distance,
are you not ashamed before Yánlíng?"
This refers to the Wáng clan being expelled while the Dīng and Fù families gained favor and prominence.
If one were to ascend to a height and look at Chéng Dì's imperial tomb,
would one not feel ashamed concerning the entrusted matters?
The middle son of Chéngdū Hóu Shāng, Yì, was re-enfeoffed as Chéngdū Hóu.
In Suíhé second year,
Shāng's son Kuàng was deprived of his marquisate due to a crime;
now Yì inherits the title.
中,
read as 'zhòng'.
6 Zhū Bó also memorialized, saying:
"According to the Han dynasty's precedents,
regional inspectors (cìshǐ) were appointed,
with low rank but generous rewards.
(In Han,
a cìshǐ's rank was only six hundred shí.)
After serving in the region for nine years,
they were promoted to governors or chancellors (shǒuxiàng),
with a rank of two thousand shí;
those with exceptional talent and outstanding achievements were immediately promoted.
Shī Gǔ says: 'quàn gōng' means to encourage oneself to achieve merit.
樂,
read as 'luò'.
Later, provincial governors (zhōumù) were established,
the matter can be found in volume 32, Chéng Dì, Suíhé first year.
更,
read as 'gōng héng fān'.
Their position was next to the Nine Ministers (jiǔ qīng);
if a Nine Minister position was vacant,
it would be filled by a high-ranking candidate;
those with average abilities would merely maintain their positions,
fearing that their effectiveness would decline.
Shī Gǔ says: 'líng yí'
means to gradually fall into disuse.
Your servant requests to abolish the provincial governors
and reinstate the regional inspectors as before."
The Emperor followed his advice.
7 In the sixth month,
on the day Gēngshēn,
Empress Dowager Dīng
passed away. An edict was issued for her to be buried
in the garden of Dìngtáo Gòng Huáng,
following her husband.
Gòng Huáng was buried in his state.
Xián says: it is in the north of modern Cáozhōu Jìyīn Xiàn.
共,
read as 'gōng'.
近郡國 refers to the commanderies and states near Dìngtáo.
The notes to the Former Han History say: 'chuān fù tǔ'
refers to the matter of digging a pit and filling it in.
It means that after the coffin was placed,
the earth was used to form the mound again,
hence 'fù tǔ'.
近,
read as 'qí jìn fān'.
8 Initially,
during the reign of Chéngdì,
Gān Zhōngkě of Qí falsely created the *Tiānguān Lì* and the *Bāoyuán Tàipíng Jīng* in twelve scrolls,
stating that the Hàn house was facing the great end of heaven and earth,
and that it should receive a new mandate from Heaven.
He taught this to Xià Hèliáng and others from Bóhǎi.
The Zhōnglěi Xiàowèi, Liú Xiàng, memorialized that Gān Zhōngkě was pretending to be a divine being,
deceiving the emperor and deluding the masses.
Gān Zhōngkě falsely claimed,
"The Heavenly Emperor sent the Perfected Man Chìjīngzǐ down to teach me."
Therefore, Liú Xiàng memorialized against him.
He was punished;
his deception was the reason.
Lower,
*xiá jià fān*.
He died of illness.
Xià Hèliáng and others continued to privately teach each other.
When the emperor ascended the throne,
Sīlì Xiàowèi Xiè Guāng and Qí Dūwèi Lǐ Xún presented Xià Hèliáng and others,
who were all appointed as attendants in the Huángmén.
Yīng Shào said: Those summoned for their skills and talents,
who have not yet received a formal office,
are called "attendants" (dài zhào).
Dǒng Bā said: Huángmén [refers to]
the imperial yellow gate.
They expounded
that "the Hàn dynasty's calendar is in decline,
and it is time for a new mandate.
Chéngdì did not respond to Heaven's mandate,
and thus died without an heir.
Now Your Majesty has been ill for a long time,
and strange phenomena have occurred repeatedly.
This is Heaven's warning to man.
It is fitting that you should urgently change the reign title and imperial designation.
Only then can you prolong your life and increase your longevity,
and a royal son will be born,
and disasters will cease.
If the Way is attained but not acted upon,
Shīgǔ said: It means knowing the Way but being unable to practice it.
great floods will appear,
and disastrous fires will arise,
cleansing the people."
The emperor had been ill for a long time.
Bān Gù said: The emperor was paralyzed when he ascended the throne,
and it worsened in his later years.
He consequently followed the advice of Xià Hèliáng and others,
issuing an edict for a general amnesty throughout the realm,
making the second year of Jiànpíng the first year of Tàichū,
and taking the title
"Chén Shèng Liú Tàipíng Huángdì."
Lǐ Fēi said: Chén means to expound;
it means that the divine Way and the sage are Liú.
Rú Chún said: Chén [refers to]
the descendant of Shùn.
Wáng Mǎng [was]
a descendant of Chén.
This is a mistaken statement that Chén should be established, but without knowing it.
Wéi Zhāo said: To expound and display the virtue of the sagely Liú.
Shīgǔ said: Rú and Wéi's two explanations are correct.
I believe Wéi's explanation does not deviate from the correct,
while Rú's explanation verges on shamanism.
Yán believes both explanations are correct;
which one should one follow?
Shīgǔ said: The old clepsydra
totaled one hundred *kè* for day and night.
Now twenty *kè* have been added.
9 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
the Yǒnglíng Tíngbù in the northwest plateau of Wèichéng was designated as the Chūlíng,
and the people of the commanderies were not to be moved.
10 After the emperor changed his title for more than a month,
his illness remained unchanged.
Xià Hèliáng and others again wished to arbitrarily alter governmental affairs,
but the grand ministers unanimously argued that it should not be permitted.
Xià Hèliáng and others memorialized,
"The grand ministers all do not understand the Mandate of Heaven.
The chancellor and imperial censor should be dismissed,
and Xiè Guāng and Lǐ Xún should assist in governance."
As the emperor found their words without proof,
in the eighth month,
he issued an edict saying:
"The attendants Xià Hèliáng and others proposed changing the reign title and imperial designation,
and increasing the markings on the clepsydra,
which they claimed could bring lasting peace to the state.
I, being not firm in my belief in the Way,
mistakenly listened to their words,
Shīgǔ said: Guò means mistake.
and ultimately received no auspicious response.
Indeed, to err and not to change
is to err truly!
This is a saying of Confucius recorded in the *Analects*.
The *jiǎzǐ*
(non-amnesty edict)
shall all be revoked."
Rú Chún said: He regretted that the previous amnesty did not bring blessings,
so he withdrew the edict.
Minister Zàn said: Changing the reign title and imperial designation,
and issuing a general amnesty,
to seek prolonged blessings without receiving them,
Àidì regretted it,
so he issued another decree,
revoking all matters not related to the amnesty.
This means the change of system and designation
are now all restored to their former state.
Shīgǔ said: Rú's explanation is wrong;
Zàn's explanation is correct.
Only the amnesty edict is not changed;
the rest are all revoked.
Their treachery shall be thoroughly investigated."
They were all imprisoned
and executed.
Lǐ Xún and Xiè Guāng had their death penalty commuted by one degree,
and were exiled to Dūnhuáng commandery.
This was the Hàn law known as "reducing death penalty and exiling to the frontier."
"Reduced rank" means a crime meriting death, but specifically mitigated.
Commuting the death penalty by one degree
meant being sentenced to *chéngdàn* or *chōng*.
11 Due to his illness,
the emperor
fully restored all the ancestral shrines that had been established in previous generations, totaling over seven hundred.
At the beginning of Jiànshǐ during Chéngdì's reign,
Kuāng Héng and Zhāng Tán memorialized to abolish shrines that did not conform to ritual.
Now all are restored.
With many shrines,
some had five annual sacrifices,
and some had four annual sacrifices,
hence the number was so great.
12 Fù Tàihòu's resentment towards Fù Xǐ did not cease,
and she sent Kǒngxiāng Hóu
to instruct Chancellor Zhū Bó to memorialize for Fù Xǐ's dismissal from his marquisate.
Zhū Bó discussed it with Yùshǐ Dàfū Zhào Xuán.
Zhào Xuán said:
"The matter has already been decided previously,"
meaning it was previously decided to send him back to his fief,
and there should be no heavier punishment.
Shīgǔ said: Dé wú is equivalent to wú nǎi.
"I have already promised Kǒng Hóu.
Even commoners who make a promise
are willing to die for it,
let alone the Most Honored!"
"Most Honored" refers to Fù Tàihòu.
While grand ministers serve their lord with the Way,
Zhū Bó served his private relations with death,
doing so out of a desire for power and leverage.
Zhū Bó disliked being the only one to denounce Fù Xǐ,
so because the former Dàsīkōng, Fànxiāng Hóu Hé Wǔ, was also previously removed from office and sent to his fief due to transgression,
as seen in the second year of Suíhé in the previous scroll,
he jointly memorialized:
"Fù Xǐ and Hé Wǔ, when previously in office,
were of no benefit to governance.
Although they have already been dismissed,
their enfeoffment with titles and land
is improper.
We request that both be dismissed as commoners."
The emperor knew that Fù Tàihòu had long resented Fù Xǐ,
and suspected that Zhū Bó and Zhào Xuán were acting on her instructions.
He immediately summoned Zhào Xuán to the Shàngshū to question him about the situation,
and Zhào Xuán confessed.
The chancellor and imperial censor jointly memorialized,
but only Zhào Xuán was summoned for questioning,
because Zhū Bó was strong-willed, resourceful, and cunning,
making it difficult to immediately ascertain his true intentions,
while Zhào Xuán was easier to interrogate thoroughly.
"Zuǒ Jiāngjūn Péng Xuān and those in the central court jointly questioned him,"
and Péng Xuān and others impeached,
"Zhū Bó, Zhào Xuán, and Yàn are all unrighteous
and disrespectful.
We request that they be summoned to the Tíngwèi's prison by imperial edict."
The emperor commuted Zhào Xuán's death penalty by three degrees,
and cut Yàn's households by one quarter.
Commuting the death penalty by three degrees
meant being sentenced to *lìchén qiè*.
Yàn was enfeoffed with five thousand households,
and one thousand two hundred fifty were cut.
Zhū Bó committed suicide,
and his marquisate was abolished.
13th day of the 9th month,
Píng Dāng (平當), the Grand Master of Ceremonies, was made Grandee Secretary.
In winter,
the 10th month,
on the jiǎyín (甲寅) day,
he was promoted to Chancellor.
Because it was winter,
he was provisionally granted the noble title of Marquis within the Passes.
Rú Chún (如淳) said: According to the Hàn Yí Zhù (漢儀注),
when a Grandee Secretary becomes Chancellor,

He was to go to the palace gate, remove his cap, and walk barefoot to apologize.
On the day of Jǐwèi,
Mǎng sent an attendant with the Grand Empress Dowager's edict to dismiss Xián right at the palace gate.
Shīgǔ said: Jí,
means to approach.
"Xián is young,
and has not yet experienced many affairs,
and as Dàsīmǎ,
he does not accord with the hearts of the multitude.
Therefore, his Dàsīmǎ seal and ribbon are to be collected,
and he is to be dismissed and returned to his residence!"
On the same day,
Xián and his wife both committed suicide;
their family, in panic,
buried them at night.
Mǎng suspected that he might have faked his death;
the responsible officials submitted a memorial requesting to open Xián's coffin,
and examine it in prison.
Shīgǔ said: this means to open the tomb and take out his coffin.
Zhěn,
means to verify;
pronounced zhěn.
The Grand Empress Dowager issued an edict:
"The dukes and ministers are to recommend a suitable Dàsīmǎ."
Mǎng had previously been Dàsīmǎ,
but had resigned his position to avoid Dīng and Fù,
and the common people had praised him as worthy;
this event is recorded in chapter 33, in the second year of Suīhé.
From Dàsītú Kǒng Guāng downwards,
the entire court recommended Mǎng.
Only the former Jiāngjūn Hé Wǔ and Zuǒjiāngjūn Gōngsūn Lù conspired together,
believing that
"In the past, during the reigns of Huì and Zhāo,
the imperial relatives Lǚ, Huò, and Shàngguān held power,
nearly endangering the state;
now Xiàochéng and Xiàoāi have died without heirs in successive generations,
and we are about to select a close relative
as a child emperor.
It is not appropriate for imperial relatives and powerful ministers to hold power.
Imperial relatives and powerful ministers
refers to Wáng Mǎng.
Qīn,
refers to imperial relatives.
Shū,
refers to those of a different surname who served as generals or dukes and ministers.
Shīgǔ said: Cuò,
means mixed and intermingled.
For the good of the country,
only this is beneficial."
Lù also recommended Wǔ.
On the day of Gēngshēn,
the Grand Empress Dowager personally appointed Mǎng as Dàsīmǎ and concurrently in charge of Shàngshū affairs.
The Grand Empress Dowager discussed with Mǎng the establishment of an heir.
Ānyánghóu Wáng Shùn,
Mǎng's paternal cousin,
was a cultivated and disciplined man
whom the Grand Empress Dowager trusted and loved.
Mǎng proposed to appoint Shùn as Chējì Jiāngjūn.
In autumn,
in the seventh month,
Shùn was dispatched with Dàhónglú Zuǒ Xián, bearing official credentials, to welcome Zhōngshānwáng Jīzǐ to be established as heir.
Shǐchíjiézhě
were envoys who carried official credentials;
from Wèi and Jìn onwards, this became an official title.
Lú,
is pronounced líng rú fān.
Sì,
is pronounced xiáng lì fān.
Wáng Mǎng again reported to the Grand Empress Dowager,
who issued an edict to the officials stating that the Empress Dowager
and her younger sister, Zhāoyí, had enjoyed exclusive favor, leading to the sealing off of the sleeping quarters (gù qǐn).
Gù
means to block.
The path for attendance in the rear palace was blocked,
preventing their advancement for imperial service.
For details, see Jiànpíng First Year in the previous volume.
They were moved to live in the Northern Palace.
Also, because the Queen Dowager of Dìngtáo Gòng Wáng and Kǒngxiāng Hóu Yàn were of one mind and conspired together,
betraying kindness and forgetting their origins,
acting willfully and unlawfully,
Empress Xiào'āi was moved to withdraw to Guì Gōng.
The Fù and Dīng clans were all dismissed from their offices and titles and returned to their old commanderies.
Wáng Mǎng, having been in retirement for many years,
once he gained power,
stopped at nothing.
The Fù clan was
from Hénèi.
The Dīng clan was
from Shānyáng.
He alone issued an edict praising Fù Xǐ, saying:
"Gāowǔ Hóu Xǐ
has an upright and honest character.
Shīgǔ said: Què
means cautious,
pronounced 'kǒu-jué' (音口角翻).
Although he is related to the former Queen Dowager of Dìngtáo,
he never followed her misguided instructions or went astray,
standing firm and maintaining his integrity,
which is why he was banished to his fiefdom.
For Xǐ's banishment to his fiefdom, see Jiànpíng Second Year in the previous volume.
Shīgǔ said: The Analects record Confucius's words
to illustrate a person of integrity.
He is appointed as a special minister (tèjìn)
and serves at court (fèng cháoqǐng)."
Although Xǐ was outwardly praised and rewarded,
he was isolated, worried, and fearful.
Later, he was again sent to his fiefdom
and died of old age.
Wáng Mǎng also demoted Fù Tàihòu's title to Dìngtáo Gòng Wáng Mǔ,
and Dīng Tàihòu's title to Dīng Jī.
Wáng Mǎng further memorialized that Dǒng Xián's father and son were arrogant, self-indulgent, extravagant, and presumptuous.
He requested that their wealth and property be confiscated by the government,
and all those who had been appointed to office by Xián be dismissed.
His father Gōng, younger brother Kuānxìn, and their family members were moved to Hépǔ,
while his mother returned separately to her old commandery, Jùlù.
The common people in Cháng'ān were clamorous,
going to his residence to weep,
almost plundering it.
Shīgǔ said: They went to weep for him,
but in reality wanted to steal.
Huān (讙) is pronounced 'xǔ-yuán' (音許爰翻).
Xiāng (鄉)
is read 'xiàng' (讀曰嚮).
Jǐ (幾)
is read 'jì' (讀曰冀).
The total was forty-three hundred million (sìshísān wànwàn).
Zhū Xǔ of Pèi, an official whom Xián favored, impeached himself and left the Grand Marshal's office,
bought a coffin and clothes,
and collected Xián's body to bury him.
Wáng Mǎng heard of this
and killed Xǔ for another crime.
Wáng Mǎng considered Grand Minister of Works Kǒng Guāng a renowned Confucian scholar,
who had served three emperors (xiàng sān zhǔ).
Chéng, Āi, and Píng Dì were the three emperors.
The world trusted him.
Therefore, Wáng Mǎng greatly honored and served Guāng,
appointing Guāng's son-in-law, Zhēn Hán, as Attendant Official (shìzhōng) and Mounted Escort Commander (fèngchē dūwèi).
For all those whom Wáng Mǎng disliked,
he fabricated charges against them,
drafted memorials,
and had Hán take them to Guāng.
Under the guise of the Empress Dowager's instruction, he hinted to Guāng
(Shīgǔ said: Cǎo (草)
refers to the draft of a document.
Fēng (風)
is read 'fèng' (讀曰諷))
that he dared not not submit them.
Wáng Mǎng reported to the Empress Dowager,
and she always approved his memorials.
Thereupon, he impeached Hē Wǔ and Gōngsūn Lù for mutually recommending each other,
and both were dismissed from office.
Wǔ was sent to his fiefdom.
He also memorialized that Dǒng Hóng's son, Gāochāng Hóu Wǔ, and his father were treacherous and evil,
and their titles were stripped.
Hóng's treachery and evil
referred to his request to establish Dīng Jī as Empress Dowager.
He handled the case of Empress Dowager Féng of Zhōngshān,
wrongly implicating the innocent.
Guānnéi Hóu Zhāng Yóu falsely accused his relatives,
and Central Palace Steward Shǐ Lì and Tàishān Administrator Dīng Xuán wrongly condemned people to capital punishment.
All these matters are found in Jiànpíng First Year of Volume 33.
Pì (辟)
is pronounced 'pí-yì' (毗亦翻).
The matter is found in Jiànpíng Fourth Year of the previous volume.
They were all deemed unsuitable to hold positions in the Central Plain (zhōngtǔ),
dismissed as commoners,
and moved to Hépǔ.
In the case of Zhōngshān,
Lì and Xuán originally presided over the investigation,
but only signed memorials jointly with Lóng.
Wáng Mǎng had admired Lóng and sought his friendship in his youth,
but Lóng was not very supportive,
so Wáng Mǎng used this matter to squeeze him out.
Hóngyáng Hóu Lì,
the Empress Dowager's own younger brother,
although not holding office,
Wáng Mǎng, as his paternal cousin, inwardly respected and feared him.
He feared Lì might casually speak to the Empress Dowager,
preventing him from acting arbitrarily.
So he again had Guāng memorialize Lì's crimes:
"He previously knew that Dìnglíng Hóu Cháng had committed a crime of great treason,
yet spoke on his behalf and misled the court.
The matter is found in Suīhé First Year of Chéng Dì in Volume 32.
Wèi (為)
is pronounced 'yú-wèi' (于偽翻).
Misled the court
means misled the imperial court.
Cháo (朝)
is pronounced 'zhí-yáo' (直遙翻).
There were many rumors saying: 'The Lǚ clan and the young emperor have reappeared,'
referring to Empress Lǚ naming another's child as Emperor Huì's son.
The matter is found in Volume 13.
It is difficult to show to future generations,
achieving the merit of a swaddled infant (chéng qiángbǎo zhī gōng)."
This means it is difficult to achieve the merit of assisting an infant ruler.
The Empress Dowager did not listen.
Wáng Mǎng said:
"Now the Hàn imperial house is in decline,
and for generations there has been no heir.
The Empress Dowager alone governs on behalf of the young ruler,
which is truly cause for awe and fear.
Even if one strives to be just and impartial above all others,
there is still fear that it will not be followed.
Shīgǔ said: Lì (力)
means to make an effort.
Xiān (先)
is pronounced 'xī-jiàn' (悉薦翻).
If this continues,
all beneath will become corrupt and perverse,
and chaos will arise from this.
It is advisable to temporarily send him to his fiefdom,
and after things settle (ān hòu), recall him."
Shīgǔ said: Ān (安)
is like xú (徐, slowly).
I say ān (安)
means settled.
Ān hòu
means after the matter is settled.
So Lì was sent to his fiefdom.
All of Wáng Mǎng's methods for coercing those above and below
were of this type.
Thereupon, those who supported Wáng Mǎng were promoted,
and those who opposed and resented him were punished and eradicated.
He took Wáng Shùn and Wáng Yì as his trusted confidants (fùxīn),
Zhēn Fēng and Zhēn Hán as those who made decisive judgments (zhǔ jīduàn),
Píng Yàn as the one who managed important affairs (lǐng jīshì)
(Yàn
was Dāng zhī zǐ),
and Sūn Jiàn as his enforcers (zhuǎyá).
Fēng's son Xún, Xiù's son Fēn,
and Cuī Fā of Zhuō Jùn
(Xìngpǔ: Son of Qí Dīng Gōng,
who received a fief in Cuī,
hence the surname)
were all part of this. Wáng Mǎng's demeanor was stern, but his words were outwardly upright.
Shīgǔ said: He outwardly showed a severe expression,
but falsely made upright statements.
When he subtly showed his inclination,
his partisans understood his intentions and explicitly memorialized them.
Wáng Mǎng would kowtow and weep,
firmly declining and yielding,
thereby confusing the Empress Dowager above,
and demonstrating his sincerity to the common people below.
In the eighth month,
Wáng Mǎng again reported to the Grand Empress Dowager,
deposing Empress Xiàochéng and Empress Xiào'āi as commoners,
and sending them to their gardens.
This refers to the gardens of the sleeping temples of Xiàochéng and Xiào'āi.
Fù (復)
is pronounced 'fú-yòu' (扶又翻).
Both committed suicide.
Kǎoyì says: In Hàn Chūnqiū,
"Eighth month,
jiǎyín,"
but it is unknown what source Hú Dàn based this on.
6 The Grand Minister of Works, Péng Xuān 彭宣, seeing Wáng Mǎng 王莽 monopolize power,
thereupon submitted a memorial saying:
"The Three Dukes are like a tripod supporting the ruler;
if one leg is not up to the task,
then the beautiful food will be overturned and scattered.
Shī Gǔ 師古 says: 'Beautiful food'
refers to the contents of the tripod.
The 'Dǐng Guà' 鼎卦 (The Cauldron Hexagram) of the Yì Jīng 易經 (Book of Changes), in the nine-four line statement, says: 'The tripod's leg is broken,
overturning the duke's soup.'
Sù 餗
means food.
Therefore, Xuān 宣 cited this as his statement.
Rèn 任,
pronunciation 'rén'.
My years are old and my eyes are dim.
Shī Gǔ 師古 says: Mào 眊
is the same as mào 耄.
Zhèng Xuán 鄭玄 says: Mào 耄
means confused and forgetful.
Being muddled and forgetful,
I wish to return the seals and cords of Grand Minister of Works and Marquis of Chángpíng 長平,
and beg for my bones to return to my hometown,
awaiting burial in a ditch or ravine."
Sī 竢
is the ancient form of the character sì 俟.
Zhèn 窴
is the same as tián 填.
He was sent to his fief.
Mǎng 莽 resented Xuān's 宣 request to retire,
and therefore did not bestow gold, an elegant carriage, or a team of four horses.
Xuān 宣 lived in his fief for several years,
then passed away.
Bān Gù 班固's eulogy says: Xuē Guǎngdé 薛廣德 preserved the honor of his suspended carriage,
Píng Dāng 平當 hesitated with a sense of shame,
Péng Xuān 彭宣 saw danger and stopped;
how different they are from those who are anxious about losing what they have!
Xuē Guǎngdé's 薛廣德 suspended carriage
was in the first year of Yuán Dì's 元帝 Yǒngguāng 永光 era.
Píng Dāng 平當 refused the enfeoffment
in the third year of Jiànpíng 建平.
The Tōngjiàn 通鑑, because of Péng Xuān's 彭宣 affair, appended Bān 班's eulogy here.
Xuàn 縣
is read as xuán 懸.
7 On the day wùwǔ 戊午,
Wáng Chóng 王崇, the General of the Right, became Grand Minister of Works;
Mǎ Gōng 馬宮 of Dōnghǎi 東海, the Grand Master of Ceremonies, became General of the Right.
According to Bān Shū 班書 (History of the Former Han),
Mǎ Gōng's 馬宮 original surname was Mǎshǐ 馬矢;
when Gōng 宮 pursued scholarship,
he called himself Mǎ 馬.
He was promoted to Lieutenant-General with the additional post of Left Chief Clerk.
8 In the ninth month,
on the day xīnyǒu 辛酉,
the King of Zhōngshān 中山 ascended the imperial throne.
Gòng Fù 貢父 says: The day xīnyǒu 辛酉
was sixty-four days after the death of Āi Dì 哀帝.
In the ninth year of Píng Dì 平帝,
the Grand Empress Dowager attended court,
and the Grand Minister of War, Mǎng 莽, held political power.
All officials consolidated their own duties to listen to Mǎng 莽.
He cited the ancient system where, when the Son of Heaven was in mourning, all officials consolidated their own duties to listen to the Grand Steward,
in order to usurp power.
Shī Gǔ 師古 says: Jùshù 聚束 is called zǒng 總;
the sound is zǒng 摠.
Zhū Xī 朱熹 says: It means each takes charge of their own duties.
Kǒng Guāng 孔光, in fear and apprehension,
not knowing what to do,
submitted a memorial begging for his bones to return.
Mǎng 莽 reported to the Grand Empress Dowager,
"The Emperor is young;
it is fitting to appoint a teacher and mentor."
He transferred Guāng 光 to be the Grand Tutor to the Emperor,
ranking among the Four Counsellors.
The Jì 記 (Records) says: "The Yú 虞, Xià 夏, Shāng 商, and Zhōu 周 dynasties had teachers and protectors,
they had 'yí' 疑 and 'chéng' 丞,
and they established the Four Counsellors and Three Dukes."
Mǎng 莽 imitated this to position Kǒng Guāng 孔光,
and the changing of official titles began from this point.
He was to take charge of the palace guards and provisions,
and inspect inside
Shī Gǔ 師古 says: Xíng nèi 行內,
inside the palace where the emperor resides,
is akin to saying 'within the Forbidden Palace'.
and examine the emperor's clothing, carriages, and food.
Shī Gǔ 師古 says: Shěng 省
means 'to inspect'.
I believe that 'inspecting the internal offices and doors' should be one phrase,
this relates to the palace guards; 'examining the emperor's clothing, carriages, and food' then relates to provisions.
The sentence structure is very clear.
Shī Gǔ 師古 incorrectly broke the sentence,
and thus contrived an explanation for it.
Xíng 行
is pronounced 'xià mèng' (xíng).
Shěng 省
is pronounced 'xī jǐng' (shěng).
Zhēn Fēng 甄豐 became General of the Right.
9 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the day rén'yín 壬寅,
Emperor Xiào'āi 孝哀 was buried in Yìlíng 義陵.
Minister Zàn 瓚 says: From his death to his burial was a total of one hundred and five days.
Yìlíng 義陵 was in Fúfēng 扶風,
forty-six lì 里 from Cháng'ān 長安.
Kǎo Yì 考異 (Textual Differences Examined) says: The Āi Jì 哀紀 (Annals of Emperor Ai) states
"In the ninth month,
on the day rén'yín 壬寅,
buried in Yìlíng 義陵."
According to the perpetual calendar,
the first day of that month was xīnyǒu 辛酉;
there was no rén'yín 壬寅.
Rén'yín 壬寅 was the twelfth day of the tenth month.
Also, Minister Zàn's 瓚 note says:
"From his death to his burial was a total of one hundred and five days."
According to this, the Emperor died on the day wùwǔ 戊午 in the sixth month,
so it is certain that the burial was in the tenth month.
It seems the month in the main annals was mistaken.
Emperor Xiào Píng 孝平
Xún Yuè 荀悅 says: The taboo name
'Kàn' 衎
refers to the character
'Lè' 樂.
Yìng Shào 應劭 says: The谥法 (Rules for Posthumous Titles) states: "One who establishes principles and governs records is called Píng 平."
I observe that the Emperor's original name was Jīzǐ 箕子,
and he only changed his name to Kàn 衎 in the second year of Yuánshǐ 元始.
First year of Yuánshǐ 元始
(Xīnyǒu 辛酉, one)
1 In spring,
in the first month,
Wáng Mǎng *fèng* Yìzhōu,
ordering the barbarians beyond the frontier to declare themselves Yuèsháng Shì and present, through multiple interpreters, one white pheasant and two black pheasants.
The note on Yuèsháng has already been seen in Volume 28, Yuán Dì's Chūyuán second year.
Referring to the explanations of various scholars,
the land of Yuèsháng is not beyond the frontier of Yìzhōu.
Mǎng, deeming himself an assistant to the young sovereign,
wished to use the arrival of distant people as a meritorious achievement comparable to that of Zhōu Gōng to delude the populace,
and therefore did this.
Shī Gǔ said: Yuèsháng
is a distant southern country.
*Yì*
refers to transmitting speech.
The roads are extremely distant,
and customs are vastly different,
hence it requires repeated translations before communication is possible.
*Fèng*
is read as *fěng*.
The white pheasants were offered to the ancestral temple.
Thereupon, the various officials profusely enumerated Mǎng's merits and virtues,
"attributing the auspicious omen of the white pheasant to Zhōu Chéng;

At that time, the various officials said
that it is the law of the sagely kings
that when a minister has great accomplishments, he is given a noble title during his lifetime,
and they cited the matter of Zhōu Gōng as evidence.
He increased the number of households and equalized the爵 *jué* and 邑 *yì*."

unless it was the initial enfeoffment,

*Chóu*
means "equal";

Xián said: *Chóu*
means "equal";

ought to have his fief households increased,

Mǎng submitted a memorial saying:
"Your subject, along with Kǒng Guāng, Wáng Shùn, Zhēn Fēng, and Zhēn Hán, jointly formulated the strategy;

setting aside your subject Mǎng,
and not including him in the same rank."
*Jìn*
means to stop.
*Qǐn*
means to set aside.
"'Without partiality, without factionalism,
the royal way is vast and open.'
Shī Gǔ said: These are words from the *Shàngshū Hóngfàn*.
*Dàngdàng* describes a vast and level appearance;
therefore it is quoted.
It is not permissible to conceal and not proclaim [your merits] because of kinship;
Your Majesty, you must not refuse!"
Mǎng again submitted memorials, firmly declining several times,
claiming illness and not rising.
His attendants reported to the Empress Dowager,
"It is advisable not to thwart Mǎng's intention,

Only then did Mǎng agree to rise.
In the second month,
on the *bǐngchén* day,
the Empress Dowager issued an edict:

I note that what the *Kǎoyì* refers to as the *Wángzǐhóu* stating enfeoffment on the *bǐngchén* day of the second month,
refers to Xūan Dì's great-great-grandson Xìn and others.
From a current examination,
this cannot be without doubt.
See note below.
"Enfeoff Guangyáng Hóu;
The *Ēnzé Hóu Biǎo* says: Guǎngyáng Hóu

The *Ēnzé Hóu Biǎo* says: Chéngyáng Hóu
was established in Rǔnán.
Shī Gǔ said: *Chéng*
is pronounced *zhēng*.
Mǎng had not yet risen.
The various officials again memorialized:
"Although Mǎng declines,
what the court ought to display
means what the imperial court should make manifest.
*Cháo*
is read *zhí yáo* fan.
Clearly emphasizing his primordial merit,
let not the numerous officials and the common people be disappointed!"
The Empress Dowager then issued an edict:
"Let the Grand Marshal, Marquis of Xīndū, Mǎng, be made Grand Tutor,
to manage the affairs of the Four Supports,

Shī Gǔ said: *Jǐ*
means sufficient.
*Jiājǐ* means every household is self-sufficient.
The various officials again contended,

It means that when households are provided for and people are sufficient,

And he proposed the commendation and reward of the imperial clan and various officials,
establishing Kǎimíng, the太子 *tàizǐ* of the former King Yún of Dōngpíng, as King;
in the second year of Āi Dì's Jiànpíng era,
Yún died,
and his state was abolished,

To maintain the lineage of Xiào Wáng;
Dōngpíng Sī Wáng,
was Yǔ, son of Xūan Dì;
the Emperor entered to serve the Grand宗 *zōng*,
therefore Chéngdū was established to maintain the lineage of Xiào Wáng.
The Grand Steward Wáng Yùn and twenty-five others were all granted the title of Guānnèi Hóu.
Yùn and others had previously deliberated on the honorary title of Empress Dowager Fù of Dìngtáo,
upheld the classical law,
and did not yield to perverse intentions, thereby being granted titles.
*Yùn*
is pronounced *yú fěn* fan.
All were permitted to be successors;

To appoint the Duke as Zǎihéng;

Mǎng submitted a sealed memorial, stating:

means 'to be equal to'.

Mǎng then rose to attend to his duties,
only reducing the land of Zhàolíng, Huángyóu, and Xīnyě.
Mǎng again used the ten million in additional tribute money he received to reward those attending to and supporting the Empress Dowager.
Although Mǎng held absolute power,
he employed countless methods to deceive, flatter, and serve the Empress Dowager,
extending even to the surrounding chamber attendants,
bribing them with tens of millions.
He repeatedly requested to honor the Empress Dowager's sisters with the title of Jūn,
and grant them soup and bath towns.
Her elder sister, Jiá, was made Guǎng'ēnjūn;
Jūn Lì was made Guǎnghuìjūn;
and her younger sister, Dì, was made Guǎngshījūn.
Mǎng also knew that the Empress Dowager, being a woman,
was weary of dwelling in the deep palace,
and Mǎng wished to entertain her to gain influence.
So, he ordered the Empress Dowager's carriage to make seasonal tours of the four suburbs.
Zhāng Yàn said: "Gaining influence"
means exchanging the pleasure of sightseeing for power,
like a merchant trading.
Shī Gǔ said: "Yú"
is the same as "yú" (to entertain).
"Outside the city walls is called the suburbs,"
about twenty *lǐ* away.
Zhòng Fēng said: "To speak of 'suburbs'
does not necessarily mean twenty *lǐ*."
Wherever they arrived in the subordinate counties,
he would always bestow favors,
giving money, silk, cattle, and wine to the people,
making it a regular practice each year.
The Empress Dowager's favorite child-attendant became ill,
in an outer dwelling.
Fú Qián said: "The children born to palace maids and attendants

This shows how much he desired to please the Empress Dowager.
Tàibǎo Shùn reported, stating:

means to retreat.
Yú and Ruì
are names of two states,
both east of the Yellow River.
The rulers of the two states disputed a piece of land unfairly,

they went to him to settle the matter;
upon entering the border of Zhōu,
farmers yielded their fields,

They then said to each other:
"We are petty men;

So they yielded to each other,

Shī Gǔ said: "There were seventeen kinds of food.
This means he would enter the court once every ten days,
receiving this esteemed treatment,

7 Wáng Mǎng 奏起明堂、辟雍、靈臺.
Yìng Shào 曰: “明堂 is for rectifying the four seasons
and disseminating education.
The 明堂 is round above and square below,
with eight windows and four thoroughfares.
It is the palace for administering government,
located on the south side of the capital. The eight windows above symbolize the eight winds,
the four thoroughfares symbolize the four seasons,
the nine chambers symbolize the nine provinces,
the twelve types [of plants] symbolize the twelve months,
the thirty-six doors symbolize the thirty-six rains,
and the seventy-two windows symbolize the seventy-two winds.
The Yellow Emperor called it 合宮 (Hégōng),
Yǒu Yú called it 總章 (Zǒngzhāng),
the Yīn called it 陽館 (Yángguǎn),
and the Zhōu called it 明堂 (Míngtáng).
辟雍 (Bìyōng)
is shaped like a jade bi disk;
it is encircled by water,
symbolizing the widespread flow of education.
The Dà Dài Lǐ says: ‘The 明堂
is covered with thatch,
round above and square below.’
The Son of Heaven's [observatory] is called 靈臺 (Língtái),
while that of the feudal lords is called 觀臺 (Guāntái),
used for observing cosmic energies
and recording celestial phenomena.
Its construction was extremely grand.”
He established a canon of music;
increased the number of Erudites,
five for each classic.
He summoned throughout the empire those who were proficient in a single art and taught more than eleven disciples,
as well as those who possessed lost rituals, ancient books, astronomy, and prognostic charts.
Zhāng Héng 曰: “Prognostic charts are false and absurd,
not the method of the Sages.”
Liú Xiàng and his son oversaw the collation of secret documents,
reviewing and categorizing the Nine Schools,
and found no record of prognostications.
It was only after the reigns of Chéng and Āi
that they began to be heard of.
Mèng Kāng 曰: “史籀 (Shǐ Zhòu)'s work consisted of fifteen chapters of ancient script.”
Shī Gǔ 曰: “It refers to the Great Seal Script created by the Grand Scribe 史籀 (Shǐ Zhòu) of King Xuān of Zhōu.”
籀 (Zhòu)
is pronounced like “zhí jiù fān.”
All were to report to the Public Carriages Office.
He cast a wide net across the empire for men of unusual talent;
those who arrived, before and after, numbered in the thousands.
He ordered them all to record and explain their views in the court,
intending to rectify errors
and unify diverse opinions.
“He ordered each to present themselves in court and record their explanations.”
He also summoned hundreds of people skilled in water conservancy for the Yellow River.
Among the most divergent opinions, Guān Bìng of Pínglíng, a Commandant of Long Waters, said:
The Surname Compendium says: Guān (關) are descendants of Guān Lóngfēng, a Grandee of the Xià dynasty.
The Fēngsú Tōng says: They are descendants of Guān Lìngyǐn Xǐ.
“The Yellow River frequently breaches [its banks] in the vicinity of Píngyuán and Dōngjùn.
Its terrain there is low and the soil loose and poor.
I have heard that when Yǔ regulated the river,
he originally left this area vacant,
believing that if the water became too abundant, it would overflow,
and if less, it would naturally recede.
Although it occasionally shifted its course,
it could not deviate from this area.
Ancient times are difficult to ascertain.
Recently, observing since the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
the river has breached in the region of Cáo and Wèi.
The Hàn territories of Jìyīn and Dìngtáo
were formerly the state of Cáo.
Dōngjùn and Líyáng in Wèijùn
were ancient Wèi territory.
This land should be left vacant,
and not used for official posts or private dwellings.”
The Censor Hán Mù of Línhuái believed:
“It would be advisable to dig channels generally in the locations of Yǔ's Nine Rivers mentioned in the Yǔgòng.
Even if it is impossible to create nine,
just four or five [channels]
should be beneficial.”
Wáng Héng, an Aide to the Grand Minister of Works, said:
“The land where the Yellow River enters Bohai
is higher than the places Hán Mù proposes to dig.
In the past, there were continuous rains
and northeast winds,
causing the sea to overflow,
surging southwest
for hundreds of Lǐ.
The land of the Nine Rivers has already been submerged by the sea.
Yǔ's regulation of the river water
originally followed the foot of the Western Mountains, flowing northeast.
Shī Gǔ 曰: “行 (xíng)” here means “to flow through.”
If the river shifts,
then the current course is not what Yǔ dug.
Moreover, when Qín attacked Wèi,
it breached the river to inundate its capital.
This event is recorded in Volume 7, Qín Shǐhuáng's twenty-second year.
It cannot be repaired.
It would be advisable to move it back to a flat and stable area and open a new empty course,
making it follow the foot of the Western Mountains,
utilizing high ground to flow northeast into the sea.
Only then will there be no water disaster.”
“The Western Mountains” refers to the mountains west of Líyáng.
He said to Zhēn Fēng:

“This would relieve the people's suffering.”

8 His attendants reported,
saying,
“In the past, the Duke of Zhōu served as regent for seven years,
and only then were institutions established.
Now, the Duke of Ānhàn has assisted in government for four years,
and the great work of 'two phrases' has been completed.
He ought to be promoted to the position of Grand Chancellor, ranking above all feudal kings.”
An imperial edict stated:
“Granted.”
He then ordered discussion on the rites of the Nine Bestowals.
Yìng Shào 曰: “The Nine Bestowals are:
first, carriages and horses;
second, ceremonial robes;
third, musical instruments;
fourth, vermillion doors;
fifth, an entry ramp;
sixth, a hundred Tiger Warriors;
seventh, axes and hatchets;
eighth, bows and arrows;
ninth, black millet wine.
These are all institutions of the Son of Heaven.
To show reverence for him,
these items are bestowed one by one,
but in smaller numbers.”
Zhāng Yàn 曰: “The Nine Bestowals are not mentioned in the classics.
The Zhōu Lǐ refers to them as the Nine Appointments,
and they are mentioned in the Chūnqiū commentaries.”
Chén Zàn 曰: “The Nine Bestowals are comprehensive objects,
a grand ceremony for hegemons.
Even Duke Huán of Qí and Duke Wén of Jìn could not fully obtain them.”
Zhèng Xuán 曰: “According to my examination, the name 'Nine Bestowals' does not exist in antiquity.
The Wáng Zhì states: ‘The Three Dukes receive one appointment to wear the dragon robe.’
If there is an addition,
it is a gift, not exceeding nine appointments.”
Kǒng Yǐngdá 曰: “Zhèng Xuán's intention is that, in addition to the Nine Appointments,
there are separate Nine Gifts.
According to the Lǐ Wěi Hán Wén Jiā,
it first lists the distinctions of the Nine Bestowals,
and then states: ‘They are what the four directions look up to and what the sons of feudal lords hope for.’
Sòng Jūn's commentary says: ‘The Nine Gifts are what are commonly seen by the four directions, and what dukes, marquises, counts, viscounts, and barons hope for.’
Kǒng's citation of the Hán Wén Jiā concerning the Nine Bestowals is the same as Yìng Shào's,
except that for musical instruments, it says 'musical ear' (樂則耳).
Sòng Jūn's commentary says: ‘For having propriety in advancing and retreating, and moderation in walking,
carriages and horses are bestowed to replace their walking.
For having achievements in writing and setting a standard in conduct,
ceremonial robes are bestowed to manifest their virtue.
For being skilled in teaching and harboring utmost benevolence within,
musical instruments are bestowed to transform their people.
For maintaining an orderly dwelling and a clean interior,
vermillion doors are bestowed to signify their distinction.
For having禮 (lǐ) in actions,
an entry ramp is bestowed to ensure their comfort.
For being brave, fierce, and resolute in upholding righteousness,
a hundred Tiger Warriors are bestowed to guard against emergencies.
For displaying awe-inspiring military might and being dedicated to guarding the state,
axes and hatchets are bestowed, granting them the power to execute unilaterally.
For harboring benevolence within and steadfastly upholding righteousness,
bows and arrows are bestowed, granting them the power to launch expeditions unilaterally.
For being filial and kind to parents,
black millet wine is bestowed to be offered to ancestors.’”

the tomb of Empress Dowager Bó, Emperor Wén's mother.
Yúnlíng was
the tomb of Empress Dowager Zhào, Emperor Zhāo's mother.
10 Wáng Mǎng, believing that he had civilized the Xiōngnú in the north,
reached overseas in the east,
and pacified Huángzhī in the south,
personally submitted a memorial stating: the Yuèshāng clan, through multiple interpreters, presented white pheasants;
Huángzhī, from thirty thousand *lǐ* away, offered live rhinoceros;
the king of Dōngyí crossed the great sea,
presenting national treasures;
the Shànyú of the Xiōngnú followed the regulations,
abandoning his two names.
Thereupon, he dispatched Zhōnglángjiàng Píng Xiàn and others to take large amounts of gold and silk to entice the Qiāng outside the frontier,
to make them offer land and wish to become internal subjects.
Xiàn and others reported:
"The Qiāng chieftain Liáng Yuàn and his tribe, numbering about twelve thousand people,
wish to become internal subjects,
offering Xiānshuǐ Hǎi, Yǔngǔ, and the salt lake."

"Northwest of Línqiāng County in Jīnchéng Commandery, beyond the frontier,
there are Xī Hǎi and a salt lake."
Kàn Yīn says: "To the west is Bēihé Qiāng Hǎi,
which is the land offered to Wáng Mǎng to become Xīhǎi Commandery."
Lì Dàoyuán says: "The world calls it Qīnghǎi,
two hundred and fifty *lǐ* east of Xīpíng."
"All of them are to become Hàn commoners;
they themselves will occupy the precipitous places as a protective screen."
When asked about Liáng Yuàn's intention to submit,
he replied: "The Grand Empress Dowager is sagely and brilliant,
Ānhàn Gōng is utterly benevolent,
the world is peaceful,
the five grains are ripe,
some rice stalks are over a *zhàng* tall,
some single grains yield three grains of rice,
some grow without planting,
some cocoons form without silkworms;
sweet dew falls from the sky,
and sweet springs emerge from the earth;
phoenixes come in graceful array,
and divine sparrows descend and gather.
From four years ago—
meaning since Mǎng began assisting in government—
hence we desire and are pleased to become internal subjects."
"It is appropriate to settle them in due course and provide them with occupations."
*Chǔ* [處],
means to measure the land and settle them.
means to ensure each has an occupation.
rhymes with *luò*.
*Chǔ* [處],
pronounced *chāng lǚ fān*.
The matter was submitted to Mǎng,
and Mǎng further memorialized:
"Now there are already Dōnghǎi, Nánhǎi, and Běihǎi Commanderies,
I request to accept the land offered by Liáng Yuàn and others as Xīhǎi Commandery.
Divide the world into twelve provinces,
in accordance with ancient institutions."
The memorial was approved.
In winter,
Xīhǎi Commandery was established.
The *Kǎoyì* says: "The *Wáng Mǎng Zhuàn* states that Xīhǎi Commandery was established in the autumn of the following year;
we now follow the Píng Jì."
Those who committed offenses were exiled to Xīhǎi.
The exiles numbered in the tens of thousands,
and the people began to resent him.
11 Liáng Wáng Lì was impeached for colluding with the Wèi clan,
deposed,
and exiled to Nánzhèng;
he committed suicide.
The Wèi clan was
the Emperor's maternal relatives.
12 The capital was divided, and Qiánhuīguāng and Hòuchéngliè Commanderies were established.
Qiánhuīguāng likely governed the counties south of Cháng'ān,
and Hòuchéngliè likely governed the counties north of Cháng'ān.
The jurisdiction of commanderies and kingdoms was delimited,
and dismissals, establishments, and alterations were numerous,
causing much trouble throughout the empire,
which officials could not keep track of.
1 In spring,
the first month,
the *xiá* sacrifice was performed at Míngtáng;

every five years there are two grand sacrifices,
one *dì* and one *xiá*."
The *xiá* sacrifice means
that the spirit tablets of demolished temples are all offered food together with the Great Ancestor.
Shī Gǔ says: "*Xiá* [祫],
pronounced *hé*."
One hundred and twenty marquises
and over nine hundred imperial kinsmen
were summoned to assist in the sacrifice.
After the rituals were completed,
all were given additional households, titles, gold and silk, increased ranks, and appointments as officials, each according to their station.

those with titles received gold and silk,

2 Ānhàn Gōng also proposed restoring the southern and northern suburbs of Cháng'ān.
Within a period of thirty-odd years,
the altars to Heaven and Earth were moved five times.

the early Hàn dynasty.

the fourth month,

means to complete.
In the fifth month,
an imperial edict commanded Wáng Mǎng (王莽), the Ānhàn Gōng (安漢公), to be granted the Nine Bestowals.
Wáng Mǎng prostrated himself twice,

the *gǔnmiǎn* (袞冕),

*Fú* (韍)

*wéi* (韡)

is a type of jade.
The ornaments of a sword worn at the waist,

*bì* (珌)

is the sword sheath.
*Běng* (琫)
is the upper ornament of the sword worn at the waist;
*bì* (珌)

The *Ěryǎ* (爾雅) says: Gold is called *dàng* (璗).

refers to beautiful gold that is the same color as jade.
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: *Yáng* (瑒)
is pronounced *dàng* (蕩).
*Běng* (琫)
is pronounced *bùkǒng* (布孔翻).
*Bì* (珌)
is pronounced *bì* (必).
Mèng Kāng (孟康) says: These are the decorations on the front of current Qí (齊) sacrifice shoes,
protruding three inches from the shoe.

*Gōu* (句)
is pronounced *jùjū* (巨俱翻).
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: *Luánlù* (鸞路) refers to a carriage equipped with bells.
Four horses are called a *chéng* (乘),
pronounced *shízhèng* (食證翻).
The *Zhōulǐ* (周禮) says: A flag with intertwining dragons is a *qí* (旂).
The *Ěryǎ* (爾雅) says: A flag with bells is a *qí* (旂).
*Liú* (旒)
refers to the streamers hanging from the end of a flag.
The *rónglù* (戎路) and *chéngmǎ* (乘馬),
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: *Rónglù* (戎路)
is a war chariot.
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: *Tóng* (彤)
is red.
*Lú* (盧)
is black.
On the right stood a golden *qī* (戚).
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: *Yuè* (鉞) and *qī* (戚)
are both types of axes.
*Zhòu* (冑)
is a helmet.
*Jùchàng* (秬鬯)
is fragrant wine.
The *Zhōulǐ* (周禮) *Chūnguān Chàngrén Zhù* (周禮春官鬯人註) says: It is wine brewed from *jù* (秬);
*jù* (秬) is like black millet,
with two grains per husk.
Lù Diàn Bīyǎ (陸佃埤雅) says: The *Shuōwén* (說文) says: *Chàng* (鬯) is brewed with *jù* (秬), and *yùcǎo* (鬱草) is fragrant,
used to serve and invite the spirits.
Old sayings: Fragrant and flowing freely,
thus called *chàng* (鬯);

Cuī Bào's Gǔjīn Zhù: Whales (jīng),
large ones are a thousand lì long,
small ones several zhàng long.
They give birth to tens of thousands of offspring in a lifetime,
and usually come to the shore in the fifth or sixth month to give birth.
By the seventh or eighth month, they lead their young back to the vast ocean,
beating waves to create thunder,
and spraying foam to make rain.
Aquatic creatures are astonished and terrified,
all fleeing and hiding,
none daring to resist.
The female is called ní,
and large ones are also a thousand lì long.
It is probably because jīngní are powerful
and can drive and devour small fish,
hence they are used as a metaphor for the strong and violent who bully the weak.
And leading tens of thousands of offspring,
rampaging in the vast ocean,
also carries the meaning of being a chieftain or leader.
Yú[AS-FBED]jiāng
is the ancient character for jīng,

enfeoffed as Zhāngxīn Gōng;
