enfeoffed as Lóngxīn Gōng;
these were the Sāngōng (Three Dukes).
The Grand A, Yòufú, Grand Minister of Works Zhēn Fēng was made Gēngshǐ Jiāngjūn (General Who Initiates Reforms),
enfeoffed as Guǎngxīn Gōng;
Wáng Xīng of Jīngzhào was made Wèijiāngjūn (General of the Guards),
enfeoffed as Fèngxīn Gōng;
the Light Chariot General Sūn Jiàn was made Lìguó Jiāngjūn (General Who Establishes the State),
enfeoffed as Chéngxīn Gōng;
Wáng Shèng of Jīngzhào was made Qiánjiāngjūn (General of the Vanguard),
enfeoffed as Chóngxīn Gōng;
these were the Sìjiàng (Four Generals).
In total, there were eleven dukes.
Wáng Xīng
was formerly a city gate clerk;
a city gate clerk
served the city gate commandant
and was in charge of documents.
(He was also) a pastry seller;
the Shìmíng says: Bǐng
means to combine,
referring to flour mixed and combined.
Steamed cakes, boiled noodles, and the like
are named according to their shape.
The appearances of these two men matched the divination,
and they were directly appointed from commoners,
to show divine will.
On this day,
several hundred officials, including high ministers, grand masters, imperial attendants (Shìzhōng), and executive secretaries (Shàngshū), were enfeoffed and appointed.
All those of the Liú clan who were commandery governors were moved to become remonstrance grandees (Jiàndàfū).
The Míngguāng Palace was renamed Dìng'ān Guǎn (Dìng'ān Residence),
where the Dìng'ān Grand Empress Dowager resided;
the Dàhónglú Fǔ (Grand Herald's Office) was made the Dìng'ān Gōng Dì (Residence of the Duke of Dìng'ān);
all were placed under the supervision of gate guards and envoys.
The wet nurse was ordered not to speak to the infant,
who was always kept within four walls;
Mèng Kāng said: The Duke of Dìng'ān was ordered to live within four walls,
so he could not see anything.
The Hàn Guān Diǎnzhí says: All palace walls were painted with white lead,
outlined with purple silk,
and depicted ancient heroes.
The Shìmíng says: Bì
means to ward off,
to ward off wind and cold.
He could not even name the six domestic animals.
Later, Wáng Mǎng married his granddaughter, Yǔ's daughter, to him.
Yǔ was Wáng Mǎng's eldest son, so Yǔ's daughter was his granddaughter.
Qī
is pronounced qī.
Wáng Mǎng then decreed that all officials (Sī) should fulfill their duties
according to the texts of ancient edicts.
He established the Dà Sīmǎ Sīyǔn, Dà Sītú Sīzhí, and Dà Sīkōng Sīruò,
whose ranks were all Gūqīng (Solitary Ministers).
Shīgǔ said: Yǔn
means trust.
Ruò
means compliance.
I observe that in ancient times, the Sāngū (Three Solitaries) held the rank of Liùqīng (Six Ministers);
their titles and emoluments were the same as the Liùqīng, hence Gūqīng.
Later, the Nàyán was renamed;
the Dàlǐ (Grand Judge) was called Zuòshì;
the Tàicháng (Grand Minister of Ceremonies) was called Zhìzōng;
the Dàhónglú (Grand Herald) was called Diǎnyuè;
the Shàofǔ (Privy Treasurer) was called Gònggōng;
the Shuǐhéng Dūwèi (Commandant of the Waterways and Forests) was called Yǔyú;
all these were based on the official systems of Táng and Yú.
Sīqīng
refers to Sīyǔn, Sīzhí, and Sīruò.
Eighty-one Yuánshì
were appointed to oversee various functions of the central capital offices.
He also renamed the Guānglùxūn (Minister of the Imperial Household) and others as Liùjiān (Six Supervisors),
all of whom were Shàngqīng (Superior Ministers).
The Guānglùxūn was called Sīzhōng,
the Tàipú (Grand Coachman) was called Tàiyù,
the Wèiwèi (Palace Commandant) was called Tàiwèi,
the Zhí Jīnwú (Bearer of the Gilded Mace) was called Fènwǔ,
the Zhōngwèi (Chief Commandant of the Capital) was called Jūnzhèng.
He also established the Dàzhuì Guān,
in charge of the emperor's carriages and personal belongings;
later, they also commanded troops.
The Dūwèi (Commandant) was called Dàwèi,
the county magistrate (Xiànlìng, Xiànzhǎng) was called Zǎi;
the Chánglè Palace was called Chánglè Shì (Chánglè Chamber),
Cháng'ān was called Cháng'ān;
all other officials, palaces, commanderies, and counties had their names changed,
too numerous to count.
Those of Wáng Mǎng's clan who were in the Qícuī degree of mourning were enfeoffed as Marquis,
those in the Dàgōng degree as Count (Bó),
those in the Xiǎogōng degree as Viscount (Zǐ),
and those in the Sīmá degree as Baron (Nán);
their daughters were all made Rèn.
Shīgǔ said: Rèn
means to fill or hold a position.
The meaning of Nánfú (Baron's attire) is that
Nán also refers to a position;
it is pronounced rén.
"Mù"
and the women were given
"Lóng"
as their title.
Shīgǔ said: Mù and Lóng
were both the names of the enfeoffed territories, chosen for their auspicious meanings.
It was also said:
"The feudal lords of the Hàn dynasty sometimes called themselves kings,
and the Four Barbarians likewise did so.
This deviates from ancient precedents
and is contrary to the principle of a unified realm.
A king unifies the realm.
The title of 'king'
belongs to the one who possesses all under Heaven.
For feudal lords and the Four Barbarians to claim it
is not in accordance with ancient practice.
'Móu' (繆)
means 'contrary.'
All those among the Four Barbarians who presumptuously adopted the title of 'king' were to be changed to 'marquis'."
Thereupon, the thirty-two Hàn feudal kings
were all demoted to 'gōng' (公),
and the one hundred eighty-one princely marquises were all demoted to 'zǐ' (子).
Later, their titles were all stripped.
Kǎo Yì (考異) states: The tables of feudal kings
all say,
"Wáng Mǎng (王莽) usurped the throne,
and they were demoted to 'gōng' (公).
The following year,
they were abolished."
The tables of princely marquises only say
"cut off"
or
"dismissed,"
all in this year.

However, in the following year, when Guójiàngjūn Jiàn (國將軍建) proposed that the various Liú (劉) family members who had been enfeoffed as feudal lords should be differentiated into five ranks according to the size of their households,
it was not said that their titles were stripped.
The biography of Chéngyáng Wáng Zhǐ (城陽王祉) in the Hòu Hàn (後漢) record says:
"Those of the Liú (劉) clan who were marquises were all demoted to 'zǐ' (子),
and later their titles were stripped."
It is not known in which year they were stripped.

2 Wáng Mǎng (王莽) also enfeoffed descendants of Huángdì (黃帝), Shàohào (少昊), Zhuānxù (顓頊), Dìkù (帝嚳), Yáo (堯), Shùn (舜), the Xià (夏), Shāng (商), and Zhōu (周) dynasties, as well as Gāotáo (皋陶) and Yīyǐn (伊尹), all as 'gōng' (公) or 'hóu' (侯),
making each responsible for their respective sacrifices.
Yáo Xún (姚恂) was made Chūmù Hóu (初睦侯),
to offer sacrifices to the descendants of Huángdì (黃帝).
Liáng Hù (梁護) was made Xiūyuǎn Bó (脩遠伯),
to offer sacrifices to the descendants of Shàohào (少昊).
The imperial grandson Gōnglóng Gōng Qiān (功隆公千)
offered sacrifices to the descendants of Dìkù (帝嚳).
Liú Xīn (劉歆) was made Chūliè Bó (初烈伯),
to offer sacrifices to the descendants of Zhuānxù (顓頊).
The imperial tutor Liú Xīn's (劉歆) son Dié (疊) was made Yīxiū Hóu (伊休侯),
to offer sacrifices to the descendants of Yáo (堯).
Guī Chāng (媯昌) was made Shǐmù Hóu (始睦侯),
to offer sacrifices to the descendants of Emperor Yú (虞帝).
Shān Zūn (山遵) was made Bāomóu Hóu (褒謀侯),
to offer sacrifices to the descendants of Gāotáo (皋陶).
Yī Xuán (伊玄) was made Bāohéng Zǐ (褒衡子),
to offer sacrifices to the descendants of Yīyǐn (伊尹).
Jī Dǎng (姬黨), the Duke of Wèi (衞公) and descendant of Zhōu (周), was re-enfeoffed as Zhāngpíng Gōng (章平公).
Kǒng Hóng (孔弘), the Duke of Sòng (宋公) and descendant of Yīn (殷), was re-enfeoffed as Zhāngzhāo Hóu (章昭侯).
Rú Fēng (如豐) from Liáoxī (遼西), a descendant of Xià (夏), was enfeoffed as Zhānggōng Hóu (章功侯).
3 Wáng Mǎng (王莽), benefiting from the peaceful achievements of the Hàn dynasty,
the wealth of its treasuries and myriad officials,
the submission of the Hundred Barbarians,
and the tranquility of the realm,
possessed all this in one morning.
Yet his heart and mind were not satisfied.
"Not satisfied"
means not sated.
He desired to make things more expansive.
He wanted to change the institutions to accord with antiquity.
'Xiá' (陿)
is the same as 'xiá' (狹).
'Gēng' (更)
is pronounced 'gōng-héng.'
When the grandson of Qí Wáng Jiàn (齊王建), Jìběi Wáng Ān (濟北王安), lost his state,
the people of Qí (齊) called him 'Wáng Jiā' (王家),
and this became their surname.
Therefore, Huángdì (黃帝) was taken as the distant ancestor,
and Emperor Yú (虞帝) as the primal ancestor.
Chén Húgōng (陳胡公) was posthumously honored as
Chén Hú Wáng (陳胡王),
Tián Jìngzhòng (田敬仲) as Tián Jìng Wáng (田敬王),
and Jìběi Wáng Ān (濟北王安) as
Jìběi Mǐn Wáng (濟北愍王).
The descendants of Huángdì (黃帝) were divided into the Yǒu Yú Shì (有虞氏);
the descendants of Yǒu Yú (有虞) were enfeoffed in Chén (陳);
Tián Jìngzhòng (田敬仲) fled from Chén (陳) to Qí (齊),
becoming the Tián (田) clan;
and the descendants of Tián Ān (田安) became the Wáng Jiā (王家).
'Jì' (濟)
is pronounced 'zǐ-lǐ.'
There were four ancestral temples for his close relatives.
The five clans of Yáo (姚), Guī (媯), Chén (陳), Tián (田), and Wáng (王) throughout the realm were all considered imperial clans,
granted hereditary remission from labor service,
with no other obligations.
Chén Chóng (陳崇) and Tián Fēng (田豐) were enfeoffed as marquises
to offer sacrifices to the descendants of Hu Wáng (胡王) and Jìng Wáng (敬王).
All the regional governors and administrators of the realm, due to the rebellions by Zhái Yì (翟義), Zhào Péng (趙朋), and others previously,
as detailed in the previous volume, Jùshè Yuánnián (居攝元年),
'Shǒu' (守)
is pronounced 'shì-yòu';
same below.
were recognized for their loyalty and filial piety.
Governors were enfeoffed as 'nán' (男),
and administrators as 'fùchéng' (附城).
The Hàn dynasty's Gāo Miào (高廟) was designated as Wénzǔ Miào (文祖廟).
Shīgǔ (師古) says: He wanted to emulate Shùn (舜) receiving the Mandate from Wénzǔ (文祖).
It was not to be abolished,
and sacrifices were to continue as before.
The various Liú (劉) family members were not to have their labor exemptions rescinded,
but were to retain them for life;
provincial governors were to frequently inquire about them,
ensuring they suffered no infringement or injustice.
4 Wáng Mǎng (王莽), considering that the character for 'Liú' (劉) consists of
'mǎo' (卯), 'jīn' (金), and 'dāo' (刀),
issued an edict that in the first month, the auspiciousness of 'gāngmǎo' (剛卯) and 'jīndāo' (金刀) should not be observed.
Fú Qián (服虔) says: 'Gāngmǎo' (剛卯) were made on the 'mǎo' (卯) day of the first month,
worn as pendants,
three inches long,
one inch wide,
square.
Some were made of jade,
some of metal,
some of peach wood,
and worn attached to a leather belt.
There are still jade ones today,
with an inscription on one side that reads:
"First month 'gāngmǎo' (剛卯)."
'Jīndāo' (金刀) were the coins minted by Wáng Mǎng (王莽).
Jìn Zhuó (晉灼) says: 'Gāngmǎo' (剛卯) were one inch long,
five fen wide,
square,
with a hole pierced through the center.
They were adorned with colored silk tassels,
the bottom resembling the tassels on a cap string,
and inscribed on the top surface with two lines of writing.
The text reads:
"The 'gāngmǎo' (剛卯) of the first month is complete,
the spiritual staff is in the four directions,
blue, red, white, yellow,
these four colors are appropriate.
The Emperor orders Zhùróng (祝融),
to teach Kuí (夔) and Lóng (龍),
so that diseases and plagues, strong and debilitating,
dare not oppose me!"
Another inscription reads:
"On the fierce 'mǎo' (卯) day,
the Emperor orders Kuí (夔) to transform,
submit to your firm subjugation,
transform this spiritual staff,
both upright and straight,
both angular and square,
so that diseases and plagues, strong and debilitating,
dare not oppose me!"
Shīgǔ (師古) says: Today, jade 'gāngmǎo' (剛卯) are often found in the earth.
Judging by their size and inscription,
Fú Qián's (服虔) explanation is correct.
Wáng Mǎng (王莽) believed that the character 'Liú' (劉) has 'mǎo' (卯) on top,
'jīn' (金) at the bottom,
and 'dāo' (刀) on the side.
Therefore, he prohibited 'gāngmǎo' (剛卯) and 'jīndāo' (金刀).
I, Yú (余), note that the character 'Liú' (劉) originally followed '[AS-FBF9]' ( [AS-FBF9] )
and Wáng Mǎng (王莽) considered '[AS-FBF9]' ( [AS-FBF9] )
to be close to 'mǎo' (卯),
hence he said so.
Kǒng Yǐngdá (孔穎達) says: In ancient script, there was 'dāo' (刀).
'Dāo' (刀) had two types: one was 'qìdāo' (契刀),
the other was 'cuòdāo' (錯刀).
'Qìdāo' (契刀) was worth five hundred;
'cuòdāo' (錯刀) was worth one thousand.
'Qìdāo' (契刀) had no carvings, while 'cuòdāo' (錯刀) was inlaid with gold.
The 'dāo' (刀) had a coin shape but with the character 'dāo' (刀) on its edge,
which is why people still refer to coins as 'qiándāo' (錢刀).
He then made small coins,
six fen in diameter,
weighing one zhū (銖),
inscribed "small coin worth one."
These and the previous "large coin worth fifty"
constituted two types,
circulated concurrently.
To prevent the people from counterfeiting,
he prohibited the possession of copper and charcoal.
5 In summer,
fourth month,
Xúxiāng Hóu Liú Kuài (劉快) gathered several thousand people and started an uprising in his state.
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: Kuài (快)
was the son of Jiāodōng Gōng Wáng (膠東恭王).
However, Wáng Zǐ Hóu Biǎo (王子侯表) writes
“炔” (Què),
following
“火” (huǒ),
which is different from this.
I suspect Biǎo (表) is mistaken.
The former Hàn (漢) King of Jiāodōng (膠東)
was at that time Fúchóng Gōng (扶崇公).
Kuài (快) raised troops to attack Jìmò (即墨).
Jìmò (即墨)
was the capital of the Jiāodōng (膠東) state.
Yīn (殷)
was the great-grandson of Jiāodōng Kāng Wáng Jì (膠東康王寄).
He imprisoned himself.
Officials and common people resisted Kuài (快);
Kuài (快) was defeated and fled,
dying in Chángguǎng (長廣).
The “Dìlǐ Zhì” (地理志) states:
Chángguǎng (長廣) County
belonged to Lángxié (琅邪) Commandery.
He was given an increase to his state of ten thousand households,
and its territory was a hundred *lǐ* (里) square.
6 Wáng Mǎng (王莽) said:
“In ancient times, a single man tilled one hundred *mǔ* (畝),
and the tax was one-tenth.
Mèngzǐ (孟子) said: ‘The people of Zhōu (周) tilled one hundred *mǔ* (畝) and shared a portion [with the government].’
This refers to the Zhōu (周) system.
Qín (秦) destroyed the sage's system,
abolished the well-field system.
See scroll two, nineteenth year of Zhōu Xiǎn Wáng (周顯王).
壞 (huài),
pronounced *guài*.
Greed and meanness arose.
The strong enclosed thousands of *mǔ* (畝) of land,
while the weak had not even enough room to stand an awl.
Furthermore, slave markets were established,
where they were placed in the same pens as cattle and horses.
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: 闌 (lán)
means to obstruct or enclose,
like a pen for cattle and horses.
Their lives were arbitrarily controlled,
contravening the meaning of ‘Among the natures of Heaven and Earth, man is the most valuable.’
The “Xiàojīng” (孝經) says: ‘Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said: Among the natures of Heaven and Earth, man is the most valuable.’
斷 (duàn),
pronounced *dīng luàn*.
The land tax was light,
one-thirtieth,
but there were always additional levies;
even the sick and disabled had to pay.
Moreover, powerful families encroached and oppressed,
sharing fields and extorting rent.
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: Sharing fields
means that the poor who had no fields took and cultivated land from the rich,
sharing the harvest.
假 (jiǎ)
also refers to poor people renting land from rich people.
Extortion means
that the rich extorted and defrauded them of their taxes.
In reality, five-tenths was taxed.
Thus, the rich had surplus beans and grain for their dogs and horses,
became arrogant, and committed evil.
The poor did not have enough husks and dregs to eat,
became destitute, and committed crimes.
Both were trapped in guilt,
and punishments were not wrongly applied.
Now, I am renaming all land in the world ‘royal fields’ (wáng tián),
and slaves ‘private dependents’ (sī shǔ).
None may be bought or sold.
If a male household has fewer than eight members and owns more than one *jǐng* (井) of land,
the surplus land shall be distributed to their nine kin, neighbors, and fellow villagers.
Those who previously had no land and now ought to receive land
shall do so according to the system.
Anyone who dares to criticize the well-field sage system or confuse the masses with unlawful acts
shall be exiled to the four frontiers
to ward off *chīmèi* (魑魅).”
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: 魑 (chī)
is a mountain spirit.
魅 (mèi)
is the essence of an old object.
魑 (chī),
pronounced *chī*.
魅 (mèi),
pronounced *mèi*.
Shùn (舜) exiled the Four Evils to the four frontiers
to ward off *chīmèi* (魑魅).
7 In autumn,
Wáng Mǎng (王莽) dispatched the Five-Awesome Generals Wáng Qí (王奇) and twelve others.
The Five-Awesome Generals
were divided into Left, Right, Front, Rear, and Central Commanders (shuài),
whose robes, caps, carriages, apparel, and harnessed horses each corresponded to the colors and numbers of their respective directions.
將 (jiàng),
pronounced *jí liàng*.
帥 (shuài),
pronounced *suǒ lèi*;
the same below.
There were twenty-five talismans and omens,
and twelve auspicious responses.
The Five-Awesome Generals (Wǔwēi Jiāng) carried the talismans and omens,
and bore the seals and sashes.
For kings, marquises, and below, as well as officials whose titles were changed,
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: 更 (gēng),
means to change.
they were all immediately granted the seals and sashes of the new dynasty,
and the seals and sashes of the former Hàn (漢) dynasty were collected.
A general amnesty was issued throughout the world.
The Five-Awesome Generals (Wǔwēi Jiāng) rode on *gānwén* (乾文) chariots.
Zhèng Shì (鄭氏) said: Heavenly patterns were painted on the chariots.
Zhèng Shì (鄭氏) said: 坤 (kūn)
represents a mare.
Six
is the number of Earth.
Their attire was very grand.
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: 鷩 (biē) bird
is a pheasant species,
specifically the pheasant;
what is commonly called a mountain chicken today
is not it.
鷩 (biē),
pronounced *biē*.
The generals carried *jié* (節),
and the commanders carried *chuáng* (幢).
Those who went east reached Xuántú (玄菟), Lèlàng (樂浪), Gāogōulí (高句驪), and Fúyú (夫餘).
Those who went south passed beyond the frontiers,
traversed Yìzhōu (益州),
and changed the King of Gōudīng (句町) to a Marquis.
徼外 (jiào wài)
means beyond the border fortifications.
Yìzhōu (益州)
was the Yìzhōu (益州) Commandery established by Wǔ Dì (武帝).
During the reign of Zhāo Dì (昭帝),
the Gūzēng (姑繒) and Yèyú (葉榆) barbarians rebelled.
Gōudīng Hóu Wáng Bō (句町侯亡波) attacked the rebels and rendered meritorious service,
so he was made a king.
隃 (yú),
same as 踰 (yú).
徼 (jiào),
pronounced *gōng diào*.
句町 (Gōudīng),
pronounced *qú tǐng*.
They reached the Western Regions,
and all their kings were changed to marquises.
Those who went north reached the Xiongnú (匈奴) court,
bestowed a seal upon the Chányú (單于),
changed the inscription on the Hàn (漢) seal,
and removed the word
璽 (xǐ) and used 章 (zhāng).
Seal is a tally,
a token of trust,
also an indicator,
used to mark objects and entrust them.
The “Hàn Guān Yí” (漢官儀) states: For vassal kings,
a golden seal with a camel knob,
the inscription read 璽 (xǐ).
For Marquises,
a golden seal with a tortoise knob,
the inscription read 章 (zhāng).
For the Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ Dàfū),
a gold seal;
for officials of two thousand *dàn* (石) and above,
a silver seal,
with a tortoise knob,
the inscription read 章 (zhāng).
For officials from one thousand *dàn* (石) to four hundred *dàn* (石), all had copper seals,
the inscription read 印 (yìn).
This was Wáng Mǎng's (王莽) pretext for changing seals and sashes, thereby disrupting the four barbarian tribes.
去 (qù),
pronounced *qiāng lǚ*.
璽 (xǐ),
pronounced *sī shì*.
8 In winter,
there was thunder,
and tung blossoms bloomed.
9 He appointed Chén Chóng (陳崇), the Marquis of Tǒngmù (統睦), as Sīmìng (司命),
responsible for supervising and inspecting those from the rank of Shànggōng (上公) downwards.
He also appointed Cuī Fā (崔發) and others, Marquises of Shuōfú (說符), as Zhōngchéng Jiāngjūn (中城將軍) and Sìguān Jiāngjūn (四關將軍),
responsible for the twelve city gates and the fortresses of Ráoliù (繞霤), Yángtóu (羊頭), Yáomǐn (肴黽), and Qiānlǒng (汧隴).
The Zhōngchéng Jiāngjūn (中城將軍)

9 As Wáng Mǎng’s (王莽) coinage was failing to circulate,
he again issued a decree stating:
“If all precious currencies are heavy, small transactions are not accommodated;
if all are light, transport costs become burdensome.
If there are distinctions of weight, lightness, and size,
then their use is convenient and the people are content.”
Thereupon, he again created gold, silver, turtle shell, cowrie, and coin
and bù (布) currencies,
naming them “Precious Currencies” (bǎohuò 寶貨).
There were six denominations of coin currency.
The small coin (xiǎoxián 小錢) had a diameter of six fēn (分),
weighed one zhū (銖),
and was named “Small Coin Worth One” (xiǎoxián zhíyī 小錢直一);
next was seven fēn (分),
weighing three zhū (銖),
named “Miáo (么) Coin Worth Ten” (miáoxián yīshí 么錢一十);
next was eight fēn (分),
weighing five zhū (銖),
named “Yòu Coin Worth Twenty” (yòuxián èrshí 幼錢二十);
next was nine fēn (分),
weighing seven zhū (銖),
named “Zhōng Coin Worth Thirty” (zhōngxián sānshí 中錢三十);
next was one cùn (寸),
weighing nine zhū (銖),
named “Zhuàng Coin Worth Forty” (zhuàngxián sìshí 壯錢四十);
adding the previous large coin (dàqián 大錢) worth fifty,
there were six denominations.
Shīgǔ (師古) said: “Miáo (么)”
is pronounced yī yáo fān (一遙翻).
One jīn (斤) of yellow gold
was worth ten thousand coins,
constituting one denomination.

Shīgǔ (師古) said: “Zhū (朱)”

Measuring the edges on both sides of the back,

“Yuán (元)”
means “large”.
Large cowries (dàbèi 大貝), four cùn (寸) eight fēn (分) or more,

And for those implicated in buying and selling fields, houses, and slaves, or counterfeiting coins,

Zhēn Fēng and his son remained silent.

Wáng Mǎng, having usurped the throne through deceit,

The *Rítuálí* (周禮) mentions nine *zàng*.

The sub-commentary states: The five main *zàng* are
the lungs, spleen, heart, liver, and kidneys.
As for the additional stomach, bladder, large intestine, and small intestine,

making nine *zàng*.
The six *fǔ* are: stomach, small intestine, large intestine, bladder, gallbladder, and sanjiāo.
Because they receive and contain,
they are therefore called *fǔ*;
they also have the designation of *zàng*,
hence they are included in the number of nine *zàng*.
However, among the six *fǔ*, these four are chosen,
according to the *Huángdì Bāshíyī Nánjīng* (黃帝八十一難經), which says: The stomach is the *fǔ* of food and grain,
the small intestine is the *fǔ* of reception and containment,
the large intestine is the *fǔ* of passage,
and the bladder is the *fǔ* of essence and fluid.
Where *qì* (氣) is generated,
the lower *qì* resembles heaven,
thus it is discharged and not substantial,
and if substantial, not full.
If this is the case,
then they are proper *fǔ*,
hence they are included in the nine *zàng*.
The others,
the gallbladder is the *fǔ* of purity,
and the sanjiāo is an isolated *fǔ*,
not a proper *fǔ*,
hence they are not included in the nine *zàng*.

so it is fitting that the world attributes its grievances to Your Grace.
The court considers the insubordination of those far away as its utmost concern,
while I, Shēng (升), regard the discontent of those nearby as a serious worry.
'Those far away' refers to the Sìyí (四夷).
'Those nearby' refers to the people's dissatisfaction with Mǎng's (莽) laws and decrees.
Events are contrary to the Dao (道),
rushing headlong into the rut of a overturned chariot,
following in the footsteps of failed endeavors.
The later these things manifest, the more peculiar they are;
the later they are initiated, the more frightening they become!
It is the beginning of spring, the start of the year, yet you are launching distant campaigns.
Wild greens are insufficient to fill bellies,
fields lie barren and unplowed,
grain prices soar,
a *hú* (斛) reaching several thousand (coins).
Officials and common people are trapped in a sea of fire,
no longer subjects of the state.
If this continues,
then the Hú (胡) and Mò (貊) will guard the palace gates,
and the bandits of Qīng (青) and Xú (徐) will be within the imperial tents!
This means the people of the imperial capital and its environs will also revolt.
We can solve the world's desperate situation,
and free the common people from their distress;
this cannot be written down.
I wish to be granted an audience
to fully express what is in my heart."
Mǎng (莽) did not listen.
5 Yìpíng Liánshuài (翼平連率) Tián Kuàng (田況) memorialized that the assessment of people's property in the commanderies and counties was inaccurate.
The Dìlǐzhì (地理志) states: Shòuguāng (壽光) County in Běihǎi (北海),
Mǎng (莽) called it Yìpíng (翼平).
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: It means assessing the common people's property
not according to actual figures.
Shuài (率),
pronounced suǒ lèi.
Zǐ (訾)
is the same as zī (貲).
[Commentary: The twelve-line edition correctly writes
the Kǒng (孔) edition is the same.]
Mǎng (莽), considering Kuàng's (況) loyal words and concern for the state,
elevated his rank to Bó (伯) and bestowed upon him two million coins.
However, the common people all reviled him.
Many people in Qīng (青) and Xú (徐) abandoned their hometowns and fled,
the old and weak dying on the roads,
and the strong joining the bandits.
6. Sùyè Liánshuài Hán Bó
(Geography Monograph: Dōnglái Bùyè County,
Wáng Măng called it Sùyè)
reported: "There is an extraordinary man,
ten *zhàng* tall,
ten arm-spans in circumference.
He came to my residence,
wishing to vigorously attack the Hú barbarians.
He calls himself Jùwú Bà,
from Pēnglái, southeast of Five Cities, northwest of Zhāorú Sea Coast."
Shī Gǔ noted: Zhāorú
is a sea name.
*Bīn*
means shore.
(According to the immortals' accounts,
Pēnglái has five cities and twelve towers.)
"Three horses cannot carry him.
On that day, with a large carriage and four horses,
erecting a tiger banner,
I brought Bà to the palace gates.
Bà sleeps with a drum for a pillow,
eats with iron chopsticks.
This is how August Heaven assists the Xīn dynasty!
I wish Your Majesty would make him a great suit of armor, a tall carriage, and the clothes of Bēn and Yù,
and send one grand general with a hundred tiger-guards
to welcome him on the road.
If the capital's gates are not wide enough,
open them wider and taller,
to display him to the hundred barbarian tribes,
and pacify the world."
Bó's intention was to satirize Wáng Măng;
since Măng's courtesy name was Jùjūn,
he obliquely suggested that he should not usurp and dominate (*bà*).
(Fēng
is read as Fěng.)
Wáng Măng disliked him,
detained Bà at Xīnfēng,
(Shī Gǔ noted: "At the place where he was seen.")
and considered it a sign of Wénmǔ Tàihòu causing a hegemon-king.
(Shī Gǔ noted: "Măng's courtesy name was Jùjūn,
implying that Wénmǔ produced this person
and enabled me to achieve hegemony.")
(Gèng
has the sound *gǔ-héng-fān*.)
Hán Bó was imprisoned
for inappropriate speech
and executed in the marketplace.
7. In Guāndōng, famine and drought continued for years.
The followers of Diāo Zǐdū and others gradually increased
to sixty or seventy thousand.
Dìhuáng 1st Year
(Gēngchén, 20 CE)
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the *yǐwèi* day,
an amnesty was granted to the world;
the era name was changed to Dìhuáng,
following the calendar title of thirty-six thousand years.
2. Wáng Măng issued an edict saying:
"When armies are being deployed,
whoever dares to rush around noisily and violate the law shall be immediately condemned and executed,
without waiting for the proper time!"
(Shī Gǔ noted: *Qūhuān*
means rushing about and making a clamor.
*Xū*
means to wait.
*Huān*
has the sound *xǔ-yuán-fān*.)
The people were terrified,
communicating on the roads with their eyes.
(Wéi Zhāo noted: "They dared not speak,
merely glancing at each other with their eyes.")
3. Wáng Măng saw that there were many bandits in the four directions,
and again wished to suppress them.
He again issued an edict saying:
"My imperial primal ancestor, Huáng Dì, pacified the world.
He commanded troops as Grand General,
internally establishing Grand Ministers,
and externally appointing five Grand Stewards of the Army.
From Grand General to common officers, there were 738,900 people,
and 13,500,000 common soldiers.
I have received the texts of the auspicious omens,
and examining those of my predecessors,
I shall prepare them in detail."
Thereupon, he established the positions of Grand Steward of the Army of the Front, Rear, Left, Right, and Center,
and bestowed upon all provincial governors down to county magistrates the titles of Grand General, Pǐan General, Pí General, and Colonel.
Provincial governors became Grand Generals;
*Zúzheng*, *Liánshuài*, and *Dàyǐn* became Pǐan Generals;
subordinate officials and chiefs became Pí Generals;
and county magistrates became Colonels.
The daily expenses were ten times what they were before,
and there was no visible grain in the granaries to supply them.
(Shī Gǔ noted: *Jiàn*
means existing.
*Zhuàn*
has the sound *zhī-liàn-fān*.
*Jiàn*
has the sound *xián-biàn-fān*.)
Carriages and horses on the roads were conscripted.
(Shī Gǔ noted: "Those traveling on the roads
were seized to serve the purpose.")
4. In autumn,
the seventh month,
a great wind destroyed the Wánglù Hall.
(Wáng Măng had renamed the front hall of Wèiyāng Palace Wánglù Hall.
Fú Qián noted: "It is like saying 'road chamber.'
*Lù*
means great.")
Wáng Măng's edict said: "Then, on the *rénwǔ* day at *bǔ* time,
there was a violent wind, thunder, and rain, a calamity that tore off roofs and broke trees.
(*Bǔ*
means to eat.
*Bǔshí*
is mealtime.
Some say: *Bǔ*
is *būshí*;
when the sun is in *shēn*, it is *bū*.
Shī Gǔ noted: *Lièfēng*
means violent wind.
*Shé*
has the sound *ér-shè-fān*.)
I meditated for ten days,
and then my confusion cleared.
(Shī Gǔ noted: "First it mentions violent wind, thunder, and rain,
then it says the confusion cleared.
This probably alludes to Shùn not being confused by violent wind, thunder, and rain.")
He established Ān as Xīnqiān King;
Lín, who was in Luòyáng,
was made Tǒngyìyáng King.
All commentators said: 'Lín being in Luòyáng as Tǒng
means that he holds the central land as the foundation of the Xīn dynasty,
and should properly be made Crown Prince.'
From then on,
Lín suffered from a prolonged illness,
and although he recovered, he was not well.
(It means that although his illness recovered,
he could not return to his original healthy state.)
The names were not correct.
Since my ascension to the throne,
*yīn* and *yáng* have not been in harmony,
grain harvests have been scarce and depleted.
(Shī Gǔ noted: *Xiǎn*
means little.
*Hào*
means diminished.
*Xiǎn*
has the sound *xiān-jiàn-fān*.)
Bandits and criminals,
the people are restless and anxious,
at a loss as to what to do.
(Shī Gǔ noted: *Zhēngyíng*
means an agitated and uneasy state of mind.
*Cuò*
has the sound *qī-gù-fān*.)
It is due to the incorrect names.
As for establishing Ān as Xīnqiān King,
(Fú Qián noted: Ān
was Wáng Măng's third son.
*Qiān*
has the sound *xiān*.
Wáng Măng renamed Rǔnán Xīncài as Xīnqiān.
Shī Gǔ noted: '*Qiān*
is just like *xiān*,
no need for a borrowed pronunciation.)
5. Wáng Măng again issued an edict saying:
"Yellow is treasured, while red is servile."
(Fú Qián noted: "Regarding yellow as precious
is using his own element's energy.
'Servile red' means
that servants and commoners all wear red,
which is the inferior practice of the Hàn dynasty.")
(*Sī*
has the sound *sī*.)
6. Many who observed the *qì* for divination said there was an omen of earthworks;
in the ninth month,
on the *jiǎshēn* day,
Wáng Măng began building nine ancestral temples south of Cháng'ān city.
(Nine temples:
five ancestral temples,
four parental temples.)
They were seventeen *zhàng* high,
and the other temples were half that height,
with a magnificent design.
Wáng Măng extensively recruited artisans from all over the world, and officials and common people who voluntarily contributed money and grain to assist the construction,
arriving continuously on the roads;
(Shī Gǔ noted: *Luòyì*
means unceasing.)
the cost of the project was over several hundred million,
and tens of thousands of laborers died.
7. In this month,
there was heavy rain for over sixty days.
8 In Jùlù, the men Mǎ Shìqiú and others plotted to raise troops from Yān and Zhào to execute Wáng Mǎng.
Shīgǔ said: Mǎ Shì
is the surname.
Qiú
is the given name.
This was reported.
Wáng Mǎng dispatched the Sāngōng and Grandees to arrest and investigate the partisans,
implicating several thousand powerful figures from various commanderies and states,
all of whom were executed.
He enfeoffed Dān as Fǔguó Hóu.
9 Wáng Mǎng made it a capital offense to privately mint coins, and banished those who deprecated or obstructed the precious currency to the Four Frontiers.
This matter is detailed in the previous scroll, during Shǐjiànguó 2nd year.
Jǔ,
in Lǚ Fān.
This could not be fully enforced;
Shèng,
pronounced shēng.
so he lightened the law instead:
those who privately minted coins or cloth money, along with their wives and children, were confiscated as government slaves and maidservants.
Officials and neighbors who knew but did not report them
were guilty of the same crime.
For deprecating or obstructing the precious currency,
commoners were punished with one year of forced labor,
and officials were dismissed from office.
10 The Grand Tutor Píng Yàn died;
Yu Yú Táng Zūn was appointed Grand Tutor.
Táng Zūn said:
"The state is empty and the people are poor;
the fault lies in extravagance."
So he himself wore short clothes with small sleeves,
rode a mare and a straw cart,
slept on straw,
and ate and drank from earthenware vessels.
Shīgǔ said: A straw cart
is a plank cart.
Sleeping on straw
means discarding rush mats.
Xiù
is the ancient character for "sleeve."
I note that in the prosperity of the Hàn dynasty,
those who rode mares were forbidden from gathering,
and this was true even in villages and fields.
In the court and market,
it is thus evident.
Táng Zūn, as a high-ranking official, riding a mare
was also to correct the customs of the age.
When he went out
and saw men and women not taking separate paths,
Táng Zūn himself dismounted from his cart
and stained their clothes with a ochre banner used for symbolic punishment.
Shīgǔ said: Ochre banner
is a cloth banner dyed with ochre juice.
Wū,
Wū Gù Fān.
He issued an edict to caution the Gōngqīng:
"Think of aligning with him."
Shīgǔ said: This means to make them adopt the same conduct as Táng Zūn.
The Analects states that Kǒngzǐ said: "When you see a worthy person, think of emulating him,"
hence Wáng Mǎng said this.
11 Zhì Yùn of Rǔnán, who understood astronomy and calendrical calculations,
believed that the Hàn dynasty would certainly receive the Mandate again.
He submitted a memorial explaining to Wáng Mǎng:
"Heaven has sent down warnings,
wishing to enlighten Your Majesty,
to assume the position of a minister.
To receive it from Heaven
and return it to Heaven
can be called knowing fate!"
Wáng Mǎng was greatly enraged
and imprisoned Zhì Yùn in the imperial prison.
He was released after the winter
when a general amnesty was declared.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
Wáng Mǎng's wife died
and was posthumously titled Xiàomù Huánghòu.
Originally,
Wáng Mǎng's wife, because Wáng Mǎng had killed several of her sons,
wept until she lost her sight.
Wáng Mǎng ordered Crown Prince Lín to reside in the palace and care for her.
Wáng Mǎng's wife's attendant, Yuán Bì,
was favored by Wáng Mǎng,
and Lín also had an affair with her.
Fearing exposure,
they plotted to kill Wáng Mǎng together.
Lín's wife, Yīn,
daughter of the Guóshī Gōng,
was skilled in astrology.
She told Lín that there would soon be a "white-robed gathering" in the palace.
The Astronomy Treatise in the Jìn Shū: "When wood and metal combine,
it is a white-robed gathering.
When earth and metal combine,
it is also a white-robed gathering."
"In the palace" means
it is known by observing the constellations where the gathering occurs.
Yǔ,
Niú Jù Fān.
She thought their plot would soon succeed.
Later, Lín was demoted to Tǒngyì Yáng Wáng
and sent to an outer residence, becoming even more anxious and fearful.
When Wáng Mǎng's wife became gravely ill,
Lín sent a letter saying:
"Your Majesty is extremely strict with your descendants.
Previously, the eldest and middle grandsons both died at the age of thirty.
Now, your subject Lín is again approaching thirty,
and I truly fear that one day I may not be able to preserve my mother
and then I will not know where my death will be!"
Lǐ Qí said: "Zhōngshì"
refers to Lín's mother.
Jìn Zhuó said: It is the central hall of the Chánglè Palace.
Shīgǔ said: Both explanations are incorrect.
Lín himself meant that he wanted to preserve himself in the household,
but it was not possible.
Fù,
Fú Yòu Fān;
same below.
When Wáng Mǎng saw his letter,
he was greatly enraged,
suspecting Lín of ill intentions,
and did not allow him to attend the funeral.
After the burial,
Yuán Bì and others were arrested and interrogated,
and fully confessed to the adultery and murder plot.
Wáng Mǎng wished to keep it secret,
so he had the investigating official, the Sīmìng Cóngshì, killed
and buried in prison.
Sīmìng Cóngshì
is a subordinate official of the Sīmìng.
He gave Lín medicine;
Lín refused to drink it
and stabbed himself to death.
He also issued an edict to Guóshī Gōng:
"Lín originally did not understand astronomy;
the matter originated with Yīn."
Yīn also committed suicide.
2 That month,
Xīnqiān Wáng Ān died of illness.
Originally,
when Wáng Mǎng was enfeoffed as a Marquis and went to his state,
at the beginning of the Ài Emperor's reign,
Wáng Mǎng went to his state;
in Yuánshòu 1st year,
he was recalled to the capital.
He had sons Xìng and Kuāng,
both of whom remained in the state of Xīndū,
because their parentage was unclear.
Shīgǔ said: It means that the sons were born to attendants who might have had private relations with outsiders,
and their parentage could not be clearly determined.
Wáng Mǎng then sent envoys with royal chariots to welcome Xìng and Kuāng,
enfeoffing Xìng as Gōngxiū Gōng and
Kuāng as Gōngjiàn Gōng.
3 The diviner Wáng Kuàng told Wèichéng Dàyǐn Lǐ Yān:
Wáng Mǎng changed Wèijùn to Wèichéng.
"The Hàn house will rise again,
and the Lǐ clan will be its support."
He then wrote a prophetic book for Lǐ Yān,
comprising over ten thousand characters.
When the matter was discovered,
Wáng Mǎng killed them all.
4 Wáng Mǎng dispatched the Grand Tutor Xīzhòng Jǐng Shàng,
Wáng Mǎng made the Grand Tutor oversee spring,
and his subordinates were given the office of Xīzhòng.
All the Generals were given the title of Hùjūn.
The Guóshī Hézhòng Cáo Fàng assisted Guō Xìng in attacking Gōudīng.
Zàng was based on the Guóshī overseeing autumn,
so Hézhòng was appointed.
Gōudīng,
pronounced Qú Tǐng.
The army's conduct was undisciplined,
and the common people were greatly distressed.
5 Wáng Mǎng also transported grain and silk from all over the empire to Xīhé, Wǔyuán, Shuòfāng, and Yúyáng,
millions of units for each commandery,
intending to attack the Xiōngnú.
Xūbǔ Dāng died of illness.
Wáng Mǎng gave his concubine daughter as wife to Xūbǔ Dāng's son, Hòu'ān Gōng Shē.
Wáng Mǎng's daughter Jié,
born to the attendant Kāimíng,
was given as wife to Shē.
Lǐ Qí said: Shē
was originally a Marquis.
Wáng Mǎng gave his daughter to him as wife,
so he advanced his title to Duke.
Qī,
Qī Xì Fān.
He ultimately intended to deploy troops to establish him.
Shīgǔ said: It means his intentions for this plan were not limited.
Wèi,
Yú Wěi Fān;
same below.
When Wáng Mǎng was defeated,
Yún and Shē also died.
6 In autumn,
frost killed the beans,
there was a great famine east of the passes,
and locusts.
7 Wáng Mǎng, having already lightened the law on private coinage,
the offenders became even more numerous.
When five people were implicated together,
they were confiscated and made into official slaves;
their men were put in caged carts,
their women walked,
with iron chains weighing down their necks,
and were sent to
Zhōngguān in numbers of tens of thousands.
Shī Gǔ said: Lángdāng
means a long chain.
Zhōngguān
is the official in charge of minting coins.
Shī Gǔ said: It means changing and matching them,
not according to their old arrangements.
8 Chǔ Xià from Shànggǔ requested to persuade Guātián Yí to surrender;
Chǔ Xià
is a person's name.
During the Warring States period,
Qí had Chǔ Zǐ.
Wáng Mǎng sought his corpse and buried it,
erected a tomb and a memorial hall for him,
and posthumously titled him Guāníng Shāngnán.
This 'shāng'
is not a 'shāng' for someone who died before adulthood,
but for someone who died violently.
This is what the Chǔ Cí refers to as Guóshāng.
9 In the intercalary month,
on the day Bǐngchén,
there was a general amnesty.
10 Láng Yángchéng Xiū presented an auspicious omen,
his surname was Yángchéng,
his given name Xiū,
and his official title was Láng.
It also said:
"The Yellow Emperor attained immortality with one hundred and twenty women."
Han Confucians said that the Son of Heaven had three Fūren, nine Pín, twenty-seven Shìfù, and eighty-one Yùqī,
which also amounts to one hundred and twenty women.
The "Bǎi Guān Zhì" states: A Zhōngsàn Dàfū holds a salary of six hundred shí.
At that time, it was subordinate to Sīzhōng.
They widely sought out and nominated noble women from the villages.
11 Wáng Mǎng detested the spirits of the Han Emperor Gāo's temple,
and sent Hǔbēn warriors into the Gāo temple,
striking it from
all four sides.
Shī Gǔ said: This refers to being condemned in a dream.
Tí
means to throw,
pronounced as tú-jì fān.
Shī Gǔ said: It means to chop and destroy it with an axe.
Huài
is pronounced as guài.
Shī Gǔ said: Sprinkling it with peach water,
and lashing it with a vermilion whip.
Zhě
means red.
The Han dynasty had the Hǔbēn Xiàowèi in charge of light chariots.
This Qīngchē Xiàowèi
was established by Wáng Mǎng.
12 In this year,
Qín Fēng of Nánjùn gathered nearly ten thousand people;
Chí Zhāopíng, a woman from Píngyuán, also gathered several thousand people in the river-blocked area.
The "Xìng Pǔ" states: Chí
is a surname,
descended from Fán Chí,
taking their grandfather's courtesy name as their clan name.
One account says: Descended from the ancient worthy Chí Rèn.
All said:
"These are prisoners of heaven, walking corpses,
their lives are like leaking clocks."
Meaning they had offended heaven,
and would die in an instant;
their frantic thievery
was merely the action of corpses.
Lù said:
"The Grand Astrologer Zōng Xuān,
of the Zōng clan,
a descendant of Jìn Bózōng.
Bózōng originally came from Sòng Huángōng.
He observed atmospheric changes,
mistook ill omens for good,
disturbed astronomy,
and misled the court;
the Grand Tutor, Pínghuà Hóu Zūn,
adorned falsehoods to steal fame and position,
harming the sons of others;
the National Preceptor, Jiāxìn Gōng Xiù,
'xìn'
should be written as
'xīn'.
He destroyed the teaching methods,
causing scholars to be bewildered;
the Illuminating Scholar Nán Zhāng Hán and the Geographical Marquis Sūn Yáng,
created the well-field system,
making the people abandon their agricultural work;
Xīhé Lǔ Kuāng,
established the six monopolies to impoverish merchants and artisans;
the Explaining Talisman Marquis Cuī Fā,
flattered and sought favor,
preventing the sentiments of the lower classes from reaching the top;
these few individuals should be executed to appease the world!"
He also said:

Your servant fears that the new dynasty's worries are not with the Xiongnu but within its own borders."
Wáng Mǎng was enraged,
and ordered Hǔbēn to escort Lù out.
Lù's words were indeed straightforward,
but as an old official of Han, to engage in discussions with Wáng Mǎng's court,
in his conduct and silence,
was it in accordance with righteousness?
Serving a ruler like Gōng Shèng would be appropriate.
Lǔ Kuāng was demoted to Wǔyuán Zúzheng,
because the common people complained and criticized;
the six monopolies were not solely created by Kuāng,
Wáng Mǎng, appeasing public sentiment, brought them out.
Initially,
everywhere people suffering from hunger, cold, poverty, and sorrow rose up to become bandits.
Gradually
they gathered,
always hoping for a good harvest so they could return to their hometowns.
Although their numbers reached tens of thousands,
they dared not seize cities or towns.
They merely lived day by day.
Shīgǔ said: “Què
means ‘to exhaust,’
to be exhausted day by day.”
This means that the bandits only used what they plundered
to sustain themselves daily.
Què,
pronounced kōng xué fān.
The bandits did not dare to kill him (Wáng Mǎng),
yet Mǎng never understood the reason.
Shīgǔ said: “He did not understand this intention.”
The Shepherd of Jīngzhōu dispatched twenty thousand conscripts to suppress the Lùlín bandits.
The bandit leaders, Wáng Kuāng and others, led their forces to meet and engage them at Yúndù.
Xián said: “Yúndù
is a county name,
part of Jiāngxià Commandery.
Its ancient city is located northwest of present-day Miǎnyáng County, Fùzhōu.”
Dù Yòu said: “Yìngchéng County, Ānzhōu,

They killed several thousand people

The Shepherd wanted to retreat northward,
but Mǎ
Wǔ and others again ambushed him.
They hooked the Shepherd’s carriage, tearing its bǐngní.

is decorated with scarlet oil and

The bandits then attacked and captured Jìnglín.
Xián said: “Jìnglín
is a county name,
part of Jiāngxià Commandery;
its ancient city is south of Chángshòu County, Yǐngzhōu.”
Xián said: “Ānlù County
is part of Jiāngxià Commandery;
it is the present-day county of Ānzhōu.”
They returned to the Lùlín mountains,
reaching a total of over fifty thousand people.
The commanderies and counties could not control them.
Furthermore,
Lěi Sīmǎ Shì investigated a case in Yùzhōu.
Shīgǔ said: “When someone formally accuses another,
he goes and investigates the matter.”
Yùzhōu Department included Yǐngchuān, Rǔnán, Pèijùn, Liángguó, and Lǔguó.
The bandits handed him over to the county.
Shì returned
and submitted a detailed report.
Mǎng was furious,
thinking it was a fabrication.
He then issued a decree rebuking the Seven Dukes, saying:
The Seven Dukes
refer to the Four Aides and the Three Excellencies.
“An official
is one who governs.
To spread virtue and manifest kindness,
to shepherd and nourish the people,
is the way of benevolence.
To suppress the strong and oversee the wicked,
Shīgǔ said: “Dū
means to observe and inspect.”
is the principle of righteousness.
But now it is not so.
When bandits arise, they are not immediately caught,
even forming gangs to intercept and rob officials traveling by post-carriage.
Those officials who escape then falsely claim: ‘I reproached the bandits,
saying, “Why are you acting like this?”
The bandits replied,
“It is only because of poverty.”
The bandit leader then released me.’
Now, most common people who discuss this speak like this.
Only the impoverished, cold, and hungry commit crimes and wrongdoing.
The major ones become bandits,
the minor ones commit petty theft by burrowing.
Shīgǔ said: “Xuè
refers to digging through walls to steal.”
Now, they conspire and form gangs by the thousands and hundreds.
This is the greatest rebellion and disorder;
how can it be called hunger and cold!
Let the Seven Dukes strictly command their ministers, grandees, military commanders, chief commanders, and myriad magistrates
to diligently shepherd and nourish the good people,
and to swiftly capture and exterminate the bandits!
If anyone is not of one mind and exerts joint effort to hate the cunning bandits,
but falsely claims they act out of hunger and cold,
they shall be immediately arrested and imprisoned,
and their crime shall be requested for judgment!”
Meaning, to request that their crime be judged.
No one dared to report the true situation of the bandits,
and the commanderies and counties were also unable to freely dispatch troops.
Thus, the bandits could not be controlled.
Meaning, they could not be suppressed.
Only Tián Kuàng (田況), the Administrator of Yìpíng (翼平) Commandery, was naturally courageous and decisive.
He mobilized over 40,000 commoners aged eighteen and above,
armed them with weapons from the arsenal,
and made a sworn agreement with them by carving it in stone.
When Fán Chóng (樊崇) and others heard of this,
they dared not enter the commandery.
Kuàng (況) then impeached himself in a memorial to the throne, saying,
"Impeached"
is pronounced 'hù gài' (戶㮣).
"I dispatched troops without receiving a tiger tally;
this is to play with military power,
and the crime is equivalent to failing to raise an army."
Shīgǔ (師古) said: The crime of unauthorized troop dispatch
is on the same level as failing to raise military supplies.
Therefore, do not punish me for now.
Later, Kuàng (況) himself requested to go out of the commandery to attack the bandits,
and wherever he advanced, he defeated them.
Wáng Mǎng (王莽) issued an imperial decree by seal, appointing Kuàng (況) to oversee the affairs of Qīng (青) and Xú (徐) provinces.
Kuàng (況) then submitted a memorial, stating:
"When bandits first arise,
their origins are very small,
and they can be captured by local officials and commoners."
"Local officials"
refers to officials who track down bandits,
such as the bandit officials in commanderies, patrol leaders in counties, and heads of xiāng (鄉) and tíng (亭).
Shīgǔ (師古) said: "Commoners"
refers to people from the same five-household group,
like today's neighborhood watch.
"Counties deceive their commanderies,
and commanderies deceive the imperial court;
reporting ten when there are a hundred,
and a hundred when there are a thousand.
The imperial court neglects them,
failing to supervise and demand accountability promptly,
leading to the spread of the problem across provinces.
Then generals and commanders are dispatched,
and many envoys are sent,
to supervise and urge each other on.
Commanders and counties exert themselves to please their superiors,
responding and fending off interrogations."
Shīgǔ (師古) said: "Exert" (力)
means to be diligent.
"Fend off" (塞)
means to confront.
"Fend off" (塞)
is pronounced 'xī zé' (悉則).
"Interrogations" (詰)
is pronounced 'qù jí' (去吉).
"They gather supplies and resources,
hoping to avoid execution by beheading."
Shīgǔ (師古) said: They mutually fear the punishment of being beheaded.
"Gather" (共)
is read as 'gōng' (供).
"Beheaded" (斷)
is pronounced 'dīng guǎn' (丁管),
and also 'dīng luàn' (丁亂).
"Generals and commanders, moreover, cannot personally lead their officers and soldiers.
In battle, they are defeated by the bandits,
the morale of the officers is gradually damaged,
and the common people are needlessly burdened.
Recently, we were fortunate to receive an amnesty,
and the bandits desired to disband;
but some were intercepted and attacked,
causing them to flee into mountains and valleys,
spreading the word among themselves.
Consequently, the surrendered bandits in the commanderies and counties were all alarmed again,
fearing they would be tricked and annihilated.
Due to famine, they were easily incited,
and in just ten days, their numbers swelled by over a hundred thousand,
this is why the bandits are so numerous.
Now, east of Luòyáng (洛陽),
a shí (石) of rice costs two thousand coins.
I secretly saw an imperial edict planning to dispatch Grand Preceptor Wáng Kuàng (王匡) and General Gēngshǐ (更始).
These two are trusted high officials;
they will bring many followers,
and the roads will be depleted."
This refers to the lack of provisions.
"It would be better to urgently select governors and administrators,
clarify their rewards and punishments,
and gather those who have left their homes.
For small states without city walls,"
"Small states"
refers to the states of various marquises.
"They should accumulate grain and food,
and concentrate their efforts on strong defense.
If bandits come to attack the cities,
they will be unable to capture them.
With no food where they pass,
they will naturally be unable to gather.
In this way,
if we recruit them, they will surely surrender;
if we attack them, they will be annihilated.
Now, to needlessly send out more generals and commanders
would cause distress to the commanderies and counties,
even worse than the bandits.
It would be appropriate to recall all envoys traveling by post-horse
to give the commanderies and counties a respite,
and to entrust me, your subject Kuàng (況), with the task of pacifying the bandits in these two provinces."
Wáng Mǎng (王莽) feared and disliked Kuàng (況).
He feared and disliked his abilities.
"Disliked" (惡)
is pronounced 'wū lù' (烏路).
He dispatched an envoy to bestow upon Kuàng (況) an imperial decree by seal.
When the envoy arrived,
he met Kuàng (況),
and then ordered him to take over command of his troops,
sending Kuàng (況) west to Cháng'ān (長安),
where he was appointed Grand Master of the Household (師尉大夫).
After Kuàng (況) left,
the situation in Qí (齊) deteriorated.
1. In spring,
the first month,
the Nine Temples were completed,
and the spirit tablets were installed.
These were wooden tablets.
The imperial carriage was drawn by six horses,
adorned with five-colored wool woven into dragon patterns,
and green horns,
three chì (尺) long.
Shīgǔ (師古) said: This was to cover the horses.
"Green" (綠)
is pronounced 'zhì lüè' (陟略).
"Long" (長)
is pronounced 'zhí liàng' (直亮).
The *Gǔjīn Zhù* (古今註) states: The Flowered Canopy (華蓋) was made by the Yellow Emperor.
When the Yellow Emperor fought Chíyóu (蚩尤) in the plains of Zhuōlù (涿鹿),
there were always clouds with a golden branch and jade leaves;
thus, the Flowered Canopy was created.
"Heavy" (重)
is pronounced 'zhí lóng' (直龍).
It was carried on a four-wheeled cart;
those pulling it all shouted
"Ascend to immortality!"
Wáng Mǎng (王莽) came out
and ordered it to be placed in front.
All the officials secretly said:
"This resembles a funeral hearse,
not an immortal object."
2. In the second month,
Fán Chóng (樊崇) and others killed Jǐng Shàng (景尚).
Jǐng Shàng (景尚) was the one dispatched last year.
3. People east of the Pass resorted to cannibalism.
4. In summer,
the fourth month,
Grand Preceptor Wáng Kuàng (王匡) and General Gēngshǐ (更始) Lián Dān (廉丹) were dispatched eastward to suppress the various bandits.
Initially,
as the followers of Fán Chóng (樊崇) and others grew increasingly numerous,
they made an agreement among themselves:
"Those who kill will die;
those who injure will compensate for the wounds."
Among them, the most respected were called Sānlǎo (三老),
next were Cóngshì (從事),
and next were Zúshǐ (卒史).
Shīgǔ (師古) said: This means they did not take grand titles.
I believe Sānlǎo (三老), Cóngshì (從事), and Zúshǐ (卒史) were all county and commandery officials.
Chóng (崇) and others rose from among the common people, and this was all they knew.
Later, as their faction grew daily,
and their power expanded daily,
they attacked Cháng'ān (長安)
and enthroned Péngzǐ (盆子);
it was not that they initially refused to take grand titles.
Fearing that their troops would be confused with Wáng Mǎng's (王莽's) soldiers,
they all dyed their eyebrows red to identify each other,
and were thus called "Red Eyebrows" (Chìméi 赤眉).
Kuàng (匡) and Dān (丹) combined forces, leading over a hundred thousand elite soldiers,
who plundered recklessly wherever they went.
The people of the east coined a saying:
"Better to meet the Red Eyebrows,
than to meet the Grand Preceptor!
The Grand Preceptor is still tolerable,
but General Gēngshǐ will kill us!"
It turned out just as Tián Kuàng (田況) had said.
5. Wáng Mǎng (王莽) also dispatched many grandees and envoys to instruct the people to boil herbs and wood to make fermented paste.
Fú Qián (服虔) said: Boil wood fruits.
Or it is said,
it is like today's *ěr zhú* (餌朮) and similar things.
Rú Chún (如淳) said: It is like making apricot paste and similar things.
Shīgǔ (師古) said: Rú Chún's (如淳's) explanation is correct.
This again incurred trouble and expense.
6 The Lǜlín (綠林) bandits were struck by an epidemic,
and almost half of them died.
They then dispersed and withdrew.
Wáng Cháng (王常) and Chéng Dān (成丹) headed west into Nánjùn (南郡),
calling themselves
the "Xiàjiāng (下江) soldiers."
Wáng Fèng (王鳳), Wáng Kuāng (王匡), Mǎ Wǔ (馬武), and their associates Zhū Wěi (朱鮪), Zhāng Áng (張卬), and others headed north into Nányáng (南陽),
calling themselves
the "Xīnshì (新市) soldiers."
According to the Jùnguózhì (郡國志),
Xīnshì (新市) County belonged to Jiāngxià (江夏) Commandery.
The Shuǐjīngzhù (水經註) states: The seat of Xīnshì (新市) County was Dùchéng (杜城),
which belonged to Jìnglíng (竟陵) Commandery.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: The old city of Hàn's (漢) Xīnshì (新市) County
was northeast of Fùshuǐ (富水) County in Yǐngzhōu (郢州).
Wáng Mǎng (王莽) dispatched Sīmìng Dàjiàngjūn (司命大將軍) Kǒng Rén (孔仁) to manage Yùzhōu (豫州),
and Nàyán Dàjiàngjūn (納言大將軍) Yán Yóu (嚴尤) and Zhìzōng Dàjiàngjūn (秩宗大將軍) Chén Mào (陳茂) to attack Jīngzhōu (荊州).
Wáng Mǎng (王莽) bestowed the title of Dàjiàngjūn (大將軍) on all Sīqīng (司卿) and Liùqīng (六卿).
They traveled by post-carriage to their assigned regions to recruit soldiers.
Yán Yóu (嚴尤) said to Chén Mào (陳茂):
"To dispatch a general without the military tally,
requiring him to first ask for permission before acting,
is like tying up a Hán Lú (韓盧) hound and then expecting it to catch prey."
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: Xiè (紲) means
to tie up.
Hán Lú (韓盧) was
a famous dog from the ancient state of Hán (韓).
Black is called Lú (盧).
Xiè (紲)
is pronounced sī liè fān.
7 Locusts came from the east,
flying so thick they covered the sky.
8 Hundreds of thousands of displaced people entered the passes.
Officials for feeding and relief were set up to provide them with food.
Envoys supervised them,
and together with minor officials, they stole their provisions.
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: "Stole their provisions"
means stole the things that were distributed.
Earlier,
Wáng Mǎng (王莽) had sent Zhōnghuángmén (中黃門) Wáng Yè (王業) to manage market purchases in Cháng'ān (長安),
buying cheaply from the people.
The people greatly suffered from this.
Wáng Yè (王業) was credited with saving expenses
and was granted the peerage of Fùchéng (附城).
Wáng Mǎng (王莽) heard of the famine in the city
and questioned Wáng Yè (王業).
Wáng Yè (王業) said:
"They are all displaced people."
He then bought millet rice and meat soup from the market,
brought them in, and showed them to Wáng Mǎng (王ǎng), saying:
"The residents' food is all like this."
Wáng Mǎng (王莽) believed him.
9 In the autumn,
seventh month,
the Xīnshì (新市) bandit Wáng Kuāng (王匡) and others advanced to attack Suí (隨).
Xián (賢) said: Suí (隨) County
belonged to Nányáng (南陽) Commandery;
it is now Suízhōu (隨州) County.
Liào Yuán (廖元) and Chén Mù (陳牧)
formed the "Pínglín (平林) soldiers"
to respond to them.
The Xìngpǔ (姓譜) states: Liào (廖)
are descendants of Bóliáo (伯廖), the son of Zhōu Wénwáng (周文王).
The Fēngsútōng (風俗通) states: In ancient times there was Liào Shú'ān (廖叔安),
whose name is written as
"Liáo (飂)" in the Zuǒzhuàn (左傳);
presumably, they are his descendants.
The Shuǐjīngzhù (水經註) states: The Zhāngshuǐ (章水) flows south past the west of the old city of Pínglín (平林) County in Suíjùn (隨郡),
which is popularly known as Jiāngpíchéng (將陂城),
bordering Xīnshì (新市).
Xián (賢) said: Liào (廖)
is pronounced lì diào fān.
Pínglín (平林)
is a place name,
located northeast of present-day Suí (隨) County in Suízhōu (隨州).
Fù (復)
is pronounced fú yòu fān.
10 Wáng Mǎng (王莽) issued an imperial edict rebuking Lián Dān (廉丹), saying:
"The granaries are empty,
the treasuries are bare.
It is time to be enraged!
It is time to fight!
General, you bear the heavy responsibility of the state;
if you do not sacrifice yourself in the field,
you will have no way to repay the kindness and fulfill your duty!"
Lián Dān (廉丹) was terrified.
That night,
he summoned his aide Fēng Yǎn (馮衍)
and showed him the letter.
Fēng Yǎn (馮衍) then advised Lián Dān (廉丹), saying:
"Zhāng Liáng (張良) served Hán (韓) for five generations as chancellor,
and struck Qín Shǐhuáng (秦始皇) in Bólàng (博浪).
This event is found in volume 7, Qín Shǐhuáng (秦始皇) 29th year.
Shuō (說)
is pronounced yù ruì fān.
Xiàng (相)
is pronounced xī liàng fān.
You are a trusted minister of Hàn (漢).
Xián (賢) said: Lián Bāo (廉褒),
a native of Xiāngwǔ (襄武),
was Hòujiàngjūn (後將軍) during the reign of Xuāndì (宣帝),
and was an ancestor of Lián Dān (廉丹).
Outstanding heroes do not attach themselves to him.
Now the realm is in chaos,
people cherish Hàn (漢)'s virtue
even more than the people of Zhōu (周)
longed for Shàogōng (召公).
Shàogōng's (召公) teachings
were made clear in the southern states;
the people of Zhōu (周) longed for him
and composed the Gāntáng (甘棠) ode.
Shào (召)
is pronounced Shào.
Heaven will surely follow them.
Xián (賢) said: The Shī Xiǎoyá (詩小雅) states: 'Though you have no virtue to give to me,
yet I sing and dance.'
This means that people sing and dance
for the virtue of the Hàn (漢) house.
The Shū (書) states: 'What the people desire,
Heaven will surely follow.'
There is nothing better than to establish yourselves in a large commandery,
to pacify and comfort the officials and soldiers,
to sharpen your integrity,
to attract heroic and outstanding men,
to seek counsel from loyal and wise strategies,
to promote the welfare of the state,
and to remove the harm to the myriad people.
Then blessings and emoluments will flow endlessly,
and your achievements and merits will be imperishable.
Why would you let your army be destroyed in the central plains,
your body lie exposed in the wilderness,
your achievements fail, your name perish,
bringing shame upon your ancestors!"
Lián Dān (廉丹) did not listen.
Fēng Yǎn (馮衍)
was the great-grandson of Zuǒjiàngjūn (左將軍) Fèng Shì (奉世).
In winter,
Wúyán (無鹽) natives Suǒlú Huī (索盧恢) and others raised troops,
rebelled in the city, and joined the bandits.
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: Suǒlú (索盧)
is a surname.
Huī (恢)
is a given name.
The Lǚshì Chūnqiū (呂氏春秋) states: Qín Huálí (禽滑釐) had a disciple named Suǒlú Cān (索盧參).
Fǎnchéng (反城) means
to hold the city in rebellion.
Another explanation says: Fǎn (反)
is pronounced fān,
and in current speech, rebels are still called fānchéng (幡城).
Suǒ (索)
is pronounced xiān gè fān.
I believe the latter explanation is correct.
Xián (賢) said: Wúyán (無鹽) County
belonged to Dōngpíng (東平) Commandery;
its old city is now east of Xūchāng (須昌) County in Yùnzhōu (鄆州).
More than ten thousand heads were severed.
Wáng Mǎng (王莽) sent Zhōnglángjiàng (中郎將) to present an imperial letter to commend Lián Dān (廉丹) and Wáng Kuāng (王匡),
promoting them to the rank of Gōng (公).
More than ten officials and soldiers who had rendered meritorious service were enfeoffed.
The Chìméi (赤眉) separate commander Dǒng Xiàn (董憲) and others, with several tens of thousands of troops, were in Liángjùn (梁郡).
Wáng Kuāng (王匡) wanted to advance and attack them.
Lián Dān (廉丹) believed that after recently capturing a city, the troops were exhausted
and should rest to regain their morale.
Wáng Kuāng (王匡) did not listen,
and led his troops forward alone.
Lián Dān (廉丹) followed him.
They fought a combined battle at Chéngchāng (成昌).
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: Chéngchāng (成昌)
is a place name.
I believe, based on the Hòuhànshū (後漢書),
it should also be within the Wúyán (無鹽) County area.
Wáng Kuāng (王匡) fled.
Lián Dān (廉丹) ordered an officer to take his seal, sash, and tally and give them to Wáng Kuāng (王匡),
saying:
"A young man may flee,
but I cannot!"
He then remained,
and died in battle.
School captains Rú Yún (汝雲), Wáng Lóng (王隆), and more than twenty others fought separately.
Rú (汝)
is a surname.
The Zuǒzhuàn (左傳) mentions: Jìn (晉) grandee Nǚ Qí (女齊).
Lù Démíng (陸德明) said: Nǚ (女)
is pronounced Rú.
All of them said:
"Lián Gōng (廉公) is dead,
for whom shall we live!"
They charged towards the bandits
and all died in battle.
Guójiàng (國將) Āi Zhāng (哀章) personally requested to pacify Shāndōng (山東).
Wáng Mǎng (王莽) dispatched Āi Zhāng (哀章) to rush east and combine forces with Tàishī (太師) Wáng Kuāng (王匡).
He also sent Dàjiàngjūn (大將軍) Yáng Jùn (陽浚) to guard Áocāng (敖倉);
Sītú (司徒) Wáng Xún (王尋) led over ten myriad troops to garrison Luòyáng (洛陽),
and镇南宫 (Zhènnángōng);
Dàsīmǎ (大司馬) Dǒng Zhōng (董忠) raised soldiers and practiced archery in the Zhōngjūn Běilěi (中軍北壘).
It should probably be written as
"Běijūn Zhōnglěi (北軍中壘)."
11 Initially,
Chángshā Dìng Wáng gave birth to Chōnglíng Jiéhóu Mǎi,
Mǎi gave birth to Dàihóu Xióngqú,
Xióngqú gave birth to Kǎohóu Rén.
Rén, considering the south to be low and humid,
relocated his fief to Báishuǐ Xiāng in Nányáng,
and went there with his clan to settle.
Xián says: Chōnglíng
is a乡 (xiāng, township) name,
originally belonging to Línglíng Língdào Xiàn,
located north of modern-day Yǒngzhōu Tángxīng Xiàn;
in Yuándì's time,
it was moved to Nányáng,
and still called Chōnglíng;
its old city is in the east of modern-day Suízhōu Zǎoyáng Xiàn.
Dù Yòu says: Zǎoyáng
was Càiyáng Xiàn in the Later Hàn dynasty;
the old city of Hàn Chōnglíng is in the east of the present county.
His son Chǎng succeeded;
when Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
the state was abolished.
Jiéhóu's youngest son Wài became the Administrator of Yùlín.
Xián says: Yùlín Jùn
is modern-day Chēnzhōu Xiàn.
I (Yú) note that Tang dynasty Chēnzhōu had no Yùlín Xiàn,
but the Tang dynasty Guì, Liǔ, Yù, Yōng, Xiàng, Yàn, Xún, Nán, Yǐn, Lè, Róng, Bīn and other prefectures
were all territories of Hàn Yùlín Jùn.
Xián says: Jùlù Jùn
is modern-day Xíngzhōu Xiàn.
I (Yú) note that Tang dynasty Xíngzhōu indeed had Jùlù Xiàn,
and both Tang dynasty Xíng and Zhào prefectures were territories of Hàn Jùlù Jùn.
Xián says: Nándùn Xiàn
belonged to Rǔnán Jùn;
its old city is west of modern-day Chénzhōu Xiàngchéng Xiàn.
Guōdì Zhì: Chénzhōu Nándùn Xiàn
was the ancient State of Dùnzǐ;
pressured by Chén,
it moved south,
hence it was called Nándùn.
Húyáng Xiàn
belonged to Nányáng Jùn.
Sòng Bái says: Húyáng Xiàn
was the land of the ancient State of Liǎo.
Zhòng,
Xiù,
brothers, were orphaned early,
and raised by their uncle Liáng.
Yǎn was resolute and firm by nature,
generous and with great integrity.
Since Wáng Mǎng usurped the Hàn throne,
he was always indignant,
harboring thoughts of restoring the imperial rule.
He did not concern himself with family business,
but spent his fortune and broke his family
to associate with heroes and outstanding men from all over the land.
Xiù had a high nose and a sun-like forehead.
Xián says: Lóng
means high.
Xǔ Fù said: The tip of the nose is called zhǔn.
Zhèng Xuán's commentary on the Shàngshū Zhōnghóu says: Rìjiǎo (sun-like forehead)
refers to a prominent bone on the forehead resembling the sun.
Xián says: Sowing is called jià,
harvesting is called sè.
He was compared to Gāozǔ's elder brother Zhòng.
Xián says: Zhòng
was Héyánghóu Xǐ,
who was skilled in managing property.
Gāozǔ, when offering a toast to Tàishànghuáng, said: "Initially, my father always said I could not manage property
as well as Zhòng;
now, regarding what I have achieved,
who has more, me or Zhòng?"
Xiù once went with Chén to visit Cài
Shǎogōng, a man from Ráng.
Shǎogōng, who had studied mantic charts and prognostication texts,
said,
"Liú Xiù is destined to be the Son of Heaven."
Someone asked,
"Is it Guóshīgōng Liú Xiù?"
Xiù joked,
"How do you know it isn't me?"
Everyone sitting there burst into laughter.
Chén was secretly pleased.
Lǐ Shǒu, a man from Wǎn,
was fond of astronomy, calendars, and prognostication texts.
He was Wáng Mǎng's Zōngqīngshī.
Xián says: In the fifth year of Píngdì,
Wáng Mǎng served as acting regent,
and Zōngshī were appointed in commanderies and states to oversee the imperial clan.
Perhaps they were honored at that time, hence called Zōngqīngshī.
I (Yú) note that Mǎng appointed Zōngshī
only to oversee the Hàn imperial clan.
This Zōngqīngshī
was appointed by Mǎng when he usurped the throne.
"The Liú clan shall rise,
and the Lǐ clan shall assist."
When the New City (Xīnshì) and Pinglin (Pínglín) troops rose,
Nányáng was in turmoil.
Lǐ Tōng's cousin Yì said to Tōng:
"Now the four directions are in chaos,
and the Hàn dynasty is about to be restored.
Among the Nányáng imperial clan,
only Liú Bóshēng and his brothers are broad-minded and accommodating to the masses.
We can conspire with them for a great undertaking."
Yǎn's
courtesy name was Bóshēng.
"This is my intention!"
It so happened that Xiù was selling grain in Wǎn.
Tōng sent Yì to welcome Xiù,
and they met.
Yì then fully explained the matter of the prognostication texts,
and they made an agreement
and settled on a plan.
Tōng wanted to, on the day of the autumn official trial for the cavalry,
seize the Former Division (Qiánduì) Grandee (Dàfū) Zhēn Fù and the Subordinate Director (Shǔzhèng) Liángqiū Cì.
Mǎng renamed Nányáng "Former Division,"
and established the position of Grandee (Dàfū) like an Administrator (Tàishǒu),
and the position of Subordinate Director (Shǔzhèng) like a Commandant (Dūwèi).
Shīgǔ says: Duì
is pronounced suì.
Zhēn
is pronounced like zhī-rén.
He ordered Yì and Xiù to return to Chōnglíng to raise troops to respond.
Thereupon, Yǎn summoned the heroes and outstanding men to deliberate, saying:
"Wáng Mǎng is tyrannical,
and the people are scattered and broken.
Now, continuous drought for years
and widespread military uprisings
signify the time of Heaven's destruction
and the restoration of Gāozǔ's legacy,
establishing the autumn of ten thousand generations!"
He meant establishing the empire to be passed down for ten thousand generations,
and that this was the time.
Thereupon, he dispatched his trusted associates to various counties to raise troops,
and Yǎn himself mobilized the youths from Chōnglíng.
The youths from various families were frightened
and all fled into hiding,
saying:
"Bóshēng will kill us!"
But when they saw Xiù in his crimson robe and great crown,
Dǒng Bā's Yúfú Zhì says: The great crown
was worn by military officers.
Dōngguān Jì: At that time, the emperor's crimson robe and great crown
were the general's attire.
They said: "Even the cautious and honest are doing it!"
Then they gradually felt at ease.
Altogether, they gathered seven or eight thousand youths
and organized their retainers and guests,
calling themselves
"Zhùtiān Dūbù" (Pillars of Heaven General Command).
Xián says: Zhùtiān
means like the pillars of heaven.
Dūbù means to command all the troops.
Before Lǐ Tōng could act,
the matter was discovered,
and he fled.
His father Shǒu and sixty-four family members were implicated and executed.
Yǎn sent his clansman Jiā to persuade the Xīnshì and Pínglín troops,
and with their leaders Wáng Fèng and Chén Mù,
attacked Chángjù to the west.
They advanced and massacred Tángzǐ Xiāng.
Xián says: Tù (屠) means to kill many.
Tángzǐ Xiāng has Tángzǐ Shān,
southwest of modern-day Tángzhōu Húyáng Xiàn.
The division of spoils in the army was unequal,
and the troops were resentful
and wanted to turn against the Liú clan.
Liú Xiù collected all the items his clansmen had obtained
and distributed them to the troops,
who then were pleased.
They advanced and captured Jíyáng.
Xián says: Zǎoyáng
is a county name,
belonging to Nányáng Jùn,
located north of Jíshuǐ.
It was the ancient State of Xiè;
its old city is northwest of modern-day Tángzhōu Húyáng Xiàn.
Jí
is pronounced jì-lì.
Yán Yóu and Chén Mào defeated the Xiàjiāng troops.
Chéng Dān, Wáng Cháng, Zhāng Áng and others gathered the scattered soldiers and entered Lóuxī,
plundering the area between Zhōng and Lóng,
and their forces revived.
They led their army to battle the Administrator of Jīngzhōu at Shàngtáng.
Xián says: Shàngtáng
is a乡 (xiāng, township) name; its old city is northeast of modern-day Suízhōu Zǎoyáng Xiàn.
Shuǐjīng Zhù: Shàngtáng was originally Shàngtáng Xiāng of Càiyáng Xiàn,
and the State of Táng during the Spring and Autumn period.
a comet appeared in Zhāng.
Xián says: Zhāng
is a southern constellation.
Xùhàn Zhì says: Zhāng represents the territory of Zhōu.
Jìnshū Tiānwén Zhì: Zhāng has six stars,
north of the Heavenly Temple.
Bèi is pronounced pú-nèi.
14 Liú Yǎn (劉縯) wanted to advance and attack Wǎn (宛).
When they reached Xiǎocháng'ān Jù (小長安聚),
Xián (賢) said: The *Xù Hànshū* (續漢書) states: In Yùyáng Xiàn (淯陽縣) there is Xiǎocháng'ān Jù (小長安聚).
The old city is now south of Nányáng Xiàn (南陽縣) in Dèngzhōu (鄧州).
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: Nányáng (南陽),
was Wǎn Xiàn (宛縣) in the Hàn (漢) dynasty;
thirty-seven *lǐ* (里) south of the county seat is Xiǎocháng'ān (小長安).
At that time, the sky was covered in dense fog,
and the Hàn (漢) army suffered a great defeat.
Liú Xiù (秀) fled on a lone horse.
He met his younger sister Bó Jī (伯姬),
and they rode together to escape.
Continuing forward,
he again saw his elder sister Yuán (元).
He urged her to get on the horse,
but Yuán (元) waved her hand and said:
"Go!
I cannot be saved,
there's no need for both of us to perish!"
Just then, the pursuing soldiers arrived.
Yuán (元) and three other women all died.
Liú Yǎn's (縯) younger brother Zhòng (仲) and dozens of relatives also died.
Liú Yǎn (縯) again gathered his troops,
and returned to defend Jíyáng (棘陽).
Zhēn Fù (甄阜) and Liángqiū Cì (梁丘賜), emboldened by their victory, left their baggage train at Lánxiāng (藍鄉).
Xián (賢) said: Bǐyáng Xiàn (比陽縣) has Lánxiāng (藍鄉).
重 (zhòng),
read *zhí yòng fān*.
Xián (賢) said: Lì Dàoyuán's (酈道元) *Shuǐjīng Zhù* (水經註) states: The waters of the two lakes flow into [each other],
combining to form the Huángshuǐ (黃水);
further south, it passes through Huángchún Jù (潢淳聚) in Jíyáng Xiàn (棘陽縣),
also called Huángchún Shuǐ (潢淳水).
It is now in Húyáng Xiàn (湖陽縣) in Tángzhōu (唐州).
*Shuǐjīng Zhù* (水經註): The Bǐshuǐ (沘水) emerges from Mount Dàhú (大胡山) northeast of Bǐyáng Xiàn (沘陽縣),
and flows south to meet the Lǐshuǐ (澧水),
which is called Pàishuǐ (派水).
In the past, Hàn Guāngwǔ (漢光武) defeated Zhēn Fù (甄阜) and Liángqiū Cì (梁丘賜) at
the west of Bǐshuǐ (沘水),
and slew them at this river.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: The old city of Hàn Wǔyáng (漢舞陽) is north of Bìyáng Xiàn (泌陽縣) in Tángzhōu (唐州);
there is the Bìshuǐ (泌水),
south of the county,
where Guāngwǔ (光武) defeated Fù (阜) and Cì (賜).
They broke the bridge behind them,
showing no intention of returning.
Xīnshì (新市) and Pínglín (平林) saw the Hàn (漢) army defeated several times,
and the armies of Fù (阜) and Cì (賜) arrived in great numbers,
so they each wanted to disband and leave.
Liú Yǎn (縯) was very worried about this.
Just then, over five thousand soldiers from Xiàjiāng (下江) arrived at Yíqiū (宜秋).
Xián (賢) said: Yíqiū (宜秋) is a settlement name,
in Bǐyáng Xiàn (沘陽縣).
I checked the *Xù Hàn Zhì* (續漢志),
and there is Yíqiū Jù (宜秋聚) in Píngshì Xiàn (平氏縣) of Nányáng (南陽).
"We wish to see an able general from Xiàjiāng (下江)
to discuss important matters."
The crowd nominated Wáng Cháng (王常).
Liú Yǎn (縯) met Wáng Cháng (常),
and persuaded him of the benefits of alliance.
Xián (賢) said: To ally for mutual benefit is *cóng* (從).
說 (shuō),
read *shū ruì fān*;
same below.
從 (cóng),
read *zǐ róng fān*.
"Wáng Mǎng (王莽) is cruel and tyrannical;
the people long for the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
Now the Liú (劉) clan is rising again,
they are the true ruler.
If you sincerely dedicate yourself to their cause,
and help achieve this great accomplishment,
then, should the cause succeed," Liú Yǎn (縯) said,
"how could I dare to enjoy it alone!"
So he and Wáng Cháng (常) formed a deep bond and Wáng Cháng (常) departed.
Wáng Cháng (常) returned,
and fully recounted this to the other generals, Chéng Dān (成丹) and Zhāng Áng (張卬).
Wáng Cháng (常) had met Liú Yǎn (縯),
while the other two generals were in the army.
為 (wèi),
read *yú wěi fān*.
將 (jiàng),
read *jí liàng fān*.
"When a true man rises,
he should each be his own master.
Why should we be controlled by others?"
Wáng Cháng (常) then slowly enlightened and persuaded his commanders, saying:
"Wáng Mǎng (王莽) is harsh and cruel,
and has long lost the hearts of the people.
The people's lamentations and longing for the Hàn (漢)
is not a matter of a single day.
This is why we have been able to rise.
That which the people resent,
Heaven abandons;
that which the people long for,
Heaven grants.
To undertake a great enterprise,
one must certainly follow the will of the people below,
and accord with the will of Heaven above,
only then can success be achieved.
If one relies on strength and courage,
acting on impulse and indulging desires,
even if one gains the world,
one will certainly lose it again.
With the power of Qín (秦) and Xiàng (項),
they still ended in ruin.
How much more so for us, commoners gathered in the wilds,
to act in such a way,
that is the path to destruction.
Now, the various Liú (劉) families of Nányáng (南陽) have raised
troops.
Observing those who came to discuss,
they all have profound strategies and great foresight,
the talent of kings and dukes.
If we unite with them,
we will certainly achieve great success.
This is how Heaven is assisting us!"
Although the generals from Xiàjiāng (下江) were stubborn and lacked insight,
屈強 (qūqiáng) means
stubborn and perverse.
屈 (qū),
pronunciation *jū wù fān*.
強 (qiáng),
pronunciation *qí liǎng fān*.
少 (shǎo),
pronunciation *shī zhǎo fān*.
They all acknowledged and said:
"Without General Wáng (王將軍),
we would have almost fallen into injustice!"
They immediately led their troops to join the Hàn (漢) army, Xīnshì (新市), and Pínglín (平林).
Thereupon, all the divisions united with one heart and one mind,
and their morale grew stronger.
Liú Yǎn (縯) gave a great feast to the soldiers,
established an alliance,
rested the troops for three days,
and divided them into six divisions.
On the last day of the twelfth month,
they secretly moved their army during the night,
attacked and captured Lánxiāng (藍鄉),
seizing all its baggage train.
