後 學 天 台
Huáiyáng Wáng (淮陽王)
His given name was Xuán (玄),
courtesy name Shènggōng (聖公),
he was a paternal cousin of Guāngwǔ (光武).
*Dìwáng Shìjì* (帝王世紀) states: Chōnglíng Dàihóu Xióngqú (舂陵戴侯熊渠) begat Cāngwǔ Tàishǒu Lì (蒼梧太守利);
Lì (利) begat Zǐzhāng (子張);
Zǐzhāng (子張) begat Xuán (玄).
Later, he was defeated,
and surrendered to the Chìméi (赤眉).
Guāngwǔ (光武) issued an edict to enfeoff him as Huáiyáng Wáng (淮陽王).
The first year of Gēngshǐ (更始)
1 Spring,
first month.
On the *jiǎzǐ* (甲子) day, the first day of the month,
the Hàn (漢) army and the Xiàjiāng (下江) army jointly attacked Zhēn Fù (甄阜) and Liángqiū Cì (梁丘賜),
beheaded them,
and killed over twenty thousand soldiers.
Wáng Mǎng's (王莽) Nàyán Jiāngjūn Yán Yóu (納言將軍嚴尤) and Zhìzōng Jiāngjūn Chén Mào (秩宗將軍陳茂) led their troops, intending to occupy Wǎn (宛).
Liú Yǎn (劉縯) fought them below Yùyáng (淯陽).
The *Xù Hàn Zhì* (續漢志) states:
Yùyáng Xiàn (淯陽縣) belonged to Nányáng Jùn (南陽郡).
Xián (賢) said: The old city is now south of Nányáng Xiàn (南陽縣) in Dèngzhōu (鄧州), on the sunny side (*yáng*) of the Yùshuǐ (淯水),
hence the name.
淯 (yù),
pronunciation *yù*.
Then they besieged Wǎn (宛).
Before this,
although the bandits from Qīng (青) and Xú (徐) numbered in the hundreds of thousands,
they utterly lacked official documents,
commands, banners, or organized divisions.
Shīgǔ (師古) said: 文 (wén)
refers to writings.
號 (hào)
refers to great titles.
Another says: 號 (hào)
refers to commands.
先 (xiān),
read *xī jiàn fān*.
They all called themselves generals,
attacked cities and seized territory,
and sent letters of persuasion.
"Letters of persuasion"
means enumerating Wáng Mǎng's (王莽) crimes.
They initially feared [Wáng Mǎng].
Liú Xuán 劉玄, great-grandson of the Marquis Dài 戴 of Chūnlíng 舂陵, was among the Pínglín 平林 troops
and was styled General Gēngshǐ 更始.
At this time, the Hàn 漢 forces already numbered over 100,000.
The generals deliberated that with so many troops and no unified command,
they wished to establish a member of the Liú 劉 clan to satisfy popular expectation.
The powerful figures of Nányáng 南陽 and Wáng Cháng 王常 and others all wished to establish Liú Yǎn 劉縯.
However, the generals of Xīnshì 新市 and Pínglín 平林, who delighted in license,
feared Yǎn’s 縯威명 awe-inspiring reputation,
and coveted Xuán’s 玄懦弱 weakness and pliability.
They first together decided on a strategy to establish him,
and then summoned Yǎn 縯 to show him their deliberation.
Yǎn 縯 said:
"It is indeed generous of you generals to wish to honor and establish a member of the imperial clan!
Very generous!
However, the Chìméi 赤眉 (Red Eyebrows) have risen in Qīng 青 and Xú 徐,
numbering several hundred thousand.
If they hear that the imperial clan has been established in Nányáng 南陽,
I fear the Chìméi 赤眉 will also establish someone."
Later, the Chìméi 赤眉 indeed established Pénzǐ 盆子.
"Fù 復"
is pronounced "fú yòu fān" 扶又翻.
"This casts doubt on the empire and diminishes our own authority."
This means that if members of the imperial clan contend for power,
then the empire will not know whom to follow,
which casts doubt on the hearts of the people and diminishes their own authority.
"Chūnlíng 舂陵 is only three hundred *lǐ* 里 from Wǎn 宛.
To hastily establish ourselves
as the standard for the empire,
allowing future generations to inherit our weaknesses,
is not a good plan.
It would be better to temporarily claim the title of king to issue commands;
the power of a king is also sufficient to execute generals.
If the one established by the Chìméi 赤眉 is worthy,
we will lead our forces to follow him,
and he will surely not seize our titles and positions.
If they have established no one,
then after defeating Wáng Mǎng 王莽
and pacifying the Chìméi 赤眉,
to then assume the exalted title
would not be too late."
Many generals said,
"Excellent!"
Zhāng Áng 張卬 drew his sword and struck the ground,
According to *Kǎoyì* 考異, Sīmǎ Biāo’s 司馬彪 *Xù Hànshū* 續漢書
writes "Áng" 卬
as
"Yìn" 印;
Yuán Hóng’s 袁宏 *Hòuhàn Jì* 後漢紀 writes
"Jīn" 斤.
Both are errors.
We follow Fàn Yè’s 范曄 *Hòuhànshū* 後漢書.
"Hesitating in action accomplishes nothing!"
This is from *Zhànguócè* 戰國策,
the words of Féiyì 肥義 to Zhào Wǔlíng Wáng 趙武靈王.
"There can be no second thought!"
All the assembled troops followed this.
In the second month,
on the *xīnsì* 辛巳 day which was the first day of the month,
an altar was set up on the sands by the Yùshuǐ 淯水.
*Shuǐjīng Zhù* 水經註 says: The Yùshuǐ 淯水 originates from Gōnglí Shān 攻離山 in Lúshì Xiàn 盧氏縣, Hóngnóng 弘農.
It flows southeast past the northwest of Xī’è Xiàn 西鄂縣, Nányáng 南陽,
then east past the south of Wǎn Xiàn 宛縣.
The generals established the "Sacred Duke" (Shènggōng 聖公) beside this water.
He stood facing south,
receiving the homage of his officials.
Ashamed and sweating,
he raised his hands but could not speak.
Thereupon, a general amnesty was declared,
and the reign era was changed.
His clan elder Liáng 良 was made Grand Elder of the State (Guósānlǎo 國三老).
Wáng Kuāng 王匡 was made Senior Duke Stabilizing the State (Dìngguó Shànggōng 定國上公).
Wáng Fèng 王鳳 was made Senior Duke Establishing the State (Chéngguó Shànggōng 成國上公).
Zhū Wěi 朱鮪 was made Grand Minister of War (Dà Sīmǎ 大司馬).
Liú Yǎn 劉縯 was made Grand Minister of Education (Dà Sītú 大司徒).
Chén Mù 陳牧 was made Grand Minister of Works (Dà Sīkōng 大司空).
The rest were all Nine Ministers (Jiǔ Qīng 九卿) and Generals.
Kuāng 匡 and Fèng 鳳 were both given the rank of Senior Duke (Shànggōng 上公) and honored with the fine titles of Dìngguó 定國 and Chéngguó 成國.
"Nine Ministers and Generals" (Jiǔ Qīng Jiāngjūn 九卿將軍) means
their official positions were Nine Ministers,
each bearing the title of General,
following Wáng Mǎng’s 王莽 system.
Many were displeased.
The powerful figures had wished to establish Yǎn 縯, but now Xuán 玄 was established,
hence their disappointment.
Wáng Mǎng 王莽, wishing to outwardly show his composure,
dyed his beard and hair,
and established a daughter of Shǐ Chén 史諶 of Dùlíng 杜陵 as empress.
He set up a harem,
with one hundred and twenty positions, whose ranks were equivalent to Dukes, Ministers, Grandees, and Senior Scholars (Gōng 公, Qīng 卿, Dàfū 大夫, Yuánshì 元士).
The Three Ladies (Sān Fūrén 三夫人) were equivalent to the Three Dukes (Sān Gōng 三公).
The Nine Concubines (Jiǔ Pín 九嬪) were equivalent to the Nine Ministers (Jiǔ Qīng 九卿).
The Twenty-seven Court Ladies (Èrshíqī Shìfù 二十七世婦) were equivalent to the Twenty-seven Grandees (Èrshíqī Dàfū 二十七大夫).
The Eighty-one Imperial Wives (Bāshíyī Yùqī 八十一御妻) were equivalent to the Eighty-one Senior Scholars (Bāshíyī Yuánshì 八十一元士).
Mǎng 莽 issued a general amnesty throughout the empire,
declaring:
"Wáng Kuāng 王匡,
Āi Zhāng 哀章, and others are attacking the bandits in Qīng 青 and Xú 徐.
Yán Yóu 嚴尤, Chén Mào 陳茂, and others are attacking the ugly captives of the vanguard.
Clearly proclaim to them the promise of life and a clean slate."
Shī Gǔ 師古 says: "Life" (shēnghuó 生活)
means that those who surrender will not be killed.
"A clean slate" (dānqīng zhī xìn 丹青之信)
means it is clearly stated.
"I will dispatch the Grand Minister of Works (Dà Sīkōng 大司空), the Duke Lóngxīn (Lóngxīn Gōng 隆新公), to lead an army of a million to utterly exterminate them."
In the third month,
Wáng Fèng 王鳳, together with the Grand Master of Ceremonies and Partial General (Tàicháng Piānjīangjūn 太常偏將軍) Liú Xiù 劉秀 and others, marched through Kūnyáng 昆陽, Dìnglíng 定陵, and Yǎn 郾,
and captured them all.
Xián 賢 says: Kūnyáng 昆陽, Dìnglíng 定陵, and Yǎn 郾
are all county names,
all belonging to Yǐngchuān Jùn 潁川郡.
The old city of Kūnyáng 昆陽
is located twenty-five *lǐ* 里 north of Yè Xiàn 葉縣, Xǔzhōu 許州 today.
Yǎn 郾 is
today’s Yǎnchéng Xiàn 郾城縣, Yùzhōu 豫州.
Dìnglíng 定陵 is
northwest of today’s Yǎnchéng 郾城.
"Yǎn" 郾
is pronounced "yú jiàn fān" 於建翻.
I, Yu 余, note that according to the old *Tángshū* 唐書,
in the winter of the second year of Xiánhēng 咸亨 of Gāozōng 高宗,
he held a hunting expedition on the southern bank of the Kūnshuǐ 昆水 in Yè Xiàn 葉縣, Xǔzhōu 許州.
Wáng Mǎng 王莽, upon hearing of the defeat of Yán Yóu 嚴尤 and Chén Mào 陳茂,
dispatched Minister of Works (Sīkōng 司空) Wáng Yì 王邑 by rapid relay,
together with Minister of Education (Sītú 司徒) Wáng Xún 王尋, to raise troops and pacify the region east of the mountains (Shāndōng 山東).
He summoned sixty-three families expert in military law to serve as army officers,
and appointed the giant Jù Mǔbà 巨毋霸 as rampart commandant (lěiwèi 壘尉).
Zhèng Xuán 鄭玄 says: A military encampment is called a *lěi* 壘.
Xián 賢 says: A *lěiwèi* 壘尉
is in charge of matters concerning ramparts and encampments.
When Yì 邑 arrived at Luòyáng 洛陽,
each province and commandery selected elite troops,
and the regional governors themselves led them.
The number of those who had assembled reached forty-three
million men,
styled a "million-strong army" (bǎiwàn 百萬).
As for the rest still on the road,
their banners and pennants, and their baggage train,
stretched for a thousand *lǐ* 里 without break.
Xián 賢 says: *Zhōulǐ* 周禮 says: Feathers are split to make a *jīng* 旌,
bears and tigers are used for a *qí* 旗.
*Zī* 輜
is a type of cart.
*Shìmíng* 釋名 says: *Zī* 輜
means "to pile up" (cè 廁),
referring to military provisions and various items piled up and loaded;
because of their heavy load,
they are called *zīzhòng* 輜重 (baggage train).
"Zhòng" 重
is pronounced "zhí yòng fān" 直用翻.
In the fifth month,
Xún 尋 and Yì 邑 marched south into Yǐngchuān 潁川,
and joined forces with Yán Yóu 嚴尤 and Chén Mào 陳茂.
When the generals saw the formidable forces of Xún 尋 and Yì 邑,
they all turned and fled,
entering Kūnyáng 昆陽.
They were terrified,
worried about their wives and children,
and wanted to disperse and return to various cities.
Liú Xiù 劉秀 said:
"Now our troops and provisions are few
while the enemy outside is powerful.
If we combine our strength to resist them,
we might still achieve success.
If we wish to disperse,
there is no way for all of us to survive.
Moreover, Wǎnéng Chéng 宛城 has not yet been taken."
Xián 賢 says: This refers to Bóshēng’s 伯升 (Liú Yǎn 劉縯) siege of Wǎn 宛 which had not yet been taken.
"If Kūnyáng 昆陽 is captured,
within a day,
all our other divisions will also be annihilated.
Will you now not be of one heart and mind to jointly achieve fame and glory,
but instead wish to guard your wives, children, and possessions?"
The generals angrily said:
"How dare General Liú 劉 speak like this!"
Xiù 秀 smiled and stood up.
Just then, a scout returned,
reporting:
"A large army is about to arrive north of the city.
Their formation stretches for hundreds of *lǐ* 里.
Its rear is out of sight."
The generals had always looked down upon Xiù 秀,
but now that they were in dire straits,
they said to each other:
"Let us again ask General Liú 劉 for his plan."
Xiù 秀 again outlined a strategy for victory or defeat,
and all the generals said:
"Yes."
At that time, there were only eight or nine thousand men in the city.
Xiù 秀 ordered Wáng Fèng 王鳳 and the Grand General of the Court of Justice (Tíngwèi Dàjiāngjūn 廷尉大將軍) Wáng Cháng 王常 to defend Kūnyáng 昆陽,
while he himself, with the General of Five Military Prowesses (Wǔwēi Jiāngjūn 五威將軍) Lǐ Yì 李軼 and thirteen riders,
went out at night
Xián 賢 says: Wáng Mǎng 王莽 established the Five Military Prowess Generals (Wǔwēi Jiāngjūn 五威將軍).
Their clothing followed the colors of the five directions,
to awe the empire.
When Lǐ Yì 李軼 first rose,
he still borrowed this title.
I, Yu 余, say that titles like Grand Master of Ceremonies and Partial General (Tàicháng Piānjīangjūn 太常偏將軍) and Grand General of the Court of Justice (Tíngwèi Dàjiāngjūn 廷尉大將軍)
were also like Mǎng’s 王莽 Grand General of the Master of Words (Nàyán Dàjiāngjūn 納言大將軍) and Grand General of the Minister of Rites (Zhìzōng Dàjiāngjūn 秩宗大將軍);
these are what were previously referred to as "Nine Ministers and Generals" (Jiǔ Qīng Jiāngjūn 九卿將軍).
to gather troops outside.
At that time, Wáng Mǎng's (王莽) troops, numbering almost 100,000, arrived beneath the city walls.
Liú Xiù (劉秀) and the others almost failed to get out.
Wáng Xún (王尋) and Wáng Yì (王邑) then unleashed their troops to surround Kūnyáng (昆陽).
Yán Yóu (嚴尤) advised Wáng Yì (王邑), saying:
"Kūnyáng (昆陽) is a small but strong city.
The one falsely claiming to be emperor is now in Wǎn (宛).
'The one falsely claiming to be emperor'
refers to Gēngshǐ Dàdì (更始大帝).
He will surely flee there;
if Wǎn (宛) falls,
Kūnyáng (昆陽) will submit on its own."
Wáng Yì (王邑) replied:
"When I besieged Zhái Yì (翟義) in the past,
I failed to capture him alive.
(The incident involving Zhái Yì (翟義) can be found in Volume 36, in the second year of Wáng Mǎng's (王莽) regency.)
(Xián (賢) said: Zuò (坐),
pronounced wò.)
Now I lead a million troops;
if I encounter a city and cannot take it,
that is not the way to display my might.
We should first slaughter this city,
advance through blood,
singing in front and dancing behind.
Is that not exhilarating?!"
So they surrounded it with dozens of layers of troops,
setting up hundreds of camps.
The sound of gongs and drums could be heard for tens of lǐ (里).
Some dug tunnels and used battering rams to assault the city.
(Xián (賢) said: Chōng (衝)
refers to a battering ram (橦車);
the Shī Jīng (詩經) says: '臨衝閑閑'.)
(Xǔ Shèn (許慎) said: Píng (輣)
refers to a siege tower (樓車).)
(Píng (輣)
is pronounced bù gēng.)
(Zhuàng (撞)
is pronounced zhàng jiāng.)
Arrows fell like rain,
and the people inside the city drew water by taking shelter behind doors.
Wáng Fèng (王鳳) and others begged for surrender,
but it was not granted.
Wáng Xún (王尋) and Wáng Yì (王邑) considered their victory to be a matter of time,
and were not concerned with military affairs.
Yán Yóu (嚴尤) said:
"The Art of War states: 'When besieging a city, leave a gap.' "
(Shīgǔ (師古) said: This is a quote from the Art of War.)
(Quē (闕)
means 'incomplete'.)
(Sūn Zǐ (孫子) said: 'When besieging an army, leave a gap.')
(Cáo Cāo (曹操) noted: 'The Sīmǎ Fǎ (司馬法) says: Surround three sides of it,
leaving one side open,
to show a path to life.')
Wáng Yì (王邑) still did not listen.
Zēn Péng (岑彭), the Administrator (守長) of Jíyáng (棘陽),
(The Xìng Pǔ (姓譜) states: Cén (岑)
are descendants of the ancient Cénzǐ (岑子) State.)
(The Lǚ Shì Chūnqiū (呂氏春秋) states: King Wén (文王) of Zhōu (周) enfeoffed Qú (渠), the son of Yào (耀) (his half-brother), as Cénzǐ (岑子).)
(Its territory is the Cén Tíng (岑亭) of Liáng Guó (梁國).)
(Péng (彭) was from Jíyáng (棘陽),
and served as the Administrator (守長) of his home county.)
(Zhǎng (長)
is pronounced zhī liǎng.)
(Èr (貳)
means 'deputy'.)
(Wáng Mǎng (王莽) appointed him as deputy to Zhēn Fù (甄阜), the Dàfū (大夫) of the vanguard.)
The Hàn (漢) army attacked it for several months.
The people in the city resorted to cannibalism,
and then surrendered the entire city.
Gēngshǐ (更始) then made it his capital.
The generals wanted to kill Zēn Péng (岑彭),
but Liú Yǎn (劉縯) said:
"Zēn Péng (岑彭)
is a high official of the commandery.
To steadfastly hold his position
is a mark of his integrity.
Now that we are undertaking a great endeavor,
we should honor righteous men.
It would be better to enfeoff him."
Gēngshǐ (更始) then enfeoffed Zēn Péng (岑彭) as Guīdé Hóu (歸德侯).
(Xián (賢) said: Guīdé (歸德)
is a county name,
belonging to Běidì Jùn (北地郡).)
(Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Huáchí Xiàn (華池縣) in Qìngzhōu (慶州)
was originally the land of Hàn (漢) Guīdé Xiàn (歸德縣).)
(Also,
northwest of Tōngyuǎn Jūn (通遠軍) is Guīdé Chuān (歸德川).)
Liú Xiù (劉秀) arrived at Yǎn (郾) and Dìnglíng (定陵),
and mobilized all the troops from the various camps.
The generals were greedy and cherished their wealth and goods,
wishing to divide their troops to guard them.
Liú Xiù (劉秀) said:
"If we defeat the enemy now,
our treasures will multiply ten thousandfold, and great achievements can be made.
If we are defeated,
not even our heads will remain.
What wealth and goods would there be then?!"
So he mobilized all of them.
In the sixth month,
on the day of Jǐmǎo (己卯) at the new moon,
Liú Xiù (劉秀) advanced with all the camps.
He personally led over a thousand infantry and cavalry as the vanguard,
arraying them four or five lǐ (里) from the main army.
Wáng Xún (王尋) and Wáng Yì (王邑) also sent several thousand troops to engage in battle.
Liú Xiù (劉秀) charged them,
beheading dozens.
(Xián (賢) said: According to Qín (秦) law,
beheading one person
conferred one rank of nobility.
Hence, 'beheading' was referred to as 'level' or 'rank'.)
"General Liú (劉將軍) is usually timid when facing a small enemy,
but now he is brave when facing a large enemy.
This is very strange!
Let me take the front again;
I ask to assist the general!"
Liú Xiù (劉秀) advanced again,
and Wáng Xún (王尋) and Wáng Yì's (王邑) troops retreated.
The various units jointly pressed on them,
beheading several hundred to a thousand.
(From several hundred ranks up to a thousand ranks.)
(Fù (復)
is pronounced fú yòu.)
As they advanced,
the generals' courage grew stronger,
and each one was able to contend with a hundred.
Liú Xiù (劉秀) then led three thousand 'dare-to-die' soldiers from the west side of the city along the water to charge into their strong center.
(Xián (賢) said: 'Dare-to-die'
refers to those who are brave and willing to die.)
(In all military matters,
the commander of the central army is supreme,
and supported by the strongest and sharpest forces,
hence it is called the 'strong center'.)
(I believe 'dare-to-die' refers to
those who dare to commit themselves to death.)
He personally led over ten thousand troops in a formation.
(Shīgǔ (師古) said: To patrol the military formation.)
(Xíng (行)
is pronounced xià gēng.)
(Chén (陳)
is read as zhèn;
same below.)
Wáng Xún (王尋) fought alone against the Hàn (漢) army,
but was at a disadvantage.
The main army dared not move to rescue him.
Wáng Xún (王尋) and Wáng Yì's (王邑) formation was in disarray,
and the Hàn (漢) army, seizing the momentum, shattered them,
subsequently killing Wáng Xún (王尋).
The people inside the city also beat drums and shouted as they came out.
The forces from within and without united,
their thunderous roars shaking heaven and earth.
Wáng Mǎng's (王莽) army suffered a great rout;
those who fled trampled over each other,
with corpses covering over a hundred lǐ (里).
At that moment, there was a great thunderstorm and wind;
roof tiles all flew off,
and rain poured down.
The Zhìchuān (滍川) river overflowed greatly.
(The Shuǐ Jīng (水經) states: The Zhì Shuǐ (滍水) originates from Mount Yáo (堯山) west of Lǔyáng Xiàn (魯陽縣) in Nányáng (南陽),
flows southeast passing north of Kūnyáng Chéng (昆陽城),
and enters the Rǔ (汝) to the east.)
(Zhì (滍)
is pronounced zhí lǐ.)
Tens of thousands of soldiers drowned in the water.
(Xián (賢) said: The number exceeded ten thousand,
so it is expressed as 'tens of thousands'.)
Wáng Yì (王邑), Yán Yóu (嚴尤), and Chén Máo (陳茂) used light cavalry to cross the water over the dead bodies and escape.
All their military supplies and heavy baggage were captured,
too numerous to count.
It took months to carry them away,
and some of the remainder was burned.
The soldiers fled,
each returning to their own commandery.
Wáng Yì (王邑) alone returned to Luòyáng (洛陽) with several thousand brave men from Cháng'ān (長安) whom he commanded.
The Guānzhōng (關中) region was terrified upon hearing this.
Thereupon, heroes and magnates throughout the realm responded enthusiastically,
(Yǐngxiǎng (響應) means 'to respond like an echo'.)
proclaiming themselves generals,
and using the Hàn (漢) era name to await imperial decrees.
Within ten days or a month,
this spread throughout the world.
When Wáng Mǎng (王莽) heard the Hàn (漢) army claim that he had poisoned and killed Emperor Xiàopíng (孝平皇帝),
he assembled the Gōngqīng (公卿) in Wánglù Táng (王路堂),
and opened the golden casket documents for which he had requested a mandate for Emperor Píng (平帝).
(This matter can be found in Volume 36, in the sixth year of Emperor Píng's (平帝) Yuánshǐ (元始) reign.)
(Wéi (為)
is pronounced yú wěi.)
9 Liú Xiù (劉秀) again campaigned in Yǐngchuān (潁川).
He attacked Fùchéng (父城) but could not take it.
Xián (賢) said: Fùchéng (父城)
is a county name.
Its old city is in the northeast of today’s Yèxiàn (葉縣), Xǔzhōu (許州).
Rúzhōu (汝州)’s Jiāchéngxiàn (郟城縣) also has a Fùchéng (父城).
Fù (復)
is pronounced Fú Yòu;
the same below.
Xián (賢) said: Jīnchē (巾車)
is a village name,
within the borders of Fùchéng (父城).
It was captured by the Hàn (漢) army.
Yì (異) said:
"I have an old mother in Fùchéng (父城).
I wish to return
and hold five cities to demonstrate my merit and repay your kindness!"
Xiù (秀) agreed.
Yì (異) returned
and said to Miáo Méng (苗萌), the prefect of Fùchéng (父城):
"Many generals are violent and unruly,
but only General Liú (劉) does not plunder wherever he goes.
Observing his words and actions,
he is no ordinary man!"
Thereupon, he and Méng (萌) led five counties to surrender.
10 The generals of Xīnshì (新市) and Pínglín (平林) saw that the prestige of Liú Yǎn (劉縯)’s brothers was growing,
and secretly encouraged Gēngshǐ (更始) to eliminate them.
Xiù (秀) said to Yǎn (縯):
"Things are about to turn bad."
Meaning Gēngshǐ (更始) intended to plot against them.
"It's always like this."
Gēngshǐ (更始) held a grand assembly of generals
and took Yǎn (縯)’s precious sword to examine it.
The embroidered-robed censor Shēntú Jiàn (申徒建) then presented a jade *jué* (玦).
Shēntú (申徒)
is Shēntú (申屠).
Xián (賢) said: *Jué* (玦)
means *jué* (決), to decide quickly.
Yǎn (縯)’s maternal uncle Fán Hóng (樊宏) said to Yǎn (縯):
"Could Jiàn (建) not have the intention of Fàn Zēng (范增)?"
The story of Fàn Zēng (范增) is found in Volume 9, Emperor Gāo (高) Year 1.
Lǐ Yì (李軼) was initially friendly with Yǎn (縯)’s brothers,
but later fawned upon the new favorites.
New favorites
refers to Zhū Wěi (朱鮪) and others.
"This person cannot be trusted again!"
Yǎn (縯) did not listen.
Yǎn (縯)’s subordinate general Liú Jì (劉稷)
was the bravest in the three armies.
Hearing that Gēngshǐ (更始) had been enthroned,
he angrily said:
"The ones who originally raised troops for a great cause
were Bóshēng (伯升) and his brothers.
What is Gēngshǐ (更始) doing now?!"
Gēngshǐ (更始) appointed Jì (稷) as General Kàngwēi (抗威),
but Jì (稷) refused to accept the appointment.
He refused to bow and accept the order of Kàngwēi (抗威).
So, Jì (稷) was arrested first,
and was about to be executed.
Yǎn (縯) strongly argued against it.
Lǐ Yì (李軼) and Zhū Wěi (朱鮪) then persuaded Gēngshǐ (更始) to also arrest Yǎn (縯)
and killed him that very day.
His paternal cousin, the Grand Minister of the Household, Cì (賜), was made Grand Minister of Works.
Cì (賜) was of the same ancestry as Gēngshǐ (更始), the Administrator of Cāngwú (蒼梧), Lì (利).
Xiù (秀) rode from Fùchéng (父城) to Wǎn (宛) to apologize.
Xián (賢) said: Because Bóshēng (伯升) was killed,
he felt uneasy,
so he apologized.
He was Yǎn (縯)’s official.
He returned due to suspicion.
He took the blame upon himself.
He also dared not mourn for Yǎn (縯),
and ate, spoke, and laughed as usual.
Gēngshǐ (更始) was ashamed of this,
and appointed Xiù (秀) as General-in-Chief Pòlǔ (破虜),
and enfeoffed him as Marquis Wǔxìn (武信).
11 The Daoist Xīmén Jūnhuì (西門君惠) said to Wáng Mǎng (王莽)’s General of the Guards, Wáng Shè (王涉):
"The *chèn* texts say the Liú (劉) clan will revive,
and the name of the State Preceptor Gōng (公) matches this."
Shè (涉) then conspired with State Preceptor Gōng (公) Liú Xiù (劉秀), Grand Marshal Dǒng Zhōng (董忠), and Sìzhōng Dàzhuì (司中大贅) Sūn Jí (孫伋),
to use their subordinate troops to force Mǎng (莽) to surrender to Hàn (漢),
to save their clans.
Shè (涉) wanted to save the Wáng (王) clan.
Jiàng (降)
is pronounced Hù Jiāng.
In the seventh month,
Jí (伋) reported their plot to Mǎng (莽).
Mǎng (莽) summoned Zhōng (忠) and interrogated him,
then struck and killed him.
He ordered the Tiger-swift guards to chop Zhōng (忠) with "horse-chopping swords,"
arrested his clan members,
and buried them together in one pit with strong vinegar, poison, white blades, and thorny brambles.
Xiù (秀) and Shè (涉) both committed suicide.
Mǎng (莽), considering them his kin and old ministers,
was afraid of internal collapse,
so he concealed their execution.
Shīgǔ (師古) said: Wáng Shè (王涉) was kin;
Liú Xīn (劉歆) was an old minister.
I note from Mǎng (莽)’s biography
that Shè (涉) was
the son of Quányáng Hóu (曲陽侯) Gēn (根).
È (惡)
is pronounced Wū Lù.
When high officials rebelled internally,
he had no one left and right he could trust.
In ancient times, the words *wáng* (亡) and *wú* (無) were interchangeable.
So, he recalled Wáng Yì (王邑)
to be Grand Marshal,
made Grand Chamberlain Zhāng Hán (張邯) Grand Minister of Works,
Cuī Fā (崔發) Grand Minister of War,
and Sìzhōng Shòuróng (司中壽容) Miáo Xīn (苗訢) State Preceptor.
Mǎng (莽) was so depressed he could not eat,
only drank wine
and ate *guǐfù* (蜭鰒) fish.
When tired from reading military documents,
he would lean on his desk and doze off,
no longer using a pillow.
12 Wěi Cuī (隗崔) and Wěi Yì (隗義) of Chéngjì (成紀).
Chéngjì (成紀) county
belonged to Tiānshuǐ (天水) Commandery.
Xián (賢) said: Its old city is in the northwest of today’s Lǒngchéngxiàn (隴城縣), Qínzhōu (秦州).
Pí (陴) is a surname
originating from the Chìdí (赤狄).
Shàngguī (上邽) county
belonged to Lǒngxī (隴西) Commandery.
Xián (賢) said: The old Guīróng (邽戎) settlement
is now Qínzhōu (秦州) county.
Jì (冀) county
belonged to Tiānshuǐ (天水) Commandery.
Qín Wǔgōng (秦武公) attacked the Jìróng (冀戎)
and then established a county there.
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Qínzhōu (秦州) is administered from Lǒngchéngxiàn (隴城縣),
which is the old Jìchéng (冀城).
They attacked Píngxiāng (平襄)
and killed Mǎng (莽)’s Zhenróng Dàyǐn (鎮戎大尹) Lǐ Yù (李育).
Xián (賢) said: Píngxiāng (平襄)
is a county name,
belonging to Tiānshuǐ (天水) Commandery. Its old city is in the northwest of today’s Fúqiāngxiàn (伏羌縣), Qínzhōu (秦州). Wáng Mǎng (王莽) renamed Tiānshuǐ (天水) Commandery to Zhenróng (鎮戎).
He was famous for his integrity
and fond of classics.
Cuī (崔) and others jointly elected him as Supreme General.
Cuī (崔) became White Tiger General,
and Yì (義) became Left General.
Cuī (崔) originally appointed himself Right General;
the White Tiger is located on the right,
and he started his rebellion in the west,
which the White Tiger governs,
so he changed the title of Right General to White Tiger General.
They made him Army Advisor.
Xián (賢) said: Pínglíng (平陵)
is Emperor Zhāo (昭)’s mausoleum,
and a county was named after it.
Its old city is in the northwest of today’s Xiányángxiàn (咸陽縣).
When King Wǔ (武) attacked Zhòu (紂),
he made Tàigōng (太公) his teacher and revered father.
Tián Dān (田單), defending Jìmò (即墨),
made a single soldier a divine teacher.
Hán Xìn (韓信), after defeating Zhào (趙),
took Lǐ Zuǒchē (李左車) as his teacher.
All were army advisors.
Later, it became an official title.
It is east of Píngxiāngyì (平襄邑).
Shuō (說)
is pronounced Shū Ruì.
On the *jǐsì* day,
they offered sacrifices to Gāozǔ (高祖), Tàizōng (太宗), and Shìzōng (世宗).
Xiāo (囂) and others all declared themselves subjects and performed their duties,
slaughtered horses to form an alliance,
to revive and assist the Liú (劉) clan.
They sent proclamations to commanderies and kingdoms,
enumerating Mǎng (莽)’s crimes.
They commanded an army of 100,000
and attacked and killed Chén Qìng (陳慶), the Inspector of Yōngzhōu (雍州), and Wáng Xiàng (王向), the Grand Administrator of Āndìng (安定).
Mǎng (莽) renamed the Hàn (漢) Liángzhōu (涼州) to Yōngzhōu (雍州).
Xiàng (向)
was the son of Píng’ā Hóu (平阿侯) Wáng Tán (王譚).
*Kǎoyì* (考異) says: Wáng Mǎng (王莽)’s biography writes
"Zuòzhèng (卒正) Wáng Xún (王旬)";
Yuán Jì (袁紀) writes
"Grand Administrator Wáng Xiàng (王向)";
we now follow Fàn (范)’s book.
All of them were captured.
13 At first,
Gōngsūn Shù (公孫述) of Máolíng (茂陵) was the Chief of Qīngshuǐ (清水).
Xián (賢) says: Qīngshuǐ (清水)
is a county name,
belonging to Tiānshuǐ (天水) Commandery;
it is now the county of Qínzhōu (秦州).
He was promoted to Colonel of Dǎojiāng (導江) Front Troops,
governing Línqióng (臨邛).
Xián (賢) says: Wáng Mǎng (王莽) renamed Shǔ (蜀) Commandery as Dǎojiāng (導江).
Línqióng (臨邛)
is now the county of Qióngzhōu (邛州).
Bān Zhì (班志) states that
Línqióng (臨邛) County belonged to Shǔ (蜀) Commandery.
Qióng (邛)
is pronounced Qúróng (渠容) fān.
Zōng Chéng (宗成) of Nányáng (南陽) and the merchant Wáng Cén (王岑) raised troops to plunder Hànzhōng (漢中) in response to Hàn (漢).
Zōng Chéng (宗成)
was a native of Nányáng (南陽).
The Dìlǐ Zhì (地理志) states that
Shāng (商) County
belonged to Hóngnóng (弘農) Commandery.
Xián (賢) says: This is now the Shāngluò (商雒) County of Shāngzhōu (商州).
Their combined forces numbered several tens of thousands.
Shù (述) sent envoys to welcome Chéng (成) and others.
When Chéng (成) and others reached Chéngdū (成都),
the Dìlǐ Zhì (地理志) states that
Chéngdū (成都) County
belonged to Shǔ (蜀) Commandery.
Shù (述) summoned the local magnates and said:
"The whole world suffers from the Xīn (新) dynasty
and has longed for the Liú (劉) clan for a long time.
Therefore, when they heard of the arrival of the Hàn (漢) general,
they rushed to welcome him on the roads.
Now innocent commoners have their wives and children seized and captured.
These are bandits,
not righteous troops."
So he sent someone to falsely claim to be a Hàn (漢) envoy,
who bestowed upon Shù (述) the seals and ribbons of General Who Assists Hàn (輔漢將軍), Administrator of Shǔ (蜀) Commandery, and concurrently Governor of Yìzhōu (益州).
He selected elite troops and attacked Chéng (成) and others to the west,
killing them.
According to this, Línqióng (臨邛) is southwest of Chéngdū (成都).
Shù's (述) troops marched from Línqióng (臨邛) to intercept Zōng Chéng (宗成) and others,
which was not westward.
This follows the error in Fàn Shǐ (范史).
14 Previously, Liú Wàng (劉望), Marquis of Zhōngwǔ (鍾武), raised troops in Rǔnán (汝南).
According to the Wángzǐ Hóu Biǎo (王子侯表): Zhōngwǔ Jié Hóu Dù (鍾武節侯度),
grandson of Chángshā Dìng Wáng (長沙定王),
was enfeoffed as marquis in the second year of Yuányán (元延) of Emperor Chéng (成帝).
His descendants are not mentioned.
Perhaps Wàng (望) was the son of his descendant?
Zhōngwǔ (鍾武) is within the boundary of Yìyáng (義陽) Commandery.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù (水經註) says: The Shī (師) River flows past Yìyáng (義陽) Commandery city
and eastward past the south of the old city of Zhōngwǔ (鍾武).
Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Wáng Mǎng Zhuàn (王莽傳) writes
"Liú Shèng (劉聖),"
but we follow the Liú Xuán Zhuàn (劉玄傳) in Fàn Shū (范書) here.
In the eighth month,
Wàng (望) ascended the throne as emperor,
appointing Yóu (尤) as Grand Marshal and
Mào (茂) as Chancellor.
15 Wáng Mǎng (王莽) sent Grand Tutor Wáng Kuāng (王匡) and State General Āi Zhāng (哀章) to defend Luòyáng (洛陽).
Gēngshǐ (更始) sent Dìngguó Shànggōng (定國上公) Wáng Kuāng (王匡) to attack Luòyáng (洛陽),
and Xīpíng Dàjiāngjūn (西屏大將軍) Shēntú Jiàn (申屠建) and Chéngxiàng Sīzhí (丞相司直) Lǐ Sōng (李松) to attack Wǔguān (武關).
Lǐ Sōng (李松)
was Tōng's (通) younger cousin.
Píng (屏)
is pronounced Bìyǐng (必郢) fān.
Dèng Yè (鄧曄) and Yú Kuāng (于匡) of Xī (析) raised troops in Nánxiāng (南鄉) in response to Hàn (漢).
Shīgǔ (師古) says: Xī (析)
is a county of Nányáng (南陽).
Nánxiāng (南鄉) is the name of a xiāng (鄉) in Xī (析) County.
Sòng Bái (宋白) says: Dèngzhōu Nèixiāng (鄧州內鄉) County
is the ancient Xī (析)邑.
Xī (析)
is pronounced Xiānlì (先歷) fān.
Méng (萌) surrendered;
they advanced to attack the Right Column Grandee Sòng Gāng (宋綱),
killing him.
Mǎng (莽) renamed Hóngnóng (弘農) Commandery as Yòuduì (右隊).
Shīgǔ (師古) says: Hú (湖)
is a county of Hóngnóng (弘農),
originally belonging to Jīngzhào (京兆).
The source is unknown.
Cuī Fā (崔發) said:
"In ancient times, when a state faced a great disaster,
they would weep to ward it off."
Shīgǔ (師古) says: The duty of the priestesses among the officials of the Spring Office in the Zhōulǐ (周禮) states: "Whenever there is a great disaster in the state,
they sing and weep to pray."
Weeping is
a way to express sorrow.
In the Zuǒshì Zhuàn (左氏傳) of the Chūnqiū (春秋): In the twelfth year of Xuān (宣),
the Chu (楚) ruler besieged Zhèng (鄭) for seventeen days.
The people of Zhèng (鄭) wailed greatly,
and all those guarding the parapets wept.
Therefore, Fā (發) quoted this as his words.
Yàn (厭)
is pronounced Yīyè (一葉) fān.
Mǎng (莽) then led his officials to the southern suburb,
presented the full account of his auspicious omens,
cried out to Heaven,
and when his breath was exhausted,
he prostrated himself and kowtowed.
Scholars and commoners gathered morning and evening to weep,
and they were provided with meals and gruel.
Those who grieved most profoundly
were appointed as Láng (郎),
numbering over five thousand people.
Mǎng (莽) appointed nine generals,
all given the title Hǔ (虎) (Tiger).
He sent several tens of thousands of elite troops from the Northern Army eastward,
placing their wives and children in the palace as hostages.
At that time, there were still over six hundred thousand catties of gold in the palace,
and other valuables in proportion.
Mǎng (莽) cherished it even more,
granting each of the Nine Tiger officers four thousand coins.
The masses heavily resented this
and had no will to fight.
The Nine Tigers reached Huáyīn (華陰) Huíxī (回谿).
Xián (賢) says: Huíxī (回谿)
is what is now popularly called Huíhéng (回阬),
northeast of Yǒngníng (永寧) County in Luòzhōu (洛州).
The gully is four lǐ (里) long,
two zhàng (丈) wide,
and two zhàng (丈) five chǐ (尺) deep.
Huá (華)
is pronounced Hùhuà (戶化) fān.
Yú Kuāng (于匡) and Dèng Yè (鄧曄) attacked them,
and six Tigers fled.
Two Tigers went to the palace gate to face death,
and Mǎng (莽) sent envoys to demand where the dead were;
they all committed suicide.
The other four Tigers escaped.
The two Tigers who committed suicide were
Shǐ Xióng (史熊) and Wáng Kuàng (王況).
As for the four Tigers who escaped,
their names are omitted in history.
The three Tigers were
Guō Qīn (郭欽), Chén Huī (陳翬), and Chéng Zhòng (成重).
Shīgǔ (師古) says: Jīngshī Cāng (京師倉)
is at Guànběi Wèikǒu (灌北渭口) in Huáyīn (華陰).
Dèng Yè (鄧曄) opened Wǔguān (武關) to welcome the Hàn (漢) troops.
Lǐ Sōng (李松), with over three thousand men, reached Hú (湖),
and together with Yè (曄) and others attacked Jīngshī Cāng (京師倉),
but it had not yet fallen.
Yè (曄) appointed Wáng Xiàn (王憲), a clerk from Hóngnóng (弘農), as Commandant,
leading several hundred men to cross the Wèi (渭) River northward
and enter the territory of Zuǒfēngyì (左馮翊).
Lǐ Sōng (李松) sent General Piān (偏將軍) Hán Chén (韓臣) and others directly westward to Xīnfēng (新豐) to attack
Mǎng's (莽) Bōshuǐ (波水) General.
According to the Dòu Róng Zhuàn (竇融傳),
Mǎng (莽) appointed Róng (融) as Bōshuǐ (波水) General.
The Qián Shū Yīnyì (前書音義) says: Bōshuǐ (波水)
is south of Cháng'ān (長安).
Wáng Xiàn (王憲) went north to Pínyáng (頻陽),
and all those he passed welcomed him and surrendered.
Shīgǔ (師古) says: Wherever he passed,
people all came to welcome and submit to him.
He led his troops to follow Xiàn (憲).
Lǐ Sōng (李松) and Dèng Yè (鄧曄) led their armies to Huáyīn (華陰),
while troops from around Cháng'ān (長安) converged on the city.
They also heard that Kuí (隗) of Tiānshuǐ (天水) was about to arrive,
and all vied to
enter the city,
eager for great achievements and the spoils of plunder.
It means entering the city to execute Mǎng (莽),
thereby achieving great merit and obtaining plunder;
they were greedy for both benefits.
They were all given weapons,
killed a pig,
drank its blood,
and swore an oath, saying:
"Anyone who does not serve the Xīn (新) dynasty
shall be recorded by the spirits of the earth!"
They made Gēngshǐ (更始) General Shǐ Chén (史諶) lead them.
They crossed the Wèi (渭) Bridge,
but all scattered and fled,
and Chén (諶) returned empty-handed.
The soldiers excavated the tombs of Mǎng's (莽) wife, son, father, and ancestors,
burned their coffins and outer coffins, as well as the Nine Temples, Míngtáng (明堂), and Bìyōng (辟雍),
and the fire lit up the city.
In the ninth month,
on the day Wùshēn,
the soldiers entered through the Xuānpíng city gate.
Shīgǔ said: “This is the first gate at the northern end of the eastern side of Cháng’ān City.”
Wáng Yì, Wáng Lín, Wáng Xún, Tuǒyùn, and others divided their troops to resist the attack beneath the northern watchtower.
By dusk,
government offices and private residences were all abandoned.
On the day Jǐyǒu,
city youths Zhū Dì and Zhāng Yú, fearing plunder,
rushed and shouted in unison.
Shīgǔ said: “The crowd moved boisterously, echoing each other.”
Huān
is pronounced Xǔyuán.
Hé
is pronounced Hūwò.
Chéng Dàchāng said: “Zhàozuòshì refers to places like the weaving and punishment workshops northwest of Wèiyāng Gōng,
which the Huángtú calls the workshops of Shàngfāng.
The Zuòshì Mén was the gate for artisans to enter and exit,
presumably a side gate of Wèiyāng Gōng.”
Shīgǔ said: “Jìngfǎ
is the name of a hall.
Tà
means a small gate.
It refers to chopping them with axes.”
“Rebellious usurper Wáng Mǎng,
why do you not surrender!”
The fire reached Yètíng and Chéngmíng.
This was where Huánghuángshìzhǔ resided.
Huánghuángshìzhǔ said:
“How can I face the Hàn family!”
She threw herself into the fire and died.
Mǎng avoided the fire in the Xuānshì Qiándiàn,
but the fire invariably followed him.
Mǎng wore a deep blue uniform.
Shīgǔ said: “Gàn
is a deep blue with a reddish hue.
Jūn
means pure, purely a deep blue garment.”
Jūn
is pronounced Jūn,
and also Yìxún.
“How could Yú Dì have a dagger?”
This was Mǎng’s own doing to fool his consort.
Shīgǔ said: “Shì
is used to predict times and days.
Tiānwén Láng
is a modern-day user of the shì.”
He said:
“Heaven bestows virtue upon me,
what can the Hàn forces do to me!”
Mǎng quoted Confucius’s words to compare himself.
On the day Gēngxū
at dawn,
his attendants supported Mǎng from the Qiándiàn to the Jiàntái.
Dukes, ministers, and officials, more than a thousand people, followed him.
Wáng Yì had fought day and night,
utterly exhausted;
nearly all his soldiers were dead or wounded;
he galloped into the palace,
and with difficulty reached the Jiàntái.
Shīgǔ said: “Jiānguān
is synonymous with qíqū,
meaning circuitous or arduous.”
Yì shouted at them,
ordering them to return,
and father and son jointly guarded Mǎng.
Soldiers entered the hall,
heard that Mǎng was on the Jiàntái,
and together surrounded it in several hundred layers.
On the platform, they still shot arrows at each other.
When the arrows were exhausted,
they engaged in close combat;
Wáng Yì and his son, Tuǒyùn, and Wáng Xún died in battle.
Mǎng entered a room.
At xiàbū time,
the soldiers ascended the platform.
Būhòu
is called xiàbū.
According to the “Tiānwén Zhì” of the former history: from dawn to shíshí,
from shíshí to rìyì,
from rìyì to bū,
from bū to xiàbū,
from xiàbū to rìrù.
The merchant Dù Wú killed Mǎng,
and Commandant Dōnghǎi Gōngbīn Jiù decapitated Mǎng.
Shīgǔ said: “Gōngbīn is the surname,
Jiù is the given name.
The Fēngsú Tōng says: he was a descendant of Lǔ Grand Master Gōngbīn Gēng.”
Wáng Mǎng was fifty-one when he became regent,
fifty-four when he truly ascended the throne,
and sixty-eight when he was executed.
His body was dismembered and cut into pieces,
and dozens of people fought and killed each other over them;
Gōngbīn Jiù took Mǎng’s head to Wáng Xiàn.
Xiàn declared himself the Hàn Grand General,
and tens of thousands of soldiers in the city all submitted to him;
he lodged in the Dōnggōng,
Shīgǔ said: “Shè
means to reside or lodge.”
and used his carriages and attire.
On the day Guǐchǒu,
Lǐ Sōng and Dèng Yè entered Cháng’ān,
and Generals Zhào Méng and Shēntú Jiàn also arrived;
because Wáng Xiàn had obtained the imperial seals and ribbons but did not present them,
and kept many palace women,
and erected the Son of Heaven’s drums and banners,
they arrested and executed him.
Mǎng’s head was sent to Wǎn,
and displayed in the marketplace;
the common people collectively struck it,
and some even cut off and ate his tongue.
Bān Gù’s eulogy says: Wáng Mǎng initially rose as an imperial maternal relative,
humbled himself and diligently acted to gain reputation.
When he held office and assisted in governance,
he worked hard for the state,
and acted with integrity.
Was he not one of those “who seize benevolence in appearance but act contrary to it”?
Shīgǔ said: “This is recorded in the Analects, Confucius’s reply to Zǐzhāng.
An inhumane person assumes the appearance of a humane person,
but his actions contradict it.”
Xíng
is pronounced Xiàmèng.
Moreover, he exploited the power accumulated over generations by his four ancestors,
encountered the Hàn dynasty in decline,
with its succession thrice broken.
Chéng, Āi, and Píng all had no heirs.
He became their spiritual leader,
and thus was able to unleash his treachery to achieve the disaster of usurpation.
Judging from this,
it was also a matter of opportune timing (Heaven’s will),
not merely the result of human effort!
When he usurped the throne and faced south,
the danger of overthrow was more perilous than that of Jié and Zhòu,
yet Mǎng remained at ease, believing himself to be Huáng Dì and Yú Shùn reborn.
Huáng Dì and Yú Shùn were Mǎng’s ancestors.
Fù
is pronounced Fúyòu.
He unleashed his power and deceit,
spreading poison throughout Zhūxià,
and extending chaos to the Mán and Hé barbarians,
yet it was still not enough to satisfy his desires.
Therefore, within the four seas,
everyone loudly lost their joy in life.
Shīgǔ said: “Xiāorán
describes the worried appearance of many mouths, pronounced Wúgāo.”
Sàng
is pronounced Xīlàng.
Both near and far revolted,
city walls were unguarded,
the body politic was dismembered,
and thus the cities and towns of the realm became desolate,
harm spread to all living beings.
Among the treacherous ministers and rebellious sons recorded in historical texts,
examining their ruinous failures,
none were as extreme as Mǎng’s!
In ancient times, Qín burned the Odes and Documents to establish private doctrines;
Mǎng recited the Six Arts to embellish his wicked words.
Shīgǔ said: “He used the affairs of the Six Classics to adorn his wicked words.”
Both met their demise,
all were merely driven away by the Sage King.
Sū Lín said: “The Sage King is Guāngwǔ,
driven away for Guāngwǔ.”
Shīgǔ said: “It means to expel and purge in anticipation of a sage.”
16 Dìngguó Shànggōng Wáng Kuāng captured Luòyáng,
and took Mǎng’s Grand Preceptor Wáng Kuāng and Āi Zhāng alive,
executing them both.
In winter,
the tenth month,
General Fènwēi Dà Jiāngjūn Liú Xìn attacked and killed Liú Wàng in Rǔnán.
Xìn
was the son of Dà Sītú Cì’s elder brother Xiǎn.
All commanderies and counties surrendered.
17 Gēngshǐ planned to make Luòyáng his capital.
He appointed Liú Xiù acting Sīlì Xiàowèi
and sent him ahead to organize and repair the imperial palace and government offices.
The Sīlì Xiàowèi inspected the Sānfǔ, Sānhé, and Hóngnóng areas,
hence he was tasked with organizing and repairing the imperial palace and government offices.
He wrote official documents,
and the Dōngguān Jì states: "Wénshū Yí refers to documents transferred to subordinate counties."
Everything was as in previous regulations.
The Xù Hànshū states: "The Sīlì office had twelve Cóngshì Shǐ,
each with a salary of one hundred shí,
who were responsible for overseeing documents
and investigating illegal activities."
When seeing generals commit transgressions,
they all wore juànzè and women's clothing.
The Hàn Guān Yí states: "A zé
was worn by the lowly and those who did not wear caps in ancient times."
The Fāngyán states: "A head covering is called a zé,
or sometimes Chénglù."
Liú Zhāo Zhì states: "When Qín dominated the feudal lords,
they added a head ornament for military generals,
making it a jiàngpà to distinguish noble from common;
later, it was gradually made into yántí.
When Hàn arose,
they continued the yán,
pushed the luǒ back,
applied a jīn,
connected the tí and covered it,
naming it zé.
The zé
was a zé (meaning 'complexion' or 'seriousness'),
making the head and face solemn and serious.
By the time of Xiàowén,
the yántí was raised,
the jīn was elevated,
made into a roof,
joined at the back,
and fastened both above and below.
All officials, noble and common, wore it;
civil officials had long ears,
and military officials had short ears."
When they saw the Sīlì's subordinates,
everyone was so delighted that they couldn't contain themselves.
Some old clerks shed tears, saying:
"We never expected to see the awe-inspiring presence of Hàn officials again today!"
Because of this, all who recognized him placed their trust in him.
Gēngshǐ moved his capital north to Luòyáng,
and dispatched envoys to tour the commanderies and kingdoms,
saying:
"Those who surrender first will have their titles and positions restored!"
When an envoy reached Shànggǔ,
the Hàn Shànggǔ Commandery,
whose seat was Jǔyáng,
he presented the seal and ribbon.
The envoy accepted it,
stayed for one night,
and showed no intention of returning it.
The Gōngcáo, Kòu Xún, led soldiers to see the envoy,
and asked for it back.
The Xìngpǔ states: "Sū Fènshēng was Sīkòu for King Wǔ of Zhōu,
and his descendants adopted Kòu as their surname based on the office."
The Bǎiguān Zhì states: "The Jùn Gōngcáo was responsible for selecting and evaluating meritorious deeds,
and was above all other Cáo."
The envoy said:
"You are the Heavenly King's envoy;
does the Gōngcáo intend to threaten you?!"
Xún said:
"I do not dare to threaten Your Excellency.
I am merely concerned that your plan is not well considered.
Today, the world is newly settled.
Your Excellency carries credentials and a mandate,
and all commanderies and kingdoms eagerly await your arrival.
Now, you have just arrived in Shànggǔ and have already broken a great trust.
How then will you issue commands to other commanderies?"
The envoy did not respond.
Xún shouted at his attendants to summon Kuàng by the envoy's order.
When Kuàng arrived,
Xún stepped forward, took the seal and ribbon, and placed it on Kuàng.
The envoy, having no other choice,
then officially issued an edict to him.
Kuàng accepted it and returned.
Péng Chǒng from Wǎn and Wú Hàn, who were exiles in Yúyáng,
had Hán Hóng, a fellow villager, become Gēngshǐ's envoy,
touring the northern provinces.
He officially appointed Chǒng as acting Piānjiāngjūn,
managing the affairs of the Yúyáng Tàishǒu,
thus laying the groundwork for Péng Chǒng to hold Yúyáng.
Xián said: "Ānlè
is a county name,
belonging to Yúyáng Commandery.
Its ancient city is northwest of modern Yōuzhōu Lù Xiàn.
Lè
is pronounced Luò."
Gēngshǐ sent envoys to pacify the Chìméi.
He dispatched envoys to persuade and pacify them,
asking them to surrender and lay down their arms;
this is inferred later.
Jiàng (surrender)
is pronounced Hù Jiāng fān.
He kept their soldiers,
and
about twenty of their leaders accompanied the envoys to Luòyáng.
Gēngshǐ enfeoffed them all as Lièhóu.
However, since Chóng and the others had no actual territories,
and their remaining troops gradually began to desert,
they returned to their camp.
Chóng and the others were camped in Púyáng at the time.
This laid the groundwork for the Chìméi to attack Gēngshǐ.
18 Wáng Mǎng's Lújiāng Liánshuài, Lǐ Xiàn from Yǐngchuān, held his commandery and defended himself,
proclaiming himself King of Huáinán.
19 Yǒng, the son of the former King Lì of Liáng, went to Luòyáng;
Lì's death is mentioned in volume 36, Píngdì Yuánshǐ fourth year.
His capital was Suīyáng.
This laid the groundwork for Yǒng to occupy Liáng and gather bandits.
Suī
is pronounced suī.
20 Gēngshǐ wanted to send his close generals to campaign in Héběi.
Dà Sītú Cì said:
"Among the family members, only Wénshū is suitable."
Zhūjiāzǐ refers to the various clan members from Nányáng.
Guāngwǔ's personal name was Xiù,
and his courtesy name was Wénshū.
Gēngshǐ was hesitant,
but Cì strongly urged him;
Gēngshǐ then appointed Liú Xiù acting Dà Sīmǎ,
to hold the jié and cross the Yellow River north,
to pacify and comfort the provinces and commanderies.
This laid the groundwork for Guāngwǔ to stabilize the world from Héběi.
21 He appointed Dà Sītú Cì as Chéngxiàng,
ordering him to first enter Guānzhōng to repair the ancestral temples and palaces.
He planned to make Cháng'ān his capital.
22 When Dà Sīmǎ Xiù arrived in Héběi,
in every commandery and county he passed through,
he investigated officials,
promoted the capable and dismissed the incompetent,
released prisoners,
and abolished Wáng Mǎng's harsh policies.
Xián said: "The Shuōwén says: 'Kē is a small grass;'
it implies that the decrees were numerous and detailed."
Officials and common people rejoiced,
competing to bring cattle and wine to welcome and entertain him,
but Xiù refused them all.
Nányáng’s Dèng Yǔ (鄧禹) held his staff and followed Xiù (秀),
catching up with him at Yè (鄴).
Xiù said:
"I can personally bestow titles and appointments.
You have come a long way.
Do you wish to serve in an official capacity?"
Yǔ said:
"I do not."
Xiù said:
"If that is the case,
what do you wish to do?"
Yǔ said:
"I only wish that your illustrious general's (mínggōng 明公) might and virtue spread throughout the four seas,
and that Yǔ (禹) may contribute his small measure,
leaving his achievements and fame on bamboo and silk (zhúbó 竹帛)!"
In the early Hàn (漢) dynasty, there was no paper,
so writing was done on bamboo slips and fine silk (jiānsù 縑素);
hence the phrase "bamboo and silk (zhúbó 竹帛)."
He then stayed the night and conversed privately (jiānyǔ 間語).

Xián says: Liáo
means to roast.
Proceeding to the west of Xiàbó city,
Xián said: Xiàbó Xiàn,
belonged to Xìndū Guó;
being below the Bó Shuǐ,
it was therefore called Xiàbó;
its old city was south of the present-day Xiàbó Xiàn in Jìzhōu.
There was an old man in white clothes by the roadside,
Xián said: He was probably a divine being.
There is a shrine west of present-day Xiàbó Xiàn.
"Strive on!
Xìndū Jùn is defending Cháng'ān Chéng,"
Xián said: Xìndū Jùn,
is present-day Jìzhōu.
為 (wèi),
pronounced yú wěi.
Xiù immediately hastened to it.
At this time, all the commanderies and kingdoms had already surrendered to Wáng Láng,
only the Administrator of Xìndū, Rèn Guāng from Nányáng, and the Administrator of Héróng, Pī Róng from Xìndū, refused to comply.
The Dōngguān Jì says: Wáng Mǎng divided Xìndū into Héróng,
located in Xiàqūyáng.
Pī Róng Zhuàn writes
"Héchéng".
The character Chéng is correct.
The Fēngsú Tōng says: Xī Zhòng was the Carriage Master for Xià,
enfeoffed in Pī,
his descendants took this as their clan name. Tóng,
pronounced yú zhōng.
"I fear we cannot keep it intact,"
Xián said: Being defended alone without reinforcements,
hence the fear.
Greatly rejoiced;
the officials and common people all cheered, "Long live!"
Pī Róng also came from Héróng to meet them.
Many of the deliberators said that they could use the Xìndū troops to escort themselves,
and return west to Cháng'ān.
Pī Róng said;
"The officials and common people have been longing for the Hàn for a long time,
hence when Gēngshǐ raised his imperial title, the empire responded,
the Sānfǔ cleared the palaces and roads to welcome him.
Now this diviner Wáng Láng,
using a false name and taking advantage of circumstances,
has gathered a disorderly rabble,
and thus shaken the lands of Yān and Zhào.
Zhèn,
means to raise.
Your Excellency must rally the troops of the two commanderies to campaign against him.
The two commanderies,
are Xìndū and Héchéng.
If we abandon this now and return,
not only would we lose Héběi for nothing,
but we would certainly alarm the Sānfǔ again,
damaging our prestige and authority;
this is not a good plan.
If Your Excellency has no intention of further campaigning,
then even the Xìndū troops
would be difficult to gather.
Why?
Once Your Excellency goes west,
Hándān's power will be established,
the people will not abandon their parents and turn their backs on an established ruler to escort Your Excellency a thousand *lǐ*.
This refers to Guāngwǔ returning west,
then Wáng Láng's position and title would be settled,
hence called an established ruler.
Bèi,
pronounced pú mèi.
The Kǎoyì says: Fàn Shū Pī Tóng Zhuàn:
"Hándān is established,
the people will not turn their backs."
The characters "chéng zhǔ"
are all written as
"chéng".
Yuán Jì writes
"Hándān and Chéng,
the people will not abandon Héchéng to escort Your Excellency a thousand *lǐ*."
The Hàn Chūnqiū writes
"the people of Hándān cannot abandon their parents and turn their backs on an established ruler."
According to the text's meaning,
"chéng"
should all be written as
"chéng" (成).
"Hándān chéng" means Hándān's power is established.
"Chéng zhǔ" means Wáng Láng is an already established ruler.
Xiù then stopped.
Xiù, considering the two commanderies' troops to be weak,
wished to join the armies of Chéngtóu Zǐlù and Lì Zǐdū:
Yuán Zēng raised an army in Lúchéngtóu,
Zēng's courtesy name was Zǐlù,
hence he was called Chéngtóu Zǐlù.
The Kǎoyì says: Fàn Shū writes
"Lì Zǐdū".
Liú Bān, a co-editor, said:
"Lì"
should be
"Diāo",
pronounced diāo.
So he mobilized the surrounding counties,
obtaining four thousand elite soldiers,
and appointed Rèn Guāng as Grand General of the Left,
Lǐ Zhōng, the Commandant of Xìndū, as Grand General of the Right,
and Pī Róng as Grand General of the Rear;
the Administrator of Héróng remained as before,
and Wàn Xiū, the Magistrate of Xìndū, as General of the Vanguards.
Wàn,
is a surname.
Among Mèngzǐ's disciples was Wàn Zhāng.
He left Zōng Guǎng from Nányáng to manage the affairs of the Administrator of Xìndū,
and ordered Rèn Guāng, Lǐ Zhōng, and Wàn Xiū to lead troops to follow him.
Pī Róng led troops at the front,
and Rèn Guāng then extensively composed proclamations saying:
"Grand Marshal Liú Gōng, leading Chéngtóu Zǐlù and Lì Zǐdū's million troops, is coming from the east
to strike all the rebellious barbarians!"
He dispatched cavalry to speed into the border region of Jùlù.
Officials and common people received the proclamations,
and spread the word among themselves.
Xiù entered the border of Tángyáng at dusk,
Xián said: Tángyáng Xiàn,
belonged to Jùlù Jùn,
located on the south bank of the Táng Shuǐ;
its old city was south of the present-day Lùchéng Xiàn in Jìzhōu.
The marsh was completely filled with people,
and Tángyáng immediately surrendered;
he then attacked Shè Xiàn,
and made it surrender.
Chéngtóu Zǐlù was
Yuán Zēng from Dōngpíng,
who plundered the area between the Hé and Jì rivers,
and had a host of over two hundred thousand;
Lì Zǐdū had a host of sixty to seventy thousand,
thus Xiù wished to rely on them.
Liú Zhí from Chāngchéng gathered several thousand troops and occupied Chāngchéng,
welcoming Xiù;
Xián said: Chāngchéng Xiàn,
its old city was northwest of present-day Jìzhōu.
Dù Yòu said: Its old city was north of Xìndū Xiàn in Jìzhōu.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù quotes Yìng Shào as saying: It was thirty *lǐ* north of Tángyáng Xiàn.
Gěng Chún led his clan and retainers, over two thousand people,
the old and sick among them all carried wooden coffins with them,
Xián said: The Zuǒ Zhuàn says: "If she marries under such circumstances,
she will soon go to her coffin."
Mù (木),
refers to a coffin.
The old and sick feared death,
so they carried them to follow the army.
Xián said: Yù,
a county name;
its old city was in Jìzhōu.
I have examined the records of the Two Hàn dynasties and found no Yù Xiàn,
probably
an error for the character
"Shè".
He advanced to attack Xiàqūyáng,
and made it surrender;
his forces gradually gathered,
reaching tens of thousands,
then he again attacked Zhōngshān to the north.
Xián said: Zhōngshān Guó,
also known as Zhōngrén Tíng;
its old city was northeast of present-day Tángxiàn in Dìngzhōu.
Zhāng Yào's Zhōngshān Jì says: There was a mountain within the city,
hence it was called Zhōngshān.
Fù (復),
pronounced fú yòu.
He then sent his younger cousin Xīn to return to their home,
and burn their dwellings to cut off any hope of turning back.
Xiù 進拔 Lúnú.
Dù Yòu said: “It is Ānxǐ County of Dìngzhōu,
which was Hàn Lúnú.”
He sent dispatches to the border commanderies, calling on them to jointly attack Hándān.
The commanderies and counties responded again.
At that time, Yáng, the king of Zhēndìng, raised an army and joined Wáng Láng.
His forces numbered over a hundred thousand.
Xiù sent Liú Zhí to persuade Yáng,
and Yáng surrendered.
Yáng
was a sixth-generation descendant of Shùn, King Xiàn of Chángshān.
Shùn
was a son of Emperor Jǐng.
說
is pronounced shū ruì.
Xiù married Yáng's niece, Lady Guō, as his consort to cement the alliance.
He then advanced to attack Yuánshì and Fángzi,
capturing both.
Xián said: “Yuánshì and Fángzi belonged to Chángshān Commandery;
they are now counties in Zhàozhōu.”
防 and 房
were interchangeable in ancient script.
He attacked and beheaded Láng’s general Lǐ Yùn.
Hào County
belonged to Chángshān Commandery.
Xián said: “It is now Gāoyì County in Zhàozhōu.”
鄗
is pronounced hū gè.
惲
is pronounced yú fěn.
He again defeated Láng’s general Lǐ Yù.
Xián said: “Bǎirén
was a county name,
belonging to the State of Zhào;
it is now a county in Xíngzhōu;
its old city was in the northwest of the county.”
He attacked it
but could not take it.
Yán Cén, a man from Nánzhèng, raised an army and occupied Hànzhōng.
Yán
is the surname;
Cén
is the given name.
He had several hundred thousand troops.
Jiǎ Fù, a Commandant from Nányáng, seeing Gēngshǐ's chaotic rule,
persuaded Jiā, saying:
“Today, the world is not yet settled,
but Your Majesty is content to guard what you hold.
Is what you hold perhaps not retainable?”
“What you hold”
refers to Hànzhōng.
“Your words are grand,
but not for me to undertake.
The Grand Marshal is in Héběi,
and he will surely be able to employ you.”
He then wrote a letter recommending Fù and Chén Jùn, the Chief Clerk from Nányáng, to Liú Xiù.
Fù and others met Xiù in Bǎirén.
Xiù appointed Fù as General Who Breaks Captives,
and Jùn as Consolidating Aide.
The Biography of Liú Xuán states: “Xuán initially served as Consolidating Aide in Chén Mù’s and others’ army.”
Xián said: “Wishing to consolidate the army and its masses,
this was provisionally made an official title.”
I say that Guāngwǔ’s intention in employing Jùn
was not merely to consolidate the army and its masses,
but perhaps for the people.
掾
is pronounced yú juàn.
A servant of Xiù’s committed a crime.
Jì Zūn, the Market Prefect of Yǐngchuān, killed him on the spot.
Those who followed the army were not from one place,
so markets were set up within the army
for them to trade,
and a prefect was appointed to govern them.
The Genealogy of Surnames states: “Jì Bó, the fifth son of Duke Zhōu,
later took this as his clan name.”
Xián said: “祭
is pronounced cè jiè.”
Xiù ordered Zūn to be arrested.
The Registrar, Chén Fù, remonstrated:
“Your Lord has always wished for the armies to be orderly and disciplined.
Now Zūn has upheld the law without flinching;
this demonstrates that your commands are effective.”
Xiù then pardoned him.
Xián said: “貰
means to pardon.”
Wáng Mǎng established Left and Right Investigators of Treachery
to supervise the cunning and deceitful.
Guāngwǔ adopted this as a general's title.
“One must be wary of Jì Zūn!
If he even kills a servant from my own household for breaking the law,
he will certainly not show favoritism to you gentlemen.”
Previously,
after Wáng Mǎng had killed Bào Xuān—
(the details are in Volume 36, Píngdì Yuánshǐ Three)—
the Administrator Gǒu Jiàn protected Yǒng,
and Yǒng was thus saved.
Gēngshǐ summoned Yǒng to be Minister of the Secretariat,
acting as Grand General,
leading troops to consolidate Hédōng and Bìngzhōu.
Hédōng Commandery
originally belonged to Sīlì.
Yǒng was ordered to pacify Hédōng and the various commanderies under Bìngzhōu.
Upon arriving in Hédōng, Yǒng attacked the Qīngdú
and thoroughly defeated them.
He appointed Féng Yǎn as General Who Establishes Hàn,
stationed in Tàiyuán,
to repair armor and train soldiers with Tián Yì, the Administrator of Shàngdǎng, and others, to defend the land of Bìng.
Someone
advised Grand Marshal Xiù that defending Bǎirén was not as good as pacifying Jùlù.
Xiù then led his troops northeast and captured Guǎng'ā.
Xián said: “Guǎng'ā
was a county name,
belonging to Jùlù Commandery;
its old city was northwest of present-day Xiàngchéng County in Zhàozhōu.”
Dù Yòu said: “Zhàozhōu Zhāoqìng County
was Hàn Guǎng'ā County.”
During Emperor Wǔ's reign,
courtiers requested enfeoffments for the imperial princes.
The Censor presented an “Ordnance Map”.
Suǒyǐn said: “The earth is called 輿 (yú)
because heaven and earth have the virtue of covering and supporting,
so heaven is called Gài (cover) and earth is called Yú (carriage/support).
Therefore, a map of the earth is called an ‘Ordnance Map’.
It is likely that this name existed from ancient times,
not just from the Hàn dynasty.”
“The commanderies and states of the world are like this,
and now we have only obtained one.
You said earlier that with my deliberations, the world would not be settled.
Why is that?”
Yǔ replied:
“Currently, the world within the seas is in chaos,
and people long for an enlightened ruler
like infants yearn for a loving mother.
The success of ancient rulers depended on the depth or shallowness of their virtue,
not on the size [of their territory]!”
During the chaos
in Jìzhōng,
Gěng Yǎn became separated from Liú Xiù,
and fled north to Chāngpíng.
Xián said: “Chāngpíng County
belonged to Shànggǔ Commandery;
it is now a county in Yōuzhōu;
its old city was to the east of the county.”
He then persuaded Kuàng to attack Hándān.
At that time, Wáng Láng sent generals to campaign in Yúyáng and Shànggǔ,
urgently raising their troops.
The northern provinces were in doubt,
and many wanted to follow him.
Kòu Xún, the Merit Officer of Shànggǔ, and Mǐn Yè, the Door-side Aide,
Mǐn
is a surname.
In Lǔ, there was Grandee Mǐn Mǎfù;
among Confucius’ disciples, there was Mǐn Zǐqiān.
“Hándān has risen precipitously,”
Xián said: “拔 (bá)
means suddenly.”
“The Grand Marshal,
Liú Bóshēng’s younger brother,
honors the worthy and humbles himself before scholars;
we can pledge allegiance to him.”
Kuàng said:
“Hándān is currently flourishing,
and we cannot resist it alone.
What should we do?”
Xún replied:
“Shànggǔ is now complete and strong,
with ten thousand cavalry drawing bows.
We can carefully choose our course of action.
I request to go east and make an alliance with Yúyáng,
uniting our hearts and forces;
Hándān is not worth worrying about!”
Kuàng agreed with him,
and sent Xún east to make an alliance with Péng Chǒng,
intending for each to dispatch two thousand cavalry and one thousand infantry to Grand Marshal Xiù.
Wú Hàn, the Prefect of Ānlè, Gài Yán, the Protector-General, and Wáng Liáng, the Prefect of Húnú, also urged Chǒng to follow Xiù.
Chǒng thought it was so;
but all his subordinates wanted to join Wáng Láng,
and Chǒng could not overrule them.
Hàn went out and stopped at an outer pavilion—
an outer pavilion
is a pavilion outside the city gate—
and summoned and fed a student,
asking him about what he had heard.
The student said:
“Grand Marshal Lord Liú,
wherever he passes, is praised by the commanderies and counties;
the one who has assumed the revered title in Hándān
is truly not of the Liú clan.”
Hàn was greatly pleased,
and immediately faked a letter from Xiù,
sending dispatches to Yúyáng,
and making the student carry it to Chǒng,
instructing him to fully explain what he had heard.
Just then, Kòu Xún arrived.
Chǒng then dispatched three thousand cavalry and infantry,
with Wú Hàn acting as Chief Clerk,
leading them with Gài Yán and Wáng Liáng,
to attack Jì to the south,
killing Wáng Láng’s great general Zhào Hóng.
Xiāo Wáng 蕭王 was residing in the palace in Hándān 邯鄲.
During the day, he was sleeping in Wēnmíng Diàn 溫明殿.
Xián 賢 said: This was the palace of Zhào Wáng Rúyì 趙王如意.
The old foundation is now within Hándān Xiàn 邯鄲縣, Míngzhōu 洺州.
Shuǐ Jīng Zhù 水經註 states: Wēnmíng Diàn 溫明殿 is west of Cóngtái 叢臺.
[Gěng Yǎn 耿弇] approached the bed to request a private audience.
He then said:
"Many officers and soldiers have been killed or wounded.
I request to return to Shànggǔ 上谷 to raise more troops."
Xiāo Wáng 蕭王 said:
"Wáng Láng 王郎 has already been defeated.
Héběi 河北 is mostly pacified.
Why do we need more soldiers?"
Yǎn 弇 said:
"Although Wáng Láng 王郎 has been defeated,
the wars across the world have only just begun.
Now, envoys have come from the west,
wishing to cease military action,
but we cannot listen to them.
There are dozens of groups like the Tóngmǎ 銅馬 and Chìméi 赤眉,
each with hundreds of thousands or millions of people.
They are unstoppable wherever they go.
Shènggōng 聖公 [referring to Gēng Shǐ Dì 更始帝] cannot handle them;
his defeat is certain and not far off."
Xiāo Wáng 蕭王 sat up and said:
"You have spoken wrongly!
I will execute you!"
Yǎn 弇 said:
"Your Majesty cherishes and treats Yǎn 弇 like a son,
so I dared to reveal my innermost feelings."
Xiāo Wáng 蕭王 said:
"I was only joking with you.
Why do you say this?"
Yǎn 弇 said:
"The common people suffered under Wáng Mǎng 王莽 [referring to his dynasty, the Xīn 新 dynasty]
and longed for the Liú 劉 clan again.
When they heard that Han forces were rising,
none were not joyful,
as if escaping a tiger's mouth and returning to a kind mother.
Now Gēng Shǐ 更始 is the Son of Heaven,
but his generals are wantonly seizing power in Shāndōng 山東,
and the powerful relatives are running rampant within the capital.
They loot and plunder as they please.
The common people beat their chests in despair,
and yearn for Wáng Mǎng's 王莽's court again.
This is why I know his defeat is certain.
Your merits and fame are already established.
By righteous conquest,
the empire can be pacified with a mere proclamation.
The empire is of utmost importance;
Your Highness can take it for yourself.
Do not let another surname obtain it!"
Xiāo Wáng 蕭王 then declined by citing that Héběi 河北 was not yet pacified,
and did not heed the summons,
thus beginning to show disloyalty to Gēng Shǐ 更始.
Xián 賢 said: "Èr 貳 means to diverge or dissent."
At this time,

the various bandits Tóngmǎ 銅馬, Dàtóng 大彤, Gāohú 高湖, Chónglián 重連, Tiějìng 鐵脛, Dàqiāng 大槍, Yóulái 尤來, Shàngjiāng 上江, Qīngdú 青犢, Wǔxiào 五校, Wǔfān 五幡, Wǔlóu 五樓, Fùpíng 富平, Huòsuǒ 獲索, etc., each led their divisions.
Their combined forces numbered several hundred thousand.
Xián 賢 said: "Some bandits named themselves after mountains, rivers, or lands,
others by the strength and appearance of their armies.
The Tóngmǎ 銅馬 bandit chiefs were Dōngshān Huāngtū 東山荒禿, Shànghuái Kuàng 上淮況, and others.
The Dàtóng 大彤 leader was Fán Chóng 樊重.
The Yóulái 尤來 leader was Fán Chóng 樊崇.
The Wǔxiào 五校 bandit chief was Gāo Hù 高扈.
The Tánxiāng 檀鄉 bandit chief was Dǒng Cìzhòng 董次仲.
The Wǔlóu 五樓 bandit chief was Zhāng Wén 張文.
The Fùpíng 富平 bandit chief was Xú Shǎo 徐少.
The Huòsuǒ 獲索 bandit chief was Gǔ Shīláng 古師郎, and others.
All are mentioned in Dōng Guān Jì 東觀記."
Jìng 脛,
pronounced "xíng dìng fān" (tone for 定, then for 翻).
Fùpíng 富平,
a county name,
belonging to Píngyuán Jùn 平原郡;
now Yàncì Xiàn 厭次縣, Dìzhōu 棣州.
Xiāo Wáng 蕭王 wanted to attack them,
so he appointed Wú Hàn 吳漢 and Gěng Yǎn 耿弇 as Grand Generals,
holding imperial credentials, to go north and mobilize the cavalry from the ten commanderies of Yōuzhōu 幽州.
The ten commanderies of Yōuzhōu 幽州 were Zhuó Jùn 涿郡, Guǎngyáng 廣陽, Dài Jùn 代郡, Shànggǔ 上谷, Yúyáng 漁陽, Liáoxī 遼西, Liáodōng 遼東, Xuántú 玄菟, and Lèlàng Jùn 樂浪郡.
[He] secretly ordered the various commanderies not to respond to the mobilization.
Xián 賢 said: "Diào 調 means to mobilize."
Diào 調,
pronounced "tú diào fān" (tone for 徒, then for 弔).
Xián 賢 said: "Wúzhōng 無終 was originally the state of the Shānróng 山戎 people.
Wúzhōng 無終,
a mountain name,
was thus adopted as the state's name;
during the Han dynasty, it was a county name,
belonging to Yòuběipíng 右北平.
Its old city is in Yúyáng Xiàn 漁陽縣, Yōuzhōu 幽州 today."
At this time, Miáo Cēng Gài 苗曾蓋 governed Wúzhōng 無終.
Wú Hàn 吳漢 immediately arrested Cēng 曾 [Miáo Cēng Gài 苗曾蓋]
and executed him.
Gěng Yǎn 耿弇 arrived in Shànggǔ 上谷,
also arrested Wéi Shùn 韋順 and Cài Chōng 蔡充,
and executed them.
The northern prefectures were shaken with fear,
and thus all their troops were mobilized.
In the autumn, Xiāo Wáng 蕭王 attacked the Tóngmǎ 銅馬 at Qiāo 鄡.
Xián 賢 said: "Qiāo 鄡,
a county name,
belonging to Jùlù Jùn 鉅鹿郡;
its old city is east of Lùchéng Xiàn 鹿城縣, Jìzhōu 冀州."
Qiāo 鄡,
pronounced "kǔ yáo fān" (tone for 苦, then for 堯).
Xián 賢 said: "Qīngyáng 清陽,
a county name,
belonging to Qīnghé Jùn 清河郡;
now a county in Bèizhōu 貝州;
its old city is northwest of the prefecture."
Wú Hàn 吳漢 submitted all the military registers to the Grand Marshal's office.
Xián 賢 said: "Mò 莫 means 'grand' or 'great'."
"Bīngbù 兵簿" refers to the register of soldiers' names.
Shàng 上,
pronounced "shí zhǎng fān" (tone for 時, then for 掌).
He did not keep anything for himself,
and the King [Xiāo Wáng 蕭王] valued him even more.
The King appointed Zhū Fú 朱浮 of Pèiguó 沛國, who was a General of the Household, as Grand General and Governor of Yōuzhōu 幽州,
and sent him to govern Jìchéng 薊城.
The Tóngmǎ 銅馬 ran out of provisions,
and fled at night.
Xiāo Wáng 蕭王 pursued and attacked them at Guǎntáo 館陶,
severely defeating them.
Xián 賢 said: "Guǎntáo Xiàn 館陶縣,
belonged to Wèi Jùn 魏郡;
now a county in Wèizhōu 魏州."
Then Gāohú 高湖 and Chónglián 重連 came from the southeast,
and joined with the remnants of the Tóngmǎ 銅馬.
Xiāo Wáng 蕭王 again engaged them in a great battle at Púyáng 蒲陽,
completely defeating and pacifying them,
and enfeoffing their chiefs as marquises.
The generals could not yet trust the bandits,
and the surrendered ones also felt insecure.
The King [Xiāo Wáng 蕭王] understood their feelings,
and ordered the surrendered ones to return to their camps, organize their troops,
and he himself rode a light cavalry detachment to inspect their formations.
The surrendered men said to each other:
"Xiāo Wáng 蕭王 puts his sincere heart into others' stomachs.
How could we not commit to death for him!"
Xián 賢 said: "Tóusǐ 投死 is like saying 'to dedicate one's life to death'."
I believe Tóu 投 means 'to entrust',
meaning 'to entrust oneself to death'.
Xíng 行,
pronounced "xià mèng fān" (tone for 下, then for 孟).
Chén 陳,
read as Zhèn 陣.
Gēng 更,
pronounced "gōng héng fān" (tone for 工, then for 衡).
He then distributed the surrendered men among his generals,
and the total force grew to hundreds of thousands.
A separate division of the Chìméi 赤眉, along with the Qīngdú 青犢, Shàngjiāng 上江, Dàtóng 大彤, Tiějìng 鐵脛, and Wǔfān 五幡, numbering over 100,000, were at Shèquǎn 射犬.
Xián 賢 said: "Xù Hàn Zhì 續漢志 states that Yěwáng 野王 had Shèquǎn Jù 射犬聚;
its old city is north of Wǔdé Xiàn 武德縣, Huáizhōu 懷州 today."
[Xiāo Wáng 蕭王] severely defeated them.
He then advanced south to Hénèi 河內,
and Hénèi Tàishǒu 河內太守 Hán Xīn 韓歆 surrendered.
9 Initially,
Xiè Gōng (謝躬) and Xiāo Wáng (蕭王) together eliminated Wáng Láng (王郎).
They frequently disagreed and clashed with Xiāo Wáng.
Xiè Gōng (謝躬) constantly wished to ambush Xiāo Wáng (蕭王),

Although they were both in Hándān (邯鄲),

Nevertheless, Xiāo Wáng (蕭王)

Xiè Gōng (謝躬) was diligent in his official duties.
Xiāo Wáng (蕭王) often praised him, saying:
“Secretary Xiè (謝尚書)

Therefore, Xiè Gōng (謝躬) was not suspicious.
His wife knew about it
and often warned him, saying:
“You and Liú Gōng (劉公) have long been unable to get along,
yet you trust his empty words,
and will ultimately be controlled!”
Xiè Gōng (謝躬) did not heed her.
Subsequently, Xiè Gōng (謝躬) led his army of several tens of thousands back to garrison at Yè (鄴).
Yè (鄴) County
belonged to Wèi Jùn (魏郡).
He ordered Xiè Gōng (謝躬) to intercept and attack Yóu Lái (尤來) at Lónglǜ Shān (隆慮山).
The Dìlǐ Zhì (地理志) states: Lónglǜ (隆慮) County
belonged to Hénèi Jùn (河內郡).
Yìng Shào (應劭) said: Lónglǜ Shān (隆慮山)
is north of the county.
To avoid the name of Emperor Shāng (殤帝),

Shī Gǔ (師古) said: Lǜ (慮)
is pronounced Lú (廬).
While Xiè Gōng (謝躬) was away, Xiāo Wáng (蕭王)

Xiè Gōng (謝躬), unaware,
returned to Yè (鄴) with light cavalry.
Wú Hàn (吳漢) and the others captured and beheaded him,
and all his troops surrendered.

Chén Zūn (陳遵) argued with him,

12 Chìméi (赤眉) leader Fán Chóng (樊崇) and others led troops into Yǐngchuān (潁川).

Although the Chìméi (赤眉) won several battles,
they were exhausted and weary of war.
All of them cried day and night,
longing to return east.
Fán Chóng (樊崇) and the others deliberated,

It would be better to attack Cháng'ān (長安) to the west.
Thereupon, Fán Chóng (樊崇) and Féng Ān (逢安) went via Wǔguān (武關), and Xú Xuān (徐宣) and the others took Lùhún Guān (陸渾關).

13 Xiāo Wáng (蕭王) was about to campaign northwards into Yān (燕) and Zhào (趙).
He estimated that the Chìméi (赤眉) would surely defeat Cháng'ān (長安),

So he appointed Dèng Yǔ (鄧禹) as Qián Jiāngjūn (前將軍),

and sent them west into the pass,
ordering Dèng Yǔ (鄧禹) to select his own subordinates, from Piánpí (偏裨) and below, who could go with him.
At that time, Zhū Wěi (朱鮪), Lǐ Yì (李軼), Tián Lì (田立), and Chén Qiáo (陳僑) commanded an army of reportedly three hundred thousand,

Bào Yǒng (鮑永) and Tián Yì (田邑) were in Bīngzhōu (并州).
Xiāo Wáng (蕭王) considered Hénèi (河內) to be strategically important and prosperous.
Hénèi (河內)
had the natural barrier of Tàiháng (太行) to the north,
and controlled the strategic river crossings to the south.
Xián (賢) said: It cannot be entrusted to just anyone,
hence the difficulty.
Dèng Yǔ (鄧禹) said:
“Kòu Xún (寇恂) possesses both civil and military talents,
and has the ability to govern people and manage armies.
No one but this man can be appointed!”
So Kòu Xún (寇恂) was appointed Hénèi Tàishǒu (河內太守),
acting as Dàjiāngjūn (大將軍).
Kǎoyì (考異) says: Yuán Jì (袁紀):
“When Dèng Yǔ (鄧禹) first met the King in Yè (鄴),
he immediately spoke of wanting to occupy Hénèi (河內).”
By this point, it also says:
“Gēngshǐ's (更始) Wǔyīn Wáng (武陰王) Lǐ Yì (李軼) occupied Luòyáng (洛陽),

The King was troubled by this,
and intended to take Hénèi (河內) to pressure them.
He said to Dèng Yǔ (鄧禹): ‘
Your words about me having Hénèi (河內) are like Gāozǔ (高祖) having Guānzhōng (關中).
Without Xiāo Hé (蕭何) in Guānzhōng (關中),
who could keep one region peaceful
so that Gāozǔ (高祖) had no worries about the west?
You have already recommended Wú Hàn's (吳漢) abilities;
now recommend a Xiāo Hé (蕭何) for me.’
Dèng Yǔ (鄧禹) said: ‘Kòu Xún (寇恂) possesses both civil and military talents,
and has the ability to manage armies.
No one but Kòu Xún (寇恂) can pacify Hénèi (河內)!’”
According to this, after Shìzǔ (世祖) became Gēngshǐ's (更始) deputy,
he first gained Hénèi (河內) and Wèi Jùn (魏郡),
and then wished to hold them
to compare with Guānzhōng (關中).
It was not his original intention or a deliberate plan to immediately seize Hénèi (河èi).
Now we follow Fàn Shū's (范書) account as definitive.
“In the past, Gāozǔ (高祖) left Xiāo Hé (蕭何) in Guānzhōng (關中);
I now entrust Hénèi (河內) to you.
You must provide sufficient military provisions,
drill the soldiers and horses,
prevent and block other armies,
and not let them cross northwards, that is all!”

He was to resist Luòyáng (洛陽).
