is located on the sunny side (south) of the Fànshuǐ (范水),
belonging to Zhuó Jùn (涿郡).
The old city of Fányáng (范陽) is located southeast of present-day Yìzhōu Yìxiàn (易州易縣).
Some said he had already been killed.
The generals did not know what to do.
Wú Hàn (吳漢) said:
“You all must strive!
The King’s nephews are in Nányáng (南陽).
Why worry about having no lord!”
“Nephews”
refers to Bóshēng's (伯升) sons Zhāng (章) and Xìng (興).
After several days, order was restored.
Although the bandits won the battle,
they feared the King’s prestige,
and that night,
they withdrew.
The main army advanced again
to Āncì (安次),
fought continuously,
and defeated them.
The bandits retreated into Yúyáng (漁陽),
plundering and taking captives wherever they went.
The Strong Bow General Chén Jùn (陳俊) said to the King:
“The bandits have no supplies.
It is advisable to send light cavalry ahead of the bandits,
and make the common people fortify themselves in their strongholds to cut off their food supply.
They can then be annihilated without a battle.”
The King agreed,
and sent Jùn (俊) with light cavalry to ride ahead of the bandits.
Seeing people whose fortified strongholds were sturdy and complete,
he ordered them to hold fast.
Those scattered in the open country
were plundered.
When the bandits arrived,
they found nothing
and consequently scattered and were defeated.
The King said to Jùn (俊):
“It is the General’s (將軍) strategy that has困 (trapped) these barbarians.”
6 Féng Yì (馮異) sent a letter to Lǐ Yì (李軼),
explaining the consequences of good and ill fortune,
and persuading him to surrender to Xiāo Wáng (蕭王).
Yì (軼) knew that Cháng'ān (長安) was already in danger,
and due to Bóshēng's (伯shēng) death,
his heart was not at ease.
This event is seen in Volume One, Gēngshǐ (更始) First Year.
“Yì (軼) originally conspired with Xiāo Wáng (蕭王) to found the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
This event is seen in Volume Thirty-eight, Wáng Mǎng (王莽) Dìhuáng (地皇) Third Year.
The General (將軍) garrisoned Mèngjīn (孟津),
both controlling the vital points.
Xián (賢) said: Jī (機) refers to the trigger of a crossbow.
Zhóu (軸) refers to the axle of a chariot.
Both are crucial parts of things,
hence they are used as metaphors.
We intend to cut through metal.
The “Yì Jīng” (易經) says: Two people with one heart,
their righteousness can cut through metal.
Lù Démíng (陸德明) said: Duàn (斷) is pronounced Dīng Luàn (丁亂);
Wáng Sù (王肅) pronounced it Dīng Guǎn (丁管).
I wish to present my humble plan to assist the state and pacify the people.”
After Yì (軼) sent this letter,
he no longer contended with Yì (異),
so Yì (異) was able to attack Tiānjǐng Guān (天井關) to the north.
Liú Zhāo Zhì (劉昭志) said: Gāodū Xiàn (高都縣) in Shàngdǎng (上黨) has Tiānjǐng Guān (天井關).
Xián (賢) said: It is located south of present-day Zézhōu Jìnchéng Xiàn (澤州晉城縣),
on the Tàiháng Shān (太行山).
South of the pass there are three Tiānjǐng (天井) springs.
He also marched south to capture thirteen counties east of Hé Nán Chénggāo (河南成皋),
with over 100,000 surrendering.
Wǔ Bó (武勃) led more than 10,000 men to attack the rebels.
Yì (異) fought him below Shìxiāng (士鄉).
Xiāng Zhāo Zhì (鄉昭志): Luòyáng Xiàn (雒陽縣) in Hénán (河南) has Shìxiāng Jù (士鄉聚).
The “Xù Hàn Zhì” (續漢志) says: Shìxiāng (士鄉)
is a postal station name,
belonging to Hénán Jùn (河南郡).
Bó (勃) was beheaded.
Yì (軼) closed the city gates and did not provide aid.
Yì (異) saw his sincerity and loyalty,
and reported it fully to the King.
The King replied to Yì (異) saying:
“Jìwén (季文) is full of deceit.
Lǐ Yì's (李軼) courtesy name is Jìwén (季文).
Now
transfer his letter to inform the prefects and commandants to be vigilant.”
Everyone was surprised that the King openly publicized Yì's (軼) letter.
Zhū Wěi (朱鮪) heard of it,
and sent someone to assassinate Yì (軼).
As a result, there was disunity within the city,
and many surrendered.
Zhū Wěi (朱鮪) heard that the King was campaigning in the north and Hénèi (河內) was isolated,
so he dispatched his generals Sū Mào (蘇茂) and Jiǎ Qiáng (賈彊) with over 30,000 troops to cross the Gǒng Hé (鞏河)
and attack Wēn (溫).
Gǒng Xiàn (鞏縣) belonged to Hénán Jùn (河南郡),
and was the state of Zhōu Gǒng Bó (周鞏伯).
The Yellow River passes north of Gǒng Xiàn (鞏縣),
and is called Gǒng Hé (鞏河),
which is also the Wǔshè Jīn (五社津).
Wēn Xiàn (溫縣)
belonged to Hénèi Jùn (河內郡),
and was the fief of Zhōu Dàfū Sū Zǐ (周大夫蘇子).
Xián (賢) said: Gǒng (鞏) and Wēn (溫)
are both counties of present-day Luòzhōu (洛州).
Xián (賢) said: Píngyīn (平陰)
is a county name,
belonging to Hénán Jùn (河南郡).
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: The city of Hàn (漢) Píngyīn Xiàn (平陰縣) is fifty *lǐ* (里) north of present-day Luòyáng Xiàn (洛陽縣).
“Shuǐjīng Zhù” (水經註) says: Píngyīn (平陰)
is the shady land (陰地) of Jìn (晉),
hence it was where the Yīnróng (陰戎) resided.
Wèi Wéndì (魏文帝) renamed it Héyīn (河陰).
Zhuì (綴) means to link together.
Jiāng (將) is pronounced like Liàng (亮).
Kòu Xún (寇恂) immediately led his army out,
and at the same time sent messages to the subordinate counties,
dispatching troops to rendezvous at Wēn (溫).
The military officers all advised:
“The Luòyáng (洛陽) troops are now crossing the river,
continuously, front and back.
It is advisable to wait until all the armies have gathered
before going out.”
Xún (恂) said:
“Wēn (溫)
is the protective screen of the commandery.
If Wēn (溫) is lost, the commandery cannot be defended.”
So he rushed to it.
At dawn the next day,
battle was joined.
Féng Yì (馮異)'s relief forces and the troops from various counties arrived just then.
Xún (恂) ordered his soldiers to stand on the city walls, beat drums, and shout,
loudly proclaiming:
“Duke Liú's (劉公) troops have arrived!”
Sū Mào's (蘇茂) army heard this
and their formation wavered.
Xún (恂) then rushed to attack,
utterly defeating them.
Féng Yì (馮異) also crossed the river to attack Zhū Wěi (朱鮪),
who fled.
Yì (異) and Xún (恂) pursued them to Luòyáng (洛陽),
encircled the city once, and then returned.
From then on, Luòyáng (洛陽) was terrified,
and the city gates were closed during the day.
Yì (異) and Xún (恂) issued a proclamation stating their achievements.
The generals came to congratulate them,
and then petitioned for the conferment of an honorable title.
General Mǎ Wǔ (馬武) of Nányáng (南陽) was the first to speak, saying:
“Although Your Royal Highness insists on modesty,
what about the ancestral temples and the altars of soil and grain!
You should first ascend to the exalted position,
then proceed with the punitive expeditions.
Who are these bandits whom you are now rushing to attack?”
Xián (賢) said: Shéi (誰) means "without a lord."
The “Former Han History: Sounds and Meanings” says: To rush straight is *chí* (馳); to rush in disorder is *wù* (騖).
I believe
“Shéi zéi” (誰賊)
means, perhaps, that since the title and position are not yet established,
who can be designated as a bandit?
“What general would utter such words?
He can be executed!”
So he led his army back to Jì (薊).
He then again sent Wú Hàn (吳漢) to lead Gěng Yǎn (耿弇), Jǐng Dān (景丹), and thirteen other generals to pursue Yóulái (尤來) and others.
They beheaded over 13,000,
and then pursued them exhaustively to Jùnmí (浚靡) before returning.
The bandits scattered into Liáoxī (遼西) and Liáodōng (遼東),
and were completely plundered and attacked by the Wūhuán (烏桓) and Mòrén (貊人).
Dūhù Jiāngjūn Jiǎ Fù
Emperor Xuān of Hàn established the office of Dūhù in the Western Regions,
overseeing all the states of the Southern and Northern Roads.
When Gān Yánshòu attacked Zhìzhī,
he referred to himself as Dūhù Jiāngjūn;
the Hàn court did not yet consider it a general's title.
It was not until Guāngwǔ
that it was bestowed upon Jiǎ Fù.
Fù was severely wounded;
the King was greatly alarmed and said:
"The reason I did not let Jiǎ Fù lead a separate force
was because he was reckless in battle.
As expected,
I have lost my famous general!
I heard his wife is pregnant;
if she gives birth to a daughter,
my son shall marry her;
if she gives birth to a son,
my daughter shall marry him;
I will not let him worry about his wife and children."
Fù's illness soon healed,
and he caught up with the King at Jì,
where they met with great joy.
Returning to Zhōngshān,
the generals again urged him to accept the imperial title;
the King still refused.
When they reached Nánpíngjí,
Xián said: This is a county name,
belonging to Chángshān Jùn,
now Zhàozhōu Xiàn;
the old city was south of the county.
The King did not agree.
When the generals were about to leave,
Gěng Chún stepped forward and said:
"The scholars and officials of the realm,
who have abandoned their relatives,
forsaken their homelands,
and followed Your Majesty amidst arrows and stones,
their plan was surely to 'climb the dragon's scales'
and 'attach to the phoenix's wings'
to achieve their aspirations.
Now Your Majesty delays at this opportune moment and goes against the will of the multitude,
not regularizing your title and position.
Chún fears that the scholars and officials, their hopes dashed and schemes exhausted,
will entertain thoughts of leaving and returning,
seeing no point in enduring prolonged hardship.
Once the great army disperses,
it will be difficult to reassemble."
Chún's words were very sincere and urgent,
and the King was deeply moved, saying:
"I will consider it."
Proceeding to Hào,
Xù Hàn Zhì says: Hào Xiàn,
belonged to Chángshān Guó;
the Emperor ascended the throne here
and renamed it Gāoyì.
Hào,
pronounced as 'hú gè fān'.
He inquired about the movements in all four directions.
Yì said:
"Gēngshǐ will surely be defeated;
the worry for the ancestral temple rests with Your Majesty.
You should follow the consensus of the multitude!"
Just then, the Confucian scholar Qiáng Huá came from Guānzhōng, bearing the Chìfú Fú, and presented it to the King, saying:
"Liú Xiù raises troops to apprehend the lawless;
the four barbarians gather like clouds, dragons fight in the wild;
at the juncture of four and seven, fire is the master."
His ministers thereupon again presented their plea.
In the sixth month,
on the day Jǐwèi,
the King ascended the imperial throne south of Hào;
at that time, an altar was erected south of Hào at Qiānqiū Tíng Wǔchéng Mò.
Xián said: That place is now in Bǎixiāng Xiàn of Zhàozhōu.
Kǎo Yì says: In the biography of Guāngwǔ Běnjì,
Fèng Yì defeated Sū Mào,
and the generals urged him to accept the imperial title,
and Guāngwǔ returned to Jì,
all before the fourth month.
However, in the biography of Fèng Yì,
Yì's letter to Lǐ Yì says:
"Cháng'ān is in chaos,
Chìméi approaches the suburbs,
kings and marquises stir up trouble,
high officials are disunited,
and the rule of law is broken."
He also advised Guāngwǔ to claim the imperial title,
also saying:
"The Three Kings have rebelled,
and Gēngshǐ has been defeated and perished."
According to this, in the sixth month of this year, on Jǐwèi,
Guāngwǔ ascended the throne.
In the same month, on Jiǎzǐ,
Dèng Yǔ defeated Wáng Kuāng and others at Ānyì.
Wáng Kuāng, Zhāng Áng, and others fled back to Cháng'ān,
then plotted to seize Gēngshǐ
together at the time of the Lìqiū Chú Láo festival.
Therefore, the rebellion of the Three Kings
should have occurred after Guāngwǔ's enthronement,
at the turn of summer and autumn.
How could Fèng Yì have spoken of it before the fourth month?
Perhaps the historians embellished his words,
leading to this discrepancy!
A general amnesty was declared.
Dèng Yǔ besieged Ānyì,
but it did not fall for several months.
Gēngshǐ's Grand General Fán Cān, with tens of thousands of men, crossed Dàyáng.
Xián said: Dàyáng Xiàn,
belonged to Hédōng Jùn.
Qián Shū Yīnyì says: South of the Yellow River.
In the Spring and Autumn period, the Earl of Qín attacked Jìn,
crossing at Máojīn.
Dù Yù said: It is Dàyáng Xiàn in Hédōng.
Yǔ met and attacked him south of Jiě,
and cut him down.
Xián said: Jiě Xiàn,
belonged to Hédōng Jùn;
its old city is now southeast of Sāngquán Xiàn in Púzhōu.
Shīgǔ said: Jiě,
pronounced like 'xiè'.
They again jointly attacked Yǔ,
and Yǔ's army was at a disadvantage.
The next day,
on Guǐhài,
Kuāng and others, considering it a 'six-jiǎ exhausted day,'
did not go out.
Yǔ thus managed to reorganize his troops.
On Jiǎzǐ,
Kuāng led his entire army out to attack Yǔ;
Yǔ ordered his army not to move rashly.
When they reached the camp,
he then issued a general order to his officers.
Mèng Kāng said: It means transmitting orders throughout the army to dispatch them.
He thoroughly defeated them.
Kuāng and the others all fled.
Yǔ pursued and beheaded Jūn and the Hédōng Grand Administrator Yáng Bǎo,
thus pacifying Hédōng.
Kuāng and the others fled back to Cháng'ān.
Kǎo Yì says: Liú Xuán's biography states:
"Wáng Kuāng and Zhāng Áng defended Hédōng,
were defeated by Dèng Yǔ,
and fled back to Cháng'ān."
Dèng Yǔ's biography does not mention Zhāng Áng's name.
We follow this now.
Zhāng Áng discussed with the generals, saying:
"Chìméi will arrive any moment;
our destruction is not far off.
It is better to plunder Cháng'ān
and return east to Nányáng;
if things do not go well,
we can simply return to the lakes and swamps to be bandits!"
So they jointly entered
and tried to persuade Gēngshǐ;
Gēngshǐ was angry and did not respond,
and no one dared to speak again.
Gēngshǐ sent Wáng Kuāng, Chén Mù, Chéng Dān, and Zhào Méng to garrison Xīnfēng,
and Lǐ Sōng to guard the passes,
to resist Chìméi.
Zhāng Áng, Liáo Zhàn, Hú Yīn, and Shēntú Jiàn conspired with Kuí Xiāo,
intending to jointly seize Gēngshǐ
at the time of the Lìqiū Chú Láo festival,
and carry out their previous plan.
Kǎo Yì says: Yuán Jì states:
"Shēntú Jiàn and others urged Gēngshǐ to abdicate the imperial throne,
but Gēngshǐ did not agree;
Jiàn and others plotted to seize him."
We follow Fàn Shū now.
Gēngshǐ feigned illness and did not go out,
summoning Zhāng Áng and the others to enter,
intending to execute them all;
only Kuí Xiāo claimed illness and did not enter,
gathering his guests Wáng Zūn, Zhōu Zōng, and others to array their troops and defend themselves.
Gēngshǐ was indecisive;
Áng, Zhàn, and Yīn suspected a change,
and thus burst out.
Only Shēntú Jiàn remained,
and Gēngshǐ beheaded Jiàn,
and sent the Zhí Jīn Wǔ Dèng Yè to lead troops to surround Kuí Xiāo's residence.
Áng, Zhàn, and Yīn arrayed their troops and burned the gates,
entering and fighting in the palace.
Gēngshǐ was greatly defeated;
Xiāo also broke through the encirclement
and fled back to Tiānshuǐ.
The next morning,
Gēngshǐ fled east to Zhào Méng at Xīnfēng.
Gēngshǐ again suspected Wáng Kuāng, Chén Mù, and Chéng Dān of conspiring with Zhāng Áng and the others,
so he summoned them all.
Mù and Dān arrived first,
and he immediately beheaded them.
Wáng Kuāng was fearful,
and led his troops into Cháng'ān,
joining with Zhāng Áng and the others.
8 The Chìméi advanced to Huáyīn.
In the army, there was a Qí shaman.
A Qí shaman
was a shaman from the State of Qí.
Chéngyáng Jǐng Wáng Zhāng had the merit of executing Zhū Lǚ,
so the people of Qí sacrificed to him to seek blessings and help.
“Jǐng Wáng was greatly enraged and said: ‘I should be for the xiànguān,
why am I for rebels!’ ”
Xián said: Xiànguān
refers to the Son of Heaven.
The army was alarmed and agitated.
Fāng Wàng’s younger brother, Yáng, persuaded Fán Chóng and others, saying:
“Now, generals, you command a million troops,
marching west towards the imperial city,
yet you have no title,
and are called mere rebels.
This cannot last;
it would be better to establish a member of the imperial clan,
and, acting righteously, undertake punitive expeditions.
With this as your command,
who would dare not follow!”
Chóng and others thought this was sound,
and the shaman’s pronouncements became even more urgent.
They advanced to Zhèng.
Zhèng County
belonged to Jīngzhào.
Xián said: It is now Huázhōu County.
“We are now close to Cháng’ān,
and with the spirits acting thus,
we must seek a member of the Liú clan to jointly enthrone.”
Earlier,
the Chìméi passed through Shì.
The Geographical Treatise says:
Shì County
belonged to Tàishān Commandery.
Jìn,
its jìn fān.
Xiān,
xī jiàn fān.
Méng’s father was named Xiàn,
a fifth-generation descendant of Chéngyáng Jǐng Wáng,
son of Huāng Wáng Shùn.
During the Yuándì period, he was enfeoffed as Shìhóu.
He, along with Fán Chóng and others, surrendered to Gēngshǐ at Luòyáng.
Fán Chóng and others surrendered,
see previous volume, Gēngshǐ first year.
Jiàng,
Hù Jiāng fān.
He served as Shìzhōng,
in Cháng’ān.
Mào and Pénzǐ remained in the army,
under the command of Yòuxiào Zúshǐ Liú Xiáqīng,
in charge of herding cattle.
Hánzhù says: Zúshǐ,
ranked at one hundred dàn,
was found in the Jiǔxiāng Temple, various commanderies, and all military expeditionary units and commanderies.
Xiào,
Hù Jiào fān.
Xiá,
Hù Jiá fān.
They sought descendants of Jǐng Wáng in the army,
and found over seventy people.
Only Mào, Pénzǐ, and the former Xī’ānhóu Xiào were the closest relatives.
Chóng and others said:
“We hear that in ancient times, the Son of Heaven leading troops was called ‘Shàng Jiāngjūn’.”
So they wrote on a slip of bamboo as a tally, saying
“Shàng Jiāngjūn,”
and also placed two empty slips in a box.
Xián said: Zhá,
is a jiǎn.
Sì,
is a qiè.
They sacrificed to Chéngyáng Jǐng Wáng,
and all the Sānlǎo and Cóngshì gathered in a great assembly;
among the Chìméi leaders, the most respected were called Sānlǎo,
the next were Cóngshì.
They drew slips according to age order.
Pénzǐ was the youngest,
he drew last,
and obtained the tally;
all the generals declared themselves subjects,
and bowed.
Pénzǐ was fifteen years old at the time,
with disheveled hair and bare feet,
wearing worn-out, mud-stained clothes.
Seeing the crowd bowing,
he was frightened and wanted to cry.
Mào said to him:
“Keep the tally well!”
Pénzǐ immediately chewed and broke it,
and threw it away.
Xú Xuān was appointed Prime Minister,
Fán Chóng as Grand Imperial Secretary,
Féng Ān as Grand Minister of War of the Left,
Xiè Lù as Grand Minister of War of the Right.
The rest were all ranked as high officials and generals.
Although Pénzǐ was enthroned,
he still bowed to Liú Xiáqīng morning and evening,
and sometimes wanted to go out and play with the cowherds;
Xiáqīng angrily stopped him,
and Chóng and others no longer paid attention to him.
9 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the day Xīnwèi,
the Emperor sent an envoy with a staff of authority to appoint Dèng Yǔ as Grand Minister of Works,
enfeoffing him as Zuòhóu, with an income of ten thousand households.
Xián said: Zuò County
belonged to Nányáng Commandery.
Its ancient city is in the northeast of modern Xiāngzhōu Gǔchéng County.
Yú says that Dèng Yǔ’s accomplishments were compared to Xiāo Hé’s,
hence his enfeoffment as Zuò.
Zuò,
pronounced Zàn.
There was also a discussion to select a Grand Minister of Agriculture,
and the Emperor, based on the Chìfú Tally, said
“Wáng Liáng is to govern Wèi and act as Xuánwǔ.”
On the day Dīngchǒu,
Wáng Liáng, the magistrate of Yěwáng, was appointed Grand Minister of Agriculture.
The Emperor considered Yěwáng to be where Wèi was moved,
and Xuánwǔ to be the name of the water god.
The Grand Minister of Agriculture was an official for water and land,
so Liáng was used.
Xián said: Xuánwǔ
is the god of the north,
a composite of tortoise and snake.
Yěwáng County
belonged to Hénèi Commandery.
Sòng Bái said: Huáizhōu Hénèi County
is ancient Yěwáng.
The crowd was all displeased.
On the day Rénwǔ,
Wú Hàn was appointed Grand Marshal.
Initially,
Gēngshǐ had appointed Fú Zhàn of Lángyé as Administrator of Píngyuán.
Xìngpǔ says: The Fú clan originally descended from Fúxī.
In the early Hàn, there was Fú Shēng of Jìnán.
Shǒu,
shì yòu fān.
Zhàn alone remained calm,
nurturing and comforting the common people.
When a menxiàdū plotted to raise troops for Zhàn, Zhàn captured and executed him;
various commanderies each had menxiàdū,
in charge of military guards.
Wéi,
yú wěi fān.
The entire region of Píngyuán relied on Zhàn to be preserved.
The Emperor summoned Zhàn to be Shàngshū,
and tasked him with establishing the old regulations.
And because Dèng Yǔ was on a western expedition,
Zhàn was appointed Sīzhí,
acting as Grand Minister of Works;
the Sītú of the Eastern Capital was the Prime Minister of the Western Capital;
Sīzhí
was the Chancellor's Sīzhí.
He was always stationed to guard.
10 Dèng Yǔ crossed the Yellow River from Fényīn,
entering Xiàyáng.
Fényīn County
belonged to Hédōng.
Xiàyáng County
belonged to Féngyì.
The Geographical Treatise says:
The Left Assistant Commandant governed Gāolíng.
Xián said: The Left Assistant
is the Left Féngyì.
All three Fǔ had Commandants.
Yá,
a county name,
belonged to the Left Féngyì.
Its ancient city is in the northeast of modern Tóngzhōu Báishuǐ County.
The Zuǒzhuàn says: Qín and Jìn fought at Péngyá,
which is this place.
Gōngchéng
is a surname,
derived from a Qín aristocratic rank.
Chéng,
Shéng Zhèng fān.
Xī,
Xǔ Jí fān.
Liú Mào of the imperial clan gathered a multitude between Jīng and Mì.
Mào
was the paternal cousin of Yuánshì Wáng Xī.
Xián said: Jīng County
belonged to Hénán Commandery,
the capital of Zhèng;
its ancient city is in the southeast of modern Zhèngzhōu Xíngyáng County.
Mì County
belonged to Hénán Commandery;

Pèiguó.

Sì (wait),

Húyáng Gōngzhǔ had recently become a widow.

Shandong (山東) people on official journeys,

I have consulted Fàn's (范) book,

"The Sānfǔ region suffered from the chaos of Wáng Mǎng and Gēngshǐ,

Yì bowed his head and received the order,

Your servant Guāng says: In ancient times, the people of Zhōu praised the virtue of King Wǔ, saying:

Observing how Guāngwǔ captured Guānzhōng,

hence Zhāng Bù was able to exclusively gather forces in Qí Dì
and occupy twelve commanderies.
Bù occupied Chéngyáng, Lángyá, Gāomì, Jiāodōng, Dōnglái, Běihǎi, Qí, Qiānchéng, Jǐnán, Píngyuán, Tàishān,
and Zīchuān—twelve commanderies.
The Emperor visited Huái.
Wú Hàn led Gěng Yǎn and Gài Yán to attack the Qīngdú west of Zhǐ,
greatly defeating and subduing them.
Xián said: Zhǐ Xiàn
belonged to Hénèi Jùn;
its old city is southeast of modern Jìyuán Xiàn in Luò Zhōu.
Gài,
pronounced gǔ hé.
In the third month,
on the rén yín day,
Sīzhí Fú Zhàn was made Dà Sītú.
The Administrator of Zhuō Jùn, Zhāng Fēng, rebelled,
and the Jùn Guó Zhì says: Zhuō Jùn
is eighteen hundred lǐ northeast of Luòyáng.
He allied with Péng Chǒng.
Zhū Fú, because the Emperor did not personally campaign against Péng Chǒng,
submitted a memorial requesting aid.
The imperial reply said:
"Last year, the Chìméi were arrogant and unrestrained in Cháng'ān,
Xián said: Báhù means tyrannical and unrestrained.
They indeed came and submitted.
Now, I assess that these rebellious bandits
cannot long remain intact;
among them, there will surely be those who kill each other from within.
Currently, our military resources are not sufficient,
so we must wait until after the wheat harvest!"
Xū
means 'to wait'.
People resorted to cannibalism.
Coincidentally, Gěng Kuàng sent cavalry to rescue him,
and Fú was thus able to escape and flee.
Jìchéng then surrendered to Péng Chǒng.
The Kǎo Yì says: In Zhū Fú's biography:
"Shàngshū Lìng Hóu Bà memorialized: 'Fú caused disorder in Yōu Zhōu,
formed an alliance with Chǒng's crimes,
fruitlessly exhausted the military,
and could not die for his integrity.
His crime deserves execution.' "
According to records, Bà did not become Shàngshū Lìng until the following year;
this was probably a posthumous impeachment.
Péng Chǒng attacked and captured several counties in Yòuběipíng and Shànggǔ,
bribed the Xiōngnú,
borrowed troops for assistance;
he also allied with Zhāng Bù and the various bandits of Fùpíng and Huòsuǒ in the south,
all of whom communicated with him.
11The emperor himself led a campaign against Dèng Fèng,
reaching Dǔyáng;
Dǔyáng County
belonged to Nányáng Commandery.
Dù Yòu said: Táng Prefecture's Fāngchéng County
was Hàng Dǔyáng County.
Yīng Shào said: Dǔyáng
was renamed Shùnyáng by Jǐngdì.
The two accounts differ.
Dǒng Xīn surrendered.
In summer,
the fourth month,
the emperor pursued Fèng to Xiǎocháng'ān,
fought him,
and utterly defeated him;
Fèng, baring his torso, surrendered through Zhū Hù.
Last year Fèng captured Hù,
now he surrendered through Hù.
Fèng
was the elder nephew of Dèng Chén.
The details are in the previous scroll, last year.
Cén Péng and Gěng Yǎn admonished:
"Dèng Fèng, ungrateful, rebelled
and kept his forces exhausted for a year.
When Your Majesty arrived,
he showed no remorse or intention to reform,
but personally stayed on the battlefield.
Only after defeat did he surrender.
If Fèng is not executed,
there will be no means to deter evil!"
Thereupon, he was beheaded.
Zhū Hù's position was restored.
12Yán Cén, after defeating the Chìméi,
immediately appointed and established regional governors and commandery administrators,
intending to occupy Guānzhōng.
At that time, numerous bandits in Guānzhōng were still rampant:
Cén occupied Lántián,
Wáng Xīn occupied Xiàguī,
Xián said: Qín Wǔgōng attacked the Guī Róng and established it.
Since there was Shàngguī in Lǒngxī,
this is called Xià.
Fāng
is a surname.
The Fēngsútōng mentions Fāng Chéng, Hàng Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ.
Zhāng Hán occupied Cháng'ān,
Gōngsūn Shǒu occupied Chánglíng,
Yáng Zhōu occupied Gǔkǒu,
Lǚ Wěi occupied Chéncāng,
Jiǎo Hóng occupied Qiān,
Jiǎo
is a surname;
Hàn had Jiǎo Shànshū.
Qiān,
pronounced kǔ jiān.
Rèn Liáng occupied Hù,
Rǔ Zhāng occupied Huáilǐ,
Rǔ
is a surname.
Shāng had Rǔ Jiū, Rǔ Fāng.
In the Chūnqiū period,
Jìn had Rǔ Qí, Rǔ Kuān.
Those commanding many troops numbered over ten thousand,
the fewer ones several thousand,
and they attacked each other constantly.
Féng Yì fought and marched,
stationing his army in the Shànglín Yuàn.
Yì, after the victory at Xiáogǔ,
led his troops westward,
fighting and marching,
and advanced to encamp in the Shànglín Yuàn.
Yì;
Yì attacked,
utterly defeating them.
All the camps and strongholds that had allied with Cén came and surrendered.
Bǎo is the same as bǎo (fort).
At that time, the common people were starving;
one jīn of gold could be exchanged for five shēng of beans.
Roads were cut off,
and supplies could not reach them.
Féng Yì's soldiers subsisted entirely on fruits and nuts.
An imperial edict appointed Zhào Kuāng of Nányáng as Right Fúfēng,
to lead troops to assist Yì,
and also sent silk and grain.
As Yì's troops and provisions gradually increased,
he then gradually executed and attacked the powerful figures who did not obey orders,
and rewarded those who surrendered or were meritorious.
He sent all the various camp leaders to the capital,
dispersed their followers to return to their former occupations,
and established his authority throughout Guānzhōng.
Only Lǚ Wěi, Zhāng Hán, and Jiǎng Zhèn sent envoys to surrender to Shǔ;
the rest were all pacified.
13Wú Hàn, leading Grand General of Swift Cavalry Dù Mào and six other generals, besieged Sū Mào at Guǎnglè;
Zhōu Jiàn gathered over a hundred thousand men to relieve him.
Zhōu Jiàn was Liú Yǒng's general.
Disadvantaged,
Wú Hàn fell from his horse and injured his knee,
returning to camp;
Quī is the same as xī (knee).
The generals said to Hàn:
"A formidable enemy is before us,
and you, sir, are injured and confined to bed;
the hearts of the multitude are afraid!"
The morale of the three armies is dependent on the general,
hence this was said.
He slaughtered oxen to feast his soldiers,
encouraging and motivating them.
The soldiers' morale doubled.
The next day,
Sū Mào and Zhōu Jiàn led out their troops and surrounded Hàn;
Hàn fought vigorously,
utterly defeating them.
Mào fled back to Húlín.
The people of Suīyáng rebelled, opened the city gates, and welcomed Liú Yǒng.
Gài Yán, leading his generals, besieged them;
Wú Hàn left Dù Mào and Chén Jùn to guard Guǎnglè,
and personally led his troops to assist Yán in besieging Suīyáng.
14The imperial carriage returned from Xiǎocháng'ān,
ordering Cén Péng to lead Fù Jùn, Zāng Gōng, Liú Hóng, and over thirty thousand others to attack Qín Fēng in the south.
In the fifth month,
on the Jǐyǒu day,
the imperial carriage returned to the palace.
15On the last day of the Yǐmǎo cycle,
there was a solar eclipse.
16In the sixth month,
on the Rénxū day,
there was a general amnesty.
17Yán Cén attacked Nányáng,
capturing several cities;
Grand General of Establishing Might Gěng Yǎn fought him at Ráng.
The Dìlǐzhì states: Ráng County
belonged to Nányáng Commandery.
Cén fled with several cavalry to Dōngyáng,
where he joined Qín Fēng;
Fēng gave him his daughter as wife.
Grand General of Establishing Righteousness Zhū Hù, leading Jì Zūn and others, fought Cén at Dōngyáng,
defeating him;
Xián said: Dōngyáng is a gathering place's name;
its old city was south of today's Dèng Prefecture.
Línhuái Commandery also had a Dōngyáng County,
which is not this place.
I rely on the Jùn Guó Zhì,
Nányáng's Yùyáng County had Dōngyáng Jù.
Hù then went south and joined Cén Péng's army.
Yán Cén's Protector of the Army, Dèng Zhòngkuàng, held troops and occupied Yīn County.
Xián said: Yīn County
belonged to Nányáng Commandery;
its old city was north of today's Gǔchéng County in Xiāng Prefecture.
The Shuǐjīngzhù states: The Miǎn River flows south past east of Gǔchéng,
then south past west of Yīn County.
Sòng Bái said: Today's Guānghuà Military Prefecture
was originally Yīn County territory.
Former Court Attendant Sū Jìng of Fúfēng wrote to persuade him,
before this, the emperor had used Jìng as Court Attendant.
Shuì is pronounced shū ruì.
Jìng ultimately did not boast of his accomplishments,
hid himself, delighted in the Dao,
and died of old age at home.
Qín Fēng resisted Cén Péng at Dèng.
The Dìlǐzhì states: Dèng County
belonged to Nányáng Commandery;
it was the State of Dèng during the Chūnqiū period.
In the seventh month,
Péng attacked and defeated him.
He advanced to besiege Fēng at Líqiū,
and separately dispatched General of Massed Crossbows Fù Jùn to lead troops to secure Jiāngdōng,
and Yáng Prefecture was completely pacified.
18Gài Yán besieged Suīyáng for a hundred days.
Liú Yǒng, Sū Mào, and Zhōu Jiàn broke out,
intending to flee to Cuó;
this is Cuó County of Pèi Commandery.
Xián said: Today's Bó Prefecture County;
the sound is zā.
Yǒng's general Qìng Wú beheaded Yǒng and surrendered.
The Xìngpǔ states: Descendants of Qíng, a grandee of Qí.
The Jùn Guó Zhì states: Pèi Commandery's Shānsāng County had Chuíhuì Jù.
Xián said: In today's Bó Prefecture's Shānsāng County northwest,
also named Lǐchéng.
Dù Yòu's Tōngdiǎn states: Chuíhuì Jù is in Bó Prefecture's Méngchéng County northwest.
Jiǎo Qiáng fled to secure Xīfáng.
19In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Rénshēn day,
the emperor visited Chōnglíng,
and offered sacrifices at the ancestral temples.
These were the ancestral temples of Chōnglíng Jiéhóu and his four generations of descendants.
20 Gěng Yǎn calmly spoke to the Emperor,
requesting permission to go north and gather the unmobilized Shanggǔ troops,
pacify Péng Chǒng in Yúyáng,
capture Zhāng Fēng in Zhuójùn,
then return to reclaim Fùpíng and Huòsuǒ,
attack Zhāng Bù to the east,
and thus pacify Qí.
The Emperor admired his spirit
and granted his request.
21 In the eleventh month,
on the Yǐwèi day,
the Emperor returned from Chōnglíng.
22 In this year,
Lǐ Xiàn proclaimed himself Emperor,
appointed all officials,
held nine cities,
and commanded over one hundred thousand troops.
Of the twelve cities in Lújiāng,
Xiàn had only taken nine.
23 The Emperor said to Grand Master of the Palace Lái Shè:
(Family register: Lái,
of the Zǐ surname,
a collateral descendant of Shang,
given the fief of Lái,
and thus took it as their clan name;
later, to avoid calamity, the radical 邑 (yì) was removed.
The Han List of Meritorious Officials includes the Marquis of Dà, Lái Cāng.)
(Shè,
read Xǔjí Fān.)
"Now Xīzhōu has not yet submitted.
(Xīzhōu refers to Wěi Xiāo.)
(Zǐyáng is Gōngsūn Shù's courtesy name.)
As all the generals are currently occupied in Guāndōng,
I am contemplating a strategy for Xīzhōu,
but am unsure what it should be."
Shè replied:
"I once met Wěi Xiāo in Cháng'ān.
When he first rose up,
he took 'Hàn' as his banner.
(Details can be found in Volume 39, Gēngshǐ First Year.)
If you open up to him with a sincere promise,
(Yáng Zǐ said: The words of a sage
are as clear as red and blue.)
then Gōngsūn Shù's inevitable downfall
will not be worth planning against!"
The Emperor agreed
and then ordered Shè to go as envoy to Xiāo.
Xiāo had already rendered service to Hàn,
and had also accepted Dèng Yǔ's titles and appointments.
(Details can be found in the previous volume, First Year.)
Xiāo then submitted a memorial to the court.
The Emperor replied with extraordinary courtesy,
addressing him by his courtesy name,
using the etiquette reserved for an equal state,
thereby comforting and treating him with great generosity.
(Xián said: Wèi,
means 'to pacify'.
Jiè,
means 'to recommend'.
It means to comfort, pacify, and recommend him.)
1 In the first month,
on the Jiǎshēn day,
there was a great amnesty.
2 In the second month,
on the Rénzǐ day,
the Emperor went to Huái;
on the Rénshēn day,
he returned to Luòyáng.
3 Yán Cén again raided Shùnyáng;
(The Record of Commandaries and States says: Shùnyáng County belongs to Nányáng Commandery.
The Shùn River flows southeast into the Cài River.
The Record of Geography says: The old city of Shùnyáng
is thirty lǐ west of Ráng County, Dèng Prefecture,
and was the Xún fief of Chǔ.)
(Fù,
read Fúyòu Fān;
same below.)
Cén fled to Hànzhōng;
Gōngsūn Shù appointed Cén as Grand Marshal
and enfeoffed him as King of Rǔníng.
4 Tián Róng heard that Qín Fēng had been defeated,
became fearful,
and wished to surrender.
His wife's elder brother, Xīn Chén, enumerated the commanderies and states acquired by Péng Chǒng, Zhāng Bù, Dǒng Xiàn, Gōngsūn Shù, and others, and showed them to Róng, saying:
"Luòyáng is as small as a palm!"
(As a palm, meaning its narrowness.)
Róng said:
"Even with King Qín's strength,
he was still besieged by the General Who Conquers the South;
my surrender is decided!"
(Cén Péng was then the General-in-Chief Who Conquers the South, hence Róng's statement.)
He personally led troops along the river, ascending the Miǎn River to Líqiū.
(From Yílíng, one goes down the river
to Miǎnkǒu;
from Miǎnkǒu, one ascends the Miǎn River,
and can reach Líqiū.)
(Shàng,
read Shízhǎng Fān.)
He took a secret path and first surrendered to Cén Péng,
then sent a letter to Róng, saying:
"You should surrender in good time,
do not be bound by your previous plans!"
Róng suspected Chén of betraying him,
burned a turtle shell for divination,
and the omen for surrender showed a central crack.
(Zhōulǐ, Chuí Shì: For all divinations,
a bright fire is used to burn a tortoise shell until it scorches,
then the burning ember is blown,
and cuts are made and given to the diviner.
Zhèng Xuán said: Jiāo Jùn refers to the use of thorn branches or similar.
The omen
is the shape that appears on the tortoise shell
from the fire
and can be interpreted.)
(Chuí,
read Shísuǐ Fān.)
(Jiāo,
read Zāiyuē Fān.)
(Jùn,
read Jùn,
also Zǐcùn Fān.)
He allied with Qín Fēng;
Cén Péng attacked and defeated them,
and Róng fled back to Yílíng.
5 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the Dīngsì day,
the Emperor went to Yè;
on the Jǐsì day,
he went to Língpíng.
(Xián said: A county name,
belonging to Jùlù Commandery,
its old city is southeast of present-day Gǔchéng County, Dìng Prefecture.)
In Gélì County, five clans jointly drove out the acting magistrate,
occupied the city, and rebelled;
(Xián said: Gélì County belongs to Píngyuán Commandery,
its old city is northwest of present-day Dé Prefecture.
The five clans
were likely powerful local gentry and magnates.)
(Gélì,
read Gé.)
(I believe "shǒuzhǎng" refers to an acting Gélì county magistrate,
not a regular official.)
(Zhǎng,
read Zhīliǎng Fān;
same below.)
Wú Hàn said:
"Those who caused Gélì to rebel
are the acting magistrate's fault.
Anyone who dares to rashly advance troops shall be executed!"
He then issued a proclamation to the commandery, ordering the arrest of the acting magistrate,
and sent someone to offer apologies;
the five clans in the city were greatly pleased,
and immediately led their people to surrender.
The generals then submitted,
saying:
"To take a city without battle
is beyond what the common multitude can achieve!"
6 In the fifth month,
the Emperor went to Yuánshì;
then went to Lúnú,
intending to personally lead a campaign against Péng Chǒng.
Fú Zhàn admonished him, saying:
"Now Yǎn, Yù, Qīng, and Jì are
the heartland of the Central Plains,
yet bandits run rampant,
and they have not yet submitted to transformation.
Yúyáng is a barren border region.
(Border region means bordering foreign tribes.)
For Your Majesty to abandon what is near and pursue what is far,
to discard what is easy and seek what is difficult,
is truly what bewilders your servant!"
The Emperor then returned.
7 The Emperor dispatched the Suggestion Grand General Zhū Hù (朱祜), the Establishing Might Grand General Gěng Yǎn (耿弇), the Conquering Barbarians General Jì Zūn (祭遵),
and the Valiant Cavalry General Líu Xǐ (劉喜) to attack Zhāng Fēng (張豐) in Zhuójùn (涿郡).
Jì Zūn arrived first,
swiftly attacked Fēng,
and captured him.
Previously,
Fēng was fond of esoteric arts.
A Daoist priest told Fēng that he was destined to be emperor.
In Xīdū (西都) there were Fangshi (方士),
and in Dōngdū (東都) they were therefore called Daoists.
Hǎo (好) is pronounced "hū dào".
He said,
"There is an imperial seal in the stone."
Fēng believed him
and thus rebelled.
After he was captured
and about to be executed,
he still said,
"There is an imperial seal in the elbow stone."
People nearby broke it open with a hammer for him.
Fēng then realized he had been deceived
and sighed, looking up at the sky,
"I am about to die, with no regrets!"
The Emperor issued an edict for Gěng Yǎn to advance and attack Péng Chǒng (彭寵).
Gěng Yǎn considered that his father Kuàng (況) had achieved the same merit as Péng Chǒng.
Kuàng and Péng Chǒng both had rendered aid to the Hàn (漢) dynasty;
this is recorded in the previous volume, chapter 39, under Gèngshǐ (更始) 2nd year.
He dared not advance alone
and requested to go to Luòyáng (雒陽).
The edict replied,
"General, your whole family has served the state,
and your achievements are especially notable.
What suspicion or doubt do you have
that you wish to be summoned back?"
Kuàng heard this
and instead sent Yǎn's younger brother, Guó (國), to serve at court.
At this time, Jì Zūn was stationed in Liángxiāng (良鄉),
and Líu Xǐ was stationed in Yángxiāng (陽鄉).
Xián (賢) said: Liángxiāng and Yángxiāng
are both county names,
and both belonged to Zhuójùn (涿郡).
The old city of Yángxiāng
is in the northwest of present-day Gù'ān (故安) County, Yōuzhōu (幽州).
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Liángxiāng,
in Yān (燕) it was Zhōngdū (中都),
in Hàn (漢) it was Liángxiāng County.
Gěng Kuàng sent his son Shū (舒) to raid and defeat the Xīongnú (匈奴) soldiers,
beheading two kings.
Péng Chǒng then retreated.
8 In the sixth month,
on the xīn-hài (辛亥) day,
the imperial carriage returned to the palace.
9 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the dīng-hài (丁亥) day,
the Emperor visited Qiáo (譙).
Kǎoyì (考異) says: Yuánjì (袁紀) states,
"In the sixth month he visited Qiáo."
Now we follow Fànshū (范書).
10Dǒng Xiàn's (董憲) general Bēn Xīu (賁休) surrendered with Lánlíng (蘭陵).
Xiàn heard of this
and personally besieged him from Tán (郯).
Xián (賢) said: Tán County
belonged to Dōnghǎi (東海) Commandery;
its old city is in the northeast of present-day Xiàpī (下邳) County, Sīzhōu (泗州).
Tán (郯) is pronounced "tán".
Chǔ (楚) is Péngchéng (彭城).
The Emperor ordered:
"You can go directly and attack Tán."
Xián (賢) said: Dǎo (擣)
means to strike.
I think Dǎo (擣)
means to strike where it is empty;
this is what military strategists call attacking where one is certain to rescue.
Yán (延) and others, seeing Bēn Xīu's city was in danger,
therefore went to his aid first.
Xiàn met them in battle and feigned defeat and retreated.
Yán and others then broke the siege and entered the city.
The next day,
Xiàn brought out a large army and again surrounded them.
Yán and others, in fear,
hastily broke out and fled,
and then went to attack Tán.
The Emperor reproached them, saying:
"The reason I wanted to attack Tán first earlier
was because of its unexpectedness!
Now that you have fled,
the enemy's plan is already set.
How can the siege be lifted?"
Yán and others reached Tán,
but indeed could not conquer it.
And Dǒng Xiàn then captured Lánlíng
and killed Bēn Xīu.
11In the eighth month,
on the wù-wǔ (戊午) day,
the Emperor visited Shòuchūn (壽春).
The Dìlǐzhì (地理志) states: Shòuchūn County
belonged to Jiǔjīang (九江) Commandery.
Xián (賢) said: Now Shòuzhōu (壽州) County.
In the ninth month,
Xiàn (憲) was besieged in Shū (舒).
The Dìlǐzhì (地理志) states: Lújiāng (廬江) Commandery
had its seat in Shū County.
Xián (賢) said: Its old city is in the west of present-day Lújiāng (廬江) County, Lúzhōu (廬州).
Huì (會) is pronounced "gǔ wài".
At the end of Wáng Mǎng's (王莽) reign,
the world was in chaos,
but Hénán (河南) Marquis Hóu Bà (侯霸), the Grand Administrator of Línhuái (臨淮), alone was able to preserve his commandery intact.
The Jùnguózhì (郡國志) states: Línhuái Commandery was one thousand four hundred lǐ (里) east of Luòyáng (雒陽).
He was appointed Shàngshūlìng (尚書令).
At that time, the court had no established code of laws
and few old officials.
Hóu Bà was thoroughly familiar with past precedents,
collected surviving documents,
and memorialized the good governance and laws of previous generations,
which were then implemented.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the jiǎ-yín (甲寅) day,
the imperial carriage returned to the palace.
12Wēi Xiāo (隗囂) sent Mǎ Yuán (馬援) to observe Gōngsūn Shù (公孫述).
Mǎ Yuán had previously lived in the same neighborhood as Gōngsūn Shù
and they were on good terms.
Mǎ Yuán and Gōngsūn Shù were both from Màolíng (茂陵).
The Shuōwén (說文) says: Hàn (閈)
means a neighborhood;
pronounced "hóu hàn".
Mǎ Yuán expected to shake hands and rejoice as in their ordinary lives.
However, Gōngsūn Shù grandly arranged imperial guards and attendants to usher Mǎ Yuán in.
After they bowed and completed the ceremony, he ordered Mǎ Yuán to leave and go to his guesthouse.
For Mǎ Yuán, he even ordered the creation of a plain robe made of dùbù (都布)
Hé Chéngtiān's (何承天) Zuǎnwén (纂文) says: Dū (都), zhì (致), cuò (錯), lǚ (履), wújí (無極)
are all names of fabrics.
The Fāngyán (方言) says: Chányī (禪衣),
in the region between the Jiāng (江) and Huái (淮) rivers and Southern Chǔ (楚) it is called dié (褋);
west of the Pass it is called chányī (禪衣).
Wéi (為) is pronounced "yú wěi".
and convened all officials in the ancestral temple,
establishing a place for his old acquaintance.
Gōngsūn Shù, with his luánqí (鸞旗) and máoqí (旄騎),
The note for luánqí (鸞旗) is in volume 13, Wéndì (文帝) 1st year.
Máojí (旄騎)
means cavalry with yak-tail banners.
When Qín (秦) Duke Mù (穆) attacked the great catalpa tree in Nánshān (南山),
a blue ox ran out
and entered the Fēngshuǐ (豐水) river.
