pronounced *yú kuàng* (于況).
1 In spring,
the first month,
Wú Hàn (吳漢) again led the General Who Captures Enemies, Wáng Bà (王霸), and three other generals with 60,000 men out of Gāoliǔ (高柳) to attack Jiǎ Lǎn (賈覽).
Several thousand Xiōngnú (匈奴) cavalry came to rescue him,
and a continuous battle was fought below Píngchéng (平城).
Píngchéng (平城) county
belonged to Yànmén (鴈門) commandery.
2 The Marquis of Xiàyáng (夏陽), Féng Yì (馮異), and others
The biography of Féng Yì (馮異) says: He was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yángxià (陽夏).
Xián (賢) says: Xià (夏)
is pronounced *jiǎ* (賈).
The end of Mǎ Wǔ’s (馬武) biography lists the official positions and names of the twenty-eight generals,
stating "Marquis of Xiàyáng (夏陽), Féng Yì (馮異)."
Yángxià (陽夏) county belonged to Huáiyáng (淮陽) commandery.
Xiàyáng (夏陽) county belonged to Zuǒfēngyì (左馮翊).
It is not known which is correct.
The *xià* (夏) in Xiàyáng (夏陽)
is pronounced *hù yǎ* (戶雅).
All were beheaded.
Wěi Chún (隗純) had not yet surrendered.
The generals wanted to return temporarily and rest their troops.
Yì (異) firmly held his ground.
They jointly attacked Luòmén (落門).
In Jì (冀) county, Tiānshuǐ (天水), there was Luòmén (落門) settlement,
and Luòmén (落門) mountain.
Xián (賢) says: It is in the southeast of today’s Lǒngxī (隴西) county, Wèizhōu (渭州).
In summer,
Yì (異) died in the army.
3 In autumn,
the eighth month,
on the *jǐhài* (己亥) day,
the emperor visited Cháng'ān (長安).
4 Originally,
Wěi Xiāo’s (隗囂) general, Gāo Jùn (高峻) of Āndìng (安定), held troops and occupied the Dìyī (第一) region of Gāopíng (高平).
When the emperor went to Lǒng (隴),
he sent Mǎ Yuán (馬援) to persuade Jùn (峻) to surrender.
When Wú Hàn (吳漢) and the other armies retreated,
Jùn (峻) fled back to his old camp,
and again helped Xiāo (囂) resist Lǒngdǐ (隴坻).
For one year, it could not be taken.
The emperor personally led a campaign against him.
Kòu Xún (寇恂) advised, saying:
"Cháng'ān (長安) is centrally located.
Xián (賢) says: From Luòyáng (雒陽) to Gāopíng (高平), Cháng'ān (長安) is in the middle.
Āndìng (安定) and Lǒngxī (隴西) will surely be shaken with fear.
If we calmly stay in one place,
we can control the four directions.
Now our soldiers and horses are weary,
and we are about to traverse dangerous terrain.
This is not a secure position for a monarch.
Last year's situation in Yǐngchuān (潁川)
can serve as a grave warning."
The emperor did not heed him,
and advanced
to Qǐan (汧).
Jùn (峻) still did not surrender.
The emperor sent Kòu Xún (寇恂) to persuade him to surrender.
Xún (恂) delivered the imperial letter to Dìyī (第一).
Jùn (峻) sent his military advisor Huángfǔ Wén (皇甫文) to meet him,
whose words and demeanor showed no submission.
Xún (恂) was enraged
and was about to execute him.
The generals advised, saying:
"Gāo Jùn (高峻) has 10,000 elite soldiers,
mostly equipped with powerful crossbows.
He blocks the Lǒng (隴) road to the west,
and has not surrendered for years.
Now we want him to surrender, but instead we kill his envoy.
Is this not unacceptable?"
Xún (恂) did not reply,
and immediately beheaded him.
He sent his deputy back to inform Jùn (峻), saying:
"Your military advisor was disrespectful,
and has already been executed!
If you wish to surrender,
surrender quickly;
if not,
then hold fast!"
Jùn (峻) was terrified,
and on that very day opened the city gates and surrendered.
All the generals congratulated him,
and then asked:
"May we ask why you killed his envoy but made his city surrender?"
Xún (恂) said:
"Huángfǔ Wén (皇甫文) was Jùn’s (峻) confidant,
the one from whom he sought counsel.
Now that he came,
his words and attitude showed no submission,
indicating he definitely had no intention of surrendering.
If we had kept him alive, Wén (文) would have carried out his plan;
by killing him, we shattered their courage."
This means that when Wén (文) died, Jùn (峻) lost his courage.
All the generals said:
"This is beyond our comprehension!"
5 In winter,
the tenth month,
Lái Xiá (來歙) and the generals attacked and broke through Luòmén (落門).
Zhōu Zōng (周宗), Xíng Xún (行巡), Gǒu Yǔ (苟宇), Zhào Huī (趙恢), and others surrendered with Wěi Chún (隗純).
Wáng Yuán (王元) fled to Shǔ (蜀).
The Wěi (隗) clan was resettled east of the capital.
Wěi Chún (隗純) surrendered, but his clan was relocated,
because they were a powerful clan in Xīzhōu (西州),
and it was feared they might later cause trouble again.
Upon reaching Wǔwēi (武威),
he was captured
and executed.
6 The Xiānlíng Qiāng (先零羌) and various other tribes raided Jīnchéng (金城) and Lǒngxī (隴西).
Lái Xiá (來歙) led Gài Yán (蓋延) and others to attack them,
utterly defeating them,
beheading and capturing several thousand people.
Thereupon, granaries were opened to relieve the hungry and destitute.
Lǒngyòu (隴右) thus became peaceful,
and the route to Liángzhōu (涼州) was cleared.
All the commanderies of Liángzhōu (涼州) on their way to the capital
had to pass through Lǒng (隴).
When Lǒngyòu (隴右) was peaceful,
the road to Liángzhōu (涼州) became open.
7 On the *gēngyín* (庚寅) day,
the emperor's carriage returned to the palace.
1 In spring,
the third month,
on the *jǐyǒu* (己酉) day,
the emperor visited Nányáng (南陽).
*Kǎoyì* (考異) says: Imperial Annals:
"On the *jǐyǒu* (己酉) day,
he visited Nányáng (南陽).
On the *gēngwǔ* (庚午) day,
the imperial carriage returned to the palace."
Above, there is
"the second month, *jǐmǎo* (己卯)."
Yuán (袁) Annals:
"The third month, on the *jǐyǒu* (己酉) day,
he visited Nányáng (南陽)."
Comparing with the perpetual calendar,
the *rénshēn* (壬申) day was the first day of the second month,
and the *jǐmǎo* (己卯) day was the eighth day.
Both the *jǐyǒu* (己酉) and *gēngwǔ* (庚午) days
were in the third month.
It seems that in the Imperial Annals,
above "the *jǐyǒu* (己酉) day,"
the characters
"the third month"
were omitted.
We now follow the Yuán (袁) Annals.
On the *gēngwǔ* (庚午) day,
the imperial carriage returned to the palace.
2 Cén Péng (岑彭) garrisoned at Jīnxiāng (津鄉)
and repeatedly attacked Tián Róng (田戎) and others,
but failed.
The emperor sent Wú Hàn (吳漢) leading the General Who Executes Enemies, Liú Lóng (劉隆), and two other generals,
dispatching a total of over 60,000 Jingzhōu (荊州) soldiers and 5,000 cavalry,
to meet Péng (彭) at Jīngmén (荊門).
Péng (彭) prepared several thousand
warships.
Wú Hàn (吳漢) considered that the oarmen from various commanderies consumed too much grain,
and wanted to dismiss them.
Oarmen (*zhuózú*) were those who rowed boats with oars.
Unable to send them away,
he submitted a memorial explaining the situation.
The emperor replied to Péng (彭), saying:
"The Grand Marshal (Dàsīmǎ) is accustomed to using infantry and cavalry,
and is not skilled in naval warfare.
The matter at Jīngmén (荊門)
is entirely dependent on the Commander-in-Chief Who Conquers the South (Zhēngnán Gōng) to manage as crucial."
Péng (彭) was the Grand General Who Conquers the South,
hence he was referred to as Commander-in-Chief Who Conquers the South.
In the intercalary month,
Cén Péng ordered his army to recruit volunteers to attack the pontoon bridge,
promising the highest rewards to the first to ascend.
Thereupon, the partial general Lǔ Qí volunteered and advanced.
At that time, the east wind was furious and strong.
Lǔ Qí’s boat went upstream against the current
and sped directly towards the pontoon bridge.
The clustered stakes had reversed grappling hooks.
These reversed grappling hooks,
once they hooked an enemy ship,
would prevent it from retreating,
and also resist it from advancing.
Qí and his men, seizing the advantage, fought desperately.
They used flying torches to set it ablaze.
With the wind raging and the fire intensifying,
the bridge towers collapsed and burned.
Cén Péng advanced his entire army with the wind,
sweeping aside all opposition.
The Shǔ troops were thrown into great disarray,
and several thousand drowned.
They beheaded Rèn Mǎn
and captured Chéng Fàn alive,
while Tián Róng fled to garrison Jiāngzhōu.
Péng recommended Liú Lóng for appointment as the Administrator of Nánjùn;
he had first appointed Lóng to govern Nánjùn and then submitted his memorial.
Shàng (上),
at that time, was pronounced like ‘fān’.
The Huáyáng Guózhì states: Bā and Chǔ attacked each other,
hence Jiāngguān was established.
It was formerly in Chìjiǎ Chéng,
later moved to the south bank of Jiāngzhōu,
opposite Báidì Chéng.
The old city was in what is now Qúizhōu Yúfù Xiàn to the south,
which is the ancient Hànguān.
Dù Yòu said: Bāshān Xiàn,
ancient Hànguān.
If so, this is a different place.
Wherever they passed, the common people offered oxen and wine to welcome and entertain them.
Péng again declined to accept them;
the people were greatly pleased
and vied to open their gates and surrender.
An imperial edict appointed Péng as the Inspector of Yìzhōu,
and in any commandery he entered, he was to act as the Administrator.
If Péng left the border,
the title of Administrator was to be transferred to the subsequent general.
The subsequent general
was the one who led troops to follow Péng and advance.
When Péng arrived at Jiāngzhōu,
judging its city strong and its provisions plentiful,
and difficult to capture quickly,
he left Féng Jùn to guard it.
He himself led his army, taking advantage of the favorable situation, directly to Diànjiāng,
attacking and breaking Píngqǔ.
Xián said: Diànjiāng,
a county name,
belonging to Bājùn,
is now Zhōngzhōu Xiàn.
According to Sòng Bái’s Xù Tōngdiǎn: Zhōngzhōu Diànjiāng Xiàn was originally the land of Línjiāng Xiàn in the Later Hàn.
Later, Emperor Gōng of the Northern Wèi divided Línjiāng to establish Diànjiāng Xiàn.
Hézhōu Shíjìng Xiàn
was the original Hàn Diànjiāng Xiàn.
All counties under the jurisdiction of Hézhōu
were Hàn Diànjiāng territory.
Diàn (墊),
pronounced like ‘tú xié’ in reverse.
Píngqǔ (平曲),
location missing.
Wú Hàn remained at Yílíng,
preparing exposed oars for continued advance.
The Éryǎ says: ‘Jí’ is called ‘ráo’.
Lùráo (露橈)
means the oars are exposed outside,
while people are inside the boat.
Ráo (橈),
pronounced ‘ráo’.
3 In summer,
the Xiānlíng Qiāng raided Líntáo.
Líntáo Xiàn
belonged to Lǒngxī Jùn.
Líng (零),
pronounced ‘lián’.
Táo (洮),
pronounced ‘tāo’.
The Jùnguó Zhì states: Lǒngxī Jùn,
2,220 *lǐ* west of Luòyáng.
They were severely defeated.
4 Gōngsūn Shù appointed Wáng Yuán as general
and sent him with Lǐngjūn Huán Ān to resist Héchí.
The Xìngpǔ states: Huán (環),
a surname,
descendants of Huán Liè Yǐn of Chǔ;
also, Chǔ had the worthy man Huán Yuān.
Héchí Xiàn
belonged to Wǔdū Jùn.
Lái Xī and Gài Yán and others advanced to attack Yuán and Ān,
severely defeating them,
then captured Xiàbiàn,
and continued to advance with their victory.
The Shǔ people were greatly alarmed
and sent an assassin to stab Xī.
He had not yet died.
“Had not yet died”
means not yet ceased.
Kècì (客刺),
pronounced ‘qī yì’ in reverse.
Yán saw Xī
and, bowing down, grieved,
unable to look up.
Xī shouted at Yán, saying:
“How dare Hǔyá act thus!
Yán was Hǔyá Dàjiāngjūn,
hence he was referred to as Hǔyá.
Since I have nothing to repay the state,
I call out to Jùqīng,
wishing to entrust military affairs to you.
Gài Yán,
courtesy name Jùqīng.
Shǔ (屬),
pronounced ‘zhī yù’ in reverse.
Even if the blade is in my body,
can I not command troops to execute you, sir!”
Yán wiped his tears and forced himself to rise,
receiving his instructions.
Xī personally wrote a memorial, saying:
“Your servant, after people had settled down at night,
that is, after sunset when activities ceased,
hence the first watch of the night is called ‘people settled down’.
was struck in a vital spot.
‘What person’
means not knowing who the person was.
I truly regret that my service has not been commensurate,
bringing shame to the imperial court.
Indeed, governing the state is fundamentally about obtaining worthy individuals.
Tàizhōng Dàfū Duàn Xiāng
is upright and trustworthy.
Xián said: Gǔgěng (骨鯁)
means upright.
The Shuōwén says: Gěng (鯁),
fish bone;
when a bone gets stuck in the throat while eating, it is gěng.
Also, my brothers are unworthy,
and I fear they will eventually incur punishment.
May Your Majesty pity them
and frequently bestow instruction and guidance.”
He threw down his brush, drew the blade, and died.
For anyone who is stabbed by an assassin,
even with the blade in the body, one has not yet died.
Drawing the blade causes one to expire.
Greatly surprised,
the Emperor read the letter, wiping away tears;
he appointed Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn Mǎ Chéng to act as Zhōngláng Jiāng in his stead.
When Xī’s coffin returned to Luòyáng,
the Emperor in a plain carriage attended the mourning,
and sent off the funeral procession.
5 Zhào Wáng Liáng followed the Emperor in sending off Xī’s coffin and returned.
Upon entering the Xiàchéng Mén,
there were twelve city gates in Luòyáng, the Xià Mén was located at the *hài* position (northwest).
he shouted at Hándān to turn his carriage around.
He also questioned and reprimanded the gate guard.
The Bǎiguān Zhì states: The Chéngmén Xiàowèi was in charge of the twelve city gates of Luòyáng,
with one gate guard for each gate.
Hán (邯),
pronounced ‘hù gān’ in reverse.
The Sīlì Xiàowèi Bào Yǒng impeached him in a memorial, stating:
“Liáng showed no respect befitting a feudal vassal,
a great disrespect.”
Liáng was a noble relative and highly esteemed,
yet Yǒng impeached him,
which made the court solemn.
Yǒng appointed Bào Huī of Fúfēng as Dūguān Cóngshì.
The Bǎiguān Zhì states: The Sīlì Xiàowèi had twelve Cóngshì Shǐ.
The Dūguān Cóngshì
was primarily responsible for investigating and reporting officials who violated the law.
Cài Zhì’s Hàn Yí states: The Dūguān presided over court assemblies in Luòyáng,
together with the *yuàn* officials of the Three Bureaus.
He did not avoid the powerful or resistant.
The Emperor often said:
“Even noble relatives should restrain themselves to avoid the two Bàos.”
From Yǒngxíng county to Bālíng,
the Sīlì Xiàowèi
commanded Sānhé, Sānfǔ, and Hóngnóng.
Bālíng county
belonged to Jīngzhào.
Xíng
is pronounced Xiàmèng.
[He] bowed down,
wept with full grief, and then departed;
westward, he reached Fúfēng,
slaughtered an ox, and offered it at Gǒu Jiàn's tomb.
The matter of Gǒu Jiàn protecting Bào Yǒng is seen in volume 36, Gēngshǐ Year 2.
Shàng
is pronounced Shípáng.
[He] felt displeased
and asked the high officials:
"Is performing a mission like this
acceptable?"
Emperor Wǔ established thirteen regional inspectors (cìshǐ),
all of whom were envoys (bùshǐzhě).
The Sīlì (Commissioner of Servants) now went beyond his department,
hence the mention of performing a mission.
Shǐ
is pronounced Shūlì.
"[The benevolent one]
is the master of conduct,
and the loyal one
is the lord of righteousness;
benevolence does not abandon old friends,
and loyalty does not forget the ruler—
these are the highest forms of conduct."
The Emperor's displeasure then subsided.
6 The Emperor personally led the expedition against Gōngsūn Shù;
in the autumn, seventh month,
he arrived at Cháng'ān.
7 Gōngsūn Shù sent his generals Yán Cén, Lǚ Wěi, Wáng Yuán, and Gōngsūn Huī with all their forces to resist in Guǎnghàn and Zīzhōng.
Guǎnghàn county
belonged to Guǎnghàn Commandery.
Xián said: Zīzhōng
is a county name,
belonging to Jiānwéi Commandery;
its territory is in present-day Zīzhōu, Zīyáng county.
Sòng Bái said: All counties of Zīzhōu
are the territory of Han Zīzhōng;
Pánshí county,
the seat of Zīzhōu,
is the old city of Han Zīzhōng.
Xián said: It is Huángshítān.
The commentary to the Water Classic states: The Jiāngshǔi river flows east from Fúlíng for a hundred *lǐ* and reaches Huángshí.
It is in present-day Fúzhōu, Fúlíng county.
Dù Yòu said: Today it is called Héngshítān.
From Fúshuǐ up to Píngqū,
[he] resisted Yán Cén,
then divided his troops to sail down the river back to Jiāngzhōu,
and upstream along the Dūjiāng.
Xián said: Dūjiāng
is Chéngdū Jiāng.
Sòng Bái said: Píjiāng,
also named Dūjiāng,
and also named Chéngdū Jiāng.
[He] greatly defeated them;
then, day and night, he doubled his march for over two thousand *lǐ*,
and directly captured Wǔyáng.
Xián said: Wǔyáng county
belonged to Jiānwéi Commandery,
its old city is in the east of present-day Lóngzhōu, Lóngshān county;
he also said: Its old city is in present-day Méizhōu.
Liú Xù said: Táng Língzhōu's Rénshòu county
was the territory of Han Wǔyáng county;
some say: Present-day Méizhōu's Méishān and Péngshān counties
were originally the territory of Han Wǔyáng county.
Dù Yòu said: The old city of Han Wǔyáng county
is in the east of Jiāzhōu, Suíshān county.
A few dozen *lǐ* from Chéngdū,
Xián said: Guǎngdū
is a county name,
belonging to Shǔ Commandery,
its old city is in the southeast of present-day Yìzhōu, Chéngdū county.
Sòng Bái said: The *Shǔ Zhì* states that Han Guǎngdū county was established in Yuánsò year 2;
in Suí Rénshòu year 1,
to avoid Emperor Yáng's taboo name,
it was changed to Shuāngliú;
in Táng Lóngshuò year 3,
Shuāngliú county was divided,
and Guǎngdū county was re-established twelve *lǐ* south of the old county.
Wherever [Péng] went, they scattered and fled.
Initially,
Shù, hearing that Han troops were in Píngqū,
had sent a large army to intercept them.
When Péng reached Wǔyáng,
circling around to the rear of Yán Cén's army,
Shǔ was shaken.
Shù was greatly alarmed
and struck the ground with his staff, saying:
"What kind of god is this!"
Yán Cén had amassed troops at Yuánshuǐ.
The Emperor's Annals (Dì Jì) write
"Chénshuǐ,"
while this text writes
"Yuán,"
following the error in the biography of Zāng Gōng.
Xián said: The commentary to the Water Classic states: Chénshuǐ flows out of Guǎnghàn county
and enters Fúshuǐ downstream.
Some original texts writing
"Chénshuǐ"
or
"Yuánshuǐ"
are
both incorrect.
I rely on the present-day Tóngchuān Fǔ, Tōngquán county having Chénshuǐ to its north.
Supplies did not arrive,
and all who surrendered wished to scatter and revolt against the commanderies and counties,
regrouping to observe the outcome.
Gōng wanted to retreat,
fearing he would be
attacked from the rear;
coincidentally, the Emperor sent an envoy with troops to Cén Péng,
who had seven hundred horses.
Gōng forged an imperial edict and took them for his own use,
advancing day and night,
spreading out many banners and flags,
ascending the mountains and raising war cries,
with infantry on the right and cavalry on the left,
drawing along boats.
Their shouts echoed through the valleys.
Cén did not expect the Han army to arrive suddenly,
climbed the mountain to observe,
and was greatly terrified;
Gōng then launched an attack,
severely defeating them,
beheading and drowning over ten thousand people,
so that the water became turbid.
Yán Cén fled to Chéngdū,
and all his forces surrendered,
yielding all their soldiers, horses, and treasures.
From then on, [he] pursued the retreating enemy with victory,
Xián said: People prefer yang and dislike yin,
and the north is a dark, secluded place,
so those who are defeated in battle are all said to "go north."
The *Shǐ Jì*, *Yuè Shū* says: "Běi" (north)
means "bài" (defeat);
in recent times, "běi" is pronounced "bèi" (back),
losing its original meaning.
The army reached Yángxiāng.
The biography of Zāng Gōng writes
"Píngyángxiāng,"
this text omits
the character
"Píng."
The commentary to the Water Classic states: Zāng Gōng ascended the Fú river to Píngyáng,
where Gōngsūn Shù's general Wáng Yuán surrendered,
and then captured Miánzhú.
The Fúshuǐ river flows north of Miánzhú county,
so Píngyángxiāng must be within Miánzhú county's borders.
The Emperor wrote a letter to Gōngsūn Shù,
explaining the fortune and misfortune
and showing him a trustworthy pledge.
Shù read the letter and sighed deeply,
showing it to his close associates.
The Grand Courtier Cháng Shǎo and the Minister of the Imperial Household Zhāng Lóng both urged Shù to surrender.
Shù said:
"Rise and fall
are fate;
how could there be a Son of Heaven who surrenders!"
His attendants dared not speak again.
Shǎo and Lóng both died of sorrow.
8 The Emperor returned from Cháng'ān.
9 In winter,
the tenth month,
Gōngsūn Shù sent assassins disguised as runaway slaves,
who surrendered to Cén Péng,
and at night
assassinated Péng;
the Grand Master of Remonstrance and Supervisor of the Army Zhèng Xīng took command of his camp,
awaiting Wú Hàn's arrival to hand it over.
Péng maintained his army in perfect order,
not violating even a single hair.
Qiónggǔ King Rèn Guì, hearing of Péng's prestige and trustworthiness,
sent envoys from thousands of *lǐ* away to offer surrender;
The matter of Rèn Guì surrendering to Shù is seen in volume 40, Year 1.
Qióng
is pronounced Qúgōng.
Rèn
is pronounced Rén.
The Emperor gave all that Rèn Guì had presented to Péng's wife and children.
The people of Shǔ built a temple to sacrifice to him.
10 Mǎ Chéng and others captured Héchí,
then pacified Wǔdū.
The *Jùn Guó Zhì* says: Wǔdū Commandery is one thousand nine hundred *lǐ* west of Luòyáng.
[They] gathered to raid and plunder,
blocking the Hàohàimín Pass.
Chéng and Mǎ Yuán advanced deeply to attack them,
greatly defeating them,
and resettled the surrendered Qiāng people in Tiānshuǐ, Lǒngxī, and Fúfēng.
At this time,
the court officials considered that Jīnchéng was west of Pòqiāng.
Pòqiāng Xiàn belonged to Jīnchéng Jùn.
Xián said: The old city was west of today's Shànzhōu Huángshuǐ Xiàn.
Sòng Bái said: Huángshuǐ Xiàn was originally the land of Hàn Pòqiāng Xiàn.
Later, the Wèi acquired Qīang territory
and established Xīdū Xiàn here.
The Suí changed its name to Huángshuǐ.
They deliberated on abandoning it.
Mǎ Yuán memorialized, saying:
"West of Pòqiāng,
the cities are mostly strong and secure,
easily defensible.
Its fields and soil are fertile.
Xián said: 'Rǎng' means without clods.
If the Qiāng were to remain in
Huángzhōng,
then the harm would be incessant.
It cannot be abandoned."
The Emperor followed his advice.
Over three thousand people returned.
Yuán appointed chief officials for them,
repaired the city walls,
and erected signal towers.
The Zìlín says: 'Wù'
is a small barricade.
The character is sometimes written
pronounced Gǔ.
He encouraged them to farm and raise livestock,
and the people in the commandery lived in contentment.
He also recruited and pacified the Dī and Qiāng outside the passes,
all of whom came to surrender.
Yuán requested that their Hou, Wang, Jun, and Chang titles be reinstated;
the Emperor granted all his requests.
Then the forces of Mǎ Chéng were dismissed.
11. In the twelfth month,
Wú Hàn led thirty thousand men from Yílíng upstream along the river
to attack Gōngsūn Shù.
12. Guō Jí was appointed Píngzhōu Mù.
When he passed through the capital,
the Emperor asked him about gains and losses.
Jí said:
"In selecting and appointing various officials,
one should choose the most talented from all under Heaven,
and not exclusively use people from Nányáng."
At this time, many in office were from the Emperor's hometown and old acquaintances,
which is why Jí mentioned it.
Róng Zhàozǔ punctuated, Gù Jiégāng and Niè Chóngqí re-collated.
Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial command.
Hòuxué Tiāntái
Shìzǔ Guāngwǔ Huángdì Zhōng Zhī Xià
Jiànwǔ Shí’èr Nián
(Bǐngshēn, 36)
1. In spring,
the first month,
Wú Hàn defeated Gōngsūn Shù's generals Wèi Dǎng and Gōngsūn Yǒng at Yúfú Jīn.
The Xù Hànshū says: Jiànwéi Jùn Nán'ān Xiàn has Yúfú Jīn,
which is north of the county
and borders the great river.
The Nánzhōng Zhì says: Yúfú Jīn is several hundred paces wide.
Fú,
pronounced fú.
Shù sent his son-in-law Shǐ Xīng to rescue them.
Hàn intercepted and attacked them,
defeating them,
and then entered Jiànwéi's territory.
All the counties defended their cities.
An edict ordered Hàn to proceed directly to Guǎngdū
and occupy its heartland.
Hàn then advanced to attack Guǎngdū,
capturing it.
In Wǔdì Yuánshuò second year,
Guǎngdū Xiàn was established,
belonging to Shǔ Jùn.
Xián said: Shìqiáo
is one of the Qīxīng Qiáo.
Lǐ Yīng's Yìzhōu Jì: Chōngxīng Qiáo,
formerly Shìqiáo,
is four lí southwest of present-day Chéngdū Xiàn.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù: In Chéngdū,
the two rivers have seven bridges.
The one outside Shíniúmén to the southwest is called Shìqiáo.
Day and night, people defected and rebelled.
Although Shù executed their families,
he still could not stop it.
The Emperor was determined to make him surrender
and issued another edict to persuade Shù, saying:
"Do not be suspicious because Lái Xī and Cén Péng suffered harm.
If those two had suffered harm
(see upper volume, last year),
Xī,
pronounced xū jí.
then your clan would be complete.
Imperial edicts personally written
are not often to be had."
Shù ultimately had no intention of surrendering.
2. In autumn,
the seventh month,
Féng Jùn captured Jiāngzhōu
and seized Tián Jiè.
3 The Emperor cautioned Wú Hàn
saying: "Chéngdū has over a hundred thousand troops,
they are not to be taken lightly.
You should firmly hold Guǎngdū,
await their attack,
and not engage them directly.
If they dare not come,
you may move your camp closer to pressure them,
and only when their strength is exhausted,
can you attack them."
Hàn, taking advantage of his victory,
personally led twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to advance and press Chéngdū;
about ten *lǐ* from the city,
he set up camp north of the river,
and
built a pontoon bridge.
He sent his deputy, General Wǔwēi Liú Shàng, to lead over ten thousand men and encamp south of the river,
with the camps about twenty *lǐ* apart.
The Emperor, hearing of this, was greatly alarmed
and reprimanded Hàn, saying:
"I have given you countless instructions,
why do you act so rashly when faced with the actual situation!
You have lightly advanced deep into enemy territory,
and also set up a separate camp from Shàng.
If there is any urgency,
you will not be able to support each other.
If the bandits send troops to hold you in check,
and attack Shàng with a large force,
once Shàng is defeated,
you will also be defeated.
I am fortunate there were no other consequences—
this means fortunate there were no other worries,
not leading to defeat and loss.
Before the imperial edict arrived,
in the ninth month,
Shù indeed sent his Grand Minister of Works, Xiè Fēng, and Superintendent of the Guards, Yuán Jí, to lead about a hundred thousand troops—
'about a hundred thousand'
is an approximation.
They marched out to attack Hàn,
and sent a separate general to lead over ten thousand men to cut off Liú Shàng,
preventing them from aiding each other.
Hàn fought a great battle for a day,
but his army was defeated
and retreated into the fort.
Fēng then surrounded him.
Hàn then summoned his generals and encouraged them
saying:
"Lì means to exert oneself."
Máo Huǎng said: "Lì, in 'exert and encourage',
has the meaning of 'embellish and rouse'."
"We, along with you all, have crossed perilous obstacles,
fought battles for a thousand *lǐ*,
and thus penetrated deep into enemy territory,
reaching their city walls.
But now Liú Shàng and I are both under siege in two separate places,
our forces are not connected,
and the disaster is immeasurable.
I intend to secretly move our troops to join Shàng south of the river,
combining our forces to resist them.
If we can be of one heart and one mind,
each man fighting for himself,
great success can be achieved;
if not,
defeat will be utter.
The pivot of success or failure
rests on this one action."
All the generals said:
"Yes."
Thereupon, they feasted the soldiers and fed the horses,
closed their camp for three days and did not sally forth.
Then they set up many banners,
kept the smoke and fires burning,
and at night,
with gags in their mouths, led their troops to join forces with Liú Shàng.
Fēng and others did not realize it.
The next day,
they divided their forces to defend the north of the river,
and Fēng personally led the attack south of the river.
Hàn engaged them with all his forces,
and from dawn until dusk,
utterly defeated them,
beheading Fēng and Jí.
Thereupon, he withdrew to Guǎngdū,
leaving Liú Shàng to resist Shù,
and reported the situation in detail,
while deeply reproaching himself.
The Emperor replied:
"Your return to Guǎngdū
is very appropriate.
Shù will certainly not dare to bypass Shàng and attack you.
Xián says: 'Luè'
is similar to 'to pass by'.
You should lead all your infantry and cavalry from Guǎngdū, fifty *lǐ* away, to rush to his aid,
just when he is in a precarious situation,
and you will surely defeat him!"
From then on, Hàn fought Shù between Guǎngdū and Chéngdū,
winning all eight battles,
and eventually camped within its outer city.
This refers to the outer city of Chéngdū.
Zāng Gōng captured Zǐtóng,
and defeated Fúchéng.
Fúxiàn
belonged to Guǎnghàn Commandery.
Xián says: Fúchéng
is now Zǐtóng County.
Sòng Bái says: Miánzhōu's Bāxī County was formerly Han Fúxiàn.
Huī
was Shù's younger brother.
He joined Wú Hàn at Chéngdū.
Xián says: Fán
is a county name,
belonging to Shǔ Commandery.
Fán
is a river name,
hence the county name.
Its old city is north of present-day Yìzhōu Xīnfán County.
Pí
is a county name,
belonging to Shǔ Commandery.
Its old city is north of present-day Yìzhōu Pí County.
Pí
is pronounced "pí".
4 Lǐ Tōng wished to avoid power and influence,
and requested to retire;
after two years,
the Emperor finally allowed him to resign the seal and ribbon of Grand Minister of Works,
and bestowed upon him the special rank of Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, with the privilege of attending court.
Later, when officials proposed enfeoffing imperial princes,
the Emperor, moved by Tōng's initial major strategic proposal—
the event is recorded in volume thirty-eight, Wáng Mǎng, Dìhuáng third year —
enfeoffed Tōng's youngest son, Xióng, as the Marquis of Zhàolíng.
5 Gōngsūn Shù, in dire straits,
said to Yán Cén:
"What should we do?"
Cén replied:
"A man should seek life amidst death;
how can we just sit here and be impoverished!
Wealth is easily gathered,
we should not be stingy."
Shù then distributed all his gold and silks,
recruiting over five thousand dare-to-die soldiers to assign to Cén.
Cén falsely erected banners at Shìqiáo,
beat drums and challenged the enemy,
while secretly sending elite troops to attack Wú Hàn's army from behind and defeat Hàn.
Hàn fell into the water
but climbed out by clinging to a horse's tail.
Hàn's army had only seven days of provisions left,
and secretly prepared boats,
intending to flee.
Zhāng Kān of Nányáng, the Administrator of Shǔ Commandery—
at that time Chéngdū had not yet fallen, he was first appointed Administrator of Shǔ Commandery to recruit and pacify the people of Shǔ —
advised that Shù was bound to fail and that retreating was not a suitable strategy.
He [Kān] spoke
as the character (shuō, persuade) is written.
He then feigned weakness to provoke the enemy.
In winter,
the eleventh month,
Zāng Gōng’s army was at Xiányángmén;
Zāng Gōng’s biography has it written
“Xiánmén”.
Xián said: it was the east-facing gate on the north side of the Chéngdū city wall.
The character
“Yáng”
is superfluous here.
“Dōng” [east]
is sometimes written
“Xī” [west].
On the day Wùyín,
Gōngsūn Shù personally led tens of thousands of men to attack the Hàn forces,
and sent Yán Cén to resist Zāng Gōng.
In a great battle,
Yán Cén won all three engagements.
From dawn until noon,
the soldiers could not eat,
and were all exhausted.
The Hàn then sent their protectors of the army, Gāo Wǔ and Táng Hán, with tens of thousands of elite troops to strike them.
Gōngsūn Shù’s army fell into great disorder;
Gāo Wǔ rushed forward and stabbed Gōngsūn Shù,
penetrating his chest and causing him to fall from his horse.
His attendants carried him into the city.
Gōngsūn Shù entrusted his army to Yán Cén,
and that night,
he died;
the next morning,
Yán Cén surrendered the city.
On the day Xīnsì,
Wú Hàn exterminated Gōngsūn Shù’s wife and children,
completely wiped out the Gōngsūn clan,
and also put Yán Cén’s entire clan to death.
Then he let his soldiers plunder extensively,
and burned Gōngsūn Shù’s palaces.
The Emperor was enraged when he heard of this,
and reprimanded Wú Hàn.
He also rebuked Liú Shàng, saying:
“The city surrendered three days ago,
the officials and people submitted,
there were tens of thousands
of children and elderly mothers.
To suddenly unleash soldiers and set fires –
hearing of it makes one feel a profound sorrow.
You, Shàng, are a descendant of the imperial clan,
and have served as an official;
how could you bear to do this!
Look up at the sky,
look down at the earth,
consider releasing the fawn and drinking the broth:
which of the two is more benevolent?
Hánzǐ said: Mèngsūn hunted and caught a fawn,
and ordered Qín Xībā to hold it.
Its mother followed and called out,
Qín Xībā could not bear it,
so he released it to its mother.
Mèngsūn was angry and drove Xībā away;
but later he reinstated him,
and made him the tutor to his son.
The Zhànguócè says: Yuè Yáng was a general,
and was attacking Zhōngshān for Wèi Wénhóu.
The ruler of Zhōngshān cooked Yuè Yáng’s son and sent him the broth.
Yuè Yáng sat under his tent and drank it,
finishing the cup.
Wénhóu said to Chǔshī Zàn:
‘Yuè Yáng ate the flesh of his own son for my sake.’
He replied:
‘Since you [the son] could eat it,
who wouldn’t eat it!’
After Zhōngshān was taken,
Wénhóu rewarded his achievement but doubted his sincerity.”
Previously,
Gōngsūn Shù had summoned Lǐ Yè of Guǎnghàn to be a Bóshì,
but Lǐ Yè firmly claimed illness and did not rise.
Lǐ Yè,
during Emperor Píng’s Yuánshǐ era, was appointed Láng.
When Wáng Mǎng assumed regency,
he left office due to illness,
and sealed his gate, not responding to summonses from the provinces and commanderies.
Wáng Mǎng appointed Lǐ Yè as a Jiǔshì,
but he did not take up the post due to illness.
He then hid in mountains and valleys,
completely concealing his name and traces.
Since he would not serve Wáng Mǎng,
how could he be willing to rise for Gōngsūn Shù!
Gōngsūn Shù sent the Grand Minister of the Court Protocol, Yǐn Róng, with an imperial edict to coerce Lǐ Yè, saying,
“If you accept, you will receive the position of duke or marquis;
if you do not, you will be granted poisoned wine.”
Yǐn Róng explained the intent, saying:
“At present, the world is in chaos;
who knows right from wrong,
and would risk his insignificant life in an unfathomable abyss!
The court yearns for renowned virtue,
and has had vacant official posts for
seven years now.
The four seasons’ rare provisions
are not forgotten by the ruler;
“Zhēnyù”
refers to the provision of rare delicacies.
For your descendants below,
and your reputation and person to be complete,
would that not be excellent!”
Lǐ Yè then sighed, saying:
“The ancients did not enter a perilous state,
nor reside in a chaotic state;
the Analects records the words of Kǒngzǐ.
A gentleman, seeing danger, gives his life;
the Analects records the words of Zǐzhāng.”
Yǐn Róng said:
“You should call your family to discuss it.”
Lǐ Yè said:
“A man has long made his decision in his heart,
what concern is it of his wife and children!”
Thereupon, he drank the poison and died.
Gōngsūn Shù was ashamed to have the reputation of killing a worthy man,
so he sent an envoy to offer condolences and sacrifices,
and bestowed one hundred rolls of silk.
Lǐ Yè’s son, Lǐ Huī, fled
and refused to accept.
Gōngsūn Shù also invited Qiáo Xuán of Bājùn.
The Xìngpǔ says: the grandee of Cáo took his fief in Qiáo,
and thus took it as his surname.
Qiáo Xuán,
in the fourth year of Emperor Píng’s Yuánshǐ era, was an Xìuyī Shǐzhě,
traveling throughout the empire
to observe local customs.
When Wáng Mǎng assumed regency,
he abandoned his envoy’s carriage
and returned home to live in seclusion.
Gōngsūn Shù also sent an envoy to coerce him with poison.
The Grand Administrator personally visited Qiáo Xuán’s hut
and urged him to accept,
but Qiáo Xuán said:
“To preserve my aspirations and maintain my integrity,
what regret is there even in death!”
Thereupon, he accepted the poison.
Qiáo Xuán’s son, Qiáo Yīng, wept blood and kowtowed to the Grand Administrator,
offering ten million in family money to ransom his father from death.
The Grand Administrator interceded for him,
and Gōngsūn Shù agreed.
Gōngsūn Shù also summoned Wáng Hào and Wáng Jiā of Shǔjùn.
During Emperor Píng’s time,
Wáng Hào was the magistrate of Měiyáng,
and Wáng Jiā was a Láng.
When Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
they both abandoned their offices and returned west.
Gōngsūn Shù first imprisoned their wives and children.
The envoy said to Wáng Jiā:
“Hurry and prepare,
your wife and children can be spared.”
He replied:
“Even dogs and horses recognize their master,
how much more so humans!”
Meaning that as a Hàn minister,
how could he not remember his former master!
He offered his head to the envoy.
Gōngsūn Shù was enraged,
and then executed Wáng Hào’s family.
Wáng Jiā heard this and sighed, saying:
“I am too late!”
Then, facing the envoy, he fell on his sword and died.
Fèi Yí of Jiànwéi refused to serve Gōngsūn Shù;
he lacquered his body to appear leprous,
feigning madness to avoid him.
Rèn Yǒng and Féng Xìn, both from the same commandery, feigned glaucoma to decline the summons.
“Qīngmáng” refers to a condition where
the pupil is not clear,
and one cannot see objects.
Rèn
is pronounced as Rén.
An edict posthumously granted Cháng Shǎo the title of Tàicháng,
and Zhāng Lóng the title of Guānglùxūn.
Cháng Shǎo and Zhāng Lóng’s deaths were mentioned in the previous year of the preceding volume.
They were sacrificed to with a Zhōngláo,
Shīgǔ said: Zhōngláo
is Xiǎoláo,
meaning a sheep and a pig.
And Lǐ Yè’s village was honored with a plaque.
Fèi Yí, Rèn Yǒng, and Féng Xìn were summoned,
but Rèn Yǒng and Féng Xìn died of illness,
only Fèi Yí served as the Grand Administrator of Hépǔ.
The Jùnguózhì says: Hépǔ Commandery
is nine thousand one hundred and ninety-one li south of Luòyáng.
They were all promoted and employed.
Thereupon, the people of the western lands were all pleased,
and all submitted their hearts.
At first,
Wáng Mǎng (王莽) appointed Wén Qí (文齊) of Guǎnghàn (廣漢) as the Grand Administrator of Yìzhōu (益州) Commandery.
The *Jùn Guó Zhì* (郡國志) states: Yìzhōu (益州) Commandery
is five thousand five hundred *lǐ* west of Luòyáng (雒陽).
He pacified and gathered the *Yí* (夷) people,
and gained their harmony greatly.
During Gōngsūn Shù’s (公孫述) time,
Qí (齊) steadfastly defended the dangerous terrain.
Shù (述) detained his wife and children,
promising him a marquisate,
but Qí (齊) did not surrender.
Hearing that the Emperor had ascended the throne,
he secretly sent an envoy to report his situation.
When Shǔ (蜀) was pacified,
he was summoned and made General who Guards from Afar,
and ennobled as Hóu (侯) of Chéngyì (成義).
6. In the twelfth month,
on the *xīnmǎo* (辛卯) day,
General who Displays Martial Might, Mǎ Chéng (馬成), acted as Grand Minister of Works.
7. In this year,
the Cānláng Qiāng (參狼羌) and various other tribes raided Wǔdū (武都).
The Cānláng Qiāng (參狼羌)
were descendants of Wúyì Yuánjiàn (無弋爰劍).
Yuánjiàn’s (爰劍) grandson Qióng (邛)
led his people south and migrated several thousand *lǐ* west of the Cìzhī (賜支) River bend.
Later, his descendants separated
and each formed their own tribes: some became the Máoniú (氂牛) tribe,
which were the Yuèsuī Qiāng (越巂羌);
some became the Báimǎ (白馬) tribe,
which were the Guǎnghàn Qiāng (廣漢羌);
and some became the Cānláng (參狼) tribe,
which were the Wǔdū Qiāng (武都羌).
Yuánjiàn’s (爰劍) great-grandson Rěn (忍) and his brother Wǔ (舞) remained in Huángzhōng (湟中),
becoming the various Qiāng (羌) tribes of Huángzhōng (湟中).
The character *zhǒng* (種)
is pronounced *zhāng yǒng*.
More than ten thousand of them surrendered,
and thus the region west of Lǒng (隴) became peaceful.
Yuán (援) cultivated kindness and trust,
treating his subordinates with leniency.
He entrusted officials with their duties,
only managing the general outline of affairs.
His door was daily filled with guests and old acquaintances.
When the various clerks occasionally reported on external matters,
Yuán (援) would always say,
“This is the responsibility of the Assistant and Clerks;
why bother me with it!
The *Bǎi Guān Zhì* (百官志) states: A Grand Administrator has one Assistant,
and various Clerks (*yuán*) and Scribes (*shǐ*) for the different bureaus.
There is a Registrar of Merits (*gōngcáoshǐ*) who is responsible for selecting and appointing based on merit;
there are Five Section Clerks (*wǔguānyuán*) who oversee the Registrar of Merits and various other bureaus;
the rest include the Consultation Bureau (*yìcáo*), Legal Bureau (*fǎcáo*), Bandit Bureau (*zéicáo*), Judgment Bureau (*juécáo*), Treasury Bureau (*jīncáo*), Granary Bureau (*cāngcáo*), etc.
The character *yuán* (掾)
is pronounced *yú juàn*.
Let them enjoy their leisure.
If influential families oppress common people,
or cunning officials disobey orders,
then these are truly the Grand Administrator’s affairs.”
Once, in a neighboring county,
there was a case of revenge.
The officials and people were alarmed, saying the Qiāng (羌) had revolted.
The common people rushed into the city.
The Chief of Díwén (狄道) went to the gate
and requested that the city gates be closed and troops dispatched.
Xián (賢) says: Díwén (狄道) County
belonged to Lǒngxī (隴西) Commandery,
and is now Lánzhōu (蘭州) County.
Yu (余) explains that the capital of Lǒngxī (隴西) was Díwén (狄道),
hence he could go to the gate to report to the Grand Administrator.
The character *zhǎng* (長)
is pronounced *zhī liǎng*.
He (referring to Yuán (援)) burst out laughing and said,
“How dare the barbarians attack us again!
Advise the Chief of Díwén (狄道)
to return and guard his official residence.
Xián (賢) says: *xiǎo* (曉)
means to explain.
*Sìshè* (寺舍)
means official residence.
You can lie down under your bed!”
Afterwards, order gradually returned,
and the commandery admired him.
8. An imperial edict stated:
“If border officials lack the strength to fight, they should defend.
When pursuing enemies or estimating their strength, they are not to be constrained by the law against delay.
Xián (賢) says: According to Hàn (漢) law,
those who delay or show timidity while on military campaigns are executed.
Whether pursuing enemies is near or far,
and advancing or retreating based on estimating the enemy’s strength,
they are not to be constrained by military law,
but simply make it their business to defeat the enemy.
9. The Marquis of Jiésāng (節桑), Wáng Cháng (王常), the Marquis of Mùpíng (牟平), Gěng Kuàng (耿況), and the Marquis of Dōngguāng (東光), Gěng Chún (耿純), all passed away.
The *Shìfǎ* (諡法) states: “One who loves integrity and restrains himself is called *jié* (節)”;
“One who has achievements and brings peace to the people is called *liè* (烈).”
Hè Chēn (賀琛) says: “One who assists the prime minister and dies in office is called *chéng* (成)”;
“One who is generous, honest, and firm is called *chéng* (成).”
The Emperor frequently visited them in person,
and again appointed Yǎn’s (弇) brothers Guǎng (廣) and Jǔ (舉) as Commanders of the Gentlemen of the Household.
Yǎn (弇) had six brothers:
Yǎn (弇), Shū (舒), Guó (國), Guǎng (廣), Jǔ (舉), and Bà (霸).
There were six brothers in total.
He personally attended to their medicines,
which was considered a great honor at the time.
10. Lú Fāng (盧芳) allied with the Xiongnú (匈奴) and Wūhuán (烏桓)
and repeatedly raided the border.
The Emperor sent Grand General of Cavalry Dù Mào (杜茂) and others to lead troops to garrison the northern border
and repair the Fēihú (飛狐) Road.
He repaired the Fēihú (飛狐) Road to facilitate the movement of troops from Zhào (趙) and Wèi (魏) to reinforce the northern border.
He repaired the beacon towers.
In total, there were dozens or hundreds of battles, large and small, against the Xiongnú (匈奴) and Wūhuán (烏桓),
but they could not be ultimately defeated.
11. The Emperor decreed that Dòu Róng (竇融) and the Grand Administrators of the five commanderies enter court.
Róng (融) and the others followed the decree,
with their officials, guests, and retainers accompanying them.
Their carriages numbered over a thousand,
and their horses, cattle, and sheep covered the fields.
Upon arrival,
they proceeded to the city gate
and surrendered their official seals and ribbons.
An edict sent envoys to return their marquisate seals and ribbons,
granted them an audience,
and bestowed awards and favors,
which astonished the capital.
Soon after, Róng (融) was appointed Provincial Governor of Jìzhōu (冀州).
Jìzhōu (冀州) Prefecture included Wèijùn (魏郡), Jùlù (鉅鹿), Chángshān (常山), Zhōngshān (中山), Xìndū (信都), Héjiān (河間), Qīnghé (清河), Zhàoguó (趙國), and Bóhǎi (勃海).
Kǒng Fèn (孔奮), the Chief of Gūzàng (姑臧), was made Assistant of Wǔdū (武都) Commandery.
Gūzàng (姑臧) was the most prosperous and fertile place west of the Héxī (河西) region.
Gūzàng (姑臧) County
belonged to Wǔwēi (武威) Commandery.
Liú Xù (劉昫) says: Gūzàng (姑臧) County
was where the Yuèzhī (月氏) *róng* (戎) of Qín (秦) resided.
The Xiongnú (匈奴) called it Gàicáng (蓋藏) City,
and the name was corrupted to Gūzàng (姑臧) City.
The character *zhǎng* (長)
is pronounced *zhī liǎng*.
Many scholars did not maintain their integrity.
Those who served in the county would accumulate vast wealth within a few months.
Fèn (奮), however,
served for four years and diligently practiced honesty and cleanliness,
which was mocked by many
who thought he was in a place of fat and grease but couldn't enrich himself.
The *Shuōwén* (說文) states: “Fat from horned animals is *zhī* (脂),
fat from hornless animals is *gāo* (膏).”
The character *chǔ* (處)
is pronounced *chāng lǚ*.
The wealth of the various Grand Administrators and Magistrates
filled their carriages and spread across rivers and marshes.
Only Fèn (奮) had no assets,
taking to the road in a single carriage.
The Emperor rewarded him for this.
The Emperor appointed Rèn Yán (任延), the Magistrate of Suīyáng (睢陽), as Grand Administrator of Wǔwēi (武威).
The Emperor personally saw him
and warned him, saying,
“Serve your superiors well,
and do not lose your good reputation.”
Yán (延) replied,
“I have heard that a loyal minister does not curry favor,
and a fawning minister is not loyal.
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) states: Yán’s (延) biography has it as
‘a loyal minister has no private interests,
and a minister with private interests is not loyal.’
However, Gāo Jùn’s (高峻) unofficial history has it as
‘a loyal minister does not curry favor,
and a fawning minister is not loyal.’
This meaning is more profound
and corresponds to the preceding sentence.
Therefore, we follow this.
This is the principle for a minister and son.
If superiors and subordinates echo each other,
it is not a blessing for Your Majesty.
The *Qūlǐ* (曲禮) says: ‘Do not echo others like thunder.’
Zhèng’s (鄭氏) commentary says: When thunder sounds,
nothing fails to respond simultaneously;
human speech should come from oneself,
and not necessarily be like that.
I dare not obey your edict.”
The Emperor sighed and said,
“Your words are right!”
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the *gēngshēn* (庚申) day,
Grand Minister of Agriculture Hóu Bà (侯霸) passed away.
2 On the day of Wùzǐ,
an imperial edict stated:
“As for the rare delicacies presented by commanderies and states,
order the Tàiguān to cease receiving them!
The Bǎiguān Zhì says: The Tàiguān Lìng is one person,
with a salary of six hundred shí,
in charge of the emperor's meals and drinks.
Fù,
pronounced Fú Yòu Fān.
Return to the old system.”
The Hàn Guān Yí says: Kǒushí [means]
matters concerning delicacies.
A horse that traveled a thousand lǐ a day,
and a precious sword were also presented,
valued at a hundred jīn.
An edict bestowed the sword upon a knight,
and the horse was harnessed to a drum-chariot.
The Yúfú Zhì says: Behind the emperor's Fǎjià were golden gongs, yellow yuè-axes, and a Huángmén drum-chariot.
Hands did not hold pearls or jade.
Once, while out hunting,
the imperial carriage returned at night,
but the guard of the Shàngdōngmén, Zhì Yùn of Rǔnán, refused to open the gate.
Xián says: Shàngdōngmén [was]
the northern gate on the east side of Luòyáng city.
Yùn,
pronounced Yú Fěn Fān.
Yùn said:
“The firelight is distant and unclear.”
Thus he did not accept the edict.
The emperor then turned back
and entered through the Dōngzhōngmén.
Xián says: The middle gate on the east side.
Yùn submitted a memorial in remonstrance, saying:
“In the past, King Wén did not dare to indulge in hunting excursions,
so that the myriad people might have their rightful provisions.
This is from the Wúyì chapter of the Shàngshū.
Pán,
means pleasure.
If night is joined to day,
what will become of the altars of the state and the ancestral temples!”
When the memorial was presented,
Yùn was bestowed a hundred bolts of cloth,
and the Dōngzhōngmén guard was demoted to Cānfēng Wèi.
Luòyáng had twelve city gates,
each with one guard,
with a salary of six hundred shí.
Cānfēng County
belonged to Lángxié Commandery.
3 In the second month,
General Pǔlú Mǎ Wǔ was dispatched to garrison Hūtuóhé to guard against the Xiōngnú.
4 Lú Fāng attacked Yúnzhōng,
but it did not fall for a long time.
His general Suí Yù remained to guard Jiǔyuán,
intending to compel Fāng to surrender;
Fāng knew this,
and with more than ten horsemen, fled into the Xiōngnú territory.
His troops all returned to Suí Yù,
who then went to the palace to surrender.
An edict appointed Yù as Wǔyuán Tàishǒu,
and he was enfeoffed as Juānhú Hóu.
5 Zhū Hù submitted a memorial:
“In ancient times, when a minister was enfeoffed,
they were not granted the rank of king.”
On the day of Bǐngchén,
an edict demoted Chángshā Wáng Xīng, Zhēndìng Wáng Dé, Héjiān Wáng Shào, and Zhōngshān Wáng Mào all to the rank of Hóu:
Emperor Gāo had enfeoffed various vassal kings,
but none of their descendants existed concurrently with the Hàn dynasty.
Emperor Wén enfeoffed the Kings of Liáng, Chéngyáng, and Zīchuān.
Emperor Jǐng enfeoffed the Kings of Héjiān, Chángshā, Zhōngshān, and Chángshān.
Emperor Zhāo enfeoffed the Kings of Guǎngyáng, Guǎnglíng, and Gāomì.
These several states were abolished when Wáng Mǎng usurped the Hàn.
Only the enfeoffment of Chángshā, Zhēndìng, Héjiān, and Zhōngshān [is mentioned here]
because they were of the same lineage as the emperor, descended from Emperor Jǐng.
Chángshā was
the main branch of Chōnglíng;
Zhēndìng was a re-enfeoffment of the descendants of Chángshān Wáng Xiàn.
Now they are again demoted to the rank of Hóu,
as their relationship of allegiance
has become distant.
On the day of Dīngsì,
Zhào Wáng Liáng was made Zhào Gōng,
Tàiyuán Wáng Zhāng was made Qí Gōng,
and Lǔ Wáng Xīng was made Lǔ Gōng.
Liáng was
the emperor's paternal uncle;
Zhāng and Xīng were
the emperor's nephews.
In total, one hundred thirty-seven members of the imperial clan and rulers of extinguished states were enfeoffed as Hóu.
Fùpíng Hóu Zhāng Chún was
the fourth-generation descendant of Ānshì.
Throughout Wáng Mǎng's reign,
he preserved his former enfeoffment due to his prudence, conscientiousness, and adherence to agreements;
at the beginning of Jiànwǔ,
he was the first to come to the palace
and was reinstated as Hóu.
Thereupon, officials submitted a memorial:
“Marquises who are not of the imperial clan should not have their states restored.”
The emperor said:
“Zhāng Chún has served as an imperial guard for over ten years,
he should not be abolished!”
He was re-enfeoffed as Wǔshǐ Hóu,
receiving half of Fùpíng's revenue.
Xián says: Wǔshǐ County
belonged to Wèijùn;
Fùpíng County
belonged to Píngyuán Commandery.
6 On the day of Gēngwǔ,
Shàojiā Gōng Kǒng Ān was made Sòng Gōng,
and Chéngxīu Gōng Jī Cháng was made Wèi Gōng.
During the Yuánshǐ fourth year,
Shàojiā Gōng was changed to Sòng Gōng,
and Chéngxīu Gōng to Zhèng Gōng.
Now Zhèng is changed to Wèi.
7 In the third month,
on the day of Xīnwèi,
Hán Xīn, the Tàishǒu of Pèi Commandery, was made Dàsītú.
The Jùn Guó Zhì states
that Pèi Commandery was one thousand two hundred lǐ southeast of Luòyáng.
8 On the day of Bǐngzǐ,
the acting Dàsīkōng Mǎ Chéng was reinstated as Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn.
9 Wú Hàn returned with his troops from Shǔ,
and upon reaching Wǎn,
an edict allowed him to visit his home and ancestral tombs, and bestowed upon him twenty thousand hú of grain;
in the summer, fourth month,
he arrived at the capital.
Thereupon, a great banquet was held for the generals, soldiers, and meritorious officials.
Three hundred sixty-five people in total
had their territories increased or were re-enfeoffed,
and forty-five members of the imperial family by marriage or those favored by grace were enfeoffed.
Dèng Yǔ was formally enfeoffed as Gāomì Hóu,
receiving four counties;
Yǔ received Chāng'ān, Yí'ān, Chúnyú, and Gāomì, four counties.
Xián says: Gāomì,
a state name,
is now Mìzhōu County.
I [the commentator] believe that during the Western Hàn, Gāomì was a kingdom,
and during the Eastern Hàn, it was a marquisate,
belonging to Běihǎi Kingdom.
What Xián referred to was likely the marquisate.
Jiǎ Fù was enfeoffed as Jiāodōng Hóu,
receiving six counties;
Gùshǐ Hóuguó
belonged to Rǔnán Commandery;
it was formerly Qǐn County.
The emperor renamed it.
The Shǐjì Zhèngyì says: Sūn Shú'áo
took Qǐnqiū land for his enfeoffment because Qǐn was barren.
Lǐ Tōng also admired Shú'áo for receiving this territory,
and Guāngwǔ praised him,
renaming it Gùshǐ.
Jiāodōng,
which was a kingdom during the Western Hàn,
was made a marquisate by the emperor,
and entirely belonged to Běihǎi,
receiving Yùzhì, Zhuàngwǔ, Xiàmì, Jímò, Tǐnghú, and Guānyáng,
a total of six counties.
For those who had already passed away, their sons and grandsons were granted additional enfeoffments,
or distant relatives were re-enfeoffed.
The emperor had been engaged in warfare for a long time,
was weary of military matters,
and moreover knew that the world was exhausted.
He longed for peace and rest,
and after Lǒng and Shǔ were pacified,
unless there was an urgent emergency,
he never again spoke of military campaigns.
The crown prince once asked about matters of attack and warfare.
The emperor said:
“In the past, when Wèi Líng Gōng asked about battle formations,
Kǒngzǐ did not answer.”
The Lúnyǔ says: Wèi Líng Gōng asked Kǒngzǐ about battle formations.
Kǒngzǐ said:
“As for matters of sacrificial vessels and ceremonies,
I have heard of them;
as for matters of military campaigns,
I have not studied them.”
Chén is
read as Zhèn.
Dèng Yǔ and Jiǎ Fù knew that the emperor wished to put away his weapons
and cultivate civil virtues,
and did not want meritorious officials to gather troops in the capital.
So they cast aside their armor and weapons
and devoted themselves to Confucian learning.
The emperor also considered
preserving the titles and territories of meritorious officials,
not wishing them to incur faults due to their official duties,
fearing they might lose their titles and estates because of errors in their official responsibilities.
Gěng Yǎn and others also submitted their seals and ribbons as Grand Generals and Generals,
and all were enfeoffed as marquises and returned to their residences,
granted the rank of Tèjìn,
and served at court.
Dèng Yǔ's inner conduct was pure and complete.
He had thirteen sons,
each of whom he made to specialize in one art.
He kept his household in order,
educated and raised his sons and grandsons,
all of whom could serve as models for later generations.
He used the income from his state and city,
and did not pursue productive profit.
All his expenses were covered by the income from his state and city,
and he did not engage in production, work, or profit-making.
Jiǎ Fù was a person of firm resolve and straightforwardness,
possessing many great principles.
After returning to his private residence,
he closed his gates and maintained his authority and gravity.
Zhū Hù and others recommended that Fù was suitable to be prime minister,
but the emperor was then holding the Three Excellencies accountable for administrative affairs,
so none of the meritorious officials were employed.
At this time,
among the marquises, only the three marquises of Gāomì, Gùshǐ, and Jiāodōng participated with the high officials in discussing state affairs,
and their favor was extremely generous.
Although the emperor controlled his meritorious officials,
he was always able to accommodate them.
"Huíróng" (回容)
is like what is now called "huíhù" (回護).
Xián said: "Huí" (回)
means "to bend" or "to deviate,"
meaning to bend the law to accommodate.
When precious delicacies were contributed from distant regions,
they were always first distributed to all the marquises,
with nothing left for the imperial kitchen,
thus all of them preserved their good fortune and emoluments,
and none were punished or reprimanded.
Yìzhōu sent over Gōngsūn Shù's blind musicians, instruments for the suburban altars and ancestral temples, "bǎo" (葆) chariots, and imperial carriages.
It was then that the ritual objects were first made complete.
Xián said: "Gǔ" (瞽)
means a person without eyes.
As a music master,
the idea was that being unable to see,
they were precise in sound.
"Xiàomiào zhī qì" (效廟之器) refers to
items like zūn (樽) and yí (彞) vessels.
"Yuèqì" (樂器) refers to
items like bells and chimes.
A "bǎo" (葆) chariot
refers to one with a "yǔbǎo" (羽葆) or feather canopy built on top;
an assembly of five-colored feathers
is called a "bǎo" (葆).
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: "Yǔbǎo" (羽葆)
means inserting raven feathers onto a handle like a canopy,
which is called a "yǔbǎo" (羽葆),
meaning a canopy.
"Yú" (輿)
is a general term for a carriage.
"Niǎn" (輦)
is a carriage pulled by people.
"Fǎwù" (法物) refers to
the imperial chariot processional regulations and rituals.
At the time, things were just being established, and there was no time,
but now they were obtained and made complete.
I think "fǎwù" (法物)
refers to the aforementioned musical instruments, "bǎo" chariots, and imperial carriages.
"Chuán" (傳)
is read as "zhí liàn."
There were few affairs in the empire,
and the documents for conscription
aimed at simplicity and brevity,
to the extent that only one in ten was kept.
On the Jiǎyín day,
Dòu Róng, the Governor of Jìzhōu, was appointed Grand Minister of Works (Dà Sīkōng).
Róng considered himself not an old official,
and suddenly entering the court,
taking precedence over the meritorious officials,
at every court
assembly and audience,
his demeanor and tone
were excessively humble and respectful,
which made the emperor even closer and more favorable towards him.
Róng was cautious
and felt uneasy for a long time,
repeatedly declining his rank and position,
submitting a memorial saying:
"Your subject Róng has sons,
whom I teach and guide daily in the classics and arts,
not allowing them to observe astronomy
or read prophecies and omens.
I sincerely wish for them to be respectful and cautious in affairs,
diligently adhering to the Dao,
not desiring them to have talent or ability,
let alone to inherit continuous cities and vast lands,
enjoying the former domains of feudal kings!"
He then again requested a private audience,
but the emperor did not permit it.
Later, after the court session,
he lingered behind the seats.
"Qūnxún" (逡巡)
describes a retreating appearance.
He then sent his attendants to convey an order for him to leave.
This means he was given an imperial decree to make Róng leave.
Receiving the imperial edict, Róng said:
"I knew the other day that you wished to resign your post and return to your home territory."
Xián said: "Rìzhě" (日者)
is like "wǎng rì" (往日), meaning "the other day" or "formerly."
"Now that we meet,
we should discuss other matters,
and you must not speak of it again."
Róng did not
dare to reiterate his request.
In the fifth month,
the Xiōngnú raided Hédōng.
In summer,
Rèn Guì, the King of Qiónggǔ, sent envoys to present a three-year report,
and was immediately appointed Grand Administrator of Yuèsuí.
The "Jùnguó Zhì" (郡國志) states: Yuèsuí Commandery
is four thousand eight hundred *lǐ* west of Luòyáng.
"Suí" (巂)
is pronounced "suǐ."
"Qióng" (邛)
is pronounced "qú róng."
"Rèn" (任)
is pronounced "rén."
"Shàng" (上)
is pronounced "shí zhǎng."
In autumn,
Kuàijī experienced a great plague.
The "Jùnguó Zhì" (郡國志) states: Kuàijī Commandery
is three thousand eight hundred *lǐ* east of Luòyáng.
"Kuài" (會)
is pronounced "gǔ wài."
Xián, the King of Shāchē,
and Ān, the King of Shànshàn, both sent envoys to offer tribute.
The Western Regions suffered from the heavy levies of the Xiōngnú,
and all wished to become vassals of Hàn,
and to re-establish the Protector-General;
but the emperor, considering that China had just been pacified,
did not permit it.
4 Tàizhōng Dàfū Liáng Tǒng (梁統) submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant stealthily observed that in the fifth year of Chūyuán (初元) of Yuán Dì (元帝),
thirty-four capital offenses were leniently reduced;
and in the first year of Jiànpíng (建平) of Āi Dì (哀帝),
eighty-one capital offenses were leniently reduced;
of these, for forty-two cases where individuals committed murder,
the penalty was reduced by one degree from death.
From that time onward,
this was established as a regular standard.
Therefore, people lightly violated the law,
and officials easily committed murder.
Your servant has heard that the principle of establishing a ruler
is centered on benevolence and righteousness.
The benevolent love people,
and the righteous rectify principles.
Loving people means making it one's duty to eliminate evil,
and rectifying principles means having the heart to remove chaos.
Punishments should be moderate;
there is no benefit in making them light.
'Zhōng' (衷),
means 'middle';
it means 'appropriate'.
When laws and regulations are established,
they should genuinely achieve their proper measure.
When Gāo Dì (高帝) entered the Pass,
he established the Three-Chapter Law.
Later, Xiāo Hé (蕭何) established the Nine-Chapter Law.
In the first year of Wén Dì (文帝),
the law of collective punishment for families (shōunú xiāngzuò 收孥相坐) was abolished;
in the thirteenth year,
corporal punishments (ròuxíng 肉刑) were abolished.
By the time Āi (哀) and Píng (平) succeeded to the throne,
they had been in power for only a short time,
and their judgments were still few.
Chéngxiàng Wáng Jiā (王嘉) lightly made arbitrary changes,
diminishing and removing the old established laws of the former emperors.
(However, Wáng Jiā's (王嘉) biography and the Treatise on Penal Law (Xíngfǎ Zhì 刑法志) contain no such record of this matter.
Liáng Tǒng (梁統) and Wáng Jiā (王嘉) lived in contemporary times,
so what he cited was certainly not groundless,
but Bān Gù (班固) merely omitted to record it.)
(Some laws were not expedient for governance,
others did not satisfy the people's hearts.)
Your servant respectfully presents those that are particularly harmful to the political system,
attaching them for your consideration.
refers to the political system.
pronounced like 'fù' (附).
May Your Majesty carefully select the good ones,
and establish unchangeable statutes! "
The matter was submitted to the Gōng Qīng (公卿).
Guānglù Xūn Dù Lín (杜林) memorialized, saying:
"When the Great Hàn (漢) first rose,
it abolished harsh governance,
and the whole realm rejoiced.
But after that,
laws gradually multiplied.
Lǎozi (老子) said: 'The more laws and ordinances are promulgated,
the more thieves and robbers there will be.'
When minor matters are accumulated to form serious offenses,
though they cause no harm to righteousness,
they are treated as major crimes.
To the point where laws cannot prohibit,
and edicts cannot stop,
superiors and inferiors evade each other,
and the abuses become ever deeper.
Xián (賢) said: 'Dùn' (遁),
is like avoiding.
The Former Hàn History (Qián Shū 前書) says: 'Superiors and inferiors conceal each other,
and use textual loopholes to evade the law.'
This should not be altered. "
Liáng Tǒng (梁統) again submitted a statement, saying:
"What your servant has memorialized
is not to advocate for severe punishments.
The Classic (Jīng 經) says: '
Therefore, the common people were regulated, based on the moderation of punishments.'
This is from the Lǚ Xíng (呂刑) chapter of the Shàng Shū (尚書).
It means neither too light nor too heavy.
From Gāo Zǔ (高祖) to Xiào Xuān (孝宣),
the realm was called well-governed.
But by Chūyuán (初元) and Jiànpíng (建平), robbers and thieves increased significantly.
This was all due to punishments not being moderate,
making it easy for ignorant people to commit offenses.
From this perspective,
the creation of lenient punishments
on the contrary gives rise to great calamities,
bestowing favor upon villains and transgressors,
while harming the good and upright! "
The matter was shelved,
with no response.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the day Xīnchǒu (辛丑),
Dàsītú Hán Xīn (韓歆) was dismissed.
Hán Xīn (韓歆) was fond of speaking directly,
without concealment or avoidance.
The emperor was often unable to tolerate him.
Hán Xīn (韓歆), before the emperor, testified that the year would bring famine and disaster,
pointing to heaven and drawing on the earth, speaking with great force and directness.
Therefore, he was dismissed and returned to his hometown.
The emperor was still not appeased,
and again sent an envoy to issue an edict rebuking him.
Hán Xīn (韓歆) and his son Yīng (嬰) both committed suicide.
Hán Xīn (韓歆) had always enjoyed a great reputation,
and his death was not for his crimes;
the multitudes were greatly displeased.
Thereupon, the emperor posthumously bestowed money and grain,
to conduct his burial with proper rites.
Xián (賢) said: 'Chénglǐ' (成禮),
means to complete the rites;
it means that his funeral rites were not downgraded because of an unnatural death.
Your servant Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光) says: In ancient times, Gāo Zōng (高宗) instructed Yuè (說) saying:
"If medicine does not cause dizziness and nausea,
the illness will not be cured."
Indeed, direct and cutting words
are not beneficial to the minister,
but they are a blessing to the state.
Therefore, rulers seek them day and night,
fearing only that they will not hear them.
Alas,
that in the era of Guāngwǔ (光武), Hán Xīn (韓歆) died for his forthright remonstrance,
how could this not be a blemish on a benevolent and wise ruler!
2 On the day Dīngwèi (丁未),
a comet appeared in Mǎo (昴).
Mǎo (昴) consists of seven stars,
and is a constellation in the west.
It governs legal affairs;
it is also called Máotóu (旄頭),
which is a barbarian star.
The space between Mǎo (昴) and Bì (畢) is called Tiānjiē (天街),
through which the ecliptic passes.
'Bèi' (孛),
pronounced 'pú nèi fān'.
3 Ouyáng Shè (歐陽歙), the Administrator of Rǔnán (汝南), was appointed Dàsītú (大司徒).
The Guanzhongzhi (郡國志) says: Rǔnán (汝南) Commandery
is six hundred fifty lǐ (里) south of Luòyáng (雒陽).
'Shè' (歙),
pronounced 'xǔ jí fān'.
4 The Xiongnú (匈奴) raids and plundering became increasingly severe,
and the prefectures and commanderies could not stop them.
In the second month,
Wú Hàn (吳漢) was dispatched to lead Mǎ Chéng (馬成), Mǎ Wǔ (馬武), and others to attack the Xiongnú (匈奴) in the north.
Six tens of thousands of officials and people from Yànmén (鴈門), Dàijùn (代郡), and Shànggǔ (上谷) were relocated to east of Jūyōng (居庸) and Chángshān (常山) passes,
to avoid the Hu (胡) bandits.
The Guanzhongzhi (郡國志) says: Yànmén (鴈門) Commandery
is one thousand five hundred lǐ (里) north of Luòyáng (雒陽).
