and was captured only three years later.
Zhú Zhī Fúnán Jì (竺芝扶南記) says: Mountain streams and rapids are called Jiū (究).
Xián (賢) said: This place is now Xīnchāng Xiàn (新昌縣), Cénzhōu (岑州).
I note that the Táng Zhì (唐志) says: Xīnchāng Xiàn (新昌縣) belonged to Fēngzhōu (豐州);
the character "Cén" (岑)
is an error.
4 In summer,
fourth month,
on the day of Jiǎxū (甲戌),
the imperial carriage returned to the palace.
5 On the day of Wùshēn (戊申),
the Emperor journeyed to Hénèi (河內).
On the day of Wùzǐ (戊子),
he returned to the palace.
6 In the fifth month,
there was a drought.
7 Lú Fāng (盧芳) returned from Chāngpíng (昌平),
feeling self-doubt and fear.
He then rebelled again,
attacking Mǐn Kān (閔堪) for several months.
The Xiōngnú (匈奴) sent several hundred cavalry to welcome Fāng (芳) out of the frontier.
Fāng (芳) remained among the Xiōngnú (匈奴) for more than ten years,
and died of illness.
8 Wú Hàn (吳漢) dispatched troops from the three commanderies of Guǎnghàn (廣漢), Bā (巴), and Shǔ (蜀).
The Jùnguó Zhì (郡國志) says: Guǎnghàn Jùn (廣漢郡)
is three thousand lǐ (里) west of Luòyáng (雒陽).
Bā Jùn (巴郡)
is two thousand seven hundred lǐ (里) west of Luòyáng (雒陽).
Shǔ Jùn (蜀郡)
is three thousand one hundred lǐ (里) west of Luòyáng (雒陽).
In autumn,
seventh month,
he captured it
and beheaded Shǐ Xīn (史歆) and others.
Hàn (漢) then crossed the water using rafts
(made of bamboo and wood woven together to cross water;
large ones are called fá (筏),
small ones called fú (桴)).
Yáng Wěi (楊偉) and others were terrified and dispersed.
Hàn (漢) executed their chieftains
and relocated several hundred families of their faction to Nánjùn (南郡) and Chángshā (長沙) before returning.
9 In winter,
tenth month,
on the day of Gēngchén (庚辰),
the Emperor journeyed to Yíchéng (宜城).
Xián (賢) said: Yíchéng Xiàn (宜城縣)
belonged to Nánjùn (南郡),
it was the Yān Yì (鄢邑) of Chǔ (楚).
Its old city is now south of Shuàidào Xiàn (率道縣), Xiāngzhōu (襄州).
He offered sacrifices at Zhānglíng (章陵).
In the twelfth month,
he returned to the palace.
10 In this year,
the position of Zhōu Mù (州牧) was abolished,
and Cìshǐ (刺史) was established.
The establishment of Zhōu Mù (州牧) was first seen in volume thirty-two, in the first year of Suīhé (綏和) of Chéngdì (成帝).
Until the second year of Jiànpíng (建平) of Āidì (哀帝),
it reverted to Cìshǐ (刺史).
In the second year of Yuánshòu (元壽),
it reverted to Mù (牧).
11 Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiàng Zhāng Chún (張純) and Tàipú Zhū Fú (朱浮) presented a memorial:
“According to the Rites,
a son,
when serving the main branch of the family,
should lower his private familial ties.
The four existing temples to one’s immediate family should be abolished
and replaced with the four temples to the former emperors.”
Dàsītú Shè (涉) and others memorialized
to “erect four temples to Yuán (元), Chéng (成), Āi (哀), and Píng (平) [emperors].”
The Emperor himself, following the order of zhāomù (昭穆),
ought to be the successor to Emperor Yuán (元).
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the day Gēngzǐ (庚子),
Emperor Xuān (宣) was posthumously honored as Zhōngzōng (中宗).
Sacrifices to Emperors Zhāo (昭) and Yuán (元) began at the Grand Ancestral Temple.
Xián (賢) said: “The Hànpinyin Guāngwǔ (光武) was the twelfth son,
but in terms of father-son succession,
he was a brother to Emperor Chéng (成),
an uncle to Emperor Āi (哀),
and a grandfather to Emperor Píng (平);
none of these could be succeeded by him.
Emperor Yuán (元) was a father to Guāngwǔ (光武),
hence the Emperor succeeded Emperor Yuán (元) as the ninth generation.
Thus the Hétú (河圖) says: ‘The red nine will gather and prosper,’
referring to Guāngwǔ (光武).
Therefore, Emperor Xuān (宣) was his ancestor,
and Emperor Zhāo (昭) was his great-grandfather,
hence they were posthumously honored and sacrificed to.
Chōnglíng Jiéhóu (舂陵節侯) and those below him were to be enshrined at Zhānglíng (章陵);
at Cháng'ān (長安) and Zhānglíng (章陵),
the Tàishǒu (太守), lìng (令), and zhǎng (長) were all to attend the sacrifices.
The Jìsì Zhì (祭祀志) says: ‘At that time, an edict stated:
“The location of the ancestral temples has not yet been decided.
For now, the gāomiào (高廟) will perform the xiáji (祫祭).
Emperors Chéng (成), Āi (哀), and Píng (平) will for now be sacrificed to at the former gāomiào (高廟) in Cháng'ān (長安).
As for Chōnglíng (舂陵) in Nányáng (南陽),
sacrifices will for now be performed at their respective former garden temples during the seasonal rites.
For garden temples far from the Tàishǒu’s (太守) seat of governance,
the local lìng (令) or zhǎng (長) shall act as Tàishǒu (太守) to attend the sacrifices.”’
Rú Chún (如淳) said: ‘For ancestral temples located in Zhānglíng (章陵),
the Nányáng Tàishǒu (南陽太守) acts as an envoy to offer sacrifices;
not allowing marquises or kings to sacrifice is because
feudal lords may not be ancestors of the Son of Heaven.
Anyone attending ancestral temple sacrifices
is considered to be attending the sacrifice.’”
2 Mǎ Yuán (馬援) beheaded Zhēng Cè (徵側) and Zhēng Èr (徵貳).
3 The bandit leaders Dān Chén (單臣) and Fù Zhèn (傳鎮) gathered and entered Yuánwǔ (原武) city,
proclaiming themselves generals.
An edict ordered Tàizhōng Dàfū Zāng Gōng (臧宮) to lead troops to besiege them;
after several attacks failed,
soldiers were killed and wounded.
The Emperor summoned the gōngqīng (公卿) and various kings to ask for strategies.
They all said:
“Their rewards should be increased.”
Only Dōnghǎi Wáng Yáng (東海王陽) said:
“Sorcerers kidnapping each other
cannot stand for long.
Among them, there must be those who regret and wish to escape,
but the outside encirclement is too tight,
preventing their escape.
It would be advisable to slightly loosen the siege
to allow them to flee.”
Xián (賢) said: “‘Tǐng (挺)’ means ‘to loosen.’
I refer to the Lǐjì Yuèlìng (禮記月令),
which says ‘tǐng (挺) heavy prisoners.’
‘Tǐng (挺)’ means ‘to relax,’
pronounced ‘dài dǐng fān’ (待鼎翻).”
“Then a single tíngzhǎng (亭長) would be enough to capture them.”
The Emperor agreed,
and immediately ordered Gōng (宮) to withdraw the siege and relax the pressure on the bandits.
The bandit group dispersed.
In summer, the fourth month,
Yuánwǔ (原武) was captured, and Chén (臣), Zhèn (鎮), and others were beheaded.
4 Mǎ Yuán (馬援) advanced to attack the remaining followers of Zhēng Cè (徵側), such as Dū Yáng (都陽) and others.
When he reached Jūfēng (居風),
they surrendered.
Xián (賢) said: “Jūfēng (居風)
is a county name,
belonging to Jiǔzhēn Jùn (九真郡),
now Áizhōu (愛州).
The Jiāozhōu Jì (交州記) says: ‘Jūfēng (居風) has a mountain
from which golden oxen emerge.
They are often seen at night,
glowing for ten *lǐ*.’
The mountain has a ‘Wind Gate,’
where it is always windy.
Xián (賢) said: ‘Qiáo (嶠) refers to mountain ranges (lǐngqiáo, 嶺嶠).
The Éryǎ (爾雅) says: A sharp and high mountain is called a qiáo (嶠);
pronounced jūmiào fān (居廟翻).’
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: ‘Mǎ Yuán’s (馬援) biography writes
“Dū Yáng (都陽)”;
the Imperial Annals write
“Dū Yáng (都陽)”;
we now follow the Annals.
Also, the Imperial Annals say:
“In the fourth month of the eighteenth year,
Mǎ Yuán (馬援) was sent to attack Jiāozhǐ (交趾).
In the fourth month of the nineteenth year,
Zhēng Cè (徵側) and Zhēng Èr (徵貳) were beheaded,
and then Dū Yáng (都陽) and others were attacked
and surrendered.”
Mǎ Yuán’s (馬援) biography says:
“In the seventeenth year,
he was appointed Fúbō Jiāngjūn (伏波將軍)
to campaign against Zhēng Cè (徵側) and Zhēng Èr (徵貳).
In the spring of the eighteenth year,
his army reached Làngbó (浪泊).
In the first month of the following year,
Zhēng Cè (徵側) and Zhēng Èr (徵貳) were beheaded.”
Perhaps what is recorded in the Annals
is the time when Mǎ Yuán (馬援) memorialized his victory over Zhēng Cè (徵側) and Zhēng Èr (徵貳) and when their heads reached Luò (雒).
Shěn Huáiyuǎn’s (沈懷遠) Nányuè Zhì (南越志) says:
“Zhēng Cè (徵側) fled into the Jīnxī (金溪) cave,
and was only captured two years later.”
Mǎ Yuán’s (馬援) biography is closer to this,
so we follow it now.
Thereafter, the Luòyuè (駱越) people followed the precedents set by General Mǎ (馬).
Xián (賢) said: ‘Luò (駱)
is another name for Yuè (越).
The Línyì Jì (林邑記) says: Rìnán (日南), Lúróng (盧容), Pǔtōng (浦通), and Tónggǔ (銅鼓) are Outer Yuè (越).
Tónggǔ (銅鼓) is Luòyuè (駱越);
it has bronze drums,
hence its name.
Mǎ Yuán (馬援) took their drums
to cast bronze horses.’”
5 In the intercalary month,
on the day Wùshēn (戊申),
the dukes of Zhào (趙), Qí (齊), and Lǔ (魯) were all advanced to the rank of king.
6 After Empress Guō (郭) was deposed,
Crown Prince Qiáng (彊) felt uneasy.
Zhì Yùn (郅惲) advised the Crown Prince, saying:
“To remain in a precarious position for too long
is to violate filial piety towards the emperor above
and to approach danger below.
It would be better to resign your position to attend to your mother.”
The Crown Prince followed this advice,
and on several occasions, through his attendants and various kings, expressed his sincere desire
to be appointed as a vassal lord.
The Emperor could not bear to agree, delaying for several years.
In the sixth month,
on the day Wùshēn (戊申),
an edict stated:
“According to the meaning of the Chūnqiū (春秋),
a son is established based on the nobility of his mother.
The Chūnqiū Gōngyáng Zhuàn (春秋公羊傳) says:
‘The legitimate heir is established by seniority, not by virtue;
a son is established by the nobility of his mother, not by seniority.’
Why was Duke Huán (桓) noble?
Because his mother was noble.
If the mother is noble, the son is noble;
the son is noble because of the mother,
and the mother is noble because of the son.
The son of the Empress
should properly inherit the great succession.
Crown Prince Qiáng (彊),
with great humility and retreat,
wishes to be made a vassal lord.
The sentiment between father and son
makes it difficult to repeatedly deny him.
‘Zhòng (重)’ here means ‘difficult.’
Let Yáng (陽) be established as the Crown Prince,
and his name changed to Zhuāng (莊).”
Yuán Hóng (袁宏) remarked:
“Establishing a Crown Prince
is for the purpose of emphasizing the imperial lineage
and unifying the people’s hearts;
unless there is great wickedness evident to the world,
it should not be changed.
When Shìzǔ (世祖) restored the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
he ought to have followed the righteous path to set a precedent for later generations.
Now, the Crown Prince’s virtue has not outwardly diminished,
but with many internal favorites,
to move the legitimate son from his position
can be called a mistake.
However, Dōnghǎi (東海) returned to his fief,
his humble and respectful heart shining ever brighter;
Emperor Míng (明), inheriting the succession,
his fraternal affection grew stronger.
The Lúnyǔ (論語) states: ‘Confucius said: Only those who are filial and fraternal to their brothers.’
Though the rise and fall differ,
the profound nature of father and son, brother and brother,
remains unbroken.
If one were to apply the Way of the Three Dynasties to this, what could surpass it!”
7 The emperor appointed Tài zǐ’s maternal uncle, Yīn Shí, to guard the Zhí jīn wú,
and Yīn Xīng as Wèi wèi.
Both assisted and guided the Heir Apparent.
Yīn Shí’s nature was loyal and honest;
when in court, although he spoke very frankly in righteous discussions,
when conversing with guests,
he never touched upon state affairs.
The emperor respected him greatly,
often pointing to Yīn Shí to admonish and warn imperial relatives,
and to motivate his attendants.
Although Yīn Xīng honored the virtuous and was fond of giving,
his gates were free of wandering knights-errant.
In the late Western Hàn period,
Wàn Zhāng, Lóu Hù, Chén Zūn, and others all associated with powerful and prominent families;
by this time,
there were also people like Dù Bǎo and Wáng Pán.
好 (Hǎo)
is pronounced “hū dào.”
施 (Shī)
is pronounced “shì chì.”
俠 (Xiá)
is pronounced “hù jiá.”
According to the Xìng pǔ (Genealogy of Surnames): Xiān Yú
originally derived from the Zǐ surname.
King Wǔ of Zhōu enfeoffed Jī Zǐ in Cháo Xiān.
His son (a branch line), Zhòng, received the fief of Yú,
and thus adopted Xiān Yú as his clan name.
裒 (Póu)
is pronounced “pú hóu.”
It means to praise one’s strengths and recommend them.
His friends Zhāng Sì and Dù Qín
were very close to Yīn Xīng.
Thinking that they were outwardly splendid but lacked substance,
he secretly
gave them money,
but never spoke of them (to the emperor);
for this reason, the world praised his loyalty.
The emperor appointed Huán Róng of Pèi Guó as a Yì láng.
Pèi Guó
is Pèi Jùn.
In the twentieth year of Jiàn wǔ,
King Fǔ of Zhōng Shān was relocated and enfeoffed in Pèi,
which then became a guó (principality).
The Xù Hàn zhì states: All láng guān were in charge of taking turns holding halberds,
guarding the various palace gates overnight,
and serving as charioteers when the emperor went out;
only the Yì láng was not among those on duty.
A Yì láng’s rank was six hundred dàn of grain.
The imperial carriage visited the Grand Academy,
where various erudites were gathered to debate before him.
Huán Róng clarified the meaning of the classics,
always seeking to satisfy others with礼 letdowns and courtesies,
and not winning over others by length of discourse;
no other scholar could match him,
and he received special rewards.
The emperor also ordered the students to sing refined songs and strike stone chimes,
only dismissing them at the end of the day.
The emperor sent Zuǒ zhōng láng jiàng Zhōng Xīng of Rǔ Nán to teach the Heir Apparent and the imperial clan princes the Chūn qiū.
Zhōng Xīng taught the Gōng yáng Chūn qiū,
which was of the Yán school.
Zhōng Xīng declined, citing lack of merit.
The emperor said,
"Is educating and instructing the Heir Apparent and the various princes
not a great merit?"
Zhōng Xīng replied,
"My teacher is the Shào fǔ Dīng Gōng."
Thereupon, Dīng Gōng was re-enfeoffed,
and Zhōng Xīng firmly declined the appointment.
8 Dǒng Xuān of Chén Liú became the Prefect of Luò yáng.
The household servant of Princess Hú yáng committed murder in broad daylight,
and then hid in the princess’s residence,
so the officials could not apprehend him.
When the princess went out,
with the slave riding in her carriage,
Dǒng Xuān waited for her at Xià mén Tíng.
Of Luò yáng’s twelve city gates,
Xià mén was located in the hài position.
Cài Zhì’s Hàn Yí states: Luò yáng had twelve city gates,
and each gate had a pavilion.
Xián says: Xià mén was the westernmost gate on the northern side of Luò yáng city,
and outside the gate was Wàn shòu Tíng.
乘 (Chéng)
is pronounced “shéng zhèng.”
叩 (Kòu)
means near.
He loudly enumerated the princess’s faults;
then he yelled at the slave to get out of the carriage,
and subsequently struck and killed him.
The princess immediately returned to the palace to complain to the emperor.
The emperor was furious,
summoned Dǒng Xuān,
and wanted to beat him to death with a rod.
Dǒng Xuān kowtowed and said,
"I beg to speak one word before I die."
The emperor said,
"What do you wish to say?"
Dǒng Xuān said,
"Your Majesty’s sagely virtue has brought about a restoration,
yet you indulge a slave who commits murder.
How will you govern the world then?
I do not need a rod;
please allow me to kill myself!"
He then struck his head against a pillar.
楹 (Yíng)
means pillar.
The emperor ordered his Xiǎo huáng mén to hold him.
Xiǎo huáng mén
were eunuchs
belonging to the Shào fǔ.
Dǒng Xuān refused to comply;
when forced to prostrate,
Dǒng Xuān braced himself with both hands on the ground,
absolutely refusing to bend.
The princess said,
"When Wén Shū was a commoner,
he concealed fugitives and hid those who committed capital crimes.
亡 (Wáng)
refers to fugitives;
死 (Sǐ)
refers to those who committed capital crimes.
Now that he is the Son of Heaven,
can his authority not enforce a single command?"
The emperor smiled and said,
"The Son of Heaven is not the same as a commoner!"
He then commanded,
"Let the 'Hard-necked Prefect' go out!"
Xián says: 強項 (Qiáng xiàng)
means not bending or yielding.
Dǒng Xuān distributed all (the imperial gifts) among his officers.
From then on, he was able to contend with powerful and influential families,
and the capital was filled with awe and trepidation.
"慓" (Piào)
should be written
慓 (Piào)
is pronounced “pǐ miào.”
The Qián shū yīn yì states: 慓 (Piào)
means swift;
this is not the meaning here.
【In the twelve-line edition,
it is indeed written
the Kǒng edition is the same.
9 In the ninth month,
on the day Rén shēn,
the emperor traveled to Nán yáng;
he then proceeded to the county residence of Nán dùn in Rǔ Nán,
where he held a banquet,
bestowed gifts upon officials and commoners,
and remitted the land tax for Nán dùn for one year.
The elders came forward, kowtowed, and said,
"The late Emperor resided here for a long time,
and Your Majesty is familiar with the temples and residences.
Xián says: Guāng wǔ once visited Nán dùn with the late Emperor,
hence his familiarity with the official residences and buildings.
Fēng sú tōng says: 寺 (Sì)
means succession;
officials who manage affairs succeed one another within it.
It also says: 寺 (Sì)
means to manage;
all places where official residences are located are called sì.
We beg for a remission for ten years."
The emperor said,
"The world is a heavy vessel;
I constantly fear I am not capable enough to bear it.
Day by day,
how dare I promise such a distant term of ten years!"
The officials and commoners again said,
"Your Majesty is truly frugal with it (the remission);
why speak of humility!"
The emperor laughed heartily,
and increased the remission by one more year.
He then proceeded to Huái yáng, Liáng, and Pèi.
10 The Dòng Cán of the Southwest Yi rebelled,
killing the chief official.
An edict ordered Wǔ wēi Jiāng jūn Liú Shàng to suppress them.
On his route through Yuè Suī,
Qióng Gǔ Wáng Rèn Guì feared that once Liú Shàng had pacified the southern border,
his authority and laws would certainly be enforced,
and he himself would not be able to act unrestrainedly.
He then gathered troops and set up camps,
brewed much poisonous wine,
intending to first "comfort" the army,
and then launch a surprise attack on Liú Shàng.
Liú Shàng knew of his plan,
and immediately divided his troops to first occupy Qióng Dū.
The administrative seat of Yuè Suī Jùn was Qióng Dū,
which Rèn Guì occupied.
Sòng Bái says: Hàn Qióng Dū Xiàn
became Cuī Zhōu Yuè Suī Xiàn in Táng dynasty.
He then executed Rèn Guì.
1 In spring,
the second month,
on the day Wù zǐ,
the imperial carriage returned to the palace.
2 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day Gēngchén,
Dà Sītú Dài Shè was imprisoned and died for having falsely accused the former Tàicāng Lìng Xī Shè of a crime.
To falsely accuse an innocent person is called 'rù' (入).
The Bǎiguān Zhì says: The Tàicāng Lìng belongs to the Dà Sīnóng,
and is in charge of receiving grain transported by rivers from commanderies and kingdoms.
His rank is 600 dàn of grain.
Xià (下),
pronounced xiá jià.
Dà Sīkōng Dòu Róng was dismissed from office.
3 Guǎngpíng Zhōnghóu Wú Hàn was gravely ill,
and the emperor personally visited him.
When asked what he wished to say,
he replied:
“Your minister is foolish
and knows nothing,
I only wish that Your Majesty will be careful not to grant pardons lightly.”
In the fifth month,
on the day Xīnhài,
Wú Hàn passed away.
An imperial edict ordered his funeral to follow the precedent of Dà Jiàngjūn Huò Guāng.
This event is recorded in Volume 24, Xuāndì, Dìjié second year.
Wú Hàn was strong and resolute by nature.
Whenever he participated in campaigns,
if the emperor had not yet rested,
he would always stand on the side with one foot slightly raised.
When other generals saw that the battle formation was unfavorable,
many would become alarmed
and lose their composure.
Wú Hàn, however, remained calm and composed,
and would set about organizing and sharpening weapons
and rousing his officers and soldiers.
At that time, the emperor sent someone to observe what Dà Sīmǎ Wú Hàn was doing.
The messenger returned and reported that he was preparing implements for attack and defense.
The emperor then sighed and said:
“Duke Wú is indeed quite capable and satisfies expectations;
he is a hidden bulwark like an enemy state!”
Xián says: Yǐn (隱)
describes a weighty and imposing appearance,
meaning his gravitas and influence are like that of an enemy state.
He would receive an imperial edict in the morning
and set out on the road by evening,
never spending a day
making preparations.
When in court,
he was scrupulously cautious and meticulous,
which was evident in his demeanor.
The Éryǎ says: Míngmíng and Jīnjīn
mean to observe carefully.
Lǐ Xún says: Jīnjīn
means to observe with meticulous detail.
Sūn Yán says: It means to observe with caution.
Jīn (斤)
is pronounced jìn.
When his wife and children bought land and property while he was away,
Wú Hàn returned
and reproached them, saying:
“The army is out on campaign,
and officers and soldiers lack sufficient provisions,
why have you bought so much land and houses?!”
He then distributed all of it among his brothers and relatives on his wife's side.
Thus, he was able to fulfill his duties and end his life with honor and success.
4 The Xiongnú raided Shàngdǎng and Tiānshuǐ,
and then advanced to Fúfēng.
The Jùnguó Zhì says: Shàngdǎng Jùn
is 1,500 lǐ north of Luòyáng.
Tiānshuǐ Jùn
is 2,000 lǐ west of Luòyáng.
5 The emperor suffered from vertigo
and was severely ill.
He appointed Yīn Xīng to lead the Shìzhōng,
and received his dying instructions in the Yúntái Guǎngshì.
Xián says: The Shàngshū says: When King Chéng was about to collapse,
he commanded Zhàogōng to compose a 'Gùmìng'.
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary says: Dying instructions are called Gùmìng.
Gù (顧)
is pronounced gǔ.
In the Southern Palace of Luòyáng, there are Yúntái and Guǎngdé Diàn.
I believe Guǎngshì refers to
the imperial bedchamber.
According to the Jìnshū, Yuándì Jì, an official memorialized that the Tàijí Diàn Guǎngshì should be furnished with crimson curtains,
but the emperor ordered light green silk curtains in summer
and light green cloth in winter,
which clearly shows that Guǎngshì was the bedchamber.
He summoned Yīn Xīng
and wished to appoint him as Dà Sīmǎ to replace Wú Hàn.
Yīn Xīng kowtowed and wept, firmly declining,
saying:
“Your minister dares not spare himself,
but this would truly detract from Your Sacred Virtue,
and I cannot presumptuously accept!”
His sincerity from the heart
moved those around him,
and the emperor eventually agreed.
Tàizǐ Tàifù Zhāng Zhàn,
since the deposition of Empress Guō,
claimed illness and did not attend court.
The emperor compelled him to rise
and wanted to make him Sītú.
Zhāng Zhàn firmly declined, saying his illness was severe
and he could no longer manage court affairs.
He was then dismissed.
In the sixth month,
on the day Gēngyín,
Cài Mào of Hénèi, the Grand Administrator of Guǎnghàn, was appointed Dà Sītú.
Tàipú Zhū Fú was appointed Dà Sīkōng.
On the day Rénchén,
Zuǒ Zhōnglángjiàng Liú Lóng was appointed Piàojí Jiàngjūn,
and acted as Dà Sīmǎ.
6 On the day Yǐwèi,
Zhōngshān Wáng Fǔ was transferred to become Pèi Wáng.
Guō Kuàng was appointed Dà Hónglú.
The emperor frequently visited his residence,
and bestowed upon him gold and silk,
such generosity was unparalleled.
Guō Kuàng
was the younger brother of Empress Guō.
His frequent favors towards Guō Kuàng
were to comfort the empress's heart.
Shù (數)
is pronounced suò jiǎo.
“Jīn Xué” (金穴) (golden lair).
7 In autumn,
in the ninth month,
Mǎ Yuán returned from Jiāozhǐ.
Pínglíng Mèng Jì went to welcome and comfort him.
Mǎ Yuán said:
“Currently, the Xiongnú and Wūhuán are still disturbing the northern border.
I wish to volunteer to attack them.
A man should die in the borderlands,
with his body wrapped in horsehide for burial.
How can one lie on a bed, dying in the hands of women and children?!”
Mèng Jì said:
“Indeed!
A valiant man should be like this!”
8 In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the day Jiǎwǔ,
the emperor traveled to Lǔ, Dōnghǎi, Chǔ, and Pèi Guó.
These were all the enfeoffed states of the imperial princes.
Later, Dōnghǎi Wáng Qiáng concurrently ruled Lǔ Jùn and made his capital in Lǔ,
but at this time it was still Lǔ Wáng Xìngguó.
9 In the twelfth month,
the Xiongnú raided Tiānshuǐ, Fúfēng, and Shàngdǎng.
10On the day Rén Yín,
the emperor returned to the palace.
11Mǎ Yuán volunteered to attack the Xiongnú.
The emperor permitted it
and ordered him to encamp at Xiāngguó.
Xián says: Xiāngguó
is a county name,
belonging to Zhàoguó,
now Lónggāng Xiàn in Xíngzhōu.
Mǎ Yuán said to Huángmén Láng Liáng Sōng and Dòu Gù:
“Generally, when people become rich and noble,
they should be able to return to being humble.
If you wish never to be humble again,
you must maintain your integrity when in high positions.
Strive to remember my humble words!”
Liáng Sōng
was the son of Liáng Tǒng.
Dòu Gù
was the son of Dòu Yǒu.
12Liú Shàng advanced his troops and fought continuously with Dòngcán and others,
defeating them all.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
they pursued them to Bùwéi.
Sūn Shèng's Shǔ Pǔ says: Initially,
Qín moved Lǚ Bùwéi's sons, younger brothers, and clan to Shǔ.
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn, the southwest barbarians were opened up,
commanderies and counties were established,
and the Lǚ clan was moved there to populate them,
thus Bùwéi Xiàn was established.
The Huáyáng Guó Zhì says: Emperor Wǔ opened the Bónán Shān road,
established Bùwéi Xiàn,
and moved Lǚ Jiā's (Prime Minister of Nányuè) descendants and clan there to settle it,
thus naming it Bùwéi
to signify the evil deeds of their ancestors.
The Jùnguó Zhì says: It originally belonged to Yìzhōu Jùn.
In the second year of Yǒngpíng of Emperor Míng,
Yǒngchāng Jùn was separated and established,
with its seat of government in Bùwéi.
The Shǐjì Zhèngyì says: Bùwéi Xiàn
is 600 lǐ north of Yèyú.
All the southwestern barbarians were pacified.
2 The Wūhuán, allied with the Xiōngnú and Xiānbēi, plundered as bandits.
Dàijùn and areas east suffered especially from the Wūhuán's depredations.
They lived close to the frontier forts;
leaving their yurts in the morning,
they would reach cities and towns by evening.
The common people of the five commanderies
all suffered at their hands.
The five commanderies
were Dàijùn, Shànggǔ, Yúyáng, Yòuběipíng, and Liáoxī.
The populace fled,
and the border regions became desolate,
devoid of human traces.
In autumn,
in the eighth month,
the Emperor dispatched Mǎ Yuán and an Acolyte to jointly construct fortifications
and gradually establish commanderies and counties.
Sometimes, Grand Administrators, Chiefs, and Wardens were appointed to vacant posts
to encourage the return of the people.
Among the Wūhuán, those dwelling outside Shànggǔ's frontier forts, at Bái Shān, were the strongest and wealthiest.
Mǎ Yuán led three thousand cavalry to attack them
but returned without success.
Kǎoyì says: Liú Zhāo’s commentary to the supplements of the Hòuhànshū Zhì is also called Xùhànzhì.
Its Jùnguózhì commentary states
“Colonel Mǎ Yuán,”
which is incorrect.
The Dìjì states:
“In winter, the tenth month,
Mǎ Yuán was sent out of the frontier to attack the Wūhuán.”
Mǎ Yuán’s biography states:
“In the twelfth month,
he encamped at Xiāngguó.
In the autumn of the following year,
he led three thousand cavalry out of Gāoliǔ.”
Yuánjì places this before Jì Róng's event in the eighth month.
We follow this now.
3 More than ten thousand Xiānbēi cavalry raided Liáodōng.
The Grand Administrator, Jì Róng, led several thousand men to meet and attack them,
personally donning armor and plunging into the enemy lines.
The invaders scattered in a great rout,
more than half dying by drowning.
He then pursued them relentlessly beyond the frontier forts.
The invaders, in desperation,
abandoned their weapons and fled naked in disarray.
Thereafter, the Xiānbēi were terrified
and feared Jì Róng,
daring not to again approach the frontier.
4 In winter,
the Xiōngnú raided Shànggǔ and Zhōngshān.
5 The King of Shāchē, Xián, became increasingly arrogant and oppressive.
Desiring to annex the Western Regions,
he frequently attacked various kingdoms
and heavily demanded taxes,
causing the kingdoms to be anxious and fearful.
The former King of Chēshī, along with Shànshàn, Yānqí, and eighteen other kingdoms, all sent their sons to serve at court
and presented their treasures.
When they were granted an audience,
they all wept and prostrated themselves,
requesting a Protector-General.
The Emperor, considering that the Central Plains had only recently been pacified
and the northern frontier was not yet subdued,
returned all their hostage-sons.
This is what historians call "assessing the times and measuring one's strength."
When the kingdoms heard that no Protector-General would be sent
and that all their hostage-sons were being returned,
they became greatly worried and fearful.
They then sent a communiqué to the Grand Administrator of Dūnhuáng, stating:
“We wish to retain our hostage-sons to show Shāchē,
saying that the hostage-sons are being held,
and a Protector-General will soon be dispatched,
hoping to temporarily halt their military actions.”
Péi Zūn reported the situation,
and the Emperor granted permission.
1 In spring,
the intercalary first month,
on the day Bǐngxū,
the Emperor visited Cháng’ān.
In the second month,
on the day Jǐsì,
he returned to Luòyáng.
2 In summer,
the fifth month,
on the last day Yǐwèi,
there was a solar eclipse.
3 In autumn,
the ninth month,
on the day Wùchén,
there was an earthquake.
4 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day Rénzǐ,
Grand Minister of Works Zhū Fú was dismissed.
On the day Guǐchǒu,
Dù Lín, the Minister of the Imperial Clan, was made Grand Minister of Works.
Previously,
Liú Kūn of Chénliú served as the Chief of Jiānglíng County.
When there was a fire in the county,
Kūn bowed his head towards the fire,
and the fire soon extinguished.
Jiānglíng County
belonged to Nánjùn.
Tigers all carried their young across the river.
The Emperor heard of this and was astonished.
He summoned Kūn to replace Lín as Minister of the Imperial Clan.
The Emperor asked Kūn:
“Previously in Jiānglíng, you quelled a fire by turning the wind.
Later, while governing Hóngnóng,
tigers crossed the river northwards.
What virtuous policies did you implement to achieve these things?”
He replied:
“It was merely by chance.”
Those around him all laughed,
but the Emperor sighed, saying:
“This is truly the speech of a noble man!”
He then ordered it to be recorded in the bamboo slips.
Cè refers to
jiǎncè,
which are bamboo slips bound together.
According to Hàn regulations, imperial edicts recorded on cè
were two chǐ long.
National histories also used jiǎncè.
Here, “shū zhū cè” means to record it in the historical records.
The Shàngshū, an ancient document, used eight-cùn slips.
5 In this year,
Qīngzhōu suffered a locust plague.
Qīngzhōu prefecture included Jìnán, Píngyuán, Lè'ān, Běihǎi, Dōnglái, and Qíguó.
6 The Xiōngnú Chányú Yú died.
His son, the Left Worthy Prince Wūdá Dīhóu, succeeded him.
He too died,
and his younger brother, the Left Worthy Prince Púnú, succeeded him.
In Xiōngnú territory, there were consecutive years of drought and locusts.
The ground was scorched for several thousand lǐ.
“Red ground”
means that all vegetation on the ground was destroyed.
More than half the population died.
Xián says: "Two-thirds of a whole is more than half."
They then sent an envoy to Yúyáng to request peace and kinship through marriage.
The Emperor dispatched Colonel Lǐ Mào to reciprocate the mission.
Kǎoyì says: The Dìjì states:
“In this year, the Xiōngnú Rìzhú Wáng Bǐ sent an envoy to Yúyáng to request peace and kinship through marriage;
Lǐ Mào was sent to reciprocate the mission.”
However, the following year there is another entry:
“Bǐ sent an envoy to Xīhé to offer allegiance.”
Therefore, the one Lǐ Mào reciprocated
was not Bǐ.
We now follow the Nánxiōngnú Zhuàn.
7 The Wūhuán took advantage of the Xiōngnú’s weakness
to attack and defeat them.
The Xiōngnú migrated north several thousand lǐ,
leaving the land south of the desert empty.
An edict ordered the disbanding of guards, stations, and garrisons in the various frontier commanderies,
and silk and cloth were used to entice the Wūhuán to surrender.
8 The hostage-sons of the Western Regions kingdoms, having long stayed in Dūnhuáng,
were all distressed and longed to return.
The King of Shāchē, Xián, knowing that no Protector-General would arrive,
attacked and defeated Shànshàn
and assaulted and killed the King of Qiūcí.
King Ān of Shànshàn submitted a memorial:
“We wish to again send our sons to serve at court
and once more request a Protector-General.
If no Protector-General comes out,
we are truly pressured by the Xiōngnú.”
The Emperor replied:
“Currently, our envoys and great army are unable to go forth.
If the various kingdoms feel that their strength is insufficient,
they are free to do as they wish, east, west, north, or south.”
Giving them freedom to choose their course.
Bān Gù (班固) commented: During the reign of Xiào Wǔ (孝武),
plans were made to control the Xiōngnú (匈奴).
It was feared that they would combine with the Western Regions,
forming a party with the Southern Qiāng (羌).
Southern Qiāng (南羌)
refers to the various Qiāng (羌) tribes in Huángzhōng (湟中).
Cóng (從),
pronounced Ziróng (子容).
The four commanderies were Wǔwēi (武威), Zhāngyè (張掖), Jiǔquán (酒泉), and Dūnhuáng (敦煌).
Communication with the Western Regions
was to sever the right arm of the Xiōngnú (匈奴),
isolating the Southern Qiāng (南羌) and Yuèzhī (月氏).
The Chányú (單于), deprived of aid,
consequently fled far away,
and there was no royal court south of the desert.
Having encountered the profound tranquility of Wén (文) and Jǐng (景),
the people were nurtured for five generations.
Gāo (高), Huì (惠), Empress Lǚ (呂后), Wén (文), and Jǐng (景) comprised the five generations.
The soldiers and horses were strong and prosperous,
thus enabling them to see rhinoceros hides and [AS-827B] tortoiseshell,
leading to the establishment of the seven commanderies of Zhūyá (珠厓).
Feeling the effects of kǒujiàng (蒟醬) and bamboo staffs,
they opened up Zāngkē (牂柯) and Yuèsuí (越巂).
Hearing of "Heavenly Horses" and grapes (pútáo),
they established communication with Dàyuān (大宛) and Ānxī (安息).
From then on, exotic products from distant lands
arrived from all four directions.
Thereupon, imperial parks were opened,
palaces were expanded,
splendid curtains and tents were set up,
beautiful clothing and ornaments were crafted,
and wine ponds and meat forests were arranged to feast guests from the Four Barbarian Tribes.
Fish-dragon and horn-butting performances were staged for their entertainment.
In addition, bribes, gifts, and presentations
were exchanged over ten thousand *lǐ*,
and the expenses of armies and travel
were countless.
When expenditures became insufficient,
wine sales were monopolized,
salt and iron were managed by the government,
white gold was minted,
deer-skin currency was created,
taxes were levied on vehicles and boats,
and rent was collected on livestock.
The strength of the people was exhausted,
and financial resources were depleted.
Coupled with years of famine,
bandits rose everywhere,
roads became impassable.
The "directly appointed envoys" then began to appear,
dressed in embroidered robes and wielding axes,
carrying out executions in the commanderies and kingdoms,
only then gaining control.
Therefore, in his later years, Wǔ (武) abandoned the land of Lúntái (輪臺) and issued an edict of profound sorrow.
Was this not a regret for a benevolent and sagacious ruler?
All these matters are found in the "Annals of Emperor Wǔ."
Moreover, in opening up the Western Regions,
nearby there was Lóngduī (龍堆),
and far away there were the Cōnglǐng (葱嶺) mountains.
The hardships of intense heat, headaches, and perilous crossings,
as discussed by Huáinán (淮南), Dù Qīn (杜欽), and Yáng Xióng (揚雄),
all considered these to be the natural boundaries that separate regions,
dividing inner and outer.
The various states of the Western Regions
each had their own rulers,
their forces divided and weak,
with no unified leadership.
Although they belonged to the Xiōngnú (匈奴),
they were not intimate or attached.
The Xiōngnú (匈奴) could obtain their horses, livestock, and felt blankets, but could not command them,
advancing and retreating with them.
Separated from Han,
and the journey being long,
gaining them would not be an advantage,
abandoning them would not be a loss.
Our great virtue lies with us,
we have nothing to gain from them.
Therefore, since Jiànwǔ (建武),
the Western Regions have admired Han's (漢) might and virtue,
all happily wishing to be incorporated.
They frequently sent envoys to pledge hostages to Han (漢),
requesting a Protector-General.
The sagacious Emperor, looking far back into ancient and modern times,
and considering the exigencies of the moment,
declined and did not permit it.
Even Yǔ's (禹) ordering of the Western Róng (戎),
Zhōu Gōng's (周公) refusal of the white pheasant,
and Tài Zōng's (太宗) turning back of the tribute horses,
exemplify this principle!
The Yǔ Gòng (禹貢) states: "The Western Róng (戎) were then ordered."
Jì (即),
meaning "to go to";
Xù (序),
meaning "to arrange."
Yǔ (禹) went and arranged them,
not valuing military might to subdue them
and make them present tribute.
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: In ancient times, when Zhōu Gōng (周公) assisted King Chéng (成王),
the Yuèshāng (越裳) clan, after nine translations, presented a white pheasant.
King Chéng (成王) asked Zhōu Gōng (周公),
and the Duke said:
"If virtue is not extended to them,
then a gentleman does not accept their pledge.
If governance is not applied to them,
then a gentleman does not treat those far off as his subjects.
How can I obtain this object?"
The interpreter said:
"I received an order from our national elder Huáng Gǒu (黃耇) saying: 'For a long time, there have been no fierce winds, thunder, or rain from heaven.
Does this mean there is a sage in the Central Kingdom?'"
Then it was returned to the king,
attributing it to the spiritual power of the former kings,
to be offered in the ancestral temple.
The incident of turning back the tribute horses is found in volume 13, first year of Emperor Wén (文帝).
Collated by Wáng Chóngwǔ (王崇武) (punctuated), Róng Zhàozǔ (容肇祖), and Niè Chóngqí (聶崇岐) (proofread).
Compiled by Imperial Edict
by Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光).
Later
Emperor Shìzǔ Guāngwǔ (世祖光武) (part 2)
Jiànwǔ (建武) 23rd year
(Dīngwèi (丁未), 47 CE)
1 Spring,
1st month,
the Southern Mán (蠻) in Nánjùn (南郡) rebelled.
The "Treatise on Commanderies and Kingdoms" states: Nánjùn (南郡)
is one thousand five hundred *lǐ* south of Luòyáng (雒陽).
Mán (蠻)
refers to the various Mán (蠻) tribes in the mountains along the Miǎn (沔) River.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: At that time, the Púshān (潳山) Mán (蠻) of Nánjùn (南郡) revolted.
Liú Shàng (劉尚) attacked and defeated them,
relocating over seven thousand of their people
to an area within Jiāngxià (江夏).
The Mán (蠻) of Miǎnzhōng (沔中) are their descendants.
2 Summer,
5th month,
on the Dīngmǎo (丁卯) day,
Grand Minister of Works Cài Mào (蔡茂) passed away.
3 Autumn,
8th month,
on the Bǐngxū (丙戌) day,
Grand Minister of Construction Dù Lín (杜林) passed away.
4 9th month,
on the Xīnwèi (辛未) day,
Yù Kuàng (玉況) of Chénliú (陳留)
was appointed Grand Minister of Works.
5 Winter,
10th month,
on the Bǐngshēn (丙申) day,
Grand Steward Zhāng Chún (張純) was appointed Grand Minister of Construction.
6 The Wǔlíng Mán (武陵蠻), led by Jīngfū Xiāng Dānchéng (精夫相單程) and others, rebelled.
King Zhāo (昭王) of Qín (秦) sent Bái Qǐ (白起) to attack Chǔ (楚),
seizing the Mán (蠻) and Yí (夷) lands,
and first established Qiánzhōng (黔中) Commandery.
When Han (漢) arose,
it was changed to Wǔlíng (武陵).
The Fàn Shū (范書) states: The tribal chief of the Chángshā (長沙) Wǔlíng Mán (武陵蠻) was named Jīngfū (精夫),
a descendant of Pánhù (槃瓠).
Xián (賢) said: The Yuán (沅) River originates from the former Jǔlán (且蘭) in Zāngkē (牂柯),
flows northeast through Chénzhōu (辰州), Tánzhōu (潭州), and Yuèzhōu (岳州),
then through Dòngtíng Hú (洞庭湖) into the Jiāng (江) River.
Wǔxī (武谿)
is located about one hundred eighty *lǐ* west of present-day Lúxī (盧谿) County, Chénzhōu (辰州),
and is one of the Five Xī (谿).
Yuán (沅),
pronounced *yuán*.
The Mán (蠻), taking advantage of the treacherous terrain, ambushed them,
and Shàng's (尚) entire army was annihilated.
7 At first,
Shànyú Yú's 輿 younger brother, the Right Gūlǐwáng 谷蠡王 Zhīyáshī 知牙師, was next in line to become the Left Xiánwáng 賢王.
The Left Xiánwáng 賢王, in turn, was next in line to become Shànyú 單于.
The Shànyú 單于 wished to pass the position to his son,
so he killed Zhīyáshī 知牙師.
Wūzhūliú Chányú 烏珠留單于 had a son named Bǐ 比,
who was the Right Àojiàn Rìzhúwáng 薁鞬日逐王,
leading eight southern tribes.
When Bǐ 比 saw that Zhīyáshī 知牙師 had died,
he spoke resentfully, saying:
"If we speak of brothers,
the Right Gūlǐwáng 谷蠡王 was next in line to be enthroned.
If we speak of sons,
I am the eldest son of the previous Shànyú 單于,
so I should be enthroned!"
Hūhánxié Shànyú 呼韓邪單于 had made a pact with his sons that the succession should pass among brothers in order.
But Shànyú Yú 輿 killed his brother Zhīyáshī 知牙師 and enthroned his own son,
disrupting Hūhánxié's 呼韓邪 pact.
And Bǐ 比 was Wūzhūliú's 烏珠留 eldest son.
Bǐ 比 told himself that if the succession were to pass from father to son,
then upon Wūzhūliú's 烏珠留 death,
Bǐ 比 should have been enthroned as Shànyú 單于.
Why wait until Yú 輿 to begin passing it to his son?
Shīgǔ 師古 said: Gǔ 谷
is pronounced Lù 鹿.
Lǐ 蠡
is pronounced Lú Xī fān 盧奚翻.
Court meetings were rare and infrequent.
The Xiongnu 匈奴 kings would gather at the Shànyú's 單于 court in the first month of each year.
So they sent two Gǔdūhóu 骨都侯 to supervise the soldiers of Bǐ's 比部.
When Shànyú Púnú 單于蒲奴 was enthroned,
Bǐ 比's resentment and ambition grew.
He secretly sent a Han Chinese man, Guō Héng 郭衡, with a map of Xiongnu 匈奴 territory to the Grand Administrator of Xīhé 西河, seeking to submit.
The Jùn Guó Zhì 郡國志 says: Xīhé 西河 Commandery
is 1,200 lǐ 里 north of Luòyáng 雒陽.
Shǒu 守
is pronounced Shì Yòu fān 式又翻.
At the dragon sacrifice in the fifth month,
the Xiongnu 匈奴 kings would gather at Lóngchéng 龍城 for the sacrifice every fifth month of the year.
The Nán Xiongnu Zhuàn 南匈奴傳 says: The Xiongnu 匈奴 customarily had three dragon sacrifices a year,
always on the Wù day 戊日 of the first, fifth, and ninth months.
Bǐ's 比 younger brother, Jiàn Jiāng Wáng 漸將王, was under the Shànyú's 單于 tent.
The Nán Xiongnu Zhuàn 南匈奴傳: The high-ranking ministers are the Left Xiánwáng 賢王,
next the Left Gūlǐwáng 谷蠡王,
next the Right Xiánwáng 賢王,
next the Right Gūlǐwáng 谷蠡王,
who are called the "Four Horns."
Next are the Left and Right Rìzhúwáng 日逐王,
next the Left and Right Wēnyúshīwáng 溫禺鞮王,
next the Left and Right Zhǎnjiāngwáng 斬將王,
these are the "Six Horns."
"Jiàn" 漸
should be
"Zhǎn" 斬;
a copying error added the "water" radical.
He rode to report to Bǐ 比.
Bǐ 比 then gathered 40,000 to 50,000 soldiers from the eight tribes,
waiting for the two Gǔdūhóu 骨都侯 to return,
intending to kill them.
When the Gǔdūhóu 骨都侯 were about to arrive,
they learned of his plan
and fled.
The Shànyú 單于 sent 10,000 cavalry to attack him,
but seeing Bǐ's 比 host was strong,
they dared not advance and returned.
8 That year,
Gē Hóu Zhū Hù 鬲侯朱祜 died.
Fàn Shū Zhū Hù Zhuàn 范書朱祜傳: Died in the 24th year.
He esteemed Confucian scholarship;
as a general, he accepted many surrenders,
taking the subjugation of cities and towns as his primary goal,
and not caring for the merit of severed heads.

All the generals prostrated themselves, not daring to respond.
Jūn said:
"Indeed, when a loyal minister goes beyond the border,
if there is something that can bring peace to the state,
he may act on his own authority."
The Gōng-Yáng Zhuàn states: In the etiquette of diplomatic missions,

If, when he is beyond the border, there is something that can secure the altars of earth and grain
and preserve the state,
then he may act on his own authority.
Jìng
is pronounced as 'jìng.'
He ordered Zhǒng Fèng to bring the imperial edict into the barbarian camp

The barbarians were shocked and terrified.
In the tenth month of winter,

Thereupon, Jūn entered the bandit camp,
dispersed their forces,
sent them back to their respective commanderies,
appointed chief officials for them, and then returned.
The southern barbarians were thus pacified.
Before Jūn arrived,

The Emperor commended his achievements,

Having received a command and departed,

Ordering him to visit home and offer sacrifices at his ancestral tomb

Shàng

5 In this year,

An examination of discrepancies states: The Imperial Annals (帝紀) already recorded the Wūhuán (烏桓) coming to court this spring.
At year-end, it again records the Wūhuán (烏桓) paying tribute and submitting in this year.
Perhaps initially only the great chief came to court,

They were settled within the frontier,

Xián (賢) says: Perhaps it was a temporary arrangement at the time.
"Jiàng" (降),

It is intended to show that the higher one's position, the lower one's aspirations should be,

Chénliú and Xiāngyì presented them.

From the empress and king down to commoners,

Qín changed the ancient system;

Hàn inherited the Qín practices,
for over two hundred years,

After the restoration,
Emperor Míng then began to collect information from the Zhōu Guān, Lǐ Jì, Shàngshū, and various Confucian records and explanations,
to complete the gǔnmiǎn robes.
The Son of Heaven's carriages, robes, and caps

those of gōng, qīng, and below

He ascended the Língtái

The Chūnqiū Zuǒ Shì Zhuàn says: At the solstices, equinoxes, and the beginning and end of seasons,

Dù Yù's commentary says: Cloud phenomena
are atmospheric colors and unusual changes.
One should observe portents and omens
in advance to prepare for them.
The Qián Shū Tiānwén Zhì says: On the first day of the first month of the year,
from dawn until shǐ (around 9 am) is for wheat;
from shǐ until rìyì (around 1 pm) is for millet;
from rìyì until bū (around 3 pm) is for broomcorn millet;
from bū until xiàbū (around 5 pm) is for soybeans;
from xiàbū until sunset is for hemp.
At each of these times, based on the color of the clouds,
one can predict what crops are suitable for planting.

They set up tiger, bear, and leopard targets,

In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day Rénzǐ,
the Emperor went to the Bìyōng,
and for the first time performed the ceremony of nourishing the elderly.
Lǐ Gōng was appointed as the Three Elders (Sānlǎo),
and Huán Róng as the Five Reverends (Wǔgēng).
The Sānlǎo wore robes of Dūzhù silk,
and Jìnxián crowns,
and carried jade staffs.
The Wǔgēng also wore similar attire,
but did not carry staffs.
When the imperial carriage arrived at the Bìyōng ritual hall,
the Emperor sat in the eastern wing.
He sent an envoy with an An-chē carriage to welcome the Sānlǎo and Wǔgēng from the Tàixué lecture hall.
The Son of Heaven welcomed them at the entrance screen,
and they exchanged greetings.
The Emperor proceeded by the Zùjiē (eastern steps),
and the Sānlǎo ascended by the Bīnjiē (western steps).
When they reached the steps,
the Son of Heaven bowed as per ritual.
The Sānlǎo ascended,
facing east.
The Sāngōng set up tables,
and the Jiǔqīng arranged their shoes.
The Son of Heaven personally bared his arm to carve the sacrificial animal,
and held the sauce to feed them.
To "feed"
means to present food.
Sauce
is the principal flavor of food,
hence it was held while feeding.
The minister for preventing choking (zhùgěng) was in front,
and the minister for preventing indigestion (zhùyì) was behind.

and made peace with him.
This set the stage for Guǎngdé to kill Xián.
Wáng Chóngwǔ punctuated, Róng Zhàozǔ and Niè Chóngqí re-collated.
Sīmǎ Guāng
Compiled by imperial command.
Later Academy
Tiāntái
Emperor Xiǎnzōng Xiàomíng, Part Two
Yǒngpíng Fourth Year
(Xīnyǒu, 61 CE)
1 Spring,
the emperor recently went out to view city residences.
Chéng,
Luòyáng city.
Dì,
residence.
Xián said: There are ranks of A and B,
hence it is called *dì*.
Hénèi Commandery
was one hundred twenty *lǐ* north of Luòyáng.
The emperor, having read the memorial,
immediately returned to the palace.
2 Autumn,
ninth month,
on the day *Wùyín*,
King Āi of Qiānchéng, Jiàn, passed away.
Having no son,
the kingdom was abolished.
3 Winter,
tenth month,
on the day *Yǐmǎo*,
Sītú Guō Dān and Sīkōng Féng Fáng were dismissed.
Fàn Qiān of Pèiguó, Hénán Yǐn, was appointed Sītú,
and Tàipú Fú Gōng was appointed Sīkōng.
Gōng
was Zhàn's elder brother's son.
4 Liáng Sōng, Marquis of Língxiāng, was imprisoned and died for resentment and for "flying letters" (anonymous slander) and libel.
Sōng inherited his father Tǒng's title as Marquis of Língxiāng.
*Xiàn*,
read *xuán*.
*Xià*,
read *xiájià*.
Initially,
when the present emperor was crown prince,
Zhòng, son of Tàizhōng Dàfū Zhèng Xìng, was famous for his mastery of the classics.
“Famous” means
he was well-known at the time,
everyone knew him.
Zhòng said:
"The Crown Prince is the heir apparent,
and there is no principle of foreign relations for him;
Chú,
means deputy.
Feudal kings should not privately communicate with guests."
Sōng said:
"The intention of the elder [prince]
cannot be defied."
Zhòng said:
"To violate prohibitions and incur crimes
is not as good as upholding righteousness and dying."
So he did not go.
When Sōng was defeated,
many guests were implicated,
but only Zhòng was not tainted by the words.
5 King Guǎngdé of Yútián led thirty thousand soldiers from various kingdoms to attack Shāchē.
He lured King Xián of Shāchē,
killed him,
and annexed his kingdom.
The Xiōngnú sent soldiers from various kingdoms to besiege Yútián,
and Guǎngdé requested to surrender.
The Xiōngnú established Xián's hostage son Bùjūzhēng as King of Shāchē,
but Guǎngdé attacked and killed him again,
and re-established his younger brother Qílí as King of Shāchē.
6 Cāng, King of Dōngpíng, felt uneasy,
believing that he, as a close relative, was assisting in governance.
Cāng assisted in governance,
starting in the second year of Zhōngyuán, as recorded in the previous scroll.
He repeatedly submitted memorials, stating:
"Since the Hàn dynasty began,
no imperial clansman has been allowed to hold a position among the Three Excellencies or ministers.
I beg to return the seal and sash of the Grand General of Cavalry,
and retire to my feudal kingdom."
His words were very earnest,
so the emperor permitted Cāng to return to his kingdom,
but did not allow him to return the seal and sash of the Grand General.
1 Spring,
second month,
Cāng resigned and returned to his feudal domain.
The Kingdom of Dōngpíng
was six hundred seventy-two *lǐ* east of Luòyáng.
His *yuán* were made Middle Grandees,
and his *lìshǐ* were made Royal Household Gentlemen.
The "Treatise on Official Ranks" states: one Chief Clerk of the General,
rank one thousand *shí*;
twenty-nine *yuánshǔ*,
rank equivalent to four hundred *shí* down to two hundred *shí*;
thirty-one *lìshǐ* and *yùshǔ*,
one hundred *shí*.
The emperor specially appointed forty *yuán* and *shǐ* for Cāng.
The Grand Tutor of a kingdom had a rank of two thousand *shí*,
Middle Grandees equivalent to six hundred *shí*,
and Gentlemen two hundred *shí*.
*Yuán*,
read *yújuàn*.
One hundred thousand bolts of cloth.
2 Winter,
tenth month,
the emperor traveled to Yè;
that month,
he returned to the palace.
3 Eleventh month,
the Northern Xiōngnú raided Wǔyuán;
twelfth month,
they raided Yúnzhōng,
and the Southern Chányú repelled them.
4 That year,
border residents who were in the inner commanderies were dispatched,
and given two thousand *wàn* in travel expenses per person.
The money was given for travel preparations.
5 Dài Hóu Dòu Róng of Ānfēng was old,
and his children and grandchildren were unrestrained and
largely lawless.
His eldest son, Dòu Mù, was married to Princess Nèihuáng.
Nèihuáng County
belonged to Wèijùn.
Dòu Mù made Liú Xū, Marquis of Liù'ān, divorce his wife
and married his own daughter to him.
Liù'ān State
belonged to Lújiāngjùn.
Xián said: “This is today’s Lúzhōu.”
Examining the Former Hàn, Liù'ān was a kingdom;
in the Later Hàn, Liù'ān was a marquisate
belonging to Lújiāngjùn.
It is acceptable for Xián to equate Tang’s Lúzhōu with Hàn’s Lújiāngjùn,
but Hàn’s Liù'ān Marquisate was actually within the borders of Tang’s Shòuzhōu.
Liú Xù’s Dìlǐzhì states: “In Shòuzhōu’s Ānfēng County,
the old city of Hàn’s Liù'ān State is south of the county.”
This can be relied upon.
After this, in the second year of Yuánhé of Emperor Zhāng,
Gōng, King of Jiānglíng, was moved to become King of Liù'ān,
and Lújiāngjùn became his state.
Then Xián’s note could be used.
妻 (qī),
pronounced qī.
The Emperor was furious,
dismissing Mù and others from all their offices.
All the Dòu family who were officials
returned with their families to their home commandery.
The Dòu clan
was originally from Pínglíng, Fúfēng.
Only Dòu Róng was kept in the capital;
Dòu Róng soon died.
A few years later,
Mù and others were again implicated in an incident and, along with his sons Xūn and Xuān, were all imprisoned and died.
After a long time,
an edict allowed Dòu Róng’s wife and one young grandson to live in Luòyáng.
1 In spring,
the second month,
a precious tripod was discovered on Wángluòshān
and presented to the Emperor.
According to the Běnjì,
Wángluòshān was in Lújiāngjùn.
On the Jiǎzǐ day,
an edict declared:
“Auspicious signs descend
in response to those with virtue.
At present, our governance is often flawed,
so how could this be achieved?
The Yìjīng says: ‘The tripod symbolizes the Sāngōng.’
The Sāngōng support the monarch like the three legs of a tripod,
hence the saying.
This is a phrase from the Yìwěi.
Therefore, bestow fifty bolts of silk upon the Sāngōng,
and half that amount upon the Jiǔqīng and officials of two thousand dàn.
An edict from the former emperor
forbade people from using the word ‘shèng’ (sage) when submitting memorials,
seen in volume forty-two, Jiànwǔ seventh year of Guāngwǔ.
上 (shàng),
pronounced shàng.
From now on, if there are excessive or false praises,
the Shàngshū should suppress them and not review them,
to show that we are not flattered by sycophants.”
蚩 (chī),
means to mock.
2 In winter,
the tenth month,
the Emperor traveled to Lǔ;
in the twelfth month,
he returned to Yángchéng.
Yángchéng County
belonged to Yǐngchuān.
On the Rénwǔ day,
he returned to the palace.
3 This year,
Nán Chányú Shì died.
Sū, son of Chányú Mò, was enthroned
as Qiūchúchēlíndī Chányú;
a few months later,
he also died.
Cháng, younger brother of Chányú Shì, was enthroned
as Húxiéshīzhúhóudī Chányú.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the Guǐmǎo day,
Empress Dowager Yīn died.
In the second month,
on the Gēngshēn day,
Empress Guāngliè was buried.
All empresses in the Western Capital followed the Emperor’s posthumous name,
except for Empress Wèi Sī and Empress Xǔ Gōng'āi, who did not die a natural death and were separately given posthumous titles.
The practice of following the Emperor’s posthumous name and adding an extra character
began with Empress Yīn.
Fàn Yè said: “Empresses of the Hàn dynasty all adopted the Emperor’s posthumous name as their title.
Emperor Míng first established the title ‘Guāngliè,’
and thereafter all empresses were matched by their virtue,
so that the wise and the foolish, the excellent and the inferior,
were all indiscriminately included.”
Xián said: “According to the posthumous naming system: ‘He who holds virtue and follows his profession is called Liè.’”
2 The Northern Xiōngnú were still powerful
and frequently raided the borders.
They sent envoys to request trade.
The Emperor hoped that their communication
would prevent them from raiding again,
so he agreed.
3 Zōng Jūn, Administrator of Dōnghǎi, was appointed Shàngshūlìng.
Previously,
when Zōng Jūn was Administrator of Jiǔjiāng,
Jiǔjiāngjùn
was one thousand five hundred lǐ southeast of Luòyáng.
He dismissed all his subordinates (yuán and shǐ)
and closed the Dūyóufǔ (Inspector’s office) inside.
There were no incidents in the subordinate counties.
A commandery had five departments of Dūyóu,
supervising the subordinate counties.
He closed them within the office
for fear that their function of inspection
would harass the subordinate counties,
thereby causing more trouble.
Jiǔjiāng previously suffered much from tiger depredations,
and traps and snares were regularly set.
Xián said: “檻 (kǎn)
refers to a trap mechanism for catching beasts.
穽 (jǐng)
means digging a pit to ensnare them.”
Zōng Jūn then issued a notice to the subordinate counties, saying:
“The fierce beasts in the Jiāng and Huái regions
are like chickens and pigs in the northern lands.
If they now harm the people,
the fault lies with corrupt officials.
Yet, efforts are made to set up traps.
張 (zhāng),
means to set up.
To set up traps and snares to await birds and beasts is called zhāng.
As in Péi Yán’s Xīngxīng Míng,
‘The slave wants to trap me’
— that is it.
Therefore, strive to remove corrupt and greedy officials,
and think of promoting loyal and good ones.
Then the traps and snares can be removed at once,
and the quota system abolished.”
Thereafter, there were no more tiger troubles.
The Emperor heard of Zōng Jūn’s reputation,
and thus entrusted him with crucial affairs of state.
Zōng Jūn said to others:
“The state favors legalists and incorruptible officials,
believing that this is sufficient to stop corruption.
However, legalistic officials are accustomed to deceit,
and incorruptible officials are pure only in themselves,
bringing no benefit to the suffering common people or the harm caused by bandits.
I wish to prostrate myself and argue this point,
but now is not the time for change.
After a long time, when they themselves experience hardship,
then I can speak!”
Before he could speak,
he was transferred to Sīlì Xiàowèi.
Later, the Emperor heard his words
and retrospectively approved of them.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the Jǐmǎo day,
Sītú Fàn Qiān died.
2 In the third month,
on the Xīnmǎo day,
Yú Yán, Tàiwèi, was appointed Sītú,
and Zhào Xī, Wèiwèi, acted as Tàiwèi.
3 Zhèng Zhòng, Yuèqí Sīmǎ, was sent as an envoy to the Northern Xiōngnú.
A Sīmǎ of the Yuèqí Xiàowèi command was a single individual
with a rank of one thousand dàn.
Zhèng Zhòng did not yield.
The Chányú besieged him,
denying him water and fire.
Zhèng Zhòng drew his sword and swore an oath to himself.
He swore to die
rather than yield to the Chányú.
Then the Chányú sent another envoy
to return to the capital with Zhèng Zhòng.
At first,
the Grand Minister of Agriculture, Gěng Guó (耿國), memorialized:
"It would be advisable to establish a General Who Crosses the Liao (Dù Liáo Jiāngjūn, 度遼將軍) to garrison Wǔyuán (五原)
to prevent the Southern Xiōngnú (南匈奴) from defecting."
The imperial court did not follow this advice.
The Southern Xiōngnú, Xūbǔ Gǔdūhóu (須卜骨都侯) and others, knowing that Hàn (漢) and the Northern barbarians (Běilǔ, 北虜) were exchanging envoys,
harbored resentment internally
and wished to rebel.
The Xiōngnú (匈奴) foreign-named ministers
were the Zǔo (左) and Yòu (右) Gǔdūhóu (骨都侯).
Furthermore, there were the foreign clans Hūyǎn (呼衍氏), Xūbǔ (須卜氏), Lìlín (立林氏), and Lán (蘭氏),
all prominent clans within the Xiōngnú (匈奴) state,
who regularly intermarried with the Chányú (單于).
[They] ordered troops to welcome them.
Zhèng Zhòng (鄭衆) went beyond the frontier
and suspected something amiss;
he watched,
and indeed captured an envoy from Xūbǔ (須卜).
He then memorialized:
"It would be advisable to appoint a new Grand General
to prevent communication between the two barbarian groups."
From this, the Dù Liáo (度遼) camp was first established,
with Grand Master of Ceremonies Wú Táng (吳棠) acting as General Who Crosses the Liao (Dù Liáo Jiāngjūn, 度遼將軍),
leading the Límíng Hǔyá (黎陽虎牙) camp soldiers to garrison Màn Bǎi (曼柏) in Wǔyuán (五原).
The Hàn Guān Yí (漢官儀) states: Guāngwǔ (光武) used the troops from Yōu (幽) and Jì (冀) to conquer and pacify the empire,
hence a camp was established at Límíng (黎陽),
with an Usher (Yèzhě, 謁者) overseeing it,
comprising a thousand soldiers and cavalry.
Xián (賢) states: Emperor Zhāo (昭帝) appointed Fàn Míngyǒu (范明友) as General Who Crosses the Liao (Dù Liáo Jiāngjūn, 度遼將軍),
and it was re-established now.
Màn Bǎi (曼柏) county
is within the present-day territory of Yínchéng (銀城) county, Shèngzhōu (勝州).
4. Autumn,
great floods in fourteen commanderies and states.
5. Winter,
tenth month,
the Northern Palace (Běigōng, 北宮) was completed.
6. On the day Bǐngzǐ (丙子),
death-row prisoners were recruited to the Dù Liáo (度遼) camp;
those who had committed crimes and fled
were allowed to atone for their sins, each according to a different scale.
King Yīng (英) of Chǔ (楚) presented yellow pongee and white plain silk to the Chancellor of the state (Guóxiàng, 國相), saying:
Emperor Chéng (成帝) of Hàn (漢) abolished the Intendant (Nèishǐ, 內史) in kingdoms,
allowing the Chancellor (Xiàng, 相) to govern the people,
with duties like a Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu, 太守)
and a salary of two thousand bushels.
Wán (紈) is modern-day silk.
Shīgǔ (師古) says: Wán (紈) is plain white silk;
jiān (縑) is silk woven with doubled threads.
Xiàng (相) is pronounced xī liàng fān.
"Entrusted to be a vassal and supporter,
my faults and evils have accumulated.
Rejoicing in the great grace,
I humbly offer pongee and silk
to redeem my transgressions."
The Chancellor (Guóxiàng, 國相) reported this,
and an imperial edict replied:
"King Yīng (英) of Chǔ (楚) recites the subtle words of Huáng (黃) and Lǎo (老),
and reveres the benevolence and compassion of Fútú (浮屠).
He has purified himself for three months,
swearing an oath to the spirits.
What suspicion or doubt
could there be for regret or remorse!
Return his redemption offerings
to assist in the lavish feasts for Yīpúsài (伊蒲塞) and Sāngmén (桑門)."
At first,
the Emperor heard that in the Western Regions there was a deity
named Fó (佛).
He then sent envoys to Tiānzhú (天竺) to seek its Way,
obtaining its scriptures and some Shāmén (沙門).
The core of its scriptures was centered on emptiness and non-being,
valuing compassion and non-killing;
it held that when a person dies,
their spirit is not extinguished,
but is reborn in another form;
the good and evil deeds performed during life
all have retribution.
Therefore, what is valued is the cultivation of the spirit
to become a Fó (佛).
It excels at grand and magnificent words
to persuade and entice the common people.
Those who are proficient in its Way
are called Shāmén (沙門).
Thus, the art began to spread in China,
and its images were drawn,
and among the kings, dukes, and nobles,
King Yīng (英) of Chǔ (楚) was the first and foremost to favor it.
Yuán Hóng (袁宏)'s Hàn Jì (漢紀) states: Fútú (浮屠) is Fó (佛).
In the Western Regions, in the land of Tiānzhú (天竺), there is the Way of Fó (佛).
Fó (佛),
in Hàn (漢) means "enlightened,"
to awaken all sentient beings.
Its teachings primarily emphasize cultivating goodness and a compassionate heart,
not killing living beings,
and exclusively pursuing purity and tranquility.
Those who are proficient are called Shāmén (沙門).
Shāmén (沙門),
in Hàn (漢) means "rest."
It means to rest the mind and remove desires to return to non-action.
[The golden man was] sixteen feet tall,
golden in color.
At first,
Emperor Míng (明帝) dreamed of a tall golden man,
and asked his ministers about it.
Someone said:
"There is a deity in the West
named Fó (佛).
Could what Your Majesty dreamed
not be this?"
Thereupon, he sent envoys to Tiānzhú (天竺),
to inquire about its teachings and depict its image.
Xián (賢) says: Yīpúsài (伊蒲塞)
is Yōupósāi (優婆塞),
which is translated in China as "one who lives nearby,"
meaning one who has received precepts and whose conduct is worthy of living near monks.
Sāngmén (桑門) is Shāmén (沙門).
In Sanskrit, it is "śramaṇa,"
sometimes called Sāngmén (桑門).
In Táng (唐) it means "diligent rest,"
in Qín (秦) it was translated as "diligent practice,"
and also "good awakening."
Wèi Shōu (魏收) says: Emperor Wǔ (武帝) of Hàn (漢) sent Huò Qùbìng (霍去病) to attack the Xiōngnú (匈奴),
capturing the golden man of King Xiūtú (休屠王),
which was considered a great deity,
and placed in Gānquán Palace (甘泉宮).
It was not offered sacrifices,
but only incense was burned and obeisance made.
This was the gradual spread of the Way of Fó (佛).
Zhāng Qiān (張騫) on his mission to Dàxià (大夏)
reported that nearby was the state of Shēndú (身毒),
also named Tiānzhú (天竺).
It was then first heard that there was the teaching of Fútú (浮屠).
In the first year of Yuánshòu (元壽) of Emperor Āi (哀帝),
the doctoral disciple Qín Jǐngxiàn (秦景憲) received the oral transmission of the Fútú (浮屠) scriptures from Yīcún (伊存), an envoy of the King of Dàyuèzhī (大月氏).
China heard of it,
but did not fully believe it.
Later, Emperor Míng (明帝) dreamed of a golden man at night,
with white light around its neck,
flying in the palace courtyard.
He then asked his ministers,
and Fù Yì (傅毅) was the first to answer with "Fó (佛)."
The Emperor sent Langzhong Cài Yīn (郎中蔡愔) and others as envoys to Tiānzhú (天竺),
to copy the surviving models of Fútú (浮屠),
and then returned east to Luòyáng (洛陽) with the Shāmén (沙門) Shè Móténg (攝摩騰) and Zhú Fǎlán (竺法蘭).
The method of kneeling and bowing for Shāmén (沙門) in China began from this.
When Cài Yīn (蔡愔) returned,
he arrived carrying scriptures on a white horse.
Hàn (漢) consequently established the Báimǎ Sì (白馬寺) to the west of Yōngguān (雍關) in Luòchéng (洛城).
Hǎo (好) is pronounced hū dào fān.
7. On the last day of Rén'yín (壬寅),
there was a solar eclipse,
which was total.
Jì (既) means "completely."
[This] speaks plainly without concealment.
Thereupon, all those in office submitted sealed memorials,
each speaking of gains and losses;
the Emperor reviewed the memorials,
deeply taking the blame himself,
and showed the submitted memorials to all officials.
The edict said:
"What all officials have said
are all My faults.
The people's grievances cannot be redressed,
and corrupt officials cannot be restrained;
yet I lightly use the people's labor,
renovating palace buildings,
being extravagant in expenditures,
and excessively swayed by joy and anger.
Constantly recalling past warnings,
I am filled with awe and trepidation;
I merely fear that with My meager virtue,
over time I will become negligent!"
Only a ruler who can earnestly examine himself
can then utter such words.
8 Although the Northern Xiongnú sent envoys to offer tribute,
their raiding and plundering did not cease,
and border cities were closed during the day.
The Emperor discussed sending an envoy to reciprocate their envoy.
Zhèng Zhòng submitted a memorial admonishing:
"Your servant has heard that the reason the Northern Chányú desires to compel a Hàn envoy to come
is to alienate the multitudes of the Southern Chányú
and to strengthen the hearts of the Thirty-Six Kingdoms;
Xián said: Emperor Wǔ opened up the Western Regions,
which originally comprised the Thirty-Six Kingdoms.
Your servant believes 'strengthen their hearts'
means to make them exclusively attached to the Xiongnú.
[They wish to] boast to neighboring enemies,
making those in the Western Regions who wish to be assimilated hesitate and be suspicious,
and those who cherish their homeland despair of China.
Once a Hàn envoy arrives,
they become arrogant and self-confident.
If we send another one,
the captives will certainly consider their strategy successful.
'Successful strategy,'
means having achieved their plan.
pronounced Fú Yòu;
same below.
Xián said: 'Bó Yì' (駁議)
means to persuade the Chányú to return to Hàn.
pronounced Běi Jiǎo.
The Southern Court will be shaken,
and the Wūhuán will become disloyal.
The Southern Chányú's court was in Měijì, Xīhé.
'Shaken'
means desiring to leave the frontier and go north.
The Wūhuán were originally allied with the Xiongnú.
Hàn established a Commandant to oversee and protect them,
preventing them from communicating with the Xiongnú.
'Disloyal'
means their hearts are not loyal to Hàn but are divided with the Xiongnú.
Once they fully understand the situation,
they will utterly splinter and break away,
soon becoming a border menace.
Fortunately, we now have the forces of Dùliáo displaying their might on the northern frontier.
Even if we do not reply,
they would not dare to cause trouble."
The Emperor did not comply.
He again dispatched Zhòng.
Zhòng then stated:
"When your servant previously served as an envoy,
I did not bow to the Xiongnú.
The Chányú resented it,
and sent soldiers to surround your servant.
Now if I again bear the imperial command,
I will surely be humiliated and insulted.
Your servant truly cannot bear to hold the great Hàn's diplomatic credentials and bow alone to those in felt and furs.
The 'Biography of the Xiongnú' in the previous book states: 'From the monarchs downwards,
all eat animal meat,
wear their skins and furs,
and are clad in felt and furs.'
'Zhān' (旃)
is the same as 'zhān' (氈).
This will certainly harm the might of great Hàn."
The Emperor did not listen.
Zhòng had no choice.
After his departure,
he repeatedly submitted memorials on the road to resolutely argue against it.
An imperial edict severely rebuked Zhòng,
recalled him,
and imprisoned him at the Tíngwèi.
He was released in a general amnesty
and returned home.
Afterward, the Emperor, upon seeing Xiongnú visitors,
heard about Zhòng's dispute with the Chányú over protocol,
and then recalled Zhòng to be a Jūnsīmǎ.
The Hàn system: a Grand General's camp had five divisions,
each with one Commandant (Xiàowèi),
ranking equivalent to two thousand dàn of grain;
and one Jūnsīmǎ,
ranking equivalent to one thousand dàn of grain.
For divisions without a Commandant,
there was only one Jūnsīmǎ.
The Emperor recalled Zhòng to be a Jūnsīmǎ,
and had him join Mǎ Gēng in attacking Chēshī.
1 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the Jiǎchén day,

an imperial edict instructed the Sīlì Xiàowèi and the various Cìshǐ to annually recommend one Mòshòu Chánglì who had served for three years or more and whose governance was exceptionally outstanding, to be submitted along with the annual accounting,
and also to report those whose governance was particularly poor.
Dù Yòu said: The thirteen prefectures (zhōu bù) of the Later Hàn were: Sīlì governed Hénán,
which is the present prefecture;
