Fàn (范)
was the grandson of Dān (丹).
Lián Dān (廉丹) was a general for Wáng Mǎng (王莽).
1 In spring,
the first month,
the Emperor was to pay respects at Yuánlíng (原陵).
That night,
he dreamt of the late Emperor and Empress Dowager as if they were alive and joyful.
Upon waking,
he was too sorrowful to sleep.
He immediately consulted the calendar,
and the next morning was an auspicious day,
so he led the hundred officials to the mausoleum.
On that day,
sweet dew fell on the mausoleum trees.
Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Dìjì (帝紀) states:
"Sweet dew fell at Gānlíng (甘陵)."
The Huánghòu Jì (皇后紀) states:
"Paying respects at Yuánlíng (原陵),
sweet dew fell on the trees."
Therefore, it indeed fell at Yuánlíng (原陵).
The Dìjì (帝紀) mistakenly used
"Gān" (甘)
for
"Yuán" (原).
When the ceremony was over,
the Emperor knelt before the mat and leaned on the imperial bed,
looking at the Empress Dowager's mirror and cosmetic box.
He was moved to sorrow and tears,
and ordered the emollients and toiletries to be replaced.
All his attendants wept,
unable to look up.
Shěn Yuē (沈約) said: Before the Three Dynasties, there were no tomb sacrifices.
It was not until the Qín (秦) that the "sleeping chamber" (qǐn) first appeared,
built beside the tomb.
The Hàn (漢) followed the Qín (秦) practice;
all mausoleums had garden-sleeping chambers (yuánqǐn), hence the term "sleeping hall" (qǐndiàn).
The daily necessities and clothes
symbolized those of a living person;
this was the intent of the ancient qǐn.
2 Běihǎi Jìng Wáng Mù (北海敬王睦) passed away.
Mù (睦)
was the son of Běihǎi Jìng Wáng Xīng (北海靖王興).
Guāngwǔ (光武) and the present Emperor both loved him.
He once sent a Zhōngdàfū (中大夫) to the capital for court greetings.
Xián (賢) said: Zhōngdàfū (中大夫)
was an official of a kingdom,
responsible for presenting the king's greetings to the capital
and offering jade discs for the New Year.
Cháo (朝),
read zhíyáo (直遙).
"The imperial court questioned your humble servant,
Xián (賢) said: Cháotíng (朝廷) refers to the Son of Heaven.
The envoy said:
"Your Majesty is loyal, filial, benevolent, and kind,
respectful of the worthy, and fond of scholars."
Yuè (樂)
read luò (洛).
Mù (睦) said:
"Alas! You are endangering me!
These were merely my youthful actions to advance myself.
Tell the Grandee that since I inherited my title,
my ambitions have dwindled,
my will has weakened,
I indulge in music and women,
and am fond of dogs and horses.
That would be showing affection for me."
Such was his wisdom and cautious deliberation.
At that time, restrictions on vassal kings were strict,
and the laws were quite severe,
hence Mù (睦) considered this.
3 In the second month,
on the yǐsì (乙巳) day,
Sītú (司徒) Wáng Mǐn (王敏) passed away.
4 In the third month,
on the guǐchǒu (癸丑) day,
Bào Yù (鮑昱), the Grand Administrator of Rǔnán (汝南 Tàishǒu), was appointed Sītú (司徒).
Yù (昱)
was the son of Yǒng (永).
5 The Inspector of Yìzhōu (益州 Cìshǐ), Zhū Fǔ (朱輔) of Liángguó (梁國),
Yìzhōu (益州) Department comprised Hànzhōng (漢中), Bājùn (巴郡), Guǎnghàn (廣漢), Shǔjùn (蜀郡), Jiànwéi (犍為), Zāngkē (牂柯), Yuèsuí (越巂), Yìzhōu (益州), Yǒngchāng (永昌) and other commanderies.
The Yìzhōu Cìshǐ (益州剌史) governed from Luò Xiàn (雒縣) in Guǎnghàn Jùn (廣漢郡).
won over distant barbarians through his prestige.
West of Wénshān (汶山),
Wénshān (汶山) is in the west borderlands of Jiāndī Dào (湔氐道) in Shǔjùn (蜀郡),
where the Jiāngshuǐ (江水) originates.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: Máozhōu (茂州) was the Hàn (漢) Wénshān Xiàn (汶山縣).
Wén (汶),
Jìnshū (晉書) reads it as Mín (岷).
Jiān (湔),
Péi Sōngzhī (裴松之) reads it as Jiǎn (剪).
where the imperial calendar had not yet reached,
over a hundred states, including the Báiláng (白狼) and Pánmù (槃木),
all presented themselves as vassals and offered tribute.
Báiláng Wáng Táng Zōu (白狼王唐菆) composed three poems,
eulogizing the virtues of the Hàn (漢).
Fǔ (輔) dispatched Yóu Gōng (由恭), an aide from Jiànwéi Jùn (犍為郡), to translate and present them.
Jiànwéi Jùn (犍為郡)
is three thousand two hundred and seventy lǐ west of Luòyáng (雒陽).
The barbarian language did not communicate with that of the Central Plains,
hence they were translated before being presented.
Jiàn (犍),
read jūyán (居言).
Yuàn (掾),
read yújuàn (俞絹).
Yóu (由)
is a surname.
There was Yóu Yú (由余) in Qín (秦);
some say: descendants of Chǔ Wáng Sūn Yóu Zǐ (楚王孫由子).
6 Initially,
the king of Qiūcí (龜茲), Jiàn (建), was established by the Xiōngnú (匈奴).
Relying on the barbarian's power,
he seized control of the Northern Route,
attacked and killed the king of Shūlè (疏勒),
and installed his minister Dōutí (兜題) as the king of Shūlè (疏勒).
Bān Chāo (班超) traveled a secret path to Shūlè (疏勒),
ninety lǐ from Pántuó Chéng (槃橐城), where Dōutí (兜題) resided.
He sent officer Tián Lǜ (田慮) ahead to demand surrender,
instructing Lǜ (慮) thus:
"Dōutí (兜題) is not originally of the Shūlè (疏勒) lineage;
the people of the state will surely not obey him.
If he does not surrender immediately,
you may seize him."
When Lǜ (慮) arrived,
Dōutí (兜題), seeing Lǜ (慮) was slight and weak,
showed no intention of surrendering.
Lǜ (慮), taking advantage of Dōutí's (兜題) unpreparedness,
stepped forward and seized Dōutí (兜題), binding him.
Dōutí's (兜題) attendants, caught off guard,
were all startled and fled.
Lǜ (慮) quickly reported to Chāo (超).
Chāo (超) immediately rushed there,
summoned all the Shūlè (疏勒) generals and officials,
explained the wicked deeds of Qiūcí (龜茲),
and then enthroned Zhōng (忠), the nephew of the former king, as king.
Kǎoyì (考異) says: Yuán Jì (袁紀) states:
"He sought out the closest kin of the former king,
found his elder brother Yúlè (榆勒) and installed him,
renaming him Zhōng (忠)."
Xùhànshū (續漢書) states:
"He sought out the former king's nephew Yúlè (榆勒) and installed him,
renaming him Zhōng (忠)."
We now follow Chāo Zhuàn (超傳).
Chāo (超) asked Zhōng (忠) and his officials:
"Should Dōutí (兜題) be killed,
or should he be sent away alive?"
They all said:
"He should be killed."
Chāo (超) said:
"Killing him will be of no benefit to the matter.
We should let Qiūcí (龜茲) know the might and virtue of Hàn (漢)."
Thereupon, he released and sent him away.
7. In summer,
in the fifth month,
on the day Wùzǐ,
the Gōngqīng (Grandees) and hundreds of officials, believing in the Emperor's majestic virtue and ability to win over distant lands,
and the manifest auspicious omens,
gathered in the imperial court to offer a toast of longevity.
Bān Gù's Xīdū Fù (Rhapsody on the Western Capital) states: "Within the left and right courts,
where the hundreds of officials of the court assemble,
Xiāo, Cáo, Bǐng, and Wèi deliberated above;
this was indeed on the left and right of the palace courtyard."
Xián remarked: "Longevity
is what people desire,
thus, inferiors offering a goblet and presenting wine
all speak of 'offering longevity' (shàngshòu)."
Cháo (朝),
pronounced as zhí yáo.
"Heaven produces divine objects
to respond to the king;
distant people admire civilization,
truly because of (my) virtue.
How can I, so humble and unworthy,
enjoy this!
It is only by the sagely virtue of Gāozǔ and Guāngwǔ that this is brought about.
I dare not decline.
Reverently raise your goblets,
and the Tàicháng (Grand Master of Ceremonies) shall choose an auspicious day to make a proclamation to the ancestral temples."
Thereupon, he extended grace by bestowing ranks and grain upon the people, with distinctions.
At that time, all male commoners in the realm were granted two ranks;
Sānlǎo, Xiàotì, and Lìtián were granted three ranks;
displaced persons without official registration who wished to register were granted one rank;
widowers, widows, orphans, childless elderly, the severely infirm, and the poor who could not support themselves
were given three hú of grain per person.
8. In winter,
in the eleventh month,
he dispatched Fèngchē Dūwèi Dòu Gù, Fùmǎ Dūwèi Gěng Bǐng, and Jì Dūwèi Liú Zhāng to go out from Dūnhuáng and Kūnlún Sài,
to attack Xīyù (Western Regions).
Xián remarked: "Kūnlún
is the name of a mountain,
which was then used for the pass.
It is in the southwest of modern Sùzhōu Jiǔquán Xiàn.
The mountain has the form of Kūnlún,
hence its name.
King Mù of Zhōu met the Queen Mother of the West on this mountain;
there are stone chambers and a Queen Mother's Terrace."
It also states: "The Former Hàn History records that Dūnhuáng Jùn Guǎngzhì Xiàn has Kūnlún Zhàng,
where the Yíhé Dūwèi resided.
The old city of Guǎngzhì
is to the east of modern Guāzhōu Chánglè Xiàn."
Dūn (敦),
pronounced as tú mén.
Lún (侖),
pronounced as lú kūn.
Fú and Chuán
are both combined to serve as a token of trust.
Fú
refers to a military tally.
Zhāng Yàn said: "A Chuán
is like today's guòsuǒ (pass document)."
Rú Chún said: "Two lines written on silk,
with one part held,
to pass through gates,
when combined, one could pass,
this was called Chuán.
This Chuán
was likely also used as a token of trust in military operations,
not the Chuán used for passing through gates."
A commanding general would have both Fú and Chuán.
Now, entrusting the army to Gù,
these were omitted.
Qù (去),
pronounced as qiāng lǚ.
Chuán (傳),
pronounced as zhū liàn.
(They) attacked and defeated the Báishān Lǔ (White Mountain Barbarians) by the PúLèi Sea,
and then advanced to attack Chēshī.
The Former King of Chēshī
was the son of the Later King;
their courts were separated by over five hundred lǐ.
The Former King of Chēshī resided in Jiāohé Chéng,
and the Later King resided in Wùtú Gǔ.
The valleys were deep,
and the soldiers suffered from cold and hardship. They wanted to attack the Former King.
Bǐng believed that by first attacking the Later King,
and concentrating forces on the root,
the Former King would submit on his own.
Gù's plan was undecided.
Bǐng stood up bravely and said:
"Please let me go first."
He then mounted his horse and led his troops north.
The main army had no choice but
to advance together,
beheading several thousand.
The Later King, Āndé, was terrified,
ran out to meet Bǐng,
removed his cap,
embraced the horse's feet, and surrendered.
Bǐng took him to Gù;
the Former King also submitted,
and thus Chēshī was pacified, and they returned.
Thereupon, Gù memorialized to re-establish the Xīyù Dūhù (Protector-General of the Western Regions) and the Wù and Jǐ Xiàowèi (Commandants).
Xuāndì established the Dūhù,
Yuándì established the Wù and Jǐ Xiàowèi.
Since Wáng Mǎng's rebellion,
Xīyù had been cut off from Zhōngguó (China),
and these positions were no longer established.
Now, with Xīyù reconnected,
they were re-established.
Kǎoyì stated: "Yuán Jì
has 'Mù' (睦)
instead of 'Mù' (穆).
Now we follow Fàn Shū."
(They) garrisoned the Later King's domain at Jīnpú Chéng.
Xián remarked: "Jīnpú Chéng
was the court of the Later King of Chēshī,
which is now the city of Púchāng Xiàn in Tíngzhōu."
Dù Yòu said: "Jīnpú Chéng
is Wùtú Gǔ, where the Later King of Chēshī governed.
It is now Púlèi Xiàn in Běitíng Fǔ."
(They) garrisoned the Former King's domain at Liǔzhōng Chéng.
Xián remarked: "Liǔzhōng
is now Xīzhōu Xiàn."
Kǎoyì stated: "Yuán Jì has 'Zhézhōng'
instead,
now we follow Fàn Shū."
Gōng
was the grandson of Kuàng.
Gěng Kuàng joined Guāngwǔ from Shànggǔ,
and his descendants achieved many great merits.
1. In spring,
in the second month,
an edict ordered Dòu Gù and others to cease military operations and return to Jīngshī (the capital).
2. The Northern Chányú dispatched the Zuǒ Lùlí Wáng (Left Lùlí King) to lead twenty thousand cavalry to attack Chēshī.
Gěng Gōng dispatched his Sīmǎ (Major) to lead three hundred soldiers to rescue them,
but they were all captured.
The Xiōngnú then defeated and killed Āndé, the Later King of Chēshī, and attacked Jīnpú Chéng.
Gōng applied poison to his arrows,
and said to the Xiōngnú:
"The arrows of the Hàn house are divine;
those wounded by them will surely experience something extraordinary."
The barbarians who were hit by arrows
saw their wounds all bubble,
and were greatly astonished.
Coincidentally, a violent storm erupted,
and they attacked amidst the rain,
killing and wounding many.
The Xiōngnú were terrified,
saying to each other:
"The Hàn soldiers are divine,
truly formidable!"
They then withdrew.
3. In summer,
in the sixth month,
on the day Jǐwèi,
a comet appeared in Tàiwēi.
Jìn Tiānwén Zhì (Treatise on Astronomy of the Jìn Dynasty) states: "Tàiwēi
is the court of the Son of Heaven,
and the residences of the twelve feudal lords."
Bèi (孛),
pronounced as pú nèi.
4. Gěng Gōng, finding a stream near Shuīlè Chéng that could be fortified,
led his troops to occupy it.
This Shuīlè Chéng was in the rear part of Chēshī,
not the capital city of the kingdom of Shuīlè.
According to Xīyù Zhuàn (Annals of the Western Regions),
the kingdom of Shuīlè was five thousand lǐ from where the Chángshǐ (Chief Clerk) resided,
while the rear part was five hundred lǐ from where the Chángshǐ resided.
Gěng Gōng moved from Jīnpú Chéng in the rear part to occupy Shuīlè Chéng.
Later, Fàn Qiāng also came from Jiāohé Chéng in the front part, traveling north of the mountains to Shuīlè to welcome Gōng.
Carefully examining the details,
it is clear that it was not the capital city of the kingdom of Shuīlè.
In the seventh month,
the Xiōngnú attacked again,
damming the stream.
Gōng dug a well fifteen zhàng deep within the city,
but could not find water.
The officers and soldiers suffered from thirst,
even squeezing horse dung juice to drink.
Gōng personally led his men to pull up a basket.
Shortly after,
a spring gushed forth,
and everyone cheered, "Long live!"
He then ordered his officers and soldiers to splash water to show the barbarians.
The barbarians were taken by surprise,
thinking it was divine intervention,
and consequently withdrew.
5 In the eighth month,
on the day Rén-zǐ,
the emperor collapsed in the front hall of the Eastern Palace,
aged forty-eight.
His dying edict stated:
“Do not construct a funerary temple.
The ancestral tablet should be stored in the separate dressing room of Empress Guāngliè.”
Xián said: According to ritual, ancestral tablets are stored in a temple.
Since no funerary temple was to be erected,
it was therefore stored in the Empress’s separate dressing room.
Gēng [更]
means yì [易] (to change).
Gēng [更],
from the fanqie “gōng héng fān”;
the same applies below.
The emperor followed the system of Jiànwǔ,
making no changes.
The Empress’s relatives were not permitted to be enfeoffed as marquises or participate in government.
When Princess Guǎntáo requested an official post for her son,
Princess Guǎntáo,
who was Gǔangwǔ’s daughter Hóng Fū,
she sent Fùmǎ Dūwèi Hán Guāng.
Yǔ [與],
read as yù.
Wèi [為],
from the fanqie “yú wěi fān”.
He instead bestowed ten million cash and
said to his close ministers:
“Official posts of láng [郎] correspond to the constellations above.
The Shǐjì says: The twenty-five stars behind the Tàiwēi Palace
are the positions of the láng.
Sù [宿],
pronounced xiù.
If they are not the right people,
then the people will suffer calamity.
Therefore, I find it difficult.”
As the Bureau of Public Conveyances did not accept memorials on "reverse-branch days,"
the Yīnyáng Shū says: For all "reverse-branch days,"
the first day of the month is taken as the standard: if the new moon is Xū or Hài,
the 1st day is a "reverse-branch day";
if the new moon is Shēn or Yǒu,
the 2nd day is a "reverse-branch day";
if the new moon is Wǔ or Wèi,
the 3rd day is a "reverse-branch day";
if the new moon is Chén or Sì,
the 4th day is a "reverse-branch day";
if the new moon is Yín or Mǎo,
the 5th day is a "reverse-branch day";
if the new moon is Zǐ or Chǒu,
the 6th day is a "reverse-branch day."
“People neglect agriculture and sericulture,
traveling from afar to present themselves at the palace gates,
only to be further constrained by prohibitions and taboos.
How can this be the intention of governance!”
Thereupon, he abolished that regulation.
Shàngshū Yán Zhāng had two younger sisters who were Guìrén.
Zhāng was energetic and well-versed in old institutions.
After long service, he ought to have been promoted to an important position,
but because he was a relative of the Empress’s inner court,
the emperor ultimately did not use him.
Because of this, officials found their proper place,
the people enjoyed their livelihoods,
those near and far respected and submitted,
and the population prospered.
6 The Crown Prince ascended the throne,
aged eighteen.
He honored the Empress as Empress Dowager.
When Emperor Míng first passed away,
the Mǎ clan brothers contended to enter the palace.
The Běigōng Wèishìlìng Yáng Rén, clad in armor and wielding a halberd,
strictly ordered the gate guards,
and no one dared to advance lightly.
The Eastern Capital’s Southern and Northern Palaces each had one Wèishìlìng,
with a rank of six hundred dàn of grain,
each in charge of their palace guards.
The Hàn Guān says: The Northern Palace had seventy-two staff members,
and four hundred seventy-one guards;
the Zhūjué Sīmǎ was in charge of the Southern Side Gate,
with four staff members
and one hundred twenty-four guards;
the Dōngmíng Sīmǎ was in charge of the Eastern Gate,
with thirteen staff members
and one hundred eighty guards;
the Shuòpíng Sīmǎ was in charge of the Northern Gate,
with five staff members
and one hundred seventeen guards: all staff members were team leaders and assistants.
All those residing in the palace
had their names registered at the gates of the respective palaces with two characters,
as iron seal documents.
Only after examining the documents were they allowed in.
If an outsider needed to enter the palace for a matter,
the senior official would provide a sealed kǎi-pass.
For those with official ranks,
their escorts would state their official positions.
Hú Guǎng said: The document was made of wood,
about two cùn long,
sealed with an iron stamp.
Bèi [被],
from the fanqie “pí yì fān.”
Due to his strictness,
the emperor recognized his loyalty and
favored him even more,
appointing him as Shífāng Magistrate.
Shífāng County [什邡縣]
belonged to Guǎnghàn Commandery.
This is the Shífāng where Emperor Gāo enfeoffed Yōng Chǐ.
Fāng [邡],
read as fāng.
7 On the day Rén-xū,
Emperor Xiàomíng was buried at Xiǎnjié Mausoleum.
The Dìwáng Jì says: Xiǎnjié Mausoleum
was formerly Fùshòu Pavilion,
thirty-seven lǐ northwest of Luòyáng.
8 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day Dīng-wèi,
a general amnesty was declared.
9 An edict appointed Jiéxiāng Hóu Xī, who was acting Tàiwèi, as Tàifù,
and Sīkōng Róng as Tàiwèi,
both concurrently supervising Shàngshū affairs.
Emperor Guāngwǔ did not empower the Sāngōng;
affairs were managed by the departments and bureaus.
Only those supervising Shàngshū affairs had slightly heavier responsibilities.
From then until the Qí and Liáng dynasties,
they were called Lù Gōng.
Xián said: Emperor Wǔ first appointed Zhāng Zǐrú to lead Shàngshū affairs.
The supervision of Shàngshū affairs began from this.
The Jìn Bǎiguān Zhì says: During the time of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
the Zuǒyòucáo and various officials divided and managed Shàngshū memorials.
Those who knew the key matters began to lead Shàngshū affairs.
Zhāng Ānshì as Chējì Jiāngjūn, Huò Guāng as Dàjiāngjūn, Wáng Fèng as Dà Sīmǎ, and Shī Dān as Zuǒ Jiāngjūn all led Shàngshū affairs.
Later, Emperor Zhāng of Hàn appointed Tàifù Zhào Xī and Tàiwèi Móu Róng to concurrently supervise Shàngshū affairs.
The Shàngshū having the title of “supervising” began from this.
It was also the responsibility of leading Shàngshū in the Western Capital,
akin to the important post of Dàlù in Táng and Yú.
Shěn Yuē said: In the Eastern Capital of Hàn,
whenever an emperor ascended the throne,
a Tàifù and one supervising Shàngshū affairs were appointed.
Upon the emperor’s death, they were abolished.
10 In the eleventh month,
on the day Wù-xū,
Wǔlún, the Administrator of Shǔjùn Commandery, was appointed Sīkōng.
Lún was publicly upright in his commandery,
and many of the officials he recommended were suitable.
Therefore, the emperor appointed him from a distant commandery.
The Xù Hàn Zhì says: Shǔjùn Commandery
is three thousand one hundred lǐ west of Luòyáng.
Shǒu [守],
from the fanqie “shì yòu fān.”
11 Yānqí and Qiūcí attacked and overran Dūhù Chén Mù.
The Northern Xiōngnú besieged Guān Chǒng at Liǔzhōng City.
As there was a great mourning in the Central Plains,
no relief troops arrived.
Chēshī rebelled again,
and together with the Xiōngnú, attacked Gěng Gōng.
Gōng led his brave soldiers to defend against them.
After several months,
food ran out and they were in dire straits,
so they boiled armor and crossbows,
eating their tendons and leather.
Gōng and his soldiers were utterly sincere and shared life and death,
so none had disloyal thoughts.
However, they gradually died off,
leaving only several tens of people.
The Chányú knew Gōng was in distress
and wanted to compel his surrender.
He sent an envoy to persuade Gōng, saying:
“If you surrender,
you will be enfeoffed as King Báiwū.”
Lǐ Xún’s commentary to the Éryǎ states that
among the Five Dí, there is a type called Báiwū.
Jiàng [降],
from the fanqie “hù jiāng fān.”
Gōng lured the envoy up the city wall,
personally struck and killed him,
and roasted him on the city wall.
The Chányú was greatly enraged,
and increased his troops to besiege Gōng,
but could not take the city.
Guān Chǒng (關寵) submitted a memorial asking for help.
An edict ordered the *gōngqīng* (公卿) to convene a meeting.
Sīkōng (司空) Lún (倫) believed it was inadvisable to rescue them.
Sītú (司徒) Bào Yù (鮑昱) said:
"Now, if we send people to a place of danger and difficulty,
and abandon them when they are in urgent need,
externally, this will encourage the brutality of the barbarians;
internally, it will harm ministers who bravely face death.
It would indeed be a temporary expedient
if no border incidents were to occur thereafter.
But if the Xiōngnú (匈奴) again violate the frontier and act as bandits,
how will Your Majesty then be able to command generals!
Moreover, the soldiers of the two detachments number only a few tens each.
Xián (賢) said: 'The two detachments refer to Guān Chǒng (關寵) and Gōng (恭).'
They have held out for a whole month without falling,
which demonstrates their fewness and their utmost effort.
*Lì jìn* (力盡)
is like saying 'exhausting one's strength'.
Increase their flags and banners,
march day and night to relieve their emergency;
the exhausted troops of the Xiōngnú (匈奴)
will surely not dare to resist.
Within forty days, they can return and re-enter the frontier."
The Emperor agreed with him.
He then dispatched Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn (征西將軍) Gěng Bǐng (耿秉) to garrison Jiǔquán (酒泉),
acting as *Tàishǒu* (太守).
He sent the *Tàishǒu* (太守) of Jiǔquán (酒泉), Duàn Péng (段彭).
*Kǎoyì* (考異) notes: The biography of Gěng Gōng (耿恭) states
"Qín Péng (秦彭),"
but here we follow the Imperial Annals.
The *Xìngpǔ* (姓譜) states: In Sòng (宋), there was Huángfǔ Chōngshí (皇甫充石),
a ducal clan of Sòng (宋).
In early Hàn (漢), there was Huángfǔ Luán (皇甫鸞),
who moved from Lǔ (魯) to reside in Màolíng (茂陵),
changing *fù* (父) to *fǔ* (甫).
I note that in the *Shī* (詩),
there was also a *qīngshì* (卿士) named Huángfǔ (皇父) in Zhōu (周).
On the 12th day, *jiǎchén* (甲辰) of the last day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
The Queen Mother's brothers, Hǔbēn Zhōngláng (虎賁中郎) Liáo (廖), and Huángménláng (黃門郎) Fáng (防) and Guāng (光)
The *Bǎiguān Zhì* (百官志) states: *Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng* (給事黃門侍郎), 600 *dàn* (石) salary,
responsible for attending to the emperor's left and right.
The *Hàn Jiùyí* (漢舊儀) states: *Huángménláng* (黃門郎) are subordinate to the *Huángmén Lìng* (黃門令);
at dusk,
they enter to report and bow at the Qīngsuǒ Mén (青瑣門),

The Emperor appointed Liáo (廖) as Wèiwèi (衞尉),
Fáng (防) as Zhōnglángjiàng (中郎將),
and Guāng (光) as Yuèqí Xiàowèi (越騎校尉).
Liáo (廖) and others devoted themselves to building connections,
and high-ranking officials flocked to them.
Dìwǔ Lún (第五倫) submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant heard the *Shū* (書) say: 'Ministers should not practice tyranny or authoritarianism;
this will harm your household,
and bring ill fortune to your state.'
These are words from the *Hóngfàn* (洪範) chapter of the *Shàngshū* (尚書).
Yet, the Yīn (陰) clan was suppressed,
and not granted power.
This refers to Empress Yīn (陰) not seeking positions for her relatives.
There were mutual illegal acts,
and when Emperor Míng (明) ascended the throne,
he eventually executed many of them.
This refers to Liáng Sōng (梁松), Dòu Mù (竇穆), and others.
There were no longer powerful relatives;
requests and solicitations in writing
were all cut off.
He also admonished his maternal relatives, saying: 'To exert oneself to treat scholars well
is not as good as working for the state.
Holding a basin to look at the sky,
one cannot do two things at once.'
Sīmǎ Qiān (司馬遷)'s *Shū* (書) states: 'How can one look at the sky while holding a basin?'
He again used the Mǎ (馬) family as an example.
I secretly heard that Wèiwèi (衞尉) Liáo (廖) gave three thousand bolts of cloth,
and Chéngmén Xiàowèi (城門校尉) Fáng (防) gave three million cash,
to privately support the gentry of Sānfǔ (三輔);
known or unknown,
none were left without provisions.
I also heard that on the *Là* (臘) day, he also gave five thousand cash each to those who were in Luò (雒) at the time.
Yuèqí Xiàowèi (越騎校尉) Guāng (光),
for the *Là* (臘) festival, used three hundred sheep,
four hundred *hú* (斛) of rice,
and five thousand *jīn* (斤) of meat.
Your ignorant servant believes this does not conform to the principles of the classics,
and in fear and trepidation,
dares not fail to report it.
Although Your Majesty desires to treat them generously,
you should also find a way to secure them.
My speaking of this now,
is truly out of loyalty to Your Majesty above,
and to preserve the Empress's family below."
This year,
Yìshī (亦師) and Yǎn (兗), Yù (豫), Xú (徐) Provinces suffered severe drought.
Yǎnzhōu (兗州) Department included Chénliú (陳留), Dōngjùn (東郡), Dōngpíng (東平), Tàishān (泰山), Jìběi (濟北), Shānyáng (山陽), Jìyīn (濟陰) and other commanderies and kingdoms.
Yùzhōu (豫州) Department included Rǔnán (汝南),
Yǐngchuān (潁川) two commanderies,
Liáng (梁), Pèi (沛), Chén (陳), Lǔ (魯) and other kingdoms.
Xúzhōu (徐州) Department included Dōnghǎi (東海), Lángyá (琅邪), Péngchéng (彭城), Guǎnglíng (廣陵), Xiàpéi (下邳) and other commanderies and kingdoms.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: Yǎnzhōu (兗州) is probably named after the Yǎn (沇) River.
Also, the meaning of *Yǎn* (兗) is "straight" [or "upright"] (端)
and "trustworthy" (信).
*Duān* (端)
refers to the *yáng* (陽) *qì* (氣) being upright,
hence its *qì* (氣) is sharp and reducing.
Xúzhōu (徐州) probably takes its meaning from "leisurely and gentle" (舒緩),
or some say: it is named after Xúqiū (徐丘).
Punctuation by Wáng Chóngwǔ (王崇武), collated by Róng Zhàozǔ (容肇祖) and Niè Chóngqí (聶崇岐).
Sīmǎ Guāng (司馬光)
compiled by imperial decree.

Sùzōng Xiàozhāng Huángdì (肅宗孝章皇帝), Part One.
His personal name was Dá (炟).
He was the fifth son of Xiǎnzōng (顯宗).
His mother was Consort Jiǎ (賈貴人),
but he was adopted by Empress Mǎ (馬后) and raised as her legitimate son,
then ascended the throne.
The *Shìfǎ* (諡法) states: "Warm, gentle, and of exemplary conduct is called Zhāng (章)."
*Fú Hóu Gǔjīn Zhù* (伏侯古今註) states:
The character "Dá" (炟)
is pronounced as "Zhù" (著).
Jiànchū (建初) First Year
(*bǐngzǐ* (丙子), 76 CE)
1. Spring,
first month.
An edict ordered Yǎn (兗), Yù (豫), and Xú (徐) three provinces to provide provisions to the famine-stricken people.
The Emperor asked Sītú (司徒) Bào Yù (鮑昱):
"How can the drought disaster be eliminated and restored?"
*Xiāofù* (消復) means
to eliminate anomalies and restore normalcy.
"[Though] Your Majesty has just ascended the throne,
even if there have been successes or failures,
they are not enough to cause such an anomaly.
Your servant previously served as *Tàishǒu* (太守) of Rǔnán (汝南),
presiding over the affairs of Chǔ (楚).
Xián (賢) said: 'In the thirteenth year of Yǒngpíng (永平),
Chǔ Wáng Yīng (楚王英) plotted rebellion,
and those implicated were in Rǔnán (汝南).
Yù (昱) at that time was primarily responsible for their prosecution.'
*Zhì* (治) is pronounced *zhí* (直).
I fear I could not fully assign their guilt.
When a great trial begins,
more than half of those accused are innocent.
Moreover,
the relatives of those exiled are separated,
and their lonely souls are un-worshipped.
It is appropriate to return all exiled families,
abolish their prohibitions and disqualifications,
so that the living and the dead may find their proper place,
and then harmonious *qì* (氣) can be achieved."
The Emperor adopted his suggestion.
The Grand Scribe, Yáng Zhōng 楊終, presented a memorial, saying:
"Recently, campaigning northward against the Xiōngnú 匈奴,
and opening up the Thirty-six States to the west,
the common people have served in forced labor year after year,
and the transportation costs have been burdensome;
the suffering and distressed people are sufficient to move Heaven and Earth.
Your Majesty should pay attention and examine this! "
The Hàn 漢 Lántái 蘭臺
at that time, scholars and literary men
were made to collate and proofread within it,
hence there was the office of Collator,
such as Liú Xiàng 劉向 and Yáng Xióng 揚雄 and their like.
In the Eastern Capital, a Secretary was appointed to the Lántái 蘭臺,
to manage and collate secret documents.
Those officials who held this post
were called Collators.
Zhōng 終 was summoned to the Lántái 蘭臺,
and appointed Collator.
Shěng 省
is pronounced 'xǐ jǐng'.
Dìwǔ Lún 第五倫 also agreed with Zhōng’s 終 proposal.
Móu Róng 牟融 and Bào Yù 鮑昱 both believed:
"A filial son does not alter his father's way,"
citing Kǒngzǐ's 孔子 words from the Analects.
"Stationing troops in the Western Regions
was established by the late emperor,
and should not be changed."
Zhōng 終 again presented a memorial, saying:
"Qín 秦 built the Great Wall,
with numerous labor projects;
Hú Hài 胡亥 did not reform it,
and consequently lost the whole empire."
This event is recorded in the Qín Jì 秦紀.
Fù 復
is pronounced 'fú yòu'.
Zú 卒
is pronounced 'zǐ xù'.
This event is recorded in Volume 28, the second year of Chūyuán 初元 of Yuándì 元帝.
This event is recorded in Volume 43, the twenty-second year of Jiànwǔ 建武 of Guāngwǔ 光武.
Xián 賢 said: Jièlín 介鱗
refers to distant barbarians,
whose people are no different from fish and turtles.
Yīcháng 衣裳
refers to Zhōngguó 中國 (China).
Yáng Xióng’s 揚雄 Fǎyán 法言 says: "The cessation of Zhūyá 珠厓
was due to the effort of abandoning it;
otherwise, the scaled creatures would replace our garments."
The Chūnqiū 春秋 ridiculed this, saying: " 'Our ancestors established it, and then destroyed it;
it would have been better not to have occupied it at all,'
because it caused no harm to the people;
Xiānggōng 襄公 raised three armies,
and Zhāogōng 昭公 disbanded them.
The noble man praised his return to antiquity,
believing that not disbanding them would have harmed the people.
Now the campaign at Yīwú 伊吾,
and the garrisoning of troops at Lóulán 樓蘭 —
Dòu Gù 竇固 and others took Yīwú 伊吾,
see previous volume, Yǒngpíng 永平 sixteenth year.
Lóulán 樓蘭
is Shànshàn 鄯善;
these troops probably refer to the officers and soldiers led by Bān Chāo 班超.
— are not the will of Heaven."
The Emperor accepted this.
2 On the day Bǐngyín 丙寅,
an edict was issued:
"Officials of two thousand shí 石 should diligently encourage agriculture and sericulture;
for crimes not punishable by death,
investigations should await autumn.
Officials concerned with appointments should be clear and careful in their selections,
promoting the gentle and good,
and dismissing the greedy and treacherous,
following the seasonal commands,
and rectifying unjust cases."
At this time, following the precedents of Yǒngpíng 永平,
the administration of officials was still severe and strict,
and the judgments of the Grand Secretariat
often inclined towards severity.
Chén Chǒng 陳寵 of Pèiguó 沛國, a Grand Secretariat official, believing that the Emperor had newly ascended the throne,
and that it was fitting to change the harsh customs of the previous era,
thereupon presented a memorial, saying:
"Your servant has heard that the governance of the former kings
rewarded without excess and
punished without abuse;
if one must err,
it is better to reward excessively than to punish abusively."
This is a saying of Shēngzǐ 聲子, a grandee of Cài 蔡, recorded in the Zuǒzhuàn 左傳.
"This is to deter evil and wickedness;
once evil and wickedness are pacified,
it is certainly appropriate to alleviate with leniency.
Your Majesty, upon ascending the throne,
has generally followed this principle,
repeatedly issuing edicts to all officials,
broadly promoting harmony and gentleness."
Xián 賢 said: Yànyàn 晏晏
means gentle and mild.
The Shàngshū Kǎolíngyào 尚書考靈耀 says: "Yáo 堯 was intelligent, clear-minded, accomplished, profound, and gentle."
Shù 數
is pronounced 'suǒ jiǎo'.
"Yet the harshness remains;
those who judge cases are eager to inflict the pain of flogging and severe torture."
Xián 賢 said: Bàng 篣
is the same as bǎng 榜,
ancient characters were used interchangeably.
The Shēnglèi 聲類 says: "It means to flog."
The Shuōwén 说文 says: Gé 格
means to strike.
"Some even use public office for private gain,
indulging in their power and influence.
Governing is like tuning a qín 秦 and sè 瑟;
if the large strings are too tight, the small strings will break."
Xián 賢 said: The Xīnxù 新序 states: Zāng Sūn 臧孫,
a grandee of Lǔ 魯,
implemented harsh policies.
Zǐgòng 子貢 criticized him, saying: "Indeed, governance is like tuning a qín 秦 and sè 瑟;
if the large strings are too tight, the small strings will break."
"Therefore, it is said: 'If punishments are just, then treachery and evil will cease;
if rewards are just, then the common people will rejoice.'
Abolish troublesome and harsh laws,
lighten flogging and torture to save all lives,
and expand great virtue to conform to the will of Heaven!"
The Emperor deeply accepted Chǒng’s 寵 words,
always striving for leniency and generosity in all matters.
3 Duàn Péng 段彭, Administrator of Jiǔquán 酒泉, and other commanders gathered their forces at Liǔzhōng 柳中,
attacked Chēshī 車師,
and assaulted Jiāohé Chéng 交河城.
Xián 賢 said: The Qiánshū 前書 states,
the former king of Chēshī 車師 resided in Jiāohé Chéng 交河城.
The river divided its waters, flowing around the city,
hence it was called Jiāohé 交河.
It was 8,100 *lǐ* 里 from Cháng'ān 長安.
The old city is in today's Xīzhōu Jiāohé Xiàn 西州交河縣.
They captured over three thousand people.
The Northern Xiōngnú 匈奴 were alarmed and fled,
and Chēshī 車師 surrendered again.
At that time, Guān Chǒng 關寵 had already died,
and Royal Messenger Wáng Méng 王蒙 and others wanted to lead their troops back;
Gěng Gōng’s 耿恭 army officer Fàn Qiāng 范羌,
who was then in the army —
Earlier,
Gōng 恭 had dispatched Qiāng 羌 to Dūnhuáng 敦煌 to receive winter clothing for the soldiers,
and he then accompanied Wáng Méng’s 王蒙 army out of the pass.
The generals dared not advance,
so they allotted two thousand men to Qiāng 羌,
to meet Gōng 恭 from north of the mountains.
They encountered heavy snow over a *zhàng* 丈 (ten feet) deep,
and the army barely managed to reach.
Inside the city, they heard the sounds of soldiers and horses at night,
thinking it was the barbarians coming,
and were greatly alarmed.
Qiāng 羌 called out from afar, saying:
"I am Fàn Qiāng 范羌,
the Hàn 漢 has sent troops to welcome the Commander!"
Everyone in the city cried out "Long live!"
They opened the gates,
and held each other, weeping.
The next day,
they consequently followed him back together.
The barbarian troops pursued them,
fighting and marching,
and the officers and soldiers were already starved and exhausted.
When they set out from Shuōlè 疏勒,
there were still twenty-six people;
many died along the way.
After three months, they reached Yùmén 玉門.
Xián 賢 said: Yùmén 玉門
is a pass name,
belonging to Dūnhuáng Jùn 敦煌郡,
in today's Shāzhōu 沙州.
Your servant Xián 賢 notes: Jiǔquán Jùn 酒泉郡 also has a Yùmén Xiàn 玉門縣.
According to the Dōngguānjì 東觀記,
it says they reached Dūnhuáng 敦煌,
clearly meaning Yùmén Guān 玉門關.
Their clothes and shoes were torn and tattered,
and their faces were emaciated.
Zhèng Zhòng 鄭衆, Colonel of the Guard, had a bath prepared for Gōng 恭 and his men,
and changed their clothes and hats.
Zhòng 衆 had previously, as Army Marshal, attacked Chēshī 車師 with Mǎ Liáo 馬廖,
and upon reaching Dūnhuáng 敦煌,
was appointed Colonel of the Guard.
Wèi 為
is pronounced 'yú wěi'.
"Gōng 恭, with isolated troops, defended an isolated city,
against tens of thousands of Xiōngnú 匈奴,
for months and over a year,
exhausting his mind and strength,
digging wells in the mountains,
and boiling crossbows for food.
He killed and wounded hundreds of thousands of vile barbarians,
and ultimately preserved his loyalty and courage,
not bringing shame upon the Great Hàn 漢.
He ought to receive high honors
to encourage commanders."
When Gōng 恭 arrived in Luòyáng 雒陽,
he was appointed Cavalry Commandant.
An edict was issued to abolish all posts of Colonels Wù and Jǐ (戊己校尉) and Protector-General,
these two offices having been established in the seventeenth year of Yǒngpíng 永píng under Míngdì 明帝.
Chāo was about to leave and return.
The entire kingdom of Shūlè was filled with sorrow and fear.

"The Hàn envoy is abandoning us.
We will surely be annihilated by Qiūcí again.
Truly, I cannot bear to see the Hàn envoy depart."
Thereupon, he used a knife to cut his own throat.
As previously recorded,
among the officials of the kingdom of Shūlè were the Shūlè Hóu,
Jīhú Hóu,
Fǔguó Hóu,
and Dūwèi.
Fù (復)
is pronounced fú yòu.

The kings, marquises, and all below them wept loudly,

"We rely on the Hàn envoy as on our parents.

the kingdom of Wèitóu was located in Wèitóu Gǔ,
8,650 *lǐ* from Cháng'ān,

4. On the *jiǎyín* day,

The emperor replied in writing, saying,
"Recently, officials and commoners submitting memorials have also made such statements.
But my wisdom is shallow and limited,

Receiving your majesty's profound strategy,

Huīrán (恢然)

[It was] upheld and followed.
This matter is found in the previous volume, Míngdì's Yǒngpíng 14th year.
This was considered a peak.
Your ignorant servant believes that the establishment of garden-cities [around tombs]

[If] those below undertake useless projects,

Yúshùn was filial to his parents,

Your servant Cāng truly laments that the pure virtue and beauty of the two emperors are not extended to infinity!"
The emperor then stopped.
From then on, whenever the court had a questionable policy,

eighth month,

In the ninth month,

Fáng (魴)
is pronounced jiān fáng.

9. Gāolín Wēnyúdú Wáng of the Northern Xiōngnú led his followers back to reside in Zhuóxié Shān.

In Yǒngpíng 16th year,
Jì Róng and others campaigned north,

The Southern [Xiōngnú] suffered

1. Spring,
third month,
on the *jiǎchén* day,
the garrison troops at Yīwúlú were withdrawn.

but if an official is punished for corruption,
he is abandoned for life."
'Zāng' (臧)
is the same as 'cáng' (藏) (corruption).
Thereafter, his brother became incorruptible.
Jūn served as a Shàngshū
but was later dismissed and returned home.
The Emperor issued an edict to praise and favor Yì and Jūn,
granting each a thousand *hú* of grain,
and ordering chief officials to inquire about their well-being every August,
additionally bestowing sheep and wine.
Kǎoyì states: Yì's biography says
"during the Jiànchū period,"
but we follow Jūn's biography here.
12. Mèng Yún, the Grand Administrator of Wǔwēi, submitted a memorial, stating:
"The Běi Xiōngnú again wish to trade with our officials and people."
An edict granted permission.
The Běi Xiōngnú Grand Jūqú Yīmòzī Wáng and others
drove over ten thousand cattle and horses to trade with Hàn.
The Nán Chányú dispatched light cavalry from Shàngjùn to plunder them,
returning with a great haul.
13. The Emperor again dispatched Acting Cavalry Commander Hé Gōng and others.
The Xìngpǔ says: The clan Hé originally descended from Xī Hé;
another account says from Biàn Hé.
Chāo then raised troops from Shūlè and Yútián to attack Shāchē.
Shāchē used bribes to entice King Zhōng of Shūlè.
Zhōng then rebelled
and joined them,
retreating west to defend Wūjí Chéng.
Chāo then appointed Chéng Dà, the Administrator of the King's establishment, as the new King of Shūlè.
He mobilized all those who had not rebelled to attack Zhōng.
He also sent someone to persuade the King of Kāngjū to capture Zhōng and return him to his own country.
Chāo had previously installed Zhōng as King of Shūlè;
see the entry for the seventeenth year of Emperor Míng's Yǒngpíng reign in the previous volume.
'Shuō' (說)
is pronounced *shūruì fān*.

4. The Tàichū Calendar had been in use for over a hundred years,

This means that the movements of the seven luminaries

and the new moons, full moons, and quarter moons did not align.
The Sìfēn Calendar was created;

On the day *Jiǎyín*,

*Yuàn* (掾),

9 Autumn,
seventh month,
on the gēng-zǐ day,
an edict stated:
"The Chūnqiū emphasizes the three 'corrects' [zhèng]
and carefully observes the three 'subtleties' [wēi]."
Xián said: "The three 'corrects' [sān zhèng]
refer to the correct alignments of Heaven, Earth, and Man.
The reason for these three [corrects]
is due to the months of the three 'subtleties' [sān wēi],
which rulers ought to observe and perfect.
The Lǐjì says: 'The calendar and first day of the month are changed three times,
and the cultural style, whether plain or refined, is reverted twice.'
The three 'subtleties' are
the beginning of the three 'corrects';
all things are subtle,
and their colors differ,
hence rulers take them as a model.
In the eleventh month,
the yang energy begins to exert its influence beneath the Yellow Springs,
and all colors are red;
red is the color of yang energy,
hence the Zhōu dynasty took Heaven's Correctness,
and revered the color red.
In the twelfth month,
all things begin to sprout and their color is white;
white is the color of yin energy,
hence the Yīn dynasty took Earth's Correctness,
and revered the color white.
In the thirteenth month,
all things emerge from their sheaths,
and their color is black;
people can then apply their efforts and expand their enterprises;
hence the Xià dynasty took Man's Correctness,
and revered the color black.
The Shàngshū Dàzhuàn says: 'The Xià dynasty took the thirteenth month as its 'correct' month,
and dawn as the first day;
the Yīn dynasty took the twelfth month as its 'correct' month,
and cock-crow as the first day;
the Zhōu dynasty took the eleventh month as its 'correct' month,
and midnight as the first day.'
The reason for invariably taking the months of the three 'subtleties' as the 'correct' month
is that at such times,
all things are still subtle.
When a ruler receives the mandate,
they should assist the subtle and govern the weak,
this being the meaning of observation and succession.
It should only refer to the early winter tenth month."

the Southern Chányú sent troops to fight the Northern Lǔ Wēnyúdú Wáng at Zhuóxié Shān,

Mèng Yún, the Administrator of Wǔwēi, submitted a memorial stating:

A decorous and harmonious debate
is the proper conduct,

1. In the spring,
first month,
on the day Bǐngshēn,
the emperor made a northern inspection tour.
On Xīnchǒu,
he plowed in Huái.
In the second month,
on Yǐchǒu,
an edict was issued to the Shìyùshǐ and Sīkōng, stating:
"Wherever the spring tour passes,
no felling or killing is permitted.
If chariots can be diverted,
divert them.
If outrider horses can be unharnessed,
unharness them."
The Shìyùshǐ
was in charge of impeachments,
and the Sīkōng
was in charge of public works.
When the imperial carriage was on a tour,
the Shìyùshǐ was responsible for impeaching those whose conduct on the roads was not in accordance with regulations.
The Sīkōng led artisans and laborers to build roads
and repair bridges.
Therefore, both were issued the edict.
Xián said: The horses harnessed between the shafts are called fúmǎ;
those outside the fúmǎ are called pīmǎ.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: A chariot has one shaft,
and four horses are harnessed to it.
The two central horses that flank the shaft are called fúmǎ,
and the two on the sides are called pīmǎ.
They are also called cānmǎ.
Pī
has the sound "fēi".
On Wùchén,
the emperor proceeded to Zhōngshān,
and exited the Great Wall.
Xián said: According to the Shǐjì,
Méng Tián built the Great Wall for Qín,
extending from Líntáo in the west
to the sea in the east.
I believe this is not the Qín Great Wall,
but probably the Great Wall built by Zhào.
On Guǐyǒu,
he returned
and visited Yuánshì.
In the third month,
on Jǐmǎo,
he proceeded to Zhào.
The state of Zhào
was 1,100 *lǐ* north of Luòyáng.
On Xīnmǎo,
he returned to the palace.
2. The Grand Commandant Zhèng Hóng repeatedly criticized the excessive power of the Palace Attendant Dòu Xiàn in strong and direct terms.
Dòu Xiàn resented this.
Coincidentally, Zhèng Hóng impeached Dòu Xiàn's associates, Shàngshū Zhāng Lín and Luòyáng Magistrate Yáng Guāng, for corruption and cruelty in office.
When the memorial was submitted,
a clerk who was an old acquaintance of Yáng Guāng
secretly informed him,
and Yáng Guāng reported it to Dòu Xiàn.
Dòu Xiàn then impeached Zhèng Hóng, a high official,
for leaking confidential matters.
The emperor interrogated and reproached Zhèng Hóng.
In the summer,
fourth month,
on Bǐngyín,
Zhèng Hóng's seal and ribbon were confiscated.
Zhèng Hóng went to the Court of Judicial Review himself,
but an imperial edict ordered his release.
He then requested to retire and return home due to old age,
but this was not granted.
As his illness worsened,
he submitted a memorial expressing his gratitude and stating:
"Dòu Xiàn's wickedness
reaches heaven and earth;
the people within the seas are perplexed,
and both the wise and the foolish abhor evil,
saying, 'What methods does Dòu Xiàn employ to bewitch the emperor!
The recent calamity of the Wáng clan
is clearly visible.'
This refers to the Wáng clan using their imperial affinity to usurp the throne.
Bǐng
has the sound 'bǐng'.
To protect the throne for myriad generations
yet trust sycophantic and treacherous officials,
without considering the critical juncture of survival or ruin—
though my life hangs by a thread,
I will not forget my loyalty even in death.
I wish Your Majesty would execute the crimes of the Four Villains,
to satisfy the hopes of both humans and spirits who are filled with indignation!"
The emperor reviewed the memorial
and dispatched a physician to examine Zhèng Hóng's illness.
By the time the physician arrived,
he had already passed away.
3. Sòng Yóu, the Grand Minister of Agriculture, was appointed Grand Commandant.
4. Sīkōng Dìwǔ Lún requested to retire due to old age and illness.
To dedicate oneself to serving the ruler
means one's body is no longer one's own.
Therefore, when old, one requests to retire;
this is called "requesting one's body,"
which is synonymous with "requesting one's bones."
On Bǐngzǐ,
he was granted an edict dismissing him
and was allowed to keep the salary of a two-thousand-dan official for the rest of his life.
Dìwǔ Lún upheld public duty and was utterly devoted,
speaking without wavering or hesitation.
"Wavering or hesitation"
refers to opinions that are indecisive, accepting both possibilities.
He had little literary talent,
but was praised for his integrity and purity while in office.
Someone once asked Dìwǔ Lún:
"Do you have any private interests?"
He replied:
"Once, someone offered me a thousand-*lǐ* horse.
Although I did not accept it,
whenever the Three Dukes made selections,
I could not forget it in my heart,
though
I ultimately did not use him.
In such a case,
how can it be said that I have no private interests!"
Yuán Ān, the Grand Coachman, was appointed Sīkōng.
5. In the autumn,
eighth month,
on Yǐchǒu,
the emperor visited Ānyì
and viewed the salt lakes.
Ānyì county
belonged to Hédōng Commandery.
The salt lake was southwest of the county.
Yáng Quánqí's Luòyángjì states:
The Hédōng salt lake is seventy *lǐ* long
and seven *lǐ* wide;
the vapor above its water is purple.
Xǔ Shèn said: The Hédōng salt lake is fifty-one *lǐ* in length,
seven *lǐ* in width,
with a circumference of one hundred sixteen *lǐ*.
Lì Dàoyuán said: The Ānyì salt lake
receives salt water from above.
The water emerges from Báo Shān to the southeast,
flows northwest past the north of Wūxián Shān,
then past the south of the old city of Ānyì,
and then flows westward,
emptying into the salt lake.
The water produces rock salt,
which forms naturally.
What is taken in the morning is replenished by evening,
with no reduction.
Only when there are violent mountain rains,
bringing sweet dew,
and torrents rush forth,
does the salt lake's output decrease.
Therefore, both public and private efforts block the water channels
to prevent overflow.
Thus, it is called "salt water"
and also "blocked water."
West of the lake there is another lake,
called Nǚyán Zé,
twenty-five *lǐ* from east to west,
and twenty *lǐ* from north to south,
located south of the old city of Yīshì.
The local people customarily draw water to soak and split hemp,
then divide and irrigate fields in the plains and wilds.
When the water in the irrigated fields dries up,
the earth naturally forms salt,
which is what is called *xiánsà*,
but it tastes bitter.
Xián said: It is now west of Yúxiāng County, Púzhōu.
He returned to the palace.
6. The Qiāng of Shāodāng, Míwú, rebelled again with his brother Hàowú and other tribes.
Hàowú first made a shallow incursion
and raided the border of Lǒngxī.
The Director of Beacon Affairs, Lǐ Zhāng, pursued him.
The Director of Beacon Affairs
was a commandery clerk in charge of beacons.
He was taking Hàowú to the commandery.
Hàowú said:
"Killing me alone
will not harm the Qiāng.
If I can truly return alive,
I will certainly disband all troops
and not violate the frontier again."
The Administrator of Lǒngxī, Zhāng Yú, released him,
and the Qiāng immediately dispersed,
each returning to their original territory.
Míwú retreated to Guīyìchéng north of the Yellow River.
"North of the Yellow River"
refers to the north of the Fēngliú Great River.
Guīyìchéng
was originally built by Hàn
to attract and settle the Qiāng who submitted.
7 The King of Shūlè, Zhōng, borrowed troops from the King of Kāngjū,
and re-occupied Sǔnzhōng.
Zhōng's rebellion is mentioned in the first year of the previous volume.
Xián says: Sǔnzhōng,
is not fully understood;
the Dōngguān Jì writes
"Dùnzhōng,"
while the Xù Hànshū and Huá Jiào Shū both write
"Sǔnzhōng."
The original sometimes writes
"Zhēn,"
and it is unknown which is correct.
I note that in the Xīyù Zhuàn,
in the third year of Jiànníng of Emperor Líng,
the Inspector of Liángzhōu, Méng Tuó,
dispatched troops to attack Shūlè,
and attacked the city of Zhēnzhōng.
"Zhēnzhōng"
is correct.
Chāo knew of their deception but feigned agreement.
Zhōng went to Chāo with light cavalry.
Chāo beheaded him,
and then attacked and routed his forces.
The southern route was thus opened.
8 Empress Dowager Xǔ of Chǔ passed away.
When Yīng, King of Chǔ, was relocated,
Empress Dowager Xǔ remained in the Chǔ palace.
She was posthumously ennobled with the title of Chǔ Lìhóu.
The Shìfǎ states: "Lì" signifies killing the innocent.
9 The Emperor appointed Guō Gōng of Yǐngchuān as Grand Judge (Tíngwèi).
In deciding cases and sentencing,
he often leaned towards leniency and clemency.
He listed forty-one severe cases that could be treated lightly,
presented them to the throne,
and all were implemented.
10 Dr. Cáo Bāo of Lǔguó submitted a memorial,
believing that
"it is appropriate to establish the ritual system [wénzhì]
and complete the Hàn rites."
Grand Minister of Ceremonies (Tàicháng) Cháo Kān
(Cháo is a surname,
descended from the Yǒucháoshì.
In the Chunqiu, there was Cháo Niúchén.)
said: "A great canon for a whole generation
cannot be established by Bāo alone,"
meaning Bāo alone is not capable of establishing it.
The Emperor knew that the various scholars were constrained
and difficult to consult for a new beginning.
Xián says: Jūluán means constrained or restricted.
It was proper to establish it in due course,
so he appointed Bāo as Imperial Household Grandee (Shìzhōng).
Xuánwǔ Sīmǎ Bān Gù believed that

2 Dòu Xiàn was about to campaign against the Xiongnú.

Sòng Yóu became fearful

Everyone was anxious and fearful for them,
but Ān and Kuí maintained their serious demeanor as usual.
The Imperial Censor Lǔ Gōng submitted a memorial, saying:
“The state has recently suffered a great sorrow, and Your Majesty is still in mourning.

and for three seasons, the sounds of imperial processions have not been heard.

The emperor’s outings were announced with a ‘jǐng’ (警), and his entries with a ‘bì’ (蹕).

means warning or alert;
‘bì’ means

Now, those accompanying the imperial carriage on its exit

Emperor Hé ascended the throne in the second month of the second year of Zhānghé.
In the spring of the following year, the discussion arose to attack the Xiongnú.
The Emperor was in mourning and did not go out,
hence for three seasons, the sounds of imperial processions were not heard.
It is as if they seek something but cannot find it.

Yán Dīng was good at observing mourning rites;

he was flustered as if seeking something but unable to find it.

To disturb the whole world to deal with the barbarians

or to reform the era and rectify the times,
from the interior to the exterior.
The myriad people
are begotten by Heaven;

just as parents love their children.
If even a single creature does not find its proper place,
then the qi of Heaven will be in disharmony,

Therefore, those who love the people will surely receive heavenly recompense.

they are the disparate qi of the four directions,

was merely to keep them loosely bound but not cut off.
The ‘Zìshū’ says: ‘Jī’ (羈)
is a horse’s halter.

They are hidden far away, west of the Shǐhóu River,

Now, the conscription has just begun,

To look up at Heaven’s heart
and look down at human will
is sufficient to know the success or failure of an undertaking.
I fear that Zhōngguó will cease to be Zhōngguó;
how can it merely be about the Xiongnú!”
The Director of the Imperial Secretariat Hán Líng, the Commandant of Cavalry Zhū Huī, and the Remonstrance Official Jīngzhào Yuè Huī

The Imperial Censor Hé Chǎng submitted a memorial, saying:

is mentioned in Volume 11, Gao Dì Year 7.

‘hǎo’ (好)

The memorial was submitted

Dòu Xiàn once sent a student with a letter to the Secretary and Grandee Remonstrant, Zhì Shòu,

Hé Chǎng submitted a memorial, saying:

It is why I, at the risk of death, speak without seeing clearly.
The Analects say: ‘To serve a gentleman has three faults;
to speak without seeing his expression is called blindness.’
A loyal minister exhausts his loyalty

Though I do not know Shòu,

I truly do not wish for the sagely court to carry out a slanderous execution

Zhèng Xuán’s commentary on the Shàngshū Kǎolíngyào says: ‘Broad tolerance and covering all creation is called peaceful and harmonious.’

The memorial was presented,

supporting the Southern Chányú costs over 109 million in expenses annually,
and the Western Regions cost 74.8 million annually.
Now, the northern court is even more distant,
and its expenses would be more than double.
This would exhaust the empire's resources and is not a crucial policy."
The emperor ordered his proposal to be debated.
Ān again debated and refuted Xiàn.
Xiàn was aggressive and relied on his power,
his words were arrogant and slanderous,
even defaming Ān,
citing the precedent of Emperor Guāngwǔ executing Hán Xīn and Dài Shè.
Hán Xīn's death is found in volume forty-three, in the fifteenth year of Jiànwǔ.
Dài Shè's death is found in the same volume, in the twentieth year.
However, the emperor ultimately followed Xiàn's plan.
The "Kǎoyì" says: "The biography of Yuán Ān states:
'Xiàn requested to enthrone the Left Lùlí King Ātōng as the Northern Chányú.
Ān thought it was not permissible,
but Xiàn eventually enthroned the Right Gǔlí King Yúchújiàn.'
According to this,
Ātōng and Yúchújiàn are two different people.
The 'Yuán Jì' writes
'Āxiū,'
and the 'Biography of the Southern Xiōngnú' only mentions the Right Gǔlí King Yúchújiàn,
without the name Ātōng.
We follow this.
The 'Yuán Jì' also says:
'Sòng Yóu, Dīng Hóng, and Yǐn Mù believed that Āxiū was the son of a regicide,
and also an enemy to the Wūhuán and Xiānbēi, who were kin to his father and brother,
and thus should not be enthroned.
The Southern Chányú was established by the former emperor,
and now he has initiated the defeat of the Northern barbarians,
achieving great merit.
He should be ordered to take command of the surrendered populace.'
This differs from Fàn Shū.
It also says
'ultimately followed Ān's proposal,'
which is probably an error.
We now follow the 'Biography of Yuán Ān.'"

Later Study Terrace
Emperor Xiàohé, part 2
Fourth Year of Yǒngyuán
(Rénchén, 92 CE)
1 In spring,
in the first month,

following the precedent of the Southern Chányú.
In the beginning,
Zhōu Róng of Lújiāng was appointed to Yuán Ān's mansion.
Ān impeached Dòu Jǐng.
The matter is found in the first year of the previous volume.
See the previous year in the upper volume.
Xú Yǐ, the Taìwèi's Aide and a client of the Dòu clan, deeply detested this,
and threatened Róng, saying:
"You, as Yuán Gōng's confidant,

Róng replied:
"I, Róng,

This is truly what I desire!"
He then instructed his wife and children:
Chì (敕)
means to warn.
"If you should suddenly encounter an unforeseen disaster,

2 In the third month,
on the Guǐchǒu day,
Sītú Yuán Ān passed away.

5 In the sixth month,

Dīng Hóng (丁鴻) submitted a memorial, saying:
“In the past, the Zhū Lǚ (諸呂) seized power,

Jī (幾) [meaning 'almost'],
pronounced Jū Xī.
The ancestral temples were left without blood sacrifices.
This event is recorded in the Wáng Mǎng Jì (王莽紀);
Hóng (鴻) cites this event to allude to the hidden danger.
They could not wield their power.
Xián (賢) says: This means that if the emperor esteems the worthy and values the venerable,
he can then govern.
They dared not overstep their bounds;
however, people near and far throughout the empire
were all terrified and obeyed their will.
When Cìshǐ (刺史) and Èrqiānshí (二千石) were first appointed,
they had to announce their arrival and seek an audience, awaiting a reply.
To announce their arrival when first appointed,
and to take leave when going to their posts.
“Seeking an audience” means
seeking to present their names;
“awaiting a reply” means
whether they were granted or denied an audience,

They received edicts from the Imperial Secretariat.
The seals were used as credentials.
Those newly appointed went to the Shàngshū Tái (尚書臺) to receive edicts.
Xǐ (璽) [meaning 'seal'],
pronounced Sī Shì.
For a long time, sometimes up to several tens of days,
they turned their backs on the imperial court
and faced the private gate,
this indicates that the imperial authority is diminished,
and the power of those below is ascendant.
When human ways are perverse below,
the verification appears in the heavens.
Even if there are hidden schemes,
the spirits illuminate their true nature,
manifesting omens as a warning,
to inform the ruler.
To prohibit what is subtle is easy;
to remedy what is advanced is difficult.
No one fails to overlook what is subtle and minor, thereby allowing it to become great.
Benevolence cannot bear to instruct,
righteousness cannot bear to sever.
After the event has passed,
it serves as a clear mirror of what was to come.
This means that disaster lies hidden in subtle ways,
which people often overlook,
but once it is revealed,
it is clear and undeniable,
thus serving as a clear mirror of what was to come.
If he is not firm, the three luminaries will not be bright;
the King cannot be weak,
if he is weak, the chief ministers will act recklessly.
It is fitting, in light of this great anomaly,
to reform governance and correct errors,
to appease the will of Heaven!”
6 On the Bǐngchén day,

7 There was a drought,
and locusts.
8 The Dòu (竇) clan, father, son, and brothers, were all Qīng (卿) and Jiào (校).
Qīng (卿) refers to the Jiǔ Qīng (九卿);
Jiào (校) refers to
the various Xiàowèi (校尉).
Jiào (校) [meaning 'officer'],
pronounced Hù Jiào.

Dèng Tù (鄧拓), the Ráng Hóu (穰侯), and Dèng Lěi (鄧磊), his younger brother and Bùbīng Xiàowèi (步兵校尉), as well as Yuán (元), their mother, and Guō Jǔ (郭舉), the husband of Xiàn's (憲) daughter and Shèshēng Xiàowèi (射聲校尉), and Guō Huáng (郭璜), Jǔ's (舉) father and Chánglè Shàofǔ (長樂少府), conspired together.
Xián (賢) says: The Empress Dowager resided in Chánglè Gōng (長樂宮),
hence there was a Shàofǔ (少府),
whose salary was Èrqiānshí (二千石).
Lè (樂) [in Chánglè],
pronounced Luò.
Jǔ (舉) gained the Empress Dowager's favor,

a conspiracy of regicide.
At this time,
Xiàn's (憲) brothers monopolized power,
and the Emperor had no means of direct contact with internal and external officials and ministers;
those he resided with were only eunuchs.
Yānhuàn (閹宦) [meaning 'eunuch'],
in the Zhōu Lǐ (周禮) it is called Yǎn (奄).
Zhèng Xuán (鄭玄) noted: Yǎn (奄)
are those whose essence is hidden and concealed;
today they are called Huànrén (宦人).
Yān (閹) [meaning 'eunuch'],
pronounced Yī Lián,
also Yī Jiǎn.
Only Zhèng Zhòng (鄭衆), the Zhōngchángshì Gōudùn Lìng (中常侍鉤盾令),
was cautious, diligent, and perceptive.
Bǎiguān Zhì (百官志) says: Gōudùn Lìng (鉤盾令),
salary six hundred shí (石),
eunuchs held this position,
in charge of nearby pools, gardens, parks, and places of recreation,
subordinate to the Shàofǔ (少府).
Jī (幾) [meaning 'perceptive'],
refers to matters;
xīnjī (心幾) [meaning 'perceptive'],

today people who are said to have 'something on their mind' are said to be perceptive.
Zhāo (朝) [meaning 'court'],
pronounced Zhí Yáo.
Dùn (盾) [in Gōudùn],
pronounced Shí Yǐn.
Jī (幾) [meaning 'perceptive'],
pronounced Jū Xī.
So he and Zhòng (衆) decided to execute Xiàn (憲),
since Xiàn (憲) was outside [the capital],

They held back and did not act;
then Xiàn (憲) and Dèng Tù (鄧拓) both returned to the capital.
At this time, Qīnghé Wáng Qìng (清河王慶)
was exceptionally favored.
Wò (渥) [meaning 'exceptionally'],
means thick and moist.
Shěng (省) [meaning 'court'],
means within the forbidden palace.
He wanted to obtain the Wàiqī Zhuàn (外戚傳),
Xián (賢) says: The Former Han History's "Biographies of Imperial Relatives."
Zhuàn (傳) [meaning 'biography'],
pronounced Zhí Liàn.
He dared not make the request himself,
but ordered Qìng (慶) to privately ask the Qiānchéng Wáng (千乘王).
Qiānchéng Wáng Kàng (千乘王伉)
was the Emperor's eldest brother.
Chéng (乘) [in Qiānchéng],
pronounced Shéng Zhèng.
He was the only one allowed inside.
He also ordered Qìng (慶) to relay a message to Zhèng Zhòng (鄭衆),
asking for old precedents.
Xián (賢) says: This refers to the precedents of Wén Dì (文帝) executing Bó Zhāo (薄昭)
and Wǔ Dì (武帝) executing Dòu Yīng (竇嬰).
Suǒ (索) [meaning 'ask for'],
pronounced Shān Kè.
On the Gēngshēn day,
the Emperor went to the Běi Gōng (北宮).
He issued an edict to the Zhí Jīnwú (執金吾) and the Wǔ Jiàowèi (五校尉) to mobilize troops to garrison and guard the Nán (南) and Běi Gōng (北宮).
The Zhí Jīnwú (執金吾) was in charge of outer palace security and extraordinary situations,
the Wǔ Jiàowèi (五校尉) of the Northern Army commanded the soldiers of the five camps,
therefore he ordered them to mobilize troops to garrison and guard.
Guō Huáng (郭璜), Guō Jǔ (郭舉), Dèng Tù (鄧拓), and Dèng Lěi (鄧磊) were arrested
and all died in prison.
He sent the Yèzhě Púshè (謁者僕射) to seize Xiàn's (憲) Dà Jiàngjūn (大將軍) seal and sash,
and re-enfeoffed him as Guànjūn Hóu (冠軍侯).
Xiàn (憲) had previously been enfeoffed as Guànjūn Hóu (冠軍侯),
but had not accepted it;
now he was re-enfeoffed,
with the instruction to proceed to his fiefdom.
Gèng (更) [meaning 're-'],
pronounced Jū Mèng.
Huái (懷) [referring to the Emperor's intention].
The Emperor, on account of the Empress Dowager,
did not wish to explicitly execute Xiàn (憲),
meaning he did not wish to execute him by name.
When Xiàn (憲), Dǔ (篤), and Jǐng (景) arrived at their fiefdoms,
they were all compelled to commit suicide.
At first,
Zhāng Pú,
the Yǐn of Hénán, frequently used proper law to discipline and govern Dòu Jǐng.
When the Dòu clan failed,
Pú submitted a memorial, saying:
“When Fāng Xiàn and others were honored and favored,
all ministers flattered and attached themselves, fearing they would fall short.
They all said that Xiàn received the trust of the dying command [from the emperor],
and harbored the loyalty of Yī and Lǚ.
They even compared Dèng Fūrén to Wénmǔ.
Xián says: Dèng Fūrén
is the mother of Ráng Hóu, Dèng Yuán.
Zhāng Pú's discussion of Xiàn also includes his faction,
calling Dèng Fūrén
is like in the former book where Huò Guāng’s wife is called Huò Xiǎn,
or Qí Dàbómǔ is called Qí Fūrén, and similar cases.
Fù,
pronounced fú yòu.
They all said they deserved death,
not
considering their past and present,
or examining their true intentions.
I humbly observe that Xiàyáng Hóu Liú Huái consistently maintained loyalty and goodness.
Previously, when speaking with me,
he always expressed a desire to serve with utmost devotion,
and restrained his guests,
never violating the law.
I have heard that in royal governance, for punishments concerning kin,
there is the principle of three pardons.
The Lǐjì says: When a member of the ducal clan commits a crime,
and the case is concluded,
the officer in charge reports to the duke, saying:
‘So-and-so’s crime warrants a major execution.’
The duke says:
‘Pardon him.’
The officer again says:
‘It warrants a major execution.’
The duke again says:
‘Pardon him.’
The officer again says:
‘It warrants an execution.’
The duke again says:
‘Pardon him.’
When the three pardons are not responded to,
he (the officer) rushes out,
and carries out the punishment through the executioner.
The duke then sends someone to pursue him, saying:
‘He must be pardoned.’
The officer replies:
‘It is too late.’
Returning to report to the duke,
the duke wears plain clothes,
as if mourning for someone of his own rank.
Now, the deliberators wish to select a strict and capable chancellor for Liú Huái.
I fear that if he is pressed too hard,
he will certainly not escape unharmed.
It is advisable to grant a degree of leniency and pardon,
to uphold profound virtue.”
The emperor was moved by his words,
and because of this, Liú Huái alone was spared.
All members of the Dòu clan, guests, and those who held office because of Xiàn,
were dismissed and returned to their native commanderies.
At first,
Bān Gù’s servant, while drunk, once insulted Zhǒng Jīng,
the Magistrate of Luòyáng.
Xìng Pǔ says: Zhǒng was originally Zhòng Shì,
changed to avoid calamity.
Gù was arrested and
died in prison.
Gù had been writing the Hànshū,
but it was not yet finished. An imperial edict commanded Gù’s younger sister Zhāo,
wife of Cáo Shòu, to complete it.
Zhāo is Cáo Dàjiā.
Huà Qiáo’s commentary says: Gù’s narration of events
is neither excessively flamboyant
nor suppressed and resistant.
Xián says: Jī,
to extol.
Guǐ,
to disparage.
Yì,
to withdraw.
Kàng,
to advance.
I believe jīguǐ yìkàng
all refer to the flaw of a historian intentionally crafting the text.
Huà,
pronounced hù huà.
It is detailed yet structured,
making those who interpret it tireless and unwearied.
Indeed, he was able to achieve renown!
Gù criticized Sīmǎ Qiān, saying his judgments of right and wrong greatly deviated from the sages.
Xián says: Referring to Qiān’s judgments of right and wrong being at odds with the sages,
meaning revering Huáng-Lǎo and disdaining the Six Classics,
slighting benevolence and righteousness and disparaging those who uphold integrity.
He often disparaged those who died for their principles,
referring to cases like Gōng Shèng said to have died of old age.
Referring to cases like Wáng Líng and Jí Àn’s foolishness.
Referring to not establishing biographies for the loyal and righteous.
He indeed greatly disparaged those who upheld integrity!
9 At first,
when Dòu Xiàn took a wife,
all commanderies and kingdoms under heaven sent congratulatory gifts.
Hánzhōng Jùn was also supposed to send an official.
Hánzhōng Jùn is located one thousand nine hundred ninety lǐ west of Luòyáng.
The commandery had a household office,
which managed households, sacrifices, agriculture, and sericulture.
Hé,
pronounced gē gé.
“General Dòu is a relative of the imperial family,
but he does not cultivate virtue and propriety, instead monopolizing power and acting arrogantly and wantonly.
The calamity of ruin and destruction
can be awaited by standing on tiptoe;
Qiáo,
to lift.
Do not associate with him.”
The grand administrator still sent the official,
but Hé could not stop him.
He requested to go himself,
and was granted permission.
Hé then intentionally delayed his journey wherever he went to observe the changing situation.
When he reached Fúfēng,
Pān Yuè’s Guānzhōng Jì says: The Three Fǔ originally governed from inside Cháng'ān city,
with senior officials each residing in their county to govern the people.
After the Eastern Capital,
Fúfēng moved its administration to Huáilǐ,
and Féngyì moved its administration to Gāolíng.
All those who had associated with Dòu Xiàn were dismissed from office,
but the Grand Administrator of Hánzhōng alone was not included.
The emperor bestowed upon Qīnghé Wáng Qìng
slaves, carriages, horses, money, silk, and precious treasures,
filling his residence to overflowing.
When Qìng was occasionally unwell,
the emperor inquired about him morning and evening,
and provided food and medicine,
showing extreme attentiveness.
Qìng also was cautious, respectful, and filial.
Considering himself deposed,
he was especially fearful of matters and careful of laws,
thus he was able to preserve his favor and emolument.
10 The emperor appointed Yuán Ān’s son Shǎng as a Láng,
and Rén Kuí’s son Tún as Bùbīng Xiàowèi,
because Ān and Kuí upheld integrity and did not align with the Dòu clan.
Rén,
pronounced rén.
Kuí,
pronounced wǔ zuì.

with a salary of two thousand dàn of grain,

and to follow the empress when she went out.
Zhāng Yàn says: The empress’s minister.
Shī Gǔ says: Qiū means
the time of harvest,
Cháng means
lasting and enduring,
hence it was used as the empress’s official title.
Zhòng often declined much and accepted little.

The use of power by eunuchs began from this time.
11 Autumn,
seventh month,
on the day Jǐchǒu,

12 Eighth month,
on the day Xīnhài,

tenth month,

15 The Mán of Wǔlíng, Línglíng, and Lǐzhōng rebelled.
16. Hùqiāng Xiàowèi Dèng Xùn 鄧訓 died.
Officials, common people, Qiāng 羌, and Hú 胡 came to mourn day and night, numbering several thousand daily.
Some Qiāng 羌 and Hú 胡 even cut themselves with knives,
and stabbed their dogs, horses, cattle, and sheep to death,
saying:
"Lord Dèng Shǐjūn 鄧使君 is dead;
we too shall all die!"
Former Wūhuán 烏桓 officials and soldiers all fled along the roads.
Xián 賢 said: These were the officials and soldiers during Dèng Xùn's 鄧訓 previous tenure as Wūhuán Xiàowèi 烏桓校尉.
The officials seized them,
but they did not comply.
The matter was reported to Xiàowèi Xú Yǎn 徐傿.
Xú Yǎn 徐傿 sighed and said:
"This is an act of righteousness!"
So he released them.
Thereupon, every family erected a shrine for Dèng Xùn 鄧訓,
and whenever there was illness,
they would pray for blessings.
Shǔjùn Tàishǒu Niè Shàng 聶尚 replaced Dèng Xùn 鄧訓 as Hùqiāng Xiàowèi 護羌校尉.
Desiring to win over the various Qiāng 羌 with kindness,
he sent interpreters to summon Mítáng 迷唐,
instructing him to return to reside in Dà Yúgǔ 大榆谷 and Xiǎo Yúgǔ 小榆谷.
Mítáng's 迷唐 departure from Dà Yúgǔ 大榆谷 and Xiǎo Yúgǔ 小榆谷
is mentioned in the previous volume, Zhānghé 章和 second year.

but Niè Shàng 聶尚 summoned him,
intending to reverse Dèng Xùn's 鄧訓 policies.
Niè 聶,
(missing character)
(missing character)
shǐ 使,
rhymes with shū lì.

1. Spring,
first month,

"Zhēn 貞" means maintaining purity and integrity;

fourth month,
on the Rénzǐ 壬子 day,

after Dòu Xiàn 竇憲 had established Yúchújiàn 於除鞬 as the Northern Chányú 北單于,
