9. When Gěng Kuí 耿夔 defeated the Northern Xiōngnú 北匈奴,
this matter is mentioned in the previous volume, third year.
The Tuòbá 拓拔 clan migrated south from the northern wilderness,
probably at this time.
They all proclaimed themselves Xiānbēi 鮮卑;
the Xiānbēi 鮮卑 thus gradually grew powerful.
10. Winter,
tenth month,
on the Xīnwèi 辛未 day,
Tàiwèi Yǐn Mù 尹睦 died.
11. Eleventh month,
on the Yǐchǒu 乙丑 day,
Tàipú Zhāng Pú 張酺 became Tàiwèi 太尉.
Zhāng Pú 張酺, along with Shàngshū Zhāng Mǐn 尚書張敏 and others, memorialized:
"Shèshēng Xiàowèi Cáo Bāo 射聲校尉曹褒,
in composing the Hàn 漢 rites,
has disrupted the sagely methods,
and should be punished with execution."
They submitted five memorials in total.
The Emperor knew that Zhāng Pú 張酺 adhered to his family's learning but was not well-versed.
This refers to adhering to his family's specific scholarly tradition.
And so, the Hàn 漢 rites were not implemented.
Cáo Bāo's 曹褒 work on rites
is mentioned in the previous volume, Zhāngdì 章帝 Zhānghé 章和 first year.
12. In this year,
the Wǔlíng Jùn 武陵郡 troops defeated the rebellious Mán 蠻,
who then surrendered.
13 Liáng Wáng Chàng (梁王暢) and his retinue member Biàn Jì (卞忌) offered sacrifices to pray for blessings.
The Xìngpǔ (姓譜) states: The Biàn (卞) clan originated from Zhōu Cáo Shú Zhènduó (周曹叔振鐸).
A collateral descendant of Cáo (曹) was enfeoffed at Xià (下),
and subsequently established the clan there.
I note that Lǔ (魯) had Biàn Zhuāngzǐ (卞莊子),
and Chǔ (楚) had Biàn Hé (卞和).
"The spirit said that the king would become the Son of Heaven."
Chàng (暢) engaged in a corresponding dialogue,
and was impeached by the judicial officials,
who requested his summons to the imperial prison.
The Emperor did not permit it,
but merely curtailed two counties, Chéngwǔ (成武) and Shànfù (單父).
Chéngwǔ (成武) and Shànfù (單父) counties
originally belonged to Shānyáng (山陽),
later to Jìyīn (濟陰).
Emperor Zhāng (章帝) added them to the Liáng (梁) kingdom.
Xián (賢) said: Chéngwǔ (成武)
is now a county in Cáozhōu (曹州);
Shànfù (單父)
is now a county in Sòngzhōu (宋州).
Shàn (單)
is pronounced "shàn".
He submitted a memorial deeply reproaching himself, saying:
"Your subject is by nature wild and foolish,
unaware of prohibitions,
and has implicated himself in a capital crime,
deservedly facing public execution.
Your Majesty's sagely virtue
has bent the law to render a fair judgment."
Xián (賢) said: Qūpíng (曲平) means
bending the law to extend grace,
and fairly dealing with the crime.
"You have suffered defilement for your subject."
Héng (橫)
is pronounced "hú mèng fān".
Wū (汙)
means 'evil'.
The world would consider pardoning Chàng (暢) as accepting defilement,
meaning accepting defilement for Chàng (暢).
Wéi (為)
is pronounced "yú wěi fān".
"I swear to restrain myself and my family,
not daring to again deviate from the rules in my comings and goings,
not daring to again incur any extravagant expenses.
My rental income has a surplus;
I beg to be allowed to retain the five counties of Suīyáng (睢陽), Gǔshú (穀熟), Yú (虞), Méng (蒙), and Nínglíng (寧陵) for sustenance,
and return the remaining four counties that I currently hold.
The four counties are Xiàyì (下邑), Wèishì (尉氏), Bó (薄), and Yǎn (郾).
Suī (睢)
is pronounced "suī".
All those who are not legitimate wives
are concubines.
I wish to return them to their original families.
I will personally select two hundred prudent and disciplined male and female servants.
The remaining Hubēn (虎賁) guards, official cavalry, and various artisans, musicians, head-shorn servants, and slaves
I received,
as well as weapons and warhorses,
shall all be returned to their original departments."
Hubēn (虎賁) guards
belonged to the Hubēn Zhōnglángjiàng (虎賁中郎將).
Guānjì (官騎) were Zōují (騶騎).
The Hàn Guānyí (漢官儀) states: Zōují (騶騎),
called Guānjì (官騎) in royal households,
along with warhorses,
all belonged to the Tàipú (太僕).
Gōngjì (工技) belonged to the Shàngfāng (尚方).
Gǔchuī (鼓吹) belonged to the Huángmén (黃門).
Cāngtóu (倉頭) and male/female servants
belonged to the Yǒngxiàng (永巷), Yùfǔ (御府), Xīguān (奚官) and other officials.
Bīngnǔ (兵弩)
belonged to the Kǎogōnglìng (考工令).
Each had its original department.
Bēn (賁)
is pronounced "bēn".
Jì (技)
is pronounced "qú qǐ fān".
Chuī (吹)
is pronounced "chāng ruì fān".
Shàng (上)
is pronounced "shí zhǎng fān".
"I have disturbed the sagely transformation
and defiled the clear stream.
Now that I have been allowed to live,
I truly have no face to again reside in the grand palace
with my wickedness,
consume a large kingdom's resources,
command officials,
or hoard miscellaneous goods."
Xián (賢) said: In ancient times, when an army marched,
ten men formed a 'shí' (什),
and their tableware and similar items were shared,
hence they were called 'shíwù' (什物) or 'shíjù' (食具).
Today, people generally refer to tools for livelihood as 'shíwù' (什物).
Fù (復)
is pronounced "fú yòu fān".
The Emperor issued a gracious edict, not consenting.
14 Hùqiāng Xiàowèi (護羌校尉) Guàn Yǒu (貫友)
Guàn (貫)
is a surname. In early Hàn (漢), there was Zhào Xiàng Guàn Gāo (趙相貫高).
He lured them with wealth,
and thus they dispersed.
Then he dispatched troops out of the frontier,
attacked Mítáng (迷唐) in Dà-Xiǎoyúgǔ (大、小榆谷),
captured over eight hundred heads and prisoners,
collected tens of thousands of hu (斛) of wheat,
and then built walled forts on both sides of the Féngliú Dàhé (逢留大河).
This Dàhé (大河) is the Yellow River.
The river here is known as Féngliú (逢留),
north of the two Yúgǔ (榆谷).
He built a river bridge,
intending to cross troops to attack Mítáng (迷唐).
Lì Dàoyuán's Shuǐjīngzhù (酈道元水經註) says: A bridge was built where the river was narrow.
Háng (航)
is pronounced "hù gāng fān".
He relied on the Cìzhī Héqǔ (賜支河曲).
The Xīqiāngzhuàn (西羌傳) says: Cìzhī (賜支) is what the Yǔgòng (禹貢) calls Xīzhī (析支).
The Qiāng (羌) lived southwest of Hégūan (河關),
bordering Cìzhī (賜支),
extending to the source of the river,
a land of a thousand lì (里).
Sīmǎ Biāo (司馬彪) said: The Xīqiāng (西羌) from Xīzhī (析支) westward bordered the source of the river,
dwelling on the right bank.
The river bends and flows northeastward,
passing through the land of Xīzhī (析支),
which is the Héqu (河曲).
Yīng Shào (應劭) said: The Yǔgòng's Xīzhī (析支) belonged to Yōngzhōu (雍州),
west of Hégūan (河關),
over a thousand lì (里) east of Hégūan (河關),
the dwelling place of the Qiāng (羌) people,
called the Héqu Qiāng (河曲羌).
15 Chányú Túntúhé (單于屯屠何) died,
and Chányú Xuān's (單于宣) younger brother Ānguó (安國) ascended the throne.
Ānguó (安國) was initially the Zuǒxiánwáng (左賢王),
with no commendations.
When he became Chányú (單于),
Chányú Shì (單于適)'s son, the Yòugǔlìwáng (右谷蠡王) Shīzǐ (師子), was in turn appointed Zuǒxiánwáng (左賢王).
Shīzǐ (師子) was always brave, cunning, and resourceful.
Both Chányú Xuān (單于宣) and Túntúhé (屯屠何) loved his decisive spirit,
frequently sending him to lead troops out of the frontier
to surprise attack Běitíng (北庭).
Upon his return,
he received rewards and gifts,
and the Son of Heaven also bestowed special honors upon him.
Because of this, everyone in the state respected Shīzǐ (師子) and did not adhere to Ānguó (安國).
Ānguó (安國) wanted to kill him.
The newly surrendered Hú (胡) people
had previously been plundered by Shīzǐ (師子) outside the frontier.
"Outside the frontier"
refers to the time when they belonged to the northern tribes.
Jiàng (降)
is pronounced "hù gāng fān".
Ānguó (安國)
entrusted his plans to the surrendered ones
and conspired with them.
Shīzǐ (師子), aware of their plot,
moved to reside separately in the Wǔyuán (五原) border.
Whenever the Lóngtíng (龍庭) held a meeting,
the Xiongnu's Lóngtíng (龍庭)
was originally outside the frontier.
At this time, the Southern Chányú (單于) resided within the frontier,
and his dwelling was also called Lóngtíng (龍庭).
Dùliáo Jiāngjūn (度遼將軍) Huángfǔ Léng (皇甫稜) knew about this
and protected Shīzǐ (師子), not sending him away.
The Chányú's (單于) resentment grew even stronger.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
Huángfǔ Léng was dismissed.
Zhū Huī, the Grand Master of the Gilded Effulgence (zhí jīn wú), was appointed acting General Overseeing the Liao (dù liáo jiāng jūn).
At this time, the Chányú was not on good terms with the Colonel (zhōng láng jiàng) Dù Chóng,
and so he submitted a memorial accusing Chóng.
Chóng secretly instructed the Administrator (tài shǒu) of Xīhé to cut off the Chányú's memorial.
The Colonel
was the Colonel-Protector of the Southern Xiongnú (shǐ xiōng nú zhōng láng jiàng).
Duàn
means "to cut off."
The Chányú resided in Měijì, Xīhé Commandery,
hence the instruction to the Administrator to cut off his memorial,
preventing it from reaching the emperor.
Chóng then, with Zhū Huī, memorialized:
“The Southern Chányú Ānguó,
estranged from the old Hú,
and close to the newly surrendered,
intends to kill the Left Worthy King (zuǒ xián wáng) Shīzǐ and the Left Grand Chéqú (zuǒ tái qiě qú) Liú Lì and others.
Furthermore,
the surrendered from the Right Division
are conspiring to coerce Ānguó into raising troops and rebelling.
We request that Xīhé, Shàngjùn, and Āndìng be put on alert for this.”
The Emperor sent the matter down to the Grandees (gōng qīng) for deliberation.
They all opined:
“Although the fickle nature of the 'barbarians' (mányí)
is difficult to predict,
a large military assembly
will surely not dare to move yet.
Now, an envoy with strategy and foresight should be sent to the Chányú's court.
Zhī
means 'to go.'
Shǐ
is pronounced shū lì fān.
Observe his movements.
If there are no other changes,
Chóng and others can be ordered to meet with Ānguó and his chief ministers,
to hold them accountable for their subordinates' violent acts harming the border regions,
and jointly execute those found guilty.
They should jointly determine their crimes
and execute those who deserve execution.
Héng
is pronounced hù mèng fān.
This should be a temporary expedient.
After the matter is concluded,
rewards and gifts should be distributed judiciously.
Xián said: To measure and bestow gifts,
not giving too much.
Thereupon, Huī and Chóng immediately dispatched troops to his court.
Ānguó, hearing of the Han army's arrival at night,
was greatly alarmed
and abandoned his tent to flee.
Zhàng
refers to the Chányú's residence,
also called a qiónglú
or lúzhàng.
Shīzǐ, having been forewarned,
led all his encampments into Mánbó City.
Mánbó County
was under Wǔyuán Commandery.
The gates were closed,
and he could not enter.
Zhū Huī sent an officer to reason
and reconcile with him,
but Ānguó refused to listen.
As the city would not surrender,
he then led his troops to garrison Wǔyuán.
Chóng and Huī then dispatched cavalry from various commanderies to give urgent chase.
Everyone was greatly terrified.
Ānguó's maternal uncle, the Gǔdōu Marquis Xǐ Wéi, fearing they would all be executed,
then assassinated Ānguó
and established Shīzǐ as Tíngdúshīzhúhóudī Chányú.
2 On the day Jǐmǎo,
Minister of Works (sī tú) Dīng Hóng passed away.
3 In the second month,
on the day Dīngwèi,
Minister of Works (sī kōng) Liú Fāng was appointed Minister of Works (sī tú),
and Grand Messenger (tài cháng) Zhāng Fèn was appointed Minister of Works (sī kōng).
4 In summer,
in the fifth month,
Huái Prince of Chéngyáng, Shú, passed away.
Having no son,
his state was abolished.
5 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
the capital suffered a drought.
6 Bān Chāo, the Protector-General of the Western Regions (xī yù dū hù), mobilized troops from Kūcí, Shànshàn, and eight other states, totaling over 70,000 men,
to attack Yānqí.
Upon reaching its city walls,
he enticed Guǎng, King of Yānqí, and Fàn, King of Wèilí, to Chén Mù's old city,
beheaded them,
and sent their heads to the capital.
He then unleashed his troops to plunder,
beheading over 5,000,
capturing 15,000 people,
and establishing Yuán Méng, the Left Marquis of Yānqí, as King of Yānqí.
The state of Yānqí had Left and Right Generals,
and Left and Right Marquises.
Gēng
is pronounced gōng héng fān.
He then pacified them.
Thereupon, over fifty states in the Western Regions all submitted hostages and became internal dependencies,
extending to the seashore.
This refers to the shore of the Western Sea,
namely the various states of Tiáozhī, Dàqín, Méngqí, Dōulè.
Zhì
is pronounced yī zhì.
All of them sent tribute through multiple interpreters.
7 When the Southern Chányú Shīzǐ was established,
five or six hundred surrendered Hú attacked Shīzǐ by night.
Wáng Tián, the Administrator of Pacification (ān jí yuàn), leading his bodyguard, fought
and defeated them.
The Colonel-Protector of the Southern Xiongnú appointed Administrators (yuàn),
who served according to need.
The Administrator of Pacification
was so named for pacifying the Xiongnú.
Guāngwǔ, when in Héběi,
also established Administrators of Pacification
because the empire was not yet settled,
to pacify its people.
In the twenty-sixth year of Jiànwǔ,
the Colonel-Protector of the Southern Xiongnú established an Administrator and Scribe of Pacification (ān jí yuàn shǐ),
who commanded fifty pardoned criminals
armed with weapons and crossbows to follow the Chányú wherever he resided,
to participate in legal disputes
and observe his movements.
Yuàn
is pronounced yú juàn fān.
Over 200,000 people from fifteen tribes all rebelled,
coercing Fènghóu, the Chányú of Yùdī Rìzhú, son of the former Chányú Túntúhé, to be their Chányú.
“Dī”
should be
“Jiān.”
Xián said: The former
“Dī”
and
“Jiān”
are interchangeable;
it is acceptable not to change it now.
Yù
is pronounced yú liù fān.
Jiān
is pronounced jiǔ yán fān.
They burned post stations and tents,
and led their heavy wagons towards Shuòfāng,
intending to cross north of the desert.
In the ninth month,
on the day Guǐchǒu,
Dèng Hóng, the Grand Master of the Palace (guāng lù xūn), was appointed acting General of Chariots and Cavalry (chē qí jiāng jūn),

and with Féng Zhù, the Colonel of Valiant Cavalry (yuè qí xiào wèi), and Zhū Huī, the acting General Overseeing the Liao, led the Left and Right Feathered Forest Guards (yǔ lín), the soldiers of the Five Camps of the Northern Army (běi jūn wǔ xiào), as well as the tracker archers (jì shè) from commanderies and kingdoms, and border troops.
Xián said: The Han had tracker archers,
meaning they tracked and shot.
At this time, the Southern Chányú and Colonel Dù Chóng were besieged in Mùshī City.
There was a Mùshī Park in a Han border commandery for raising horses;
this was Mùshī Park City,
which should be within the borders of Měijì County, Xīhé Commandery.
In winter,
in the eleventh month,
Dèng Hóng and others arrived at Měijì.
Fènghóu then lifted the siege and left,
heading towards Hànyí Valley.
The Southern Chányú sent his son leading ten thousand cavalry, and Dù Chóng led four thousand cavalry,
to join Dèng Hóng and others in pursuing Fènghóu at Dàchéng Stockade.
Dàchéng County formerly belonged to Xīhé Commandery;
in the "Records of Commanderies and Kingdoms," it belonged to Shuòfāng Commandery.
Rèn Shàng led Xiānbēi and Wūhuán forces to intercept Fènghóu in Mǎnyí Valley,
and
again inflicted a great defeat,
altogether beheading over 17,000 in total.
Fènghóu then led his followers out of the pass,
and the Han army, unable to pursue, returned.
8 Chén Chǒng, the Grand Minister of Agriculture (dà sī nóng), was appointed Commandant of Justice (tíng wèi).
Chǒng was naturally benevolent and compassionate,
and frequently deliberated on difficult cases.
He always adhered to the classics,
striving for leniency and forgiveness,
and the harsh and oppressive practices
consequently diminished.
9 The Emperor appointed Huáng Xiāng of Jiāngxià, the Prefect of the Masters of Writing (shàng shū lìng), as Administrator of Dōngjùn.
Xiāng declined, saying:
“Administering a commandery and governing is not suited to my talent.
I beg to remain as a supernumerary official,
be granted a minor supervisory position,
and be entrusted with the troublesome affairs of the Palace and Chancery.”
Gōng
refers to the imperial palace;
tái
refers to the Chancery (shàng shū tái).
The Masters of Writing received and issued imperial edicts,
hence the phrase "troublesome affairs of the Palace and Chancery."
His salary was increased by two thousand piculs (shí).
According to the "Records of Officialdom,"
the Prefect of the Masters of Writing had a salary of one thousand piculs.
Now, it was specially increased by two thousand piculs
because Xiāng had been in the Chancery for a long time
and had also declined the commandery appointment.
Therefore, he was retained as Prefect of the Masters of Writing
but received the salary of a commandery administrator.
Xiāng also diligently performed his duties,
worrying about public affairs as if they were his own family's.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
Dèng Hóng (鄧鴻) and others' armies returned.
Féng Zhù (馮柱), leading the Hǔyá (虎牙) battalion, remained stationed in Wǔyuán (五原).
Hóng (鴻) was imprisoned and died for delaying and suffering a defeat.
Later, the Emperor learned that Zhū Huī (朱徽) and Dù Chóng (杜崇) had alienated the Hú (胡) tribes,
and had also forbidden them from submitting memorials,
which led to the Hú (胡) rebellion.
They were both summoned,
imprisoned, and died.
2 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the *xīnhài* (辛亥) day of the new moon,
there was a solar eclipse.
3 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the *yǐsì* (乙巳) day,
the ground cracked in Yìyáng (易陽).
I note that according to the *Dìlǐ Zhì* (地理志) and *Jùnguó Zhì* (郡國志),
Yìyáng (易陽) County belonged to Zhào Guó (趙國).
Yīng Shào (應劭) said: the Yì Shuǐ (易水) river originates in Gù'ān (故安) of Zhuō Jùn (涿郡).
Shī Gǔ (師古) and Xián (賢) both said the county was on the south bank of the Yì Shuǐ (易水),
but this is all based on Yīng Shào's (應劭) error.
The Yì Shuǐ (易水) is on the southern border of Yān (燕),
and in Hàn (漢) times belonged to Hèjiān Jùn (河間郡).
At this time, Zhào Guó (趙國) only comprised the lands of Tángxíng (唐邢) and Míng (洺) prefectures.
How could it have a subordinate county so far to the south of the Yì Shuǐ (易水)?
The *Wǔdài Shǐzhì* (五代史志) states: Línmíng (臨洺) County of Míng Zhōu (洺州)
was formerly called Yìyáng (易陽);
it was abolished in the Later Qí (齊) dynasty
and incorporated into Xiāngguó (襄國) County;
in the Later Zhōu (周) dynasty, it was renamed Yìyáng (易陽) County,
and Xiāngguó (襄國) County was established separately;
in the sixth year of Kāihuáng (開皇) in the Suí (隋) dynasty,
Yìyáng (易陽) County was renamed Hándān (邯鄲) County;
in the tenth year,
Hándān (邯鄲) County was renamed Línmíng (臨洺) and Hándān (邯鄲) County was established separately.
From this, we can see that
Hàn (漢) Yìyáng (易陽) County must have been between Hándān (邯鄲) and Xiāngguó (襄國) counties.
4 In the ninth month,
on the *guǐmǎo* (癸卯) day,
there was an earthquake in the capital.
5 Lèchéng Wáng Dǎng (樂成王黨) was imprisoned for robbery and murder,
and the counties of Dōngguāng (東光) and Què (鄡) were removed from his domain.
Dōngguāng (東光) County
originally belonged to Bóhǎi Jùn (勃海郡);
Què (鄡) County
originally belonged to Jùlù Jùn (鉅鹿郡).
Emperor Zhāng (章帝) added them to Lèchéng Guó (樂成國).
Què (鄡),
pronounced *qiāng yáo fān*.
It was an old rule that palace women who married out
could not marry into the various kingdoms.
There was a former Yè Tíng (掖庭) entertainer named Āi Zhì (哀置) whose husband was Zhāng Chū (章初).
Dǎng (黨) summoned her to the palace and had relations with her.
Chū (初) wanted to submit a memorial to report this,
so Dǎng (黨) bribed Āi Zhì's (哀置) sister Zhāo (昭) to kill Chū (初).
1 In spring,
in the second month,
Consort Yīn (陰氏) was made Empress.
The Empress
was the great-granddaughter of Shí (識).
2 In summer,
in the fourth month,
Lèchéng Jìng Wáng Dǎng (樂成靖王黨) died.
His son, Āi Wáng Chóng (哀王崇), succeeded him,
but soon died.
He had no son,
so the kingdom was abolished.
3 In the fifth month,
there was a locust plague in Hénèi (河內) and Chénliú (陳留).
4 The Southern Xiōngnú (匈奴) Right Wēnyúdú Wáng Wūjū Zhàn (右溫禺犢王烏居戰) rebelled and left the frontier.
Xián (賢) said: Wēnyúdú Wáng (溫禺犢王) was named Wūjū Zhàn (烏居戰).
In the seventh month,
General Dùliáo (度遼) Páng Fèn (龐奮) and Commandant of Yùqí (越騎) Féng Zhù (馮柱) pursued and defeated him,
relocating his remaining followers and over twenty thousand surrendered Hú (胡) to Āndìng (安定) and Běidì (北地).
Āndìng Jùn (安定郡)
was one thousand seven hundred *lǐ* west of Luòyáng (雒陽).
Běidì Jùn (北地郡)
was one thousand one hundred *lǐ* west of Luòyáng (雒陽).
5 The king of Chēshī (車師) Later Division, Zhuōdī (涿鞮), rebelled,
attacking the Former King Wèibìdà (尉畢大)
and capturing his wife and children.
"Wèibìdà (尉畢大)"

It can be settled without battle."
Zōng approved his words
and immediately ceased military operations.
When the bandits heard this,
they were greatly pleased
and returned the people they had plundered.
However, the Dōnglái Commandery forces had not yet disarmed,
so the bandits were again startled and frightened,
fleeing to Liáodōng,
stopping on a sea island.
It indeed turned out as Fǎ Xióng had said.
15 Autumn,
seventh month,
on the *yǐyǒu* day,
three commanderies suffered great floods.
16. Rèn Rén (任仁), a Cavalry Commandant (騎都尉), repeatedly lost battles against the Qiāng (羌).
His soldiers were undisciplined and unruly.
He was brought in a cage cart to the Grand Judge (廷尉)
and died.
Dùan Xǐ (段禧), the Protector of the Qiāng (護羌校尉), passed away.
The former Protector Hóu Bà (侯霸) was again appointed to replace him.
He moved to Zhāngyè (張掖).
In the second year of Yǒngchū (永初) [108 CE],
Hóu Bà (侯霸) was dismissed because many Qiāng (羌) rebelled.
The Protector of the Qiāng (護羌校尉) was at that time residing in Dídao (狄道).
According to the commentary on the Shuǐjīng (水經註),
the Qiāng (羌) River flows out from the mountains southwest of Huángzhōng (湟中),
passing east of Hùqiāng Chéng (護羌城),
where the Protector of the Qiāng (護羌校尉) once governed,
then east again past the west of Línqiāng Chéng (臨羌城).
The Protector of the Qiāng (護羌校尉) likely governed within the borders of Línqiāng (臨羌) County, Jīnchéng (金城) Commandery.
However, Emperor Xuān (宣) established the Protector of the Qiāng (護羌校尉),
who originally governed Lìngjū (令居) in Jīnchéng (金城).
After the pacification of Hé (河) and Lǒng (隴) by the Eastern Capital,
the Protector of the Qiāng (護羌校尉) governed Ānyí (安夷) County.
Soon after, they moved from Ānyí (安夷) to Línqiāng (臨羌).
Hóu Bà (侯霸) first resided in Dídao (狄道) in Lǒngxī (隴西),
because the Qiāng (羌) rebellion made Línqiāng (臨羌) uninhabitable.
Now he moved to Zhāngyè (張掖),
because Lǒngxī (隴西) was devastated
and he crossed the river again to the west.
17. In the ninth month,
on the day of Jiǎshēn (甲申),
Yìzhōu (益州) Commandery experienced an earthquake.
Xián (賢) said: The old city of Yìzhōu (益州) Commandery
is in modern Kūnzhōu (昆州), Jìnníng (晉寧) County.
18. The Empress Dowager's (皇太后) mother, the Lady of Xīnyě (新野君), fell ill.
The Xùhàn Zhì (續漢志) states: For women enfeoffed as lords (封君),
their ceremonial rank is comparable to that of princesses (公主).
They use oiled quivers and closed carriages (油鞬軿車),
wear ribbons (綬),
and have sashes (緄帶) made of colored cords (采組),
each matching the color of their ribbon.
A golden bìxié (辟邪) adorns the head as part of the sash.
She stayed for several days;
the Three Excellencies (三公) submitted memorials strongly protesting,
so she returned to the palace.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day of Jiǎxū (甲戌),
the Lady of Xīnyě (新野君) died.
The Minister of Works (司空) was sent to oversee the funeral arrangements,
with ceremonies comparable to those of Gōng (恭) Prince of Dōnghǎi (東海).
For the Gōng (恭) Prince,
see Volume 44, Yǒngpíng (永平) first year of Emperor Míng (明).
The Empress Dowager (太后) intended not to allow it,
and asked Cáo Dàjiā (曹大家).
Dàjiā (大家) submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your concubine has heard that among the virtues,
humility and yielding are the greatest.
Now, the four maternal uncles (四舅) deeply adhere to loyalty and filial piety,
withdrawing themselves.
Xián (賢) said: The four maternal uncles (四舅)
refer to Zhì (騭), Kūi (悝), Hóng (弘), and Chāng (閶).
If you refuse and do not permit it,
should there be even a slight transgression after today,
I truly fear that the reputation for humility and yielding cannot be regained."
Xián (賢) said: This means that if there is a minute fault,
the beauty of humility and yielding is lost.
When the mourning period ended,
an imperial edict ordered Zhì (騭) to return and assist in government affairs,
and he was again granted his former enfeoffment.
At the beginning of the Emperor's (帝) accession,
Zhì (騭), Kūi (悝), Hóng (弘), and Chāng (閶) were enfeoffed,
but they all declined the offer.
So it was stopped.
Thereupon, they all served at court,
their rank below the Three Excellencies (三公),
but above the Special Advance (特進) and Marquis (侯).
Xián (賢) said: Above the Special Advance (特進) and Marquis (侯).
Qǐng (請)
is pronounced cái xìng (才性) [qièyīn, an ancient phonetic notation], also as written.
They then went to the court hall
and participated in discussions with the dukes and ministers (公卿).
19. The Empress Dowager (太后) decreed that all family members of Empress Yīn (陰后) should return to their ancestral commandery.
The matter of Empress Yīn's (陰后) family moving south is found in the previous volume, Yǒngyuán (永元) fourteenth year of Emperor Hé (和).
Returning to their ancestral commandery
means returning to Nányáng (南陽).
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the Gēngchén (庚辰) new moon,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the day of Bǐngxū (丙戌),
ten commanderies and kingdoms experienced earthquakes.
On the day of Jǐchǒu (己丑), Grand Commandant (太尉) Zhāng Yǔ (張禹) was dismissed.
On the day of Jiǎshēn (甲申),
Lǐ Xiū (李脩) of Yǐngchuān (潁川), the Minister of the Imperial Household (光祿勳), was appointed Grand Commandant (太尉).
4. The Xiānlíng Qiāng (先零羌) raided Hédōng (河東),
reaching Hénèi (河內).
The common people panicked,
many fled south across the river.
Zhū Chǒng (朱寵), the Central Inspector of the Northern Army (北軍中候), was sent to lead the soldiers of the five camps to garrison Mèngjīn (孟津).
The Central Inspector of the Northern Army (北軍中候)
was in charge of overseeing the five camps: Tunqí (屯騎), Yuèqí (越騎), Bùbīng (步兵), Chángshuǐ (長水), and Shèshēng (射聲).
The Xùhàn Zhì (續漢志) states: Formerly there was a Zhōnglěi School Commandant (中壘校尉),
who managed the Northern Army's (北軍) camps and fortifications;
during the Restoration (中興),
the Zhōnglěi (中壘) position was abolished,
and only the Zhōnghòu (中候) was established to oversee the five camps.
Hóng Shì Lìshì (洪氏隸釋) states: According to Zhù Mù Hòubēi (祝睦後碑), it is written as
"Northern Army Army Central Inspector" (北軍軍中候),
from which we know that this is also an abridged text.
Four commanderies,
all belonging to Jìzhōu (冀州).
Fearing that the Qiāng (羌) would enter Jìzhōu (冀州) territory from Hédōng (河東) and Hénèi (河內) in the north,
defensive strongholds were built to guard against them.
However, many of the Two-Thousand-Picul (二千石) officials, county magistrates (令), and chiefs (長) along the border were from inner commanderies
and had no intention of defending or fighting.
They all eagerly requested to move their commanderies and counties to avoid the invaders.
In the third month,
an edict ordered Lǒngxī (隴西) to move to Xiāngwǔ (襄武).
Lǒngxī (隴西) Commandery originally governed Dídao (狄道).
The Kǎoyì (考異) states: Above it says
"Jīnchéng (金城) moved to Xiāngwǔ (襄武),"
and here it again says
"Lǒngxī (隴西) moved to Xiāngwǔ (襄武),"
which is consistent in the annals and biographies.
Perhaps both commanderies temporarily governed from Xiāngwǔ (襄武)!
Běidì (北地) moved to Chíyáng (池陽).
Shàngjùn (上郡) governed
Yá (衙).
Xián (賢) said: Āndìng (安定) Commandery
is modern Jìngzhōu (涇州).
The old city of Měiyáng (美陽)
is north of modern Wǔgōng (武功) County.
Běidì (北地) Commandery
is modern Níngzhōu (寧州).
The old city of Chíyáng (池陽) County
is north of modern Jīngyáng (涇陽) County.
Shàngjùn (上郡)
is modern Suízhōu (綏州).
The old city of Yá (衙) County
is northeast of modern Báishuǐ (白水) County, Tóngzhōu (同州).
The battle between Qín (秦) and Jìn (晉) at Péngyá (彭衙) in the Zuǒzhuàn (左傳)
refers to this place.
I (the annotator) also note from the Jùnguó Zhì (郡國志) that
Měiyáng (美陽) County
belonged to Fúfēng (扶風);
Chíyáng (池陽) and Yá (衙) two counties
belonged to Féngyì (馮翊).
Yá (衙)
is pronounced yá.
Unwilling to leave their old homes,
they proceeded to cut down their crops,
dismantle their houses,
flatten their camps and walls,
and destroy their stored provisions.
At that time, there were continuous droughts, locusts, and famine,
and then they were driven away, oppressed, and plundered.
They were scattered and wandered,
dying along the roads.
Some abandoned the old and weak,
others became servants or concubines.
More than half were lost.
Cuò (䠞)
is the same as cù (蹙).
Sàng (喪)
is pronounced sì làng (息浪) [fān, an ancient phonetic notation].
They attacked the Qiāng (羌) at Yángtóu Shān (羊頭山) in Shàngdǎng (上黨)
and defeated them.
Xián (賢) said: Yángtóu Shān (羊頭山)
is in Gǔyuǎn (穀遠) County, Shàngdǎng (上黨) Commandery.
Fù (復)
is pronounced fú yòu (扶又) [fān];
same below.
King Fúyú (夫餘) raided Lèlàng (樂浪).
This is when Fúyú (夫餘) began its raids.
Fū (夫)
is pronounced fú.
Lèlàng (樂浪)
is pronounced luò láng.
6. In summer,
the intercalary fourth month,
on the day of Dīngyǒu (丁酉),
a general amnesty was granted to Liángzhōu (涼州) and the four commanderies west of the river.
7. The sea pirate Zhāng Bólù (張伯路) again raided Dōnglái (東萊).
Fǎ Xióng (法雄), the Inspector of Qīngzhōu (青州), attacked and defeated him.
The pirate fled back to Liáodōng (遼東).
Lǐ Jiǔ (李久) and others from Liáodōng (遼東) jointly beheaded him.
Zhāng Bólù (張伯路) caused unrest in the third year of Yǒngchū (永初)
and was now finally pacified.
8. In autumn,
the ninth month,
Dù Qí (杜琦) and his younger brother Jìgòng (季貢) from Hànyáng (漢陽), along with Wáng Xìn (王信) and others from the same commandery, colluded with the Qiāng (羌).
They gathered a crowd and occupied the city of Shàngguī (上邽).
In winter, the twelfth month,
Zhào Bó (趙博), the Administrator of Hànyáng (漢陽), sent his retainer Dù Xí (杜習) to assassinate Qí (琦).
Xí (習) was enfeoffed as the Marquis for Suppressing Treachery (討姦侯).
Dù Jìgòng (杜季貢), Wáng Xìn (王信) and others led their followers and occupied Chūquán Yíng (樗泉營).
9 That year,
locusts plagued Jiǔzhōu,
and eight commanderies and kingdoms suffered from floods.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the day of Jiǎyín,
an edict stated:
“The presentation of new flavors [to the court]
often occurs out of season,
or they are forced to ripen prematurely.
This refers to using an earth chamber with fire,
causing the earth’s vapor to steam and cultivate them,
forcing them to mature.
The Former Han History, Biography of Zhào Xìnchén, states: ‘The imperial garden planted winter-grown onions, leeks, and vegetables,
covered them with shelters,
and kept fires burning day and night,
waiting for the warmth to make them grow.’
‘強 (qiáng)’ [meaning ‘to force’]
has two pronunciations.
When flavors are forced and their growth stunted,
how can this be in accordance with the seasons and nurturing of things?
The Biographies state: ‘Do not eat what is not in season.’
Xián states: The Analects say: ‘Do not eat what is not in season.’
It means that if something is not in season,
then one should not eat it.
The Former Han History,
Zhào Xìnchén said: ‘Things not in season
are harmful to people
and should not be offered for sustenance.’
All must be offered only when in season.”
“Only when ripe should they be presented.”
‘上 (shàng)’ [meaning ‘to present’]
has the pronunciation ‘shì zhǎng’.
2 In the third month,
locusts plagued ten prefectures.
3 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day of Yǐchǒu,
Sīkōng Zhāng Mǐn was dismissed.
On the day of Jǐmǎo,
Liú Kǎi, the Tàicháng, was appointed Sīkōng.
4 An edict commanded that the twenty-eight meritorious generals of Jiànwǔ be all enfeoffed by their descendants.
5 In the fifth month,
there was a drought.
6 On the day of Bǐngyín,
an edict ordered that all officials from Zhōngèrqiānshí down to Huángshòu
should have their ranks restored.
Dǒng Bā’s Yúfúzhì states: Zhōngèrqiānshí wore a green sash;
Sìbǎishí and Èrbǎishí wore a yellow sash.
Four years prior,
the salaries of officials had been reduced;
now they were restored.
7 In the sixth month,
on the day of Rénchén,
Mount Yuán in Yuánxī, Yùzhāng, collapsed.
Yùzhāng Commandery
is two thousand seven hundred lǐ south of Luòyáng
and belongs to Yángzhōu.
8 On the day of Xīnsì,
there was a general amnesty.
9 Shìyùshǐ Táng Xǐ attacked the Hányáng bandit Wáng Xìn
and defeated and beheaded him.
Dù Jìgòng fled
and joined Diān Líng.
That year,
Diān Líng died,
and his son Líng Chāng was established.
He was still young.
His kinsman Láng Mò planned for him
and appointed Jìgòng as general,
who then resided separately at Dīngxī City.
According to Dōngguānjì,
Dīngxī City is in Língzhōu County, Běidì Commandery.
1 In spring,
in the second month,
on the day of Bǐngwǔ,
earthquakes occurred in eighteen commanderies and kingdoms.
2 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day of Yǐwèi,
Píngyuán Huáiwáng Shèng passed away
without a son;
the Empress Dowager enthroned Dé, the son of Lè’ān Yíwáng Chǒng, as Píngyuán Wáng.
3 On the last day of Bǐngshēn,
there was a solar eclipse.
4 In autumn,
Hùqiāngxiàowèi Hóu Bà and Jìdūwèi Mǎ Xián attacked the Láoqiāng, a separate branch of the Xiānlíng, in Āndìng
and captured over a thousand heads and prisoners.
5 Locusts.
Yuánchū First Year
(Jiǎyín, 114 CE)
1 In spring,
in the first month,
on the day of Jiǎzǐ,
the reign title was changed.
2 In the second month,
on the day of Yǐmǎo,
the ground in Rìnán split open,
over a hundred lǐ long.
Dōngguānjì states: The split was one hundred eighty-two lǐ long
and fifty-six lǐ wide.
‘長 (cháng)’ [meaning ‘long’]
has the pronunciation ‘zhí liàng’.
3 In the third month,
on the day of Guǐhài,
there was a solar eclipse.
Kǎoyì states: The Dìjì
says, “In the second month, on the day of Jǐmǎo,
the ground in Rìnán split open.
In the third month, on the day of Guǐyǒu,
there was a solar eclipse.”
Both Běnzhì and Yuán Jì state
“In the third month, on the day of Jǐmǎo,
the ground in Rìnán split open.”
According to Chánglì,
the new moon of the second month of that year was on Rénchén,
so there was no Jǐmǎo;
the new moon of the third month was on Rénxū,
and Guǐyǒu was the twelfth day,
so a solar eclipse should not have occurred.
The second month should be Yǐmǎo,
and the third month should be Guǐhài.
4 An edict ordered troops to be stationed in thirty-six
strategic locations in Tōnggǔ, Hénèi,
where all made entrenched forts
and set up signal drums
to guard against Qiāng invaders.
From the north of Tàiháng to Mount Héng,
which separates Bìng and Jì,
there are many valley paths connecting them.
Now, entrenched forts are made in these strategic locations to guard against Qiāng invaders.
5 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day of Dīngyǒu,
there was a general amnesty.
6 The capital and five commanderies and kingdoms suffered from drought
and locusts.
7 In the fifth month,
the Xiānlíng Qiāng plundered Yōngchéng.
This is the city of Yōng County, Yòufúfēng.
‘雍 (yōng)’ [meaning ‘Yong’]
has the pronunciation ‘yū yòng’.
8 The Yí of Shǔ
Commandery plundered Cánlíng
and killed the county magistrate.
Cánlíng County belongs to Shǔ Commandery.
Xián states: The old city of Cánlíng is now west of Yìshuǐ County, Yìzhōu.
There is Cánlíng Mountain,
hence the name.
9 In the ninth month,
on the day of Yǐchǒu,
Tàiwèi Lǐ Xiū was dismissed.
10 The Qiāng chieftain Hàoduō and various tribes looted Wǔdū, Hànzhōng, and Bājùn.
The Bǎnshǔn Mán came to their rescue.
According to Fàn Shū,
the Bǎnshǔn Mán ethnic group,
during the time of Qín Zhāoxiāng Wáng, had rendered meritorious service by shooting and killing a white tiger.
King Zhāoxiāng exempted the Yí people’s cultivated land from rent
and their ten wives from taxation.
Those who injured others were judged,
and those who killed could redeem their lives with a ransom fee.
When Gāozǔ was King of Hàn,
he conscripted the Yí people to pacify Sānqín
and exempted their seven chieftain clans from taxes and levies.
The remaining households paid annual cōng money,
forty per person.
They were called the Bǎnshǔn Mán Yí.
There is the Yú River in Lángzhōng,
and its people mostly lived along the river.
They were naturally strong and brave,
often breaking enemy formations,
and enjoyed singing and dancing.
Gāozǔ created the Bāyú dance for them.
The Mán likely fought with board shields,
hence their name.
‘楯 (shǔn)’ [meaning ‘shield’]
has the pronunciation ‘shí yǐn’.
‘倓 (tán)’ [meaning ‘ransom’]
has the pronunciation ‘tú làn’.
‘賨 (cóng)’ [meaning ‘con’]
has the pronunciation ‘cáng zōng’.
The Bǎiguānzhì states: A commandery has five guān yuán,
who manage gōngcáo and various cào matters.
‘掾 (yuán)’ [meaning ‘clerk’]
has the pronunciation ‘yú juàn’.
They cut off the Lǒng Pass
and joined Líng Chāng.
Hóu Bà and Mǎ Xián fought them at Páohǎn
and defeated them.
Páohǎn County belongs to Lǒngxī Commandery
and was Táng dynasty’s Hézhōu.
‘枹 (páo)’ [meaning ‘Pao’]
is pronounced ‘fū’.
11th year, Xīnwèi.
Sīmǎ Bāo (司馬苞) of Shānyáng (山陽), Grand Minister of Agriculture, was made Grand Commandant.
12th year. Winter,
10th month,
on the day Wùzǐ (戊子), which was the first day of the lunar month,
there was a solar eclipse.
13th year. Pí Yáng (皮楊), Inspector of Liángzhōu (涼州).
The Pí Xìng Pǔ (皮姓譜) says: The Pí (皮) clan are descendants of Fán Zhòng Pí (樊仲皮);
also, in Zhèng (鄭), there was a high minister Zǐ Pí (子皮),
who was from the Hǎn (罕) clan.
(He) suffered a great defeat,
with over eight hundred men killed.
The Kǎoyì (考異) says: The Jì (紀) records it as
"Pí Yáng (皮陽)" ;
we follow the Xīqiāng Zhuàn (西羌傳) here.
I (the compiler) note that the old seat of the Lǒngxī (隴西) Commandery was Dídào (狄道).
Last year it was moved to Xiāngwǔ (襄武),
so that territory had already been abandoned and was no longer held.
14th year. This year,
fifteen commanderies and states experienced earthquakes.
1st month. Spring,
Páng Cān (龐參), Colonel Protector of the Qiāng (羌), by his benevolence and trustworthiness, attracted and enticed various Qiāng (羌) tribes.
Hàoduō (號多) and others led their multitudes to surrender;
Cān (參) sent them to the imperial court.
Hàoduō (號多) was granted the seal of a marquis,
and sent back.
Cān (參) first returned to govern at Língjū (令居),
having moved back to Língjū (令居) from Zhāngyè (張掖).
2nd month. Língchāng (零昌) divided his troops to raid Yìzhōu (益州),
and Zhōnglángjiàng (中郎將) Yǐn Jiù (尹就) was dispatched to suppress him.
3rd month. Summer,
4th month,
on the day Bǐngwǔ (丙午),
the noble lady, the Yán (閻) clan of Xíngyáng (滎陽), was established as Empress.
The Empress Yán’s (閻) mother
was the uterine sister of Dèng Hóng’s (鄧弘) wife,
and thus she was able to be established.
Lady Lǐ (李) of the imperial harem bore the imperial prince Bǎo (保),
and the Empress poisoned Lady Lǐ (李) to death.
This laid the groundwork for the later deposition of Bǎo (保).
Bǎo (保) was later enthroned,
he was Shùn Dì (順帝).
4th month. 5th month,
the capital was in drought.
Hénán (河南) and nineteen commanderies and states suffered from locusts.
Hénán (河南)
was the capital region itself.
5th month. 6th month,
on the day Bǐngxū (丙戌),
Grand Commandant Sīmǎ Bāo (司馬苞) died.
6th month. Autumn,
7th month,
on the day Xīnsì (辛巳),
Mǎ Yīng (馬英) of Tàishān (泰山), Grand Coachman, was made Grand Commandant.
7th month. 8th month,
the Xiānbēi (鮮卑) of Liáodōng (遼東) besieged Wúlǜ (無慮);
Wúlǜ (無慮) County
belonged to Liáodōng (遼東) Commandery.
Yīng Shào (應劭) says: Lǜ (慮)
is pronounced lǘ.
Shīgǔ (師古) says: It is what is called Yīwúlǘ (毉無閭).
According to the Jùn Guó Zhì (郡國志),
Wúlǜ (無慮) County
at that time belonged to Liáodōng Shǔguó (遼東屬國).
They also attacked Fūlí (夫犂) Camp,
and killed the county magistrate.
Xián (賢) says: Fūlí (夫犂) County
belonged to Liáodōng Shǔguó (遼東屬國),
its old city is now southeast of Yíngzhōu (營州).
I (the compiler) note that in the chronicles of both Han dynasties,
neither Liáodōng (遼東) Commandery nor Liáodōng Shǔguó (遼東屬國) had a Fūlí (夫犂) County.

Fàn Yè (范曄) said: During the Hàn (漢) dynasty, empresses had no posthumous titles;
they were all named after the emperor's posthumous title.
Even during Lǚ's (呂) usurpation of power
and Shàngguān's (上官) regency,
there were no special designations.
In the Restoration,
Emperor Míng (明) first established the title of Guāngliè (光烈).
Thereafter, they were all paired with virtue,
and regardless of their wisdom or foolishness, superiority or inferiority,
they were all treated uniformly.
Thus, Empresses Mǎ (馬) and Dòu (竇)
were both called "Virtuous."
For other emperors' biological mothers and princes who succeeded to the throne,
due to the weight of posthumous honors,
special titles were created for them,
such as Gōnghuái (恭懷) and Xiàochóng (孝崇).
In the Chūpíng (初平) period,
Cài Yōng (蔡邕) first officially rectified the posthumous title of Héxī (和熹).
Subsequently, titles like Ānsī (安思) and Shùnliè (順烈) were added accordingly.
Xián (賢) noted: Cài Yōng's (蔡邕) Collection of Posthumous Title Deliberations states: Empresses of the Hàn (漢) dynasty had no posthumous titles.
Emperor Míng (明) first established the title of Guāngliè (光烈).
Thereafter, they were given the character "Dé" (德) based on the emperor's title,
treating all, high and low, superior and inferior,
uniformly.
This violated the ritual
"great deeds receive great names, small deeds receive small names"
system.
The posthumous title law states: "To pacify the people with merit is called Xī (熹)";
the emperor and empress are one body,
and the rites should also be the same.
The late Empress Dowager should be called Héxī (和熹).
Since the Empress Dowager presided over the government,
there were droughts and floods for ten years,
foreign tribes invaded from outside,
and bandits rose up internally.
Whenever she heard of people suffering from famine,
she would sometimes stay awake until dawn,
personally reducing her own expenses
referring to reducing meals, removing entertainment, and similar actions.
Thus, the empire was again peaceful,
and the harvests were abundant again.
The governance of Héxī (和熹) while presiding over the court
could be described as "the hen crowing at dawn,"
bringing ruin to the household.
The Emperor began to personally attend to government affairs.
Shàngshū (尚書) Chénzhōng (陳忠) recommended recluses and upright scholars, such as Dùgēn (杜根) of Yǐngchuān (潁川) and Chéngyìshì (成翊世) of Píngyuán (平原), among others.
The Emperor accepted and employed them all.
Chénzhōng (陳忠) was the son of Chénchǒng (寵).

The Empress Dowager was furious,

For three days,

"In the past, when he encountered disaster,

Having risen from humble origins,

"According to the established system,

The previously mentioned Cháoyáng Hóu (朝陽侯) Liú Hù's (劉護) second cousin, Liú Huái (劉懷), was enfeoffed and inherited Hù’s (護) peerage as a marquis;

"In the past, the favor shown to the Dòu (竇) and Dèng (鄧) clans

比 (bǐ),

In the past, Emperor Wén (文帝) treasured one hundred catties of gold, refusing to build a raised platform,

1 In spring,

in the fourth month,
on the day Jiǎxū,

6 The Emperor wished to establish an Huánghòu,

The names of the four individuals were written on lots,
prayers were offered to the spirits, and then the lots were drawn.
The one whose lot was drawn would be selected.
"[I] humbly observe the imperial edict,
that the matter of establishing an Hòu is significant.
Your Majesty, in your humility, does not wish to decide independently,
and intends to use lots and strategies,
to resolve doubts with divine spirits.
What is recorded in the scriptures,
the precedents of our ancestors,
has never included such a practice.
Relying on divination
may not necessarily select the truly virtuous;
even if the right person is found,
it is still not a selection based on virtue.
Truly, intelligence and discernment manifest naturally.
It is appropriate to consult good families,
and select the virtuous.
If virtues are equal, consider age;
if ages are equal, consider appearance.
Review the canonical scriptures,

The Emperor agreed to this.
The daughter of Chéngshì Hóu Shāng, a junior relative of Gōnghuái Huánghòu,

This concubine asks to be spared from fault."
The Emperor, because of this, esteemed her as virtuous.

(`rénshēn`, 132)

Xián (賢) said: This refers to competing to promote the prognosticators (chènjiā 讖家).

Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: The ceremony for conferring titles upon princes and the Three Ducal Ministers (Sāngōng 三公) in the Later Hàn (後漢) was as follows:
All officials assembled,
took their positions,
and the court attendant (yèzhě 謁者) led the Grand Master of Ceremonies (Guānglùxūn 光祿勳) forward.
The court attendant (yèzhě 謁者) then led the recipient forward,
who prostrated before the hall.
The Grand Master of Ceremonies (Guānglùxūn 光祿勳) bowed once,
raised his hands, and said:
"An imperial edict proclaims,
'Let so-and-so be appointed to so-and-so office.'"
After the edict was read, the recipient declared himself a subject
and bowed twice.
The Secretary of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Láng 尚書郎) handed the seal and ribbon (xīnyìnshòu 璽印綬) to the Imperial Secretary (Shìyùshǐ 侍御史),
who then stood forward to receive the seal and ribbon.
The recipient bowed twice and kowtowed,
offering three praises.
The court attendant (yèzhě 謁者) said:
"Prince so-and-so, subject so-and-so, newly enfeoffed;
Grandee so-and-so, newly appointed,
expresses gratitude."
The inner court attendant (zhōngyèzhě 中謁者) responded,
"Gratefully acknowledged."
The praiser stood and said:
"The Emperor rises for the Grandee."
They resumed their seats.
The recipient bowed in thanks,
rose,
and took his place.
The ceremony concluded.
Since the Hàn (漢) dynasty, only Wèi Qīng (衞青) was appointed General-in-Chief (Dàjiāngjūn 大將軍) in the military for his achievements.
Never before had there been an instance of an appointment made at a residence,

He was modest and fond of scholars,

Lǐ Gù, believing that Liáng Shāng was gentle and self-preserving, and unable to make reforms,

In Fàn Shū, the biography of Lǐ Gù,
'形 (xíng)'

These two sayings are also likely based on apocryphal texts.
They should be treated with reverence and awe.
Xián says: Zhī (祗)

It means that Heaven shows no partiality,

With the Way practiced and loyalty established,
Your Excellency follows the noble example of Bóchéng Zigāo.
Zhuāngzǐ says: Bóchéng Zigāo

How could you be compared and discussed with those ordinary relatives of the imperial family who indulge in glory and covet positions!"
Shāng was unable to act on it.

Liáng Jì found his words agreeable.
The next day,

Liáng Jì's demeanor was menacing.
'Xiōngxiōng'
refers to a malicious and violent demeanor.
From Hú Guǎng and Zhào Jiè downwards, none were not intimidated and fearful.
They all said:

Only Lǐ Gù and Dù Qiáo steadfastly upheld their original proposal.
Liáng Jì sternly said:
"Dismiss the meeting!"
Lǐ Gù still hoped that public sentiment could prevail,
because public sentiment favored Qīnghé Wáng,
he still hoped it could be established.
Liáng Jì became even more enraged.
On Dīnghài day,
Liáng Jì persuaded the Empress Dowager

This laid the groundwork for killing Lǐ Gù and Dù Qiáo.
On Wùzǐ day,

Tāng
was Ān's grandson.

there,

The Empress Dowager still presided over court affairs.
6 In autumn,
seventh month,
on Yǐmǎo day,

This is like leaning against Nánshān and sitting on a flat plain,

Shìfǎ: 'Mù' means 'to spread virtue and uphold righteousness';

tenth month,

is pronounced 'wū lù'.

The first part of Emperor Xiàohuán's annals.

The character "Zhì"

"Yì".
In the first year of Jiànhé
(Dīnghài, 147):

the first month,
on the Xīnhài day,

2. On the Wǔwǔ day,
a general amnesty was granted.
3. In the third month,
a dragon was seen in Qiáo.

belonged to Péiguó commandery.
"Jiàn"
is pronounced xián biàn fān.

the fourth month,

The kingship of Fùlíng, passed down by Yán, continued for five generations,
until Dài.
When Dài died
without a son,
the state was abolished.
Now Biàn was appointed to continue the enfeoffment.
"Qiú"
is pronounced cái yóu fān.
6. In the sixth month,
Grand Commandant Hú Guǎng was dismissed,
and Grand Minister of Ceremonies Dù Qiáo became Grand Commandant.
Kǎoyì says: The Emperor's Annals state:
"Grand Minister of Agriculture Dù Qiáo."
Qiáo's biography says: Qiáo rose from Minister of Agriculture to Grand Minister of the Court of Dependencies, then Grand Minister of Ceremonies,
and then became Grand Commandant.
Yuán Jì says the same.
Xún Shú's biography says:
"Grand Minister of Ceremonies Dù Qiáo recommended Shú as upright."
We follow this account.
The court was disheartened,
and the ministers stood on tiptoe (in fear);
only Qiáo maintained a serious demeanor and did not yield.
Xián says: "Huí"
means crooked.
"Ráo"

"Ráo"

the seventh month,

Yǐngyáng county

Jì's son Yìn as Marquis of Xiāngyì,
Hú Guǎng as Marquis of Ānlè —
According to Guǎng's biography,
he was enfeoffed with Ānlè township in Yùyáng county.
"Lè"

and Yuán Tāng as Marquis of Ānguó.

Dù Qiáo remonstrated, saying:
"The enlightened rulers of antiquity

The rulers who lost their states,
how could their courts not have loyal and upright ministers?
'Zhēn'
is interchangeable with 'zhēn';
'gàn'
is interchangeable with 'gàn'.
Building a wall requires pillars and beams,

'Cháo'

This refers to the decrees and edicts for enfeoffment and titles,

To conceal writings and not apply their teachings,
to hear of goodness and not believe in its righteousness,

Your Majesty, having ascended the throne from a regional lord,
with Heaven and man aligning their hearts,
you do not prioritize the rites for loyal and worthy officials, but first enfeoff your intimates.
The Liáng clan,
and the insignificant offspring of the eunuchs,

How perverse and excessive this is,

If those with merit are not rewarded,

Should one not be careful! "

Kǎoyì says: The Empress's Annals and Yuán Jì both state the eighth month but no specific day.

Yǐwèi."

Yǐwèi

Probably the Emperor's Annals omitted

Dù Qiáo held firmly to the old rites

The old customs in the Hàn Shū state: when formally proposing to an empress,

"Zàng"

The officials impeached and memorialized about (Qīnghé) Wáng (王),

(Qīnghé Wáng) committed suicide.

(Lǐ Gù) debated with Jì (冀);

(Mǎ Róng) rose

7. The Xiongnu 匈奴 Hūyǎn Wáng 呼衍王 of the North raided Yīwú 伊吾,
defeated Yīwú's Sīmǎ 司馬 Máo Kǎi 毛愷,
and attacked Yīwú's garrison city.
An imperial edict ordered Dūnhuáng 敦煌 Grand Administrator Mǎ Dá 馬達 to lead troops to relieve them;
upon reaching Púléi Hǎi 蒲類海,
Hūyǎn Wáng 呼衍王 withdrew.
8. In autumn,
in the seventh month,
the Wǔlíng Mán 武陵蠻 rebelled.
9. In winter,
in the tenth month,
Sīkōng 司空 Hú Guǎng 胡廣 retired.
10. In the eleventh month,
on the day of Xīnsì 辛巳,
there was an earthquake in the capital.
An imperial edict ordered all officials to recommend men of outstanding integrity.
Zhuójùn 涿郡 recommended Cuī Shí 崔寔,
who went to the Gōngchē 公車,
claimed illness,
and did not answer the policy questions;
he then withdrew and discussed current affairs,
entitling his work Zhènglùn 政論.
Its words say:
"The reason why the world is not governed well
is often due to the ruler enjoying long periods of peace,
customs gradually deteriorating without being noticed,
governance slowly declining without being reformed,
becoming accustomed to chaos and comfortable with danger,
heedlessly unaware.
Some are infatuated with desires,
disregarding the myriad affairs of state;
others are deaf to admonitions,
weary of falsity and neglectful of truth;
Xián Yuē 賢曰: Yànyù jiānwěi 厭飫姦偽 means to be fed up with treachery and falsehood,
and to lightly disregard the ultimate truth.
(They) do not know which path to follow;
Ěryǎ 爾雅: A road that branches into two is called Qí 岐.
Guō Pú 郭璞 says: Qí 岐 means a road that branches out.
This means the ruler's vision is unclear,
and regarding the good or evil of people, and the right or wrong of matters,
he does not know which to choose.
Shì 適,
pronunciation: dì lì fān.
(They) keep their mouths shut and cling to their salaries;
Xián Yuē 賢曰: The Yì 易 says: 'Guōnáng 括囊 (keeping one's mouth shut), no blame, no praise.'
Guō 括 means to tie.
Tying the sack means not speaking,
merely holding onto one's salary.
Words are discarded because of low status;
thus the Imperial order is lax above,
and wise scholars are frustrated below.
Xián Yuē 賢曰: Yùyī 鬱伊 describes an inability to express oneself.
The Chǔ Cí 楚辭 says: 'Lonely and depressed, to whom can I speak?'"
4 Autumn,
seventh month.
Locusts afflicted thirty-two commanderies and kingdoms.
The Yellow River overflowed.
Several hundred thousand households of common people were starving, impoverished, and displaced,
especially severely in Jìzhōu.
An imperial edict appointed Attendant Imperial Censor Zhū Mù as Inspector of Jìzhōu.
When the county magistrates and chiefs of the Jì region heard that Mù had crossed the Yellow River,
more than forty of them resigned their seals and ribbons and departed.
Upon his arrival,
he impeached and prosecuted corrupt officials in various commanderies;
some even committed suicide,
or died in prison.
The eunuch Zhào Zhōng's father died,
and he was buried in Ānpíng.
The kingdom of Ānpíng
was subordinate to Jìzhōu.
During the funeral,
there was extravagant ostentation.
Mù ordered the commandery to investigate and verify.
The officials, fearing his strictness,
proceeded to exhume the grave, open the coffin,
and display the corpse.
When the emperor heard this,
he was furious.
He summoned and shackled Mù to the Court of the Commandant of Justice,
and sentenced him to penal labor in the Zuǒxiào.
The emperor did not consider Zhào Zhōng's jade casket an act of extravagance,
but rather viewed Zhū Mù's exhumation of the grave as a crime.
How could a dim-witted ruler truly distinguish right from wrong!
Xián said: Zuǒxiào
is a name of an office,
subordinate to the Jiàngzuò (Superintendent of Works),
in charge of the artisans on the left.
校 (xiào),
pronounced as hù jiào.
"Your servant humbly observes that the pardoned convict Zhū Mù,
who dedicated himself to public service and cared for the nation,
on the day he was appointed to the province,
was determined to eradicate evil.
Indeed, as the Regular Attendants were powerful and favored,
with their fathers, sons, and brothers spread throughout the provinces and commanderies,
competing to be like tigers and wolves,
devouring the common people,
Mù therefore upheld the heavenly net,
mended its torn meshes,
and ensnared the vicious and harmful,
to fulfill Heaven's will.
Because of this, all the inner officials collectively hated and resented him.
Inner officials
are the same as middle officials.
恚 (huì),
pronounced as yú bì.
Slander and discord continuously arose,
leading to his extreme punishment and chastisement,
sentenced to penal labor in the Zuǒxiào.
All discerning people in the world
consider Mù to be like Yǔ and Jì, who toiled diligently but were subjected to the hostility of Gòng and Gǔn.
If the dead have consciousness,
then Emperor Táng would be angry on Chóngshān,
and Chónghuá would be resentful at Cāngmù!
Xián said: The Shàngshū says: 'Banish Huāndōu to Chóngshān.'
Kǒng Ānguó's commentary says: Chóngshān
is in the southern borderlands.
The Shānhǎi Jīng says: 'There is the country of Huāntóu,
where Emperor Yáo was buried.'
Guō Pú's commentary says: Huāntóu
is Huāndōu.
The Lǐjì says: 'Shùn was buried in the wilderness of Cāngwú.'
Though I secretly hold the reins of the state,
grasp royal titles in my hands,
and utter heavenly decrees from my mouth,
Heavenly decrees
are the royal laws;
meaning punishments and executions issue from his mouth.
Xián said: 運 (yùn),
means to act.
The Lúnyǔ says: 'The Jì clan was richer than the Duke of Zhōu.'
噏 (xī),
the same as 吸 (xī).
It is not that I detest glory and love disgrace,
or detest life and love death;
it is merely that I am moved by the disarray of the royal order.
Xián said: 攝 (shè),
means to connect.
I say 攝 (shè)
means to put in order and rectify.
Thus, I pour out my heart in sorrow,
making deep plans for the emperor.
Your servant wishes to be tattooed on the forehead and shackled at the feet,
Xián said: 黥首 (qíng shǒu)
means to carve the forehead and tattoo it with ink.
繫趾 (jì zhǐ)
means to shackle one's feet.
To bind the feet with iron is called 釱 (dài).
to serve."
The emperor read his memorial,
and then pardoned him.
5 Winter,
tenth month.
Grand Commandant Yuán Tāng was dismissed;
Grandee Secretary Hú Guǎng was made Grand Commandant.
Minister of Works Wú Xióng and Grand Secretary Zhào Jiè were dismissed;
Grand Coachman Huáng Qióng was made Minister of Works,
and Superintendent of the Imperial Household Fáng Zhí was made Grand Secretary.
6 The Wǔlíng Man barbarians, led by Zhān Shān and others, rebelled.
Yīng Fèng of Rǔnán, the Grand Administrator of Wǔlíng, persuaded them to surrender.
7 Araduò, King of the Later State of Jūshī, was not on good terms with Yán Hào, the Marquis of the Wù Department.
The Wù and Jǐ Departments each had a colonel,
and each had a departmental marquis.
The Xīyù Zhuàn says: Emperor Hé established the Marquis of the Wù Department,
residing in the city of the Marquis of the Later State of Jūshī.
They attacked and besieged the military farms,
killing and injuring officers and soldiers.
Tànzhē, the Marquis of the Later Department, led the remaining people to rebel against Araduò
and surrendered to the Han officials.
The previous book says: The Later State of Jūshī had a Marquis for Attacking Hu,
who was granted a seal and ribbon by Han.
降 (jiàng),
pronounced as hù jiāng;
the same below.
Araduò fled with over a hundred riders into the Northern Xiōngnú.
Sòng Liàng, the Grand Administrator of Dūnhuáng, memorialized to establish Bēijūn, the hostage son of the former king Jūnjìu, as king.
Later, Araduò returned from the Xiōngnú
and contended with Bēijūn for the kingdom,
gathering many of his countrymen.
The Commander Yán
carefully considered that Araduò's enticing the northern barbarians
would bring chaos to the Western Regions,
so he issued a reassuring proclamation.
開信 (kāi xìn) means
to make a clear and trustworthy statement.
Araduò then went to Yán and surrendered.
Thereupon, Araduò was re-established as king,
and Bēijūn was taken back to Dūnhuáng,
and given three hundred tents of the people of the Later Department.
The Xīyù Zhuàn says: 帳 (zhàng)
is equivalent to
the number of households in China.
將 (jiāng),
as is.
1 Spring,
first month.
On the day of Jiǎwǔ,
a general amnesty was proclaimed.
2 Second month.
On the day of Xīnchǒu,
inspectors and officials with salaries of two thousand dàn were again permitted to observe three years of mourning.
In the first year of Jiànguāng of Emperor Ān,
the observance of three years of mourning was abolished,
as recorded in volume 49.
3 On the day of Guǐmǎo,
there was an earthquake in the capital.
4 Summer,
locusts.
5 Qúshān in Dōnghǎi collapsed.
Xián said: Qúshān is now in Qúshān County, Hǎizhōu, to the south.
6 On the day of Yǐmǎo,
Mǎ Huìzǐchū, the wet nurse, was enfeoffed as a marquis.
7 Autumn,
ninth month.
On the first day of Dīngmǎo,
there was a solar eclipse.
8 Grand Commandant Hú Guǎng was dismissed;
Minister of Works Huáng Qióng was made Grand Commandant.
Intercalary month.
Superintendent of the Imperial Household Yǐn Sòng was made Minister of Works.
9 Winter,
eleventh month.
On the day of Jiǎchén,
the emperor conducted a hunt in the Shànglín Park,
and then proceeded to Hángǔ Guān.
10 Bandits Gōngsūn Jǔ and Dōngguō Dòu and others from Tàishān and Lángyá rebelled,
killing high officials.
Yǒngshòu First Year
(Yǐwèi, 155)
1 Spring,
first month.
On the day of Wùshēn,
a general amnesty was proclaimed,
and the reign era was changed.
2 Second month.
Sīlì and Jìzhōu suffered from famine;
people resorted to cannibalism.
3 The Grand Student Liú Táo (劉陶) submitted a memorial on current affairs, saying:
"Heaven and the Emperor,
the Emperor and the people,
are like the head and the feet;
they depend on each other to function.
Your Majesty's eyes do not see the affairs of Míngtiáo (鳴條),
nor do your ears hear the sound of the tánhcē (檀車).
Xián (賢) says: Míngtiáo (鳴條)
is a place name,
west of Ānyì (安邑).
Tāng (湯) fought Jié (桀) in the plain of Míngtiáo (鳴條).
Tánhcē (檀車)
refers to war chariots.
The Shī (詩) says: 'Tánhcē (檀車) roll with thunder.'
I note that the poem from the Dàyǎ (大雅) 'Dàmíng' (大明) says: 'Mùyě (牧野) was vast and wide,
the tánhcē (檀車) shone bright.
There was Grand Mentor Shàngfù (尚父),
who was like an eagle soaring,
assisting King Wǔ (武),
thus he conquered the great Shāng (商).'
Táo (陶) likely used this 'tán' (檀) event
to say that Jié (桀) and Zhòu (紂), though noble as Sons of Heaven,
offended Heaven
and poisoned the people,
so Tāng (湯) and Wǔ (武) attacked them.
The matters of fallen states do not reach the Emperor's ears and eyes,
so the Emperor does not know to take them as a warning.
Maó Shì Shī Zhuàn (毛氏詩傳) says: 'Tán' (檀)
is a strong and tough wood.
Lù Jī (陸璣) in his commentary says: 'The bark of the tán (檀) tree is pure green,
smooth and lustrous,
similar to jìmí (檕迷).
Also similar to bómǎ (駮馬).'
Bómǎ (駮馬) is zǐqín (梓檎).
Thus the local saying: 'If you cut tán (檀) carelessly, you get jìmí (檕迷);
if you get jìmí (檕迷), you can still get bómǎ (駮馬).'
Jìmí (檕迷)
is also called qiècóng (挈橀).
Thus the Qí (齊) people's proverb says: 'Go up the mountain to cut tán (檀),
qiècóng (挈橀) will be exhausted first.'
This is because tán (檀) wood is strong and tough,
suitable for making war chariots.
'Chān' (嘽)
is pronounced tǔ dān (吐丹).
'Liáng' (涼)
is pronounced lì shàng (力尚).
Earthquakes and eclipses do not immediately harm the sacred body,
'earthquakes and eclipses'
refers to earthquakes and solar eclipses.
[You] lightly regard Heaven's wrath.
I humbly reflect that Gāozǔ (高祖) rose
from commoner status,
gathered the scattered and supported the injured,
successfully established the imperial enterprise,
his diligence was extreme.
He bestowed blessings and bequeathed his inheritance,
down to Your Majesty.
Your Majesty is unable to further illuminate the path of your eminent ancestors,
but instead neglects the diligence of Gāozǔ (高祖).
You recklessly lend powerful instruments,
and hand over the reins of the state,
allowing vile
and ugly convicts
to cut down the common people,
tigers and leopards make lairs in fawns' fields,
jackals suckle in spring pastures.
The wealthy become the souls of the deeply wronged,
the poor and hungry become hungry and cold ghosts.
This means that rich or poor, none die a natural death.
Dù Yù (杜預) says: 'Zhūn' (窀)
means thick.
'Xī' (穸)
means night.
'Thick night'
is like 'long night'.
'Zhūn' (窀)
is pronounced zhū lún (株倫).
This is what your foolish servant laments with deep sorrow and long sighs!
Moreover, when Qín (秦) was about to fall,
those who offered honest remonstrance were executed,
those who flattered were rewarded.
Auspicious words were confined to loyal tongues,
state decrees came from slanderous mouths.
Yán Lè (閻樂) lived in Xiányáng (咸陽),
Zhào Gāo (趙高) was given charge of the imperial carriage house.
Yán Lè (閻樂) was the Magistrate of Xiányáng (咸陽),
Zhào Gāo (趙高) was the Chief of the Imperial Carriage House.
Prestige abandoned them without regret.
Ancient and modern times follow one rule,
success and failure share the same course.
I wish Your Majesty would look back at the fall of the powerful Qín (秦),
and observe the changes in the reigns of Āi (哀) and Píng (平).
The gains and losses are clear,
and the misfortunes and blessings can be seen.
Your servant also hears that danger cannot be supported without benevolence,
and chaos cannot be saved without wisdom.
I secretly observe that the former Inspector of Jìzhōu (冀州), Zhū Mù (朱穆) of Nányáng (南陽), and the former Colonel of the Wūhuán (烏桓), Lǐ Yīng (李膺) of my own commandery,
both uphold righteousness and are upright and impartial,
pure and lofty beyond common ways.
These are truly excellent assistants for a restoration,
and pillar-ministers of the state.
They should be recalled to the imperial court
to assist the royal house.
The year before last, Zhū Mù (朱穆) fell into disgrace,
Lǐ Yīng (李膺) was also dismissed and resided in Lúnshì (綸氏) at that time.
Xián (賢) says: 'Bù shí' (不時)
means not conforming to the times.
It will surely lead to annihilation.
Your servant first grieves for what is lamentable in the world,
and now the world also grieves for your servant's foolishness!"
The memorial was presented,
but not heeded.
4 In summer,
Nányáng (南陽) experienced severe flooding.
5 Sīkōng (司空) Fáng Zhí (房植) was dismissed;
Tàicháng (太常) Hán Yǎn (韓縯) was made Sīkōng (司空).
6 Mountains collapsed in Bā Jùn (巴郡) and Yìzhōujùn (益州郡).
7 In autumn,
the Southern Xiōngnú (匈奴) Zuǒ yùjiān (左薁鞬), Táiqí (臺耆), Qiejú Bódé (且渠伯德) and others rebelled,
plundering Měijì (美稷).
The Eastern Qiāng (羌) tribes again rose in response.
Āndìng Shǔguó Dūwèi (安定屬國都尉), Zhāng Huàn (張奐) of Dūnhuáng (敦煌), had just arrived at his post.
Xián (賢) says: 'Shǔguó Dūwèi (屬國都尉)'
had a rank equivalent to two thousand dàn (石).
The Shuǐjīngzhù (水經註) says: 'The seat of the Āndìng Shǔguó Dūwèi (安定屬國都尉) was in Sānshuǐ (三水) County.'
Upon hearing this,
he immediately led out his troops.
The military officials thought his strength was no match,
and bowed their heads, trying to stop him.
Huàn (奐) did not listen,
and proceeded to garrison Chángchéng (長城).
This is the Great Wall built by Qín (秦)'s Méng Tián (蒙恬),
located in the commandery of Shàngjùn (上郡).
He sent General Wáng Wèi (王衞) to entice the Eastern Qiāng (羌),
and then occupied Guīcí (龜茲) County.
The earlier record states,
'Guīcí (龜茲) County in Shàngjùn (上郡)
was the seat of the Shàngjùn Shǔguó Dūwèi (上郡屬國都尉).'
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: 'People from Guīcí (龜茲) Kingdom who came to surrender were settled here,
hence the name.'
The chieftains of the Eastern Qiāng (羌) then led their followers to jointly attack Yùjiān (薁鞬) and others with Huàn (奐),
defeating them.
Bódé (伯德) was terrified,
and led his multitude to surrender.
The commandery became peaceful.
The Qiāng (羌) chieftains presented Huàn (奐) with twenty horses
and eight jin of gold.
Huàn (奐) poured wine on the ground in front of the Qiāng (羌) people
and said:
"Even if horses were as common as sheep,
I would not accept them into my camp;
even if gold were as common as millet,
I would not take it into my bosom."
He returned it all to them.
Before this, the eight Dūwèi (都尉) were fond of wealth,
which troubled the Qiāng (羌).
But when Huàn (奐) corrected himself and kept himself pure,
none were displeased, and they all submitted willingly.
His moral influence spread widely.
1 In spring,
the third month,
the barbarians of Shǔjùn (蜀郡) Shǔguó (屬國) rebelled.
In the first year of Yánguāng (延光),
the Commander of Shǔjùn (蜀郡) Western Division was made Shǔguó Dūwèi (屬國都尉).
2 Originally,
Tánshíhuái (檀石槐) of the Xiānbēi (鮮卑)
was brave, robust, and had strategic intelligence.
His tribes feared and obeyed him,
so he established laws and prohibitions,
arbitrated disputes fairly,
and no one dared to violate them.
Thus he was elected as Dàrén (大人).
Tánshíhuái (檀石槐) established his court on Mount Táwū (彈汙山) by the Chuòchóu (歠仇) River.
"Wū" (汙)
is written as "Hán" (汗) in Fàn Shū (范書).

Chuò (歠)
is pronounced chāng yuè (昌悅).
His army was very strong;
the Dàrén (大人) of the eastern and western regions all submitted to him.
He then raided the southern borders,
repelled the Dīnglíng (丁零) to the north,
pushed back the Fúyú (夫餘) to the east,
and attacked the Wūsūn (烏孫) to the west,

Autumn,
seventh month,
Tánshíhuái 寇 Yúnzhōng.
Lǐ Yīng, former Commander of the Wūhuán, was appointed General Who Crosses the Liao.
When Yīng arrived at the border,
the Qiāng and Hú were all awed and submitted,

3 Gōngsūn Jǔ, Dōngguō Dòu, and others gathered a multitude of up to thirty thousand people,
raiding the three prefectures of Qīng, Yǎn, and Xú,

They were attacked for several years,
but could not be overcome.
The Department of State Affairs selected someone capable of governing a difficult region,

治,
zhí zhī fān.
掾,
yú juàn fān.
長,
zhī liǎng fān.

Over ten thousand households of displaced people from other counties entered the county's borders;

主者 means
the officials in charge of the granary's grain.
"Even if I save those in the ditches,

長,

4 In the beginning,
when the Xiānbēi raided Liáodōng,
Duàn Jiǒng, the Commandant of the Dependent State, led his troops to rush to their aid.
Later, fearing the bandits would be alarmed and flee,

Jiǒng pretended to retreat on the road,

Jiǒng then unleashed his troops in a major offensive,

and was due to receive a heavy penalty;
due to his merits,
he was sentenced to Sīkòu;
after the punishment was completed,

a two-year prison sentence.
璽,
sī shì fān.

Sīkòu Yǐn Sòng recommended Jiǒng.
Duàn Jiǒng's biography writes

"Sòng" (頌);
writing
"Sòng" (頌)
is correct.
He attacked Jǔ, Dòu, and others,

1 Spring,
first month,

According to the Commentary on the Zhōu Lǐ: Zhèng Zhòng (鄭衆) said: "The six palaces are one empress in front and five behind."
Among the king's 120 women: one empress (hòu),

is a word for concealment.
The empress mirrors the king;

The fūrén and below

the remaining three nine-pín concubines,
nine shìfù,
and twenty-seven nǚyù

Those who attend the empress

Fūrén are like the Sān Gōng (三公);

This is what the rites refer to as
"being arranged to be attended by the king at the appropriate time."
Zhèng Xuán (鄭玄) also said: "Generally, the method of presentation for imperial attendance
is symbolized by the moon and the empress;
the lower-ranked should be first,
and the higher-ranked should be later.
The eighty-one nǚyù account for nine nights,
the twenty-seven shìfù account for three nights,
the nine pín account for one night,
the three fūrén account for one night,
and the empress accounts for one night,
completing a full cycle every fifteen days.
After the full moon, the cycle reverses."
According to what the two Zhèngs said,

In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the day of Bǐngwǔ,
Empress Liáng (Liáng Shì) passed away.
On the day of Yǐchǒu,
Empress Yìxiàn was buried at Yìlíng.
Xián (賢) said: "In the posthumous naming system (shìfǎ): 'gentle, harmonious, sacred, and good' is called Yì (懿);
'intelligent, bright, and wise' is called Xiàn (獻)."
The Liáng Jì family,
successively had seven marquises,
three empresses.
Jì's ancestor, Yōng 雍, was enfeoffed as Chéngshì Hóu 乘氏侯.
Jì 冀 was enfeoffed as Xiāngyì Hóu 襄邑侯.
Later he inherited the title of Chéngshì Hóu 乘氏侯,
and also enfeoffed his son Yìn 胤 as Xiāngyì Hóu 襄邑侯,
his younger brother Bùyí 不疑 as Yǐngyáng Hóu 潁陽侯,
Méng 蒙 as Xīpíng Hóu 西平侯.
Bùyí's 不疑 son Mǎ 馬 was Yǐngyīn Hóu 潁陰侯.
Yìn's 胤 son Táo 桃 was Chéngfù Hóu 城父侯.
These are the seven enfeoffed marquises.
The three empresses were Gōnghuái Gōnghuái 恭懷, Shùnliè Shùnliè 順烈, and Yìxiàn Yìxiàn 懿獻.
There were two Grand Generals,
seven ladies and daughters who were granted fiefs and titles of "Jūn" 君,
three who married princesses,
and the rest, fifty-seven in total, were Ministers (Qīng 卿), Generals (Jiàng 將), Prefects (Yǐn 尹), or Commandants (Xiào 校).
Qīng 卿
refers to the Nine Ministers (Jiǔ Qīng 九卿).
Jiàng 將
refers to the Commandant of Cavalry (Zhōnglángjiàng 中郎將).
Yǐn 尹
refers to the Prefects of Hénán 河南 and Jīngzhào 京兆.
Xiào 校
refers to various Commandants (Xiàowèi 校尉).
Xiào 校,
pronounced as "hù jiào".
Liáng Jì's 梁冀
fierce and unrestrained arrogance grew daily.
He planted his trusted associates
throughout the palace guards and among the close attendants,
Xián 賢 says: Shù 樹 means "to set up".
Even the smallest details were known to him.
When supplies were requisitioned from all directions
or tributes were offered seasonally,
all the finest items
were first delivered to Jì 冀.
Xián 賢 says: Shàngdì 上第 means "the first rank".
Officials and common people who carried goods to seek office or request pardon for crimes
filled the roads,
stretching as far as the eye could see.
Qǐng zuì 請罪 refers to requesting to be exempted from punishment.
All of them first arrived at Jì's 冀 gate
with written petitions (jiānxi 牋檄) to express their gratitude.
The dictionary says: Jiān 牋
means "memorial,"
"note,"
"letter."
In the biography of Zuǒ Xióng 左雄,
it is said that civil officials were evaluated by their memorials (jiānzòu 牋奏).
Speaking from later generations,
zòu 奏 was used to report to the Son of Heaven,
jiān 牋 was used for the empress's palace, the crown prince's palace, and for addressing generals, prime ministers, and high ministers,
and xí 檄 was used for summoning and transmitting orders.
It was not for expressing gratitude.
My thorough understanding is that after Cài Lún 蔡倫 invented paper,
writings on paper were called jiān 牋,
and writings on wood were called xí 檄.
Therefore, it says "jiānxi 牋檄 to express gratitude."
Wú Shù 吳樹 of Xiàpī 下邳 was appointed Prefect of Wǎn 宛.
When he left for his post, he bid farewell to Jì 冀.
Jì's 冀 retainers were spread throughout the county,
and they entrusted their concerns to Shù 樹.
Shù 樹 said:
"These petty men are treacherous parasites;
every household could be punished.
As a sagacious general, you occupy the position of a supreme commander,
and you should promote the worthy and virtuous to fill the gaps in the court.
Since I have been in attendance,
I have not heard you praise a single worthy person,
but you have entrusted many to unworthy individuals.
This is truly something I dare not hear!"
Jì 冀 was silent and displeased.
When Shù 樹 arrived at the county,
he proceeded to execute dozens of Jì's 冀 retainers who had harmed people.
Later, Shù 樹 became Inspector of Jīngzhōu 荊州.
When he bid farewell to Jì 冀,
Jì 冀 poisoned him.
He left,
and died in his carriage.
Hóu Měng 侯猛, the Administrator of Liáodōng 遼東, when first appointed,
did not pay respects to Jì 冀.
Jì 冀 falsely accused him of another matter and had him cut in half at the waist.
Yuán Zhù 袁著 of Rǔnán 汝南, a Gentleman of the Interior,
at nineteen years old,
went to the palace gate and submitted a memorial, saying:
"Indeed, in the cycle of the four seasons,
once success is achieved, one should withdraw,
this is the saying of Cài Zé 蔡澤.
Few avoid disaster.
Now the Grand General's position is at its peak and his achievements complete,
this can serve as a great warning.
It is advisable to follow the ritual of 'withdrawing the carriage,'
and 'rest with a high pillow,' nourishing your spirit.
The Analects say: 'When a tree's fruits are too numerous, its branches will break, harming its heart.'
Fàn Suī 范睢 said: 'When a tree grows too densely, its branches spread out,
and when its branches spread out, its heart is wounded.'
You will not be able to preserve your own body!"
Jì 冀 heard this and secretly sent men to arrest him.
Zhù 著 then changed his name,
feigned illness and pretended to die.
He wove reeds into a human figure,
bought a coffin, and arranged a funeral procession.
Jì 冀 knew it was a trick,
sought him out and found him,
and then had him flogged to death.
Hǎo Jié 郝絜 and Hú Wǔ 胡武 of Tàiyuán 太原,
fond of dangerous words and lofty discussions,
were good friends with Zhù 著.
Jié 絜 and Wǔ 武 once jointly submitted a memorial to the Three Ducal Ministers,
recommending eminent scholars from across the land,
but did not visit Jì 冀.
Jì 冀, still angry,
ordered the Metropolitan Prefecture Office to issue a summons to capture them.
The Commander of the Capital (Sīlì Xiàowèi 司隸校尉) was in charge of the Metropolitan Prefecture Office with 1,200 convicts.
Jì 冀 probably ordered the Metropolitan Prefecture Administrator (Dūguān Cóngshì 都官從事) to issue the summons to capture them.
Over sixty people died.
Jié 絜 initially fled,
but knowing he could not escape,
he then had a coffin carried to Jì's 冀 gate and submitted a memorial.
After the memorial was taken in,
he swallowed poison and died.
His family was then spared.
When Empress Ān's 安嫡母, Noble Lady Gěng 耿貴人, passed away,
Jì 冀 requested precious items from Noble Lady Gěng's 耿貴人 cousin, Chéng 承, Marquis of Línlǜ 林慮.
Unable to obtain them,
Jì 冀 became angry
and executed over ten people from his entire clan.
Cuī Qí 崔琦 of Zhuōjùn 涿郡 was well-regarded by Jì 冀 for his literary talent.
Qí 琦 wrote the "Exhortation for Empress's Relatives" (Wàiqī Zhēn 外戚箴) and "Rhapsody on a White Swan" (Báihú Fù 白鵠賦) to subtly admonish him.
The "Exhortation for Empress's Relatives" (Wàiqī Zhēn 外戚箴) says:
"Illustrious empress's relatives,
their splendor and favor resplendent.
In ancient times, during Emperor Shùn's 帝舜 reign,
virtue was magnified by Yīng 瑛 and Huáng 皇. The Zhōu 周 dynasty rose with three mothers,
Yǒuxīn 有莘 elevated Tāng 湯.
King Xuān 宣王 rose late,
Queen Jiāng 姜后 removed her hairpin.
Duke Huán 桓 of Qí 齊 loved music,
Lady Wèi 衞姬 remained silent.
All assisted their lords with propriety,
supported their rulers with benevolence,
promoted talent and advanced goodness,
using righteousness to save themselves.
Down to later generations,
things gradually decayed and declined.
The fish-like order was broken,
the nine concubines in disarray.
The disaster of the state of Jìn 晉,
calamity arose from Lì 麗.
The utter ruin of the family,
the hen crowing at dawn.
Monopolizing power and indulging in love,
exalting oneself and obscuring others,
oppressing elders and alienating old friends,
destroying and stripping close relatives.
Setting up empresses in parallel and equals to the principal wife,
the licentious woman brought about the death of Chén 陳.
Those who were not virtuous were exalted,
becoming Ministers of Education.
Carrying honor and riding in state,
enjoying the revenues of famous cities.
People of the time criticized them,
their virtue was not admirable.
Tyrant Xīn 辛 was infatuated with women,
rejecting remonstrance and isolating himself.
With a viper's heart,
he unleashed poison upon the innocent.
He killed his uncles,
and disemboweled pregnant women.
Heaven was enraged and Earth indignant,
men plotted and ghosts schemed.
On the morning of Jiǎzǐ 甲子,
body and head were separated.
He was initially the Son of Heaven,
then became a mere human monster in autumn.
It was not only indulging in lust,
but empress dowagers were especially so.
They did not guide each other with propriety,
but competed to encourage power,
laughing first and weeping later,
eventually ending in disgrace and destruction.
Families and states perished,
ancestral temples burned.
Mòxī 妺喜 ruined Xià 夏,
Bāosì 褒姒 brought down Zhōu 周,
Dájǐ 妲己 destroyed Yīn 殷,
and Zhào Língwáng 赵灵王 was at Shāqiū 沙丘.
Consort Qī 戚姬 was made a human swine,
and the Lǚ 呂 clan was destroyed because of it.
Empress Chén 陳后 practiced sorcery,
and eventually died in exile.
Huò 霍 desired to poison her son,
but she herself suffered ruin.
Therefore it is said,
'Do not claim your nobility,
Heaven will humble you.'
'Do not rely on constant favor,
beauty has its ebb and decline.'
'Do not cling to perpetual good fortune,'
Love can wane;
do not say "I am capable,"
for you violate heaven and man.
Calamity arises from a lack of virtue;
blessings come from careful timing.
The sun does not always stay at its zenith;
the moon, when full, has its wane.
Those who adhere to the Dao are secure;
those who rely on power are in peril.
Your humble servant, who manages the imperial family,
dares to declare this. "
These admonitions deeply convey the dangers of imperial relatives,
thus they are fully recorded here.
Hū,

Fèng,

In the eighth month,

Yùn,

Jì and his wife, Shòu, both committed suicide on that very day;

All the relatives of the Liáng and Sūn clans, both internal and external, were arrested and sent to the imperial prison.
Regardless of age, all were executed in the marketplace;

Tàiwèi Hú Guǎng, Sītú Hán Yǎn, and Sīkōng Sūn Lǎng were all implicated for flattering Liáng Jì,
and not guarding the palace,

Their death sentences were commuted by one degree,

More than three hundred former officials and retainers were dismissed and degraded;
the imperial court was left empty.
At this time,
the events suddenly erupted from within,

and the government offices and markets were in an uproar.
It was only after several days that order was restored;

Jì's wealth and goods were confiscated,
and the county officials sold them off,

The land tax and rent throughout the empire were reduced by half.
His imperial gardens and parks were counted,

On the 7th day, the rénwǔ day,

The emperor disliked the Liáng clan,
