and its introductory preface also narrates his flight and hardship.
3 In the intercalary month,
the remaining Qīng Qiāng tribes, along with the great chieftain Shāohé, again raided Zhāngyè.
In the morning,
they approached Commandant Duàn Jiǒng's army.
Jiǒng dismounted and fought fiercely.
By midday, his saber was broken and his arrows exhausted,
and the barbarians also retreated.
Jiǒng pursued them,
fighting and marching,
attacking day and night,
cutting meat to eat with snow,
for over forty days.
They finally reached Jīshí Shān.
The *Jùn Guó Zhì* says: Jīshí Shān
is southwest of Héguān County, Lǒngxī Commandery.
Xián said: Jīshí Shān
is south of present-day Lóngzhī County, Shànzhōu.
The *Yǔ Gòng* says: Yu guides the Hé from Jīshí,
this is it.
They beheaded the great chieftain Shāohé,
accepted the surrender of his remaining followers, and returned.
4 In summer,
the fifth month,
on the day Jiǎxū,
a mountain in Hànzhōng collapsed.
5 In the sixth month,
on the day Xīnchǒu,
the Minister of Works, Zhù Tián, passed away.
6 In autumn,
the seventh month,
Shèng Yǔn, the Grand Minister of Agriculture, was appointed Minister of Works,
and Yú Fàng, the Grand Master of Ceremonies, was appointed Grand Minister of Agriculture.
7 The Mán of Chángshā rebelled,
stationing themselves at Yìyáng.
The Mán of Línglíng raided Chángshā.
8 The remaining bandits of Jiǔzhēn occupied Rìnán,
and their numbers grew stronger.
An edict re-appointed Xià Fāng, Administrator of Guìyáng, as Inspector of Jiāozhǐ.
Fāng's prestige and benevolence were well-known.
In winter, the eleventh month,
over twenty thousand bandits from Rìnán
came in groups to Fāng and surrendered.
9 The Lèjiě and Língwú tribes of Qiāng besieged Yǔnjiē.
Duàn Jiǒng attacked and defeated them.
The bandits of Tài-Shān, Shū-Sūn Wú-Jì, attacked and killed the Commandant Hóu Zhāng;
Zhōng-Láng-Jiàng Zōng Zī was dispatched to suppress and defeat them.
An imperial edict summoned Huáng-Fǔ Guī,
who was appointed Tài-Shān Tàishǒu.
Upon arriving at his post,
Guī extensively implemented strategies,
and the bandits and rebels were all pacified.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the day Xīn-Yǒu,
the Jiā-Dé Hall in the Nán-Gōng caught fire;
on the day Wù-Zǐ,
the Bǐng-Shǔ caught fire.
The Bǎi-Guān-Zhì states: The Bǐng-Shǔ had seven chiefs,
with a salary of four hundred shí of grain,
wearing yellow ribbons,
and eunuchs served as their officials.
They were in charge of the empress's separate quarters.
2 There was a great plague.
3 In the second month,
on the day Rén-Chén,
the Wǔ-Kù caught fire.
4 Sī-Tú Shèng Yǔn was dismissed,
and Dà-Sī-Nóng Zhǒng Gǎo was appointed Sī-Tú.
The Kǎo-Yì states: Yuán's record places this in the previous year.
However, after Zhù Tián's death, there was Shèng Yǔn,
and after Yǔn's dismissal,
Gǎo became Sī-Tú;
a period of half a year separated these events,
so Yuán's record is incorrect.
We now follow Fàn's book.
5 In the third month,
Tài-Wèi Huáng Qióng was dismissed;
in summer,
the fourth month,
Tàicháng, Liú Jǔ of Pèi-Guó, was appointed Tài-Wèi.
Initially,
Jǔ was the magistrate of Yōng-Qiū.
Yōng-Qiū
belonged to Chén-Liú Jùn,
which was a former state.
Whenever there were litigants,
he would always bring them before him,
pull their ears and instruct them,
saying that anger and resentment could be tolerated,
but one should not enter the county yámen,
and he would send them home to reconsider.
The litigants, moved by this,
would each withdraw and leave.
6 On the day Jiǎ-Yín,
Bó, the son of King Xiào of Hé-Jiān and Marquis of Sān-Hù-Tíng, was enfeoffed as King of Rèn-Chéng,
to continue the lineage of King Xiào.
Xián says: Dù Yù's commentary on the Zuǒ-Zhuàn states: "North of the present Dān-Shuǐ county, there is Sān-Hù-Tíng;
its old city is in the southwest of the present Nèi-Xiāng county, Dèng-Zhōu."
In the first year of Yuán-Jiā,
King Chóng of Rèn-Chéng died without an heir,
and the state was abolished.
Now Bó is enfeoffed to continue the lineage.
King Xiào of Hé-Jiān was Kāi.
King Xiào of Rèn-Chéng was Shàng.
7 In the fifth month,
on the day Xīn-Yǒu,
a comet appeared in the constellation Xīn.
The Jìn-Shū Tiān-Wén-Zhì states: "The three stars of Xīn: the middle star is called Míng-Táng,
the position of the Son of Heaven;
the front star is the Crown Prince;
the rear star is the common son."
Bèi (孛) means "a comet."
8 On the day Dīng-Mǎo,
the Cháng-Shòu Gate of the Yuán-Líng caught fire.
The Yuán-Líng was the tomb of Guāng-Wǔ.
9 On the day Jǐ-Mǎo,
it hailed in the capital.
10 In the sixth month,
Jīng-Zhào, Fú-Fēng, and Liáng-Zhōu experienced earthquakes.
11 On the day Gēng-Zǐ,
Tài-Shān and Bó Yóu-Lái-Shān both collapsed and split.
Tài-Shān is northwest of Bó county.
Xián says: Cú-Lái-Shān is also called Yóu-Lái-Shān.
Bó is the present Bó-Chéng county.
"I base this on the fact that both mountains are within the borders of Bó county,
and Tài-Shān is mentioned first;
the reason Yóu-Lái-Shān is linked to Bó is that
everyone knows Tài-Zōng (Tài-Shān),
but it is possible that some might not know that Yóu-Lái-Shān is in Bó county,
hence the writing style is thus."
12 On the day Jǐ-Yǒu,
there was a general amnesty.
13 Sī-Kōng Yú Fàng was dismissed,
and former Tài-Wèi Huáng Qióng was appointed Sī-Kōng.
14 The Yi of Qián-Wéi Shǔ-Guó raided the common people.
In the first year of Yǒng-Chū,
the southern commandant of Qián-Wéi was made the commandant of Qián-Wéi Shǔ-Guó,
overseeing the two counties of Zhū-Tí and Hàn-Yáng.
15 The Líng-Wú Qiāng and various Xiān-Líng tribes rebelled,
raiding Sān-Fǔ.
16 In autumn,
the seventh month,
there was a rain-making ceremony in the capital.
The Gōng-Yáng-Zhuàn says: "Yú (雩) is a sacrifice for drought."
17 The stipends of the Gōng-Qīng and lower officials were reduced,
and half the rent was borrowed from kings and marquises.
Kǒng Yǐng-Dá says:
"Yǐ" (已)
and
"Yǐ" (以)
were originally the same character.
Hóng's Lì-Shì says: Mèng Yù, the Tàishǒu of Jì-Yīn, repaired the Yáo Temple Stele,
and its text includes
"not for displaying divine holiness" (非所以表神聖),
and
"to sacrifice with one grand animal in spring and autumn" (以一太牢春秋秩祠),
and
"thus followers of the Dao gathered from distant lands" (是以好道之徒自遠方集);
all these characters are written as
It also says
"already manifested sacred virtue" (已章聖德),
and
"to strengthen our virtue,
to encourage our benevolence" (敦我已德，厲我已仁);
these characters are all written as
"Yǐ" (已) and "Yǐ" (以) have the same meaning,
but their character structures are different;
this is sufficient to know that from Han to Tang,
the two characters 已 and 以 were used interchangeably.
Fèng (奉) means "stipend."
Tuò (貣) means "to borrow,"
a loanword.
Hǔ-Bēn, Yǔ-Lín Tí-Qí, camp soldiers, and the Wǔ-Dà-Fū each had varying amounts of money.
18 In the ninth month,
Sī-Kōng Huáng Qióng was dismissed,
and Dà-Hóng-Lú Liú Chǒng of Dōng-Lái was appointed Sī-Kōng.
Chǒng had served as the Tàishǒu of Kuài-Jī.
He simplified and eliminated excessive regulations,
prohibited and investigated illegal activities,
and the prefecture was greatly well-governed;
he was summoned to be Jiàng-Zuò-Dà-Jiàng.
In Shān-Yīn county, there were five or six old men
who emerged from the valleys of Mount Ruò-Yé.
Xián says: Ruò-Yé is in the southeast of the present Kuài-Jī county, Yuè-Zhōu.
Yé is read as 'yē'.
(They said,) "We, crude men from the mountain valleys,
have never known the prefectural court.
During the time of other prefects,
officials would demand things from the common people,
ceaselessly until night,
and dogs would bark all night,
so the people could not rest.
Since you, our bright lord, took office,
dogs do not bark at night,
and the people do not see officials.
We are old and have encountered such enlightened governance.
Now we hear that you are to leave,
so we have come to support ourselves and bid you farewell."
Chǒng said:
"How can my governance be as you say!
My hard-working elders!"
He chose one large coin for them and accepted it.
The Qían-Qīng town, forty-five lǐ west of the present Yuè-Zhōu city,
is where the elders bade Chǒng farewell.
In the winter of the 19th year [of Yánxī, 176 CE],
the Xiānlíng and Shěndī Qiāng, along with various other Qiāng bandits, plundered and occupied Bìng and Liáng provinces.
Commandant Duàn Gǒng led the Yìcóng from Huángzhōng to suppress them.
In Huángzhōng, there were Yìcóng Hú,
who were the Xiǎo Yuèzhī Hú.
Cóng,
pronounced cái yòng.
They were held fast in Gǒng's army.
Xián said: Jīgù,
means to remain or stay.
The Yìcóng, having served for a long time, yearned for their homes and old ways,
and all revolted and returned.
Guō Hóng attributed the blame to Gǒng,
and Gǒng was summoned, imprisoned,
and sentenced to forced labor at the Zuǒxiào.
Hú Hóng, the Administrator of Jìnán, replaced him as commandant.
Hú Hóng lacked prestige and strategy,
so the Qiāng became even more unruly,
overturning and capturing encampments and forts.
They recruited and joined forces with each other,
raiding various commanderies,
and the bandit menace grew stronger.
Huángfǔ Guī, the Administrator of Tàishān, submitted a memorial stating:
"Now the cunning bandits are almost eradicated,
and Tàishān is largely pacified.
I hear again that the various Qiāng have all revolted.
I grew up in Bīnqí,
and am fifty-nine years old.
In the past, as a commandery official,
I twice experienced Qiāng rebellions,
and in planning for these matters,
I made some accurate predictions.
This refers to knowing that Mǎ Xián would certainly be defeated. The event is found in volume fifty-two, during the fifth year of Yǒnghé under Emperor Shùn.
Gēng,
pronounced gōng héng.
Zhòng,
pronounced zhú zhòng.
Fearing that my dog and horse years will end [my life will run out] without repaying the great imperial favor,
I wish to request a supernumerary position,
to serve as a single envoy with one cart,
to bring comfort and reassurance to the Sānfǔ,
to proclaim the nation's power and benevolence,
and to assist the various armies with my knowledge of topography and military strategy.
Living in a precarious and isolated situation,
I have observed the commandery generals for several decades.
From Niǎoshǔ to Dōngdài,
their ailment is one and the same."
Xián said: Jùn jiàng,
means commandery governor.
Niǎoshǔ,
is a mountain name,
west of present-day Wèizhōu,
which is where the Xiānlíng Qiāng plundered.
Dōngdài refers to Tàishān,
where Shūsūn Wúfú revolted.
All these problems are caused by commandery governors failing to pacify and soothe the populace,
leading to revolts.
Their ailment is one and the same.
The Éryǎ Yì says: In the midst of Niǎoshǔ Tóngxué,
the Wèishuǐ river originates;
its bird is the tú,
and its mouse is the tuō.
The tuō resembles a domestic mouse but with a short tail,
the tú resembles a quail but is smaller,
yellowish-black,
burrowing three to four chi deep into the ground,
with the mouse inside [the burrow]
and the bird outside.
It is in Shǒuyáng county of Lǒngxī.
The Shāzhōu Jì says: Hánlǐng is thirty lǐ from Tàiyángchuān,
and there is a mountain called Niǎoshǔ Tóngxué Zhī Shān.
Jiàng,
pronounced jì liàng.
"It is better to have peace and order;
diligently studying Sūn Wú's [art of war]
is not as good as upholding the law."
Xián said: This means that if you seek a fierce enemy,
it is not as good as pacifying them with policies of peace and order;
being skilled in military treatises
is not as good as commandery governors upholding the law,
preventing them from revolting.
"I am truly grieved by this."
Xián said: Qī,
means worry.
The former change,
refers to the Qiāng revolt.
An edict appointed Guī as Zhōngláng Jiàng,
holding the staff of authority to supervise the Guānxī army and suppress the Língwú and others.
In the eleventh month,
Guī attacked the Qiāng,
defeating them and beheading eight hundred.
The various Xiānlíng Qiāng tribes admired Guī's prestige and trustworthiness,
encouraging each other to surrender, with over ten thousand doing so.
In the 1st year [of Xīpíng, 172 CE], spring,
in the first month,
on the day Rénwǔ, the Nángōng Bǐngshǔ caught fire.
In the 2nd year, third month,
the Shěndī Qiāng raided Zhāngyè and Jiǔquán.
Huángfǔ Guī dispatched the various Xiānlíng Qiāng tribes
to jointly attack Lǒngyòu,
but the roads were cut off,
and a great epidemic broke out in the army,
killing three or four tenths of the men.
Guī personally entered the thatched huts.
Ān,
a thatched cottage.
Lú,
a temporary shelter.
Máo Huǎng said: A structure made of interwoven grass and wood is called ān; when in the wilderness, it is called lú.
The entire army was moved and pleased.
The Eastern Qiāng then sent envoys to surrender,
and Liángzhōu was once again accessible.
Previously, Sūn Jùn, the Administrator of Āndìng, had engaged in rampant corruption.
Lǐ Xī, the Dūwèi of Shǔguó, and Zhāng Bǐng, the Dūjūn Yùshǐ, had killed many surrendered Qiāng.
Lǐ Xī,
was probably the Dūwèi of the Āndìng Shǔguó,
however, the record does not mention Āndìng Shǔguó.
As a Censor overseeing the army,
he was therefore called Dūjūn Yùshǐ.
Xiān,
pronounced xí jiàn.
The Éryǎ Yì says: Láng,
is a fierce meat-eating beast;
when things are piled up in disorder,
it is called lángjí.
They all relied on powerful and influential figures,
and did not follow the laws.
When Guī arrived,
he itemized and impeached their crimes,
some were dismissed, some executed;
when the Qiāng people heard this,
they all spontaneously reformed.
The great chieftains of the Shěndī, Diānchāng, Jītián, and others, numbering over one hundred thousand people, again came to Guī to surrender.
In the 3rd year, summer,
in the fourth month,
bandits arose in Chángshā,
raiding Guìyáng and Cāngwú.
On the day Yǐchǒu,
the Eastern Que of Gōnglíng caught fire.
Gōnglíng,
is Emperor Ān's mausoleum.
On the day Wùchén,
the Hǔbēn Yèmén caught fire.
In the fifth month,
the Kānglíng Yuánqǐn caught fire.
Kānglíng,
is Emperor Shāng's mausoleum.
Bandits from Chángshā and Línglíng entered Guìyáng, Cāngwú, and Nánhǎi.
The Cìshǐ of Jiāozhǐ and the Tàishǒu of Cāngwú fled at the mere rumor.
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Shèng Xiū was dispatched to supervise the commanderies and prefectures in recruiting troops to suppress them,
but they could not overcome them.
On the day Yǐhài,
there was an earthquake in the capital.
On the day Jiǎshēn,
the Lùshǔ of the Zhōngzàng Fǔchéng caught fire.
The Bǎiguān Zhì says: The Zhōngzàng Fǔ
managed the imperial treasury's silks, gold, silver, and various goods.
On the day Jǐwèi,
the Nángōng Chéngshàntà caught fire.
The Wūwú Qiāng raided Hànyáng.
Troops from Lǒngxī, Jīnchéng, and other commanderies attacked and defeated them.
9 Thieves from Ài Xiàn attacked the commanderies of Chángshā.
Ài Xiàn
belonged to Yùzhāng Commandery.
Xián said: The old city was in what is now Jiànchāng Xiàn of Hóng Zhōu.
According to records, what is now Fēnnìng in Hóng Zhōu
was originally the Hàn Ài Xiàn.
Also, according to Sòng Bái’s Xù Tōngdiǎn: Fēnnìng Xiàn was originally Wǔníng Xiàn,
and Wǔníng Xiàn was originally Hàn Xī’ān Xiàn.
Xī’ān Xiàn
was established in the Jiàn’ān period of the Later Hàn, by dividing off from Hǎihūn Xiàn;
while Jiànchāng Xiàn was established in the Yǒngyuán period by dividing off from Hǎihūn,
which was before Jiàn’ān.
At that time,
Ài Xiàn still existed.
In the second year of Yuánjiā of the Sòng dynasty,
Hǎihūn was abolished and Jiànchāng was moved there.
The old city of Ài was within the borders of Jiànchāng,
so Xián’s commentary is correct.
The rebels numbered over ten thousand people.
The Palace Attendant Mǎ Mù supervised Liú Dù, the Inspector of Jīng Zhōu, in attacking them.
The army was defeated,
and Mù and Dù fled.
The Mán of Línglíng also revolted.
In the winter, tenth month,
the Mán of Wǔlíng revolted,
plundering Jiānglíng.
Lǐ Sù, the Administrator of Nán Commandery, fled.
Hú Shuǎng, the Chief Clerk, clutched his horse’s head and remonstrated, saying:
“The Mányí see that the commandery is unprepared,
and so dare to seize the opportunity and advance.
My lord is a great minister of the state,
with a thousand *lǐ* of linked cities,
raising flags and beating drums,
ten thousand would respond to your call.
How can you abandon the heavy responsibility of your seals and command,
and become a fugitive!?”
Sù drew his blade towards Shuǎng and said:
“Officer, hurry and go!
The Administrator is in dire straits now,
how can there be time for such advice!”
Shuǎng embraced the horse and insisted on his remonstrance.
Sù then killed Shuǎng and fled.
When the Emperor heard of it,
he summoned Sù,
and had him executed in the marketplace.
Dù and Mù had their sentences reduced by one degree from death.
Shuǎng’s gate and residence were restored,
and one person from his family was appointed as a Gentleman.
Shàngshū Zhū Mù recommended Dù Shàng of Shānyáng, the Right Director of Works, to be Inspector of Jīng Zhōu.
The Right Director of Works
was in charge of the right-wing artisans,
with a salary of six hundred *dàn* of grain,
and was subordinate to the Grand Architect.
Zhào Míngchéng’s Jīnshí Lù contains a stele for Dù Shàng, the Inspector of Jīng Zhōu, which states: His ancestors came from Zhuānxù,
and shared the same surname as Chǔ,
being descendants of Xióng Quē.
It also says: They governed the laws and regulations of the state.
According to Yuánhé Xìngzuǎn: Ancient officials in charge of *dù* (measurements/regulations)
adopted this as their clan name,
it does not say they shared the same surname as Chǔ.
On the day Xīnchǒu,
Fēng Gǔn, the Grand Master of Ceremonies, was appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry,
and led over ten thousand soldiers to attack the Wǔlíng Mán.
Previously,
the generals and commanders who were dispatched often had their military funds embezzled by eunuchs,
and were frequently condemned for it.
Gǔn requested that one Palace Regular Attendant supervise military expenses.
Shàngshū Zhū Mù memorialized,
“Gǔn, by being suspicious of money,
has lost the propriety of a great minister.”
An imperial edict ordered no impeachment.
Gǔn requested Yìng Fèng, the former Administrator of Wǔlíng, to accompany him,
and appointed him Aide-de-camp.
When a general goes on campaign, the Aide-de-camp participates in planning and deliberation.
When Gǔn’s army reached Chángshā,
the rebels heard of it,
and all came to the camp to beg for surrender.
He then attacked the Wǔlíng Mányí,
beheading over four thousand,
and accepting the surrender of over one hundred thousand people.
Jīng Zhōu was pacified.
An imperial edict bestowed a hundred million cash,
but he steadfastly declined to accept it.
He marched his troops back to the capital,
attributed the success to Yìng Fèng,
and recommended him as Colonel Director of Retainers.
He then submitted a memorial requesting to retire due to old age,
but the court did not permit it.
10 The Diānnà Qiāng plundered Wǔwēi, Zhāngyè, and Jiǔquán.
11 Liú Jǔ, the Grand Commandant, was dismissed.
Yáng Bǐng, the Grand Master of Ceremonies, was appointed Grand Commandant.
12 Huángfǔ Guī, holding the imperial credential, acted as a general.
Returning to supervise his home area,
he neither showed private favoritism,
but made many impeachments,
and also detested eunuchs,
not associating with them.
Consequently, both the court and external factions resented him,
and thus conspired to falsely accuse Guī of bribing the Qiāng,
making them perform a fake surrender.
Xián said: This means a superficial surrender based on official records,
not a sincere one.
*Jiàng*,
read *hù jiāng fān*.
Guī submitted a memorial defending himself, saying:
“In the autumn of the fourth year,
the barbarian hordes were stirring and rebellious.
Xián said: *Chǔn*,
means movement.
*Lì*,
means contrary.
The old capital,
refers to Cháng’ān.
Your subject brought forth the awe-inspiring power of the state,
and the Qiāng and Róng bowed their heads.
The expenses saved amounted to over one hundred million.
Considering the duty of a loyal subject not to boast of effort,
the Xiǎo Yǎ of the Shī Jīng says: 'Diligently engage in affairs,
dare not boast of effort,
without fault or crime,
slanderous mouths clamor.'
However, comparing this to previous events,
Xián said: Previous events,
refers to the defeated generals of earlier generations.
Earlier, when I entered the provincial borders,
I first impeached Sūn Jùn, Lǐ Xī, and Zhāng Bǐng;
upon returning from the southern campaign,
I further impeached Guō Hóng and Zhào Xī,
detailing their transgressions and wickedness,
and holding them accountable for capital punishment.
All these five officials,
their factions constituted half the nation.
As for the officials with black seals, down to the petty clerks,
those implicated numbered over a hundred.
Officials used the resentment of reporting generals.
The Administrator was called the Commander of the Commandery.
*Fù*,
read *fú yòu fān*.
*Jiāng*,
read *jí liàng fān*.
They carried gifts and rode in chariots,
packed provisions and walked,
conspiring with powerful families,
competitively spreading slanders and calumnies,
claiming that your subject privately rewarded the Qiāng,
repaying them with money and goods.
If your subject used private funds,
then my household would have nothing to carry.
If the goods came from the government,
then the accounts would be easy to verify.
Even if your subject were foolish and confused,
and it were as the accusers say,
previous generations still gave palace ladies to the Xiongnú.
This refers to Emperor Yuán bestowing Wáng Zhāojūn upon Hūhánxié Chányú.
*Yí*,
read *yú jì fān*.
This refers to Emperor Wǔ marrying Xìjūn, daughter of Jiāngdū King Jiàn, to Kūnmò, King of Wūsūn.
Then what crime, disloyalty, or unreasonableness
would there be in such talent and strategy of a good minister,
which is valued by military strategists!
Since Yǒngchū,
not a few generals have been dispatched,
and five armies have been destroyed.
This refers to Dèng Zhì’s defeat in western Jì,
Rèn Shàng’s defeat at Píngxiāng,
Sīmǎ Jūn’s defeat at Dīngxī Chéng,
Mǎ Xián’s defeat at Shègū Shān,
and Zhào Chōng’s defeat at Zhānyīn Hé.
There are those who returned with their chariots and seals intact,
Xián said: This means that generals whose armies were destroyed,
on the day of their return,
carried many treasures,
with their seals intact,
and then entered the powerful households.
I believe this means that the gold and currency supplied by the court for the army
were delivered to powerful households without breaking the seals.
Yet their achievements were celebrated,
and they were generously ennobled.
Now your subject returns to his native land,
impeaches various commanderies,
severs ties and separates from kin,
and humiliates old acquaintances.
It is only natural
that various slanders and covert harm
The emperor then summoned Huángfǔ Guī back.
He was appointed Yìláng,
and on account of his achievements, he was due for enfeoffment.

Bǐng impeached Hóu Lǎn."
Thus, this occurred in this year.)
(The "Biographies of Eunuchs" states:
"Hán Yǎn impeached Jù Yuàn; Yuàn was deprived of his state and made a Xiāng Hóu."
This is clearly the same event as the "Biography of Bǐng" mentions regarding the curtailment of Yuàn's state.)
(However, Yuán Jì records it in the spring of the previous year,
which differs from Fàn.)
(Now we follow Fàn's book.)
All were stripped of their noble titles and territories.
Liú Pǔ and others were demoted to Guānnèi Hóu,
and Yǐn Xūn and others were also all stripped of their titles.
6 The emperor had many imperial favorites,
with palace women reaching five or six thousand.
Those driven to labor or serving as retainers were more than double this number.
(Those "driven to labor" were favored and powerful individuals who exploited their influence to abduct commoners
to serve as private laborers in the Yè Tíng.)
(Those "serving as retainers" were individuals who sought power and influence,
and were happy to serve them.)
(Fù,
transcribed as 扶又翻.)
The emperor and his favored Guō Guìrén frequently slandered each other.
On the day Guǐhài
the empress, Dèng Shì, was deposed
and sent to the Bàoshì,
where she died of grief.
(The Hàn Guān Yí states: The Bàoshì
was within the Yè Tíng.
It had one official, a chéng,
who was in charge of palace women who were ill.
Empresses and noble consorts who committed crimes
were also sent to this chamber.)
7 Hù Qiāng Xiàowèi Duàn Jiǒng attacked the Hǎnjiě Qiāng
and defeated them.
8 In the third month,
on the day Xīnsì,
there was a general amnesty throughout the realm.
9 Wǎnlíng's prominent family, the Yáng Yuánpǐng, were dismissed from Běihǎi Jùn.
(Wǎnlíng Xiàn
belonged to Hénán Yǐn.)
The commandery office's latrine was uniquely elaborate.
(Xián says: Hùnxuān
is a latrine building.)
Hénán Yǐn Lǐ Yīng memorialized to investigate their crimes.
Yuánpǐng bribed the eunuchs,
and Yīng was ultimately accused of the very crime he was investigating.
(Fǎnzùo means to be accused of the crime one is investigating and fail to prosecute it,
but instead be charged oneself.)
He was imprisoned for the crime.
Tíngwèi Féng Gǔn tortured him to death.
(He was interrogated and tortured until he received the death penalty.)
(Gǔn,
transcribed as 古本翻.)
Together, they presented a joint memorial falsely accusing Gǔn of crimes.
Zhōng Chángshì Sū Kāng and Guǎn Bà
forcibly seized fertile lands and good properties throughout the empire.
(Gù means to seize and fortify.)
Dà Sīnóng Liú Yòu sent letters to the relevant areas,
ordering the confiscation of these properties according to law.
The emperor was furious
and had Yīng and Gǔn both assigned to penal labor at Zuǒxiào.
10 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the day Jiǎyín,
the Ānlíng funerary park caught fire.
(Ānlíng was Emperor Huì Dì's mausoleum.)
11 On the day Dīngsì,
an edict ordered the destruction of all illicit shrines in the commanderies and states,
specifically preserving only the two shrines in Luòyáng for Wáng Huàn and in Mìxiàn for Zhuó Mào.
12 In the fifth month,
on the day Bǐngxū,
Tàiwèi Yáng Bǐng passed away.
Bǐng was a man of
integrity and few desires.
He once famously said,
"I have three things I am not confused by: wine, women, and wealth."
After Bǐng had died,
the virtuous and upright who he had recommended, such as Liú Yú (劉瑜) of Guǎnglíng (廣陵), came to the capital and submitted a memorial, saying:
“The eunuchs should not be equated with those enfeoffed with territory,
vying to establish heirs,
succeeding to titles and inheriting ranks.
In the fourth year of Yángjiā (陽嘉), under Emperor Shùn (順),
an edict was issued allowing eunuchs to adopt sons to succeed to their titles.
Favored women fill the palace,
idly consuming provisions in the empty palace.
To eat without doing anything
is called 'idly consuming provisions'.
'Róng' (宂)
is read ‘ér lǒng’ (而隴).
Furthermore,
the number of mansions has increased,
pushed to the limits of exotic ingenuity,
digging into mountains and working stones,
hastened by severe punishments.
The officials of the prefectures and commanderies,
each examine cases,
where illicit affairs and bribes
all serve as bait for the officials.
The people are troubled and distressed,
rising up to join bandit gangs,
and officials immediately raise troops to punish and suppress their crimes.
Impoverished people,
sometimes sell their heads to claim rewards,
fathers and elder brothers mutilating themselves in turns,
wives and children watching each other be torn apart.
Moreover,
Your Majesty likes to make secret visits to the homes of your close attendants,
privately favoring the residences of eunuchs.
Guests and market traders
blaze a trail on the roads,
and in consequence, they become violent and unrestrained,
nothing being forbidden.
We only hope that Your Majesty will broaden the path of remonstrance.
The 'path of remonstrance' (諫道)
refers to the channel for speaking out.
Distance yourself from treacherous and evil people,
banish the music of Zhèng (鄭) and Wèi (衞),
and then governance will achieve peace,
and virtue will inspire auspicious winds.”
The Xiàojīng Yuánshénqì (孝經援神契) says: When virtue reaches the eight directions,
then auspicious winds arrive.
The presiding officials wished to make Yú equivocate in his words,
and so they questioned him on other matters.
Yú again spoke wholeheartedly for over eight thousand words,
which were even more incisive than before.
He was appointed Yìláng (議郎).
13 The troops of Jīngzhōu (荊州), Zhū Gài (朱蓋) and others, rebelled,
and together with the bandits of Guìyáng (桂陽), Hú Lán (胡蘭) and others, they again attacked Guìyáng.
The Administrator Rèn Yìn (任胤) abandoned the city and fled.
The bandit multitude then reached tens of thousands.
They turned to attack Línglíng (零陵).
The Administrator, Chén Qiú (陳球) of Xiàpī (下邳), firmly defended against them.
Línglíng (零陵) was low and damp,
with a city built of intertwined wood.
Línglíng Commandery (零陵郡)
was established by Emperor Wǔ (武).
Sòng Bái (宋白) says: The ancient seat of the commandery is seventy-eight *lǐ* (里) south of present-day Qīngxiāng County (清湘縣) in Quánzhōu (全州);
the ancient city still exists there.
The clerks and secretaries advised Qiú to send his family to safety.
Qiú angrily said:
“As Administrator, holding the tiger tally of a state,
appointed to one region,
how could I consider my wife and children and thus dampen the nation's prestige!
Anyone who speaks of it again will be beheaded!”
Thereupon, he strung large wooden planks to make bows,
feathered spears as arrows,
and operated mechanisms to launch them,
killing and injuring many.
This is similar to the wheeled crossbows of today.
Qiú immediately took advantage of the terrain within,
and in turn, breached the water to flood the bandits.
They resisted for more than ten days, and the city could not be taken.
At that time, Dù Shàng (度尚) was recalled to the capital.
An edict appointed Shàng as Zhōnglángjiāng (中郎將),
to lead over twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to rescue Qiú.
Troops from various commanderies were mobilized to join forces and attack,
greatly defeating them,
beheading over three thousand heads of Lán (蘭) and others.
Shàng was again appointed Cìshǐ (刺史) of Jīngzhōu (荊州).
Zhāng Xù (張敘), Administrator of Cāngwú (蒼梧), who was captured by bandits,
and Rèn Yìn (任胤) were both summoned and executed in the marketplace.
The remaining followers of Hú Lán (胡蘭) fled south to Cāngwú (蒼梧).
Zhāng Pán (張磐), Cìshǐ (刺史) of Jiāozhǐ (交趾), attacked and defeated them.
The bandits then returned into the borders of Jīngzhōu (荊州).
Dù Shàng (度尚) feared that he would be held accountable.
'Fù' (負)
means 'blame' or 'guilt'. [He] feared being blamed for not completely annihilating the remaining bandits.
Therefore, Pán (磐) was summoned to the Tíngwèi (廷尉).
Before his plea was properly registered,
he happened to be pardoned by an amnesty.
Pán (磐) refused to leave prison,
instead holding fast to his shackles and wooden constraints.
'Jié' (節) refers to sections made of bamboo.
'Xiéjié' (械節) also refers to the carved sections of shackles.
*Kǎo Yì* (考異) says: According to this, Zhāng Pán (張磐) was pardoned by an amnesty.
Checking the imperial annals,
there was no amnesty after this,
so I don't know which amnesty it was.
There was an amnesty in the third month of the sixth year,
two years before this;
and an amnesty in the sixth month of the first year of Yǒngkāng (永康),
two years after this.
I now follow the imperial annals.
“The imperial grace is boundless,
and yet you do not come out,
is this acceptable?”
Pán (磐) said:
“Pán (磐) holds the position of a regional governor.
In ancient times,
there were eight regions and eight governors.
The Han Cìshǐ (刺史) (Inspector) holds the ancient role of a regional governor.
Yet I suffer punishment in prison.
Affairs have their truth and falsehood,
laws have their right and wrong.
Pán (磐) is truly innocent,
so an amnesty has nothing to pardon;
if I endure this to merely escape,
I will forever bear the shame of being insulted,
living as a corrupt official,
and dying as a wretched ghost.
I beg that Shàng (尚) be summoned to the Tíngwèi (廷尉),
using a post-carriage to summon him to the Tíngwèi (廷尉).
'Chuán' (傳)
is read ‘zhū liàn’ (株戀) or
‘zhí liàn’ (直戀).
This would fully clarify the truth and falsehood.
If Shàng (尚) is not summoned,
Pán (磐) will bury his bones in this prison cell,
and will never leave in vain,
suffering injustice without resistance!”
The Tíngwèi (廷尉) submitted his statement.
An imperial edict summoned Shàng (尚).
Upon reaching the Tíngwèi (廷尉),
he ran out of excuses,
and was found guilty,
but was pardoned due to his previous merits.
14 In the intercalary month,
on the *jiǎwǔ* (甲午) day,
there was a fire at the Shuòpíng (朔平) office of the Nángōng (南宮).
This was the Shuòpíng Sīmǎ (朔平司馬) office.
The *Bǎiguān Zhì* (百官志) says: The Shuòpíng Sīmǎ (朔平司馬)
was in charge of the northern gate of the Northern Palace.
15 Duàn Jiǒng (段熲) defeated the Western Qiāng (西羌),
advanced his troops in relentless pursuit,
moving through mountains and valleys,
from spring to autumn,
not a day passed without battle.
The barbarians were finally defeated and scattered.
In total, twenty-three thousand heads were taken,
tens of thousands of captives were seized,
and over ten thousand households surrendered.
Jiǒng (熲) was enfeoffed as Dūxiānghóu (都鄉侯).
16 In autumn,
seventh month,
Chén Fān (陳蕃), a Tàizhōng Dàfū (太中大夫), was appointed Tàiwèi (太尉).
Fān (蕃) declined in favor of Hú Guǎng (胡廣), the Tàicháng (太常), Wáng Chàng (王暢), the Yìláng (議郎), and Lǐ Yīng (李膺), a pardoned convict,
but the emperor refused.
Chàng
was Gōng's
son. Wáng Gōng served Emperor Ān and became a Duke.
He detested the abundance of powerful relatives and influential clans,
so upon taking office,
he displayed fierce determination and might.
When a prominent clan committed an offense,
he would sometimes order his subordinates to demolish their houses and chop down their trees,
filling in their wells and leveling their stoves.
This would ruin their family businesses.
"Wén Wēng, Zhào Fù, Zhuó Mào, and their like,
all governed with warmth and generosity,
and their reputations reached later generations.
Demolishing houses and felling trees
will be perceived as harsh and severe.
Although you may wish to punish evil,
it will be difficult for your reputation to spread far.
Nà was the old capital,
a domain of Marquises and royal lands.
In ancient times, the Son of Heaven's system
stipulated a square of a thousand *lǐ*
as the royal domain (*diānfú*);
and beyond that, another five hundred *lǐ*,
as the Marquis domain (*hóufú*).
Guāng Wǔ arose in Nányáng,
which was later called the Southern Capital (*Nándū*).
Moreover, Luòyáng was within the Marquis and royal domains,
hence the saying.
The three Empresses were born in Xīnyě."
Xián said: "The four ancestral temples above Nándùn Jūn are in Zhānglíng.
Empress Guāngliè, Empress Yīn of Emperor Hé, and Empress Dèng were all from Xīnyě.
Meritorious officials and generals
flourished for generations.
I believe that diligently applying punishments
without knowing how to extend kindness,
and assiduously seeking out villains,"
*Zīzī*
means the same as *jíjí*.
"When Shùn appointed Gāo Yáo,
the unkind kept their distance."
The *Lúnyǔ* records Zǐxià's words.
*Táo*
is pronounced *yáo*.
"It is not about applying punishments."
Chàng deeply accepted his words,
and instead promoted lenient governance,
causing education and transformation to become widespread.
17. In the eighth month,
on the *Wùchén* day,
an order was first issued for commanderies and kingdoms to levy a tax of money per *mǔ* of land for those who owned fields.
Xián said: "Ten coins per *mǔ*."
Yu said, based on the *Huànzhě Zhuàn*: "Zhāng Ràng and others persuaded Emperor Líng to levy a tax on all fields in the empire,
ten coins per *mǔ*.
This was not an event of this time.
The Han land tax was one thirtieth,
but the calculation of collecting money per *mǔ*
began from this time."
18. In the ninth month,
on the *Dīngwèi* day,
there was an earthquake in the capital.
19. In winter,
in the tenth month,
Sīkōng Zhōu Jǐng was dismissed;
Tàicháng Liú Máo was appointed Sīkōng.
Máo
was Kǎi's son.
Liú Kǎi was highly respected at the time for yielding the country,
and his position reached that of a Duke.
20. Lángzhōng Dòu Wǔ,
a great-great-grandson of Róng,
had a daughter who became a noble lady (*guìrén*).
The palace woman Tián Shèng was favored by the Emperor,
and the Emperor intended to establish her as Empress.
Sīlì Xiàowèi Yīng Fèng submitted a memorial saying:
"The importance of the Empress
is the cause of rise and fall.
The Han established Fēiyàn,
and the imperial lineage was cut off."
The matter is recorded in Chapter 33, Emperor Āi's Jiànpíng First Year.
"The *Guānjū* song delights in finding a virtuous lady to match a gentleman."
The *Hán Shī Wàizhuàn* says: "There are five types of women one should not marry: one should not marry the eldest daughter of a family that has suffered mourning,
because she does not receive destiny;
one should not marry a woman from a family with inherited severe illness,
because they are abandoned by Heaven;
one should not marry a woman from a family with criminals,
because they are abandoned by men;
one should not marry a woman from a disordered family,
because their kind is not upright;
one should not marry a woman from a rebellious family,
because they abandon human relations."
*Yuǎn*,
pronounced *yú yuàn*.
The Dòu clan was a good family,
and they strongly contended for this.
The Emperor had no choice,
and on the *Xīnsì* day,
he established Lady Dòu as Empress,
appointed Wǔ as Tèjìn and Chéngmén Xiàowèi,
and enfeoffed him as Huáilǐ Hóu.
21. In the eleventh month,
on the *Rénzǐ* day,
the Northern Temple of the Yellow Gates caught fire.
22 Chén Fān repeatedly spoke about the injustice suffered by Lǐ Yīng, Féng Gǔn, and Liú Yòu,
requesting their pardon and rehabilitation,
and their promotion to official posts.
His words were earnest and repetitive,
sincere and heartfelt,
even to the point of tears;
the Emperor did not listen.
Yīng Fèng submitted a memorial, saying:
"Loyal and worthy generals
are the heart and backbone of the state.
I have observed that Féng Gǔn, Liú Yòu, Lǐ Yīng, and others, who were formerly sentenced to hard labor,
rooted out wicked officials
and exposed them to the law.
Xián says: 'Sì'
means 'to display.'
Yet they were unjustly accused and slandered,
leading to loyal ministers being implicated in the same guilt as chief villains.
From spring until winter,
they have not received leniency,
causing sighs of lamentation
among observers far and wide.
The essence of establishing governance
is to record achievements and forget failings.
This is why Emperor Wǔ spared
Hán Ān-guó who was among convicts.
Xián says: During Emperor Jǐng's reign,
Hán Ān-guó was a Grand Master of Liáng,
and was condemned to punishment by law;
later, when the Intendant of Liáng was vacant,
he was promoted from among convicts to an official of two thousand *dàn*.
This mention of Emperor Wǔ
is a mistake.
The event is recorded in Volume 27, Gānlù First Year of Emperor Xuān.
Equalize the merits of Jífǔ.
The *Shī* says: 'How grandly Fang Shú! He campaigned against the Xiǎnyǔn,
and the Man and Jīng came to acknowledge his might.'
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states: Fang Shú previously campaigned with Jífǔ against the Xiǎnyǔn;
now he is specifically campaigning against the Man and Jīng,
making them all submit to King Xuān's authority.
Gǔn had merit during Emperor Shùn's time for suppressing the Wǔlíng and Chángshā barbarians,
thus he is compared to Jífǔ.
They possessed the virtue of neither swallowing nor spitting.
Xián says: This refers to Yòu's impeachment of Liáng Jì's brother, Mín,
and how, as Commandant of the Capital,
he was feared by powerful magnates.
The *Shī* says: 'Though soft, they do not swallow;
though hard, they do not spit.'
'Shù'
is pronounced 'suò.'
Their enduring love reached Duólíao.
Yīng was the Administrator of Yúyáng
and the Colonel of the Wūhuán,
both in the Yōu region.
The General Who Crosses the Liao [Duólíao]
was stationed in the Bīng region.
These were places where he displayed his might and left a legacy of love.
As the royal army has not yet flourished,
I beg for the pardon of Yīng and the others,
to be prepared for unforeseen circumstances."
After the memorial was presented,
all their sentences were commuted.
After some time,
Lǐ Yīng was again appointed Commandant of the Capital.
At that time, Zhāng Ràng's younger brother, Shuò, a Lesser Yellow Gate, was the Magistrate of Yěwáng.
He was greedy, cruel, and lawless.
Fearing Yīng's formidable authority,
he fled back to the capital.
Yěwáng county belonged to Hénèi Commandery,
and Hénèi Commandery was under the jurisdiction of the Capital region.
Fearing Yīng would investigate his crimes,
he therefore fled back to the capital.
When two pieces of wood are joined to form a pillar,
how can it be sufficient to contain a person?
'Joined pillar'
refers to where two pillars stand directly opposite each other,
where two roofs meet.
Yīng led his officers and soldiers to break open the pillar to seize Shuò,
and delivered him to Luòyáng prison.
After the interrogation was complete,
he immediately executed him.
Ràng complained of injustice to the Emperor.
The Emperor summoned Yīng
and questioned him as to why he had executed Shuò without first seeking permission.
He replied:
"In the past, Zhòngní [Confucius] served as the Minister of Crime of Lǔ,
and executed Shǎozhèng Mǎo in seven days.
Now I have been in office for more than ten days;
I privately feared being faulted for procrastination,
and did not expect to be accused of acting too quickly.
I truly know my offense and responsibility,
and am prepared to die immediately.
I only beg for five more days
to eliminate the chief villains,
after which I will willingly face the cauldron;
this is my lifelong wish."
The Emperor had nothing further to say.
He turned to Ràng and said:
"This is the fault of your brother,
what offense has the Commandant of the Capital committed?"
Then he dismissed Yīng.
From then on, all the yellow gates and regular attendants bowed and held their breath,
not daring to leave the palace on their days off.
The Emperor, surprised, asked the reason.
They all kowtowed and wept, saying:
"We fear Commandant Lǐ."
At that time, the imperial court was in daily chaos,
and the moral order was in decline.
Yet Yīng alone upheld moral principles,
exalting himself through his reputation.
Those scholars who received his welcome and patronage
were said to have "ascended the Dragon Gate."
Xián says: This uses fish as a metaphor.
Dragon Gate [Lóngmén]
is the mouth where the Yellow River descends,
in present-day Lóngmén County, Jiàngzhōu.
Xīn Shì's *Sān Qín Jì* says: The Hékǒu pass,
also called Dragon Gate,
where the water is treacherous and impassable,
no fish or turtles can ascend it.
Thousands of large fish from rivers and seas
gather at the foot of Dragon Gate,
unable to ascend.
If they ascend, they become dragons.
'Bèi'
is pronounced 'píyì.'
23 Liú Kuān, the Administrator of Dōnghǎi, was summoned to be the President of the Imperial Secretariat.
Kuān
was the son of Qí.
Liú Qí served Emperor Shùn
as Grand Minister of Works.
'Qí'
is pronounced 'qiūyí.'
Xián says: This refers to the Administrator of Zhēn, the great-grandson of Qiáng, the King of Dōnghǎi.
According to Kuān's biography, it says: In this year, he was summoned from Administrator of Dōnghǎi to be President of the Imperial Secretariat,
then transferred to be Administrator of Nányáng,
having successively held office in three commanderies.
Even in urgent situations,
he never spoke harshly or showed an angry countenance.
When officials or common people committed errors,
he merely punished them with a reed whip.
In ancient times, whips were made of raw hide.
He never inflicted severe suffering.
Whenever he met elders,
he comforted them with words about farming and village life.
To the young,
he exhorted them with teachings of filial piety and brotherly respect.
Everyone was pleased and transformed by him.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the xīnmǎo day,
there was a solar eclipse.
An edict commanded the Gōngqīng and commanderies and kingdoms to recommend filially pious individuals.
Xún Shuǎng, recommended by Tài Cháng Zhào Diǎn, presented a policy brief, stating:
“In ancient times, the Sages established the center of Heaven and Earth and called it Lǐ.
Among all rituals,
the wedding ritual (hūnlǐ) is paramount.
The Yáng nature is pure and capable of bestowing,
while the Yīn essence is compliant and capable of transformation.
By regulating pleasure with ritual,
their energies are moderated and released.
Shuǎng’s words point directly to the emperor having too many internal consorts.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn states: When Jìn Hóu was ill,
Yī Hé examined him
and said:
‘This illness is incurable!
It is like gǔ;
it is neither ghost nor food,
but confusion leading to loss of will.’
The Duke asked:
‘Should women not be approached?’
He replied:
‘Control it.
The music of the former kings
was used to regulate all affairs.
Heaven has six qì;
when excessive, they become disasters.
Thus, their qì must be moderated and released.’
Shī is pronounced like shì zhì.
To achieve the blessing of long life.
But by the end of the Three Dynasties,
there was excessive indulgence without restraint.
Yáng was exhausted above,
and Yīn was blocked below.
Therefore, the Duke of Zhōu’s admonition said: ‘
At such times, none were able to live long.’
These are words from the Shàng Shū chapter Wú Yì.
‘Even the sparrow hawk,
who says it is foolish?
What is it compared to this man,
who seeks to ruin his body?’
This is truly lamentable.
Xián said: Shì means ‘to follow,’
meaning the folly of destroying one’s body
is worse than that of the sparrow hawk.
Sàng is pronounced like xī làng.
Furthermore, there are attendants and servants outside [the palace],
who impose burdens on innocent people
to support useless women.
The common people are impoverished outside,
and Yīn and Yáng are blocked within.
Therefore, the harmonious qì is disturbed,
and calamities and anomalies frequently arrive.
Your humble servant believes that all those who have not yet been favored [by the emperor]
should be sent out and allowed to marry.
This would truly be a great blessing for the nation.”
An edict appointed him Lángzhōng.
2 Sīlì and Yùzhōu suffered famine;
four or five out of ten people died,
even to the point where entire households were wiped out.
Hù refers to those registered in the government census.
To wipe out a household means
that neither old nor young survive,
all dying of hunger,
leaving no descendants.
3 An edict summoned Zhāng Huàn to be Dà Sīnóng,
and again appointed Huángfǔ Guī to replace him as Dùliáo Jiāngjūn.
Guī, feeling he had held high positions for too long,
wished to retire.
He repeatedly reported illness
but was not granted leave.
When the funeral of a friend arrived,
Guī crossed the border to meet it.
He then secretly instructed his guest to inform Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ Hú Fāng
that Guī had left his distant military camp without authorization,
and that he should be immediately impeached.
Fāng said:
“Wēimíng wishes to avoid the path of officialdom.
The Dùliáo Jiāngjūn is stationed on the border of Xīhé,
which is under the jurisdiction of the Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Huángfǔ Guī’s courtesy name is Wēimíng.
Xián said: It means he wants to return home and avoid the path of officialdom.
I should cherish talent for the imperial court;
how could I carry out this man’s scheme?”
So, he did not question it.
4 In summer,
the fourth month,
