*Kǎo Yì* (考異) says: Fàn Shū (范書) states:
"He ascended the throne
at thirteen years old."
Yuán Jì (袁紀), the imperial edict issued upon his initial establishment as heir, states:
"He is twelve years old."
In the second year of Jiànníng (建寧) when the factionalists were executed,
it states he was fourteen.
Yuán Jì (袁紀) is correct.
Emperor Xiào Líng (孝靈皇帝) (First Part, Upper)
His personal name was Hóng (宏).
According to the *Shì Fǎ* (諡法): "Chaos but no harm is called Líng (靈)."
Fú Hóu Gǔjīn Zhù (伏侯古今註):
The character "Hóng" (宏)
is pronounced as
Jiànníng (建寧) First Year
(*wùshēn*, 168 CE)
1 Spring,
first month,
on *rénwǔ* (壬午) day,
Dòu Wǔ (竇武), the City Gate Commandant, was made Grand General.
*Kǎo Yì* (考異) says: Yuán Jì (袁紀):
"In the ninth year of Yánxī (延熹),
fourth month,
on *wùyín* (戊寅) day,
Dòu Wǔ (竇武), a Special Advanced Official, was made Grand General.
Wǔ (武) feigned illness and firmly declined
dozens of times;
it was not permitted."
Fàn Shū (范書) places this in the first month of this year,
on *rénwǔ* (壬午) day.
Wǔ's (武) biography
also states that his appointment as Grand General was after the welcoming and enthronement of Emperor Líng (靈).
We follow this.
*Kǎo Yì* (考異) says: The Imperial Annals state
that Fán (蕃) was appointed Grand Tutor after his enthronement;
the biography places it before.
Due to the words "was reprimanded by Fán (蕃) for his memorials" etc.,
we know that following the biography is correct.
Three people are called *cān* (參).
At that time,
the state had just suffered a great loss,
and the imperial heir had not yet been established.
The various Shàngshū were fearful
and many feigned illness, not attending court.
Chén Fān sent a letter rebuking them, saying:
"The ancients, in establishing their integrity,
served the deceased as if they were still alive."
Xián said: It means that although the ruler has passed away,
the laws and regulations still exist,
and should be followed as if he were still alive.
Therefore, it is said "as if existing."
I believe
"serving the dead as serving the living,
serving the deceased as serving the present"
is a text from the Zhōngyōng,
meaning that even if the ruler is dead, one should serve him as if he were alive.
Political affairs are daily dwindling.
How can you, gentlemen, abandon the bitterness of *túliǎo*
and rest in bed?
The Guófēng of the Shījīng says: "Who says *tú* is bitter?
Its sweetness is like *jì*."
The Zhōusòng says: "Unable to bear the many difficulties at home,
I again gather *liǎo*."
The Xiǎoyǎ says: "Some rest reclining on their forms."
The various Shàngshū, in awe and fear,
all rose and attended to their duties.
On the *Jǐhài* day,
the Marquis of Jiědú Pavilion arrived at Xìamén Pavilion.
Dòu Wǔ was ordered to carry the *jié* (imperial insignia)
and, with a royal blue-canopied carriage, welcome him into the palace.
On the *Gēngzǐ* day,
he ascended the imperial throne
and changed the reign title.
In the second month,
on the *Xīnyǒu* day,
Emperor Xiàohuán was buried at Xuānlíng.
Xián said: Xuānlíng
is thirty *lǐ* southeast of Luòyáng.
On the *Xīnwèi* day,
a general amnesty was declared throughout the empire.
Initially,
the Protector of the Qiāng, Duàn Jiǒng, had pacified the Western Qiāng
(Last year, Jiǒng pacified the Western Qiāng).
The General Who Crosses the Liao, Huángfǔ Guī, and the Colonel, Zhāng Huàn, had been recruiting them for years,
but after submitting, they rebelled again.
In the fourth year of Yánxī of Emperor Huán,
Huángfǔ Guī recruited and pacified the Eastern Qiāng.
In the sixth year,
Guī recommended Zhāng Huàn.
By the first year of Yǒngkāng,
within seven years,
the Qiāng's submission and rebellion were unpredictable.
"When they submit,
the households (Qiāng) flock back.
(Same below.)
The Xiānlíng and Eastern Qiāng commit evil and rebel,
but Huángfǔ Guī and Zhāng Huàn each command strong forces
and do not pacify them in a timely manner.
It is desired to order Jiǒng to move his troops to the east to attack them.
We are unsure of the appropriateness of this,
so deliberate on the strategy."
Jiǒng submitted a memorial, saying:
"I humbly observe that although the Xiānlíng and Eastern Qiāng have rebelled repeatedly,
those who have submitted to Huángfǔ Guī
already number about twenty thousand households.
Good and evil are now separated,
and the remaining rebels are few.
The reason Zhāng Huàn hesitates and does not advance for a long time
(Chóuchú
means to hesitate,
also to stop one's feet)
is that if troops move, they will surely be alarmed.
Moreover, from winter to spring,
they are camped and do not disperse.
Both people and livestock are weary and emaciated,
having the potential for self-destruction.
We wish to recruit them again and pacify the strong enemy by sitting still.
I believe that the 'wolf cubs' (Qiāng) have a wild nature
and are difficult to incorporate with kindness.
Even if they submit when their power is exhausted,
they will stir again when the troops depart.
Only by long spears threatening their flanks
and white blades pressed against their necks
can they be dealt with!
It is estimated that the remaining Eastern tribes number over thirty thousand households.
They live close within the frontier,
and the roads have no dangerous turns.
They do not have the 'vertical and horizontal' strategic advantage of Yān, Qí, Qín, or Zhào.
Yet they have long disrupted Bīng and Liáng,
and repeatedly encroached upon the Sānfǔ.
Xīhé and Shàngjùn have already been moved inland
(Details can be found in Volume 52, Yǒnghé fifth year of Emperor Shùn),
reaching a critical point again.
From Yúnzhōng and Wǔyuán
west to Hànyáng, over two thousand *lǐ*,
the Xiōngnú and various Qiāng
all occupied their lands.
This is like a hidden ulcer,
lodged under the ribs.
If not punished,
it will turn and grow larger.
If five thousand cavalry, ten thousand infantry, and three thousand chariots are deployed,
in three winters and two summers,
it will be enough to break and pacify them.
The total cost is estimated to be 5.4 billion coins.
Xián said: Wúlǜ
means altogether or in total.
Máo Huàng said: A total calculation is called wúlǜ,
meaning there is no doubt that the amount is such.
Then the Qiāng can be completely destroyed,
the Xiōngnú will submit permanently,
and the internally relocated commanderies and counties
can return to their native lands.
I humbly observe that in the middle of Yǒngchū,
the various Qiāng rebelled
for fourteen years,
costing 24 billion coins
(Details can be found in Volume 50, Yuánchū fifth year of Emperor Ān).
After another seven years,
over 8 billion coins were spent
(Details can be found in Volume 52, Yǒngjiā first year of Emperor Chōng).
Yet they were not completely exterminated,
and the remaining remnants rose again,
causing harm up to now.
If the people are not temporarily fatigued now,
then there will be no end to lasting peace.
Your humble servants will exert their meager abilities,
awaiting your command."
The Emperor assented
and allowed everything as submitted.
Jiǒng then led over ten thousand troops,
carrying fifteen days' provisions,
from Péngyáng directly to Gāopíng.
Xián said: Péngyáng and Gāopíng
are both county names,
belonging to Āndìng Commandery.
Péngyáng County
is today's Péngyuán County in Yuánzhōu.
Gāopíng County
is today's Yuánzhōu.
Xián said: The mountain is in today's Pínggāo County, Yuánzhōu.
Dù Yòu said: Pínggāo County
is the Gāopíng of the Hàn dynasty.
Jiǒng's troops were all afraid.
Jiǒng then ordered long arrowheads and sharp knives in the army
(The Fàn Shū, Duàn Jiǒng Biography, has
"stretching arrowheads and sharp knives").
With strong crossbows,
he arrayed light cavalry as left and right wings,
and said to his officers and soldiers:
"Now we are thousands of *lǐ* from home.
Advance, and the task will be accomplished;
flee, and all will surely die.
Strive together for glory!"
Thereupon, he shouted loudly,
and all responded with shouts, leaping forward.
Cavalry galloped alongside,
charging and attacking them.
The rebel forces were greatly routed,
and over eight thousand heads were taken.
The Empress Dowager bestowed an imperial edict of praise, saying:
"Once the Eastern Qiāng are fully pacified,
all merits and efforts shall be recorded.
For now, Jiǒng is granted 200,000 coins,
and one person from his family is made a Lángzhōng."
She commanded the Zhōngzàng Fǔ to allocate gold, money, and colored silks to augment military expenses.
The Bǎiguān Zhì says: The director of the Zhōngzàng Fǔ
belongs to the Shǎofǔ and is in charge of imperial silks, gold, silver, and various goods.
(Diào
is *tuódiào* in transcription.
Zàng
is *jǔlàng* in transcription.)
In the intercalary month,
on the *Jiǎwǔ* day,
the imperial ancestor was posthumously honored as Emperor Xiàoyuán,
(Shěn Yuē said: The posthumous title Xiàoyuán
is not recorded in the Shìfǎ.
Now, according to the Shìfǎ of Duke Zhōu:
'One who can think and discern the multitude is called Yuán;'
'One whose righteous conduct pleases the people is called Yuán;'
'One who upholds righteousness and practices virtue is called Yuán;'
'One who pacifies the people with laws is called Yuán.')
and the imperial father as Emperor Xiàorén.
(Shìfǎ:
'One who values the worthy and cherishes kin is called Rén.')
The imperial ancestor was Shú,
the Marquis of Jiědú Pavilion.
The imperial father was Cháng,
the Marquis.
Xián said: Shènyuán
is southeast of today's Lèshòu County, Yíngzhōu.
They wished to call them the Two Imperial Mausoleums.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the *Wùchén* day,
Grand Commandant Zhōu Jǐng died.
Minister of Works Xuān Fēng was dismissed.
Wáng Chàng, the Commander of the Chánglè Guard, was appointed Minister of Works.
8 In the fifth month,
on the *Dīngwèi* day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
9 Liú Jǔ, a Grand Master of the Palace, was appointed Grand Commandant.
10In the sixth month,
the capital experienced severe flooding.
11On the *Guǐsì* day,
in recognition of the meritorious service in establishing the sovereign,
Dòu Wǔ was enfeoffed as Marquis of Wénxǐ.
His son, Wǔ Jī, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Wèiyáng.
Upon examining the annals of the two Hàn dynasties, there is no Wèiyáng county;
it was probably named a feudal state due to the kinship with his maternal uncle.
Jìng was enfeoffed as Marquis of Xīxiāng.
The Palace Regular Attendant, Cáo Jié, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Cháng'ān Township.
There were eleven marquises in total.
Lú Zhí of Zhuōjùn submitted a memorial to persuade Dòu Wǔ, saying:
"Your Excellency's position in the Hàn court
is like that of Dàn and Shì in the Zhōu house.
You have established a sagely ruler,
and all within the Four Seas are in order.
Commentators believe that your son's achievements
are of the utmost importance in this matter.
Now, the succession is among those of the same clan,
by examining maps and records,
and establishing them in order,
what merit is there in this?
Since Emperor Hé had no heir,
Emperor Ān, as a grandson of Sùzōng, was enthroned.
Chōng and Zhì had short reigns,
and Emperor Huán, as a great-grandson of Sùzōng, was enthroned.
Emperor Huán had no heir,
and again, a great-great-grandson of Sùzōng was enthroned.
This is the succession of those of the same clan,
establishing them in order.
A 'map' (tú)
is a depiction of the clan members according to the closeness or distance of their kinship.
A 'record' (dié)
is a genealogical register.
It would be proper to decline the great reward
to preserve your reputation."
Dòu Wǔ could not adopt this advice.
Lú Zhí was eight *chǐ* and two *cùn* tall,
his voice was like a bell,
his nature was firm and resolute,
and he possessed great integrity.
In his youth, he served Mǎ Róng.
Mǎ Róng was extravagant and indulgent,
often having female entertainers sing and dance before him.
Lú Zhí attended lectures for many years,
never once glancing away.
Mǎ Róng respected him for this.
The Empress Dowager, considering Chén Fán's long-standing virtue,
specifically enfeoffed him as Marquis of Gāoyáng Township.
Chén Fán submitted a memorial declining, saying:
"I have heard that territorial enfeoffments
are for meritorious service.
Although I do not possess conduct of inherent purity,
I secretly admire the saying of the *jūnzǐ*: 'If it is not obtained by the right way,
one does not dwell in it.'
Confucius said: 'Wealth and honor
are what people desire,
but if they are not obtained by the right way,
one does not dwell in them.'
To accept it with averted face,
the *Shī* says: 'He who accepts a rank without declining,
it will lead to his own ruin.'
Calamity will flow down to the common people,
and as for my own person,
where can I find refuge?"
The Empress Dowager did not permit it.
Chén Fán steadfastly declined,
submitting ten memorials in total,
and ultimately did not accept the enfeoffment.
12Duàn Gǒng led light troops to pursue the Qiāng.
He emerged from Qiáomén.
According to the *Dōngguān Jì*,
Qiáomén
is a valley name.
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* states: "Qiáomén
is the Great Wall gate of Qiáoshān."
He engaged them in battle at Shēyán Zé, Luòchuān, and on the waters of Lìngxiān.
Xián says: "This is within the borders of Shēyán County in Shàngjùn."
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù*: "The Shēyán River flows out from the red sand dunes southwest of Shēyán County,
and flows eastward into the Yellow River."
Luòchuān is south of the Shēyán River.
Xián says: "Lìngxiān
is a river name,
located in the current Gānzhōu Zhāngyè County area.
It is also called Hélí Shuǐ,
and also Qiānggǔ Shuǐ."
I have examined that after the initial victory at Xiānshuǐ,
the pursuit and battle continued at Língwǔ Gǔ.
This Xiānshuǐ is clearly not the Xiānshuǐ of Gānzhōu,
but should be in the northern part of Shàngjùn.
They also fought at Língwǔ Gǔ.
Xián says: "Língwǔ
is a county name,
with a valley,
located northwest of the current Língzhōu Huáiyuǎn County."
Based on the geographical treatises of previous histories,
Běidì Commandery has Língwǔ County,
and Língwǔ Gǔ should be within the borders of this county,
not the Língwǔ County of Táng Língzhōu.
In autumn,
seventh month,
Duàn Gǒng arrived at Jīngyáng.
Jīngyáng County
was subordinate to Āndìng Commandery.
Xián says: "The old city is south of the current Yuánzhōu Píngliáng County."
The Qiāng
all scattered into the mountains and valleys of Hányáng.
Hù-Xiōngnú Zhōnglángjiàng Zhāng Huàn
submitted a memorial saying: “Although the Dōngqiāng have been defeated,
it is difficult to completely eliminate the remaining tribes.
Duàn Jiǒng’s nature is impulsive and reckless;
I fear that defeat and failure will not be constant.
It is advisable to temporarily win them over with benevolence,
so as to avoid future regret.”
An imperial edict was sent to Jiǒng,
who again submitted a memorial saying:
“I originally knew that although the Dōngqiāng were numerous,
they were soft and weak and easily controlled.
Therefore, I repeatedly presented my humble thoughts,
hoping to devise a plan for lasting peace.
However, Zhōnglángjiàng Zhāng Huàn asserted that the barbarians were strong and difficult to defeat,
and that it was advisable to use appeasement to bring them to surrender.
The sagacious court, with its clear discernment,
trusted and accepted my humble words,
thus my strategy was implemented,
and Huàn’s plan was not used.
The circumstances are now the opposite,
leading to suspicion and resentment.
Believing the accusations of the rebellious Qiāng,
he embellished his words,
saying that my troops ‘have repeatedly suffered setbacks’
(Xián says: ‘Shāngbài’ [傷敗] means to be wounded and defeated; ‘niè’ [衂] is pronounced niǔ-lùo fān [女六翻]),
‘cannot be completely exterminated’
(Xián says: He means that the Qiāng also derive their life from the one qi of Heaven, and thus cannot be entirely exterminated),
‘cannot bring about empty tranquility,
with blood flowing to defile the wilderness,
harming harmony and causing disaster.’
I humbly recall that during the transition between the Zhōu and Qín dynasties,
the Róng and Dí caused harm.
Since the restoration,
the Qiāng bandits have been most prevalent.
They cannot be completely exterminated;
even if they surrender, they rebel again.
Now, the various tribes of the Xiānlíng
have repeatedly vacillated,
thus they attack and occupy counties and towns,
plunder people and goods,
dig up graves and expose corpses,
bringing disaster to both the living and the dead.
Heaven is enraged,
lending a hand to execute punishment.
In the past, Xíng was lawless,
and the state of Wèi attacked it.
As the army set out, it rained;
(Zuǒzhuàn says: Wèi suffered a great drought.
Divination was made to perform sacrifices to mountains and rivers,
but it was not auspicious.
Níng Zhuāngzǐ said:
‘In ancient times, when Zhōu suffered famine,
it conquered Yīn and the harvest was bountiful.
Now Xíng is lawless,
does Heaven wish Wèi to punish Xíng?’
They followed this advice,
and as the army set out, it rained.)
Continuous sweet rain was received,
the harvests were abundant year after year,
and people were free from disease.
Observing Heaven’s will above,
there was no disaster or harm;
examining human affairs below,
the people were harmonious and the army victorious.
From Qiáomén westward to Luòchuān eastward,
the old towns and counties
are now interconnected
(Dù Yòu says: West of Qiáomén and east of Luòchuān is today’s Jīnchéng, Huìníng, Píngliáng commanderies).
Chariots and cavalry travel safely,
without any need for setbacks.
Considering that Huàn is a Hàn official,
holding a military post,
he was stationed with troops for two years,
yet could not pacify the bandits.
(In the ninth year of Huán Dì’s Yánxī reign,
Huàn commanded three provinces and two camps.)
His claim of appeasing fierce enemies
(Xián says: ‘Guǎng’ [獷] means evil appearance.
Pronounced gè-měng fān [各猛翻])
is presumptuous and unsubstantiated.
(Zuǒzhuàn: Zāng Huì divined whether it was sincere or presumptuous.
Dù Yù’s commentary says: ‘Jiàn’ [僭] means not trustworthy.)
In the past, when the Xiānlíng caused banditry,
Zhào Chōngguó ordered them to be moved inland
(During the reign of Xuān Dì,
Zhào Chōngguó attacked the Western Qiāng;
over 30,000 surrendered,
who were moved to Jīnchéng
and settled in the Jīnchéng Subordinate State.
‘Lìng’ [令] means to order,
pronounced líng [零]).
Mǎ Yuán moved them to Sānfǔ,
but they first submitted then rebelled,
and remain a constant trouble to this day
(Xián says: ‘Gěng’ [鯁] is the same as ‘gěng’ [梗].
‘Gěng’ [梗] means ailment.
Dàyǎ says: ‘to this day a constant trouble’),
causing deep concern.
Now, the neighboring commanderies have sparse populations,
and have been repeatedly harmed by the Qiāng.
To wish to have the surrendered barbarians live among them
is like planting thorny bushes in fertile fields,
or raising snakes and vipers inside one’s house.
Therefore, I uphold the might of the Great Hàn,
and establish a long-term strategy,
desiring to sever their roots,
preventing them from being able to reproduce
(Xián says: ‘Zhí’ [殖] means to grow.
Zuǒzhuàn says: ‘See evil as a farmer strives to remove weeds,
severing their roots,
so they cannot reproduce’).
Fifty-four billion [cash] have been spent;
now, just one year has passed,
and less than half has been consumed,
yet the remaining bandits are mere embers
(Dù Yù says: ‘Jìn’ [燼] means charred wood remaining after a fire).
I always receive imperial edicts that the army should not be controlled from within
(Xián says: ‘Yù’ [御] means to control.
Huáinánzǐ says: ‘A state cannot be governed from outside,
nor can an army be controlled from within’).
Entrusting everything to me,
I will adapt to circumstances as appropriate,
without missing opportune moments.”
13In the eighth month,
Sīkōng Wáng Chàng was dismissed,
and Zōngzhèng Liú Chǒng became Sīkōng.
14Originally,
Chén Fān had been instrumental in Dòu Tàihòu’s enthronement.
(Details can be found in Volume 55, Huán Dì’s Yánxī eighth year.)
All matters, great and small, were entrusted to Fān.
Fān and Dòu Wǔ worked with one heart and exerted their utmost effort
to support the imperial house.
They summoned famous and virtuous men from across the empire, such as Lǐ Yīng, Dù Mì, Yǐn Xūn, Liú Yú, and others,
and all were appointed to the court,
participating together in governmental affairs.
Consequently, the scholars of the empire
all craned their necks, longing for an era of great peace.
However, the emperor’s wet nurse Zhào Ráo and various imperial female secretaries
(Xián says: Nǚ Shàngshū [女尚書] are inner court officials.
‘Ráo’ [嬈] is pronounced nǎi-liǎo fān [乃了翻]),
along with Zhōng Chángshì Cáo Jié, Wáng Fǔ, and others, formed cliques,
flattering the empress dowager.
The empress dowager trusted them,
frequently issuing imperial edicts
for appointments and promotions.
Fān and Wǔ detested this.
Once, they met in the court hall,
and Fān privately said to Wǔ:
“Cáo Jié, Wáng Fǔ, and their ilk
have manipulated state power since the previous emperor’s reign,
corrupting and bringing chaos to the realm.
If we do not execute them now,
it will certainly be difficult to deal with them later.”
Wǔ deeply agreed with this.
Fān was greatly pleased,
pushing his
mat as he stood up.
Wǔ then gathered like-minded individuals, such as Shàngshū Lìng Yǐn Xūn, to jointly devise a strategy.
There was an eclipse of the sun.
Dù Fān said to Chén Wǔ:
“In the past, Xiāo Wàngzhī was troubled by Shí Xiǎn alone.
The matter can be found in volume 28, in the second year of Yuán Dì’s Chūyuán reign.
I am eighty years old,
and wish to eliminate harm for the General.
Now, we can use the solar eclipse as an opportunity to dismiss the eunuchs,
to rectify the celestial anomaly.”
Chén Wǔ then reported to the Empress Dowager, saying:
“According to precedent,
the Yellow Gate officials and Regular Palace Attendants are only supposed to attend to matters within the palace
gates,
and manage the property of the nearby offices;
‘within the palace’
refers to the Forbidden Enclosure.
‘Property of the nearby offices’
refers to the Central Storehouse, the Imperial Workshop, and the Inner Offices, all under the jurisdiction of the Lesser Minister.
They hold heavy power,
their sons and younger brothers are widely distributed,
and they specialize in greed and tyranny.
The empire is agitated
precisely because of this.
They should all be punished and abolished to clear the court.”
The Empress Dowager said:
“According to precedents since the Hàn Yuán era,
‘Hàn Yuán’
means the early Hàn dynasty.
Only those who are guilty should be punished.
How can they all be abolished?”
At that time, the Central Regular Palace Attendant Guǎn Bà
had considerable talent and strategy,
and held exclusive control within the palace.
Chén Wǔ first reported to arrest Guǎn Bà and other Central Regular Palace Attendants like Sū Kāng,
all of whom were executed.
Chén Wǔ repeatedly reported to execute Cáo Jié and others,
but the Empress Dowager hesitated and could not bear to,
and the matter was not pursued for a long time.
Dù Fān submitted a memorial, saying:
“Now the capital is in an uproar,
and the roads are noisy with rumors,
saying that Hóu Lǎn, Cáo Jié, Gōngchéng Xīn, Wáng Fǔ, Zhèng Sà, and others,
along with Lady Zhào and various Imperial Secretaries, are jointly bringing chaos to the empire.
‘Gōngchéng’
was a Qin noble rank.
This family took their rank as their surname.
乘,
read as ‘shéng zhèng.’
昕,
read as ‘xǔ jīn.’
Lady Zhào is Zhào Ráo.
颯,
read as ‘lì.’
Those who oppose them are slandered and harmed.
Suddenly, the officials are like floating wood in the river,
drifting east and west,
greedy for gain and fearful of harm.
If Your Majesty does not promptly execute these individuals now,
they will certainly cause rebellion and chaos,
endangering the state.
Their calamity will be immeasurable.
I wish that my memorial be published and shown to those around you,
and also let all wicked people in the world know of my hatred for them.”
The Empress Dowager did not accept it.
In the same month,
Venus violated the ‘General’ star of the Fáng constellation,
and entered the Tàiwēi enclosure.
The *Jìn Shū Astrological Treatise* states: The four stars of Fáng represent the Míngtáng,
the palace where the Son of Heaven dispenses governance,
and also the Four Assistants.
The first star
is the Senior General;
the next
is the Secondary General;
the next
is the Secondary Chancellor;
the uppermost star
is the Senior Chancellor.
Tàiwēi is
the court of the Son of Heaven.
Tiānguān,
means astronomy.
The *Shǐjì Tiānguān Shū* is similar to later astronomical treatises.
惡,
read as ‘wū lù.’
A memorial was submitted to the Empress Dowager, saying:
“According to astrological texts: The palace gates should be closed,
generals and chancellors will suffer misfortune,
and treacherous people are near the ruler;
I urge you to guard against this quickly.”
A letter was also sent to Chén Wǔ and Dù Fān,
stating that due to the unfavorable arrangement of the stars,
the high officials should swiftly decide on a major plan.
Thereupon, Chén Wǔ and Dù Fān appointed Zhū Yǔ as the Grand Administrator of Sīlì,
Liú Yòu as the Governor of Hénán,
and Yú Qí as the Magistrate of Luòyáng.
Chén Wǔ submitted a memorial to dismiss the Prefect of the Yellow Gate, Wèi Biāo,
and replaced him with his close confidant, the Lesser Yellow Gate officer Shān Bīng.
The *Xìngpǔ* states: During the Zhōu dynasty, there was an official called Shān Shī,
whose descendants took the official title as their surname.
Some say: They are descendants of Lièshān Shì.
The Chánglè Imperial Secretary
was probably established because the Empress Dowager was in regency,
to manage the submission of memorials and documents from the outer court and various matters.
樂,
read as ‘luò’;
same below.
Dù Fān said to Chén Wǔ:
“These individuals should be immediately arrested and killed.
Why bother to interrogate them?”
Chén Wǔ did not agree,
and ordered Shān Bīng, along with Yǐn Xūn and Palace Remonstrator Zhù [AS-89E3], to jointly interrogate Zhèng Sà.
His confession implicated Cáo Jié and Wáng Fǔ.
Yǐn Xūn and Shān Bīng immediately reported and arrested Cáo Jié and others,
and sent Liú Yú to submit the memorial internally.
In the ninth month,
on the day Xīnhài,
Dòu Wǔ returned to his residence after an overnight stay.
The officer in charge of the Central Secretariat had already informed Zhū Yǔ, the Wǔguān Historian of Chánglè.
Yǔ secretly opened Wǔ's memorial.
Chánglè [Palace]
was the Empress Dowager's palace.
In the Empress Dowager's palace, there were five female Palace Secretaries (nǚ shàngshū),
and the Wǔguān Historian was in charge of them.
The Kǎoyì says:
Fàn Shū's Imperial Annals records
"Dīnghài,"
while Yuán Jì records
"Xīnhài."
According to the Chánglì,
in this year,
the ninth month
began on Yǐsì,
and there was no Dīnghài.
We now follow Yuán Jì.
"Those eunuchs who indulge themselves
may certainly be executed,
but what crime have we committed
that we should all face extermination of our clans?"
Thereupon, he shouted loudly:
"Chén Fán and Dòu Wǔ memorialized the Empress Dowager to depose the Emperor,
which is high treason!"
That night, he summoned seventeen strong and trusted Chánglè Attendant Officers (cóngguānshǐ) he knew, including Gōng Pǔ and Zhāng Liàng.
The Chánglè Attendant Officers
were in charge of the attendant officers of the Empress Dowager's palace.
Cóng
is pronounced as "cái yòng fān."
Gōng
is pronounced as "gōng."
They plotted to execute Wǔ and others.
Cáo Jié reported to the Emperor, saying:
"Outside, there is much alarm!"
Qīqiè
means "urgent" or "pressing."
He made the Emperor draw his sword and leap about,
had wet nurses Zhào Ráo and others guard him on either side,
took the tally,
and closed all the palace gates.
Xián says: Qǐ
is a tally with a feathered halberd pattern.
The Hàn Guān Yí says: All who reside in the palace
are registered at the Yèmén (Side Gate).
Those whose names correspond and are permitted to enter
receive a sealed qǐ from their respective offices,
which is verified by an official seal,
before they are admitted.
He threatened [the Emperor] with drawn blades
and made him issue an imperial rescript.
Wáng Fǔ was appointed Yellow Gate Prefect (Huángmén Lìng).
The imperial rescript
was what was known as a "chǐyī."
Yǐn Xūn and Shān Bīng were arrested.
Bīng, suspicious,
refused the edict.
Fǔ stabbed him to death,
and also killed Xūn.
Zhèng Sà was released,
and the soldiers were sent to coerce the Empress Dowager
and seize her seals and ribbons.
The palace attendant (zhōngyèzhě) was ordered to guard the Southern Palace,
closing the gates and cutting off the covered walkways.
The palace attendants (yèzhě) were in charge of guarding the gates and doors.
When Emperor Wén entered and ascended the throne from his princely residence,
there were ten yèzhě
holding halberds to guard the Duānmén (Front Gate) – this is an example.
There were covered walkways connecting the Southern and Northern Palaces in Luòyáng.
Wǔ refused the imperial edict,
and galloped into the Infantry Camp (Bùbīng Yíng).
Together with his nephew, the Infantry Commandant (Bùbīng Xiàowèi) Sháo, he shot the envoy to death.
He summoned several thousand soldiers from the Five Northern Army Garrisons to encamp at the Dūtíng.
This was the Dūtíng of Luòyáng.
Jiào
is pronounced as "hù jiào fān."
"The Yellow Gate attendants and Regular Attendants (Chángshì) have rebelled!
Those who exert themselves will be enfeoffed as marquises and richly rewarded."
Chén Fán, hearing of the trouble,
led over eighty officials and students (zhūshēng).
They all drew their blades and broke into the Chéngmíng Gate,
reaching the gate of the Secretariat (Shàngshū Mén).
They rolled up their sleeves and shouted:
"The Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn) is loyal in defending the state!
The Yellow Gate attendants are rebelling!
Why do you say the Dòu clan is unprincipled?"
Wáng Fǔ happened to come out and meet Fán at that moment.
Just hearing his words,
he reprimanded Fán, saying:
"The former Emperor has just passed away,
and his mausoleum is not yet completed.
What功 merits has Dòu Wǔ achieved
that his brothers, sons, and nephews were all enfeoffed as three marquises?
This refers to Wǔ's son Jī being enfeoffed as Marquis of Wèiyáng,
his nephew Sháo as Marquis of Hù,
and Sháo's younger brother Jìng as Marquis of Xīxiāng.
They took many palace women from the Yèting,
and within ten days,
accumulated vast wealth.
For a high official to be like this,
is this principled?
This means, 'if this is not unprincipled, then what is it?'
If you just blindly form factions,
what else can you ask of the rebels?"
He ordered swordsmen to arrest Fán.
Fán drew his sword and shouted at Fǔ,
his words and expression becoming even more severe.
Thereupon, Fán was seized
and sent to the Northern Temple Prison (Běisì Yù).
The Kǎoyì says: Fàn Shū's biography of Fán says:
"Fán drew his sword and shouted at Fǔ,
and Fǔ's soldiers dared not approach.
So, more men were added to surround him dozens deep,
and thereupon Fán was seized and sent to prison."
We now follow Yuán Jì.
"You old hag!
Can you still diminish our number of officials or take away our stipends and leave?!"
Bǐng
means "to provide."
Jiǎ
means "to borrow" or "leave."
Bù
is pronounced as "fǔ jiǔ fān."
He killed him.
At that time, Zhāng Huàn, the Protector General of the Southern Xiongnú (Hù Xióngnú Zhōnglángjiāng), had been recalled to the capital.
Cáo Jié and others, knowing that Huàn was new and unaware of their original plot,
falsely issued an imperial decree appointing Zhōu Jìng, the Lesser Minister of the Treasury (Shǎofǔ), as acting General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chējì Jiāngjūn) with extra authority (jiājié).
They ordered him and Huàn to lead the soldiers of the Five Garrisons to attack Wǔ.
When the night watches had ended,
meaning it was almost dawn,
they emerged and encamped at the Zhùquè Yèmén.
The southern side-gate of the Northern Palace was called the Zhùquè Mén.
Jiāng
is pronounced as "jí liàng fān."
Soon after, the entire army assembled beneath the palace gate,
facing Wǔ's forces.
Fǔ's forces gradually grew stronger.
He ordered his soldiers to shout loudly at Wǔ's army:
"Dòu Wǔ has rebelled!
You are all imperial guards,
whose duty is to guard the palace.
Why are you following a rebel?
Those who surrender first will be rewarded!"
The soldiers of the camps and offices (yíngfǔ bīng) had always feared and obeyed the eunuchs.
Yíngfǔ
refers to the commandants of the Five Garrisons.
From dawn until mealtime,
almost all the soldiers surrendered.
Wǔ and Sháo fled.
The various armies pursued and surrounded them.
They all committed suicide.
Their heads were displayed at the Dūtíng in Luòyáng.
Their relatives by clan, guests, and in-laws were arrested
and all executed.
The Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) Liú Yú and the Cavalry Commandant (Túnqí Xiàowèi) Féng Shù
also had their entire clans exterminated.
The eunuchs further slandered Liú Shú of Héjiān, the Commandant of Tiger Guards (Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiāng), and Wèi Lǎng of Kuàijī, a former Secretary (Shàngshū),
claiming they had conspired with Wǔ and others.
They both committed suicide.
The Empress Dowager was moved to the Southern Palace.
Wǔ's family members were exiled to Rìnán.
All those from high officials to commoners who had been recommended by Fán or Wǔ, as well as their disciples and former subordinates,
were dismissed from office and prohibited from holding future positions (jìngù).
Bā Sù of Bóhǎi, a Grand Master of the Remonstrance (Yìláng).
The Xìng Pǔ says: Bā
is a descendant of the Bā kingdom.
In the Later Hàn, there was also Bā Zhī, the Inspector of Yángzhōu.
Cáo Jié and others did not know,
so he was merely subjected to jìngù. Later, they learned and arrested him.
Sù loaded himself onto a cart and proceeded to the county office.
Sù was a native of Gāochéng County in Bóhǎi.
[His friend] entered the gate,
removed his seal and ribbon,
and wished to leave together with him.
Sù said:
"As a minister,
one should not conceal one's plans,
nor flee punishment for one's crimes.
Since I did not conceal my plans,
how could I dare to flee my punishment?"
Thereupon, he was executed.
Cáo Jié was promoted to Chánglè Guard Commander (Chánglè Wèiwèi)
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Yùyáng.
Yùyáng County
belonged to Nányáng Commandery.
He retained his position as Yellow Gate Prefect.
Zhū Yǔ, Gōng Pǔ, Zhāng Liàng, and six others were all made marquises (lièhóu).
Eleven others were made Marquises of Guānnèi.
At this, all the petty men achieved their ambitions,
and the scholar-officials were all disheartened.
Fān's friend, Zhū Zhèn of Chénliú, collected and buried Fān's corpse.
He hid Fān's son, Yì.
When the matter was discovered,
he was imprisoned,
and his entire household was shackled.
Zhèn endured torture and interrogation,
swearing he would rather die than speak,
and Yì was thus spared.
Hú Téng of Guìyáng, a staff member of the military prefecture (Wǔfǔ yuàn), interred Wǔ's corpse
and conducted the funeral rites.
He was sentenced to perpetual banishment (jìngù) for this.
Wǔ's grandson, Fǔ,
was two years old.
Téng falsely claimed him as his own son.
Together with the Clerk (Lìngshǐ) Zhāng Chǎng of Nányáng—
The Bǎiguān Zhì states: For the Grand General's (Dàjiàngjūn) office,
there were thirty-one Clerks and Imperial Attendants (Yùshǔ).
—Fǔ also managed to escape harm.
Zhāng Huàn was promoted to Grand Minister of Agriculture (Dàsīnóng).
He was to be ennobled as a marquis for his achievements.
Huàn was deeply distressed that he had been exploited by Cáo Jié and others,
so he firmly declined the honor.
The Grand Tutor (Tàifù) Hú Guǎng was appointed Grand Tutor,
overseeing the affairs of the Secretariat (Shàngshū Shì).
The Minister of Works (Sīkōng) Liú Chǒng was appointed Minister of Education (Sītú),
and the Grand Herald (Dàhónglú) Xǔ Xù was appointed Minister of Works.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
on the last day of the month, Jiǎchén,
there was a solar eclipse.
In the eleventh month,
the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) Liú Jǔ was dismissed.
Wénrén Xí of Pèiguó, the Grand Coachman (Tàipú), was appointed Grand Commandant.
Wénrén
is a surname.
The Fēngsú Tōng says: "Shàozhèng Mǎo was a prominent figure (wénrén) in Lǔ,
and his descendants took this as their surname."
In the twelfth month,
the Xiānbēi and Huìmò raided Yōu and Bìng provinces.
In this year,
Jìfù Hé, the uncle of the king of Shūlè, killed his king and established himself.
Among the Wūhuán, the elder (Dàrén) Nánlóu of Shànggǔ had over nine thousand settlements (luò),
and Qiūlìjū of Liáoxī had over five thousand settlements,
proclaiming themselves kings.
Sūpúyán of Liáodōng had over one thousand settlements,
proclaiming himself King Qiào.
Wūyán of Yòuběipíng had over eight hundred settlements,
proclaiming himself King Hánlǔ.
The histories say the Wūhuán were strong and flourishing.
In spring,
in the first month,
on Dīngchǒu,
there was a general amnesty throughout the empire.
The Emperor welcomed Noble Lady (Guìrén) Dǒng from Héjiān.
In the third month,
on Yǐsì,
she was honored as Empress Xiàorén
and resided in the Yǒnglè Palace.
Her elder brother, Chǒng, was appointed Bearer of the Golden Mace (Zhíjíngwú),
and her nephew, Zhòng, was appointed Commandant of the Five Offices (Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiàng).
In summer,
in the fourth month,
on Rénchén,
a green snake was seen on the Emperor's seat.
On Guǐsì,
there was a strong wind,
hail,
and thunderbolts.
Pīlì means "thunder and lightning."
The Kǎoyì states: The Dìjì records:
"In the second year of Jiànníng,
in the fourth month, on Guǐsì,
there was a strong wind and hail."
The Yáng Cì Zhuàn records:
"In the first year of Xīpíng,
a green snake was seen on the Emperor's seat."
The Xù Hàn Zhì records:
"In the first year of Xīpíng,
in the fourth month,
on Jiǎwǔ,
a green snake was seen on the Emperor's seat."
The Yuán Jì records:
"In the second year of Jiànníng,
in the fourth month,
on Rénchén,
a green snake was seen;
on Guǐsì,
there was a strong wind."
According to Zhāng Huàn's biography,
the discussion of Chén and Dòu recommending Wáng and Lǐ
corresponds to the Yuán Jì.
We now follow this.
An imperial edict commanded all officials, from the Dukes (Gōng) and Ministers (Qīng) down, to submit sealed memorials.
The Grand Minister of Agriculture (Dàsīnóng) Zhāng Huàn submitted a memorial stating:
"In ancient times, when the Duke of Zhōu was not buried according to proper rites,
Heaven thereupon showed its wrath.
The Shàngshū Dàchuán says: 'When the Duke of Zhōu died,
King Chéng wished to bury him in Chéngzhōu.
Heaven then sent thunder and lightning with wind,
all the grain lay flattened,
and large trees were uprooted.
The people of the state were greatly alarmed.
The King buried the Duke of Zhōu in Bì,
to show that he dared not treat him as a subject.'
If these matters are not clearly pardoned,
the coming of omens and calamities
is all due to this.
It is imperative to promptly arrange for their burial,
return their families,
and completely abolish
the perpetual banishment (jìngù) imposed on those implicated.
Furthermore,
although the Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu) resides in the Southern Palace (Nángōng),
she receives no affectionate courtesies,
and no court official speaks of it.
Those near and far are disappointed.
It is fitting to consider a great discussion on the recompense of 'gù fù'."
Xián said: Gù
means to look back.
Fù
means to turn over and over again.
The Xiǎoyǎ says: 'Father gave me life,
Mother nurtured me,
they looked after me, they turned to me,
they carried me in their bosoms coming and going.'
When this was presented to the Chamberlains (Chángshì),
all on the left and right disliked it,
and the Emperor could not follow it himself.
Huàn also, along with Secretariat Director (Shàngshū) Liú Měng and others, jointly recommended Wáng Chàng and Lǐ Yīng as suitable candidates for the Three Dukes (Sāngōng).
Cáo Jié and others hated their words even more,
and an imperial edict was consequently issued, severely reprimanding them.
Huàn and the others all imprisoned themselves in the Court of the Grand Judge (Tíngwèi).
After several days,
they were released,
but had to redeem their offense with three months' salary.
The Gentleman of the Household, Xiè Bì 謝弼 from Dōngjùn 東郡, submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant has heard, 'Only snakes and vipers,
are omens for women.'
This is a line from the poem "Wúyáng" 無羊 in the Xiǎoyá 小雅 of the Shījīng 詩經.
Zhèng Xuán 鄭玄's commentary says: 'Vipers and snakes dwell in holes,
they are omens of the yin.'
To establish a sagely and enlightened ruler,
the Shūjīng 書經 says: 'Fathers and sons, brothers,
their crimes do not extend to each other.'
The Zuǒzhuàn 左傳 says: Xū Chén 胥臣 said: 'The Kānggào 康誥 says:
"If a father is not benevolent,
a son is not filial,
an elder brother is not friendly,
a younger brother is not respectful,
their crimes do not extend to each other."'
Now, the Shàngshū Kānggào 尚書康誥 does not contain this phrase.
How can blame be extended to the empress dowager?
If she is confined to a desolate palace,
and the heavens are all moved,
should she suffer from an illness like mist or dew,
what face will Your Majesty have to meet the world?
Xiàohé Huángdì 孝和皇帝 did not cut off the favor towards the Dòu 竇 clan;
this event is recorded in volume 47, Yǒngyuán Yongyuan 9th year.
The Lǐjì 禮記 says: 'One who becomes an heir is considered a son.'
Now, considering Huán Dì 桓帝 as a father,
how can one not consider the empress dowager as a mother?
Your Majesty, I wish you would look up to and emulate the 'steaming and advancing' transformation of Yǒuyú 有虞 [Shùn 舜],
and the compassion of the 'Kǎifēng' 凱風
for comforting one's mother.
The "Shùndiǎn" 舜典 of the Shūjīng 書經 says: 'He made progress (zhēng zhēng 烝烝) in governance,
not reaching villainy.'
Kǒng Ānguó 孔安國's commentary says: 'Zhēng zhēng 烝烝
means "steadily advancing."
It refers to Shùn's 舜 progress in the path of goodness.'
The poem "Kǎifēng" 凱風 says: 'Though there are seven sons,
none comforts the mother's heart.'
'Do not employ petty men,'
this is from the top six line of the Guà 卦 'Shī' 師 in the Yìjīng 易經.
Not yet having received rank or emolument,
by the empress mother's private favor,
they enjoyed great enfeoffments;
great winds, rain, and hail
are also due to this.
Furthermore,
the late Grand Tutor Chén Fān 陳蕃,
diligently served the royal house,
yet was entrapped by wickedness,
and was summarily exterminated,
the cruelty and excess of which
shocked the entire world;
and his disciples and former subordinates
were all banished and ostracized.
Lī 離 means
to suffer.
How can a hundred men redeem him?
The poem "Huángniǎo" 黃鳥 in the Guófēng 國風 says: 'If he could be redeemed,
a hundred men for his body.'
Release them from the net of prohibitions.
The three highest ministers are weighty instruments,
the fate of the nation depends on them.
Of the four dukes now,
only Sīkōng Liú Chǒng 司空劉寵 is resolute and holds to goodness;
the others are all men who consume salaries without merit and bring about disaster.
They will surely face the misfortune of a broken leg and overturned food cauldron.
Xián 賢 commentary says: 'The four dukes
refer to Liú Jǔ 劉矩 as Tàiwèi 太尉, Xǔ Xùn 許訓 as Sītú 司徒, Hú Guǎng 胡廣 as Tàifù 太傅, and Chǒng 寵.'
The Shūjīng 書經 says: 'If there is one resolute minister,
resolute and having no other skill.'
Kǒng Ānguó 孔安國's commentary says: 'Duànduàn 断断 refers to
a devoted and single-minded minister.'
Sù 素 means
empty;
to eat one's salary without virtue is called sùcān 素餐.
The Yìjīng 易經 says: 'Carrying a burden and riding in a carriage,
brings robbers.'
It also says: 'The cauldron's leg breaks,
overturning the duke's food cauldron.'
The cauldron is used as a metaphor for the three dukes;
sù 餗 is the food in the cauldron;
'broken leg and overturned sù' means
they are not competent for their position.
According to this year, Wénrén Xí 聞人襲 had already replaced Liú Jǔ 劉矩 as Tàiwèi 太尉,
and the other three dukes also do not match Xián's 賢 commentary.
Duàn 断,
pronounced as Dīng luàn fān 丁亂翻.
Zhé 折,
pronounced as Ér shè fān 而設翻.
Sù 餗,
pronounced sù 速.
All should be dismissed,
and the former Sīkōng Wáng Chàng 司空王暢 and Chánglè Shǎofǔ Lǐ Yīng 長樂少府李膺 be summoned to handle affairs of government.
Then calamities and changes may be averted,
and the national destiny will be long-lasting."
The attendants at court disliked his words,
and he was sent out to be Guǎnglíng Fǔchéng 廣陵府丞.
Fǔchéng 府丞
is the same as Jùnchéng 郡丞.
He returned home.
Cáo Jié's 曹節 nephew, Shào 紹, who was Dōngjùn Tàishǒu 東郡太守,
arrested Bì 弼 on another charge,
and he was flogged to death in prison.
The emperor questioned Guānglùxūn Yáng Cì 光祿勳楊賜 about the snake omen.
Cì 賜 submitted a memorial, saying:
"Good fortune does not come without reason,
and disaster does not arise in vain.
When the sovereign has a thought in his mind,
even if it has not yet manifested in his expression,
the five planets shift according to it,
and yin and yang change their patterns because of it.
If the imperial ultimate principle (huángjí 皇極) is not established,
then there will be the calamity of dragons and snakes.
Xián 賢 commentary says: 'The Hóngfàn Wǔxíng Zhuàn 洪範五行傳 says: Huáng 皇
means great;
jí 極
means center;
jiàn 建
means to establish;
niè 孽
means disaster.
If the ruler does not conform to the great center,
this is called 'not established.'
Snakes and dragons
are yin creatures.
'Omens for women.'
Your Majesty, I wish you would reflect on the way of qian (heavenly, masculine) firmness,
distinguish between what is proper for internal and external affairs,
suppress the power of the Huángfǔ 皇甫 clan,
and cut off your affection for seductive consorts.
Xián 賢 commentary says: 'Yànqī 豔妻 (seductive consort)
refers to Bāo Sì 褒姒, Queen of Zhōu Yōu Wáng 周幽王.
The officials of the Huángfǔ 皇甫 clan
are all partisans of the empress,
holding positions due to her favoritism.'
The Shījīng 詩經 says: 'Huángfǔ 皇甫, the minister,
and the seductive consort are stirring up trouble.'
Bié 別,
pronounced as Pī liè fān 彼列翻.
Then auspicious omens will immediately appear."
Cì 賜 was
Bǐng's 秉 son.
4 In the fifth month,
Tàiwèi Wénrén Xí 太尉聞人襲
and Sīkōng Xǔ Xǔ 司空許栩 were dismissed;
in the sixth month,
Sītú Liú Chǒng 司徒劉寵 was made Tàiwèi 太尉,
Tàicháng Xǔ Xùn 太常許訓 from Rúnán 汝南 was made Sītú 司徒,
and Tàipú Liú Xiāo 太僕劉囂 from Chángshā 長沙 was made Sīkōng 司空.
Xiāo 囂 had always been close to the various regular attendants,
which is why he attained the position of one of the three ducal ministers.
5 An imperial edict dispatched the court attendant FÉNG Chán to persuade the scattered Qiāng of Hànyáng to surrender.
Duàn Jiǒng believed that in spring,
when the common people were spread across the fields for agriculture,
although the Qiāng might surrender temporarily,
the government lacked provisions.
They would inevitably become bandits again,
so it was better to seize the opportunity to launch an attack.
"Launching an attack"
means letting loose soldiers to strike the Qiāng.
Duàn Jiǒng therefore advanced his camp,
positioning it forty to fifty *lǐ* from Fántíngshān, where the Qiāng were encamped.
Wèi Shōu's *Dìxíngzhì* states:
In Qúnyīn Xiàn of Āndìng Commandery, there is Fántíng.
Dù Yòu wrote Wǎtíngshān.
The commentary says: Wǎtíngshān
is in modern-day Píngliáng Dūxiāoguān Xiàn.
He attacked and defeated them.
The Qiāng forces scattered and fled eastward,
regrouping at Shèhǔgǔ.
They divided their troops to guard the upper and lower entrances of the valley.
Duàn Jiǒng planned to annihilate them in one swift action,
not wishing to let them scatter and escape again.
In autumn, the seventh month,
Duàn Jiǒng sent a thousand men to Xī Xiàn to construct a wooden palisade.
Xī Xiàn
belonged to Lǒngxī Jùn in the Former Hàn Dynasty
and to Hànyáng Jùn in the Later Hàn Dynasty.
Consult the two gazetteers.
Both state that the county has Bōzhǒngshān,
from which the Xīhànshuǐ originates.
This is the place from which
"Bōzhǒng guides the Yàng,
flowing eastward to become the Hàn"
(as mentioned in the *Yǔgòng*) originates.
Duàn Jiǒng's campaign against the Qiāng began at Gāopíng, Āndìng;
when the Qiāng were defeated,
he pursued them to Shēyán, Shàngjùn,
and after a major defeat at Língwǔgǔ,
he pursued them to Qíngyáng, Āndìng.
The various Qiāng scattered into the valleys of Hànyáng
and gathered at Fántíngshān.
After Fántíng was broken,
they regrouped at Shèhǔgǔ,
whereupon Duàn Jiǒng built a palisade at Xī Xiàn to block them.
Judging from the direction of the Qiāng's flight,
Shèhǔgǔ was northeast of Xī Xiàn,
and Fántíngshān must have been northeast of Shèhǔgǔ.
It seems the Eastern Qiāng, pursued by Duàn Jiǒng's army,
intended to flee west again, out of the pass,
to their old nests,
but were annihilated in this valley.
Xián says: The old city of Xī Xiàn
is southwest of modern-day Qínzhōu Shàngguī Xiàn.
The palisade was forty *lǐ* long, blocking them.
He dispatched Yàn, Yù, and others to lead seven thousand men, holding gags, to ascend the Western Mountain at night,
establish a camp, and dig trenches, about one *lǐ* from the enemy.
He also sent Commander Zhāng Kǎi and others to lead three thousand men up the Eastern Mountain,
at which point the enemy became aware of them.
Duàn Jiǒng then, with Kǎi and others, attacked from both the Eastern and Western Mountains,
letting loose his troops in a fierce assault,
defeating them.
He pursued them to the upper and lower entrances of the valley,
and in the depths of the mountains and valleys,
he defeated them everywhere,
beheading nineteen thousand heads, from their chieftains down.
The four thousand people whom FÉNG Chán and others had persuaded to surrender
were settled separately in the three commanderies of Āndìng, Hànyáng, and Lǒngxī.
Thus, the Eastern Qiāng were completely pacified.
Duàn Jiǒng fought a total of one hundred and eighty battles,
beheading more than thirty-eight thousand heads,
capturing more than four hundred and twenty-seven thousand miscellaneous livestock,
with expenses of forty-four *yì* (4.4 billion),
and over four hundred soldiers killed.
He was further enfeoffed as the Marquis of Xīnfēng Xiàn,
with an estate of ten thousand households.
Your servant Guāng says: The *Shū* states,
"Heaven and Earth
are the parents of all things.
Humans are the most intelligent of all things,
truly bright and wise,
they become the great rulers;
the great rulers become the parents of the people."
This is a passage from the *Tàishì* in the *Zhōushū*.
*Dǎn* means "truly."
Though their categories of *qì* differ,
their pursuit of benefit and avoidance of harm,
their love of life and hatred of death,
are the same as humans.
If they are governed correctly,
they will attach themselves and obey;
if the way is lost,
they will rebel and invade.
This is naturally so.
Therefore, the governance of the former kings was:
if they rebelled, suppress them;
if they submitted, embrace them.
They were settled in the Four Borders.
*Yì* means "border."
*Chǔ* is pronounced *chānglǚ fān*.
But to regard them as mere plants and animals,
making no distinction between good and bad,
not discerning those who stay or leave,
and slaughtering them all –
how can this be the intention of being the parents of the people?
Moreover, the reason the Qiāng rebelled

"Wronged and oppressed"
means being exploited and harboring grievances.
This was because the generals and commanders were not the right people.
If only good generals were sent to drive them out beyond the pass,

How could one exclusively find pleasure in excessive killing?
If one fails to govern them correctly,

Therefore, Duàn Jìmíng's conduct as a general

Their raids and disturbances in commanderies and counties

Afterwards, Sūn Wú completely took over their territory,

Prince Wán fled to Qí

When Chén and Dòu gained power,

When Chén and Dòu were executed,

The eunuchs, hating Lǐ Yīng and others,

Hóu Lǎn bore an even greater grudge against Zhāng Jiǎn

One who had been dismissed by Zhāng Jiǎn,

forming a faction,

An imperial edict ordered the publication of a proclamation to arrest Zhāng Jiǎn and others.
"Kānzhāng" (刊章) means
to remove the names and then publish the proclamation.
In the tenth month,
the Grand Minister of the Household, Cáo Jié, consequently prompted the officials to memorialize:

Xián states: "Gōu" (鉤)
means to be implicated or dragged in.
At this time, the emperor was fourteen years old.
He asked Cáo Jié and others:
"What does it mean to be a partisan?"
They replied:
"Those who are 'gōudǎng' (鉤黨)

The emperor said:
"What evil have partisans committed that you wish to execute them?"
They replied:
"They all recommend their own kind,

The emperor said:

They replied:

The emperor then approved their memorial.
"Guǐ" (軌)
means laws and regulations.
A ruler as a ruler,
a minister as a minister,
this is what is called the law.
For a minister to wish to endanger the state

But these eunuchs used this crime to accuse upright gentlemen,
and the emperor did not realize it.
Looking at how Emperor Yuán did not understand what caused him to summon and imprison those in the Ministry of Justice,
the darkness was even worse!
How detestable!
Someone said to Lǐ Yīng:
"You should leave!"
He replied:
"One does not evade difficulty in affairs,
nor does one escape punishment for crimes;
this is a minister’s integrity.
The 'Zuǒ Zhuàn' says, Yángshé Chì's words were: One does not shun difficulty in serving the ruler,
nor does one escape punishment for crimes.
Life and death are fated;
where would I go if I were to leave!"
So he proceeded to the imperial prison,

His disciples and former subordinates were all banned from holding office.
Jǐng Yì of Shǔjùn, a Censor, had a son, Gù, who was a student of Lǐ Yīng.
As he had not yet had his name recorded in the registry,

"Lù" (錄)
means to record.
"Dié" (牒)
means a register.
At that time, many gathered students and taught them,
with some numbering in the thousands.
Each recorded their names in a registry.
Jǐng Yì said: "Originally, I considered Lǐ Yīng to be worthy and sent my son to study under him.
How can I simply seek temporary safety

Thereupon, he memorialized to resign and return home.
Wú Dǎo, the Superintendent of Posts in Rǔnán, received the edict to arrest Fàn Pāng.
Upon reaching Zhēngqiāng,
he held the imperial edict and closed himself in the relay station.
Zhēngqiāng county
belonged to Rǔnán commandery.
It was originally Dāngxiāng county.
Since the time of Guāngwǔ, Xī Hán had achieved merit in pacifying the Qiāng,
and it was changed to Zhēngqiāng Marquisate to enfeoff him,

Fàn Pāng was a native of the county.
Xián states: "Chuán" (傳)
means a relay station.
The pronunciation is "zhī liàn fān".
The old city of Zhēngqiāng is now southeast of Yǎnlíng county in Yùzhōu.
The people of the county did not know what to do.
Fàn Pāng heard of it and said:
"It must be for me."
He immediately went to the prison himself.
The county magistrate, Guō Yī, was greatly astonished.
He came out,
removed his seal and sash,

"The world is vast; why are you here!"
Fàn Pāng replied:

His mother came to bid him farewell.
Fàn Pāng said to his mother:
"Zhòngbó is filial and respectful,
sufficient for your support.
Zhòngbó
is the courtesy name of Fàn Pāng’s younger brother.
"Gōng" (供)
is pronounced "jù yòng fān".
"Yǎng" (養)
is pronounced "yáng shàng fān".
The living and the dead will each find their place.
I only ask that you, mother, cut off this unbearable affection,

Zhòngbó
was Fàn Pāng’s younger brother.
Lóngshū Jūn
refers to Fàn Pāng’s father, Xiǎn, the Chancellor of Lóngshū Marquisate.
His mother said:
"Now you have achieved fame equal to Lǐ Yīng and Dù Mì.
What regret is there in dying!
Lǐ Yīng and Dù Mì refer to Lǐ Yīng and Dù Mì.
Can one seek both longevity
and achieve both?"
Fàn Pāng knelt to receive her instruction,
bowed twice, and took his leave.
He looked at his son and said:
"I would want you to do evil,
but evil is not to be done;
I would want you to do good,
but then I would not have done evil."
Those on the road who heard this
could not help but shed tears.
In total, more than a hundred partisans died,
and their wives and children were all exiled to the borders.
All heroes and scholars of integrity throughout the realm
were indiscriminately labeled as partisans by the eunuchs.
Those with grievances or enmities
would then entrap and harm others.
Even trivial grudges
led to people being wrongly included in the partisan list.
The provinces and commanderies, following orders,
even those who had never interacted,
also suffered the calamity.
"Lí" (離)
is the same as "lí" (罹),
meaning to suffer.
"Fèijìn" (廢禁)
means to be dismissed and banned from office.
Guō Tài, upon hearing of the deaths of the partisans,

"The 'Shī Jīng' says: 'When the people are gone,

The Hàn dynasty is doomed, but we do not yet know

This is a line from "Zhèngyuè" in the "Xiǎoyǎ" section of the "Shī Jīng".

Zhèng Shì says: Observing the crow perching on the roof of a wealthy person

Yuán Hóng's chronicle attributes it to grieving over the "Three Lords" and "Eight Talents",
which we follow here.
And he did not speak critically or argue vehemently.
"Hé" (覈)
means to deeply investigate the truth,
to scrutinize.
Zhāng Jiǎn (張儉) was a fugitive, in dire straits.
He would arrive at a gate
and throw himself upon its inhabitants,

Families would break up their households to accommodate him.
Later, he drifted to Dōnglái (東萊),

Máo Qīn (毛欽), the magistrate of Wàihuáng (外黃), arrived at the door with soldiers.

Máo Qīn (毛欽) was likely the magistrate of Huáng (黃) County;

Cāo (操),
pronounced qiān gāo.
"Zhāng Jiǎn (張儉) is guilty and a fugitive.

Qīn (欽) then stood up and patted Dú (篤), saying:

Dú (篤) said:

Xián (賢) says: "Míngtíng (明廷)"

Among those he encountered,

His clan relatives were all exterminated,

He did not meet him.

means to return.
(Yǒng's (褎) brother) Róng (融), at sixteen,

"He came seeking me;

The official asked their mother,

When the party prohibitions were lifted,

A year or so later,

(Another man, Fù (馥),) sighed:

is the same as xū (鬚).

At first,

Initially,

At that time, the Central Regular Attendant Yuán Shè (袁赦)

their carriages,

Hóng (閎) saw that the times were dangerous and chaotic,

Your subject Guāng says: When the world has the Way,
the gentlemen proclaim in the royal court to rectify the crimes of the petty men,
and none dare to disobey.
When the world lacks the Way,
the gentlemen keep silent to avoid the calamity of the petty men,

The sixth-four line of Kūn,
residing near the position of the fifth but lacking the meaning of mutual affinity,

Guài uses five yangs to decide one yin;

and the way of the gentlemen flourishes,

If one is not in that position,
and the four seas are in chaos,
and yet desires to save the situation with mere words,
judging people,
stirring the turbid and exalting the clear,
poking the head of a viper,
and kicking
the tail of a tiger or wolf,
to the point of suffering cruel punishments,
with calamity extending to friends,
the class of scholars being exterminated and the state consequently perishing,
is this not tragic!
Only Guō Tài was both discerning and wise,
thus preserving his life.
Just as Yǐn Jífǔ praised Zhòngshānfǔ, so too do I praise Guō Tài.
“Not waiting until the end of the day,”
refers to Shēntú Pán obtaining the sixth-two line of Yù.
Jǐ,
read jū xī.
9 On the last day of the Gēngzǐ month,
there was a solar eclipse.
10 In the eleventh month,
Grand Commandant Liú Chǒng was dismissed;
Guō Xǐ of Fúgōu, Grand Coachman, became Grand Commandant.
11 The Xiānbēi raided Bìngzhōu.
12 Chánglè Grand Coachman Cáo Jié was critically ill,
and an imperial edict appointed him General of Chariots and Cavalry.
A short while later,
his illness healed,
he returned his seal and ribbon,
and was reinstated as Central Regular Attendant,
with the title of Special Advanced,
and a salary of two thousand bushels (dàn) of grain.
13 King Bógù of Gāogōulí raided Liáodōng,
and the Grand Administrator of Xuántú, Gěng Lín, attacked and made him surrender.
1 Spring,
third month,
on the last day of the Bǐngyín month,
there was a solar eclipse.
2 Duàn Jiǒng was summoned back to the capital,
and appointed Palace Attendant.
Jiǒng had been on the frontier for over ten years,
never sleeping on a mat for a single day,
sharing hardships with his generals and soldiers;
thus, they were all willing to fight to the death,
achieving success wherever they went.
3 Summer,
fourth month,
Grand Commandant Guō Xǐ was dismissed;
Wénrén Xí, Grand Master of the Palace, became Grand Commandant.
4 Autumn,
seventh month,
Minister of Works Liú Xiāopí died;
eighth month,
Qiáo Xuán of Liángguó, Grand Herald, became Minister of Works.
The Xìngpǔ states: The Yellow Emperor was buried on Qiáoshān,
and his descendants guarded the tomb,
thus taking the surname.
5 Ninth month,
Dǒng Chǒng, Commander of the Capital, was imprisoned and died
for falsely claiming to have received a request from Empress Dowager Yǒnglè.
6 Winter,
Grand Administrator of Yùlín, Gǔ Yǒng, by means of kindness and trust, induced over one hundred thousand Wūhǔ people to surrender.
Wàn Zhèn said: "The land of Wūhǔ
is south of Guǎngzhōu
and north of Jiāozhōu."
Xián said: "Wūhǔ
is the name of a southern barbarian tribe."
The Guǎngzhōujì states: "Their custom is to eat people,
drink wine through their noses,
and still eat with their mouths as before."
Liú Xù said: "Guìzhōu Yùpíng County,
the Han-era Yùlín Guǎngyù County land,
was formerly inhabited by the Xī'ōu and Luòyuè.
Gǔ Yǒng recruited the Wūhǔ to surrender,
and established seven counties,
which are these."
Dù Yòu said: "The Wūhǔ land is southwest of today's Nánhǎi Commandery,
and managed by Běishuòníng Commandery, Ānnán Prefecture."
Hǔ,
read hū gǔ.
They received official robes,
and seven counties were established.
7 Mèng Tuó of Fúfēng, Inspector of Liángzhōu,
sent his subordinate Rèn Shè to lead five hundred soldiers from Dūnhuáng,
along with Wùjǐ Commandant
Cáo Kuān and Western Regions Chief Clerk Zhāng Yàn leading the forces of Yānqí, Qiūcí, and the Anterior and Posterior Cheshī,
totaling over thirty thousand men, to attack Shūlè,
because in the first year Shūlè had assassinated its king.
Rèn,
sound like rén.
Dūn,
read tú mén.
Jiào,
read hù jiào.
Qiūcí,
sound like qiū cí.
After more than forty days,
they could not subdue it,
and withdrew.
Thereafter, the kings of Shūlè successively murdered each other,
and the imperial court was unable to regain control.
Initially,
the Central Regular Attendant Zhāng Ràng had a supervisor-slave
who managed his household affairs,
and whose power and influence were resounding.
Mèng Tuó, being wealthy,
befriended this slave,
exhaustively offering gifts and asking about his desires,
holding nothing back.
Meaning his affection was broad and he left nothing out.
He asked him what he desired.
Mèng Tuó said:
“I only hope that you will bow to me once!”
At that time, hundreds or thousands of carriages of guests sought an audience with Zhāng Ràng.
When Mèng Tuó arrived at Zhāng Ràng’s residence,
he came late
and could not enter.
The supervisor-slave then led the various servants to greet and bow to him on the road,
and together they carried his carriage into the gate.
The guests were all surprised,
thinking that Mèng Tuó was greatly favored by Zhāng Ràng,
and all vied to bribe him with treasures and curiosities.
Mèng Tuó divided these and presented them to Zhāng Ràng,
who was greatly pleased.
Because of this, Mèng Tuó was appointed Inspector of Liángzhōu.
1 Spring,
first month,
on the day Jiǎzǐ,
the Emperor underwent the capping ceremony (came of age),
and granted a general amnesty to the empire,

2 Second month,
on the day Guǐmǎo,

3 Third month,
on the first day of the Xīnyǒu month,

4 Grand Commandant Wénrén Xí was dismissed;
Lǐ Xián of Rǔnán, Grand Coachman, became Grand Commandant.
5 There was a great epidemic.
Sītú Xǔ Xùn 許訓 was dismissed;
Sīkōng Qiáo Xuán 橋玄 was made Sītú;
In summer,
in the fourth month,
Tài Cháng Nányáng Lái Yàn 南陽來豔 was made Sīkōng.
6 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
Sīkōng Lái Yàn 來豔 was dismissed.
7 On *Guǐchǒu* 癸丑,
the noble lady Sòng shì 宋氏 was established as empress.
The empress
was the daughter of Zhí Jīn Wú Fēng 酆.
8 Sītú Qiáo Xuán 橋玄 was dismissed;
Tài Cháng Nányáng Zōng Jù 南陽宗俱 was made Sīkōng,
and the former Sīkōng Xǔ Xǔ 許栩 was made Sītú.
9 Because Empress Dowager Dòu 竇 太后 had the merit of assisting in his enthronement,
in winter,
in the tenth month,
on the first day of *Wùzǐ* 戊子,
the Emperor led his officials to pay respects to the Empress Dowager at Nángōng 南宮,
personally offering a longevity feast.
Huáng Mén Lìng Dǒng Méng 董萌 thereupon repeatedly pleaded the Empress Dowager's grievances,
and the Emperor deeply accepted them.
Her provisions and allowances
were increased beyond what they had been before.
Cáo Jié 曹節 and Wáng Fǔ 王甫 resented this,
and falsely accused Dǒng Méng 董萌 of slandering Yǒnglè Gōng 永樂宮,
which was where the Emperor's mother, Xiàorén Dǒng Tàihòu 孝仁董太后, resided.
*Lè* 樂
is pronounced *luò*.

Xīpíng 熹平 First Year

1 In spring,
in the first month,
the imperial carriage went to Yuánlíng 原陵.
Sītú Yuán Chénliú Cài Yōng 司徒掾陳留蔡邕 said:
"I have heard that in antiquity, there were no tomb sacrifices.
The court has the rite of going to the imperial mausoleum,
which I initially thought could be reduced;
now, seeing the solemnity of the ceremony,
and observing its original intent,
I realize that Emperor Xiàomíng 孝明 was profoundly filial and compassionate,
and it cannot be easily changed.
According to the *Lǐyí Zhì* 禮儀志,
the Western Capital historically had the practice of ascending the imperial mausoleum;
by the Eastern Capital, the ceremonial forms became even more complete;
a brief account is found in volume 44, Yǒngpíng 永平 First Year.
*Shàng* 上
is pronounced *shǎng*.
*Yuán* 掾
is pronounced *juàn*.
*Yì* 易
is pronounced *yì*.
This is what is meant."
2 In the third month,
on *Rénxū* 壬戌,
Tàifù Hú Guǎng 胡廣 passed away,
at the age of eighty-two.
Hú Guǎng 胡廣 circulated through the four Ducal offices:
Tàifù, Tàiwèi, Sītú, Sīkōng.
Xián 賢 said:
Hú Guǎng 胡廣 was made Sīkōng in the first year of Hàn'ān 漢安 under Emperor Shùn 順;
he passed away in the first year of Xīpíng 熹平,
making it thirty-one years.
(Emperors) Ān 安, Shùn 順, Chōng 沖, Zhì 質, Huán 桓, Líng 靈.
He was never dismissed for a full year
before being promoted again.
Most of those he appointed were renowned scholars of the realm,
and he, along with his former subordinates Chén Fān 陳蕃 and Lǐ Xián 李咸, were simultaneously among the Sān Sī 三司.
Sān Sī 三司
refers to the Sān Gōng 三公.
He had a clear understanding of court regulations,
hence a proverb in the capital said:
"If nothing can be managed,
ask Bóshǐ 伯始;
if the world is in harmony,
there is Duke Hú 胡公."
Hú Guǎng 胡廣,
courtesy name Bóshǐ 伯始.
If it is already said,
"If nothing can be managed, ask Bóshǐ 伯始,"
then the expectations and responsibilities at that time were also heavy,
how could his thirty-plus years circulating through the four Ducal offices be considered an honor!
Xián 賢 said: *Zhōng* 中
means harmony.
*Yōng* 庸
means constant.
Harmony and constancy are virtues that can always be practiced.
He always spoke humbly and showed respectful demeanor to curry favor with the times,
lacking the spirit of loyalty and uprightness,
and the world consequently thought little of him.
3 In the fifth month,
on *Jǐsì* 己巳,
a general amnesty was declared,
and the reign era was changed.
4 Chánglè Tàipú Hóu Jué 長樂太僕侯覺 was dismissed for abusing power and being extravagant,
had his seals and cords confiscated by imperial edict,
and committed suicide.
Chánglè Tàipú 長樂太僕
was an official of the Empress Dowager's palace;
in charge of chariots,
eunuchs served in this role.
His rank was 2,000 *dàn* (bushels).
*Lè* 樂
is pronounced *luò*.
5 In the sixth month,
the capital experienced severe flooding.
6 Empress Dowager Dòu's 竇太后 mother died in Bǐjǐng 比景.
The Empress Dowager fell ill from grief and sorrow,
and on *Guǐsì* 癸巳,
she passed away in Yúntái 雲臺.
The eunuchs, having accumulated resentment towards the Dòu 竇 clan,
transported the Empress Dowager's corpse in a clothing cart and placed it in a market stall south of the city.
After several days,
Cáo Jié 曹節 and Wáng Fǔ 王甫 wanted to inter her with the rites of a noble lady.
The Emperor said:
"The Empress Dowager personally enthroned me
and oversaw the great undertaking,
how can she conclude as a noble lady!"
Thereupon, a funeral was held and the rites completed.
Cáo Jié and others wanted to bury the empress dowager separately,
and have Noble Lady Féng enshrined and interred with Huán Dì.
Xián said: "To be enshrined and interred"
means for a recently deceased sovereign to be enshrined in the temple of an earlier deceased one,
or for a wife to be enshrined with her husband,
or for an enshrined concubine to be enshrined with her concubine-ancestress.
He ordered the Regular Palace Attendant Zhào Zhōng to oversee the discussion.
The Grand Commandant Lǐ Xián was ill at the time,
but he rose, supported,
pounding pepper to take with him.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: "The 'Explanation of Woods' states:
'Huì
is large pepper.'
Guō Pú said: 'Today, pepper trees grow in clumps,
and those with large fruits are called huì.'
Lù Jī's commentary says:
'Pepper trees are like zhūyú,
with thorns,
and firm, smooth leaves.
People in Shǔ make tea,
and people in Wú make tea,
both boiling their leaves to make it fragrant.
Currently, there is pepper in the mountains of Chénggāo,
called bamboo leaf pepper;
its tree is also like Shǔ pepper,
with less toxicity and heat,
unsuitable for compounding medicine,
but it can be added to food
and used to steam chicken and pork,
providing the best fragrance.
There are also pepper trees on the islands of Dōnghǎi;
their branches and leaves are all similar,
but their fruits are long rather than round,
very fragrant,
and their taste resembles orange peel.'
The 'Materia Medica' also states: 'Pepper
is very hot
and toxic.'
According to Lǐ Xián pounding pepper to take with him,
Qí Míngdì, when he was about to kill the descendants of Gāo Wǔ,
ordered the Grand Steward to boil two bushels of pepper,
presumably because its poison could kill.
'If the empress dowager is not permitted to share the sacrifice with Huán Dì,
I will not return alive!'
He intended to dispute it to the death.
Hundreds of people were seated,
each looking around for a long time,
none willing to speak first.
Zhào Zhōng said:
'The deliberation should be decided now!'
The Grand Judge Chén Qiú said:
'The empress dowager, with her abundant virtue and good family,
presided over the realm as mother.
It is fitting for her to share the sacrifice with the late emperor.
There should be no doubt about this.'
Zhōng laughed and said:
'Grand Judge Chén should immediately take up his brush.'
Qiú then submitted his deliberation, saying:
'The empress dowager, while in the pepper chamber,
possessed the virtue of intelligent motherly conduct. She encountered an unfortunate era,
but supported and established the sagacious and enlightened emperor to inherit the ancestral temple.
Her merits were extremely weighty.
After the late emperor passed away,
she encountered a great imprisonment,
and was moved to an empty palace.
Unhappily, she died early.
Although her family incurred guilt,
the matter was not the empress dowager's fault.
If she is now buried separately,
it would truly disappoint the expectations of the world.
Moreover, Noble Lady Féng's tomb was once exhumed,
her bones exposed,
sharing a corpse with bandits,
her spirit defiled.
Xián said: "Duàn Jiǒng, when he was the Magistrate of Hénán,
had a bandit excavate Noble Lady Féng's tomb,
and was demoted to Counsellor Remonstrant.
I conclude that Jiǒng entered as a Court Attendant in the third year of Yánxī,
then transferred to Bearer of the Golden Mace and Magistrate of Hénán.
Thus, the tomb excavation occurred around this year."
"Bèi"
is read as Pí Yì.
How can she be fittingly enshrined with the most esteemed one!'
Zhōng read Qiú's deliberation,
changed his expression and looked up and down,
scoffing at Qiú:
'Grand Judge Chén's proposal is quite strong!'
"Chī"
means to laugh.
'Since the Chéns and Dòus were wronged,
and the empress dowager was unjustly imprisoned,
I have always felt pain,
and the world has expressed indignation!
To speak of it today,
and then retire to suffer punishment,
is my long-cherished wish!'
Lǐ Xián said:
'I originally thought it should be so;
it truly accords with my intention.'
Thereupon, all officials from the dukes and ministers down followed Qiú's deliberation.
Cáo Jié and Wáng Fǔ still disputed,
believing that:
'The family of Empress Liáng committed grave wickedness,
and she was buried separately in Yìlíng.
Empress Liáng died before Huán Dì and was buried in Yìlíng.
After Liáng Jì was executed,
the mausoleum was first abolished and became a tomb for a noble lady.
And Lady Lǐ was enshrined with the sacrifice.
During the rebellion of the deposed crown prince,
Emperor Wǔ issued an edict deposing his mother, Empress Wèi,
and the empress committed suicide.
When Emperor Wǔ died,
Huò Guāng, following the emperor's private intention,
had Lady Lǐ enshrined with the sacrifice.
How can she be interred with the late emperor!'
Lǐ Xián again submitted a memorial, saying:
'I humbly recall that Empress Dòu of Zhāngdé cruelly harmed Gōnghuái,
and Empress Yán of Ānsī's family committed grave wickedness.
The matter of Empress Dòu is found in volume 46, in the eighth year of Jiànchū under Emperor Zhāng.
The matter of Empress Yán is found in volumes 50 and 51, in the third and fourth years of Yángguāng under Emperor Ān.
"Fù"
is read as Fú Yòu.
Yet there was no text from the court to degrade or demote them.
As for Empress Wèi,
Emperor Xiàowǔ himself deposed her,
so she cannot be used as a comparison.
Now, the Empress Dowager Chánglè holds her esteemed title,
and personally acted as regent,
moreover, she supported and established the sagacious and enlightened emperor,
glorifying the imperial throne.
The empress dowager regards Your Majesty as her son,
how can Your Majesty not regard the empress dowager as your mother!
A son does not depose his mother,
a minister does not demean his sovereign.
It is fitting to inter her with the late emperor in Xuānlíng,
entirely following the old system.'
The emperor read the memorial
and followed it.
In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the Jiǎyín day,
Empress Huánsī was buried in Xuānlíng.
7 Someone wrote on the Zhūquè Gate Tower:
"Ancient and Modern Notes": "In the eleventh month of the second year of Yǒngpíng,
the Northern Palace was first built.
Zhūquè
refers to the gate tower of the Southern Sīmǎ Gate,

'The world is in great chaos,
Cáo Jié and Wáng Fǔ secretly murdered the empress dowager,

and there are no loyal speakers.'

After more than a month,

Duàn Jiǒng, the Censor-in-Chief, was appointed to replace him.

Previously,
the Colonel Director of Retainers, Wáng Yù, relying on eunuchs,

Huàn once competed with Duàn Jiǒng in attacking the Qiāng,

The matter is found in the previous volume, in the first year of Jiànníng.
He wanted to drive Huàn back to Dūnhuáng and harm him;
Huàn moved to the jurisdiction of Hóngnóng. The matter is found in the previous volume, in the first year of Yǒngkāng under Emperor Huán.
"Dūn"

Only then was he spared.
Initially,
Lǐ Hǎo of Wèi Jùn, serving as the Sīlì Xiàowèi,
killed Sū Qiān of Fúfēng due to an old grudge.
Qiān's son, Bùwéi, buried but did not inter him,
changed his name,
and gathered followers to seek revenge.
When Hǎo was promoted to Dàsīnóng,
Bùwéi hid in a granary,
dug through the ground to reach Hǎo's bedchamber.
The *Shuōwén* says: *kuí* (廥)
is a storehouse for hay and straw,
pronounced *gōngwài fān*.
Hǎo was greatly frightened,
laid planks on the ground,
and moved nine times in one night.
Bùwéi also dug up Hǎo's father's tomb,
severed his head,
and displayed it in the market.
Hǎo sought to apprehend him but failed,
and in his indignation and rage,
he vomited blood and died.
Bùwéi received a pardon and returned home,
then buried his father and observed mourning rites.
Zhāng Huàn had always been close to the Sū clan,
while Duàn Jiǒng was on good terms with Hǎo.
Jiǒng appointed Bùwéi as a Sīlì Cóngshì.
Bùwéi, in fear,
claimed illness and did not report for duty.
Jiǒng was enraged,
and ordered Cóngshì Zhāng Xián to go to Bùwéi's house and kill him,
first giving poison to Xián's father, saying:
"If Xián fails to get Bùwéi,
then you may drink this!"
Xián then apprehended Bùwéi,
and executed his entire household of over sixty people.
All were put to death.
8 When Wáng Lǐ of Bóhǎi was demoted to Yǐngtáo,
he sought reinstatement through the Zhōng Chángshì Wáng Fǔ,

But he did not return to pay the money.
Zhōng Chángshì Zhèng Sà and Zhōng Huángmén Dǒng Téng frequently communicated with Lǐ.
Fǔ secretly observed them and reported to Duàn Jiǒng.
In winter,
tenth month,
Sà was arrested and sent to Běisì Yù.

to commit suicide.
His eleven concubines, seventy children, and twenty-four entertainers all died in prison,

*Gòu* (句),
