Lì
was the Emperor's cousin.)
pronounced *zǐlǐ fān*.)
5 Sūn Jiān of Fùchūn, Sīmǎ of Wú Jùn, recruited brave and skilled men,
obtaining over a thousand,
to assist the commanderies and counties in suppressing Xǔ Shēng.
(The *Bǎiguān Zhì* states that commanderies had a Céng and a Chángshǐ,
but no Sīmǎ.
This was probably because at that time, with the rise of bandits,
a Sīmǎ was appointed to oversee military affairs.
Fùchūn county
belonged to Wú Commandery.
Xián says: This is today's Fùyáng County in Hángzhōu.
To avoid the personal name of Empress Dowager Zhèng, mother of Emperor Jiǎnwén of Jìn,
it was renamed Fùyáng.)
In the eleventh month,
Zāng Mín and Chén Yín severely defeated Shēng in Kuàijī
and beheaded him.
6 Rènchéngwáng Bó died.
Having no son,
the kingdom was cut off.
(In the fourth year of Yánxī of Emperor Huán,
Bó inherited the enfeoffment of Rènchéng Kingdom.)
7 In the twelfth month,
the Xiānbēi entered Běidì.
Tàishǒu Xià Yù led the Túgè in pursuit and attack,
defeating them.
Yù was promoted to Hù Wúhuán Xiàowèi.
The Xiānbēi again raided Bìngzhōu.
8 Sīkōng Táng Zhēn was dismissed;
Shǎofǔ Xǔ Xùn of Yǒnglè was made Sīkōng.
(The Shǎofǔ of Yǒnglè
was an official of Empress Dowager Dǒng's palace.)
pronounced *luò*.)
1. In the spring,
in the third month,
an imperial edict commanded all Confucian scholars to correct the text of the Five Classics.
The Counselor, Cài Yōng, was ordered to inscribe them in three scripts: Guwén, Zhuàn, and Lì.
These were carved into stone tablets
and erected outside the gate of the Imperial Academy.
The Luòyáng Jì (Record of Luòyáng) states: The Imperial Academy was located outside the Kāiyáng Gate, south of the city of Luòyáng.
Its lecture hall was ten zhàng long
and two zhàng wide.
In front of the hall were four sections of stone classics,
consisting in total of forty-six stele.
Going west,
the Shàngshū, Zhōuyì, and Gōngyángzhuàn were preserved on sixteen stele,
while twelve stele were destroyed.
Going south,
the fifteen stele of the Lǐjì had all collapsed and broken.
Going east,
three stele of the Lúnyǔ were destroyed.
The names of Jiànyì Dàfū Mǎ Rìdī and Yìláng Cài Yōng were on the Lǐjì stele.
Guwén
is also called Kēdòu Shū (tadpole script).
Zhuàn
is Dàzhuàn (Great Seal script).
Lì
is what is now called Bāfēn Shū (eight-part script).
Jiāng Shì of the Later Wèi dynasty said: "When Fúxīshì arose, the eight trigrams shaped his strokes.
When Xuānyuánshì flourished, the divine tortoise revealed its patterns.
The ancient historian Cāngjié observed the patterns of the two primary forces (heaven and earth)
and studied the tracks of birds and beasts,
then he created characters
to replace knotted cords.
By the time of the Three Dynasties,
their forms differed considerably.
Although they were created based on classifications,
they could not surpass the methods of Master Cāng.
The Zhōulǐ (Rites of Zhōu) states: The Baoshì taught the noble sons of the state the six types of writing: first, Zhǐshì (indicative);
second, Xiàngxíng (pictographic);
third, Xíngshēng (picto-phonetic);
fourth, Huìyì (associative compound);
fifth, Zhuǎnzhu (transferring meaning);
sixth, Jiǎjiè (phonetic loan).
These were probably the surviving methods of Shǐ Xié.
Later, during the reign of King Xuān, the Grand Historian Shǐ Zhòu wrote fifteen chapters of Dàzhuàn,
which were sometimes similar to Guwén and sometimes different;
people at the time called it Zhòushū.
Kǒngzǐ (Confucius) edited the Six Classics,
and Zuǒ Qiūmíng narrated the Chūnqiū (Spring and Autumn Annals),
all using Guwén.
When the Seven States had different systems,
their writing varied;
when Qín unified the realm,
Lǐ Sī proposed to abolish anything that did not conform to Qín script.
Sī wrote the Cāngjié Piān,
Chēfǔ Lì Zhào Gāo wrote the Yuánlì Piān,
and Tàishǐ Lì Húmǔ Jìng wrote the Bóxué Piān.
All of them drew upon Shǐ Zhòu's work,
with some simplifications and revisions.
This is what is called Xiǎozhuàn (Small Seal script).
When Qín burned the classics
and abolished old customs,
the number of officials and prisoners increased,
leading to a demand for simplicity and ease;
thus, Lìshū (clerical script) began to be used,
and Guwén consequently ceased.
Lìshū
was created by Chéng Miǎo of Xiàdù, whom Shǐhuáng (First Emperor) ordered to adapt Xiǎozhuàn.
People of the time, considering Miǎo a mere clerk,
called it Lìshū.
Thus, Qín had eight types of writing: first, Dàzhuàn;
second, Xiǎozhuàn;
third, Fúshū (tally script);
fourth, Chóngshū (insect script);
fifth, Móyìn (seal engraving script);
sixth, Shǔshū (official document script);
seventh, Shūshū (weapon script);
eighth, Lìshū.
With the rise of Hàn, there was the Wèilǜ Xué,
which taught Zhòushū
and also practiced the eight types.
There was also Cǎoshū (cursive script),
whose origin is unknown.
Although its form lacked fixed rules,
it was also a temporary adaptation.
During the reign of Emperor Xiàoxuān,
those who mastered the reading of Cāngjié were summoned,
and only Zhāng Chǎng received the transmission.
The Inspector of Liángzhōu, Dù Yè, and Yuán Lǐ of Pèi, and the Great Scholar Qín Jìn were also able to explain it.
During the reign of Emperor Xiàopíng,
Lǐ and over a hundred others were summoned to explain characters in the Wèiyāng Palace.
The Palace Attendant Yáng Xióng collected these and compiled the Xùnzǎn.
During Wáng Mǎng's interim regency,
he ordered the Grand Marshal Zhēn Fēng to collate the sections of characters,
and he significantly revised Guwén.
At that time, there were six types of writing: first, Guwén,
which was the text found in Kǒngzǐ's wall;
second, Qíjì (unusual characters), which were variations of Guwén;
third, Zhuànshū,
said to be Xiǎozhuàn;
fourth, Zuǒshū,
which was Qín Lìshū;
fifth, Miàozhuàn (seal script for seals),
used for engraving seals;
sixth, Niǎochóng (bird and insect script),
used for writing on banners and tallies.
The "text from the wall" refers to
King Gōng of Lǔ demolishing Kǒngzǐ's residence
and discovering the Shàngshū, Chūnqiū, Lúnyǔ, and Xiàojīng.
Also, Marquis Běipíng, Zhāng Cāng, presented the Chūnqiū Zuǒshìzhuàn,
whose script was similar to that of the Kǒng family,
and which was thus the Guwén of previous generations.
In the Later Hàn,
the Palace Gentleman Cáo Xǐ of Fúfēng was known as a master of Zhuàn (seal script).
His method differed slightly from Lǐ Sī's,
but it was extremely refined and skillful.
Thereafter, later scholars
all followed his method.
An imperial edict also ordered the Palace Attendant Jiǎ Kuí to revise old texts.
Diverse arts and unique techniques,
being a single aspect of royal instruction,
if there was anything that could benefit the state,
nothing was not thoroughly collected.
Kuí
was the teacher of the ancient studies of Xǔ Shèn of Rǔnán.
Shèn lamented the contemporary fascination with novelty
and deplored the superficiality of common scholars,
so he compiled the Shūowén Jiězì in fifteen chapters.
It categorized and grouped characters,
being comprehensive yet not exceeding bounds,
and is most worthy of discussion.
The Left Commander of the Palace Guard, Cài Yōng of Chénliú, adopted the methods of Lǐ Sī and Cáo Xǐ
to create various ancient and modern forms.
An imperial edict ordered stone tablets to be erected at the Imperial Academy,
on which the Five Classics were inscribed,
with their titles written in the standard script.
Most of these were by Yōng.
Later, when the Hóngdū Academy was opened,
extraordinary talents in calligraphy and painting flocked to it.
At that time, many regions offered their seal scripts,
but none surpassed Yōng's.
In the early Wèi dynasty,
the Erudite Zhāng Yī of Qīnghé authored the Pí Cāng, Guǎng Yǎ, and Gǔjīn Zìgǔ.
He gathered omissions
and expanded categories of affairs,
which certainly benefited literature.
However, his Gǔjīn Zìgǔ, compared to Xǔ Shèn's work,
sometimes correctly captured and sometimes missed the ancient and modern forms and uses.
Hándān Chún of Chénliú was also contemporary with Yī.
He excelled in the character explanations of Cāng, Yǎ, and Xǔ Shì.
He deeply studied and mastered the principles of the eight styles and six types of writing.
He was as famous as Yī.
He also erected the three-character stone classics west of the Hàn stele.
Compared to the Shūowén's seal and clerical scripts, they were largely similar,
but the ancient characters showed minor differences.
There were also Wéi Dàn of Jīngzhào and Wèi Jì of Hédōng, two families
both known as masters of seal script.
At that time, the inscriptions on palace and pavilion plaques, and on precious vessels,
were all by Dàn.
They were passed down through generations of his descendants,
and their artistry was praised by the world.
During the Jìn dynasty,
Lǚ Chén, the Director of Sacrifices for the King of Yìyáng, presented the Zìlín in six volumes.
Examining its nature and purpose,
it was based on Xǔ Shèn's Shūowén;
but by arranging chapters and sentences,
he subtly distinguished ancient, Zhòu, rare, and confusing characters.
The text adopted standard clerical script
without deviating from the seal script's intent.
Chén's younger brother Jìng separately followed the method of the former Director of the Left Bureau, Lǐ Dēng's, Shēnglèi,
and composed the Yùnjí in five volumes,
where Gōng, Shāng, Yuè, Lù, Zhǐ, and Yǔ each constituted a chapter.
However, his characters differed from his brother's like Lǔ and Wèi,
and his pronunciations varied like Chǔ and Xià,
sometimes showing discrepancies.
The Imperial Wèi succeeded the last of many kings.
Times changed and customs shifted,
and characters were altered.
Seal forms were confused and incorrect,
clerical script forms lost their authenticity.
Vulgar learning and crude habits
further added fabricated characters.
Artful speakers and eloquent debaters
created doubts based on their own ideas,
confusing the public at the time,
making rectification difficult.
For example, they said,
"追 (zhuī, to chase) is 'guī' (to return),
巧言 (qiǎoyán, artful words) is 'biàn' (to debate),
小免 (xiǎomiǎn, small rabbit) is 'tù' (rabbit),
神虫 (shénchóng, divine insect) is 'cán' (silkworm)."
Such instances are very numerous,
and all are inconsistent with Kǒngshì's Guwén, Shǐ Zhòu's Dàzhuàn, Xǔ Shì's Shūowén, and the three-character stone classics.
Shì's account of character studies
is quite detailed in its origins and developments,
hence it is fully recorded here.
Zhào Míngchéng's Jīnshílù states: The stone classics
were erected in the fourth year of Xīpíng during the reign of Emperor Líng of Hàn.
The characters are Cài Yōng's small characters in Bāfēn script;
The preface to the Rúlín Zhuàn (儒林傳) in the Hòuhàn Shū (後漢書) states
"they were the three scripts of gǔwén (古文), zhuàn (篆), and lì (隸),"
which
is incorrect.
The script written by Yōng (邕) was bāfēn (八分),
while the Sāntǐ Shíjīng (三體石經) was erected during the Wèi (魏) period.
Hóng (洪) Shì's (氏) Lìxù (隸續) states: The stone classics are mentioned in Fàn (范) Shǐ's (史) Dìjì (帝紀), Rúlín (儒林), and Huànzhě Zhuàn (宦者傳),
all referring to the Wǔjīng (五經).
Cài Yōng (蔡邕) and Zhāng Xùn's (張馴) biographies, however, mention the Liùjīng (六經).
Only the Rúlín Zhuàn (儒林傳) says: "They were the gǔwén (古文), zhuàn (篆), and lì (隸) styles of calligraphy."
Lì (酈) Shì's (氏) Shuǐjīng (水經) states: The Hàn (漢) erected stone classics at the Tàixué (太學).
In the Zhèngshǐ (正始) era of Wèi (魏),
the Sānzì Shíjīng (三字石經) in gǔwén (古文), zhuàn (篆), and lì (隸) scripts was again carved.
The Táng Zhì (唐志) lists two kinds of Sānzì Shíjīng (三字石經) and gǔzhuàn (古篆),
namely the Shàngshū (尚書)
and the Zuǒzhuàn (左傳).
Only the Suí Zhì (隋志) records variations;
its catalog includes seven types of Yīzì Shíjīng (一字石經)
and three types of Sānzì Shíjīng (三字石經).
Since it considers the Qī Jīng (七經) to be Cài Yōng's (蔡邕) writing,
and then says Wèi (魏) erected the Yīzì Shíjīng (一字石經),
this is its error.
In Fàn Wèizōng's (范蔚宗) time,
the Sāntǐ Shíjīng (三體石經) and those carved in Xīpíng (熹平) were placed side by side in the Academy,
hence the historian mistakenly recorded the matter,
and later generations copied his incorrect words,
or, not having seen the stone carvings,
had no means to verify them.
Although Zhào (趙) Shì (氏) attributed the Yīzì (一字) to Zhōngláng (中郎)'s writing,
he had not seen the Sāntǐ (三體).
Ōuyáng (歐陽) Shì (氏) considered the Sāntǐ (三體) to be a Hàn (漢) stele,
but had never seen the Yīzì (一字).
In recent times, Fāng Sháo (方勺) wrote Bózé Biān (泊宅編),
which records his brother Táo's (匋) colophon to the stone classics,
also misled by Fàn Shǐ (范史) and Suí Zhì (隋志),
identifying the Sāntǐ (三體) as Hàn (漢) characters.
Regarding the Gōngyáng Bēi (公羊碑), which bears names like Mǎ Rìdī (馬日磾) and others,
it is said that people used the corrected version established by them,
and thus their names were preserved.
This can be called a fallacious argument.
Jiāng Shì (江式) in Běi Shǐ (北史) states: Wèi (魏) Hándān Chún (邯鄲淳) taught calligraphy to the imperial princes,
and erected the Sānzì Shíjīng (三字石經) to the west of the Hàn (漢) stele.
According to this, this stele was erected in the Zhèngshǐ (正始) years.
The Hàn Shū (漢書) states: In the first year of Yuánjiā (元嘉),
Dù Shàng (度尚) ordered Hándān Chún (邯鄲淳) to compose the Cáo É Bēi (曹娥碑).
At that time, Chún (淳) was already of age (weak冠),
and from Yuánjiā (元嘉) to Zhèngshǐ (正始) was over ninety years.
That Shì (式) considered the Sānzì (三字) to be a Wèi (魏) stele is correct;
to say it was written by Hándān Chún (邯鄲淳)
is incorrect.
When the stele was first erected,
those who came to view and copy it numbered over a thousand carriages daily,
filling the streets.
2 In the beginning,
the court deliberated that as prefectures and commanderies formed factions,
people were clannish,
so they enacted a regulation that families by marriage and people from two different provinces could not supervise each other.
By this time, the Sānhù Fǎ (三互法) was revived.
Xián (賢) says: Sānhù (三互)
means that families by marriage and people from two different provinces could not hold official positions interchangeably.
Fù (復)
is pronounced fú yòu;
same below.
Selection and appointment were difficult, and the two provinces of Yōu (幽) and Jì (冀) were long left with vacancies.
Cài Yōng (蔡邕) submitted a memorial, saying:
"I humbly observe that the old lands of Yōu (幽) and Jì (冀)
are where armor and horses come from.
Xián (賢) says: Kǎi (鎧)
means armor.
The Zhōulǐ Kǎogōng Jì (周禮考工記) says: Yān (燕) has no hán (函).
Hán (函)
also means armor.
It means that in the land of Yōu (幽) and Yān (燕),
every household can make hán (函),
hence there are no armor makers.
The Zuǒzhuàn (左傳) says: The northern land of Jì (冀)
is where horses are born.
They have gradually become empty and depleted.
Now, offices have been vacant for some time,
and officials and common people are longing for appointments,
but the three ministries' selections
remain undecided for over a month.
I was puzzled and asked the reason,
and was told it was to avoid the Sānhù (三互) restriction.
Eleven provinces are subject to this prohibition.
Only two provinces can be selected from.
Moreover,
the gentlemen from these two provinces are sometimes further limited by years and months,
causing hesitation and delay,
leaving both provinces empty,
desolate for thousands of miles,
with no one to oversee them.
I foolishly believe that the Sānhù (三互) prohibition
is a minor restriction.
If we merely assert imperial authority
and clarify its decrees,
with officials supervising each other—
people from Jìzhōu (冀州) inspecting Yōuzhōu (幽州) and people from Yōuzhōu (幽zhou) inspecting Jìzhōu (冀州) —
this is what is meant by 'officials supervising each other.'
What is there to object to
about the Sānhù (三互)?
In the past, Hán Ānguó (韓安國) rose from a prisoner.
Hán Ānguó (韓安國),
a man from Liáng (梁),
was convicted and sentenced by law.
When the position of Intendant of Liáng (梁) became vacant,
the emperor sent an envoy to appoint him as Intendant of Liáng (梁),
rising from a prisoner to an official of two thousand shí (石).
Zhū Mǎichén (朱買臣),
a man from Wú (吳),
was poor
and sold firewood to support himself.
Later, he followed a reporting official to Cháng'ān (長安),
was appointed Grand Administrator of Kuàijī (會稽),
and returned to govern his home region.
How could they have been constrained by the Sānhù (三互)
or bound by minor regulations?
I beg Your Majesty to look to the former emperors
and abolish these recent prohibitions.
For those provincial inspectors whose talents can be exchanged,
do not be constrained by months and years,
and let the Sānhù (三互)
be adjusted appropriately."
The court did not comply.
Your servant Guāng (光) says: Shū Xiàng (叔向) said:
"When a state is about to perish,
its regulations are many."
This is from Shū Xiàng (叔向)'s letter to Zǐchǎn (子產) in the Zuǒzhuàn (左傳).
If one diligently selects the loyal and worthy and appoints them,
and for all officials, both within and outside the court,
rewards those with merit
and punishes those with faults,
without favoritism,
then laws and regulations are not burdensome, and the world is greatly governed.
Why is this so?
Because the fundamental principles are upheld.
When it declines,
the various officials cannot select the right people,
and prohibitions become more numerous,
and defenses more stringent.
Those with merit are not rewarded due to obstructive regulations.
Hé (閡)
is the same as ài (礙).
Both superiors and subordinates are troubled, and the world falls into great disorder.
Why is this so?
Because they pursue superficial matters.
In the time of Xiàolíng (孝靈),
the provincial inspectors and officials of two thousand shí (石) were as greedy as jackals and tigers,
brutally destroying the common people,
yet the court was still adhering to the Sānhù (三互) prohibition.
Looking back now,
is this not utterly ridiculous and a deep warning for us?
3 Fēng (封) the grandson of Héjiān (河間) Wáng (王) Jiàn (建), Tuó (佗), as Rènchéng (任城) Wáng (王).
Tuó (佗)
was the son of the Emperor's paternal cousin.
Tuó (佗)
is pronounced tuó hé.
Rèn (任)
has the sound of rén.

fourth month,

on the dìngmǎo (丁卯) day,

is the mausoleum of Chéngdì (成帝).

severely defeating them,
and killed their king.
The Wùjǐ Xiàowèi (戊己校尉) and Xīyù Chángshǐ (西域長史) each dispatched troops to assist in establishing Jūmí (拘彌)'s attendant prince Dìngxīng (定興) as king,

1 Summer,
fourth month,
on the guǐhài (癸亥) day,
there was a general amnesty.
2 The Yí (夷) people of Yìzhōujùn (益州郡) rebelled,
and the Grand Administrator Lǐ Yǒng (李顒) suppressed them.
3 There was a great prayer for rain (yú).
4 Fifth month,
Grand Commandant Chén Dān (陳耽) was dismissed;
Sīkōng (司空) Xǔ Xùn (許訓) was made Grand Commandant.
5 In the intercalary month,
Cáo Luán (曹鸞), the Administrator of Yǒngchāng (永昌), submitted a memorial, saying:
“As for the Factionals (Dǎng rén),
some are of venerable age and profound virtue,
some are wise and eminent scholars in their prime;
all are fit to be the arms and legs of the imperial house,
assisting in great state affairs.
Yet, for a long time they have been subjected to the banishment (jìngù),
suffering humiliation in the mud.
Even those guilty of rebellion and high treason are granted pardon,
what crime have the Factionals committed
that they alone are not shown clemency?
Therefore, natural disasters have repeatedly appeared,
and droughts and floods have arrived one after another,
all due to this.
It is fitting to grant a generous pardon,
to accord with the will of Heaven.”
The Emperor, upon reviewing the memorial,
became greatly enraged.
He immediately issued an edict to the Sīlì (司隸) and Yìzhōu (益州) to arrest Luán (鸞) in a cage-cart,
send him to Huáilǐ (槐里) prison,
and flog him to death.
Yǒngchāng (永昌) Commandery
was subordinate to the Inspector (cìshǐ) of Yìzhōu (益州).
However, Huáilǐ (槐里) County in Fúfēng (扶風)
was subordinate to the Sīlì (司隸).
The edict was to Yìzhōu (益州) to arrest Luán (鸞),
but it was the Sīlì (司隸) who sent him to Huáilǐ (槐里) prison.
The character "掠" (liáo)
is pronounced liàng.
All those stripped of their offices and subjected to banishment (jìngù)
were pardoned, extending to their five degrees of relatives.
Xián (賢) says: This refers to zhǎncuī (斬衰), qícuī (齊衰), xiǎogōng (小功), dàgōng (大功), and sīmá (緦麻).

the seventh month,
Xu Xùn (許訓), the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi), was dismissed;
Liú Kuān (劉寬), the Minister of the Imperial Household (Guānglùxūn), was appointed Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).

the tenth month,
Yuán Wěi (袁隗), the Minister of the Masses (Sītú), was dismissed;
in the eleventh month,
on the day Liǎngxū (兩戌),
Yáng Cì (楊賜), the Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Guānglù Dàfū), was appointed Minister of the Masses (Sītú).

the Xiānbēi (鮮卑) raided Yōuzhōu (幽州).
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the day Xīnchǒu (辛丑),
a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
2 In summer,
the fourth month,
there was a great drought,
and locusts afflicted seven provinces.
An edict was issued for the Three Ducal Ministers (Sāngōng) to memorialize about local officials who were harsh, cruel, corrupt, and greedy,
and to dismiss them.
Yáng Qiú (陽球) of Yúyáng (漁陽), the Chancellor of Píngyuán (平原), was summoned to the Palace Assistant Imperial Censor (Tíngwèi) for his harshness and cruelty.

12 The Emperor hunted in Shànglínyuàn,
passed through Hángǔguān,
and then hunted in Guǎngchéngyuàn.
In the twelfth month,
he returned
and visited the Grand Academy.
13 Huán Diǎn served as Palace Assistant Imperial Censor,
and the eunuchs feared him.
Diǎn often rode a dappled horse,
and the capital had a saying for him:
"Keep going, but then stop;
avoid the dappled horse Censor!"
A dappled horse is
a mix of blue-gray and white.
He was the grandson of Yān.
In the early Yǒngjiàn reign of Emperor Shùn,
Yān was Grand Tutor.
Yān was
the grandson of Róng.
1 In spring,
the third month, on the day Xīnwèi,
a general amnesty was granted throughout the empire.
2 In summer,
there was a great drought.
3 The Empress Dowager's mother was ennobled as Wǔyángjūn.
4 In autumn,
the Yellow River in Jīnchéng overflowed for more than twenty *lǐ*.
5 The mountain banks in Wǔyuán collapsed.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The *Běnjì* states:
"There was a great harvest."
According to the great drought this summer,
even if there was a good autumn harvest,
it could not be considered a great harvest.
Therefore, it is not included here.
6 Initially,
Zhāng Jiǎo of Jùlù served Huáng-Lǎo (Yellow Emperor and Laozi Daoism),
teaching with sorcery,
and was called
"Táipíngdào" (Way of Great Peace).
He cured illnesses with enchanted water and talismans,
ordering the sick to kneel and confess their sins.
Sometimes, the illnesses were cured,
and the masses revered and believed in him as divine.
Jiǎo dispatched his disciples to travel in all directions,
spreading deception and enticement.
Within ten years,
his followers numbered in the hundreds of thousands,
and people from the eight provinces of Qīng, Xú, Yōu, Jì, Jīng, Yáng, Yǎn, and Yù
all responded.
Some abandoned and sold their property,
migrating and rushing to join,
filling the roads,
and tens of thousands died of illness before even arriving.
The commanderies and counties did not understand his true intentions,
instead stating that Jiǎo taught good morals and was embraced by the people.
Grand Commandant Yáng Cì, who was then Minister of Works,
(Cì became Minister of Works
in Xīpíng fifth year).
said,
"Jiǎo is deceiving and dazzling the common people,
and despite pardons, he does not repent,
but rather his influence spreads.
If we now order the provinces and commanderies to arrest and suppress them,
I fear it will cause further disturbance
and hasten the onset of disaster.
It is advisable to strictly instruct the regional inspectors and two-thousand-bushel officials
to identify the transient population
and protectively return each to their original commandery,
thereby isolating and weakening their faction.
Then, execute their chieftains.
This can be achieved without effort."
It happened that Cì left his post,
and the matter remained pending.
Xián says: This means the matter discussed remained within the palace,
and was not implemented.
I note that Cì was dismissed in Xīpíng sixth year.
'Shuài'
is pronounced suǒ lèi fān.
'Yuàn'
is pronounced yú juàn fān.
'Fù'
is pronounced fú yòu fān.
"Jiǎo and others' secret plots grew more severe,
with private rumors spreading in all directions,
saying that Jiǎo and others had secretly entered the capital
to spy on court affairs.
With the voices of birds and the hearts of beasts,
they secretly called out to each other;
the provinces and commanderies, out of taboo,
did not want to hear about it,
but merely circulated warnings among themselves,
none daring to report it publicly.
An imperial edict should be issued
to heavily reward those who report Jiǎo and others,
with land as a prize.
Anyone daring to shield them
will be guilty of the same crime."
The Emperor paid little attention,
instead summoning Táo to organize the *Chūnqiū* regulations.
Táo was skilled in the *Chūnqiū*
and provided interpretations for it,
hence the imperial order to organize its regulations.
Jiǎo then established thirty-six "fang";
a "fang"
was like a general.
Large "fang" had over ten thousand people,
and small "fang" had six or seven thousand.
The *Kǎoyì* says: Yuán Jì writes
"fāng" (坊),
but we follow Fàn Shū here.
A rumor spread:
"The Azure Heaven is dead,
the Yellow Heaven is to be established.
The year is Jiǎzǐ,
and there will be great prosperity under Heaven."
They wrote the character "Jiǎzǐ"
with white earth on the gates of the capital's temples.
Temple gates
refer to the gates of various official temples in the capital.
All wrote
the character "Jiǎzǐ".
The Grand "Fang" leader Mǎ Yuányì and others first gathered tens of thousands of people from Jīng and Yáng,
planning to launch their uprising in Yè.
Yuányì frequently traveled to the capital,
with Zhong Chángshì Fēng Xǔ and Xú Fèng and others as internal contacts,
agreeing to launch the uprising both inside and outside on the fifth day of the third month.
Zhōngpíng first year
(Jiǎzǐ, 184). The reign year was changed in the twelfth month of this year.
1. In the spring,
Jiǎo's disciple, Táng Zhōu from Jǐnán, submitted a memorial accusing him.
Thereupon, Mǎ Yuányì was arrested
and torn apart by chariots in Luòyáng.
The Kǎoyì states: Yuán Jì says:
"In the fifth month, on the day Yǐmǎo,
Mǎ Yuányì and others conspired rebellion in the capital
and were executed."
We now follow Fàn Shū.
Over a thousand people were put to death;
a pursuit was launched into Jìzhōu to capture Jiǎo and his followers.
When Jiǎo and his group realized their plot was exposed,
they rode day and night to dispatch orders to all regions,
rising up simultaneously.
They all wore yellow scarves as their emblem,
hence contemporary people called them
"Yellow Turban rebels."
In the second month,
Jiǎo proclaimed himself General of Heaven (Tiāngōng Jiāngjūn),
his younger brother Bǎo proclaimed himself General of Earth (Dìgōng Jiāngjūn),
and Bǎo's younger brother Liáng proclaimed himself General of Humanity (Réngōng Jiāngjūn).
The Kǎoyì states: Sīmǎ Biāo's Jiǔzhōu Chūnqiū says:
"Jiǎo's younger brother was Liáng,
and Liáng's younger brother was Bǎo."
Yuán Jì says
"Jiǎo's younger brothers were Liáng and Bǎo."
We now follow Fàn Shū.
They plundered and gathered in settlements;
prefectures and commanderies lost their grip,
and many chief officials fled.
Within a matter of days,
the whole empire responded,
and the capital was shaken.
People from Ānpíng and Gānlíng each seized their respective kings to align with the rebels.
In the third month,
on the day Wùshēn,
Hé Nán Yǐn Hé Jìn was appointed General-in-Chief (Dàjiāngjūn),
enfeoffed as Marquis of Shèn.
Shèn County
belonged to Rǔnán Commandery.
Weapons and equipment were repaired
to guard the capital.
Commandants were established for the eight passes: Hángǔ, Tàigǔ, Guǎngchéng, Yīquè, Huányuán, Xuánmén, Mèngjīn, and Xiǎopíngjīn.
Hángǔ Pass
was in Hé Nán Gǔchéng County.
Xián says: Tàigǔ
was east of Luòyáng.
Guǎngchéng
was in Hé Nán Xīnchéng County.
Jīng Xiāngfán says: Yīquè
was fifty *lǐ* southwest of Luòyáng.
Huányuán Pass
was southeast of Gōushì County.
The Shuǐjīngzhù says: Xuánmén Pass
was ten *lǐ* southwest of Chénggāo County.
Mèngjīn
was south of Hénèi Héyáng County.
Xiǎopíngjīn
was north of Hé Nán Píng County.
Xián says: It is now northwest of Gǒng County.
Dù Yòu says: Northeast of Luòzhōu Xīn'ān County are the Eight Passes Fortifications of Han.
The Emperor summoned his officials for a meeting.
The Administrator of Běidì, Huángfǔ Sōng, suggested that the party prohibitions should be lifted
and more money from the imperial treasury and horses from the Western Garden be issued to the soldiers.
The head of the Central Treasury (Zhōngcáng Fǔlìng)
belonged to the Household Department (Shàofǔ),
and eunuchs held the position.
"Central Treasury money"
was what the Han called "forbidden money."
"Horses from the Western Garden"
refers to *lǜjì* horses.
"Cáng"
is pronounced *cú làng fān*.
He was Guī's nephew.
The Emperor sought advice from the Palace Regular Attendant (Zhōngchángshì) Lǚ Qiáng,
who replied:
"The party proscriptions have long been in place,
and people's hearts are resentful.
If they are not pardoned,
they might easily conspire with Zhāng Jiǎo,
causing the rebellion to grow larger,
and regret will be of no avail.
I request that we first execute the corrupt officials around Your Majesty,
grant a great amnesty to the partisans,
and select competent or incompetent Inspectors (Cìshǐ) and officials with salaries of two thousand *dàn*.
Then there will be no bandits left unpacified."
The Emperor, fearing, followed his advice.
On the day Rénzǐ,
an amnesty was granted to all partisans in the empire,
and those who had been exiled were returned.
This refers to the wives and children of partisans who had been exiled to the borders.
Elite troops from across the empire were mobilized,
and the Colonel of the Northern Department (Běizhōnglángjiāng), Lú Zhí, was dispatched to suppress Zhāng Jiǎo.
The Han had three offices of Colonels:
Wǔguān and Zuǒ-Yòu offices.
There was also a Colonel-Protector of the Xiongnu (Shǐxiōngnú Zhōnglángjiāng).
The Colonel of the Northern Department was first established at this time,
probably for suppressing the Yellow Turbans north of the river.
At this time, the Palace Regular Attendants Zhào Zhōng, Zhāng Ràng, Xià Yùn, Guō Shèng, Duàn Guī, Sòng Diǎn, and others were all enfeoffed as marquises and highly favored.
The Emperor often said:
"Regular Attendant Zhāng is my father,
and Regular Attendant Zhào is my mother."
Because of this, the eunuchs had no fear or apprehension,
and they all built mansions
designed to rival imperial palaces.
The Emperor once wanted to ascend the Hòutái (Watchtower) of Yǒng'ān.
According to the Xù Hàn Zhì: Yǒng'ān Palace was northeast of the Northern Palace,
and there was a watchtower within the palace.
The palace name in Luòyáng was Yǒng'ān Palace,
with a circumference of six hundred ninety-eight *zhàng*.
Its former foundations are within the old city of Luòyáng.
Then the Senior Grandee (Zhōng Dàrén) Shàng Dàn remonstrated, saying:
Xián says: Shàng
is the surname;
Dàn
is the given name.
The Xìngpǔ says: Descendants of Shī Shàngfǔ.
In the Later Han, there were Shàng Shì and Shàng Zǐpíng.
"The Son of Heaven should not ascend to great heights;
ascending to great heights causes the common people to scatter."
From then on, the Emperor dared not ascend towers and pavilions again.
To observe Emperor Líng, who, due to Shàng Dàn's words, no longer dared to ascend towers and pavilions,
truly feared that the common people would scatter.
Can it be said that he had no love for the people?
If he had trusted the words of gentlemen as he trusted Shàng Dàn,
then the fate of the Han
might not have been known.
Xián says: The Chūnqiū Qiántánbā states: "The Son of Heaven should not build high towers and pavilions;
if he builds high towers and pavilions, those below will rebel against him."
This was probably used to mislead the Emperor.
"Fù"
is pronounced *fú yòu fān*;
the same below.
The Emperor questioned and reproached the Regular Attendants, saying:
"You often said that the partisans intended to commit treason,
and so they were all imprisoned,
or some were executed.
Now the partisans are being used by the state;
you, on the contrary, are colluding with Zhāng Jiǎo.
Are you not deserving of execution?"
They all kowtowed and said:
"This was the doing of Wáng Fǔ and Hóu Lǎn!"
Thereupon, all the Regular Attendants individually requested to retire,
and each summoned back their relatives and younger brothers who were in the prefectures and commanderies.
Zhào Zhōng, Xià Yùn, and others then jointly slandered Lǚ Qiáng,
saying he conspired with the partisans about court affairs
and frequently read the biography of Huò Guāng.
This implied he intended to plot a deposition and enthronement.
"Shù"
is pronounced *suǒ jiǎo fān*.
The Emperor sent a Yellow Gate Attendant (Zhōnghuángmén) with soldiers to summon Qiáng.
When Qiáng heard the Emperor's summons,
he angrily said:
"If I die,
chaos will erupt!
A man who wishes to be loyal to the state
how can he face a prison official?"
So he committed suicide.
Zhōng and Yùn again slandered him, saying:
"Qiáng, upon being summoned, without knowing what he was asked, went outside and screened himself (committed suicide)."
Xián says: "Self-screening"
means committing suicide.
"Bǐng"
is pronounced *bì yǐng fān*.
Consequently, his relatives were arrested,
and their property was confiscated.
The Grandee Remonstrant, Xiàng Xǔ [向栩] of Hénèi [河內], submitted proposals for convenient policies,
criticizing those around the emperor.
Zhāng Ràng [張讓] falsely accused Xǔ [栩] of being in league with Zhāng Jiǎo [張角],
intending to act as an inside supporter.
He was arrested and sent to the Huángmén Běisì Yù [黃門北寺獄],
where he was killed.
The Gentleman of the Palace, Zhāng Jūn [張鈞] of Zhōngshān [中山], submitted a memorial saying:
"I secretly believe that the reason Zhāng Jiǎo [張角] was able to raise an army and cause rebellion,
and why the myriad people were happy to join him,
is entirely due to the Ten Regular Attendants allowing their fathers, elder brothers, sons, younger brothers, in-laws, and guests to hold positions in and control the provinces and commanderies,
monopolizing wealth and profit,
and plundering the common people.
The grievances of the common people
had no place to be heard,
hence they plotted rebellion
and gathered as bandits.
It is fitting to behead the Ten Regular Attendants
and display their heads in the southern suburbs,
to apologize to the common people."
According to the biographies of the eunuchs,

at this time, Zhāng Ràng [張讓], Zhào Zhōng [趙忠], Xià Yùn [夏惲], Guō Shèng [郭勝], Sūn Zhāng [孫璋], Bì Lán [畢嵐], Lì Sōng [栗嵩], Duàn Guī [段珪], Gāo Wàng [高望], Zhāng Gōng [張恭], Hán Kuí [韓悝], and Sòng Diǎn [宋典], twelve people,
were all Central Regular Attendants.
"Ten Regular Attendants"
is an approximate number.
"Xiàn" [縣],
pronounced "xuán".
The *Kǎoyì* [考異] says: "Fàn Shū [范書]’s 'Biographies of the Eunuchs' lists twelve names of Regular Attendants at the beginning,
but then refers to them as 'Ten Regular Attendants.'
This is unclear."
"Thus, without needing an army, the great bandits will naturally disappear."
The Emperor showed Jūn's [鈞] memorial to the Regular Attendants.
They all removed their caps, went barefoot, and prostrated themselves,
begging to be sent to the Luòyáng [雒陽] Imperial Prison
and offering to contribute their family wealth to aid military expenses.
An imperial edict was issued,
allowing them all to wear their caps and shoes and attend to their duties as before.
The Emperor angrily said to Jūn [鈞]:
"This is truly a madman!
Among the Ten Regular Attendants, is there not even one good person?"
The Imperial Censor, acting on the Emperor's will,
then falsely accused Jūn [鈞] of studying the Huángjīn Dào [黃巾道].
He was arrested, tortured,
and died in prison.
On the day *gēngzǐ*,
Zhāng Mànchéng [張曼成] of the Nányáng [南陽] Huángjīn [黃巾] attacked and killed the Administrator Chǔ Gòng [褚貢].
The Emperor questioned the Grand尉 Yáng Cì [楊賜] about the Huángjīn [黃巾] affair.
Cì's [賜] reply was direct and pointed,
which displeased the Emperor.
In summer,
the fourth month,
Cì [賜] was dismissed due to the bandits.
Dèng Shèng [鄧盛] of Hóngnóng [弘農], the Grand Coachman, was made Grand尉.
Later, the Emperor reviewed historical records
and found the memorial submitted by Cì [賜] and Liú Táo [劉陶] concerning Zhāng Jiǎo [張角].
Thereupon, Cì [賜] was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Línjìn [臨晉].
Línjìn [臨晉] county
belonged to Fēngyì [馮翊].
Xián [賢] says: "Its old city is in the southwest of modern Tóngzhōu Cháoyì [同州朝邑] county."
"Shàng" [上],
read "shízhǎng".
The Minister of Works, Zhāng Jì [張濟], was dismissed;
the Grand Minister of Agriculture, Zhāng Wēn [張溫], was made Minister of Works.
Huángfǔ Sōng [皇甫嵩] and Zhū Jùn [朱儁] combined their forces of over forty thousand men
to jointly attack Yǐngchuān [潁川].
The Rǔnán [汝南] Huángjīn [黃巾] defeated the Administrator Zhào Qiān [趙謙] at Shàolíng [邵陵].
Shàolíng [邵陵] county
belonged to Rǔnán [汝南] Commandery.
Xián [賢] says: "Its old city is in the east of modern Yùzhōu Yǎnlíng [豫州郾陵] county."
"Bài" [敗],
read "bǔmài".
Bō Cái [波才] besieged Huángfǔ Sōng [皇甫嵩] at Chángshè [長社].
Sōng's [嵩] troops were few,
and everyone in the army was afraid.
The bandits built their camps amidst the grass.
Just then, a strong wind arose.
Sōng [嵩] ordered his soldiers to bind torches and climb onto the city walls.
He sent elite soldiers to secretly break out of the encirclement,
set fire, and shout loudly.
Those on the city walls raised torches in response.
Sōng [嵩], beating drums and shouting, sallied forth from the city,
attacking the bandit formation.
The bandits were startled
and fled in disorder.
Just at that moment, Cáo Cāo [曹操] of Pèiguó [沛國], the Cavalry Commandant, arrived with his troops.
In the fifth month,
Sōng [嵩], Cāo [操], and Zhū Jùn [朱儁] joined forces,
fought the bandits again,
severely defeating them,
beheading tens of thousands of their men.
Sōng [嵩] was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Dūxiāng [都鄉].
Cāo's [操] father, Sōng [嵩],
was the adopted son of the Central Regular Attendant Cáo Téng [曹騰].
The full details of his true parentage are unclear.
Some say he was a son of the Xiàhóu [夏侯] clan.
The *Cáo Màn Zhuàn* [曹暪傳] by a Wú [吳] person and Guō Bān's [郭頒] *Shìyǔ* [世語]
both state that Sōng [嵩]
was a son of the Xiàhóu [夏侯] clan,
and the uncle of Xiàhóu Dūn [夏侯惇],
making Cāo [操] and Dūn [惇] paternal cousins.
He had stratagems and schemes,
but was also chivalrous and unrestrained,
not focusing on a profession.
People of his time did not find him extraordinary;
only the Grand尉 Qiáo Xuán [橋玄] and Hé Yǒng [何顒] of Nányáng [南陽] regarded him as exceptional.
Xuán [玄] said to Cāo [操]:
"The world will soon be in chaos;
without a talent born for this era,
it cannot be saved.
The one who can bring peace to it
will perhaps be you!"
Yǒng [顒], upon seeing Cāo [操],
sighed and said:
"The Hàn [漢] dynasty is about to perish;
the one who will bring peace to the world
must be this man."
Xuán [玄] said to Cāo [操]:
"You are not yet renowned;
you can associate with Xǔ Zǐjiāng [許子將]."
Zǐjiāng [子將]
refers to Shào [劭], the paternal cousin of Xǔ Xùn [許訓].
Xǔ Shào [許劭],
courtesy name Zǐjiāng [子將].
Xǔ Xùn [許訓] was Duke,
see volume above, Xīpíng [熹平] years 3 and 4.
"Cóng" [從],
read "cáiyòng".
He appreciated and recognized many people,
and together with his paternal cousin Jìng [靖], had a high reputation.
They enjoyed discussing and evaluating local figures,
and each month they would revise their classifications,
which is why the custom of "Yuèdàn Píng" [月旦評] (Monthly Character Assessments) existed in Rǔnán [汝南].
Later, the establishment of the Zhongzheng [中正] system in provinces and commanderies was based on this.
"Hǎo" [好],
read "hūdào".
"Gēng" [更],
read "gōnghéng".
When people in the court heard of this,
none failed to change their conduct and adorn their actions.
Cáo Cāo [曹操] went to visit Shào [劭] and asked him,
saying:
"What kind of person am I?"
Shào [劭] disdained his character
and did not answer.
Cāo [操] then coerced him.
Shào [劭] said:
"You,
in a time of peace, are an able minister;
in a time of chaos, a treacherous hero."
This indicates his extraordinary talent.
If the world is in order, he will exhaust his abilities for the benefit of the age;
if the world is in chaos, he will display his wisdom to become a hero of the time.
The story of Cáo Cāo [曹操] begins here.
When Zhū Jùn was attacking the Yellow Turbans,
his Military Protector (hùjūn sīmǎ) Fù Xiè from Běidì presented a memorial, saying:
A Military Protector
holds the office of Sīmǎ,
and is tasked with overseeing an entire army.
“I have heard that the calamities of the empire do not arise from without,
but all originate from within.
This is why Yú Shùn first eliminated the Four Felons,
and then employed the Sixteen Worthies.
The Shàngshū says: Shùn exiled Gònggōng to Yōuzhōu,
banished Huāndōu to Chóngshān,
drove Sānmíáo to Sānwēi,
and slew Gǔn at Yǔshān.
With these four punishments, the empire was all subdued.
The Zuǒzhuàn says: Gāoyángshì had eight talented sons:
Cāngshū, Tuīyǐ, Táoyǐn, Dàlín, Pángjiàng, Tíngjiān, Zhòngróng, Shúdá.
They were called the Eight Primordials (Bāyuán).
Gāoxīnshì had eight talented sons:
Bófèn, Zhòngkān, Shúxiàn, Jìzhòng, Bóhǔ, Zhòngxióng, Shúbào, Jìlí.
They were called the Eight Harmonious (Bākǎi).
Shùn, when serving Yáo,
banished the four wicked clans
and promoted the sixteen worthies.
Otherwise, good people would have no means of advancement.
Now Zhāng Jiǎo has risen in Zhào and Wèi,
and the Yellow Turbans are causing chaos in six prefectures.
These are all troubles that started within the royal court (xiāosháng) and have spread calamity throughout the four seas.
I have received a military commission
to carry out punishment against crime.
Upon first arriving in Yǐngchuān,
every battle was victorious;
though the Yellow Turbans are numerous,
they are not cause for concern for the imperial court.
What I truly fear
is that when managing a flood, one does not trace it to its source,
and the downstream flow only grows wider.
Your Majesty is benevolent, virtuous, and tolerant,
with much that you cannot bear to punish,
hence the eunuchs wield power,
and loyal officials are not advanced.
Even if Zhāng Jiǎo were indeed beheaded
and the Yellow Turbans changed their clothes,
(meaning their followers submitted, changing out of their yellow turbans and resuming the clothing of ordinary people of the time)
(Xiāo,
read as jiān Yáo fān.
Xiāo Yí
means to behead and exterminate.)
the trouble would only deepen.
Why?
Because the wicked and the righteous are not suited to govern the same state,
just as ice and charcoal cannot be kept in the same vessel.
They (the wicked) know that the achievements of righteous people become prominent, and the omens of their (the wicked's) own peril and demise appear;
thus they will all resort to cunning words and deceptive theories,
jointly fostering falsehood.
When a filial son is doubted repeatedly,
even Zēngmǔ throws her shuttle.
(This story is found in volume 3, year 7 of King Nǎn of Zhōu.)
Hánzǐ says: Páng Gòng was held hostage with the Crown Prince of Wèi in Hándān.
Gòng said to the King of Wèi:
‘If one person says there is a tiger in the market,
would Your Majesty believe it?’
The King said:
‘No.’
‘If two people say it,
would you believe it?’
The King said:
‘No.’
‘If three people say it,
would you believe it?’
The King said:
‘I would believe it.’
Gòng said:
‘It is clear there is no tiger in the market,
yet if three people say there truly is a tiger in the market
now Hándān is further from Wèi than the market,
and those who slander me are more than three.
I hope Your Majesty will observe carefully!’
Loyal officials will again face the execution at Dùyóu!
(The story of Bái Qǐ is found in volume 5, year 58 of King Nǎn of Zhōu.)
Fù,
read as fú yòu fān.
Yóu,
pronounced yóu.)
Swiftly carry out punishment against slanderers and sycophants,
then good people will desire to advance,
and treachery and wickedness will cease of their own accord.”
Zhào Zhōng saw his memorial and detested it.
Xiè had achieved great merit in fighting the Yellow Turbans
and was due for enfeoffment,
but Zhōng slandered him.
The Emperor recognized Xiè’s words
and he was spared punishment,
but ultimately not enfeoffed.
8 Zhāng Mánchéng had garrisoned at Wǎn for over a hundred days.
In the sixth month,
Qín Xié, the Administrator of Nányáng, attacked Mánchéng
and beheaded him.
9 Jiāozhǐ was rich in precious goods,
and previous governors (cìshǐ) often lacked integrity in their conduct,
their personal finances amply supplied,
and would then seek transfers.
Consequently, the officials and people resented and rebelled,
seizing the governor and the Administrator of Hépǔ, Lái Dá,
and proclaimed themselves Pillar-of-Heaven General (Zhùtiān Jiāngjūn).
The Three Ducal Offices (sānfǔ) selected Jiǎ Cóng of Dōngjùn, a magistrate (jīnglìng) of Jīng County, to be the governor of Jiāozhǐ.
(Jīng County
belonged to Hénányǐn.)
(Cóng,
read as zǔ zōng fān.)
He inquired into the reasons for their rebellion,
and all said,
“The taxes and levies were excessively heavy,
leaving none of the common people anything.
The capital is far away,
and there is nowhere to report our grievances.
The people cannot make a living,
and so they gathered as bandits.”
Cóng immediately issued a proclamation,
instructing everyone to settle in their professions,
attracting and pacifying the scattered populace,
remitting and restoring corvée labor,
executing the ringleaders who were major malefactors,
and selecting good officials to temporarily administer various counties.
Within a year, order was restored,
and the people were at peace.
The streets and alleys sang a song about him:
“Father Jiǎ arrived late,
causing us to rebel first;
now that there is peace,
officials dare not dine!”
(Meaning officials dared not eat in commoners’ homes.)
(Fàn,
read as fú wǎn fān.)
10 Huángfǔ Sōng and Zhū Jùn, capitalizing on their victory, advanced to attack the Yellow Turbans in Rǔnán and Chénguó.
They pursued Bō Cái to Yángzhái
and attacked Péng Tuō at Xīhuá.
(Xìngpǔ says: Bō
is a surname.
Their ancestors served Wáng Mǎng as the General of Bōshuǐ,
and their descendants took this as their surname.)
(Yángzhái County
belonged to Yǐngchuān Commandery.)
(Xīhuá County
belonged to Rǔnán Commandery.)
(Xián says: The old city of Xīhuá
is west of present-day Xiàngchéng County, Chénzhōu;
it is also said
to be northwest of present-day Yǐnshuǐ County.)
The remaining bandits surrendered and dispersed,
and the three commanderies were all pacified.
Sōng then reported the situation,
attributing the credit to Jùn.
Thereupon, Jùn was promoted to Marquis of Xīxiāng
and transferred to General Who Suppresses Bandits (Zhènzéi Zhōnglángjiàng).
(This office was established to suppress the remaining Yellow Turban bandits.)
Jùn proceeded to campaign in Nányáng.
The Northern Chief Commandant (Běi Zhōnglángjiàng) Lú Zhí repeatedly defeated Zhāng Jiǎo in battle,
slaying and capturing over ten thousand people.
Jiǎo and others fled to protect Guǎngzōng.
(Guǎngzōng County
belonged to Jùlù Commandery.)
(Xián says: It is present-day Zōngchéng County, Bèizhōu.)
He built cloud ladders
and was about to capture it.
(Chuí
means almost.)
(Qiàn,
read as qī yàn fān.)
Someone advised Zhí to bribe Fēng (the eunuch),
but Zhí refused.
Fēng returned
and told the Emperor:
“The bandits in Guǎngzōng are easy to defeat,
but Chief Commandant Lú is merely holding his ground and resting his troops,
waiting for heavenly retribution.”
The Emperor was enraged,
had Zhí summoned in a caged cart,
reducing his punishment by one degree from death;
and dispatched the Eastern Chief Commandant (Dōng Zhōnglángjiàng) Dǒng Zhuó from Lǒngxī to replace him.
(Lú Zhí was previously Northern Chief Commandant,
and Zhuó was Eastern Chief Commandant.)
(The system of four Chief Commandants began at this point.)
In the 11th year,
Zhāng Xiū
of Bā Jùn used sorcery to heal people's illnesses.
His methods were roughly similar to those of
Zhāng Jiǎo.
He required sick families to provide five dòu
of rice,
and was
thus called
"Master of Five Dòus of Rice."
In autumn,
the 7th month,
Xiū gathered a crowd
and rebelled,
plundering commanderies and counties.
People at the time
called them
"Rice Rebels."
The *Kǎo Yì* states: Fàn Shū's *Líng Dì Jì* mentions this Zhāng Xiū.
Chén Shòu's *Wèi Zhì: Zhāng Lǔ Chuán* has "Liú Yān's Sīmǎ Zhāng Xiū."
Liú Ài's *Diǎn Lüè* has "Zhāng Xiū of Hànzhōng."
Péi Sōngzhī believed that "Zhāng Xiū"
should be "Zhāng Héng,"
and that it was either an error in the *Diǎn Lüè* or a mistake in transcription.
According to the *Lǔ Chuán*, it states:
"His grandfather Líng and
father Héng were both followers of the Five Dòu Rice Way.
When Héng died,
Lǔ continued the practice."
Liú Yān's Sīmǎ Zhāng Xiū attacked Hànzhōng together with Lǔ.
Lǔ attacked and killed Xiū;
he was not Lǔ's father.
This record is based on Fàn Shū.
In the 12th year,
the 8th month,
Huángfǔ Sōng fought the Yellow Turbans at Cāngtíng.
Cāngtíng is in the vicinity of Fàn Xiàn, Dōng Jùn.
Dǒng Zhuó attacked Zhāng Jiǎo without success
and was punished.
On the day *Yǐsì*,
an edict ordered Sōng to suppress Jiǎo.
In the 13th year,
the 9th month,
Ánpíng Wáng Xù was executed for unrighteous conduct.
In the first year of Ān Dì's Yánguāng era,
the state of Lèchéng was renamed Ánpíng,
and the filial king's descendant was allowed to inherit the enfeoffment.
Xù was the son of Dé.
Previously, Xù had been captured by the Yellow Turbans.
The people of his state ransomed him, and he was able to return.
The court debated restoring his state.
Counselor Lǐ Xiè said:
"Xù, as a frontier vassal, was not competent
and brought disgrace upon the sagely court.
He should not have his state restored."
The court did not heed him.
Xiè was punished for slandering the imperial clan
and sent to labor at Zuǒxiào.
Before a year had passed,
the king was executed for his crimes,
and Xiè was reinstated as Counselor.
A saying circulated in the capital:
"The father refused to establish an emperor,"
referring to Lǐ Gù's refusal to establish the two emperors Zhì and Huán.
In the 14th year,
winter,
the 10th month,
Huángfǔ Sōng fought against Zhāng Jiǎo's brother Liáng at Guǎngzōng.
Liáng's forces were elite and brave,
and Sōng could not defeat them.
The next day,
he closed his camp and rested his soldiers to observe the situation.
Realizing that the rebels' morale was gradually slackening,
he secretly assembled his troops at night.
At cock-crow,
he swiftly attacked their formation.
They fought until dusk,
utterly defeating them,
beheading Liáng,
and capturing 30,000 heads.
About 50,000 people drowned in the river.
Jiǎo had already died of illness earlier;
his coffin was opened, his corpse mutilated,
and his head sent to the capital.
In the 11th month,
Sōng again attacked Jiǎo's brother Bǎo at Xiàqūyáng,
beheading him.
Xiàqūyáng County
belonged to Jùlù Commandery.
Since Chángshān had Shàngqūyáng,
this place was called Xiàqūyáng.
Fù (復) is pronounced "fú yòu."
Sōng was immediately appointed General of the Left Chariots and Cavalry,
concurrently Governor of Jì Zhōu,
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Huáilǐ.
Sōng was able to care for and comfort his soldiers.
Whenever the army stopped during a march,
he would wait for the camp tents to be properly set up
before going to his own quarters.
After all the soldiers had eaten,
he would then taste his own meal.
Ér (爾) means "thus."
In the 15th year,
the Xiānlíng Qiāng of Běidì and the bandits of Bāohǎn and Héguān rebelled.
Héguān and Bāohǎn were both counties
belonging to Lǒngxī Commandery.
Líng (零) is pronounced "lián."
Bāo (枹) is pronounced "fū."
Běigōng,
whose clan name was derived from their dwelling place.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* has Wèi Grandee Běigōng Wénzǐ.
The *Mèngzǐ* has Běigōng Yǒu.
Cóng (從) is pronounced "cái yòng."
Biān Zhāng and Hán Suì, people of Jīnchéng, were already renowned in the Western Region.
The bandits enticed and coerced them,
making them exclusively responsible for military and political affairs.
They killed Chén Yì, the Administrator of Jīnchéng,
and attacked and burned commanderies and counties.
Previously, the Administrator of Wǔwēi
relied on his powerful connections
and acted with greed and brutality.
The name of the Administrator of Wǔwēi has been lost by historians.
The Inspector Liáng Hú was afraid
and wanted to kill Zhènghé to absolve himself of blame.
He consulted Gài Xūn, the Chief Clerk of Hányáng and Dūnhuáng.
The *Xù Hàn Zhì* states: A commandery administrator appoints one assistant.
For commanderies on the frontier,
the assistant serves as chief clerk.
Dūn (敦) is pronounced "tú mén."
Gài (蓋) is pronounced "tú gài."
Some advised Xūn to seize this opportunity to take revenge.
Xūn said:
"To plot to kill a good man
is not loyalty;
to take advantage of another's danger
is not benevolence."
He then admonished Hú, saying:
"If you tie up and feed a hawk,
desiring its ferocity,
and it responds,
'Xiàn said: Xiè means to tie.
*Guǎngyǎ* says: Zhì means to seize.
Take its ability to subdue and seize all birds.
Sǔn is pronounced "sǒng yǐn."
Shí (食) is read as *sì*.
'What purpose would it serve?'"
Hú then stopped.
Zhènghé went to Xūn to apologize,
but Xūn refused to see him,
saying:
"I advise Lord Liáng;
I do not act for Sū Zhènghé."
His resentment remained as before.
Later, the Inspector, Zuǒ Chāng, stole tens of thousands of army provisions.
Xūn remonstrated with him.
Zuǒ Chāng was enraged
and dispatched Xūn, along with subordinates Xīn Zēng and Kǒng Cháng, to garrison Àyáng separately to resist the rebels.
Àyáng County
belonged to HànYáng Commandery.
Xūn repeatedly achieved military successes.
When Běigōng Bóyù attacked Jīnchéng,
Xūn urged Zuǒ Chāng to relieve it,
but Zuǒ Chāng refused to comply.
After Chén Yì's death,
Biān Zhāng and others advanced and besieged Zuǒ Chāng in Jì.
Zuǒ Chāng summoned Xūn and others to rescue him.
Xīn Zēng and others were hesitant and unwilling to go.
Xūn angrily said:
"In the past, Zhuāng Jiǎ was late,
and Ráng Jū brandished his sword.
During the time of Qí Jǐnggōng,
Yān and Jìn invaded Qí.
Jǐnggōng appointed Sīmǎ Ráng Jū as general
to repel them,
and ordered his favored minister Zhuāng Jiǎ to supervise the army.
Ráng Jū set a meeting for the next morning.
Zhuāng Jiǎ, always arrogant and noble,
only arrived in the evening.
Ráng Jū summoned the army's legal officer and asked:
'According to military law,
what is the penalty for being late for an appointed time?'
He replied:
'They should be executed.'
Thereupon, he executed Zhuāng Jiǎ and paraded his head before the entire army."
Xīn Zēng and the others, terrified, followed him.
When Xūn arrived in Jì,
he rebuked Biān Zhāng and others for their crime of rebellion;
they all said:
"If Lord Zuǒ had followed your words earlier
and brought troops against us,
perhaps we could have reformed ourselves;
now our crimes are already grave,
and we cannot surrender."
Then they lifted the siege and departed.
The rebellious Qiāng besieged Colonel Xià Yù at Xùguān.
The previous biography of Yǐn Wēngguī discusses the crime of being exiled to the supervisor of animal husbandry.
The commentary says: The Right Fúfēng,
where animal husbandry was located,
had officials like the Yùanshī,
hence it was called Xùguān.
Xù
is pronounced "xǔ jiù fān".
Arriving at Húpán,
during the Jìn dynasty,
Qín Fúshēng buried Yáo Yìzhòng at Húpán.
The chronicle states: It is in Jì County, Tiānshuǐ.
Xūn's remaining forces numbered less than a hundred men.
He suffered three wounds on his body,
but sat steadfastly without moving,
pointing to a wooden marker and saying:
"Bury me here!"
Diān Wú of the Jùjiù tribe of Qiāng, held back his men and said:
Xián says: Jùjiù
is a distinct branch of the Qiāng.
Jù
is pronounced "gǔ hóu fān".
Jiù
is pronounced "zhāng yǒng fān".
Diān
is pronounced "diān".
"The Director is a worthy man.
For you to kill him would be to defy Heaven."
Xūn looked up and cursed:
"You dead rebel!
What do you know?
Hurry up and kill me!"
The men looked at each other in astonishment.
Diān Wú dismounted and offered his horse to Xūn,
but Xūn refused to mount it,
and was consequently captured by the Qiāng.
The Qiāng admired his righteousness and courage,
dared not harm him,
and sent him back to HànYáng.
Later, Inspector Yáng Yōng memorialized to appoint Xūn as the Prefect of HànYáng.
The remaining partisans of Zhāng Mánchéng again took Zhào Hóng as their leader.
Their forces swelled again,
reaching over a hundred thousand,
occupying Wǎnchéng.
Zhū Jùn, together with Jīngzhōu Inspector Xú Qiú and others, combined their forces and besieged them.
From June to August, they could not capture it;
officials memorialized to summon Zhū Jùn.
Sīkōng Zhāng Wēn submitted a memorial, saying:
"In ancient times, Qín employed Bái Qǐ,
and Yān entrusted Yuè Yì.
Both spent years and months
before they could conquer the enemy.
The Records of the Grand Historian state: Bái Qǐ served Qín Zhāowáng as a Dàliángzào.
He attacked Wèi
and defeated it.
Five years later,
he attacked Zhào
and captured Guāngláng City.
Seven years later,
he attacked Chǔ
and captured the five cities of Yān and Dèng.
The next year,
he captured Yǐng,
burned Yílíng,
and then advanced east to Jìnglǐng.
Yuè Yì served Yān Zhāowáng
as the Supreme General.
He campaigned against Qí,
entered Línzī,
campaigned throughout Qí for five years,
and captured over seventy cities.
With his army pointing south,
his strategy is already set;
changing generals while facing the enemy
is what military strategists forbid.
It is advisable to grant him more time
and hold him accountable for success."
The emperor then stopped the order.
Zhū Jùn attacked Zhào Hóng
and beheaded him.
The rebel leader Hán Zhōng again occupied Wǎn to resist Zhū Jùn.
Zhū Jùn beat drums and attacked their southwest;
the rebels committed all their forces to meet him.
Zhū Jùn personally led elite troops to surprise their northeast
and entered by scaling the city walls.
Hán Zhōng then retreated and held a small city,
fearfully begging for surrender.
All the generals wanted to accept it.
Zhū Jùn said:
"Warfare often has situations that appear similar but whose underlying circumstances differ.
In the past, during the era of Qín and Xiàng,
the people had no fixed ruler,
so rewards were given to those who joined to encourage others to come.
Now, the whole country is unified;
only the Yellow Turbans are rebelling.
Accepting surrender does not encourage good,
but punishing them is enough to deter evil.
If we accept them now,
it will further open the door to rebellious thoughts.
If the rebels find it advantageous, they will advance and fight;
if they are at a disadvantage, they will beg for surrender.
Letting the enemy grow stronger
is not a good strategy!"
Thereupon, he launched an urgent assault,
fighting continuously but without success.
Zhū Jùn ascended an earthen mound to observe,
and looking at his Sīmǎ, Zhāng Chāo, said:
"I understand now.
The rebels are now completely surrounded externally,
and their internal camp is pressed hard.
They beg for surrender but are refused;
they wish to escape but cannot.
This is why they fight to the death.
If ten thousand men are of one mind,
they are still irresistible,
let alone a hundred thousand!
It is better to lift the siege
and combine our forces to enter the city.
When Hán Zhōng sees the siege lifted,
he will certainly come out.
When he comes out, his morale will be scattered.
This is the way
to defeat them."
Immediately after, he lifted the siege.
Hán Zhōng indeed came out to fight.
Zhū Jùn then attacked,
greatly defeating him,
and beheading over ten thousand.
The Grand Administrator of Nányáng, Qín Xié, killed Hán Zhōng.
The remaining rebels again enthroned Sūn Xià as their leader
and returned to garrison Wǎn.
Zhū Jùn urgently attacked them.
Sīmǎ Sūn Jiān led his troops and was the first to scale the walls.
On the Guǐsì day,
Wǎnchéng was captured.
Sūn Xià fled.
Zhū Jùn pursued him to Jīng Shān in Xī'è.
Xī'è County
belonged to Nányáng Commandery.
Xián says: The old city is south of Xiàngchéng County in modern Dèngzhōu;
Jīng Shān is to its south.
Over ten thousand were beheaded.
Thereupon, the Yellow Turbans were shattered and dispersed.
Of those executed by other prefectures and commanderies,
several thousand were in one commandery.
In the twelfth month,
on the Jǐsì day,
a general amnesty was declared throughout the empire,
and the reign era was changed.
The Grand Administrator of Yùzhōu, Wáng Yǔn of Tàiyuán, defeated the Yellow Turbans.
He obtained letters from Zhāng Ràng's retainers
that showed communication with the Yellow Turbans,
and he submitted them to the emperor.
The emperor angrily reprimanded Ràng;
Ràng kowtowed and apologized,
and was ultimately not punished.
Ràng consequently used this matter to accuse Wáng Yǔn,
who was then summoned and imprisoned.
Xián said: "傳 (zhuàn)
means to arrest.
傳 (zhuàn) is pronounced as
株戀 (zhūliàn) .
下 (xià) is pronounced as
遐稼 (xiágà) ."
Wáng Yǔn returned to his post as Grand Administrator;
within ten days,
he was again arrested for another offense.
Yáng Cì did not want him to suffer such torture and humiliation again.
Xián said: "更 (gēng)
means to experience.
楚 (chǔ) means
pain and suffering.
更 (gēng) is pronounced as
工衡 (gōnghéng) ."
"Because of Zhāng Ràng's affair,
you have been summoned twice in one month.
His wickedness is immeasurable.
Please consider a deep plan!"
Xián said: "Deep plan
means to let him die by his own hand."
Together, they tearfully offered medicine and presented it to him.
Wáng Yǔn sternly said:
"As a subject,
having offended my sovereign,
I should submit to the great penalty to apologize to all under Heaven.
How can I take medicine to seek death?!"
In an earlier text, Wáng Jiā Zhuàn states: "What is meant by 咀藥而死 (jǔyào'érsǐ - chewing medicine to die)?"
乳 (rǔ)
should be 咀 (jǔ) .
He then went out to the cage-cart.
Upon arrival,
Grand General Hé Jìn, along with Yáng Cì and Yuán Wěi, jointly submitted a memorial to plead for him,
and he was granted a reduced sentence, escaping death.
Kǎo Yì says: "Wáng Yǔn Zhuàn states
'Grand Commandant Yuán Wěi, Minister of Works Yáng Cì.'
However, Wěi and Cì did not hold these offices at the time,
so this is probably a mistake."
1 In spring,
in the first month,
there was a great epidemic.
2 In the second month,
on the day of Jǐyǒu,
the Yúntái of the Nángōng was struck by fire.
On Gēngxū,
the Yuèchéng Mén was struck by fire.
According to Xù Hàn Zhì: "This was probably the gate of Yuèchéng Diàn.
'城 (chéng)'
should be
'成 (chéng)'."
Wǔ Xíng Zhì writes it as
"Yuèchéng Mén."
Liú Zhāo said: "It was the middle gate of the Nángōng."
The Regular Palace Attendants Zhāng Ràng and Zhào Zhōng persuaded the emperor to levy a tax on all fields in the empire,
ten coins per *mǔ*,
to repair the palaces
and cast bronze statues.
Lè'ān Grand Administrator Lù Kāng submitted a memorial advising against it, saying:
"In the past, when Duke Xuān of Lǔ taxed *mǔ*s, a locust plague arose of its own accord.
Gōngyáng Zhuàn says: 'What is "initial *mǔ* tax"?
It is to tax based on measuring the *mǔ*s.'
Hé Xiū's commentary says: 'Duke Xuān had no benevolence or trust with the people;
the people were unwilling to exert their full strength on public fields,
so he went around inspecting the *mǔ*s,
taxing those with good grain.'
蝝 (yuán)
refers to young locusts.
The commentary says: 'In winter,
locusts are born.'
Why does it say 'locusts are born'?
This signifies that the ruler altered ancient customs and changed established practices.
The commentary says: '上 (shàng) refers to
the ruler.'
This means Duke Xuān altered the old public field system and taxed *mǔ*s.
蝝 (yuán) is pronounced as
余專 (yúzhuān) .
Zuǒ Zhuàn: Jì Sūn wanted to implement a field tax,
and sent Rǎn Yǒu to consult Zhòng Ní.
Zhòng Ní privately told Rǎn Yǒu: 'If Master Jì Sūn wishes to act according to the law,
then the statutes of Duke Zhōu exist;
if he wishes to act haphazardly,
then why consult me?'
Why abandon the admonitions of the sages
and personally adopt the laws of fallen kings!"
The emperor's inner favorites slandered Kāng, saying he invoked fallen states to metaphorically criticize the enlightened emperor,
which was a great disrespect. He was taken in a cage-cart to the Court of Judicial Review.
The Imperial Censor Liú Dài submitted a memorial to explain and defend him,
and he was allowed to return to his village.
Kāng was the grandson of Xù.
The affairs of Lù Xù
can be found in Volume 45, Emperor Míng's Yǒngpíng 14th year.
An edict was also issued to requisition timber and decorative stone from the provinces and commanderies,
to be transported to the capital.
The Yellow Gate Regular Attendants would often condemn and reprimand those materials that were not up to standard,
then forcibly buy them at cheap prices,
receiving only one-tenth of their original value.
After this, when the goods were delivered,
the eunuchs
would not immediately accept them,
so timber accumulated and rotted,
and the palaces were not completed for years.
The Grand Administrators and Administrators again imposed additional private levies,
causing the common people to sigh and lament.
Furthermore, the Zhōu of Xīyuán were ordered to divide and lead groups to supervise and urge the provinces and commanderies,
creating fear and unrest,
and receiving many bribes.
When Grand Administrators, Officials of Two Thousand *Shí*, and those promoted as *Màocái* and *Xiàolián* were transferred or appointed,
they were all forced to pay "military aid" and "palace repair" money.
For large commanderies, this amounted to twenty or thirty million,
with differing amounts for others.
Those about to take office
all had to first go to Xīyuán to negotiate the price
before they could depart.
Xián said: "諧 (xié)
means to agree upon and fix the price."
They were all compelled and then dispatched.
At that time, Sīmǎ Zhí of Hénèi, the newly appointed Grand Administrator of Jùlù,
was known for his integrity,
and his demanded amount was reduced by three million.
Upon receiving the edict, Sīmǎ Zhí
sighed mournfully, saying:
"To be a parent to the people yet instead exploit them to satisfy current demands,
I cannot bear it."
He claimed illness;
but was not allowed.
When he arrived at Mèngjīn,
he submitted a memorial thoroughly outlining the mistakes of the current era,
and then swallowed poison and committed suicide.
When the memorial was presented,
the emperor temporarily halted the collection of palace repair money.
3 Zhū Jùn was appointed Right General of Chariots and Cavalry.
4 Since the rebellion of Zhāng Jiǎo,
bandits arose everywhere, including Zhāng Niújiǎo of Bólíng, Chǔ Fēiyàn of Chángshān, and others such as Huáng Lóng, Zuǒ Xiào, Yú Dīgēn, Zhāng Báijí, Liú Shí, Zuǒ Zīwénbā,
Pínghàn Dàjì, Sīlì Yuánchéng, Léi Gōng, Fú Yún, Bái Què, Yáng Fèng, Yú Dú, Wǔ Lù, Lǐ Dàmù, Bái Rào, Suī Gù, and Kǔqiú—
their numbers were countless.
Zhū Jùn Zhuàn says: "Those who were nimble were called Fēiyàn (Flying Swallow)."
Yú Dīgēn:
Xián's commentary says: "Zuǒ Zhuàn says: 'Yú Sī, Yú Sī.'
Dù Yù says: 'Yú Sī describes
the appearance of having many whiskers.'"
Those who rode white horses were called Zhāng Báijí (White Rider Zhāng).
Those with loud voices were called Léi Gōng (Thunder Duke).
Those with large eyes were called Dàmù (Big Eyes).
"Zuǒ Zīwénbā"
is written as
"Zuǒ Zīzhàngbā" (Eight-Foot Bearded Zuǒ).
校 (xiào) is pronounced as
戶教 (hùjiào) .
