mostly rebelled and returned to their native lands.
Zhāng Chún was indignant at not being allowed to lead,
so he allied with Zhāng Jǔ, the former Administrator of Tàishān from the same commandery, and the Wūhuán chieftain Qiūlìjū and others.
They plundered Jìzhōng
and killed Gōngqí Chóu,
the Commandant Protector of the Wūhuán.
(Gōngqí is a compound surname.)
Their forces reached over ten myriad,
encamping at Féirú.
(Féirú County belonged to Liáoxī Commandery.
Yìng Shào says: Féi Zǐ fled to Yàn,
and Yàn enfeoffed him here.
Xián says: The ancient city is now in Píngzhōu.)
Chún proclaimed himself General of the Firmament and King of Āndìng,
sending letters to the provinces and commanderies,
stating that Jǔ was to replace Hàn
and instructing the Son of Heaven to abdicate,
ordering the grandees and ministers to welcome him.
In winter,
tenth month,
Qū Xīng, a rebel from Chángshā, proclaimed himself general,
with over ten thousand followers.
An imperial edict appointed Councillor Sūn Jiān as Administrator of Chángshā
to suppress and pacify them.
Jiān was enfeoffed as Marquis of Wūchéng.
(Wūchéng County belonged to Wújùn.
This laid the groundwork for Jiān to suppress Dǒng Zhuó with Chángshā forces.)
In the eleventh month,
Grand Commandant Cuī Liè was dismissed;
Grand Minister of Agriculture Cáo Sōng was made Grand Commandant.
In the twelfth month,
the Túcū Hú rebelled.
(The Túcū Hú were the Xiōngnú.
Tú: read as Zhí Yú Fān.)
In this year,
the title of Guānnèi Hóu was sold
for five million cash.
10 Formerly, the Chief of Tàiqiū, Chén Shí, died.
Over thirty thousand people from within the seas came to mourn.
When Shí was in his home village,
he dealt with matters fairly and impartially.
When there were disputes or lawsuits,
he would always seek to decide and rectify them.
Pàn (判),
means fēn (分),
to separate or divide.
It means to analyze and discern the correct principle.
Those who left bore no grudges;
they even sighed, saying:
"I would rather be subjected to punishment
than be criticized by Lord Chén!"
Yáng Cì and Chén Dān,
whenever they were appointed to high official positions,
all their colleagues congratulated them.
They would sigh that Shí had not yet reached such a high office,
and felt ashamed to have preceded him.
Punctuation by Róng Zhàozǔ; collated by Wáng Chóngwǔ and Niè Chóngqí.
Sīmǎ Guāng
Compiled by imperial order
Later, students, Tiāntái
Emperor Xiàolíng, Part Two
Zhōngpíng Fifth Year
(Wùchén, 188 CE)
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the Dīngyǒu day,
an amnesty was granted to all under heaven.
2 In the second month,
a comet appeared in the Zǐgōng (Purple Palace) constellation.
Zǐgōng
is Táiwēi.
Within the twelve stars that encompass and guard it
is all called Zǐgōng,
the palace of the Son of Heaven.
Bèi (孛),
pronounced "pú nèi fān".
3 The remaining Yellow Turban rebels, Guō Dà and others, rose up in the Báibō Valley in Héxī.
The Dìjì (Imperial Annals) record it as
"Xīhé";
this should be followed.
Furthermore, according to Sòng Bái's Xù Tōngdiǎn,
Héqīng County in Hénán Prefecture
is now governed from Báibō Town.
How can this valley near Mèngjīn be Héxī?
4 In the third month,
the Túgè Hú attacked and killed Zhāng Yì, the Inspector of Bìngzhōu.
5 The Grand Astrologer Jiāngxià Liú Yān, seeing that the royal house faced many difficulties,
suggested:
"The widespread military threats and bandits
are due to the Inspectors' weak authority.
They can neither suppress them
nor employ the right people,
leading to defection and rebellion.
It is fitting to reorganize and appoint牧伯 (mùbó),
selecting officials of clear reputation and significant standing to fill these posts."
Yān secretly desired to become the Governor of Jiāozhǐ.
He believed that Jiāozhǐ was remote,
and thus he could avoid disaster.
He was skilled in interpreting prophecies and omens.
Hé Jìn recommended him,
and he was summoned and appointed as Attendant at the Palace Gate.
"The capital is about to descend into chaos,
and the Yìzhōu division of the heavens has the aura of an emperor."
Cài Yōng's Yuèlìng Zhāngjù states: From Wēi ten degrees to Bì eight degrees,
is called the division of Shǐwéi,
the field of Wèi.
From Bì eight degrees to Wèi one degree,
is called the division of Jiànglóu,
the field of Lǔ.
From Wèi one degree to Bì six degrees,
is called the division of Dàliáng,
the field of Zhào.
From Bì six degrees to Jǐng ten degrees,
is called the division of Shíshěn,
the field of Jìn.
From Jǐng ten degrees to Liǔ three degrees,
is called the division of Qúnshǒu,
the field of Qín.
From Liǔ three degrees to Zhāng twelve degrees,
is called the division of Qúnhuǒ,
the field of Zhōu.
From Zhāng twelve degrees to Zhěn six degrees,
is called the division of Qúnwěi,
the field of Chǔ.
From Zhěn six degrees to Kàng eight degrees,
is called the division of Shòuxīng,
the field of Zhèng.
From Kàng eight degrees to Wěi four degrees,
is called the division of Dàhuǒ,
the field of Sòng.
From Wěi four degrees to Dǒu six degrees,
is called the division of Xīmù,
the field of Yān.
From Dǒu six degrees to Xūnǚ two degrees,
is called the division of Xīngjì,
the field of Yuè.
From Xūnǚ two degrees to Wēi ten degrees,
is called the division of Xuánxiāo,
the field of Qí.
The Jìnshū Tiānwénzhì uses what Chén Zhuó, the Grand Astronomer of the Later Wèi, stated about the celestial divisions corresponding to commanderies and kingdoms;
it is also recorded here: From Zhěn twelve degrees to Dī four degrees is Shòuxīng,
corresponding to the chén (辰) earthly branch,
the division of Zhèng,
belonging to Yǎnzhōu.
From Dī five degrees to Wěi nine degrees is Dàhuǒ,
corresponding to the mǎo (卯) earthly branch,
the division of Sòng,
belonging to Yùzhōu.
From Wěi ten degrees to Nándǒu eleven degrees is Xīmù,
corresponding to the yín (寅) earthly branch,
the division of Yān,
belonging to Yōuzhōu.
From Nándǒu twelve degrees to Xūnǚ seven degrees is Xīngjì,
corresponding to the chǒu (丑) earthly branch,
the division of Wú and Yuè,
belonging to Yángzhōu.
From Xūnǚ eight degrees to Wēi fifteen degrees is Xuánxiāo,
corresponding to the zǐ (子) earthly branch,
the division of Qí,
belonging to Qīngzhōu.
From Wēi sixteen degrees to Kuí four degrees is Zōuzī,
corresponding to the hài (亥) earthly branch,
the division of Wèi,
belonging to Bìngzhōu.
From Kuí five degrees to Wèi six degrees is Jiànglóu,
corresponding to the xū (戌) earthly branch,
the division of Lǔ,
belonging to Xúzhōu.
From Wèi seven degrees to Bì eleven degrees is Dàliáng,
corresponding to the yǒu (酉) earthly branch,
the division of Zhào,
belonging to Jìzhōu.
From Bì twelve degrees to Dōngjǐng fifteen degrees is Shíshěn,
corresponding to the shēn (申) earthly branch,
the division of Wèi,
belonging to Yìzhōu.
From Dōngjǐng sixteen degrees to Liǔ eight degrees is Qúnshǒu,
corresponding to the wèi (未) earthly branch,
the division of Qín,
belonging to Yōngzhōu.
From Liǔ nine degrees to Zhāng sixteen degrees is Qúnhuǒ,
corresponding to the wǔ (午) earthly branch,
the division of Zhōu,
belonging to Sānhé.
From Zhāng seventeen degrees to Zhěn eleven degrees is Qúnwěi,
corresponding to the sì (巳) earthly branch,
the division of Chǔ,
belonging to Jīngzhōu.
Fēn (分),
pronounced "fú wèn fān".
At that time, Xí Jiǎn, the Inspector of Yìzhōu, was vexing the people with frequent levies,
and the rumors spread far.
Moreover, Gěng Bǐ and Zhāng Yì had both been killed by bandits.
Thus, the imperial court followed Yān's proposal,
selecting high officials and Imperial Secretaries to be State Governors,
each taking up the post according to their original rank.
High officials were
ranked at two thousand shi;
Imperial Secretaries were
only ranked at six hundred shi.
After the Eastern Capital,
the responsibilities of Imperial Secretaries became more important than those of high officials.
Huáng Wǎn, the Grand Coachman, became the Governor of Yùzhōu;
Liú Yú of Dōnghǎi, the Grand Master of Ceremonies, became the Governor of Yōuzhōu.
The importance of these provincial posts
began from this point.
Yān
was a descendant of King Gōng of Lǔ;
Yú
was a fifth-generation descendant of King Gōng of Dōnghǎi.
Yú had previously served as Inspector of Yōuzhōu,
and the people and barbarians cherished his benevolence and trustworthiness,
which is why he was appointed.
Dǒng Fú and Zhào Wěi, the Prefect of Tàicāng,
Bǎiguānzhì: Prefect of Tàicāng,
rank six hundred shi,
responsible for receiving grain transported by commanderies and kingdoms,
subordinate to the Grand Minister of Agriculture.
Wěi (韙),
pronounced "yǔ guǐ fān".
followed Yān into Shǔ.
6 An imperial edict ordered troops from the Southern Xiongnú to be dispatched to assist Liú Yú in suppressing Zhāng Chún.
The Chányú Qiāngqú sent the Zuǒxiánwáng with cavalry to Yōuzhōu.
The people of the kingdom feared there would be no end to military levies.
Thereupon, the right-wing Xīluò rebelled.
During the Jiànwǔ era,
the right-wing Yùjiàn Rìzhúwáng Bǐ came to surrender
and was established as the Xīluò Shīzhúdī Chányú.
The right-wing Xīluò
were likely a collateral branch
residing in the western part
and thus adopted that as the name of their tribe.
䤈 (Xī):
pronounced similar to "xīn xī fān".
Over one hundred thousand people
attacked and killed Qiāngqú.
A textual variant states: According to the Dìjì (Annals of the Emperors):
"The Túcă Hú attacked and killed the governor of Bìngzhōu, Zhāng Yì,
and then joined with the Left-wing Hú of the Southern Xiongnú,
killing their Chányú."
We follow the Xiongnú Biography here.
Xián says: Yúfúluó
was the ancestor of Liú Yuān of Former Zhào,
and was thus the progenitor of the chaos that afflicted Jìn.
7 Summer,
in the fourth month,
Grand Commandant Cáo Sōng was dismissed.
8 In the fifth month,
Fán Líng of Nányáng, formerly Yonglè Shǎofǔ, was appointed Grand Commandant;
in the sixth month,
he was dismissed.
9 Bandits Mǎ Xiāng and Zhào Zhī from Yìzhōu raised troops in Mízhu county.
Mízhu county
belonged to the Guǎnghàn Commandery.
Xián says: Its old city is in the east of present-day Yìzhōu Mízhu county.
They killed the Inspector Xì Jiǎn,
advanced to attack Bājùn and Jiānwéi,
and within ten days to a month,
destroyed three commanderies.
They had tens of thousands of followers
and
proclaimed themselves Son of Heaven.
The provincial aide Jiǎ Lóng led officials and commoners to attack Mǎ Xiāng and others.
Within several days, they were defeated and routed,
and the provincial border became peaceful.
Lóng then selected officials and soldiers to welcome Liú Yān.
Yān moved his administration to Mízhu,
pacifying and assimilating the rebellious and the disaffected,
diligently implementing lenient and benevolent policies,
to win over the hearts of the people.
This laid the foundation for Liú Yān's autocratic rule in Yìzhōu.
10 Seven commanderies and kingdoms suffered great floods.
11 Chén Yì, the son of the former Grand Tutor Chén Fān, and the geomancer Xiāng Kǎi met at the residence of Wáng Fēn, the Inspector of Jìzhōu.
Kǎi said:
"The celestial phenomena are unfavorable to the eunuchs;
the Huángmén and Chángshì will truly have their clans exterminated."
Yì was pleased.
Fēn said:
"If that is the case,
Fēn wishes to sweep them away!"
He then gathered other prominent figures,
submitting a memorial stating that the Hēishān bandits were raiding commanderies and counties,
intending to use this as a pretext to raise an army.
At that time, the Emperor wished to make a northern tour to his old residence in Héjiān.
The Emperor was formerly the Marquess of Jiědú Tíng,
and had an old residence in Héjiān.
Their plan was to execute all the Chángshì and Huángmén,
then depose the Emperor,
and enthrone the Marquess of Héféi.
He confided this plan to the Palace Gentleman for Consultation, Cáo Cāo.
That he confided this plan to Cāo
likely indicates he also knew Cāo was a hero of his time.
"[Cáo Cāo said:] Indeed, the matter of deposing and establishing an emperor
is the most inauspicious undertaking in the world.
The ancients who weighed success and failure, and assessed significance before acting,
were Yī and Huò.
Such words
are beyond the reach of ordinary people!
Relying on the authority of prime ministers,
wielding the power of government,
and aligning with the desires of the populace,
they were thus able to have their plans adopted and their deeds accomplished.
Now, you gentlemen merely see how easy it was in the past,
but have not recognized the difficulty of the present.
To undertake extraordinary measures,
hoping for certain victory,
is this not perilous!"
Fēn also summoned Huà Xīn of Píngyuán and Táo Qiūhóng to collectively decide on the plan.
Hóng wished to proceed,
but Xīn stopped him, saying:
"The great matter of deposing and establishing an emperor
was difficult even for Yī and Huò.
Fēn is careless by nature and not martial;
this will surely not succeed."
Hóng then desisted.
Coincidentally, at midnight in the north, a red aura appeared,
extending across the sky from east to west.
The Grand Astrologer reported:
"There is a conspiracy in the north;
it is not advisable to travel north."
The Emperor then stopped.
He ordered Fēn to disband his troops,
and shortly thereafter summoned him.
Fēn, in fear,
discarded his official seal and fled,
and upon reaching Píngyuán,
committed suicide.
12 Autumn,
in the seventh month,
Mǎ Rìdī, Colonel of Archers, was appointed Grand Commandant.
Rìdī
was a grand-nephew of Róng.
13 In the eighth month,
the Eight Colonels of the Western Garden were first established.
Jiǎn Shuò, Little Yellow Gate, was appointed Colonel of the Upper Army.
The Xìngpǔ (Genealogies) states: Jiǎn
is a surname.
The Zuǒzhuàn mentions Jiǎn Shū, a grandee of Qín.
Bào Hóng, Colonel of Agile Cavalry, was appointed Colonel of the Lower Army.
Cáo Cāo, Palace Gentleman for Consultation, was appointed Colonel Supervising the Army.
Zhào Róng was appointed Assistant Colonel of the Left Army.
Féng Fāng was appointed Assistant Colonel of the Right Army.
Xià Móu, Grandee Remonstrant, was appointed Colonel of the Left.
Chúnyú Qióng was appointed Colonel of the Right.
All were under the command of Jiǎn Shuò.
A textual variant states: Fàn Shū (Book of the Later Hàn) in the biography of Yuán Shào says,
"Shào was Colonel Assisting the Army,"
and in the biography of Hé Jìn, "Chúnyú Qióng was Colonel Assisting the Army."
We follow the Shānyánggōng Zàijì by Lè Zī here.
He (the Emperor) focused on military affairs;
Shuò was strong and skilled in military strategy,
and the Emperor personally trusted him.
Even the Grand General was subordinate to him.
14 In the ninth month,
Minister of Works Xǔ Xiāng was dismissed;
Minister of Agriculture Dīng Gōng was appointed Minister of Works.
Liú Hóng of Nányáng, Minister of the Household, was appointed Minister of Agriculture.
15 Dǒng Zhòng, Marquess of Tiáo and Minister of the Guards, was appointed General of Agile Cavalry.
Zhòng
was the nephew of the Empress Dowager Yǒnglè.
16 Winter,
in the tenth month,
the Yellow Turbans of Qīng and Xú again rose,
plundering commanderies and counties.
17 Prognosticators who observed vital energies believed that a great battle would occur in the capital,
with blood flowing in both palaces.
The Emperor wished to suppress this omen,
so he extensively mobilized troops from all four directions,
conducting military exercises below the Píngluò Guān.
The Shuǐjīngzhù states: The Gǔshuǐ river flows southeast from Báimǎ Sì past Píngluò Guān,
which is outside the upper west gate.
樂 (Luò):
pronounced luò.
觀 (Guān):
pronounced guàn.
A twelve-tiered ornate canopy was erected above,
ten zhàng high;
to the northeast of the altar, a smaller altar was built,
and a nine-tiered ornate canopy was again erected,
nine zhàng high.
Tens of thousands of infantry and cavalry were arrayed,
forming camps in formation.
On the day of Jiǎzǐ,
the Emperor personally came out to review the army,
standing beneath the great ornate canopy;
the Grand General advanced to stand beneath the smaller ornate canopy.
The Emperor personally donned armor,
mounted his horse,
proclaimed
"Supreme General,"
circled the formation three times, and returned,
entrusting the troops to Jìn.
The Emperor asked Gài Xūn, Colonel Who Quells Barbarians:
"My military exercise is like this,
how is it?"
He replied:
"I have heard that the ancient kings displayed virtue, not military might.
The Guóyǔ records the words of Jì Gōng Mòufù.
It is not sufficient to manifest decisive bravery."
The Zuǒzhuàn says: "To listen with decisive bravery" is called military prowess.
Killing enemies is decisiveness;
achieving decisiveness is bravery.
The Emperor said:
"Excellent!
I regret meeting you so late;
my fawning ministers have never uttered such words."
Xūn said to Yuán Shào:
"The Emperor is very intelligent,
but merely obscured by his close attendants."
He plotted with Shào to jointly execute the Emperor's favorites.
Jiǎn Shuò, in fear,
sent Xūn out to be Minister of Jīngzhào.
18 In the eleventh month,
Wáng Guó besieged Chéncāng.
An imperial edict re-appointed Huángfǔ Sōng as General of the Left,
to oversee the Former General Dǒng Zhuó,
combining their forces of forty thousand men to resist him.
In the 19th year [of the Zhōngpíng reign], Zhāng Chún and Qiū Lìjū plundered the four provinces of Qīng, Xú, Yōu, and Jì.
An imperial edict ordered the Cavalry Commandant Gōngsūn Zàn to suppress them.
Zàn fought them at Shímén in the Commandery of the Dependent State.
The Commandery of the Dependent State
was the Commandery of the Dependent State of Liáodōng.
Xián said: Shímén
is a mountain name,
located southwest of modern-day Liǔchéng County, Yíngzhōu.
Zàn,
pronounced zàng hàn.
He abandoned his wife and children
and fled beyond the frontier,
recovering all the men and women who had been captured.
Zàn penetrated deeply without reinforcements
and was instead surrounded by Qiū Lìjū and others at Guǎnzǐchéng in Liáoxī.
After more than two hundred days,
his provisions ran out and his forces disintegrated.
Five or six tenths of his soldiers died.
In the 20th year [of the Zhōngpíng reign], Dǒng Zhuó said to Huángfǔ Sōng:
"Chéncāng is in dire straits;
please rescue it quickly."
Sōng said:
"No.
A hundred battles and a hundred victories
are not as good as subduing the enemy's army without fighting.
Though Chéncāng is small,
its defenses are solid and prepared.
It cannot be easily captured.
Though Wáng Guó's forces are strong,
if they attack Chéncāng and fail to take it,
their troops will surely be exhausted.
To strike them when they are exhausted
is the way to complete victory.
Why should we rescue it?"
Wáng Guó attacked Chéncāng for more than eighty days
but failed to take it.
1. In the spring,
second month,
Wáng Guó's forces were exhausted and debilitated.
They lifted the siege and departed.
Huángfǔ Sōng advanced his troops and attacked them.
Dǒng Zhuó said:
"No!
Military strategy dictates:
do not press a cornered foe,
and do not pursue a retreating army."
Xián said: These words are from Sīmǎ's military strategy.
"Not so.
Previously, I did not attack
to avoid their keen edge.
Now I attack
to await their decline.
Those I strike are exhausted troops,
not a retreating army.
Wáng Guó's forces are about to flee,
having no will to fight.
To attack disorder with order
is not to press a cornered foe."
Thereupon, he alone advanced to attack them,
making Zhuó serve as a rear guard.
After continuous battles,
he thoroughly defeated them,
beheading over ten thousand.
Zhuó was greatly shamed and resentful,
and from then on, a rift formed between him and Sōng.
This laid the groundwork for Zhuó's fear of Sōng in the second year of Chūpíng under Emperor Xiàn.
Hán Suì and others jointly deposed Wáng Guó
and coerced Yán Zhōng of Hànyáng, the former magistrate of Xìndū, to supervise and command all the tribes.
Zhōng died of illness.
Suì and others gradually vied for power
and killed each other,
and from this, they gradually declined.
2. Liú Yú, the Inspector of Yōuzhōu, arrived at his post.
He sent envoys to the Xiānbēi,
informing them of the advantages and disadvantages,
and demanded they send the heads of Zhāng Jǔ and Zhāng Chún,
offering generous rewards.
Qiū Lìjū and others, hearing of Yú's arrival,
were pleased
and each sent interpreters to submit.
Jǔ and Chún fled beyond the frontier;
the rest surrendered and dispersed.
Yú memorialized to disband the garrisons,
leaving only the Commandant of Surrendering Captives, Gōngsūn Zàn,
with ten thousand infantry and cavalry stationed at Yòuběipíng.
Zàn, due to his victory at Shímén,
was promoted from Cavalry Commandant to Commandant of Surrendering Captives.
Jiàng,
pronounced hù jiāng.
Jiào,
pronounced hù jiào.
Wáng Zhèng, Zhāng Chún's retainer, killed Chún
and sent his head to Yú.
Gōngsūn Zàn's ambition was to annihilate the Wūhuán,
while Yú wished to attract them to surrender with kindness and trust.
From this, a rift formed between him and Zàn.
This laid the groundwork for Zàn's killing of Yú in the fourth year of Chūpíng.
3. In the summer,
fourth month,
on the bǐngzǐ new moon,
there was a solar eclipse.
4. The Grand Commandant Mǎ Rìdī was dismissed.
An envoy was sent to immediately appoint Liú Yú, Inspector of Yōuzhōu, as Grand Commandant
and enfeoff him as Marquis of Róngqiū.
Róngqiū County
belonged to Dōnghǎi Commandery.
A textual study states: Yuán's Chronicle says:
"On jǐchǒu in the third month,
Liú Yú, Cavalier-Attendant-in-Ordinary, became Sīmǎ
and held the post of Inspector of Yōuzhōu."
We now follow Fàn Shū.
5. Jiǎn Shuò was jealous of the General-in-Chief Jìn.
He and the eunuch attendants together persuaded the Emperor to send Jìn west to attack Hán Suì.
The Emperor agreed.
Jìn secretly knew of their plot,
so he memorialized to send Yuán Shào to collect troops from Xú and Yǎn provinces,
and that he would go west after Shào returned,
thereby delaying the departure date.
6. Originally,
the Emperor had repeatedly lost imperial sons.
Empress Hé had given birth to Prince Biàn,
who was raised in the home of the Daoist Shǐ Zǐmiǎo,
and was called
"Marquis Shǐ."
Xián said: Dàorén refers to a person with Daoist arts.
Empress Dowager Dǒng raised Prince Xié herself,
and he was called
"Marquis Dǒng."
The inner ministers requested the establishment of an heir apparent.
The Emperor, considering Biàn frivolous and lacking in solemnity,
wished to establish Xié,
but remained undecided.
He then fell gravely ill
and entrusted Xié to Jiǎn Shuò.
On bǐngchén,
the Emperor passed away at Jiādé Palace.
He was thirty-four years old.
Jiādé Palace was inside Jiǔlóng Gate of the Southern Palace.
Wishing to first execute Hé Jìn and establish Xié,
he sent someone to summon Jìn,
intending to consult with him on matters.
Jìn immediately set out.
Pān Yǐn, Jiǎn Shuò's Sīmǎ, had a long-standing friendship with Jìn.
He met Jìn and winked at him.
Jìn was startled,
galloped back to his camp via a detour,
and led his troops to garrison at the Bǎijùndǐ.
There were over a hundred commanderies and states in the empire,
all of which had residences in the capital.
It was called Bǎijùndǐ because
all hundred commanderies were collectively one residence.
On wǔwǔ,
Imperial Prince Biàn ascended the throne,
aged fourteen.
A textual study states: The imperial annals say
"aged seventeen,"
but Zhāng Fán's Hàn Chronicles say
"the Emperor was fourteen years old."
We now follow this.
The Empress Dowager attended to court affairs.
An amnesty was granted to the empire,
and the era name was changed to Guāngxī.
Imperial Prince Xié was enfeoffed as King of Bóhǎi.
Xié was nine years old.
Yuán Wěi, the General of the Rear, was appointed Grand Tutor
and, with General-in-Chief Hé Jìn, participated in managing the affairs of the Imperial Secretariat.
As Jìn 晉 now held court authority,
he resented Jiǎn Shuò 蹇碩 for plotting against him
and secretly planned to execute him.
Yuán Shào 袁紹, through Jìn's 晉 close associate Zhāng Jīn 張津,
urged Jìn 晉 to execute all the eunuchs.

Another account says that inside the Son of Heaven's gate, there were two layers of eyebrow-grilles,
and the inner blue paintings were called suǒ.
Kǎoyì says: Hé Jìn's biography states
"Jiǔlóngmén."
We follow Yuán Jì here.
Ràng and others went in to report to the Empress Dowager,
saying that the Grand General's troops had rebelled,
burned the palace,
and attacked the Shàngshūtá,
the Shàngshūtá
being the gate of the Shàngshū office.
They went from the covered walkway to the Northern Palace.
'Jiāng' (將),
as written,
means xié (攜, to carry) or xiá (挾, to hold).
They pulled Dùan Guī;
Guī was frightened,
and released the Empress Dowager.
The Empress Dowager threw herself from the chamber
and was
spared.
Yuán Shào and his uncle Wěi forged an edict to summon Fán Líng and Xǔ Xiàng,
and executed them.
Shào and Hé Miáo led troops to encamp below Zhūquè Què,
captured Zhào Zhōng and others,
and executed them.
Wú Kuāng and others had long resented Miáo for not being of one mind with Jìn,
and also suspected him of conspiring with the eunuchs.
They then ordered the army, saying:
"The one who killed the Grand General is
the Chēqí!"
At this time, Miáo was Chēqí Jiāngjūn.
All wept, saying:
"We are willing to die!"
Kuāng then led his troops with Dǒng Zhuó's younger brother, Fèngchē Dūwèi Mín, to attack and kill Miáo,
abandoning his corpse in the imperial garden.
Shào then closed the gates of the Northern Palace,
commanded his troops to hunt down all the eunuchs,
killing them all regardless of age,
over two thousand people in total.
Some without beards were mistakenly killed.
is interchangeable with the ancient character for 'beard' (鬚).
Some went up to the roof of Dūanmén
to attack the palace interior.
The main south gate of the palace was called Dūanmén,
a forbidden area.
On the day gēngwǔ,
Zhāng Ràng, Duàn Guī, and others, cornered and desperate,
then took the Emperor and the King of Chénliú, with several tens of others,
and walked out through Gǔmén.
Gǔmén,
located at 'zǐ' (north),
was the main north gate of Luòchéng.
They reached Xiǎopíngjīn.
Xián said: Xiǎopíngjīn is in the northwest of present-day Gǒngxiàn.
Dù Yòu said: Northwest of Gǒngxiàn is the old city of Xiǎopíngxiàn,
and further north is a ford called Xiǎopíngjīn.
No high officials could follow them,
only Shàngshū Lú Zhí and Hénán Zhōngbù Yuàn Mǐn Gòng arrived at the river at night.
The Hàn Guānyí states: All commanderies established five Dūyóu to supervise subordinate counties;
the Hénán Yǐn established four Dūyóu,
and the Zhōngbù was a Yuàn.
'Yuàn' (掾),
pronounced yú juàn.
And said:
"If you don't die quickly now,
I will kill you!"
He then wielded his sword and cut down several people.
Ràng and others were terrified,
clasped their hands, bowed twice,
and prostrated themselves before the Emperor, saying in farewell:
"Your servants die,
may Your Majesty take care!"
They then threw themselves into the river and died.
Gòng Fú Dì and the King of Chénliú walked out at night, following the light of fireflies, heading south.
Wanting to return to the palace,
after walking several *lǐ*,
they found a commoner's open cart.
An open cart
has no canopy on top
and no curtains on the four sides.
It was merely a cart used by commoners to transport goods.
They stopped at Luòshè.
Luòshè
is a place name,
located north of Běimáng.
On the *Xīnwèi* day,
the Emperor rode a horse alone,
while the King of Chénliú and Gòng Fú rode a horse together.
They traveled south from Luòshè,
and gradually, *gōngqīng* began to arrive.
Dǒng Zhuó arrived at Xiǎnyáng Yuàn.
Xiǎnyáng Yuàn
was built in the second year of Yánxī during the reign of Emperor Huán,
located west of Luòyáng.
Knowing that a change had occurred,
he led his troops to advance rapidly.
Before dawn,
he reached the west of the city.
Hearing that the Emperor was in the north,
he then went with the *gōngqīng* to welcome and receive him at the foot of Běimáng Bǎn.
When the Emperor saw Dǒng Zhuó leading his soldiers,
he was terrified and wept.
Yì Gōng said to Dǒng Zhuó:
"There is an imperial edict to withdraw the troops."
Dǒng Zhuó said:
"You gentlemen are great ministers of the state,
but you could not rectify the royal house,
to the point where the state is scattered and turbulent."
Dōng Dū Yì Chén refers to the Son of Heaven as "the state."
Dǒng Zhuó spoke with the Emperor,
but the conversation could not be understood.
*Liǎo*
means to understand.
When asked about the cause of the disaster and chaos,
the King answered,
from beginning to end,
omitting nothing.
Dǒng Zhuó was greatly pleased,
considering the King virtuous,
and moreover, he was raised by Empress Dowager Dǒng.
Dǒng Zhuó considered himself of the same clan as the Empress Dowager,
and thus had the intention to depose and enthrone.
On that day,
the Emperor returned to the palace,
issued a general amnesty,
and changed Guāngxī to Zhāoníng.
The Imperial Seal of the State was lost,
which lays the groundwork for Sūn Jiān obtaining the seal in the second year of Chūpíng, in the time of the later Emperor Xiàn.
*Xǐ*
is pronounced *sī shì fān*.
Dīng Yuán was appointed Zhí Jīnwú.
Bāo Xìn, the Cavalry Commandant, who had recruited troops from Tài Shān, happened to arrive
and said to Yuán Shào:
"Dǒng Zhuó commands strong troops
and harbors ulterior motives.
If we do not plan early now,
we will surely be controlled by him.
While he is newly arrived and fatigued,
if we attack him,
he can be captured!"
Yuán Shào feared Dǒng Zhuó
and dared not act.
Bāo Xìn then led his troops back to Tài Shān.
When Dǒng Zhuó entered,
his cavalry and infantry numbered no more than three thousand.
He felt his forces were too few
and feared he would not be obeyed by those near and far.
So every four or five days, he would secretly lead his army out to nearby camps at night,
and at dawn,
he would display many banners and drums as they returned,
giving the impression that more western troops had arrived,
though no one in Luò [yáng] knew the truth.
Soon, his younger brother Miáo's forces all returned to Dǒng Zhuó.
Dǒng Zhuó also secretly sent Lǚ Bù, the Commander of Wǔyuán, from Dīng Yuán's forces, to kill Dīng Yuán and incorporate his troops.
Dǒng Zhuó's forces thus greatly increased.
He then suggested to the court
that due to prolonged rain,
Sīkōng Líu Hóng should be dismissed and replaced by him.
Initially,
Cài Yōng was exiled to Shuòfāng.
This event is recorded in volume 57, first year of Guānghé.
Wáng Zhì, the Administrator of Wǔyuán,
who was the younger brother of Fǔ,
impeached Cài Yōng for slandering the court.
Cài Yōng then fled and lived in the jiānghǎi region
for twelve years.
Dǒng Zhuó heard of his reputation and summoned him,
but Cài Yōng feigned illness and did not comply.
Dǒng Zhuó was enraged
and cursed, saying:
"I can exterminate clans!"
Cài Yōng, in fear, accepted the summons.
Upon arrival,
he was appointed Jìjiǔ,
and was greatly respected.
He was promoted to Gāodì,
and within three days,
he had served in all three bureaus.
Cài Yōng was promoted to Gāodì,
appointed Shì Yùshǐ,
then transferred to Zhì Shū Yùshǐ,
and promoted to Shàngshū.
Within three days,
he had served in all three bureaus.
Dǒng Zhuó said to Yuán Shào:
"The ruler of the realm
should be wise and enlightened.
Every time I think of Emperor Líng,
it fills me with indignation!"
Xián said: *Dú*
means hatred.
"Now I wish to enthrone him,
can he surpass Shǐ Hóu?
Some people have little wisdom and great foolishness,
and they do not know what is right.
Moreover,
the Líu clan's lineage is not worth preserving!"
*Qiě ěr*
means "and so it is."
Dǒng Zhuó intended to depose the Hàn emperor and enthrone himself.
"The Hàn house has ruled the realm for approximately four hundred years,
and its grace and favor have been profound,
so the common people support it.
The present emperor is in the prime of his youth,
and no unrighteousness has been proclaimed throughout the realm.
If you wish to depose the legitimate heir and enthrone a collateral one,
I fear the populace will not follow your counsel!"
Dǒng Zhuó gripped his sword and shouted at Yuán Shào:
"You brat, how dare you say that!"
*Gǎnrán*
means "dare to do so."
"Is it not up to me?
If I wish to do it,
who dares to disobey?
Do you think Dǒng Zhuó's sword is not sharp?"
Yuán Shào flared up and said:
"Are the strong men of the realm only Dǒng Gōng!"
He drew his sword,
made a horizontal bow,
and left directly.
Dǒng Zhuó, being newly arrived,
and seeing that Yuán Shào was from a prominent family,
therefore dared not harm him.
Yuán Shào hung his *jié* at Shàng Dōngmén.
*Xiàn* refers to the *jié* of Sīlì that he temporarily held.
Shàng Dōngmén
is located in the *yín* direction.
Xián said: It is the northernmost gate on the east side of Luòyáng city.
*Xiàn*
is read as *xuán*.
In the ninth month,
on the *Guǐyǒu* day,
Dǒng Zhuó convened a great assembly of all officials,
and raising his head, he spoke, saying:
"The Emperor is dark and weak,
and cannot serve the ancestral temple
or be the lord of the realm.
Now I wish to follow the precedents of Yī Yǐn and Huò Guāng
and enthrone the King of Chénliú instead.
What do you think?"
The *gōngqīng* and those below were all terrified
and dared not reply.
Dǒng Zhuó then spoke loudly, saying:
Xián said: *Kàng*
means high.
"In the past, Huò Guāng made the decision,
and Yánnián gripped his sword.
This event is recorded in volume 24, first year of Yuánpíng during the reign of Emperor Zhāo.
All actions were carried out according to military law!"
Those seated were shaken.
Only Shàngshū Lú Zhí said:
"In the past, when Tài Jiǎ was enthroned, he was unenlightened;
Chāngyì's transgressions numbered over a thousand,
hence there were acts of deposition and enthrone.
The present emperor is in the prime of his youth,
and has committed no moral lapses.
This is not comparable to previous cases."
Dǒng Zhuó was greatly enraged
and dismissed the assembly.
He was about to kill Lú Zhí,
but Cài Yōng pleaded on his behalf,
and Yìláng Péng Bó also admonished Dǒng Zhuó, saying:
"Shàngshū Lú is a great scholar within the seas,
and a man of hope for the people.
If you harm him first now,
the whole realm will be terrified."
Dǒng Zhuó then stopped,
merely dismissing Lú Zhí from office.
Lú Zhí then fled and hid in Shànggǔ.
Dǒng Zhuó showed his proposal for deposition and enthronement to Tàifù Yuán Wěi,
and Yuán Wěi reported agreement with the proposal.
On the *jiǎxū* day,
Dǒng Zhuó again convened his officials in the Former Hall of Chóngdé.
He then coerced the Empress Dowager into issuing an edict to depose the Young Emperor,
saying:
“The Emperor is in mourning
without the heart of a filial son,
and his demeanor is not that of a ruler.
He is now to be deposed as King of Hóngnóng,
and Xié, the King of Chénliú, is to be enthroned as Emperor.”
Yuán Wěi untied the imperial seals and ribbons
and presented them to the King of Chénliú.
He helped the King of Hóngnóng down from the hall,
where he faced north and declared himself a subject.
The Empress Dowager choked back tears,
unable to utter a sound,
only sobbing and weeping.
No one dared to speak.
Dǒng Zhuó further deliberated:
“The Empress Dowager pressed the Empress Yǒnglè
until she died of grief,
violating the proper conduct between a daughter-in-law and her mother-in-law.”
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* states: “A daughter-in-law
is one who nurtures her mother-in-law;
to harm one’s mother-in-law to benefit oneself as a daughter-in-law
is the greatest transgression.”
An amnesty was granted to the empire,
and the era name Zhāoníng was changed to Yǒnghàn.
On the *bǐngzǐ* day,
Dǒng Zhuó poisoned Empress Dowager Hé.
Below the rank of high ministers, people did not wear full mourning attire,
but attended the funeral
in plain clothes only.
Dǒng Zhuó also exhumed Hé Miáo’s coffin,
took out his corpse,
dismembered and jointed it,
and discarded it by the roadside.
He killed Miáo’s mother, Lady Wǔyáng,
and abandoned her body among the *zhǐluò* in the park.
*Luò*
refers to a fence.
*Zhǐ*
resembles a thorn bush,
with many thorns.
South of the Yangtze, it is called *jú* (orange),
north of the Yangtze, it is called *zhǐ* (trifoliate orange).
People use it to make fences.
13An imperial edict appointed sons and younger brothers of high ministers and below as palace gentlemen (*láng*),
to fill the positions of eunuchs
and attend in the palace hall.
14On the *yǐyǒu* day,
Liú Yú, Grand Commandant, was appointed Grand Minister of War (*Dà Sīmǎ*),
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Xiāngbēn.
Xiāngbēn County
belonged to Dōnghǎi Commandery.
Yīng Shào said: “*Bēn*
is pronounced *fēi*.”
He was put in charge of the affairs of the Former General,
and granted the *jiéchuán* (credentials), battle-axe, and *hǔbēn* (Tiger Bannermen),
and further enfeoffed as Marquis of Méi.
15On the *bǐngxū* day,
Yáng Biāo, Grand Master of the Palace (*Tàizhōng Dàfū*), was appointed Minister of Works (*Sīkōng*).
16On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
Huáng Wǎn, Governor of Yùzhōu, was appointed Minister over the Masses (*Sītú*).
17Dǒng Zhuó led the high ministers to submit a memorial,
rehabilitating Chén Fān, Dòu Wǔ, and other partisans,
restoring all their titles and ranks,
sending envoys to offer condolences and sacrifices,
and promoting their descendants.
18From the sixth month until this month, it had been raining.
19In winter,
tenth month,
on the *yǐsì* day,
Empress Língsī was buried.
20The White Wave Bandits plundered Hédōng.
The *Kǎoyì* says: The Imperial Annals state:
“In the ninth month of the fifth year,
the Southern Chányú rebelled
and, with the White Wave Bandits, plundered Hédōng.”
According to the *Xiōngnú Zhuàn*,
after the Emperor’s demise,
Yúfúluó then allied with the White Wave Bandits to plunder.
The Annals are mistaken;
we now follow the *Zhuàn*.
Initially,
after Yúfúluó was established as the Southern Chányú,
those among his countrymen who had killed his father rebelled,
and Chányú Qiāngqú was killed.
The event is seen in the previous volume, Middle Peace (*Zhōngpíng*) fifth year.
Yúfúluó went to the imperial court to plead his case.
Coinciding with Emperor Líng’s death,
the empire fell into great chaos.
Yúfúluó, leading several thousand cavalry, joined forces with the White Wave Bandits to plunder commanderies and counties.
At that time, the people all gathered together for protection,
so there was no profit from raiding,
and the army was consequently frustrated and injured.
He wanted to return to his country,
so he settled in Píngyáng, Hédōng.
but his countrymen did not accept him,
and the Southern Court then left the position vacant,
allowing an old king to manage state affairs.
21In the eleventh month,
Dǒng Zhuó was appointed Grand Chancellor (*Xiàngguó*).
Since Xiāo Hé, the Hàn had not again appointed anyone as Grand Chancellor.
He was allowed to enter the court without hurrying,
and wear his sword and shoes into the hall.
22In the twelfth month,
on the *wùxū* day,
Huáng Wǎn, Minister over the Masses, was appointed Grand Commandant;
Yáng Biāo, Minister of Works, was appointed Minister over the Masses;
and Xún Shuǎng, Minister of the Imperial Household (*Guānglù Xūn*), was appointed Minister of Works.
Initially,
Zhōu Bì of Wǔwēi, an Imperial Secretary,
and Wǔ Qióng of Rǔnán, Commandant of the City Gates,
persuaded Dǒng Zhuó to rectify the administration of Huán and Líng
and promote eminent scholars from the empire to win public support.
Dǒng Zhuó agreed,
ordering Bì, Qióng, along with Zhèng Tài, an Imperial Secretary, and Hé Yǒng, a Chief Clerk, among others, to purge the corrupt
and elevate the obscure.
Thereupon, reclusive scholars Xún Shuǎng, Chén Jì, Hán Róng, and Shēntú Pán were summoned.
Shuǎng was again appointed Prefect of Píngyuán,
and upon reaching Wǎnlíng –
Wǎnlíng County belonged to Hénán Yǐn,
east of Luòyáng –
he served for three days
before being promoted to Minister of Works.
From being summoned to taking office as one of the Three Ducal Ministers,
a total of ninety-three days passed.
Jì was also appointed Colonel of the Five Offices,
and Róng was appointed Grand Herald.
Jì
was the son of Shí;
Róng
was the son of Sháo.
Shuǎng and others, fearing Dǒng Zhuó’s brutality,
all dared not refuse.
Only Shēntú Pán received the summons,
and when people urged him to go,
Pán laughed without answering.
Dǒng Zhuó ultimately could not compel him,
and he died of old age
at over seventy years old.
Dǒng Zhuó also appointed Hán Fù, an Imperial Secretary, as Governor of Jìzhōu;
Liú Dài, an Attendant in Ordinary, as Inspector of Yǎnzhōu;
Kǒng Zhòu of Chénliú as Inspector of Yùzhōu;
Zhāng Miǎo of Dōngpíng as Administrator of Chénliú;
and Zhāng Zī of Yǐngchuān as Administrator of Nányáng.
Those whom Dǒng Zhuó personally favored
were not placed in prominent positions,
but only as generals and commandants.
*Jiàngxiào*
refers to Colonels and Commandants.
*Chǔ*
is pronounced *chānglǚ fān*.
23An imperial edict abolished the three era names Guāngxī, Zhāoníng, and Yǒnghàn.
After abolishing the three names,
the era was again referred to as Middle Peace (*Zhōngpíng*) sixth year.
24Dǒng Zhuó was cruel and ruthless.
Once he monopolized power,
seizing the nation’s arms, treasures,
and shaking the world with his might,
his desires knew no bounds.
He said to his guests:
“My rank of Grand Chancellor
is supreme, beyond compare!”
He claimed he was not a minister but a ruler,
so rebellious was he.
*Yǔ*
is pronounced *niújù fān*.
*Xiàng*
is pronounced *xīliàng fān*.
He did not remove his sword,
disturbing the dragon (referring to the imperial court),
his surname,
presumably descended from the ancient Rǎolóng clan.
At this time,
the noble and powerful families in Luòyáng
had mansions facing each other,
and their gold, silk, and property
were abundant in every household.
Dǒng Zhuó let his soldiers loose,
storming their residences,
plundering their valuables,
and seizing women,
without sparing the noble and powerful;
people were terrified,
unsure of survival from day to day.
Dǒng Zhuó sought to arrest Yuán Shào urgently.
Zhōu Bì and Wǔ Qióng advised Dǒng Zhuó, saying:
“The great matter of dethroning and enthroning [an emperor]
is not something ordinary people can handle.
Yuán Shào did not grasp the larger situation
and fled in fear,
he has no other ambitions.
If you urgently seek to arrest him now,
circumstances will inevitably lead to rebellion.
The Yuán clan has spread its benevolence for four generations;
from Yuán Ān to Shào, it has been four generations.
If he gathers heroes and assembles a multitude,
and heroes rise because of him,
then the region east of the mountains will not belong to you, my lord.
It is better to pardon him,
appoint him as a Commandery Administrator.
Shào, happy to be absolved of his crime,
will surely cause no trouble.”
Dǒng Zhuó considered this sound,
and immediately appointed Shào as Administrator of Bóhǎi
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Dǎngxiāng.
He also made Yuán Shù General of the Rear
and Cáo Cāo as Commandant of Agile Cavalry.
Shù, fearing Dǒng Zhuó,
fled to Nányáng.
Cáo Cāo changed his name
and traveled secretly eastward,
passing through Zhōngmóu.
Zhōngmóu County
was subordinate to Hénán Yǐn.
Jiàn
is pronounced 'xiàn'.
He was arrested and brought to the county [magistrate].
At that time, the county had already received Dǒng Zhuó’s warrant.
Only the Merit Officer (Gōngcáo) knew in his heart that it was Cáo Cāo,
and believing that the world was about to be in chaos
and that it was inappropriate to detain a national hero,
he spoke up and had him released.
Bái refers to the Magistrate of Zhōngmóu.
He dispersed his family wealth
and gathered five thousand men to form an army.
At this time,
many heroes wished to raise armies to punish Dǒng Zhuó.
Yuán Shào was in Bóhǎi.
Hán Fù, Governor of Jìzhōu, sent several departmental clerks to guard him,
preventing him from taking action.
Bùcóngshì refers to
departmental clerks of commanderies and states.
To guard Bóhǎi, a single commandery,
he sent several departmental clerks to watch over it,
fearing Shào would raise an army.
He forged a letter from the Three Excellencies in the capital to the provinces and commanderies,
detailing Dǒng Zhuó’s wickedness,
saying:
“We are being coerced
and cannot save ourselves.
We eagerly await righteous armies
to resolve the nation’s troubles.”
Fù received the letter
and asked his subordinate officials:
“Should we now assist the Yuán clan
or assist the Dǒng clan?”
Liú Zǐhuì, the Administrator of Governance, said:
“Now we raise an army for the nation,
what is this talk of Yuán or Dǒng!”
Fù showed a look of shame.
Zǐhuì further said:
“Warfare is a terrible thing
and one should not be the first to initiate it.
Now, it is advisable to observe other provinces;
if there are those who make a move,
then we can join them.
Jìzhōu is not weak compared to other provinces,
and no one else’s achievements surpass those of Jìzhōu.”
Fù agreed.
Fù then wrote a letter to Shào,
recounting Dǒng Zhuó’s evils,
and permitting him to raise an army.
Kǎoyì says: Both Fàn Shū and Wèi Zhì record this event.
Fàn Shū places it after the army was raised,
Wèi Zhì places it before the army was raised.
If it was after the army was raised,
Shào was already the盟主 (alliance leader),
how would Fù dare to forbid him from raising an army?
If it was before the army was raised,
then it is closer to the truth.
Here, we follow Wèi Zhì.
Emperor Xiàndì
—his personal name was Xié.
According to the rules for posthumous titles: “Intelligent and wise” is called Xiàn.
Gǔjīn Zhù says:
The character
“Xié”
is also written as
“Hé”. Zhāng Fán Jì says: Emperor Líng believed the Emperor resembled himself,
hence he was named Xié. Dìwáng Jì says: Xié,
courtesy name Bóhé.
Shǔ posthumously named the Emperor Mǐn,
Wèi posthumously named the Emperor Xiàn.
This follows the Wèi posthumous title,
because Wèi taking the imperial abdication from Hàn is considered orthodox.
The first year of Chūpíng
(Gēngwǔ, 190 CE).
1 Spring,
first month.
All the commanderies and provinces east of the passes raised armies to attack Dǒng Zhuó,
and acclaimed Yuán Shào, Administrator of Bóhǎi, as their alliance leader.
Shào styled himself General of Chariots and Cavalry.
All the generals were provisionally granted official titles by him.
At that time, Dǒng Zhuó held the Son of Heaven,
so Shào and others had no one to receive orders from,
hence they provisionally granted official titles.
Hán Fù, Governor of Jìzhōu, remained in Yè,
supplying their army provisions.
Kǒng Zhòu, Inspector of Yùzhōu, was stationed in Yǐngchuān.

Liú Dài, Inspector of Yǎanzhōu, Zhāng Miǎo, Administrator of Chénliú, Miǎo’s younger brother Chāo, Administrator of Guǎnglíng, Qiáo Mào, Administrator of Dōngjùn, Yuán Yí, Administrator of Shānyáng, and Bào Xìn, Chancellor of Jìběi, were all stationed together with Cáo Cāo at Suānzǎo.
Suānzǎo County was subordinate to Chénliú Commandery.
Mào
is pronounced “mào”.
Lǔyáng County
was subordinate to Nányáng Commandery.
Many heroes gravitated towards Yuán Shào.
Only Bào Xìn said to Cáo Cāo:
“Truly, strategies are not born often in this world.
You are the one who can suppress chaos and restore order.
If it is not the right person,
even if strong, they will surely perish.
Are you perhaps one whom Heaven has enlightened?”
2 On the day of Xīnhài,
there was a general pardon throughout the realm.
3 On the day of Guǐyǒu,
Dǒng Zhuó ordered the Minister of the Household (Lángzhōnglìng) Lǐ Rú to poison and kill King of Hóngnóng Biàn.
4 Dǒng Zhuó deliberated on raising a large army to attack the region east of the mountains.
Zhèng Tài, Grand Secretary (Shàngshū), said:
“Truly, governance lies in virtue,
not in numbers.”
Dǒng Zhuó was displeased and said:
“According to your words,
are soldiers useless?”
Zhèng Tài said:
“I do not mean it to be so;
I mean that there is no need to send a large army to the region east of the mountains.
You, my lord, hail from Xīzhōu,
and have been a general since your youth,
proficient in military affairs.
Yuán Běnchū is the son of high officials,
born and raised in the capital.
Zhāng Mèngzhuó is a respected elder from Dōngpíng,
who sits without peeking into the hall.
Kǒng Gōngxù engages in pure discussions and elevated discourse,
breathing life into the withered and blowing life out of the living.
Kǒng Zhòu,
courtesy name Gōngxù.
Xián says: breathing life into the withered means making the withered come to life,
blowing life out of the living means making the living wither;
it refers to his discussions having both praise and criticism.
Facing a spear-point and deciding victory or defeat
is not their equal to you, my lord.
This means facing the military front and deciding victory or defeat with the enemy.
Their ranks are without order.
If they rely on numbers and boast of strength,
they will each stand like chess pieces, observing success and failure,
unwilling to be of one mind and courage,
and advance and retreat together.
These few sentences,
though Gōngyè used them to explain to Dǒng Zhuó,
nevertheless accurately describe the attitudes of the generals east of the passes.
The people are not accustomed to war.
Guānxī recently suffered from Qiāng raids;
even women there can wield bows and fight.
Those whom the world fears
are none other than the people of Bīng and Liáng, and the allied Qiāng and Hú.
And you, my lord, command them as your claws and teeth.
This is like driving tigers and rhinoceroses against dogs and sheep,
or raising a fierce wind to sweep away dead leaves—
who dares to resist them?
There is no need to levy troops and alarm the world,
causing the people burdened by service to gather and commit evil,
abandoning virtue and relying on numbers,
thereby diminishing your own prestige and authority.”
Dǒng Zhuó was then pleased.
5 Dǒng Zhuó, seeing that the troops in Shāndōng were numerous,
wanted to move the capital to avoid them.
All the Duke-Ministers were unwilling but dared not speak.
They feared his brutality.
An envoy summoned Jùn for an appointment,
but Jùn declined,
unwilling to accept.
He then said:
"If the state moves west,
it will certainly isolate the hopes of the whole realm.
'Gū' (孤)
means 'fù' (負, to turn one's back on).
Your servant does not see how this is acceptable."
The envoy said:
"You were summoned to accept an appointment, but you refused;
you were not asked about the relocation, yet you expounded on it.
Why is this?"
Jùn said:
"The position of Vice Grand Chancellor is not something your servant is capable of holding;
moving the capital is not a good plan, and it is an urgent matter.
Declining what I am incapable of,
and speaking on what is urgent,
is proper for your servant."
Because of this, he was stopped from becoming Vice Grand Chancellor.
Zhuó assembled all the Duke-Ministers for a discussion,
saying:
"Gāozǔ established his capital in Guānzhōng,
for eleven generations.
Guāngwǔ established his palace in Luòyáng,
and now it has also been eleven generations.
According to the 'Shíbāo Chèn' (石包讖),
in addition to the contemporary apocryphal texts,
there was also the 'Shíbāo Shìchèn' (石包室讖).
This was probably appended and created by people of the time,
similar to the 'Kǒngzǐ Bìfáng Jì' (孔子閉房記) and such.
To accord with the will of heaven and man."
All the officials remained silent.
Sītú Yáng Biāo said:
"Moving the capital and changing the system are
great affairs of the realm.
Thus, when Pángēng moved to Bó,
the Yin people resented each other.
The 'Shū Xù' (書序) states: Pángēng moved five times,
intending to govern Bó,
and the Yin people sighed and resented each other.
Therefore, Guāngwǔ re-established the capital in Luòyì,
and many years have passed since then.
The common people are at peace and happy.
Now, to abandon the ancestral temples without cause,
and forsake the imperial tombs,
I fear that the common people will be alarmed and stirred,
and there will certainly be a chaotic upheaval like boiling porridge.
Xián (賢) states: like boiling porridge.
The 'Shī' (詩) says: like boiling, like soup.
How can inauspicious and perverse books
be trusted and used!"
Zhuó said:
"Guānzhōng is fertile and rich,
which is why Qín was able to annex the six states.
Moreover, timber comes naturally from Lǒngyòu,
and Dùlíng has the Emperor Wǔ's pottery kilns.
If we work together to build it,
it can be accomplished in a single day.
What concern are the common people to discuss!
If anyone holds back,
I will drive them with a large army,
and they can be made to go to Cānghǎi."
Xián (賢) states: meaning they dare not avoid danger and difficulty.
"To stir the realm is extremely easy,
but to pacify it is extremely difficult.
May you, Illustrious Duke, consider this!"
Zhuó changed his expression and said:
"Do you intend to obstruct the state's plan!"
Tàiyù Huáng Wǎn said:
"This is a great matter of the state.
Sir Yáng's words,
are they not worthy of thought!"
Zhuó did not answer.
Sīkōng Xún Shuǎng, seeing Zhuó's determined intent,
feared harm to Biāo and others,
and so calmly said:
"How could the Grand Chancellor enjoy this!
The Shāndōng armies have risen,
and they cannot be restrained in a single day.
Therefore, it is appropriate to relocate to plan against them.
This is the strategy of Qín and Hàn."
Referring to Qín and Hàn establishing their capitals in Guānzhōng,
utilizing the mountainous and riverine terrain to control the realm.
Wǎn retired,
and again presented a dissenting opinion.
In the second month,
on the day Yǐhài,
Zhuó, citing unusual calamities, memorialized to dismiss Wǎn, Biāo, and others.
He appointed Guānglùxūn Zhào Qiān as Tàiyù,
and Tàipú Wáng Yǔn as Sītú.
Chéngmén Jiàowèi Wǔ Qióng and Dūjūn Jiàowèi Zhōu Bì strongly advised against moving the capital.
Zhuó was furious and said:
"When Zhuó first entered court,
these two gentlemen advised using virtuous scholars,
so Zhuó followed.
But when these gentlemen arrived at their posts,
they raised troops to plot against me!
These two gentlemen have betrayed Zhuó!
How can Zhuó be ungrateful to them!"
On the day Gēngchén,
Qióng and Bì were arrested
and beheaded.
Yáng Biāo and Huáng Wǎn were terrified,
and went to Zhuó to apologize.
Zhuó also regretted killing Qióng and Bì,
and so re-appointed Biāo and Wǎn as Guānglù Dàfū.
6 Zhuó summoned Jīngzhàoyǐn Gài Xūn to be Yìláng.
At this time, Zuǒ Jiāngjūn Huángfǔ Sōng was leading three thousand troops, garrisoned in Fúfēng.
Pān Yuè's 'Guānzhōng Jì' (關中記) states: The former administrations of the Sānfǔ were within Cháng'ān city,
and each chief magistrate governed the people in his own county seat.
After Guāngwǔ moved the capital east,
Fúfēng moved its administration to Huáilǐ,
and Féngyì moved its administration to Gāolíng.
At the same time, Zhuó also summoned Sōng to be Chéngmén Jiàowèi.
Sōng's Chángshǐ Liáng Yǎn persuaded Sōng, saying:
"Dǒng Zhuó has plundered the capital region,
and establishes and deposes as he pleases.
Now he summons the General;
at worst, it means disaster, at best, humiliation.
Now, while Zhuó is in Luòyáng,
and the Son of Heaven has come west,
with the General's forces, you can welcome the Supreme One,
receive orders to suppress the rebel,
recruit soldiers and gather commanders.
The Yuán clan presses him from the east,
and the General pressures him from the west.
This will make him a captured bird!"
Sōng did not follow,
and consequently went to answer the summons.
Sōng previously failed to listen to his nephew Lì's words,
and now again did not follow Yǎn's strategy.
This was because he felt his own talent was insufficient to control Zhuó.
He also returned to the capital.
Zhuó appointed Xūn as Yuèqí Jiàowèi.
Hé'nán Yǐn Zhū Jùn presented military matters to Zhuó.
Zhuó rebuked Jùn, saying:
"I have fought a hundred battles and won a hundred victories;
I have made up my mind.
Sir, do not speak recklessly,
lest you defile my blade!"
Gài Xūn said:
"In ancient times, the sagacity of Wǔdīng
still sought counsel and remonstrance.
Xián (賢) states: Wǔdīng
was King Gāozōng of Yīn.
He said to Fù Yuè:
'Open your heart,
and water my heart.'
Yuè replied to the King, saying:
'Only wood that follows the line is straight;
a ruler who follows remonstrance is sagely.'
I say that Gài Xūn was a loyal and upright scholar.
At the time, Zhuó was plotting usurpation,
so it would not be appropriate to mention the deeds of Wǔdīng.
According to the 'Guóyǔ',
Chǔ Zuǒshǐ Yǐ Xiāng said: 'In the past, Duke Wǔ of Wèi, when he was ninety-five years old,
still admonished and warned the state, saying:
"Do not say I am old and senile and abandon me.
You must be respectful and diligent at court,
and admonish me morning and evening.
When you hear one or two words,
you must remember and accept them,
to instruct and guide me."'
When he died,
he was called Duke Rèishèng Wǔ.
Xūn likely used the deeds of Duke Wǔ of Wèi to admonish Zhuó.
The historical texts were mistakenly transmitted,
taking 'Gōng' (公)
for 'Dīng' (丁).
And do you wish to block people's mouths?"
Zhuó then apologized to him.
7 Zhuó dispatched troops to Yángchéng.
They happened upon the people gathered at the altar for a community meeting.
This was an event of the second month.
Yángchéng County belonged to Yǐngchuān Commandery.
The soldiers hitched their heavy wagons,
loaded with women,
tied their heads to the wagon shafts,
sang and shouted as they returned to Luòyáng,
claiming they had attacked bandits and gained a great victory.
Zhuó burned their heads,
and gave the women to his armed soldiers as concubines.
"Jiǎbīng" (甲兵)
refers to armed soldiers.
8 On the Dīnghài day,
the imperial chariot moved west.
Dǒng Zhuó seized all wealthy families,
executed them for various crimes,
confiscated their properties,
the number of dead was incalculable.
He forcibly relocated several million of the remaining people to Cháng'ān.
Horsemen and foot soldiers drove and pushed them,
treading on each other,
suffering from hunger, and plundering,
corpses filled the roads.
Dǒng Zhuó himself remained stationed in the Bìguī Yuàn,
burning down all palaces, temples, government offices, and residences.
Within two hundred *lǐ*,
houses were completely destroyed,
without even chickens or dogs remaining.
He also ordered Lǚ Bù to excavate the imperial mausoleums and the tombs of high-ranking officials and nobles,
and collect their treasures.
When Dǒng Zhuó captured soldiers from Shāndōng,
he coated more than ten *pǐ* of cloth with human fat,
wrapped it around their bodies,
and then burned them,
starting from their feet.
9 In the third month,
on the Yǐsì day,
the imperial chariot entered Cháng'ān.
A textual variant note says: Yuán Jì records it as
"Jǐsì,"
but we follow Fàn Shū here.
Shīgǔ says: *Sānfǔ Huángtú* states: The Jīngzhào Fǔ was on Shàngguān Qián Jiē,
entering the former Zhōngwèi Fǔ to the east.
At that time, Dǒng Zhuó had not yet arrived,
and all matters of the court, large and small, were entrusted to Wáng Yǔn.
Wáng Yǔn outwardly appeased,
but inwardly planned for the royal house,
showing great ministerial bearing.
From the Son of Heaven to the court, all relied on Wáng Yǔn.
Wáng Yǔn condescended to humor Dǒng Zhuó,
and Dǒng Zhuó also greatly trusted him.
10 Because of Yuán Shào,
on the Wùwǔ day, Dǒng Zhuó
killed Grand Tutor Yuán Kuí and Grand Coachman Yuán Jī,
and more than fifty members of their household, from infants upwards.
"Chǐkǒu"
refers to infants.
11 Initially,
the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, Wáng Ruì,
Péi Sōngzhī says: Ruì was the uncle of Jìn Grand Tutor Xiáng.
Líng and Guì refer to Línglíng and Guìyáng.
spoke rather lightly of him.
When the regional and commandery forces raised armies to attack Dǒng Zhuó,
Wáng Ruì and Sūn Jiān also raised armies.
Wáng Ruì had always been on bad terms with the Administrator of Wǔlíng, Cáo Yín,
and openly declared he would kill Cáo Yín first.
Cáo Yín, afraid,
falsely forged a document from an inspecting envoy to Sūn Jiān,
detailing Wáng Ruì's faults,
ordering his arrest.
After the execution was completed,
he reported the situation.
Sūn Jiān, receiving the document,
immediately led his troops to attack Wáng Ruì.
Wáng Ruì, hearing the troops approaching,
ascended a tower to look,
and sent to ask,
"What do you want to do?"
Sūn Jiān's vanguard replied,
"Our soldiers have been fighting for a long time and are weary.
We wish to seek provisions from the governor."
According to *Wú Lù*,
"zīzhí" means
the cost of clothing and provisions.
"The soldiers are asking for rewards themselves,
why is Lord Sūn among them?"
Sūn Jiān said,
"I have been ordered by the envoy to execute you!"
Wáng Ruì said,
"What crime have I committed?"
Sūn Jiān said,
"For being ignorant!"
Wáng Ruì, in desperation,
scraped gold and drank it, and died.
Táo Hóngjǐng says: Raw gold is poisonous;
if not refined,
consuming it kills a person.
His army already numbered tens of thousands.
The Administrator of Nányáng, Zhāng Zī, refused to supply military provisions,
so Sūn Jiān lured and beheaded him.
Chén Shòu's *Zhì* says: Sūn Jiān lured him with oxen and wine.
*Wú Lì* says: Sūn Jiān feigned illness to lure him.
There was nothing he asked for that he did not obtain.
Before arriving at Lǔyáng,
Lǔyáng County belonged to Nányáng Commandery.
Yuán Shù thus was able to occupy Nányáng.
A textual variant note says: Fàn Shū's biography of Shù states:
"Liú Biǎo recommended Shù as Administrator of Nányáng."
Liú Biǎo's biography states:
"Shù blocked the way with troops and was stationed in Lǔyáng,
so Liú Biǎo could not reach Jīngzhōu."
*Wèi Zhì*'s biography of Shù:
"Sūn Jiān killed Zhāng Zī,
and Shù was able to occupy Nányáng."
*Wèi Wǔdì Jì*,
for the second month of this year, already says Shù was stationed in Nányáng.
Perhaps Shù initially fled to Lǔyáng,
then Sūn Jiān took Nányáng this spring,
and Shù then occupied it,
still taking Lǔyáng as his administrative seat.
An imperial edict appointed Liú Biǎo, the Commander of the Northern Army, as Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
At that time, bandits and rebels ran rampant,
and roads were blocked.
Liú Biǎo entered Yíchéng alone on horseback,
Xián says: Yíchéng County belonged to Nánjùn,
originally Yān,
renamed Yíchéng in the third year of Emperor Huì.
and conspired with them, saying:
"Currently, the clan bandits in Jiāngnán are very numerous,
Xián says: Clan members who jointly became bandits.
if Yuán Shù relies on them,
disaster will surely come.
I want to recruit soldiers,
but I fear they cannot be gathered.
What is the strategy?"
Kuǎi Liáng said:
"Those who do not attach themselves lack benevolence;
those who attach themselves but are not governed lack righteousness.
If the way of benevolence and righteousness is practiced,
the common people will flock to it like water flowing downwards,
why worry that soldiers will not be gathered?"
Kuǎi Yuè said:
"Yuán Shù is arrogant and lacks strategy,
most of the clan bandit leaders are greedy and violent,
causing suffering to their subordinates.
If we send people to show them profit,
they will surely come with their forces.
If you, my lord, execute the lawless among them,
and then pacify and utilize the others,
the people of the entire province will have a desire to survive,
and upon hearing of your prestige and virtue,
they will surely come carrying their children on their backs.
With soldiers gathered and people attached,
holding Jiānglíng in the south,
and guarding Xiāngyáng in the north,
the eight commanderies of Jīngzhōu can be settled with a mere proclamation,
*Jùn Guó Zhì*: Jīngzhōu department had seven commanderies: Nányáng, Nánjùn, Jiāngxià, Línglíng, Guìyáng, Chángshā, Wǔlíng.
*Hàn Guān Yí* considers Zhānglíng as the eighth commandery.
no one will be able to do anything."
Yuán Shù,
courtesy name Gōnglù.
"Excellent!"
So, he sent Kuǎi Yuè to lure the clan bandit leaders.
Fifty-five people came,
and he executed all of them and took their forces.
He then moved his administration to Xiāngyáng,
the Inspector of Jīngzhōu originally governed from Wǔlíng Hànshòu.
Xiāngyáng County belonged to Nánjùn.
Jiāngnán was entirely pacified.
The parts of Jīngzhōu in Jiāngnán were the four commanderies of Chángshā, Wǔlíng, Línglíng, and Guìyáng.
This laid the foundation for Liú Biǎo's exclusive control over Jīngzhōu.
18 Wáng Kuāng (王匡) was stationed at Héyángjīn (河陽津).
Héyángjīn (河陽津)
is Méngjīn (孟津).
He was utterly defeated.
19 The Left Central Protector, Cài Yōng (蔡邕), proposed,
"For those who held the temple title of Zōng (宗) from Xiàohé Dì (孝和帝) onwards,
all should have it removed
to follow earlier precedents."
This was adopted.
According to ritual,
Zǔ (祖) is for those with merit, while Zōng (宗) is for those with virtue.
From Hé Dì (和帝) onwards, there was no virtue to warrant the title of Zōng (宗),
hence it was removed.
Qù (去) (removed) is pronounced qiāng lǚ fān.
Qiāng lǚ fān.
A "Kǎo Yì" (考異) note states: Yuán Jì (袁紀) places this in the following year.
We follow Fàn Shū (范書) here.
20 The Central Protector, Xú Róng (徐榮), recommended Gōngsūn Dù (公孫度), a former Inspector of Jìzhōu (冀州) from his same commandery, to Dǒng Zhuó (董卓).
Zhuó (卓) appointed him as Grand Administrator of Liáodōng (遼東).
Upon arriving in office,
Dù (度) executed over a hundred powerful families and prominent gentry in the commandery according to law.
The commandery trembled with fear.
He then attacked Gāogōulí (高句驪) to the east,
and struck the Wūhuán (烏桓) to the west.
He said to his trusted officials, Liǔ Yì (柳毅) and Yáng Yí (陽儀), among others,
"The Hàn (漢) dynasty's mandate is about to expire.
I must plan with you gentlemen to rectify
things."
Thereupon, he divided Liáodōng (遼東) into Liáoxī (遼西) and Zhōngliáo (中遼) commanderies,
appointing grand administrators for each.
He crossed the sea to take control of the various counties of Dōnglái (東萊),
and established a Governor of Yíngzhōu (營州).
He declared himself Marquis of Liáodōng (遼東) and Shepherd of Píngzhōu (平州),
erected temples to the two founding emperors of Hàn (漢),
and, acting on his own authority,
offered sacrifices to Heaven and Earth in the suburbs,
and personally ploughed the ceremonial field.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: Jiè (藉) means to borrow.
It means to borrow manpower to manage it,
to encourage and lead all under Heaven,
making them devoted to agriculture.
The Spring and Autumn Annals says: After the suburban sacrifice, one ploughs.
Thus, borrowing manpower to complete the annual work,
it is therefore called the Emperor's ploughing.
Minister Zàn (瓚) said: Qīngēng (親耕) means to personally plough,
it should not be taken to mean borrowing.
Jiè (藉) means to tread.
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: Zàn's (瓚) explanation is correct.
The Shuōwén (說文) says:
The emperor ploughs a thousand *mǔ*.
Jiè (藉) is pronounced qín xī fān.
He established standards with yak tails and feathered cavalry.
Feathered cavalry
refers to Yǔlín (羽林) cavalry.

Study, Tiāntái (天台)
Emperor Xiàoxiàn (孝獻皇帝) Year Yǐ (乙)
Chūpíng (初平) Second Year
(Xīnwèi (辛未), 191 CE)
1. Spring,
First month,
Xīnchǒu (辛丑),
a general amnesty was declared.
2. The various generals east of the pass deliberated: The court's young emperor
was oppressed by Dǒng Zhuó (董卓),
separated by distant passes.
Passes
refer to Hángǔ Guān (函谷關) and Táolín Sài (桃林塞).
Liú Yú (劉虞), the Governor of Yōuzhōu (幽州),
a wise and capable member of the imperial clan,
wished to jointly enthrone him as their lord.
Cáo Cāo (曹操) said:
"The reason we raised armies and received responses from near and far
is because we acted righteously.
Now the young emperor is weak
and controlled by a treacherous minister.
He does not have the flaws of Chāngyì (昌邑) that led to the ruin of a state.
Chāngyì (昌邑)
refers to Prince Hè (賀) of Chāngyì (昌邑).
Who in the world would approve of this!
You gentlemen face north,
I will face west."
Yōuzhōu (幽州) is in the north,
Cháng'ān (長安) is in the west,
hence Cāo (操) said this.
"The emperor is not the son of Xiàolíng (孝靈),
and they want to follow the precedent of Jiàng (絳) and Guàn (灌) in deposing a young ruler and enthroning the Prince of Dài (代),
to enthrone Grand Marshal Yú (虞) as emperor."
Shù (術) secretly harbored disloyal ambitions;
it was not beneficial for the state to have a mature ruler,
so he outwardly claimed public righteousness to reject this.
Shào (紹) again wrote to Shù (術), saying:
"Now the western court has a young ruler
who is not of their bloodline,
meaning the emperor is not the son of Líng Dì (靈帝).
Fù (復)
is pronounced fú yòu fān;
same below.
How can he be trusted again!
We should merely send troops to garrison crucial passes,
and they will all starve to death;
enthrone a sagely ruler in the east,
and great peace can be hoped for.
Why hesitate!
Moreover, your family was executed,
do you not remember Zǐxū (子胥)?
Referring to Zǐxū's (子胥) ability to avenge his father and brother.
This attributes the killing of Yuán Wěi (袁隗) and others to the emperor.
"The sagely ruler is intelligent and sagacious,
possessing the qualities of Zhōu Chéng (周成).
The villain Zhuó (卓) took advantage of a time of crisis and chaos,
and awed and subdued all officials.
This is merely a minor misfortune for the Hàn (漢) house.
To say that the present emperor 'is not of their bloodline,'
is that not a slander!
And to say, 'Your family was executed,
how can you again face north,'
this was done by Zhuó (卓),
how could it be the state's doing!
My sincere loyalty
is focused on destroying Zhuó (卓),
I know nothing else!"
Fù (馥) and Shào (紹) eventually sent the former Grand Administrator of Lèlàng (樂浪), Zhāng Qí (張岐), and others, bearing the proposal to offer the imperial title to Yú (虞).
When Yú (虞) saw Qí (岐) and the others,
he sternly rebuked them, saying:
"Now the world is in chaos,
the emperor is in distress.
I have received great favors,
yet have been unable to clear the national shame.
You gentlemen each occupy a province or commandery;
you should collectively exert your utmost efforts for the imperial house,
and instead you conspire rebelliously to defile each other!"
He firmly rejected them.
Fù (馥) and others again asked Yú (虞) to oversee the affairs of the Secretariat and
to confer titles and appointments on his own authority.
Again he refused,
wishing to flee to the Xiongnú (匈奴) to cut himself off;
only then did Shào (紹) and the others desist.
3. Second month,
Dīngchǒu (丁丑),
Dǒng Zhuó (董卓) was made Grand Preceptor,
his rank above that of kings and princes.
4. Sūn Jiān (孫堅) moved his encampment to Liángdōng (梁東),
was defeated by Zhuó's (卓) general Xú Róng (徐榮),
then rallied his scattered troops and advanced to station at Yángrén (陽人).
Xián (賢) said: Liáng (梁) county
belongs to Hénán (河南) Commandery,
now Rǔzhōu (汝州) county.
The old city of Yángrén Jù (陽人聚)
is west of Liáng (梁) county.
Lǚ Bù (呂布) was made Commander of Cavalry.
Zhěn (軫) and Bù (布) were not on good terms.
Jiān (堅) attacked,
utterly defeating them,
and beheaded their commander Huà Xióng (華雄).
Someone said to Yuán Shù (袁術):
"If Jiān (堅) takes Luò (雒),
he will be uncontrollable.
This would be getting rid of a wolf only to gain a tiger."
Shù (術) became suspicious
and did not transport military provisions.
Jiān (堅) rode swiftly by night to see Shù (術).
Yángrén (陽人) is over a hundred *lǐ* from Lǔyáng (魯陽).
"The reason I expose myself without regard
is, above, to eliminate bandits for the state,
and below, to comfort your family's private vendetta.
Jiān (堅) and Zhuó (卓) have no personal animosity,
yet you listen to insidious words.
Insidious slander
comes from The Analects.
Why is this?"
Shù (術) was flustered
and immediately dispatched military provisions.
Sūn Jiān (孫堅) returned to camp.
Dǒng Zhuó (董卓) sent his general Lǐ Què (李傕) to persuade Sūn Jiān (孫堅),
wishing to establish a marital alliance [with him],
and promising to appoint Sūn Jiān’s (孫堅) distant relatives and younger brothers as刺史 (cìshǐ) and郡守 (jùnshǒu) [if Sūn Jiān (孫堅) listed them],
and authorize their use.
Sūn Jiān (孫堅) said:
“Dǒng Zhuó (董卓) is a rebel against Heaven, without principle.
If I do not now exterminate your three clans and display them to the four seas,
then I shall die with my eyes open.
How could I form a marital alliance with you!”
The character乃 (nǎi) [in the original text]
here means 汝 (rǔ) (you).
[The battle occurred] ninety *lǐ* (里) from Luò (雒).
Xián (賢) said: Dàgǔkǒu (大谷口)
is eighty-five *lǐ* (里) northwest of the old Sōngyáng (嵩陽),

here means 至 (zhì) (to).
[Dǒng Zhuó (董卓)] fought Sūn Jiān (孫堅) among the various tombs,

Zhēnguān (甄官)
was in charge of the carving of stone and firing of pottery.
This set the stage for Yuán Shù (袁術) to seize the seal in the first year of Jiàn'ān (建安) [196 CE].
The character 璽 (xǐ)

Dǒng Zhuó (董卓) said to his長史 (zhǎngshǐ) Liú Ài (劉艾):
“The Guāndōng (關東) armies have been defeated many times;
they all fear me
and can do nothing.
Only Sūn Jiān (孫堅) is a little foolish.

Duàn Wēi (段煨),中郎將 (Zhōnglángjiàng), to garrison Huàyīn (華陰);
and Niú Fǔ (牛輔),中郎將 (Zhōnglángjiàng), to garrison Ānyì (安邑).

5 In summer,

[The character] 怖 (bù)
is pronounced *pǔ bù fān*.

[Someone] addressed him as尚父 (Shàngfù).
Dǒng Zhuó (董卓) asked Cài Yōng (蔡邕) about this,

“My lord’s (明公) might and virtue
are indeed immense,
however, compared to Tàigōng (太公),

One should wait until Guāndōng (關東) is pacified
