Dǒng Zhuó (董卓) then stopped.

Dǒng Zhuó (董卓) ordered Sīlì Xiàowèi (司隸校尉) Liú Xiāo (劉囂) to register officials and common people who were unfilial to their parents, disloyal to their lords, corrupt as officials, or disobedient as younger brothers.
All were to be executed,
and their property confiscated by the state.
Consequently, people falsely accused each other,
and thousands died unjustly.
The common people were agitated and distressed,
communicating with each other through their eyes on the roads.
6 In the sixth month,
on the day Bǐngxū (丙戌),
there was an earthquake.
7 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
Sīkōng (司空) Zhǒng Fú (种拂) was dismissed;
Chúnyú Jiā (淳于嘉) of Jìnán (濟南),光祿大夫 (Guānglù Dàfū), was made Sīkōng (司空).
Tàiwèi (太尉) Zhào Qiān (趙謙) was dismissed;
Mǎ Rìdī (馬日磾), Tàicháng (太常), was made Tàiwèi (太尉).
8 Earlier,
Hé Jìn (何進) had sent Zhāng Yáng (張楊) of Yúnzhōng (雲中) back to Bīngzhōu (幷州) to recruit soldiers.
When Hé Jìn (何進) was defeated,
Zhāng Yáng (張楊) remained in Shàngdǎng (上黨),
with several thousand followers.
Yuán Shào (袁紹) was in Hénèi (河內),
so Zhāng Yáng (張楊) went to join him,
and along with the Southern Chányú (單于) Yú Fúluó (於扶羅), he camped by the Zhāngshuǐ (漳水).
The Zhuózhāngshuǐ (濁漳水) originates in Chángzǐ (長子) of Shàngdǎng (上黨) and flows eastward past Yè (鄴).
Yè (鄴) was where Hán Fù (韓馥) resided.
Yuán Shào (袁紹) was wary of him;
secretly reducing and cutting his army's provisions,
wishing to cause his troops to disperse.
Coincidentally, Hán Fù’s (韓馥) general Qū Yì (麴義) rebelled.
The *Xìng Pǔ* (姓譜) says: During the Hàn (漢) dynasty, there was Jū Tán (鞠譚) of Píngyuán (平原).
His son Bì (閟) avoided disaster
and changed his name to the Qū (麴) clan,
which later became a prominent clan in Xīpíng (西平).
Yuán Shào (袁紹) then allied with Qū Yì (麴義).
Shào's guest, Péng Jì, said to Shào:
"General, you are undertaking a great enterprise, yet you rely on others for resources.
If you do not seize a province,
you will have no way to secure yourself."
Shào said:
"Jìzhōu's army is strong,
and my soldiers are hungry and exhausted.
If we cannot manage this,
we will have no place to stand."
Jì said:
"Hán Fù is a mediocre talent.
We can secretly invite Gōngsūn Zàn
to attack Jìzhōu.
Fù will certainly be terrified.
Then send an eloquent debater to explain the advantages and disadvantages.
Fù, pressed by the urgency,
will surely be willing to yield."
Shào approved of this,
and immediately sent a letter to Zàn.
Zàn then led his troops and arrived,
outwardly claiming to be attacking Dǒng Zhuó but secretly planning to assault Fù.
Fù fought him but was unsuccessful.
At this time, Dǒng Zhuó had entered the pass,
and Shào had returned his army to Yánjīn.
According to the *Xù Hàn Zhì*,
there is Yánjīn north of Sǎnzǎo County.
"Gōngsūn Zàn is leading the troops of Yān and Dài, advancing south on his victory,
and all the commanderies are responding to him.
His vanguard is irresistible.
Yuán Chēqí is leading his army eastward,
from Hénèi to Yánjīn,
which is called 'eastward'.
I secretly worry for the General!"
Fù was terrified,
and said:
"In that case, what should we do?"
Xún Chén said:
"How do you assess your own benevolence and capacity to accommodate the multitude, making you someone the world would attach itself to,
compared to the Yuán clan?"
Fù said:
"I am not as good."
"In times of danger, to speak with decisive resolution—
'Tǔjué' refers to speaking with extraordinary decisiveness.
How do you compare to the Yuán clan?"
Fù said:
"I am not as good."
"In terms of spreading kindness and virtue throughout the generations,
so that every household in the world benefits from it,
how do you compare to the Yuán clan?"
Fù said:
"I am not as good."
Xún Chén said:
"The Yuán clan are heroes of their time.
General, with three disadvantages in your favor,
if you remain above them for long,
they will certainly not serve beneath you.
Indeed, Jìzhōu
is a vital asset to the empire.
If they were to combine forces with Gōngsūn Zàn to seize it,
ruin and death could be expected immediately.
The Yuán clan
are old friends of the General,
and moreover, are allies.
This refers to their alliance in attacking Dǒng Zhuó.
If you were to offer Jìzhōu to the Yuán clan,
they would certainly greatly appreciate the General's virtue,
and Zàn would also be unable to contend with them.
Thus, the General would have the reputation of yielding to the worthy,
and your person would be as safe as Mount Tài."
Fù, being timid and cowardly by nature,
consequently approved of his plan.
Fù's Chief Clerk Gěng Wǔ, Assistant Administrator Mǐn Chún, and Registrar Lǐ Lì heard of this and remonstrated, saying:
The *Kǎo Yì* states that *Jiǔzhōu Chūnqiū* writes
"Gěng Yù,"
but we follow Fàn's book, *Wèi Zhì*, and *Yuán Jì* here.
Also, Fàn's book mentions
Cavalry Commandant Jǔ Shòu remonstrated,
but not Lǐ Lì.
We follow *Wèi Zhì* and *Yuán Jì* here.
"Jìzhōu has a million armored soldiers
and enough grain for ten years.
Yuán Shào is a lone guest with a poor army,
depending on our every breath.
'Bíxī' refers to the moment of a single exhalation and inhalation.
The breath exhaled from the nose is warm,
and inhaled is cold,
hence the expression.
Medical texts say: blood is the pulse,
qi is the breath.
The terms 'pulse' and 'breath' are distinguished from this.
Respiration
is the bellows of qi;
movement and response
are the waves of blood.
Its channels, when measured by body-inches,
total sixteen zhang and two chi.
In one exhalation, the pulse moves twice;
in one inhalation, the pulse moves twice.
In a complete respiration, the pulse moves five times,
and with a 'great breath,' six times.
One movement is one inch,
so one breath makes the pulse travel six inches.
Ten breaths, six chi;
one hundred breaths, six zhang;
two hundred breaths, twelve zhang;
seventy breaths, four zhang and two chi.
A total of two hundred seventy breaths,
in the time it takes for two *ke* of water to drain, completes sixteen zhang and two chi,
encompassing the entire body.
Within one hundred *ke*, fifty circuits are completed.
Thus it is said that the pulse travels twenty-five degrees in the yang
and twenty-five degrees in the yin.
Breath is measured by respiration.
One day totals thirteen thousand five hundred breaths.
As the advance and retreat of breath are slower than the pulse,
it takes one day and one night to complete the sixteen zhang and two chi of channels,
and qi circulates throughout the body,
gathering at the Fēngfǔ point.
The pulse belongs to yin,
and yin moves quickly,
like the Taiyin completing its circuit in one month.
Breath belongs to yang,
and yang moves slowly,
like the Taiyang completing its circuit in one year.
This corresponds to the constant measure of Heaven.
"Rùn"
should be
"Jiàn."
Cut off his sustenance,
and he can be starved to death instantly.
Why do you wish to give the province to him?"
Fù said:
"I am an old subordinate of the Yuán clan,
and my talent is not equal to Běnchū's.
To yield based on assessing virtue
is esteemed by the ancients.
What is wrong with you gentlemen alone?"
Earlier,
Fù's subordinates Zhào Fú and Chéng Huàn, commanding ten thousand strong crossbows, were stationed at Mèngjīn.
Hearing of this, they led their troops and rushed back.
At that time, Shào was at Qīngshuǐ in Cháogē.
According to the *Shuǐ Jīng*,
Qīngshuǐ originates in Xiūwǔ County, Hénèi,
passes through Huòjiā and Jí counties,
and flows into the Yellow River,
not reaching Cháogē.
Only the Qí River flows through Cháogē.
Perhaps locals also called the Qí River "Qīngshuǐ."
According to *Jiǔzhōu Chūnqiū*,
Shào was then at the mouth of Qīngshuǐ in Cháogē.
Fú and others traveled eastward from Mèngjīn,
meaning both armies were traveling by boat on the Yellow River towards Yè.
The Qīngshuǐ mouth is the Qí mouth,
and the south bank is Yánjīn.
With several hundred boats
and over ten thousand men,
they arrayed their troops and sounded their drums,
passing Shào's camp by night.
Shào was greatly displeased by this.
When Fú and the others arrived,
they said to Fù:
"Yuán Běnchū's army has no provisions,
and his men have already dispersed.
Although Zhāng Yáng and Yú Fúluó have newly joined him,
they are not yet willing to be used
and are not worth fighting.
We, your humble subordinates, request to use the existing troops to resist him.
Within ten days,
he will surely collapse like crumbling earth and shattered tiles.
You, Illustrious General, simply need to open your gates and sleep soundly.
What is there to worry or fear?"
Fù again did not listen,
but instead vacated his position,
went to live in the former residence of the Chief Eunuch Zhào Zhōng,
and sent his son to deliver his seal and sash to yield to Shào.
When Shào was about to arrive,
ten of Fù's subordinates scrambled to abandon him,
but only Gěng Wǔ and Mǐn Chún stood with drawn swords to resist him.
They could not be stopped,
so they ceased;
Shào killed them all.
Shào then took command as the Governor of Jìzhōu.
Acting by imperial authority, he made Fù General of Martial Awe,
but without any troops to command
or any official staff.
Shào appointed Jǔ Shòu of Guǎngpíng as General of Martial Prowess.
Guǎngpíng County belonged to Jùlù Commandery.
"Jǔ"
is pronounced "qiān yú" (Q164) and also "zhū" (Q52).
It is a surname,
descended from Jǔ Sòng, the Yellow Emperor's historian.
He was treated with great favor.
Shěn Pèi of Wèijùn and Tián Fēng of Jùlù were both upright but had not found favor with Hán Fù.
Shào made Tián Fēng an Assistant Administrator
and Shěn Pèi a Registrar.
Xǔ Yōu of Nányáng, Péng Jì,
and Xún Chén of Yǐngchuān
Shào appointed Zhū Hàn [Zhū Hàn] of Hénèi [Hénèi] as his Dūguān Cóngshì [Dūguān Cóngshì].
Shào established the Dūguān Cóngshì [Dūguān Cóngshì] position,
which was like holding the office of Sīlì Xiàowèi [Sīlì Xiàowèi].
Wishing to curry favor with Shào [Shào],
[Zhū] Hàn [Hàn] sent out troops to besiege Fù’s [Fù] residence,
drew their blades and climbed onto the roof.
Fù [Fù] fled upstairs,
and they captured Fù’s [Fù] eldest son,
breaking both his legs with a club;
Shào [Shào] immediately arrested Hàn [Hàn]
and killed him.
Fù [Fù] was still anxious and terrified,
so he asked Shào [Shào] for permission to leave,
and went to rely on Zhāng Miǎo [Zhāng Miǎo].
Later, Shào [Shào] sent an envoy to Miǎo [Miǎo]
to discuss some matters,
and whispered in Miǎo’s [Miǎo] ear;
"whispering in the ear" [ěr yǔ]
means speaking close to the ear.
[Fù] thought he was being plotted against,
and not long after,
he rose and went to the latrine,
where he committed suicide with a writing knife.
Bào Xìn [Bào Xìn] said to Cáo Cāo [Cáo Cāo]:
“Yuán Shào [Yuán Shào], as the盟主 [méngzhǔ] (alliance leader),
is exploiting his power for personal gain [quán zhuān lì],
and will inevitably stir up trouble,
thus becoming another Zhuó [Zhuó].
If we try to restrain him,
our strength will be insufficient to control him,
and we will only encounter difficulty.”
*Gòu [Gòu]*
is the same as *gòu [gòu]*.
*Nán [Nán]*,
read *nǎi dàn*.
Cāo [Cāo] approved of this.
At that time, the Black Mountain bandits, Yú Dú [Yú Dú], Bái Rào [Bái Rào], Suī Gù [Suī Gù] and others, numbering over a hundred thousand, raided Dōngjùn [Dōngjùn],
and Wáng Gōng [Wáng Gōng] could not repel them.
Cáo Cāo [Cáo Cāo] led his troops into Dōngjùn [Dōngjùn],
attacked Bái Rào [Bái Rào] at Púyáng [Púyáng],
and defeated them.
Yuán Shào [Yuán Shào] then formally appointed Cāo [Cāo] as the Grand Administrator of Dōngjùn [Dōngjùn],
governing from Dōngwǔyáng [Dōngwǔyáng].
Dōngwǔyáng [Dōngwǔyáng] County [xiàn]
belonged to Dōngjùn [Dōngjùn].
Yìng Shào [Yìng Shào] said: The county is south of the Wǔ [Wǔ] River.
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù [Shuǐjīng Zhù]* says: The Wǔ [Wǔ] River is the Luò [Luò] River.
Xián [Xián] said: The old city is south of today’s Xīn [Xīn] County [xiàn] in Wèizhōu [Wèizhōu].
*Shǒu [Shǒu]*,
read *shì yòu*.
9 The Southern Chányú [Chányú] abducted Zhāng Yáng [Zhāng Yáng] and rebelled against Yuán Shào [Yuán Shào],
encamping at Líyáng [Líyáng].
Dǒng Zhuó [Dǒng Zhuó] appointed Yáng [Yáng] as Jiànyì Jiāngjūn [Jiànyì Jiāngjūn] and Grand Administrator of Hénèi [Hénèi].
10 The Grand Astrologer [Tàishǐ] observed the *wàng qì* (auspicious vapors),
saying that a high official was destined to be executed;
Dǒng Zhuó [Dǒng Zhuó] sent someone to falsely accuse Wèi Wèi [Wèi Wèi] Zhāng Wēn [Zhāng Wēn] of communicating with Yuán Shù [Yuán Shù].
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day *rénxū [rénxū]*,
Wēn [Wēn] was flogged to death in the marketplace to fulfill the prophecy.
It is lamentable that Zhāng Wēn [Zhāng Wēn] was unable to execute Zhuó [Zhuó] during the Western Expedition [Xīzhēng] and instead died by Zhuó’s [Zhuó] hand.
11 The Qīngzhōu [Qīngzhōu] Yellow Turbans [Huángjīn] raided Bóhǎi [Bóhǎi],
numbering 300,000,
intending to join with the Black Mountain bandits.
Gōngsūn Zàn [Gōngsūn Zàn] led 20,000 infantry and cavalry to meet and attack them south of Dōngguāng [Dōngguāng],
severely defeating them.
Dōngguāng [Dōngguāng] County [xiàn]
belonged to Bóhǎi [Bóhǎi].
Xián [Xián] said: It is today’s Cāngzhōu [Cāngzhōu] County [xiàn].
The bandits abandoned their baggage train [zīzhòng]
and fled across the river;
Zàn [Zàn] attacked them while they were halfway across,
and the bandits were again severely defeated,
with tens of thousands killed,
so much blood that it made the water red.
It means the water became red.
The chariots, armor, and wealth were immeasurable,
and his prestige greatly spread.
12 Liú Yú’s [Liú Yú] son Hè [Hè] was a Shìzhōng [Shìzhōng].

Fàn’s [Fàn] book is mistaken.

When Yú [Yú] received the letter,

Gōngsūn Zàn [Gōngsūn Zàn] knew Shù [Shù] had other intentions,
and tried to stop him,
but Yú [Yú] did not listen.
Zàn [Zàn] feared Shù [Shù] would hear of this and resent him,

but secretly advised Shù [Shù] to seize Hè [Hè]

From this, a rift formed between Yú [Yú] and Zàn [Zàn].
There was already a rift between Yú [Yú] and Zàn [Zàn] before this,

Hè [Hè] was again detained by Yuán Shào [Yuán Shào].
At this time, the states and commanderies east of the passes [Guāndōng zhōu, jùn] were striving to annex each other to strengthen themselves,

and become estranged.
Shù [Shù] had sent Sūn Jiān [Sūn Jiān] to attack Dǒng Zhuó [Dǒng Zhuó] and he had not yet returned.
Shào [Shào] appointed Zhōu Áng [Zhōu Áng] of Kuàijī [Kuàijī] as the Inspector of Yùzhōu [Yùzhōu],

Yángchéng [Yángchéng] County [xiàn]
belonged to Yǐngchuān [Yǐngchuān] Commandery.
Jiān [Jiān], holding the title of Inspector of Yùzhōu [Yùzhōu],
was garrisoned at Yángchéng [Yángchéng].
“We raised a righteous army together,
intending to save the imperial altars [shèjì];
the rebel chief is almost defeated,
yet each acts like this.
With whom shall I exert my strength?!”
He led his troops to attack Áng [Áng]
and put him to flight.
Yuán Shù [Yuán Shù] sent Gōngsūn Yuè [Gōngsūn Yuè] to assist Jiān [Jiān] in attacking Áng [Áng],
and Yuè [Yuè] was struck and killed by a stray arrow.
Gōngsūn Zàn [Gōngsūn Zàn] angrily said:

So he mobilized his army and encamped at Pánhé [Pánhé].
The *Shuǐjīng* (Classic of Waterways) states: The old channel of the Great River [Dàhé] flows northeast past the old city north of Xīpíngchāng [Xīpíngchāng] County [xiàn],
branching off eastward into Bān [Bān] County [xiàn],
becoming the Bānhé [Bānhé].
I follow Xián’s [Xián] commentary;
*Bān [Bān]*,
pronunciation *bǔ mǎn fān*.
Here it is written as
"Pán [Pán]",
and should be read as such.
Xián [Xián] also said: Bān [Bān] is the Gōupánhé [Gōupánhé] of the Nine Rivers [Jiǔhé] mentioned in the *Ěryǎ [Ěryǎ]*.
Its dry riverbed is southeast of today's Lèlíng [Lèlíng] County [xiàn] in Cāngzhōu [Cāngzhōu].
The *Wèi Shōu Dìxíng Zhì* (Wei Shou's Treatise on Geography) states that Bān [Bān] County [xiàn] in Āndé [Āndé] Commandery had the old Bānhé [Bānhé].
He advanced his troops to attack Shào [Shào].
Many cities in Jìzhōu [Jìzhōu] rebelled against Shào [Shào] and sided with Zàn [Zàn].
Shào [Shào] was afraid,
and bestowed the seal and ribbon of the Grand Administrator of Bóhǎi [Bóhǎi] that he wore upon Zàn’s [Zàn] cousin Fàn [Fàn],
sending him to the commandery,
but Fàn [Fàn] subsequently betrayed Shào [Shào]
and commanded the Bóhǎi [Bóhǎi] troops to assist Zàn [Zàn].
Zàn [Zàn] then personally appointed his generals Yán Gāng [Yán Gāng] as Inspector of Jìzhōu [Jìzhōu],
Tián Kǎi [Tián Kǎi] as Inspector of Qīngzhōu [Qīngzhōu],
and Shàn Jīng [Shàn Jīng] as Inspector of Yǎnzhōu [Yǎnzhōu],

At first,
Liú Bèi from Zhuōjùn
was a descendant of King Jìng of Zhōngshān.
The Shǔ Book states: Bèi
was a descendant of Zhēn, Marquis of Lùchéngtíng, who was the son of Shèng, King Jìng of Zhōngshān.
However, his lineage from his grandfather upwards
cannot be verified.
With his mother, he made a living by selling straw sandals.
He was seven *chǐ* and five *cùn* tall,
with hands that hung down past his knees,
and he could see his own ears when he looked back.
He had great ambitions,
spoke little,
and did not show his emotions of joy or anger.
He once studied under Lú Zhí with Gōngsūn Zàn,
and because of this, he went to rely on Zàn.
Zàn sent Bèi with Tián Kǎi to pacify Qīngzhōu, where they achieved merit,
and he was thus made Administrator of Píngyuán.
From a young age, Bèi was close friends with Guān Yǔ from Hédōng and Zhāng Fēi from Zhuōjùn.
He appointed Yǔ and Fēi as Assistant Officers of Separate Commands,
giving them command over different units.
Bèi and the two of them slept in the same bed,
their affection like that of brothers,
yet in crowded places and large assemblies,
they would stand attending all day,
following Bèi everywhere,
fearless of hardship and danger.
Zhào Yún from Chángshān, as a commander of his home county, led troops to Gōngsūn Zàn.
Zàn said:
"I hear that all the people of your province wish to join the Yuán clan.
Those who wish to submit should have the character 'cóng' (follow) in their name."
Yún replied:
"The world is in turmoil,
and it is unclear who is right.
The people are in dire straits.
The discussion in my humble province is
to follow wherever benevolent governance resides.
It is not to disregard Yuán Gōng
or to privately favor the General."
Liú Bèi saw him and found him remarkable,
warmly receiving him.
Yún then followed Bèi to Píngyuán,
becoming Bèi's cavalry commander.
Liú Bèi's career began here.
13 At first,
when Yuán Shù obtained Nányáng,
it had a population of several million households.
But Shù was extravagant, wanton, and self-indulgent,
collecting taxes without restraint.
The common people suffered from this
and gradually dispersed.
Having already developed a rift with Yuán Shào,
each formed factions and sought allies to scheme against the other.
Shù allied with Gōngsūn Zàn, while Shào connected with Liú Biǎo.
Many heroes attached themselves to Shào.
Shù angrily said:
"These youngsters do not follow me, but follow my household slave!"
According to Yuán Shānsōng's book,
Shào
was the illegitimate son of Sīkōng Fèng,
and was adopted by his paternal uncle Chéng.
Thus, Shù said this.
"Shào is not a son of the Yuán clan."
Shào was furious when he heard this.
Shù sent Sūn Jiān to attack Liú Biǎo.
Biǎo dispatched his general Huáng Zǔ to meet them in battle between Fán and Dèng.
Dèng County
belonged to Nányáng Commandery.
Fánchéng
was the city of Zhōu Zhòngshān Fǔ,
north of the Hàn River.
Dù Yòu said: Fánchéng
is now Ānyǎng County of Xiāngzhōu.
Liú Xùn said: Dèngchéng County was
Dèng County of Hàn,
and the ancient Fánchéng. Sòng changed it to Ānyǎng County;
in the first year of Tiānbǎo it was changed to Línhàn County;
in the twenty-first year of Zhēnyuán, the county seat was moved to ancient Dèngchéng,
and it was then renamed Dèngchéng County.
Jiān then besieged Xiāngyáng.
Biǎo secretly sent Huáng Zǔ out at night to rally troops.
As Zǔ was leading his troops back,
Jiān intercepted and engaged him in battle.
Zǔ was defeated and fled,
hiding in Mt. Xiàn.
Mt. Xiàn is ten *lǐ* from Xiāngyáng.
Xiàn,
pronounced hù diǎn fān.
Jiān pursued Zǔ at night.
Zǔ's subordinate
soldiers ambushed Jiān from among the bamboo and trees,
killing him.
Huán Jiē of Chángshā, whom Jiān had recommended as a *xiàolián*, went to Biǎo to request Jiān's corpse.
Biǎo, out of righteousness, granted the request.
Jiān's nephew Bēn led his soldiers and followers to Yuán Shù.
Shù again appointed Bēn as Inspector of Yùzhōu.
Due to this, Shù was unable to defeat Biǎo.
14 At first,
when Dǒng Zhuó entered the pass,
he left Zhū Jùn to guard Luòyáng.
However, Jùn secretly conspired with the various generals east of the mountains.
Fearing an attack by Zhuó,
he fled to Jīngzhōu.
Zhuó appointed Yáng Yì of Hóngnóng as Administrator of Hénán.
Jùn then led his troops back to Luò,
attacked Yì,
and drove him away.
As Hénán was ravaged and had no resources,
Jùn then moved his garrison east to Zhōngmóu,
sending letters to the provinces and commanderies
requesting troops to punish Zhuó.
Táo Qiān, the Inspector of Xúzhōu, memorialized to appoint Jùn as acting General of Chariots and Cavalry,
sending three thousand elite troops to assist him.
Other provinces and commanderies also provided support.
Qiān was
a native of Dānyáng.
Dānyáng County
belonged to Dānyáng Commandery,
now a county in Rùnzhōu.
Qiān was appointed as Inspector.
When Qiān arrived,
he attacked the Yellow Turbans,
utterly defeating and routing them,
bringing peace to the provincial borders.
Initially,
Xún Shú (荀淑) had a grandson named Yù (彧).
From a young age, he possessed talent and a good reputation.
Hé Yóng (何顒) saw him and was greatly impressed,
saying,
"He is a talent fit to be a king's aide!"
When chaos erupted throughout the land,
Yù (彧) said to the elders of his clan,
"Yǐngchuān (潁川) is a land vulnerable on four sides."
This means its terrain is flat,
making it susceptible to attack from all directions.
"Many of our fellow villagers are attached to their homes and cannot bear to leave.
I alone will lead my clan to seek refuge with Hán Fù (韓馥)."
It so happened that Yuán Shào (袁紹) had already seized Fù's (馥) position,
and treated Yù (彧) with the courtesy due to an honored guest.
Yù (彧) judged that Shào (紹) would ultimately be unable to accomplish a great enterprise.
Hearing that Cáo Cāo (曹操) possessed great strategic ability,
he left Shào (紹) and followed Cāo (操).
When Cāo (操) conversed with him,
he was greatly pleased,
saying,
"He is my Zǐfáng (子房)!"
comparing him to Zhāng Liáng (張良).
Cāo (操), having just raised his army as General Fènwǔ (奮武),
therefore appointed Yù (彧) as Fènwǔ Sīmǎ (奮武司馬).
Many were killed by Guō Jué (傕), Fàn Sì (汜), and others.
3 Yuán Shào (袁紹) personally went out to resist Gōngsūn Zàn (公孫瓚),
and fought Zàn (瓚) twenty *lǐ* (里) south of Jièqiáo (界橋).
The *Shuǐ Jīng* (水經) says: "The right channel of the Great River flows northeast, passing south of the old city of Guǎngzōng (廣宗) county in Jùlù (鉅鹿) commandery,
then northeast, passing north of Jièchéng (界城) pavilion,
then northeast, passing east of the old city of Wǔqiáng (武強) county in Xìndū (信都) commandery."
This suggests a bridge was built over the river channel.
The commentary also says: "The Qīnghé (清河) river flows northeast, passing east of Jièchéng (界城) pavilion.
There is a great bridge over the water,
called Jièchéngqiáo (界城橋)."
Xián (賢) says: "Today, near Zōngchéng (宗城) county in Bèizhōu (貝州), there is an ancient Jièchéng (界城).
This city is near the dry Zhāngshuǐ (漳水) river.
Jièqiáo (界橋) must have been over this river."
Dù Yòu (杜佑) says: "Jièqiáo (界橋) is east of Zōngchéng (宗城) county in Bèizhōu (貝州)."
His vanguard was very sharp.
Shào (紹) ordered Qū Yì (麴義) to lead eight hundred elite soldiers as the vanguard,
supported by a thousand strong crossbows on either flank.
Zàn (瓚), underestimating their small numbers,
unleashed his cavalry to charge them.
Yì's (義) soldiers remained motionless, crouching under their shields.
When the cavalry was within ten-odd paces,
they all fired at once,
their shouts shaking the earth.
Zàn's (瓚) army was utterly defeated.
They beheaded Yán Gāng (嚴綱), his appointed Governor of Jìzhōu (冀州).
The *Kǎoyì* (考異) says: The *Jiǔzhōu Chūnqiū* (九州春秋) records
"Liú Gāng" (劉綱).
We follow the *Fàn Shū* (范書) and *Wèi Zhì* (魏志) here.
Pursued to Jièqiáo (界橋),
Zàn (瓚) regrouped his forces and fought again.
Yì (義) defeated him once more,
then advanced to Zàn's (瓚) camp
and pulled down his *yámén* (牙門).
Xián (賢) says: The *Zhēnrén Shuǐjìng Jīng* (真人水鏡經) says: "Whenever an army sets out,
it must be complete and firm;
if there is any breakage,
it is unfavorable for the general."
The *yámén* (牙門) flagstaff
is the essence of the army.
This is what the *Zhōu Lǐ* (周禮) says in the Sīzhí (司職) section:
"When military forces gather, a flag-gate is erected,"
which refers to this.
Initially,
Liú Dài (劉岱), the Governor of Yǎnzhōu (兗州), was allied with Shào (紹) and Zàn (瓚).
Shào (紹) had his wife and children reside with Dài (岱),
and Zàn (瓚) also sent his subordinate Fàn Fāng (范方) with cavalry to assist Dài (岱).
When Zàn (瓚) defeated Shào's (紹) army,
he told Dài (岱) to send Shào's (紹) wife and children away,
and separately instructed Fàn Fāng (范方):
"If Dài (岱) does not send Shào's (紹) family away,
return with your cavalry!
Once I have settled Shào (紹),
I will attack Dài (岱)."
Dài (岱) deliberated with his officials
for several days without reaching a decision.
Hearing that Chéng Yù (程昱) of Dōngjùn (東郡) possessed wisdom and strategy,
he summoned and questioned him.
Yù (昱) said,
"If you abandon the nearby aid of Shào (紹) and seek the distant help of Zàn (瓚),
this is like the saying of borrowing someone from Yuè (越) to save a drowning child."
This means the forces cannot reach each other.
The people of Yuè (越) are skilled in water,
hence they are thought capable of saving someone from drowning.
*Nì* (溺)
is pronounced *nuólì* (奴歷).
"Although Zàn (瓚) has now defeated Shào's (紹) army,
he will ultimately be captured by Shào (紹)."
Dài (岱) followed his advice.
Fàn Fāng (范方) returned with his cavalry,
but before he arrived, Zàn (瓚) was defeated.
4 Cáo Cāo's (曹操) army was stationed at Dùnqiū (頓丘).
Dùnqiū (頓丘) county
belonged to Dōngjùn (東郡).
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: "The county is named after the mound."
"A single mound forms a Dùnqiū (頓丘),
meaning it is formed in one heap."
Or it is said: "Chéng (成)
means 'heavy,'
so it is a single heavy mound."
Cāo (操) led his troops west into the mountains
to attack Dú (毒) and others' main encampment.
Dú (毒) and others were at that time plundering Wèijùn (魏郡),
encamped in the western mountains.
Cāo (操) said,
"If the bandits hear I am going west and return,
Wǔyáng (武陽) will relieve itself;
if they do not return,
I can defeat their main encampment,
and the bandits will certainly not be able to take Wǔyáng (武陽)."
So he proceeded.
Dú (毒) heard of this
and abandoned Wǔyáng (武陽) to return.
Cāo (操) then attacked Suī Gù (眭固) and the Xiongnú (匈奴) Yúfúluó (於扶羅) at Nèihuáng (內黃).
Nèihuáng (內黃) county belonged to Wèijùn (魏郡);
Chénliú (陳留) had Wàihuáng (外黃),
hence "Nèi" (內) was added.
*Suī* (眭)
is pronounced *xīsuí* (息隨).
5 Dǒng Zhuó (董卓) made his younger brother Mín (旻) Left General,
and his nephew Huáng (璜) Central Army Commandant.
Both commanded military affairs,
and his relatives, both inner and outer, were all arrayed in the imperial court.
Zhuó's (卓) concubines, even those holding infants in their arms, were all enfeoffed as marquises,
and given golden seals and purple ribbons to play with.
Zhuó's (卓) carriages and attire usurped those of the Son of Heaven.
He summoned the Sāntái (三臺).
Sāntái (三臺): the Secretariat (Shàngshūtái 尚書臺), the Censorate (Yùshǐtái 御史臺), and the Credential Office (Fújiétái 符節臺).
The *Jìn Shū* (晉書) says: "Han officials: The Secretariat (Shàngshū) was the Central Terrace (Zhōngtái 中臺),
the Censor (Yùshǐ) was the Constitutional Terrace (Xiàntái 憲臺),
and the Herald (Yèzhě) was the Outer Terrace (Wàitái 外臺);
these were called the Sāntái (三臺)."
He also built a stronghold in Méi (郿).
The *Yīngxióng Jì* (英雄記) says: Méi (郿) is two hundred sixty *lǐ* (里) from Cháng'ān (長安).
The *Hàn Shū* (漢書):
Méi (郿),
pronounced *méi* (媚),
a place name.
He accumulated enough grain for thirty years' storage,
saying himself,
"If I succeed,
I will dominate the world;
if not,
guarding this will be enough to live out my old age."
Zhuó (卓) was ruthless in executions.
If any generals made a slip in their words,
they were immediately executed before him,
and people could not live in peace.
Sītú (司徒) Wáng Yǔn (王允), together with Sīlì Xiàowèi (司隸校尉) Huáng Wǎn (黃琬), Púyè (僕射) Shìsūn Ruì (士孫瑞), and Shàngshū (尚書) Yáng Zàn (楊瓚), secretly plotted to execute Zhuó (卓).
Zhōnglángjiàng (中郎將) Lǚ Bù (呂布)
was skilled with bow and horse,
and possessed extraordinary physical strength.
*Lǚ* (膂) means the backbone.
Zhuó (卓) always kept Bù (布) as his personal guard when moving about,
and trusted him greatly,
swearing to be father and son.
However, Zhuó's (卓) nature was rigid and narrow-minded.
Once, Bù (布) slightly displeased Zhuó (卓),
and Zhuó (卓) pulled out a hand-halberd and threw it at Bù (布).
A hand-halberd (shǒujǐ 手戟)
is a small halberd,
convenient for striking and stabbing.
"Courageous strength" is *quán* (拳),
"swift and rapid" is *jié* (捷).
Bù (布) quickly changed his expression and apologized,
and Zhuó's (卓) anger also subsided.
Because of this, Bù (布) secretly resented Zhuó (卓).
Zhuó (卓) also made Bù (布) guard the inner chambers,
but privately committed adultery with Bù's (布) maidservant,
making Bù (布) feel even more insecure.
Wáng Yǔn (王允) had always treated Bù (布) well.
When Bù (布) saw Yǔn (允),
he recounted how Zhuó (卓) had almost killed him.
Yǔn (允) then revealed his plot to execute Zhuó (卓) to Bù (布),
and had him act as an inside accomplice.
Bù (布) said,
"What about our father-son relationship?"
Yǔn (允) replied,
"Your surname is Lǚ (呂);
you are not his biological kin.
Now you are worried about death and have no time for other thoughts.
What 'father-son relationship' is there to speak of?
At the moment he threw the halberd,
was there any father-son affection?!"
Bù (布) then agreed.
In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the dìnsì day,
the Emperor, having recently recovered from an illness,
held a grand assembly in the Wèiyāng Diàn.
Dǒng Zhuó, dressed in court attire, entered by carriage.
Wèi’s Mìshūjiān, Qín Jìng, said: "The Hàn dynasty, following the Qín, changed the system of six crowns;
for court attire, it was merely a dark cap and a crimson robe.
The Jìn dynasty called it the 'Five Seasons Court Attire.'
There was also the 'Four Seasons Court Attire,'
and then simply 'Court Attire.'
From the camp to the palace,
with infantry on the left and cavalry on the right,
the garrisons circled,
and Lǚ Bù and others were ordered to guard the front and rear."
Wáng Yǔn had Shìsūn Ruì personally write an imperial edict to give to Lǚ Bù.
The reason for having the Shàngshū Púyè personally write the edict
was fear of its leakage.
The Kǎoyì states: "Yuán Jì wrote
'Lǐ Shùn,'
but now we follow Fàn Shū and Wèi Zhì."
Shǒu Běi Yèmén was kept closed to await Dǒng Zhuó.
When Dǒng Zhuó entered the gate,
Sù stabbed him with a halberd;
Dǒng Zhuó was wearing inner armor,
so it did not penetrate.
“Zhōngjiǎ” means
wearing armor underneath,
with clothing on top of the armor.
He fell from his carriage
and looked back, shouting loudly:
“Lǚ Bù, where are you?!”
Lǚ Bù said:
“There is an imperial edict to punish the traitorous minister!”
Dǒng Zhuó cursed loudly:
“You useless dog!
How dare you do this?!”
Lǚ Bù immediately responded by holding a spear and stabbing Dǒng Zhuó,
then quickly ordered soldiers to behead him.
The Chief Clerk Tián Yí and Dǒng Zhuó’s former "warehouse heads" rushed to his body;
Lǚ Bù also killed them,
making a total of three people killed.
Lǚ Bù then pulled out the imperial edict tablet from his bosom and announced to the officers and soldiers:
“The edict is only to punish Dǒng Zhuó;
all others will not be questioned.”
The officers and soldiers all stood still and upright,
shouting “Long live!”
The common people sang and danced in the streets,
and the gentlemen and women in Cháng’ān sold their pearls, jade, and clothing to buy wine and meat to celebrate,
filling the streets and markets.
His brother Mín, Huáng, and others, as well as his clan’s old and young in Méi,
were all hacked and shot to death by his former retainers.
Dǒng Zhuó’s corpse was exposed in the market.
The weather was just beginning to get hot,
and Dǒng Zhuó was naturally corpulent;
his fat flowed onto the ground.
The officers guarding the corpse used it to make large wicks,
“zhù” means
lamp,
that which holds the ember.
The light illuminated until dawn,
continuing for several days like this.
Yuán’s retainers collected Dǒng’s corpse,
burned it to ashes, and scattered them on the road.
In his stronghold, there were two or three tens of thousands of catties of gold,
eight or nine tens of thousands of catties of silver,
and brocades, silks, and rare curiosities piled up like hills.
Wáng Yǔn was appointed Lù Shàngshū Shì (Recorder of Affairs of the Secretariat),
and Lǚ Bù was made Fènwēi Jiāngjūn, Jǐajié, and accorded status equal to the Sān Sī.
The title Fènwēi Jiāngjūn first appeared in the Hàn Yuándì era, when Rèn Qiānqiū was appointed to it.
Shěn Yuè said: “Lǚ Bù was Fènwǔ Jiāngjūn, accorded status equal to the Sān Sī,
which is similar to Yítóng Sān Sī.”
Wēn Xiàn
belonged to Hénèi Jùn,
it was the fief of Zhōu Grandee Sū Fènshēng.
When Dǒng Zhuó died,
Cài Yōng, the Zuǒ Zhōnglángjiàng and Gāoyáng Hóu, was sitting with Wáng Yǔn.
Gāoyáng Xiàn
belonged to Zhuó Jùn;
there was also a Gāoyáng Tíng in Chénlíu’s Yǔ Xiàn.
“Zuò”
is pronounced “cú wò fān.”
Wáng Yǔn flared up
and rebuked him, saying:
“Dǒng Zhuó was a great villain of the state,
who nearly destroyed the Hàn dynasty.
As a minister of the King,
you should have shared in the common hatred,
yet you harbor private gratitude for his treatment,
and instead mourn him.
Are you not complicit in his rebellion?!”
He immediately had him arrested and handed over to the Tíngwèi.
Cài Yōng apologized, saying:
“Though I may be disloyal,
the great principles of antiquity and the present,
which I am accustomed to hearing
and often recite,
would I ever turn my back on the state and align myself with Dǒng Zhuó?
I beg to have my head tattooed and my feet amputated,
so that I may continue to compile the Hàn History.”
Originally,
Cài Yōng was exiled to Shuòfāng.
From his exile, he submitted a memorial,
pleading to continue the treatises of the Hàn History.
This was presumably where his studies and aspirations lay.
He was unable to achieve it.
Tàiwèi Mǎ Rìdī said to Wáng Yǔn:
“Bójiē is a rare talent, appearing once in a generation.
Cài Yōng’s courtesy name was Bójiē.
He should continue to complete the later history,
making it a great canon for an era.
His offense is so minor;
to execute him,
would it not disappoint public expectation?”
Wáng Yǔn said:
“In the past, Wǔdì did not kill Sīmǎ Qiān,
which allowed him to write slanderous books that circulated in later generations.
Xián said: ‘All historians must record both good and evil.
It means that what Sīmǎ Qiān recorded was only the unpleasant affairs of the Hàn imperial family,
all of which were considered slander.
This does not solely refer to Emperor Wǔ himself,
but also matters like Gāozǔ’s praise for the family steward,
and Wǔdì’s tax on wealth and monopoly on liquor, and so on.’
Bān Gù’s collected works state: ‘Sīmǎ Qiān wrote a book, establishing his own school of thought,
even to the point of suffering mutilation.
Therefore, he subtly satirized and criticized,
denigrating the contemporary era,
which is not the act of a righteous scholar.
With warhorses on the outskirts,
we cannot allow a flattering minister to hold the brush beside the young emperor,
as it would neither benefit the sagely virtue
nor prevent our party from being slandered and criticized.”
Mǎ Rìdī withdrew and told others:
“Will Wáng Gōng have no descendants?!
Good people are the pillars of the state;
literary works are the canons of the state.
To destroy the pillars and abolish the canons,
how can one last long?!”
Cài Yōng subsequently died in prison.
Originally,
Huángmén Shìláng Xún Yōu, along with Shàngshū Zhèng Tài and Shìzhōng Zhǒng Jí, conspired, saying:
“Dǒng Zhuó is arrogant, cruel, and without affection.
Although he commands strong troops,
he is truly but a single common man.
He can be directly assassinated.”
The plot was almost complete when it was discovered.
Xún Yōu was arrested and imprisoned,
while Zhèng Tài fled to Yuán Shù.
Xún Yōu’s speech and appetite remained normal.
When Dǒng Zhuó died,
he was released.
The Qīngzhōu Yellow Turbans raided Yǎnxzhōu.
Liú Dài wished to attack them.
Jìběi Xiàng Bāo Xìn advised:
“Now the bandit multitude numbers a million;
the common people are all terrified,
and the soldiers have no will to fight.
They cannot be resisted directly.
However, the bandit army lacks baggage trains,
relying solely on plunder for supplies.
It would be better now to conserve the strength of our troops
and first establish a strong defense.
If they wish to fight but cannot,
and attack but are unable,
their forces will surely disperse.
Then, we can select our elite forces,
occupy strategic points, and attack them,
and they can be defeated.”
Liú Dài did not heed him,
and consequently engaged in battle,
and was indeed killed by them.
Cáo Cāo's general of Dōngjùn, Chén Gōng, said to Cāo:
"The province now has no master,
and the royal mandate is cut off.
I request to persuade the provincial disciplinary officials.
'Disciplinary officials'
refers to the provincial Assistant Inspector (biéjià) and Chief Secretary (zhìzhōng) and other officers.
'Suì' (說),
pronounced shū ruì (輸芮) (fanqie);
same below.
'Mù zhī' (牧之)
means to be made the provincial Inspector (mù).
This is the enterprise of a hegemon."
Gōng then went to persuade the Assistant Inspector and Chief Secretary, saying:
"Today the empire is fractured and the province has no master.
Cáo of Dōngjùn
is a talent destined to emerge.
If we welcome him to govern the province,
he will surely bring peace to the people."
Bào Xìn and others also thought so,
and so with provincial officials Wàn Qián and others, they went to Dōngjùn
to welcome Cāo to assume the post of Yǎnzhōu Inspector (cìshǐ).
Cāo then advanced his troops to attack the Yellow Turbans east of Shòuzhāng,
but was unsuccessful.
The bandits were fierce and strong,
while Cāo's troops were few and weak.
Cāo soothed and encouraged them,
clearly setting out rewards and punishments,
seizing opportunities to deploy surprise tactics,
fighting day and night.
In every battle, they captured enemies,
and the bandits eventually retreated.
Bào Xìn died in battle.
Cāo offered a reward to find his body but could not.
So he carved wood in Xìn's likeness,
offered sacrifices, and wept for him.
An imperial edict appointed Jīngzhào Jīn Shàng as Yǎnzhōu Inspector.
When Shàng led his division there,
Cāo counter-attacked him,
and Shàng fled to Yuán Shù.
This sets the stage for Shàng's refusal to yield to Shù in the second year of Jiàn'ān.
7 Fifth month.
Kǎoyì says: Fànshū states,
"On the dìngyǒu day,
a general amnesty was declared."
Yuán Jì states,
"On the dìngwèi day,
a general amnesty was declared."
According to this, in the first month of this year,
on the dīngchǒu day,
a general amnesty was declared.
And when Lǐ Què sought an amnesty,
Wáng Yùn said:
"There cannot be two amnesties in one year."
Therefore, there certainly could not have been an amnesty in the fifth month.
8 Initially,
Lǚ Bù urged Wáng Yùn to execute all of Dǒng Zhuó's retainers.
Yùn said:
"These people are innocent;
it is not permissible."
Bù wished to distribute Zhuó's wealth and goods to the grandees and generals.
Yùn again did not agree.
Yùn had always treated Bù as a mere swordsman.
Bù, confident in his achievements,
often boasted about himself.
Having lost his expectations,
he gradually felt resentful.
Yùn's nature was resolute and he detested evil.
Initially, fearing Dǒng Zhuó,
he had humbled himself before him.
Once Zhuó was exterminated,
he believed he had no more troubles,
and became rather arrogant.
Because of this, his subordinates did not become very attached to him.
Yùn first discussed with Shìsūn Ruì
specifically issuing an edict to pardon Zhuó's retainers.
But then he had doubts, saying:
"Retainers merely follow their master.
If we now brand them as wicked and then pardon them,
I fear it will only make them deeply suspicious of us,
which is not the way to appease them."
So he stopped.
He also discussed completely disbanding their armies.
Someone persuaded Yùn, saying:
"The people of Liángzhōu have always feared the Yuán clan and the Guāndōng region.
If we suddenly disband their troops and open the passes,
everyone will surely feel insecure.
We could appoint Huángfǔ Yìzhēn as a general,
have him take command of their forces,
and then keep them in Shǎn to pacify them."
Yùn said:
"No.
Those in Guāndōng who raised righteous armies
are all our allies.
If we now occupy strategic passes and garrison Shǎn,
although it would secure Liángzhōu,
it would create suspicion in the hearts of Guāndōng.
This cannot be done."
At that time, the common people spread rumors that all people from Liángzhōu would be executed.
Zhuó's former generals and officers then became mutually terrified,
and all held onto their troops to defend themselves,
saying to each other:
"Cài Bójiē was merely close to Duke Dǒng and still suffered implication;
now that they have not pardoned us and wish us to disband our troops,
if we disband our troops today,
tomorrow we will again be treated as fish and meat."
Lǚ Bù sent Lǐ Sù to Shǎn
with an imperial edict to execute Niú Fǔ.
Fǔ and others fought back against Sù,
Sù was defeated
and fled to Hóngnóng.
Bù executed him.
Fǔ was timid and lost control.
It happened that the camp was alarmed for no reason.
Fǔ wanted to flee,
but was killed by his attendants.
Lǐ Què and others returned.
Què and others returned from Chénliú and Yǐngchuān.
Què and others had no one to rely on.
They sent envoys to Cháng'ān to seek a pardon.
Wáng Yùn said:
"An amnesty cannot be granted twice in one year."
He did not permit it.
Què and others became even more frightened
and did not know what to do.
They wished to disperse and
covertly return to their hometowns.
The Colonel Who Suppresses Barbarians (Tǎolǔ Xiàowèi), Jiǎ Xǔ of Wǔwēi, said:
"If you gentlemen abandon your armies and go alone,
then even a single head of a courier station can tie you up.
It is better to lead your forces westward
to attack Cháng'ān
and avenge Duke Dǒng.
If the enterprise succeeds,
we will uphold the state to rectify the empire.
If it does not go as planned,
'bùhé' (不合)
means the enterprise does not succeed,
not aligning with the original plan.
Què and others agreed with him.
So they formed an alliance
and led several thousand troops,
traveling westward day and night.
Wáng Yùn, seeing Hú Wéncái and Yáng Zhěngxiū were both prominent figures from Liángzhōu,
Xián says: 'Dàrén' (大人)
refers to powerful and wealthy families.
It also says: 'Dàrén' (大人)
is a term of respect for elders,
meaning to show reverence.
He explained to them,
without offering a warm countenance,
saying:
"Guāndōng rats!
What do you want to do?
You go summon them!"
So the two went,
but in reality, they gathered troops and returned.
Què collected troops along the way.
By the time they reached Cháng'ān,
they already numbered over a hundred thousand.
Together with Zhuó's former retainers Fán Chóu, Lǐ Méng, and others, they surrounded Cháng'ān City.
The city walls were high and difficult to attack,
so they besieged it for eight days.
Kǎoyì says: Wèizhì says ten days.
Now following Fànshū.
Xián says: 'Sōubīng' (叟兵) refers to Shǔ soldiers.
The Hàn dynasty called Shǔ 'Sōu' (叟).
On the wùwǔ day,
Què's forces were led into the city,
and the soldiers were let loose to plunder.
Bù fought within the city but
was defeated.
He took several hundred cavalrymen, tied Zhuó's head to his saddle, and fled out of the city.
He halted his horse outside the Qīngsuǒ Gate.
Wèi Guàn says: Qīngsuǒ
refers to the blue carvings by the door.
Another says: Inside the Son of Heaven's gate, there are two layers of brow-bars,
the inner one painted blue is called suǒ.
Yùn said:
"If, by the grace of the altars of earth and grain,
the state can be made secure,
that is my wish.
If that cannot be achieved,
then I will sacrifice myself and die for it.
The imperial court is young and vulnerable,
'cháotíng' (朝廷)
refers to the Son of Heaven.
To save myself by fleeing in a time of crisis,
I cannot bear.
Strive to express my gratitude to the various dukes of Guāndōng,
and diligently keep the state in your thoughts!"
The Grand Minister of Ceremonies (Tàicháng), Zhǒng Fú, said:
"As a great minister of the state,
I cannot suppress violence and resist insult,
allowing blades to be pointed at the palace.
Where would I go if I were to leave?"
Thereupon he fought and died.
Jué and Sì were encamped at the Nángōng Yèmén.
They killed Tàipú Lǔ Kuí,
Dàhónglú Zhōu Huàn,
Chéngmén Xiàowèi Cuī Liè, and Yuèqí Xiàowèi Wáng Qí.
Over ten thousand officials and common people died,
their bodies scattered across the roads.
Wáng Yǔn helped the Emperor ascend the Xuānpíngmén to avoid the soldiers.
The Sānfǔ Huángtú states: "The northernmost gate on the east side of Cháng'ān city was called Xuānpíngmén."
"Shàng,"
a variant of "zhǎng fān."
The Emperor said to Jué and the others:
"You and your soldiers are running amok;
what do you intend to do?"
Jué and the others replied:
"Dǒng Zhuó was loyal to Your Majesty,
yet was causelessly killed by Lǚ Bù.
Your servants are avenging Zhuó;
we dare not be rebellious.
We request to report to the Tíngwèi to receive punishment once our task is complete."
Jué and the others surrounded the gate tower
and jointly submitted a memorial requesting Sītú Wáng Yǔn to come out,
asking,
"What was Grand Preceptor Dǒng Zhuó's crime?"
Yǔn, cornered and desperate,
then descended to meet them.
On the day Jǐwèi,
a general amnesty was declared throughout the realm.
Lǐ Jué was appointed Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn,
and Guō Sì was appointed Yángliè Jiāngjūn.
The title Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn began in the early Jiànwǔ era,
with Mǎ Chéng holding it.
The title Yángliè Jiāngjūn probably began at this time.
Jué and the others apprehended Sīlì Xiàowèi Huáng Wǎn
and killed
him.
Earlier,
Wáng Yǔn had appointed Sòng Yì, from the same commandery, as Zuǒ Fēngyì,
and Wáng Hóng as Yòu Fúfēng.
Yǔn was
a Tàiyuán native.
Fearing trouble from the two commanderies,
he first summoned Yì and Hóng.
Hóng sent an envoy to Yì, saying:
"Guō Sì and Lǐ Jué have not yet harmed Lord Wáng because we two are outside.
'Wēi'
means 'to kill.'
Tomorrow, our clans will all be exterminated.
What plan shall we devise?"
Yì said:
"Although fortune and misfortune are hard to predict,
a royal command
cannot be evaded!"
Hóng said:
"The righteous armies east of the pass are in an uproar,
wanting to punish Dǒng Zhuó.
Now that Zhuó is dead,
his partisans are easy to control.
If we raise an army to attack Jué and the others,
and respond to those in Shāndōng,
this would be a plan to turn disaster into fortune."
Yì did not comply,
and Hóng could not act alone,
so they both proceeded to the summons.
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
Jué apprehended Yǔn, Yì, and Hóng,
and killed them all;
Yǔn's wife and children all died.
As Hóng faced death, he reviled,
"Sòng Yì is an insignificant pedant,
unfit to discuss grand plans!"
Xián said: "Shù"
refers
to being lowly and inferior, like a page boy.
No one dared to collect his body,
but his former subordinate, Zhào Jiǎn, the Magistrate of Pínglíng from Jīngzhào, abandoned his office, collected his body, and buried it.
Initially,
Yǔn monopolized the credit for Dǒng Zhuó's extermination.
Shìsūn Ruì attributed his merits to others and did not seek enfeoffment,
thus he was spared from the disaster.
Your servant Guāng says: The Yìjīng states,
"A modest gentleman who has rendered service will have good fortune in the end."
The Yìjīng Xì Cí states: "To labor without boasting,
to have achievements without flaunting virtue,
is the height of generosity."
It speaks of one who places himself below others despite his accomplishments.
"Dé" speaks of abundance,
"lǐ" speaks of reverence.
"Qiān" [modesty]
is to maintain one's position with reverence.
Chéng Yí's commentary states: "One who has rendered service and can be modest,
and moreover acts as a gentleman,
will have good fortune in the end."
Indeed, to delight in being superior and to revel in victory
is human nature.
To be modest in peaceful times
is already rare,
let alone when one has venerable accomplishments!
Even if one knows the virtue of modesty
and strives to practice it,
if the heart of arrogance and conceit is not forgotten,
then it cannot last long,
and one cannot achieve "good fortune in the end."
Only a gentleman can comfortably maintain modesty and compliance,
and thus remain unchanged over time;
this is what is meant by "good fortune in the end."
To preserve oneself in this way,
can it not be called wisdom?
9 Jué and the others made Jiǎ Xǔ Zuǒ Fēngyì
and wanted to enfeoff him.
Xǔ said:
"This was a plan to save our lives;
what merit is there?"
He firmly declined.
They then offered him the position of Shàngshū Púyè.
Xǔ said:
"The Shàngshū Púyè is the chief of officials,
on whom the whole realm relies.
My reputation is not renowned,
which is not how one commands people's respect."
So they made him Shàngshū.
10Lǚ Bù fled from Wǔguān to Nányáng.
Yuán Shù treated him very generously.
Bù, presuming his service to the Yuán clan,
believed that killing Dǒng Zhuó was avenging the Yuán clan.
Shù became troubled by him,
and Bù felt uneasy,
so he left to join Zhāng Yáng in Hénèi.
Lǐ Jué and others urgently sought to apprehend Bù,
so Bù again fled back to Yuán Shào.
11On the day Bǐngzǐ,
Zhào Qiān, formerly a General, was made Sītú.
13Autumn,
seventh month,
on the day Gēngzǐ,
Tàiwèi Mǎ Rìdī was made Tàifù
and Lù Shàngshū Shì.
In the eighth month,
Chējì Jiāngjūn Huángfǔ Sōng was made Tàiwèi.
14An imperial edict ordered Tàifù Mǎ Rìdī and Tàipú Zhào Qí, bearing insignia, to pacify and settle the region east of the pass.
15Ninth month,
Lǐ Jué was made Chējì Jiāngjūn,
acting Sīlì Xiàowèi, and granted imperial authority (Jiǎjié);
Guō Sì was made Hòujiāngjūn,
Fán Chóu was made Yòujiāngjūn,
and Zhāng Jì was made Piàojì Jiāngjūn.
All were enfeoffed as marquises.
Jué, Sì, and Chóu controlled court affairs.
"Guǎn"
is synonymous with "guǎn."
16Sītú Zhào Qiān was dismissed.
17On the day Jiǎshēn,
Sīkōng Chúnyú Jiā was made Sītú,
and Guānglù Dàfū Yáng Biāo was made Sīkōng
and Lù Shàngshū Shì.
18Earlier,
when Dǒng Zhuó entered the pass,
he persuaded Hán Suì and Mǎ Téng to jointly plan against Shāndōng.
Suì and Téng led their forces to Cháng'ān.
Coincidentally, Zhuó died,
so Lǐ Jué and others made Suì Zhènxī Jiāngjūn
and sent him back to Jīnchéng;
Téng was made Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn
and sent to garrison Méi.
The Jìn Shū Zhígūan Zhì states: "The Four Generals of the Expedition (Sìzhēng) originated in the Han dynasty,
while the Four Generals of the Garrisons (Sìzhèn) were for pacifying distant regions."
19Winter,
tenth month.
Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ Liú Biǎo sent envoys with tribute.
Biǎo was appointed Zhènnán Jiāngjūn, Jīngzhōu Mù,
and enfeoffed as Chéngwǔ Hóu.
Chéngwǔ county
belonged to Shānyáng Commandery in the Former Han,
and to Jìyīn Commandery in the Later Han.
20Twelfth month,
Tàiwèi Huángfǔ Sōng was dismissed.
Guānglù Dàfū Zhōu Zhōng was made Tàiwèi
and Cān Lù Shàngshū Shì.
21Cáo Cāo pursued the Yellow Turbans to Jìběi
and completely subdued them.
He gained over 300,000 soldiers
and over a million men, women, and children.
He selected the elite among them
and called them the Qīngzhōu Troops.
Those who surrendered were the Yellow Turbans of Qīngzhōu,
hence they were called the Qīngzhōu Troops.
Cáo Cāo appointed Máo Jiè of Chénliú as Zhìzhōng Cóngshì.
Máo Jiè said to Cáo Cāo:
"Today, the world is in chaos and disintegration.
The imperial carriage is adrift.
The common people have abandoned their livelihoods.
Famine, starvation, and displacement are rampant.
The government has no reserves for even a year,
and the common people have no desire for peace and stability.
It is difficult to last long.
Those who fight righteously are victorious."
Wèi Xiàng once cited this saying.
The Yì Dàzhuàn says: "What gathers people?
Wealth.
What maintains a position?
Benevolence."
Cultivating farming and planting to accumulate military provisions
is how Cáo Cāo eliminated the warlords.
It lay in welcoming the Son of Heaven to the capital at Xǔ and establishing military colonies to accumulate grain, and that is all.
Máo Jiè initiated the strategy for these two matters.
Then the hegemonic enterprise can be achieved."
Cáo Cāo adopted his words
and sent an envoy to Zhāng Yáng, the Grand Administrator of Hénèi,
wanting to borrow a route to the west to Cháng'ān;
Zhāng Yáng did not agree.
Dǒng Zhāo of Dìngtáo persuaded Zhāng Yáng, saying:
"Though Yuán and Cáo are considered one family,
their power will not last long.
Although Cáo Cāo is now weak,
he is truly a hero of the world;
you should deliberately ally with him.
'Deliberately' [Gù 故]
refers to the reason for forming an alliance,
meaning to ally based on circumstances.
It is advisable to transmit his reports to the court
and simultaneously submit a memorial recommending him.
If the matter succeeds,
it will become a deep bond forever."
Zhāng Yáng then transmitted Cáo Cāo's reports
and thereupon submitted a memorial recommending Cáo Cāo.
Dǒng Zhāo wrote letters for Cáo Cāo to Lǐ Jué, Guō Sì, and others,
expressing sincere regards with varying degrees of emphasis.
When Lǐ Jué and Guō Sì saw Cáo Cāo's envoy,
they thought the lords east of the pass wanted to establish their own Son of Heaven,
and that although Cáo Cāo had an envoy,
he was not sincere;
they discussed detaining Cáo Cāo's envoy.
Huángmén Shìláng Zhōng Yáo persuaded Lǐ Jué and Guō Sì, saying:
"Currently, heroes are rising simultaneously,
each forging decrees and acting autocratically.
Only Cáo Yǎnzhōu is truly loyal to the imperial house.
To reject his loyal intentions
is not the way to fulfill the hopes for the future!"
Lǐ Jué and Guō Sì then gave a generous reply.
At this time,
Dǒng Zhāo was in Hénèi,
and Zhōng Yáo was in Cháng'ān.
Cáo Cāo could not employ them,
yet each of them paved the way for Cáo Cāo.
They probably heard of his heroic strategy
and preemptively served him to forge a connection.
He was the great-grandson of Zhōng Hào.
The account of Zhōng Hào is found in volume 53, under the third year of Jiànhé of Emperor Huán.
Xúzhōu Cìshǐ Táo Qiān and various administrators and chancellors jointly submitted a memorial,
promoting Zhū Jùn to Tàishī,
and thereupon dispatched a manifesto to the provincial governors,
intending to jointly attack Lǐ Jué and others
and welcome the Son of Heaven.
Coincidentally, Lǐ Jué, using the counsel of Tàiwèi Zhōu Zhōng and Shàngshū Jiǎ Xǔ,
summoned Zhū Jùn to court.
Zhū Jùn then declined Táo Qiān's proposal and accepted the summons,
again becoming Tàipú.
Gōngsūn Zàn again sent troops to attack Yuán Shào,
reaching Lóngcòu.
Lóngcòu
is a place name
in Píngyuán Commandery.
The Hàn Jìn Chūnqiū records a letter from Yuán Shào to Gōngsūn Zàn, saying:
"At the Lónghé crossing,
your weary troops were sent forward as bait.
Before the main army could cross,
your courage broke and your forces scattered,
defeated without a drumbeat."
So Lóngcòu was probably a river ford.
Upon careful consideration of Shào's letter,

The Emperor sent envoys to mediate,
but he did not comply.
Hán Suí led his forces to mediate between Téng and Jué;
subsequently, he re-allied with Téng.
Suí knew that Jué was not someone to be allied with.
Fù (復),
pronounced 'fú yòu'.
He acted as an internal confederate
to eliminate Jué and others.
On the day Rénshēn,
Téng and Suí led troops to garrison at Chángpíngguān.
The plot of Shào and others was exposed;
they fled to Huáilǐ.
Jué dispatched Fán Chóu, Guō Sì, and his nephew Lì to attack them.
Téng and Suí were defeated and fled,
returning to Liángzhōu.
Huáilǐ was also attacked,
and Shào and others all died.
On the day Gēngshēn,
an edict pardoned Téng and others.
Jué and others were unable to subdue Téng by force,
so they consequently issued an edict to pardon him.
In the fourth month,
Téng was appointed General Āndí,
and Suí was appointed General Ānjiàng.
These two general titles
were temporarily established at that time only;
they were not re-established in later generations.
Jiàng (降),
pronounced 'hù jiāng'.
6 Cáo Cāo sent his Sīmǎ, Xún Yù, and the Magistrate of Shòuzhāng, Chéng Yù, to guard Zhēnchéng.
Zhēnchéng County
belonged to Jìyīn Commandery.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: 'The former seat of Yǎnzhōu.'
Wèi Wǔ's founding of his enterprise began here.
It was a city on the Yellow River,
and extremely strong and fortified.
Zhēn (甄)
should be written as
'Jùan' (鄄).
The Supplement to the Book of Hàn Records: 'The Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ had his seat in Chāngyì.'
Sòng Bái said: 'Emperor Xiàn of Hàn established Yǎnzhōu in Jùanchéng.'
Cáo Cāo probably began his administration as Cìshǐ here.
Then he seized territory as far as Lángyá and Dōnghǎi,
destroying everything in his path.
Upon returning, he defeated Liú Bèi east of Tán.
Qiān was afraid
and wished to flee back to Dānyáng.
Qiān was a native of Dānyáng.
Cāo then withdrew his army.
Previously,
Zhāng Miǎo, when he was young,
enjoyed chivalry,
and Yuán Shào and Cáo Cāo were both on good terms with him.
When Shào became the Alliance Head,
he displayed arrogance.
The matter of the Alliance Head
is found in Volume 59, Chūpíng first year.
Shào was angered
and ordered Cāo to kill him.
Cāo did not obey,
saying:
"Mèngzhuó
is a close friend.
One should tolerate right and wrong from such a person.
The empire is not yet settled;
how can we endanger each other?"
Cāo's previous attack on Táo Qiān
is found in the previous volume, previous year.
He instructed his family, saying:
"If I do not return,
go and rely on Mèngzhuó."
Later, when he returned and saw Miǎo,
they wept together.
Qì (泣)
means to shed tears.
Gāo Róu of Chénliú said to his fellow villagers:
"Although General Cáo occupies Yǎnzhōu,
he originally has plans for the four directions,
and cannot sit securely and defend it.
However, Prefect Zhāng relies on the resources of Chénliú
and will take the opportunity to cause trouble.
What do you think about us avoiding him?"
The people all considered Cáo and Zhāng to be close,
and Róu was also young,
so they did not believe his words.
Róu's elder cousin Gàn called Róu from north of the Yellow River.
Róu took his entire clan and followed him.
Gāo Gàn was with Yuán Shào north of the Yellow River.
When Lǚ Bù left Yuán Shào to join Zhāng Yáng,
the events are detailed in the previous volume, same year.
At their parting,
they clasped hands and swore an oath.
Shào heard of this,
and greatly resented it, fearing that Cáo Cāo would eventually kill him,
and his heart was not at ease.
The former Grand Administrator of Jiǔjiāng, Biān Ràng of Chénliú, had once criticized and debated Cáo Cāo.
Cāo heard of it and killed him,
along with his wife and children.
Ràng had always had talent and renown,
and because of this, the literati and officials of Yǎnzhōu all became fearful.
Chén Gōng, being firm, upright, and valorous by nature,
also became suspicious inwardly.
So he conspired to rebel against Cáo Cāo with his Staff Officer, Xǔ Sì, Wáng Kǎi, and [Cáo] Mǎo’s younger brother Chāo.
Gōng persuaded Mǎo, saying:
"Today the world is in turmoil,
heroes are rising in unison.
You, with a multitude of a thousand *li*,
occupy a strategically vital territory,
brandishing your sword and looking around,
you are indeed a mighty hero.
Yet you are controlled by others,
is this not contemptible?
Now the provincial army is campaigning in the east,
meaning Cáo Cāo’s army is campaigning in Xúzhōu.
Lǚ Bù is a valiant warrior,
skillful in battle and unsurpassed.
If you were to temporarily welcome him,
and together govern Yǎnzhōu,
observe the world’s situation,
and await the changes of the times,
this would also be a moment for expansion and maneuvering."
Mǎo agreed.
At that time, Cáo Cāo had dispatched Gōng to lead troops and garrison Dōngjùn.
Gōng then secretly welcomed Lǚ Bù with his forces to become the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu.
When Bù arrived,
Mǎo sent his partisan Liú Yì to inform Xún Yù, saying:
"General Lǚ has come to assist Commander Cáo in attacking Táo Qiān.
It is proper to quickly supply his army with provisions."
The multitude was suspicious.
Yù knew Mǎo was causing trouble,
and immediately marshaled troops and prepared defenses.
He urgently summoned Xiàhóu Dūn, the Grand Administrator of Dōngjùn, from Púyáng.
When Dūn arrived,
Lǚ Bù then occupied Púyáng.
At this time, Cáo Cāo had taken his entire army to attack Táo Qiān,
leaving few troops to guard.
And many of his commanders and high-ranking officials were in league with Mǎo and Gōng.
*Dūjiàng* (督將),
those who lead troops;
*Dàlì* (大吏),
those who generally manage provincial and commandery affairs.
*Jiàng* (將),
is pronounced *liàng* (亮翻).
That night,
several tens of those plotting rebellion were executed,
and the populace was then settled.
Guō Gòng, the Inspector of Yùzhōu, led tens of thousands of troops and arrived beneath the city walls.
Some said he was in league with Lǚ Bù,
and the populace was greatly fearful.
Gòng requested to see Xún Yù.
Yù was about to go,
but Dūn and others said:
"You are the bulwark of an entire province,
meaning the entire province relies on him for its stability.
You must not go."
Yù said:
"Gòng and Mǎo are
not long-standing confederates.
His arrival is sudden,
so his plans must not yet be settled.
While they are unsettled, if I persuade him,
even if he is not used,
he can be made to remain neutral.
Xián says: Do not let him commit to any side.
*Shuō* (說),
pronounced *shū ruì* (輸芮翻);
same below.
If I do not go, he will become angry and firm up his plans."
Gòng saw that Yù had no fear,
and believed that Juànchéng was not easy to attack.
So he withdrew his troops and left.
At this time,
the commanderies and counties of Yǎnzhōu all responded to Lǚ Bù,
only Juànchéng, Fàn, and Dōng'ā remained unmoved.
Xián says: Fàn County belonged to Dōngjùn,
now Púyáng County.
Dōng'ā County belonged to Dōngjùn,
now Jìzhōu County.
"Chén Gōng wanted to personally lead troops to take Dōng'ā,
and also sent Fàn Yì to take Fàn."
The officials and people were all afraid.
Chéng Yù was originally from Dōng'ā.
Yù said to Yù:
"Now the entire province has rebelled,
only these three cities remain.
Gōng and others are bringing heavy forces against them.
If there is nothing to deeply secure their loyalty,
these three cities will surely fall.
You are
the hope of the people,
you should go and pacify them."
Yù then returned, passing through Fàn,
and persuaded its magistrate, Jìn Yǔn, saying:
"I hear Lǚ Bù has seized your mother, younger brother, wife, and children.
A filial son truly cannot bear this in his heart.
Now the world is in great chaos,
heroes are rising together.
There must be one destined by Heaven to quell the world's chaos.
This is what a wise person should carefully choose.
Those who gain the right lord prosper,
those who lose the right lord perish.
Chén Gōng rebelled and welcomed Lǚ Bù, and a hundred cities responded.
He seems capable of achieving something.
However, in your opinion,
what kind of person is Bù?
Bù is crude and lacks intimates,
stern but without propriety,
merely a hero among common men.
Gōng and others are merely temporarily allied by circumstance,
they cannot truly serve him as their lord.
*Xiàng* (相),
as written.
It means they cannot establish the relationship of lord and subject with him.
In the end, nothing will be achieved.
Commander Cáo's wisdom and strategy are unprecedented,
probably bestowed by Heaven.
You must firmly hold Fàn,
and I will defend Dōng'ā.
Then the achievement of Tián Dān can be accomplished.
Tián Dān,
his deeds are seen in Volume 5, during the 36th year of King Nǎn of Zhōu.
Only you consider this thoroughly!"
Yǔn wept and said:
"I dare not have a divided heart."
At that time, Fàn Yì was already in the county.
Yǔn then met Yì,
hid soldiers, and stabbed him to death.
He returned
and marshaled troops to defend himself.
Xú Zhòng commented: Yǔn and Cáo Gōng had not yet formed a lord-subject relationship;
his mother was his closest kin,
according to righteousness, he should have gone [to rescue her].
Gōngzǐ Kāifāng of Wèi served Qí,
and did not return for years.
Guǎn Zhòng believed that if one does not cherish one's kin,
how can one love one's lord!
Duke Huán of Qí asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"What about Kāifāng?"
He replied:
"Abandoning kin to serve a lord is not human nature;
he is difficult to trust."
Yǔn should have first rescued his closest kin.
When Xú Shù's mother was captured by Cáo Gōng,
Liú Bèi sent Shù to return north,
showing compassion for a son's feelings, as one who wishes to rule the world should.
The events are seen in the later Volume 65, the 13th year of Jiàn'ān.
7 Yù also dispatched separate cavalry to cut off the crossing at Cāngtíng Jīn,
Shuǐjīng Zhù: The Yellow River passes north of Dōng'ā County.
The Yellow River flows northeast of Fàn County,
forming Cāngtíng Jīn.
Shùzhēng Jì says: Cāngtíng Jīn is within Fàn County,
sixty *li* from Dōng'ā.
to prevent crossing.
When Yù arrived at Dōng'ā,
Zǎo Zhī of Yǐngchuān, the Magistrate of Dōng'ā, had already led and inspired officials and people to firmly defend the city.
Yǐngchuān Wénshì Chuán: The Zǎo clan was originally named Jí,
and changed it to avoid disaster.
When Cáo Cāo returned,
he took Yù's hand and said:
"Without your strength,
I would have nowhere to return."
He memorialized Yù as Chancellor of Dōngpíng,
garrisoning Fàn.
Lǚ Bù attacked Juànchéng but could not take it,
and moved west to garrison Púyáng.
Cáo Cāo said:
"Lǚ Bù, having suddenly gained a province,
failed to occupy Dōngpíng,
cut off the roads to Kàngfù and Tài Shān,
and exploit the dangerous terrain to constrain me.
Dōngpíng Commandery,
controls the roads to Kàngfù and Tài Shān.
Kàngfù originally belonged to Dōngpíng,
in the first year of Yuánhé of Emperor Zhāng,
it was divided to belong to Rènchéng.
Xián says: The old city of Kàngfù is now in Rènchéng County of Yǎnzhōu.
*Duàn* (斷),
pronounced *dīng guǎn* (丁管翻).
*Kàngfù* (亢父),
pronounced *kàng fǔ* (抗甫).
*Yāo* (要),
pronounced *yī yáo* (一遙翻).
I know he is incapable of anything."
Then he advanced to attack him.
8 In the fifth month,
Guō Sī was appointed General of the Rear, with the title General Who Spreads Martial Might.
Fán Chóu was appointed General of the Right, with the title General Who Pacifies and Gathers.
The title General Who Pacifies and Gathers
was also a temporary appointment at that time.
Together, they formed the Six Bureaus.
At that time, Grand Tutor Mǎ Rìdī was on an envoy mission.
Lǐ Jué, as General of Chariots and Cavalry, established a bureau.
Sī and Chóu also established bureaus,
which, together with the Three Excellencies, formed the Six Bureaus.
Lǐ Jué and the others each wanted to employ those they had recommended.
If one of their recommendations was not followed,
they would become indignant and express their displeasure.
The officials in charge were troubled by this,
so they eventually employed the recommended individuals in sequence.
The "officials in charge"
were likely the Imperial Secretaries.
Guō Sī's recommendations came first,
followed by Fán Chóu's,
while those recommended by the Three Excellencies
were ultimately never used.
9 The four commanderies west of the Yellow River were far from the seat of administration for Liángzhōu,
separated by river bandits.
The Inspector of Liángzhōu originally governed Jì County in Hànyáng Commandery.
At that time, numerous bandits arose,
leading to the isolation of the region west of the Yellow River.
The "river bandits" were probably bandits who obstructed the river and became brigands.
In the sixth month,
on the day Bǐngzǐ,
an edict appointed Hándān Shāng of Chénliú as Inspector of Yōngzhōu,
to govern that region.
The Fēngsú Tōng states
that Hándān adopted his surname from a state.
I believe Hándān was not a state,
but rather he adopted his surname from a city.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn mentions
Jìn had Hándān Wǔ.
Yōngzhōu was established at that time,
with its seat of governance in Wǔwēi.
"治" (zhì)
is pronounced "zhí zhī fān."
10On the day Dīngchǒu,
there was an earthquake in the capital.
On the day Wùyín,
there was another earthquake.
11On the last day of the month, Yǐyǒu,
there was a solar eclipse.
12In the autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the day Rénzǐ,
Grand Commandant Zhū Jùn was dismissed.
13On the day Wùwǔ,
Yáng Biāo, the Grand Astrologer, was appointed Grand Commandant
and given supervision over the affairs of the Imperial Secretariat.
14On the day Jiǎzǐ,
Yáng Dìng, General Who Guards the South, was appointed General Who Pacifies the West
and allowed to establish a bureau like the Three Excellencies.
15From the fourth month until this month, there was no rain.
One *hú* of grain cost 500,000 cash,
and people in Cháng'ān resorted to cannibalism.
The Emperor ordered Palace Censor Hóu Wèn to distribute rice and beans from the imperial granary to make gruel for the poor.
However, people continued to die of starvation as before.
The Emperor suspected that the distribution was not carried out honestly.
"稟" (bǐng)
means "to give."
"賦" (fù)
means "to grant."
He received only two basins.
So he had Wèn beaten fifty times with a staff.
Thereupon, everyone was fully saved.
From this,
it can be seen that Emperor Xiàn was not ignorant or foolish.
However, he ultimately lost the empire
because his power and authority had left him, and small favors were not enough to win the people's support.
16In the eighth month,
the Qiāng bandits in Fèngyì attacked the dependent counties.
Guō Sī, Fán Chóu, and others led their troops to defeat them.
17Lǚ Bù had a separate encampment west of Púyáng.
Cáo Cāo launched a night raid and defeated it,
but before he could return,
Lǚ Bù arrived.
He personally engaged in battle.
From dawn until early afternoon,
they fought dozens of rounds,
locked in an intense struggle.
Cáo Cāo recruited men to break the enemy lines.
The Commander (Sīmǎ) Chén Wéi of Chénliú led the volunteers forward to confront them.
Diǎn was his surname,
Wéi his given name.
Arrows fell like rain.
Diǎn Wéi did not look,
and said to the "people of equal rank" (děngrén):
"People of equal rank" are
those who stand equally to recruit people,
and those who are equal,
are called "people of equal rank."
Or it means: "People of equal rank"
refers to a group of volunteers of equal standing.
"When the barbarians are ten paces away,
then report it to me."
The "people of equal rank" said:
"They are ten paces away!"
He then said:
"Report it when they are five paces away."
The "people of equal rank" were afraid,
and quickly exclaimed:
"The barbarians are upon us!"
Diǎn Wéi, holding a *jǐ*, roared and charged.
Whomever he struck fell immediately,
and Lǚ Bù's forces retreated.
As night fell,
Cáo Cāo was able to withdraw.
He appointed Diǎn Wéi a Commandant (Dūwèi),
and ordered him to always lead several hundred personal guards,
surrounding the main tent.
The Tián clan, a prominent family in Púyáng, acted as a double agent.
Cáo Cāo managed to enter the city
and burned its east gate,
showing no intention of defection.
During the battle,
his army was defeated.
Lǚ Bù's cavalry captured Cáo Cāo but did not recognize him.
They asked:
"Where is Cáo Cāo?"
Cáo Cāo said:
"The one riding the yellow horse and running is him."
Lǚ Bù's cavalry then released Cáo Cāo and pursued the one on the yellow horse.
Cáo Cāo broke out through fire,
and upon reaching his camp,
personally rallied his troops,
ordering the army to quickly prepare siege equipment.
He advanced
and attacked again.
He personally rallied his troops
and urged the army to advance and attack
because he feared that after the defeat,
the morale of the soldiers would decline.
"勞" (láo)
is pronounced "lì dào fān."
"復" (fù)
is pronounced "fú yòu fān."
Locusts arose,
and the common people suffered greatly from hunger.
Lǚ Bù's provisions also ran out,
and both sides withdrew.
In the ninth month,
Cáo Cāo returned to Juǎnchéng.
Lǚ Bù arrived at Chéngshì.
Chéngshì County
belonged to Jìyīn Commandery.
Yīng Shào said: In the Spring and Autumn period,
Lǔ defeated the Sòng army at Chéngqiū,
which is this place.
Sòng Bái said: The old city of Chéngshì, fifty-seven *lǐ* southwest of present-day Jìzhōu Jùyě County, is it.
"乘" (chéng)
is pronounced "shéng zhèng fān."
He then encamped east of Shānyáng.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
Cáo Cāo arrived at Dōng'ē.
Yuán Shào sent someone to persuade Cáo Cāo,
wishing for Cáo Cāo to send his family to Yè.
Cáo Cāo had recently lost Yǎnzhōu,
and his army's provisions were exhausted,
so he was about to agree.
Chéng Yù said:
"It seems that the General is perhaps afraid when facing the matter,
otherwise,
why would your considerations not be deeper?
Yuán Shào indeed has the ambition to unite the world,
but his wisdom cannot accomplish it.
Does the General believe he can be subordinate to him?
With the General's might like a dragon and a tiger,
can he be like Hán Xìn and Péng Yuè to Yuán Shào?
Although Yǎnzhōu is now devastated,
there are still three cities,
and no fewer than ten thousand able-bodied soldiers.
With the General's divine martial prowess,
and with Wénruò and me to gather and utilize them,
Xún Yù,
whose courtesy name is Wénruò.
I implore the General to reconsider!"
Cáo Cāo then stopped.
18In the twelfth month,
Minister of Works Chúnyú Jiā was dismissed.
Zhào Wēn, the Commander of the Imperial Guards, was appointed Minister of Works
and given supervision over the affairs of the Imperial Secretariat.
19 When Mǎ Tēng attacked Lǐ Quē,
Liú Yān's two sons, Fàn and Dàn, both died.
Councillor Páng Xī of Hénán,
who had always been on good terms with Yān,
recruited Yān's grandsons and brought them into Shǔ.
It happened that a heavenly fire burned down the city,
so Yān moved his administration to Chéngdū.
Liú Yān initially resided in Jū.

is a chronic carbuncle.
They jointly nominated Zhāng to be Inspector of Yìzhōu,

Zhāng's generals Shěn Mí, Lóu Fā, and Gān Níng rebelled,
attacking Zhāng.
They were unsuccessful
and fled into Jīngzhōu.
An imperial edict then appointed Zhāng as Governor of Yìzhōu.
Zhāng appointed Wěi as General of the Household, Pacifying the East,
and he led his troops to attack Liú Biǎo,
stationing them at Qúnín.
Qúnín County
belonged to Bājùn.
Shī Gǔ said: Qú [朐],
is pronounced qú.
The Jìnshū Yīnyì says: Qú [朐],
is pronounced chún.
Nín [䏰],
is pronounced rúyǔn.
Xián said: The old city of Qúnín
is in the west of present-day Kúizhōu Yún'ān County;
it is the old city of Wànhù.
Nín [䏰],
is pronounced rùn.
Liú Xǔ said: Kāizhōu Shèngshān County
is the land of Hàn Qúnín.
I hold that the present-day Yún'ān Commandery
is the land of Hàn Qúnín County.
The land is low and wet,
with many Qúnín worms,
hence the name.
Liú Yǔxī said: Qúnín [朐䏰]
is an earthworm.
Péi Sōngzhī said: Nín [䏰],
is pronounced rúzhèn.
20 Xúzhōu Governor Táo Qiān was gravely ill
and said to Mi Zhú of Dōnghǎi, his Administrative Assistant:
The Xìngpǔ says: A Grand Master of Chǔ was enfeoffed at Mí Tíng in Nánjùn,
and thus adopted it as his surname.
Some say he was a descendant of Gōngyǐn Mí,
who adopted his given name as his surname.
"Only Liú Bèi can bring peace to this province."
When Qiān died,
Zhú led the people of the province to welcome Bèi.
Bèi did not dare to accept at first,
saying:
"Yuán Gōnglù is nearby in Shòuchūn.
Yuán Shù,
styled Gōnglù.
Chén Dēng of Xiàpéi, Agricultural Superintendent, said:
According to Péi Sōngzhī's commentary to the Sānguó Zhì, Táo Qiān memorialized Dēng as Agricultural Superintendent.
The Wèizhì says: Cáo Gōng established the Agricultural Superintendent,
with a salary equivalent to two thousand dàn of grain.
This office already existed,
and Cáo Gōng merely increased its salary.
"Gōnglù is arrogant and tyrannical,
not a ruler who can govern in times of chaos.
Now, I wish to gather a hundred thousand infantry and cavalry for your Excellency,
who can, on the one hand, assist the Lord and save the people,
and on the other hand, carve out territory and defend its borders.
Observing Dēng's words,
he was indeed a talent not easily dismissed.
Dēng also did not dare to heed your Excellency."
Kǒng Róng, Administrator of Běihǎi, said to Bèi:
"How can Yuán Gōnglù be someone who worries for the state and forgets his family!
He is but a dry bone in a tomb,
what is there to be concerned about!
According to Chén Shòu's Zhì,
Bèi said to Zhú and others:
'Yuán Gōnglù is nearby in Shòuchūn.
This gentleman's family has held high office for four generations and five nobles,
you can give the province to him.'
Róng's words:
'A dry bone in a tomb,
what is there to be concerned about.'
were precisely in response to 'four generations and five nobles'.
The common people support the capable;
if Heaven gives and you do not take,
regret will be irreversible."
The Yì says: The plans of men and ghosts,
the common people support the capable.
Meaning, the common people only support the capable.
The Qiánshū says: If Heaven gives and you do not take,
you will instead suffer calamity.
21 Initially,
Grand Tutor Mǎ Rìdī and Zhào Qí were both sent as imperial envoys to Shòuchūn.
Qí upheld his principles unyieldingly,
and Yuán Shù feared him.
Rìdī had some requests from Shù,
and Shù insulted and belittled him.
He borrowed Rìdī's staff of authority to examine it,
then seized it and did not return it.
He listed more than ten people from his army
and ordered Rìdī to urgently appoint them.
Rìdī asked Shù to leave,
but Shù kept him and would not let him go,
also wanting to force him to become his military advisor.
Rìdī was so distressed by this loss of integrity
that he vomited blood and died.
Dù Yù said: Bìng [病],
means to consider it one's own illness.
22 Initially,
Sūn Jiān married Lady Wú of Qiántáng,
and they had four sons:
Cè, Quán, Yì, Kuāng, and one daughter.
Jiān was on military campaign abroad,
leaving his family in Shòuchūn.
Cè, at over ten years old,
had already befriended well-known individuals.
Zhōu Yú of Shū, the same age as Cè,
was also brilliant and precocious.
Sù [夙],
means early.
He came from Shū to visit Yān,
and immediately formed a bond of friendship,
persuading Cè to move his residence to Shū.
Cè followed his advice.
Yú then offered Cè a large house by the roadside,
ascended the hall to pay respects to his mother,
and shared everything they had.
When Jiān died,
Cè was seventeen,
and returned to bury him in Qū'ē.
Qū'ē County
belonged to Wújùn.

The Emperor ordered the palace attendants and ministers, Lǐ Qué and Guō Sī,
