Guō Sì was appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chēqí Jiāngjūn);
Yáng Dìng was appointed General of the Rear (Hòu Jiāngjūn);
Yáng Fèng was appointed General Who Rises in Righteousness (Xīngyì Jiāngjūn): all were enfeoffed as marquises.
Yáng Fèng, having assisted the Emperor as a former leader of the Báibō bandits,
was thus honored with the title Xīngyì.
The Shǔ Zhì states: Chéng
was the maternal uncle of Emperor Xiàn.
Péi Sōngzhī states: Chéng
was the nephew of Empress Dowager Dǒng, mother of Emperor Líng,
and thus a "father-in-law" (zhàngrén) to Emperor Xiàn;
it is probably because the term zhàngrén was not used in ancient times,
hence he was referred to as "maternal uncle" (jiù).
Guō Sì wanted the imperial carriage to proceed to Gāolíng.
Gāolíng County
belonged to Fēngyì Commandery.
A great meeting was held to discuss this,
but no decision was reached.
The Emperor sent an envoy to instruct Guō Sì, saying:
“Hóngnóng is near the imperial ancestral temples,
there should be no doubt!”
Guō Sì did not comply.
The Emperor then did not eat for the entire day.
When Guō Sì heard this, he said:
“He can at least proceed to a nearby county for now.”
In the eighth month,
on the jiǎchén day,
the imperial carriage proceeded to Xīnfēng.
On the bǐngzǐ day,
Guō Sì again plotted to abduct the Emperor back to Mèi.
Attendant Zhǒng Jí, knowing of this,
secretly informed Yáng Dìng, Dǒng Chéng, and Yáng Fèng to meet at Xīnfēng.
Guō Sì, knowing his plot was exposed,
abandoned his army and entered the Southern Mountains.
From Xīnfēng, Mount Lí westward connects to Mount Zhōngnán,
which is called the Southern Mountains.
9 Cáo Cāo besieged Yōngqiū.
Zhāng Miǎo went to Yuán Shù to seek aid,
but before he arrived,
he was killed by his subordinates.
10 In winter,
the tenth month,
Cáo Cāo was appointed Governor of Yǎnzhōu.
11 On the wùxū day,
Guō Sì’s partisans Xià Yù and Gāo Shuò conspired to force the imperial carriage to travel west.
Attendant Liú Ài saw that fires were breaking out incessantly,
and requested the Emperor to move to one of the camps to avoid the fires.
At this time, Guō Sì, Yáng Dìng, Dǒng Chéng, and Yáng Fèng each had their own camps.
Liú Ài dared not specify,
so he requested to move to the camp of one of the generals,
whichever the Emperor preferred.
Xià Yù and others mustered their troops, intending to stop the imperial carriage,
but Yáng Dìng and Yáng Fèng fought vigorously,
defeating them,
and thus they were able to get out.
On the rénbǐng day,
the imperial entourage arrived at Huáyīn.
General Who Calms and Harmonizes (Níngjí Jiāngjūn) Duàn Wēi prepared imperial clothing, carriages, and provisions for the high officials and others,
wishing for the Emperor to proceed to his camp.
The title Níngjí
is similar to Ānjí (General Who Brings Peace and Order),
and was also temporarily established at that time.
Wēi
is pronounced wéi (烏回翻).
Zhǒng Jí and Zuǒ Líng, Yáng Dìng’s partisans, claimed that Duàn Wēi intended to rebel.
Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) Yáng Biāo, Minister of Works (Sītú) Zhào Wēn, Attendant Liú Ài, and Minister of the Secretariat (Shàngshū) Liáng Shào all said:
“Duàn Wēi will not rebel.
We, your servants, dare to guarantee this with our lives.”
Dǒng Chéng and Yáng Dìng coerced the Inspector (Dūyóu) of Hóngnóng to say that Guō Sì was in Duàn Wēi’s camp.
The Emperor suspected this,
and so encamped in the open south of the road.
Camping outdoors without shelters
is called "lù cì" (open encampment).
On the dīngwèi day,
Yáng Fèng, Dǒng Chéng, and Yáng Dìng were about to attack Duàn Wēi,
and sent Zhǒng Jí and Zuǒ Líng to request the Emperor to issue an edict.
The Emperor said:
“Duàn Wēi’s crime is not yet evident.
If Fèng and the others attack him,
do you then wish me to issue an edict?”
Zhǒng Jí insisted,
until midnight,
but the Emperor still did not consent.
Yáng Fèng and the others then proceeded to attack Duàn Wēi’s camp,
but could not take it for more than ten days.
Duàn Wēi supplied the imperial meals
and provided for all the officials,
without any duplicity.
An edict was sent by the Attendants and Ministers of the Secretariat to inform Yáng Dìng and the others,
ordering them to make peace with Duàn Wēi.
Yáng Dìng and the others obeyed the edict and returned to their camps.
Lǐ Què and Guō Sì regretted letting the imperial carriage proceed east.
Hearing that Yáng Dìng was attacking Duàn Wēi,
they called upon each other to rescue him,
and then intended to abduct the Emperor and go west.
Yáng Dìng, hearing that Lǐ Què and Guō Sì had arrived,
wished to return to Lántián,
but was intercepted by Guō Sì.
He fled alone on horseback to Jīngzhōu.
Zhāng Jì and Yáng Fèng and Dǒng Chéng were not on good terms,
so he rejoined Lǐ Què and Guō Sì.
In the twelfth month,
the Emperor proceeded to Hóngnóng.
Zhāng Jì, Lǐ Què, and Guō Sì jointly pursued the imperial carriage,
and a great battle took place at the eastern gorge of Hóngnóng.
The armies of Dǒng Chéng and Yáng Fèng were defeated.
The number of officials and soldiers who died
was uncountable.
Imperial regalia, talismans, records, and archives
were almost entirely abandoned.
All objects for imperial use and apparel
are called "yù wù" (imperial regalia).
Fú (talismans)
are like bronze tiger talismans and bamboo envoy tallies.
The word fú means "to support" (fú),
meaning two halves supporting each other without discrepancy.
It also means: fú
is "to assist" (fǔ),
that which assists in trustworthiness;
and also "to match" (hé),
to verify.
Cè (records)
are made of bound bamboo slips.
In ancient times, all imperial pronouncements were written on cè.
Under the Hàn system,
the Emperor’s cè were two feet long.
Diǎnjí (archives)
are like inner court maps and records, and precedents from the Secretariat.
Shèng (勝)
is pronounced shēng.
Lǐ Què asked his attendants:
“Can we still live?”
Jùn cursed him, saying:
“You ruthless rebels,
you have coerced the Son of Heaven,
caused high officials to be harmed,
and palace women to be scattered.
There have never been such rebellious subjects and traitorous sons
as you!”
Lǐ Què then killed him.
On the rénshēn day,
the Emperor encamped in the open at Cáoyáng.
Xián says: Cáoyáng
is the name of a gorge,
seven lǐ southwest of present-day Shǎnzhōu,
commonly called Qīlǐjiàn.
Cuī Hào says: it extends from the Southern Mountains north to the Yellow River.
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi renamed it Hàoyáng.
Dù Yòu says: forty-five lǐ west of Shǎnjùn is Cáoyángjiàn.
Judging from the text below,
Dù Yòu’s statement is correct.
Secretly, a messenger was dispatched to Hédōng,
to summon the former Báibō leaders Lǐ Lè, Hán Xiān, Hú Cái,
and the Right Worthy King (Yòuxiánwáng) Qùbēi of the Southern Xiōngnú;
they all led several thousand cavalry to come
and, together with Dǒng Chéng and Yáng Fèng, attacked Lǐ Què and others,
greatly defeating them,
and beheading several thousand people.
Thereupon, Dǒng Chéng and others, having just defeated Guō Jué and the others,
thought they could lead the emperor east again.
On Gēngshēn day,
the imperial carriage set off eastward,
departing from Cáoyáng and heading east.
Hú Cái, Yáng Fèng, Hán Xiān, and the Xiongnu Right Worthy King (Yòu Xiánwáng) acted as a rearguard.
Guō Jué and the others came to fight again,
and Yáng Fèng's forces suffered a great defeat,
with more deaths than at Dōngjiàn.
Guānglù
Dèng Yuān, Tíngwèi Xuān Fán,
Shǎofǔ Tián Fēn, and Dàsīnóng Zhāng Yì all died.
Sītú Zhào Wēn, Tàicháng Wáng Jiàng, Wèiwèi Zhōu Zhōng, and Sīlì Xiàowèi Guǎn Hé were intercepted by Guō Jué,
who intended to kill them.
Jiǎ Xǔ said:
"These are all high officials,
how can you harm them?"
So he stopped.
Lǐ Lè said:
"The situation is urgent,
Your Majesty should ride a horse."
The emperor said:
"I cannot abandon the hundred officials and leave.
What crime have they committed?"
Observing this statement from the emperor,
uttered at a time of extreme danger,
how can one treat him as a ruler of a fallen state?
He was merely controlled by powerful ministers.
"Shě"
is read as "shě".
They managed to reach Shǎn.
Dù Yòu said: Shǎn
was the land of the Guó state during the Spring and Autumn period,
the so-called Northern Guó.
At that time, after the devastation,
the Hǔbēn (Tiger Guards) and Yǔlín (Feathered Forest Guards) numbered less than one hundred men.
Guō Jué and Fàn Sì's soldiers surrounded the camp, shouting,
causing the officials and soldiers to lose color in their faces,
each having thoughts of dispersing.
Lǐ Lè was afraid,
and wanted the imperial carriage to cross the Dǐzhù by boat,
and exit at Mèngjīn.
The commentary to the "Shuǐ Jīng" (Classic of Waterways) says: The Yellow River flows south past Dàyáng Xiàn,
then east past the Dǐzhù narrows.
Dǐzhù
is a mountain name.
In ancient times, when Yǔ controlled the great flood,
he chiseled through mountains and hills that obstructed the water,
thus breaking mountains to open up the river.
The river branched into streams,
flowing around the mountain,
which appeared in the water like a pillar,
hence it was called Dǐzhù.
After the three passages were opened,
the water flow was dispersed.
Its shape was marked by three openings,
so it was also called Sānmén Shān;
it is northeast of Guóchéng,
and east of Dàyángchéng.
From Dǐzhù down to Wǔhù Tān,
a distance of one hundred and twenty *lǐ*,
there are nineteen rapids (*hàn*),
where the water flows swiftly and rapidly,
breaking boats and ships,
which has been a problem since ancient times.
The Yellow River then flows east past the north of Píngyīn Xiàn,
and then east past the south of Héyáng Xiàn,
which is Mèngjīn.
It was not suitable for the Son of Heaven to cross.
So, Lǐ Lè was sent to cross at night,
secretly preparing boats
and lighting a fire as a signal.
The emperor and the *gōngqīng* (high-ranking officials) walked out of the camp.
Empress Fú's brother, Fú Dé, supported the Empress,
holding ten bolts of silk in one hand.
Dǒng Chéng ordered the Fújié Lìng Sūn Huī to strike him amid the crowd.
The "Bǎiguān Zhì" (Treatise on Officials) says: The Fújié Lìng
belonged to the Shǎofǔ,
with a salary of six hundred *shí*.
He was the head of the Fújié Tái
and was in charge of imperial tallies and credentials.
Whenever an envoy was dispatched,
he was responsible for presenting the credentials.
Blood splattered on the Empress's clothes.
The river bank was more than ten *zhàng* high,
making it impossible to descend.
So, silk was used to make a litter,
with people carrying the emperor in front,
and the rest crawling down.
Some even threw themselves down from above,
their hats and caps all ruined.
Upon reaching the riverside,
the soldiers rushed to the boats,
and Dǒng Chéng and Lǐ Lè struck them with *gē* (halberds).
The fingers in the boats could be scooped up by the handful.
The "Zuǒ Zhuàn" says:
When Jìn's Xún Línfù led his army to battle at Bì and was defeated,
the central army and the lower army fought for boats,
and the fingers in the boats could be scooped up by the handful.
Those who crossed successfully
numbered only a few tens, including the Empress and Yáng Biāo.
The palace women, officials, and common people who could not cross
were all plundered by the soldiers,
their clothes completely taken,
their hair also cut off,
and the number of those who froze to death was countless.
Wèiwèi Shìsūn Ruì was killed by Guō Jué.
Guō Jué saw fire north of the river
and sent cavalry to investigate.
They happened to see the emperor crossing the river
and shouted:
"Are you taking the Son of Heaven away?!"
Dǒng Chéng, fearing an attack, shot at them,
using blankets as a barrier.
Fearing that Guō Jué's soldiers would shoot at them,
they used blankets as a barrier
to ward off arrows.
"Màn"
is pronounced *mòbàn* (in fanqie),
meaning "curtain".
"Shè"
is pronounced *ér yì* (in fanqie).
Xián said: Dàyáng Xiàn
belonged to Hédōng Jùn.
The "Qián Shū Yīnyì" (Pronunciation and Meaning of the Former Han History) says: It is on the sunny side of the Great River,
which is today's Shǎnzōu Héběi Xiàn.
The Hénèi Tàishǒu Zhāng Yáng sent several thousand men carrying rice to offer as provisions.
On Yǐhài day,
the emperor rode in an ox-cart
and proceeded to Ānyì.
Ānyì Xiàn
belonged to Hédōng Jùn.
He distributed provisions to the *gōngqīng* and below.
"Fù"
means "to give",
"to distribute".
He appointed Hú Cái as Zhēngdōng Jiāngjūn,
and Zhāng Yáng as Ānguó Jiāngjūn.
The title of Ānguó Jiāngjūn
probably began here.
The chieftains of the various stockades competed to be appointed to offices,
and there were not enough seals to be carved,
to the extent that they had to be drawn with an awl.
The imperial carriage was in an enclosure of thorn hedges,
with no gates or closures.
When the emperor met with his ministers,
soldiers would lie on top of the hedges to watch,
pressing against each other and laughing.
The emperor also sent Tàipú Hán Róng to Hóngnóng to make peace with Guō Jué and Fàn Sì.
Guō Jué then released the *gōngqīng* and various officials,
and largely returned the plundered palace women and imperial carriages and attire.
Afterwards, grain ran out,
and all the palace women ate vegetables and fruits.
On Yǐmǎo day,
Zhāng Yáng came from Yěwáng to pay his respects.
Yěwáng Xiàn
belonged to Hénèi Jùn;
during the Suí and Táng dynasties, it was Hénèi Xiàn.
The various generals would not listen,
so Yáng returned to Yěwáng.
At this time,
Cháng'ān city was empty for more than forty days.
The strong scattered in all directions,
and the weak ate each other.
Within two or three years,
there were no longer any human traces in Guānzhōng.
Jǔ Shòu
persuaded Yuán Shào, saying:
"Your Excellency's family has for generations served in the highest offices of the state,
and for generations upheld loyalty and righteousness.
Now the imperial court is scattered and displaced.
Bō means
'to flow,'
or 'to move.'
Yuè means
'to fall,'
or 'to flee.'
Xián says: Bō
means 'to move';
Yuè
means 'to escape';
indicating a loss of dwelling place.
Shuì (說) is pronounced
as shū ruì fān;
similarly below.
I observe that although the various zhōus and jūn (郡) externally claim to be righteous armies,
they are in fact plotting against each other internally,
and none have the intention of worrying about the nation or showing compassion for the people.
Now that the zhōuyù (州域) is roughly settled,
zhōuyù refers to the territory of Jì Zhōu (冀州).
Cū (粗) is pronounced
as zuò wǔ fān.
If we welcome the great imperial chariot from the west,
and establish the capital in Yè (鄴),
jí means
'to settle.'
accumulate soldiers and horses,
and punish those who are not in court,
bùtíng (不庭) refers to those who do not attend court.
Dù Yù
says: When inferiors serve superiors,
all rituals are performed in the court.
Another interpretation says: Tíng
means 'straight';
bùtíng means 'those who are not straight.'
Guō Tú (郭圖) and Chún Yú Qióng (淳于瓊) of Yǐng Chuān (潁川) said:
"The Hàn (漢) imperial house has been in decline
for a long time now.
Wáng Sù's (王肅) commentary on Jiāyǔ (家語) says: It is like a gradual winding descent of a hill.
Is this not difficult?
Moreover, heroes are rising simultaneously,
each occupying zhōus and jūn,
gathering followers and amassing crowds,
with tens of thousands in each movement.
It is said, 'When Qín (秦) lost its deer,
the first to get it became king.'
Now, if we welcome the Son of Heaven to be near us,
every action will be reported to him.
If we obey him, our authority will be diminished;
if we defy him, we will be resisting his mandate.
This is not a good strategy."
Shòu (授) said:
"To welcome the imperial court now
is righteous,
and timely.
If we do not decide quickly,
someone else will surely do it first."
Shào (紹) did not follow this advice.
Shào was unable to follow Shòu's words,
and indeed, Cáo Cāo (曹操) got there first.
After the Emperor had already established his capital in Xǔ (許),
Shào then wanted to move him closer to himself.
Was it not too late?
Xiān (先) is pronounced
as xī jiàn fān.
Kǎoyì (考異) states: The Wèi Zhì (魏志) biography of Shào says:
"When the Son of Heaven was in Hé Dōng (河東),
Shào sent Guō Tú (郭圖) as an envoy.
Upon returning, Tú persuaded Shào to welcome the Son of Heaven and establish the capital in Yè (鄴),
but Shào did not agree."
Now, we follow Fàn Shū (范書).
12 In the beginning,
Zhū Zhì (朱治) of Dān Yáng (丹陽) had once served Sūn Jiān (孫堅) as a xiàowèi (校尉).
Zhì followed Jiān to suppress the bandits in Cháng Shā (長沙), Líng (零), and Guì (桂),
and was appointed Dūwèi (都尉) by imperial decree.
He also followed in defeating Dǒng Zhuó (董 Zhuó) at Yáng Rén (陽人),
and was appointed Dūjūn Xiàowèi (督軍校尉) by imperial decree.
He advised Sūn Cè (孫策) to return and take over Jiāng Dōng (江東).
At that time, Wú Jǐng (吳景) was attacking Fán Néng (樊能), Zhāng Yīng (張英) and others,
but failed to overcome them for over a year.
Cè (策) said to Shù (術):
"My family has old favors in the east.
I wish to assist my uncle in attacking Héng Jiāng (橫江).
Once Héng Jiāng is captured,
I will then return to my homeland to recruit soldiers.
I can gather thirty thousand troops
to assist the enlightened lord in pacifying the empire."
Cè was originally from Jiāng Dōng,
hence he referred to it as his homeland.
This refers to his promise to grant Jiǔ Jiāng (九江) and Lú Jiāng (廬江), but then not employing them.
Wáng Lǎng (王朗) was in Kuàijī (會稽).
Thinking that Cè (策) might not be able to stabilize the situation,
he then agreed to it,
and by imperial decree appointed Cè as Zhéchōng Xiàowèi (折衝校尉).
Cè led over a thousand soldiers and several tens of cavalry,
and as he marched, he gathered more troops.
By the time he reached Lì Yáng (歷陽),
his forces numbered five or six thousand.
At that time, Zhōu Yú's (周瑜) paternal uncle, Shàng (尚), was the Grand Administrator of Dān Yáng (丹陽).
Yú led his troops to welcome him,
and also provided him with provisions.
Cè was greatly pleased,
and said:
"With you,
I succeed!"
Xié (諧) means
'to match,'
or 'to accord.'
The historian says that the establishment of their deep friendship
should be viewed at this point,
and here one should distinguish the two characters of 'deep friendship.'
Heroes meeting in the wilderness,
in an instant,
readily dedicated themselves to service.
How could this be achieved by mere voice, laughter, and appearance?
Cè (策) defeated them all.
Fán Néng (樊能) and Zhāng Yīng (張英) were defeated and fled.
Cè crossed the river and continued fighting,
conquering everywhere he went.
No one dared to stand against his vanguard.
When the common people heard that Sūn Láng (孫郎) had arrived,
they all lost their composure.
Jiāng Biǎo Zhuàn (江表傳) says: Although Cè was young,
and held titles,
the people of Wú (吳) all called him Sūn Láng.
They hid in the mountains and grasses.
Shān Cǎo (山草) means
'amidst deep mountains and dense vegetation.'
Lǐ Gù (李固) said in a memorial:
"Your servant is hiding among the mountains and grasses,
feeling heartbroken and pained."
Thus, the two characters shāncǎo
were a common expression at the time.
Cháng (長) is pronounced
as zhī liǎng fān.
The soldiers followed orders,
not daring to plunder.
Chickens, dogs, vegetables, and roots—
they committed no offenses whatsoever.
Rú (茹) also means
'vegetables.'
People competed to offer oxen and wine to reward the army.
Cè (策) was a person
of handsome appearance,
who could laugh and speak well,
was broad-
minded in listening and receiving,
and skilled in employing people.
Therefore, all soldiers and common people who met him gave their utmost,
and were happy to die for him.
Cè (策) attacked Liú Yáo's (劉繇) camp at Niú Zhǔ (牛渚).
The Jùn Guó Zhì (郡國志) says: South of Mò Líng Xiàn (秣陵縣) in Dān Yáng Jùn (丹陽郡),
there is Niú Zhǔ.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) says: Niú Zhǔ Qí (牛渚圻),
which is Cǎi Shí (采石) in Dāng Tú Xiàn (當塗縣) of Xuān Chéng Jùn (宣城郡).
Today, thirty lǐ north of Dāng Tú Xiàn (當塗縣) in Tài Píng Zhōu (太平州), there is Niú Zhǔ Shān (牛渚山), which is it.
Dǐ (邸) means
'to arrive,'
referring to the destination.
Gé (閣) means
'to store.'
Dǐ Gé (邸閣) refers to
a place where transported goods arrive and are stored.
Lǐ (禮) occupied Mò Líng Chéng (秣陵城).
Shěn Yuē (沈約) says: Mò Líng's
land was originally named Jīn Líng (金陵).
Its original seat of government was sixty lǐ from the imperial capital,
which is the present-day Gù Zhì Cūn (故治村).
Yuán Fēng Jiǔ Yù Zhì (元豐九域志) says: In Jiāng Níng Fǔ (江寧府), Jiāng Níng Xiàn (江寧縣) has Mò Líng Zhèn (秣陵鎮).
Dīng Dù's (丁度) Jí Yùn (集韻) says: Zuó (笮)
is pronounced cè gé qiē,
and is a surname.
Fēng Sú Tōng (風俗通) says: Chǔ (楚) had Zuó Lún (笮倫).
Cè (策) defeated them all.
He also defeated Yáo's (繇) separate general at Méi Líng (梅陵).
The Táng Shū Dì Lǐ Zhì (唐書地理志) says,
Xuān Zhōu (宣州), Nán Líng Xiàn (南陵縣) has Méi Gēn Zhèn (梅根鎮),
and today there is Méi Gēn Gǎng (梅根港).
He captured them all.
The Jùn Guó Zhì (郡國志) says,
Dān Yáng Jùn (丹陽郡) has Hú Shú (湖孰) and Jiāng Chéng (江乘) two xiàn.
Yuán Fēng Jiǔ Yù Zhì (元豐九域志) says, Jiāng Níng Fǔ (江寧府), Shàng Yuán Xiàn (上元縣) has Hú Shú Zhèn (湖孰鎮).
Tái Shǐ Cí (太史慈), from the same commandery, at this time came from Dōnglái (東萊) to visit Liú Yáo (劉繇).
Tàishǐ (太史)
was taken as a surname due to the office held.
Liú Yáo (劉繇) and Tái Shǐ Cí (太史慈) were both Dōnglái (東萊) people.
省
is pronounced xǐjǐng.
Some advised Liú Yáo (劉繇) that he could make Tái Shǐ Cí (太史慈) a great general.
Liú Yáo (劉繇) said:
"If I were to employ Zǐyì (子義),
Tái Shǐ Cí's (太史慈) courtesy name was Zǐyì (子義).
This refers to his accurate assessment of people.
At that time, he alone, with a single cavalry soldier, encountered Sūn Cè (孫策) at Shéntíng (神亭).
Shéntíng (神亭)
is in the present-day Dānyáng (丹陽) county of Zhènjiāng Fǔ (鎮江府).
