it was moved to Qiántáng,
becoming the Western part.
During the Yuándǐng era,
an Eastern Dūwèi was also established,
administered from Yě.
Guāngwǔ renamed Huípǔ as Zhāng'ān,
and established Dōnghòuguān at Yě."
Sūn Liàng's biography in the *Wú Shū* states: "During the Wǔfèng era,
the eastern part of Kuàijī was made Línhǎi Commandery."
Sūn Xiū's biography states: "During the Yǒng'ān era,
the southern part of Kuàijī was made Jiàn'ān Commandery."
Shěn Yuē's *Sòng Zhì* states: "The Administrator of Dōngyáng was originally the Western Dūwèi of Kuàijī."
It also states: "The Administrator of Línhǎi was originally the Eastern Dūwèi of Kuàijī."
The *Qián Hàn* Dūwèi was administered from Yín.
The *Hòu Hàn* divided Kuàijī into Wú Commandery.
It is suspected that the Dūwèi's seat was moved to Zhāng'ān.
The *Xù Hàn Zhì* states: "Zhāng'ān was formerly Yě;
Guāngwǔ renamed it."
The *Jìn Tàikāng Jì* states: "It was originally Huípǔ Township in the southern part of Yín County,
established by Emperor Zhāng."
It is unclear which is correct.
It also says: "Sīmǎ Biāo said: Zhāng'ān is the former Yě."
If so, Línhǎi is also Yě territory.
Zhāng Bó's *Wú Lù* states: "This was the place where Gōujiàn smelted and cast metals.
Later, it was divided into the Eastern and Southern Dūwèi of Kuàijī: the Eastern part
is Línhǎi;
the Southern part
is Jiàn'ān."
Dù Yòu's *Tōng Diǎn* states: "The Latter Hàn renamed Yě County as Hòuguān Dūwèi.
Later, Yě County was divided into the Eastern and Southern Dūwèi of Kuàijī.
Today's Fúzhōu is the Southern part,
and Táizhōu is the Eastern part."
It also states: "During the two Hàn dynasties, the Western Dūwèi of Kuàijī administered Wùzhōu."
The various accounts differ,
each having omissions and errors.
I have previously collated and corrected them.
Since Qín established Kuàijī Commandery,
its seat was in present-day Wúmén.
By Emperor Shùn's time, Wú Commandery was separately established,
and Kuàijī's commandery seat was moved to Shānyīn.
The Zhèjiāng River served as the boundary between the two commanderies.
Therefore, Qiántáng belonged to Kuàijī during the Western Hàn,
which is why it was the seat of the Western part.
When Kuàijī moved east of the Zhèjiāng River,
the Western part also moved to Wùnǚ.
Huípǔ was later renamed Zhāng'ān,
and was the eastern part of Kuàijī.
Today's Táizhōu is likely that territory.
Yě County was the southern part,
belonging to Jiàn'ān Commandery in Wú,
and later becoming Fúzhōu in Táng.
The *Tàikāng Jì* once stated: "Huípǔ was originally the southern township of Yín."
Or it is said that the Eastern part was administered from Yín,
which led to Xiūwén's confusion.
However, Yín and Huípǔ were both county names in the Western Hàn.
To say that the Western Hàn carved out Yín to establish the county
may not be known.
By Emperor Zhāng's time,
Huípǔ was no longer a township.
What the *Tàikāng Jì* recorded
is also an error.
The former *Zhì* noted that Kuàijī's Yě County was "originally Mǐnyuè territory."
The *Xù Zhì* states: "Zhāng'ān,
formerly Yě,
Mǐnyuè territory,
Guāngwǔ renamed it."
Due to the omission of several characters in between,
Liú Zhāo's supplementary note was misled by the *Tàikāng Jì*,
and Xiūwén was again unable to distinguish them.
It should say: Zhāng'ān was formerly Huípǔ,
Emperor Zhāng renamed it;
Dōnghòuguān was formerly Yě,
Mǐnyuè territory,
Guāngwǔ renamed it:
then the text is complete.
At the end of this commandery, there are
the four characters "Dōngbù Hòuguó,"
which are extraneous text.
*Hóu* (侯) and *hòu* (候) are similar,
and it was administered by the southern part,
hence the confusion in the text.
Bān Gù's *Shǐ* noted Huípǔ as the southern part.
Sīmǎ Biāo said Zhāng'ān was the former Yě.
Zhāng Bó said Yě was divided into Eastern and Southern Dūwèi.
Dù Yòu said the Western part of the two Hàn dynasties was all in Wùnǚ.
The *Tú Jīng* took Yě to be the Eastern part.
All are mistaken.
I found Hóng's explanation very detailed.
His statement that Qiántáng
belonged to Kuàijī during the Western Hàn,
and was therefore the seat of the Western part,
this statement,
I fear, may still have an insecure point.
Sūn Cè utterly defeated them,
and Wáng Lǎng then went to Sūn Cè and surrendered.
Sūn Cè personally took charge as Administrator of Kuàijī,
and again appointed Yú Fān as *Gōngcáo*,
treating him with the courtesy due to a friend.
Sūn Cè enjoyed hunting.
Yú Fān remonstrated, saying:
"Your Excellency is fond of going out lightly and incognito.
Your attendants do not have time to be strict,
and the officers and soldiers often suffer from it.
Indeed, a ruler who is not dignified will not possess authority.
'Dignified'
means respected.
'Authority'
means prestige.
It means that if one is not respected,
one will have no prestige.
You might be harmed like that by Yùqiě.
This is a phrase from Zhāng Héng's *Dōngjīng Fù*.
The commentary states: The *Shuō Yuàn* says: King Wú wished to drink with the common people.
Wǔ Zǐxū remonstrated, saying:
'No, you must not.
Once, a white dragon descended into the clear, cold abyss,
transforming into a fish.
A fisherman named Yùqiě shot it in the eye.
The white dragon ascended to complain to the Heavenly Emperor.
The Emperor asked: "At that time,
how did you position your form?"
The white dragon replied: "I descended into the clear, cold abyss
and transformed into a fish."
The Heavenly Emperor said: "A fish is naturally something that people shoot.
What crime has Yùqiě committed!"
Now, the white dragon
was a noble animal of the Heavenly Emperor,
and Yùqiě
was a humble servant of the State of Sòng.
If the white dragon had not transformed,
Yùqiě would not have shot it.
If you now abandon your position of ten thousand chariots to drink with commoners,
your minister fears you may suffer the calamity of Yùqiě."
The king then stopped.
'Qiě'
is pronounced 'zǐyú' (子余).
Liú Jì was harmed by this.
The event is found in Volume 7, Second Year of Qín Èrshì.
Sūn Cè said:
"Your words are correct."
However, he could not change.
This serves as the groundwork for Sūn Cè's death from going out lightly.
In the ninth month,
Sītú Chúnyú Jiā, Tàiwèi Yáng Biāo, and Sīkōng Zhāng Xǐ were all dismissed.
When the imperial carriage moved east,
Yáng Fèng wanted to intercept it from Liáng,
but failed.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Cáo Cāo campaigned against Yáng Fèng.
Yáng Fèng fled south to Yuán Shù,
who then attacked his Liáng garrison
and captured it.
12 An imperial edict was sent down to Yuán Shào,
reproaching him
with, "Having vast territory and numerous troops,
yet you exclusively build up your own faction,
and no army to aid the emperor has been heard of.
You merely attack and punish each other."
This refers to his attacks on Gōngsūn Zàn.
On the day Wùchén,
Shào was appointed Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi)
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Yè.
Shào was ashamed to be ranked below Cáo Cāo
and angrily said,
"Cáo Cāo should have died many times,
but I always saved and preserved him.
After Cāo's defeat at Xíngyáng and Biànshuǐ,
he gathered his troops and followed Shào in Hénèi.
Shào memorialized for him to be made Administrator of Dōngjùn.
When Lǚ Bù attacked and seized Yǎnzhou,
Shào again allied with Cāo,
wishing to have him send his family to live in Yè."
Cāo declined the appointment in a memorial.
Cāo, afraid,
requested to yield the title of General-in-Chief (Dà Jiāngjūn) to Shào.
On the day Bǐngxū,
Cāo was appointed Minister of Works (Sīkōng),
acting as General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chēqí Jiāngjūn).
Cāo appointed Xún Yù as Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng)
and Defender of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Lìng).
Cāo asked Yù about strategists,
and Yù recommended his nephew, Xún Yōu, Administrator of Shǔjùn.
Yōu had escaped the calamity of Dǒng Zhuó,
was again recruited into a ducal office,
was nominated as a High Scholar,
and promoted to Chancellor of Rèncchéng,
but did not take up the post.
Considering Shǔ to be perilous and secure,
with a thriving population,
he requested to be Administrator of Shǔjùn.
The road was cut off,
so he could not reach it,
and stayed in Jīngzhōu.
(To follow,
cái yòng fān;
same below.)
Cāo summoned Yōu to be a Minister of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū).
When he spoke with him,
Cāo was greatly pleased,
saying,
"Gōngdá,
is no ordinary man!
(Xún Yōu,
courtesy name Gōngdá.)
What worry can there be for the world!"
He appointed him Military Advisor.
Initially,
Guō Jiā went to see Yuán Shào.
Shào treated him with great respect.
After several tens of days,
Jiā said to Shào's advisors Xīn Píng and Guō Tú,
"A wise man carefully assesses his lord;
thus, he is completely safe, and fame and success can be established.
Lord Yuán merely wishes to emulate the Duke of Zhōu in humble treatment of scholars,
but does not know the opportune moment for employing men.
He has many schemes but few essentials,
is fond of planning but lacks resolve.
It will be difficult to overcome the great difficulties of the world
and establish the enterprise of a hegemon with him.
I will seek another lord.
Why don't you also leave!"
The two men said,
"The Yuán clan has been benevolent and virtuous to the world,
and many people rally to them.
Moreover, they are currently the strongest.
Where will we go if we leave!"
Jiā knew they did not understand,
so he spoke no more,
and thereupon departed.
Cāo summoned him,
and discussed affairs of the world with him.
Cāo rejoiced, saying,
"The one who will help me achieve great things
must be this man!"
When Jiā came out,
he also rejoiced, saying,
"He is truly my lord!"
Cāo memorialized for Jiā to be Sīkōng Jìjiǔ.
Chén Shòu's Sānguó Zhì reads
"Sīkōng Jūnjìjiǔ"
(Minister of Works' Military Libationer);
this is missing
the character "jūn" (military).
The Jìn Zhì states: "When the ruling power achieved its ambition,
pacifying all of China,
they first established the Military Libationer (Jūnshī Jìjiǔ)
to participate in managing military regulations."
Cāo appointed Mǎn Chǒng of Shānyáng as Magistrate of Xǔ.
Cāo's cousin Hóng
had retainers who frequently violated the law in the Xǔ district.
Chǒng arrested and prosecuted them.
Hóng wrote to Chǒng.
("Bào" means
to inform.
The previous text,
Huò Xiǎn said,
'Young Master, please inform me of the matter.')
(Shù,
suǒ jiǎo fān.)
(Zhì,
zhí zhī fān.)
Hóng reported this to Cāo.
Cāo summoned the person in charge of Xǔ.
(The "person in charge" was
the chief clerk of Xǔ county.)
Thereupon, he quickly had them killed.
Cāo rejoiced, saying,
"Should one in office not act like this!"
13 Kǒng Róng, Administrator of Běihǎi,
relied on his lofty spirit
and was intent on pacifying the troubles,
but his talent was shallow and his ambition grand,
and ultimately he achieved no success.
(Qì means
ultimately,
or finally.)
(Nàn,
nǎi dàn fān.)
His writings overflowed in official documents,
his words and manner were pure
and elegant,
enjoyable to read and recite.
But in discussing matters and examining facts,
it was difficult to implement everything.
He could only cast wide nets,
but his reasoning was very lax.
He could win people's hearts quickly,
but after a long time, they were unwilling to attach themselves to him.
Those he employed
sought novelty and peculiarity,
and were mostly light-minded, minor talents.
As for honoring the famous Confucian Zhèng Xuán,
treating him with the rites due to a grandparent,
and changing the name of his local district to Zhèng Gōng Xiāng,
(Xuán's biography states: Róng deeply revered Xuán,
and instructed Gāomì County to specially establish a district for Xuán,
saying,
"In ancient Qí, there was a Scholar District,
and Yuè had a Gentleman Army;
both were for honoring worthies.
Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān, Grand Judge Wú Gōng, and Usher-Commander Dèng Gōng
were all famous officials of Han.
Moreover, the Four Graybeards of Mount Nánshān,
namely Yuán Gōng and Xià Huánggōng,
whose nobility was praised by their generation,
were all addressed as 'Gōng' (Duke).
Therefore, 'Gōng' is
the proper title for benevolence and virtue,
not necessarily restricted to the Three Ducal Ministers.
Now, Mr. Zhèng's district
should properly be called Zhèng Gōng Xiāng.")
All of this was merely to have him present in the assembly;
he did not discuss political affairs with him,
saying,
"This is the hope of the people;
it cannot be lost!"
When the Yellow Turbans came to raid,
Róng was defeated in battle
and fled to take refuge in Dūchāng.
(Xián says: Dūchāng County
belonged to Běihǎi Commandery.
Its ancient city was in the northeast of modern Línqú County, Qīngzhōu.)
Róng's troops were weak and provisions scarce.
He was isolated in a corner
and had no communication with others.
Zuǒ Chéngzǔ advised Róng to align himself with a strong state,
but Róng did not listen and killed him.
Liú Yìxùn abandoned him and left.
Yuán Tán, Inspector of Qīngzhōu, attacked Róng.
From spring to summer,
only a few hundred soldiers remained.
Stray arrows rained down,
yet Róng still leaned on his desk and read,
talking and laughing as usual.
The city fell during the night,
and he fled to Dōngshān.
(This was the Dōngshān of Dūchāng County.)
Cáo Cāo had an old acquaintance with Róng,
and summoned him to be Grand Minister of Works (Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng).
When Yuán Tán first arrived in Qīngzhōu,
its territory, west of the river,
did not extend beyond Píngyuán.
Tán pushed back Tián Kǎi to the north.
(Tián Kǎi
was appointed Inspector of Qīngzhōu by Gōngsūn Zàn.)
His might and benevolence were very evident.
Later, however, he trusted petty individuals
and indulged in extravagance and debauchery,
and his prestige consequently declined.
Since the middle of the Jiànníng (建寧) period in the 14th year,
the world had fallen into chaos and separation.
The people abandoned agriculture,
and various armies arose.
They generally lacked provisions of grain,
had no plans for the year's end,
and would plunder when hungry,
then discard the surplus when full.
They scattered and drifted apart,
with countless instances of armies breaking themselves without an enemy.
It was impossible to count them all.
Yuán Shào (袁紹) was in Hébĕi (河北),
and his soldiers subsisted on mulberry fruits.
Yuán Shù (袁術) was in Jiānghuái (江淮),
relying on cattail roots and shellfish for sustenance.
Many people resorted to cannibalism,
and the provinces and villages were desolate.
The Yǔlín (羽林) Supervisor, Zăo Zhī (棗祗), requested the establishment of agricultural garrisons (túntián 屯田).
An intellectual from Yĭngchuān (潁川) recorded: "The Zăo (棗) clan
was originally surnamed Jí (棘),
but changed it to avoid disaster."
A Hàn (漢) official description states: "The Yǔlín (羽林) had Left and Right Supervisors,
with a rank of 600 dàn (石) of grain,
subordinate to the Guānglùxūn (光祿勳)."
Zăo Zhī (棗祗) was appointed Túntián Dūwèi (屯田都尉),
and the Qí Dūwèi (騎都尉) Rèn Jùn (任峻) was appointed Diǎnnóng Zhōnglángjiàng (典農中郎將).
The Wèi Zhì (魏志) states: "Cáo Gōng (曹公) established Diǎnnóng Zhōnglángjiàng (典農中郎將),
with a rank of 2,000 dàn (石) of grain;
Diǎnnóng Dūwèi (典農都尉),
with a rank of 600 or 400 dàn (石);
Diǎnnóng Xiàowèi (典農校尉),
with a rank equivalent to 2,000 dàn (石) of grain,
whose duties were like those of a Zhōnglángjiàng (中郎);
the duties were divided and the scope was smaller for a Xiàowèi (校尉)."
A million hù (斛) of grain were obtained.
Thereupon, the prefectures and commanderies uniformly established agricultural officials,
accumulating grain everywhere,
and the granaries were all full.
Thus, when Cāo (操) campaigned in the four directions,
he had no labor of transporting provisions,
and was able to annex all the heroes.
The prosperity of the army and state
began with Zăo Zhī (棗祗) and was completed by Rèn Jùn (任峻).
Yuán Shù (袁術) feared that Lǚ Bù (呂布) would harm him,
so he sought a marriage alliance for his son,
and Bù (布) again agreed to it.
Shù (術) sent his general Jì Líng (紀靈) and others with 30,000 infantry and cavalry to attack Liú Bèi (劉備),
and Bèi (備) sought help from Bù (布).
His generals said to Bù (布):
"General, you have always wanted to kill Liú Bèi (劉備);
now you can use Shù (術) to do it."
Bù (布) said:
"Not so.
If Shù (術) defeats Bèi (備),
then he will connect northward with the generals in Tàishān (泰山).
The generals in Tàishān (泰山) refer to the likes of Zāng Bà (臧霸), Sūn Guān (孫觀), Wú Dūn (吳敦), and Yĭn Lĭ (尹禮).
We cannot but save him."
So he led over a thousand infantry and cavalry and galloped to their aid.
When Jì Líng (紀靈) and others heard of Bù's (布) arrival,
they all withdrew their troops and stopped.
Bù (布) encamped southwest of Pèi (沛) city,
and sent a Língxià (鈴下) to invite Jì Líng (紀靈) and others.
Língxià (鈴下)
means a soldier,
positioned beneath the bell-gate.
When an alert came, they would pull the bell to summon,
hence the name.
The Xù Hàn Zhì (續漢志) states: "The Wŭbăi (五百) and Língxià (鈴下),
attendants in the pavilions, gate-ramparts, deployments, and street runners,
all had regulated grades and ranks,
their number varying with their assigned duties."
Chéng Dàchāng's (程大昌) Xù Yănfánlù (續演繁露) states: "The Língxià (鈴下) in their awe-inspiring presence
are perhaps like today's officials for receiving guests."
Bù (布) went to them,
and they dined together with Bèi (備).
Bù (布) said to Jì Líng (紀靈) and others:
"Xuándé (玄德)
is my brother.
Liú Bèi's (劉備) courtesy name is Xuándé (玄德).
That is why I came to save him.
My nature is not to enjoy causing conflict;
I only enjoy resolving conflicts."
It means he did not like to bring people into conflict,
but liked to resolve people's conflicts.
Xǐ (喜)
is pronounced with the third tone.
Bù (布) drew his bow and looked around, saying:
"Gentlemen, watch me shoot the small branch of the halberd.
Xián (賢) said: The Zhōu Lǐ Kăogōng Jì (周禮考工記) states: 'For a halberd,
the blade is two inches wide,
the 'nèi' is twice that,
the 'hú' is three times it,
and the 'yuán' is four times it.'
Zhèng's (鄭) commentary states: 'Yuán (援) is the straight blade,
Hú (胡) is its small side blade.'
Xiăozhī (小支)
refers to Hú (胡),
which is today's curved side branch of a halberd.
Zhí (植),
pronounced with the second tone,
means to stand.
Shè (射),
pronounced with the fourth tone.
If I don't hit it, you can stay and fight it out."
Bù (布) immediately shot an arrow,
which struck directly the branch of the halberd.
Jì Líng (紀靈) and others were all astonished,
saying:
"General, this is heavenly might!"
The next day they held another joyous gathering,
and then each departed.
Bèi (備) gathered his troops and obtained over ten thousand men.
Bù (布) disliked this,
and personally led his troops to attack Bèi (備);
Bèi (備) was defeated and fled,
returning to Cáo Cāo (曹操).
Cāo (操) treated him generously,
appointing him Governor of Yùzhōu (豫州).
Someone said to Cāo (操):
"Bèi (備) has heroic ambitions.
If you do not deal with him early,
he will certainly become a problem later."
Cāo (操) asked Guō Jiā (郭嘉) about this,
and Jiā (嘉) said:
"That is true.
However, you raised an army of righteousness
to eliminate tyranny for the people,
and recruit exceptional talents by demonstrating sincerity and trustworthiness.
You still fear that this is not enough.
Now, Bèi (備) has a reputation as a hero;
if he returns to you in distress and you harm him,
this will be known as harming the worthy.
If this happens,
then wise scholars will become suspicious,
change their minds and choose another lord.
With whom will you then pacify the world?
Eliminating the trouble of one man at the cost of discouraging the hopes of the entire world
is a critical juncture for security or danger;
it must not be overlooked."
Cāo (操) laughed, saying:
"You have understood it!"
So he increased Bèi's (備) troops,
supplied him with provisions,
and sent him east to Pèi (沛)
to gather scattered soldiers and plan against Lǚ Bù (呂布).
Originally,
when Bèi (備) was in Yùzhōu (豫州),
he nominated Yuán Huàn (袁渙) from Chénjùn (陳郡) as Màocái (茂才).
In the sixth year of Wǔdì's (武帝) Yuánfēng (元封) reign,
an imperial edict commanded prefectures and commanderies to nominate Màocái (茂才).
Màocái (茂才)
is the same as Xiùcái (秀才);
to avoid the given name of Guāngwǔ (光武),
historians consequently wrote it as Màocái (茂才).
Bù (布) wanted Huàn (渙) to write a letter insulting Bèi (備),
but Huàn (渙) refused.
Bù (布) forced him repeatedly,
but he did not consent.
Bù (布) became furious
and threatened Huàn (渙) with soldiers, saying:
"Do it, and you live;
don't do it, and you die!"
Huàn's (渙) expression did not change;
he smiled and replied:
"I have heard that only virtue can humiliate a person,
not insults!
If he is truly a gentleman,
then he will not be shamed by the General's words;
if he is truly a petty man,
then he will return the General's sentiment.
It means if Bù (布) insults Bèi (備) in writing,
and Bèi (備) is a gentleman,
he will certainly not be shamed by the insult;
if he is a petty man,
he will return the insult in writing to Bù (布).
Moreover, my service to General Liú (劉) in the past
is like my service to the General today.
If I were to leave here one day
and then insult the General,
would that be acceptable?"
Bù (布) was ashamed and stopped.
Zhāng Jì (張濟), leading his troops from Guānzhōng (關中), entered the territory of Jīngzhōu (荊州),
attacking Rángchéng (穰城).
Ráng (穰) county
belonged to Nányáng (南陽) Commandery.
Jīngzhōu (荊州) officials all offered congratulations,
but Liú Biǎo (劉表) said:
"Jì (濟) came here in distress.
The host was discourteous.
It means there was no courtesy of welcoming them at the outskirts and providing lodging.
This is not my intention as Governor.
I accept condolences,
but not congratulations."
He sent people to receive Zhāng Jì's (張濟) multitude;
when the multitude heard this, they rejoiced
and all pledged their loyalty to him.
Jì's (濟) nephew, Jiànzhōng Jiāngjūn (建忠將軍) Zhāng Xiù (張繡), took over command of his forces
and garrisoned at Wăn (宛).
At first,
when the Emperor had left Cháng'ān,
Xuānwēi Jiāngjūn Jiǎ Xǔ surrendered his seals and ribbons,
and went to rely on Duàn Wēi in Huáyīn.
Jiǎ Xǔ had long been famous,
and was highly regarded by Duàn Wēi's army.
Duàn Wēi treated him with great courtesy and generosity.
Jiǎ Xǔ secretly planned to go over to Zhāng Xiù.
Someone asked:
"Duàn Wēi treats you very well,
where will you go if you leave him?"
Jiǎ Xǔ said:
"Duàn Wēi is by nature suspicious,
and has intentions to be wary of me.
Although his courtesy is great,
it cannot be relied upon for long;
I will be plotted against.
Since I am highly regarded by Duàn Wēi's army,
then I will certainly be feared by Duàn Wēi.
If I stay long, Duàn Wēi will fear that I will seize his army,
and will certainly plot to kill me.
Moreover, he hopes that I will establish strong external support,
and will certainly treat my wife and children well.
Zhāng Xiù has no strategist,
and also wishes to obtain me. Thus, my family and I will both be safe."
Jiǎ Xǔ then departed.
Zhāng Xiù treated him with the courtesy due to a son or grandson.
Duàn Wēi indeed treated Jiǎ Xǔ's family well.
Jiǎ Xǔ advised Zhāng Xiù to ally with Liú Biǎo,
and Zhāng Xiù followed his advice.
Jiǎ Xǔ went to see Liú Biǎo,
who treated him with the courtesy due to a guest.
Jiǎ Xǔ said:
"Liú Biǎo
has the talent of a Sāngōng in peaceful times,
but he does not perceive changes in events,
is often suspicious and indecisive.
He will achieve nothing!"
Liú Biǎo loved the people and nurtured scholars,
calmly preserving himself.
There were no troubles within his borders,
and scholars from Guānxī, Yǎn, and Yù who returned to him numbered in the thousands.
Liú Biǎo then established schools,
expounding on classical arts and doctrines.
He ordered the former Yǎyuè Láng, Dù Kuí from Hénán, to compose court music.
Cài Yōng said: "Han music has four categories:
first is Tàiyǔ Yuè, used for suburban sacrifices, ancestral temples, imperial tombs, and palace ceremonies;
second is Zhōusòng Yǎyuè, used for Bìyōng, banquets, archery contests, the Six Zōng, and altars of Soil and Grain;
third is Huángmén Gǔchuī,
which the Son of Heaven uses to entertain his officials;
fourth is Duǎnxiāo Náogē,
which is military music."
Liú Biǎo wished to observe it in his courtyard.
Dù Kuí said:
"Currently, the General's title is not that of the Son of Heaven.
To combine music and perform it in the courtyard,
would that not be improper?"
Liú Biǎo then stopped.
Ní Héng from Píngyuán,
young, possessed talent and eloquence,
but was arrogant and haughty.
Kǒng Róng recommended him to Cáo Cāo.
Ní Héng insulted Cáo Cāo.
Cáo Cāo summoned Ní Héng to be a drummer,
and was again insulted by Ní Héng.
Cáo Cāo said to Kǒng Róng:
"Ní Héng, that boy,
if I kill him,
it would be like killing a sparrow or a mouse!
But this man has an undeserved reputation,
and people far and near will say that I cannot tolerate him."
So he sent him to Liú Biǎo.
Liú Biǎo extended him courtesy and treated him as an honored guest.
Ní Héng praised Liú Biǎo's virtues to no end,
but loved to mock and criticize his retainers.
Thereupon, his retainers slandered him based on his actions, saying:
"Ní Héng praises the General's benevolence,
saying Xībó was no better.
He only believes you cannot make decisions,
and will ultimately fail,
and that this is precisely why."
These words actually pointed out Liú Biǎo's shortcomings,
but were not what Ní Héng had said.
Liú Biǎo was angered by this,
and knowing that Huáng Zǔ, the Grand Administrator of Jiāngxià, was impetuous,
sent Ní Héng to him.
Huáng Zǔ also treated him well.
Later, Ní Héng publicly insulted Huáng Zǔ,
and Huáng Zǔ killed him.
Cáo Cāo, angered by Ní Héng, sent him to Liú Biǎo,
still considering Liú Biǎo to be broad-minded and fond of scholars,
observing whether he could tolerate him or not.
Liú Biǎo, angered by Ní Héng, sent him to Huáng Zǔ,
knowing that Huáng Zǔ was impetuous,
and would certainly not be able to tolerate Ní Héng.
This was simply to put him to death.
Both men used cunning and stratagem,
but Liú Biǎo was shallow.
1 In spring,
the first month,
Cáo Cāo attacked Zhāng Xiù.
His army was at Yùshuǐ.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: Yùshuǐ flows from Gōnglí Mountain in Lúshì County, Hóngnóng,
and passes south of Wǎn County to the east,
which is where Cáo Cāo's army was defeated.
Yù
is pronounced yù.
Cáo Cāo took Zhāng Jì's wife,
and Zhāng Xiù resented it.
Cáo Cāo also gave gold to Zhāng Xiù's fierce general Hú Chē'ér.
Zhāng Xiù, hearing this, became suspicious and fearful,
and launched a surprise attack on Cáo Cāo's army,
killing Cáo Cāo's eldest son, Áng.
Cáo Cāo was hit by a stray arrow
and fled in defeat.
School Captain Diǎn Wéi fought fiercely against Zhāng Xiù's forces.
Almost all his左右 guards died or were wounded.
Diǎn Wéi suffered dozens of wounds.
Zhāng Xiù's soldiers pressed forward to grapple with him.
Diǎn Wéi, holding two men under his arms, killed them,
glared with wide eyes, cursed loudly, and died.
Cáo Cāo gathered his scattered troops
and returned to Wǔyīn.
Wǔyīn County
belonged to Nányáng Commandery.
Cáo Cāo defeated Zhāng Xiù,
who fled back to Ráng,
and reunited with Liú Biǎo.
At this time,
the various armies were in great disorder.
Pínglǔ Xiàowèi Yú Jìn from Tàishān alone kept his troops organized and returned.
On the way, he encountered Qīngzhōu soldiers looting people.
Yú Jìn enumerated their crimes and attacked them.
The Qīngzhōu soldiers fled
and went to Cáo Cāo to complain.
After Yú Jìn arrived,
he first established camp and fortifications,
and did not immediately go to see Cáo Cāo.
Someone said to Yú Jìn:
"The Qīngzhōu soldiers have already accused you.
You should hurry to His Lord and explain."
Yú Jìn said:
"The enemy is still behind us,
and may pursue us at any time.
If we do not first prepare,
how can we face the enemy?
Moreover, His Lord is intelligent,
how can slander succeed?"
Slowly, he dug trenches and secured the camp. After this was done,
he then entered to see Cáo Cāo
and fully explained the situation.
Cáo Cāo was pleased
and said to Yú Jìn:
"In the disaster at Yùshuǐ,
I was still in disarray.
General, in the midst of chaos, you were able to keep order,
punish the violent and strengthen your defenses.
'Punish the violent'
refers to attacking the looters.
'Strengthen your defenses'
refers to first digging trenches and securing the camp.
Even ancient famous generals,
how could they surpass this!"
Thereupon, Cáo Cāo recorded Yú Jìn's past and present merits,
and enfeoffed him as Yìshòu Tínghóu.
Cáo Cāo led his army back to Xǔ.
2 Yuán Shào sent a letter to Cáo Cāo,
its language arrogant and rude.
Cáo Cāo said to Xún Yù and Guō Jiā:
"Now I am about to punish the unrighteous, but my strength is not equal to his.
What should I do?"
They replied:
"That Liú Bāng and Xiàng Yǔ were not equally matched
is known to you, my lord.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn only surpassed Xiàng Yǔ in wisdom,
thus though Yǔ was strong,
he was eventually captured by him.
Now, Shào has ten weaknesses,
and you, my lord, have ten strengths.
Although Shào is strong,
he can accomplish nothing.
Shào is excessively formal and ceremonial,
while you, my lord, act naturally and are at ease;
this is a victory of the Way.
Shào acts perversely,
while you, my lord, uphold righteousness to lead the world;
it means upholding the Son of Heaven to lead the world,
which is righteous in principle.
Since the time of Huán and Líng,
government has erred on the side of leniency.
Shào remedies leniency with more leniency,
thus he cannot control himself.
Shè
means to manage.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says: 'It was recorded for the attack on Qín,'
meaning it was managed.
Dù Yù's commentary says: 'Able to control and manage oneself.'
Superiors and subordinates know their limits;
this is a victory in governance.
Shào is outwardly lenient but inwardly jealous,
he uses people but doubts them,
relying only on relatives and younger brothers.
You, my lord, are outwardly simple and easygoing but inwardly sharp and clear-sighted,
you use people without doubt,
only considering what is appropriate for their talent,
without distinguishing between near and far;
this is a victory of magnanimity.
Shào has many schemes but little resolution,
failing in subsequent matters.
You, my lord, act immediately upon forming a plan,
responding to changes endlessly;
this is a victory of strategy.
Shào engages in lofty discussions and shows deference to gain fame and reputation.
Many scholars who are good at superficial embellishment flock to him.
You, my lord, treat people with sincerity,
not engaging in false courtesies.
Loyal, upright, far-sighted, and substantial scholars all wish to serve you;
this is a victory of virtue.
Shào, seeing people cold and hungry,
shows concern for them,
manifest in his countenance.
What he does not see,
his consideration may not reach.
You, my lord, sometimes overlook
small matters before your eyes,
but when it comes to major affairs,
reaching all corners of the land,
the grace you bestow
always exceeds their expectations.
Even what you do not see,
your consideration is unfailingly thorough;
this is a victory of benevolence.
Shào's chief ministers contend for power,
and slanderous words cause confusion.
You, my lord, govern your subordinates with the Way,
insidious slanders do not prevail;
this is a victory of discernment.
The Lún Yǔ says: 'When insinuating slander does not prevail,
one may be called discerning.'
It means those who slander others are like water soaking in gradually.
What you, my lord, approve, you advance with propriety;
what you disapprove, you rectify with law;
this is a victory of refinement.
Shào loves to put on an empty show of power,
and does not understand the essentials of military affairs.
Xún Zǐ discussed military essentials with Línwǔ Jūn before King Xiàochéng of Zhào.
The King said:
'May I ask about the essentials of warfare?'
You, my lord, use troops like a god,
your soldiers rely on you,
and your enemies fear you;
this is a victory of military prowess."
Cáo Cāo smiled and said:
"If it is as you, my lords, say,
what virtue do I possess to merit such praise!"
Guō Jiā further said:
"Shào is about to attack Gōngsūn Zàn in the north.
You can take advantage of his distant campaign
to seize Lǚ Bù in the east.
If Shào becomes an enemy,
and Bù supports him,
this would be a serious harm."
Xún Yù said:
"If Lǚ Bù is not taken first,
Héběi will not be easy to conquer."
Shào attacked Gōngsūn Zàn,
and Cáo Cāo seized the opportunity to take Lǚ Bù in the east.
Cáo Cāo attacked Liú Bèi,
and Shào could not raid Xǔ.
This is why he failed.
Yì,
pronounced like shǐ.
"However,"
Cáo Cāo continued, "what troubles me is
that I also fear Shào might invade and harass Guānzhōng,
stir up trouble among the Qiāng and Hú in the west,
and lure Shǔ Hàn in the south.
This would mean I alone would resist five-sixths of the world with Yǎn and Yù.
What should my generals do?"
Xún Yù replied:
"There are dozens of generals and commanders in Guānzhōng,
none of whom can unite them.
Only Hán Suí and Mǎ Téng are the strongest.
Seeing the contention in Shāndōng,
they will surely each gather their forces to protect themselves.
If you now appease them with kindness and virtue,
send envoys to form an alliance,
although it cannot last long,
it will be sufficient for you, my lord, to stabilize Shāndōng
without their interference.
Suí
and Téng's defection and submission
eventually turned out as Xún Yù predicted.
Bǐ,
pronounced like bì mèi.
If you entrust them with the western affairs,
you, my lord, will have no worries."
Cáo Cāo then memorialized Yáo to be appointed as Grandee Remonstrant and acting Commandant of the Capital,
holding a staff of authority to supervise all armies in Guānzhōng,
with special permission to disregard regulations.
When Yáo arrived in Cháng'ān,
he sent letters to Téng, Suí, and others.
Yí
means to send.
Téng and Suí each sent their sons to serve at court.
3 Yuán Shù proclaimed himself emperor in Shòuchūn,
calling his dynasty Zhòngjiā.
He appointed the Administrator of Jiǔjiāng as the Governor of Huáinán,
established dukes, ministers, and all officials,
and performed sacrifices to heaven and earth in the suburbs.
Chén Guī, the Administrator of Pèi,
a disciple of Qiú,
had been acquainted with Shù in his youth.
Shù summoned Guī by letter,
and also seized his son as a hostage,
determined to compel Guī to come.
Guī replied by letter, saying:
"General Cáo is restoring the old order,
and will clear away the wicked and violent.
I thought Your Excellency would exert yourself with one heart
to assist the Hàn court.
Instead, you secretly plot rebellion,
bringing disaster upon yourself.
You want me to seek personal gain and fawn upon you?
I would rather die!"
Shù wanted to make Jīn Shàng, the former Inspector of Yǎnzhōu, Grand Commandant,
but Shàng refused and fled.
Shù killed him.
Jīn Shàng's flight to Shù is seen in Volume 60, Chūpíng year 3.
4 In the third month,
an imperial edict appointed Kǒng Róng, the Grand Architect, to hold a staff of authority and formally appoint Yuán Shào as Commander-in-Chief,
concurrently overseeing the four provinces of Jì, Qīng, Yōu, and Bīng.
5 In summer,
the fifth month,
there was a locust plague.
6 Yuán Shù sent the envoy Hán Yìn to inform Lǚ Bù of his imperial proclamation,
and then asked for a bride for his son.
Bù sent his daughter with him.
Chén Guī feared that Xú and Yáng would form an alliance,
and the troubles would be endless.
Shù governed Yángzhōu,
Bù governed Xúzhōu.
Cóng,
pronounced like zī róng.
Nàn,
pronounced like nǎi dàn.
(Guī said:) "Duke Cáo welcomes the Son of Heaven,
assisting in national governance.
The general should cooperate with him in strategy,
and together preserve the great plan.
Now, if you form a marriage alliance with Yuán Shù,
you will surely gain a name for unrighteousness,
and face a danger like eggs piled up!"
Bù also resented that Shù had not accepted him initially;
this event is seen in Volume 60, Chūpíng year 3.
So he recalled his daughter and broke off the marriage,
arrested Hán Yìn,
and displayed his head in Xǔ market.
Chén Guī wished to send his son Chén Dēng to meet Cáo Cāo,
but Lǚ Bù adamantly refused.
It happened that an imperial edict appointed Lǚ Bù Left General.
Cáo Cāo then sent Lǚ Bù a handwritten letter,
offering deep solace and acceptance.
Lǚ Bù was greatly pleased,
and immediately dispatched Chén Dēng to present a memorial of thanks for the imperial favor,
and also to reply to Cáo Cāo's letter.
When Chén Dēng met Cáo Cāo,
he took the opportunity to state that Lǚ Bù was brave but lacked strategy,
was light in his loyalties,
and that he should be dealt with swiftly.
Cáo Cāo said:
"Lǚ Bù is a wolf-cub with a wild heart,
truly difficult to keep for long.
Without you, none could discern his true character."
He immediately increased Chén Guī's rank to two thousand *dàn* (石) (Middle Two Thousand *Dàn*).
According to the Hàn system: the Chancellor (*xiàng*) of a kingdom held the rank of two thousand *dàn*.
To increase the rank to Middle Two Thousand *Dàn*
meant the rank was equivalent to that of the Nine Ministers (*jiǔ qīng*).
As they parted,
Cáo Cāo held Chén Dēng's hand and said:
"The affairs of the East
I now entrust to you."
He ordered him to secretly gather his forces to act as an internal aid.
Initially,
Lǚ Bù had sought the governorship of Xúzhōu through Chén Dēng but did not obtain it.
When Chén Dēng returned,
Lǚ Bù was enraged.
He pulled out a *jǐ* (halberd) and chopped at a table, saying:
"Your father persuaded me to ally with Cáo Cāo
and break off the marriage alliance with Gōnglù (Yuán Shù's courtesy name);
now I have gained nothing of what I sought,
while you and your father are both prominently honored.
I have simply been sold out by you!"
Chén Dēng did not change his expression,
and slowly replied:
"I told Duke Cáo: 'Nurturing General Lǚ Bù is like nurturing a tiger;
one must sate it with meat,
for if it is not sated, it will surely devour people.'
The Duke said: 'What you say is not so.
It is like nurturing a hawk;
when it is hungry, it is useful,
but when it is full, it will fly away.'
Such were his words."
Lǚ Bù's anger then dissipated.
Yuán Shù dispatched his major generals Zhāng Xūn, Qiáo Ruì, and others, who joined forces with Hán Xiān and Yáng Fèng,
and with tens of thousands of infantry and cavalry, headed for Xiàpī,
attacking Lǚ Bù via seven routes.
At that time, Lǚ Bù had three thousand soldiers
and four hundred horses.
Fearing he could not resist them,
he said to Chén Guī:
"The arrival of Yuán Shù's army
is your doing.
What is to be done?"
Chén Guī said:
"Xiān and Fèng, and Shù,
are but a hastily assembled force.
Their plans are not pre-determined,
and they cannot hold together.
Your son Dēng's strategy regarding them
likens them to 'tied-together chickens',
unable to roost together.
The *Zhàn Guó Cè* states: King Huì of Qín said:
'The inability of the feudal lords to unite
is like tied-together chickens being unable to all get onto the roost.' "
Lǚ Bù adopted Chén Guī's plan,
and sent a letter to Xiān and Fèng saying:
"You two generals personally rescued the Grand Chariot (Emperor),
and I, Lǚ Bù, personally killed Dǒng Zhuó.
We both established great achievements.
How can we now conspire with Yuán Shù and act as bandits?
It is better that we combine our strength to defeat Shù
and rid the nation of this menace."
He also promised to give them all of Yuán Shù's military resources.
Xiān and Fèng were greatly pleased,
and immediately reversed their strategy and sided with Lǚ Bù.
Lǚ Bù advanced his army,
stopping a hundred paces from Zhāng Xūn's camp.
Xiān and Fèng's soldiers simultaneously shouted
and advanced on Zhāng Xūn's camp.
Zhāng Xūn and his men scattered and fled.
Lǚ Bù's soldiers pursued and attacked,
beheading ten of their generals.
Nearly all of those killed, wounded, or drowned in the water perished.
Lǚ Bù then joined forces with Xiān and Fèng and marched towards Shòuchūn,
advancing by both land and water.
When they reached Zhōnglí,
Zhōnglí county,
belonged to Jiǔjiāng Commandery,
over two hundred *lǐ* from Shòuchūn.
They then crossed back north of the Huái River,
and left a letter insulting Yuán Shù.
Yuán Shù personally led five thousand infantry and cavalry, displaying his forces along the Huái River.
Lǚ Bù's cavalry all laughed loudly at him from the north bank of the river before returning.
Zāng Bà, the leader of the bandits in Tàishān, attacked Xiāo Jiàn, the Chancellor of Lángyá, at Jǔ.
In the Former Hàn, Jǔ county
belonged to Chéngyáng Kingdom;
in the Later Hàn, it belonged to Lángyá Kingdom.
*Shuài* (帥),
pronounced *suǒ lèi fān*.
Zāng Bà obtained Xiāo Jiàn's resources
and promised to bribe Lǚ Bù but had not yet sent it.
Lǚ Bù went personally to demand it.
His commander Gāo Shùn remonstrated:
"Your general's formidable reputation is widespread,
feared by near and far.
Is there anything you cannot obtain
that you must personally go to demand a bribe?
If, by any chance, you do not succeed,
would it not be a loss of face!"
Lǚ Bù did not heed him.
When they arrived at Jǔ,
Zāng Bà and his men could not discern his intent
and resolutely held their ground and resisted him.
He returned without gaining anything.
Gāo Shùn was a man of integrity and dignity,
with few words.
The more than seven hundred soldiers he commanded
were disciplined and well-ordered.
Each battle he fought, he surely won,
earning him the name
"Breaker of Formations Camp."
Lǚ Bù later alienated Gāo Shùn.
Because Wèi Xù was related to him both inside and outside the family,
he took Gāo Shùn's troops and gave them to Wèi Xù.
Yet when it came to attacking and fighting,
he would again order Gāo Shùn to lead.
Gāo Shùn, however, never bore any resentment.
Lǚ Bù alienated Gāo Shùn yet favored Wèi Xù;
it was Wèi Xù who later seized Gāo Shùn, leading to Lǚ Bù's defeat.
*Jiāng* (將),
pronounced *jí liàng fān*.
Lǚ Bù's actions were inconsistent,
and Gāo Shùn often admonished him, saying:
"General, in your actions,
you are unwilling to consider deeply.
Suddenly there are gains and losses,
and you always say 'it was a mistake'.
How can mistakes be counted so often!"
Lǚ Bù knew of his loyalty but could not follow his advice.
Cáo Cāo dispatched the Imperial Counselor (Yìláng) Wáng Bù
with an imperial edict to appoint Sūn Cè as Commandant of Cavalry (*Jì Dūwèi*)
and hereditary Marquis of Wūchéng.
Sūn Cè's father, Sūn Jiān,
was enfeoffed as Marquis of Wūchéng for his meritorious service in suppressing bandits.
Wūchéng county
belonged to Wú Commandery,
now Ānjí Prefecture.
*Kǎo Yì* states: *Jiāng Biǎo Zhuàn* says:
"In the summer of the second year of Jiàn'ān [197 CE],
Wáng Bù presented an imperial edict of *Wùchén* to Sūn Cè."
The specific month is unknown.
The envoy was also to work with Lǚ Bù and Chén Yǔ, the Administrator of Wú Commandery, to jointly attack Yuán Shù.
Sūn Cè wished to obtain a general's title to enhance his standing,
and Wáng Bù, acting on imperial authority, provisionally appointed Sūn Cè General Who Makes the Hàn Manifest (*Míng Hàn Jiāngjūn*).
General Who Makes the Hàn Manifest
was also a provisional title created for expediency,
meaning to clarify loyalty and disloyalty
and acknowledge the veneration of the Hàn dynasty.
Similarly below for "Assistant to the Hàn".
Sūn Cè prepared his equipment.
*Yán* (嚴),
means "to prepare".
Qiántáng county,
in the Former Hàn, belonged to Kuàijī Commandery;
in the Later Hàn, its territory was abolished,
and it should have belonged to Wú Commandery.
*Qiántáng Jì* states: In the past, Huá Xìn, a Judicial Officer of the Commandery, proposed building this dike to prevent the sea,
recruiting those who could bring one *hú* of earth,
and offering one thousand coins.
Within ten days or a month, those who came gathered like clouds.
Before the dike was completed, no more earth was collected,
so those carrying earth and stones
all abandoned them and left.
The dike was thus completed,
hence the name Qiántáng (Money Dike).
He secretly allied with Zǔ Láng, Yán Báihǔ, and others,
to act as internal supporters.
Sūn Cè realized this,
and sent his generals Lǚ Fàn and Xú Yì to attack Chén Yǔ at Hǎixī.
Chén Yǔ was defeated
and fled alone on horseback to Yuán Shào.
8 Initially,
Chén Wáng Chǒng (陳王寵) was courageous
and skilled in crossbow archery.
Chǒng (寵)
was the great-grandson of Míng Dì (明帝)'s son, Chén Jìng Wáng Xiàn (陳敬王羨).
Chǒng (寵) raised troops to defend himself,
and the people of his state feared him,
not daring to rebel.
The state chancellor, Kuàijī Luò Jùn (會稽駱俊), had always commanded respect and kindness.
At this time, kings and marquises no longer received rents or salaries,
and were often captured and plundered.
Some ate only every other day,
and many died in ditches.
However, Chén (陳) alone was rich and strong,
and many people from neighboring commanderies came to him,
having a force of over 100,000.
When the provincial and commandery troops rose,
Chǒng (寵) led his forces to garrison Yángxià (陽夏).
Xián (賢) said: Yángxià (陽夏) County
belonged to Huáiyáng (淮陽) State.
Xià (夏)
is pronounced "gōng yǎ fān."
Yuán Shù (袁術) sought grain from Chén (陳),
but Luò Jùn (駱俊) refused him.
Shù (術) became enraged,
and sent assassins to murder Jùn (俊) and Chǒng (寵).
Chén (陳) was thus defeated.
9 In autumn,
the ninth month,
Sīkōng (司空) Cáo Cāo (曹操) marched east to attack Yuán Shù (袁術).
When Shù (術) heard of Cāo (操)'s arrival,
he abandoned his army and fled,
leaving his general Qiáo Ruí (橋蕤) and others at Qíyáng (蘄陽) to resist Cāo (操).
Xián (賢) said: Qí (蘄) River originates from the northern mountains of Qíchūn (蘄春) County in Jiāngxià (江夏).
The "Shuǐ Jīng Zhù" (水經註) says: This is Qí Shān (蘄山) itself.
It flows southwest past Qí Shān (蘄山),
then south opposite Qíyáng (蘄陽),
emptying into the Great River.
It is also called Qíyáng Kǒu (蘄陽口).
I, based on "Sān Guó Zhì" (三國志),
believe that Shù (術) was invading Chén (陳) at the time,
Cāo (操) marched east to attack him,
Shù (術) left Ruí (蕤) and others to resist Cāo (操),
Ruí (蕤) and others were defeated and died,
and Shù (術) then fled across the Huái (淮) River.
Thus, the battle must have been fought outside the Huái (淮),
how could it have reached Qíyáng (蘄陽) of Jiāngxià (江夏)!
This must be Qí (蘄) County of Pèi (沛) Commandery.
Fàn Shǐ (范史) erroneously used the character Yáng (陽),
and the "Tōng Jiàn" (通鑑) followed it.
All were executed.
The "Kǎo Yì" (考異) says: The "Fàn Shū" (范書) biography of Lǚ Bù (呂布) says:
"Bù (布) defeated Zhāng Xūn (張勳) at Xiàpī (下邳)
and captured Qiáo Ruí (橋蕤) alive."
Is this another Qiáo Ruí (橋蕤), or was general Ruí (蕤) captured and then returned?
However, the "Wèi Zhì" (魏志) biography of Lǚ Bù (呂布) has no mention of Qiáo Ruí (橋蕤).
This must be an error in the "Fàn Shū" (范書).
At that time, there was a drought and a famine,
and the soldiers and common people suffered from cold and hunger.
Shù (術) consequently declined.
Cāo (操) invited Hé Kuí (何夔) of Chén (陳) State to be his aide.
He asked him what he thought of Yuán Shù (袁術).
Kuí (夔) replied:
"What Heaven aids is compliance;
what people aid is trustworthiness.
Shù (術) lacks the substance of trustworthiness and compliance, yet he hopes for the aid of Heaven and men.
How can he achieve it!"
Cāo (操) said:
"A state that loses its worthy men perishes.
You were not employed by Shù (術),
so his downfall
is not inappropriate, is it!"
Cāo (操) was severe by nature,
and his aides were often flogged for official matters.
Kuí (夔) always kept poison,
vowing to die rather than be disgraced,
and thus was never affected.
Xǔ Chǔ (許褚) of Pèi (沛) Commandery,
whose bravery and strength surpassed others,
gathered several thousand young men and relatives,
fortified their walls to resist foreign invaders.
The area between Huái (淮), Rǔ (汝), Chén (陳), and Liáng (梁) all feared him.
Cāo (操) marched through Huái (淮) and Rǔ (汝),
and Chǔ (褚) submitted to Cāo (操) with his forces.
Cāo (操) said:
"This is my Fán Kuài (樊噲)!"
On that day, he was appointed Dūwèi (都尉)
and brought into the imperial guard.
All the chivalrous men who followed Chǔ (褚)
were made "Tiger Warriors."
10 The former Tàiwèi (太尉) Yáng Biāo (楊彪) was related by marriage to Yuán Shù (袁術).
According to Biāo (彪)'s biography,
Biāo (彪)'s son Xiū (脩)
was Yuán Shù (袁術)'s nephew.
Biāo (彪) must have married into the Yuán (袁) clan.
He was falsely accused of attempting to depose and enthrone an emperor,
arrested and imprisoned,
and impeached for high treason.
Jiāngzuò Dàjiàng (將作大匠) Kǒng Róng (孔融) heard of this,
and without even changing into court attire,
went to see Cāo (操) and said:
"Duke Yáng (楊公) comes from four generations of pure virtue—
Zhèn (震), Bǐng (秉), Cì (賜), and Biāo (彪)—
four generations renowned for their integrity.
The 'Zhōu Shū' (周書) states that
fathers, sons, and brothers
are not implicated in each other's crimes.
How much less can one implicate Duke Yáng (楊公) with the Yuán (袁) clan's crimes!"
Cāo (操) said:
"This is the intention of the state."
Guójiā (國家)
refers to the Emperor.
"If King Chéng (成王) had killed Shào Gōng (召公),
could Zhōu Gōng (周公) have claimed ignorance!"
Cāo (操) ordered Xǔ Lìng (許令) Mǎn Chǒng (滿寵) to preside over Biāo (彪)'s case.
Róng (融) and Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令) Xún Yù (荀彧) both instructed Chǒng (寵), saying:
"Simply take down his statements,
do not apply torture."
Chǒng (寵) reported nothing,
and interrogated him according to the law.
After several days,
he sought an audience with Cāo (操)
and said:
"During Yáng Biāo (楊彪)'s interrogation,
there were no other statements.
This man is famous throughout the realm.
If his guilt is not made clear,
it will greatly disappoint the people.
I secretly regret this for you, illustrious Duke."
Cāo (操) immediately pardoned and released Biāo (彪) that day.
Initially,
Yù (彧) and Róng (融) were both angry
when they heard that Chǒng (寵) had tortured Biāo (彪).
But when Biāo (彪) was released because of this,
they became even more favorably disposed towards Chǒng (寵).
Biāo (彪), seeing the decline of the Hàn (漢) dynasty
and that power lay with the Cáo (曹) clan,
feigned a leg ailment,
and for over ten years did not walk,
thus escaping misfortune.
11 When Mǎ Rìdī (馬日磾)'s coffin arrived in the capital,
Rìdī (日磾) died,
see volume 61, Xīngpíng (興平) first year.
Dī (磾)
is pronounced "dīng xī fān."
Kǒng Róng (孔融) said:
"Rìdī (日磾), with the esteemed rank of Tàishī (太師) (the highest of the three ducal ministers)
and bearing the insignia of an envoy,
yet crookedly flattered treacherous ministers
and was led by them.
How can high officials of the imperial house
use being coerced as an excuse!
His Majesty sympathizes with old officials
and cannot bear to investigate further,
so it is not appropriate to bestow more rites upon him."
The court followed this.
When Jīn Shàng (金尚)'s coffin arrived in the capital,
an edict ordered all officials to mourn and offer sacrifices,
and appointed his son Wěi (瑋) as Lángzhōng (郎中).
12 In winter,
the eleventh month,
Cáo Cāo (曹操) again attacked Zhāng Xiù (張繡),
capturing Húyáng (湖陽).
Húyáng (湖陽) County
belonged to Nányáng (南陽) Commandery.
He also attacked Wǔyīn (舞陰)
and took it.
13 Hán Xiān (韓暹) and Yáng Fèng (楊奉) were at Xiàpī (下邳),
plundering between Xú (徐) and Yáng (揚).
Their army was starving,
so they bade farewell to Lǚ Bù (呂布),
intending to go to Jīngzhōu (荊州).
Bù (布) did not permit it.
Fèng (奉), knowing that Liú Bèi (劉備) had a long-standing grudge against Bù (布),
secretly contacted Bèi (備),
wishing to attack Bù (布) together.
Bèi (備) pretended to agree.
Fèng (奉) led his army to Pèi (沛).
Bèi (備) invited Fèng (奉) into the city.
Before half the meal was finished,
he bound Fèng (奉) at the table
and executed him.
Xiān (暹), having lost Fèng (奉),
was isolated.
He returned to Bìngzhōu (幷州) with over ten horsemen
and was killed by Zhùqiū (杼秋) Magistrate Zhāng Xuān (張宣).
Zhùqiū (杼秋) County,
in the Former Hàn (漢) belonged to Liáng (梁) State,
in the Later Hàn (漢) belonged to Pèi (沛) Commandery.
Shīgǔ (師古) said: Zhù (杼)
is pronounced "shí rǔ fān."
Cáo Cāo (曹操)'s enemy,
Lè (樂), died of illness.
Guō Sì (郭汜) was killed by his general Wǔ Xí (伍習).
14 Dù Xí, Zhào Yǎn, Fán Qīn of Yǐngchuān, fleeing the turmoil, took refuge in Jīngzhōu,
and Liú Biǎo treated them all with guest rites.
Qīn was repeatedly recognized by Biǎo for his unusual talent.
Xí admonished him, saying:
"The reason I came with you
is simply to preserve ourselves and wait for the right moment.
How could we expect Governor Liú to be the lord who restores order and entrust ourselves to him as a worthy elder?
If you don't cease displaying your abilities,
you are not one of my kind,
and I will break off with you!"
Qīn said with a sigh,
"I shall respectfully obey!"
When Cáo Cāo welcomed the Son of Heaven to the capital at Xǔ,
Yǎn said to Qīn,
"General Zhèn Dōng Cáo will surely be able to restore and save Huáxià."
(The following is the same.)
"I know where to return!"
So, he returned to Cāo,
and Cāo appointed Yǎn as the Chief of Lánglíng.
Lánglíng county
belonged to Rǔnán commandery.
(Zhǎng,
pronounced "zhī liǎng fān.")
Lǐ Tōng of Jiāngxià, Commandant of Yáng'ān, had a maternal uncle who committed a crime.
Cāo divided two counties of Rǔnán to establish the Commandant of Yáng'ān.
He was condemned to death.
At that time, the power of life and death
was decided by the governors and prefects.
Tōng's wife and children wept and pleaded for his life.
Tōng said,
"I am currently working with Lord Cáo;
it would be unrighteous to forsake public duty for private interests!"
He admired Yǎn for upholding the law impartially
and became close friends with him.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
Cáo Cāo returned to Xǔ.
(He had attacked Zhāng Xiù and then returned.)
He was about to attack Zhāng Xiù again.
Xún Yōu said,
"Xiù and Liú Biǎo rely on each other for strength;
however, Xiù, as a mobile force, depends on Biǎo for provisions,
and Biǎo cannot supply him.
Their alliance will inevitably break down.
It is better to slow our advance and wait for this to happen;
we can lure him out.
If we press him,
they will inevitably come to each other's rescue."
Cāo did not follow this advice
and besieged Xiù at Ráng.
2 In summer,
in the fourth month,
he sent the Court Attendant 僕射 (Púshè) Péi Mào.
(Family genealogy: A descendant of Bó Yì,
enfeoffed in Xiāng,
thus taking it as his surname.
Later moved and enfeoffed in Jiěyì,
so he removed
"yì"
and adopted
exterminated his three clans.
Thus, all of Dǒng Zhuó's faction
was eliminated.
(Wēi,
pronounced "wū huí fān."
Què,
pronounced "gǔ yuè fān.")
He was enfeoffed as Marquis of Wénxiāng.
3 Previously,
whenever Yuán Shào received imperial edicts,
he worried about those that were not convenient for him.
He wanted to move the Son of Heaven closer to himself,
so he sent someone to persuade Cáo Cāo that Xǔxià was low and damp,
and Luòyáng was ruined.
It would be better to move the capital to Juǎnchéng to achieve full security.
Cāo rejected this.
Tián Fēng persuaded Shào, saying,
"Since the plan to move the capital
has not been adopted,
you should quickly plan to attack Xǔ,
welcome the Son of Heaven,
and act by imperial edicts
to issue commands to all within the seas.
This is the best strategy.
Otherwise,
you will eventually be captured by others,
and regret will be useless."
Shào did not follow.
At this time, some of Shào's deserters went to Cāo
and said that Tián Fēng had advised Shào to attack Xǔ.
Cāo lifted the siege of Ráng and returned,
and Zhāng Xiù led his troops to pursue him.
In the fifth month,
Liú Biǎo sent troops to aid Xiù,
stationing them at Ānzhòng
to guard the dangerous pass and cut off the army's rear.
(Shuǐ Jīng Zhù: Méixī River originates from Zǐshān north of Wǎn county, Nányáng,
flows south past the east of Dùyǎn county.
The land is low-lying,
and rapid streams flow into it.
Ancient people dammed it at Ānzhòng
to collect the circulating water,
calling it Ānzhònggǎng.
Jùn Guó Zhì: Nányáng Commandery has Ānzhòng侯國 (Hóuguó).)
"When I reach Ānzhòng,
I will surely defeat Xiù."
When he arrived at Ānzhòng,
Cāo's army was attacked from front and rear.
Cāo then secretly dug through the dangerous terrain at night and feigned retreat.
Biǎo and Xiù pursued with their entire armies.
Cāo deployed elite cavalry and infantry for a pincer attack,
decisively defeating them.
Another day,
Xún Yù asked Cāo,
"Why were you so certain of victory against the enemy with your previous strategy?"
Cāo said,
"The enemy blocked our retreating army
and placed us in a death trap.
The Art of War says, 'Do not obstruct a returning army.'
It also says, 'Place them in a death trap, and they will live.'"
When Xiù pursued Cāo,
Jiǎ Xǔ stopped him, saying,
"Do not pursue;
if you pursue, you will surely be defeated."
Xiù did not listen,
advanced his troops into battle,
was utterly defeated, and returned.
Xǔ ascended the city wall and said to Xiù,
"Hurry and pursue them again;
another battle will surely result in victory."
Xiù apologized, saying,
"Because I did not heed your words,
I have come to this point.
Now that I am defeated,
why pursue again?"
(Fù,
pronounced "fú yòu fān";
same below.)
"The military situation has changed;
hurry and pursue!"
(He meant that military situations are not constant;
if one accurately perceives the change,
then one can turn defeat into victory.)
So, Xiù gathered his scattered troops and pursued again,
engaged in battle,
and indeed returned victorious.
(This was also only a small victory.)
"When Xiù pursued the retreating army with elite troops, you said he would surely be defeated.
When he attacked the victorious army with defeated troops, you said he would surely conquer.
Everything happened as you said.
Why is this?"
Xǔ said,
"This is easy to understand.
Although the general is skilled in warfare,
he is no match for Lord Cáo.
Lord Cáo's army had just retreated and would surely personally guard the rear,
so I knew you would surely be defeated.
Lord Cáo attacked the general,
made no miscalculations,
had not exhausted his strength, and yet suddenly retreated,
so there must have been some domestic incident.
(Having an incident
means there was a change.)
He would surely advance rapidly with light forces,
leaving his generals to guard the rear.
Although these generals are brave,
they are no match for the general,
so even using defeated troops, you were sure to win the battle."
Xiù was then convinced.
4 Lǚ Bù resumed communication with Yuán Shù,
sending his Zhonglangjiang Gāo Shùn and the Administrator of Běidì, Zhāng Liáo of Yànmén, to attack Liú Bèi.
(Bù merely remotely appointed Liáo as Administrator of Běidì.)
They were defeated by Shùn and others.
In autumn,
in the ninth month,
Shùn and others captured Péichéng,
seized Bèi's wife and children,
and Bèi fled alone.
Cáo Cāo (曹操) wished to personally attack Lǚ Bù (呂布).
All the generals said:
"Liú Biǎo (劉表) and Zhāng Xiù (張繡) are behind us,
yet we would launch a distant assault on Lǚ Bù (呂布).
This would surely be perilous."
Xún Yōu (荀攸) said:
"Biǎo (表) and Xiù (繡) have just been defeated;
they dare not move.
Bù (布) is fierce and mighty,
and moreover relies on Yuán Shù (袁術).
If he were to roam between the Huái (淮) and Sì (泗) rivers,
heroes would surely respond to him.
Now, while he has just rebelled,
and the hearts of his multitude are not yet united,
we can go and defeat him."
Cāo (操) said:
"Excellent!"
Before they set off,
Zāng Bà (臧霸), Sūn Guān (孫觀), Wú Dūn (吳敦), Yǐn Lǐ (尹禮), Chāng Xī (昌豨) and others, the commanders of Tàishān (泰山) garrisons, all defected to Bù (布).
Cāo (操) and Liú Bèi (劉備) met at Liáng (梁),
then advanced to Péngchéng (彭城).
Chén Gōng (陳宮) said to Bù (布):
"You should meet them with an attack,
and, being rested, await their fatigue;
there will be no failure."
Bù (布) said:
"It is better to wait for them to come,
and push them into the Sì (泗) River."
In winter,
the tenth month,
Cāo (操) massacred Péngchéng (彭城).
Chén Dēng (陳登), the Administrator of Guǎnglíng (廣陵), led the commandery troops as Cāo's (操) vanguard,
advancing to Xiàpī (下邳).
Bù (布) personally led his forces in several battles with Cāo (操),
but was greatly defeated each time,
and retreated to defend the city,
not daring to sally forth.
Cāo (操) sent a letter to Bù (布),
explaining the good and bad fortunes;
Bù (布) was afraid,
and wanted to surrender.
Chén Gōng (陳宮) said:
"Cáo Cāo (曹操) has come from afar;
his forces cannot last long.
If the General leads the cavalry and infantry out to garrison outside,
I, Gōng (宮), will lead the remaining troops to defend within.
If they attack the General,
I, Gōng (宮), will lead my troops to attack their rear;
if they only attack the city,
then the General can relieve it from outside.
In no more than ten days or a month,
Cāo's (操) army will run out of provisions,
and we can attack them,
and defeat them."
Bù (布) agreed with this,
wanting Gōng (宮) and Gāo Shùn (高順) to guard the city,
while he would personally lead the cavalry to cut Cāo's (操) supply lines.
Bù's (布) wife said to Bù (布):
"Gōng (宮) and Shùn (順) have always been at odds.
Once the General goes out,
Gōng (宮) and Shùn (順) will certainly not be of one mind in defending the city.
If there is any mishap,
where will the General establish himself?
Moreover, the Cáo (曹) clan treated Gōngtái (公臺) like their own child,
yet he still abandoned them and returned to us.
Chén Gōng's (陳宮) courtesy name is Gōngtái (公臺);
the matter of his return to Bù (布)
can be seen in the previous volume, Xīngpíng (興平) first year.
舍 shě,
pronounced shě.
Yet you wish to entrust the entire city,
abandon your wife and children,
and go out alone with an isolated army.
If suddenly there is a change,
how can your concubine ever again be the General's wife!"
Bù (布) then stopped;
he secretly dispatched his subordinates Xǔ Sì (許汜) and Wáng Kǎi (王楷) to seek aid from Yuán Shù (袁術).
Shù (術) said:
"Bù (布) did not give me his daughter,
so it is right that he should fail.
Why do you come again?"
Sì (汜) and Kǎi (楷) said:
"If the Illustrious Master (明上) does not save Bù (布) now,
you will defeat yourself;
when Bù (布) is broken,
the Illustrious Master (明上) will also be broken."
Shù (術) had at that time usurped the imperial title,
hence he was referred to as Illustrious Master (明上).
Bù (布) feared that Shù (術) would not send aid because of the daughter incident,
and thus would not send rescue troops.
He wrapped his daughter's body with silk and tied her to a horse,
then personally sent her out at night.
He clashed with Cāo's (操) garrison soldiers,
fought and shot but could not get through,
so he returned to the city.
Zhāng Yáng (張楊), the Administrator of Hénèi (河內), had always been on good terms with Bù (布),
and wished to save him,
but could not.
So he moved his troops to the Eastern Market,
which was the Eastern Market of Yěwáng (野王) County.
In the eleventh month,
Yáng Jiàng (楊將) and Yáng Chǒu (楊醜) killed Yáng (楊) in response to Cāo (操).
Another general, Suī Gù (眭固), then killed Chǒu (醜),
and led his troops north to join Yuán Shào (袁紹).
Yáng (楊) was by nature kind and gentle,
without awe-inspiring punishment.
When his subordinates plotted rebellion and were discovered,
he would shed tears before them,
and always forgive them without questioning,
hence he met with calamity.
Cāo (操) dug trenches and besieged Xiàpī (下邳).
As time dragged on,
the soldiers were exhausted,
and he wished to return.
Xún Yōu (荀攸) and Guō Jiā (郭嘉) said:
"Lǚ Bù (呂布) is brave but without strategy;
now, having been repeatedly defeated,
his morale is low.
The three armies depend on their general as their core;
if the core is weak, the army has no will to fight.
Chén Gōng (陳宮) is intelligent but slow.
Now, while Bù's (布) morale has not yet recovered,
and Gōng's (宮) plans are not yet settled,
attack them swiftly,
and Bù (布) can be overcome."
So they diverted the Yí (沂) and Sì (泗) rivers to inundate the city.
The Sì (泗) River flows southeast,
passing west of Xiàpī (下邳) County.
The Yí (沂) River flows south,
also reaching west of Xiàpī (下邳) County,
and then enters the Sì (泗) River to the south.
Therefore, both rivers were diverted to inundate the city.
The commentary to the 'Shuǐ Jīng' (水經) states: The Yí (沂) River, north of Xiàpī (下邳) County,
flows west and divides into two streams: one stream flows southwest to the north of the city and enters the Sì (泗),
the other stream passes east of the city, bends from the south of the county,
and also flows into the Sì (泗),
called the Lesser Yí (沂) River.
There is a bridge over this water,
where Zhāng Liáng (張良) met Huáng Shígōng (黃石公).
Cāo (操) here diverted the Yí (沂) and Sì (泗) rivers to inundate the city.
Bù (布) was increasingly hard-pressed.
The 'Kǎo Yì' (考異) states: Fàn Shū (范書) and Bù's (布) biography say
"inundated his city for three months,"
and the 'Wèi Zhì' (魏志) biography also says
"besieged for three months."
According to records, Cāo (操) arrived at Xiàpī (下邳) in the tenth month,
and Bù (布) was killed,
all within one season,
so it cannot be said to be three months.
This follows the 'Wèi Zhì Wǔ Jì' (魏志武紀).
"Gentlemen, do not torment me,
I shall surrender myself to the Illustrious Duke (明公)."
Chén Gōng (陳宮) said:
"The rebel bandit Cáo Cāo (曹操),
what kind of Illustrious Duke (明公) is he!
To surrender to him today
is like throwing an egg at a stone;
how can one possibly be preserved!"
Hóu Chéng (侯成), one of Bù's (布) generals, had lost his famous horse,
but later recovered it.
The other generals gathered for a feast to congratulate Chéng (成).
Chéng (成) divided wine and meat and first presented them to Bù (布).
Bù (布) angrily said:
"I have forbidden wine, yet you gentlemen brew it.
Is it that you wish to conspire against me over wine!"
Chéng (成) was resentful and fearful.
In the twelfth month,
on the day Guǐyǒu (癸酉),
Chéng (成) and the other generals Sòng Xiàn (宋憲), Wèi Xù (魏續) and others jointly seized Chén Gōng (陳宮) and Gāo Shùn (高順),
and led their troops to surrender.
Bù (布) and his subordinates ascended the White Gate Tower.
The commentary to the 'Shuǐ Jīng' (水經) states: The south gate of Xiàpī (下邳) city is named White Gate.
The 'Sòng Wǔ Běi Zhēng Jì' (宋武北征記) states: Xiàpī (下邳) city has three concentric walls.
The great city wall was four li in circumference,
which Lǚ Bù (呂布) defended.
Wèi Wǔ (魏武) captured Bù (布) at the White Gate,
which was a gate of the great city.
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: The inner city of Xiàpī (下邳),
its south side faced the White Tower Gate.
Bù (布) ordered his attendants to take his head to Cāo (操),
but his attendants could not bear to,
so he descended.
Lǚ Bù saw Cáo Cāo and said:
"From today onwards,
the world will be at peace."
Cáo Cāo said:
"Why do you say that?"
Lǚ Bù said:
"What My Lord worries about is nothing more than me,
and now I have submitted.
If you let me lead the cavalry
and My Lord lead the infantry,
the world would not be difficult to pacify."
He then turned to Liú Bèi and said:
"Xuándé,
you are a guest seated at the banquet,
while I am a captured prisoner.
The ropes bind me too tightly,
can you not say a word for me?"
Cáo Cāo laughed and said:
"When binding a tiger, one cannot but do it tightly."
He then ordered Lǚ Bù's bonds to be loosened.
Liú Bèi said:
"No!"
A textual examination states: "The Xiàndì Chūnqiū says:
