After capturing Shèquǎn (射犬),
he captured Wèi Zhǒng (魏種) alive.
Cáo Cāo (曹操) said:
"It is only for his talent!"
He released him from his bonds and employed him,
making him Administrator of Héneì (河內)
and entrusting him with affairs north of the Yellow River.
3. Appointed General of the Guards Dǒng Chéng (董承) as General of Chariots and Cavalry.
4 Yuán Shù
had already declared himself emperor. His
extravagance and debauchery intensified. He had hundreds of concubines and attendants,
all of whom wore fine silks
and ate rich foods.
Meanwhile, his subordinates suffered from hunger
and received no relief.
Eventually, his resources were exhausted,
and he could no longer sustain himself.
So, he burned his palaces
and fled to Qíanshān to his subordinates Chén Jiǎn and Léi Bó.
Qíán County
belonged to Lújiāng Commandery
and had Tiānzhù Mountain.
Xián commented: “It is the mountain in Qíán County.”
Qíán
is now Huòshān County in Shòuzhōu.
Qíán
is pronounced qián.
He then fell into great distress,
his soldiers dispersed and fled,
and he was so worried and frustrated that he didn't know what to do.
He then sent an envoy to return his imperial title to his cousin Shào.
Shào and Shù shared the same ancestor Yuán Tāng.
By kinship, he was his cousin;
by age, he was his elder brother.
“The Hàn dynasty's mandate has long departed.
The Yuán clan is destined to rule as kings;
the auspicious signs are clear.
Now you possess four provinces.”
Xián commented: “Qīng,
Jì, Yōu, and Bīng.”
“I respectfully return the great mandate.
May you bring it to fruition!”
Yuán Tán came from Qīngzhōu to meet Shù,
intending to pass north through Xiàpī.
Cáo Cāo dispatched Liú Bèi and General Zhū Líng of Qīnghé to intercept him.
Shù could not pass
and fled back to Shòuchūn.
In the sixth month,
he arrived at Jiāngtíng,
sat on a bamboo mat, and sighed,
“Has Yuán Shù come to this!”
Xián commented: “Cè is
dì;
it means without a cushion or mat.”
He vomited blood and died.
Shù’s younger cousin Yìn feared Cáo Cāo
and dared not remain in Shòuchūn.
He led his subordinates, carrying Shù’s coffin and his wife and children, to Lújiāng Administrator Liú Xūn in Wǎnéng.
Wǎn County
belonged to Lújiāng Commandery
and is now Shūzhōu.
Shīgǔ commented: “Wǎn,
pronounced hú guǎn fān;
Dù Yòu said: pronounced huàn.”
Kǎoyì commented: “The ‘Biography of Sūn Cè’ in the Wú Zhì states:
‘After Shù died, his Chief Clerk Yáng Hóng, General Zhāng Xūn, and others led his forces
and wished to join Cè.
The Administrator of Lújiāng, Liú Xūn, intercepted and attacked them,
capturing them all
and seizing their treasures to take back.’
This differs from other records.
We now follow Fàn Shū, the ‘Biography of Shù’ in the Chén Zhì, and the Jiāng Biǎo Zhuàn.”
(Presented in submission).
5 After Yuán Shào defeated Gōngsūn Zàn,
his arrogance grew,
and his tribute to the emperor became sparse and perfunctory.
His Chief Clerk Gěng Bāo secretly memorialized Shào,
suggesting that he should respond to the will of Heaven and man
and assume the imperial title.
Shào showed Bāo’s memorial to his military headquarters.
Bái shì:
the matter that was memorialized.
Bāo deserved execution.
Shào, having no choice,
killed Bāo to clear himself.
Shào selected 100,000 elite infantry and 10,000 cavalry
intending to attack Xǔ.
Jū Shòu advised:
“Recently, in campaigning against Gōngsūn Zàn,
our army has been out for years,
the people are exhausted,
and our granaries are empty.
It is not yet time to move.
We should focus on agriculture and let the people rest.
First, send an envoy to present our victory to the Son of Heaven;
if communication is blocked,
then impeach Cáo Cāo for obstructing our royal road.
Afterwards, advance and garrison Líyáng,
gradually establish camps south of the Yellow River,
build more ships,
repair weapons and equipment,
and dispatch elite cavalry to raid their borders,
preventing them from having peace.
We will then take advantage of their exhaustion.
If we do this,
we can settle the matter sitting down.”
Guō Tú and Shěn Pèi said:
“With your enlightened lord’s divine might,
leading the strong forces of Héshuò
to attack Cáo Cāo,
it will be as easy as turning over one’s hand.
Why go to such lengths!”
Shòu said:
“Indeed, an army that suppresses rebellion and punishes tyranny
is called a righteous army;
one that relies on numbers and presumes strength
is called an arrogant army.
The righteous are invincible,
while the arrogant are destroyed first.”
The former Hàn statesman Wèi Xiàng submitted a memorial saying: “A righteous army triumphs,
an arrogant army is destroyed.”
“Now, moving our army south
would violate righteousness.
Moreover, the strategy for victory in the ancestral temple
does not lie in strength or weakness.
Cáo Cāo’s laws are well-enforced,
and his soldiers are well-trained.
He is not like Gōngsūn Zàn, who sits and waits to be attacked.
Now to abandon a strategy of perfect safety and raise an unnamed army –”
The former Hàn scholar Dǒng Gōng said: “An army without a just cause
will fail.”
Tú and Pèi said:
“King Wǔ’s campaign against Zhòu
was not unrighteous;
how can an army against Cáo Cāo be called unnamed!
Furthermore, with the lord’s current strength,
and his officers and soldiers eager to fight,
if we do not seize this moment to establish our great enterprise,
it is what is called ‘Heaven gives, but one does not take,
and instead suffers calamity.’
These are the words of Fàn Lǐ in Shǐ Jì.
This was the reason for Wú’s destruction.
The Supervising General’s plan is about being cautious.”
Shào made Shòu supervise all the generals,
hence he was called Supervising General.
Chí láo
is like what southerners today call bǎ wěn (being steady).
Jiān,
pronounced gǔ xián fān.
Shào adopted Tú’s advice.
Tú and others then slandered Shòu, saying:
“Shòu supervises both internal and external affairs,
his prestige shakes the three armies.
If his influence grows unchecked,
how will we control him!
For a minister to be equal to his lord leads to ruin;
this is what Huáng Shí warned against.”
“A minister being equal to his lord” means
he wields authority and influence with no distinction from the lord.
Huáng Shí
refers to the book Zhāng Liáng obtained from the bridge at Xiàpī.
“He should not know internal affairs.”
Shào then divided Shòu’s command into three chief governorships,
making Shòu, Guō Tú, and Chúnyú Qióng each lead one army.
Cavalry Commandant Cuī Yǎn of Qīnghé advised:
“The Son of Heaven is in Xǔ.
The people hope for a restoration of order.
We must not attack!”
Shào did not listen.
When the generals in Xǔ heard that Shào was going to attack Xǔ,
they were all afraid.
Cáo Cāo said:
“I know Shào’s character.
His ambition is great, but his wisdom is small;
his appearance is stern, but his courage is weak;
he is envious and critical but lacks authority;
his troops are numerous, but his divisions are unclear;
his generals are arrogant, and his commands are not unified.
Although his territory is vast
and his provisions abundant,
it is just enough to serve as tribute for me.”
Kǒng Róng said to Xún Yù:
“Shào has vast territory and strong forces.
Tián Fēng and Xǔ Yōu are wise men who plan for him.
Shěn Pèi and Féng Jì are loyal ministers
who manage his affairs.
Yán Liáng and Wén Chǒu are brave generals who command his troops.
It will probably be difficult to defeat him!”
Yù said:
“Although Shào’s troops are numerous, their discipline is lax.
Tián Fēng is rigid and offends his superiors.
Xǔ Yōu is greedy and undisciplined.
Shěn Pèi is authoritarian and lacks foresight.
Féng Jì is resolute but self-serving.
These several individuals
are incompatible
and will inevitably cause internal strife.
Yán Liáng and Wén Chǒu
are merely individually brave;
they can be captured in a single battle.”
Autumn.
In the eighth month,
Cáo Cāo advanced his army to Líyáng.
He sent Zāng Bà and others to lead elite troops into Qīngzhōu to defend the east.
Zāng Bà rose in Tàishān
and dominated the eastern region;
therefore, Cáo Cāo made him the defender.
Even if Yuán Shì wanted to move east from Píngyuán,
they would be powerless.
In the ninth month,
Cáo Cāo returned to Xǔ
and divided his troops to guard Guāndù.
Xián said: Péi Sōngzhī's Běizhēng Jì (Record of the Northern Expedition) states: The terrace at Zhōngmóu
overlooks the Biànshǔi River,
which is Guāndù.
Yuán Shào and Cáo Cāo's fortifications still exist there.
It is located north of modern Zhōngmóu County, Zhèngzhōu.
According to the Shuǐjīng Zhù (Commentary on the Water Classic),
the Biànshǔi River is the same as the Lángdàng Qú Canal.
Dù Yòu said: Twelve lǐ north of Zhōngmóu County, Zhèngzhōu,
there is Zhōngmóu Tái,
which is Guāndù City,
the place where Yuán and Cáo confronted each other.
Yuán Shào sent someone to recruit Zhāng Xiù,
and also sent a letter to Jiǎ Xǔ to establish good relations.
Zhāng Xiù intended to agree,
but Jiǎ Xǔ, in Zhāng Xiù's presence,
openly spoke to Yuán Shào's envoy, saying:
“Go back and tell Yuán Běnchū
that even brothers cannot tolerate each other,”
referring to the enmity with Yuán Shù,
“and that they each gathered factions to plot against each other.”
“Xiǎn” means
to say it clearly among many people.
Zhāng Xiù was startled and fearful, saying:
“How could it come to this!”
He secretly asked Jiǎ Xǔ:
“If this is the case,
where should we turn?”
Jiǎ Xǔ said:
“It is better to follow Cáo Gōng.”
Zhāng Xiù said:
“Yuán Shào is strong and Cáo Cāo is weak,
and we were previously enemies with Cáo Cāo,”
referring to the battle at Yùshuǐ,
where Zhāng Xiù killed Cáo Cāo's son.
Jiǎ Xǔ said:
“This is precisely why you should follow him.
Cáo Gōng upholds the Son of Heaven to command the world;
this is the first reason to follow him.
Yuán Shào is strong and powerful;
if we, with our small force, follow him,
he will surely not value us.
Cáo Gōng's forces are weak,
and he will surely be pleased to gain us;
this is the second reason to follow him.
A person with the ambition of a hegemon or king
will naturally set aside private grievances to manifest his virtue to the four seas;
this is the third reason to follow him.
General, please have no doubts!”
Winter.
In the eleventh month,
Zhāng Xiù led his forces to surrender to Cáo Cāo.
Cáo Cāo held Zhāng Xiù's hand
and celebrated with a joyful banquet.
He took Zhāng Xiù's daughter for his son, Cáo Jūn,
and appointed Zhāng Xiù as Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn.
He recommended Jiǎ Xǔ as Zhí Jīn Wǔ
and enfeoffed him as Dūtíng Hóu.
All administrative centers of commanderies, kingdoms, counties, and districts
had a Dūtíng.
The generals in Guānzhōng, seeing Yuán Shào and Cáo Cāo contending,
all remained neutral and watched.
Wéi Duān, the Inspector of Liángzhōu, sent his subordinate Yáng Fù of Tiānshuǐ to Xǔ.
When Yáng Fù returned,
the generals in Guānyòu asked:
“Between Yuán Shào and Cáo Cāo, who will win and who will lose?”
Yáng Fù said:
“Yuán Gōng is lenient but indecisive,
fond of deliberation but lacking in resolution.
Without decisiveness, he lacks authority;
lacking resolution, he delays matters.
Though he is strong now,
he will ultimately fail to achieve a great enterprise.
Cáo Gōng possesses heroic talent and far-reaching strategy,
resolves critical moments without doubt,
his laws are consistent, and his troops are elite.
He can utilize extraordinary individuals,
and those he employs fully exert their abilities.
He will surely be able to accomplish great things.”
Cáo Cāo sent Wèi Jì of Hédōng, a Censor-in-Chief of the Imperial Secretariat, to govern and pacify Guānzhōng.
At that time, many people from the four directions returned,
and the Guānzhōng generals mostly attracted them to become their private troops.
Wèi Jì wrote to Xún Yù, saying:
“Guānzhōng is a fertile land,
but it has recently suffered from chaos.
Over one hundred thousand households migrated to Jīngzhōu.
Hearing that their homeland is peaceful,
they all long to return.
However, those who return have no means to support themselves,
and the generals all compete to recruit and retain them as private troops.
The commanderies and counties are poor and weak,
unable to contend with them.
The military families thus grow strong,
and once there is a change,
there will surely be future troubles.
Salt
is a great treasure of the state.
It was abandoned during the chaos,
and it is advisable to restore the old system of appointing envoys to supervise its sale.
With the proceeds, more plowing oxen should be purchased.
If there are returning people,
these should be supplied to them,
encouraging diligent farming and accumulating grain to enrich Guānzhōng.
Distant people, hearing of this,
will surely compete to return day and night.
Furthermore, sending the Colonel Director of Retainers to reside in Guānzhōng to be its chief
would daily diminish the generals' power and daily increase the government's and people's prosperity.
This is the benefit of strengthening the foundation and weakening the enemy.”
Xún Yù reported this to Cáo Cāo,
and Cáo Cāo followed it.
He first sent an Attendant Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat to supervise the salt officials.
The Yánchí Salt Pool in Ānyì, Hédōng,
formerly had salt officials.
The profit from salt was substantial.
Qí used Guǎn Zǐ's method of selling salt and iron to become a hegemon.
When Jìn established its capital,
the great ministers insisted on its proximity to salt.
During the time of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
it was used to assist military expenditures.
During the Án Lùshān and Shǐ Sīmíng Rebellion in Táng,
Dìwǔ Qí monopolized salt to provide for national expenses.
From then on, it became a regular tax,
its profit accounting for half of the nation's annual income.
Jiān (監),
pronounced as 'gōng xián fān'.
At that time, Zhōng Yáo was appointed as Colonel Director of Retainers.
According to Wèilüè and Sānguó Zhì,
Zhōng Yáo actually governed Luòyáng.
Presumably, he temporarily governed Hóngnóng
to recruit and pacify Guānzhōng.
Yuán Shào (袁紹) sent someone to request aid from Liú Biǎo (劉表).
Biǎo (表) promised to help but ultimately did not arrive,
nor did he assist Cáo Cāo (曹操).
The Commissioner-Colonel (從事中郎) Hán Sōng (韓嵩) of Nányáng (南陽) said:
"According to Han regulations,
only the Colonel Director of Retainers (司隸校尉) had a Commissioner-Colonel (從事中郎).
By the end of the Han dynasty,
provincial governors (州牧) also had Commissioner-Colonels (從事中郎).
'Now that two heroes are locked in struggle,
the fate of the empire rests with the General (將軍).
If you wish to achieve something,
you could seize their weakness and act.
If not,
you should certainly choose whom to follow.
How can you, with a hundred thousand armored troops,
sit idly by and watch their success or failure,
unable to help when aid is sought,
and unwilling to pledge allegiance when a worthy leader appears!
These two resentments will surely converge on you, General (將軍),
and I fear you will not be able to remain neutral.
Cáo Cāo (曹操) is skilled in military matters,
and many talented individuals are returning to him.
His power will surely overcome Yuán Shào (袁紹),
and then he will move his troops towards the Jiāng (江) and Hàn (漢) rivers.
I fear, General (將軍), you will not be able to resist him.
The best plan now –
'best plan' (勝計)
means among all plans,
this plan is the superior one –
is that Cáo Cāo (曹操) will surely highly value you, General (將軍).
You will long enjoy good fortune,
extending to your descendants.
This is a perfectly safe strategy.'"
Kuǎi Yuè (蒯越) also urged him.
Biǎo (表) was indecisive and hesitant,
so he sent Sōng (嵩) to Xǔ (許), saying:
"The empire's fate is still uncertain today,
but Cáo Cāo (曹操) holds the Son of Heaven (天子) in Xǔ (許).
You go observe his weaknesses for me."
Sōng (嵩) replied:
"A sage adapts to circumstances;
a lesser man adheres to principles.
In the *Zǔo Zhuàn* (左傳),
these are the words of Prince Xīnshí (欣時) of Cáo (曹).
I am one who adheres to principles.
The relationship between lord and minister is fixed by name [and duty];
one defends it with death.
Now that I have registered my name and offered my pledge,
*zhì* (質)
as written.
Even if I have to go through boiling water or tread on fire,
I will not refuse death.
From my perspective,
Duke Cáo (曹公) will surely achieve his ambitions in the empire.
If you, General (將軍), can align yourself with the Son of Heaven (天子) above
and submit to Duke Cáo (曹公) below,
then sending me is acceptable.
But if you still hesitate,
when I arrive at the capital,
the Son of Heaven (天子) will grant me an office,
and I will not be able to decline the appointment.
I will then become a minister of the Son of Heaven (天子),
merely your former subordinate.
If you are my lord,
I will obey the command of the Son of Heaven (天子),
and it would be against righteousness for me to die for you again.
Please reconsider carefully;
do not wrong me!"
Biǎo (表) thought he was reluctant to go on the mission
and forced him.
Thinking he was reluctant to go to Xǔ (許),
he compelled him to go.
*Shǐ* (使),
pronounced *shū lì fān*.
An imperial edict appointed Sōng (嵩) a Palace Attendant (侍中) and Administrator of Línglíng (零陵太守).
When he returned,
he lavishly praised the court and the virtues of Duke Cáo (曹公),
advising Biǎo (表) to send a son to serve at court.
Biǎo (表) was furious,
thinking he harbored disloyal intentions.
He convened a grand meeting of his staff,
arrayed troops,
and holding the imperial credential,
intended to execute him.
Holding the imperial credential
showed that he intended to execute,
yet he still dared not execute without authority,
preserving the Han system.
"How dare Hán Sōng (韓嵩) harbor disloyal intentions!"
Everyone was afraid and wanted Sōng (嵩) to apologize.
Sōng (嵩) remained unmoved,
and calmly said to Biǎo (表):
"You, General (將軍), have wronged me;
I have not wronged you, General (將軍)!"
And he recounted his previous words.
Biǎo's (表) wife, Lady Cài (蔡氏), advised:
"Hán Sōng (韓嵩) is a respected figure in Chǔ (楚);
moreover, his words are straightforward.
There is no justification for executing him."
Biǎo (表) was still angry and
interrogated and killed those who accompanied him.
Finding no other intentions,
he did not execute Sōng (嵩) but imprisoned him.
The chieftain of the Yángzhōu (揚州) bandits, Zhèng Bǎo (鄭寶), wanted to abduct residents and move to Jiāngbiǎo (江表).
Liú Yè (劉曄) of Huáinán (淮南),
a prominent person of high lineage –
Yè (曄) descended from the imperial clan of Han,
and along with Jiǎng Jì (蔣濟) and Hú Zhì (胡質) was a famous scholar of Yángzhōu (揚州) –
was troubled by this.
It happened that Cáo Cāo (曹操) sent an envoy to the province
to investigate something.
Yè (曄) invited him to his home.
Bǎo (寶) came to visit the envoy.
Yè (曄) detained him and feasted with him,
then personally killed him with a blade.
He cut off his head and ordered Bǎo's (寶) troops, saying:
"Duke Cáo (曹公) has issued an order:
whoever dares to make a move
will be guilty of the same crime as Bǎo (寶)!"
His several thousand followers were all awestruck and submitted,
and they acclaimed Yè (曄) as their leader.
Yè (曄) handed over his followers to Liú Xún (劉勳), the Administrator of Lújiāng (廬江).
Xún (勳) was puzzled by this,
and Yè (曄) said:
"Bǎo (寶) disregarded the law,
and his followers traditionally profited from looting and raiding.
I have no previous standing
meaning he had no prior status to provide for them.
*Chāo* (鈔),
pronounced *chǔ jiāo fān*.
They will surely harbor resentment and be difficult to control for long,
so I gave them to you!"
During times of chaos in the empire,
if one is unfortunately acclaimed by the masses,
one should take Liú Yè (劉曄) as a model.
Xún (勳) could not provide for them sufficiently,
so he sent his younger cousin Xié (偕) to seek grain from the clan leaders at Shàngliáo (上繚).
He could not obtain the full amount.
He could not obtain the quantity he sought.
*Liáo* (繚),
read as *liáo*.
Sūn Cè (孫策) detested Xún (勳)'s strong army.
He feigned humility in his address to Xún (勳), saying:
"The Zōng (宗) clan of Shàngliáo (上繚) has repeatedly bullied my humble district.
I wish to attack them,
but the road is inconvenient.
Shàngliáo (上繚) is very rich and fertile.
I ask you, my lord, to attack them.
I will send out troops to act as an external reinforcement."
He also bribed Xún (勳) with pearls, jewels, and gěyuè (葛越).
Wénxuǎn Zhù (文選註) says: Gěyuè (葛越)
is grass cloth.
Today, hemp cloth is called gěyuè (葛越),
and white cloth is called báiyuè (白越).
Everyone, inside and out, congratulated him,
except for Liú Yè (劉曄).
Xún (勳) asked him why,
and he replied:
"Although Shàngliáo (上繚) is small,
its city walls are strong and its moats deep.
It is difficult to attack and easy to defend.
It cannot be taken in ten days.
With the army exhausted outside and the interior of the state empty,
if Cè (策) takes advantage of this emptiness to attack us,
then the rear will not be able to hold out alone.
This means the general will be hampered by the enemy in advancing,
and have nowhere to return in retreating.
If the army must go out,
disaster will strike today."
Xún (勳) did not listen,
and proceeded to attack Shàngliáo (上繚).
When he reached Hǎicūn (海昏),
the Zōng (宗) leaders, knowing this,
all abandoned their fortified camps and fled,
and Xún (勳) gained nothing.
At that time, Cè (策) led his troops west to attack Huáng Zǔ (黃祖).
When he reached Shíchéng (石城),
Hǎicūn (海昏) county
belonged to Yùzhāng (豫章) commandery.
It was at the mouth of the great river of Yùzhāng (豫章).
There was a place called Gǎikǒu (慨口).
During the Yǒngyuán (永元) era,
Jiànchāng (建昌) county was established by dividing Hǎicūn (海昏).
Shàngliáo (上繚)
was within the borders of Jiànchāng (建昌).
Shíchéng (石城) county
belonged to Dānyáng (丹楊) commandery.
Xián (賢) says: It is southwest of modern Sūzhōu (蘇州).
I refer to Shuǐjīng (水經): Shíchéng (石城) county is east of Niúzhǔ (牛渚).
Lì Dàoyuán (酈道元)'s commentary also says: Niúzhǔ (牛渚) is five hundred *lǐ* (里) less than east of Shíchéng (石城).
It is unknown which is correct.
Also according to Wǔdài Zhì (五代志),
Xuānchéng (宣城)'s Qiūpǔ (秋浦) county was
formerly called Shíchéng (石城).
Sòng Bái (宋白) says: Chízhōu (池州)'s Guìchí (貴池) and Shídài (石埭) two counties
were both the territory of Hàn (漢)'s Shíchéng (石城) county.
Cè (策) then dispatched his elder cousins Bēn (賁) and Fǔ (輔) with eight thousand men to garrison Péngzé (彭澤).
Sòng Bái (宋白) says: Péngzé (彭澤) county
was named after Pénglǐ Zé (彭蠡澤).
During the Hàn (漢) dynasty, it belonged to Yùzhāng (豫章) commandery.
Today, Jiāngzhōu (江州)'s Péngzé (彭澤) county and Nánkāng (南康) army's Dūchāng (都昌) county are both territories of Hàn (漢)'s Péngzé (彭澤) county.
He conquered it [Péngzé],
obtaining Xún (勳)'s wives and children and over thirty thousand men from his army.
He memorialized to appoint Lǐ Shù (李術) of Rǔnán (汝南) as the Grand Administrator of Lújiāng (廬江),
providing him with three thousand soldiers to guard Wǎnchéng (皖城),
which laid the groundwork for Lǐ Shù (李術)'s later disloyalty to the Sūn (孫) clan.
Xún (勳) returned to Péngzé (彭澤).
Sūn Bēn (孫賁) and Sūn Fǔ (孫輔) intercepted and attacked him,
defeating him.
Xún (勳) fled to guard Liúyí (流沂).
Liúyí (流沂)
is a place name,
near Xīsài (西塞).
Xīsài Shān (西塞山)
is thirty *lǐ* (里) northeast of modern Shòuchāng (壽昌) army.
Zǔ (祖) sent his son, Shè (射), leading five thousand naval troops to assist Xún (勳).
The naval troops
are the same as the navy.
They were utterly defeated.
Xún (勳) fled north to Cáo Cāo (曹操),
and Shè (射) also escaped.
Cè (策) obtained over two thousand of Xún (勳)'s soldiers
and a thousand ships.
He then advanced to attack Huáng Zǔ (黃祖).
In the twelfth month,
on the *Xīnhài* (辛亥) day,
Cè (策)'s army reached Shāxiàn (沙羡).
Shāxiàn (沙羡) county
belonged to Jiāngxià (江夏) commandery.
Jìn Zhuó (晉灼) says: Xiàn (羡)
is pronounced *yí* (夷).
Shuǐjīng Zhù (水經註) says: Púqí (蒲圻),
in the river there is Shāyáng Zhōu (沙陽洲),
the seat of Shāyáng (沙陽) county.
The county was originally Jiāngxià (江夏)'s Shāxiàn (沙羡).
In the Tàikāng (太康) era of Jìn (晉),
it was renamed Shāyáng (沙陽) county.
[He] brought five thousand long spears to save Zǔ (祖).
On the *Jiǎyín* (甲寅) day,
Cè (策) fought with them
and utterly defeated them,
beheading Xī (晞).
Zǔ (祖) escaped alone,
while his wives and children were captured, along with six thousand ships,
and tens of thousands of soldiers were killed or drowned.
Cè (策) amassed his troops to march into Yùzhāng (豫章).
He encamped at Jiāojiū (椒丘).
Jiāojiū (椒丘)
was several tens of *lǐ* (里) from Yùzhāng (豫章)'s Nánchāng (南昌) county.
"Huà Zǐyú (華子魚) has his own name" –
Huà Xīn (華歆),
courtesy name Zǐyú (子魚).
"Has his own name"
means his fame was well-known at the time.
"If you do not open the gates and yield the city,
when the war drums sound,
there will inevitably be casualties.
You go ahead,
and fully convey my intentions."
Fān (翻) then went to see Huà Xīn (華歆) and said:
"I have humbly heard that Your Excellency's fame is equal to that of the former Prefect Wáng (王) of our humble commandery in Zhōngzhōu (中州).
You are revered by all within the seas.
Though I am in the eastern frontier,
I have always looked up to you with admiration."
Xīn (歆) said:
"I am not as good as Wáng (王) of Kuàijī (會稽)."
Wáng Lǎng (王朗) was the Grand Administrator of Kuàijī (會稽),
defeated by Cè (策).
Kuài (會),
pronounced *kuài fān* (工外翻).
"I wonder how Yùzhāng (豫章)'s provisions, weapons,
and the bravery of its soldiers and people
compare to our humble commandery?"
Xīn (歆) said:
"They are far inferior."
Fān (翻) said:
"Your Excellency says you are not as good as Wáng (王) of Kuàijī (會稽) –
that is merely a humble remark.
The *Yì* (易) says: 'Humility gives dignity and brilliance.'
Tán (譚),
same as *tán* (談).
It is truly as your esteemed teaching implies.
Sūn Tǎonì (孫討逆)'s wisdom and strategy surpass the world;
his use of troops is like a god.
He previously drove away Liú Yángzhōu (劉揚州),
whom you personally witnessed;
Liú Yángzhōu (劉揚州)
refers to Liú Yáo (劉繇).
And you have also heard of him.
Our humble commandery
refers to Kuàijī (會稽).
Judging our own provisions,
we already know they are insufficient.
If we do not make plans early,
regret will be too late.
Now the great army has already arrived at Jiāojiū (椒丘).
I will return now.
If a welcoming proclamation does not arrive by midday tomorrow,
I shall bid you farewell."
Xīn (歆) said:
"Having been in Jiāngbiǎo (江表) for a long time,
I have always wished to return north.
When Sūn Kuàijī (孫會稽) comes,
I will then leave."
So that night he drafted a proclamation.
The next morning,
he sent an official to deliver it as a welcome.
Cè (策) then advanced his army.
Xīn (歆), wearing a hemp turban, welcomed Cè (策).
Kǎo Yì (考異) says: Huà Qiáo (華嶠)'s *Pǔ Xù* (譜叙) says:
"Sūn Cè (孫策) had taken Yángzhōu (揚州),
and with a large army, he advanced into Yùzhāng (豫章).
The entire commandery was greatly alarmed.
His officials asked to go out to the suburbs to welcome him.
Xīn (歆) said: 'Do not do that.'
Cè (策) gradually advanced.
Again, they petitioned to deploy troops.
He again did not consent.
When Cè (策) arrived,
the entire administration went to the inner gates,
requesting to go out and avoid him.
He then smiled and said:
'He will come himself now.
Why rush to avoid him?'
A moment later,
a doorman announced: 'General Sūn (孫) has arrived,'
and requested an audience.
He then came forward and sat with Xīn (歆),
discussing for a long time.
Only at night did he depart.
When righteous scholars heard of this,
they all sighed deeply and were convinced in their hearts."
This account is too far from human nature,
so it is not adopted here.
"Your Excellency's age, virtue, and reputation
are respected far and wide.
Cè (策) is young and inexperienced,
and should observe the rites of a younger relative."
He then bowed to Xīn (歆),
treating him as a most honored guest.
Sūn Shèng 曰: Xīn 既無夷、皓韜邈之風，
又失王臣匪躬之操，
夷、皓，
謂 Bó Yí、四皓也。
易曰：
「王臣蹇蹇，
匪躬之故。 」
言 Huá Xīn 不能高尚其志，
又失蹇蹇匪躬之節也。
交臂於陵肆之徒，
位奪節墮，
咎孰大焉！
7 Cè 分 Yùzhāng 為 Lúlínɡ 郡，
以 Sūn Bēn 為 Yùzhāng 太守，
Sūn Fǔ 為 Lúlínɡ 太守。
會 Tónɡ Zhī 病，
Fǔ 遂進取 Lúlínɡ，
Tónɡ Zhī 據 Lúlínɡ 事見上卷上年。
Péi Sōngzhī 曰：按 Sūn Cè 于時始得 Yùzhāng、Lúlínɡ，
尚未能得定 Jiāngxià。
Yú 之所鎮，
應在今 Bāqiū 縣也，
與後所屯 Bāqiū 處不同。
余據 Jìn 地理志，
Lúlínɡ 郡有 Bāqiū 縣。
Shěn Yuē 曰：Jìn 立。
今 Fǔzhōu Chóngrén 縣即其地。
Liáng 改 Bāqiū 曰 Bāshān。
Sūn Cè 之克 Wǎnéng 也，
撫視 Yuán Shù 妻子；
及入 Yùzhāng，
收載 Liú Yáo 喪，
善遇其家。
士大夫以是稱之。
Kuàijī 功曹 Wèi Ténɡ 嘗迕 Cè 意，
Cè 將殺之，
衆憂恐，
計無所出。
Cè 母 Wú Fūrén 倚大井謂 Cè 曰：
「汝新造 Jiāngnán，
其事未集，
方當優賢禮士，
捨過錄功。
Wèi Gōngcáo 在公盡規，
汝今日殺之，
則明日人皆叛汝。
吾不忍見禍之及，
當先投此井中耳！ 」
Cè 大驚，
遽釋 Ténɡ。
初，
Wú Jùn 太守 Kuàijī Shèng Xiàn 舉 Gāo Dài 孝廉，
Xǔ Gòng 來領郡，
Dài 將 Xiàn 避難於營帥 Xǔ Zhāo 家。
Wūchéng Zōu Tuó、Qián Tóng 及 Jiāxīng Wáng Shèng 等
各聚衆萬餘或數千人，
不附 Sūn Cè。
Cè 引兵撲討，
皆破之，
進攻 Yán Báihǔ。
Báihǔ 兵敗，
奔 Yúháng，
Yúháng 縣，
前 Hàn 屬 Kuàijī 郡，
後 Hàn 分屬 Wú Jùn。
Chéng Pǔ 請擊 Zhāo，
Cè 曰：
「Xǔ Zhāo 有義於舊君，
有誠於故友，
此丈夫之志也。 」
Péi Sōngzhī 曰：Xǔ Zhāo 有義於舊君，
謂濟 Shèng Xiàn 也；
有誠於故友，
則受 Yán Báihǔ 也。
8 Cáo Cāo 復屯 Guāndù。
Cāo 常從士 Xú Tā 等謀殺 Cāo，
常從士，
常隨從在左右者也。
從，
才用翻。
他，
徒何翻。
見校尉 Xǔ Chǔ，
色變，
Chǔ 覺而殺之。
車騎將軍 Dǒng Chéng 稱受帝衣帶中密詔，
與 Liú Bèi 謀誅 Cáo Cāo。
Cāo 從容謂 Bèi 曰：
「今天下英雄，
惟使君與 Cāo 耳，
Běnchū 之徒，
不足數也！ 」
Bèi 方食，
失匕箸；
Bèi 以 Cāo 知其英雄，
懼將圖已，
故驚失匕筯也。
匕，
匙也；
箸，
挾也。
箸，
遲助翻。
Bèi 因曰：
「聖人云『迅雷風烈必變』 ，
論語記 Kǒngzǐ 之容。
遂與 Chéng 及長水校尉 Zhǒng Jí、將軍 Wú Zǐlán、Wáng Fú 等同謀。
會 Cāo 遣 Bèi 與 Zhū Líng 邀 Yuán Shù，
Chéng Yù、Guō Jiā、Dǒng Zhāo 皆諫曰：
「Bèi 不可遣也！ 」
Cāo 悔，
追之，
不及。
Shù 既南走，
Zhū Líng 等還。
Bèi 遂殺 Xúzhōu 刺史 Chē Zhòu，
留 Guān Yǔ 守 Xiàpī，
行太守事，
身還 Xiǎopèi。
Dōnghǎi 賊 Chāng Xī 及郡縣多叛 Cāo 為 Bèi。
據 Shǔ Zhì，
Chāng Xī 即 Chāng Bà。
豨，
許豈翻，
又音希。
Lǚ Bù 之敗，
Tàishān 諸屯帥皆降於 Cáo Cāo，
獨 Xī 反側於其間，
蓋自恃其才略過於 Zāng Bà 之徒也。
遣使與 Yuán Shào 連兵，
Cāo 遣司空長史 Pèiguó Liú Dài、中郎將 Fúfēng Wáng Zhōng 擊之，
不克。
Bèi 謂 Dài 等曰：
「使汝百人來，
無如我何；
Cáo Gōng 自來，
未可知耳！ 」
正月，
Dǒng Chéng 謀洩；
Rénzǐ ，
Cáo Cāo 殺 Chéng 及 Wáng Fú、Zhǒng Jí，
皆夷三族。
Cāo 欲自討 Liú Bèi，
諸將皆曰：
「與 Gōng 爭天下者，
Yuán Shào 也。
今 Shào 方來而棄之東，
言 Shào 方來寇，
乃棄而不顧而東征 Bèi 也。
若何？ 」
Cāo 曰：
「Liú Bèi，
人傑也，
今不擊，
必為後患。 」
Guō Jiā 曰：
「Shào 性遲而多疑，
來必不速。
Bèi 新起，
衆心未附，
急擊之，
必敗。 」
Cāo 師遂東。
Jìzhōu 別駕 Tián Fēng 說 Yuán Shào 曰：
「Cáo Cāo 與 Liú Bèi 連兵，
未可卒解。
Gōng 舉軍而襲其後，
可一往而定。 」
Shào 辭以子疾，
未得行。
Fēng 舉杖擊地曰：
「嗟乎！
遭難遇之時，
而以嬰兒病失其會，
惜哉，
事去矣！ 」
Cáo Cāo attacked Liú Bèi.
He defeated him.
Kǎoyì says: The Wèi Shū says:
"Bèi said that Cáo was engaged with a major enemy,
and would not be able to come east.
Then scout cavalry suddenly arrived,
saying that Grandee Cáo was coming.
Bèi was greatly alarmed,
but still did not believe it.
He personally led several tens of cavalry out to observe the Grandee's army.
Seeing their banners and pennants,
he abandoned his troops and fled."
It is believed that Bèi would certainly not have gone to such an extent;
the Wèi Shū contains many falsehoods.
[Cáo Cāo] advanced and captured Xiàpī,
seizing Guān Yǔ.
He then attacked Chāng Xī,
and defeated him.
Bèi fled to Qīngzhōu,
and through Yuán Tán, returned to Yuán Shào.
When Shào heard that Bèi had arrived,
he went two hundred *lǐ* from Yè to welcome him.
Shào went far out to welcome Bèi,
showing his great respect.
The lost soldiers gradually returned to him.
Cáo Cāo returned his army to Guāndù.
Shào then discussed attacking Xǔ.
Tián Fēng said:
"Since Cáo Cāo has defeated Liú Bèi,
Xǔ is no longer empty.
Moreover, Cáo is skilled in warfare,
constantly changing his tactics.
Although his forces are few,
they should not be underestimated.
It is better now to hold out for a long time.
The General holds the strongholds of mountains and rivers,
possesses the armies of four provinces.
He should externally ally with heroes,
and internally cultivate agriculture and military preparation.
Then, select his elite troops,
and divide them into 'surprise forces'.
Sūnzi's Art of War says: 'In all battles,
use the orthodox to engage,
and the unorthodox to win.'
The commentary says: 'The orthodox [zhèng]
confronts the enemy;
the unorthodox [qí]
attacks where they are unprepared.
If they save their right, strike their left;
if they save their left, strike their right.
This will exhaust the enemy by making them rush to respond,
the people will not be able to settle in their work,
we will not be tired while they are already distressed.
In less than three years,
we can sit back and conquer them.
Now, abandoning the 'temple-victory strategy'
(A strategy decided in the ancestral temple and winning a victory a thousand *lǐ* away is called a 'temple-victory'.)
Sūnzi says: 'Before battle, if the temple-victory is achieved,
the calculations are many;
before battle, if the temple-victory is not achieved,
the calculations are few.)
If it does not go as planned,
regret will be too late."
Shào did not listen.
Fēng strongly remonstrated, offending Shào.
Shào considered this dispiriting the troops
and had him shackled.
Thereupon, he issued a proclamation to the prefectures and commanderies,
enumerating Cáo's crimes.
In the second month,
he advanced his army to Líyáng.
Jǔ Shòu, before his departure,
gathered his clan members,
distributed his wealth to them,
and said:
"If our power remains, our prestige will be all-encompassing;
if our power is lost, I will not even preserve my own person.
Alas!"
His younger brother Zōng said:
"Cáo Cāo's soldiers and horses are no match;
why are you afraid, my lord!"
Shòu said:
"Given Cáo Cāo's intelligence and strategy,
and also that he holds the Son of Heaven as his resource,
although we have defeated Bóguī,
(Gōngsūn Zàn,
courtesy name Bóguī.)
the defeat of our army
will be in this campaign.
Yáng Xióng said: 'The Six States, foolish,
weakened Jī for Yíng.'
Is this not what applies now!"
Xián says: This is from the Fǎ Yán.
Yíng
is the surname of Qín;
Jī
is the surname of Zhōu.
Fāng Yán says: Chī
means foolish.
The Six States were foolish and deluded,
invading and weakening the Zhōu court,
eventually being annexed by Qín.
Wèi
is pronounced yú wěi.
The General who Manifests Awe, Chéng Yù,
Shěn Yuē says: The title General who Manifests Awe
began in the early Eastern Hàn,
with Sòng Dēng being the first.
Cáo Cāo wanted to add two thousand soldiers to Yù's command,
but Yù refused,
saying:
"Yuán Shào possesses a hundred thousand troops,
and considers himself invincible.
Now, seeing Yù with few soldiers,
he will certainly take it lightly
and not attack.
If Yù's troops are increased,
exceeding a certain number, he will have no choice but to attack.
If he attacks, he will certainly be victorious.
This would only diminish our strength on both sides.
I hope the Duke will have no doubts."
Shào heard that Yù had few soldiers,
and indeed did not go.
Cáo said to Jiǎ Xǔ:
"Chéng Yù's courage
surpasses that of Bēn and Yù!"
Yuán Shào sent his general Yán Liáng to attack Liú Yán, the Administrator of Dōngjùn, at Báimǎ.
Xián says: Báimǎ County
belonged to Dōngjùn,
and is now a county in Huázhōu.
The old city was east of the present county.
"[Yán] Liáng is narrow-minded and irritable,
though brave and fierce,
he cannot be relied upon alone."
Shào did not listen.
In summer,
the fourth month,
Cáo Cāo marched north to relieve Liú Yán.
Xún Yōu said:
"Our present forces are few and no match.
We must divide their strength to succeed.
When the Duke arrives at Yánjīn,
(Dù Yù says: North of Suānzǎo County in Chénliú,
there is Yánjīn.
In the Táng dynasty, Xīnxiāng County in Wèizhōu had Yánjīnguān.
The pass was on the north bank of Yánjīn;
Cáo Cāo's destination
was the south bank of Yánjīn.)
Shào will certainly move west to respond.
Then, with light troops, we can attack Báimǎ,
catching them unprepared,
and Yán Liáng can be captured."
Cáo followed this advice.
Shào heard that troops had crossed the river,
and immediately divided his forces to intercept them in the west.
Cáo then led his army, marching quickly towards Báimǎ.
Before they had reached ten *lǐ* away,
Liáng was greatly surprised,
and came to meet them in battle.
Cáo sent Zhāng Liáo and Guān Yǔ to lead the charge and attack him.
Yǔ saw Liáng's banners and parasol
(A war chariot
used by a great general,
equipped with standards and banners,
and an open parasol.)
and cut off his head, then returned.
Shào's army could not resist him.
Thus, the siege of Báimǎ was lifted,
its people relocated,
and they moved west along the river.
Shào crossed the river to pursue them.
Jǔ Shòu remonstrated, saying:
"The changes in victory and defeat
must be thoroughly considered.
Now, we should remain garrisoned at Yánjīn,
and divide our forces to Guāndù.
If we achieve victory there,
it will not be too late to return and welcome them.
(To return and welcome the large army garrisoned.)
The troops must not return."
Shào did not listen.
Shòu sighed at the ford, saying:
"The superior's ambition is full,
the inferior's efforts are for merit.
Oh, vast Yellow River,
will I cross it?"
He then excused himself due to illness.
Shào did not permit it and resented him,
then reassigned his command
entirely to Guō Tú.
Shào’s army reached the south of Yánjīn.
Cáo lined up his troops and encamped at the foot of the southern slope.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: Báimǎ county has the Shénmǎ Pavilion.
It is truly a layered peak,
two hundred paces from north to south,
and fifty-odd paces from east to west.
Outside, it was cultivated, cleared,
leveled, and removed completely.
Directly to the south is the Zhìtú mound.
The steps are perfectly aligned.
It is about twenty *lǐ* west of Báimǎ Fords,
and about fifty *lǐ* south of the old city of Báimǎ county.
This is the Báimǎ Shān mentioned in the Kāishān Tú.
The southern slope – is it on the south side of the mountain?
At this time, Cáo’s troops, following the river, had already entered the territory of Suānzǎo.
This needs to be investigated.
He said:
“About five or six hundred cavalry.”
A moment later,
it was reported again:
“The cavalry are gradually increasing,
and the infantry are innumerable.”
Cáo said:
“Do not report again.”
He ordered the cavalry to dismount and release their horses.
At this time,
Báimǎ’s baggage train was on its way.
The generals believed that the enemy cavalry were numerous,
and it would be better to return and defend the camp.
Xún Yōu said:
“This is how we bait the enemy;
how can we leave it?”
Cáo looked at Xún Yōu and smiled.
Shào’s cavalry general Wén Chǒu, together with Liú Bèi, arrived with five or six thousand cavalry, one after another.
The generals reported again,
“We should mount our horses.”
Cáo said:
“Not yet.”
A moment later,
more cavalry arrived,
some of them splitting off to attack the baggage train.
Cáo said:
“Now we can.”
Then they all mounted their horses.
At this time, the cavalry numbered less than six hundred,
so they unleashed their troops to attack,
utterly defeating them,
and beheading Chǒu.
Chǒu and Yán Liáng
were both Shào’s famous generals.
In two battles,
they were all captured.
Shào’s army lost its morale.
For any army, morale is primary;
if morale is lost, the army cannot recover.
At first,
Cáo admired Guān Yǔ’s character,
but perceived that his heart had no intention of remaining long.
He sent Zhāng Liáo to inquire about his feelings.
Yǔ sighed, saying:
“I deeply know that Cáo Gōng treats me generously;
however, I have received grace from General Liú,
and have sworn to die with him;
I cannot betray him.
I will ultimately not stay;
I must achieve something to repay Cáo Gōng before I leave.”
Liáo reported Yǔ’s words to Cáo,
and Cáo respected his integrity.
When Yǔ killed Yán Liáng,
Cáo knew he would definitely leave,
and generously increased his rewards.
Yǔ sealed all that he had been given,
bowed with a letter of resignation,
and hastened to Liú Bèi amidst Yuán’s army.
This was Yuán Shào’s army.
Cáo said:
“Each serves his own lord;
do not pursue him.”
Cáo returned his army to Guāndù.
Yán Róu sent an envoy to Cáo,
and Cáo appointed Yán Róu as Wūhuán Commandant.
Xiānyú Fǔ personally met Cáo at Guāndù,
and Cáo appointed Fǔ as Right General Who Pacifies the Liao,
to return and garrison Yōutǔ.
At this time,
Yōuzhōu was controlled by Shào,
and was far from Xǔ.
Yet Róu and Fǔ had already pledged their loyalty to Cáo.
The Hàn General Who Pacifies the Liao began with Fàn Míngyǒu;
after the restoration,
a General Who Pacifies the Liao was established to protect the Southern Xiōngnú,
stationed in Xīhé.
Now, sending Xiānyú Fǔ back to garrison Yōutǔ,
he was therefore made Right General Who Pacifies the Liao.
From Zhōngguó northward,
Xīhé was previously considered left,
and Yōutǔ right.
2 Chén Dēng, the Administrator of Guǎnglíng, governed Shèyáng.
Shèyáng County,
in the Former Hàn, belonged to Línhuái Commandery;
in the Later Hàn, it belonged to Guǎnglíng Commandery.
Yīng Shào said: It is on the north bank of the Shè River.
Today, Chǔzhōu's Shānyáng County has Shèyáng Lake,
which is that very place.
Xián said: Shèyáng is east of modern Chǔzhōu's Ānyí County.
Dēng enticed Yán Báihǔ's remaining followers,
intending them to become a future menace.
Cè returned to attack Dēng.
His army reached Dāntú.
Dāntú County,
in the Former Hàn, belonged to Kuàijī Commandery;
in the Later Hàn, it was divided and belonged to Wú Commandery.
In the Spring and Autumn period, it was Zhūfāng.
During the Qín era, those who observed the qi said
that the land had the qi of an emperor.
Shǐhuáng sent two thousand convicts to excavate the city to undermine its potential,
and renamed it Dāntú.
A 'Discrepancy Investigation' says: This incident comes from the Jiāngbiǎo Zhuàn.
According to Cè's biography, it says:
"Cè planned to attack Xǔ,
but died before he could launch it."
Chén Jiǎo's biography says:
"Dēng was besieged by Sūn Quán at Kuāngqí.
Dēng ordered Jiǎo to seek aid from Tàizǔ.
Tàizǔ dispatched help.
After the Wú army retreated,
Dēng set up an ambush and pursued them,
greatly defeating them."
The Xiānxián Xíngzhuàng says:
"Dēng harbored the ambition to annex Jiāngnán.
Sūn Cè sent an army to attack Dēng at Kuāngqí City.
Dēng decisively defeated them,
slaying tens of thousands of captives.
The bandits, infuriated by their loss,
soon again raised a large army to march against Dēng.
Dēng sent his Registrar, Chén Jiǎo, to seek aid from Tàizǔ."
These several accounts
are inconsistent.
Sūn Shèng's Yìtóng Píng says:
"According to Yúan Shào reaching Líyáng in the fifth year of Jiàn'ān (200 CE),
Cè was killed in the fourth month.
However, the record states: Cè heard that Cáo Gōng and Shào were confronting each other at Guāndù,
which is incorrect.
The statement about attacking Dēng is thus substantiated."
We will follow this now.
Originally,
Cè killed Xǔ Gòng, the Administrator of Wú Commandery.
A 'Discrepancy Investigation' says: The Jiāngbiǎo Zhuàn says:
"Originally,
Gòng submitted a memorial to the Hàn Emperor,
stating that Cè was fierce and heroic,
and should be summoned back to the capital;
if left outside, he would surely become a generational menace.
A scout obtained the memorial and showed it to Cè.
Cè reproached Gòng with it.
Gòng denied having submitted the memorial.
Cè ordered his warriors to strangle him."
It notes: Gòng was previously forced out by Zhū Zhì,
and had already left the commandery to join Yán Báihǔ.
How could he have done so again?
Presumably, Cè killed Gòng when he defeated Báihǔ.
(Gòng's retainers) wished to avenge Gòng.
Cè was fond of hunting,
often going out on horseback.
His mount was swift and excellent,
and his retinue could not possibly keep up.
Suddenly, he encountered three of Gòng's retainers,
who shot Cè in the cheek.
His cavalry arrived shortly after
and killed all of them.
Cè's wound was severe.
He summoned Zhāng Zhāo and others and said:
"The Central Plains are in chaos.
With the populace of Wú and Yuè,
and the natural defenses of the Three Rivers—
Wéi Zhāo said: The Three Rivers
refer to the Wúsōng Jiāng, Qiántáng Jiāng, and Pǔyáng Jiāng.
The Wú Dìjì says: The Sōng Jiāng flows seventy lǐ northeast
to the mouth of the Three Rivers.
The northeast branch entering the sea is the Lóu Jiāng,
and the southeast branch entering the sea is the Dōng Jiāng.
Together with the Sōng Jiāng, they form the Three Rivers.
You all must guide my younger brother well!"
He called Quán,
bestowed upon him the seal and sash,
and said:
"To command the forces of Jiāngdōng,
to decide strategy between two battle lines,
and to contend for supremacy under Heaven—
'Héng' [衡],
is used to balance weight;
'contend for supremacy' [爭衡] means that in a divided world,
where military might is applied,
the balance of power under Heaven is shifted.
and to appoint the worthy and employ the capable,
each exhausting their hearts to preserve Jiāngdōng,
I am not as good as you."
On the day Bǐngwǔ,
Cè died.
A 'Discrepancy Investigation' says: Yú Xǐ's Zhìlín states that Cè died on the fourth day of the fourth month,
hence this placement.
Chén Zhì's Cè Zhuàn:
"Cè secretly intended to attack Xǔ
and welcome the Hàn Emperor,
secretly preparing his troops.
Before the deployment could be launched,
he was killed by a retainer of Xǔ Gòng."
Guō Jiā's biography says:
"When Cè crossed the river
to attack Xǔ from the north,
everyone who heard was afraid.
Jiā predicted: 'Cè is reckless and unprepared,
and will surely die at the hand of a common man.'
He was indeed killed by Gòng's retainers."
Although Jiā had foresight,
how could he have known that Cè would die before attacking Xǔ?
Presumably, people at the time saw Cè preparing troops along the river
and suspected he would attack Xǔ.
Jiā merely predicted he would not succeed.
Quán wailed in sorrow,
not yet attending to affairs.
Zhāng Zhāo said:
"Xiàolián!
Is this a time for crying?!"
Sūn Quán was first the Prefect of Yángxiàn.
The commandery nominated him as Xiàolián,
hence he was addressed as such.
He helped him mount his horse
and sent him out to inspect the troops.
Zhāo led the officials
to submit a memorial to the imperial court,
issued orders to subordinate cities,
and instructed all military officers, both central and regional,
to fulfill their duties.
Zhōu Yú came from Bāqiū with troops to attend the funeral,
and then remained in Wú,
serving as Central Protector of the Army, sharing responsibility for all affairs with Zhāng Zhāo.
Qín established the Commander of the Army Protector;
Hàn followed suit.
Gāozǔ appointed Chén Píng as Central Commander of the Army Protector.
Wǔdì again made him Commander of the Army Protector,
subordinate to the Grand Marshal.
During the Three Kingdoms' struggle,
the office of Central Protector of the Army first appeared.
The Dōngguān Jì says: When the Hàn Grand General went on campaign,
one Central Protector of the Army was appointed.
After Wèi and Jìn,
those of lesser rank served as Central Protector of the Army,
while those of higher rank served as General of the Army Protector.
However, Wú also had Left and Right Protectors of the Army,
so the Wú system itself divided them into three departments: Central, Left, and Right.
Yet, the deeply dangerous regions
were not entirely pacified,
and transient scholars
were all concerned with their safety and whether to stay or leave,
without a fixed loyalty between ruler and subject.
However, Zhāng Zhāo, Zhōu Yú, and others believed that Quán could achieve great things,
and so devoted themselves to serving him.
3 Autumn,
seventh month.
Imperial Prince Féng was established as the Prince of Nányáng;
on the day Rénwǔ,
Féng died.
4 Liú Pì and other Yellow Turbans in Rǔnán rebelled against Cáo Cāo and sided with Yúan Shào.
Shào sent Liú Bèi with troops to assist Pì,
and many commanderies and counties joined them.
Shào sent an envoy to appoint Lǐ Tōng, Commandant of Yáng'ān, as General Who Conquers the South.
Liú Biǎo also secretly tried to recruit him,
but Tōng rejected both.
Someone advised Tōng to follow Shào.
Tōng pressed his sword and shouted at him:
"Cáo Gōng is wise and intelligent;
he will surely bring peace to the world.
Although Shào is powerful,
he will eventually become his captive.
I will not be disloyal, even unto death."
He immediately beheaded Shào's envoy
and sent the seal and sash to Cāo.
Tōng hastily levied household taxes.
The chief of Lǎnglǐng, Zhào Yǎn, saw Tōng and said,
"Currently, all the various commanderies are rebelling.
Only Yáng'ān remains loyal.
If you again press to collect its silks,
the common people, who enjoy disorder,
may find this unbearable, may they not?"
Tōng said,
"The Duke (Cáo Cāo) is in a very urgent standoff with Yuán Shào.
The surrounding commanderies and counties are rebelling to such an extent.
If the silks are not levied and sent,
those watching and listening will surely think that we are wavering,
waiting for something."
Yǎn said,
"It is indeed as you perceive,
but one must weigh the relative importance of things.
If the levy is slightly delayed,
I will alleviate this problem for you."
He then wrote to Xún Yù, saying,
"Currently, the people of Yáng'ān Commandery are impoverished,
and neighboring cities are all rebelling.
They are easily swayed and prone to collapse.
This is a crucial moment for the stability of an entire region.
Moreover, the people of this commandery uphold loyalty and integrity,
remaining steadfast in danger.
We believe the state should offer comfort and reassurance;
but instead, there is an urgent collection of silks.
How can this encourage good conduct!"
Yù immediately reported to Cáo Cāo,
who returned all the silks to the people.
Both superiors and subordinates were delighted,
and the commandery subsequently became peaceful.
Tōng attacked the bandits Qú Gōng and others,
defeating them all.
Qú
is a surname;
Wáng Sēngrú's Bǎijiā Pǔ includes Qú Bǎo of Cāngwú.
At that time, Cáo Cāo established new laws,
which were sent down to the provinces and commanderies.
They were considerably more severe,
and the collection of silks was particularly urgent.
Hán Kuí, the Administrator of Chángguǎng,
(Chángguǎng County
belonged to Lángyé Commandery in the Former Hàn,
and to Dōnglái Commandery in the Later Hàn.
This was probably a commandery newly established after Cáo Cāo dispatched Yuè Jìn into Qīngzhōu.)
"The ancient kings distinguished the tribute of the Nine Regions to differentiate between near and far.
The Zhōu Officer 'Zhífāngshì' distinguished the states of the Nine Regions:
an area of a thousand lǐ was called the royal domain (Wángjī);
beyond that, an area of five hundred lǐ was called the domain of the feudal lords (Hóufú);
beyond that, an area of five hundred lǐ was called the agricultural domain (Diànfú);
beyond that, an area of five hundred lǐ was called the domain of the baron (Nánfú);
beyond that, an area of five hundred lǐ was called the domain of the fiefs (Cǎifú);
beyond that, an area of five hundred lǐ was called the domain of the guards (Wèifú);
beyond that, an area of five hundred lǐ was called the domain of the barbarians (Mánfú);
beyond that, an area of five hundred lǐ was called the domain of the Yí tribes (Yífú);
beyond that, an area of five hundred lǐ was called the domain of the garrisons (Zhènfú);
beyond that, an area of five hundred lǐ was called the domain of the tributaries (Pánfú).
The Zhōu Officer 'Dàsīkòu' was in charge of establishing the three canons of the state,
to assist the king in governing the states with penalties:
first, for newly established states, light penalties were used;
second, for peaceful states, moderate penalties were used;
third, for rebellious states, severe penalties were used.
(Zhì, read 'zhí lì'.)
For minor matters among the people,
let the chief officials act temporarily as appropriate,
not deviating from the correct laws above,
and below, in accordance with the hearts of the common people.
Wait until three years have passed,
when the people are settled in their occupations,
and only then can they be regulated by law."
Cáo Cāo followed this advice.
Liú Bèi raided the area between Rǔ and Yǐng.
South of Xǔ,
officials and common people were uneasy,
and Cáo Cāo was troubled by this.
Cáo Rén said,
"The south believes that the Great General
is currently in urgent difficulty,
and cannot come to their aid.
Liú Bèi approaches them with strong forces,
so their rebellion is understandable.
Bèi has newly taken command of Shào's troops,
and has not yet mastered their use.
If we attack him,
he can be defeated."
Cáo Cāo then sent Rén with cavalry to attack Bèi.
They defeated and routed him,
and recovered all the rebellious counties before returning.
Bèi returned to Shào's army,
secretly wishing to separate from Shào.
He then persuaded Shào to form an alliance with Liú Biǎo in the south.
Shào sent Bèi, leading his original troops, back to Rǔnán,
where he joined with the bandit Gōng Dū and others,
numbering several thousand men.
Cáo Cāo sent General Cài Yáng to attack them,
but he was killed by Bèi.
Yuán Shào's army was at Yángwǔ.
(Yángwǔ County
belonged to Hénán Yǐn,
north of the Guāndù River.)
"Although the northern army is numerous, their vigor and courage are not equal to the south.
The southern army has little grain, and its provisions are inferior to the north.
The south benefits from a quick battle;
the north benefits from a slow campaign.
It is advisable to be patient and enduring,
to prolong it for months and days."
Shào did not follow this advice.
In the eighth month,
Shào advanced his camps slightly,
establishing garrisons along the sand dunes,
stretching for dozens of lǐ east and west.
Cáo Cāo also divided his camps to match.
5 In the ninth month,
on the day Gēngwǔ of the first quarter,
there was a solar eclipse.
6 Cáo Cāo led his troops out to battle Yuán Shào,
but was not victorious.
He returned
and fortified his ramparts.
Shào constructed tall watchtowers.
(Xián says: The Shìmíng states: A lǔ [watchtower] is uncovered at the top, without a roof.)
He shot into Cáo Cāo's camp,
so everyone in the camp moved around covered by shields.
Cáo Cāo then made 'thunderclap chariots.'
(Xián says: Because the sound of their launching stones was fierce and shaking,
they were called 'thunderclaps.'
These are today's catapults (pàochē).
Zhāng Yàn says: Fàn Lǐ's military treatise states that flying stones weighing twelve jīn
are launched by a mechanism,
traveling three hundred paces.
Cáo Cāo probably adopted his ancient method.
The Wèishì Chūnqiū says: In antiquity there were arrow-stones.
It is also transmitted that: The huì moves and the drum beats.
This explanation says: Huì
means launching stones;
hence, stone-launching chariots were invented.
Chē, read 'chǐ zhē'.)
These chariots
destroyed them all;
Shào again built tunnels to attack Cáo Cāo.
Cáo Cāo then dug long trenches inside to resist them.
Cáo Cāo's forces were few, their provisions were exhausted,
and the soldiers were fatigued.
The common people were distressed by conscription and levies,
many rebelling and defecting to Shào.
Cáo Cāo was troubled by this.
He wrote to Xún Yù,
discussing his intention to return to Xǔ,
to draw Shào's army away.
(Xián says: Zhì
means 'to cause to arrive.'
The Art of War says: Those skilled in battle
make others come to them,
and are not made to come to others.)
"Shào has gathered all his forces at Guāndù,
intending to decide victory or defeat with Your Grace.
Your Grace is facing the strongest with the weakest;
if you cannot control them,
you will surely be overwhelmed.
This is a great opportunity for the empire.
Moreover, Shào
is merely a hero in civilian clothes;
he can gather people but cannot use them.
With Your Grace's divine martial prowess and clear wisdom,
and aided by great compliance,
what can you not achieve!
Although provisions are scarce now,
it is not yet like the situation between Chǔ and Hàn at Xíngyáng and Chénggāo.
At that time, neither Liú nor Xiàng was willing to retreat first,
believing that to retreat first would be to lose momentum.
Your Grace, with one-tenth of the enemy's forces,
(Xián says: this speaks of the disparity with Shào's forces.)
(Xián says: this speaks of drawing a line and creating a barrier.)
has held them for half a year already.
Their true intentions are revealed, their strength exhausted;
there will surely be a change.
This is the time to employ extraordinary tactics;
it must not be missed."
Cáo Cāo followed this advice,
and so he fortified his ramparts and held his ground.
When Cáo Cāo saw the carriers,
he patted them and said:
"After fifteen days
(què,
later),
the people of Jìn often used
the character 'shǎo què'
in their letters,
meaning '
a little retreat'
You need not labor anymore."
Yuán Shào transported several thousand grain wagons to Guāndù.
Xún Yōu said to Cáo Cāo:
"Yuán Shào's transport wagons will arrive any moment.
His general, Hán Méng, is keen but underestimates the enemy.
Attack him,
and you can defeat him!"
Cáo Cāo asked:
"Who can be sent?"
Xún Yōu replied:
"Xú Huǎng can."
Thereupon, he dispatched the Partial General Xú Huǎng of Hédōng
(according to Shěn Yuè's Zhì,
Cáo Wèi established forty general titles,
with Partial General and Vice General at the bottom)
who routed him
and burned his baggage train.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Yuán Shào again sent wagons to transport grain,
dispatching his general Chúnyú Qióng and others with over ten thousand soldiers to escort them,
encamping forty lǐ north of Yuán Shào's camp.
Jū Shòu advised Yuán Shào:
"You should send Jiǎng Qí to form a separate supporting army externally
to cut off Cáo Cāo's raids."
Yuán Shào did not listen.
Xǔ Yōu said:
"Cáo Cāo's forces are few, and he has committed his entire army to resist us.
The remaining defenses in Xǔ are
necessarily weak and empty.
If we dispatch light troops,
traveling by night to surprise-attack (xīng xíng,
means traveling under the stars),
if Xǔ is captured,
then by welcoming the Son of Heaven to attack Cáo Cāo,
Cáo Cāo will be captured.
If he has not yet collapsed,
we can make him rush back and forth,
and his defeat is certain."
Yuán Shào did not listen,
saying:
"I must first capture Cáo Cāo."
At this time, Xǔ Yōu's family committed a crime,
and Shěn Pèi arrested and imprisoned them.
Xǔ Yōu was enraged
and consequently defected to Cáo Cāo.
(Kǎo Yì says: The Wèi Zhì's Wǔ Jì says:
"Xǔ Yōu was greedy for wealth,
and Yuán Shào could not satisfy him,
so he came to defect."
We follow Fàn Shū's Shào Zhuàn here.)
When Cáo Cāo heard of Xǔ Yōu's arrival,
he went out barefoot to greet him,
clapped his hands, and laughed, saying:
"Zǐqīng has come from afar,
my affairs are settled!"
(Xǔ Yōu,
courtesy name Zǐyuǎn.
Calling him Zǐqīng here
is a way of showing respect.
Some say: Cáo Cāo addressed Xǔ Yōu, saying:
"Zǐyuǎn,
now that you have come,
my affairs are settled."
This makes more sense in the text.)
Xǔ Yōu said to Cáo Cāo:
"Yuán's army is mighty,
how will you withstand them?
How many provisions do you have now?"
Cáo Cāo replied:
"We can still last a year."
Xǔ Yōu said:
"No,
tell me again!"
Cáo Cāo then said:
"We can last half a year."
Xǔ Yōu said:
"Does Your Excellency not wish to defeat the Yuán clan,
why do you not speak truthfully!"
Cáo Cāo said:
"I was joking just now.
In truth, we have provisions for one month.
What should we do?"
Xǔ Yōu said:
"Your Lordship is holding out alone with an isolated army,
with no external reinforcements and grain supplies exhausted.
These are days of great peril.
Yuán's baggage train of over ten thousand wagons
is at Gùshì and Wūcháo.
(According to Shuǐ Jīng,
Wūcháo marsh
is southeast of Sūnzǎo County in Chénliú.)
If you raid it with light troops,
arriving unexpectedly,
burning their amassed provisions,
within three days,
the Yuán clan will defeat themselves."
Cáo Cāo was overjoyed,
and thus left Cáo Hóng and Xún Yōu to guard the camp.
He personally led five thousand infantry and cavalry,
all bearing Yuán's army banners,
gagging their mouths and tying up their horses' mouths,
exiting at night through a hidden path.
Each man carried a bundle of firewood.
When asked along the way,
they replied:
"Duke Yuán fears Cáo Cāo will raid the rear army,
so he has sent troops to strengthen defenses."
Those who heard them believed it to be true
and remained unconcerned.
When they arrived,
they surrounded the camp,
setting a great fire,
causing chaos and panic within the camp.
At dawn,
Chúnyú Qióng and others saw Cáo Cāo's forces were few
and came out beyond the formation gate.
Cáo Cāo immediately attacked them.
Chúnyú Qióng retreated to defend his camp,
and Cáo Cāo then attacked it.
When Yuán Shào heard that Cáo Cāo was attacking Chúnyú Qióng,
he said to his son Yuán Tán:
"Even if Cáo Cāo defeats Chúnyú Qióng,
if I capture his camp,
then he will have nowhere to return!"
(Jiù,
means 'even if';
it means, even if Cáo Cāo defeats Chúnyú Qióng,
and I capture his camp,
he will have nowhere to return.)
Zhāng Hé said:
"Duke Cáo's elite troops are gone;
they will certainly defeat Chúnyú Qióng and the others.
If Chúnyú Qióng and the others are defeated,
then our cause will be lost.
Please let us go to their rescue first."
Guō Tú insisted on attacking Cáo Cāo's camp.
Zhāng Hé said:
"Duke Cáo's camp is strong;
attacking it will surely not capture it.
If Chúnyú Qióng and the others are captured,
all of us will become captives."
Yuán Shào only sent light cavalry to rescue Chúnyú Qióng,
but used heavy forces to attack Cáo Cāo's camp,
and could not take it.
Yuán Shào's cavalry reached Wūcháo.
Some of Cáo Cāo's entourage said,
"The enemy cavalry are getting closer,
please divide our forces to resist them."
Cáo Cāo angrily said:
"The enemy is at our back,
yet you report this!"
The soldiers all fought desperately,
and consequently, they greatly defeated them,
beheading Chúnyú Qióng and others,
burning all their grain supplies.
They cut off the noses of over a thousand
soldiers,
and severed the lips and tongues of their oxen and horses,
to display to Yuán Shào's army.
Yuán Shào's officers and soldiers were all terrified.
Guō Tú was ashamed of the failure of his plan,
and again slandered Zhāng Hé to Yuán Shào, saying:
"Zhāng Hé was pleased by the army's defeat."
Zhāng Hé, enraged and fearful,
then, with Gāo Lǎn, burned their siege equipment
and went to Cáo Cāo's camp to surrender.
Cáo Hóng was doubtful and dared not accept them.
Xún Yōu said:
"Zhāng Hé's plan was not used,
and he came in anger to defect.
What doubts do you have, sir!"
Thereupon, he accepted them.
Thereupon, Yuán Shào’s 紹 army was terrified and
suffered a great defeat.
Yuán Shào 紹 and Tán 譚, among others, wrapped their heads with scarves and rode on horseback.
Fù Zǐ 傅子 says: In the late Hán 漢 dynasty,
many dukes and nobles discarded formal attire
and considered wearing scarves elegant.
Thus, people like Yuán Shào 袁紹 and Cuī Bào 崔豹,
though they were generals,
all wore silk scarves.
Wèi Tàizǔ 魏太祖, seeing the world in chaos
and resources scarce,
imitated the ancient píbàn 皮弁 cap,
cutting silk fabric to make jiá 帢 caps.
This aligned with the principle of simplicity and adapting to the times,
and their colors distinguished ranks.
This is still in practice today.
These could be called military attire,
but not national attire.
Cáo Cāo 曹操 pursued but could not catch them,
and seized all their baggage, books, and treasures.
As for the remaining soldiers who surrendered,
Cáo Cāo 曹操 buried them all alive,
killing more than seventy thousand people in total.
Kǎoyì 考異 says: Fàn Shū Shào Zhuàn 范書紹傳 says:
“Eighty thousand people were killed.”
According to Xiàndì Qǐjūzhù 獻帝起居注: Cáo Gōng 曹公 reported,
“A total of over seventy thousand heads were captured.”
Jū Shòu 沮授 did not cross the river with Yuán Shào 紹
and was captured by Cáo Cāo’s 曹操 army.
He then cried out loudly:
“I, Shòu 授, do not surrender,
I am merely captured!”
Cáo Cāo 曹操 had an old acquaintance with him,
and welcomed him, saying:
“The division of constellations is different.
Therefore, it is ruined.
The twenty-eight lunar mansions are arranged in the sky,
each with its own position and measure.
The celestial sphere is three hundred sixty-five and one-quarter degrees,
divided into twelve sections.
Bān Gù 班固 correlated the twelve sections of the Sāntǒng Lì 三統曆 with the twelve terrestrial divisions,
and thus the theory of terrestrial divisions became prevalent.
Fèi Zhí’s 費直 explanation of the Zhōu Yì 周易 and Cài Yōng’s 蔡邕 Yuèlìng Zhāngjù 月令章句 mentioned things somewhat sequentially.
Wèi Tàishǐlìng Chén Zhuó 魏太史令陳卓 further spoke of the celestial positions corresponding to various commanderies and states,
and thus the theory of terrestrial divisions became detailed.
Huángfǔ Mì 皇甫謐 says: The Yellow Emperor devised the division of stars and sections to establish laws and measures.
Heaven has twelve sections,
where the sun and moon reside;
Earth has twelve divisions,
where kings and lords establish their states.
Fēn 分,
read Fú Wèn 扶問.
“Pǐ 圮”
should be
“Pǐ 否”;
Pǐ 否 means
separated.
Jū Shòu 沮授 said:
“Jìzhōu 冀州 made a strategic error
and brought defeat upon itself.
Yuán Shào 紹 was the Administrator of Jìzhōu 冀州,

Qiàn,

The text is too long to include in full.
