Yù said:
“Dù Jī of Jīngzhào, the Administrator of Xīpíng,
during the late Hàn, Xīpíng Commandery was established by dividing Jīnchéng.
His wisdom is sufficient to respond to changes.”
Cāo Cāo then appointed Jī as Administrator of Hédōng.
Zhōng Yáo urged Wáng Yì to hand over his seal,
the commandery seal.
And proceed directly from Hébĕi to Xǔ to surrender.
Hébĕi County
belonged to Hédōng Commandery.
Sòng Bái said: Pínglù County of Shǎnzōu
was originally the land of Dàyáng County in the Hàn dynasty,
and in the Later Hàn it was changed to Hébĕi County.
Wèi Gù and the others sent several thousand soldiers to block Shǎnjīn.
The commentary to the Water Classic says: The Hé Shuǐ flows east past the north of Shǎn County,
and Hébĕi faces Máochéng,
called Máojīn,
also called Shǎnjīn.
Shǎn,
pronounced shì rǎn fān.
For several months, they could not cross.
Cāo Cāo sent Xiàhóu Dūn to campaign against Gù and the others.
Before he arrived,
Jī said:
“Hédōng has thirty thousand households,
not all of whom wish to cause trouble.
Now that troops are pressing hard,
those who wish to do good have no leader
and will surely fear and obey Gù.
If Gù and the others have absolute power,
to campaign against them and not win
will mean the trouble continues;
if we campaign and win,
it means devastating the people of an entire commandery.
Moreover, Gù and the others have not openly defied the imperial mandate;
outwardly they use the pretext of requesting their former lord to stay.
They will certainly not harm the new lord.
I will go alone in my carriage,
taking them by surprise.
Gù is a man of many schemes but indecisive,
so he will surely pretend to accept me.
If I can stay in the commandery for a month,
and use stratagems to tie them down,
that will be enough.”
So he took a deceptive route and crossed at Dòujīn.
The commentary to the Water Classic says: The Hé Shuǐ flows east past the north of the old city of Hú County,
then east to merge with the Bó Gǔ Shuǐ,
then further east to merge with the Mén Shuǐ on the right.
At this point, the Hé Shuǐ has the name Dòujīn.
Dòu,
pronounced dòu.
Fàn Xiān 范先 initially wanted to kill Jī 畿 to awe the crowd,
and also to observe Jī’s 畿 disposition.
He executed over thirty people, including the clerk, outside the gate,
but Jī 畿 remained composed.
Thereupon, Gù 固 firmly said:
“Killing him would do no harm,
but would only earn a bad name;
moreover, control is in our hands.”
So they honored him.
Jī 畿 said to Gù 固 and Xiān 范先:
“Wèi 衛 and Fàn 范
are the hopes of Hédōng 河東.
I merely look to you for completion.
However, the relationship between ruler and minister has a fixed meaning,
and success or failure are likewise determined by it.
Important matters should be discussed and decided together.”
He appointed Gù 固 as Dūdū 都督 (Commander),
acting Chéngshì 丞事 (Assistant Administrator),
and also in charge of Gōngcáo 功曹 (Merit Officer).
He had already made him Dūdū 都督,
and also ordered him to act as Jùnchéngshì 郡丞事 (Prefectural Assistant Administrator),
and also to take charge of Gōngcáo 功曹.
The Dūdū 都督 commanded troops;
the Chéng 丞 deputized the Tàishǒu 太守 (Grand Administrator),
and was involved in all prefectural affairs;
the Gōngcáo 功曹 was in charge of selecting and appointing based on merit.
Ostensibly, he gave all prefectural power to them.
All of this was overseen by Fàn Xiān 范先.
Gù 固 and the others were pleased,
and although they outwardly deferred to Jī 畿,
they did not take him seriously.
Gù 固 wanted to raise a large army,
but Jī 畿 was worried about this.
He persuaded Gù 固, saying:
“If we raise a large army now,
public sentiment will surely be disturbed.
It is better to gradually recruit soldiers with funds.”
Gù 固 thought this was reasonable
and agreed,
resulting in very few soldiers being recruited.
Recruiting soldiers with funds
meant the prefecture's finances were insufficient to sustain them,
hence very few soldiers were obtained.
“People are attached to their homes.
The various generals and clerks
can be sent out in shifts to rest,
and it will not be difficult to summon them back in times of urgency or leisure.”
Gù 固 and the others, fearing to go against public sentiment,
also agreed.
Consequently, good people were outside,
secretly forming his support;
bad people were dispersed,
each returning to their homes.
At this time, Bái Qí 白騎 attacked Dōngyuán 東垣.
Bái Qí 白騎 refers to
Zhāng Báiqí 張白騎’s followers who banded together as bandits.
Yuán Xiàn 垣縣
belonged to Hédōng Jùn 河東郡.
The character “Dōng 東”
is superfluous.
According to the Xù Hàn Zhì 續漢志 (Continued History of the Han Dynasty),
Yuán Xiàn 垣縣,
a note says: the mountains are to the east,
shaped like a wall (yuán 垣).
It is likely that the name Dōngyuán 東垣 already existed at this time.
Qí 騎
is pronounced Qí or Jì.
Huòzé Xiàn 濩澤縣
belonged to Hédōng Jùn 河東郡.
Xián 賢 says: now Zézhōu Xiàn 澤州縣.
Shīgǔ 師古 says: Huò 濩
is pronounced Wūháo 烏號.
Jī 畿 then went out,
leading only dozens of cavalry,
and hurried to defend a strong fortification.
Many officials and common people offered their cities to assist Jī 畿;
“offered their cities”
means offering the cities of the dependent counties.
He gained over four thousand people.
Gù 固 and the others, along with Gāo Gàn 高幹 and Zhāng Shèng 張晟, jointly attacked Jī 畿,
but failed to take him.
They plundered various counties
but gained nothing.
Cáo Cāo 曹操 sent the Yìláng 議郎 (Court Discussant) Zhāng Jì 張既 to campaign westward against the various generals in Guānzhōng 關中, such as Mǎ Téng 馬騰, etc.
All of them led their troops to converge and attack Shèng 晟 and the others,
defeating them.
They decapitated Gù 固 and Yǎn 琰, etc.
Their remaining partisans
were all pardoned.
Thereupon, Dù Jī 杜畿 governed Hédōng 河東,
diligently promoting leniency and benevolence.
When people had lawsuits,
Jī 畿 explained the principles of justice to them,
and sent them home to consider carefully.
The elders all blamed and rebuked each other,
not daring to litigate.
He encouraged farming and sericulture,
and urged livestock raising.
Every household among the common people became prosperous.
Then, he established schools,
promoted filial piety and brotherly respect,
repaired military affairs,
and lectured on military preparedness.
Hédōng 河東 thus became peaceful.
Jī 畿 was in Hédōng 河東 for sixteen years,
consistently ranking as the best in the realm.
This laid the foundation for Cáo Cāo 曹操 to use Hédōng's 河東 resources and wealth to pacify Guānzhōng 關中.
Dù Jī 杜畿's son was Dù Shù 杜恕,
and Shù's 恕 son was Dù Yù 杜預.
His governance of Hédōng 河東,
observing his strategies,
indeed shows he was an extraordinary talent.
I secretly believe that the Dù 杜 clan, serving Wèi 魏 and Jìn 晉,
was noble and prosperous for generations,
and must have had family traditions.
Historians recorded them accordingly,
perhaps sometimes exaggerating their actual achievements.
5. Bìshūjiān, Shìzhōng Xún Yuè.
In the second year of Yánxī of Emperor Huán,
the office of Bìshūjiān was established,
with a rank of six hundred dàn of grain.
(Xún Yuè) presented a memorial.
Yuè
was the elder brother's son of Xún Shuǎng.
At that time, political power lay with the Cáo family,
and the Son of Heaven "恭己 (gōngjǐ, deferring to others in governance)."
The phrase "gōngjǐ nánmiàn" originally meant merely sitting facing south in a dignified manner,
without interfering in political affairs.
Kǒngzǐ said: "He who governs by doing nothing,
surely that was Shùn!
What did he do?
He merely sat reverently facing south."
Later generations came to understand "gōngjǐ" as political power resting with powerful ministers, and oneself having no involvement.
Was Shùn's "gōngjǐ"
truly like this?
(A ruler should) accept what is good and reject what is bad.
Therefore, (Xún Yuè) wrote this book.
Its general outline states:
"The art of governance
first requires eliminating four harms,
then upholding five policies.
Falsehoods disturb customs,
self-interest corrupts laws,
indulgence exceeds boundaries,
extravagance ruins institutions:
if these four are not removed,
then governance has no way to proceed.
These are called the four harms.
Promoting agriculture and sericulture to sustain life,
discerning good and evil to rectify customs,
proclaiming cultural education to manifest transformation,
establishing military preparations to wield authority,
clarifying rewards and punishments to unify laws:
these are called the five policies.
If people do not fear death,
they cannot be deterred by punishment;
if people do not enjoy life,
they cannot be encouraged to do good.
Therefore, those in power
must first enrich the people's wealth to stabilize their will.
This is called 'nurturing life.'
This theory
cannot be changed for ten thousand generations.
'樂 (yuè),'
pronounced 'luò' (music).
Praise and blame should be based on verification.
The Shū Jīng says: 'Do not listen to groundless words.'
Investigate names and examine facts,
lest deceit and falsehoods mislead the hearts of the multitude.
'蕩 (dàng)'
means to move or stir.
If people are moved by deceit and falsehood,
then their hearts will also be moved by deceit and falsehood,
in response to their superiors.
If the people have no corrupt customs,
this is called 'rectifying customs.'
Honor and disgrace
are the essence of rewards and punishments.
Therefore, ritual education, honor, and disgrace are applied to gentlemen,
to transform their emotions;
shackles, cangues, and floggings are applied to commoners,
to transform their behavior.
If education and transformation are abandoned,
ordinary people are pushed down into the realm of commoners;
if education and transformation are practiced,
ordinary people are led into the path of gentlemen.
This is called 'manifesting transformation.'
Those in power must have military preparations to guard against unforeseen events.
In times of peace, it is entrusted to internal administration.
The Guó Yǔ states: 'Guǎn Zhòng, as prime minister to Qí Huán Gōng,
established internal administration to integrate military commands.'
This is called 'wielding authority.'
Rewards and punishments
are the handles of governance.
A ruler does not arbitrarily reward,
not because he begrudges his wealth,
but if rewards are given arbitrarily,
then good deeds will not be encouraged;
he does not arbitrarily punish,
not because he pities the person,
but if punishments are given arbitrarily,
then evil will not be deterred.
Rewards not encouraging (good)
is called 'stopping good';
punishments not deterring (evil)
is called 'indulging evil.'
If those in power can avoid preventing their subordinates from doing good,
and avoid indulging their subordinates in doing evil,
then the national laws will be established.
This is called 'unifying laws.'
Once the four harms are eliminated,
and the five policies are established,
implement them with sincerity,
guard them with firmness,
be concise but not negligent,
be broad but not missing anything,
and then, with folded hands and humble gestures,
the whole world will be at peace."
Xún Yuè's Shēn Jiàn,
its argumentation is precise and incisive,
concerning the general pattern of a state's rise and fall,
surpassing Xún Yù and Xún Yōu;
however, regarding assessing the world's situation,
responding to enemies and setting up stratagems
to achieve temporary victory,
Yuè might not have been capable.
Cáo Cāo, a cunning hero,
deeply trusted Yù and Yōu,
while Yuè was by the Son of Heaven's side.
Yuè was not comparable to Yù and Yōu,
and Cāo did not fear him,
probably knowing that Yuè could only offer theories,
and his talent was certainly not for practical execution.
Alas!
In the late Eastern Hàn,
Xún Shú was renowned for his virtue,
and Yù and Yōu succeeded with their wisdom and strategy.
Xún Yuè probably only had a faint resemblance to his grandfather!
His talent was insufficient to serve the world,
and his words are merely seen in this book.
Later rulers of states and the empire,
if they examine his era,
and deeply ponder his words,
will then know Yuè's loyalty to the Hàn dynasty,
and his contribution to the empire and the state.
'蠲 (juān),'
pronounced 'jí xuán.'
Punctuation by Hé Zīquán, collated by Róng Zhàozǔ and Niè Chóngqí.
Sīmǎ Guāng
Compiled by Imperial Edict
Hòu Xué Tiāntái
Xiàoxiàn Huángdì Gēng
The 11th year of Jiàn'ān
(Bǐngxū, 206 CE)
1. Spring,
first month,
a comet appeared near the Běidǒu.
The Jìn Tiānwén Zhì states: "The seven stars of the Běidǒu
are north of Tàiwēi: the first is Tiānshū,
the second is Xuán,
the third is Jī,
the fourth is Quán,
the fifth is Yùhéng,
the sixth is Kāiyáng,
the seventh is Yáoguāng;
the first to fourth form the 'Khuí' (dipper bowl),
and the fifth to seventh form the 'Sháo' (dipper handle)."
'孛 (bèi),'
pronounced 'pú nèi.'
2. Cáo Cāo personally led an attack on Gāo Gàn,
leaving his heir Cáo Pī to guard Yè,
and appointing Biejia Cóngshì Cuī Yǎn as his tutor.
Cāo besieged Húguān.
In the third month,
Húguān surrendered.
Gāo Gàn personally entered the Xiōngnú territory to seek aid,
but the Chányú did not receive him.
Gàn fled alone with a few horsemen,
intending to flee south to Jīngzhōu.
However, the Shàngluò Dūwèi Wáng Yǎn captured and beheaded him.
Shàngluò County,
in the Former Hàn, belonged to Hóngnóng,
and in the Later Hàn, belonged to Jīngzhào.
The Yáoguān Pass was northwest of the county,
hence a Dūwèi was stationed there.
Liú Xù says: "It is named because the county is located upstream of the Luò River."
Cáo Cāo sent Chénjùn’s Liáng Xí, as a Bìebù Sīmǎ, to lead Bìngzhōu as Cìshǐ.
At that time, after years of chaos and famine,
the Hú and Dí were powerful and dominant.
Officials and common people fled and defected to their tribes.
The Southern Xiōngnú tribes were all within Bìngzhōu’s borders.
Each became a menace.
This refers to the local magnates who had gathered followers to protect themselves.
He enticed and recruited them,
summoning all their magnates with courtesy.
Gradually, he recommended and promoted them,
sending them to the headquarters.
Once the magnates were all gone,
he then conscripted all able-bodied young men to form "righteous followers."
This means they joined the army out of righteousness.
From,
read "cái yòng fān."
He ordered his generals to divide and request them as brave and strong men.
After the officials and soldiers had departed,
he gradually moved their families,
sending them to Yè one after another,
totaling tens of thousands of mouths.
For those who did not obey,
he raised an army to attack them,
beheading thousands,
and gaining tens of thousands of surrenders.
The Shànyú became submissive and obedient,
and the Míngwáng kowtowed.
Míngwáng refers to the kings of the various Xiōngnú tribes.
Jiàng,
read "hù jiāng fān."
Jī,
read "qǐ."
They became the same as registered households.
Biān,
means "to arrange in order."
They were listed in the common people's registers,
hence called "biānhù."
The common people spread out across the fields,
diligently encouraged farming and sericulture,
and his commands were carried out, and prohibitions observed.
If he commanded, it was done;
if he prohibited, it ceased.
Cáo Cāo thought that among all the Cìshǐ he had heard of or known,
none was like Xí.

Xí then recommended and brought forward renowned scholars who had sought refuge within the province's borders: Cháng Lín, Yáng Jùn, Wáng Xiàng, Xún Wěi of Hénèi, and Wáng Líng of Tàiyuán, among others.
Cáo Cāo appointed them all as Xiànzhǎng.
Later, they all became famous in the world.
Earlier,
Zhòngcháng Tǒng of Shānyáng, while studying, traveled to Bìngzhōu.
He visited Gāo Gàn.
Zhòngcháng is a compound surname.
Guò,
read "gōng hé fān."
He inquired about worldly affairs.
Tǒng said to Gàn:
"You have grand ambitions but lack the grand talent;
you like scholars but cannot select the right people.
This is what I deeply warn you against."
Gàn was inherently conceited,
thinking himself very talented.
Tǒng then left him.
After Gàn died,
Xún Yù recommended Tǒng as Shàngshū Láng.
The Bǎiguān Zhì states: There were thirty-six Shàngshū Shìláng,
with a salary of four hundred dàn.
Six people per section,
mainly responsible for drafting documents.
Cài Zhì's Hàn Yí says: A Shàngshū Láng,
initially comes from the Three Bureaus to the Grand Secretariat for trial.
Upon first ascending to the Grand Secretariat,
one is called Shǒu Shàngshū Lángzhōng.
After a year,
one is called Shàngshū Láng.
After three years,
one is called Shìláng.
Kǒng Ānguó said: Chāng,
means "appropriate."
Appropriate words.
The Lüè states:
"Those heroes destined by Heaven
have never had a share of the empire.
Without a share of the empire,
wars thus arise in contention.
Those who compete in wisdom all reach their limits,
and those who compete in strength all lose.
Jiǎo,
means "to compete,"
and "to compare."
When their power is no longer sufficient to contend,
they then begin to bridle their heads and tether their necks,
submitting to my bit and halter.
Xián said: Xián,
means "bridle."
Xiè,
means "halter."
Xiè,
read "xī liè fān."
Once the heroes' hopes are dashed,
and the will of the gentry and common people is settled,
it is valued to have a constant ruling house,
and honor resides in one person.
At such a time,
even if a person of the lowest talent occupies that position,
they can still make their benevolence equal to Heaven and Earth,
and their might comparable to spirits and gods.
Zhōu and Kǒng, even if they numbered thousands, would have nothing to contend in their sageliness,
and Bēn and Yù, even if millions, would have nowhere to exert their courage.
Those foolish rulers of later generations,
seeing that none dared to oppose them in the world,
thought themselves as indestructible as Heaven and Earth.
They then indulged in their private pleasures,
gave free rein to their wicked desires,
and rulers and ministers publicly engaged in licentiousness.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn,
Xìe Yě said:
'When dukes and ministers publicly engage in licentiousness,
the people have nothing to emulate.'
Dù Yù said: Xuān,
means 'to show.'
They abandoned all administrative affairs,
and forgot about capable people.
Those they trusted and loved
were all sycophants and flatterers.
Those who received great favor and honor
were all relatives of empresses and concubines.
This eventually led to exhausting the fat and marrow of the empire,
and hacking away at the bones and marrow of the living people.
Grievances and poison were unbearable,
disasters and chaos arose together,
the Central Plains were disturbed and tumultuous,
the four barbarian tribes invaded and rebelled.
Like crumbling earth and shattering tiles,
it was gone in a morning.
Those who were once our suckling children and grandchildren
are now all our blood-drinking enemies.
Even when the tides shift and power departs,
those who still do not awaken—
is it not because wealth and honor breed inhumanity,
and indulgence leads to foolishness and illness!
Survival and demise alternate because of this,
and order and chaos cycle back from this.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn: Good and evil, when they reach their peak, always return;
this is the way of Heaven."
3. In the autumn,
seventh month,
Zhāng Měng, the Tàishǒu of Wǔwēi, killed Hándān Shāng, the Cìshǐ of Yōngzhōu.
In the first year of Xīngpíng (194 CE),
the four commanderies west of the Yellow River in Liángzhōu were separated to establish Yōngzhōu.
Yōng,
read "yú yòng fān."
Měng was the son of Huàn.
4. In the eighth month,
Cáo Cāo marched east to attack the sea bandit Guǎn Chéng.
He reached Chúnyú.
Chúnyú County belonged to Běihǎi Commandery.
Xián said: Its old city is in the northeast of present-day Ānqiū County, Mìzhōu.
Chéng fled into a sea island.
5. Chāng Xī rebelled again.
Cáo Cāo dispatched Yú Jìn to attack and execute him.
6 That year,
the son of the deceased Prince Rángxié, Róng, Xī, was established as Prince Rángxié.
The eight states of Qí, Běihǎi, Fùlíng, Xiàpī, Chángshān, Gānlíng, Jìyīn, and Píngyuán were all abolished.
Róng
was the great-great-grandson of Guāngwǔ's son, Prince Rángxié Xiào, Jīng.
After Róng's death,
the state was dissolved,
but now his son was re-established.
Qí
was a descendant of Guāngwǔ's elder brother, Prince Wǔ, Yǎn.
Běihǎi
was a descendant of Yǎn's youngest son, Prince Jìng, Xīng.
Fùlíng
was a descendant of Guāngwǔ's son, Prince Zhì, Yán.
Xiàpī
was a descendant of Míngdì's son, Prince Huì, Yǎn.
Chángshān
was a descendant of Míngdì's son, Prince Qǐng, Bǐng.
Gānlíng
was a descendant of Zhāngdì's son, Prince Qīnghé Xiào, Qìng.
Jìyīn:
Míngdì's son, Prince Dào, Cháng, died without an heir,
and that state was abolished long ago.
According to Fàn Shǐ,
it should be Jìběi,
a descendant of Zhāngdì's son, Prince Huì, Shòu,
whose state was also abolished in this year.
Píngyuán:
Hédì's son, Prince Huái, Shèng, was enfeoffed initially,
and died without an heir.
Yì, son of Prince Héjiān, Kāi, succeeded him.
Yì was deposed as Marquis Líwú,
and his son Zhì was established as Emperor Huán.
Then Shòu, the Emperor's elder brother, was re-established as Prince Píngyuán,
to continue Yì's line.
By this time, that state was also abolished.
All eight states were abolished,
but Xī alone was established to succeed Rángxié. This was because
Róng had previously sent his younger brother, Miǎo, to Cháng'ān to offer tribute.
Cáo Cāo was then in Dōngjùn,
and Miǎo greatly praised Róng's loyalty and sincerity.
Cáo Cāo appreciated Róng for this,
and therefore established an heir for Róng.
The abolition of the eight states
was a gradual weakening of the Hàn imperial clan.
濟,
pronounced as "zǐ lǐ" (齊禮).
7 The Wūhuán took advantage of the chaos in the empire,
seizing over a hundred thousand Hàn households.
Yuán Shào established their chieftains as Chányú,
and gave daughters of his own household
to them in marriage.
Tàdùn of the Xīliáo Wūhuán was particularly powerful,
and was highly favored by Shào.
Therefore, Shàng and his brothers returned to him,
repeatedly raiding within the frontier
in an attempt to help Shàng reclaim his former territory.
Cáo Cāo was about to attack them.
He dug the Pínglǔ Canal and Quánzhōu Canal to facilitate transport.
Cāo Jì says: The canal was dug
from Hūtúo, entering the Páishǔi,
named Pínglǔ Canal.
Also, from the Kùhé River mouth,
it was dug to enter the Lùhé River,
named Quánzhōu Canal,
to connect to the sea.
泒,
pronounced "gū".
泃,
pronounced "jù".
Xián says: The Hūtúo River
was formerly south of Ráoyáng.
When Cáo Cāo used the old course of the Ráohé,
he diverted it to flow north into the new canal,
which is why it is now north of Ráoyáng County.
Shuōwén says: The Páishǔi
originates from the Jùnrénshùfū Mountain in Yànmén,
and flows northeast into the sea.
Shuǐjīngzhù says: The Kùshuǐ
originates from the western mountain of Wúzhōng County, Yòuběipíng.
It flows northwest,
passes Pínggǔ County and then flows southeast,
then flows south into the Lùhé River,
and further east joins the mouth of the Quánzhōu Canal,
which was dug by Cáo Cāo.
The canal extends east to the south of Lè'ān Pavilion in Hǎiyáng County, where it joins the Rúshuǐ,
and then enters the sea.
Quánzhōu and Pínggǔ two counties
both belonged to Yúyáng Commandery.
Xián says: The old city of Quánzhōu
is now south of Yōngnú County in Yōuzhōu.
Hǎiyáng County
belonged to Liáoxī Commandery.
葰,
pronounced "xiāng wéi".
8 Sūn Quán attacked the mountain bandits of Má and Bǎo two strongholds,
and pacified them.
Shuǐjīngzhù says: The Jiāngshuǐ passes Lùkǒu and flows east,
on the left it reaches the Mátúnkǒu,
directly south of Púqízhōu.
The water enters northward for over a hundred *lǐ*;
this was where Wú stationed its troops.
1 In spring,

懾 (shè),

harbor private concerns and

At that time, Cáo Cāo's army

"Sù is brave and resourceful,

Quán (權) appointed Lǔ Sù (魯肅) as Fierce Might Colonel,

I fear Cáo (操) would not have reacted to this extent,

Chángshā (長沙) was divided to form Hànchāng (漢昌) Commandery.
Póyáng (鄱陽) is present-day Ráozhōu (饒州) territory.

In the eighth year of Wǔdé (武德) of the Táng (唐) dynasty (625 CE),

The Shuǐ Jīng (水經) says: The Jiāng (江) river flows west past the south of Wūlín (烏林).

on the right bank, is Pújīkǒu (蒲磯口),

enters north of Púqí (蒲圻) County,

At first,
Quán (權) said to Lǚ Méng (呂蒙):

Quán (權) said:
"Do I want you to study the classics and become a scholar?
You just need to skim through them

Shīgǔ (師古) says: Shè (涉) is like wading through water;
liè (獵) is like hunting beasts.
It means to browse through them without specializing.
Zhì (治) is pronounced zhí zhī.
Who is like me?
I constantly read books,
and consider it to be of great benefit."
Méng (蒙) then began to study.
When Lǔ Sù (魯肅) passed through Xúnyáng (尋陽)

belonged to Guìyáng (桂陽) Commandery.

Tǒng (統) was dismissed from office.

Zhūgě Liàng (諸葛亮) also spoke of this.
Bèi (備) met Tǒng (統),
and had good conversations with him,
greatly appreciating him.
"Good conversations" means debating current affairs.
Tán (譚) is the same as Tán (談).
His 친 (親) and treatment were second only to Zhūgě Liàng (諸葛亮),
and he served alongside Liàng (亮) as Army Advisor General of the Household.
At first,
Cāngwú (蒼梧) scholar Xiè (燮) was the Administrator of Jiāozhǐ (交趾).
The Inspector of Jiāozhōu (交州), Zhū Fú (朱符), was killed by barbarian rebels,

Xiè (燮) memorialized for his younger brother Yī (壹) to lead Hépǔ (合浦) Commandery,
Méi (䵋) to lead Jiǔzhēn (九真) Commandery,

Xiè (燮) had a generous and magnanimous character,
and many scholars from the central plains went to rely on him.
He dominated the entire prefecture,
being far away by ten thousand li (裡).
His authority was supreme and unrivaled.
As the empire was in turmoil,
Xiè (燮) held a stronghold in a remote prefecture.
People only knew his supreme authority
and no longer knew of an emperor.
Zhǎng (長) is pronounced zhī liǎng.
He subdued the myriad barbarians.
The imperial court sent Zhāng Jīn (張津) of Nányáng (南陽) as the Inspector of Jiāozhōu (交州).
Jīn (津) was fond of matters concerning ghosts and spirits.
He always wore a crimson headscarf,
played the qín (琴), burned incense,
and read Daoist texts,
claiming it could aid in transformation.
He was killed by his general Qū Jǐng (區景).
Liú Biǎo (劉表) sent Lài Gōng (賴恭) of Línglíng (零陵) to replace Jīn (津) as Inspector.
The Xìng Pǔ (姓譜) says: The Lài (賴) state was destroyed by Chǔ (楚),

The imperial court bestowed upon Xiè (燮) an imperial edict,
appointing Xiè (燮) as General of the Household Who Pacifies the South,
overseeing the seven commanderies,
and retaining his position as Administrator of Jiāozhǐ (交趾) as before.
Jù (巨) and Gōng (恭) fell out.
Jù (巨) raised troops to drive out Gōng (恭),
and Gōng (恭) fled back to Línglíng (零陵).
Sūn Quán appointed Bù Zhì (步騭) of Lín-Huái (臨淮), Grand Administrator of Póyáng (鄱陽), as Governor of Jiāozhōu (交州).

who held a fief in Bù (步),
and thus took Bù as his surname.
番,
read Pú Hè.
騭,
read Zhí Rì.
Wú Jù (吳巨) was outwardly submissive but inwardly rebellious.
Bù Zhì (步騭) lured and then executed him,
and his prestige greatly increased.
Quán (權) promoted Xiè (燮) to General of the Left,
and Xiè (燮) sent his son to serve as a hostage.
From this, the region south of the mountains began to submit to Quán (權).
