and never served as the Chancellor's deputy.
2 In the third month,
Cāo (操) dispatched Zhōng Yáo (鍾繇), Commandant of the Capital, to attack Zhāng Lǔ (張魯),
and sent Xiàhóu Yuān (夏侯淵) and others, the Protector of the Western Expedition, to lead troops out of Hédōng (河東),
to meet with Yáo (繇).
Yuān's (淵) clan
was the one Cāo (操) himself came from;
he was entrusted with the vanguard mission for the western expedition.
As his rank and seniority had not yet qualified him to be General of the Western Expedition,
he was therefore given the title of Protector.
The Secretariat Section of the Grand Excellency's Office
was in charge of granaries and grain matters;
it had clerks
and subordinates.
"With a large army marching west,
Hán Suí (韓遂) and Mǎ Chāo (馬超) will suspect they are being attacked,
and will surely incite each other.
It is advisable to first rally the Three Commanderies.
If the Three Commanderies are pacified,
Hànzhōng (漢中) can be settled by merely sending a proclamation."
Cāo (操) did not follow this advice.
The various generals in Guānzhōng (關中) indeed suspected this.
Cāo (操) abandoned Guānzhōng (關中) for a distant campaign against Zhāng Lǔ (張魯);
this was a stratagem to attack Guó (虢) by borrowing the way through Yú (虞).
He wanted to attack Chāo (超) and Suí (遂) but lacked a pretext,
so he first made a show of attacking Lǔ (魯) to provoke their rebellion,
and then he would deploy his troops.
Their army of 100,000 men
was stationed at Tóngguān (潼關).
Tóngguān (潼關)
is in Huáyīn (華陰) County, Hóngnóng (弘農).
The Shuǐjīng Zhù (水經註) states: The river flows south within the pass,
the Tóng (潼) river vigorously strikes the pass mountain,
hence it is called Tóngguān (潼關).
This is what the Jìn (晉) called the stronghold of Táolín (桃林),
and what Qín (秦) called Yánghuá (陽華).
The Jìn Báiguān Zhì (晉百官志) states: The Four Pacifiers began in early Wèi (魏).
This refers to the Generals Pacifying the East, West, South, and North.
He ordered the Commandant of the Five Offices, Pī (丕), to remain and guard Yè (鄴),
and appointed Chéng Yù (程昱), General Spreading Martial Might, to participate in Pī's (丕) military affairs.
Shěn Yuè (沈約) states: The General Spreading Martial Might
began in the late Han.
The Monxià Dū (門下督) was an inspector of generals who resided within the Monxià (門下) (literally, "under the gate").
Guó Yuān (國淵) of Lè'ān (樂安) was appointed Chief Clerk of the Residency Office,
to oversee all remaining affairs.
The Xìngpǔ (姓譜) states: In Qí (齊), there was the Guó (國) clan,
who were hereditary Senior Ministers.
Also, descendants of Zhèng (鄭) Qīmùzǐ Guó (七穆子國)
took the surname Guó (國).
In the seventh month,
Cāo (操) personally led an attack on Chāo (超) and others.
Many strategists said:
"The Guānxī (關西) troops are skilled with long spears;
without carefully selected vanguards,
they cannot be withstood."
Cāo (操) said:
"The battle depends on me,
not on the enemy.
Although the enemy is skilled with long spears,
I will ensure they cannot use them to stab.
Gentlemen, just observe."
"It depends on me and not on the enemy,"
therefore one can achieve victory;
this is not something easily explained to ordinary people.
刺,
read Qī Yì;
same below.
In the eighth month,
Cāo (操) arrived at Tóngguān (潼關) and encamped facing Chāo (超) and others across the pass.
Cāo (操) held them in check tightly,
while secretly sending Xú Huǎng (徐晃) and Zhū Líng (朱靈) with four thousand infantry and cavalry
to cross the Púbǎnjīn (蒲阪津) ford
and establish a camp on the west bank of the river.
Púbǎnjīn (蒲阪津)
is west of Púbǎn (蒲阪) County.
The west bank of the river is the Pújīn Guān (蒲津關) of the Táng (唐) dynasty.
The Kǎo Yì (考異) states: The biography of Huǎng (晃) says:
"When Grand Ancestor arrived at Tóngguān (潼關),
fearing he could not cross,
he summoned Huǎng (晃) and asked him.
Huǎng (晃) said: 'My lord has a large army here,
yet the enemy has not separately guarded Púbǎn (蒲阪);
this shows their lack of strategy.
If you now lend me elite troops to cross Púbǎnjīn (蒲阪津)
and establish a forward position to cut off their rear,
the enemy can be captured.'
Grand Ancestor said: 'Excellent.'"
However, the biography of Emperor Wǔ (武帝) states
that secretly sending two generals to cross Púbǎn (蒲阪)
was entirely Grand Ancestor's plan,
while Huǎng's (晃) biography attributes it entirely to Huǎng's (晃) strategy.
Probably Chén (陳) [Shòu] wished to praise their respective achievements,
not considering the other.
Cāo (操) crossed the river north from Tóngguān (潼關).
Most of the troops crossed first;
Cāo (操) alone remained on the south bank with over a hundred tiger warriors to cover the rear.
Mǎ Chāo (馬超) led over ten thousand cavalry and infantry to attack them;
arrows fell like rain.
Cāo (操) still sat on his folding stool, unmoved.
Xǔ Chǔ (許褚) helped Cāo (操) onto a boat;
the boatman died from a stray arrow in midstream.
Chǔ (褚) held up a horse saddle with his left hand to shield Cāo (操),
and steered the boat with his right.
Commandant Dīng Fēi (丁斐)
released cattle and horses to bait the enemy;
the enemy fell into disarray,
seizing the cattle and horses,
and Cāo (操) was then able to cross.
He then crossed the Western River from Púbǎn (蒲阪),
following the river to build a covered path southward.
Chāo (超) and others retreated to block the mouth of the Wèi (渭) River.
The former text states
that the Wèi (渭) River flows into the (Yellow) River at Chuánsīkōng (船司空).
The Later Han abolished Chuánsīkōng (船司空)
and placed it under Huáyīn (華陰) County.
East of the mouth of the Wèi (渭)
is Tóngguān (潼關).
He secretly transported troops by boat into the Wèi (渭) River,
built a pontoon bridge,
and at night
divided his forces to establish camps south of the Wèi (渭) River.
Chāo (超) and others attacked the camps at night,
but the hidden troops ambushed and defeated them.
Chāo (超) and others encamped south of the Wèi (渭) River,
sent envoys to request peace by ceding the territory west of the river,
but Cāo (操) refused.
In the ninth month,
Cāo (操) advanced his army,
completely crossing the Wèi (渭) River.
Chāo (超) and others repeatedly challenged him,
but he still refused;
they earnestly requested to cede territory
and offer hostages.
Jiǎ Xǔ (賈詡) thought it was permissible to feign agreement.
Cāo (操) again asked for strategy,
and Xǔ (詡) said:
"Just sow discord among them."
Cāo (操) said:
"I understand!"
Hán Suí asked to meet with Cáo Cāo.
Cáo Cāo and Suí had an old acquaintance,
so they met on horseback and spoke for a long time.
When Suí met with Fán Chóu on horseback and spoke,
he was able to kill Chóu.
When he met with Cáo Cāo on horseback and spoke,
he brought about his own ruin.
Only then did people realize that the way Suí treated Chóu
was not due to any special stratagem.
If Mǎ Chāo and others suspected Suí,
it was just like Lǐ Jué suspecting Chóu.
They merely spoke of old acquaintances in the capital
and clapped hands, laughing joyfully.
At that time, the Qín and Hú spectators
were numerous, crowding front and back.
Cáo Cāo laughed and said to them,
"Do you wish to see Cáo Gōng?
He is just a man,
not one with four eyes and two mouths,
but merely one with much wisdom!"
After they had parted,
Mǎ Chāo and the others asked Suí,
"What did Cáo Gōng say?"
Suí replied,
"He said nothing."
Mǎ Chāo and the others grew suspicious.
Another day,
Cáo Cāo again wrote a letter to Suí,
making many alterations and emendations,
as if Suí had revised it.
Mǎ Chāo and the others became even more suspicious of Suí.
Both of these were means to sow discord between them.
The "Kǎo Yì" says: "Xǔ Chǔ Zhuàn" says:
"Tài Zǔ met with Hán Suí, Mǎ Chāo, and others.
None of his attendants were allowed to follow,
except for General Chǔ.
Mǎ Chāo, relying on his strength,
secretly intended to rush forward and assault Tài Zǔ.
Having long heard of Chǔ's bravery,
he suspected that the attendant was Chǔ,
and asked, 'Where is Cáo Gōng's Tiger Marquis?'
Tài Zǔ looked back and pointed at Chǔ.
Chǔ glared at him,
and Mǎ Chāo dared not move."
I hold that Mǎ Chāo was not with Suí at that time,
hence I doubt the veracity of this statement.
To "kè rì" means
to fix the day.
The battle lasted for a long time,
then the tiger cavalry was unleashed to attack from both sides,
greatly defeating them.
Chéng Yí, Lǐ Kān, and others were beheaded.
Suí and Chāo fled to Liángzhōu,
Yáng Qiū fled to Āndìng.
The generals asked Cáo Cāo,
"Initially,
when the bandits guarded Tóngguān,
the road north of the Wèi River was cut off.
‘Què’ means
that it was cut off and unprepared.
Why did you delay for days before crossing to the north?"
Cáo Cāo replied,
"The bandits were guarding Tóngguān.
If I had entered Hédōng,
the bandits would surely have moved to guard all the fords,
and then Xīhé would have been impossible to cross.
So I concentrated my forces towards Tóngguān.
When the bandits moved all their forces to guard the south,
the defenses of Xīhé were empty.
Therefore, the two generals were able to capture Xīhé.
Then I led the army to cross to the north.
The reason the bandits could not contend with me for Xīhé
was because of the armies of the two generals.
The two generals
were Xú Huǎng and Zhū Líng.
‘Jiàng’ is pronounced
as ‘liàng’.
To construct a covered pathway and move south
was to first make oneself invincible.
The 'Art of War' states:
First make yourself invincible to await the enemy's vulnerability.
Crossing the Wèi River and establishing firm fortresses,
not engaging the barbarians when they arrived,
was to make them arrogant.
Thus, the bandits did not build fortresses and instead sought to cede land.
My agreeing to their terms
was to comply with their wishes,
making them feel secure and unprepared.
Taking advantage of this, I preserved the strength of my soldiers,
and attacked them suddenly,
which is what is meant by 'swift thunder leaves no time to cover the ears'.
This is a saying from the 'Huáinánzǐ'.
Indeed, there was no single path."
At first,
whenever a contingent of the various generals from Guānzhōng arrived,
Cáo Cāo would show a joyful expression.
The generals asked him the reason.
Cáo Cāo said,
"Guānzhōng is vast and distant.
If the bandits each relied on dangerous terrain,
to conquer them
would take no less than one or two years.
Now they have all gathered.
Although their numbers are great,
none submit to each other.
The army has no single master.
They can be eliminated in one fell swoop,
making the accomplishment relatively easy.
This is why I am happy."
At this time,
the forces of Guānxī were the most elite and powerful,
but they were defeated by Cáo Cāo
because their laws and regulations were not unified.
"Yì" is pronounced
as "shì".
In winter,
the tenth month,
Cáo Cāo marched north from Cháng'ān to attack Yáng Qiū,
and besieged Āndìng.
Yáng Qiū surrendered,
and Cáo Cāo restored his rank and title,
sending him back to govern his people.
In the twelfth month,
Cáo Cāo returned from Āndìng,
leaving Xiàhóu Yuān to garrison Cháng'ān.
He appointed Yìláng Zhāng Jì as Jīngzhàoyǐn.
Zhāng Jì won over the displaced people
and restored the counties and townships.
The common people cherished him.
When Suí and Chāo rebelled,
many counties and townships in Hóngnóng and Féngyì responded to them,
but the people of Hédōng alone had no disloyal intentions.
Cáo Cāo and Mǎ Chāo and the others built camps along the Wèi River,
and the army's provisions entirely depended on Hédōng.
When Mǎ Chāo and the others were defeated,
there were still over 200,000 hú of provisions remaining.
Cáo Cāo then increased the salary of Dù Jī, the Administrator of Hédōng, to that of two thousand shí.
3 Fúfēng Fǎ Zhèng was Liú Zhāng's Jūnyì Xiàowèi.
Jūnyì Xiàowèi
was an officer who discussed military affairs.
It is understood that at that time, everyone would advocate for Fǎ Zhèng's skill in strategizing,
but Liú Zhāng could appoint him to office but not make use of him.
Moreover, he was scorned by those from his hometown who were also transient guests.
Fǎ Zhèng was discontented and unhappy.
"Qiáo" means
to be a guest,
to reside temporarily.
"Bǐ" means
to disparage.
"Yìyì" means
unhappy.
He had high self-regard for his talent,
and considered Liú Zhāng not worth accomplishing anything with.
"Cǔn" means
to estimate,
to ponder.
"Cǔn" is pronounced
as "cùn běn".
Sōng advised Liú Zhāng to ally with Liú Bèi.
Liú Zhāng asked,
"Who can be sent as an envoy?"
Sōng then recommended Fǎ Zhèng.
Liú Zhāng sent Fǎ Zhèng,
who initially declined,
but feigned that he had no choice but to go.
Upon his return,
he told Sōng that Liú Bèi possessed great ambition and strategy,
and secretly plotted to support and make him the ruler of the province.
At that time, Cáo Cāo dispatched Zhōng Yáo towards Hànzhōng.
Zhāng heard of this,
and was inwardly filled with fear.
Sōng therefore said to Zhāng:
"General Cáo's army is unrivaled under Heaven.
If he were to take the lands of Shǔ, using Zhāng Lǔ's resources,
who could resist him?
Liú Yùzhōu
is your clan kinsman and Cáo Gōng's deep enemy;
he is skilled in warfare.
If you send him to attack Lǔ,
Lǔ will certainly be defeated.
When Lǔ is defeated,
Yìzhōu will be strong.
Even if Cáo Gōng comes,
he will be able to do nothing!
Now, the
various generals of the province, Páng Xī and Lǐ Yì, etc.,
all rely on their merits and are arrogant and powerful.
According to Péi Sōngzhī's commentary,
Páng Xī rescued Zhāng's sons from danger,
and Lǐ Yì killed Zhào Wěi,
hence each relied on their merit.
It is said that their intention was to attach themselves to external forces.
Then if the enemy attacks from without,
and the people attack from within,
it is a certain path to defeat!"
Zhāng agreed with him
and sent Fǎ Zhèng with four thousand men to welcome Bèi.
The Chief Clerk, Huáng Quán of Bāxī, admonished him, saying:
The Bā Jì by Qiáo Zhōu says: Liú Zhāng divided Bājùn, taking Diànjiāng and areas above it to form Bāxī Jùn.
"General of the Left Liú has a reputation for bravery.
Cáo Cāo submitted a memorial appointing Bèi as General of the Left,
hence he is called such.
Xiāo
is pronounced jiān yáo fān.
If you treat him as a subordinate,
his heart will not be satisfied.
If you treat him with the courtesy due to a guest,
then one country cannot accommodate two lords.
If the guest enjoys the stability of Mount Tài,
then the host will be in peril like stacked eggs.
It would be better to close the borders and await a clear time."
Zhāng did not listen,
and sent Quán out as the Prefect of Guǎnghàn.
Guǎnghàn County
belonged to Guǎnghàn Commandery.
Zhǎng
is pronounced zhī liǎng fān.
Hú Yì suspended himself upside down at the provincial gate to remonstrate,
but Zhāng accepted nothing.
Fǎ Zhèng arrived at Jīngzhōu
and secretly presented a plan to Liú Bèi, saying:
"With the sagacious General's heroic talent,
taking advantage of Governor Liú's weakness;
Zhāng Sōng
is the province's vital support;
the Vice Prefect
is the province's highest aide,
hence called vital support.
To take Yìzhōu
is as easy as turning over one's hand."
Kǎo Yì says: Wéi Yào's Wú Shū says:
"Bèi first met Zhāng Sōng,
then later met Fǎ Zhèng,
both of whom he received with great kindness and virtue,
showing them his utmost sincerity and joy.
He then asked about the width and narrowness of Shǔ,
its weapons and armories,
the number of men and horses,
and the distances of various strategic roads;
Sōng and others fully informed him."
However, according to the biographies of Liú Zhāng and Liú Bèi,
Sōng never met Bèi first;
the Wú Shū is mistaken.
Páng Tǒng said to Bèi:
"Jīngzhōu is desolate and ruined,
its people exhausted.
To the east is Sūn Chēqí;
Bèi submitted a memorial appointing Quán as General of Chēqí,
hence he is called such.
It is difficult to achieve your ambition here.
Now Yìzhōu has a population of a million households,
fertile land and abundant wealth.
If you can truly use this as resources,
a great enterprise can be accomplished!"
Bèi said:
"The one who is like fire and water to me now
is Cáo Cāo.
'Fire and water' means their natures are opposite.
I am lenient;
Cāo is tyrannical.
I am benevolent;
Cāo is cunning.
I am loyal.
By always doing the opposite of Cāo,
things can be accomplished.
Now, how can I sacrifice trust and righteousness to the world
for a small gain?"
Tǒng said:
"In times of chaos and separation,
it is certainly not one single path that can bring stability.
Moreover, to combine against the weak and attack the ignorant,
these are the words of Zhòng Huǐ in the Shàng Shū.
In the Qián Shū, Lù Jiǎ says:
'Tāng and Wǔ seized power through rebellion but governed with righteousness.'
If, after the matter is settled,
you enfeoff him with a great state,
what harm is there to your trustworthiness?
If you do not take it today,
it will ultimately become someone else's gain."
Bèi considered it to be so.
He then left Zhūgě Liàng, Guān Yǔ, and others to guard Jīngzhōu,
and appointed Zhào Yún as the Commander of the Retained Camp.
The Commander of the Retained Camp
was in charge of military affairs of the retained camp.
Sūn Quán heard that Bèi had gone west,
and sent boats to welcome his sister.
However, the Lady wished to take Bèi's son, Shàn, back to Wú.
Zhāng Fēi and Zhào Yún led troops to intercept them at the river,
and thus Shàn was returned.
Liú Zhāng敕 supplied and prepared everything for Liú Bèi,
so Bèi felt at home upon entering the territory.
The gifts he received before and after amounted to billions.
When Bèi arrived at Bá Jùn,
the Administrator of Bá Jùn, Yán Yán, thumped his chest and sighed,
"This is what they call 'sitting alone in a remote mountain
and letting a tiger guard oneself.'"
Bèi proceeded north from Jiāng Zhōu along the Diàn Jiāng River to Fú.
Bá Jùn
had its administrative seat in Jiāng Zhōu.
Diàn Jiāng Xiàn
belonged to Bá Jùn.
Fú Xiàn
belonged to Guǎng Hàn Jùn.
The Diàn Jiāng River
is probably the same as the Fú Nèi River.
Yǔ Zhòngyōng said: Jiāng Zhōu County faces two river mouths;
to the right is the Fú Nèi River,
and to the left is the Shǔ Wài River.
Diàn
is pronounced "dié."
Fú
is pronounced "fú."
Xián said: The old city of Fú Xiàn
is now Mián Zhōu City.
Diàn Jiāng Xiàn
was Hè Zhōu in the Táng dynasty.
Carriages, armor, and tents
gleamed brilliantly, shining in the sun,
as they went to the meeting.
Zhāng Sōng ordered Fǎ Zhèng to inform Bèi
to attack Zhāng at the meeting.
Bèi said,
"This matter cannot be rushed!"
Páng Tǒng said,
"If we seize him at the meeting now,
then the General will have no need for the toil of war and will calmly settle the province."
Bèi said,
"Having just entered another's country,
my kindness and trustworthiness are not yet established;
this cannot be done."
Zhāng promoted Bèi to acting Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ)
and appointed him Governor of the Capital Region (Sī Lì Xiàowèi);
Bèi, in turn, promoted Zhāng to acting General who Guards the West (Zhèn Xī Dà Jiāngjūn)
and appointed him Provincial Governor of Yì Zhōu (Yì Zhōu Mù).
The Jìn Bǎi Guān Zhì says: The Four Generals who Guard (Sì Zhèn) are for pacifying distant lands.
These refer to the Generals who Guard the East, West, South, and North.
They reciprocated with each other.
Zhī
means "to go."
Gèng
is pronounced "gōng héng fān."
Zhāng increased Bèi's troops
and generously supplied him,
sending him to attack Zhāng Lǔ,
and also made him supervise the Bái Shuǐ army.
Bái Shuǐ Guān
was in Bái Shuǐ Xiàn, Guǎng Hàn,
where Liú Zhāng stationed troops to guard it,
which were the armies of Yáng Huái and Gāo Pèi.
Dù Yòu said: Jīn Niú Xiàn, Liáng Zhōu,
was the land of Jiā Méng Xiàn in the Hàn dynasty;
south of the county was the old Bái Shuǐ Guān.
The chariots, armor, weapons, and provisions were very abundant.
Zhāng returned to Chéng Dū,
and Bèi went north to Jiā Méng.
Jiā Méng Xiàn
belonged to Guǎng Hàn Jùn.
Xián said: Jiā Méng
is now Yì Chāng Xiàn, Lì Zhōu.
Yì Shào said: Jiā
is pronounced "jiā."
Shī Gǔ said: Méng
is pronounced "máng."
The King of Shǔ enfeoffed his brother Jiā Méng here,
and thus the place was named after him.
The Former Lord (Liú Bèi) renamed it Hàn Shòu.
He generously cultivated kindness and virtue to win the hearts of the people.
1. In the spring,
the first month,
Cáo Cāo returned to Yè.
An imperial edict granted Cāo the privilege of bowing without being announced by name,
entering court without hurrying,
and wearing his sword and shoes into the palace,
just like Xiāo Hé in earlier times.
2. When Cāo campaigned in the west,
the people of Hé Jiān, Tián Yín and Sū Bó, rebelled,
stirring up Yōu and Jì.
The Heir Apparent (Wǔ Guān Jiāng) Pī wanted to personally suppress them.
The Senior Clerk (Gōng Cáo) Cháng Lín said:
According to Cháng Lín's biography, he was then the Senior Clerk for the Heir Apparent.
"The officials and people of the north
enjoy peace and dislike chaos,
having been accustomed to civilization for a long time,
and most are virtuous.
Yín and Bó are merely a band of dogs and sheep,
incapable of causing harm.
At present, the main army is far away,
and there are strong enemies outside.
The General is the bulwark of the realm
(referring to his remaining behind to guard Yè).
Even if you win, it would not be a martial feat."
Thereupon, he sent General Jiǎ Xìn to suppress them,
and they were immediately crushed.
Over a thousand remaining rebels requested to surrender.
The deliberators all said,
"The Duke (Cáo Cāo) has an old law:
those who surrender after being besieged are not pardoned."
Chéng Yù said,
"That was during a time of turmoil,
a temporary expediency.
Now that the realm is largely settled,
they cannot be executed.
Even if they were to be executed,
it should first be reported."
The deliberators all said,
"Military matters can be decided on the spot without asking for instructions."
Yù said,
"Those who act on their own authority
are only referred to when there is an urgent matter at hand.
Now these rebels are in Jiǎ Xìn's hands,
which is why this old minister does not wish the General to proceed with it."
Pī said,
"Good."
He immediately reported to Cāo,
and Cāo indeed did not execute them.
Afterwards, he heard of Yù's counsel
and was very pleased,
saying,
"You are not only astute in military strategy,
but also skillful in mediating between father and son."
(This was to encourage Pī not to execute them on his own authority).
Chǔ
is pronounced "chāng lǚ fān."
In an earlier incident: In documents reporting victory over rebels,
one was recorded as ten;
Guó Yuān, when submitting the count of severed heads,
reported the actual number.
Guó Yuān was then in charge of retained matters.
Shàng
is pronounced "shí zhǎng fān."
Yuān said,
"Indeed, when campaigning against foreign invaders,
exaggerating the number of slain and captured
is intended to magnify military might
and awe the populace.
Hé Jiān is within our borders,
and Yín and others' rebellion,
though overcome with success,
I am secretly ashamed of it."
Cáo was greatly pleased.
3. In the summer,
the fifth month,
on the day Guǐ Wèi,
the Commandant of the Guards (Wèi Wèi) Mǎ Téng was executed,
and his three clans were exterminated.
(Mǎ Téng had gone to Yè to meet him, see volume 13, year [of the reign]).
4. In the sixth month,
on the day Gēng Yín, the last day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
5. In the autumn,
the seventh month,
there was a locust plague.
6. The remaining forces of Mǎ Chāo and others were stationed at Lán Tián,
and Xiàhóu Yuān attacked and pacified them.
The bandits of Fū
in Fūxiàn,
under the Former Hàn, belonged to Zuǒ Fēngyì,
but were abolished under the Later Hàn.
Shīgǔ said: Fū,
pronounced fū.
All the counties were in fear,
and all moved their administration to the commandery seat.
Some deliberated that they should move to a safer, more rugged terrain.
Zhèng Hún, the Zuǒ Fēngyì, said:
"Xīng and his ilk are scattered and broken,
hiding in mountains and valleys.
Although some follow them,
they are mostly coerced.
We should now widely open paths for surrender,
proclaim our might and trustworthiness.
To guard ourselves in fortified places shows weakness."
So, he gathered officials and common people,
built city walls,
made defensive preparations,
and recruited commoners to pursue the bandits.
For any property, goods, or women recovered,
seven-tenths would be rewarded.
The people were greatly pleased,
and all wished to capture bandits.
Those bandits whose wives and children had been returned
sought to surrender.
Hún demanded they hand over any other women they had acquired
before their families were returned.
Thereupon, they turned to plunder each other,
and their factions dispersed.
He also sent officials and commoners known for their benevolence and trustworthiness to spread out in the mountains and valleys to issue proclamations to them.
Those who came out arrived in continuous streams.
Then he ordered the chief officials of all the counties to return to their original seats
to settle and pacify the people.
Xīng and his followers were afraid,
and gathered their remaining forces in Fūchéng.
Cáo Cāo dispatched Xiàhóu Yuān to assist Hún in suppressing them.
Consequently, Xīng was beheaded,
and the remaining factions were all pacified.
Hún
was the younger brother of Tà.
Zhèng Tà
was employed by Dǒng Zhuó but sought to plot against Zhuó.
7 In the ninth month,
on the gengxu day,
Imperial Prince Xī was established as the King of Jìyīn,
Yī as the King of Shānyáng,
Miǎo as the King of Jìběi,
and Dūn as the King of Dōnghǎi.
At this time, Xǔ Jìng was in Shǔ.
Hearing of the establishment of the princes,
he said:
"If one intends to contract it,
one must first expand it;
if one intends to take it away,
one must first give it.
This must be what Mèngdé means."
Jì,
pronounced like zǐlǐ.
8 Initially,
Zhāng Hóng, seeing the excellent natural features of Mòlíng,
urged Sūn Quán to make it his administrative seat.
When Liú Bèi traveled east through Mòlíng,
he also advised Quán to reside there.
Quán then built Shítóuchéng
and moved his administration to Mòlíng,
renaming Mòlíng to Jiànyè.
Mòlíng,
belonged to Dānyáng Commandery,
was originally Jīnlíng,
renamed by Qín Shǐhuáng.
Sūn Quán renamed it Jiànyè.
Later, to avoid the taboo name of Jìn Mǐndì,
it was renamed Jiànkāng.
Shítóuchéng
is two lǐ west of the present-day Jiànkāng city.
Jīnlíng Zhì: Shítóuchéng is nine lǐ from Táichéng,
and in the south connects with the Qínhuái River.
Zhāng Shùnmín said: Shítóuchéng is a natural city wall,
like a fortress,
on Fùzhōu Shān, north of Qīngliáng Sì.
Those traveling by river from the north
follow Shítóuchéng
and turn into the Qínhuái.
Lù Yóu said: Looking at Shítóu Shān from Lóngwān,
it is not very high,
but it stands sheer in the river,
winding like a wall.
Qīngliáng Sì is more than a lǐ from Shítóu.
Looking west, one sees Xuānhuà Dù and the various mountains of Lìyáng.
Sòng Bái said: When Jìn pacified Wú,
it was divided into two districts.
South of the Huái River was Mòlíng,
and north was Jiànyè.
Jiāngbiǎo Zhuàn: Hóng said to Quán:
"Mòlíng,
established by Chǔ Wǔwáng,
was named Jīnlíng.
Its terrain has hills and mounds connected to Shítóu.
In the past, Qín Shǐhuáng, during his eastern tour,
passed through this county.
Those who observed the qi said that
Jīnlíng's topography
possessed the qi of a king's capital.
Therefore, he dug and severed the connected ridges,
renaming it Mòlíng.
Now the site still exists,
and it is suitable for a capital."
Xiàndì Chūnqiū also records Quán saying:
"Mòlíng has a small river over a hundred lǐ long
where large ships can anchor.
I am preparing my navy,
and should move to occupy it."
Also, according to Jìn Shū, Xī Lóng Zhuàn,
Lóng was the Cǐshǐ of Yángzhōu,
garrisoned at Mòlíng.
Qí Wáng Jiǒng issued a檄令 (edict) for him to go and attack Zhào Wáng Lún.
Lóng delayed the edict and did not follow it.
At that time, Wáng Suì was garrisoned at Shítóu.
Many of Lóng's troops wished to go west to Suì.
Lóng sent an attendant to Niúzhǔ to forbid them,
but they could not be stopped.
The officers and soldiers, supporting Suì, attacked and killed Lóng.
This indicates that Shítóu was west of Niúzhǔ.
Upon careful examination of this matter,
the Mòlíng army, wanting to go to Suì,
wished to proceed west from Niúzhǔ to support the king.
Shítóu was naturally east of Niúzhǔ.
9 Lǚ Méng, hearing that Cáo Cāo intended to move his troops eastward,
persuaded Sūn Quán to construct fortified encampments at the mouth of the Rúxū waterway.
All the generals said:
"We will land and attack the enemy,
and wash our feet before re-entering the ships.
What use are encampments?"
Méng said:
"Troops have strengths and weaknesses,
and battles are not always victorious.
If by chance
the enemy's infantry and cavalry press in,
people will not have time to reach the water.
How could they get into the ships?"
Quán said:
"Excellent!"
So, the Rúxū encampments were built.
In the 10th winter,
in the tenth month,
Cáo Cāo (曹操) attacked Sūn Quán (孫權) in the east.
Dǒng Zhāo (董昭) spoke to Cáo Cāo, saying:
"From ancient times until now,
among subjects who have brought order to the world,
none has achieved the merit you have today;
and those who have achieved such merit,
have never long remained in the position of a subject.
Now, your Excellency feels shame at possessing an unseemly virtue,
and delights in preserving your reputation and integrity;
however, to hold the power of a great minister,
causing people to suspect you of great ambitions,
is truly something one cannot but consider carefully."
Then, he discussed with the marquises and generals,
proposing that the Chancellor should be promoted to the rank of Guó Gōng (國公),
with the nine bestowments fully presented,
to make his extraordinary achievements manifest.
Xián (賢) said: The Lǐ Hán Wén Jiā (禮含文嘉) states: The nine bestowments
are: first, carriages and horses;
second, robes and apparel;
third, musical instruments;
fourth, vermilion doors;
fifth, the nābì (納陛) (a ceremonial ramp);
sixth, one hundred Hǔbēn (虎賁) guards;
seventh, battle-axes;
eighth, bows and arrows;
ninth, fragrant millet wine.
They are called the nine bestowments (jǐu xí, 九錫),
xí (錫)
means to give;
the nine bestowments are all given according to one's virtue.

The Zuǒ Zhuàn (左傳) states: Lǔ Gōng (魯公) was bestowed with a grand carriage, a grand banner, the huáng (璜) jade pendant of the Xià Hòushì (夏后氏), the Fán Ruò (繁弱) bow of Fēng Fù (封父), Zhù Zōng (祝宗), Bǔ Shǐ (卜史), and an array of ceremonial objects and records.
"Cáo Gōng (曹公) originally raised an army of righteousness to stabilize the court and pacify the nation,
upholding sincerity and loyalty,
and maintaining the reality of modesty and yielding;
a nobleman loves others with virtue,"
(The Tán Gōng (檀弓) records that
Zēng Zǐ (曾子) said: A nobleman loves others with virtue,
while a petty person loves others with indulgence.)
Cāo (操) was displeased by this.
When he attacked Sūn Quán (孫權),
he sent a memorial requesting Xún Yù (荀彧) to comfort the troops at Qiáo (譙),
then detained Yù (彧),
appointing him Shìzhōng (侍中), Guānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫), bearer of the jié (節) (imperial staff), and military advisor to the Chancellor.
Zhé (輒)
means to act presumptuously.
Yù (彧) stayed at Shòuchūn (壽春) due to illness,
drank medicine, and died.
The Xún Yù Zhuàn (彧傳) says: Cāo (操) sent him a food box;
when he opened it,
it was an empty container,
whereupon he drank medicine and died.
The Kǎo Yì (考異) states: Chén Zhì (陳志) Xún Yù Zhuàn (彧傳) says:
"He died of sorrow."
Fàn Shū (范書) Xún Yù Zhuàn (彧傳) says:
"Cāo (操) sent him a food box;
when he opened it,
it was an empty container,
whereupon he drank medicine and died."
Sūn Shèng's (孫盛) Wèi Shì Chūnqiū (魏氏春秋) also says the same.
Examining Yù's (彧) death,
Cāo (操) concealed his execution.
Chén Shòu (陳壽) said he died of sorrow,
which was probably to leave the matter doubtful.
If we do not state clearly that he drank medicine,
I fear that future superiors
might believe that covert executions can be carried out.
He was good at recommending worthy scholars and promoting talented individuals,
which is why people of the time all grieved for him.
Your servant Guāng (光) says: Kǒngzǐ's (孔子) words on benevolence were profound.
Even Zǐlù (子路), Rǎn Qiú (冉求), Gōngxī Chì (公西赤), the foremost among his disciples,
and Lìng Yǐn (令尹) Zǐwén (子文), Chén Wénzǐ (陳文子), virtuous grandees of various states,
were not deemed sufficient to embody it,
yet he alone praised Guǎn Zhòng's (管仲) benevolence.
Was it not because he assisted Qí Huán (齊桓)
and greatly benefited the common people?
The Lúnyǔ (論語): Mèng Wǔbó (孟武伯) asked:
"Is Zǐlù (子路) benevolent?"
The Master said:
"I do not know."
He asked again.
The Master said:
"Yóu (由) [Zǐlù's (子路) given name]
can be tasked with administering the levies of a state of a thousand chariots,
but I do not know if he is benevolent."
"What about Qiú (求) [Rǎn Qiú's (冉求) given name]?"
He replied:
"Qiú (求)
can be appointed as governor of a town of a thousand households, or a family of a hundred chariots,
but I do not know if he is benevolent."
"What about Chì (赤) [Gōngxī Chì's (公西赤) given name]?"
He replied:
"Chì (赤)
can, dressed in formal attire, stand in court
and converse with guests and visitors,
but I do not know if he is benevolent."
Zǐ Zhāng (子張) asked:
"Lìng Yǐn (令尹) Zǐwén (子文)
served as Lìng Yǐn (令尹) thrice without showing joy;
he was dismissed thrice without showing resentment.
He always informed the new Lìng Yǐn (令尹) of the policies of the previous Lìng Yǐn (令尹).
What do you think?"
The Master said:
"He was loyal."
He asked:
"Was he benevolent?"
He replied:
"I do not know,
how could he be benevolent?"
"When Cuī Zǐ (崔子) assassinated the ruler of Qí (齊),
Chén Wénzǐ (陳文子), who had ten chariots,
abandoned them and left,
arriving in another state,
he said, 'They are still like our grandee Cuī Zǐ (崔子),'
and left it.
Arriving in another state,
he again said, 'They are still like our grandee Cuī Zǐ (崔子),'
and left it.
What do you think?"
The Master said:
"He was pure."
He asked:
"Was he benevolent?"
He replied:
"I do not know,
how could he be benevolent?"
Zǐgòng (子貢) said:
"Was Guǎn Zhòng (管仲) not benevolent?
When Huán Gōng (桓公) killed Gōngzǐ Jiū (公子糾),
he could not die (for his former master)
and moreover served him as prime minister."
The Master said:
"Guǎn Zhòng (管仲) assisted Huán Gōng (桓公)
to become hegemon among the feudal lords,
bringing order to the whole world;
the people have received his blessings even to this day.
If not for Guǎn Zhòng (管仲),
we would be wearing our hair unbound and clothes fastened on the left!
How can he be compared to the petty faithfulness of common men and women,
who would hang themselves in a ditch without anyone knowing of it!"
Zǐlù (子路) said:
"Huán Gōng (桓公) killed Gōngzǐ Jiū (公子糾);
Zhào Hū (召忽) died for him,
but Guǎn Zhòng (管仲) did not.
May I say he was not benevolent?"
The Master said:
"Huán Gōng (桓公) united the feudal lords nine times,
not with military chariots,
but through Guǎn Zhòng's (管仲) strength!
Such was his benevolence!
Such was his benevolence!"
Guǎn Zhòng (管仲) was not ashamed to serve as prime minister,
his intention was probably that without Huán Gōng (桓公), the common people could not have been saved.
At the end of the Hàn (漢) dynasty, there was great chaos,
and the people were in utter misery;
without talent surpassing the age, none could save them.
If so, then whom else should Xún Yù (荀彧) have served but Wèi Wǔ (魏武) [Cáo Cāo (曹操)]!
At the time of Qí Huán (齊桓),
although the Zhōu (周) house was in decline,
it was not like the beginning of Jiàn'ān (建安).
At the beginning of Jiàn'ān (建安),
the four seas were overturned,
and not an inch of land or a single person
belonged to Hàn (漢).
Xún Yù (荀彧) assisted Wèi Wǔ (魏武) in raising an army,
recommending the worthy and employing the capable,
training soldiers and sharpening weapons,
making crucial decisions and devising strategies,
conquering in all four directions;
thus he was able to turn weakness into strength,
chaos into order,
possessing eight-tenths of the empire.
How could his achievements be inferior to Guǎn Zhòng's (管仲)?
Guǎn Zhòng (管仲) did not die for Gōngzǐ Jiū (公子糾), but Xún Yù (荀彧) died for the Hàn (漢) house;
his benevolence, moreover, surpasses that of Guǎn Zhòng (管仲)!
However, Dù Mù
believed that Xún Yù's
"advice to Wèi Wǔ to take Yǎnzhōu likened him to Gāo [Zǔ] and Guāng [Wǔdì]; his not allowing [him to] return to Xǔ at Guāndù likened him to Chǔ and Hàn.
When the task was accomplished and the merit completed,
he then sought fame from the Hàn dynasty.
This is like teaching a thief to dig through walls and break open chests, but not sharing in the spoils;
how can he not be a thief!"
Your servant believes that Kǒngzǐ said,
"When refinement surpasses substance, it becomes [mere] history,"
as seen in the *Lúnyǔ*.
There must be some means of refinement.
Therefore, likening Wèi Wǔ to Gāo [Zǔ], Guāng [Wǔdì], Chǔ, and Hàn,
is the historian's literary embellishment;
how could it all be Xún Yù's spoken words!
To denigrate Xún Yù on this basis
is not his fault.
Moreover, if Wèi Wǔ became emperor,
then Xún Yù would be a founding minister of great merit,
enjoying the same rewards as Xiāo Hé;
if Xún Yù did not desire this but instead desired to sacrifice himself to gain fame,
how could that be human nature!
11th month, 12th moon.
A comet appeared in Wǔ Zhūhóu.
The *Jìn Tiānwén Zhì* says: The Wǔ Zhūhóu are five stars
north of Dōngjǐng.
Also, in the southern barrier of Tàiwēi,
one star northeast of the Zǔ Zhífǎ is called Yèzhě.
Three stars northeast of Yèzhě are called Sān Gōng.
Three stars north of Sān Gōng are called Jiǔ Qīng.
Five stars west of Jiǔ Qīng are called Nèi Wǔ Zhūhóu.
They attend the Son of Heaven internally
and do not go to their states.
*Bèi* is pronounced
pú nèi fān.
12th month. Liú Bèi was in Jiāměng.
Páng Tǒng said to Liú Bèi:
"Now, secretly select elite troops,
travel day and night,
directly attack Chéngdū.
Liú Zhāng is not martial,
and has always been unprepared.
When a large army suddenly arrives,
it will be settled in one stroke.
This is the best strategy.
Yáng Huái and Gāo Pèi
are Zhāng's famous generals,
each commanding strong forces,
holding the pass,
which is the Báishuǐ pass.
Send word that the General should return to Jīngzhōu.
Let the General send word to them,
saying that Jīngzhōu is in an emergency
and he wishes to return to save it.
Also, have everyone pack up,
outwardly appearing to be returning.
These two men are already impressed by the General's renowned name,
and will also be pleased by the General's departure.
They will surely come to meet the General on light cavalry.
Seize them in this way,
take their troops,
then advance towards Chéngdū.
This is the medium strategy.
Retreat to Báidì.
Báidì
is the city of Yúfù County in Bādōng.
Gōngsūn Shù occupied Chéngdū,
called himself Báidì,
and renamed Yúfù as Báidì Chéng.
Slowly plan again.
This is the inferior strategy.
If you hesitate and do not leave,
it will lead to great difficulties;
you cannot stay long."
Liú Bèi assented to the medium strategy.
When Cáo Cāo attacked Sūn Quán,
Sūn Quán called on Liú Bèi for help.
Liú Bèi sent a letter to Liú Zhāng, saying:
"The Sūn clan and I are originally like lips and teeth,
but Guān Yǔ's troops are weak.
If I do not go to their aid now,
Cáo Cāo will surely take Jīngzhōu
and then invade the borders of Yìzhōu.
The borders of Yìzhōu
refer to the Yìzhōu borders.
Those who merely defend themselves are rogues
and are not worth worrying about."
He then requested an additional ten thousand troops and provisions.
Liú Zhāng only promised four thousand troops,
and provided only half of the rest.
Liú Bèi then incited his troops, saying:
"I am conquering a formidable enemy for Yìzhōu,
and my army is toiling tirelessly,
yet wealth is hoarded and rewards are withheld.
How can I make the scholar-officials fight to the death!"
Zhāng Sōng wrote to Liú Bèi and Fǎ Zhèng, saying:
"The great task is imminent;
how can you abandon this and leave!"
Zhāng Sōng's elder brother, Zhāng Sù, the Grand Administrator of Guǎnghàn,
feared that calamity would reach him,
and thus revealed Zhāng Sōng's plot.
Thereupon, Liú Zhāng arrested and executed Zhāng Sōng,
and commanded the generals at the passes and garrisons that no more documents were to be exchanged with Liú Bèi.
Liú Bèi was greatly angered,
summoned Yáng Huái and Gāo Pèi, the White Water Army supervisors under Liú Zhāng,
reproached them for their impoliteness,
and executed them;
he reproached them for not observing guest-host etiquette.
He absorbed their troops
and advanced to occupy Fúchéng.
This was using Páng Tǒng's medium strategy.
1st year. Spring,
1st month.
Cáo Cāo advanced his army to Rúxūkǒu,
numbering 400,000 infantry and cavalry,
and attacked and destroyed Sūn Quán's camp west of the river.
The Great River flows northeast,
hence the area from Lìyáng to Rúxūkǒu is all called west of the river,
and Jiànyè is called east of the river.
Sūn Quán led a force of 70,000 to defend against him,
and they faced each other for over a month.
Cáo Cāo saw Sūn Quán's boats, weapons, and military formations were orderly and disciplined,
and sighed, saying:
"If one has a son, he should be like Sūn Zhòngmóu;
Sūn Quán,
courtesy name Zhòngmóu.
As for my sons, they are mere pigs and dogs!"
Sūn Quán sent a letter to Cáo Cāo,
saying:
"The spring waters are rising;
Your Grace should depart quickly."
On a separate sheet, he said:
"If you do not die,
I cannot be at peace."
Cáo Cāo said to his generals:
"Sūn Quán does not deceive me."
Thereupon, he withdrew his army and returned.
2nd year. Gēngyín day.
An edict merged the fourteen prefectures,
restoring them to nine prefectures.
The fourteen prefectures were
Sī, Yù, Jì, Yǎn, Xú, Qīng, Jīng, Yáng, Yì, Liáng, Yōng, Bīng, Yōu, and Jiāo.
To restore them to nine prefectures meant: the Hedōng, Hénèi, Fēngyì, and Fúfēng regions of Sīzhōu, and the two prefectures of Yōu and Bīng, were all incorporated into Jìzhōu;
all territories under Liángzhōu
were incorporated into Yōngzhōu,
and the Jīngzhào region of Sīzhōu was also included;
furthermore, the Hóngnóng and Hénán regions of Sīzhōu were incorporated into Yùzhōu,
and Jiāozhōu was merged into Jīngzhōu.
Thus, Sī, Liáng, Yōu, and Bīng were abolished, restoring the Nine Prefectures of Yǔ Gòng.
This was Cáo Cāo himself taking the position of Shepherd of Jìzhōu,
wanting to expand his jurisdiction to control the whole realm.
3rd year. Summer,
4th month.
Cáo Cāo arrived in Yè.
4 In the beginning,
Cáo Cāo was in Qiáo.
Fearing that the riverside commanderies and counties would be seized by Sūn Quán,
he wished to relocate their inhabitants inland.
He consulted Yángzhōu's别駕 jiàng Jǐ,
asking:
"In the past, when I confronted Yuán Běnchū at Guāndù,
I relocated the people of Yān and Báimǎ.
The people could not flee,
and the bandits also dared not plunder.
This event is recorded in volume 63, Jiàn'ān 5th year.
Yān County and Báimǎ County
both belonged to Dōngjùn.
Yān
was the State of Nányān in the Spring and Autumn period.
Xián said: The old city of Yān is now Zuòchéng County in Huázhōu.
鈔 chāo,
pronounced as Chǔ Jiāo fan.
燕 Yān,
pronounced as Yú Xián fan.
What do you think?"
Jǐ replied:
"At that time, our army was weak and the enemy strong;
if we had not relocated them, we would certainly have lost them.
Since defeating Yuán Shào,
Your Lordship's prestige has shaken the world.
The people have no other ambitions.
Human nature holds affection for one's homeland,
so they would truly be unwilling to relocate.
I fear it would surely cause unrest."
Cáo did not follow his advice.
Soon after, the people began to panic and spread fear among themselves.
From Lújiāng, Jiǔjiāng, Qíchūn, and Guǎnglíng,
over ten myriad households all crossed the river eastward.
Qíchūn County
originally belonged to Jiāngxià Commandery.
Shěn Yuè said: Wú established Qíchūn Commandery.
This is written according to the Records of Wú.
蘄 Qí,
pronounced Qí.
South of Héféi,
only Wǎnchéng remained.
Wǎn County
belonged to Lújiāng Commandery.
Xián said: It is now Huáiníng County in Shūzhōu.
Shīgǔ said: 皖 Wǎn,
pronounced as Hú Guǎn fan.
Cáo met them,
and laughed loudly, saying:
"I originally only wanted them to avoid the bandits,
but instead I have driven them all away!"
He appointed Jǐ as the Grand Administrator of Dānyáng.
Dānyáng Commandery already belonged to Sūn Quán, so Jǐ could not take office there.
5 In the fifth month,
on the day Bǐngshēn,
Cáo Cāo was enfeoffed as Wèi Gōng with ten commanderies in Jìzhōu.
At this time, Hédōng, Hénèi, Wèijùn, Zhàoguó, Zhōngshān, Chángshān, Jùlù, Ānpíng, Gānlíng, and Píngyuán, totaling ten commanderies in Jìzhōu, were made the State of Wèi.
He was also granted the Nine Bestowals: one grand chariot and one military chariot,
two teams of black oxen;
a yǎnmiǎn ceremonial robe,
with a pair of red slippers;
Máo Cháng said: Red slippers
are the formal footwear of a ruler;
釋舄 shì xì means a slipper.
Zhèng Xuán said: Slippers are worn over other footwear.
Zhèng Zhòng said: There are three grades of slippers,
with red slippers being the highest,
for use with the ceremonial robe.
the dance of six lines;
The Rites of Zhōu state: Regarding the arrangement of musical instruments,
the King uses "palace suspension" (gōngxuán),
and feudal lords use "angled suspension" (xuánxuán).
Zhèng Zhòng said: "Palace suspension"
means suspended on all four sides;
"angled suspension"
means one side is removed.
縣 xián
is pronounced xuán.
The number of dancers in a formation (yì)
is eight for the Son of Heaven,
and six for feudal lords.
Dù Yù said: Eight yì
means 8x8 = 64 people;
six yì
means 6x6 = 36 people.
Fú Qián said: The Son of Heaven has eight-eights,
feudal lords six-eights,
grandees four-eights,
and gentlemen two-eights.
Sòng Fù Lóng said: The Earl of Zhèng presented two eights of female musicians to Duke Dào of Jìn,
and Jìn gave one eight to Wèi Jiàng.
This is proof that music formations were counted in units of eight people.
佾 yì,
pronounced yì.
an inclined path for ascent;
three hundred Imperial Bodyguards;
one battle-axe and one ceremonial axe;
one red bow,
one hundred red arrows,
ten black bows,
and one thousand black arrows;
玈 lú is the same as 盧 lú,
meaning black.
a jade tablet and a libation ladle.
6 Heavy rain and flooding.
7 Zhèng Dù of Guǎnghàn, an aide in Yìzhōu, heard that Liú Bèi had raised an army,
and said to Liú Zhāng:
"General of the Left is attacking us with a detached army;
his troops number less than ten thousand,
his soldiers and masses are not yet attached to him,
his army lacks baggage trains,
and he relies on wild grains for provisions.
His strategy should be to drive all the people from Bāxī and Zǐtóng inland, west of the Fú River,
Zǐtóng County
belonged to Guǎnghàn Commandery,
established in the first year of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's Yuándǐng era,
named for the county relying on the Zǐ forest and bordering the Tóng River;
in the 22nd year of Jiàn'ān,
Liú Bèi divided it to establish Zǐtóng Commandery.
The Book of Hàn Geography states:
Zǐtóng has the Wǔfù Mountain,
from which the Tuó River flows out,
entering the Fú to the south.
Yīng Shào said: The Fú River flows from Guǎnghàn,
and enters the Hàn to the south.
The River Classic states: The Fú River flows out northwest of Fú County in Guǎnghàn,
joins the Zǐtóng River in Guǎnghàn to the east,
then flows southwest,
and then south into Diànjiāng.
The note says: The Fú River flows out from beyond the border of Gāngdīdao within Guǎnghàn subordinate state;
the Zǐtóng River is the Wǔfù River,
both entering Diànjiāng,
which is what is called the 'inner water'.
Burn and clear everything,
build high ramparts and dig deep moats,
and calmly wait for him.
When he arrives,
if he requests battle,
do not grant it.
Without provisions for long,
no more than a hundred days,
he will surely retreat on his own.
When he retreats, attack him,
and he will surely be captured."
Liú Bèi heard this and disliked it,
asking Fǎ Zhèng about it.
Fǎ Zhèng said:
"Zhāng will ultimately not use it,
so there is no need to worry."
Zhāng indeed said to his subordinates:
"I have heard of resisting the enemy to pacify the people,
but I have not heard of moving the people to avoid the enemy."
He did not use Dù's plan.
Zhāng then sent his generals Liú Guì, Lěng Bāo, Zhāng Rèn, Dèng Xián, Wú Yì, and others to resist Bèi,
but they were all defeated,
and retreated to defend Luòmù.
Wú Yì went to Bèi's army and surrendered.
Zhāng again sent his Protector of the Army Lǐ Yán of Nányáng and Fèi Guān of Jiāngxià to oversee the various armies at Luòmù,
but Lǐ Yán and Fèi Guān also led their forces to surrender to Bèi.
Bèi's army grew stronger,
and he dispatched various generals to pacify the subordinate counties.
Liú Guì and Zhāng Rèn, along with Zhāng's son Xún, retreated to defend Luòchéng.
Luò County
belonged to Guǎnghàn Commandery,
where the Luò River originates;
in the Táng Dynasty, it was the seat of Hánzhōu.
Zhāng Rèn led his troops out to battle at Yànqiáo.
The Yàn River
is south of Luò County.
There were once golden geese,
hence the name Yànqiáo.
Zhāng Rèn died.
8 In autumn,
seventh month,
Wèi began to establish its altars of land and grain, and ancestral temples.
9 Wèi Gōng Cáo took three daughters as noble ladies.
From then on,
Cáo Cāo's surname was not written, but his state title preceded his name.
Cáo's three daughters were
Xiàn,
Jié,
and Huá,
the second, Jié, later became empress.
At first,
Wèi Gōng Cāo pursued Mǎ Chāo to Āndìng.
Hearing that Tián Yín and Sū Bó had rebelled,
he led his army back.
Cān Liángzhōu Jūnjì Yáng Fù said to Cāo:
"Chāo possesses the bravery of Xìn and Bù,
and has greatly won the hearts of the Qiāng and Hú.
If the main army returns
without making preparations,
the various commanderies on Lǒngshàng will no longer belong to the state."
Lǒngxī, Nán'ān, Hànyáng, and Yǒngyáng
were all commanderies on Lǒngshàng.
According to the Xiàndì Qǐjūzhù,
in the fourth year of Chūpíng,
Yǒngyáng was formed by dividing Hànyáng and Shàngjùn.
Chāo indeed led the Qiāng and Hú to attack the various commanderies and counties on Lǒngshàng,
and all the commanderies and counties responded to him,
except Jìchéng, which fortified itself with the support of the prefecture and commandery.
Jìxiàn
belonged to Hànyáng Jùn,
where the commandery and the Liángzhōu Cìshǐ were based.
Chāo commanded all the forces of Lǒngyòu.
Zhāng Lǔ again sent his great general Yáng Áng to assist him,
totaling over ten thousand men.
They attacked Jìchéng.
From the first month to the eighth month,
no relief forces arrived.
Cìshǐ Wéi Kāng sent his Biéjià Yán Wēn out
to seek urgent help from Xiàhóu Yuān.
Xiàhóu Yuān was at that time stationed in Cháng'ān.
Wēn secretly left by water at night.
The next day,
Chāo's soldiers saw his tracks
and sent pursuers who captured him.
Chāo brought Wēn to the foot of the city wall,
and made him announce to those in the city:
"There is no help from the east."
Lǒngyòu was in the west, and Cāo was in Guāndōng,
hence it was called "the east."
"The main army will not arrive for another three days.
Persevere!"
Everyone in the city wept,
shouting "Long live!"
Although Chāo was angry,
he still, because the siege had dragged on without success,
slowly tried to persuade Wēn again,
hoping he would change his mind.
Wēn said:
"To serve one's lord means death, not a divided loyalty.
How can you wish to make a respectable man utter unrighteous words!"
Chāo then killed him.
After a while, no external relief arrived.
Wéi Kāng and the Tàishǒu wished to surrender.
Yáng Fù wept bitterly and remonstrated, saying:
"Fù and others, leading our fathers, elder brothers, sons, and younger brothers, encouraged each other with righteousness,
to die rather than be disloyal,
believing we were defending this city for the Governor.
Now, how can we abandon a nearly accomplished feat
and fall into a name of unrighteousness!"
The Cìshǐ and Tàishǒu did not listen,
and opened the city gates to welcome Chāo.
Chāo entered,
and then killed the Cìshǐ and Tàishǒu,
styling himself Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn,領Bìngzhōu Mù, and Dū Liángzhōu Jūnjì.
Wèi Gōng Cāo sent Xiàhóu Yuān to relieve Jì,
but Jì fell before he arrived.
Yuān was over two hundred *lǐ* from Jì
when Chāo came to intercept and battle him,
and Yuān's army suffered a setback.
The Dī King Qiānwàn rebelled in favor of Chāo,
and stationed himself at Xīngguó.
The Dī King Qiānwàn
was of the Dī ethnic group from Lüèyáng Qīngshuǐ;
his descendants later became the Yáng of Chóuchí.
Xīngguó
is a city name.
It happened that Yáng Fù's wife died,
so he asked Chāo for leave to bury her.
Fù's maternal cousin, Tiānshuǐ Jiāng Xù, was the Fǔyí Jiāngjūn,
commanding troops stationed at Lìchéng.
The Shuǐjīngzhù states
that Lìchéng was in Xīxiàn,
one hundred and twenty *lǐ* from Chóuchí,
and was later renamed Jiàn'ān Chéng.
Dù Yòu said: Lìchéng
is seven *lǐ* west of present-day Tónggǔ Jùn,
ninety *lǐ* from Chóuchí.
Sòng Bái said: The Jìn established Chóuchí Jùn in Lìchéng.
It is now Chéngzhōu.
Fù wept and grieved profoundly.
Xù asked:
"Why are you like this?"
Fù replied:
"I could not fully defend the city,
and when my lord died, I could not die with him.
What face do I have to continue living in this world!
The time it takes for an eye to view an object,
or one inhalation and exhalation,
is but a fleeting moment.
The cruel killing of the provincial governor —
is this not only Fù's sorrow and responsibility,
but all the gentry of the province share in the shame?
You command troops and exercise sole authority, yet have no intention of punishing the rebel.
This is why Zhào Dùn was recorded as having assassinated his lord."
Zhào Dùn was the Jìn minister Zhào Xuānzǐ.
The Zuǒzhuàn states
that Zhào Chuān attacked Líng Gōng at Táoyuán,
and Xuānzǐ returned before leaving the mountain.
The Grand Historian wrote:
"Zhào Dùn assassinated his lord,"
and showed it to the court.
Xuānzǐ said:
"It is not so."
He replied:
"You are the chief minister,
you did not leave the country when your lord fled,
and you did not punish the villain when he returned.
If not you, then who!"
"There are many flaws [in Chāo's rule];
it's easy to devise a plan."
Xù's mother said with emotion:
"Hmph!
Bóyì,
when Governor Wéi met with disaster,
it was also your fault,
how can it be only Yìshān's!
Who does not die?
To die for loyalty and righteousness
is to die in the right place.
You should act quickly,
and not worry about me again;
I will bear the consequences for you myself,
and will not burden you with my remaining years."
Xù then conspired with Zhào Áng, Yǐn Fèng of the same commandery, Wǔdū Lǐ Jùn, and others to attack Chāo.
He also sent men to Jì
to ally with Āndìng Liáng Kuān and Nán'ān Zhào Qú to act as internal agents.
Chāo took Zhào Áng's son, Yuè, as a hostage.
Áng said to his wife Yì:
According to Huángfǔ Mì's Liènǚ Zhuàn,
Yì
was a woman of the Shì clan.
"My plan is like this;
the matter is sure to be perfectly safe,
but what about Yuè?"
Yì responded in a stern voice:
"To wipe away the great shame of one's lord and father,
losing one's head is not considered important,
let alone one son!"
In the ninth month,
Yáng Fù and Jiāng Xù advanced with their troops,
entering Lǔchéng.
Lǔchéng
should be between Xīxiàn and Jìxiàn.
This was to attack Mǎ Chāo.
The *Shuǐ Jīng Zhù* states: Qíshān
is seventy *xǔ* *lǐ* west of Bōzhǒng.
There is a city on the mountain,
which is extremely dangerous and fortified.
The Hànshuǐ flows past its south.
It also says: Qíshān
is two hundred forty *lǐ* southwest of Shàngguī.
Dù Yòu says: Qíshān
is ten *lǐ* east of present-day Tónggǔ Jùn’s Chángdào Xiàn.
I note that ten *lǐ* south of present-day Xīhé Zhōu’s Chángdào Xiàn there is Qíshān.
Since ancient times, there have been two mountains, north and south,
with over ten thousand households.
Zhūgě Liàng’s memorial stated:
"Qíshān is five hundred *lǐ* from Jǔ,
with ten thousand households."
This
is what he meant.
Mǎ Chāo was furious.
Zhào Qú then used a stratagem to persuade Mǎ Chāo
to personally go out and attack them.
When Mǎ Chāo left,
Zhào Qú and Liáng Kuān closed the gates of Jìchéng
and killed Mǎ Chāo’s wife and children.
Mǎ Chāo, losing his ground for advance and retreat,
then attacked Lìchéng
and captured Jiāng Xù’s mother.
Jiāng Xù’s mother cursed him, saying:
"You are an unfilial son who betrayed his father,
a cruel brigand who murdered his lord!
'Betrayed his father'
refers to Mǎ Téng being in Yè,
yet he ignored him and rebelled.
'Murdered his lord'
refers to killing Wéi Kāng.
'Bèi'
is pronounced *pú mèi fān*.
Why do you not die early?
How dare you show your face to people!"
Mǎ Chāo killed her,
and also killed Zhào Áng’s son, Yuè.
Yáng Fù fought Mǎ Chāo,
suffering five wounds on his body.
Mǎ Chāo’s army was defeated,
and he then fled south to Zhāng Lǔ.
Zhāng Lǔ appointed Mǎ Chāo as Dūjiǎng Jìjiǔ.
Zhāng Lǔ was a follower of the Wǔdòumǐ Dào,
styling himself Shī Jūn.
His followers
were initially called Guǐzú,
later Jìjiǔ,
each leading a group of people.
Dūjiǎng Jìjiǔ
refers to Zhāng Lǔ making his followers study the *Lǎozǐ Wǔqiān Wén* extensively.
He established the position of Dūjiǎng Jìjiǔ,
whose rank was second only to Shī Jūn.
Some said to Zhāng Lǔ:
"If a person is like this,
showing no love for his own kin,
how can he love others!"
Zhāng Lǔ then stopped (his plan to give Mǎ Chāo an important position).
Cáo Cāo rewarded those who had contributed to defeating Mǎ Chāo:
eleven were enfeoffed as marquises,
and Yáng Fù was granted the title of Guānnèi Hóu.
In the eleventh winter,
in the eleventh month,
Wèi first established the positions of Shàngshū, Shìzhōng, and the Six Qīng.
Xún Yōu was appointed Shàngshū Lìng,
Liáng Mào was appointed Púshè.
Liáng
is the surname;
Mào
is the given name.
Wèi established five Caos for the Shàngshū:
Lìbù, Zuǒmín, Kècáo, Wǔbīng, and Dùzhī.
From this point onward,
the Shìzhōng position was fixed at four members.
Dàlǐ was the office of the Hàn Tíngwèi.
Yuán Huàn was appointed Lángzhōng Lìng,
acting as Yùshǐ Dàfū.
Lángzhōng Lìng was the office of the Hàn Guānglù Xūn.
At that time, Yùshǐ Dàfū was considered one of the Sāngōng,
and Zhōngchéng was the head of the Yùshǐ Tái.
Yuán Huàn, upon receiving rewards,
dispersed them all.
His family had no savings.
When in need, he would take from others.
He did not engage in ostentatious acts of purity,
yet people of his time all admired his integrity.
At one time, a rumor spread that Liú Bèi had died.
All the officials congratulated Cáo Cāo,
but Yuán Huàn alone did not.
Wèi Gōng Cáo Cāo wanted to restore corporeal punishment.
He issued an order saying:
"Formerly, Chén Hónglú believed that there were death penalties that could be replaced by humane alternatives.
Can the Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng elaborate on his father’s argument?"
Chén Qún’s father, Jì, was the Hàn Dà Hónglú.
"My father, Jì, believed that the Hàn abolished corporeal punishment but increased flogging instead.
This is recorded in volume fifteen, Emperor Wén’s thirteenth year.
This is what is meant by 'light in name but heavy in reality.'
Light in name makes it easy to commit offenses,
but heavy in reality harms the people.
Moreover, 'a life for a life' conforms to ancient custom;
as for injuring people,
mutilating their bodies or cutting their hair
is not rational.
If ancient punishments were used,
making the lewd suffer castration,
and thieves have their feet amputated,
then there would forever be no lewd acts, transgressions, or illicit entries.
The 'three thousand articles' [of law]
were formulated by King Mù of Zhōu as the *Fǔ Xíng*.
The punishments of tattooing numbered a thousand,
those of nose-cutting a thousand,
those of foot-amputation five hundred,
those of castration three hundred,
and those of capital punishment two hundred,
totaling three thousand forms of the Five Punishments.
Such measures,
which troubled the times,
should be applied first.
Crimes punishable by death under Hàn law,
which humaneness cannot reach,
and other offenses leading to death,
can be replaced by corporeal punishment.
If this were done,
the lives spared would sufficiently compensate for the bodies punished."
'Mào'
means 'to exchange'.
This would mean valuing human limbs over human lives."
At that time, among those who debated,
only Zhōng Yáo agreed with Chén Qún’s view;
the rest all believed it was not yet feasible.
Cáo Cāo, because military affairs were not yet concluded,
heeded the general opinion and stopped.
He Zīquán punctuated, Róng Zhàozǔ and Niè Chóngqí re-collated.
Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial decree.
Later, Xué Tiāntái.
Emperor Xiàoxiàn, year *rén*.
Jiàn'ān nineteenth year
(Jiǎwǔ, 214 CE)
1. In spring,
Mǎ Chāo requested troops from Zhāng Lǔ
to take Liángzhōu in the north.
Zhāng Lǔ sent Mǎ Chāo back to besiege Qíshān.
Jiāng Xù
sent an urgent appeal to Xiàhóu Yuān.
The generals debated, wanting to await Wèi Gōng Cáo Cāo’s instructions.
Xiàhóu Yuān said:
"The Duke is in Yè,
a round trip of four thousand *lǐ*.
By the time we get a reply,
Jiāng Xù and the others will surely be defeated.
This is not an urgent rescue."
So he set out,
ordering Zhāng Hé to lead five thousand infantry and cavalry as the vanguard.
Mǎ Chāo was defeated and fled.
Hán Suì was at Xiǎnqīn.
Xiǎnqīn County belonged to Hànyáng Commandery.
It is not mentioned in the Bān Zhì,
but was probably established by Guāngwǔ,
and conferred upon Dòu Yǒu.
Xián said: The old city of Xiǎnqīn
is to the east of modern Qín Zhōu Chéngjì County.
Suì fled.
Yuān pursued him to Luèyáng City,
about thirty *lǐ* from Suì.
The generals wanted to attack it,
or some suggested attacking the Xīngguó Dī.
The Wèi Lǜe states: In the Jiàn'ān period,
Dī King Āguì of Xīngguó,
and Dī King Qiānwàn of Bǎiqǐng,
each had over ten thousand followers,
and rebelled with Mǎ Chāo.
After Mǎ Chāo was defeated,
Āguì was attacked and destroyed by Xiàhóu Yuān,
and Qiānwàn fled south into Shǔ.
“Suì’s troops are elite,
and Xīngguó City is strong.
It cannot be taken quickly by assault.
It would be better to attack the various Qiāng of Chánglí.
The Shuǐ Jīng Zhù states: The Wǎtíng River
flows south past Lǒngxī Chéngjì County,
then east through Chánglí Stream,
and is called Chánglí River;
the Shāodāng and other Qiāng resided there.
*Zú*
is read as *cù*.
They will surely return to rescue their families.
If Suì abandons the Qiāng and defends alone, he will be isolated.”
This means that if Suì abandons the Qiāng and does not rescue them,
but defends himself with his troops alone,
his position will be isolated.
“Then he can certainly be captured.”
Yuān then left a supervising general to guard the baggage train,
and personally led light troops to Chánglí.
He attacked and burned the Qiāng encampments.
Suì indeed came to rescue Chánglí.
When the generals saw Suì's numerous troops,
they wanted to establish a camp and dig trenches before engaging in battle.
Yuān said:
“We have fought for a thousand *lǐ*,
and if we now set up camps and dig trenches again,
our officers and men will be exhausted
and can no longer be used effectively.
Although the bandits are numerous,
they are easy to deal with.”
So he beat the drums,
and dealt a great defeat to Suì's army,
then advanced to besiege Xīngguó.
The Dī king Qiānwàn fled to Mǎ Chāo,
and the rest of the troops all surrendered.
He then turned to attack Gāopíng and Túgè,
defeating them all.
2 In the third month,
an imperial edict commanded that Wèi Gōng Cāo’s position be above that of all other feudal kings,
and granted him a golden seal, a red sash, and a yuǎnyóu crown.
The Han system: feudal kings had golden seals, red sashes, and yuǎnyóu crowns.
Dǒng Bā said: The yuǎnyóu crown
was made like the tōngtiān crown,
nine inches high,
straight and upright with a slightly slanted top,
then straightened down to form an iron rolled brim,
with an extended tube across the front,
and no shan or shù.
3 In summer,
the fourth month,
there was a drought.
In the fifth month,
there was rain.
4 Originally,
Wèi Gōng Cāo sent the Administrator of Lújiāng, Zhū Guāng, to garrison Wǎn,
where he extensively opened rice fields.
Lǚ Méng said to Sūn Quán:
“The fields in Wǎn are fertile and beautiful.
If even one harvest ripens,
their forces will certainly increase.”
“Harvest ripens” refers to the rice maturing and being harvested.
If they have provisions, they can increase their forces.
*Shú*
is an ancient variant of the character *shú*.
In the intercalary month,
Quán personally attacked Wǎnéng City.
The generals wanted to build earthen mounds
and prepare siege equipment.
Lǚ Méng said:
“Preparing siege equipment and earthen mounds
will surely take many days to complete;
once the city defenses are repaired,
external relief forces will certainly arrive,
making it impossible to capture.
Moreover, we entered taking advantage of the rain.
If we stay for several days,
the water will surely recede,
making our return difficult,
which I secretly consider perilous.
Observing this city now,
it is not very strong.
With the keen morale of our three armies,
attacking from all four sides simultaneously,
it can be captured in less than an hour;
returning while the water is high
is the way to complete victory.”
Quán followed his advice.
Méng recommended Gān Níng as the commander for ascending the city.
Níng, holding a chain,
scaled the city wall,
leading the soldiers;
Méng followed him with elite troops,
personally holding the drumsticks and beating the drum.
All the soldiers leapt forward.
They attacked at dawn,
and by breakfast time, they had broken through,
capturing Zhū Guāng and tens of thousands of men and women.
Soon after, Zhāng Liáo arrived at Jiáshí.
Jiáshí is forty-seven *lǐ* north of modern Ānqìng Fǔ Tóngchéng County,
now called Xīxiá Shān.
Then he retreated.
Quán appointed Lǚ Méng as the Administrator of Lújiāng,
and he returned to garrison Xúnyáng.
5 Zhūgě Liàng left Guān Yǔ to guard Jīngzhōu,
and with Zhāng Fēi and Zhào Yún, led troops upstream to conquer Bādōng.
Qiáo Zhōu's Bā Jì states: In the sixth year of Chūpíng,
Zhào Wěi divided Bājùn from Ānhàn downwards to form Yǒngníng Commandery.
In the sixth year of Jiàn'ān,
Liú Zhāng renamed Yǒngníng to Bādōng Commandery.
This is the land of Tang period Kuízhōu and Kāizhōu.
They defeated Yán Yán, the Administrator of Bājùn,
and captured him alive.
Fēi angrily questioned Yán:
“The great army has arrived,
why do you not surrender,
but dare to resist in battle?”
Yán replied:
“You all are ill-mannered,
invading and seizing my province.
My province only has generals who can be beheaded,
not generals who surrender!”
Fēi was enraged,
and ordered his attendants to drag him away and behead him.
Yán’s expression remained unchanged,
saying:
“Behead me, then behead me,
why be angry?”
Fēi, impressed by his bravery, released him
and treated him as an honored guest.
He then sent Zhào Yún separately along the outer water to pacify Jiāngyáng and Jiànwéi.
Jiāngyáng County
originally belonged to Jiànwéi Commandery.
Liú Zhāng divided it to establish Jiāngyáng Commandery;
in the Tang, it was Lúzhōu.
Jiànwéi Commandery,
in the Tang, was the land of Zī, Jiǎn, Jiā, and Méi.
Modern Yúzhōu is also Han Bājùn territory.
It faces the mouths of two rivers.
To the right is the Fú Nèishuǐ,
and to the left is the Shǔ Wàishuǐ.
From Yú upstream, Hézhōu to Miánzhōu,
is called the Nèishuǐ;
from Yú upstream, Róng, Lú to Shǔ,
is called the Wàishuǐ.
*Jiàn*
