Lǐcáo 理曹
did not exist in the Hàn 漢 ducal administration;
it was likely established by Cáo 曹.
Yuán 掾
is pronounced yuàn.
He investigated and brought to completion the case concerning their wives and children.
“Investigated and brought to completion” (kǎojìng 考竟)
means to thoroughly investigate and conclude.
Cáo 曹 wanted to increase the severity of their punishment,
extending it to their parents and brothers.
Róu 柔 memorialized, saying:
“That soldiers desert the army
is indeed hateful.
‘Hateful’ (jí 疾)
means ‘evil.’
The Classic of History says: ‘Do not be angry and hateful towards the stubborn.’
I believe it would be appropriate to spare their wives and children,
firstly to induce them to return.
If we follow the previous statutes,
their hopes will already be cut off;
but to further increase the punishment,
I fear that from now on, soldiers in the army,
seeing one person flee,
and punishment extend to themselves,
will also follow each other and run away,
and it will be impossible to kill them.
This severe punishment is not a way to stop desertion,
but rather a way to increase flight!”
Cáo 曹 said:
“Excellent!”
And immediately stopped the killings.
1. In spring,
in the first month,
on the day Jiǎzǐ 甲子,
Lady Cáo 曹 was established as Empress;
she was the daughter
of Duke Cáo 曹 of Wèi 魏.
2. In the third month,
Duke Cáo 曹 of Wèi 魏 personally led troops to attack Zhāng Lǔ 張魯,
intending to enter Dī 氐 territory from Wǔdū 武都.
Wǔdū 武都
was originally the dwelling place of the Báimǎ Dī 白馬氐,
and Emperor Wǔ 武 established it as a commandery.
He sent Zhāng Hé 張郃 and Zhū Líng 朱靈 to attack and break them.
In summer,
in the fourth month,
Cáo 曹 departed from Chéncāng 陳倉, passed through Sànguān 散關, and reached Héchí 河池.
Chéncāng 陳倉 county
belonged to Yòufúfēng 右扶風,
and in the Táng 唐 dynasty, to Qízhōu 岐州,
now Bǎojī 寶雞 county.
Dàsànguān 大散關
is to its southwest.
Héchí 河池 county
belonged to Wǔdū 武都 Commandery.
Yú Jù’s 虞據 Dàsànguān 大散關 is in present-day Liángquán 梁泉 county of Fèngzhōu 鳳州.
Relying on their treacherous terrain, they refused to submit.
In the fifth month,
Cáo 曹 attacked and massacred them.
The generals Qū Yǎn 麴演, Jiǎng Shí 蔣石, and others from Xīpíng 西平 and Jīnchéng 金城 jointly beheaded Hán Suì 韓遂 and sent his head.
At the end of Hàn 漢, Jīnchéng 金城 was divided to form Xīpíng 西平 Commandery.
3 In the beginning,
Liú Bèi was in Jīngzhōu.
Zhōu Yú, Gān Níng, and others repeatedly urged Sūn Quán to take Shǔ.
Quán sent an envoy to say to Bèi:
"Liú Zhāng is not warlike,
and cannot defend himself.
If Cáo Cāo were to get Shǔ,
then Jīngzhōu would be in danger.
Now I wish to first attack and take Zhāng,
then take Zhāng Lǔ,
unifying the South.
Even if there were ten Cáo Cāos,
there would be nothing to worry about."
Bèi replied:
"Yìzhōu is rich in people and its land is dangerous.
Although Liú Zhāng is weak,
he is sufficient to defend himself.
Now to send an army to Shǔ and Hàn,
transporting supplies for ten thousand *lǐ*,
wishing to achieve victory in battle and capture,
never failing in any endeavor,
this is what even Sūn and Wú found difficult.
'Sūn and Wú'
refers to Sūn Wǔ and Wú Qǐ.
It means their strength would be exhausted,
and they would have no more distant ambitions.
Now Cáo Cāo has already taken two-thirds of the empire,
and is about to water his horses in the Cāng Hǎi,
and display his troops in Wú Huì.
'Wú Huì'
refers to the Wú region as a great metropolis.
*Huì*
is read as the character itself.
Another explanation says
Wú and Huì
refer to the lands of the two commanderies of Wú and Kuàijī.
*Huì*
is pronounced 'gōng wài fān'.
Yet, allies groundlessly attack each other,
lending the pivot to Cáo Cāo.
The 'pivot'
is what allows a door to move.
It means Cáo Cāo wants to sway Wú and Shǔ but has not found the pivot;
if they attack each other,
it is lending him the pivot that can move them.
This is not a long-term plan.
Moreover, Bèi and Zhāng are related as members of the imperial clan,
hoping to rely on awe and spiritual power to assist the Hàn court.
Now that Zhāng has offended those around him,
Bèi is uniquely terrified;
this is not something I dare to hear.
I wish for him to be granted leniency."
Quán did not listen,
and sent Sūn Yú to lead a naval force to station at Xiàkǒu.
Bèi did not allow the army to pass,
saying to Yú:
"If you wish to take Shǔ,
I shall dishevel my hair and enter the mountains,
so as not to lose faith in the world."
It means that if a member of the imperial clan is attacked and he cannot save him,
he would have no face to stand in the world.
*Pī*
is pronounced 'pí yì fān'.
Zhāng Fēi was garrisoned at Zǐguī.
Zǐguī County
belonged to Nánjùn,
and was Guīzhōu in the Táng dynasty.
Nánjùn
originally had its seat in Jiānglíng.
When Wú gained Jīngzhōu,
it established Nánjùn south of the Jiāng;
when Jìn pacified Wú,
it made Jiānglíng Nánjùn,
and the Nánjùn south of the Jiāng into Nánpíng Commandery.
What Liàng occupied was probably the Nánjùn south of the Jiāng.
Quán had no choice but to recall Yú.
When Bèi later attacked Liú Zhāng in the west,
Quán said:
"That sly bandit
dared to use such deception!"
Bèi left Guān Yǔ to guard Jiānglíng.
Lǔ Sù was neighboring Yǔ's territory;
Yǔ often gave rise to suspicion and disloyalty,
but Sù always appeased him with good will.
When Bèi had already obtained Yìzhōu,
Quán ordered the Central Supervisor of the Army, Zhūgě Jǐn, to demand the Jīngzhōu commanderies from Bèi.
At that time, Quán appointed various generals with the title 'Separate Department Supervisor of the Army';
thus, 'Central Supervisor of the Army'
was probably the 'Supervisor of the Central Army'.
Jǐn transitioned from Chief Clerk to Central Supervisor of the Army;
his position and responsibilities were probably not light.
*Jǐn*
is pronounced 'qú lìn fān'.
Bèi said:
"I am now planning to conquer Liángzhōu.
When Liángzhōu is settled,
I will then give you all of Jīngzhōu."
Quán said:
"He borrowed it and does not return it,
now he wishes to prolong the years with empty words."
It means to prolong the time.
Méngzǐ said: 'To borrow for a long time and not return,
how does one know it is not theirs?'
Guān Yǔ expelled them all.
Quán was greatly enraged
and sent Lǚ Méng to command an army of twenty thousand to take the three commanderies.
Méng sent a letter to Chángshā and Guìyáng;
all surrendered at the mere sight of his might,
only the Administrator of Línglíng, Hǎo Pǔ, defended the city and did not surrender.
Liú Bèi heard of this,
and personally went from Shǔ to Gōng'ān,
sending Guān Yǔ to contend for the three commanderies.
Sūn Quán advanced to Lùkǒu,
to direct the various armies;
he sent Lǔ Sù with ten thousand men to garrison Yìyáng to resist Yǔ.
Yìyáng County belonged to Chángshā Commandery.
Yì Shào said: 'It is on the sunny side of the Yì River.'
The Yúdì Zhì says: 'Today's Ānhuà County in Tánzhōu
was originally Hàn Yìyáng County.'
Dù Yòu said: 'Yìyáng County in Tánzhōu,
its old Hàn city is east of the present county.'
Sòng Bái said: 'The old Yìyáng city is eighty *lǐ* east of today's Yìyáng County;
that city was built by Lǔ Sù.'
Méng was ordered to quickly return from Línglíng to assist Sù.
Méng received the letter,
kept it secret.
At night,
he summoned his generals and gave them strategy;
in the morning,
when about to attack Línglíng,
he turned to Hǎo Pǔ's old acquaintance, Dèng Xuánzhī of Nányáng, and said:
"Hǎo Zǐtài heard that there are acts of loyalty and righteousness in the world,
and also wishes to perform them,
but he does not know the opportune moment.
Hǎo Pǔ,
courtesy name Zǐtài.
*Hǎo*
is pronounced 'hū gè fān'.
Guān Yǔ is in Nánjùn;
His Supreme Majesty himself is overseeing him.
He is currently in a desperate situation,
struggling to save himself,
how could he have spare strength to manage this place again!
Now I have calculated the strength and considered the situation to attack this place;
it will not take even a day for the city to be broken.
After the city is broken,
you will die,
what benefit will that be to the matter,
and will cause your hundred-year-old mother, with white hair, to suffer execution?
Is that not painful!
I surmise this man cannot get outside information;
'this man'
refers to Hǎo Pǔ.
That is why he is in this situation.
You can go see him
and explain the misfortunes and blessings."
Xuánzhī saw Pǔ
and fully conveyed Méng's intention;
Pǔ was afraid and surrendered.
Méng welcomed him,
took his hand and went down to the boat with him.
After finishing speaking,
he produced the letter and showed it to him,
then clapped his hands and laughed heartily.
Pǔ saw the letter,
knew Bèi was in Gōng'ān and Yǔ was in Yìyáng,
and felt such shame and regret that he wished to sink into the earth.
Méng left Sūn Hé
to handle the aftermath.
The *Kǎoyì* says: 'According to records, Sūn Hé was already dead, perhaps it was another person with the same name.'
Lǔ Sù 欲與 Guān Yǔ 會語，
諸將疑恐有變，
議不可往。
Sù 曰：
「今日之事，
宜相開譬。
Liú Bèi 負國，
是非未決，
Yǔ 亦何敢重欲干命！ 」
乃邀 Yǔ 相見，
各駐兵馬百步上，
但諸將軍單刀俱會。
Sù 因責數 Yǔ 以不返三郡，
Yǔ 曰：
「Wūlín 之役，
左將軍身在行間，
戮力破敵，
即謂 Chìbì 之戰也。
行，
戶剛翻。
無一塊土，
而足下來欲收地邪！ 」
Sù 曰：
「不然。
始與 Yùzhōu 覲於 Chángbǎn，
事並見六十五卷十三年。
計窮慮極，
志勢摧弱，
圖欲遠竄，
謂欲投 Wú Jù 也。
主上矜愍 Yùzhōu 之身無有處所，
不愛土地士民之力，
使有所庇蔭以濟其患；
而 Yùzhōu 私獨飾情，
愆德墮好。
私獨，
謂私其一己之所獨也。
墮，
讀曰 huī。
好，
呼到翻；
下同。
謂得 Yìzhōu，
有以藉手也。
斯蓋凡夫所不忍行，
而況整領人物之主乎！ 」
Yǔ 無以答。
會聞 Wèi Gōng Cáo 將攻 Hànzhōng，
考異曰：備傳云
「Cáo Gōng 定 Hànzhōng」 ，
Sūn Quán 傳云
「入 Hànzhōng」 ，
按 Cāo 以七月入 Hànzhōng，
Bèi 未應即聞之，
而八月 Quán 已攻 Héfèi，
蓋聞 Cáo Gōng 兵始欲向 Hànzhōng，
即引兵還耳。
使使求和於 Quán。
Quán 令 Zhūgě Jǐn 報命，
更尋盟好。
遂分 Jīngzhōu，
以 Xiāngshuǐ 為界： Chángshā、 Jiāngxià、 Guìyáng 以東屬 Quán，
Nánjùn、 Línglíng、 Wǔlíng 以西屬 Bèi。
Bān Zhì，
Xiāngshuǐ 出 Línglíng Yánghǎishān，
至 Élíng 入 Jiāng，
過郡二，
行二千五百三十里。
Wú、 Shǔ 分 Jīngzhōu，
Chángshā、 Guìyáng、 Línglíng、 Wǔlíng 以 Xiāngshuǐ 為界耳；
Nánjùn、 Jiāngxià 各自依其郡界。
夏，
戶雅翻。
與其弟 Liàng 但公會相見，
退無私面。
七月，
Wèi Gōng Cāo 至 Yángpíng。
水經註：Jìnshuǐ 發 Wǔdū Dīzhōng，
南逕 Zhāng Lǔ Chéngdōng。
城因 Xiáolǐng，
周迴五里；
東臨峻谷，
杳然百尋；
西、北二面，
連峯接崖，
莫究其極；
從南為盤道，
登陟二里有餘。
Yǔ Zhòngyōng 謂山為 Báimǎ Sài，
東對 Báimǎ Chéng，
一名 Yángpíng Guān。
Jìnshuǐ 南流入 Miǎn，
謂之 Jìnkǒu。
或曰：Yángpíng Guān，
即今 Xīngyuán Bǎiláo Guān 是也。
Dù Yòu 曰：Yángpíng Guān，
在 Hànzhōng Bāochéng Xiàn Xīběi。
其弟 Wèi 不肯，
率衆數萬人拒關堅守，
橫山築城十餘里。
初，
Cāo 承 Liángzhōu 從事及 Wǔdū 降人之辭，
說
「Zhāng Lǔ 易攻，
Yángpíng Chéngxià 南北山相遠，
不可守也」 ，
信以為然。
及往臨履，
不如所聞，
乃歎曰：
「他人商度，
少如人意。 」
攻 Yángpíng Shānshàng 諸屯，
山峻難登，
既不時拔，
士卒傷夷者多，
軍食且盡，
Cāo 意沮，
便欲拔軍截山而還，
遣大將軍 Xiàhóu Dūn、 將軍 Xǔ Chǔ 呼山上兵還。
會前軍夜迷惑，
誤入 Zhāng Wèi 別營，
營中大驚退散。
Shìzhōng Xīn Pí、 Zhǔbù Liú Yè 等在兵後，
語 Dūn、 Chǔ，
言
「官兵已據得賊要屯，
賊已散走」 ，
猶不信之。
Dūn 前自見，
乃還白 Cāo，
進兵攻 Wèi，
Wèi 等夜遁。
考異曰：武帝紀曰：
「公至 Yángpíng，
Zhāng Lǔ 使弟 Wèi 等據關，
攻之不拔，
乃引還。
賊守備解散，
公乃密遣 Jiě 等乘險夜襲，
大破之。 」
Liú Yè 傳曰：
「Tàizǔ 欲還，
令 Yè 督後諸軍。
Yè 策 Lǔ 可克，
馳白 Tàizǔ，
不如致攻，
遂進兵，
Lǔ 乃奔走。 」
Guō Bān Shìyǔ：
「Lǔ 遣五官掾降，
弟 Wèi 拒王師不得進。
Lǔ 走 Bāzhōng。
軍糧盡，
Tàizǔ 將還。
Xīcáo Yuàn Guō Chén 曰： 『Lǔ 已降，
留使既未反，
Wèi 雖不同，
偏攜可攻。
縣軍深入以進必克，
退必不免。 』
Tàizǔ 疑之。
夜有野麋數千，
突壞 Wèi 營，
軍大驚，
Gāo Zuò 等誤與 Wèi 衆遇，
Wèi 以為大軍見掩，
遂降。 」
Wèi Míngchén Zòu 載 Yáng Jì 表曰：
「Wǔ Huángdì 征 Zhāng Lǔ，
以十萬之衆，
身親臨履。
Zhāng Wèi 之守，
蓋不足言。
地險守易，
雖有精兵虎將，
勢不能施。
對兵三日，
欲抽軍還。
天祚大 Wèi，
Lǔ 守自壞，
因以定之。 」
又載 Dǒng Zhāo 表。
其
「承 Liángzhōu」
以下，
皆 Zhāo 表所述，
必得實。
今從之。
Zhāng Lǔ heard that Yángpíng had fallen.
He wanted to surrender.
Yán Pǔ said:
"If we surrender now under duress,
our merit will certainly be light.
It is better to rely on Dù Hù and go to Pǔ Hú.
Dù Hù
was the Marquis of the Cóng邑.
Pǔ Hú
was the barbarian king of the seven surnames of Bā.
The remaining leaders of the Bǎnshǔn Mán, such as the Luo, Pu, Du, E, Du, Xi, and Gong, had seven surnames.
They did not pay taxes or tributes.
These were what were called the barbarian kings of the seven surnames.
The remaining households paid Cóng money annually,
forty coins per person.
Hence, there was a Cóng Marquis.
Sūn Shèng said: Pǔ
is pronounced Fú;
Hù
is pronounced Hù.
Then we can offer our allegiance.
Zhì
is read as written.
So he fled to the Southern Mountains and entered Bāzhōng.
Modern Xīngyuán Fǔ
is the ancient land of Hànzhōng.
To the south of Xīngyuán there is a great highway
connecting to Bāzhōu.
This road is perilous and steep,
taking three days to reach the summit.
Its highest point is called
'Lonely Clouds, Two Horns,
a grasp from heaven.'
Lonely Clouds and Two Horns
are the names of two mountains;
today they are the northern border of Dàngqú Xiàn, Bā Jùn, Hàn Bā.
This area is in the middle of the Three Bā lands,
hence it is called
Middle Bā.
To the north of Bā's border is Mǐcāng Shān.
Looking down at Xīngyuán,
it is truly a strategic pass.
Lǔ said:
'I originally intended to surrender to the state,
but my intention could not be realized.
My present flight to avoid the sharp vanguard
is not out of malice.
The precious treasures and granaries
belong to the state.'
He then sealed them up and left.
Cāo entered Nánzhèng.
Nánzhèng Xiàn
was the administrative seat of Hànzhōng Jùn.
As Lǔ had originally shown good intentions,
he sent someone to comfort and appease him.
The Chancellor's Chief Clerk, Sīmǎ Yì, said to Cāo:
"Liú Bèi, through deceit and force, captured Liú Zhāng.
The people of Shǔ have not yet submitted,
and he is far away contending for Jiānglíng.
This opportunity must not be missed.
Now that Hànzhōng has been conquered,
Yìzhōu is in turmoil.
If we advance our troops upon it,
the situation will certainly collapse.
Even a sage cannot go against the times,
nor should one lose an opportunity."
Cāo said:
"People are plagued by insatiability.
Having obtained Lǒng,
do they still covet Shǔ?"
Guāngwǔ issued an edict to Cén Péng and others, saying:
"People are plagued by insatiability.
Having obtained Lǒng,
they still covet Shǔ."
"Liú Bèi
is a hero among men,
he is magnanimous but slow.
He has only recently acquired Shǔ,
and the people of Shǔ do not yet trust him.
Now that Hànzhōng has been broken,
the people of Shǔ are shaken with fear,
and their power will naturally collapse.
With your sagacity,
if you press them while they are collapsing,
there is nothing that cannot be conquered.
If you delay even slightly,
Zhūgě Liàng, who is skilled in governing the state, will become prime minister,
and Guān Yǔ and Zhāng Fēi, whose bravery surpasses all armies, will become generals.
Once the people of Shǔ are settled,
and they occupy strategic passes and strongholds,
then they will be unassailable.
If we do not take it now,
it will certainly become a future worry."
Cāo did not follow.
Seven days later,
a surrenderer from Shǔ said,
"In Shǔ, there are dozens of alarms daily.
Although the defending generals execute people, they cannot restore peace."
The Kǎoyì states: The Biography of Liú Yè says,
"Although Bèi executed them,"
but according to the Biography of Bèi, it says:
"Bèi went down to Gōng'ān,
and hearing that Cáo Gōng had pacified Hànzhōng,
he returned."
If so,
Bèi was still in Gōng'ān at that time.
"Can we still attack now?"
Yè said:
"It has already stabilized slightly;
it cannot be attacked yet."
In seven days,
how could it be said to have stabilized slightly so quickly?
Yè probably observed that Bèi's defense of Shǔ was unassailable,
and thus made this statement in response to Cāo.
Xiàhóu Yuān was appointed Dūhù Jiāngjūn.
Dūhù Jiāngjūn
was a title established to oversee all generals;
Guāngwǔ first bestowed it upon Jiǎ Fù.
The Chancellor's Chief Clerk, Dù Xí, was appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi,
and remained to supervise affairs in Hànzhōng.
Xí soothed, conciliated, enlightened, and guided the people,
and the common folk happily relocated to Luò and Yè, numbering over eighty thousand households.
In the eighth month,
Sūn Quán led a force of one hundred thousand to besiege Héféi.
At that time, Zhāng Liáo, Lǐ Diǎn, and Yuè Jìn commanded over seven thousand men garrisoned at Héféi.
When Wèi Gōng Cāo was campaigning against Zhāng Lǔ,
he sent an order to Xuē Tì, the Protector of the Army at Héféi,
writing on the side of the sealed letter:
"Open when the enemy arrives."
When Quán arrived,
the order was opened.
The order said:
"If Sūn Quán arrives,
Generals Zhāng and Lǐ are to sally forth and fight;
General Yuè is to defend;
the Protector of the Army is not to engage in combat."
Cāo considered Liáo and Diǎn courageous and sharp,
so he had them fight;
Yuè Jìn was steady and cautious,
so he had him defend;
Xuē Tì was a civil official,
so he was not to engage in combat.
This caused doubt.
Zhāng Liáo said:
"The Duke is on a distant campaign.
By the time reinforcements arrive,
they will certainly have defeated us.
Therefore, the order instructs us to strike them before they fully assemble,
to break their formidable momentum,
and thus reassure the troops.
Only then can we defend."
Yuè Jìn and others did not reply.
Liáo angrily said:
"The key to success or failure
lies in this one battle.
If you gentlemen are in doubt,
Liáo will decide alone."
He wanted to sally forth and fight alone.
He said with emotion:
"This is a great matter for the state.
I am merely considering your plan.
How can I forget public duty for private grievances?
I request to follow you out."
Thereupon, Liáo recruited brave volunteers that night,
gathering eight hundred men,
and slaughtered oxen to feast them.
The next morning,
Liáo donned armor and held a halberd,
leading the charge,
breaking through the enemy lines,
killing dozens of men,
and beheading two major generals.
He shouted his name,
charged through the rampart, and reached Quán's banner.
Quán was greatly alarmed,
not knowing what to do.
He fled and climbed a high mound,
defending himself with a long halberd.
Liáo shouted at Quán to come down and fight.
Quán dared not move.
Seeing that Liáo's troops were few,
he gathered his forces and encircled Liáo multiple times.
Liáo fiercely attacked to break the encirclement,
and led dozens of his men out.

pronounced *yú róng fān*.
[The army] returned from Guǎngshí to Yángpíng.
The army was in disarray,
not knowing what to do.
The Supervising General Dù Xí
(Initially,
when Cāo returned east,
he left Xí to oversee the military affairs of Hànzhōng.)
(Shuài,
pronounced *suǒ lèi fān*.)
issued orders to all armies, saying:
"General Zhāng [Hé] is a famous general of the state,
whom Liú Bèi fears;
the situation is critical today,
and only General Zhāng can bring peace."
So, as a temporary measure, he nominated Hé as the army commander.
Hé came out,
marshaled the troops, and arranged their formations.
All the generals submitted to Hé's command,
and the morale of the multitude was thus stabilized.
The next day,
Bèi intended to cross the Hànshuǐ River to attack.
The generals, considering their forces were outnumbered,
wished to set up formation by the water to resist him.
Guō Huái said:
"This shows weakness and is insufficient to deter the enemy;
it is not a good strategy.
It would be better to form a battle line further from the water,
draw them in,
and attack them after they have half-crossed.
Bèi can then be defeated."
After the formation was set,
Bèi became suspicious
and did not cross.
Huái then held his ground firmly,
showing no intention of retreating.
He reported the situation to Wèi Wáng Cāo,
who approved of it
and sent an envoy to grant Hé a staff of authority,
and reinstated Huái as Sīmǎ.
3 In the second month,
on the last day of the *rénzǐ* cycle,
there was a solar eclipse.
4 In the third month,
Wèi Wáng Cāo departed from Cháng'ān through Xié Gǔ,
and stationed his army at Zhēyào to approach Hànzhōng.
The Xié Gǔ pass was dangerous,
and Cāo feared being intercepted by Bèi, so he first positioned his army at the key strategic points
before advancing towards Hànzhōng.
Some say: Zhēyào
is a place name.
"Though Cáo Gōng has come,
he will be able to do nothing;
I will surely possess Hànchuān!"
So he gathered his forces, occupied strategic defiles,
and never engaged in battle.
Cāo transported grain to the foot of Běi Shān.
Huáng Zhōng led his troops to seize it,
but did not return by the appointed time.
General of the Vigor-Aiding Army Zhào Yún led several tens of cavalry out of the camp to check on him.
(General of the Vigor-Aiding Army
was a title created by Bèi.)
Yún suddenly encountered them,
and thereupon charged forward, attacking their formation,
fighting and retreating.
The Wèi soldiers dispersed and then regrouped,
pursuing him to the camp.
Yún entered the camp,
and then opened the gates wide,
lowered his banners, and silenced his drums.
The Wèi soldiers suspected Yún had an ambush,
and withdrew.
Yún then beat his drums, shaking the heavens,
and only used powerful crossbows to shoot the Wèi soldiers from behind.
The Wèi soldiers were startled and terrified,
trampling each other,
and many fell into the Hànshuǐ River and died.
The next morning, Bèi personally came
to Yún's camp,
observed the previous day's battlefield,
and said:
"Zǐlóng is all courage!"
meaning his courage was great,
capable of opposing Cāo's large army with a lone force.
Cāo and Bèi stood in opposition for months.
Many Wèi soldiers deserted.
(Wáng,
means to flee.)
In the fifth month,
Cāo completely withdrew all his forces from Hànzhōng back to Cháng'ān,
and Liú Bèi thus took Hànzhōng.
Cāo feared Liú Bèi would take the Dī people of Wǔdū in the north to threaten Guānzhōng.
(Wǔdū
was originally the land of the Báimǎ Dī.)
Jì said:
"We can persuade them to move north for grain to avoid the bandits.
Those who arrive first will be generously rewarded and honored,
so those who come first will know the benefit,
and those who follow will surely emulate them."
Cāo agreed,
and sent Jì to Wǔdū,
relocating over fifty thousand Dī households to reside in Fúfēng and Tiānshuǐ prefectures.
Cāo had probably already abandoned Wǔdū and no longer possessed it.
The various Dī people were scattered throughout Qínchuān,
and the Fú clan's rebellion against Huá began from this.
5 Yán Jùn of Wǔwēi, Zhāng Hé of Zhāngyè, Huáng Huá of Jiǔquán, Qū Yǎn of Xīpíng, and others,
each occupied their respective commanderies,
proclaimed themselves generals,
and attacked each other.
Jùn sent an envoy to send his mother and son to Wèi Wáng Cāo as hostages to seek aid.
Cāo asked Zhāng Jì.
Jì said:
"Jùn and the others outwardly borrow the nation's prestige,
but inwardly breed arrogance and defiance.
Once their plans are settled and their power sufficient,
they will immediately rebel.
Currently, we are busy settling Shǔ,
so it is advisable to allow both sides to exist and fight each other,
like Biànzhuāngzǐ stabbing a tiger,
so we can reap the benefits of their exhaustion."
The Zhànguócè states: "When Biànzhuāngzǐ was about to stab a tiger,
a stable boy stopped him and said:
'Two tigers are eating an ox.
The ox is delicious, so they will surely fight.
Then the larger one will be wounded,
and the smaller one will die.
If you stab the wounded one,
you will surely gain two with one action.'
Zhuāngzǐ thought it was good,
and indeed caught two tigers."
(Cì,
pronounced *qī yì fān*.)
"Excellent!"
After more than a year,
Luán killed Jùn,
and Wǔwēi Wáng Mì then killed Luán.
6 Liú Bèi dispatched the Administrator of Yídū, Méng Dá of Fúfēng, from Zǐguī to attack Fánglíng from the north,
killing Kǔi Qí, the Administrator of Fánglíng.
Zhāng Bó's Wú Lù states: Liú Bèi divided Nánjùn to establish Yídū Commandery,
governing the three counties of Yídào, Hěnshān, and Yílíng.
Fánglíng County
originally belonged to Hànzhōng Commandery.
This commandery was probably established by Liú Biǎo,
who made Kǔi Qí its administrator;
otherwise, Qí established himself.
Kǔi,
pronounced 'kǔ guài'.
Under Dá's command,
Liú Fēng,
originally the son of Kòu Shì of Luóhóu
and the nephew of Liú Shì of Chángshā.
When Bèi arrived in Jīngzhōu,
as he had no heir yet,
he adopted him as his son.
Shēn Dān, the Administrator of Shàngyōng, surrendered with his entire commandery.
Shàngyōng County
belonged to Hànzhōng Commandery.
Xián said: The old city is west of today's Qīngshuǐ County, Fángzhōu.
Wèi Lǜe states: Shēn Dān initially gathered several thousand families
between Xīchéng and Shàngyōng,
communicating with Zhāng Lǔ;
he also sent envoys to Cáo Gōng,
who bestowed upon him the title of General
and made him Commandant of Shàngyōng.
Jiàng,
pronounced 'hù jiāng'.
He was made Administrator of Shàngyōng,
and Dān's younger brother Yí was made General Jìanxìn and Administrator of Xīchéng.
Xīchéng County
belonged to Hànzhōng Commandery,
which Bèi also divided into a commandery and granted to Yí;
in the Táng dynasty, it was Jīnzhōu.
7 Autumn,
seventh month,
Liú Bèi declared himself King of Hànzhōng,
setting up an altar at Miǎnyáng.
Miǎnyáng County
belonged to Hànzhōng Commandery.
His ministers attended,
and after the memorial was read,
he accepted the imperial seal and ribbon,
and wore the king's crown.
He then sent an urgent message
to return the seals and ribbons of the provisional General of the Left and Marquis of Yíchéng Pavilion.
General of the Left and Marquis of Yíchéng Pavilion
were both titles proposed and granted by Cáo.
Shàng,
pronounced 'shí zhǎng'.
He promoted Yíyáng's Wèi Yán, a General of the Gate, to General Zhènyuǎn,
Yámén and Zhènyuǎn
were both general titles newly established by Liú Bèi.
to guard Hánchuān.
Emperor Wén of Wèi divided Nányáng Commandery to establish Yíyáng Commandery,
and also established Yíyáng County belonging to it;
this was after Yán entered Shǔ,
the historian recorded it retrospectively.
General Zhènyuǎn
was probably newly established by Bèi.
Sòng Bái said: Yíyáng,
in Táng it was Shēnzhōu,
in Sòng it was Xìnyángjūn.
He appointed Xǔ Jìng as Grand Tutor,
Fǎ Zhèng as Director of the Department of State Affairs,
Guān Yǔ as General of the Van,
Zhāng Fēi as General of the Right,
Mǎ Chāo as General of the Left,
and Huáng Zhōng as General of the Rear.
General of the Van, Rear, Left, and Right were all Han dynasty officials.
He dispatched Fèi Shī of Jiànwéi, the Chief Clerk of the Vanguard of Yìzhōu, to personally present the seal and ribbon to Guān Yǔ.
Yǔ, upon hearing that Huáng Zhōng's position was equal to his own,
angrily said:
"A true man will never be ranked among old soldiers!"
He refused to accept the appointment.
Shī said to Yǔ:
"Indeed, those who establish royal enterprises
do not use only one kind of person.
In the past, Xiāo and Cáo were close friends of Gāozǔ since childhood,
while Chén and Hán came later as fugitives;
discussing their ranks,
Hán was highest.
This refers to Chén Píng and Hán Xìn who came from Chǔ.
Hán Xìn became a King, while Xiāo and Cáo became Marquises,
hence it is said Hán was highest.
Now the King of Hànzhōng, through his achievements of the moment,
has greatly elevated the Han imperial house;
however, in his estimation of importance,
how could it be equal to yours, my lord?
This means that Bèi temporarily ranked Zhōng with Yǔ,
but his true estimation of importance was not based on this.
Cáo Cāo once memorialized to grant Yǔ the title Marquis of Hànshòu Pavilion,
hence he is referred to as 'my lord'.
Sharing joy and sorrow,
sharing adversity and fortune;
I, your humble servant, believe it is inappropriate for you, my lord, to be concerned with the rank of official titles or the amount of emoluments.
I am but a lowly envoy,
carrying out orders.
If you, my lord, do not accept the appointment,
I will simply return as such.
I only regret this action for you,
fearing there may be future regrets."
Yǔ was greatly enlightened,
and immediately accepted the appointment.
8 An imperial edict made Madam Biàn, wife of Wèi King Cáo, Queen.
9 Sūn Quán attacked Héféi.
At that time, troops from various prefectures garrisoned Huáinán.
Wèi changed the Han Jiǔjiāng Commandery to Huáinán Commandery.
"Although there are bandits here,
they are not worth worrying about.
Now the floods are rising,
and Zǐxiào's army is isolated,
without distant preparations.
Cáo Rén,
courtesy name Zǐxiào,
was then General Quelling the South.
Xuàn,
read 'xuán'.
I fear that General Quelling the South might face an incident."
Soon after, Guān Yǔ indeed ordered Mí Fāng, the Administrator of Nánjùn, to guard Jiānglíng,
and General Fù Shìrén to guard Gōng'ān.
Yǔ himself led his troops to attack Cáo Rén at Fán.
Rén ordered General of the Left Yú Jìn and General Lìyì Páng Dé and others to encamp north of Fán.
Cáo had promoted Páng Dé to General Lìyì because he had come over from Hànzhōng.
There was heavy continuous rain,
the Han River overflowed,
the flat ground was several *zhang* deep in water,
Yú Jìn and his seven armies were all submerged.
Jìn and the other generals climbed to high ground to escape the water.
Yǔ took large boats and attacked them.
Jìn and the others were desperate
and surrendered.
Páng Dé was on the embankment,
wearing armor and holding a bow,
his arrows never missed,
they always hit the mark.
Páng,
pronounced 'pí jiāng'.
Bèi,
pronounced 'pí yì'.
By midday,
Yǔ's attack became more urgent;
arrows ran out,
and short weapons were engaged.
Dé fought with increasing fury,
his spirit grew stronger,
but the water rose even more,
and his officers and soldiers all surrendered.
Dé boarded a small boat, intending to return to Rén's camp.
The water was so high that the boat capsized.
He lost his bow and arrows,
and holding onto the overturned boat, he was in the water
when Yǔ captured him.
He stood without kneeling.
Showing no submission.
"Your elder brother is in Hànzhōng.
Wèi Lǜe states: Dé's cousin Ròu was in Shǔ.
Why did you not surrender earlier?"
Dé cursed Yǔ, saying:
"You young fellow,
what do you mean by surrender?
The King of Wèi has a million armored soldiers,
his might shakes the world;
you, Liú Bèi, are just a mediocre talent,
how can you contend with him?
I would rather be a ghost for my state
than a general for a rebel!"
Yǔ killed him.
Wèi King Cáo heard this
and said:
"I have known Yú Jìn for thirty years,
Cáo gathered troops in Yǎnzhōu,
and Jìn immediately became a general.
Could he really be inferior to Páng Dé?"
He enfeoffed Dé's two sons as Marqui.
Guān Yǔ (關羽) urgently attacked Fánchéng (樊城).
The city was inundated by water;
portions frequently collapsed,
causing widespread fear among the troops.
Someone said to Cáo Rén (曹仁):
"The danger today
cannot be withstood by force.
We can take advantage of Guān Yǔ's (關羽) encirclement not yet being complete,
board light boats, and escape by night."
Mǎn Chǒng (滿寵), Administrator (Tàishǒu 太守) of Rǔnán (汝南), said:
"The mountain waters are swift;
I hope they will not last long.
I hear Guān Yǔ (關羽) has dispatched a separate general who is already below Jiá (郟).
Chǒng (寵) served as Administrator (Tàishǒu 太守) of Rǔnán (汝南);
Cāo (操) ordered him to assist Cáo Rén (曹仁) in garrisoning Fánchéng (樊城).
Jiá Xiàn (郟縣)
belonged to Yǐngchuān Jùn (潁川郡).
Shī Gǔ (師古) says: Jiá (郟)
is pronounced 'jiá'.
The Jìn Geographical Treatise (Jìn Dìlǐ Zhì 晉地理志) states
that Xiāngchéng Jùn (襄城郡) again had a Jiá Xiàn (郟縣),
likely because it was abolished during the Eastern Hàn (東漢) and then re-established as a county during Wèi (魏) and Jìn (晉).
The common people are in turmoil.
The reason Guān Yǔ (關羽) dares not advance further
is that he fears our army might attack his rear.
If we flee now,
south of the Hónghé (洪河)
will no longer belong to the state.
Hónghé (洪河)
is the Dàhé (大河) (Yellow River).
Rén (仁) said:
"Good!"
He then sacrificed a white horse and swore an oath with his soldiers,
vowing to hold the city with one heart.
There were only a few thousand men and horses in the city.
Only a few 'boards' of the city wall were not submerged.
A 'board' (bǎn 板) refers to a height of two chi (尺) on the wall.
The encirclement was established in several layers,
completely cutting off communication between inside and out.
Guān Yǔ (關羽) also dispatched another general to besiege General Lǚ Cháng (呂常) at Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
Hú Xiū (胡脩), Inspector (Cìshǐ 刺史) of Jīngzhōu (荊州), and Fù Fāng (傅方), Administrator (Tàishǒu 太守) of Nánxiāng (南鄉), both surrendered to Guān Yǔ (關羽).
The Commentary on the Water Classic (Shuǐ Jīng Zhù 水經註) states: In the Jiàn'ān (建安) era of the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
the western part of Nányáng (南陽) was carved out to form Nánxiāng Jùn (南鄉郡),
which belonged to Jīngzhōu (荊州).
In the past, Wèi Fěng (魏諷) of Pèiguó (沛國) possessed talent for captivating the masses,
stirring Yè Dū (鄴都).
Zhōng Yáo (鍾繇), Prime Minister (Xiàngguó 相國) of Wèi (魏), recruited him as a Western Clerk (Xīcáo Yuàn 西曹掾).
This refers to the Western Clerk (Xīcáo Yuàn 西曹掾) of the Wèi (魏) Prime Minister's (Xiàngguó 相國) mansion.
[Zhōng Yáo (鍾繇)] was on good terms with Fěng (諷).
Zhèng Mào (鄭袤) of the same commandery,
son of Tài (泰),
often said to Lǎn (覽):
"Fěng (諷) is a treacherous hero and will eventually cause rebellion."
In the ninth month,
Fěng (諷) secretly gathered a party of followers
and conspired with Chánglè Wèiwèi (長樂衞尉) Chén Yī (陳禕) to attack Yè (鄴).
Before the appointed time,
Yī (禕) became afraid and reported him.
Crown Prince Pī (丕) executed Fěng (諷),
and several thousand people were implicated and died.
Zhōng Yáo (鍾繇) was dismissed from office.
In the past,
Yáng Xiū (楊脩), Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù 主簿) to the Prime Minister (Chéngxiàng 丞相),
conspired with the Dīng (丁) brothers, Dīng Yí (丁儀) and Dīng Yì (丁廙), to establish Cáo Zhí (曹植) as the heir of Wèi (魏).
Xiū (脩) was Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù 主簿) to the Hàn (漢) Prime Minister (Chéngxiàng 丞相),
an official under Cāo (操).
He used a cart to transport Wú Zhì (吳質), the Magistrate (Zhǎng 長) of Cháogē (朝歌), hidden in a discarded basket,
to conspire with him.
Xiū (脩) reported this to Wèi Wáng (魏王) Cāo (操),
but Cāo (操) did not have time to investigate.
Pī (丕) was afraid and told Zhì (質).
Zhì (質) said:
"No harm."
The next day,
Zhì (質) again entered in a cart with baskets of silk.
Xiū (脩) again reported it,
but upon investigation,
there was no one.
Tuī (推) means 'to examine'.
Fù (復) is pronounced 'fú yòu fān'.
Afterwards, Zhí (植) fell out of favor due to his arrogance and indulgence.
Zhí (植) drove his chariot along the imperial road
and privately opened the Sīmǎ Mén (司馬門) to exit,
thus incurring displeasure.
When Cáo Rén (曹仁) was besieged by Guān Yǔ (關羽),
Cāo (操) wanted to send Zhí (植) to relieve Rén (仁),
but Zhí (植) was too drunk to receive the order,
which further estranged him.
Xiū (脩) also did not dare to cut ties.
Whenever he went to Zhí (植) to deliberate on matters that might have flaws,
he would guess Cāo's (操) intentions
and pre-prepare more than ten draft replies,
instructing his household staff:
"When the order comes out,
answer according to what is asked."
Thus, as soon as an order was issued,
a reply had already been submitted.
Cāo (操) found his speed strange,
investigated,
and only then was it revealed.
Cāo (操) also disliked Xiū (脩) because he was Yuán Shù's (袁術) nephew.
So, he brought up Xiū's (脩) past leaks of instructions
and his connections with various regional lords.
Xiū's (脩) pre-prepared replies
were referred to as "leaking instructions."
His interactions with Zhí (植)
were referred to as "connecting with various regional lords."
Wèi Wáng (魏王) Cāo (操) appointed Dù Xí (杜襲) as Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ 長史) of the Provisional Government (Liúfǔ 留府),
stationed in Guānzhōng (關中).
A Provisional Government (Liúfǔ 留府) was established in Guānzhōng (關中)
to guard against Shǔ (蜀).
Xǔ Yōu (許攸) held his troops and did not submit,
and he spoke disrespectfully.
Cāo (操) was greatly enraged
and first wished to attack him.
Many loyal officials advised:
"It is advisable to persuade and embrace Yōu (攸)
to jointly attack the strong enemy."
Cāo (操) rested his horizontal sword on his lap.
Xī (膝) is the same as xī (膝).
Xí (襲) entered, intending to remonstrate.
Cāo (操) preemptively said to him:
"My plan is already decided;
do not speak again, sir!"
Xí (襲) said:
"If Your Highness's plan is correct,
then your servant will assist Your Highness in achieving it.
If Your Highness's plan is incorrect,
even if achieved,
it should be changed.
Your Highness preemptively tells your servant not to speak,
why wait for my words not to be clear/great/bright (bù chǎn 不闡)?"
Chǎn (闡) means 'to open',
'to be great',
or 'to be bright'.
"Xǔ Yōu (許攸) has insulted me;
how can I let it go (kě zhì 可置)!"
Zhì (置) means 'to abandon' or 'to let go'.
"What kind of person does Your Highness consider Xǔ Yōu (許攸) to be?"
Cāo (操) said:
"An ordinary person."
Xí (襲) said:
"Indeed, only the wise know the wise,
and only the sage knows the sage.
How can an ordinary person know an extraordinary person?
At present, when wolves block the road, yet foxes are targeted first,
people will say that Your Highness avoids the strong and attacks the weak.
Advancing is not courage,
and retreating is not benevolence.
Your servant has heard that a crossbow of a thousand jūn (鈞)
is not fired for a shūrǔ (鼷鼠) (field mouse);
a bell of ten thousand shí (石)
is not struck by a tíng (莛) (stem) to produce sound.
Thirty jīn (斤) make one jūn (鈞).
A crossbow of a thousand jūn (鈞)
means it is heavy.
Shūrǔ (鼷鼠)
is a small mouse.
The Shūowén (說文) says: It has a stinging poison.
Some call it gānshǔ (甘鼠).
Lù Diàn's (陸佃) Pí Yǎ (埤雅) says: Shūrǔ (鼷鼠) has a sweet mouth,
biting humans and birds and beasts without pain.
The Bówù Zhì (博物志) says: It is the smallest of mice.
The Běncǎo (本草) states that shūrǔ (鼷鼠) is extremely tiny,
not easily seen.
Four jīn (斤)
[jūn (鈞)]
shí (石) is one hundred and twenty jīn (斤).
Tíng (莛)
is a grass stem.
Dōngfāng Shuò (東方朔) said: 'striking a bell with a tíng (莛)'.
All this means that things of great power
are not moved by a light touch.
Shūrǔ (鼷鼠) is pronounced 'xī'.
Tíng (莛) is pronounced 'tíng'.
Zhuàng (撞) is pronounced 'zhí jiāng fān'.
Now, this insignificant Xǔ Yōu (許攸),
how is he worth bothering Your divine martial power for!"
Cāo (操) said:
"Good!"
Thereupon, he treated Yōu (攸) generously,
and Yōu (攸) immediately submitted.
In the winter,
tenth month,
Wèi Wáng (魏王) Cāo (操) arrived at Luòyáng (洛陽).
14 The common people Lùhún Mín Sūnláng 孫狼 and others revolted.
Lùhún 陸渾 county
belonged to Hóngnóng 弘農 Commandery.
Qín 秦 and Jìn 晉 moved the Lùhún 陸渾 Róng 戎 here.
Sòng Bái 宋白 said: Lùhún 陸渾
was the land of Yīyáng 伊陽 County in Hénánfǔ 河南府.
Shīgǔ 師古 said: Hún 渾
is pronounced like "hú kūn fān" 胡昆翻.
They joined Guān Yǔ 關羽 to the south.
Guān Yǔ 關羽 bestowed an official seal upon Sūnláng 孫狼,
gave him soldiers,
and he returned to become a bandit.
From Xǔ 許 southward,
many responded to Guān Yǔ 關羽 from afar,
and Guān Yǔ’s 關羽’s prestige shook Huáxià 華夏.
Wèi Wáng Cáo Cāo 魏王曹操 considered moving the capital from Xǔ 許 to avoid his formidable force.
The Prime Minister's Military Advisor Sīmǎ Yì 司馬懿 and Chief Secretary Jiǎng Jì 蔣濟 spoke to Cáo Cāo 曹操, saying:
"Yú Jìn 于禁 and others were engulfed by the floods,
which was not a failure in battle,
and thus is not enough to harm the grand strategy of the state.
Liú Bèi 劉備 and Sūn Quán 孫權
are outwardly親 but inwardly distant.
If Guān Yǔ 關羽 achieves his ambition,

Fàn Chéngdà's *Wújùn Zhì* states: Lóu County,
is now called Kūnshān County.
Three *lǐ* to the northeast, there is a village
named Lóu County.
This was probably the administrative seat of the ancient Lóu County.
Xiákǒu
is the mouth of Xīlíng Gorge.
*Yídū Jì* states: "From Huángniú Tān, entering the Xīlíng boundary to the east,
it is about one hundred *lǐ* to Xiákǒu.
The mountains and waters wind and twist.
On both banks, tall mountains rise in layered peaks.
Except at midday or midnight,
the sun and moon are not visible."
Guān Yǔ, knowing himself to be isolated and in distress,
retreated west to safeguard Màichéng.
*Jīngzhōu Jì* states: "To the southeast of Dāngyáng County in Nánjùn, there is Màichéng."
Yǔ feigned surrender,
erected banners and set up dummy figures on the city walls,
then secretly fled.
His soldiers all dispersed,
leaving only a dozen or so cavalrymen.
Quán had previously sent Zhū Rán and Pān Zhāng to block his escape routes.
In the twelfth month,
Zhāng's *sīmǎ*, Mǎ Zhōng, captured Yǔ and his son Píng at Zhāngxiāng.
*Shuǐjīng Zhù* states: "The Zhāng River flows out from Jīngshān in Línjǔ County to the east,
then south past the south of Zhāngxiāng in Línjǔ County.
Pān Zhāng captured Guān Yǔ here.
The Zhāng River then flows south past Dāngyáng County,
and then south past the east of Màichéng."
Thus, Jīngzhōu was pacified.

Before Lǚ Méng could receive his enfeoffment, he fell ill.

When acupuncture was administered,

He wanted to see his face often,

When his illness somewhat improved,

he eventually died,

and assigned three hundred families to guard his tomb.
Later, Sūn Quán discussed Zhōu Yú, Lǔ Sù, and Méng with Lù Xùn, saying,

This was one great pleasure.

Zhāng Yán led hundreds of thousands of troops, both by water and land, downstream.
'Zhāng Yán' means to speak grandly and boastfully.

He raised his whip, intending to strike Jìn.

means to raise.

is the general's achievement."
He also generously rewarded Huán Jiē,
making him a Secretary.
Cāo disliked the remaining population of Jīngzhōu and those who were settled for agriculture in Hànchuān.
This Hànchuān
refers to the area above and below Xiāng and Fán,
and to the left and right of the Hàn River.
Sīmǎ Yì said,

Cāo said,

"The Hàn's mandate has already ended;

Zhù

Cāo said,

King Wén of Zhōu held two-thirds of the world
but served the Yīn.
Your servant Sīmǎ Guāng says: Education and moral transformation
are urgent matters for the state,
yet vulgar officials neglect them.
Customs and social practices
are great matters for the world,
yet mediocre rulers disregard them.
Only enlightened and wise gentlemen,
with deep understanding and long-term vision,
can then know the greatness of their benefits and the far-reaching extent of their achievements.
Guāngwǔ encountered the decline of the Hàn,
with heroes boiling over in contention.
He rose from commoner status
to restore and revive the former lineage.
Campaigning in all directions,
he had no time to rest,
yet he was able to uphold and value classical scholarship,
invite and retain refined scholars,
expand schools,
and cultivate and clarify rites and music.
Once his military achievements were complete,
his civil virtues were also perfected.
Following him, Xiàomíng and Xiàozhāng
diligently pursued the aspirations of their predecessors.
Yù
means 'to recount'
and 'to follow.'
Yù
is pronounced yù.
They studied classics and inquired about the Way.
From the high ministers and grandees down to the county and district officials,
all were chosen from among those who were learned in the classics and cultivated in conduct.
Even the Huǒbēn palace guards studied the Classic of Filial Piety (Xiàojīng),
and Xiongnú youths also attended the Imperial University (Dàxué).
Thus, education was established at the top,
and good customs were formed below.
The loyal, honest, pure, and cultivated scholars,
how could they not be highly regarded by those in officialdom?
Jìnshēn
refers to those who insert their tablets into their belts and let their sashes hang down,
i.e., the high ministers and grandees at court.
As for the ignorant, crude, and corrupt people,
how could they not be tolerated at court,
but also rejected by their local communities?
Since the fall of the Three Dynasties (Sāndài),
there has been no period where the beauty of moral transformation
was as flourishing as during the Eastern Hàn.
However, from Xiàohé onward,
powerful relatives of the imperial family seized authority,
favored intimates held sway,
rewards and punishments were without order,
bribery was rampant,
the worthy and the foolish were mixed,
and right and wrong were inverted.
It could be called chaos.
Yet, it barely avoided ruin because
at the top there were high ministers and grandees like Yuán Ān, Yáng Zhèn, Lǐ Gù, Dù Qiáo, Chén Fān, and Lǐ Yīng, who openly remonstrated and debated in court,
using public righteousness to uphold its precarious state.
At the bottom there were commoner scholars like Fú Róng, Guō Tài, Fàn Pāng, and Xǔ Shào,
who established private opinions to rectify its failings.
'Private opinions'
means that they could not participate in court deliberations,
but privately established their views among the people below
to correct the errors of court decisions.
There were even those who dared to risk the axe and hatchet,
falling before their eyes,
yet loyal and righteous individuals rose up in succession behind them,
following one another to execution,
regarding death as returning home.
How could it be that only these few men were virtuous?
It was also the lasting influence of Guāngwǔ, Míng, and Zhāng.
At that time,
if there had been an enlightened ruler who rose up and revitalized it,

compounded by the昏虐 (hūnnüè) of Huán and Líng,
who nurtured treachery and deceit,

and annihilated loyal and good people,

Thereupon, Hé Jìn summoned the barbarians,
Dǒng Zhuó took advantage of the opportunity,
and Yuán Shào's faction followed and stirred up trouble,
thus causing the imperial carriage to wander,
the ancestral temples to become ruins,
the royal house to be overthrown,
and the common people to suffer immensely.
The great mandate was severed and destroyed,
beyond recovery.
However, the governors and commandery administrators who held troops and occupied territories,
though they devoured each other,
still always used 'honoring the Hàn' as a pretext.
Given Wèi Wǔ's tyrannical and stubborn nature,
and his great accomplishments in the world,
he had long harbored a lawless heart.
Yet, even at the cost of his life, he did not dare to abolish the Hàn and establish himself.
Was it that his ambition did not desire it?
Rather, he feared reputation and righteousness and thus restrained himself.
From this perspective,
how can education and moral transformation be neglected,
and how can customs and social practices be disregarded?

Zhōngyuán, first year
(Bǐngchén, 56)Hóng Shì's Lìshì says: In Chéngdū, there is a stele erected by Hè Jūn, the Grand Administrator of Shǔ Jùn in the Hàn dynasty, in honor of the Zūn Jiàn Pavilion.
Its end states,
"Jiànwǔ Zhōngyuán, second year, sixth month."
According to Fàn Shǐ's Basic Annals,
the Jiànwǔ era only lasted thirty-one years,
and the following year was changed to Zhōngyuán,
written directly as Zhōngyuán, first year.
Looking at this inscription,
it seems that although it was separately designated as Zhōngyuán,
it was still prefixed with Jiànwǔ,
similar to the Zhōngyuán and Hòuyuán of Wén and Jǐng.
Furthermore, the Jìsì Zhì records the imperial edict pardoning all under heaven after the Fengshàn ceremonies,
which clearly states,
"The thirty-second year of Jiànwǔ is changed to Jiànwǔ Zhōngyuán, first year."
The Dōngyí Wōguó Zhuàn states,
"In the second year of Jiànwǔ Zhōngyuán,
they came to offer tribute."
The evidence is very clear.
Sòng Jǔgōng's Jìyuán Tōngpǔ says:
"The annals and treatises both come from Fàn Shǐ,
so it must be a transmission error,
and scholars failed to scrutinize it,
deleting it based on their own ideas.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng's Dàtóng and Dàtōng both have the character 'zhōng'
(middle),
which also followed this precedent.
Sīmǎ Gōng, in compiling the Tōngjiàn,
did not adopt this view."
I note that in the Kǎoyì,
Wēn Gōng did not fail to adopt Sòng's view;
his following Yuán and Fàn in writing Zhōngyuán
was merely for simplicity.
